Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Dhammapada

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(The First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

1.

1.

Mahāmohatamonaddhe[V 1.0001][M 1.0001][P 1.0001], loke lokantadassinā;

Yena saddhammapajjoto, jālito jalitiddhinā.

The lamp of the True Dhamma was lit by him of blazing power, the seer of the world's end, in a world shrouded by the darkness of great delusion.

2.

2.

Tassa pāde namassitvā, sambuddhassa sirīmato;

Saddhammañcassa pūjetvā, katvā saṅghassa cañjaliṃ.

Having paid homage to the feet of that glorious Perfectly Enlightened One, and having honored His True Dhamma, and having made the gesture of reverence to His Sangha.

3.

3.

Taṃ taṃ kāraṇamāgamma, dhammādhammesu kovido;

Sampattasaddhammapado, satthā dhammapadaṃ subhaṃ.

Relying on this and that reason, the Teacher—skilled in what is Dhamma and what is not Dhamma, and endowed with the state of the True Dhamma—

4.

4.

Desesi [V 1.0002] karuṇāvega-samussāhitamānaso;

Yaṃ ve devamanussānaṃ, pītipāmojjavaḍḍhanaṃ.

with a mind stirred by the force of compassion, taught that beautiful Dhammapada, which indeed increases the delight and joy of gods and humans.

5.

5.

Paramparābhatā tassa, nipuṇā atthavaṇṇanā;

Yā tambapaṇṇidīpamhi, dīpabhāsāya saṇṭhitā.

The subtle and profound commentary on its meaning, handed down by a succession of teachers, was established on the island of Tambapaṇṇi in the language of that island.

6.

6.

Na sādhayati sesānaṃ, sattānaṃ hitasampadaṃ;

Appeva nāma sādheyya, sabbalokassa sā hitaṃ.

It does not bring about the fulfillment of benefit for the remaining beings; how then could it bring about the welfare of the entire world?

7.

7.

Iti āsīsamānena, dantena samacārinā;

Kumārakassapenāhaṃ, therena thiracetasā.

Therefore, by the Elder Kumārakassapa—who was aspiring, with tamed faculties, of balanced conduct, and of firm mind—

8.

8 .

Saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena[P 1.0002], sakkaccaṃ abhiyācito;

Taṃ bhāsaṃ ativitthāra-gatañca vacanakkamaṃ.

and who desired the stability of the True Dhamma, I was earnestly requested regarding that language and sequence of words which had become overly extensive.

9 .

9 .

Pahāyāropayitvāna[M 1.0002], tantibhāsaṃ manoramaṃ;

Gāthānaṃ byañjanapadaṃ, yaṃ tattha na vibhāvitaṃ.

To abandon that language and render it into the delightful canonical Māgadhī language, and to clarify whatever word or phrase of the verses was not made clear therein.

10.

10.

Kevalaṃ taṃ vibhāvetvā, sesaṃ tameva atthato;

Bhāsantarena bhāsissaṃ, āvahanto vibhāvinaṃ;

Manaso pītipāmojjaṃ, atthadhammūpanissitanti.

Having clarified only that which was unclear, while for the rest relying on the meaning just as it is, I shall explain it in another language, bringing delight and joy to the minds of the wise, being dependent on the meaning and the Dhamma.

1. Yamakavaggo

1. The Chapter of the Pairs

1. Cakkhupālattheravatthu

1. The Story of the Elder Cakkhupāla

1.

1.

“Manopubbaṅgamā [V 1.0003][P 1.0003] dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā;

Manasā ce paduṭṭhena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ dukkhamanveti, cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti. –

All phenomena are preceded by mind, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If, with a corrupted mind, one speaks or acts, then suffering follows one, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox.

Ayaṃ dhammadesanā kattha bhāsitāti? Sāvatthiyaṃ. Kaṃ ārabbhāti? Cakkhupālattheraṃ.

Where was this Dhamma teaching given? In Sāvatthī. Concerning whom was it given? Concerning the Elder Cakkhupāla.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira mahāsuvaṇṇo nāma kuṭumbiko ahosi aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo aputtako. So ekadivasaṃ nhānatitthaṃ nhatvā natvā āgacchanto antarāmagge sampannapattasākhaṃ ekaṃ vanappatiṃ disvā “ayaṃ mahesakkhāya devatāya pariggahito bhavissatī”ti tassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ sodhāpetvā pākāraparikkhepaṃ kārāpetvā vālukaṃ okirāpetvā dhajapaṭākaṃ ussāpetvā vanappatiṃ alaṅkaritvā añjaliṃ karitvā “sace puttaṃ vā dhītaraṃ vā labheyyaṃ, tumhākaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karissāmī”ti patthanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

In Sāvatthī, it is said, there was a householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa, who was wealthy, of great riches, of great possessions, but without a son. One day, having gone to the bathing place and bathed, while returning, he saw along the way a forest tree with abundant leaves and branches. Thinking, 'This must be possessed by a deity of great power,' he had the area beneath it cleared, had a surrounding wall built, had sand strewn, had flags and banners raised, and having adorned that forest tree and circumambulated it from the right, he made a wish: 'If I should obtain a son or a daughter, I will make a great offering to you.' Having made this wish, he departed.

Athassa na cirasseva bhariyāya kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā [P 1.0004] gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tassa ārocesi. So tassā gabbhassa parihāramadāsi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ nāmaggahaṇadivase [M 1.0003] seṭṭhi attanā pālitaṃ vanappatiṃ nissāya laddhattā tassa pāloti nāmaṃ akāsi. Sā aparabhāge aññampi puttaṃ labhi. Tassa cūḷapāloti nāmaṃ katvā itarassa mahāpāloti nāmaṃ akāsi. Te vayappatte gharabandhanena bandhiṃsu. Aparabhāge mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Sabbampi vibhavaṃ itareyeva vicāriṃsu.

Then, not long after, a conception was established in his wife's womb. When she knew that a conception had been established, she informed him. He provided care for her pregnancy. After the passing of ten months, she gave birth to a son. On the naming day, the wealthy man, because the son was obtained by relying on the forest tree he had protected, gave him the name Pāla. Later, she got another son. Having named him Cūḷapāla, he gave the other the name Mahāpāla. When they came of age, they were bound with the bond of household life. Later, their parents passed away. The two brothers alone managed all the wealth.

Tasmiṃ samaye satthā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbenāgantvā anāthapiṇḍikena mahāseṭṭhinā catupaṇṇāsakoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā kārite jetavanamahāvihāre viharati mahājanaṃ saggamagge ca mokkhamagge ca patiṭṭhāpayamāno. Tathāgato hi mātipakkhato asītiyā, pitipakkhato [V 1.0004] asītiyāti dveasītiñātikulasahassehi kārite nigrodhamahāvihāre ekameva vassāvāsaṃ vasi, anāthapiṇḍikena kārite jetavanamahāvihāre ekūnavīsativassāni, visākhāya sattavīsatikoṭidhanapariccāgena kārite pubbārāme chabbassānīti dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ guṇamahattataṃ paṭicca sāvatthiṃ nissāya pañcavīsativassāni vassāvāsaṃ vasi. Anāthapiṇḍikopi visākhāpi mahāupāsikā nibaddhaṃ divasassa dve vāre tathāgatassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti, gacchantā ca “daharasāmaṇerā no hatthe olokessantī”ti tucchahatthā na gatapubbā. Purebhattaṃ gacchantā khādanīyabhojanīyādīni [P 1.0005] gahetvāva gacchanti, pacchābhattaṃ gacchantā pañca bhesajjāni aṭṭha ca pānāni. Nivesanesu pana tesaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ bhikkhusahassānaṃ niccaṃ paññattāsanāneva honti. Annapānabhesajjesu yo yaṃ icchati, tassa taṃ yathicchitameva sampajjati. Tesu anāthapiṇḍikena ekadivasampi satthā pañhaṃ na pucchitapubbo. So kira “tathāgato buddhasukhumālo khattiyasukhumālo, ‘bahūpakāro me, gahapatī’ti mayhaṃ dhammaṃ desento kilameyyā”ti satthari adhimattasinehena pañhaṃ na pucchati. Satthā pana tasmiṃ nisinnamatteyeva “ayaṃ seṭṭhi maṃ arakkhitabbaṭṭhāne rakkhati. Ahañhi kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ attano sīsaṃ chinditvā akkhīni uppāṭetvā hadayamaṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā pāṇasamaṃ puttadāraṃ pariccajitvā pāramiyo pūrento paresaṃ dhammadesanatthameva pūresiṃ. Esa maṃ arakkhitabbaṭṭhāne rakkhatī”ti ekaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathetiyeva.

At that time, the Teacher, having set rolling the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, arrived in due course and was dwelling in the great Jetavana monastery—built by the great wealthy man Anāthapiṇḍika who had spent fifty-four crores of wealth—establishing the great populace on the path to heaven and the path to liberation. Indeed, the Tathāgata dwelt for only one rains-retreat in the great Nigrodha monastery built by the eighty thousand clans of his mother's side and the eighty thousand clans of his father's side. He dwelt for nineteen rains-retreats in the great Jetavana monastery built by Anāthapiṇḍika, and for six rains-retreats in the Pubbārāma built by Visākhā through the donation of twenty-seven crores of wealth. Thus, depending on Sāvatthī, he dwelt for twenty-five rains-retreats, on account of the greatness of the virtue of these two families. Both Anāthapiṇḍika and the great laywoman disciple Visākhā regularly went to attend upon the Tathāgata twice a day. And when going, thinking, 'The young novices will look at our hands,' they never went empty-handed. When going before the meal, they would take various foods, both hard and soft. When going after the meal, they would take the five kinds of medicines and the eight kinds of drinks. Moreover, in their homes, seats were always kept prepared for two thousand monks each. Among foods, drinks, and medicines, whatever a monk desired, that was available to him just as he wished. Among them, Anāthapiṇḍika had never once asked the Teacher a question. He thought, 'The Tathāgata is delicately bred as a Buddha, delicately bred as a Khattiya. If he were to teach me the Dhamma, he might become weary.' Thus, out of excessive affection for the Teacher, he did not ask a question. The Teacher, however, as soon as he was seated there, would think: 'This wealthy man protects me where I do not need to be protected. Indeed, for four incalculable periods and more than one hundred thousand eons, I fulfilled the perfections—cutting off my own adorned head, tearing out my eyes, tearing out the flesh of my heart, and giving away my wife and children who were dear as life itself—solely for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to others. This man protects me where I do not need to be protected.' And so, he would invariably give a Dhamma discourse.

Tadā [M 1.0004] sāvatthiyaṃ satta manussakoṭiyo vasanti. Tesu satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā pañcakoṭimattā manussā ariyasāvakā jātā, dvekoṭimattā manussā puthujjanā. Tesu ariyasāvakānaṃ dveyeva kiccāni ahesuṃ – purebhattaṃ dānaṃ denti, pacchābhattaṃ gandhamālādihatthā vatthabhesajjapānakādīni gāhāpetvā dhammassavanatthāya gacchanti. Athekadivasaṃ mahāpālo ariyasāvake gandhamālādihatthe [P 1.0006] vihāraṃ gacchante disvā “ayaṃ mahājano kuhiṃ gacchatī”ti pucchitvā “dhammassavanāyā”ti sutvā “ahampi gamissāmī”ti gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā parisapariyante nisīdi.

At that time, seven crores of people lived in Sāvatthī. Among them, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma talk, approximately five crores of people became noble disciples, and approximately two crores became ordinary persons. Among them, the noble disciples had only two duties: in the time before the meal, they gave alms; and in the time after the meal or in the evening, holding perfumes, flowers, and so on in their hands, and having caused robes, cloth, medicine, drinks, and so on to be taken, they went for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma. Then one day, Mahāpāla saw the noble disciples going to the monastery holding perfumes, flowers, and so on in their hands and asked, “Where is this great crowd of people going?” Having heard, “For the purpose of listening to the Dhamma,” he said, “I too will go.” Having gone, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat at the edge of the assembly.

Buddhā ca nāma dhammaṃ desentā saraṇasīlapabbajjādīnaṃ upanissayaṃ oloketvā ajjhāsayavasena dhammaṃ desenti, tasmā taṃ divasaṃ satthā tassa upanissayaṃ oloketvā dhammaṃ desento anupubbikathaṃ kathesi. Seyyathidaṃ – dānakathaṃ, sīlakathaṃ, saggakathaṃ, kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ, okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi. Taṃ sutvā mahāpālo kuṭumbiko cintesi – “paralokaṃ gacchantaṃ puttadhītaro vā bhātaro vā bhogā vā nānugacchanti, sarīrampi attanā [V 1.0005] saddhiṃ na gacchati, kiṃ me gharāvāsena pabbajissāmī”ti. So desanāpariyosāne satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Atha naṃ satthā – “atthi te koci āpucchitabbayuttako ñātī”ti āha. “Kaniṭṭhabhātā me atthi, bhante”ti. “Tena hi taṃ āpucchāhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā gehaṃ gantvā kaniṭṭhaṃ pakkosāpetvā – “tāta, yaṃ mayhaṃ imasmiṃ gehe saviññāṇakampi aviññāṇakampi dhanaṃ kiñci atthi, sabbaṃ taṃ tava bhāro, paṭipajjāhi na”nti. “Tumhe pana kiṃ karissathā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ satthu santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ kathesi bhātika, tvaṃ me mātari matāya mātā viya, pitari mate pitā viya laddho, gehe te mahāvibhavo, sakkā gehaṃ ajjhāvasanteheva puññāni kātuṃ[P 1.0007], mā evaṃ karitthā”ti. “Tāta, ahaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā gharāvāse vasituṃ na sakkomi. Satthārā hi atisaṇhasukhumaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇo dhammo desito, na sakkā so agāramajjhe vasantena pūretuṃ[M 1.0005], pabbajissāmi, tātā”ti. “Bhātika, taruṇāyeva tāvattha, mahallakakāle pabbajissathā”ti. “Tāta, mahallakassa hi attano hatthapādāpi anassavā honti, na attano vase vattanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana ñātakā, svāhaṃ tava kathaṃ na karomi, samaṇapaṭipattiṃyeva pūressāmi”.

The Buddhas, indeed, teach the Dhamma after considering the supporting condition for the refuges, precepts, ordination, and so on, and they teach the Dhamma according to the inclination of beings. Therefore, on that day, the Teacher, having looked at his supporting condition, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke a graduated discourse. That is to say: a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven; he pointed out the danger, the baseness, and the defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation. Having heard this, Mahāpāla the householder thought: “When one goes to the next world, neither sons nor daughters, nor brothers, nor wealth follow. Even the body does not go with oneself. What use is the household life to me? I shall go forth.” At the end of the discourse, he approached the Teacher and requested the going forth. Then the Teacher asked him: “Do you have any relative who should be asked leave of?” “I have a younger brother, Venerable Sir.” “In that case, ask leave of him.” Having agreed, saying, “Very well,” he paid homage to the Teacher, went to his house, and had his younger brother summoned, saying: “Dear brother, whatever wealth of mine there is in this house, whether animate or inanimate, all of it is your burden. Manage it.” The younger brother asked, “But what will you do?” “I will go forth in the presence of the Teacher.” “What are you saying, brother? When our mother died, you were like a mother to me; when our father died, you were like a father. You have great wealth at home. It is possible to make merit while living at home. Do not do this.” “Dear brother, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, I am not able to live in the household life. Indeed, by the Teacher, a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, the middle, and the end was taught, applying it to the three characteristics which are subtle and fine. It is not possible for one living in the midst of a household to fulfill it. I will go forth, dear brother.” “Brother, you are still young. Wait for now. You can go forth in old age.” “Dear brother, indeed, for an old person, even their own hands and feet are not compliant; they are not under their own control. What then to say of relatives? Therefore, I will not do according to your word. I will fulfill only the practice of a recluse.”

“Jarājajjaritā honti, hatthapādā anassavā;

Yassa so vihatatthāmo, kathaṃ dhammaṃ carissati”. –

When one grows decrepit with age, one's hands and feet become unresponsive; with one's strength destroyed, how can one practice the Dhamma?

Pabbajissāmevāhaṃ, tātāti tassa viravantasseva satthu santikaṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā laddhapabbajjūpasampado ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike pañca vassāni vasitvā vuṭṭhavasso pavāretvā satthāramupasaṅkamitvā vanditvā pucchi – “bhante, imasmiṃ sāsane kati dhurānī”ti? “Ganthadhuraṃ, vipassanādhuranti dveyeva dhurāni bhikkhū”ti. “Katamaṃ pana, bhante, ganthadhuraṃ, katamaṃ vipassanādhura”nti? “Attano paññānurūpena ekaṃ vā dve vā nikāye sakalaṃ vā pana tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā tassa dhāraṇaṃ, kathanaṃ, vācananti [P 1.0008] idaṃ ganthadhuraṃ nāma, sallahukavuttino pana pantasenāsanābhiratassa attabhāve khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sātaccakiriyavasena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaggahaṇanti idaṃ vipassanādhuraṃ nāmā”ti. “Bhante, ahaṃ mahallakakāle pabbajito ganthadhuraṃ pūretuṃ na sakkhissāmi, vipassanādhuraṃ pana pūressāmi, kammaṭṭhānaṃ me kathethā”ti. Athassa satthā yāva arahattaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi.

“Dear brother, I will certainly go forth!” Thus, while his brother was still wailing, he went to the Teacher’s presence, requested the going forth, and received the going forth and the higher ordination. Having lived in the presence of his teachers and preceptors for five years, and having completed the rains-residence and performed the Pavāraṇā, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and asked: “Venerable sir, in this Dispensation, how many duties are there?” “Bhikkhu, there are only two duties: the duty of study and the duty of insight.” “But what, venerable sir, is the duty of study, and what is the duty of insight?” “To learn one or two Nikāyas, or the entire Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, in accordance with one’s own wisdom, and then to bear it in mind, to teach it, and to recite it—this is called the duty of study. But for one of light livelihood, who delights in secluded dwellings, who establishes the contemplation of arising and passing away in his own being, and develops insight by means of continuous practice to the point of grasping Arahantship—this is called the duty of insight.” “Venerable sir, I went forth in old age; I will not be able to fulfill the duty of study, but I will fulfill the duty of insight. Please teach me a meditation subject.” Then the Teacher taught him a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship.

So satthāraṃ vanditvā attanā sahagāmino bhikkhū pariyesanto saṭṭhi bhikkhū labhitvā tehi [V 1.0006] saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā vīsayojanasatamaggaṃ gantvā ekaṃ mahantaṃ paccantagāmaṃ patvā tattha saparivāro piṇḍāya pāvisi. Manussā vattasampanne bhikkhū disvāva pasannacittā āsanāni paññāpetvā nisīdāpetvā paṇītenāhārena parivisitvā, “bhante, kuhiṃ ayyā gacchantī”ti pucchitvā “yathāphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ upāsakā”ti vutte paṇḍitā manussā “vassāvāsaṃ senāsanaṃ pariyesanti bhadantā”ti ñatvā, “bhante, sace ayyā imaṃ temāsaṃ idha vaseyyuṃ, mayaṃ saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya sīlāni gaṇheyyāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Tepi “mayaṃ imāni kulāni nissāya bhavanissaraṇaṃ karissāmā”ti adhivāsesuṃ.

Having paid homage to the Teacher, he sought for bhikkhus to go together with him and found sixty bhikkhus. Having set out together with them, he traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas and reached a large border village. There, with his retinue, he entered for alms-food. The people, as soon as they saw the bhikkhus who were accomplished in their duties, with pleased minds, prepared seats, had them sit down, and served them with excellent food. Having asked, “Venerable sirs, where are the noble ones going?” and when it was said, “Lay disciples, to a suitable place,” the wise people understood, “The venerable ones are searching for a dwelling for the rains-residence.” They said: “Venerable sirs, if the noble ones were to live here for these three months, we would become established in the refuges and undertake the precepts.” Those bhikkhus also consented, thinking, “Relying on these families, we will bring about release from existence.”

Manussā [M 1.0006] tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ paṭijaggitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni sampādetvā adaṃsu. Te nibaddhaṃ tameva gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisanti. Atha ne eko vejjo upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, bahūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne aphāsukampi nāma hoti, tasmiṃ uppanne mayhaṃ katheyyātha, bhesajjaṃ karissāmī”ti pavāresi. Thero vassūpanāyikadivase te bhikkhū āmantetvā pucchi, “āvuso[P 1.0009], imaṃ temāsaṃ katihi iriyāpathehi vītināmessathā”ti? “Catūhi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ panetaṃ, āvuso, patirūpaṃ, nanu appamattehi bhavitabbaṃ”? “Mayañhi dharamānakassa buddhassa santikā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā āgatā, buddhā ca nāma na sakkā pamādena ārādhetuṃ, kalyāṇajjhāsayena te vo ārādhetabbā. Pamattassa ca nāma cattāro apāyā sakagehasadisā, appamattā hothāvuso”ti. “Kiṃ tumhe pana, bhante”ti? “Ahaṃ tīhi iriyāpathehi vītināmessāmi, piṭṭhiṃ na pasāressāmi, āvuso”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, appamattā hothā”ti.

The people, accepting their promise, prepared the monastery, and having furnished places for the night and day, they made the offering. Those monks would regularly enter that very village for alms-food. Then a certain physician approached them and invited them, saying: "Venerable sirs, in a place where many dwell, discomfort can arise. When it arises, you should inform me. I will prepare medicine." On the day of entering the rains-residence, the Elder addressed those monks and asked: "Friends, with how many postures will you pass these three months?" "With four, venerable sir," they replied. "But friends, how is this proper? Should you not be diligent? For we have come after receiving a meditation subject from the presence of the living Buddha. And Buddhas, indeed, cannot be pleased through negligence; they are to be pleased by you with a wholesome intention. For one who is negligent, the four states of woe are like his own home. Be diligent, friends!" he said. "And what about you, venerable sir?" they asked. "I will pass the time with three postures; I will not stretch out my back, friends," he said. "Good, venerable sir. Be diligent," they said.

Atha therassa niddaṃ anokkamantassa paṭhamamāse atikkante majjhimamāse sampatte akkhirogo uppajji. Chiddaghaṭato udakadhārā viya akkhīhi assudhārā paggharanti. So sabbarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā aruṇuggamane gabbhaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Bhikkhū bhikkhācāravelāya therassa santikaṃ gantvā, “bhikkhācāravelā, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. “Tena hi, āvuso, gaṇhatha pattacīvara”nti. Attano pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā nikkhami. Bhikkhū tassa akkhīhi assūni paggharante disvā, “kimetaṃ, bhante”ti pucchiṃsu. “Akkhīni me, āvuso, vātā vijjhantī”ti. “Nanu, bhante, vejjena pavāritamhā, tassa kathemā”ti. “Sādhāvuso”ti [P 1.0010] te vejjassa kathayiṃsu. So telaṃ pacitvā pesesi. Thero nāsāya telaṃ āsiñcanto nisinnakova āsiñcitvā antogāmaṃ pāvisi. Vejjo taṃ disvā āha – “bhante, ayyassa kira akkhīni vāto vijjhatī”ti? “Āma, upāsakā”ti. “Bhante, mayā telaṃ pacitvā pesitaṃ, nāsāya vo telaṃ āsitta”nti? “Āma, upāsakā”ti. “Idāni [V 1.0007] kīdisa”nti? “Rujjateva upāsakā”ti. Vejjo “mayā ekavāreneva vūpasamanasamatthaṃ telaṃ pahitaṃ, kiṃ nu kho rogo na vūpasanto”ti cintetvā, “bhante, nisīditvā vo telaṃ āsittaṃ, nipajjitvā”ti pucchi. Thero tuṇhī ahosi, punappunaṃ pucchiyamānopi na kathesi. So “vihāraṃ gantvā therassa [M 1.0007] vasanaṭṭhānaṃ olokessāmī”ti cintetvā – “tena hi, bhante, gacchathā”ti theraṃ vissajjetvā vihāraṃ gantvā therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ olokento caṅkamananisīdanaṭṭhānameva disvā sayanaṭṭhānaṃ adisvā, “bhante, nisinnehi vo āsittaṃ, nipannehī”ti pucchi. Thero tuṇhī ahosi. “Mā, bhante, evaṃ karittha, samaṇadhammo nāma sarīraṃ yāpentena sakkā kātuṃ, nipajjitvā āsiñcathā”ti punappunaṃ yāci. “Gaccha tvaṃ tāvāvuso, mantetvā jānissāmī”ti vejjaṃ uyyojesi. Therassa ca tattha neva ñātī, na sālohitā atthi, tena saddhiṃ manteyya? Karajakāyena pana saddhiṃ mantento [P 1.0011] “vadehi tāva, āvuso pālita, tvaṃ kiṃ akkhīni olokessasi, udāhu buddhasāsanaṃ? Anamataggasmiñhi saṃsāravaṭṭe tava akkhikāṇassa gaṇanā nāma natthi, anekāni pana buddhasatāni buddhasahassāni atītāni. Tesu te ekabuddhopi na pariciṇṇo, idāni imaṃ antovassaṃ tayo māse na nipajjissāmīti temāsaṃ nibaddhavīriyaṃ karissāmi. Tasmā te cakkhūni nassantu vā bhijjantu vā, buddhasāsanameva dhārehi, mā cakkhūnī”ti bhūtakāyaṃ ovadanto imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then, for the Elder who was not succumbing to sleep, when the first month of the rains-residence had passed and the middle month arrived, an eye disease arose. Like streams of water from a pierced pot, streams of tears flowed from his eyes. He, having practiced a recluse's duties for the entire night, entered his cell at the rising of the dawn and sat down. At the time for the alms-round, the monks went to the Elder's presence and said, "Venerable sir, it is time for the alms-round." "Well then, friends, take the bowl and robe," he said. Having had his own bowl and robe taken, he went out. The monks, seeing tears streaming from his eyes, asked, "What is this, venerable sir?" "Friends, winds are piercing my eyes," he said. "Venerable sir, were we not invited by the physician? Let us tell him." "Good, friends," he said. They told the physician. He prepared oil and sent it. The Elder, pouring the oil into his nose, applied it while sitting and entered the village. The physician, seeing him, said, "Venerable sir, is it true that wind is piercing the noble one's eyes?" "Yes, lay follower." "Venerable sir, I prepared and sent oil. Was the oil applied to your nose?" "Yes, lay follower." "How is it now?" "It is still painful, lay follower." The physician thought, "I sent an oil capable of curing with just one application. Why indeed has the disease not subsided?" and asked, "Venerable sir, was the oil applied by you while sitting, or while lying down?" The Elder became silent. Though asked again and again, he did not speak. The physician, thinking, "I will go to the monastery and observe the Elder's dwelling place," dismissed the Elder, saying, "Well then, venerable sir, you may go." He went to the monastery, and while observing the Elder's dwelling place, he saw only a place for walking and a place for sitting; not seeing a place for sleeping, he asked, "Venerable sir, was it applied by you while sitting, or while lying down?" The Elder was silent. "Venerable sir, do not do thus. A recluse's duties can be performed by one who sustains the body. Please apply it while lying down," he requested again and again. "Go for now, friend. Having consulted, I will decide," he said, dismissing the physician. Now, the Elder had neither relatives nor kinsmen there. With whom could he consult? Consulting, however, with his own physical body, he said: "Speak now, friend Pālita! Will you look after your eyes, or the Buddha's Dispensation? For in this beginningless round of rebirth, the count of your times of blindness is indeed without number. Moreover, many hundreds of Buddhas, thousands of Buddhas, have passed away. Among them, not even one Buddha has been attended to by you. Now, during this rains-residence, for these three months, I will not lie down. I will make a constant effort for three months. Therefore, let your eyes be destroyed or let them be broken! Uphold only the Buddha's Dispensation, not the eyes!" Admonishing his physical body thus, he spoke these verses:

“Cakkhūni hāyantu mamāyitāni,

Sotāni hāyantu tatheva kāyo;

Sabbampidaṃ hāyatu dehanissitaṃ,

Kiṃ kāraṇā pālita tvaṃ pamajjasi.

Let these cherished eyes decay, let the ears decay, and likewise this body. Let all this that is dependent on the body decay. For what reason, Pālita, are you negligent?

“Cakkhūni jīrantu mamāyitāni,

Sotāni jīrantu tatheva kāyo;

Sabbampidaṃ jīratu dehanissitaṃ,

Kiṃ kāraṇā pālita tvaṃ pamajjasi.

Let these cherished eyes grow old, let the ears grow old, and likewise this body. Let all this that is dependent on the body grow old. For what reason, Pālita, are you negligent?

“Cakkhūni bhijjantu mamāyitāni,

Sotāni bhijjantu tatheva kāyo;

Sabbampidaṃ [V 1.0008] bhijjatu dehanissitaṃ,

Kiṃ kāraṇā pālita tvaṃ pamajjasī”ti.

Let these cherished eyes be broken, let the ears be broken, and likewise this body. Let all this that is dependent on the body be broken. For what reason, Pālita, are you negligent?

Evaṃ [M 1.0008][P 1.0012] tīhi gāthāhi attano ovādaṃ datvā nisinnakova natthukammaṃ katvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Vejjo taṃ disvā “kiṃ, bhante, natthukammaṃ kata”nti pucchi. “Āma, upāsakā”ti. “Kīdisaṃ, bhante”ti? “Rujjateva upāsakā”ti. “Nisīditvā vo, bhante, natthukammaṃ kataṃ, nipajjitvā”ti. Thero tuṇhī ahosi, punappunaṃ pucchiyamānopi na kiñci kathesi. Atha naṃ vejjo, “bhante, tumhe sappāyaṃ na karotha, ajjato paṭṭhāya ‘asukena me telaṃ pakka’nti mā vadittha, ahampi ‘mayā vo telaṃ pakka’nti na vakkhāmī”ti āha. So vejjena paccakkhāto vihāraṃ gantvā tvaṃ vejjenāpi paccakkhātosi, iriyāpathaṃ mā vissajji samaṇāti.

Thus, having given himself counsel with three verses, while still sitting, he performed the nasal treatment and entered the village for alms. The physician, seeing him, asked, "Venerable sir, has the nasal treatment been performed?" "Yes, lay follower." "How is it, venerable sir?" "It is still painful, lay follower." "Venerable sir, was the nasal treatment performed by you while sitting, or while lying down?" The Elder became silent; though asked again and again, he said nothing. Then the physician said to him, "Venerable sir, you do not do what is suitable. From today onwards, do not say, ‘The oil was prepared for me by such-and-such a person,’ and I too will not say, ‘I will prepare oil for you.’” He, rejected by the physician, went to the monastery and admonished himself, saying, "You have been rejected even by the physician, O recluse; do not abandon the posture!"

“Paṭikkhitto tikicchāya, vejjenāpi vivajjito;

Niyato maccurājassa, kiṃ pālita pamajjasī”ti. –

Rejected from treatment, and abandoned by the physician; you are certainly bound for the King of Death. Why, Pālita, are you heedless?

Imāya gāthāya attānaṃ ovaditvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Athassa majjhimayāme atikkante apubbaṃ acarimaṃ akkhīni ceva kilesā ca bhijjiṃsu. So sukkhavipassako arahā hutvā gabbhaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi.

Having admonished himself with this verse, he practiced the recluse's duty. Then, when the middle watch of the night had passed, simultaneously both his eyes and the defilements were destroyed. Having become a dry-insight Arahant, he entered his cell and sat down.

Bhikkhū bhikkhācāravelāya āgantvā “bhikkhācārakālo, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. “Kālo, āvuso”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Tena hi gacchathā”ti. “Kiṃ tumhe pana, bhante”ti? “Akkhīni me, āvuso, parihīnānī”ti. Te tassa akkhīni oloketvā assupuṇṇanettā hutvā, “bhante, mā cintayittha, mayaṃ [P 1.0013] vo paṭijaggissāmā”ti theraṃ samassāsetvā kattabbayuttakaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Manussā theraṃ adisvā, “bhante, amhākaṃ ayyo kuhi”nti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā yāguṃ pesetvā sayaṃ piṇḍapātamādāya gantvā theraṃ vanditvā pādamūle parivattamānā roditvā, “bhante, mayaṃ vo paṭijaggissāma, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti samassāsetvā pakkamiṃsu.

The monks, having come at the time for the alms-round, said, "Venerable sir, it is time for the alms-round." "Is it time, friends?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Then go." "But what about you, venerable sir?" "My eyes have failed, friends." They looked at his eyes and, their own eyes filled with tears, comforted the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, do not worry; we will attend to you." Having performed the duties and services that ought to be done, they entered the village for alms. The people, not seeing the Elder, asked, "Venerable sirs, where is our noble one?" and having heard what had happened, they sent rice gruel. Taking almsfood themselves, they went to the Elder, paid homage, and rolling about at his feet, they wept. Comforting him, they said, "Venerable sir, we will attend to you; do not worry," and then they departed.

Tato paṭṭhāya nibaddhaṃ yāgubhattaṃ vihārameva pesenti. Theropi itare saṭṭhi bhikkhū nirantaraṃ ovadati. Te tassovāde ṭhatvā upakaṭṭhāya pavāraṇāya sabbeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu[V 1.0009]. Te vuṭṭhavassā ca pana satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmā hutvā theramāhaṃsu, “bhante, satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmamhā”ti[M 1.0009]. Thero tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “ahaṃ dubbalo, antarāmagge ca amanussapariggahitā aṭavī atthi, mayi etehi saddhiṃ gacchante sabbe kilamissanti, bhikkhampi labhituṃ na sakkhissanti, ime puretarameva pesessāmī”ti. Atha ne āha – “āvuso, tumhe purato gacchathā”ti. “Tumhe pana bhante”ti? “Ahaṃ dubbalo, antarāmagge ca amanussapariggahitā aṭavī atthi, mayi tumhehi saddhiṃ gacchante sabbe kilamissatha, tumhe purato gacchathā”ti. “Mā, bhante, evaṃ karittha, mayaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃyeva gamissāmā”ti. “Mā vo, āvuso, evaṃ ruccittha, evaṃ sante mayhaṃ aphāsukaṃ bhavissati, mayhaṃ kaniṭṭho pana tumhe disvā pucchissati, athassa mama cakkhūnaṃ [P 1.0014] parihīnabhāvaṃ āroceyyātha, so mayhaṃ santikaṃ kañcideva pahiṇissati, tena saddhiṃ āgacchissāmi, tumhe mama vacanena dasabalañca asītimahāthere ca vandathā”ti te uyyojesi.

From that day onwards, they regularly sent rice gruel and food to the monastery. The elder also continuously admonished the other sixty monks. Abiding in his instruction, when the Pavāraṇā was near, they all attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having completed the rains-residence, they wished to see the Teacher and said to the elder, 'Venerable sir, we wish to see the Teacher.' Hearing their words, the elder reflected: 'I am weak, and on the way there is a wilderness possessed by non-human beings. If I go with them, all will become weary, and they will not be able to obtain alms. I shall send them on ahead.' Then he said to them, 'Friends, you go on ahead.' 'But what about you, venerable sir?' 'I am weak, and on the way there is a wilderness possessed by non-human beings. If I go with you, all of you will become weary. You go on ahead.' 'Venerable sir, do not do so. We will go only with you.' 'Friends, do not approve of this. If it is so, it will be uncomfortable for me. My younger brother will see you and ask. Then you should inform him of the loss of my sight. He will send someone to me, and I will come with that person. By my word, pay homage to the One with Ten Powers and to the eighty great elders.' Thus, he sent them off.

Te theraṃ khamāpetvā antogāmaṃ pavisiṃsu. Manussā te disvā nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ datvā “kiṃ, bhante, ayyānaṃ gamanākāro paññāyatī”ti? “Āma, upāsakā, satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmamhā”ti. Te punappunaṃ yācitvā tesaṃ gamanachandameva ñatvā anugantvā paridevitvā nivattiṃsu. Tepi anupubbena jetavanaṃ gantvā satthārañca asītimahāthere ca therassa vacanena vanditvā punadivase yattha therassa kaniṭṭho vasati, taṃ vīthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Kuṭumbiko te sañjānitvā nisīdāpetvā katapaṭisanthāro “bhātikatthero me, bhante, kuhi”nti pucchi. Athassa te taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. So taṃ sutvāva tesaṃ pādamūle parivattento roditvā pucchi – “idāni, bhante, kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Thero ito kassaci āgamanaṃ paccāsīsati, tassa gatakāle tena saddhiṃ āgamissatī”ti. “Ayaṃ me, bhante, bhāgineyyo pālito nāma, etaṃ pesethā”ti. “Evaṃ pesetuṃ na sakkā, magge paripantho atthi, taṃ pabbājetvā pesetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Evaṃ katvā pesetha, bhante”ti. Atha naṃ pabbājetvā aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ pattacīvaraggahaṇādīni sikkhāpetvā maggaṃ ācikkhitvā pahiṇiṃsu.

Having taken leave of the elder, they entered the village. Seeing them, the people had them take a seat, offered alms, and asked, 'Venerable sirs, does it appear that the noble ones are undertaking a journey?' 'Yes, lay followers, we wish to see the Teacher.' The people pleaded with them again and again, but knowing their firm desire to go, they accompanied them for a distance, lamented, and then turned back. They, in due course, arrived at Jetavana and, by the elder's word, paid homage to the Teacher and the eighty great elders. The next day, they entered the street where the elder's younger brother lived for alms. The householder recognized them, had them take a seat, and after exchanging friendly greetings, asked, 'Venerable sirs, where is my brother, the elder?' Then they told him what had happened. As soon as he heard it, he fell rolling at their feet, wept, and asked, 'Venerable sirs, what is to be done now?' They replied, 'The elder expects someone to come from here; when that person arrives, he will come with him.' 'Venerable sirs, this is my nephew named Pālita. Please send him.' 'It is not possible to send him as he is; there is danger on the road. It is proper to give him the going forth and then send him.' 'Having done so, venerable sirs, please send him.' Then, having given him the going forth, they had him train for about half a month in matters such as the taking of the bowl and robes, explained the way to him, and sent him off.

So anupubbena taṃ gāmaṃ patvā gāmadvāre ekaṃ mahallakaṃ disvā, “imaṃ gāmaṃ nissāya koci āraññako vihāro atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Ko nāma tattha vasatī”ti? “Pālitatthero nāma, bhante”ti. “Maggaṃ me ācikkhathā”ti. “Kosi tvaṃ, bhante”ti? “Therassa bhāgineyyomhī”ti. Atha [M 1.0010] naṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ [P 1.0015] nesi. So theraṃ vanditvā aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā theraṃ sammā paṭijaggitvā, “bhante, mātulakuṭumbiko me tumhākaṃ [V 1.0010] āgamanaṃ paccāsīsati, etha, gacchāmā”ti āha. “Tena hi imaṃ me yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. So yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ gahetvā therena saddhiṃ antogāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā theraṃ nisīdāpetvā “kiṃ, bhante, gamanākāro vo paññāyatī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Āma, upāsakā, gantvā satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti. Te nānappakārena yācitvā alabhantā theraṃ uyyojetvā upaḍḍhapathaṃ gantvā roditvā nivattiṃsu. Sāmaṇero theraṃ yaṭṭhikoṭiyā ādāya gacchanto antarāmagge aṭaviyaṃ kaṭṭhanagaraṃ nāma therena upanissāya vuṭṭhapubbaṃ gāmaṃ sampāpuṇi, so gāmato nikkhamitvā araññe gītaṃ gāyitvā dārūni uddharantiyā ekissā itthiyā gītasaddaṃ sutvā sare nimittaṃ gaṇhi. Itthisaddo viya hi añño saddo purisānaṃ sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā ṭhātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Tenāha bhagavā –

Gradually reaching that village, he saw an old man at the village gate and asked, “Is there any forest monastery dependent on this village?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What is the name of the one who lives there?” “The elder named Pāla, venerable sir.” “Please tell me the way.” “Who are you, venerable sir?” “I am the elder’s nephew.” Then, taking him, he led him to the monastery. He paid respects to the elder and, after performing his duties and properly attending to the elder for about half a month, he said, “Venerable sir, my uncle, the householder, awaits your arrival. Come, let us go.” “In that case, take this end of my staff.” Taking the end of the staff, he entered the village with the elder. The people seated the elder and asked, “Venerable sir, does it appear that you are preparing for a journey?” “Yes, lay devotees, I will go and pay homage to the Teacher.” Though they entreated him in various ways, failing to persuade him, they sent the elder off, accompanied him halfway, and, weeping, turned back. The novice, leading the elder by the end of his staff, while proceeding on the way through a forest, reached a village named Kaṭṭhanagara, where the elder had previously dwelt. Leaving the village, he heard the singing of a woman gathering firewood in the forest and took the sound as a sign. Indeed, no other sound like a woman's voice is capable of pervading and remaining in a man’s entire body. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekasaddampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, itthisaddo”ti (a. ni. 1.2).

“Monks, I do not see any other single sound that so takes possession of a man's mind and remains there as does the sound of a woman.”

Sāmaṇero tattha nimittaṃ gahetvā yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ vissajjetvā “tiṭṭhatha tāva, bhante, kiccaṃ me atthī”ti tassā santikaṃ [P 1.0016] gato. Sā taṃ disvā tuṇhī ahosi. So tāya saddhiṃ sīlavipattiṃ pāpuṇi. Thero cintesi – “idāneva eko gītasaddo suyyittha. So ca kho itthiyā saddo chijji, sāmaṇeropi cirāyati, so tāya saddhiṃ sīlavipattiṃ patto bhavissatī”ti. Sopi attano kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā āgantvā “gacchāma, bhante”ti āha. Atha naṃ thero pucchi – “pāpojātosi sāmaṇerā”ti. So tuṇhī hutvā therena punappunaṃ puṭṭhopi na kiñci kathesi. Atha naṃ thero āha – “tādisena pāpena mama yaṭṭhikoṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthī”ti. So saṃvegappatto kāsāyāni apanetvā gihiniyāmena paridahitvā, “bhante, ahaṃ pubbe sāmaṇero, idāni panamhi gihī jāto, pabbajantopi ca svāhaṃ na saddhāya pabbajito, maggaparipanthabhayena pabbajito, etha gacchāmā”ti āha. “Āvuso, gihipāpopi samaṇapāpopi pāpoyeva, tvaṃ samaṇabhāve ṭhatvāpi sīlamattaṃ pūretuṃ nāsakkhi, gihī hutvā kiṃ [M 1.0011] nāma kalyāṇaṃ karissasi, tādisena pāpena mama yaṭṭhikoṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthī”ti āha. “Bhante, amanussupaddavo maggo, tumhe ca andhā apariṇāyakā, kathaṃ idha vasissathā”ti? Atha naṃ thero, “āvuso, tvaṃ mā evaṃ cintayi, idheva me nipajjitvā marantassāpi aparāparaṃ parivattantassāpi tayā saddhiṃ gamanaṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The novice, having taken that sound as a sign, released the end of the staff and, saying, “Wait a moment, venerable sir, I have some business,” went to her. Seeing him, she became silent. He then reached a state of corrupted virtue with her. The elder thought: “Just now, a singing voice was heard. And that woman’s voice stopped. The novice is also taking a long time; he must have reached a state of corrupted virtue with her.” Having finished his business, he returned and said, “Let us go, venerable sir.” Then the elder asked him, “Novice, have you become wicked?” He remained silent, and even when questioned repeatedly by the elder, he said nothing. Then the elder said to him, “For one as wicked as you, there is no task of holding the end of my staff.” Struck with spiritual urgency, he took off the saffron robes, dressed in the manner of a householder, and said, “Venerable sir, I was formerly a novice, but now I have become a layman. And when I went forth, I did not go forth out of faith; I went forth out of fear of dangers on the road. Come, let us go.” “Friend, the wickedness of a layman and the wickedness of an ascetic are both just wickedness. While in the state of an ascetic, you were unable to fulfill even a mere measure of morality; having become a layman, what good will you do? For one as wicked as you, there is no task of holding the end of my staff.” “Venerable sir, the road is beset by non-human dangers, and you are blind and without a guide. How will you stay here?” Then the elder said to him, “Friend, do not think so. Even if I were to lie down here, rolling back and forth until I die, there is no such thing as going with you.” And he spoke these verses:

“Handāhaṃ [V 1.0011] hatacakkhusmi, kantāraddhānamāgato;

Seyyamāno na gacchāmi, natthi bāle sahāyatā.

“Indeed, I am one whose eyes are lost, having come to a difficult wilderness road; I shall lie down, I will not go; there is no companionship with a fool.”

“Handāhaṃ [P 1.0017] hatacakkhusmi, kantāraddhānamāgato;

Marissāmi no gamissāmi, natthi bāle sahāyatā”ti.

“Indeed, I am one whose eyes are lost, having come to a difficult wilderness road; I shall die, I will not go; there is no companionship with a fool.”

Taṃ sutvā itaro saṃvegajāto “bhāriyaṃ vata me sāhasikaṃ ananucchavikaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti bāhā paggayha kandanto vanasaṇḍaṃ pakkhanditvā tathā pakkantova ahosi. Therassāpi sīlatejena saṭṭhiyojanāyāmaṃ paññāsayojanavitthataṃ pannarasayojanabahalaṃ jayasumanapupphavaṇṇaṃ nisīdanuṭṭhahanakālesu onamanunnamanapakatikaṃ sakkassa devarañño paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti olokento dibbena cakkhunā theraṃ addasa. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Hearing that, the other, becoming spiritually agitated, thought, “Indeed, I have committed a grave, reckless, and improper deed.” Wailing with upraised arms, he plunged into the forest thicket and departed just so. And by the elder's power of virtue, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of Sakka, the king of the gods—sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick, having the color of jayasumanā flowers, and by nature sinking and rising when he sat or stood—showed a sign of heat. Sakka, looking around, thought, “Who now seeks to dislodge me from my position?” and with his divine eye, he saw the elder. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Sahassanetto devindo, dibbacakkhuṃ visodhayi;

Pāpagarahī ayaṃ pālo, ājīvaṃ parisodhayi.

“The thousand-eyed lord of gods purified his divine eye; this Pāla, a censor of evil, purified his livelihood.”

“Sahassanetto devindo, dibbacakkhuṃ visodhayi;

Dhammagaruko ayaṃ pālo, nisinno sāsane rato”ti.

“The thousand-eyed lord of gods purified his divine eye; this Pāla, who respects the Dhamma, is seated, delighting in the Dispensation.”

Athassa etadahosi – “sacāhaṃ evarūpassa pāpagarahino dhammagarukassa ayyassa santikaṃ na gamissāmi, muddhā me sattadhā phaleyya, gamissāmi tassa santika”nti. Tato –

Then this thought occurred to him: “If I do not go to the presence of such a venerable one who censures evil and respects the Dhamma, my head will split into seven pieces. I will go to his presence.” Then:

“Sahassanetto devindo, devarajjasirindharo;

Taṅkhaṇena āgantvāna, cakkhupālamupāgami”. –

“The thousand-eyed lord of gods, bearer of the divine kingdom’s glory, having come in that instant, approached Cakkhupāla.”

Upagantvā [P 1.0018] ca pana therassa avidūre padasaddamakāsi. Atha naṃ thero pucchi – “ko eso”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, addhiko”ti. “Kuhiṃ yāsi upāsakā”ti[M 1.0012]? “Sāvatthiyaṃ, bhante”ti. “Yāhi, āvuso”ti. “Ayyo pana, bhante, kuhiṃ gamissatī”ti? “Ahampi tattheva gamissāmī”ti. “Tena hi ekatova gacchāma, bhante”ti. “Ahaṃ, āvuso, dubbalo, mayā saddhiṃ gacchantassa tava papañco bhavissatī”ti. “Mayhaṃ accāyikaṃ natthi, ahampi ayyena [V 1.0012] saddhiṃ gacchanto dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu ekaṃ labhissāmi, ekatova gacchāma, bhante”ti. Thero “eso sappuriso bhavissatī”ti cintetvā – “tena hi saddhiṃ gamissāmi, yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ gaṇha upāsakā”ti āha. Sakko tathā katvā pathaviṃ saṅkhipanto sāyanhasamaye jetavanaṃ sampāpesi. Thero saṅkhapaṇavādisaddaṃ sutvā “kattheso saddo”ti pucchi. “Sāvatthiyaṃ, bhante”ti? “Pubbe mayaṃ gamanakāle cirena gamimhā”ti. “Ahaṃ ujumaggaṃ jānāmi, bhante”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero “nāyaṃ manusso, devatā bhavissatī”ti sallakkhesi.

Then, having approached, he made the sound of footsteps not far from the elder. The elder asked him, “Who is that?” “I, venerable sir, am a traveler.” “Where are you going, lay follower?” “To Sāvatthī, venerable sir.” “Go, friend.” “And where, venerable sir, will you be going?” “I too am going there.” “In that case, let us go together, venerable sir.” “I, friend, am weak; for you, going with me will be a delay.” “I have no urgent business. By going with you, venerable sir, I will gain one of the ten bases of meritorious action. Let us go together, venerable sir.” The elder thought, “This must be a good person,” and said, “In that case, lay follower, take the end of my staff.” Sakka did so and, contracting the earth, brought him to Jetavana by evening. Hearing the sound of conches, drums, and so on, the elder asked, “Where is that sound from?” “From Sāvatthī, venerable sir.” “Before, when we were traveling, we took a long time to arrive.” “I know the straight path, venerable sir.” At that moment, the elder realized, “This is not a human; he must be a deity.”

“Sahassanetto devindo, devarajjasirindharo;

Saṅkhipitvāna taṃ maggaṃ, khippaṃ sāvatthimāgamī”ti.

“The thousand-eyed lord of gods, bearer of the divine kingdom’s glory, having contracted that path, quickly arrived at Sāvatthī.”

So theraṃ netvā therassevatthāya kaniṭṭhakuṭumbikena kāritaṃ [P 1.0019] paṇṇasālaṃ netvā phalake nisīdāpetvā piyasahāyakavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ gantvā, “samma, cūḷapālā”ti pakkosi. “Kiṃ, sammā”ti? “Therassāgatabhāvaṃ jānāsī”ti? “Na jānāmi, kiṃ pana thero āgato”ti? “Āma, samma, idāni ahaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā theraṃ tayā kāritapaṇṇasālāya nisinnakaṃ disvā āgatomhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Kuṭumbikopi vihāraṃ gantvā theraṃ disvā pādamūle parivattanto roditvā “idaṃ disvā ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ pabbajituṃ nādāsi”ntiādīni vatvā dve dāsadārake bhujisse katvā therassa santike pabbājetvā “antogāmato yāgubhattādīni āharitvā theraṃ upaṭṭhahathā”ti paṭiyādesi. Sāmaṇerā vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā theraṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu.

He led the elder to the leaf hut built by the younger brother householder for the elder's use, seated him on a plank, and then, in the guise of a dear friend, went to the householder's presence and called out, “Friend Cūḷapāla!” “What is it, friend?” “Do you know of the elder's arrival?” “I do not know. But has the elder come?” “Yes, friend. Just now I went to the monastery and, seeing the elder seated in the leaf hut you had built, I have come.” Having said this, he departed. The householder also went to the monastery and, upon seeing the elder, rolled at his feet, weeping, and said, “It was from foreseeing this that I, venerable sir, did not give you leave to go forth.” After saying this and more, he freed two slave boys and had them ordained in the elder’s presence, instructing them: “Bring gruel, rice, and so on from inside the village and attend to the elder.” The novices performed their major and minor duties and attended to the elder.

Athekadivasaṃ disāvāsino bhikkhū “satthāraṃ passissāmā”ti jetavanaṃ āgantvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā asītimahāthere ca, vanditvā vihāracārikaṃ carantā cakkhupālattherassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā “idampi passissāmā”ti sāyaṃ [M 1.0013] tadabhimukhā ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāmegho uṭṭhahi. Te “idāni atisāyanho, megho ca uṭṭhito, pātova gantvā passissāmā”ti nivattiṃsu. Devo paṭhamayāmaṃ vassitvā majjhimayāme vigato. Thero āraddhavīriyo āciṇṇacaṅkamano, tasmā pacchimayāme caṅkamanaṃ otari. Tadā ca pana navavuṭṭhāya bhūmiyā bahū indagopakā [P 1.0020] uṭṭhahiṃsu. Te there caṅkamante yebhuyyena vipajjiṃsu. Antevāsikā therassa caṅkamanaṭṭhānaṃ kālasseva na sammajjiṃsu. Itare bhikkhū “therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ passissāmā”ti āgantvā caṅkamane matapāṇake disvā “ko imasmiṃ caṅkamatī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Amhākaṃ upajjhāyo, bhante”ti. Te ujjhāyiṃsu “passathāvuso, samaṇassa kammaṃ, sacakkhukakāle nipajjitvā niddāyanto [V 1.0013] kiñci akatvā idāni cakkhuvikalakāle ‘caṅkamāmī’ti ettake pāṇake māresi ‘atthaṃ karissāmī’ti anatthaṃ karotī”ti.

Then one day, monks dwelling in the regions came to Jetavana, thinking, “We shall see the Teacher.” Having paid homage to the Tathāgata and the eighty great elders, they toured the monastery grounds. Reaching the dwelling place of the Elder Cakkhupāla, they thought, “We shall see this place too,” and in the evening, they went towards it. At that moment, a great cloud arose. They thought, “It is now very late in the evening, and a cloud has arisen. We shall go and see him early in the morning,” and they turned back. The rain, having fallen during the first watch of the night, ceased by the middle watch. The elder, being of aroused energy and accustomed to walking meditation, descended to his walking path in the last watch. At that time, on the ground fresh from the rain, many cochineal insects emerged. As the elder walked, they mostly perished. His resident pupils had not swept the elder's walking path early that morning. The other monks, coming to see the elder’s dwelling, saw the dead creatures on the walking path and asked, “Who walks on this path?” “Our preceptor, venerable sirs.” They criticized, saying: “See, friends, the deed of this ascetic! When he had his sight, he would lie down, sleeping and doing nothing. Now, when his eyes are impaired, thinking ‘I will walk,’ he has killed so many living beings. Thinking ‘I will do what is beneficial,’ he does what is harmful.”

Atha kho te gantvā tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ, “bhante, cakkhupālatthero ‘caṅkamāmī’ti bahū pāṇake māresī”ti. “Kiṃ pana so tumhehi mārento diṭṭho”ti? “Na diṭṭho, bhante”ti. “Yatheva tumhe taṃ na passatha, tatheva sopi te pāṇe na passati. Khīṇāsavānaṃ maraṇacetanā nāma natthi, bhikkhave”ti. “Bhante, arahattassa upanissaye sati kasmā andho jāto”ti? “Attano katakammavasena, bhikkhave”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, tena kata”nti? Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha –

Then they went and reported to the Tathāgata: “Venerable sir, the Elder Cakkhupāla, thinking ‘I will walk,’ has killed many living beings.” “But was he seen by you while killing?” “He was not seen, venerable sir.” “Just as you do not see him, so too he does not see those living beings. Monks, for those whose taints are destroyed, there is no such thing as an intention to kill.” “Venerable sir, when there was a supporting condition for Arahantship, why did he become blind?” “Because of a deed done by himself, monks.” “But what, venerable sir, was done by him?” “In that case, monks, listen –”

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ kāsiraññe rajjaṃ kārente eko vejjo gāmanigamesu caritvā vejjakammaṃ karonto ekaṃ cakkhudubbalaṃ itthiṃ disvā pucchi – “kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti? “Akkhīhi na passāmī”ti. “Bhesajjaṃ te karissāmī”ti? “Karohi, sāmī”ti. “Kiṃ me dassasī”ti? “Sace me akkhīni pākatikāni kātuṃ sakkhissasi, ahaṃ te saddhiṃ puttadhītāhi dāsī bhavissāmī”ti. So “sādhū”ti bhesajjaṃ saṃvidahi, ekabhesajjeneva akkhīni pākatikāni ahesuṃ. Sā [P 1.0021] cintesi – “ahametassa saputtadhītā dāsī bhavissāmī”ti paṭijāniṃ, “na kho pana maṃ saṇhena sammācārena samudācarissati, vañcessāmi na”nti. Sā vejjenāgantvā “kīdisaṃ, bhadde”ti puṭṭhā “pubbe me akkhīni thokaṃ rujjiṃsu, idāni pana atirekataraṃ rujjantī”ti āha. Vejjo “ayaṃ maṃ vañcetvā kiñci adātukāmā, na me etāya dinnāya [M 1.0014] bhatiyā attho, idāneva naṃ andhaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā gehaṃ gantvā bhariyāya etamatthaṃ ācikkhi. Sā tuṇhī ahosi. So ekaṃ bhesajjaṃ yojetvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā “bhadde, imaṃ bhesajjaṃ añjehī”ti añjāpesi. Athassā dve akkhīni dīpasikhā viya vijjhāyiṃsu. So vejjo cakkhupālo ahosi.

In the past, while a king of Kāsi was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a certain physician traveling through villages and towns practicing medicine saw a woman with weak eyes and asked, 'What is your discomfort?' 'I cannot see with my eyes,' she replied. 'I will prepare medicine for you,' he said. 'Please do, master.' 'What will you give me?' 'If you can restore my eyes to their normal state, I, along with my sons and daughters, will become your female slave.' Agreeing, 'Very well,' he prepared the medicine. With just one application, her eyes were restored to their normal state. She thought, 'I promised to become his female slave along with my sons and daughters, but he will not treat me with gentle and proper conduct; I will deceive him.' When the physician came and asked, 'Good lady, how are your eyes?' she replied, 'Before, my eyes ached a little, but now they ache exceedingly more.' The physician thought, 'This woman wishes to deceive me and give nothing. I have no need for any fee from her. I will make her blind right now.' Having thought this, he went home and told the matter to his wife. She remained silent. He then prepared a medicine, went to the woman, and had her apply it, saying, 'Good lady, apply this medicine.' Then her two eyes were extinguished like the flames of a lamp. That physician became Cakkhupāla.

Bhikkhave, tadā mama puttena katakammaṃ pacchato pacchato anubandhi. Pāpakammañhi nāmetaṃ dhuraṃ vahato balibaddassa padaṃ cakkaṃ viya anugacchatīti idaṃ vatthuṃ kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā patiṭṭhāpitamattikaṃ sāsanaṃ rājamuddāya lañchanto viya dhammarājā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Monks, at that time, the kamma done by my son followed close behind him. For indeed, this evil kamma follows just as the wheel follows the foot of the bullock that bears the yoke. Having related this story and made the connection, the King of Dhamma, like one sealing with a royal seal a message set in clay, spoke this verse:

1.

1.

“Manopubbaṅgamā [V 1.0014] dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā;

Manasā ce paduṭṭhena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ dukkhamanveti, cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti.

Mind is the forerunner of all states. Mind is their chief; they are mind-made. If, with a corrupted mind, one speaks or acts, then suffering follows one even as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that pulls the cart.

Tattha manoti kāmāvacarakusalādibhedaṃ sabbampi catubhūmikacittaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana pade tadā tassa vejjassa uppannacittavasena niyamiyamānaṃ vavatthāpiyamānaṃ [P 1.0022] paricchijjiyamānaṃ domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayuttacittameva labbhati. Pubbaṅgamāti tena paṭhamagāminā hutvā samannāgatā. Dhammāti guṇadesanāpariyattinissattanijjīvavasena cattāro dhammā nāma. Tesu –

Therein, 'mano' refers to all consciousness of the four planes, differentiated as sense-sphere wholesome states and so on. In this particular context, however, being defined and determined by the mind that arose in that physician at that time, only consciousness associated with aversion and accompanied by displeasure is to be taken. 'Forerunner' means they are endowed with that which goes first. 'Dhammā' refers to four things by way of: quality, teaching, scriptural learning, and that which is devoid of a being or a life-principle. Among these—

“Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”nti. (theragā. 304; jā. 1.15.386) –

Indeed, Dhamma and Adhamma

Both do not have the same result.

Adhamma leads to hell,

Dhamma leads to a good bourn.

Ayaṃ guṇadhammo nāma. “Dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.420) ayaṃ desanādhammo nāma. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ geyya”nti (ma. ni. 1.239) ayaṃ pariyattidhammo nāma. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti, khandhā hontī”ti (dha. sa. 121) ayaṃ nissattadhammo nāma, nijjīvadhammotipi eso eva. Tesu imasmiṃ ṭhāne nissattanijjīvadhammo adhippeto. So atthato tayo arūpino khandhā vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandhoti. Ete hi mano pubbaṅgamo etesanti manopubbaṅgamā nāma.

This is called the Dhamma of quality. 'Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning'—this is called the Dhamma of teaching. 'Here, monks, some sons of good family learn the Dhamma—the Suttas, the Geyyas...'—this is called the Dhamma of scriptural learning. 'At that time there are dhammas, there are aggregates'—this is called the Dhamma devoid of a being; the Dhamma devoid of a life-principle is this very same thing. Among these, in this instance, the Dhamma devoid of a being and a life-principle is intended. In meaning, this refers to the three formless aggregates: the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations. For these have mind as their forerunner, therefore they are called 'preceded by mind'.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0015] panetehi saddhiṃ ekavatthuko ekārammaṇo apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇe uppajjamāno mano pubbaṅgamo nāma hotīti? Uppādapaccayaṭṭhena. Yathā hi bahūsu ekato gāmaghātādīni kammāni karontesu “ko etesaṃ pubbaṅgamo”ti vutte yo nesaṃ paccayo hoti, yaṃ nissāya te taṃ kammaṃ karonti, so datto vā mitto vā tesaṃ pubbaṅgamoti vuccati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ [P 1.0023] veditabbaṃ. Iti uppādapaccayaṭṭhena mano pubbaṅgamo etesanti manopubbaṅgamā. Na hi te mane anuppajjante uppajjituṃ sakkonti, mano pana ekaccesu cetasikesu anupajjantesupi uppajjatiyeva. Adhipativasena pana mano seṭṭho etesanti manoseṭṭho. Yathā hi corādīnaṃ corajeṭṭhakādayo adhipatino seṭṭhā. Tathā tesampi mano adhipati manova seṭṭhā. Yathā pana dāruādīhi [V 1.0015] nipphannāni tāni tāni bhaṇḍāni dārumayādīni nāma honti, tathā tepi manato nipphannattā manomayā nāma.

How then is mind—arising together with these states in a single moment, not before and not after, having the same base and the same object—called the forerunner? By way of being a condition for their arising. For just as when many are together performing deeds such as raiding a village, and it is asked, 'Who is their forerunner?', he who is their support, depending on whom they perform that deed—be he Datta or Mitta—is called their forerunner; so should this simile be understood. Thus, by way of being a condition for their arising, mind is the forerunner for these states, therefore they are called 'preceded by mind'. For they are not able to arise when mind does not arise, but mind can indeed arise even when some mental factors do not arise. By way of dominance, however, mind is chief for these states, therefore they are called 'having mind as chief'. For just as for thieves and so on, the chief thieves are the dominant and chief ones, so too for these states, mind is dominant, mind itself is chief. And just as various goods produced from wood and so on are called 'wooden' and so on, so too these states, because they are produced from mind, are called 'mind-made'.

Paduṭṭhenāti āgantukehi abhijjhādīhi dosehi paduṭṭhena. Pakatimano hi bhavaṅgacittaṃ, taṃ apaduṭṭhaṃ. Yathā hi pasannaṃ udakaṃ āgantukehi nīlādīhi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ nīlodakādibhedaṃ hoti, na ca navaṃ udakaṃ, nāpi purimaṃ pasannaudakameva, tathā tampi āgantukehi abhijjhādīhi dosehi paduṭṭhaṃ hoti, na ca navaṃ cittaṃ, nāpi purimaṃ bhavaṅgacittameva, tenāha bhagavā – “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.49). Evaṃ manasā ce paduṭṭhena, bhāsati vā karoti vā so bhāsamāno catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritameva bhāsati, karonto tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritameva karoti, abhāsanto akaronto tāya abhijjhādīhi paduṭṭhamānasatāya tividhaṃ manoduccaritaṃ pūreti. Evamassa dasa akusalakammapathā pāripūriṃ gacchanti.

‘By a corrupted mind’ means: by a mind corrupted by adventitious faults such as covetousness and so forth. For the natural mind is the life-continuum consciousness, and that is uncorrupted. Just as clear water, when defiled by adventitious things such as blue dye, becomes a type of blue water, and yet it is neither new water nor is it just the former clear water; so too, that mind becomes corrupted by adventitious faults such as covetousness. It is neither a new mind, nor is it just the former life-continuum consciousness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘Luminous, O monks, is this mind, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.’ Thus, if with a corrupted mind one speaks or acts, then in speaking, one utters only the fourfold verbal misconduct; in acting, one performs only the threefold bodily misconduct. While not speaking and not acting, by that state of having a mind corrupted by covetousness and so forth, one fulfills the threefold mental misconduct. In this way, for that person, the ten unwholesome courses of action reach fulfillment.

Tato naṃ dukkhamanvetīti [P 1.0024] tato tividhaduccaritato taṃ puggalaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti, duccaritānubhāvena catūsu apāyesu, manussesu vā tamattabhāvaṃ gacchantaṃ kāyavatthukampi itarampīti iminā pariyāyena kāyikacetasikaṃ vipākadukkhaṃ anugacchati. Yathā kiṃ? Cakkaṃva vahato padanti dhure yuttassa dhuraṃ vahato balibaddassa padaṃ cakkaṃ viya. Yathā hi so ekampi divasaṃ dvepi pañcapi dasapi aḍḍhamāsampi māsampi vahanto cakkaṃ nivattetuṃ jahituṃ na sakkoti[M 1.0016], atha khvassa purato abhikkamantassa yugaṃ gīvaṃ bādhati, pacchato paṭikkamantassa cakkaṃ ūrumaṃsaṃ paṭihanati. Imehi dvīhi ākārehi bādhantaṃ cakkaṃ tassa padānupadikaṃ hoti; tatheva manasā paduṭṭhena tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā ṭhitaṃ puggalaṃ nirayādīsu tattha tattha gatagataṭṭhāne duccaritamūlakaṃ kāyikampi cetasikampi dukkhamanubandhatīti.

‘From that, suffering follows him’ means: from that threefold misconduct, suffering follows that person. Through the power of misconduct, whether in the four states of deprivation or among humans, as one goes to a state of darkness, resultant suffering, both bodily and mental, follows in this way. How so? ‘Like the wheel follows the foot of the one who pulls’ means: like the wheel follows the foot of the draught ox yoked to the pole, pulling the load. For just as that ox, pulling for one day, or two, or five, or ten, or half a month, or a month, is unable to turn back or abandon the wheel; rather, as it goes forward, the yoke afflicts its neck, and as it retreats, the wheel strikes its thigh-flesh. Just as the afflicting wheel follows its every footstep in these two ways, in the very same way, for a person who abides having fulfilled the three kinds of misconduct with a corrupted mind, suffering rooted in misconduct—both bodily and mental—pursues him in the hells and other states, in whatever place he goes.

Gāthāpariyosāne tiṃsasahassā bhikkhū saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sampattaparibhāyapi desanā sātthikā saphalā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the verse, thirty thousand monks attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. For the assembled congregation as well, the discourse was meaningful and fruitful.

Cakkhupālattheravatthu paṭhamaṃ

The First Story: The Account of the Elder Cakkhupāla.

2. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvatthu

2. The Story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī

2. Manopubbaṅgamā [V 1.0016] dhammāti dutiyagāthāpi [P 1.0025] sāvatthiyaṃyeva maṭṭhakuṇḍaliṃ ārabbha bhāsitā.

2. The second verse, beginning with `Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā`, was also spoken in Sāvatthī itself concerning Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira adinnapubbako nāma brāhmaṇo ahosi. Tena kassaci kiñci na dinnapubbaṃ, tena taṃ “adinnapubbako”tveva sañjāniṃsu. Tassa ekaputtako ahosi piyo manāpo. Athassa pilandhanaṃ kāretukāmo “sace suvaṇṇakāre kāressāmi, bhattavetanaṃ dātabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti sayameva suvaṇṇaṃ koṭṭetvā maṭṭhāni kuṇḍalāni katvā adāsi. Tenassa putto maṭṭhakuṇḍalītveva paññāyittha. Tassa soḷasavassikakāle paṇḍurogo udapādi. Tassa mātā puttaṃ oloketvā, “brāhmaṇa, puttassa te rogo uppanno, tikicchāpehi na”nti āha. “Bhoti sace vejjaṃ ānessāmi, bhattavetanaṃ dātabbaṃ bhavissati; kiṃ tvaṃ mama dhanacchedaṃ na olokessasī”ti? “Atha naṃ kiṃ karissasi, brāhmaṇā”ti? “Yathā me dhanacchedo na hoti, tathā karissāmī”ti. So vejjānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “asukarogassa nāma tumhe kiṃ bhesajjaṃ karothā”ti pucchi. Athassa te yaṃ vā taṃ vā rukkhatacādiṃ ācikkhanti. So tamāharitvā puttassa bhesajjaṃ karoti. Taṃ karontassevassa rogo balavā ahosi, atekicchabhāvaṃ upāgami. Brāhmaṇo [M 1.0017] tassa dubbalabhāvaṃ ñatvā ekaṃ vejjaṃ pakkosi. So taṃ oloketvāva “amhākaṃ ekaṃ kiccaṃ atthi, aññaṃ vejjaṃ pakkositvā tikicchāpehī”ti taṃ [P 1.0026] pahāya nikkhami. Brāhmaṇo tassa maraṇasamayaṃ ñatvā “imassa dassanatthāya āgatā antogehe sāpateyyaṃ passissanti, bahi naṃ karissāmī”ti puttaṃ nīharitvā bahiāḷinde nipajjāpesi.

In Sāvatthī, it is said, there was a brahmin named Adinnapubbaka. He had never given anything to anyone; for that reason, they knew him only as 'Adinnapubbaka'. He had a single son, who was dear and beloved. Then, wishing to have an ornament made for his son, he thought, 'If I have goldsmiths make it, wages will have to be given.' Therefore, he himself hammered the gold, made smooth earrings, and gave them to his son. For that reason, his son became known as Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī. When he was sixteen years of age, a pale disease arose in him. His mother, seeing her son, said, 'Brahmin, a sickness has arisen in your son; have him treated.' He replied, 'Madam, if I summon a physician, wages will have to be given. Are you not considering the destruction of my wealth?' 'Then what will you do for him, brahmin?' she asked. 'I will act in such a way that there is no destruction of my wealth.' So he went to the physicians and asked, 'For such-and-such a disease, what medicine do you prepare?' Then they told him about various things, such as tree bark. He brought them and prepared the medicine for his son. While he was preparing it, the sickness became severe and reached an incurable state. The brahmin, knowing his son's weakened state, summoned a physician. That physician, just upon seeing him, said, 'We have some business; have another physician summoned to treat him,' and abandoning him, he left. The brahmin, knowing his son's time of death was near, thought, 'Those who come to see him will see the property inside my house. I will put him outside.' Having taken his son out, he had him lie down on the outer veranda.

Taṃ divasaṃ bhagavā balavapaccūsasamaye mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya pubbabuddhesu katādhikārānaṃ ussannakusalamūlānaṃ veneyyabandhavānaṃ dassanatthaṃ buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento dasasahassacakkavāḷesu ñāṇajālaṃ patthari. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī bahiāḷinde nipannākāreneva tassa anto paññāyi. Satthā taṃ disvā tassa antogehā nīharitvā tattha nipajjāpitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “atthi nu kho mayhaṃ ettha gatapaccayena attho”ti upadhārento idaṃ addasa – ayaṃ māṇavo mayi cittaṃ pasādetvā kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsadevaloke tiṃsayojanike kanakavimāne nibbattissati, accharāsahassaparivāro bhavissati, brāhmaṇopi taṃ jhāpetvā rodanto āḷāhane vicarissati. Devaputto tigāvutappamāṇaṃ saṭṭhisakaṭabhārālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ accharāsahassaparivāraṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā “kena nu kho kammena mayā ayaṃ sirisampatti laddhā”ti oloketvā mayi [V 1.0017] cittappasādena laddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo dhanacchedabhayena mama bhesajjamakatvā idāni āḷāhanaṃ gantvā rodati, vippakārappattaṃ naṃ karissāmī”ti pitari rodante maṭṭhakuṇḍalivaṇṇena āgantvā āḷāhanassāvidūre [P 1.0027] nipajjitvā rodissati. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo “kosi tva”nti pucchissati. “Ahaṃ te putto maṭṭhakuṇḍalī”ti ācikkhissati. “Kuhiṃ nibbattosī”ti? “Tāvasiṃsabhavane”ti. “Kiṃ kammaṃ katvā”ti vutte mayi cittappasādena nibbattabhāvaṃ ācikkhissati. Brāhmaṇo “tumhesu cittaṃ pasādetvā sagge nibbatto nāma atthī”ti maṃ pucchissati. Athassāhaṃ “ettakāni satāni vā sahassāni vā satasahassāni vāti na sakkā gaṇanā paricchinditu”nti vatvā dhammapade gāthaṃ bhāsissāmi. Gāthāpariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo bhavissati, maṭṭha kuṇḍalī sotāpanno bhavissati. Tathā adinnapubbako brāhmaṇo. Iti [M 1.0018] imaṃ kulaputtaṃ nissāya mahādhammābhisamayo bhavissatīti disvā punadivase katasarīrapaṭijaggano mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā anupubbena brāhmaṇassa gehadvāraṃ gato.

On that day, at the time of the great dawn, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing the kinsmen to be tamed, who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had abundant roots of merit, and spread the net of knowledge over the ten thousand world-systems. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, in the very manner of lying on the outer veranda, appeared within His knowledge. The Teacher, seeing him and knowing that he had been taken out from the inner house and made to lie there, investigated, 'Is there a benefit for me in going there?' and He saw this: 'This young man, having made his mind confident in me, will pass away and be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva world in a golden mansion of thirty yojanas; he will be surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. The brahmin also, after having him cremated, will wander about the cremation ground, weeping. The devaputta, looking at his own form—three gāvutas in size, adorned with ornaments worth sixty cartloads, and surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs—will investigate, "By what kamma indeed have I obtained this glorious fortune?" Knowing that it was obtained through confidence of mind in me, he will think, "This brahmin, out of fear of the destruction of his wealth, did not prepare medicine for me, and now, going to the cremation ground, he weeps. I will cause him to experience distress." While his father is weeping, he will come in the guise of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, lie down not far from the cremation ground, and will weep. Then the brahmin will ask him, "Who are you?" He will declare, "I am your son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī." The brahmin will ask, "Where were you reborn?" He will say, "In the Tāvatiṃsa abode." When asked, "Having done what kamma?" he will explain that he was reborn through confidence of mind in me. The brahmin will ask me, "Is there such a thing as one who is reborn in heaven by making the mind confident in you?" Then I will say to him, "It is not possible to delimit by counting, saying so many hundreds, or so many thousands, or so many hundreds of thousands," and I will speak a verse in the Dhammapada. At the end of the verse, there will be a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī will become a stream-enterer. Likewise, the brahmin Adinnapubbaka will become a stream-enterer. Thus, knowing, "Relying on this clansman, there will be a great penetration of the Dhamma," on the next day, having attended to His bodily needs, surrounded by the great Saṅgha of monks, He entered Sāvatthī for alms-food and, in due course, went to the door of the brahmin's house.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe maṭṭhakuṇḍalī antogehābhimukho nipanno hoti. Athassa satthā attano apassanabhāvaṃ ñatvā ekaṃ rasmiṃ vissajjesi. Māṇavo “kiṃ obhāso nāmeso”ti parivattetvā nipannova satthāraṃ disvā, “andhabālapitaraṃ nissāya evarūpaṃ buddhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ vā kātuṃ dānaṃ vā dātuṃ dhammaṃ vā sotuṃ nālatthaṃ, idāni me hatthāpi anadhipateyyā, aññaṃ kattabbaṃ natthī”ti manameva pasādesi. Satthā “alaṃ ettakena cittappasādena imassā”ti pakkāmi. So tathāgate cakkhupathaṃ vijahanteyeva [P 1.0028] pasannamano kālaṃ katvā suttappabuddho viya devaloke tiṃsayojanike kanakavimāne nibbatti.

At that moment, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī was lying down, facing the interior of the house. Then the Teacher, knowing that the boy could not see Him, sent forth a ray of light. The young man, thinking, 'What is this radiance?', turned over and, while still lying down, saw the Teacher. He thought: 'Because of my blind and foolish father, I did not get to approach such a Buddha to perform bodily service, or to give alms, or to listen to the Dhamma. Now, even my hands are not under my control; there is nothing else to be done.' He just made his mind confident. The Teacher, thinking, 'This much confidence of mind is sufficient for him,' departed. Just as the Tathāgata was leaving his range of vision, he, with a confident mind, passed away and was reborn in the deva world in a golden mansion of thirty yojanas, like a man awakening from sleep.

Brāhmaṇopissa sarīraṃ jhāpetvā āḷāhane rodanaparāyaṇo ahosi, devasikaṃ āḷāhanaṃ gantvā rodati – “kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtakā”ti. Devaputtopi attano sampattiṃ oloketvā, “kena me kammena laddhā”ti upadhārento “satthari manopasādenā”ti ñatvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo mama aphāsukakāle bhesajjamakāretvā idāni āḷāhanaṃ gantvā rodati, vippakārappattameva naṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti maṭṭhakuṇḍalivaṇṇena āgantvā āḷāhanassāvidūre bāhā paggayha rodanto aṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ disvā “ahaṃ tāva puttasokena rodāmi, esa kimatthaṃ rodati, pucchissāmi na”nti pucchanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin, having had his son's body cremated, became one for whom weeping was his refuge at the charnel ground. Going daily to the charnel ground, he would weep, saying: 'Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?' The devaputta, too, observing his own prosperous state and investigating, 'By what deed was this obtained by me?' knew, 'It was obtained through mental confidence in the Teacher.' He then thought: 'This brahmin, having not arranged for medicine for me during my time of discomfort, now goes to the charnel ground and weeps. It is fitting to cause him to experience distress.' And so, having come in the guise of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, he stood not far from the charnel ground, raising his arms and weeping. The brahmin, seeing him, thought: 'I, for my part, weep out of grief for my son. For what reason does this one weep? I shall ask him.' And asking, he spoke this verse:

“Alaṅkato [V 1.0018] maṭṭhakuṇḍalī,

Māladhārī haricandanussado;

Bāhā paggayha kandasi,

Vanamajjhe kiṃ dukkhito tuva”nti. (vi. va. 1207; pe. va. 186);

“Adorned, with polished earrings, wearing garlands, anointed with yellow sandalwood, with arms upraised you weep. In the midst of the forest, why are you afflicted with sorrow?”

So [M 1.0019] māṇavo āha –

That young man said:

“Sovaṇṇamayo pabhassaro,

Uppanno rathapañjaro mama;

Tassa cakkayugaṃ na vindāmi,

Tena dukkhena jahāmi jīvita”nti. (va. 1208; pe. va. 187);

“A chariot-frame of mine has arisen, made of gold and radiant; I cannot find a pair of wheels for it, and because of that sorrow, I am giving up my life.”

Atha [P 1.0029] naṃ brāhmaṇo āha –

Then the brahmin said to him:

“Sovaṇṇamayaṃ maṇimayaṃ,

Lohitakamayaṃ atha rūpiyamayaṃ;

Ācikkha me bhadda māṇava,

Cakkayugaṃ paṭipādayāmi te”ti. (vi. va. 1209; pe. va. 188);

“Made of gold, of jewels, of ruby, or of silver; tell me, good young man, and I will provide a pair of wheels for you.”

Taṃ sutvā māṇavo “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo puttassa bhesajjamakatvā puttapatirūpakaṃ maṃ disvā rodanto ‘suvaṇṇādimayaṃ rathacakkaṃ karomī’ti vadati, hotu niggaṇhissāmi na”nti cintetvā “kīva mahantaṃ me cakkayugaṃ karissasī”ti vatvā “yāva mahantaṃ ākaṅkhasi, tāva mahantaṃ karissāmī”ti vutte “candimasūriyehi me attho, te me dehī”ti yācanto āha –

Hearing that, the young man thought: 'This brahmin, having not prepared medicine for his son, now sees me, who resembles his son, and while weeping says, “I will make a chariot wheel of gold and so on.” Very well, I shall subdue him.' Having thought thus, he said, 'How large a pair of wheels will you make for me?' When it was said, 'However large you desire, that large I will make,' he, requesting, said: 'I have need of the sun and moon. Give them to me.'

“So māṇavo tassa pāvadi,

Candasūriyā ubhayettha dissare;

Sovaṇṇamayo [V 1.0019] ratho mama,

Tena cakkayugena sobhatī”ti. (vi. va. 1210; pe. va. 189);

That young man said to him: 'The sun and moon are both seen here; my golden chariot is adorned by that pair of wheels.'

Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo āha –

Then the brahmin said to him:

“Bālo kho tvaṃ asi māṇava,

Yo tvaṃ patthayase apatthiyaṃ;

Maññāmi tuvaṃ marissasi,

Na hi tvaṃ lacchasi candasūriye”ti. (vi. va. 1211; pe. va. 190);

“You are indeed a fool, young man, you who desire what is unobtainable. I think you will die, for you will certainly not get the sun and moon.”

Atha [M 1.0020] naṃ māṇavo āha –

Then the young man said to him:

“Kiṃ pana paññāyamānassatthāya rodanto bālo hoti, udāhu apaññāyamānassatthāyā”ti vatvā –

Having said, 'Is one who weeps for something that is apparent a fool, or is it one who weeps for something that is not apparent?'—

“Gamanāgamanampi [P 1.0030] dissati,

Vaṇṇadhātu ubhayattha vīthiyā;

Peto kālakato na dissati,

Ko nidha kandataṃ bālyataro”ti. (vi. va. 1212; pe. va. 191);

“Their coming and going is seen, and the element of their appearance in their path; but the departed one who has passed away is not seen. Of the two who weep here, who is the greater fool?”

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo “yuttaṃ esa vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā –

Hearing that, the brahmin, realizing, 'This one speaks what is fitting,' said:

“Saccaṃ kho vadesi māṇava,

Ahameva kandataṃ bālyataro;

Candaṃ viya dārako rudaṃ,

Petaṃ kālakatābhipatthayi”nti. (vi. va. 1213; pe. va. 192) –

“Truly indeed you speak, young man. Of us who weep, I alone am the greater fool. Like a child weeping and longing for the moon, I long for my departed son who has passed away.”

Vatvā [V 1.0020] tassa kathāya nissoko hutvā māṇavassa thutiṃ karonto imā gāthā abhāsi –

Having said this, and becoming free from sorrow because of the young man's words, he uttered these verses, offering praise to the young man:

“Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

“Indeed, you have extinguished all the fever of grief for me, who was burning, just as one would douse with water a blazing fire that had been sprinkled with ghee.

“Abbahī vata me sallaṃ, sokaṃ hadayanissitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

“Indeed, you have extracted the dart of grief that was lodged in my heart—you who have dispelled the sorrow for my son, for me who was overcome by grief.

“Svāhaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna māṇavā”ti. (vi. va. 1214-1216; pe. va. 193-195);

“I am one whose dart has been extracted; I have become cool, I am at peace. I do not grieve, nor do I weep, having heard you, O young man.”

Atha [P 1.0031] naṃ “ko nāma tva”nti pucchanto –

Then, asking him, 'What is your name?', he said:

“Devatānusi gandhabbo, adu sakko purindado;

Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti. (vi. va. 1217; pe. va. 196) –

“Are you a deva, or a gandhabba? Or are you Sakka, the Giver in Former Times? Who are you, or whose son are you? How may we know you?”

Āha. Athassa māṇavo –

Then the young man said to him:

“Yañca kandasi yañca rodasi,

Puttaṃ āḷāhane sayaṃ dahitvā;

Svāhaṃ kusalaṃ karitvā kammaṃ,

Tidasānaṃ sahabyataṃ gato”ti. (vi. va. 1218; pe. va. 197) –
