“That son for whom you weep and lament, having cremated him yourself at the charnel ground—I am he. Having performed a wholesome deed, I have attained companionship with the Tidasā devas.”

Ācikkhi[M 1.0021]. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo āha –

Thus he declared. Then the brahmin said to him:

“Appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā nāddasāma,

Dānaṃ dadantassa sake agāre;

Uposathakammaṃ [V 1.0021] vā tādisaṃ,

Kena kammena gatosi devaloka”nti. (vi. va. 1219; pe. va. 198);

“We did not see you giving alms in your own home, whether little or much, nor any such observance of the Uposatha. By what deed have you gone to the world of the devas?”

Māṇavo āha –

The young man said:

“Ābādhikohaṃ dukkhito gilāno,

Ātūrarūpomhi sake nivesane;

Buddhaṃ vigatarajaṃ vitiṇṇakaṅkhaṃ,

Addakkhiṃ sugataṃ anomapaññaṃ.

“I was sick, afflicted with pain, and ailing, in a state of distress in my own home. I saw the Buddha, who is free from the dust of defilements, who has overcome all doubt, the Sugata of noble wisdom.

“Svāhaṃ muditadhano pasannacitto,

Añjaliṃ akariṃ tathāgatassa;

Tāhaṃ kusalaṃ karitvāna kammaṃ,

Tidasānaṃ sahabyataṃ gato”ti. (vi. va. 1220-1221; pe. va. 199-200);

“I, with a joyful mind and serene heart, made the añjali gesture of reverence to the Tathāgata. Having done that wholesome deed, I have attained companionship with the Tidasā devas.”

Tasmiṃ [P 1.0032] kathenteyeva brāhmaṇassa sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā paripūri. So taṃ pītiṃ pavedento –

Even as he was speaking, the brahmin's entire body was filled with joyful rapture. He, expressing that rapture, said:

“Acchariyaṃ vata abbhutaṃ vata,

Añjalikammassa ayamīdiso vipāko;

Ahampi pamuditamano pasannacitto,

Ajjeva buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ vajāmī”ti. (vi. va. 1222; pe. va. 201) –

“How wonderful it is, indeed! How marvelous it is, indeed, that such is the result of the act of making the añjali gesture! I too, with a joyful mind and serene heart, this very day go for refuge to the Buddha.”

Āha. Atha naṃ māṇavo –

Then the young man said to him:

“Ajjeva buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ vajāhi,

Dhammañca saṅghañca pasannacitto;

Tatheva [V 1.0022] sikkhāpadāni pañca,

Akhaṇḍaphullāni samādiyassu.

“This very day, go to the Buddha for refuge, and to the Dhamma and the Sangha with a devoted mind; likewise, undertake the five precepts, unbroken and unblemished.

Pāṇātipātā viramassu khippaṃ,

Loke adinnaṃ parivajjayassu;

Amajjapo mā ca musā bhaṇāhi,

Sakena dārena ca hohi tuṭṭho”ti. (vi. va. 1223-1224; pe. va. 202-203) –

“Quickly refrain from the destruction of life; in the world, avoid taking what is not given. Be one who abstains from intoxicants and do not speak falsely; be content with your own wife.”

Āha[M 1.0022]. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

He, having accepted with, “It is good,” spoke these verses:

“Atthakāmosi me yakkha, hitakāmosi devate;

Karomi tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ, tvaṃsi ācariyo mama.

“You are one who desires my welfare, O yakkha; you are one who desires my benefit, O devatā. I will do your bidding; you are my teacher.

“Upemi saraṇaṃ buddhaṃ, dhammañcāpi anuttaraṃ;

Saṅghañca naradevassa, gacchāmi saraṇaṃ ahaṃ.

“I go to the Buddha for refuge, and also to the unsurpassed Dhamma; and to the Sangha of the god among men, I go for refuge.

“Pāṇātipātā viramāmi khippaṃ,

Loke adinnaṃ parivajjayāmi;

Amajjapo no ca musā bhaṇāmi,

Sakena dārena ca homi tuṭṭho”ti. (vi. va. 1225-1227; pe. va. 204-206);

“I quickly refrain from the destruction of life; in the world, I avoid taking what is not given. I will abstain from intoxicants and not speak falsely, and I will be content with my own wife.”

Atha [P 1.0033] naṃ devaputto, “brāhmaṇa, te gehe bahuṃ dhanaṃ atthi, satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dānaṃ dehi, dhammaṃ suṇāhi, pañhaṃ pucchāhī”ti vatvā tattheva antaradhāyi.

Then the devaputta said to him, “Brahmin, in your house there is much wealth. Approach the Teacher, give alms, listen to the Dhamma, and ask a question.” Having said this, he vanished right there.

Brāhmaṇopi gehaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇiṃ āmantetvā, “bhadde, ahaṃ ajja samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nimantetvā pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, sakkāraṃ karohī”ti vatvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ neva abhivādetvā na paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito, “bho gotama, adhivāsehi ajjatanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti āha. Satthā adhivāsesi. So satthu adhivāsanaṃ viditvā vegenāgantvā [V 1.0023] sake nivesane paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyañca paṭiyādāpesi. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto tassa gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Brāhmaṇo sakkaccaṃ parivisi, mahājano sannipati. Micchādiṭṭhikena kira tathāgate nimantite dve janakāyā sannipatanti micchādiṭṭhikā “ajja samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanāya viheṭhiyamānaṃ passissāmā”ti sannipatanti, sammādiṭṭhikā “ajja buddhavisayaṃ buddhalīḷaṃ passissāmā”ti sannipatanti. Atha kho brāhmaṇo katabhattakiccaṃ tathāgatamupasaṅkamitvā nīcāsane nisinno pañhaṃ pucchi – “bho gotama, tumhākaṃ dānaṃ adatvā pūjaṃ akatvā dhammaṃ asutvā uposathavāsaṃ avasitvā kevalaṃ manopasādamatteneva sagge nibbattā nāma hontī”ti? “Brāhmaṇa, kasmā maṃ pucchasi, nanu te puttena maṭṭhakuṇḍalinā mayi manaṃ pasādetvā [M 1.0023] attano sagge nibbattabhāvo kathito”ti? “Kadā, bho gotamā”ti? Nanu tvaṃ ajja susānaṃ gantvā kandanto avidūre bāhā paggayha kandantaṃ ekaṃ māṇavaṃ disvā “alaṅkato maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, māladhārī [P 1.0034] haricandanussado”ti dvīhi janehi kathitakathaṃ pakāsento sabbaṃ maṭṭhakuṇḍalivatthuṃ kathesi. Tenevetaṃ buddhabhāsitaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

The brahmin also went home, and addressing his wife, said: “Good lady, today, having invited the ascetic Gotama, I will ask a question. Prepare a hospitable reception.” Having said this, he went to the monastery, and without paying homage to the Teacher or exchanging greetings, he stood to one side and said: “Venerable Gotama, please consent to today's meal, together with the Sangha of bhikkhus.” The Teacher consented. Knowing the Teacher's consent, he returned with haste and had excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own residence. The Teacher, surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, went to his house and sat on the prepared seat. The brahmin served respectfully, and a great crowd gathered. It is said that when the Tathāgata is invited by one of wrong view, two groups of people assemble: those of wrong view assemble thinking, “Today we will see the ascetic Gotama being harassed by questioning,” and those of right view assemble thinking, “Today we will see the Buddha's domain and the Buddha's grace.” Then the brahmin, after the meal was finished, approached the Tathāgata, sat on a low seat, and asked a question: “Venerable Gotama, are there any who, without giving alms, without making offerings, without hearing the Dhamma, and without observing the Uposatha, are reborn in the heavens by mere mental devotion alone?” “Brahmin, why do you ask me? Has not the fact of his rebirth in the heavens, by making his mind devoted to me, been told to you by your son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍali?” “When, Venerable Gotama?” “Did you not today go to the charnel ground and, while weeping, see a young man weeping nearby with arms upraised?” Making clear the conversation spoken by the two people—‘He is adorned like Maṭṭhakuṇḍali, wearing a garland, smeared with yellow sandalwood’—the Teacher then related the entire story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍali. For that very reason, this came to be called a discourse spoken by the Buddha.

Taṃ kathetvā ca pana “na kho, brāhmaṇa, ekasataṃ vā na dvesataṃ, atha kho mayi manaṃ pasādetvā sagge nibbattānaṃ gaṇanā nāma natthī”ti āha. Atha mahājano na nibbematiko hoti, athassa anibbematikabhāvaṃ viditvā satthā “maṭṭhakuṇḍalidevaputto vimāneneva saddhiṃ āgacchatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. So tigāvutappamāṇeneva dibbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitena attabhāvena āgantvā vimānato oruyha satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “tvaṃ imaṃ sampattiṃ kiṃ kammaṃ katvā paṭilabhī”ti pucchanto –

And having said that, he added, “Indeed, brahmin, it is not one hundred or two hundred, but rather, of those reborn in the celestial realm by making their minds confident in me, there is no counting.” Then the great crowd was not free from doubt. Then, knowing their state of being not free from doubt, the Teacher resolved, “Let the devaputta Maṭṭhakuṇḍali come here together with his celestial mansion!” He arrived with a personal form about three gāvutas in size, adorned with divine ornaments. Descending from his celestial mansion, he paid homage to the Teacher and stood to one side. Then the Teacher, intending to ask him, “By doing what kamma did you obtain this fortune?”—

“Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, yā tvaṃ tiṭṭhasi devate;

Obhāsentī disā sabbā, osadhī viya tārakā;

Pucchāmi taṃ deva mahānubhāva, manussabhūto kimakāsi puñña”nti. –

“With surpassing beauty you stand, O devatā, illuminating all directions like the morning star. I ask you, O deva of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human being?”

Gāthamāha. “Devaputto ayaṃ me, bhante, sampatti tumhesu cittaṃ pasādetvā laddhā”ti. “Mayi cittaṃ pasādetvā laddhā te”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. Mahājano devaputtaṃ oloketvā “acchariyā vata, bho, buddhaguṇā, adinnapubbakabrāhmaṇassa nāma putto aññaṃ [P 1.0035] kiñci puññaṃ akatvā satthari cittaṃ pasādetvā evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ paṭilabhī”ti tuṭṭhiṃ pavedesi.

He spoke the verse. The devaputta said: “Venerable sir, this fortune of mine was obtained by making my mind confident in you.” “Was it obtained by you by making your mind confident in me?” “Yes, venerable sir.” The great crowd, looking at the devaputta, expressed their delight, saying: “Oh, how wonderful, sirs, are the qualities of the Buddha! The son of the brahmin Adinnapubbaka, having done no other merit whatsoever, obtained such fortune by making his mind confident in the Teacher!”

Atha [V 1.0024] nesaṃ kusalākusalakammakaraṇe manova pubbaṅgamo, manova seṭṭho. Pasannena hi manena kataṃ kammaṃ devalokaṃ manussalokaṃ gacchantaṃ puggalaṃ chāyāva na vijahatīti idaṃ vatthuṃ kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā patiṭṭhāpitamattikaṃ sāsanaṃ rājamuddāya lañchanto viya dhammarājā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, for them, in the doing of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, mind is the forerunner and mind is the chief. For a deed done with a confident mind does not abandon a person going to the celestial realm or the human world, just as a shadow does not. Having told this story and established the connection, the King of Dhamma, as if stamping a sealed message with the royal seal, spoke this verse:

2. “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā.

2. “Mental states are preceded by mind, have mind as their chief, and are mind-made.

Manasā ce pasannena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ sukhamanveti, chāyāva anapāyinī”ti.

If one speaks or acts with a confident mind, happiness follows one like a shadow that never departs.”

Tattha [M 1.0024] kiñcāpi manoti avisesena sabbampi catubhūmikacittaṃ vuccati, imasmiṃ pana pade niyamiyamānaṃ vavatthāpiyamānaṃ paricchijjiyamānaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ labbhati. Vatthuvasena panāhariyamānaṃ tatopi somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttacittameva labbhati. Pubbaṅgamāti tena paṭhamagāminā hutvā samannāgatā. Dhammāti vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Ete hi uppādapaccayaṭṭhena somanassasampayuttamano pubbaṅgamo etesanti manopubbaṅgamā nāma. Yathā hi bahūsu ekato hutvā mahābhikkhusaṅghassa cīvaradānādīni vā uḷārapūjādhammassavanādīni vā mālāgandhasakkārakaraṇādīni vā puññāni karontesu “ko etesaṃ pubbaṅgamo”ti vutte yo tesaṃ paccayo hoti, yaṃ nissāya te tāni puññāni karonti, so tisso vā phusso vā tesaṃ pubbaṅgamoti vuccati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Iti uppādapaccayaṭṭhena mano pubbaṅgamo etesanti [P 1.0036] manopubbaṅgamā. Na hi te mane anuppajjante uppajjituṃ sakkonti, mano pana ekaccesu cetasikesu anuppajjantesupi uppajjatiyeva. Evaṃ adhipativasena pana mano seṭṭho etesanti manoseṭṭhā. Yathā hi gaṇādīnaṃ adhipati puriso gaṇaseṭṭho seṇiseṭṭhoti vuccati, tathā tesampi manova seṭṭho. Yathā pana suvaṇṇādīhi nipphāditāni bhaṇḍāni suvaṇṇamayādīni nāma honti, tathā etepi manato nipphannattā manomayā nāma.

Herein, although 'mind' (mano) is generally spoken of without distinction as all consciousness of the four planes, in this context, being specified, determined, and delimited, it is understood as the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. However, when considered in terms of the story's context, from that is understood only consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge. 'Preceded by mind' (manopubbaṅgamā) means that they are accompanied by that which goes first. 'States' (dhammā) refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Indeed, because mind accompanied by joy is their forerunner in the sense of being a condition for their arising, they are called 'preceded by mind.' For it is just as when many people, having come together, are performing meritorious deeds—such as offering robes to the great community of monks, or sublime offerings and listening to the Dhamma, or making offerings of garlands and perfumes—and it is asked, 'Who is their forerunner?' The one who is their support, relying on whom they perform those meritorious deeds, whether he is Tissa or Phussa, is called their forerunner. Thus should this analogy be understood. Therefore, in the sense of being a condition for their arising, mind is their forerunner, and so they are 'preceded by mind.' For they are unable to arise when the mind does not arise, but the mind can indeed arise even when some mental factors do not arise. In this way, by way of dominance, mind is their chief; therefore, they are 'having mind as their chief' (manoseṭṭhā). For just as a man who is the leader of a group is called the 'chief of the group' or 'chief of the guild,' so too is mind the chief of these. And just as goods produced from gold and so on are called 'golden,' so too are these called 'mind-made' (manomayā) because they are produced from the mind.

Pasannenāti anabhijjhādīhi guṇehi pasannena. Bhāsati vā karoti vāti evarūpena manena bhāsanto catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritameva bhāsati, karonto tividhaṃ kāyasucaritameva karoti, abhāsanto akaronto tāya anabhijjhādīhi pasannamānasatāya tividhaṃ manosucaritaṃ pūreti. Evamassa dasa kusalakammapathā pāripūriṃ gacchanti.

'With a confident mind' (pasannena) means with a mind made confident by virtues such as non-covetousness. As for 'one speaks or acts,' one who speaks with such a mind speaks only the fourfold verbal good conduct; one who acts performs only the threefold bodily good conduct. While not speaking and not acting, by that very confidence of mind due to non-covetousness and other virtues, one fulfills the threefold mental good conduct. In this way, for that person, the ten wholesome courses of action reach fulfillment.

Tato naṃ sukhamanvetīti tato tividhasucaritato naṃ puggalaṃ sukha manveti. Idha tebhūmikampi [V 1.0025] kusalaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā tebhūmikasucaritānubhāvena sugatibhave nibbattaṃ puggalaṃ, duggatiyaṃ vā sukhānubhavanaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ kāyavatthukampi itaravatthukampi avatthukampīti kāyikacetasikaṃ vipākasukhaṃ anugacchati, na vijahatīti attho veditabbo. Yathā kiṃ? Chāyāva anapāyinīti yathā hi chāyā nāma sarīrappaṭibaddhā sarīre gacchante gacchati, tiṭṭhante tiṭṭhati[P 1.0037], nisīdante nisīdati, na sakkoti, “saṇhena vā pharusena [M 1.0025] vā nivattāhī”ti vatvā vā pothetvā vā nivattāpetuṃ. Kasmā? Sarīrappaṭibaddhattā. Evameva imesaṃ dasannaṃ kusalakammapathānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇakusalamūlikaṃ kāmāvacarādibhedaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ gatagataṭṭhāne anapāyinī chāyā viya hutvā na vijahatīti.

As for 'From that, happiness follows one,' it means that from that threefold good conduct, happiness follows that person. Here, wholesome action of the three planes is intended. Therefore, by the power of good conduct of the three planes, resultant bodily and mental happiness follows a person reborn in a happy destination, or one situated in an unhappy destination but in a place where happiness can be experienced. This happiness—whether dependent on the physical body, on another physical basis, or without a physical basis—follows and does not abandon him. This is the meaning that should be understood. Like what? 'Like a shadow that never departs.' For a shadow is connected to the body; when the body goes, it goes; when it stands, it stands; when it sits, it sits. One is not able to make it turn back by saying, 'Turn back,' either gently or harshly, or by striking it. Why? Because it is connected to the body. In the very same way, this bodily and mental happiness, which is rooted in the wholesome practice and repeated practice of these ten wholesome courses of action, and is differentiated as sense-sphere and so forth, having become like a shadow that never departs, does not abandon one in whatever place one goes.

Gāthāpariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi, maṭṭhakuṇḍalidevaputto sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, tathā adinnapubbako brāhmaṇo. So tāvamahantaṃ vibhavaṃ buddhasāsane vippakirīti.

At the conclusion of the verse, the comprehension of the Dhamma arose for eighty-four thousand beings. The devaputta Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī was established in the fruit of stream-entry, as was the brahmin Adinnapubbaka. The brahmin then distributed his great wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation.

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Second Story: Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.

3. Tissattheravatthu

3. The Story of the Elder Tissa

Akkocchi manti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto tissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“He reviled me…”—this discourse on the Dhamma the Teacher delivered while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Tissa.

So kirāyasmā tissatthero bhagavato pitucchāputto ahosi, mahallakakāle pabbajitvā buddhānaṃ uppannalābhasakkāraṃ paribhuñjanto thūlasarīro ākoṭitapaccākoṭitehi cīvarehi nivāsetvā yebhuyyena vihāramajjhe upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ nisīdati. Tathāgataṃ dassanatthāya āgatā āgantukabhikkhū taṃ disvā “eko mahāthero bhavissatī”ti saññāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā vattaṃ āpucchanti, pādasambāhanādīni āpucchanti. So tuṇhī ahosi. Atha naṃ eko daharabhikkhu “kativassā tumhe”ti pucchitvā “vassaṃ natthi, mahallakakāle pabbajitā maya”nti vutte, “āvuso, dubbinīta, mahallaka[P 1.0038], attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsi, ettake mahāthere disvā sāmīcikammamattampi na karosi, vatte āpucchiyamāne tuṇhī hosi, kukkuccamattampi te natthī”ti accharaṃ pahari. So khattiyamānaṃ janetvā “tumhe kassa santikaṃ āgatā”ti pucchitvā “satthu santika”nti vutte “maṃ pana ‘ko eso’ti sallakkhetha, mūlameva vo chindissāmī”ti vatvā rudanto dukkhī dummano satthu santikaṃ agamāsi[V 1.0026]. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ nu tvaṃ tissa dukkhī dummano assumukho rodamāno āgatosī”ti pucchi. Tepi bhikkhū “esa gantvā kiñci āloḷaṃ kareyyā”ti teneva [M 1.0026] saddhiṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. So satthārā pucchito “ime maṃ, bhante, bhikkhū akkosantī”ti āha. “Kahaṃ pana tvaṃ nisinnosī”ti? “Vihāramajjhe upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ, bhante”ti. “Ime te bhikkhū āgacchantā diṭṭhā”ti? “Āma, diṭṭhā, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ uṭṭhāya te paccuggamanaṃ kata”nti? “Na kataṃ, bhante”ti. “Parikkhāraggahaṇaṃ āpucchita”nti? “Nāpucchitaṃ, bhante”ti. “Vattaṃ vā pānīyaṃ vā āpucchita”nti. “Nāpucchitaṃ bhante”ti? “Āsanaṃ nīharitvā abhivādetvā pādasambāhanaṃ kata”nti? “Na kataṃ, bhante”ti. “Tissa mahallakabhikkhūnaṃ sabbaṃ etaṃ vattaṃ kātabbaṃ, etaṃ vattaṃ akarontena vihāramajjhe nisīdituṃ na vaṭṭati, taveva doso, ete bhikkhū khamāpehī”ti? “Ete maṃ, bhante, akkosiṃsu[P 1.0039], nāhaṃ ete khamāpemī”ti. “Tissa mā evaṃ kari, taveva doso, khamāpehi ne”ti? “Na khamāpemi, bhante”ti. Atha satthā “dubbaco esa, bhante”ti bhikkhūhi vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva dubbaco esa, pubbepi esa dubbacoyevā”ti vatvā “idāni tāvassa, bhante, dubbacabhāvo amhehi ñāto, atīte esa kiṃ akāsī”ti vutte “tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇāthā”ti vatvā atītamāhari.

It is said that the Venerable Elder Tissa was the Blessed One’s paternal uncle's son. Having gone forth in old age, he enjoyed the gain and honor that arose in the Buddha’s Dispensation. Being of a large body, he would dress in robes that were beaten and re-beaten, and for the most part, he would sit in the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery. When visiting monks came to see the Tathāgata, they saw him and, perceiving, 'This must be a great elder,' they approached him and inquired about the customary duties, such as foot-massaging and so on. He remained silent. Then a young monk asked him, 'How many rains-retreats do you have?' When he replied, 'I have no rains-retreats; we went forth in old age,' the young monk clapped his hands at him, saying: 'Friend, you ill-disciplined old man! You do not know your own measure. Seeing so many great elders, you do not perform even the slightest act of respect. When asked about duties, you remain silent. You have no remorse at all!' Generating Khattiya-pride, Tissa asked, 'To whose presence have you come?' When they replied, 'To the Teacher’s presence,' he said, 'But as for me, what did you take me for? I will cut you off at the very root!' Weeping, sorrowful, and dejected, he went to the Teacher's presence. The Teacher then asked him, 'Tissa, why have you come, sorrowful, dejected, with a tearful face, weeping?' Those monks, thinking, 'He might go and create some disturbance,' went along with him, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. When questioned by the Teacher, Tissa said, 'Venerable sir, these monks are reviling me.' 'But where were you sitting?' 'In the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery, venerable sir.' 'Did you see these monks arriving?' 'Yes, venerable sir, I saw them.' 'Did you get up and go out to meet them?' 'No, venerable sir, I did not.' 'Did you ask to take their requisites?' 'No, venerable sir, I did not ask.' 'Did you ask about duties or offer drinking water?' 'No, venerable sir, I did not ask.' 'Did you bring out a seat, pay homage, and perform foot-massaging?' 'No, venerable sir, I did not.' 'Tissa, all these duties should be performed for senior monks. It is not proper for one who does not perform these duties to sit in the middle of the monastery. The fault is yours alone. Ask for these monks' forgiveness.' 'Venerable sir, they reviled me. I will not ask for their forgiveness.' 'Tissa, do not act so. The fault is yours alone. Ask for their forgiveness.' 'I will not ask for forgiveness, venerable sir.' Then, when the monks said, 'Venerable sir, this one is difficult to instruct,' the Teacher replied, 'Monks, not only now is this one difficult to instruct; in the past, too, he was difficult to instruct.' When they asked, 'Venerable sir, his being difficult to instruct is now known by us. What did he do in the past?' the Teacher said, 'In that case, monks, listen,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ bārāṇasiraññe rajjaṃ kārente devilo nāma tāpaso aṭṭha māse himavante vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya cattāro māse nagaramupanissāya vasitukāmo himavantato āgantvā nagaradvāre dārake disvā pucchi – “imaṃ nagaraṃ sampattapabbajitā kattha vasantī”ti? “Kumbhakārasālāyaṃ, bhante”ti. Tāpaso kumbhakārasālaṃ gantvā dvāre ṭhatvā “sace te bhaggava agaru, vaseyyāma ekarattiṃ sālāya”nti āha. Kumbhakāro “mayhaṃ rattiṃ sālāyaṃ kiccaṃ natthi, mahatī sālā, yathāsukhaṃ vasatha, bhante”ti sālaṃ niyyādesi. Tasmiṃ pavisitvā nisinne aparopi nārado nāma tāpaso himavantato āgantvā kumbhakāraṃ ekarattivāsaṃ yāci. Kumbhakāro “paṭhamaṃ āgato iminā saddhiṃ ekato vasitukāmo bhaveyya vā no vā, attānaṃ parimocessāmī”ti [P 1.0040] cintetvā “sace, bhante, paṭhamaṃ upagato rocessati, tassa ruciyā vasathā”ti āha. So tamupasaṅkamitvā “sace te, ācariya agaru, mayañcettha ekarattiṃ vaseyyāmā”ti yāci. “Mahatī sālā, pavisitvā [M 1.0027] ekamante vasāhī”ti vutte pavisitvā puretaraṃ paviṭṭhassa devilassa aparabhāge nisīdi. Ubhopi sāraṇīyakathaṃ kathetvā nipajjiṃsu.

In the past, while the king of Bārāṇasī was ruling in Bārāṇasī, an ascetic named Devila, having lived in the Himālaya for eight months, wished to live near the city for four months to partake of salt and sour victuals. Coming from the Himālaya and arriving at the city gate, he saw some boys and asked, 'Where do the renunciants who have come to this city stay?' 'In the potter's hall, venerable sir.' The ascetic went to the potter's hall and, standing at the door, said, 'Potter, if it is not burdensome for you, may we stay in the hall for one night?' The potter replied, 'I have no business in the hall at night. The hall is large; stay as you please, venerable sir,' and he assigned the hall to him. After he had entered and was seated, another ascetic named Nārada also came from the Himālaya and asked the potter for a one-night stay. The potter, thinking, 'The one who arrived first may or may not wish to stay together with this one; I shall absolve myself,' said, 'Venerable sir, if the one who first approached agrees, you may stay according to his wish.' So Nārada approached Devila and requested, 'Teacher, if it is not burdensome for you, may we too stay here for one night?' When told, 'The hall is large; enter and stay to one side,' he entered and sat down in the area behind Devila, who had entered earlier. Both, having engaged in amiable conversation, then lay down.

Sayanakāle [V 1.0027] nārado devilassa nipajjanaṭṭhānañca dvārañca sallakkhetvā nipajji. So pana devilo nipajjamāno attano nipajjanaṭṭhāne anipajjitvā dvāramajjhe tiriyaṃ nipajji. Nārado rattiṃ nikkhamanto tassa jaṭāsu akkami. “Ko maṃ akkamī”ti ca vutte, “ācariya, aha”nti āha. “Kūṭajaṭila, araññato āgantvā mama jaṭāsu akkamasī”ti. “Ācariya, tumhākaṃ idha nipannabhāvaṃ na jānāmi, khamatha me”ti vatvā tassa kandantasseva bahi nikkhami. Itaro “ayaṃ pavisantopi maṃ akkameyyā”ti parivattetvā pādaṭṭhāne sīsaṃ katvā nipajji. Nāradopi pavisanto “paṭhamaṃpāhaṃ ācariye aparajjhiṃ, idānissa pādapassena pavisissāmī”ti cintetvā āgacchanto gīvāya akkami. “Ko eso”ti ca vutte “ahaṃ, ācariyā”ti vatvā “kūṭajaṭila, paṭhamaṃ mama jaṭāsu akkamitvā idāni gīvāya akkamasi, abhisapissāmi ta”nti vutte, “ācariya, mayhaṃ doso natthi, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ evaṃ nipannabhāvaṃ na jānāmi, ‘paṭhamampi me aparaddhaṃ, idāni pādapassena [P 1.0041] pavisissāmī’ti paviṭṭhomhi, khamatha me”ti āha. “Kūṭajaṭila, abhisapissāmi ta”nti. “Mā evaṃ karittha ācariyā”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ anādiyitvā –

At bedtime, Nārada, having noted Devila's sleeping place and the door, lay down. That ascetic Devila, however, when lying down, did not lie in his own sleeping place but lay crosswise in the middle of the doorway. Nārada, going out at night, stepped on his matted locks. When it was said, “Who stepped on me?” he replied, “Teacher, it is I.” “Deceitful ascetic, having come from the forest, you step on my matted locks!” When this was said, Nārada replied, “Teacher, I did not know that you were lying here; forgive me.” Having said this, while the other was still protesting, he went outside. The other ascetic thought, “This one might step on me when entering as well,” so he turned around, placed his head where his feet had been, and lay down. Nārada, too, upon entering, thought, “Previously, I offended the teacher; now I shall enter by the side of his feet.” As he approached, he stepped on his neck. When it was said, “Who is this?” he replied, “It is I, teacher.” “Deceitful ascetic, first you stepped on my matted locks, and now you step on my neck. I shall curse you!” When this was said, Nārada replied, “Teacher, there is no fault of mine. I did not know that you were lying in this way. Thinking, ‘Previously I offended, and now I shall enter by the side of his feet,’ I entered. Forgive me.” “Deceitful ascetic, I shall curse you!” “Do not do so, teacher!” But that ascetic, not heeding his words—

“Sahassaraṃsī satatejo, sūriyo tamavinodano;

Pātodayante sūriye, muddhā te phalatu sattadhā”ti. –

“The thousand-rayed sun of limitless power, the dispeller of darkness; when the sun rises in the morning, may your head split into seven pieces!”

Taṃ abhisapi eva. Nārado, “ācariya, mayhaṃ doso natthīti mama vadantasseva tumhe abhisapatha, yassa doso atthi, tassa muddhā phalatu, mā niddosassā”ti vatvā –

He indeed cursed him. Nārada said, “Teacher, even while I am saying that there is no fault of mine, you curse me. May the head of the one who is at fault split, not the head of the one who is faultless!” Having said this—

“Sahassaraṃsī satatejo, sūriyo tamavinodano;

Pātodayante sūriye, muddhā te phalatu sattadhā”ti. –

“The thousand-rayed sun of limitless power, the dispeller of darkness; when the sun rises in the morning, may your head split into seven pieces!”

Abhisapi. So pana mahānubhāvo atīte cattālīsa, anāgate cattālīsāti asītikappe anussarati. Tasmā “kassa nu kho upari abhisapo patissatī”ti upadhārento “ācariyassā”ti ñatvā tasmiṃ anukampaṃ paṭicca iddhibalena aruṇuggamanaṃ nivāreti.

He cursed him. But that Nārada was of great power; he could recollect eighty aeons—forty in the past and forty in the future. Therefore, while investigating, “Upon whom, I wonder, will the curse fall?” and realizing that it would fall upon the teacher, on account of his compassion for him, he prevented the rising of the dawn with the strength of his psychic power.

Nāgarā [M 1.0028] aruṇe anuggacchante rājadvāraṃ gantvā, “deva, tayi rajjaṃ kārente aruṇo na uṭṭhahati, aruṇaṃ no uṭṭhāpehī”ti kandiṃsu. Rājā attano kāyakammādīni olokento kiñci ayuttaṃ adisvā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintetvā “pabbajitānaṃ vivādena bhavitabba”nti [V 1.0028] parisaṅkamāno “kacci imasmiṃ nagare pabbajitā atthī”ti pucchi. “Hiyyo sāyaṃ kumbhakārasālāyaṃ āgatā atthi devā”ti vutte taṃkhaṇaññeva rājā [P 1.0042] ukkāhi dhāriyamānāhi tattha gantvā nāradaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno āha –

When the dawn did not rise, the city-dwellers went to the king's gate and lamented, saying, “Your Majesty, while you are ruling the kingdom, the dawn does not rise. Make the dawn rise for us.” The king, looking into his own bodily conduct and so on, saw nothing improper and thought, “What, I wonder, could be the reason?” Suspecting, “It must be due to a dispute among the renunciants,” he asked, “Are there any renunciants in this city?” When it was said, “There are some who arrived at the potter's hall yesterday evening, Your Majesty,” at that very moment the king, having torches lit, went there, paid homage to Nārada, sat down to one side, and said—

“Kammantā nappavattanti, jambudīpassa nārada;

Kena loko tamobhūto, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“Nārada, for the people of Jambudīpa, work does not proceed. For what reason has the world become dark? Being asked, please explain that to me.”

Nārado sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā iminā kāraṇena ahaṃ iminā abhisapito, athāhaṃ “mayhaṃ doso natthi, yassa doso atthi, tasseva upari abhisapo patatū”ti vatvā abhisapiṃ. Abhisapitvā ca pana “kassa nu kho upari abhisapo patissatī”ti upadhārento “sūriyuggamanavelāya ācariyassa muddhā sattadhā phalissatī”ti disvā etasmiṃ anukampaṃ paṭicca aruṇassa uggamanaṃ na demīti. “Kathaṃ pana assa, bhante, antarāyo na bhaveyyā”ti. “Sace maṃ khamāpeyya, na bhaveyyā”ti. “Tena hi khamāpehī”ti vutte “eso, mahārāja, maṃ jaṭāsu ca gīvāya ca akkami, nāhaṃ etaṃ kūṭajaṭilaṃ khamāpemī”ti. “Khamāpehi, bhante, mā evaṃ karitthā”ti. “Na khamāpemī”ti. “Muddhā te sattadhā phalissatī”ti vuttepi na khamāpetiyeva. Atha naṃ rājā “na tvaṃ attano ruciyā khamāpessasī”ti hatthapādakucchigīvāsu gāhāpetvā nāradassa pādamūle onamāpesi. Nāradopi “uṭṭhehi, ācariya, khamāmi te”ti vatvā, “mahārāja, nāyaṃ yathāmanena khamāpeti, nagarassa avidūre [P 1.0043] eko saro atthi, tattha naṃ sīse mattikāpiṇḍaṃ katvā galappamāṇe udake ṭhapāpehī”ti āha. Rājā tathā kāresi. Nārado devilaṃ āmantetvā, “ācariya, mayā iddhiyā vissaṭṭhāya sūriyasantāpe uṭṭhahante udake nimujjitvā aññena ṭhānena uttaritvā gaccheyyāsī”ti āha. “Tassa sūriyaraṃsīhi saṃphuṭṭhamattova mattikāpiṇḍo sattadhā phali, so nimujjitvā aññena ṭhānena palāyī”ti.

Nārada related the entire event, saying, “For this reason, I was cursed by him. Then I, saying, ‘There is no fault of mine; may the curse fall only upon the one who has the fault,’ cursed him in return. And having cursed him, while investigating, ‘Upon whom, I wonder, will the curse fall?’ I saw that ‘at the time of sunrise, the teacher's head will split into seven pieces.’ On account of compassion for him, I am not permitting the dawn to rise.” “But how, venerable sir, might danger not befall him?” “If he were to ask forgiveness of me, it would not happen.” When the king told Devila, “Then ask for forgiveness,” Devila replied, “This man stepped on my matted locks and my neck. I will not ask forgiveness of this deceitful ascetic.” The king said, “Ask for forgiveness, venerable sir, do not act thus.” “I will not ask for forgiveness.” Even when told, “Your head will split into seven pieces,” he still would not ask for forgiveness. Then the king, saying, “You will not ask for forgiveness of your own accord,” had him seized by the hands, feet, belly, and neck, and made him bow down at Nārada's feet. Nārada said, “Rise, teacher, I forgive you,” and then added, “Great king, this one does not ask for forgiveness according to his own will. There is a lake not far from the city. Have him placed in water up to his neck with a lump of clay on his head.” The king had it done so. Nārada, addressing Devila, said, “Teacher, when my psychic power is released and the sun's heat rises, you should dive into the water, emerge in another place, and go.” As soon as the lump of clay was touched by the sun's rays, it split into seven pieces. He dived and fled by another way.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “tadā, bhikkhave, rājā ānando ahosi, devilo tisso, nārado ahamevāti evaṃ tadāpesa dubbacoyevā”ti [M 1.0029] vatvā tissattheraṃ āmantetvā, “tissa, bhikkhuno nāma ‘asukenāhaṃ akkuṭṭho, asukena pahaṭo, asukena jito, asuko kho me bhaṇḍaṃ ahāsī’ti cintentassa veraṃ nāma na vūpasammati, evaṃ pana anupanayhantasseva upasammatī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, said: “Monks, at that time, the king was Ānanda, Devila was Tissa, and Nārada was myself. Thus, even then this one was difficult to speak to.” Then, addressing the Elder Tissa, he said, “Tissa, for a monk who thinks, ‘By so-and-so I was reviled, by so-and-so I was struck, by so-and-so I was defeated, so-and-so took my belongings,’ hatred indeed does not cease. But for one who does not harbor such resentment, it ceases.” Having said this, he spoke these verses—

3.

3.

“Akkocchi [V 1.0029] maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti, veraṃ tesaṃ na sammati.

‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.’ For those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is not stilled.

4.

4.

“Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ nupanayhanti, veraṃ tesūpasammatī”ti.

‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.’ For those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is stilled.

Tattha akkocchīti akkosi. Avadhīti pahari. Ajinīti [P 1.0044] kūṭasakkhiotāraṇena vā vādapaṭivādena vā karaṇuttariyakaraṇena vā ajesi. Ahāsi meti mama santakaṃ pattādīsu kiñcideva avahari. Ye ca tanti ye keci devatā vā manussā vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā taṃ “akkocchi ma”ntiādivatthukaṃ kodhaṃ sakaṭadhuraṃ viya naddhinā pūtimacchādīni viya ca kusādīhi punappunaṃ veṭhetvā upanayhanti, tesaṃ sakiṃ uppannaṃ veraṃ na sammatīti vūpasammati. Ye ca taṃ nupanayhantīti asatiyā amanasikāravasena vā kammapaccavekkhaṇādivasena vā ye taṃ akkosādivatthukaṃ kodhaṃ tayāpi koci niddoso purimabhave akkuṭṭho bhavissati, pahaṭo bhavissati, kūṭasakkhiṃ otāretvā jito bhavissati, kassaci te pasayha kiñci acchinnaṃ bhavissati, tasmā niddoso hutvāpi akkosādīni pāpuṇāsīti evaṃ na upanayhanti. Tesu pamādena uppannampi veraṃ iminā anupanayhanena nirindhano viya jātavedo vūpasammatīti.

Herein, in those verses: `Akkocchi` means ‘he abused.’ `Avadhi` means ‘he struck.’ `Ajini` means ‘he conquered,’ either by introducing a false witness, by debate and counter-debate, or by acting with overwhelming force. `Ahāsi me` means ‘he stole something of mine,’ such as a bowl or other requisite. `Ye ca taṃ` refers to whoever—be they devas, humans, householders, or renunciants—binds that anger which has ‘he abused me’ and so on as its cause, wrapping it up again and again like binding a cart's yoke with a leather strap, or like binding rotten fish with kusa grass. For them, the hatred that has arisen even once is not stilled; that is, it is not pacified. `Ye ca taṃ nupanayhanti` refers to those who, either through lack of mindfulness, by way of inattention, or by way of reflecting on kamma and so on, do not bind that anger which has abuse and so on as its cause, thinking thus: ‘You too, though innocent now, may in a previous existence have abused someone, struck someone, defeated someone by introducing a false witness, or forcibly seized something from someone. Therefore, though being innocent, you now encounter abuse and so on.’ For them, even hatred that has arisen through negligence is pacified by this non-binding, like a forest fire without fuel. This is the meaning.

Desanāpariyosāne satasahassabhikkhū sotāpattiphalādīni [P 1.0045] pāpuṇiṃsu. Dhammadesanā mahājanassa sātthikā ahosi. Dubbacopi subbacoyeva jātoti.

At the end of the discourse, a hundred thousand monks attained the fruits beginning with Stream-entry. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial to the great assembly. The monk who was difficult to admonish became easy to admonish.

Tissattheravatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Third Story, concerning Elder Tissa, is concluded.

4. Kāḷayakkhinīvatthu

4. The Story of the Yakkhiṇī Kāḷī

Na hi verenāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ vañjhitthiṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma discourse beginning with `Na hi verena`, concerning a certain barren woman.

Eko [M 1.0030] kira kuṭumbikaputto pitari kālakate khette ca ghare ca sabbakammāni attanāva karonto mātaraṃ paṭijaggi. Athassa mātā “kumārikaṃ te, tāta, ānessāmī”ti āha. “Amma[V 1.0030], mā evaṃ vadetha, ahaṃ yāvajīvaṃ tumhe paṭijaggissāmī”ti. “Tāta, khette ca ghare ca kiccaṃ tvameva karosi, tena mayhaṃ cittasukhaṃ nāma na hoti, ānessāmī”ti. So punappunaṃ paṭikkhipitvā tuṇhī ahosi. Sā ekaṃ kulaṃ gantukāmā gehā nikkhami. Atha naṃ putto “kataraṃ kulaṃ gacchathā”ti pucchitvā “asukakulaṃ nāmā”ti vutte tattha gamanaṃ paṭisedhetvā attano abhirucitaṃ kulaṃ ācikkhi. Sā tattha gantvā kumārikaṃ vāretvā divasaṃ vavatthapetvā taṃ ānetvā tassa ghare akāsi. Sā vañjhā ahosi. Atha naṃ mātā, putta, tvaṃ attano ruciyā kumārikaṃ āṇāpesi, sā idāni vañjhā jātā, aputtakañca nāma kulaṃ vinassati[P 1.0046], paveṇī na ghaṭīyati, tena aññaṃ te kumārikaṃ ānemīti. Tena “alaṃ, ammā”ti vuccamānāpi punappunaṃ kathesi. Vañjhitthī taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “puttā nāma mātāpitūnaṃ vacanaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkonti, idāni aññaṃ vijāyiniṃ itthiṃ ānetvā maṃ dāsibhogena bhuñjissati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ sayameva ekaṃ kumārikaṃ āneyya”nti cintetvā ekaṃ kulaṃ gantvā tassatthāya kumārikaṃ vāretvā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, amma, vadesī”ti tehi paṭikkhittā “ahaṃ vañjhā, aputtakaṃ nāma kulaṃ vinassati, tumhākaṃ pana dhītā puttaṃ vā dhītaraṃ vā labhitvā kuṭumbikassa sāminī bhavissati, mayhaṃ sāmikassa naṃ dethā”ti yācitvā sampaṭicchāpetvā ānetvā sāmikassa ghare akāsi.

It is said that a certain householder's son, after his father had passed away, took care of all the duties in the fields and the house by himself and looked after his mother. Then his mother said to him, ‘Dear son, I will bring a young woman for you.’ He replied, ‘Mother, do not speak thus. I will look after you for as long as I live.’ She said, ‘Dear son, you alone perform the duties in the fields and the house, and because of that, my mind is not at ease. Therefore, I will bring one.’ After refusing again and again, he became silent. She, wishing to go to a certain family, left the house. Then her son asked her, ‘To which family are you going?’ When she said, ‘To such-and-such family,’ he forbade her to go there and pointed out a family that he himself preferred. She went there, arranged for the young woman, set the day, and brought her to his house. She turned out to be barren. Then his mother said to him, ‘Son, you had a young woman brought according to your own preference, and now she has turned out to be barren. A family known as childless perishes; the lineage is not continued. Therefore, I will bring another young woman for you.’ Although he said, ‘Enough, mother,’ she spoke of it again and again. The barren woman, hearing that conversation, thought: ‘Sons are not able to go against the word of their parents. Now he will bring another woman who can bear children and will treat me as a slave. What if I myself were to bring a young woman?’ Having so reflected, she went to a certain family and arranged for a young woman for her husband. When they refused her, saying, ‘Mother, what is this you are saying?’ she pleaded, ‘I am barren, and a family known as childless perishes. Your daughter, however, upon getting a son or a daughter, will become the mistress of the householder's wealth. Give her to my husband.’ Having gained their acceptance, she brought the young woman and had her live in her husband's house.

Athassā etadahosi – “sacāyaṃ puttaṃ vā dhītaraṃ vā labhissati, ayameva kuṭumbassa sāminī bhavissati. Yathā dārakaṃ na labhati, tatheva naṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Atha naṃ sā āha – “amma, yadā te kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāti, atha me āroceyyāsī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā gabbhe patiṭṭhite tassā ārocesi. Itarissā pana sā sayameva niccaṃ yāgubhattaṃ deti, athassā [P 1.0047] āhāreneva saddhiṃ gabbhapātanabhesajjamadāsi, gabbho pati. Dutiyampi gabbhe patiṭṭhite ārocesi[M 1.0031], itarā dutiyampi tatheva pātesi. Atha naṃ paṭivissakitthiyo pucchiṃsu – “kacci te sapatti antarāyaṃ karotī”ti? Sā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “andhabāle, kasmā evamakāsi, ayaṃ tava issariyabhayena gabbhassa pātanabhesajjaṃ yojetvā deti, tena te gabbho patati, mā puna evamakatthā”ti vuttā tatiyavāre na kathesi. Atha sā itarissā udaraṃ disvā “kasmā mayhaṃ gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ na kathesī”ti vatvā “tvaṃ maṃ ānetvā vañcetvā dve vāre gabbhaṃ pātesi, kimatthaṃ tuyhaṃ kathemī”ti vutte “naṭṭhā dānimhī”ti cintetvā tassā pamādaṃ olokentī pariṇate gabbhe okāsaṃ labhitvā bhesajjaṃ yojetvā adāsi. Gabbho pariṇatattā patituṃ asakkonto tiriyaṃ nipati, kharā vedanā uppajji, jīvitasaṃsayaṃ pāpuṇi. Sā “nāsitamhi tayā, tvameva maṃ ānetvā tvameva tayopi vāre [V 1.0031] dārake nāsesi, idāni ahampi nassāmi, ito dāni cutā yakkhinī hutvā tava dārake khādituṃ samatthā hutvā nibbatteyya”nti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā kālaṃ katvā tasmiṃyeva [P 1.0048] gehe majjārī hutvā nibbatti. Itarampi sāmiko gahetvā “tayā me kulūpacchedo kato”ti kapparajaṇṇukādīhi supothitaṃ pothesi. Sā tenevābādhena kālaṃ katvā tattheva kukkuṭī hutvā nibbattā.

Then this thought occurred to her: “If she should obtain a son or a daughter, she herself will become the mistress of the household. It is fitting to act so that she does not obtain a child.” Then she said to her: “My dear, when a fetus is established in your womb, then you should inform me.” She agreed, saying, “Very well,” and when the fetus was established, she informed her. The other woman, however, herself regularly gave her gruel and rice, and along with the food, she gave her medicine to cause an abortion; the fetus was thus aborted. A second time, when a fetus was established, she informed her, and the other woman again caused it to be aborted in the same way. Then the neighboring women asked her: “Surely your co-wife is causing you harm?” She explained the matter to them, and they said: “Blind fool, why did you act thus? She, fearing you will gain authority, prepares medicine to cause an abortion and gives it to you; because of that your fetus is aborted. Do not speak of this again.” Being told this, the third time she did not inform her. Then the other woman, seeing her belly, said: “Why did you not tell me of the establishment of the fetus?” When she replied, “You brought me here, and having deceived me, you caused the abortion of the fetus twice. For what reason should I tell you?” the other woman thought, “Now I am ruined.” Watching for her carelessness, when the fetus was mature, she found an opportunity, prepared the medicine, and gave it to her. Because the fetus was mature, it could not be aborted and lay transversely. A sharp pain arose, and she came to be in danger of her life. She made an aspiration, saying: “I have been ruined by you. You yourself brought me here, and you yourself destroyed my children on all three occasions. Now I too will perish. Having passed away from this state, may I be reborn as an ogress, able to devour your children.” Having made this aspiration, she died and was reborn in that very house as a cat. The husband, seizing the other woman, said: “You have caused the severing of my lineage,” and beat her severely with his elbows, knees, and so on. Afflicted by that very injury, she died and was reborn right there as a hen.

Kukkuṭī na cirasseva aṇḍāni vijāyi, majjārī āgantvā tāni aṇḍāni khādi. Dutiyampi tatiyampi khādiyeva. Kukkuṭī cintesi – “tayo vāre mama aṇḍāni khāditvā idāni mampi khāditukāmāsī”ti. “Ito cutā saputtakaṃ taṃ khādituṃ labheyya”nti patthanaṃ katvā tato cutā araññe dīpinī hutvā nibbatti. Itarā migī hutvā nibbatti. Tassā vijātakāle dīpinī āgantvā tayo vāre puttake khādi. Migī maraṇakāle “ayaṃ me tikkhattuṃ puttake khāditvā idāni mampi khādissati, ito dāni cutā etaṃ saputtakaṃ khādituṃ labheyya”nti patthanaṃ katvā ito cutā yakkhinī hutvā nibbatti. Dīpinīpi tatheva tato cutā sāvatthiyaṃ kuladhītā hutvā nibbatti, sā vuddhippattā dvāragāmake patikulaṃ agamāsi, aparabhāge ca puttaṃ vijāyi. Yakkhinīpi tassā piyasahāyikāvaṇṇena āgantvā “kuhiṃ me sahāyikā”ti “antogabbhe vijātā”ti vutte “puttaṃ nu kho vijātā, udāhu dhītaranti passissāmi na”nti gabbhaṃ pavisitvā passantī viya dārakaṃ gahetvā [M 1.0032] khāditvā gatā. Puna dutiyavārepi tatheva khādi. Tatiyavāre itarā garubhārā hutvā sāmikaṃ āmantetvā, “sāmi, imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekā yakkhinī mama dve putte khāditvā gatā, idāni [P 1.0049] mama kulagehaṃ gantvā vijāyissāmī”ti kulagehaṃ gantvā vijāyi.

The hen soon laid eggs, and the cat came and ate those eggs. A second and a third time, she ate them. The hen thought, “Having eaten my eggs three times, now she must want to eat me too.” Making an aspiration, “Having passed away from this state, may I be able to eat her along with her offspring,” she passed away from there and was reborn as a leopardess in the forest. The other was reborn as a doe. At the time she gave birth, the leopardess came and ate her young on three occasions. At the time of her death, the doe made an aspiration, “This one has eaten my young three times, and now she will eat me too. Having passed away from this state, may I be able to eat her along with her offspring.” Having passed away from this state, she was reborn as an ogress. The leopardess, too, passed away from there and was reborn as the daughter of a good family in Sāvatthī. When she came of age, she went to her husband’s house in a village near the gate. In time, she gave birth to a son. The ogress, too, came in the guise of a beloved friend and asked, “Where is my friend?” When told, “She has given birth in the inner chamber,” she said, “Has she given birth to a son or a daughter? I will see him,” and entering the chamber, as if looking, she took the child, devoured it, and left. Again, on the second occasion, she ate the child in the same way. On the third occasion, the other woman, being heavy with child, addressed her husband, “Husband, in this place an ogress came and devoured my two sons. Now I will go to my family’s home to give birth.” And going to her family’s home, she gave birth.

Tadā sā yakkhinī udakavāraṃ gatā hoti. Vessavaṇassa hi yakkhiniyo vārena anotattadahato sīsaparamparāya udakamāharanti. Tā catumāsaccayenapi pañcamāsaccayenapi muccanti. Aparā yakkhiniyo kilantakāyā jīvitakkhayampi pāpuṇanti. Sā pana udakavārato muttamattāva vegena taṃ gharaṃ gantvā “kuhiṃ me sahāyikā”ti pucchi. “Kuhiṃ naṃ passissasi, tassā imasmiṃ ṭhāne jātajātadārake yakkhinī āgantvā khādati, tasmā kulagehaṃ gatā”ti. Sā “yattha vā tattha vā gacchatu, na me muccissatī”ti veravegasamussāhitamānasā nagarābhimukhī pakkhandi. Itarāpi nāmaggahaṇadivase naṃ dārakaṃ nhāpetvā nāmaṃ katvā, “sāmi, idāni sakagharaṃ gacchāmā”ti puttamādāya sāmikena saddhiṃ vihāramajjhe gatamaggena gacchantī puttaṃ sāmikassa datvā vihārapokkharaṇiyā nhātvā sāmike nhāyante [V 1.0032] uttaritvā puttassa thaññaṃ pāyamānā ṭhitā yakkhiniṃ āgacchantiṃ disvā sañjānitvā, “sāmi, vegena ehi, ayaṃ sā yakkhinī, vegena ehi, ayaṃ sā yakkhinī”ti uccāsaddaṃ katvā yāva tassa āgamanaṃ [P 1.0050] saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī nivattetvā antovihārābhimukhī pakkhandi.

At that time, that ogress had gone for her turn to fetch water. For the ogresses of Vessavaṇa bring water in turn from Lake Anotatta, passing it from head to head. They are released after four or five months. Other ogresses, with their bodies exhausted, even reach the end of their lives. But she, as soon as she was freed from her water-fetching turn, quickly went to that house and asked, “Where is my friend?” They replied, “Where would you see her? In this place, an ogress comes and eats her children each time they are born. Therefore, she has gone to her family’s home.” She thought, “Wherever she may go, she will not escape me!” With a mind roused by the force of vengeance, she rushed toward the city. The other woman, on the naming day, bathed the child, gave him a name, and said, “Husband, now let us go to our own home.” Taking her son, while going with her husband along the path through the middle of the monastery, she gave the son to her husband, bathed in the monastery’s pond, and while her husband was bathing, she came out and stood nursing her son. Seeing the ogress approaching, she recognized her and cried out loudly, “Husband, come quickly! This is that ogress! Come quickly! This is that ogress!” Unable to wait until his arrival, she turned and rushed toward the inner monastery.

Tasmiṃ samaye satthā parisamajjhe dhammaṃ desesi. Sā puttaṃ tathāgatassa pādapiṭṭhe nipajjāpetvā “tumhākaṃ mayā esa dinno, puttassa me jīvitaṃ dethā”ti āha. Dvārakoṭṭhake adhivattho sumanadevo nāma yakkhiniyā anto pavisituṃ nādāsi. Satthā ānandattheraṃ āmantetvā “gaccha, ānanda, taṃ yakkhiniṃ pakkosāhī”ti āha. Thero pakkosi. Itarā “ayaṃ, bhante, āgacchatī”ti āha. Satthā “etu, mā saddamakāsī”ti vatvā taṃ āgantvā ṭhitaṃ “kasmā evaṃ karosi, sace tumhe mādisassa buddhassa sammukhībhāvaṃ nāgamissatha, ahinakulānaṃ viya acchaphandanānaṃ viya kākolūkānaṃ viya ca kappaṭṭhitikaṃ vo veraṃ abhavissa[M 1.0033], kasmā veraṃ paṭiveraṃ karotha. Verañhi averena upasammati, no verenā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly. She laid her son upon the instep of the Tathāgata's feet and said, 'I give this child to you; please grant life to my son.' The deva named Sumana, who guarded the gatehouse, did not allow the ogress to enter. The Teacher, having summoned the Elder Ānanda, said, 'Go, Ānanda, call that ogress.' The Elder called her. The other woman said, 'Venerable sir, she is coming.' The Teacher said, 'Let her come. Do not make a sound.' Then, to the ogress who had come and was standing there, he said, 'Why do you do this? If you had not come into the presence of a Buddha like me, your enmity would have become one that lasts for an entire aeon, like that between snakes and mongooses, between bears and phandana trees, and between crows and owls. Why do you return enmity for enmity? For enmity is appeased by non-enmity; it is not appeased by enmity.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

5.

5.

“Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṃ;

Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano”ti.

Enmities are never appeased by enmity in this world; by non-enmity alone are they appeased. This is an eternal law.

Tattha na hi verenāti yathā hi kheḷasiṅghāṇikādīhi asucīhi makkhitaṃ ṭhānaṃ teheva asucīhi dhovantā suddhaṃ [P 1.0051] niggandhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti, atha kho taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhiyyosomattāya asuddhatarañceva duggandhatarañca hoti; evameva akkosantaṃ paccakkosanto paharantaṃ paṭipaharanto verena veraṃ vūpasametuṃ na sakkoti, atha kho bhiyyo bhiyyo verameva karoti. Iti verāni nāma verena kismiñci kāle na sammanti, atha kho vaḍḍhantiyeva. Averena ca sammantīti yathā pana tāni kheḷādīni asucīni vippasannena udakena dhoviyamānāni nassanti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ suddhaṃ hoti sugandhaṃ; evameva averena khantimettodakena yoniso manasikārena paccavekkhaṇena verāni vūpasammanti paṭippassambhanti abhāvaṃ gacchanti. Esa dhammo sanantanoti esa averena verūpasamanasaṅkhāto porāṇako dhammo; sabbesaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavānaṃ gatamaggoti.

Therein, regarding 'Not by enmity': Indeed, just as a place smeared with impure things like spit, phlegm, and snot cannot be made clean and odorless by washing it with those same impure things—rather, that place becomes even more impure and foul-smelling; in the same way, one who abuses in return one who abuses, or strikes back at one who strikes, cannot appease enmity with enmity. Rather, one only creates more and more enmity. Thus, enmities are never appeased by enmity at any time; rather, they only increase. And regarding 'by non-enmity they are appeased': Just as those impure things like spit, when washed with very clear water, are destroyed, and that place becomes clean and fragrant; in the same way, through non-enmity—that is, with the water of patience and loving-kindness, with proper attention, and with wise reflection—enmities are pacified, calmed, and reach a state of non-existence. Regarding 'This is an ancient law': This principle, known as the appeasement of enmity through non-enmity, is an ancient law; it is the path trodden by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants.

Gāthāpariyosāne yakkhinī sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Sampattaparisāyapi dhammadesanā sātthikā ahosi.

At the end of the verse, the yakkhiṇī was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial for the assembled gathering.

Satthā [V 1.0033] taṃ itthiṃ āha – “etissā tava puttaṃ dehī”ti. “Bhāyāmi, bhante”ti. “Mā bhāyi, natthi te etaṃ nissāya paripantho”ti āha. Sā tassā puttamadāsi. Sā taṃ cumbitvā āliṅgetvā puna mātuyeva datvā rodituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ satthā “kimeta”nti pucchi. “Bhante, ahaṃ pubbe yathā vā tathā vā jīvikaṃ kappentīpi kucchipūraṃ nālatthaṃ, idāni kathaṃ jīvissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “mā cintayī”ti samassāsetvā taṃ itthimāha – “imaṃ netvā [P 1.0052] attano gehe nivāsāpetvā aggayāgubhattehi paṭijaggāhī”ti. Sā taṃ netvā piṭṭhivaṃse patiṭṭhāpetvā aggayāgubhattehi paṭijaggi, tassā vīhipaharaṇakāle musalaggena muddhaṃ paharantaṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi. Sā sahāyikaṃ āmantetvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkomi, aññattha maṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti vatvā musalasālāya udakacāṭiyaṃ uddhane nibbakose saṅkārakūṭe gāmadvāre cāti etesu ṭhānesu [M 1.0034] patiṭṭhāpitāpi idha me musalena sīsaṃ bhindantaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti, idha dārakā ucchiṭṭhodakaṃ otārenti, idha sunakhā nipajjanti, idha dārakā asuciṃ karonti, idha kacavaraṃ chaḍḍenti, idha gāmadārakā lakkhayoggaṃ karontīti sabbāni tāni paṭikkhipi. Atha naṃ bahigāme vivittokāse patiṭṭhāpetvā tattha tassā aggayāgubhattādīni haritvā paṭijaggi. Sā yakkhinī evaṃ cintesi – “ayaṃ me sahāyikā idāni bahūpakārā, handāhaṃ kiñci paṭiguṇaṃ karomī”ti. Sā “imasmiṃ saṃvacchare subbuṭṭhikā bhavissati, thalaṭṭhāne sassaṃ karohi, imasmiṃ saṃvacchare dubbuṭṭhikā bhavissati, ninnaṭṭhāneyeva sassaṃ karohī”ti sahāyikāya āroceti. Sesajanehi katasassaṃ atiudakena vā anodakena vā nassati, tassā ativiya sampajjati. Atha naṃ sesajanā, “amma, tayā katasassaṃ neva accodakena, na anudakena nassati, subbuṭṭhidubbuṭṭhibhāvaṃ ñatvā kammaṃ karosi, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti pucchiṃsu. “Amhākaṃ sahāyikā yakkhinī subbuṭṭhidubbuṭṭhibhāvaṃ [P 1.0053] ācikkhati, mayaṃ tassā vacanena thalesu ninnesu sassāni karoma, tena no sampajjati. Kiṃ na passatha? Nibaddhaṃ amhākaṃ gehato yāgubhattādīni hariyamānāni, tāni etissā harīyanti, tumhepi etissā aggayāgubhattādīni haratha, tumhākampi kammante olokessatī”ti. Athassā sakalanagaravāsino sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Sāpi tato paṭṭhāya sabbesaṃ kammante olokentī lābhaggappattā ahosi mahāparivārā. Sā aparabhāge aṭṭha salākabhattāni paṭṭhapesi. Tāni yāvajjakālā dīyantiyevāti.

The Teacher said to the woman, 'Give your son to this yakkhiṇī.' 'I am afraid, venerable sir.' 'Do not be afraid; there is no danger to you from her,' he said. She gave her son to the yakkhiṇī. The yakkhiṇī kissed him, embraced him, and then, giving him back to his mother, began to weep. Then the Teacher asked her, 'What is this?' 'Venerable sir, previously, no matter how I tried to make a living, I could not get enough to fill my belly. Now, how will I live?' Then the Teacher, having consoled her by saying, 'Do not worry,' said to the woman: 'Take this yakkhiṇī, have her live in your own house, and look after her with the first-offered rice gruel and food.' She took her and had her stay in the rafters of the house, looking after her with the first-offered rice gruel and food. At the time of pounding the paddy, it seemed to the yakkhiṇī as if her head were being struck by the end of a pestle. She called her friend and said, 'I cannot live in this place; settle me elsewhere.' And so, though she was settled in these places—in the pounding-shed, at the water-pot stand, in the kitchen, at the place where the eaves drip, on the rubbish heap, and at the village gate—she rejected them all, saying: 'Here, it feels as if my head is being smashed with a pestle; here, children pour out used water; here, children relieve themselves; here, they throw out sweepings; here, the village children play games.' Then, having settled her in a secluded spot outside the village, they brought her the first-offered rice gruel and food. That yakkhiṇī thought to herself, 'This friend of mine is now very helpful to me; I should do something in return for her.' So she told her friend, 'This year there will be abundant rain, so plant your crops on high ground. This year there will be a drought, so plant your crops only in low-lying areas.' The crops planted by other people were destroyed by either too much water or no water, but hers flourished exceedingly. Then the townspeople asked her, 'Friend, the crops you plant are not destroyed by too much water or by no water. Do you plant your crops knowing whether there will be abundant rain or a drought? What is the reason for this?' She replied, 'Our friend, the yakkhiṇī, tells us whether there will be abundant rain or a drought. We plant our crops on high and low ground according to her word, and that is why they flourish. Do you not see the rice gruel and food being constantly carried from our house? They are being taken to her. You too should take her the first-offered rice gruel and food, and she will also look after your work.' Then all the townspeople made offerings to her. From that time on, she looked after the work of everyone, attained the peak of gain, and had a large retinue. In a later time, she established eight ticket-meals. Those are given even to this day.

Kāḷayakkhinīvatthu catutthaṃ.

The fourth story: The Tale of the Yakkhiṇī Kāḷī.

5. Kosambakavatthu

5. The Story of the Monks of Kosambī

Pare [V 1.0034] ca na vijānantīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosambake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this discourse on the Dhamma beginning with the words, 'Others do not understand,' concerning the monks of Kosambī.

Kosambiyañhi ghositārāme pañcasatapañcasataparivārā dve bhikkhū vihariṃsu vinayadharo ca dhammakathiko ca. Tesu dhammakathiko ekadivasaṃ [M 1.0035] sarīravalañjaṃ katvā udakakoṭṭhake ācamanaudakāvasesaṃ bhājane ṭhapetvāva nikkhami. Pacchā vinayadharo tattha [P 1.0054] paviṭṭho taṃ udakaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā itaraṃ pucchi, “āvuso, tayā udakaṃ ṭhapita”nti? “Āma, āvuso”ti. “Kiṃ panettha āpattibhāvaṃ na jānāsī”ti? “Āma, na jānāmī”ti. “Hoti, āvuso, ettha āpattī”ti. “Tena hi paṭikarissāmi na”nti. “Sace pana te, āvuso, asañcicca assatiyā kataṃ, natthi āpattī”ti. So tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi ahosi. Vinayadharopi attano nissitakānaṃ “ayaṃ dhammakathiko āpattiṃ āpajjamānopi na jānātī”ti ārocesi. Te tassa nissitake disvā “tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo āpattiṃ āpajjitvāpi āpattibhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti āhaṃsu. Te gantvā attano upajjhāyassa ārocesuṃ. So evamāha – “ayaṃ vinayadharo pubbe anāpattīti vatvā idāni āpattīti vadati, musāvādī eso”ti. Te gantvā “tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo musāvādī”ti āhaṃsu. Te evaṃ aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu. Kato vinayadharo okāsaṃ labhitvā dhammakathikassa āpattiyā adassane ukkhepanīyakammamakāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ paccayadāyakā upaṭṭhākāpi dve koṭṭhāsā ahesuṃ, ovādapaṭiggāhakā bhikkhuniyopi ārakkhadevatāpi tāsaṃ sandiṭṭhasambhattā ākāsaṭṭhadevatāpīti yāva brahmalokā sabbepi puthujjanā dve pakkhā ahesuṃ. Cātumahārājikaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva akaniṭṭhabhāvanā pana ekaninnādaṃ kolāhalaṃ agamāsi.

Indeed, in Kosambī, at the Ghositārāma monastery, there dwelt two monks, an expert in the Vinaya and a speaker of the Dhamma, each with a retinue of five hundred monks. Among them, the speaker of the Dhamma, one day, after attending to his bodily needs, left the remaining rinsing water in a vessel in the water-closet and departed. Afterwards, the expert in the Vinaya entered there, and seeing that water, he went out and asked the other, 'Friend, was the water left by you?' 'Yes, friend.' 'Do you not know that in this matter there is an offense?' 'Indeed, I do not know.' 'Friend, in this matter there is an offense.' 'In that case, I will make amends for it.' 'If, however, friend, it was done by you unintentionally and without mindfulness, there is no offense.' He then held the view that in that matter there was no offense. The expert in the Vinaya also told his own pupils, 'This speaker of the Dhamma, though having committed an offense, does not know it.' Those pupils, seeing the pupils of the Dhamma-speaker, said, 'Your preceptor, though having committed an offense, does not know it is an offense.' They went and told their own preceptor. He said thus: 'This expert in the Vinaya, having said before, "There is no offense," now says, "There is an offense." He is a liar.' They went and said, 'Your preceptor is a liar.' Thus they increased the quarrel among one another. Thereupon, the expert in the Vinaya, having found an opportunity, performed the act of suspension against the speaker of the Dhamma for not seeing the offense. From that time onwards, their donors of requisites and attendants became two factions. The nuns who received their instruction, the guardian deities, their acquaintances and companions, the deities dwelling in the sky—all worldlings up to the Brahma-world became two factions. Beginning from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṭṭha abode, the uproar became a single clamor.

Atheko aññataro bhikkhu tathāgatamupasaṅkamitvā ukkhepakānaṃ vinayadharaantevāsikānaṃ “dhammikenevāyaṃ vinayakammena ukkhitto”ti laddhiñca, ukkhittānuvattakānaṃ [P 1.0055] dhammakathikaantevāsikānaṃ pana “adhammikeneva kammena ukkhitto”ti laddhiñca, ukkhepakehi vāriyamānānampi ca tesaṃ taṃ anuparivāretvā vicaraṇabhāvañca ārocesi bhagavā “samaggā kira hontū”ti dve vāre pesetvā “na icchanti, bhante, samaggā bhavitu”nti sutvā tatiyavāre “bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho, bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho”ti tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā ukkhepakānaṃ ukkhepane, itaresañca āpattiyā adassane ādīnavaṃ kathetvā puna tesaṃ tattheva [M 1.0036] ekasīmāyaṃ uposathādīni [V 1.0035] anujānitvā bhattaggādīsu bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ “āsanantarikāya nisīditabba”nti (mahāva. 456) bhattagge vattaṃ paññāpetvā “idānipi bhaṇḍanajātāva viharantī”ti sutvā tattha gantvā “alaṃ, bhikkhave, mā bhaṇḍana”ntiādīni vatvā, “bhikkhave, bhaṇḍanakalahaviggahavivādā nāmete anatthakārakā. Kalahaṃ nissāya hi laṭukikāpi sakuṇikā hatthināgaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesī”ti laṭukikajātakaṃ (jā. 1.5.39 ādayo) kathetvā, “bhikkhave, samaggā hotha, mā vivadatha. Vivādaṃ nissāya hi anekasatasahassā vaṭṭakāpi jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā”ti vaṭṭakajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.118) kathesi. Evampi tesu bhagavato vacanaṃ anādiyantesu aññatarena dhammavādinā tathāgatassa vihesaṃ anicchantena “āgametu, bhante bhagavā, dhammasāmi, appossukko, bhante bhagavā, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāramanuyutto [P 1.0056] viharatu, mayameva tena bhaṇḍanena kalahena viggahena vivādena paññāyissāmā”ti (mahāva. 457; ma. ni. 3.236) vutte atītaṃ āhari –

Then a certain monk approached the Tathāgata and reported the view of the disciples of the Vinaya-expert who performed the suspension, 'He was suspended by a disciplinary act that is indeed in accordance with the Dhamma,' and the view of the disciples of the Dhamma-speaker who followed the suspended one, 'He was suspended by an act that is indeed not in accordance with the Dhamma,' and also the fact that, though being prevented by those who performed the suspension, they went about following him. The Blessed One sent a messenger twice, saying, 'Let them be reconciled.' Having heard their reply, 'Venerable sir, they do not wish to be reconciled,' and then on the third occasion hearing, 'The Saṅgha is divided! The Saṅgha is divided!', he went to them. He explained the danger in the act of suspension to those who performed it, and the danger in not seeing the offense to the others. Then, having allowed them to perform the Uposatha and other observances there within a single boundary, he laid down a rule of conduct in the dining hall, saying, 'In dining halls, those who have quarreled should be seated with a space between them.' Hearing that even now they were living in a state of quarreling, he went there and said, 'Enough, monks! Do not quarrel,' and so on. He said, 'Monks, these things called quarreling, strife, conflict, and disputes are unbeneficial. Indeed, on account of a quarrel, even a small quail caused a great elephant to come to the destruction of its life.' And he related the Laṭukika Jātaka. 'Monks, be united, do not dispute. Indeed, on account of a dispute, many hundreds of thousands of quails reached the destruction of their lives.' And he related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Even so, as they did not heed the Blessed One's word, a certain monk who spoke according to the Dhamma, not wishing vexation for the Tathāgata, said, 'Venerable sir, Blessed One, Lord of the Dhamma, please wait. Venerable sir, Blessed One, may you dwell unconcerned, devoted to abiding in the happiness of the present life. We ourselves will be known by this quarreling, this strife, this conflict, and this dispute.' When this was said, the Teacher brought forth a story from the past.

Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto nāma kāsirājā ahosi. Brahmadattena dīghītissa kosalarañño rajjaṃ acchinditvā aññātakavesena vasantassa pituno māritabhāvañceva dīghāvukumārena attano jīvite dinne tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ samaggabhāvañca kathetvā “tesañhi nāma, bhikkhave, rājūnaṃ ādinnadaṇḍānaṃ ādinnasatthānaṃ evarūpaṃ khantisoraccaṃ bhavissati. Idha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, sobhetha, yaṃ tumhe evaṃ svākhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitā samānā khamā ca bhaveyyātha soratā cā”ti ovaditvāpi neva te samagge kātuṃ asakkhi. So tāya ākiṇṇavihāratāya ukkaṇṭhito “ahaṃ kho idāni ākiṇṇo dukkhaṃ viharāmi, ime ca bhikkhū mama vacanaṃ na karonti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ ekakova gaṇamhā vūpakaṭṭho vihareyya”nti cintetvā kosambiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ekakova attano pattacīvaramādāya bālakaloṇakagāmaṃ gantvā tattha bhaguttherassa ekacārikavattaṃ kathetvā pācinavaṃsamigadāye tiṇṇaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sāmaggiyānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā yena [M 1.0037] pālileyyakaṃ [P 1.0057] atthi, tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā pālileyyakaṃ upanissāya rakkhitavanasaṇḍe bhaddasālamūle pālileyyakena hatthinā upaṭṭhiyamāno phāsukaṃ vassāvāsaṃ vasi.

Once upon a time, monks, in Bārāṇasī there was a king of Kāsī named Brahmadatta. Having related the story of how Brahmadatta usurped the kingdom of Dīghīti, the king of Kosala; how Dīghīti, the father of Prince Dīghāvu, was killed while living in disguise; and how, after Prince Dīghāvu spared the king's life, from that day onwards they lived in harmony, the Blessed One admonished them, saying: 'Indeed, monks, if for those kings who wield the rod and the sword such patience and gentleness could arise, how much more fitting it would be for you, monks, who have gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, to be patient and gentle.' Yet, despite this admonition, he could not make them harmonious. Wearied by this contentious way of living, he thought: 'I am now living in discomfort amidst this strife, and these monks do not follow my word. It would be good indeed if I were to live alone, secluded from the group.' Having thought thus, he went for alms in Kosambī, and without informing the Saṅgha of monks, he took his bowl and robe and went alone to the village of Bālakaloṇaka. There, he explained the practice of solitary living to the Elder Bhagu, and in the Eastern Bamboo Grove Deer Park, he spoke of the benefits of harmony to three clansmen. Then he proceeded to where Pārileyyaka was. There, the Blessed One, depending on the village of Pārileyyaka, dwelt for the rains-residence in comfort in the protected forest grove at the foot of a beautiful sāla tree, attended by the elephant Pārileyyaka.

Kosambivāsinopi kho upāsakā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ apassantā “kuhiṃ, bhante, satthā”ti pucchitvā “pālileyyakavanasaṇḍaṃ gato”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Amhe samagge kātuṃ vāyami, mayaṃ pana na samaggā ahumhā”ti. “Kiṃ, bhante, tumhe satthu santike pabbajitvā tasmiṃ sāmaggiṃ karonte samaggā nāhuvatthā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Manussā ime [V 1.0036] satthu santike pabbajitvā tasmiṃ sāmaggiṃ karontepi samaggā na jātā, mayaṃ ime nissāya satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhimhā, imesaṃ neva āsanaṃ dassāma, na abhivādanādīni karissāmā”ti tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ sāmīcimattampi na kariṃsu. Te appāhāratāya sussamānā katipāheneva ujukā hutvā aññamaññaṃ accayaṃ desetvā khamāpetvā “upāsakā mayaṃ samaggā jātā, tumhepi no purimasadisā hothā”ti āhaṃsu. “Khamāpito pana vo, bhante, satthā”ti. “Na khamāpito, āvuso”ti. “Tena hi satthāraṃ khamāpetha, satthu khamāpitakāle mayampi tumhākaṃ purimasadisā bhavissāmā”ti. Te antovassabhāvena satthu santikaṃ gantuṃ avisahantā dukkhena taṃ antovassaṃ vītināmesuṃ. Satthā pana tena hatthinā upaṭṭhiyamāno sukhaṃ vasi. Sopi hi hatthināgo gaṇaṃ pahāya phāsuvihāratthāyeva [P 1.0058] taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pāvisi.

The lay devotees of Kosambī, going to the monastery and not seeing the Teacher, asked, 'Where, venerable sirs, is the Teacher?' 'He has gone to the Pārileyyaka forest grove.' 'For what reason?' 'He was trying to make us harmonious, but we did not become harmonious.' 'What, venerable sirs? Having gone forth in the Teacher's presence, did you not become harmonious even while he was creating harmony?' 'That is so, friends.' The lay devotees thought: 'These men, having gone forth in the Teacher's presence, did not become harmonious even while he was creating harmony. Because of them, we did not get to see the Teacher. We will not give them seats, nor will we perform acts of veneration for them.' From that time onward, they did not show them even the slightest proper respect. They, suffering from lack of food, grew emaciated. After a few days, having become upright, they confessed their transgression to one another and asked for forgiveness. Then they said to the lay devotees: 'We have become harmonious. You, too, should be towards us as you were before.' The lay devotees asked: 'But, venerable sirs, have you been forgiven by the Teacher?' 'We have not been forgiven, friends.' 'In that case, ask for the Teacher's forgiveness. When you have been forgiven by the Teacher, we too will be towards you as we were before.' They, not daring to go to the Teacher because it was the rains-residence, passed that rains-residence with difficulty. The Teacher, however, being attended by that elephant, dwelt in comfort. For that great elephant, having left the herd, had entered that forest grove for the very sake of dwelling in comfort.

Yathāha – “ahaṃ kho ākiṇṇo viharāmi hatthīhi hatthīnīhi hatthikalabhehi hatthicchāpehi, chinnaggāni ceva tiṇāni khādāmi, obhaggobhaggañca me sākhābhaṅgaṃ khādanti, āvilāni ca pānīyāni pivāmi, ogāhā cassa me uttiṇṇassa hatthiniyo kāyaṃ upanighaṃsantiyo gacchanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ekova gaṇamhā vūpakaṭṭho vihareyya”nti (mahāva. 467; udā. 35). Atha kho so hatthināgo yūthā apakkamma yena pālileyyakaṃ rakkhitavanasaṇḍaṃ bhaddasālamūlaṃ, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā pana bhagavantaṃ vanditvā olokento aññaṃ kiñci adisvā bhaddasālamūlaṃ pādeneva paharanto tacchetvā soṇḍāya sākhaṃ gahetvā sammajji. Tato paṭṭhāya soṇḍāya [M 1.0038] ghaṭaṃ gahetvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti, uṇhodakena atthe sati uṇhodakaṃ paṭiyādeti. Kathaṃ? Hatthena kaṭṭhāni ghaṃsitvā aggiṃ sampādeti, tattha dārūni pakkhipanto aggiṃ jāletvā tattha pāsāṇe pakkhipitvā pacitvā dārudaṇḍakena pavaṭṭetvā paricchinnāya khuddakasoṇḍikāya khipati, tato hatthaṃ otāretvā udakassa tattabhāvaṃ jānitvā gantvā satthāraṃ vandati. Satthā “udakaṃ te tāpitaṃ pālileyyakā”ti vatvā tattha gantvā nhāyati[P 1.0059]. Athassa nānāvidhāni phalāni āharitvā deti. Yadā pana satthā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, tadā satthu pattacīvaramādāya kumbhe patiṭṭhapetvā satthārā saddhiṃyeva gacchati. Satthā gāmūpacāraṃ patvā “pālileyyaka ito paṭṭhāya tayā gantuṃ na sakkā, āhāra me pattacīvara”nti āharāpetvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sopi yāva satthu nikkhamanā tattheva ṭhatvā āgamanakāle paccuggamanaṃ katvā purimanayeneva pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vasanaṭṭhāne otāretvā vattaṃ dassetvā sākhāya bījati, rattiṃ vāḷamigaparipanthanivāraṇatthaṃ mahantaṃ daṇḍaṃ soṇḍāya gahetvā “satthāraṃ rakkhissāmī”ti yāva aruṇuggamanā vanasaṇḍassa antarantarena vicarati, tato [V 1.0037] paṭṭhāyayeva kira so vanasaṇḍo pālileyyakarakkhitavanasaṇḍo nāma jāto. Aruṇe uggate mukhodakadānaṃ ādiṃ katvā tenevūpāyena sabbavattāni karoti.

As it is said: 'I, for my part, live crowded by elephants, she-elephants, young elephants, and elephant calves. I eat grass whose tips have been broken off, and they eat the broken branches that have been repeatedly broken. I drink turbid water, and when I am descending into the water and when I have emerged from it, the she-elephants go along rubbing their bodies against my body. It would be good indeed if I were to live alone, withdrawn from the herd.' Then that great elephant, having departed from the herd, went to the Pārileyyaka protected forest grove, to the foot of the auspicious Sāla tree, where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, and looking around and seeing no one else, he struck the foot of the auspicious Sāla tree with his foot and smoothed it, then took a branch with his trunk and swept. From then on, taking a pot with his trunk, he would set out drinking water and water for use, and when hot water was needed, he would prepare it. How? Rubbing sticks together with his trunk, he would produce fire. Placing wood in it and lighting the fire, he then placed stones in that fire. Having heated them, he rolled them with a wooden stick and threw them into a small, defined pool of water. Then, lowering his trunk to test the temperature of the water, he would go and pay homage to the Teacher. The Teacher would say, 'The water has been heated, Pārileyyaka,' and then go there to bathe. He would also bring various kinds of fruits and give them to the Teacher. When the Teacher entered a village for alms, the elephant would take his bowl and robe, place them on his head, and accompany the Teacher. When they reached the outskirts of the village, the Teacher would say, 'Pārileyyaka, from here on you cannot go. Bring me my bowl and robe,' and having had them brought, the Teacher would enter the village for alms. The elephant, too, would wait right there until the Teacher came out of the village, and upon his arrival, would go out to meet him. Taking the bowl and robe in the same way as before, he would set them down in the dwelling place, perform his duties, and fan the Teacher with a branch. At night, to ward off the danger of predatory beasts, he would carry a large club in his trunk, thinking, 'I will protect the Teacher,' and patrol within the forest grove until dawn. From then on, it is said, that forest grove became known as the Forest Grove Protected by Pārileyyaka. At dawn, beginning with offering water for washing the face, he would perform all his duties in the same manner.

Atheko makkaṭo taṃ hatthiṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya divase divase tathāgatassa ābhisamācārikaṃ karontaṃ disvā “ahampi kiñcideva karissāmī”ti vicaranto ekadivasaṃ nimmakkhikaṃ daṇḍakamadhuṃ disvā daṇḍakaṃ bhañjitvā daṇḍakeneva saddhiṃ madhupaṭalaṃ satthu santikaṃ āharitvā kadalipattaṃ chinditvā tattha ṭhapetvā adāsi[P 1.0060]. Satthā gaṇhi. Makkaṭo “karissati nu kho paribhogaṃ na karissatī”ti olokento gahetvā nisinnaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho”ti cintetvā daṇḍakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā parivattetvā upadhārento aṇḍakāni disvā tāni saṇikaṃ apanetvā puna adāsi. Satthā paribhogamakāsi. So tuṭṭhamānaso taṃ taṃ sākhaṃ gahetvā naccantova aṭṭhāsi. Athassa gahitasākhāpi akkantasākhāpi bhijjiṃsu. So ekasmiṃ khāṇumatthake patitvā niviṭṭhagatto satthari pasanneneva cittena [M 1.0039] kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane tiṃsayojanike kanakavimāne nibbatti, accharāsahassaparivāro makkaṭadevaputto nāma ahosi.

Then a certain monkey, seeing that elephant striving and making an effort day after day to perform the customary duties for the Tathāgata, thought, 'I too will make some kind of offering.' While wandering about, one day he saw a honeycomb on a stick that was without bees. Breaking the stick, he brought the honeycomb along with the stick to the Teacher. Tearing off a banana leaf, he placed the honeycomb on it and offered it. The Teacher accepted it. The monkey, watching, thought, 'Will he partake of it or not?' Upon seeing the Teacher take it and sit down, he thought, 'What could be the reason?' Taking the end of the stick, he turned it over, and upon examining it, he saw the eggs. He carefully removed them and offered it again. The Teacher partook of it. Delighted, the monkey took hold of this and that branch and stood as if dancing. Then both the branch he held and the branch he stepped on broke. Falling onto the top of a stump, his body was pierced through. With a mind full of faith in the Teacher, he died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in a golden celestial mansion of thirty yojanas. Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, he became the deva named Makkaṭa.

Tathāgatassa tattha hatthināgena upaṭṭhiyamānassa vasanabhāvo sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi. Sāvatthinagarato “anāthapiṇḍiko visākhā ca mahāupāsikā”tievamādīni mahākulāni ānandattherassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu “satthāraṃ no, bhante, dassethā”ti. Disāvāsinopi pañcasatā bhikkhū vuṭṭhavassā ānandattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “cirassutā no, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammī kathā, sādhu mayaṃ, āvuso ānanda, labheyyāma bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṃ kathaṃ savanāyā”ti yāciṃsu. Thero te bhikkhū ādāya tattha gantvā “temāsaṃ ekavihārino tathāgatassa santikaṃ ettakehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ upasaṅkamituṃ [P 1.0061] ayutta”nti cintetvā te bhikkhū bahi ṭhapetvā ekakova satthāraṃ upasaṅkami. Pālileyyako taṃ disvā daṇḍamādāya pakkhandi. Satthā oloketvā apehi “apehi pālileyyaka, mā nivārayi, buddhupaṭṭhāko eso”ti āha. So tattheva daṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇaṃ āpucchi. Thero nādāsi. Nāgo “sace uggahitavatto bhavissati, satthu nisīdanapāsāṇaphalake attano parikkhāraṃ na ṭhapessatī”ti cintesi. Thero pattacīvaraṃ bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapesi. Vattasampannā hi garūnaṃ āsane vā sayane vā attano parikkhāraṃ na ṭhapenti.

The fact of the Tathāgata's dwelling there, attended by the great elephant, became well-known throughout all of Jambudīpa. From the city of Sāvatthī, great families such as Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā the great female lay disciple sent a message to the Elder Ānanda, saying, 'Venerable sir, please show us the Teacher.'
