Also, five hundred monks from the various regions, having completed the rains-residence, approached the Elder Ānanda and requested, 'Friend Ānanda, it has been long since we heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One in person. It would be good, friend Ānanda, if we might get to hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One in person.' The Elder, taking those monks, went there but thought, 'It is not proper to approach the presence of the Tathāgata, who has been dwelling alone for three months, with so many monks.' Leaving the monks outside, he approached the Teacher alone. Pārileyyaka, seeing him, took up a club and charged. The Teacher, looking, said, 'Stand back, stand back, Pārileyyaka, do not obstruct him; this is an attendant of the Buddha.' He immediately dropped the club there and asked to receive the bowl and robe. The Elder did not give them. The great elephant thought, 'If he is one who has undertaken the duties, he will not place his own requisites on the Teacher's sitting-stone slab.' The Elder placed the bowl and robe on the ground. Indeed, those accomplished in their duties do not place their own requisites on the seats or beds of their teachers.

Thero satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā “ānanda, ekova āgatosī”ti pucchitvā pañcasatehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā “kahaṃ panete”ti vatvā [V 1.0038] “tumhākaṃ cittaṃ ajānanto bahi ṭhapetvā āgatomhī”ti vutte “pakkosāhi ne”ti āha. Thero tathā akāsi. Te bhikkhū āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā tehi bhikkhūhi, “bhante bhagavā, hi buddhasukhumālo ceva khattiyasukhumālo ca, tumhehi temāsaṃ ekakehi tiṭṭhantehi nisīdantehi ca dukkaraṃ kataṃ, vattapaṭivattakārakopi mukhodakādidāyakopi nāhosi maññe”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, pālileyyakahatthinā mama sabbakiccāni katāni. Evarūpañhi sahāyaṃ labhantena [M 1.0040] ekatova vasituṃ yuttaṃ, alabhantassa ekacārikabhāvova [P 1.0062] seyyo”ti vatvā imā nāgavagge tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The Elder approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Teacher asked, “Ānanda, have you come alone?” When told, "Venerable Sir, I have come together with five hundred monks," the Teacher, having heard of his arrival with them, said, “But where are they?” When it was said, “Not knowing Your noble intention, I left them outside and came,” He said, “Call them.” The Elder did so. Those monks came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with them, and those monks said, “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One possesses the delicacy of a Buddha and the delicacy of a Khattiya. You, by standing and sitting alone for three months, have performed a difficult deed. It seems there was no one to perform the major and minor duties, nor anyone to give water for washing the face and so forth.” When this was said, the Buddha replied, “Monks, the Pārileyyaka elephant performed all my duties. Indeed, for one who finds such a companion, it is fitting to live together with him; for one who does not, the state of wandering alone is better.” Having said this, he spoke these three verses in the Nāga Vagga:

“Sace labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ,

Saddhiṃcaraṃ sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ;

Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni,

Careyya tenattamano satīmā.

If one should find a prudent companion, one who walks together, lives righteously, and is steadfast, having overcome all dangers, one should walk with him, glad-minded and mindful.

“No ce labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ,

Saddhiṃcaraṃ sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ;

Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāya,

Eko care mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo.

If one should not find a prudent companion, one who walks together, lives righteously, and is steadfast, then like a king who has abandoned a conquered kingdom, one should walk alone, like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest.

“Ekassa caritaṃ seyyo,

Natthi bāle sahāyatā;

Eko care na ca pāpāni kayirā,

Appossukko mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo”ti. (mahāva. 464; ma. ni. 3.237; dha. pa. 328-330; su. ni. 45-46);

Better is a solitary life; there is no companionship with a fool. Let one wander alone, doing no evil, free from cares, like an elephant in the Mātanga forest.

Gāthāpariyosāne pañcasatāpi te bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Ānandattheropi anāthapiṇḍikādīhi pesitasāsanaṃ ārocetvā, “bhante, anāthapiṇḍikappamukhā te pañca ariyasāvakakoṭiyo tumhākaṃ āgamanaṃ paccāsīsantī”ti āha. Satthā “tena hi gaṇhāhi pattacīvara”nti pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā nikkhami. Nāgo gantvā gatamagge tiriyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. “Kiṃ karoti, bhante, nāgo”ti? “Tumhākaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ paccāsīsati, dīgharattaṃ kho panāyaṃ [V 1.0039] mayhaṃ upakārako, nāssa cittaṃ kopetuṃ vaṭṭati, nivattatha, bhikkhave”ti satthā bhikkhū gahetvā [P 1.0063] nivatti. Hatthīpi vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā panasakadaliphalādīni nānāphalāni saṃharitvā rāsiṃ katvā punadivase bhikkhūnaṃ adāsi. Pañcasatā bhikkhū sabbāni khepetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Bhattakiccapariyosāne satthā pattacīvaraṃ gāhetvā nikkhami. Nāgo bhikkhūnaṃ antarantarena gantvā satthu purato tiriyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. “Kiṃ karoti, bhante, nāgo”ti? “Ayañhi bhikkhave, tumhe pesetvā maṃ nivattetukāmo”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “pālileyyaka, idaṃ pana [M 1.0041] mama anivattagamanaṃ, tava iminā attabhāvena jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā maggaphalaṃ vā natthi, tiṭṭha tva”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā nāgo mukhe soṇḍaṃ pakkhipitvā rodanto pacchato pacchato agamāsi. So hi satthāraṃ nivattetuṃ labhanto teneva niyāmena yāvajīvaṃ paṭijaggeyya, satthā pana taṃ gāmūpacāraṃ patvā “pālileyyaka ito paṭṭhāya tava abhūmi, manussāvāso saparipantho, tiṭṭha tva”nti āha. So rodamāno tattheva ṭhatvā satthari cakkhupathaṃ vijahante hadayena phalitena kālaṃ katvā satthari pasādena tāvatiṃsabhavane tiṃsayojanike kanakavimāne accharāsahassamajjhe nibbatti, pālileyyakadevaputtoyevassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

At the conclusion of the verses, those five hundred monks were established in Arahantship. As for the Elder Ānanda, having announced the message sent by Anāthapiṇḍika and others, he said, 'Venerable Sir, those five koṭis of noble disciples, headed by Anāthapiṇḍika, are longing for your arrival.' The Teacher said, 'In that case, take the bowl and robe,' and having had the bowl and robe taken, he set out. The elephant went and stood across the path of his journey. 'Venerable Sir, what is the elephant doing?' 'Monks, it longs to give you alms. For a long time, this one has been helpful to me; it is not proper to trouble its mind. Turn back, monks.' The Teacher turned back, taking the monks with him. The elephant also entered the forest grove, and having collected various fruits such as jackfruit and bananas and made a pile, on the next day it gave them to the monks. The five hundred monks were not able to consume them all. At the end of the meal, the Teacher had his bowl and robe taken and set out. The elephant, going between the monks, stood across the path before the Teacher. 'Venerable Sir, what is the elephant doing?' 'Monks, this one wishes to send you away and make me turn back.' Then the Teacher said to it, 'Pārileyyaka, this journey of mine is one of no return. For you, in this existence, there is no jhāna, or vipassanā, or path and fruition. You, stay.' Hearing this, the elephant put its trunk in its mouth and, weeping, followed behind. Indeed, if it had succeeded in making the Teacher turn back, it would have attended upon him for his whole life in that very manner. But the Teacher, having reached the vicinity of the village, said, 'Pārileyyaka, from here on is not your place. The abode of humans is perilous. You, stay.' Weeping, it stood right there, and when the Teacher passed from its range of sight, it died from a broken heart. Due to its faith in the Teacher, it was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm, in a golden mansion thirty yojanas in size, amidst a thousand celestial nymphs. Its name became simply Pārileyyaka Devaputta.

Satthāpi anupubbena jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Kosambakā bhikkhū [P 1.0064] “satthā kira sāvatthiṃ āgato”ti sutvā satthāraṃ khamāpetuṃ tattha agamaṃsu. Kosalarājā “te kira kosambakā bhaṇḍanakārakā bhikkhū āgacchantī”ti sutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ mama vijitaṃ pavisituṃ na dassāmī”ti āha. “Mahārāja, sīlavantā ete bhikkhū, kevalaṃ aññamaññaṃ vivādena mama vacanaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu, idāni maṃ khamāpetuṃ āgacchanti, āgacchantu mahārājā”ti. Anāthapiṇḍikopi “ahaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ vihāraṃ pavisituṃ na dassāmī”ti vatvā tatheva bhagavatā paṭikkhitto tuṇhī ahosi. Sāvatthiyaṃ anuppattānaṃ pana tesaṃ bhagavā ekamante vivittaṃ kārāpetvā senāsanaṃ dāpesi. Aññe bhikkhū tehi saddhiṃ neva ekato nisīdanti, na tiṭṭhanti, āgatāgatā satthāraṃ pucchanti – “katamete, bhante, bhaṇḍanakārakā kosambakā bhikkhū”ti? Satthā “ete”ti dasseti. “Ete kira te, ete kira te”ti āgatāgatehi aṅgulikā dassiyamānā lajjāya sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ asakkontā bhagavato pādamūle nipajjitvā bhagavantaṃ khamāpesuṃ. Satthā “bhāriyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, kataṃ, tumhe hi nāma mādisassa buddhassa santike pabbajitvā mayi sāmaggiṃ karonte mama vacanaṃ na karittha, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi vajjhappattānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ovādaṃ [P 1.0065] sutvā tesu jīvitā voropiyamānesupi taṃ anatikkamitvā pacchā dvīsu raṭṭhesu rajjaṃ kārayiṃsū”ti vatvā punadeva [M 1.0042] kosambikajātakaṃ (jā. 1.9.10 ādayo) kathetvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, dīghāvukumāro mātāpitūsu [V 1.0040] jīvitā voropiyamānesupi tesaṃ ovādaṃ anatikkamitvā pacchā brahmadattassa dhītaraṃ labhitvā dvīsu kāsikosalaraṭṭhesu rajjaṃ kāresi, tumhehi pana mama vacanaṃ akarontehi bhāriyaṃ kata”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher also, in due course, arrived at Jetavana. The monks of Kosambī, hearing, “It is said the Teacher has come to Sāvatthī,” went there to ask for forgiveness from the Teacher. The King of Kosala, hearing, “It is said those quarrelsome monks from Kosambī are coming,” approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, I will not permit them to enter my kingdom.” “Great King, these monks are virtuous; it was merely due to a mutual dispute that they did not take my word. Now they are coming to ask for my forgiveness. Let them come, Great King.” Anāthapiṇḍika also, having said, “Venerable Sir, I will not permit them to enter my monastery,” was rejected by the Blessed One in the same way and became silent. For those who had arrived in Sāvatthī, the Blessed One had a secluded lodging prepared in a suitable place and had it given. Other monks would neither sit nor stand together with them. Visitors who arrived would ask the Teacher, “Venerable Sir, which are those quarrelsome monks from Kosambī?” The Teacher would point them out, saying, “These are they.” Being pointed at with fingers by the visitors, who said, “It seems these are they, it seems these are they,” they were unable to lift their heads out of shame. Prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, they asked for his forgiveness. The Teacher said, “Monks, you have done a grave thing. Having gone forth in the presence of a Buddha like me, you did not follow my word while I was creating harmony. The wise ones of old, having heard the advice of their parents who were condemned to death, did not transgress that word even while those parents were being executed, and later they ruled over two kingdoms.” Having said this, he then narrated the Kosambika Jātaka and said, “Thus, monks, Prince Dīghāvu, even while his parents were being executed, did not transgress their advice. Later, having obtained the daughter of Brahmadatta, he ruled over the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala. But you, by not following my word, have done a grave thing.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

6.

6.

“Pare ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase;

Ye ca tattha vijānanti, tato sammanti medhagā”ti.

Others do not realize that here we are perishing; but for those who do realize this, their dissensions are thereby calmed.

Tattha pareti paṇḍite ṭhapetvā tato aññe bhaṇḍanakārakā pare nāma. Te tattha saṅghamajjhe kolāhalaṃ karontā “mayaṃ yamāmase uparamāma vinassāma satataṃ samitaṃ maccusantikaṃ gacchāmā”ti na vijānanti. Ye ca tattha vijānantīti ye tattha paṇḍitā “mayaṃ maccusantikaṃ gacchāmā”ti vijānanti. Tato sammanti medhagāti evañhi te jānantā yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetvā medhagānaṃ kalahānaṃ vūpasamāya paṭipajjanti. Atha nesaṃ tāya paṭipattiyā te medhagā sammantīti. Atha vā pare cāti pubbe mayā “mā, bhikkhave, bhaṇḍana”ntiādīni vatvā ovadiyamānāpi mama ovādassa apaṭiggahaṇena atikkamanena amāmakā [P 1.0066] pare nāma. “Mayaṃ chandādivasena micchāgāhaṃ gahetvā ettha saṅghamajjhe yamāmase bhaṇḍanādīnaṃ vuddhiyā vāyamāmā”ti na vijānanti. Idāni pana yoniso paccavekkhamānā tattha tumhākaṃ antare ye ca paṇḍitapurisā “pubbe mayaṃ chandādivasena vāyamantā ayoniso paṭipannā”ti vijānanti, tato tesaṃ santikā te paṇḍitapurise nissāya ime dāni kalahasaṅkhātā medhagā sammantīti ayamettha atthoti.

Therein, 'pare' (others) refers to the quarrelsome ones, setting aside the wise. They, making an uproar in the midst of the Sangha, do not realize, “We are perishing, we are ceasing, we are being destroyed; we are constantly and unerringly approaching death.” ‘And those who know there’ refers to those wise ones there who understand, “We are approaching death.” ‘From that, their quarrels are calmed’ means: those who know thus, giving rise to wise reflection, practice for the calming of quarrels and disputes. Then, through that practice, those quarrels are calmed. Alternatively, ‘pare ca’ refers to those who are not my followers, who, though previously admonished by me with words such as, “Monks, do not quarrel,” transgressed by not accepting my advice. They do not realize, “We, having taken up a wrong view through the influence of desire and other causes, will perish here amidst the Sangha, striving for the increase of quarrels and such.” But now, reflecting wisely, those wise persons among you who understand, “Previously, striving under the influence of desire and other causes, we practiced unwisely”—from them, by relying on those wise persons, these quarrels, also called disputes, are now calmed. This is the meaning here.

Gāthāpariyosāne sampattabhikkhū sotāpattiphalādīsu patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the verse, the assembled monks were established in the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Kosambakavatthu pañcamaṃ.

The Fifth Story of the Monks of Kosambī.

6. Mahākāḷattheravatthu

6. The Story of Cūḷakāḷa and Mahākāḷa.

Subhānupassinti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā setabyanagaraṃ upanissāya siṃsapāvane viharanto cūḷakāḷamahākāḷe ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'One who dwells contemplating the beautiful,' while dwelling near the city of Setabyā in the Sīsapā forest, concerning Cūḷakāḷa and Mahākāḷa.

Setabyanagaravāsino [M 1.0043] hi cūḷakāḷo, majjhimakāḷo, mahākāḷoti tayo bhātaro kuṭumbikā[V 1.0041]. Tesu jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhā disāsu vicaritvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ āharanti, majjhimakāḷo ābhataṃ vikkiṇāti. Athekasmiṃ samaye te ubhopi bhātaro [P 1.0067] pañcahi sakaṭasatehi nānābhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā sāvatthiyā ca jetavanassa ca antare sakaṭāni mocayiṃsu. Tesu mahākāḷo sāyanhasamaye mālāgandhādihatthe sāvatthivāsino ariyasāvake dhammassavanāya gacchante disvā “kuhiṃ ime gacchantī”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “ahampi gamissāmī”ti cintetvā kaniṭṭhaṃ āmantetvā, “tāta, tesu sakaṭesu appamatto hohi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ gacchāmī”ti vatvā gantvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā parisapariyante nisīdi. Satthā taṃ disvā tassa ajjhāsayavasena anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathento dukkhakkhandhasuttādivasena (ma. ni. 1.163 ādayo) anekapariyāyena kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesañca kathesi. Taṃ sutvā mahākāḷo “sabbaṃ kira pahāya gantabbaṃ, paralokaṃ gacchantaṃ neva bhogā, na ñātakā ca anugacchanti, kiṃ me gharāvāsena pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā mahājane satthāraṃ vanditvā pakkante satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yācitvā satthārā “natthi te koci apaloketabbo”ti vutte, “kaniṭṭho me, bhante, atthī”ti vatvā tena hi “apalokehi na”nti vutte, “sādhu, bhante”ti vatvā gantvā kaniṭṭhaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “tāta, imaṃ sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. “Tumhe [P 1.0068] pana kiṃ karissatha bhātikā”ti? “Ahaṃ satthu santike pabbajissāmī”ti. So taṃ nānappakārehi yācitvā nivattetuṃ asakkonto “sādhu, sāmi, yathā ajjhāsayaṃ karothā”ti āha. Mahākāḷo gantvā satthu santike pabbaji. “Ahaṃ bhātikaṃ gahetvāva uppabbajissāmī”ti cūḷakāḷopi pabbaji. Aparabhāge mahākāḷo upasampadaṃ labhitvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā sāsane dhurāni pucchitvā satthārā dvīsu dhuresu kathitesu “ahaṃ, bhante, mahallakakāle pabbajitattā ganthadhuraṃ pūretuṃ na sakkhissāmi, vipassanādhuraṃ pana pūressāmī”ti yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā sosānikadhutaṅgaṃ samādāya paṭhamayāmātikkante sabbesu niddaṃ okkantesu susānaṃ gantvā paccūsakāle sabbesu anuṭṭhitesuyeva vihāraṃ āgacchati.

Indeed, in the city of Setabyā, there were three brothers who were householders: Cūḷakāḷa, Majjhimakāḷa, and Mahākāḷa. The eldest and the youngest traveled to various regions, bringing back goods with five hundred carts, while Majjhimakāḷa sold the goods they brought. On one occasion, those two brothers took five hundred carts of various goods and went to Sāvatthī, where they unyoked their carts between Sāvatthī and Jetavana. In the evening, Mahākāḷa saw the noble disciples of Sāvatthī, with flowers and perfumes in hand, going to listen to the Dhamma. He asked, 'Where are they going?' Upon hearing the reason, he thought, 'I too shall go.' He called his younger brother and said, 'Dear one, be vigilant with the carts. I am going to listen to the Dhamma.' Having said this, he went, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and sat at the edge of the assembly. The Teacher, seeing him, gave a gradual discourse in accordance with his disposition, explaining in many ways the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures by way of teachings like the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta. Hearing this, Mahākāḷa thought, 'It seems one must abandon everything and go. When going to the next world, neither wealth nor relatives follow. What use is the household life to me? I shall go forth.' After the great crowd had paid homage to the Teacher and departed, Mahākāḷa requested the going forth from the Teacher. When the Teacher asked, 'Is there no one you need to seek permission from?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, I have a younger brother.' The Teacher then said, 'Then seek his permission.' Agreeing, he went and had his younger brother summoned, saying, 'Dear one, take charge of all this property.' 'But what will you do, elder brother?' 'I will go forth in the presence of the Teacher.' Unable to dissuade him, though he pleaded in many ways, his brother said, 'Very well, master, do as you wish.' Mahākāḷa went and went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Thinking, 'I will take my brother and then disrobe,' Cūḷakāḷa also went forth. Later, Mahākāḷa received the higher ordination. Approaching the Teacher, he inquired about the duties in the Dispensation. When the Teacher had explained the two duties, Mahākāḷa said, 'Venerable sir, having gone forth in old age, I cannot fulfill the duty of study. But I will fulfill the duty of insight meditation.' Having had a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship taught to him and having undertaken the charnel-ground-dweller's practice, he would go to the charnel ground after the first watch of the night had passed, when all were asleep, and return to the monastery at dawn before anyone had risen.

Athekā [M 1.0044] susānagopikā kālī nāma chavaḍāhikā therassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ caṅkamitaṭṭhānañca disvā “ko nu kho idhāgacchati, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti pariggaṇhituṃ asakkontī ekadivasaṃ susānakuṭikāyameva dīpaṃ jāletvā puttadhītaro ādāya gantvā ekamante nilīyamānā majjhimayāme theraṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā gantvā vanditvā, “ayyo, no, bhante, imasmiṃ ṭhāne viharatī”ti āha. “Āma, upāsike”ti. “Bhante, susāne viharantehi [P 1.0069] nāma vattaṃ uggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Thero “kiṃ pana mayaṃ tayā kathitavatte vattissāmā”ti avatvā “kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati upāsike”ti āha. “Bhante, sosānikehi nāma [V 1.0042] susāne vasanabhāvo susānagopakānañca vihāre mahātherassa ca gāmabhojakassa ca kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Thero kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Katakammā corā dhanasāmikehi padānupadaṃ anubaddhā susāne bhaṇḍakaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyanti, atha manussā sosānikānaṃ paripanthaṃ karonti, etesaṃ pana kathite ‘mayaṃ imassa bhaddantassa ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ ettha vasanabhāvaṃ jānāma, acoro eso’ti upaddavaṃ nivārenti. Tasmā etesaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

Then a certain charnel ground guardian, a corpse-burner named Kālī, saw the elder’s place of standing, sitting, and walking, and thought, 'Who could be coming here? I must find out who it is.' Being unable to find out, one day she lit a lamp in the charnel ground hut, took her sons and daughters, and went to hide aside. In the middle watch of the night, seeing the elder coming, she went and paid homage, saying, 'Venerable sir, does our noble one dwell in this place?' 'Yes, lay follower.' 'Venerable sir, it is proper for those who dwell in the charnel ground to learn the observances.' The elder, without saying, 'Should we practice the observances spoken of by you?' asked, 'What is proper to do, lay follower?' 'Venerable sir, it is proper for those who practice in the charnel ground to inform the charnel ground keepers, the chief elder in the monastery, and the village headman of the fact of their dwelling in the charnel ground.' The elder asked, 'For what reason?' 'Thieves who have committed a crime, being pursued step by step by the owners of the wealth, abandon the goods in the charnel ground and flee. Then people cause harm to the charnel ground dwellers. But when these authorities are informed, they prevent the danger, saying, ‘We know that this good monk has been dwelling here for such and such a time; he is not a thief.’ Therefore, it is proper to inform them.'

“Thero aññaṃ kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Bhante, susāne vasantena nāma ayyena macchamaṃsatilapiṭṭhatelaguḷādīni vajjetabbāni, divā na niddāyitabbaṃ, kusītena na bhavitabbaṃ, āraddhavīriyena bhavitabbaṃ, asaṭhena amāyāvinā hutvā kalyāṇajjhāsayena bhavitabbaṃ, sāyaṃ sabbesu suttesu vihārato āgantabbaṃ, paccūsakāle sabbesu anuṭṭhitesuyeva vihāraṃ gantabbaṃ. Sace, bhante, ayyo imasmiṃ ṭhāne evaṃ viharanto pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ sakkhissati, sace matasarīraṃ ānetvā chaḍḍenti, ahaṃ kambalakūṭāgāraṃ āropetvā gandhamālādīhi sakkāraṃ katvā sarīrakiccaṃ karissāmi. No ce sakkhissati, citakaṃ āropetvā aggiṃ jāletvā saṅkunā ākaḍḍhitvā bahi [P 1.0070] khipitvā pharasunā koṭṭetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā aggimhi pakkhipitvā jhāpessāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ thero “sādhu bhadde, ekaṃ pana rūpārammaṇaṃ disvā mayhaṃ katheyyāsī”ti āha. Sā “sādhū”ti paccassosi. Thero yathājjhāsayena susāne samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Cūḷakāḷatthero [M 1.0045] pana uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya gharāvāsaṃ cinteti, puttadāraṃ anussarati. “Bhātiko me atibhāriyaṃ kammaṃ karotī”ti cinteti.

The Elder asked, 'What else is to be done?' 'Venerable sir, a noble one dwelling in the charnel ground should avoid fish, meat, sesame flour, oil, molasses, and so forth. One should not sleep during the day. One should not be lazy; one should be of aroused effort. Being without deceit, without guile, one should be of noble intention. In the evening, when all are asleep, one should come from the monastery. At dawn, before all have arisen, one should go to the monastery. Venerable sir, if you, dwelling thus in this place, are able to bring the task of a renunciant to its culmination, then should your dead body be brought and left here, I will place it in a great coffin with a pinnacle covered with red woolen cloth, and having made offerings with reverence with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, I will perform the bodily rites. If you are not able to, I will place it on a pyre, light it, and having dragged it with a spike, I will throw it outside, and having struck it with an axe, and having cut it into pieces, I will place it back in the fire and burn it.' Then the Elder said to her, 'Good, devout woman. However, having seen a form-object, you should tell me.' She agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The Elder, according to his inclination, practiced the ascetic's duties in the charnel ground. But the Venerable Cūḷakāḷa, arising again and again, thought of the household life; he repeatedly remembered his wife and children. He thought, 'My elder brother is undertaking an extremely heavy task.'

Athekā kuladhītā taṃmuhuttasamuṭṭhitena byādhinā sāyanhasamaye amilātā akilantā kālamakāsi. Tamenaṃ ñātakādayo dārutelādīhi saddhiṃ sāyaṃ susānaṃ netvā susānagopikāya “imaṃ jhāpehī”ti bhatiṃ datvā niyyādetvā pakkamiṃsu. Sā tassā pārutavatthaṃ apanetvā taṃmuhuttamataṃ pīṇitapīṇitaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ disvā, “imaṃ ayyassa dassetuṃ patirūpaṃ ārammaṇa”nti cintetvā gantvā theraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, evarūpaṃ nāma ārammaṇaṃ atthi, oloketha ayyā”ti āha. Thero “sādhū”ti vatvā pārupanaṃ nīharāpetvā pādatalato yāva kesaggā oloketvā “atipīṇitametaṃ [P 1.0071] rūpaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ aggimhi naṃ pakkhipitvā mahājālāhi gahitamattakāle mayhaṃ āroceyyāsī”ti vatvā sakaṭṭhānameva gantvā nisīdi. Sā tathā katvā therassa ārocesi. Thero gantvā olokesi. Jālāya pahaṭapahaṭaṭṭhānaṃ kabaragāviyā viya sarīravaṇṇaṃ ahosi, pādā namitvā olambiṃsu, hatthā paṭikuṭiṃsu, ūrunalāṭaṃ niccammaṃ ahosi[V 1.0043]. Thero “idaṃ sarīraṃ idāneva olokentānaṃ apariyantakaraṃ hutvā idāneva khayaṃ pattaṃ vayaṃ patta”nti rattiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā nisīditvā khayavayaṃ sampassamāno –

Then a certain daughter of good family, afflicted with a disease that had arisen intensely at that moment, passed away in the evening, unfaded and unstained. Her relatives, having brought that corpse to the charnel ground in the evening along with firewood, oil, and so forth, entrusted it to the female charnel ground keeper, having given a fee, saying, 'Cremate this one,' and departed. She, the keeper, having removed the cloth that covered it, saw the body, which had died just at that moment, exquisite and of a color like gold. Thinking, 'This is a suitable object to show to the noble one,' she went, paid homage to the Elder, and said, 'Venerable sirs, there is an object of such a nature. Please look.' The Elder, saying 'Good,' had the covering removed and looked from the soles of the feet up to the tips of the hair. He said, 'This form is exceedingly exquisite, of a color like gold. Having placed it in the fire, you should inform me at the very moment it is seized by great flames.' Then he went back to his own place and sat down. She, having done so, informed the Elder. The Elder went and looked. In the places struck by the flames, the color of the body became like that of a piebald cow. The feet bent and hung down, the hands curled up, and the thighs and forehead became skinless. The Elder reflected, 'This body, which just now, for those looking at it, was an object of boundless fascination, has now reached decay, has reached destruction.' He went to his place for the night, sat down, and while contemplating decay and destruction—

“Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti. (dī. ni. 2.221, 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186; 2.143; jā. 1.1.95) –

“Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned things, of the nature to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they cease; their stilling is bliss.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Having recited the verse and developed insight, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Tasmiṃ arahattaṃ patte satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ caramāno setabyaṃ gantvā siṃsapāvanaṃ pāvisi. Cūḷakāḷassa bhariyāyo “satthā kira anuppatto siṃsapāvana”nti sutvā “amhākaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti pesetvā satthāraṃ nimantāpesuṃ. Buddhānaṃ pana apariciṇṇaṭṭhāne āsanapaññattiṃ ācikkhantena ekena bhikkhunā paṭhamataraṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Buddhānañhi majjhimaṭṭhāne āsanaṃ paññāpetvā tassa dakkhiṇato [P 1.0072] sāriputtattherassa, vāmato [M 1.0046] mahāmoggallānattherassa, tato paṭṭhāya ubhosu passesu bhikkhusaṅghassa āsanaṃ paññāpetabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā mahākāḷatthero cīvarapārupanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā, “cūḷakāḷa, tvaṃ purato gantvā āsanapaññattiṃ ācikkhā”ti cūḷakāḷaṃ pesesi. Tassa diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya gehajanā tena saddhiṃ parihāsaṃ karontā nīcāsanāni saṅghattherassa koṭiyaṃ attharanti, uccāsanāni saṅghanavakassa koṭiyaṃ. Itaro “mā evaṃ karotha, nīcāsanāni upari mā paññāpetha, uccāsanāni upari paññāpetha, nīcāsanāni heṭṭhā”ti āha. Itthiyo tassa vacanaṃ asuṇantiyo viya “tvaṃ kiṃ karonto vicarasi, kiṃ tava āsanāni paññāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, tvaṃ kaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajito, kena pabbajitosi, kasmā idhāgatosī”ti vatvā nivāsanapārupanaṃ acchinditvā setakāni nivāsetvā sīse ca mālācumbuṭakaṃ ṭhapetvā, “gaccha satthāraṃ ānehi, mayaṃ āsanāni paññāpessāmā”ti pahiṇiṃsu. Na ciraṃ bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā avassikova uppabbajitattā lajjituṃ na jānāti, tasmā so tena ākappena nirāsaṅkova gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ādāya āgato. Bhikkhusaṅghassa pana bhattakiccāvasāne mahākāḷassa bhariyāyo “imāhi attano sāmiko gahito, mayampi amhākaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti [P 1.0073] cintetvā punadivase satthāraṃ nimantayiṃsu. Tadā pana āsanapaññāpanatthaṃ añño bhikkhu agamāsi. Tā tasmiṃ khaṇe okāsaṃ alabhitvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. Cūḷakāḷassa pana dve bhariyāyo, majjhimakāḷassa [V 1.0044] catasso, mahākāḷassa pana aṭṭha. Bhikkhūpi bhattakiccaṃ kātukāmā nisīditvā bhattakiccamakaṃsu, bahi gantukāmā uṭṭhāya agamaṃsu. Satthā pana nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ kari. Tassa bhattakiccapariyosāne tā itthiyo, “bhante, mahākāḷo amhākaṃ anumodanaṃ katvā āgacchissati, tumhe purato gacchathā”ti vadiṃsu. Satthā “sādhū”ti vatvā purato agamāsi. Gāmadvāraṃ patvā bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu “kiṃ nāmetaṃ satthārā kataṃ, ñatvā nu kho kataṃ, udāhu ajānitvā. Hiyyo cūḷakāḷassa purato gatattā pabbajjantarāyo jāto, ajja aññassa purato gatattā antarāyo nāhosi. Idāni mahākāḷaṃ ṭhapetvā āgato, sīlavā kho pana bhikkhu ācārasampanno, karissati nu kho tassa pabbajjantarāya”nti. Satthā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā nivattitvā ṭhito “kiṃ kathetha, bhikkhave”ti pucchi[M 1.0047]. Te tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Kiṃ pana tumhe, bhikkhave, cūḷakāḷaṃ viya mahākāḷaṃ sallakkhethā”ti? “Āma, bhante”. Tassa hi dve pajāpatiyo, imassa aṭṭha. “Aṭṭhahi parikkhipitvā gahito kiṃ karissati, bhante”ti? Satthā “mā, bhikkhave, evaṃ avacuttha, cūḷakāḷo uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya subhārammaṇabahulo viharati, papāte ṭhito dubbalarukkhasadiso. Mayhaṃ pana putto mahākāḷo [P 1.0074] asubhānupassī viharati, ghanaselapabbato viya acalo”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

When he had attained Arahantship, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, while travelling on tour, went to Setabyā and entered the Siṃsapā Grove. Hearing, 'It is said the Teacher has arrived at the Siṃsapā Grove,' the wives of Cūḷakāḷa thought, 'We will take our husband,' and sent a messenger to invite the Teacher. Now, for the Buddhas, in a place they have not frequented, it is proper for one monk to go first to announce the arrangement of seats. For the Buddhas, a seat should be prepared in the middle, with a seat for the Elder Sāriputta to his right and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna to his left, and from there, seats for the community of monks should be prepared on both sides. Therefore, the Elder Mahākāḷa, standing in the place for donning robes, sent Cūḷakāḷa, saying, 'Cūḷakāḷa, you go ahead and announce the arrangement of seats.' From the moment they saw him, the people of the house, making fun of him, spread low seats at the end for the senior monks and high seats at the end for the junior monks. The other said, 'Do not do so. Do not prepare the low seats above; prepare the high seats above and the low seats below.' The women, as if not hearing his words, said, 'What are you doing, wandering about? Is it not proper for you to prepare the seats? Having asked whom did you go forth? By whom were you made to go forth? Why have you come here?' And having snatched away his lower and upper robes, they made him wear white clothes, placed a garland-wreath on his head, and sent him off, saying, 'Go, bring the Teacher. We will prepare the seats.' Having been a monk for only a short time, without a full year's standing, and having been made to disrobe, he did not know how to be ashamed. Therefore, in that attire, without any hesitation, he went, paid homage to the Teacher, and returned, having brought the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. Then, at the conclusion of the meal for the community of monks, the wives of Mahākāḷa, thinking, 'Their husband has been taken by them; we too will take our husband,' invited the Teacher on the following day. On that occasion, however, another monk went to arrange the seats. Those women, not getting an opportunity at that moment, had the community of monks headed by the Buddha seated and gave almsfood. Now, Cūḷakāḷa had two wives, Majjhimakāḷa had four, and Mahākāḷa had eight. The monks, too, wishing to take their meal, sat down and did so; those who wished to go outside arose and went. The Teacher, however, sat and took his meal. At the conclusion of his meal, those women said, 'Venerable sir, Mahākāḷa will come after giving the blessing to us. You may go ahead.' The Teacher, saying, 'Very well,' went ahead. Having reached the village gate, the monks began to complain, 'What is this the Teacher has done? Did he do it knowingly, or did he do it not knowing? Yesterday, because Cūḷakāḷa went ahead, an obstacle to his monastic life arose. Today, because another went ahead, no obstacle arose. Now he has come, having left Mahākāḷa behind. That monk is indeed virtuous, endowed with good conduct. Will an obstacle to his monastic life arise?' The Teacher, hearing their words, turned back, stood, and asked, 'What are you talking about, monks?' They related the matter to him. 'But, monks, do you consider Mahākāḷa to be like Cūḷakāḷa?' 'Yes, venerable sir. For that one has two wives, but this one has eight. When he is surrounded and seized by eight, what will he do, venerable sir?' The Teacher said, 'Monks, do not speak thus. Cūḷakāḷa is ever stirred up and dwells with a mind given to pleasant objects, like a weak tree standing on a precipice. But my son Mahākāḷa dwells contemplating the unattractive, unshaken like a solid rock mountain.' Having said this, he spoke these verses:

7.

7.

“Subhānupassiṃ viharantaṃ, indriyesu asaṃvutaṃ;

Bhojanamhi cāmattaññuṃ, kusītaṃ hīnavīriyaṃ;

Taṃ ve pasahati māro, vāto rukkhaṃva dubbalaṃ.

One who dwells contemplating the attractive, unguarded in the senses, immoderate in eating, lazy, and of little energy—Māra indeed overcomes him, as the wind, a weak tree.

8.

8.

“Asubhānupassiṃ viharantaṃ, indriyesu susaṃvutaṃ;

Bhojanamhi ca mattaññuṃ, saddhaṃ āraddhavīriyaṃ;

Taṃ ve nappasahatī māro, vāto selaṃva pabbata”nti.

One who dwells contemplating the unattractive, with senses well-restrained, moderate in food, faithful and with aroused energy—Māra indeed does not overcome him, as the wind, a rocky mountain.

Tattha subhānupassiṃ viharantanti sutaṃ anupassantaṃ, iṭṭhārammaṇe mānasaṃ vissajjetvā viharantanti attho. Yo hi puggalo nimittaggāhaṃ anubyañjanaggāhaṃ gaṇhanto “nakhā sobhanā”ti gaṇhāti, “aṅguliyo sobhanā”ti gaṇhāti, “hatthapādā, jaṅghā, ūru, kaṭi, udaraṃ, thanā, gīvā, oṭṭhā, dantā, mukhaṃ, nāsā, akkhīni, kaṇṇā, bhamukā, nalāṭaṃ, kesā, sobhanā”ti gaṇhāti, “kesā, lomā, nakhā, dantā, taco, sobhanā”ti [P 1.0075] gaṇhāti, vaṇṇo subho, saṇṭhānaṃ subhanti, ayaṃ subhānupassī nāma. Evaṃ taṃ subhānupassiṃ viharantaṃ. Indriyesūti [V 1.0045] cakkhādīsu chasu indriyesu. Asaṃvutanti cakkhudvārādīni arakkhantaṃ. Pariyesanamattā paṭiggahaṇamattā paribhogamattāti imissā mattāya ajānanato bhojanamhi cāmattaññuṃ. Apica paccavekkhaṇamattā vissajjanamattāti imissāpi mattāya ajānanato amattaññuṃ, idaṃ bhojanaṃ dhammikaṃ, idaṃ adhammikantipi ajānantaṃ. Kāmacchandabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakkavasitāya kusītaṃ. Hīnavīriyanti nibbīriyaṃ catūsu iriyāpathesu vīriyakaraṇarahitaṃ. Pasahatīti abhibhavati ajjhottharati. Vāto rukkhaṃva dubbalanti balavavāto chinnapapāte jātaṃ dubbalarukkhaṃ viya. Yathā hi so vāto tassa dubbalarukkhassa pupphaphalapallavādīnipi pāteti, khuddakasākhāpi bhañjati, mahāsākhāpi [M 1.0048] bhañjati, samūlakampi taṃ rukkhaṃ uppāṭetvā uddhaṃmūlaṃ adhosākhaṃ katvā gacchati, evameva evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ anto uppanno kilesamāro pasahati, balavavāto dubbalarukkhassa [P 1.0076] pupphaphalapallavādipātanaṃ viya khuddānukhuddakāpattiāpajjanampi karoti, khuddakasākhābhañjanaṃ viya nissaggiyādiāpattiāpajjanampi karoti, mahāsākhābhañjanaṃ viya terasasaṅghādisesāpattiāpajjanampi karoti, uppāṭetvā uddhaṃ, mūlakaṃ heṭṭhāsākhaṃ katvā pātanaṃ viya pārājikāpattiāpajjanampi karoti, svākkhātasāsanā nīharitvā katipāheneva gihibhāvaṃ pāpetīti evaṃ evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ kilesamāro attano vase vattetīti attho.

Here, `dwelling contemplating the beautiful` means dwelling while contemplating what is beautiful; that is, dwelling by releasing the mind onto pleasing objects. For a person who grasps the sign and the details, thinking, “The nails are beautiful,” “The fingers are beautiful,” “The hands and feet, calves, thighs, waist, belly, breasts, neck, lips, teeth, mouth, nose, eyes, ears, eyebrows, forehead, and hair are beautiful,” “The hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and skin are beautiful,” “The complexion is beautiful,” and “The form is beautiful”—this is called one who contemplates the beautiful. Thus, one dwells contemplating the beautiful. Regarding `the senses`—this means the six senses beginning with the eye. `Unrestrained` means not guarding the doors of the eye and so on. Due to not knowing the measure in seeking, receiving, and consuming food, one is `immoderate in food`. Moreover, due to not knowing the measure in reflecting upon and giving away food, one is immoderate, not knowing whether this food is lawful or unlawful. One is `lazy`, being under the control of thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harm. `Lacking energy` means devoid of effort, lacking the exertion of energy in the four postures. `Overcomes` means overwhelms and subjugates. `As the wind, a weak tree` means like a strong wind overcomes a weak tree grown on a broken precipice. Just as that wind scatters the flowers, fruits, and leaves of that weak tree, breaks its small branches, breaks its large branches, and uproots that tree entirely, turning it upside down with its roots in the air and branches below, so too does the internally arisen defilement-māra overcome such a person. Like the strong wind scattering the flowers, fruits, and leaves of a weak tree, it causes one to commit minor and lesser offenses; like breaking small branches, it causes one to commit offenses requiring forfeiture; like breaking large branches, it causes one to commit the thirteen offenses requiring an initial and subsequent meeting of the Saṅgha; like uprooting and turning it upside down, it causes one to commit offenses entailing defeat, expelling one from the well-taught Dispensation and reducing one to a layperson in just a few days. Thus, the defilement-māra keeps such a person under his control—this is the meaning.

Asubhānupassinti dasasu asubhesu aññataraṃ asubhaṃ passantaṃ paṭikūlamanasikāre yuttaṃ kese asubhato passantaṃ lome nakhe dante tacaṃ vaṇṇaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ asubhato passantaṃ. Indriyesūti chasu indriyesu. Susaṃvutanti nimittādiggāharahitaṃ pihitadvāraṃ. Amattaññutāpaṭikkhepena bhojanamhi ca mattaññuṃ. Saddhanti kammassa ceva phalassa ca saddahanalakkhaṇāya lokikāya saddhāya ceva tīsu vatthūsu aveccappasādasaṅkhātāya lokuttarasaddhāya ca samannāgataṃ. Āraddhavīriyanti paggahitavīriyaṃ paripuṇṇavīriyaṃ. Taṃ veti evarūpaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ yathā dubbalavāto saṇikaṃ paharanto ekagghanaṃ selaṃ cāletuṃ na sakkoti, tathā [P 1.0077] abbhantare uppajjamānopi dubbalakilesamāro nappasahati, khobhetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā na sakkotīti attho.

One who `contemplates foulness` means one who sees any one of the ten kinds of foulness, being engaged in the practice of attending to the repulsive—seeing hair as foul, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, color, and shape as foul. Regarding `the faculties`, this means in the six faculties. `Well-restrained` means being devoid of grasping at signs and so on, having the doors closed. And `moderate in food`, by rejecting immoderation. `Faith` means being endowed with both worldly faith, which has the characteristic of belief in kamma and its result, and with supramundane faith, known as unwavering confidence in the Three Jewels. One with `aroused energy` means one who has stirred up energy, who has complete energy. `Him, indeed...` means that just as a weak wind blowing gently cannot shake a solid rock mountain, so too the weak defilement-māra arising internally cannot oppress such a person; it cannot agitate or shake him—this is the meaning.

Tāpi kho tassa purāṇadutiyikāyo theraṃ parivāretvā “tvaṃ kaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajito, idāni gihī bhavissasi na bhavissasī”tiādīni vatvā kāsāvaṃ nīharitukāmā ahesuṃ. Thero tāsaṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā nisinnāsanā vuṭṭhāya iddhiyā uppattitvā kūṭāgārakaṇṇikaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā ākāsenāgantvā satthari gāthā pariyosāpenteyeva satthu suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ abhitthavanto ākāsato otaritvā tathāgatassa pāde vandi.

Then those former wives of his surrounded the elder and, saying such things as, “Whom did you ask for leave to go forth? Now, will you become a layman or not?” they became desirous of taking away his saffron robe. The elder, perceiving their ignoble demeanor, rose from his seat and, by his psychic power, flew up into the air. He split the pinnacle of the gabled house in two, then came through the sky. Just as the Teacher was concluding the verses, he descended from the sky, praising the Teacher's golden-hued body, and paid homage at the Tathāgata's feet.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0046] sampattabhikkhū sotāpattiphalādīsu patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the verses, the monks who had arrived were established in the fruition of stream-entry and so forth.

Mahākāḷattheravatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of Cūḷakāḷa and Mahākāḷa: The Sixth.

7. Devadattavatthu

7. The Story of Devadatta

Anikkasāvoti [M 1.0049] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājagahe devadattassa kāsāvalābhaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, beginning with the words 'Anikkasāvo,' concerning Devadatta's acquisition of a saffron-dyed robe in Rājagaha.

Ekasmiñhi samaye dve aggasāvakā pañcasate pañcasate attano attano parivāre ādāya satthāraṃ āpucchitvā vanditvā jetavanato rājagahaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājagahavāsino dvepi tayopi bahūpi ekato hutvā āgantukadānaṃ adaṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ āyasmā sāriputto anumodanaṃ karonto [P 1.0078] “upāsakā eko sayaṃ dānaṃ deti, paraṃ na samādapeti, so nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne bhogasampadaṃ labhati, no parivārasampadaṃ. Eko sayaṃ na deti, paraṃ samādapeti, so nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne parivārasampadaṃ labhati, no bhogasampadaṃ. Eko sayampi na deti, parampi na samādapeti, so nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne kañjikamattampi kucchipūraṃ na labhati, anātho hoti nippaccayo. Eko sayampi deti, parampi samādapeti, so nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne attabhāvasatepi attabhāvasahassepi attabhāvasatasahassepi bhogasampadañceva parivārasampadañca labhatī”ti evaṃ dhammaṃ desesi.

Indeed, at one time, the two chief disciples, each taking their own retinue of five hundred monks, having taken leave of the Teacher and paid homage, went from Jetavana to Rājagaha. The residents of Rājagaha, whether two, three, or many, came together and gave alms to the visiting monks. Then one day, the Venerable Sāriputta, while giving a discourse of appreciation, said: 'Householders, one person gives alms themselves but does not encourage others to do so; in whatever place they are reborn, they obtain the perfection of wealth, but not the perfection of a retinue. Another does not give themselves but encourages others to give; in whatever place they are reborn, they obtain the perfection of a retinue, but not the perfection of wealth. Another neither gives themselves nor encourages others to give; in whatever place they are reborn, they do not obtain even enough rice-gruel to fill their belly; they are without refuge and without support. Yet another both gives themselves and encourages others to give; in whatever place they are reborn—whether for a hundred existences, a thousand existences, or a hundred thousand existences—they obtain both the perfection of wealth and the perfection of a retinue.' Thus he taught the Dhamma.

Tameko paṇḍitapuriso dhammaṃ sutvā “acchariyā vata bho, abbhutā vata bho dhammadesanā, sukāraṇaṃ kathitaṃ, mayā imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ sampattīnaṃ nipphādakaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā – “bhante, sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti theraṃ nimantesi. “Kittakehi te bhikkhūhi attho upāsakā”ti. “Kittakā pana vo, bhante, parivārā”ti? “Sahassamattā upāsakā”ti. “Sabbehi saddhiṃyeva sve bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatha, bhante”ti. “Thero adhivāsesi”. Upāsako nagaravīthiyaṃ caranto – “ammā, tātā, mayā bhikkhusahassaṃ nimantitaṃ, tumhe kittakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ sakkhissatha, tumhe kittakāna”nti samādapesi. Manussā attano attano pahonakaniyāmena [P 1.0079] – “mayaṃ dasannaṃ dassāma, mayaṃ vīsatiyā, mayaṃ satassā”ti āhaṃsu. Upāsako – “tena hi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samāgamaṃ katvā ekatova parivisissāma[V 1.0047], sabbe tilataṇḍulasappimadhuphāṇitādīni samāharathā”ti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samāharāpesi.

Having heard that Dhamma, a certain wise man thought: 'Oh, how wonderful, how marvelous is this Dhamma teaching! A good cause has been spoken. It is fitting for me to perform the meritorious deed that brings about these two perfections.' Having thought thus, he invited the elder: 'Venerable sir, please accept my alms-food tomorrow.' 'For how many monks do you have need, householder?' 'But how many are in your retinue, Venerable sir?' 'A thousand, householder.' 'Venerable sir, please accept the alms-food tomorrow together with all of them.' The elder consented. The householder, walking through the city streets, encouraged others: 'Mothers and fathers, I have invited a thousand monks. For how many monks will you be able to give alms-food? For how many?' The people, according to their own capacity, said: 'We will give to ten,' 'We will give to twenty,' 'We will give to a hundred.' The householder said: 'Well then, having gathered in one place, we will serve together. Everyone, bring sesame, rice, ghee, honey, molasses, and so on.' Thus, he had them brought together in one place.

Athassa [M 1.0050] eko kuṭumbiko satasahassagghanikaṃ gandhakāsāvavatthaṃ datvā – “sace te dānavattaṃ nappahoti, idaṃ vissajjetvā yaṃ ūnaṃ, taṃ pūreyyāsi. Sace pahoti, yassicchasi, tassa bhikkhuno dadeyyāsī”ti āha. Tadā tassa sabbaṃ dānavattaṃ pahosi, kiñci ūnaṃ nāma nāhosi. So manusse pucchi – “idaṃ, ayyā, kāsāvaṃ ekena kuṭumbikena evaṃ nāma vatvā dinnaṃ atirekaṃ jātaṃ, kassa naṃ demā”ti. Ekacce “sāriputtattherassā”ti āhaṃsu. Ekacce “thero sassapākasamaye āgantvā gamanasīlo, devadatto amhākaṃ maṅgalāmaṅgalesu sahāyo udakamaṇiko viya niccaṃ patiṭṭhito, tassa taṃ demā”ti āhaṃsu. Sambahulikāya kathāyapi “devadattassa dātabba”nti vattāro bahutarā ahesuṃ, atha naṃ devadattassa adaṃsu. So taṃ chinditvā sibbitvā rajitvā nivāsetvā pārupitvā vicarati. Taṃ disvā manussā “nayidaṃ devadattassa anucchavikaṃ, sāriputtattherassa anucchavikaṃ. Devadatto attano ananucchavikaṃ nivāsetvā pārupitvā vicaratī”ti vadiṃsu. Atheko [P 1.0080] disāvāsiko bhikkhu rājagahā sāvatthiṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro satthārā dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchito ādito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho bhikkhu idāneveso attano ananucchavikaṃ vatthaṃ dhāreti, pubbepi dhāresiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari –

Then a certain householder gave him a perfumed cloth for a saffron robe worth a hundred thousand, saying, 'If your provisions for the offering are not sufficient, you may relinquish this and make up what is deficient. If they are sufficient, you may give it to whichever monk you wish.' At that time, all his provisions for the offering were sufficient; there was nothing at all that was deficient. He asked the people, 'Sirs, this cloth for a robe was given by a certain householder with these instructions. It has become extra; to whom shall we give it?' Some said, 'Let us give it to the Elder Sāriputta.' Others said, 'The Elder, having come at the time of the grain harvest, is accustomed to leaving. Devadatta is our companion in auspicious and inauspicious occasions, always established like a great water jar. Let us give it to him.' By popular consensus, those who said, 'It should be given to Devadatta,' were the majority. Then they gave it to Devadatta. He had it cut, sewn, and dyed, and went about wearing it as his lower and upper robe. Seeing him, the people said, 'This is not suitable for Devadatta; it is suitable for the Elder Sāriputta. Devadatta goes about wearing what is not suitable for him.' Then a certain monk residing in another region went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthi, paid homage to the Teacher, and after exchanging courteous greetings, was asked by the Teacher about the well-being of the two chief disciples. He related that entire event from the beginning. The Teacher said, 'Monk, it is not only now that he wears a cloth unsuitable for him; in the past, too, he wore one,' and he related a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasivāsī eko hatthimārako hatthiṃ māretvā māretvā dante ca nakhe ca antāni ca ghanamaṃsañca āharitvā vikkiṇanto jīvitaṃ kappeti. Athekasmiṃ araññe anekasahassā hatthino gocaraṃ gahetvā gacchantā paccekabuddhe disvā tato paṭṭhāya gacchamānā gamanāgamanakāle jaṇṇukehi nipatitvā vanditvā pakkamanti. Ekadivasañhi hatthimārako taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā – “ahaṃ ime kicchena māremi, ime ca gamanāgamanakāle paccekabuddhe vandanti, kiṃ nu kho disvā vandantī”ti cintento – “kāsāva”nti sallakkhetvā, “mayāpi idāni kāsāvaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā ekassa paccekabuddhassa jātassaraṃ oruyha nhāyantassa tīre ṭhapitesu kāsāvesu cīvaraṃ thenetvā [M 1.0051] tesaṃ hatthīnaṃ gamanāgamanamagge sattiṃ gahetvā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā nisīdati. Hatthino taṃ disvā – “paccekabuddho”ti saññāya vanditvā pakkamanti. So tesaṃ sabbapacchato gacchantaṃ sattiyā paharitvā māretvā dantādīni gahetvā sesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ [P 1.0081] nikhaṇitvā gacchati. Aparabhāge bodhisatto [V 1.0048] hatthiyoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā hatthijeṭṭhako yūthapati ahosi. Tadāpi so tatheva karoti. Mahāpuriso attano parisāya parihāniṃ ñatvā, “kuhiṃ ime hatthī gatā, mandā jātā”ti pucchitvā, “na jānāma, sāmī”ti vutte, “kuhiñci gacchantā maṃ anāpucchitvā na gamissanti, paripanthena bhavitabba”nti vatvā, “ekasmiṃ ṭhāne kāsāvaṃ pārupitvā nisinnassa santikā paripanthena bhavitabba”nti parisaṅkitvā, “taṃ pariggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sabbe hatthī purato pesetvā sayaṃ pacchato vilambamāno āgacchati. So sesahatthīsu vanditvā gatesu mahāpurisaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā cīvaraṃ saṃharitvā sattiṃ vissajji. Mahāpuriso satiṃ uppaṭṭhapetvā āgacchanto pacchato paṭikkamitvā sattiṃ vivajjesi. Atha naṃ “iminā ime hatthī nāsitā”ti gaṇhituṃ pakkhandi. Itaro ekaṃ rukkhaṃ purato katvā nilīyi. Atha “naṃ rukkhena saddhiṃ soṇḍāya parikkhipitvā gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ pothessāmī”ti tena nīharitvā dassitaṃ kāsāvaṃ disvā – “sacāhaṃ imasmiṃ dubbhissāmi, anekasahassesu me buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavesu lajjā nāma bhinnā bhavissatī”ti adhivāsetvā – “tayā me ettakā ñātakā nāsitā”ti pucchi. “Āma, sāmī”ti. “Kasmā evaṃ bhāriyakammamakāsi, attano ananucchavikaṃ vītarāgānaṃ anucchavikaṃ vatthaṃ paridahitvā evarūpaṃ kammaṃ karontena bhāriyaṃ tayā kata”nti. Evañca pana vatvā uttaripi naṃ niggaṇhanto “anikkasāvo [P 1.0082] kāsāvaṃ…pe… sa ve kāsāvamarahatī”ti gāthaṃ vatvā – “ayuttaṃ te kata”nti vatvā taṃ vissajjesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a certain elephant-slayer dwelling in Bārāṇasī sustained his life by repeatedly killing elephants, and having brought the tusks, nails, entrails, and solid flesh, he would sell them. Then, in a certain forest, many thousands of elephants, while going to their feeding ground, saw Paccekabuddhas. From that time onwards, when coming and going, they would fall on their knees, pay homage, and depart. One day, the elephant-slayer, having seen this action, thought: 'I kill these elephants with difficulty, and these elephants pay homage to the Paccekabuddhas when coming and going. Having seen what, I wonder, do they pay homage?' Having discerned, 'They pay homage having seen the saffron robe,' he thought, 'It is proper for me also to obtain a saffron robe now.' Having stolen a robe from among the saffron robes placed on the bank by a certain Paccekabuddha who was bathing after descending into a natural lake, he sat down on the path of those elephants' coming and going, having taken a spear and having draped himself, including his head. The elephants, having seen him, paid homage with the perception 'He is a Paccekabuddha,' and departed. He, having struck with a spear the one going at the very end of them all and having killed it, took the tusks and so on, buried the rest in the ground, and went away. In a later time, the Bodhisatta, having taken rebirth in the elephant womb, became the chief of elephants, the herd-leader. At that time also, that man acted in the very same way. The Great Being, having known the decline of his retinue, asked, 'Where have these elephants gone? They have become few.' When it was said, 'We do not know, lord,' he said, 'They shall not go anywhere without asking me. There must be a danger.' Having suspected, 'The danger must be from one sitting in a certain place, draped in a saffron robe,' he thought, 'It is proper to investigate him.' Having sent all the elephants ahead, he himself came lagging behind. When the other elephants had paid homage and gone, that man, seeing the Great Being approaching, gathered up his robe and hurled his spear. The Great Being, coming while establishing mindfulness, stepped back and avoided the spear. Then, thinking, 'By this one have these elephants been destroyed,' he rushed to seize him. The other one hid, putting a tree in front of him. Then, as the Bodhisatta thought, 'I will seize him together with the tree by encircling them with my trunk and dash him on the ground,' he saw the saffron robe that was brought out and shown by that man. He then thought, 'If I were to harm this one, my respect for the many thousands of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants would be violated.' Having endured, he asked, 'Have so many of my kinsmen been destroyed by you?' 'Yes, lord.' 'Why did you do such a grave deed? By wearing a robe unsuitable for you, a robe suitable for those free from passion, and doing such a deed, a grave thing has been done by you.' And having said this, and rebuking him further, he recited the verse, 'Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ…pe… sa ve kāsāvamarahatī.' Then he said, 'An improper thing has been done by you,' and released him.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā, “tadā hatthimārako devadatto ahosi, tassa niggāhako hatthināgo ahamevā”ti jātakaṃ samodhānetvā, “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto attano ananucchavikaṃ vatthaṃ dhāresiyevā”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the elephant-slayer was Devadatta; the great elephant who subdued him was I myself.' Then, saying, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past also Devadatta wore a robe unsuitable for him,' he spoke these verses:

9.

9.

“Anikkasāvo [M 1.0052] kāsāvaṃ, yo vatthaṃ paridahissati;

Apeto damasaccena, na so kāsāvamarahati.

One who is not free from defilements, yet would wear the saffron robe, devoid of self-control and truthfulness, is not worthy of the saffron robe.

10.

10.

“Yo ca vantakasāvassa, sīlesu susamāhito;

Upeto damasaccena, sa ve kāsāvamarahatī”ti.

But one who has purged his defilements, is well-established in virtues, and is endowed with self-control and truthfulness—he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.

Chaddantajātakenāpi (jā. 1.16.122-123) ca ayamattho dīpetabbo.

This meaning should also be illustrated by the Chaddanta Jātaka.

Tattha [V 1.0049] anikkasāvoti rāgādīhi kasāvehi sakasāvo. Paridahissatīti nivāsanapārupanaattharaṇavasena paribhuñjissati. Paridhassatītipi pāṭho. Apeto damasaccenāti indriyadamena ceva paramatthasaccapakkhikena vacīsaccena ca apeto, viyutto pariccatthoti attho. Na soti so evarūpo puggalo kāsāvaṃ paridahituṃ nārahati. Vantakasāvassāti catūhi maggehi vantakasāvo chaḍḍitakasāvo pahīnakasāvo assa. Sīlesūti catupārisuddhisīlesu. Susamāhitoti suṭṭhu samāhito suṭṭhito. Upetoti indriyadamena ceva vuttappakārena ca saccena upagato. Sa veti so evarūpo puggalo taṃ gandhakāsāvavatthaṃ arahatīti.

Herein, anikkasāvo means one who is stained by the defilements of lust and so on. Paridahissati means he will use it by way of a lower garment, an upper robe, or a spread. There is also the reading paridhassati. Apeto damasaccena means devoid of both control of the senses and of verbal truth which is on the side of ultimate truth; it means separated, disjoined, and abandoned. Na so means such a person is not worthy to wear the saffron robe. Vantakasāvassa means one who has, by means of the four paths, vomited the defilements, discarded the defilements, and abandoned the defilements. Sīlesu means in the four kinds of purity of virtue. Susamāhito means well-composed, well-established. Upeto means endowed with both control of the senses and with truth of the kind already mentioned. Sa ve means such a person is indeed worthy of that perfumed saffron cloth. This is the meaning.

Gāthāpariyosāne [P 1.0083] so disāvāsiko bhikkhu sotāpanno ahosi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the verses, that monk from another region became a stream-enterer, and many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the great assembly.

Devadattavatthu sattamaṃ.

The Story of Devadatta, the Seventh.

8. Sāriputtattheravatthu

8. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta

Asāre sāramatinoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto aggasāvakehi niveditaṃ sañcayassa anāgamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at the Veḷuvana monastery, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, 'Asāre sāramatino,' concerning the non-arrival of Sañcaya, which had been reported by the chief disciples.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – amhākañhi satthā ito kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake amaravatiyā nāma nagare sumedho nāma brāhmaṇakumāro hutvā sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā mātāpitūnaṃ [M 1.0053] accayena anekakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ pariccajitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā ākāsena gacchanto dīpaṅkaradasabalassa sudassanavihārato rammavatīnagaraṃ pavisanatthāya maggaṃ sodhayamānaṃ janaṃ disvā sayampi ekaṃ padesaṃ gahetvā maggaṃ sodheti. Tasmiṃ asodhiteyeva āgatassa satthuno attānaṃ setuṃ katvā kalale ajinacammaṃ attharitvā “satthā sasāvakasaṅgho kalalaṃ anakkamitvā maṃ akkamanto gacchatū”ti nipanno. Satthārā taṃ disvāva “buddhaṅkuro esa, anāgate kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ [P 1.0084] asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ pariyosāne gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī”ti byākato. Tassa satthuno aparabhāge “koṇḍañño maṅgalo sumano revato sobhito anomadassī padumo nārado padumuttaro sumedho sujāto piyadassī atthadassī dhammadassī siddhattho tisso phusso vipassī sikhī vessabhū kakusandho koṇāgamano kassapo”ti lokaṃ obhāsetvā uppannānaṃ imesampi tevīsatiyā [V 1.0050] buddhānaṃ santike laddhabyākaraṇo, “dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyo”ti samattiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā vessantarattabhāve ṭhito pathavikampanāni mahādānāni datvā puttadāraṃ pariccajitvā āyupariyosāne tusitapure nibbattitvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā dasa sahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi sannipatitvā –

Herein is the sequential account: Our Teacher, four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons ago from this present aeon, was born as a brahmin youth named Sumedha in the city named Amaravatī. Having reached completion in all arts, after the passing of his parents, he renounced wealth of innumerable crores, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt in the Himavanta. There, having developed the meditative attainments and psychic powers, while traveling through the sky, he saw people clearing a path for the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara to enter the city of Rammavatī from the Sudassana monastery. He himself also took a section of the path to clear it. When the Teacher arrived while that section was still uncleared, Sumedha made himself a bridge, spreading his black deerskin over the mud, and lay down, thinking, 'Let the Teacher and his retinue of disciples cross by stepping on me, without stepping in the mud.' Upon seeing him, the Teacher declared, 'This one is a nascent Buddha; in the future, at the end of four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, he will become the Buddha named Gotama.' In the time after that Teacher, having received the prediction in the presence of these twenty-three Buddhas who arose illuminating the world—Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, Tissa, Phussa, Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—and having fulfilled the thirty perfections, namely the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten supreme perfections, he was established in the existence as Vessantara. Having given great gifts that caused the earth to tremble and having renounced his children and wife, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Tusita celestial realm. Having remained there for the full lifespan, the deities of the ten thousand world-systems assembled and—

“Kālo deva mahāvīra, uppajja mātukucchiyaṃ;

Sadevakaṃ tārayanto, bujjhassu amataṃ pada”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.67) –

'O Deva, great hero, the time has come! Arise in a mother's womb; delivering the world with its devas, awaken to the deathless state!'

Vutte –

When this was said and they had entreated him—

“Kālaṃ desañca dīpañca, kulaṃ mātarameva ca;

Ime pañca viloketvā, uppajjati mahāyaso”ti. –

'The time, the country, the continent, the family, and the mother as well; having observed these five, the one of great renown is born.'

Pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā tato cuto sakyarājakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā dasamāsaccayena mātukucchito vijāyi. Soḷasavassakāle tattha mahāsampattiyā parihariyamāno anukkamena bhadrayobbanaṃ patvā tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavikesu tīsu pāsādesu devalokasiriṃ [M 1.0054] viya rajjasiriṃ anubhavanto uyyānakīḷāya gamanasamaye anukkamena jiṇṇabyādhimatasaṅkhāte tayo [P 1.0085] devadūte disvā sañjātasaṃvego nivattitvā catutthavāre pabbajitaṃ disvā, “sādhu pabbajjā”ti pabbajjāya ruciṃ uppādetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha divasaṃ khepetvā maṅgalapokkharaṇītīre nisinno kappakavesaṃ gahetvā āgatena vissakammena devaputtena alaṅkatapaṭiyatto rāhulakumārassa jātasāsanaṃ sutvā puttasinehassa balavabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “yāva idaṃ bandhanaṃ na vaḍḍhati, tāvadeva naṃ chindissāmī”ti cintetvā sāyaṃ nagaraṃ pavisanto –

Having made the five great observations, he passed away from there and took conception in the royal Sakyan family. After the passing of ten months, he was born from his mother's womb. At the age of sixteen, being nurtured there in great prosperity, he gradually reached the prime of youth. Enjoying the splendor of kingship like the glory of a celestial world in three palaces suitable for the three seasons, at the time of going to the park for sport, he saw in succession the three divine messengers known as an old person, a sick person, and a dead person. With a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, he turned back. On the fourth occasion, having seen a renunciant, he generated a liking for renunciation, thinking, 'Good is the life of a renunciant!' Having gone to the park and spent the day there, while he was seated on the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond, being adorned and prepared by the deva Vissakamma who had come in the guise of a barber, he heard the news of the birth of Prince Rāhula. Knowing the powerful nature of affection for a son, he thought, 'Before this bond grows, I shall sever it.' While entering the city in the evening—

“Nibbutā nūna sā mātā, nibbuto nūna so pitā;

Nibbutā nūna sā nārī, yassāyaṃ īdiso patī”ti. –

'Surely peaceful is that mother, surely peaceful is that father, surely peaceful is that woman, who has such a husband as this.'

Kisāgotamiyā nāma pitucchādhītāya bhāsitaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā, “ahaṃ imāya nibbutapadaṃ sāvito”ti muttāhāraṃ omuñcitvā tassā pesetvā attano bhavanaṃ pavisitvā sirisayane nisinno niddopagatānaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ vippakāraṃ disvā nibbinnahadayo channaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā kaṇḍakaṃ āharāpetvā taṃ āruyha channasahāyo dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi parivuto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā [V 1.0051] anomānadītīre pabbajitvā anukkamena rājagahaṃ gantvā tattha piṇḍāya caritvā paṇḍavapabbatapabbhāre nisinno magadharaññā rajjena nimantiyamāno taṃ paṭikkhipitvā sabbaññutaṃ patvā attano vijitaṃ āgamanatthāya tena gahitapaṭiñño āḷārañca udakañca upasaṅkamitvā tesaṃ santike adhigatavisesaṃ analaṅkaritvā chabbassāni mahāpadhānaṃ padahitvā visākhapuṇṇamadivase [P 1.0086] pātova sujātāya dinnapāyasaṃ paribhuñjitvā nerañjarāya nadiyā suvaṇṇapātiṃ pavāhetvā nerañjarāya nadiyā tīre mahāvanasaṇḍe nānāsamāpattīhi divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā sāyanhasamaye sottiyena dinnaṃ tiṇaṃ gahetvā kāḷena nāgarājena abhitthutaguṇo bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha tiṇāni santharitvā “na tāvimaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmi, yāva me anupādāya [M 1.0055] āsavehi cittaṃ na muccissatī”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā puratthābhimukho nisīditvā sūriye anatthaṅgamiteyeva mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ, majjhimayāme cutūpapātañāṇaṃ patvā pacchimayāmāvasāne paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāretvā aruṇuggamane dasabalacatuvesārajjādisabbaguṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sattasattāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe vītināmetvā aṭṭhame sattāhe ajapālanigrodhamūle nisinno dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇena appossukkataṃ āpajjamāno dasasahassacakkavāḷamahābrahmaparivārena sahampatibrahmunā āyācitadhammadesano buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketvā brahmuno ajjhesanaṃ adhivāsetvā, “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti olokento āḷārudakānaṃ kālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā pañcavaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakārataṃ anussaritvā uṭṭhāyāsanā kāsipuraṃ [P 1.0087] gacchanto antarāmagge upakena saddhiṃ mantetvā āsāḷhipuṇṇamadivase isipatane migadāye pañcavaggiyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā te ananucchavikena samudācārena samudācarante saññāpetvā aññātakoṇḍaññappamukhe aṭṭhārasa brahmakoṭiyo amatapānaṃ pāyento dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā pavattitavaradhammacakko pañcamiyaṃ pakkhassa sabbepi te bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā taṃ divasameva yasakulaputtassa upanissayasampattiṃ disvā taṃ rattibhāge nibbinditvā gehaṃ pahāya nikkhantaṃ disvā, “ehi yasā”ti pakkositvā tasmiṃyeva rattibhāge sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpetvā punadivase arahattaṃ pāpetvā aparepi tassa sahāyake catupaṇṇāsa jane ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbājetvā arahattaṃ pāpesi.

Hearing this verse spoken by his paternal uncle's daughter, a woman named Kisāgotamī, and thinking, 'By her I have been made to hear the word nibbuta (cooled/extinguished),' he took off his pearl necklace, sent it to her, entered his own palace, and sat on the glorious couch. Seeing the disarray of the sleeping dancing women, his heart grew disgusted. He had the minister Channa roused, had the horse Kaṇḍaka brought, mounted it, and with Channa as his companion, surrounded by deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system, he went forth in the Great Renunciation. Having gone forth as a monk on the bank of the Anomā River, he proceeded in due course to Rājagaha. There he wandered for alms and sat on the slope of Paṇḍava Mountain. Being invited by the king of Magadha to accept the kingdom, he declined it. Having had a promise taken by the king to return to his domain after attaining omniscience, he approached Āḷāra and Udaka, but not being satisfied with the special attainment gained in their presence, he practiced the great striving for six years. On the full moon day of Visākha, early in the morning, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā, set the golden bowl afloat on the Nerañjarā River, and spent the day in the great forest grove by the bank of the Nerañjarā River, passing the time with various meditative attainments. In the evening, accepting the grass offered by Sottiya, his virtues having been extolled by Kāḷa, the Nāga king, he ascended to the Bodhi-seat, spread the grass, and made the resolve: 'I will not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.' Facing east, he sat down. Even before the sun had set, he dispelled Māra’s forces. In the first watch of the night, he penetrated the knowledge of past lives; in the middle watch, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and at the end of the last watch, he directed his knowledge to dependent origination. Adorned with the ten powers, four confidences, and all other Buddha-qualities, he fully realized omniscient knowledge. He spent seven weeks at the Bodhi-seat. In the eighth week, while sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he inclined to inaction due to contemplating the profundity of the Dhamma. Being requested by Sahampati Brahmā, who was surrounded by the great Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, to teach the Dhamma, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and accepted Brahmā’s entreaty. Considering, 'To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?' he perceived that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away. Remembering the great service of the group of five monks, he rose from his seat and, while going to the city of Kāsī, he conversed with Upaka on the way. On the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, he arrived at Isipatana in the Deer Park, the dwelling place of the group of five. Having convinced them, who were conducting themselves with unsuitable behavior, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, causing eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, with Aññāta Koṇḍañña at the forefront, to drink the nectar of the deathless. The supreme Wheel of Dhamma having been set in motion, by the fifth day of the waning fortnight, he had established all those monks in Arahantship. On that very day, seeing the perfection of supporting conditions of the young man Yasa, and seeing him coming, having left home in the night out of disgust, he called out, 'Come, Yasa.' That very night, he caused him to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and on the next day, caused him to attain Arahantship. Furthermore, he ordained Yasa’s fifty-four companions with the 'Come, monk' ordination and caused them to attain Arahantship.

Evaṃ loke ekasaṭṭhiyā arahantesu jātesu vuṭṭhavasso pavāretvā, “caratha, bhikkhave, cārika”nti saṭṭhi bhikkhū disāsu pesetvā sayaṃ uruvelaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge kappāsikavanasaṇḍe tiṃsa jane bhaddavaggiyakumāre vinesi. Tesu sabbapacchimako sotāpanno sabbuttamo anāgāmī ahosi. Te sabbepi ehibhikkhubhāveneva pabbājetvā disāsu pesetvā sayaṃ [V 1.0052] uruvelaṃ gantvā aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni dassetvā uruvelakassapādayo [P 1.0088] sahassajaṭilaparivāre tebhātikajaṭile vinetvā ehibhikkhubhāveneva pabbājetvā gayāsīse [M 1.0056] nisīdāpetvā ādittapariyāyadesanāya (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28) arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā tena arahantasahassena parivuto “bimbisārarañño dinnaṃ paṭiññaṃ mocessāmī”ti rājagahanagarūpacāre laṭṭhivanuyyānaṃ gantvā, “satthā kira āgato”ti sutvā dvādasanahutehi brāhmaṇagahapatikehi saddhiṃ āgatassa rañño madhuradhammakathaṃ kathento rājānaṃ ekādasahi nahutehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā ekanahutaṃ saraṇesu patiṭṭhāpetvā punadivase sakkena devarājena māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ gahetvā abhitthutaguṇo rājagahanagaraṃ pavisitvā rājanivesane katabhattakicco veḷuvanārāmaṃ paṭiggahetvā tattheva vāsaṃ kappesi. Tattha naṃ sāriputtamoggallānā upasaṅkamiṃsu.

Thus, when sixty-one Arahants had arisen in the world, having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Buddha sent sixty monks to the various directions, saying, “Wander on tour, monks.” He himself, while going to Uruvelā, disciplined the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes in the Kappāsika forest grove on the way. Among them, the very last became a stream-enterer, and the most excellent became a non-returner. Having ordained all of them with the ‘ehi-bhikkhu’ ordination, he sent them to the various directions. He himself went to Uruvelā, and having displayed three and a half thousand miracles, he disciplined the three matted-hair ascetic brothers—Uruvelā Kassapa and the others—who had a retinue of a thousand matted-hair ascetics. Having ordained them with the ‘ehi-bhikkhu’ ordination, he had them be seated at Gayāsīsa and, with the discourse on the Fire Sermon, established them in Arahantship. Surrounded by that thousand Arahants, thinking, “I shall fulfill the promise I made to King Bimbisāra,” he went to the Laṭṭhivana grove in the vicinity of the city of Rājagaha. Hearing that “The Teacher, it is said, has come,” the king came with twelve myriads of brahmins and householders. Speaking a sweet Dhamma talk to the king who had come, he established the king along with eleven myriads in the fruit of stream-entry, and established one myriad in the refuges. On the next day, his virtues having been extolled by Sakka, king of the devas, who had assumed the guise of a young man, he entered the city of Rājagaha. After his meal at the king’s residence, he accepted the Veḷuvana monastery and took up residence there. There Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached him.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – anuppanneyeva hi buddhe rājagahato avidūre upatissagāmo kolitagāmoti dve brāhmaṇagāmā ahesuṃ. Tesu upatissagāme sāriyā nāma brāhmaṇiyā gabbhassa patiṭṭhitadivaseyeva kolitagāme moggaliyā nāma brāhmaṇiyāpi gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Tāni kira dvepi kulāni yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā ābaddhapaṭibaddhasahāyakāneva ahesuṃ, tāsaṃ dvinnampi ekadivasameva gabbhaparihāraṃ adaṃsu. Tā ubhopi dasamāsacceyena putte vijāyiṃsu. Nāmaggahaṇadivase sāriyā brāhmaṇiyā puttassa upatissagāmake jeṭṭhakulassa puttattā upatissoti nāmaṃ kariṃsu[P 1.0089], itarassa kolitagāme jeṭṭhakulassa puttattā kolitoti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te ubhopi vuḍḍhimanvāya sabbasippānaṃ pāraṃ agamaṃsu. Upatissamāṇavassa kīḷanatthāya nadiṃ vā uyyānaṃ vā gamanakāle pañca suvaṇṇasivikasatāni parivārāni honti, kolitamāṇavassa pañca ājaññayuttarathasatāni. Dvepi janā pañcapañcamāṇavakasataparivārā honti. Rājagahe ca anusaṃvaccharaṃ giraggasamajjo nāma ahosi. Tesaṃ dvinnampi ekaṭṭhāneyeva mañcaṃ bandhanti. Dvepi ekato nisīditvā samajjaṃ passantā hasitabbaṭṭhāne hasanti, saṃvegaṭṭhāne saṃvejenti, dāyaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dāyaṃ denti. Tesaṃ imināva niyāmena ekadivasaṃ samajjaṃ passantānaṃ paripākagatattā ñāṇassa purimadivasesu viya hasitabbaṭṭhāne hāso vā saṃvegaṭṭhāne saṃvego vā dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dānaṃ vā nāhosi[M 1.0057]. Dvepi pana janā evaṃ cintayiṃsu – “kimettha oloketabbaṃ atthi, sabbepime appatte vassasate appaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gamissanti, amhehi pana ekaṃ mokkhadhammaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā nisīdiṃsu. Tato kolito upatissaṃ āha – “samma upatissa, na tvaṃ aññesu divasesu viya haṭṭhapahaṭṭho, idāni anattamanadhātukosi, kiṃ te sallakkhita”nti? “Samma kolita, etesaṃ volokane sāro natthi[V 1.0053][P 1.0090], niratthakametaṃ, attano mokkhadhammaṃ gavesituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ cintayanto nisinnomhi. Tvaṃ pana kasmā anattamanosīti? Sopi tatheva āha. Athassa attanā saddhiṃ ekajjhāsayataṃ ñatvā upatisso āha – “amhākaṃ ubhinnampi sucintikaṃ, mokkhadhammaṃ pana gavesantehi ekā pabbajjā laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Kassa santike pabbajāmā”ti?

Here is the sequential account. Indeed, even before the Buddha had arisen, not far from Rājagaha there were two brahmin villages: Upatissa village and Kolita village. In Upatissa village, on the very day a brahmin woman named Sārī conceived, a brahmin woman named Moggalī in Kolita village also conceived. It is said that these two families had been steadfastly connected friends for seven generations, and they provided the protection of pregnancy for both women on the very same day. Both gave birth to sons after ten months had passed. On the naming day, to the son of the brahmin woman Sārī they gave the name Upatissa, as he was the son of the chief family in the village of Upatissa; to the other, they gave the name Kolita, as he was the son of the chief family in the village of Kolita. Both, having grown up, reached the further shore of all the arts. When the youth Upatissa went to the river or a park for amusement, his retinue consisted of five hundred golden palanquins, while the youth Kolita had five hundred chariots yoked with thoroughbreds. Both persons had a retinue of five hundred youths each. In Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the Summit Festival. For these two, a couch was set up in the very same place. Sitting together, they would watch the festival, laughing at what was laughable, feeling a sense of urgency at what should provoke it, and giving gifts where it was appropriate. One day, as they were watching the festival in this way, because their knowledge had reached maturity, unlike on previous days there was no laughter at what was laughable, no sense of urgency at what should provoke it, and no giving of gifts where it was appropriate. Both persons then thought: “What is there to see here? All these beings, before a hundred years have passed, will arrive at a state beyond designation. We should seek a doctrine of deliverance.” Taking this as their object of thought, they sat down. Then Kolita said to Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa, you are not joyful and elated as on other days. Now you are of a discontented disposition. What have you realized?” “Friend Kolita, there is no substance in watching these people. This is meaningless. I am sitting here thinking that one should seek one's own doctrine of deliverance. But why are you discontented?” He also said the same. Then, realizing they were of one mind, Upatissa said: “Both of us have thought well. For those seeking the doctrine of deliverance, it is fitting to undertake the going forth. Under whom shall we go forth?”

Tena kho pana samayena sañcayo nāma paribbājako rājagahe paṭivasati mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ. Te “tassa santike pabbajissāmā”ti pañcamāṇavakasatāni “sivikāyo ca rathe ca gahetvā gacchathā”ti uyyojetvā ekāya sivikāya ekena rathena gantvā sañcayassa santike pabbajiṃsu. Tesaṃ pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya sañcayo atirekalābhaggayasaggappatto ahosi. Te katipāheneva sabbaṃ sañcayassa samayaṃ parimadditvā, “ācariya, tumhākaṃ jānanasamayo ettakova, udāhu uttarimpi atthī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Ettakova sabbaṃ tumhehi ñāta”nti vutte cintayiṃsu – “evaṃ sati imassa santike brahmacariyavāso niratthako, mayaṃ yaṃ mokkhadhammaṃ gavesituṃ nikkhantā, so imassa santike uppādetuṃ na sakkā, mahā kho pana jambudīpo, gāmanigamarājadhāniyo carantā addhā mokkhadhammadesakaṃ kañci ācariyaṃ labhissāmā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya, “yattha yattha paṇḍitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā atthī”ti vadanti, tattha tattha gantvā sākacchaṃ karonti. Tehi puṭṭhaṃ pañhaṃ aññe kathetuṃ [P 1.0091] na sakkonti, te pana tesaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjenti. Evaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ pariggaṇhitvā nivattitvā sakaṭṭhānameva āgantvā, “samma kolita, amhesu yo paṭhamaṃ amataṃ adhigacchati, so itarassa ārocetū”ti katikaṃ akaṃsuṃ.

Now at that time, a wanderer named Sañcaya was dwelling in Rājagaha with a large assembly of wanderers. They, thinking, “We will go forth in his presence,” sent away their five hundred young men with their palanquins and chariots. Then, having gone with a single palanquin and a single chariot, they went forth in the presence of Sañcaya. From the time of their going forth, Sañcaya attained the highest gain and fame. Within just a few days, they mastered Sañcaya's entire doctrine and asked, “Teacher, is your teaching only this much, or is there something further?” When it was said, “It is only this much; you have known everything,” they thought: “This being so, living the holy life in his presence is fruitless. The doctrine of deliverance that we went forth to seek cannot be realized in his presence. Jambudīpa is indeed vast.
