Ahaṃ tassā vacanaṃ asaddahanto ‘na mayhaṃ putto bodhiṃ appatvā kālaṃ karotī’ti paṭikkhipi”nti vutte – “idāni kiṃ saddahissatha, pubbepi aṭṭhikāni dassetvā, ‘putto te mato’ti vutte na saddahitvā”ti imissā atthuppattiyā mahādhammapālajātakaṃ (jā. 1.10.92 ādayo) kathesi. Gāthāpariyosāne rājā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Iti bhagavā pitaraṃ tīsu phalesu patiṭṭhāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto [P 1.0118] punadeva rājagahaṃ gantvā tato anāthapiṇḍikena sāvatthiṃ āgamanatthāya gahitapaṭiñño niṭṭhite jetavane vihāre tattha gantvā vāsaṃ kappesi.

Then the Blessed One thought: 'This wealth of his father that he desires follows the round of existence and is accompanied by vexation. Well then, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth obtained at the foot of the Bodhi tree and make him an heir to the supramundane inheritance.' Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Well then, Sāriputta, ordain Prince Rāhula.' The elder ordained the prince. But when the prince was ordained, extreme sorrow arose in the king. Unable to endure it, he informed the Blessed One and requested a boon: 'It would be good, venerable sir, if the noble ones would not ordain a son without the permission of his parents.' The Blessed One granted him that boon. On another day, when the Blessed One had finished his morning meal in the king's residence, the king, who was sitting to one side, said: 'Venerable sir, during the time of your difficult austerities, a certain deva approached me and said, "Your son has passed away." Not believing his words, I rejected them, thinking, "My son will not pass away without attaining enlightenment."' When this was said, the Blessed One replied: 'What would you believe now? In the past also, when shown the bones and told, "Your son is dead," you did not believe.' With this as the origin story, he related the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. At the end of the verses, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning. Thus, the Blessed One, having established his father in the three fruits, surrounded by the community of monks, went again to Rājagaha. From there, as he had given his promise to Anāthapiṇḍika to come to Sāvatthī, he went to the Jetavana monastery when it was completed and took up residence there.

Evaṃ satthari jetavane viharante āyasmā nando ukkaṇṭhitvā bhikkhūnaṃ etamatthaṃ ārocesi – “anabhirato ahaṃ, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ carāmi, na [M 1.0076] sakkomi brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissāmī”ti. Bhagavā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ pakkosāpetvā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, nanda, sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ ārocesi [V 1.0069] – ‘anabhirato, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ carāmi, na sakkomi brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissāmī’”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kissa pana tvaṃ, nanda, anabhirato brahmacariyaṃ carasi, na sakkosi brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissasī”ti? “Sākiyānī maṃ, bhante, janapadakalyāṇī gharā nikkhamantassa aḍḍhullikhitehi kesehi apaloketvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘tuvaṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī’ti, so kho ahaṃ, bhante, taṃ anussaramāno anabhirato brahmacariyaṃ carāmi, na sakkomi brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissāmī”ti.

While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda, feeling discontented, informed the monks of this matter: 'Friends, I practice the holy life without delight. I am unable to maintain the holy life. I will renounce the training and return to the lower life.' The Blessed One, hearing of this matter, had the Venerable Nanda summoned and said this: 'Is it true, Nanda, that you told many monks, "Friends, I practice the holy life without delight; I am unable to maintain the holy life; I will renounce the training and return to the lower life"?' 'It is so, venerable sir.' 'But for what reason, Nanda, do you practice the holy life without delight, are you unable to maintain the holy life, and will you renounce the training and return to the lower life?' 'Venerable sir, as I was leaving home, the Sākyan lady, Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair half-combed, looked at me and said this: "Return quickly, my lord." Remembering her, venerable sir, I practice the holy life without delight, I am unable to maintain the holy life, and I will renounce the training and return to the lower life.'

Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā iddhibalena tāvatiṃsadevalokaṃ ānento antarāmagge ekasmiṃ jhāmakkhette jhāmakhāṇuke nisinnaṃ chinnakaṇṇanāsanaṅguṭṭhaṃ ekaṃ paluṭṭhamakkaṭiṃ dassetvā tāvatiṃsabhavane sakkassa devarañño upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatāni kakuṭapādāni pañca accharāsatāni dassesi. Kakuṭapādānīti [P 1.0119] rattavaṇṇatāya pārevatapādasadisapādāni. Dassetvā ca panāha – “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, nanda, katamā nu kho abhirūpatarā vā dassanīyatarā vā pāsādikatarā vā sākiyānī vā janapadakalyāṇī, imāni vā pañca accharāsatāni kakuṭapādānī”ti? Taṃ sutvā āha – “seyyathāpi sā, bhante, chinnakaṇṇanāsanaṅguṭṭhā paluṭṭhamakkaṭī, evameva kho, bhante, sākiyānī janapadakalyāṇī, imesaṃ pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ upanidhāya saṅkhyampi na upeti, kalampi na upeti, kalabhāgampi na upeti. Atha kho imāneva pañca accharāsatāni abhirūpatarāni ceva dassanīyatarāni ca pāsādikatarāni cā”ti. “Abhirama, nanda, abhirama, nanda, ahaṃ te pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādāna”nti. “Sace me, bhante bhagavā, pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādānaṃ, abhiramissāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati brahmacariye”ti.

Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda by the arm, by his psychic power, while leading him to the Tāvatiṃsa deva world, showed him on the way, in a burnt field, a scorched she-monkey with its ears, nose, and tail cut off, sitting on a burnt stump. Then, in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, he showed him five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet who had come to attend on Sakka, king of the devas. (The term 'pigeon-like feet' refers to their feet being red in color.) Having shown them, he said: 'What do you think, Nanda? Who is more beautiful, more lovely, or more graceful: the Sākyan lady, Janapadakalyāṇī, or these five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet?' Hearing this, Nanda said: 'Venerable sir, compared to these five hundred celestial nymphs, the Sākyan lady, Janapadakalyāṇī, is like that scorched she-monkey with its ears, nose, and tail cut off. She does not amount to a fraction, nor a particle, nor a minute part in comparison. Indeed, it is these five hundred celestial nymphs that are far more beautiful, far more lovely, and far more graceful.' 'Delight, Nanda! Delight! I am your guarantor for the attainment of the five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet.' 'Venerable sir, if the Blessed One is my guarantor for the attainment of the five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet, then, venerable sir, I will delight in the holy life under the Blessed One.'

Atha [M 1.0077] kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ gahetvā tattha antarahito jetavaneyeva pāturahosi. Assosuṃ kho bhikkhū, “āyasmā kira nando bhagavato bhātā mātucchāputto accharānaṃ hetu brahmacariyaṃ carati. Bhagavā kirassa pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādāna”nti. Atha kho āyasmato nandassa sahāyakā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ bhatakavādena ca upakkitakavādena ca samudācaranti, “bhatako kirāyasmā nando, upakkitako kirāyasmā nando, accharānaṃ hetu brahmacariyaṃ carati. Bhagavā kirassa pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādāna”nti. Atha kho āyasmā nando sahāyakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [P 1.0120] bhatakavādena ca upakkitakavādena ca aṭṭiyamāno harāyamāno jigucchamāno [V 1.0070] eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto na cirasseva yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi, “khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro ca kho panāyasmā nando arahataṃ ahosi.

Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda, disappeared from there and reappeared in the Jeta Grove itself. The monks heard: “It is said that the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One’s brother and maternal aunt’s son, is practicing the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs. It is said that the Blessed One is his guarantor for the attainment of five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet.” Then the Venerable Nanda’s companion monks addressed the Venerable Nanda with the term for a hireling and the term for one who is bought: “It is said that the Venerable Nanda is a hireling; it is said that the Venerable Nanda is one who is bought. He practices the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs. It is said that the Blessed One is his guarantor for the attainment of five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet.” Then the Venerable Nanda, being annoyed, ashamed, and disgusted by the terms for a hireling and one who is bought used by his companion monks, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and with a resolute mind, before long, realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having attained it, he dwelt therein. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.” And the Venerable Nanda became one of the Arahants.

Athekā devatā rattibhāge sakalaṃ jetavanaṃ obhāsetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ārocesi – “āyasmā, bhante, nando bhagavato bhātā mātucchāputto āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti. Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādi “nando āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti. Sopāyasmā nando tassā rattiyā accayena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā etadavoca – “yaṃ me, bhante, bhagavā pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādānaṃ, muñcāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ etasmā paṭissavā”ti. “Mayāpi kho te, nanda, cetasā ceto paricca vidito ‘nando āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ [P 1.0121] paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī’ti. Devatāpi me etamatthaṃ ārocesi – ‘āyasmā, bhante, nando āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī’ti. Yadeva kho te, nanda, anupādāya āsavehi [M 1.0078] cittaṃ vimuttaṃ, athāhaṃ mutto etasmā paṭissavā”ti. Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Then a certain devatā, having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove in the latter part of the night, approached the Teacher, and after paying homage, announced: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One’s brother and maternal aunt’s son, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells having attained it.” To the Blessed One, too, knowledge arose: “Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells having attained it.” Then the Venerable Nanda, at the end of that night, approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage, said this: “Venerable sir, regarding that for which the Blessed One was my guarantor—the attainment of five hundred celestial nymphs with pigeon-like feet—I release the Blessed One, venerable sir, from that promise.” “Nanda, I too, having encompassed your mind with my mind, have known: ‘Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells having attained it.’ A devatā also informed me of this matter: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells having attained it.’ Nanda, precisely because your mind is liberated from the taints without clinging, I am now released from that promise.” Then, the Blessed One, understanding this matter, at that time uttered this solemn utterance:

“Yassa nittiṇṇo paṅko, maddito kāmakaṇṭako;

Mohakkhayaṃ anuppatto, sukhadukkhesu na vedhatī sa bhikkhū”ti. (udā. 22);

“For whom the mire is crossed over, the thorn of sensuality crushed, who has attained the destruction of delusion—that monk does not waver amidst pleasure and pain.”

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ pucchiṃsu – “āvuso nanda, pubbe tvaṃ ‘ukkaṇṭhitomī’ti vadesi, idāni te katha”nti? “Natthi me, āvuso, gihibhāvāya ālayo”ti. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū – “abhūtaṃ āyasmā nando katheti, aññaṃ byākaroti, atītadivasesu ‘ukkaṇṭhitomhī’ti vatvā idāni ‘natthi me gihibhāvāya ālayo’ti kathetī”ti gantvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā “bhikkhave, atītadivasesu nandassa attabhāvo ducchannagehasadiso ahosi, idāni succhannagehasadiso jāto. Ayañhi dibbaccharānaṃ [V 1.0071] diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya pabbajitakiccassa matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ [P 1.0122] vāyamanto taṃ kiccaṃ patto”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then one day, the bhikkhus asked the Venerable Nanda: “Friend Nanda, formerly you used to say, ‘I am discontented,’ but how is it with you now?” “Friends, there is no longing in me for the household life.” Hearing this, the bhikkhus said: “The Venerable Nanda speaks what is not true; he declares Arahantship. In past days, having said, ‘I am discontented,’ now he says, ‘There is no longing in me for the household life.’” They went and reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, in days past, Nanda’s state of being was like a poorly roofed house; now it has become like a well-roofed house. For from the time he saw the divine nymphs, striving to bring the task of one who has gone forth to its culmination, he has attained that task.” Then he spoke these verses:

13.

13.

“Yathā agāraṃ ducchannaṃ, vuṭṭhī samativijjhati;

Evaṃ abhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, rāgo samativijjhati.

“Just as rain penetrates a poorly roofed house, so lust penetrates an undeveloped mind.

14.

14.

“Yathā agāraṃ succhannaṃ, vuṭṭhī na samativijjhati;

Evaṃ subhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, rāgo na samativijjhatī”ti.

“Just as rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house, so lust does not penetrate a well-developed mind.”

Tattha agāranti yaṃkiñci gehaṃ. Ducchannanti viraḷacchannaṃ chiddāvachiddaṃ. Samativijjhatīti vassavuṭṭhi vinivijjhati. Abhāvitanti taṃ agāraṃ vuṭṭhi viya bhāvanāya rahitattā abhāvitaṃ cittaṃ rāgo samati vijjhati. Na kevalaṃ rāgova, dosamohamānādayo sabbakilesā tathārūpaṃ cittaṃ ativiya vijjhantiyeva. Subhāvitanti samathavipassanābhāvanāhi subhāvitaṃ. Evarūpaṃ cittaṃ succhannaṃ gehaṃ vuṭṭhi viya rāgādayo kilesā ativijjhituṃ na sakkontīti.

Herein, ‘a house’ (agāraṃ) means any kind of dwelling. ‘Poorly roofed’ (ducchannaṃ) means sparsely roofed, with holes and gaps. ‘Penetrates’ (samativijjhati) means the rain penetrates. ‘Undeveloped’ (abhāvitaṃ): just as rain penetrates that house, so lust penetrates an undeveloped mind, being devoid of mental development. Not only lust, but also hatred, delusion, conceit, and all other defilements thoroughly penetrate such a mind. ‘Well-developed’ (subhāvitaṃ) means well-developed through the development of serenity and insight. Just as rain cannot penetrate a well-roofed house, so defilements such as lust and so on cannot thoroughly penetrate such a mind.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. Mahājanassa desanā sātthikā ahosi.

At the conclusion of the verses, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so on. The teaching was beneficial for the great multitude.

Atha kho bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “āvuso, buddhā nāma acchariyā, janapadakalyāṇiṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito nāmāyasmā nando [M 1.0079] satthārā devaccharā āmisaṃ katvā vinīto”ti. Satthā āgantvā – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “na, bhikkhave, idāneva[P 1.0123], pubbepesa mayā mātugāmena palobhetvā vinītoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari –

Then the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, 'Friends, the Buddhas are indeed wonderful! The Venerable Nanda, who was discontented on account of Janapadakalyāṇī, was disciplined by the Teacher, who made a celestial nymph the lure.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'For this one, sir,' he said, 'Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past also, this one was disciplined by me, having been enticed by a woman.' Having said this, he related a past event:

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasivāsī kappaṭo nāma vāṇijo ahosi. Tasseko gadrabho kumbhabhāraṃ vahati, ekadivasena satta yojanāni gacchati. So ekasmiṃ samaye gadrabhabhārakehi saddhiṃ takkasilaṃ gantvā yāva bhaṇḍassa vissajjanaṃ, tāva gadrabhaṃ carituṃ vissajjesi. Athassa so gadrabho parikhāpiṭṭhe caramāno ekaṃ gadrabhiṃ disvā upasaṅkami. Sā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karontī āha – “kuto āgatosī”ti? “Bārāṇasito”ti. “Kena kammenā”ti? “Vāṇijjakammenā”ti. “Kittakaṃ bhāraṃ vahasī”ti[V 1.0072]? “Kumbhabhāra”nti? “Ettakaṃ bhāraṃ vahanto kati yojanāni gacchasī”ti? “Satta yojanānī”ti. “Gatagataṭṭhāne te kāci pādaparikammapiṭṭhiparikammakarā atthī”ti? “Natthī”ti. “Evaṃ sante mahādukkhaṃ nāma anubhosī”ti? “Kiñcāpi hi tiracchānagatānaṃ pādaparikammādikārakā nāma natthi, kāmasaṃyojanaghaṭṭanatthāya pana evarūpaṃ kathaṃ kathesi”? So tassā kathāya ukkaṇṭhi. Kappaṭopi bhaṇḍaṃ vissajjetvā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā – “ehi, tāta, gamissāmā”ti āha. “Gacchatha tumhe, nāhaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ [P 1.0124] punappunaṃ yācitvā, “anicchantaṃ paribhāsetvā naṃ nessāmī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, there was a merchant named Kappaṭa who was a resident of Bārāṇasī. He had a donkey that could carry a kumbha-load and could travel seven yojanas in a single day. On one occasion, he went to Takkasilā with loads carried by the donkey, and while his goods were being sold, he released the donkey to graze. Then his donkey, while grazing on the outer edge of the moat, saw a female donkey and approached her. She, making conversation with him, said: 'Where have you come from?' 'From Bārāṇasī.' 'For what work?' 'For the work of a merchant.' 'How much of a load do you carry?' 'A kumbha-load.' 'Carrying such a load, how many yojanas do you travel?' 'Seven yojanas.' 'In the places you go, is there anyone who performs foot-massaging or back-rubbing for you?' 'There is not.' 'That being so, you experience great suffering indeed.' (Though for animals there are indeed none who perform foot-massaging and the like, she spoke such words for the purpose of stirring the fetter of sensual desire.) He became discontented because of her words. Kappaṭa, having sold his goods, came to him and said, 'Come, my dear, let us go.' 'You go, I will not go.' Then, having pleaded with him again and again, and when he was unwilling, he thought, 'I will scold him and take him,' and spoke this verse:

“Patodaṃ te karissāmi, sāḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakaṃ;

Sañchindissāmi te kāyaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi gadrabhā”ti.

“I will make a goad for you with a sixteen-finger-long barb; I will tear your body. Know this, O donkey!”

Taṃ sutvā gadrabho “evaṃ sante ahampi te kattabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the donkey said, “That being so, I too will know what must be done to you,” and spoke this verse:

“Patodaṃ me karissasi, soḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakaṃ;

Purato patiṭṭhahitvāna, uddharitvāna pacchato;

Dantaṃ te pātayissāmi, evaṃ jānāhi kappaṭā”ti.

“You will make a goad for me with a sixteen-finger-long barb; but having stood in front and kicking backwards, I will knock out your tooth. Know this, O Kappaṭa!”

Taṃ [M 1.0080] sutvā vāṇijo – “kena nu kho kāraṇena esa evaṃ vadatī”ti cintetvā, ito cito ca olokento taṃ gadrabhiṃ disvā, “imāyesa evaṃ sikkhāpito bhavissati, ‘evarūpiṃ nāma te gadrabhiṃ ānessāmī’ti mātugāmena naṃ palobhetvā nessāmī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the merchant thought, “For what reason indeed does he speak thus?” And looking here and there, he saw that female donkey. “He must have been taught thus by her,” he thought. “I will take him by enticing him with a female, saying, ‘I will bring you such a female donkey.’” Then he spoke this verse:

“Catuppadiṃ saṅkhamukhiṃ, nāriṃ sabbaṅgasobhiniṃ;

Bhariyaṃ te ānayissāmi, evaṃ jānāhi gadrabhā”ti.

“A four-footed female with a conch-like face, beautiful in all her limbs; I will bring her as a wife for you. Know this, O donkey!”

Taṃ sutvā tuṭṭhacitto gadrabho imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the donkey, with a delighted mind, spoke this verse:

“Catuppadiṃ saṅkhamukhiṃ, nāriṃ sabbaṅgasobhiniṃ;

Bhariyaṃ me ānayissasi, evaṃ jānāhi kappaṭa;

Kappaṭa bhiyyo gamissāmi, yojanāni catuddasā”ti.

“O Kappaṭa, if you will bring for me as a wife a four-footed female with a conch-like face, beautiful in all her limbs, know this: I will go even further, fourteen yojanas!”

Atha [V 1.0073][P 1.0125] naṃ kappaṭo, “tena hi ehī”ti gahetvā sakaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. So katipāhaccayena naṃ āha – “nanu maṃ tumhe ‘bhariyaṃ te ānayissāmī’ti avocutthā”ti? “Āma, vuttaṃ, nāhaṃ attano kathaṃ bhindissāmi, bhariyaṃ te ānessāmi, vetanaṃ pana tuyhaṃ ekakasseva dassāmi, tuyhaṃ vetanaṃ dutiyassa pahotu vā mā vā, tvameva jāneyyāsi. Ubhinnaṃ pana vo saṃvāsamanvāya puttā vijāyissanti, tehipi bahūhi saddhiṃ tuyhaṃ taṃ pahotu vā mā vā, tvameva jāneyyāsī”ti. Gadrabho tasmiṃ kathenteyeva anapekkho ahosi.

Then Kappaṭa, saying, “Well then, come,” took him and went to his own place. After a few days had passed, the donkey said to him, “Did you not say to me, ‘I will bring you a wife’?” “Yes, it was said. I will not break my word; I will bring you a wife. But I will give provisions only to you alone. Whether your provisions are sufficient for a second or not, you yourself must know. Due to the two of you living together, children will be born. Whether those provisions are sufficient for you together with those many children or not, you yourself must know.” While he was still speaking, the male donkey became unconcerned.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā, “tadā, bhikkhave, gadrabhī janapadakalyāṇī ahosi, gadrabho nando, vāṇijo ahameva. Evaṃ pubbepesa mayā mātugāmena palobhetvā vinīto”ti jātakaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, concluded the Jātaka, saying: “Bhikkhus, at that time, the female donkey was Janapadakalyāṇī, the male donkey was Nanda, and the merchant was I myself. Thus, in the past also, this one was disciplined by me, having been enticed by a woman.”

Nandattheravatthu navamaṃ.

The Ninth Story, concerning the Elder Nanda.

10. Cundasūkarikavatthu

10. The Story of Cunda the Pork-butcher

Idha socetīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto cundasūkarikaṃ nāma purisaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Here he grieves”—this discourse the Teacher gave while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery, concerning a man named Cunda the pork-butcher.

So [M 1.0081] kira pañcapaṇṇāsa vassāni sūkare vadhitvā khādanto ca vikkiṇanto ca jīvikaṃ kappesi. Chātakāle sakaṭena vīhiṃ ādāya janapadaṃ gantvā ekanāḷidvenāḷimattena gāmasūkarapotake [P 1.0126] kiṇitvā sakaṭaṃ pūretvā āgantvā pacchānivesane vajaṃ viya ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ parikkhipitvā tattheva tesaṃ nivāpaṃ ropetvā, tesu nānāgacche ca sarīramalañca khāditvā vaḍḍhitesu yaṃ yaṃ māretukāmo hoti, taṃ taṃ āḷāne niccalaṃ bandhitvā sarīramaṃsassa uddhumāyitvā bahalabhāvatthaṃ caturassamuggarena pothetvā, “bahalamaṃso jāto”ti ñatvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antare daṇḍakaṃ datvā lohathāliyā pakkuthitaṃ uṇhodakaṃ mukhe āsiñcati. Taṃ kucchiṃ pavisitvā pakkuthitaṃ karīsaṃ ādāya adhobhāgena nikkhamati, yāva thokampi karīsaṃ atthi, tāva āvilaṃ hutvā nikkhamati, suddhe udare acchaṃ anāvilaṃ hutvā nikkhamati. Athassa avasesaṃ udakaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ āsiñcati. Taṃ kāḷacammaṃ uppāṭetvā gacchati. Tato tiṇukkāya lomāni jhāpetvā tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindati. Paggharaṇataṃ lohitaṃ bhājanena paṭiggahetvā maṃsaṃ lohitena madditvā pacitvā puttadāramajjhe nisinno khāditvā sesaṃ vikkiṇāti. Tassa imināva niyāmena jīvikaṃ kappentassa pañcapaṇṇāsa vassāni atikkantāni[V 1.0074]. Tathāgate dhuravihāre vasante ekadivasampi pupphamuṭṭhimattena pūjā vā kaṭacchumattaṃ bhikkhadānaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci puññaṃ nāma nāhosi. Athassa sarīre rogo uppajji, jīvantasseva [P 1.0127] avīcimahānirayasantāpo upaṭṭhahi. Avīcisantāpo nāma yojanasate ṭhatvā olokentassa akkhīnaṃ bhijjanasamattho pariḷāho hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

It is said that for fifty-five years he made his living by killing pigs, eating and selling their flesh. During a famine, he would take rice paddy in a cart to the countryside, buy village piglets for one or two nāḷis, fill his cart, and return. In his backyard, he would enclose a place like a cattle pen and keep them there. When they had grown by eating various small plants and their own excrement, he would tie immobile to a post whichever pig he wanted to kill. To make its flesh swell and become thick, he would beat it with a four-sided mallet. When he knew, “Its flesh has become thick,” he would pry open its mouth with a stick and pour boiling water from a bronze pot into it. That water would enter its belly and, carrying out the excrement, would exit from the lower part. As long as there was even a little excrement, it would exit turbidly; when the belly was clean, it would exit clear and unturbid. Then he would pour the remaining water on its back, which would cause the black skin to peel off. After that, he would singe off the hair with a grass torch and cut off its head with a sharp sword. He would collect the flowing blood in a vessel, mix the meat with the blood, cook it, and sitting amidst his wife and children, he would eat it and sell the rest. As he made his living in this very manner, fifty-five years passed. While the Tathāgata was dwelling in the monastery where he regularly dwelt, there was not for him on any single day any so-called merit, such as an offering of a handful of flowers or the gift of a ladleful of alms, or anything else. Then a disease arose in his body, and while he was still alive, the torment of the great Avīci hell manifested. The torment of Avīci is a burning heat capable of shattering the eyes of one who looks at it from a hundred yojanas away. And this was also said:

“Tassa ayomayā bhūmi, jalitā tejasāyutā;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, pharitvā tiṭṭhati sabbadā”ti. (ma. ni. 3.267; a. ni. 3.36);

“Its ground is made of iron, blazing, endowed with heat; it extends for a hundred yojanas all around, always remaining.”

Nāgasenattherena panassa pākatikaggisantāpato adhimattatāya ayaṃ upamā vuttā – “yathā, mahārāja, kūṭāgāramatto pāsāṇopi nerayikaggimhi pakkhitto khaṇena vilayaṃ gacchati, nibbattasattā panettha kammabalena [M 1.0082] mātukucchigatā viya na vilīyantī”ti (mi. pa. 2.4.6). Tassa tasmiṃ santāpe upaṭṭhite kammasarikkhako ākāro uppajji. Gehamajjheyeva sūkararavaṃ ravitvā jaṇṇukehi vicaranto puratthimavatthumpi pacchimavatthumpi gacchati. Athassa gehamānusakā taṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ pidahanti. Kammavipāko nāma na sakkā kenaci paṭibāhituṃ. So viravantova ito cito ca vicarati. Samantā sattasu gharesu manussā niddaṃ na labhanti. Maraṇabhayena tajjitassa pana bahinikkhamanaṃ nivāretuṃ asakkonto sabbo gehajano yathā antoṭhito bahi vicarituṃ na sakkoti, tathā gehadvārāni thaketvā bahigehaṃ parivāretvā rakkhanto acchati. Itaro antogeheyeva nirayasantāpena viravanto ito cito ca vicarati. Evaṃ sattadivasāni vicaritvā aṭṭhame divase kālaṃ katvā avīcimahāniraye nibbatti. Avīcimahānirayo devadūtasuttena (ma. ni. 3.261 ādayo; a. ni. 3.36) vaṇṇetabboti.

But by the Elder Nāgasena, this simile was spoken to illustrate its extreme intensity compared to the heat of an ordinary fire: “Just as, great king, even a rock the size of a gabled house, when thrown into the hell-fire, would instantly dissolve, yet the beings reborn there, by the power of their kamma, do not dissolve, just like an embryo in a mother’s womb.” When that torment manifested in him, an appearance similar to his kamma arose. Right in the middle of the house, making a sound like a pig, he wandered about on his knees, going to the eastern and western ends of the house. Then the people of his house and his neighbors seized him firmly and covered his mouth. But the so-called result of kamma cannot be prevented by anyone. Crying out, he wandered here and there. In the seven surrounding houses, people could not get any sleep. The entire household, in order to prevent him—who was threatened by the fear of death—from going outside, closed the house doors, surrounded the outside of the house, and remained on guard so that he, being inside, could not wander outside. The other, crying out with the torment of hell, wandered here and there only inside the house. Having wandered thus for seven days, on the seventh day he died and was reborn in the great Avīci hell. The great Avīci hell should be described according to the Devadūta Sutta.

Bhikkhū tassa gharadvārena gacchantā [P 1.0128] taṃ saddaṃ sutvā, “sūkarasaddo”ti saññino hutvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthu santike nisinnā evamāhaṃsu – “bhante, cundasūkaritassa gehadvāraṃ pidahitvā sūkarānaṃ māriyamānānaṃ ajja sattamo divaso, gehe kāci maṅgalakiriyā bhavissati maññe. Ettake nāma, bhante, sūkare mārentassa ekampi mettacittaṃ vā kāruññaṃ vā natthi, na vata no evarūpo kakkhaḷo pharuso satto diṭṭhapubbo”ti. Satthā – “na, bhikkhave, so ime sattadivase sūkare māreti, kammasarikkhakaṃ panassa vipākaṃ udapādi, jīvantasseva avīcimahānirayasantāpo upaṭṭhāsi. So tena santāpena satta divasāni sūkararavaṃ [V 1.0075] ravanto antonivesane vicaritvā ajja kālaṃ katvā avīcimhi nibbatto”ti vatvā, “bhante, idha loke evaṃ socitvā puna gantvā socanaṭṭhāneyeva nibbatto”ti vutte, “āma, bhikkhave, pamattā nāma gahaṭṭhā vā hontu pabbajitā vā, ubhayattha socantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The monks, passing by the door of that house, heard that sound and, perceiving it as “the sound of pigs,” went to the monastery and, sitting near the Teacher, said: “Venerable sir, having closed the door of the house of Cunda the pork-butcher, today is the seventh day that pigs are being killed. We suppose some festive ceremony must be taking place in his house. Venerable sir, for one who kills so many pigs, not a single thought of loving-kindness or a single thought of compassion exists. Indeed, we have never before seen such a harsh and cruel being.” The Teacher said: “Monks, he has not been killing pigs these seven days. Rather, a result similar to his kamma has arisen for him. While still alive, the torment of the great Avīci hell manifested. Tormented by that pain, he wandered inside his house for seven days, making a sound like a pig, and today he has died and been reborn in Avīci.” When it was said, “Venerable sir, having grieved thus in this world, he has gone and been reborn again only in a place of grief,” the Teacher replied, “Yes, monks, the heedless, whether they are householders or renunciants, grieve in both worlds.” Then he spoke this verse:

15.

15.

“Idha socati pecca socati,

Pāpakārī ubhayattha socati;

So socati so vihaññati;

Disvā kammakiliṭṭhamattano”ti.

“Here he grieves, hereafter he grieves; the evil-doer grieves in both existences. He grieves, he is afflicted, seeing the defilement of his own deeds.”

Tattha [M 1.0083] pāpakārīti nānappakārassa pāpakammassa kārako puggalo “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ, kataṃ pāpa”nti ekaṃseneva maraṇasamaye idha socati, idamassa kammasocanaṃ. Vipākaṃ anubhavanto pana pecca socati. Idamassa paraloke vipākasocanaṃ. Evaṃ so ubhayattha socatiyeva. Teneva kāraṇena jīvamānoyeva so cundasūkarikopi socati. Disvā kammakiliṭṭhanti [P 1.0129] attano kiliṭṭhakammaṃ passitvā nānappakārakaṃ vilapanto vihaññatīti.

Therein, 'the evil-doer' refers to a person who performs various kinds of evil kamma. At the time of death, he certainly grieves, thinking, 'Alas, I have not done good; I have done evil.' This is his grief for his kamma in this present life. But while experiencing the result, he grieves after death. This is his grief for the result in the next world. Thus, he grieves in both existences. For that very reason, even while living, that Cunda the pork-butcher grieved. The phrase 'seeing the defilement of his own deeds' means that upon seeing his own defiled kamma, he laments in various ways and is afflicted.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the end of the verse, many became stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Cundasūkarikavatthu dasamaṃ.

The tenth story, the story of Cunda the pork-butcher, is finished.

11. Dhammikaupāsakavatthu

11. The Story of Dhammika the Lay Follower

Idha modatīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammikaupāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Here he rejoices,' concerning the lay follower Dhammika.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira pañcasatā dhammikaupāsakā nāma ahesuṃ. Tesu ekekassa pañca pañca upāsakasatāni parivārā. Yo tesaṃ jeṭṭhako, tassa satta puttā satta dhītaro. Tesu ekekassa ekekā salākayāgu salākabhattaṃ pakkhikabhattaṃ nimantanabhattaṃ uposathikabhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ vassāvāsikaṃ ahosi. Tepi sabbeva anujātaputtā nāma ahesuṃ. Iti cuddasannaṃ puttānaṃ bhariyāya upāsakassāti soḷasa salākayāguādīni pavattanti. Iti so saputtadāro sīlavā [V 1.0076] kalyāṇadhammo dānasaṃvibhāgarato ahosi. Athassa aparabhāge rogo uppajji, āyusaṅkhāro parihāyi. So dhammaṃ [P 1.0130] sotukāmo “aṭṭha vā me soḷasa vā bhikkhū pesethā”ti satthu santikaṃ pahiṇi. Satthā pesesi. Te gantvā tassa mañcaṃ parivāretvā paññattesu āsanesu nisinnā. “Bhante, ayyānaṃ me dassanaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissati, dubbalomhi, ekaṃ me suttaṃ sajjhāyathā”ti vutte “kataraṃ suttaṃ sotukāmo upāsakā”ti? “Sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṃ satipaṭṭhānasutta”nti vutte – “ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti [M 1.0084] (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106) suttantaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. Tasmiṃ khaṇe chahi devalokehi sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā sahassasindhavayuttā diyaḍḍhayojanasatikā cha rathā āgamiṃsu. Tesu ṭhitā devatā “amhākaṃ devalokaṃ nessāma, amhākaṃ devalokaṃ nessāma, ambho mattikabhājanaṃ bhinditvā suvaṇṇabhājanaṃ gaṇhanto viya amhākaṃ devaloke abhiramituṃ idha nibbattāhi, amhākaṃ devaloke abhiramituṃ idha nibbattāhī”ti vadiṃsu. Upāsako dhammassavanantarāyaṃ anicchanto – “āgametha āgamethā”ti āha. Bhikkhū “amhe vāretī”ti saññāya tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

In Sāvatthī, it is said, there were five hundred lay followers known as the Dhammika lay followers. Each of them had an entourage of five hundred lay followers. The one who was their chief had seven sons and seven daughters. For each of them, there was one ticket-gruel, one ticket-meal, a fortnightly meal, an invitation meal, an Uposatha day meal, a meal for guests, a meal for the Sangha, and a rains-residence robe. All of them were known as worthy offspring. Thus, for the fourteen children, the wife, and the lay follower himself, sixteen portions of ticket-gruel and so forth were provided. In this way, he, together with his sons and wife, was virtuous, of good conduct, and delighted in giving and sharing. Then, in a later part of his life, an illness arose, and his life-force declined. Desiring to hear the Dhamma, he sent a message to the Teacher: 'Please send me eight or sixteen monks.' The Teacher sent them. They went, surrounded his bed, and sat on the seats that had been prepared. He said, 'Venerable sirs, seeing the noble ones will become difficult for me; I am weak. Please recite one sutta for me.' When asked, 'Which sutta do you wish to hear, lay follower?' he replied, 'The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, which is never abandoned by any of the Buddhas.' Then they began to recite the discourse: 'This, monks, is the one and only path for the purification of beings...' At that moment, from the six deva realms, six chariots arrived, adorned with all ornaments, yoked with a thousand Sindhava horses, and one hundred and fifty yojanas high. The deities standing in them said, 'We will take you to our deva realm! We will take you to our deva realm! O friend, just as one, having broken an earthen pot, takes a golden vessel, be reborn here in our deva realm to delight exceedingly! Be reborn here in our deva realm to delight exceedingly!' The lay follower, not wishing for any obstruction to his hearing of the Dhamma, said, 'Wait, wait!' The monks, thinking, 'He is stopping us,' became silent.

Athassa puttadhītaro “amhākaṃ pitā pubbe dhammassavanena atitto ahosi, idāni pana bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā sajjhāyaṃ kāretvā sayameva vāreti, maraṇassa abhāyanakasatto nāma natthī”ti viraviṃsu. Bhikkhū “idāni anokāso”ti uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu. Upāsako thokaṃ vītināmetvā satiṃ paṭilabhitvā putte pucchi – “kasmā kandathā”ti? “Tāta, tumhe bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā dhammaṃ suṇantā sayameva vārayittha, atha mayaṃ ‘maraṇassa abhāyanakasatto nāma natthī’ti kandimhā”ti[P 1.0131]. “Ayyā pana kuhi”nti? “‘Anokāso’ti uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkantā, tātā”ti. “Nāhaṃ, ayyehi saddhiṃ kathemī”ti vutte “atha kena saddhiṃ kathethā”ti. “Chahi devalokehi devatā cha rathe alaṅkaritvā ādāya ākāse ṭhatvā ‘amhāhi devaloke abhirama, amhākaṃ devaloke abhiramā’ti saddaṃ karonti, tāhi saddhiṃ kathemī”ti. “Kuhiṃ, tāta, rathā, na mayaṃ passāmā”ti? “Atthi pana mayhaṃ ganthitāni pupphānī”ti? “Atthi, tātā”ti. “Kataro devaloko ramaṇīyo”ti? “Sabbabodhisattānaṃ buddhamātāpitūnañca vasitaṭṭhānaṃ tusitabhavanaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, tātā”ti. “Tena hi ‘tusitabhavanato āgatarathe laggatū’ti pupphadāmaṃ khipathā”ti. Te khipiṃsu. Taṃ rathadhure laggitvā ākāse olambi. Mahājano tadeva passati, rathaṃ na passati. Upāsako “passathetaṃ pupphadāma”nti vatvā, “āma, passāmā”ti vutte – “etaṃ tusitabhavanato āgatarathe olambati, ahaṃ tusitabhavanaṃ gacchāmi[V 1.0077], tumhe mā cintayittha, mama santike nibbattitukāmā hutvā mayā kataniyāmeneva puññāni karothā”ti vatvā kālaṃ katvā rathe patiṭṭhāsi.

Then his sons and daughters cried out, 'Our father was previously insatiable in listening to the Dhamma, but now, having had the monks invited and having had them recite, he himself stops them. Truly, there is no being unafraid of death!' The monks, thinking, 'Now is not the time,' rose from their seats and departed. After a short while, the lay follower regained mindfulness and asked his children, 'Why are you crying?' 'Father, you invited the monks and while listening to the Dhamma, you yourself stopped them. Therefore, we cried, thinking, "Truly, there is no being unafraid of death!"' 'But where are the noble ones?' 'Thinking, "It is not the proper time," they rose from their seats and departed, father.' 'I am not speaking with the noble ones,' he said. When asked, 'Then with whom are you speaking?' he replied, 'Deities from the six deva realms, having adorned and brought six chariots, are standing in the sky and making the sound, "Delight in our deva realm! Delight in our deva realm!" I am speaking with them.' 'Where are the chariots, father? We do not see them.' 'But do I have any flower garlands?' 'Yes, father.' 'Which deva realm is delightful?' 'The Tusita realm, the dwelling place of all Bodhisattas and the mothers and fathers of Buddhas, is delightful, father.' 'In that case, throw this flower garland with the resolution, "May it catch on the chariot that has come from the Tusita realm!"' They threw it. It caught on the front of the chariot and hung suspended in the sky. The great crowd saw only the flower garland; they did not see the chariot. The lay follower, having said, 'Do you see this flower garland?' and being told, 'Yes, we see it,' said, 'This is hanging on the chariot that has come from the Tusita realm. I am going to the Tusita realm. You should not worry. If you wish to be reborn in my presence, perform meritorious deeds in the same way that I have done.' Having said this, he passed away and was established on the chariot.

Tāvadevassa [M 1.0085] tigāvutappamāṇo saṭṭhisakaṭabhārālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito attabhāvo nibbatti, accharāsahassaṃ parivāresi, pañcavīsatiyojanikaṃ kanakavimānaṃ pāturahosi. Tepi bhikkhū vihāraṃ anuppatte satthā pucchi – “sutā, bhikkhave, upāsakena dhammadesanā”ti? “Āma, bhante, antarāyeva pana ‘āgamethā’ti vāresi. Athassa puttadhītaro kandiṃsu[P 1.0132]. Mayaṃ ‘idāni anokāso’ti uṭṭhāyāsanā nikkhantā”ti. “Na so, bhikkhave, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathesi, chahi devalokehi devatā cha rathe alaṅkaritvā āharitvā taṃ upāsakaṃ pakkosiṃsu. So dhammadesanāya antarāyaṃ anicchanto tāhi saddhiṃ kathesī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Evaṃ, bhikkhave”ti. “Idāni kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti? “Tusitabhavane, bhikkhave”ti. “Bhante, idāni idha ñātimajjhe modamāno vicaritvā idāneva gantvā puna modanaṭṭhāneyeva nibbatto”ti. “Āma, bhikkhave, appamattā hi gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā sabbattha modantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that very moment, a body three gāvutas in height and adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cartloads came into existence for him; a thousand celestial nymphs surrounded him, and a golden celestial mansion of twenty-five yojanas appeared. When those monks arrived back at the monastery, the Teacher asked, “Monks, did the lay follower hear the Dhamma discourse?” “Yes, Venerable Sir, but in the middle of it, he stopped us, saying, ‘Wait.’ Then his sons and daughters wept. Thinking, ‘Now is not the proper time,’ we rose from our seats and departed.” “Monks, he was not speaking with you. Deities from the six deva worlds, having adorned and brought six chariots, were calling that lay follower. Not wishing for an interruption to the Dhamma discourse, he spoke with them.” “Is that so, Venerable Sir?” “It is so, monks.” “Where has he been reborn now?” “In the Tusita heaven, monks.” “Venerable Sir, just now he was living here rejoicing in the midst of his relatives, and having just departed, he is reborn again in a place of delight.” “Yes, monks. For the heedful, whether householders or renunciates, rejoice everywhere.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

16.

16.

“Idha modati pecca modati,

Katapuñño ubhayattha modati;

So modati so pamodati,

Disvā kammavisuddhimattano”ti.

Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices; the maker of merit rejoices in both worlds. He rejoices, he greatly rejoices, seeing the purity of his own deeds.

Tattha katapuññoti nānappakārassa kusalassa kārako puggalo “akataṃ vata me pāpaṃ, kataṃ me kalyāṇa”nti idha kammamodanena, pecca vipākamodanena modati. Evaṃ ubhayattha modati nāma. Kammavisuddhinti dhammikaupāsakopi attano kammavisuddhiṃ puññakammasampattiṃ disvā kālakiriyato pubbe idhalokepi modati, kālaṃ katvā idāni paralokepi atimodatiyevāti.

Therein, 'maker of merit' means a person who performs various kinds of wholesome deeds. Thinking, “I have certainly done no evil; I have done what is good,” one rejoices in this life through joy in that kamma, and after death, one rejoices through joy in its result. Thus one is said to rejoice in both worlds. 'Purity of kamma' means that the lay follower Dhammika, seeing his own purity of kamma, which is the accomplishment of meritorious deeds, rejoiced in this world even before his death; and having passed away, he now greatly rejoices in the next world as well.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many attained stream-entry and other fruits. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial to the great assembly.

Dhammikaupāsakavatthu ekādasamaṃ.

The eleventh story, the story of the lay follower Dhammika, is finished.

12. Devadattavatthu

12. The Story of Devadatta

Idha [V 1.0078][M 1.0086][P 1.0133] tappatīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Here he is tormented...” The Teacher spoke this Dhamma discourse concerning Devadatta while dwelling at Jetavana.

Devadattassa vatthu pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya yāva pathavippavesanā devadattaṃ ārabbha bhāsitāni sabbāni jātakāni vitthāretvā kathitaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – satthari anupiyaṃ nāma mallānaṃ nigamo atthi. Taṃ nissāya anupiyambavane viharanteyeva tathāgatassa lakkhaṇapaṭiggahaṇadivaseyeva asītisahassehi ñātikulehi “rājā vā hotu, buddho vā, khattiyaparivārova vicarissatī”ti asītisahassaputtā paṭiññātā. Tesu yebhuyyena pabbajitesu bhaddiyaṃ nāma rājānaṃ, anuruddhaṃ, ānandaṃ, bhaguṃ, kimilaṃ, devadattanti ime cha sakye apabbajante disvā, “mayaṃ attano putte pabbājema, ime cha sakyā na ñātakā maññe, kasmā na pabbajantī”ti? Kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Atha kho mahānāmo sakyo anuruddhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “tāta, amhākaṃ kulā pabbajito natthi, tvaṃ vā pabbaja, ahaṃ vā pabbajissāmī”ti āha. So pana sukhumālo hoti sampannabhogo, “natthī”ti vacanampi tena na sutapubbaṃ. Ekadivasañhi tesu chasu khattiyesu guḷakīḷaṃ kīḷantesu anuruddho pūvena parājito pūvatthāya pahiṇi, athassa mātā pūve sajjetvā pahiṇi[P 1.0134]. Te khāditvā puna kīḷiṃsu. Punappunaṃ tasseva parājayo hoti. Mātā panassa pahite pahite tikkhattuṃ pūve pahiṇitvā catutthavāre “pūvā natthī”ti pahiṇi. So “natthī”ti vacanassa asukapubbattā “esāpekā pūvavikati bhavissatī”ti maññamāno “natthipūvaṃ me āharathā”ti pesesi. Mātā panassa “natthipūvaṃ kira, ayye, dethā”ti vutte, “mama puttena ‘natthī’ti padaṃ na sutapubbaṃ, iminā pana upāyena naṃ etamatthaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti tucchaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ aññāya suvaṇṇapātiyā paṭikujjitvā pesesi. Nagarapariggāhikā devatā cintesuṃ – “anuruddhasakyena annabhārakāle attano bhāgabhattaṃ upariṭṭhapaccekabuddhassa datvā “‘natthī’ti me vacanassa savanaṃ mā hotu, bhojanuppattiṭṭhānajānanaṃ mā ‘hotū’ti patthanā katā, sacāyaṃ tucchapātiṃ passissati, devasamāgamaṃ pavisituṃ na labhissāma, sīsampi no sattadhā phaleyyā”ti. Atha [M 1.0087] naṃ pātiṃ dibbapūvehi puṇṇaṃ akaṃsu. Kassā guḷamaṇḍale ṭhapetvā ugghāṭitamattāya pūvagandho sakalanagare chādetvā ṭhito. Pūvakhaṇḍaṃ mukhe ṭhapitamattameva sattarasaharaṇīsahassāni anuphari.

The story of Devadatta has been told in detail by expanding upon all the Jātakas spoken concerning him, from the time of his ordination until his descent into the earth. Here, however, is a summary. While the Teacher was dwelling in the Anupiya mango grove near the Malla town named Anupiya, on the very day the marks of the Tathāgata were interpreted, eighty thousand sons from related families were pledged, with the thought, “Whether he becomes a king or a Buddha, he will be attended by a retinue of warriors.” When most of them had gone forth, the people saw that these six Sakyans—King Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta—had not gone forth, and they raised the matter, saying, “We have our own sons go forth. It seems these six Sakyans are not our kinsmen. Why do they not go forth?” Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached Anuruddha and said, “Dear brother, no one from our family has gone forth. Either you go forth, or I shall.” Now, Anuruddha was very delicate and of great fortune; he had never before heard the word “there is not.” For one day, while those six khattiyas were playing a game with pellets, Anuruddha lost the wager of cakes and sent for them. His mother had cakes prepared and sent them. After eating them, they played again. Again and again, he was the one who lost. His mother, having sent cakes three times upon request, on the fourth occasion sent the message, “There are no cakes.” As he had never before heard the words “there is not,” he thought, “This must be a type of cake,” and sent a messenger, saying, “Bring me a ‘no-cake.’” When his mother was told, “My lady, they say to give them a ‘no-cake,’” she thought, “My son has never heard the words ‘there is not.’ By this stratagem, I shall make him understand this matter.” She then took an empty golden bowl, covered it with another golden bowl, and sent it. The guardian deities of the city reflected: “The Sakyan Anuruddha, in his time as the treasurer Annabhāra, gave his own share of rice to the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha and made the aspiration: ‘May I never hear the words “there is not,” and may I not have to know the place where food originates.’ If he sees this empty bowl, we will not be able to enter the assembly of the devas, and our heads would split into seven pieces.” Then they filled that bowl with divine cakes. When it was placed in the gaming circle and the lid was merely lifted, the fragrance of the cakes filled the entire city. As soon as a piece of the cake was placed in his mouth, its flavor pervaded the seven thousand taste-conducting nerves.

So cintesi – “nāhaṃ mātu piyo, ettakaṃ me kālaṃ imaṃ natthipūvaṃ [P 1.0135] nāma na paci, ito paṭṭhāya aññaṃ pūvaṃ nāma na khādissāmī”ti, so gehaṃ gantvāva mātaraṃ pucchi – “amma[V 1.0079], tumhākaṃ ahaṃ piyo, appiyo”ti? “Tāta, ekakkhino akkhi viya ca hadayaṃ viya ca ativiya piyo me ahosī”ti. “Atha kasmā ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayhaṃ natthi pūvaṃ na pacittha, ammā”ti? Sā cūḷūpaṭṭhākaṃ pucchi – “atthi kiñci pātiyaṃ, tātā”ti? “Paripuṇṇā, ayye, pāti pūvehi, evarūpā pūvā nāma me na diṭṭhapubbā”ti ārocesi. Sā cintesi – “mayhaṃ putto puññavā katābhinīhāro bhavissati, devatāhi pātiṃ pūretvā pūvā pahitā bhavissantī”ti. “Atha naṃ putto, amma, ito paṭṭhāyāhaṃ aññaṃ pūvaṃ nāma na khādissāmi, natthipūvameva paceyyāsī”ti. Sāpissa tato paṭṭhāya “pūvaṃ khāditukāmomhī”ti vutte tucchapātimeva aññāya pātiyā paṭikucchitvā pesesi. Yāva agāramajjhe vasi, tāvassa devatāva pūve pahiṇiṃsu.

He thought, 'My mother does not love me. For all this time she has not cooked this so-called nothing-cake for me. From now on, I will not eat any other kind of cake.' So, having gone home, he asked his mother, 'Mother, am I dear to you or not?' 'Dear son, you are as dear to me as the eye of a one-eyed man or as my own heart.' 'Then why, mother, for all this time have you not cooked the nothing-cake for me?' She asked the junior attendant, 'Dear, is there anything in the bowl?' 'Madam, the bowl is full of cakes; I have never before seen such cakes,' he reported. She thought, 'My son must be one of great merit who has made a past resolution; the deities must have filled the bowl and sent these cakes.' Then the son said to her, 'Mother, from this day forward I will not eat any other cake; you should cook only the nothing-cake.' From then on, whenever he said, 'I wish to eat a cake,' she would simply send an empty bowl covered with another bowl. As long as he lived in the household, the deities sent him cakes.

So ettakampi ajānanto pabbajjaṃ nāma kiṃ jānissati? Tasmā “kā esā pabbajjā nāmā”ti bhātaraṃ pucchitvā “ohāritakesamassunā kāsāyanivatthena kaṭṭhattharake vā bidalamañcake vā nipajjitvā piṇḍāya carantena viharitabbaṃ. Esā pabbajjā nāmā”ti vutte, “bhātika, ahaṃ sukhumālo. Nāhaṃ sakkhissāmi pabbajitu”nti [P 1.0136] āha. “Tena hi, tāta, kammantaṃ uggahetvā gharāvāsaṃ vasa. Na hi sakkā amhesu ekena apabbajitu”nti. Atha naṃ “ko esa kammanto nāmā”ti pucchi. “Bhattuṭṭhānaṭṭhānampi ajānanto kulaputto kammantaṃ nāma kiṃ jānissatī”ti? Ekadivasañhi tiṇṇaṃ khattiyānaṃ kathā udapādi – “bhattaṃ nāma kuhiṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti? Kimilo āha – “koṭṭhe uṭṭhahatī”ti. Atha naṃ bhaddiyo “tvaṃ bhattassa uṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ na jānāsi, bhattaṃ nāma ukkhaliyaṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti āha. Anuruddho “tumhe dvepi na jānātha, bhattaṃ nāma ratanamakuḷāya suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti āha.

Not knowing even this much, what would he know of the going forth? Therefore, after asking his brother, 'What is this going forth?', and being told, 'One must live having shaved off hair and beard, wearing ochre robes, lying on a wooden pallet or a lattice bed, and wandering for alms. This is what the going forth is,' he said, 'Brother, I am delicate. I will not be able to go forth.' 'Then, dear brother, learn a trade and live as a householder. Indeed, it is not possible for both of us to remain without going forth.' Then he asked him, 'What is this trade?' Indeed, how could a clansman who does not even know where rice originates know what a trade is? For one day, a conversation arose among three princes: 'Where does rice originate?' Kimila said, 'It originates in the granary.' Then Bhaddiya said to him, 'You do not know the origin of rice; rice originates in the cooking pot.' Anuruddha said, 'Neither of you knows; rice originates in a golden bowl adorned with jewels.'

Tesu [M 1.0088] kira ekadivasaṃ kimilo koṭṭhato vīhī otāriyamāne disvā, “ete koṭṭheyeva jātā”ti saññī ahosi. Bhaddiyo ekadivasaṃ ukkhalito bhattaṃ vaḍḍhiyamānaṃ disvā “ukkhaliyaññeva uppanna”nti saññī ahosi. Anuruddhena pana neva vīhī koṭṭentā, na bhattaṃ pacantā, na vaḍḍhentā diṭṭhapubbā, vaḍḍhetvā pana purato ṭhapitameva passati. So bhuñjitukāmakāle “bhattaṃ pātiyaṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti saññamakāsi. Evaṃ tayopi te bhattuṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ na jānanti. Tenāyaṃ “ko esa kammanto nāmā”ti pucchitvā, “paṭhamaṃ khettaṃ kasāpetabba”ntiādikaṃ saṃvacchare saṃvacchare kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ sutvā, “kadā kammantānaṃ anto paññāyissati, kadā mayaṃ appossukkā bhoge bhuñjissāmā”ti vatvā kammantānaṃ apariyantatāya akkhātāya “tena hi tvaññeva gharāvāsaṃ vasa, na mayhaṃ etenattho”ti mātaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā[V 1.0080][P 1.0137], “anujānāhi maṃ, amma, pabbajissāmī”ti vatvā tāya nānappakārehi tikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā, “sace te sahāyako bhaddiyarājā pabbajissati, tena saddhiṃ pabbajāhī”ti vutte taṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “mama kho, samma, pabbajjā tava paṭibaddhā”ti vatvā taṃ nānappakārehi saññāpetvā sattame divase attanā saddhiṃ pabbajanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhi.

Among them, it is said that one day Kimila, seeing paddy being taken out from the granary, perceived, 'These are born right in the granary.' One day, Bhaddiya, seeing cooked rice being served from the pot, perceived, 'It arises from the pot itself.' But Anuruddha had never before seen paddy being pounded, nor cooked rice being cooked, nor it being served; he only saw it after it was served and placed before him. So, at the time he wished to eat, he formed the perception, 'Cooked rice arises in the golden bowl.' Thus, all three of them did not know the place where rice originates. Therefore, this one, having asked, 'What is this thing called a trade?' and having heard of the duties to be done year after year, such as, 'First, the field must be caused to be plowed,' said, 'When will an end to these tasks be seen? When will we, free from care, enjoy our wealth?' Having been told of the endlessness and inexhaustibility of the tasks, he said, 'Then you yourself live the household life. I have no need for this.' Approaching his mother, he said, 'Mother, give me permission; I will go forth.' After she had refused him three times in various ways, she said, 'If your friend, King Bhaddiya, will go forth, then you may go forth with him.' Approaching Bhaddiya, he said, 'Friend, my going forth is indeed bound up with you.' Having persuaded him in various ways, on the seventh day he received his promise to go forth together with him.

Tato bhaddiyo sakyarājā anuruddho ānando bhagu kimilo devadattoti ime cha khattiyā upālikappakasattamā devā viya dibbasampattiṃ sattāhaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavitvā uyyānaṃ gacchantā viya caturaṅginiyā senāya nikkhamitvā paravisayaṃ patvā rājāṇāya senaṃ nivattāpetvā paravisayaṃ okkamiṃsu. Tattha cha khattiyā attano attano ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā, “handa bhaṇe, upāli, nivattassu, alaṃ te ettakaṃ jīvikāyā”ti tassa adaṃsu. So tesaṃ pādamūle parivattitvā paridevitvā tesaṃ āṇaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto uṭṭhāya taṃ gahetvā nivatti. Tesaṃ dvidhā jātakāle, vanaṃ ārodanappattaṃ viya pathavīkampamānākārappattā viya ahosi. Upāli kappakopi thokaṃ gantvā nivattitvā “caṇḍā kho sākiyā, ‘iminā kumārā nippātitā’ti ghāteyyumpi maṃ. Ime hi nāma sakyakumārā evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ pahāya imāni anagghāni ābharaṇāni kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya chaḍḍetvā pabbajissanti, kimaṅgaṃ [M 1.0089][P 1.0138] panāha”nti bhaṇḍikaṃ omuñcitvā tāni ābharaṇāni rukkhe laggetvā “atthikā gaṇhantū”ti vatvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā tehi “kasmā nivattosī”ti puṭṭho tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ te ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “mayaṃ, bhante, sākiyā nāma mānanissitā, ayaṃ amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ paricārako, imaṃ paṭhamataraṃ pabbājetha, mayamassa abhivādanādīni karissāma, evaṃ no māno nimmānāyissatī”ti vatvā taṃ paṭhamataraṃ pabbājetvā pacchā sayaṃ pabbajiṃsu. Tesu āyasmā bhaddiyo teneva antaravassena tevijjo ahosi. Āyasmā anuruddho dibbacakkhuko hutvā pacchā mahāvitakkasuttaṃ (a. ni. 8.30) sutvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Āyasmā ānando sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Bhagutthero ca kimilatthero ca aparabhāge vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Devadatto pothujjanikaṃ iddhiṃ patto.

Then Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta—these six nobles, with Upāli the barber as the seventh—having experienced divine bliss for seven days like gods, departed with a fourfold army as if going to a park. Having reached another's territory, they sent the army back by the king's authority and entered that territory. There, the six nobles removed their ornaments, made a bundle of them, and said, “Now then, friend Upāli, turn back. This is sufficient for your livelihood,” and gave it to him. He rolled at their feet and lamented, but being unable to transgress their command, he rose, took it, and turned back. At the time of their separation, it was as if the forest was overcome with lamentation and the earth began to tremble. Upāli the barber, having gone a short way, turned back, thinking, “The Sakyans are fierce. They might kill me, thinking, ‘The princes have been killed by this man.’ Indeed, these Sakyan princes are abandoning such prosperity and casting away these priceless ornaments like a lump of spittle to go forth. Why then should I not go forth?” Thinking thus, he untied the bundle, hung those ornaments on a tree, and saying, “Let those who desire them take them,” he went to the princes. When asked by them, “Why have you returned?” he related the matter. Then, taking him with them, they went to the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, we are Sakyans, and we are given to pride. This man has been our attendant for a long time. Ordain him first. We will pay him reverence and so on. In this way, our pride will be eliminated.” Having said this, they had him ordained first, and afterwards, they themselves went forth. Among them, the Venerable Bhaddiya became possessed of the three knowledges within that very rains-retreat. The Venerable Anuruddha, having become a possessor of the divine eye, later heard the Mahāpurisavitakka Sutta and attained Arahantship. The Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Venerable Bhagu and the Venerable Kimila, in a later time, developed insight and attained Arahantship. Devadatta attained the psychic power of an ordinary person.

Aparabhāge satthari kosambiyaṃ viharante sasāvakasaṅghassa tathāgatassa mahanto lābhasakkāro nibbatti. Vatthabhesajjādihatthā manussā vihāraṃ pavisitvā “kuhiṃ satthā, kuhiṃ sāriputtatthero, kuhiṃ mahāmoggallānatthero, kuhiṃ mahākassapatthero, kuhiṃ bhaddiyatthero, kuhiṃ anuruddhatthero, kuhiṃ ānandatthero, kuhiṃ bhagutthero, kuhiṃ kimilatthero”ti asītimahāsāvakānaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0081] olokentā vicaranti. “Devadattatthero kuhiṃ nisinno vā, ṭhito vā”ti pucchanto nāma natthi. So cintesi – “ahampi etehi saddhiññeva pabbajito, etepi khattiyapabbajitā, ahampi khattiyapabbajito, lābhasakkārahatthā [P 1.0139] manussā eteyeva pariyesanti, mama nāmaṃ gahetāpi natthi. Kena nu kho saddhiṃ ekato hutvā kaṃ pasādetvā mama lābhasakkāraṃ nibbatteyya”nti. Athassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ kho rājā bimbisāro paṭhamadassaneneva ekādasahi nahutehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito, na sakkā etena saddhiṃ ekato bhavituṃ, kosalaraññāpi saddhiṃ na sakkā bhavituṃ. Ayaṃ kho pana rañño putto ajātasattu kumāro kassaci guṇadose na jānāti, etena saddhiṃ ekato bhavissāmī”ti. So kosambito rājagahaṃ gantvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā cattāro āsīvise catūsu hatthapādesu ekaṃ gīvāya pilandhitvā [M 1.0090] ekaṃ sīse cumbaṭakaṃ katvā ekaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā imāya ahimekhalāya ākāsato oruyha ajātasattussa ucchaṅge nisīditvā tena bhītena “kosi tva”nti vutte “ahaṃ devadatto”ti vatvā tassa bhayavinodanatthaṃ taṃ attabhāvaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā saṅghāṭipattacīvaradharo purato ṭhatvā taṃ pasādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nibbattesi. So lābhasakkārābhibhūto “ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmī”ti pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetvā saha cittuppādena iddhito parihāyitvā satthāraṃ veḷuvanavihāre sarājikāya parisāya dhammaṃ desentaṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā añjaliṃ paggayha – “bhagavā, bhante, etarahi jiṇṇo vuḍḍho mahallako, appossukko diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyuñjatu, ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmi, niyyādetha me bhikkhusaṅgha”nti [P 1.0140] vatvā satthārā kheḷāsakavādena apasādetvā paṭikkhitto anattamano imaṃ paṭhamaṃ tathāgate āghātaṃ bandhitvā pakkāmi.

Later, when the Teacher was residing at Kosambī, great gains and honor arose for the Tathāgata together with his community of disciples. People with robes, medicine, and other items in hand would enter the monastery and wander about, looking for the places where the eighty great disciples were seated, asking: “Where is the Teacher? Where is the Venerable Sāriputta? Where is the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna? Where is the Venerable Mahākassapa? Where is the Venerable Bhaddiya? Where is the Venerable Anuruddha? Where is the Venerable Ānanda? Where is the Venerable Bhagu? Where is the Venerable Kimila?” But there was no one at all asking, “Where is the Venerable Devadatta seated or standing?” He thought: “I too went forth along with them. They are of the khattiya caste who have gone forth, and I too am a khattiya who has gone forth. People with gains and honor in hand seek only them; there is no one who even mentions my name. With whom, I wonder, can I join, and whom can I win over, to generate gains and honor for myself?” Then this occurred to him: “This King Bimbisāra, at his very first sight of the Buddha, was established in the fruit of stream-entry along with one hundred and ten thousand others. It is not possible to join with him. Nor is it possible to join with the king of Kosala. But this Prince Ajātasattu, the king’s son, does not know the virtues or faults of anyone. I will join with him.” So, going from Kosambī to Rājagaha, he created the appearance of a young boy. He adorned himself with venomous snakes: four on his hands and feet, one worn around his neck, one made into a head-ring on his head, and one placed on his shoulder. With this snake-adornment, he descended from the sky and sat on Ajātasattu’s lap. When the frightened prince asked, “Who are you?” he replied, “I am Devadatta.” Then, to dispel his fear, he withdrew that form and stood before him in his robes and carrying his bowl. Having won the prince's confidence, he generated gains and honor. Overcome by gains and honor, he gave rise to the evil thought, “I will lead the community of monks.” And with the arising of that thought, he fell away from his psychic power. He approached the Teacher as he was teaching the Dhamma in the Veḷuvana monastery to the assembly including the king, paid his respects, rose from his seat, raised his hands in añjali, and said: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One is now aged, old, and advanced in years. Let him live untroubled, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life. I will take care of the community of monks. Hand over the community of monks to me.” Having said this, he was rebuked by the Teacher with the term 'spittle-swallower' and was rejected. Displeased, he departed, having conceived this first grudge against the Tathāgata.

Athassa bhagavā rājagahe pakāsanīyakammaṃ kāresi. So “pariccatto dāni ahaṃ samaṇena gotamena, idānissa anatthaṃ karissāmī”ti ajātasattuṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “pubbe kho, kumāra, manussā dīghāyukā, etarahi appāyukā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ tvaṃ kumārova samāno kālaṃ kareyyāsi, tena hi tvaṃ, kumāra, pitaraṃ hantvā rājā hohi, ahaṃ bhagavantaṃ hantvā buddho bhavissāmī”ti vatvā tasmiṃ rajje patiṭṭhite tathāgatassa vadhāya purise payojetvā tesu sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā nivattesu sayaṃ gijjhakūṭapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā, “ahameva samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitā voropessāmī”ti silaṃ pavijjhitvā ruhiruppādakakammaṃ katvā imināpi upāyena māretuṃ asakkonto puna nāḷāgiriṃ vissajjāpesi. Tasmiṃ āgacchante ānandatthero attano jīvitaṃ satthu pariccajitvā purato aṭṭhāsi. Satthā nāgaṃ dametvā nagarā nikkhamitvā vihāraṃ gantvā anekasahassehi upāsakehi abhihaṭaṃ mahādānaṃ paribhuñjitvā tasmiṃ [V 1.0082] divase sannipatitānaṃ aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhātānaṃ rājagahavāsīnaṃ anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathetvā caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamaye jāte “aho āyasmā ānando mahāguṇo, tathārūpe nāma hatthināge āgacchante attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā [M 1.0091][P 1.0141] satthu puratova aṭṭhāsī”ti therassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajiyevā”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito cūḷahaṃsa (jā. 1.15.133 ādayo; 2.21.1 ādayo) – mahāhaṃsa (jā. 2.21.89 ādayo) – kakkaṭakajātakāni (jā. 1.3.49 ādayo) kathesi. Devadattassāpi kammaṃ neva pākaṭaṃ, tathā rañño mārāpitattā, na vadhakānaṃ payojitattā na silāya paviddhattā pākaṭaṃ ahosi, yathā nāḷāgirihatthino vissajjitattā. Tadā hi mahājano “rājāpi devadatteneva mārāpito, vadhakopi payojito, silāpi apaviddhā. Idāni pana tena nāḷāgiri vissajjāpito, evarūpaṃ nāma pāpakaṃ gahetvā rājā vicaratī”ti kolāhalamakāsi.

Then the Blessed One had an act of proclamation concerning Devadatta performed in Rājagaha. Devadatta thought, “Now I have been abandoned by the ascetic Gotama; I shall bring about his misfortune.” Approaching Ajātasattu, he said, “Prince, in the past people were long-lived, but now they are short-lived. It is possible that you, while still a prince, might die. Therefore, kill your father and become king, and I shall kill the Blessed One and become a Buddha.” Having said this, when Ajātasattu was established in the kingdom, Devadatta sent men to kill the Tathāgata. But they attained the fruit of stream-entry and turned back. Then Devadatta himself climbed Mount Vulture Peak, thinking, “I myself shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.” He hurled a boulder, performing the act of drawing blood, but even by this means he could not kill him. Next, he had the elephant Nāḷāgiri unleashed. As the elephant approached, the Venerable Ānanda, giving up his own life for the Teacher, stood before him. The Teacher tamed the elephant and left the city. Returning to the monastery, he partook of a great offering brought by many thousands of lay followers. On that day, he gave a graduated discourse to the eighteen crores of inhabitants of Rājagaha who had gathered. When eighty-four thousand beings attained comprehension of the Dhamma, they said, “Oh, the Venerable Ānanda is of great virtue! When such a great elephant was approaching, he gave up his own life and stood before the Teacher.” Hearing this praise of the elder’s virtues, the Blessed One said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, he has given up his life for my sake.” Then, at the request of the monks, he recounted the Cūḷahaṃsa, Mahāhaṃsa, and Kakkaṭaka Jātakas. Devadatta's deeds had not yet become public; neither his having caused the king to be killed, nor his dispatching of assassins, nor his hurling of the boulder had become as public as his unleashing of the elephant Nāḷāgiri. For at that time, the great populace made an uproar, saying, “King Bimbisāra was also caused to be killed by Devadatta, assassins were also dispatched by him, and a boulder was also hurled. Now he has had the elephant Nāḷāgiri unleashed. King Ajātasattu associates with such an evil person!”

Rājā mahājanassa kathaṃ sutvā pañca thālipākasatāni nīharāpetvā na puna tassūpaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi, nāgarāpissa kulaṃ upagatassa bhikkhāmattampi na adaṃsu. So parihīnalābhasakkāro kohaññena jīvitukāmo satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañca vatthūni yācitvā bhagavato “alaṃ, devadatta, yo icchati, so āraññako hotū”ti paṭikkhitto kassāvuso, vacanaṃ sobhanaṃ, kiṃ tathāgatassa udāhu mama, ahañhi ukkaṭṭhavasena evaṃ vadāmi, “sādhu, bhante, bhikkhū yāvajīvaṃ āraññakā assu, piṇḍapātikā, paṃsukūlikā, rukkhamūlikā, macchamaṃsaṃ na khādeyyu”nti. “Yo dukkhā muccitukāmo, so mayā saddhiṃ āgacchatū”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tassa vacanaṃ [P 1.0142] sutvā ekacce navakapabbajitā mandabuddhino “kalyāṇaṃ devadatto āha, etena saddhiṃ vicarissāmā”ti tena saddhiṃ ekato ahesuṃ. Iti so pañcasatehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ tehi pañcahi vatthūhi lūkhappasannaṃ janaṃ saññāpento kulesu viññāpetvā viññāpetvā bhuñjanto saṅghabhedāya parakkami. So bhagavatā, “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, devadatta, saṅghabhedāya parakkamasi cakkabhedāyā”ti puṭṭho “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti vatvā, “garuko kho, devadatta, saṅghabhedo”tiādīhi ovaditopi satthu vacanaṃ anādiyitvā pakkanto āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ rājagahe piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā, “ajjatagge dānāhaṃ, āvuso ānanda, aññatreva bhagavatā, aññatra, bhikkhusaṅghā uposathaṃ karissāmi, saṅghakammaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Thero tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Taṃ viditvā satthā uppannadhammasaṃvego hutvā, “devadatto [M 1.0092] sadevakassa lokassa anatthanissitaṃ attano avīcimhi paccanakakammaṃ karotī”ti vitakketvā –

The king, having heard the people's talk, had the five hundred pots of food withdrawn and never again went to attend upon him. The citizens, too, when Devadatta went to their families, did not give him even a single portion of alms-food. Deprived of gains and honor, desiring to live by deceit, he approached the Teacher and requested five points. The Blessed One rejected him, saying, “Enough, Devadatta. Let whoever wishes be a forest-dweller.” Devadatta then said, “Friends, whose words are excellent—the Tathāgata’s or mine? For I speak from the standpoint of the most extreme practice, saying, ‘It would be good, venerable sir, if the monks for their whole lives were forest-dwellers, alms-food-eaters, rag-robe-wearers, tree-root-dwellers, and would not eat fish or meat.’” Then, saying, “Whoever wishes to be freed from suffering, let him come with me,” he departed. Hearing his words, some newly ordained monks of little wisdom thought, “Devadatta speaks what is good; we shall go about with him,” and they joined him. Thus, with five hundred monks, Devadatta, convincing people who were pleased with asceticism by means of these five points, and eating by soliciting from families, strove to cause a schism in the Sangha. When questioned by the Blessed One, “Is it true, Devadatta, that you are striving to cause a schism in the Sangha and a division in the community?” he replied, “It is true, Blessed One.” Though admonished with, “Grave, Devadatta, is the schism in the Sangha,” and so forth, he disregarded the Teacher’s words and left. Seeing the Venerable Ānanda going for alms in Rājagaha, he said, “From this day onward, friend Ānanda, apart from the Blessed One and apart from the community of monks, I shall perform the Uposatha and Sangha acts.” The elder reported the matter to the Blessed One. Knowing this, the Teacher, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, reflected, “Devadatta is performing a deed connected with what is not for the welfare of the world with its devas, a deed that will ripen for him in Avīci.”

“Sukarāni [V 1.0083] asādhūni, attano ahitāni ca;

Yaṃ ve hitañca sādhuñca, taṃ ve paramadukkara”nti. (dha. pa. 163) –

“Easy to do are things that are unwholesome and harmful to oneself; but what is wholesome and beneficial, that is exceedingly hard to do.”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā puna imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Having recited this verse, he then uttered this exclamation:

“Sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhu, sādhu pāpena dukkaraṃ;

Pāpaṃ pāpena sukaraṃ, pāpamariyehi dukkara”nti. (udā. 48; cūḷava. 343);

“Good is easy for a good person to do; good is difficult for an evil person to do. Evil is easy for an evil person to do; evil is difficult for the noble ones to do.”

Atha kho devadatto uposathadivase attano parisāya saddhiṃ ekamantaṃ nisīditvā, “yassimāni pañca vatthūni khamanti[P 1.0143], so salākaṃ gaṇhatū”ti vatvā pañcasatehi vajjiputtakehi navakehi appakataññūhi salākāya gahitāya saṅghaṃ bhinditvā te bhikkhū ādāya gayāsīsaṃ agamāsi. Tassa tattha gatabhāvaṃ sutvā satthā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ānayanatthāya dve aggasāvake pesesi. Te tattha gantvā ādesanāpāṭihāriyānusāsaniyā ceva iddhipāṭihāriyānusāsaniyā ca anusāsantā te amataṃ pāyetvā ādāya ākāsena āgamiṃsu. Kokālikopi kho “uṭṭhehi, āvuso devadatta, nītā te bhikkhū sāriputtamoggallānehi, nanu tvaṃ mayā vutto ‘mā, āvuso, sāriputtamoggallāne vissāsī’ti. Pāpicchā sāriputtamoggallānā, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gatā”ti vatvā jaṇṇukena hadayamajjhe pahari, tassa tattheva uṇhaṃ lohitaṃ mukhato uggañchi. Āyasmantaṃ pana sāriputtaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ ākāsena āgacchantaṃ disvā bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “bhante, āyasmā sāriputto gamanakāle attadutiyo gato, idāni mahāparivāro āgacchanto sobhatī”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva sāriputto sobhati, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattakālepi mayhaṃ putto mama santikaṃ āgacchanto sobhiyevā”ti vatvā –

Then Devadatta, on the Uposatha day, sat down to one side with his own assembly and said, 'Whichever monk approves of these five points, let him take a voting ticket.' When five hundred young, ungrateful monks of the Vajjian clan had taken the voting tickets, he split the Sangha. Taking those monks, he went to Gayāsīsa. Hearing that he had gone there, the Teacher sent the two chief disciples to bring those monks back. They went there and, instructing them by means of the marvel of teaching through mind-reading and the marvel of instruction through psychic power, they caused them to drink the deathless and, taking them, returned through the air. Kokālika then said, 'Rise, friend Devadatta, your monks have been led away by Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Was it not said to you by me, “Friend, do not trust Sāriputta and Moggallāna”? Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.' Having said this, he struck him with his knee in the middle of the chest, and right there hot blood gushed from his mouth. Seeing the Venerable Sāriputta approaching through the air surrounded by the community of monks, the monks said, 'Venerable sir, when the Venerable Sāriputta departed, he went with only one companion, but now, returning with a great retinue, he is resplendent.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta is resplendent. Formerly, even when born in the animal realm, my son, coming into my presence, was indeed resplendent.' Having said this,

“Hoti sīlavataṃ attho, paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ;

Lakkhaṇaṃ passa āyantaṃ, ñātisaṅghapurakkhataṃ;

Atha passasimaṃ kāḷaṃ, suvihīnaṃva ñātibhī”ti. (jā. 1.1.11) –

“There is benefit for the virtuous, for those whose conduct is hospitable. Behold Lakkhaṇa, coming, honored by his assembly of kinsmen. Then behold this Kāḷa, completely bereft of his kinsmen.”

Idaṃ [M 1.0093][P 1.0144] jātakaṃ kathesi. Puna bhikkhūhi, “bhante, devadatto kira dve aggasāvake ubhosu passesu nisīdāpetvā ‘buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desessāmī’ti tumhākaṃ anukiriyaṃ karotī”ti vutte, “na[V 1.0084], bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mama anukiriyaṃ kātuṃ vāyami, na pana sakkhī”ti vatvā –

He related this Jātaka. Again, when the monks said, “Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta, having seated his two chief disciples on either side, declares, ‘I will teach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha,’ and thus imitates you,” the Teacher replied, “Monks, it is not only now. In the past, too, he strove to imitate me, but he was not able.” Having said this:

“Api vīraka passesi, sakuṇaṃ mañjubhāṇakaṃ;

Mayūragīvasaṅkāsaṃ, patiṃ mayhaṃ saviṭṭhakaṃ.

“O Vīraka, do you see the sweet-voiced bird, with a neck like a peacock's, my graceful husband?”

“Udakathalacarassa pakkhino,

Niccaṃ āmakamacchabhojino;

Tassānukaraṃ saviṭṭhako,

Sevāle paliguṇṭhito mato”ti. (jā. 1.2.107-108) –

“Of the bird that moves on water and land, that always feeds on raw fish—imitating it, your graceful husband lies dead, entangled in the algae.”

Ādinā jātakaṃ vatvā aparāparesupi divasesu tathānurūpameva kathaṃ ārabbha –

Having related the Jātaka beginning with this, on other subsequent days as well, he began a discourse of a similar nature:

“Acāri vatāyaṃ vitudaṃ vanāni,

Kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesu asārakesu;

Athāsadā khadiraṃ jātasāraṃ,

Yatthabbhidā garuḷo uttamaṅga”nti. (jā. 1.2.120);

“Indeed, this woodpecker wandered, pecking in the forests at pithless, firewood-like trees. Then it came upon a Khadira tree, naturally possessing heartwood, whereupon the woodpecker split its own noble head.”

“Lasī [P 1.0145] ca te nipphalikā, matthako ca padālito;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, ajja kho tvaṃ virocasī”ti. (jā. 1.1.143) –

“Your brain has burst forth, and your head is split open; all your ribs are broken. Now, indeed, you are truly resplendent!”

Evamādīni jātakāni kathesi. Puna “akataññū devadatto”ti kathaṃ ārabbha –

He related Jātakas such as these. Again, beginning a discourse on the topic, “Devadatta is ungrateful,” he said:

“Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ, yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase;

Migarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase.

“We have done your task with what strength we had. Homage to you, O King of Beasts! Might we receive something?”

“Mama lohitabhakkhassa, niccaṃ luddāni kubbato;

Dantantaragato santo, taṃ bahuṃ yampi jīvasī”ti. (jā. 1.4.29-30) –

“For one who has come between the teeth of me, a blood-eater who constantly does cruel deeds—that you are still alive is a great thing indeed.”

Ādīni [V 1.0085] jātakāni kathesi. Puna vadhāya parisakkanamassa ārabbha –

He related Jātakas such as these. Again, beginning a discourse concerning his (Devadatta's) attempt to murder him:

“Ñātametaṃ kuruṅgassa, yaṃ tvaṃ sepaṇṇi siyyasi;

Aññaṃ sepaṇṇi gacchāmi, na me te ruccate phala”nti. (jā. 1.1.21) –

“It is known to this deer, O Sepaṇṇi tree, why you drop your fruit. I will go to another Sepaṇṇi tree; your fruit does not please me.”

Ādīni [M 1.0094] jātakāni kathesi. Punadivase “ubhato parihīno devadatto lābhasakkārato ca sāmaññato cā”ti kathāsu pavattamānāsu “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto parihīno, pubbepesa parihīnoyevā”ti vatvā –

He related Jātakas such as these. On the following day, when talk arose that “Devadatta is diminished in two ways: in gains and honor, and in the state of a monk,” the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is diminished; in the past, too, he was indeed diminished.” Having said this:

“Akkhī [P 1.0146] bhinnā paṭo naṭṭho, sakhigehe ca bhaṇḍanaṃ;

Ubhato paduṭṭhā kammantā, udakamhi thalamhi cā”ti. (jā. 1.1.139) –

“Your eye is blinded, your cloth is lost, and in your own house there is a quarrel. Your undertakings are ruined in both ways: on water and on land.”

Ādīni jātakāni kathesi. Evaṃ rājagahe viharantova devadattaṃ ārabbha bahūni jātakāni kathetvā rājagahato sāvatthiṃ gantvā jetavane vihāre vāsaṃ kappesi. Devadattopi kho nava māse gilāno pacchime kāle satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā attano sāvake āha – “ahaṃ satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmo, taṃ me dassethā”ti. “Tvaṃ samatthakāle satthārā saddhiṃ verī hutvā acari, na mayaṃ tattha nessāmā”ti vutte, “mā maṃ nāsetha, mayā satthari āghāto kato, satthu pana mayi kesaggamattopi āghāto natthi”. So hi bhagavā –

He related Jātakas such as these. Thus, while dwelling in Rājagaha, having related many Jātakas concerning Devadatta, he went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī and took up residence in the Jetavana monastery. Devadatta, too, after being ill for nine months, at the final time wished to see the Teacher and said to his own disciples, “I wish to see the Teacher; show him to me.” When they replied, “When you were able, you acted as an enemy toward the Teacher; we will not take you there,” he said, “Do not destroy me. Malice was harbored by me toward the Teacher, but the Teacher has not even a hair's breadth of malice toward me. For indeed, that Blessed One—”

“Vadhake devadattamhi, core aṅgulimālake;

Dhanapāle rāhule ca, sabbattha samamānaso”ti. (apa. thera 1.1.585; mi. pa. 6.6.5) –

“Toward Devadatta the murderer, toward Aṅgulimāla the robber, toward Dhanapāla and toward Rāhula—toward all he is of equal mind.”
