“Dassetha me bhagavanta”nti punappunaṃ yāci. Atha naṃ te mañcakenādāya nikkhamiṃsu. Tassa āgamanaṃ sutvā bhikkhū satthu ārocesuṃ – “bhante, devadatto kira tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgacchatī”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, so tenattabhāvena maṃ passituṃ labhissatī”ti. Devadatto kira pañcannaṃ vatthūnaṃ āyācitakālato paṭṭhāya puna buddhaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhati, ayaṃ [P 1.0147] dhammatā. “Asukaṭṭhānañca asukaṭṭhānañca āgato, bhante”ti. “Yaṃ icchati, taṃ karotu, na so maṃ passituṃ labhissatī”ti. “Bhante, ito yojanamattaṃ āgato, aḍḍhayojanaṃ, gāvutaṃ, jetavanapokkharaṇīsamīpaṃ āgato, bhante”ti. “Sacepi antojetavanaṃ pavisati, neva maṃ passituṃ [V 1.0086] labhissatī”ti. Devadattaṃ gahetvā āgatā jetavanapokkharaṇītīre mañcaṃ otāretvā pokkharaṇiṃ nhāyituṃ otariṃsu. Devadattopi kho mañcato vuṭṭhāya ubho pāde bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā nisīdi. Pādā pathaviṃ pavisiṃsu[M 1.0095]. So anukkamena yāva gopphakā, yāva jaṇṇukā, yāva kaṭito, yāva thanato, yāva gīvato pavisitvā hanukaṭṭhikassa bhūmiyaṃ paviṭṭhakāle –

“Show me the Blessed One,” he begged again and again. Then they carried him out on a stretcher. Hearing of his arrival, the monks informed the Teacher: “Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta is coming to see you.” “Monks, in that state of existence, he will not be able to see me,” the Blessed One replied. It is said that from the time he requested the five articles, Devadatta was no longer able to see the Buddha—such is the nature of things. “Venerable sir, he has reached such and such a place,” they reported. “Let him do as he wishes; he will not be able to see me,” the Blessed One said. “Venerable sir, he has come within a yojana from here, half a yojana, a gāvuta, and is now near the Jetavana lotus pond,” they continued. “Even if he enters the Jetavana monastery, he will still not be able to see me,” the Blessed One replied. Those who had brought Devadatta lowered the stretcher on the bank of the Jetavana lotus pond and went down into the pond to bathe. Devadatta also rose from the stretcher and, placing both feet on the ground, sat down. His feet sank into the earth. He sank down sequentially up to his ankles, up to his knees, up to his waist, up to his chest, and up to his neck. And at the moment his jawbone was entering the ground—

“Imehi aṭṭhīhi tamaggapuggalaṃ,

Devātidevaṃ naradammasārathiṃ;

Samantacakkhuṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ,

Pāṇehi buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ upemī”ti. (mi. pa. 4.1.3) –

“With these bones and with this life, I go for refuge to that Buddha—the foremost of beings, the Deva beyond devas, the charioteer of men to be tamed, the one with the all-seeing eye, endowed with the hundred marks of merit.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Idaṃ kira ṭhānaṃ disvā tathāgato devadattaṃ pabbājesi. Sace hi na so pabbajissa, gihī hutvā kammañca bhāriyaṃ akarissa, āyatiṃ bhavanissaraṇapaccayaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissa, pabbajitvā ca pana kiñcāpi kammaṃ bhāriyaṃ karissati, āyatiṃ bhavanissaraṇapaccayaṃ kātuṃ [P 1.0148] sakkhissatīti taṃ satthā pabbājesi. So hi ito satasahassakappamatthake aṭṭhissaro nāma paccekabuddho bhavissati, so pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīcimhi nibbatti. Niccale buddhe aparajjhabhāvena pana niccalova hutvā paccatūti yojanasatike anto avīcimhi yojanasatubbedhamevassa sarīraṃ nibbatti. Sīsaṃ yāva kaṇṇasakkhalito upari ayakapallaṃ pāvisi, pādā yāva gopphakā heṭṭhā ayapathaviyaṃ paviṭṭhā, mahātālakkhandhaparimāṇaṃ ayasūlaṃ pacchimabhittito nikkhamitvā piṭṭhimajjhaṃ bhinditvā urena nikkhamitvā purimabhittiṃ pāvisi, aparaṃ dakkhiṇabhittito nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ bhinditvā vāmapassena nikkhamitvā uttarabhittiṃ pāvisi, aparaṃ upari kapallato nikkhamitvā matthakaṃ bhinditvā adhobhāgena nikkhamitvā ayapathaviṃ pāvisi. Evaṃ so tattha niccalova pacci.

He spoke this verse. It is said that the Tathāgata, seeing this reason, ordained Devadatta. For if he had not been ordained, as a layman he would have committed heavy kamma and would not have been able to create the cause for future liberation from existence. But having been ordained, although he would commit heavy kamma, he would be able to create the cause for future liberation from existence. Therefore, the Teacher ordained him. For after one hundred thousand kappas from now, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara. He entered the earth and was reborn in Avīci. Because of his offense against the unshakeable Buddha, he is tormented, himself unshakeable. In the hundred-yojana Avīci, his body arose, itself one hundred yojanas in height. His head, up to the tips of his ears, entered the iron canopy above. His feet, up to his ankles, entered the iron ground below. An iron stake the size of a great palmyra trunk, coming out from the western wall, pierced the middle of his back, emerged from his chest, and entered the eastern wall. Another, coming out from the southern wall, pierced his right side, emerged from his left side, and entered the northern wall. Another, coming out from the canopy above, pierced his head, emerged from the lower part, and entered the iron ground. Thus, he is tormented there, completely unshakeable.

Bhikkhū “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ devadatto āgacchanto satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ alabhitvāva pathaviṃ paviṭṭho”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mayi aparajjhitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi, pubbepi paviṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā hatthirājakāle maggamūḷhaṃ purisaṃ samassāsetvā attano piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā khemantaṃ pāpitassa puna tikkhattuṃ āgantvā aggaṭṭhāne majjhimaṭṭhāne [M 1.0096] mūlehi evaṃ dante chinditvā tatiyavāre mahāpurisassa cakkhupathaṃ atikkamantassa tassa pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ –

The monks started a discussion, saying: “Devadatta, having come this far, was swallowed by the earth without getting to see the Teacher.” The Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has been swallowed by the earth after offending me; he was swallowed by it in the past as well.” And so, to show how that man had been swallowed by the earth, he told of the time when he was the elephant king. After he had comforted a man who had lost his way, placed him on his back, and brought him to a place of safety, that man returned three times and cut his tusks—at the tip, in the middle, and at the root. On the third occasion, as the man was passing beyond the range of sight of the Great Being, he was swallowed by the earth.

“Akataññussa [V 1.0087][P 1.0149] posassa, niccaṃ vivaradassino;

Sabbaṃ ce pathaviṃ dajjā, neva naṃ abhirādhaye”ti. (jā. 1.1.72; 1.9.107) –

“To an ungrateful person, who is always looking for faults, even if one were to give the entire earth, one could never please him.”

Idaṃ jātakaṃ kathetvā punapi tatheva kathāya samuṭṭhitāya khantivādibhūte attani aparajjhitvā kalāburājabhūtassa tassa pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ khantivādijātakañca (jā. 1.4.49 ādayo), cūḷadhammapālabhūte attani aparajjhitvā mahāpatāparājabhūtassa tassa pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ cūḷadhammapālajātakañca (jā. 1.5.44 ādayo) kathesi.

Having related this Jātaka, when a similar discussion arose again, in order to show how Devadatta, who had been King Kalābu, was swallowed by the earth for having offended me when I was the Khantivādī ascetic, he related the Khantivādī Jātaka. And in order to show how Devadatta, who had been King Mahāpatāpa, was swallowed by the earth for having offended me when I was Cūḷadhammapāla, he related the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka.

Pathaviṃ paviṭṭhe pana devadatte mahājano haṭṭhatuṭṭho dhajapaṭākakadaliyo ussāpetvā puṇṇaghaṭe ṭhapetvā “lābhā vata no”ti mahantaṃ chaṇaṃ anubhoti. Tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatte mate mahājano tussati, pubbepi tussiyevā”ti vatvā sabbajanassa appiye caṇḍe pharuse bārāṇasiyaṃ piṅgalaraññe nāma mate mahājanassa tuṭṭhabhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ –

When Devadatta was swallowed by the earth, the great populace was joyful and delighted. They raised banners, flags, and banana trees, set out full water pots, and celebrated a great festival, saying, “Ah, what a gain for us!” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Monks, it is not only now that the great populace rejoices at Devadatta’s death; they rejoiced in the past as well.” Then, to show how the great populace rejoiced when a king named Piṅgala, who was unloved by all people, cruel, and harsh, died in Bārāṇasī, he related the following:

“Sabbo jano hiṃsito piṅgalena,

Tasmiṃ mate paccayā vedayanti;

Piyo nu te āsi akaṇhanetto,

Kasmā tuvaṃ rodasi dvārapāla.

“All the people were tormented by Piṅgala; now that he is dead, they express their joy. Was he, the tawny-eyed one, dear to you? Why do you weep, O gatekeeper?”

“Na [P 1.0150] me piyo āsi akaṇhanetto,

Bhāyāmi paccāgamanāya tassa;

Ito gato hiṃseyya maccurājaṃ,

So hiṃsito āneyya puna idhā”ti. (jā. 1.2.179-180) –

“The tawny-eyed one was not dear to me; I am afraid of his return. For, having gone from here, he might torment the King of Death, and he, being tormented, might bring him back here again.”

Idaṃ piṅgalajātakaṃ kathesi. Bhikkhū satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu – “idāni, bhante, devadatto kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti? “Avīcimahāniraye, bhikkhave”ti. “Bhante, idha tappanto vicaritvā puna gantvā tappanaṭṭhāneyeva nibbatto”ti. “Āma, bhikkhave, pabbajitā vā hontu gahaṭṭhā vā, pamādavihārino ubhayattha tappantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

He related this Piṅgala Jātaka. The monks asked the Teacher: “Now, venerable sir, where has Devadatta been reborn?” “In the great Avīci hell, monks.” “Venerable sir, having wandered about here in torment, has he gone and been reborn in that very place of torment?” “Yes, monks. Whether they are renunciates or householders, those who live heedlessly are tormented in both states,” he said, and recited this verse:

17.

17.

“Idha [V 1.0088][M 1.0097] tappati pecca tappati, pāpakārī ubhayattha tappati;

Pāpaṃ me katanti tappati, bhiyyo tappati duggatiṃ gato”ti.

“Here he is tormented, hereafter he is tormented; the evil-doer is tormented in both states. He is tormented, thinking, ‘Evil has been done by me.’ Having gone to a woeful state, he is tormented all the more.”

Tattha idha tappatīti idha kammatappanena domanassamattena tappati. Peccāti paraloke pana vipākatappanena atidāruṇena apāyadukkhena tappati. Pāpakārīti nānappakārassa pāpassa kattā. Ubhayatthāti iminā vuttappakārena tappanena ubhayattha tappati nāma. Pāpaṃ meti so hi kammatappanena kappanto “pāpaṃ me kata”nti tappati. Taṃ appamattakaṃ tappanaṃ, vipākatappanena pana tappanto bhiyyo tappati duggatiṃ gato atipharusena tappanena ativiya tappatīti.

Therein, “here he is tormented” means that here, he is tormented by the torment of his kamma, which is a state of mental distress. “Hereafter” means that in the next world, he is tormented by the torment of the result, which is the extremely harsh suffering of the lower realms. “The evil-doer” is one who performs various kinds of evil. “In both states” means he is tormented in both states by this torment of the kind described. “Evil has been done by me” means that, being tormented by the torment of his kamma, he is tormented, thinking, “Evil has been done by me.” That torment is minor, but being tormented by the torment of the result, having gone to a woeful state, he is tormented all the more; he is tormented exceedingly by an extremely harsh torment.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the verse, many became stream-enterers and so on. The teaching was beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Devadattavatthu dvādasamaṃ.

The twelfth story, concerning Devadatta.

13. Sumanādevīvatthu

13. The Story of Sumanādevī

Idha [P 1.0151] nandatīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sumanādeviṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Here one rejoices”—this Dhamma discourse was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Sumanādevī.

Sāvatthiyañhi devasikaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa gehe dve bhikkhūsahassāni bhuñjanti, tathā visākhāya mahāupāsikāya. Sāvatthiyaṃ yo yo dānaṃ dātukāmo hoti, so so tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ okāsaṃ labhitvāva karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? “Tumhākaṃ dānaggaṃ anāthapiṇḍiko vā visākhā vā āgatā”ti pucchitvā, “nāgatā”ti vutte satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā katadānampi “kiṃ dānaṃ nāmeta”nti garahanti. Ubhopi hi te bhikkhusaṅghassa ruciñca anucchavikakiccāni ca ativiya jānanti, tesu vicārentesu bhikkhū cittarūpaṃ bhuñjanti. Tasmā sabbe dānaṃ dātukāmā te gahetvāva gacchanti. Iti te attano attano ghare bhikkhū parivisituṃ na labhanti. Tato visākhā, “ko nu kho mama ṭhāne ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisissatī”ti upadhārentī puttassa dhītaraṃ disvā taṃ attano ṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā tassā nivesane bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisati. Anāthapiṇḍikopi mahāsubhaddaṃ nāma jeṭṭhadhītaraṃ ṭhapesi. Sā bhikkhūnaṃ [M 1.0098] veyyāvaccaṃ karontī dhammaṃ suṇantī sotāpannā hutvā patikulaṃ agamāsi. Tato cūḷasubhaddaṃ ṭhapesi. Sāpi tatheva karontī sotāpannā hutvā patikulaṃ gatā. Atha sumanadeviṃ nāma kaniṭṭhadhītaraṃ ṭhapesi. Sā pana dhammaṃ sutvā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā kumārikāva hutvā tathārūpena [P 1.0152] aphāsukena āturā āhārupacchedaṃ katvā [V 1.0089] pitaraṃ daṭṭhukāmā hutvā pakkosāpesi. So ekasmiṃ dānagge tassā sāsanaṃ sutvāva āgantvā, “kiṃ, amma sumane”ti āha. Sāpi naṃ āha – “kiṃ, tāta kaniṭṭhabhātikā”ti? “Vilapasi ammā”ti? “Na vilapāmi, kaniṭṭhabhātikā”ti. “Bhāyasi, ammā”ti? “Na bhāyāmi, kaniṭṭhabhātikā”ti. Ettakaṃ vatvāyeva pana sā kālamakāsi. So sotāpannopi samāno seṭṭhidhītari uppannasokaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto dhītu sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā rodanto satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “kiṃ, gahapati, dukkhī dummano assumukho rodamāno āgatosī”ti vutte, “dhītā me, bhante, sumanadevī kālakatā”ti āha. “Atha kasmā socasi, nanu sabbesaṃ ekaṃsikaṃ maraṇa”nti? “Jānāmetaṃ, bhante, evarūpā nāma me hiriottappasampannā dhītā, sā maraṇakāle satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontī vilapamānā matā, tena me anappakaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana tāya kathitaṃ mahāseṭṭhī”ti? “Ahaṃ taṃ, bhante, ‘amma, sumane’ti āmantesiṃ. Atha maṃ āha – ‘kiṃ, tāta, kaniṭṭhabhātikā’ti? ‘Vilapasi, ammā’ti? ‘Na vilapāmi, kaniṭṭhabhātikā’ti. ‘Bhāyasi, ammā’ti? ‘Na bhāyāmi kaniṭṭhabhātikā’ti. Ettakaṃ vatvā kālamakāsī”ti. Atha naṃ bhagavā āha – “na te mahāseṭṭhi dhītā vilapatī”ti. “Atha kasmā bhante evamāhā”ti? “Kaniṭṭhattāyeva[P 1.0153]. Dhītā hi te, gahapati, maggaphalehi tayā mahallikā. Tvañhi sotāpanno, dhītā pana te sakadāgāminī. Sā maggaphalehi tayā mahallikattā taṃ evamāhā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti? “Evaṃ, gahapatī”ti. “Idāni kuhiṃ nibbattā, bhante”ti? “Tusitabhavane, gahapatī”ti. “Bhante, mama dhītā idha ñātakānaṃ antare nandamānā vicaritvā ito gantvāpi nandanaṭṭhāneyeva nibbattā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “āma, gahapati, appamattā nāma gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā idha loke ca paraloke ca nandantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, in Sāvatthī, two thousand monks ate daily in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, and likewise in the house of the great lay devotee Visākhā. In Sāvatthī, whoever wished to give alms would do so only after getting an opportunity from both of them. What was the reason? If, after asking, “Did Anāthapiṇḍika or Visākhā come to your almsgiving hall?” they were told, “They did not come,” people would criticize even an almsgiving for which a hundred thousand had been spent, saying, “What kind of almsgiving is this?” For both of them knew exceedingly well the preferences of the Saṅgha of monks and the appropriate duties. When they were managing things, the monks ate according to their liking. Therefore, all who wished to give alms would take them along. Thus, they did not get the opportunity to serve the monks in their own homes. Then Visākhā, considering, “Who, I wonder, will stand in my place and serve the Saṅgha of monks?” saw her son’s daughter and appointed her in her own place. She served the Saṅgha of monks in Visākhā’s residence. Anāthapiṇḍika also appointed his eldest daughter, named Mahāsubhaddā. While performing services for the monks and listening to the Dhamma, she became a stream-enterer and went to her husband’s home. After that, he appointed Cūḷasubhaddā. She too, doing just as her sister had, became a stream-enterer and went to her husband’s home. Then he appointed his youngest daughter, named Sumanādevī. She, however, having heard the Dhamma, attained the fruit of a once-returner. While still a young maiden, she was afflicted by such an illness that she had to stop taking food. Wishing to see her father, she had him summoned. He was at an almsgiving hall when he heard her message and came at once, asking, “What is it, my dear Sumanā?” She, in turn, said to him, “What is it, dear younger brother?” “Are you delirious, my dear?” “I am not delirious, younger brother.” “Are you afraid, my dear?” “I am not afraid, younger brother.” Having said only this much, she passed away. Though he was a stream-enterer, the great merchant was unable to endure the sorrow that arose concerning his daughter. Having had her funeral rites performed, he went weeping to the Teacher. When the Teacher asked, “Why, householder, have you come grieving, distressed, with a tearful face, and weeping?” he replied, “Venerable sir, my daughter, Sumanādevī, has passed away.” “Then why do you grieve? Is not death surely inevitable for all?” “I know this, venerable sir. But my daughter, who was so endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, died at the moment of death unable to establish mindfulness, speaking deliriously. Because of that, immeasurable distress arises in me.” “But what did she say, great merchant?” “Venerable sir, I addressed her, ‘My dear Sumanā.’ Then she said to me, ‘What is it, dear younger brother?’ ‘Are you delirious, my dear?’ ‘I am not delirious, younger brother.’ ‘Are you afraid, my dear?’ ‘I am not afraid, younger brother.’ Having said this much, she passed away.” Then the Blessed One said to him, “Great merchant, your daughter was not delirious.” “Then why, venerable sir, did she speak in that way?” “It was on account of your being younger. Indeed, householder, your daughter was your senior in terms of the path and its fruits. For you are a stream-enterer, but your daughter was a once-returner. Because she was your senior in terms of the path and its fruits, she spoke to you in that way.” “Is that so, venerable sir?” “It is so, householder.” “Where has she been reborn now, venerable sir?” “In the Tusita realm, householder.” “Venerable sir, my daughter, having lived here rejoicing among her relatives, has gone from here and been reborn in a place of rejoicing.” Then the Teacher said to him, “Yes, householder. The heedful, whether they are householders or renunciates, rejoice in this world and in the next,” and he spoke this verse:

18.

18.

“Idha [M 1.0099] nandati pecca nandati, katapuñño ubhayattha nandati;

Puññaṃ me katanti nandati, bhiyyo nandati suggatiṃ gato”ti.

Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices; one who has made merit rejoices in both places. He rejoices, thinking, 'Merit has been made by me'; having gone to a good destination, he rejoices all the more.

Tattha idhāti idha loke kammanandanena nandati. Peccāti paraloke vipākanandanena nandati. Katapuññoti nānappakārassa puññassa kattā. Ubhayatthāti idha “kataṃ me kusalaṃ, akataṃ me pāpa”nti nandati, parattha vipākaṃ anubhavanto nandati. Puññaṃ meti idha nandanto pana “puññaṃ me kata”nti somanassamatteneva kammanandanaṃ upādāya nandati. Bhiyyoti vipākanandanena pana sugatiṃ gato sattapaññāsavassakoṭiyo saṭṭhivassasatasahassāni dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanto tusitapure ativiya nandatīti.

Therein, 'idhā' means: in this world, he rejoices with the joy of action. 'Peccā' means: in the next world, he rejoices with the joy of the result. 'One who has made merit' means: a doer of various kinds of merit. 'In both places' means: here he rejoices, thinking, 'I have done good, I have not done evil,' and hereafter, while experiencing the result, he rejoices. 'Merit has been made by me' means: while rejoicing here, based on the joy of action, he rejoices with the mere mental satisfaction of 'Merit has been made by me.' 'All the more' means: with the joy of the result, having gone to a good destination, he rejoices exceedingly in the Tusita celestial realm, experiencing divine bliss for fifty-seven crores and sixty hundred thousand years.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0090][P 1.0154] bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and so on. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Sumanādevīvatthu terasamaṃ.

The thirteenth story, the Account of Sumanādevī, is concluded.

14. Dvesahāyakabhikkhuvatthu

14. The Account of the Two Companion Monks

Bahumpi ceti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve sahāyake ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Bahumpi ce,' concerning two companion monks.

Sāvatthivāsino hi dve kulaputtā sahāyakā vihāraṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā kāme pahāya sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā pañca vassāni ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike vasitvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā sāsane dhuraṃ pucchitvā vipassanādhurañca ganthadhurañca vitthārato sutvā eko tāva “ahaṃ, bhante, mahallakakāle pabbajito na sakkhissāmi ganthadhuraṃ pūretuṃ, vipassanādhuraṃ pana pūressāmī”ti yāva arahattā vipassanādhuraṃ kathāpetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Itaro pana “ahaṃ ganthadhuraṃ pūressāmī”ti anukkamena tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā gatagataṭṭhāne dhammaṃ katheti, sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇati, pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ dhammaṃ vācento vicarati. Aṭṭhārasannaṃ mahāgaṇānaṃ ācariyo ahosi. Bhikkhū satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [M 1.0100] itarassa therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tassa ovāde ṭhatvā arahattaṃ patvā theraṃ vanditvā, “satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmamhā”ti [P 1.0155] vadanti. Thero “gacchatha, āvuso, mama vacanena satthāraṃ vanditvā asīti mahāthere vandatha, sahāyakattherampi me ‘amhākaṃ ācariyo tumhe vandatī’ti vadathā”ti peseti. Te bhikkhū vihāraṃ gantvā satthārañceva asīti mahāthere ca vanditvā ganthikattherassa santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, amhākaṃ ācariyo tumhe vandatī”ti vadanti. Itarena ca “ko nāma so”ti vutte, “tumhākaṃ sahāyakabhikkhu, bhante”ti vadanti. Evaṃ there punappunaṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇante so bhikkhu thokaṃ kālaṃ sahitvā aparabhāge sahituṃ asakkonto “amhākaṃ ācariyo tumhe vandatī”ti vutte, “ko eso”ti vatvā “tumhākaṃ sahāyakabhikkhū”ti vutte, “kiṃ pana tumhehi tassa santike uggahitaṃ, kiṃ dīghanikāyādīsu aññataro nikāyo, kiṃ tīsu piṭakesu ekaṃ piṭaka”nti vatvā “catuppadikampi gāthaṃ na jānāti, paṃsukūlaṃ gahetvā pabbajitakāleyeva araññaṃ paviṭṭho, bahū vata antevāsike labhi, tassa āgatakāle mayā pañhaṃ pucchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintesi.

Indeed, in Sāvatthī, two men of good family, who were companions, went to the monastery, listened to the Teacher’s teaching, renounced sensual pleasures, dedicated themselves to the Dispensation, and went forth. After staying for five years under their teachers and preceptors, they approached the Teacher and inquired about their duties in the Dispensation. Having heard in detail about the duty of insight meditation and the duty of study, one of them said, "Venerable sir, I went forth in old age. I will not be able to fulfill the duty of study, but I will fulfill the duty of insight meditation." Having had the duty of insight meditation explained to him up to Arahantship, striving and exerting himself, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The other monk, however, thinking, "I will fulfill the duty of study," gradually mastered the three baskets of the Buddha’s word. He taught the Dhamma wherever he went, recited in a melodious voice, and traveled instructing five hundred monks. He became the teacher of eighteen great groups. Monks who received meditation subjects from the Teacher would go to the dwelling place of the other elder, follow his advice, attain Arahantship, pay homage to the elder, and say, "We wish to see the Teacher." The elder would send them off, saying, "Go, friends. Pay homage to the Teacher in my name, and also pay homage to the eighty great elders. Tell my companion elder that our teacher pays homage to you." The monks would go to the monastery, pay homage to the Teacher and the eighty great elders, and then approach the elder who was devoted to study, saying, "Venerable sir, our teacher pays homage to you." When asked, "Who is he?" they would reply, "Your companion monk, venerable sir." Though the elder repeatedly sent such messages, the monk could endure it only for a short time. Later, unable to bear it, when told, "Our teacher pays homage to you," he would ask, "Who is he?" and when told, "Your companion monk," he would ask, "Well now, what have you learned from him? Any one of the Nikāyas, such as the Dīgha Nikāya, or one of the three Piṭakas?" Then he thought, "He doesn’t even know a four-line verse. He entered the forest wearing a rag-robe right after ordination. He has gained many disciples! When he comes, it will be fitting for me to question him."

Atha aparabhāge thero satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgato. Sahāyakassa therassa santike pattacīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā [V 1.0091] gantvā satthārañceva asīti mahāthere ca vanditvā sahāyakassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paccāgami. Athassa so vattaṃ kāretvā samappamāṇaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā, “pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā “esa evarūpaṃ mama puttaṃ viheṭhetvā niraye nibbatteyyā”ti tasmiṃ anukampāya vihāracārikaṃ caranto viya tesaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Tattha tattha nisīdantā hi bhikkhū buddhāsanaṃ paññāpetvāva nisīdanti. Tena [P 1.0156] satthā pakatipaññatteyeva āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho pana ganthikabhikkhuṃ paṭhamajjhāne pañhaṃ pucchitvā tasmiṃ akathite dutiyajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā aṭṭhasupi samāpattīsu rūpārūpesu ca pañhaṃ pucchi. Ganthikatthero ekampi kathetuṃ nāsakkhi. Itaro taṃ sabbaṃ kathesi. Atha naṃ sotāpattimagge pañhaṃ pucchi. Ganthikatthero kathetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato khīṇāsavattheraṃ pucchi. Thero kathesi. Satthā “sādhu sādhu, bhikkhū”ti abhinanditvā sesamaggesupi paṭipāṭiyā [M 1.0101] pañhaṃ pucchi. Ganthiko ekampi kathetuṃ nāsakkhi, khīṇāsavo pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ kathesi. Satthā catūsupi ṭhānesu tassa sādhukāraṃ adāsi. Taṃ sutvā bhummadeve ādiṃ katvā yāva brahmalokā sabbā devatā ceva nāgasupaṇṇā ca sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ sādhukāraṃ sutvā tassa antevāsikā ceva saddhivihārino ca satthāraṃ ujjhāyiṃsu – “kiṃ nāmetaṃ satthārā kataṃ, kiñci ajānantassa mahallakattherassa catūsu ṭhānesu sādhukāraṃ adāsi, amhākaṃ panācariyassa sabbapariyattidharassa pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pāmokkhassa pasaṃsāmattampi na karī”ti. Atha ne satthā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, bhikkhave, kathethā”ti pucchitvā tasmiṃ atthe ārocite, “bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ ācariyo mama sāsane bhatiyā gāvo rakkhaṇasadiso, mayhaṃ pana putto yathāruciyā pañca gorase paribhuñjanakasāmisadiso”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then, at a later time, the elder came to see the Teacher. Having left his bowl and robe near his companion elder, he went to pay homage to the Teacher and the eighty great elders, then returned to his companion’s dwelling place. The resident monk then had the visitor perform his duties, arranged a seat of equal size, and sat down thinking, 'I will ask a question.' At that moment, the Teacher, out of compassion for him—thinking, 'This one, by harassing such a son of mine, might be reborn in hell'—walked as if on a tour of the monastery, went to where they were seated, and sat down on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat. Indeed, wherever monks sit, they first prepare a Buddha-seat and then sit down. Thus, the Teacher sat on the seat that had been prepared as was customary. After sitting down, he asked the monk devoted to the scriptures a question about the first jhāna. When that monk answered it, he proceeded to ask about the second jhāna and so on, up to the eight attainments, as well as questions on the form and formless realms. The scripturalist answered all of them. Then the Teacher asked him a question about the path of stream-entry. The elder devoted to the scriptures could not answer it. Next, he asked the elder who was an arahant. That elder answered it. The Teacher, expressing his approval with 'Excellent, excellent, monk,' then proceeded to ask questions about the remaining paths in order. The one devoted to the scriptures could not answer even one, while the arahant answered each question as it was asked. The Teacher gave his approval to him in all four instances. Hearing this, the earth deities and all the devas up to the Brahma-world, along with the nāgas and supaṇṇas, also expressed their approval. Hearing this praise, the pupils and co-residents of the scripturalist monk complained about the Teacher: 'What is this that the Teacher has done? He gave approval in all four instances to that old elder who knows nothing, but for our teacher—who has mastered all the scriptures and is the leader of five hundred monks—he did not offer even a word of praise!' Then the Teacher asked them, 'Monks, what is this you are saying?' When they explained the matter, he said, 'Monks, your teacher in my dispensation is like a cowherd hired for wages, while my son is like the owner who enjoys the five products of the cow at will.' And he spoke these verses:

19.

19.

“Bahumpi [P 1.0157] ce saṃhita bhāsamāno,

Na takkaro hoti naro pamatto;

Gopova gāvo gaṇayaṃ paresaṃ,

Na bhāgavā sāmaññassa hoti.

Though one recites many scriptures, if, being heedless, one does not act accordingly, like a cowherd counting others' cattle, one does not share in the blessings of the ascetic life.

20.

20.

“Appampi ce saṃhita bhāsamāno,

Dhammassa hoti anudhammacārī;

Rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ,

Sammappajāno suvimuttacitto.

“Anupādiyāno [V 1.0092] idha vā huraṃ vā,

Sa bhāgavā sāmaññassa hotī”ti.

Even if one recites few scriptures, but lives in accordance with the Dhamma, abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion, with right understanding and a well-liberated mind—not clinging to anything here or hereafter, one is a sharer in the blessings of the ascetic life.

Tattha saṃhitanti tepiṭakassa buddhavacanassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Taṃ ācariye upasaṅkamitvā uggaṇhitvā bahumpi paresaṃ bhāsamāno vācento taṃ dhammaṃ sutvā yaṃ kārakena puggalena kattabbaṃ, takkaro na hoti. Kukkuṭassa pakkhapaharaṇamattampi aniccādivasena yonisomanasikāraṃ nappavatteti. Eso yathā nāma divasaṃ bhatiyā gāvo rakkhanto gopo pātova niravasesaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sāyaṃ gahetvā sāmikānaṃ niyyādetvā divasabhatimattaṃ gaṇhāti, yathāruciyā pana pañca gorase paribhuñjituṃ [M 1.0102] na labhati, evameva kevalaṃ antevāsikānaṃ santikā vattapaṭivattakaraṇamattassa bhāgī hoti, sāmaññassa pana bhāgī na hoti. Yathā pana gopālakena niyyāditānaṃ [P 1.0158] gunnaṃ gorasaṃ sāmikāva paribhuñjanti, tathā tena kathitaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā kārakapuggalā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjitvā keci paṭhamajjhānādīni pāpuṇanti, keci vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggaphalāni pāpuṇanti, goṇasāmikā gorasasseva sāmaññassa bhāgino honti.

Therein, 'saṃhita' is a name for the word of the Buddha, the Tipiṭaka. Having approached teachers and learned it, though one may speak and teach it extensively to others, if one does not oneself do what ought to be done by a practitioner, one is not a doer of it. One does not arouse wise attention by way of impermanence and so forth, even for a moment as long as the flapping of a chicken's wing. Just as a cowherd who guards cattle for a wage for the whole day, having accepted them all in the morning, brings them back in the evening and hands them over to the owners, receives only the day's wage and does not get to enjoy the five products of the cow as he pleases; in the same way, that person becomes a partaker only of the performance of duties rendered by his pupils, but is not a partaker of the fruits of recluseship. And just as the owners alone enjoy the products of the cows tended by the cowherd, so too, having heard the Dhamma taught by that person, the striving individuals, practicing in accordance with the instruction—some attain the first jhāna and so on, while others develop insight and attain the paths and fruits. Just as the owners of the cattle are partakers of the products of the cow, so too do these practitioners become partakers of the fruits of recluseship.

Iti satthā sīlasampannassa bahussutassa pamādavihārino aniccādivasena yonisomanasikāre pamattassa bhikkhuno vasena paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ kathesi, na dussīlassa. Dutiyagāthā pana appassutassapi yonisomanasikāre kammaṃ karontassa kārakapuggalassa vasena kathitā.

Thus, the Teacher spoke the first verse with reference to a monk who is virtuous and learned, but who dwells heedlessly, being negligent in wise attention to impermanence and so forth—not with reference to an immoral person. The second verse, however, was spoken with reference to a practitioner who, though of little learning, engages in the practice with wise attention.

Tattha appampī ceti thokaṃ ekavaggadvivaggamattampi. Dhammassa hoti anudhammacārīti atthamaññāya dhammamaññāya navalokuttaradhammassa anurūpaṃ dhammaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ catupārisuddhisīladhutaṅgaasubhakammaṭṭhānādibhedaṃ caranto anudhammacārī hoti. So “ajja ajjevā”ti paṭivedhaṃ ākaṅkhanto vicarati. So imāya sammāpaṭipattiyā rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ sammā hetunā nayena parijānitabbe dhamme parijānanto tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ vasena suvimuttacitto, anupādiyāno idha vā huraṃ vāti idhalokaparalokapariyāpannā vā ajjhattikabāhirā vā khandhāyatanadhātuyo catūhi upādānehi anupādiyanto mahākhīṇāsavo maggasaṅkhātassa sāmaññassa vasena āgatassa phalasāmaññassa [P 1.0159] ceva pañcaasekkhadhammakkhandhassa ca bhāgavā hotīti ratanakūṭena viya agārassa arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhīti.

Therein, 'even a little' means a small amount, even just one or two chapters. As for 'one who is a follower of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma,' it means that by understanding the meaning and understanding the cause, one practices the Dhamma suitable for the nine supramundane Dhammas—that which is called the preliminary practice, distinguished as the fourfold purity of virtue, the ascetic practices, meditation on foulness, and so on. Because of such practice, one is called a follower of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. That person practices, desiring penetration, thinking, 'Today, this very day.' By this right practice, having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and fully understanding by the method with the right cause the dhammas that should be fully understood, one has a well-liberated mind by means of liberation by substitution, liberation by suppression, liberation by cutting off, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape. As for 'not clinging here or hereafter,' it means not clinging by the four kinds of clinging to the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—whether internal or external, whether included in this present life or the next. Such a one is a great Arahant. By means of the recluseship called the path and of the recluseship which is the fruit that has come from it, he becomes a partaker of the recluseship which is the five aggregates of one beyond training. Thus, like a palace with a jeweled pinnacle, He took the pinnacle of the teaching with Arahantship.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0093] bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and so on. The teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

Dvesahāyakabhikkhuvatthu cuddasamaṃ.

The fourteenth story, that of the two companion monks, is finished.

Yamakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yamaka Vagga is finished.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The first chapter is finished.

2. Appamādavaggo

2. The Chapter on Heedfulness

1. Sāmāvatīvatthu

1. The Story of Sāmāvatī

Appamādo [M 1.0103][V 1.0094][P 1.0161] amatapadanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā kosambiṃ upanissāya ghositārāme viharanto sāmāvatippamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ itthisatānaṃ, māgaṇḍiyappamukhānañca etissā pañcannaṃ ñātisatānaṃ maraṇabyasanaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling near Kosambī in the Ghositārāma monastery, taught this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless,' concerning the death and destruction of the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī, and of the five hundred relatives headed by Māgaṇḍiyā.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte allakapparaṭṭhe allakapparājā nāma, veṭhadīpakaraṭṭhe veṭhadīpakarājā nāmāti ime dve daharakālato paṭṭhāya sahāyakā hutvā ekācariyakule sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā attano attano pitūnaṃ accayena chattaṃ ussāpetvā āyāmena dasadasayojanike raṭṭhe rājāno ahesuṃ. Te kālena kālaṃ samāgantvā ekato tiṭṭhantā nisīdantā nipajjantā mahājanaṃ jāyamānañca jīyamānañca mīyamānañca disvā “paralokaṃ gacchantaṃ anugacchanto nāma natthi, antamaso [P 1.0162] attano sarīrampi nānugacchati, sabbaṃ pahāya gantabbaṃ, kiṃ no gharāvāsena, pabbajissāmā”ti mantetvā rajjāni puttadārānaṃ niyyādetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantappadese vasantā mantayiṃsu – “mayaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitā, na jīvituṃ asakkontā. Te mayaṃ ekaṭṭhāne vasantā apabbajitasadisāyeva homa, tasmā visuṃ vasissāma. Tvaṃ etasmiṃ pabbate vasa, ahaṃ imasmiṃ pabbate vasissāmi. Anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ pana uposathadivase ekato bhavissāmā”ti. Atha kho nesaṃ etadahosi – “evampi no gaṇasaṅgaṇikāva bhavissati, tvaṃ pana tava pabbate aggiṃ jāleyyāsi, ahaṃ mama pabbate aggiṃ jālessāmi, tāya saññāya atthibhāvaṃ jānissāmā”ti. Te tathā kariṃsu.

Herein, this is the story in sequence: In the past, in the country of Allakappa, there was a king named Allakapparājā, and in the country of Veṭhadīpaka, a king named Veṭhadīpakarājā. These two, having been friends from a young age, learned their craft in the household of a single teacher. After the passing of their respective fathers, they raised the royal umbrella and became kings in kingdoms of ten yojanas each. They would meet from time to time, and standing, sitting, and lying down together, they saw the great populace being born, aging, and dying. They reflected: 'There is no one who follows a person going to the next world; at the very least, not even one's own body follows. Everything must be abandoned before one goes. What use is the household life to us? We shall go forth.' Having thus deliberated, they entrusted their kingdoms to their sons and wives, went forth into the ascetic life, and while dwelling in the Himalayan region, they consulted: 'We have gone forth having abandoned our kingdoms, not because we were unable to make a living. If we live together in one place, we are just like those who have not gone forth. Therefore, we shall live separately. You live on that mountain, and I will live on this mountain. But every half-month, on the Uposatha day, we shall be together.' Then this thought occurred to them: 'Even so, there will still be association with a group for us. Instead, you should light a fire on your mountain, and I will light a fire on my mountain. By that sign, we shall know of each other's existence.' And they did so.

Atha aparabhāge veṭhadīpakatāpaso kālaṃ katvā mahesakkho devarājā hutvā nibbatto. Tato aḍḍhamāse sampatte aggiṃ adisvāva itaro “sahāyako me kālakato”ti aññāsi. Itaropi nibbattakkhaṇeyeva attano devasiriṃ oloketvā kammaṃ upadhārento nikkhamanato paṭṭhāya attano tapacariyaṃ disvā “gantvā mama sahāyakaṃ passissāmī”ti [M 1.0104] taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā maggikapuriso viya tassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ so [V 1.0095] āha – “kuto āgatosī”ti? “Maggikapuriso [P 1.0163] ahaṃ, bhante, dūratova āgatomhi. Kiṃ pana, bhante, ayyo imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekakova vasati, aññopi koci atthī”ti? “Atthi me eko sahāyako”ti. “Kuhiṃ so”ti? “Etasmiṃ pabbate vasati, uposathadivase pana aggiṃ na jāleti, mato nūna bhavissatī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Ahaṃ so, bhante”ti. “Kuhiṃ nibbattosī”ti? “Devaloke mahesakkho devarājā hutvā nibbattosmi, bhante, ‘ayyaṃ passissāmī’ti puna āgatomhi. Api nu kho ayyānaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ koci upaddavo atthī”ti? “Āma, āvuso, hatthī nissāya kilamāmī”ti. “Kiṃ vo, bhante, hatthī karontī”ti? “Sammajjanaṭṭhāne laṇḍaṃ pātenti, pādehi bhūmiyaṃ paharitvā paṃsuṃ uddharanti, svāhaṃ laṇḍaṃ chaḍḍento paṃsuṃ samaṃ karonto kilamāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana tesaṃ anāgamanaṃ icchathā”ti? “Āmāvuso”ti. “Tena hi tesaṃ anāgamanaṃ karissāmī”ti tāpasassa hatthikantavīṇañceva hatthikantamantañca adāsi. Dadanto ca pana vīṇāya tisso tantiyo dassetvā tayo mante uggaṇhāpetvā “imaṃ tantiṃ paharitvā imasmiṃ mante vutte nivattitvā oloketumpi asakkontā hatthī palāyanti, imaṃ tantiṃ paharitvā imasmiṃ mante vutte nivattitvā pacchato olokentā olokentā palāyanti, imaṃ tantiṃ paharitvā imasmiṃ mante vutte hatthiyūthapati piṭṭhiṃ upanāmento āgacchatī”ti ācikkhitvā, “yaṃ vo ruccati, taṃ kareyyāthā”ti [P 1.0164] vatvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā pakkāmi. Tāpaso palāyanamantaṃ vatvā palāyanatantiṃ paharitvā hatthī palāpetvā vasi.

Then, at a later time, the ascetic Veṭhadīpaka passed away and was reborn as a mighty deva king. When half a month had passed, not seeing the fire, the other ascetic knew, “My companion has passed away.” At the very moment of his rebirth, the other one, observing his divine glory, reflecting on his kamma, and perceiving his ascetic practice from the time of his going forth, thought, “I shall go and see my companion.” He abandoned that existence and, like a traveler, went to the ascetic's presence. Having paid homage, he stood to one side. Then the ascetic asked him, “Whence have you come?” “I am a traveler, venerable sir, who has come from afar. But, venerable sir, does the noble one dwell alone in this place, or is there anyone else?” “I have one companion.” “Where is he?” “He lives on this mountain, but on the Uposatha day he does not light the fire. Surely he must have died.” “Is that so, venerable sir?” “Yes, friend.” “I am he, venerable sir.” “Where were you reborn?” “I was reborn in the deva world as a mighty deva king, venerable sir. Thinking, ‘I shall see the noble one,’ I have come again. But is there any trouble for the noble ones dwelling in this place?” “Yes, friend. I am troubled on account of the elephants.” “What do the elephants do to you, venerable sir?” “They drop dung in the sweeping place, strike the ground with their feet, and raise up dust. I grow weary removing the dung and leveling the dust.” “Do you wish for them not to come?” “Yes, friend.” “Then I shall bring about their not coming.” He gave the ascetic a lute charming to elephants and a spell charming to elephants. As he gave them, he showed the three strings of the lute and taught the three spells: “When this string is struck and this spell is recited, the elephants will flee without even being able to turn and look back. When this string is struck and this spell is recited, they will turn back and flee while looking behind them again and again. When this string is struck and this spell is recited, the leader of the elephant herd will come, offering his back.” Having instructed him thus, he said, “Do as you please,” paid homage to the ascetic, and departed. The ascetic, reciting the spell for making them flee and striking the string for making them flee, made the elephants flee and dwelt there.

Tasmiṃ samaye kosambiyaṃ pūrantappo nāma rājā hoti. So ekadivasaṃ gabbhiniyā deviyā saddhiṃ bālasūriyatapaṃ tappamāno abbhokāsatale nisīdi. Devī rañño pārupanaṃ satasahassagghanikaṃ rattakambalaṃ pārupitvā nisinnā raññā saddhiṃ samullapamānā rañño aṅgulito satasahassagghanikaṃ rājamuddikaṃ nīharitvā attano aṅguliyaṃ pilandhi. Tasmiṃ samaye hatthiliṅgasakuṇo ākāsena gacchanto dūrato rattakambalapārupanaṃ deviṃ disvā “maṃsapesī”ti saññāya pakkhe vissajjetvā otari. Rājā [M 1.0105] tassa otaraṇasaddena bhīto uṭṭhāya antonivesanaṃ pāvisi. Devī garugabbhatāya ceva bhīrukajātikatāya ca vegena gantuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ so sakuṇo ajjhappatto nakhapañjare nisīdāpetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Te kira sakuṇā pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhārenti. Tasmā ākāsena netvā yathārucitaṭṭhāne nisīditvā maṃsaṃ khādanti. Sāpi tena nīyamānā maraṇabhayabhītā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ viravissāmi, manussasaddo nāma tiracchānagatānaṃ ubbejanīyo, taṃ sutvā maṃ chaḍḍessati. Evaṃ sante [V 1.0096] saha gabbhena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissāmi, yasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nisīditvā maṃ khādituṃ ārabhissati, tatra naṃ saddaṃ katvā palāpessāmī”ti. Sā attano paṇḍitatāya adhivāsesi.

At that time, in Kosambī, there was a king named Pūrantappa. One day, while basking in the morning sun with his pregnant queen, he sat in an open space. The queen, wearing the king's red woolen cloak worth a hundred thousand, sat conversing with the king. She removed a royal signet ring worth a hundred thousand from the king’s finger and placed it on her own. At that moment, a Hatthiliṅga bird, flying through the sky, saw the queen from a distance wrapped in the red woolen cloak and, perceiving her as a piece of meat, released its wings and descended. The king, frightened by the sound of its descent, got up and entered the inner palace. The queen, due to her heavy pregnancy and being of a timid nature, could not move quickly. Then the bird seized her, set her in the cage of its talons, and flew into the sky. It is said that these birds possess the strength of five elephants. Therefore, carrying their prey through the air, they settle in a place of their liking and eat the flesh. As she was being carried, terrified by the fear of death, the queen thought: “If I scream, the sound of a human voice is alarming to animals, and hearing it, it will drop me. In that case, I will perish along with the child in my womb. But in whatever place it settles down to begin eating me, there I will make a sound and cause it to flee.” Through her wisdom, she endured.

Tadā ca himavantapadese thokaṃ vaḍḍhitvā maṇḍapākārena [P 1.0165] ṭhito eko mahānigrodho hoti. So sakuṇo migarūpādīni tattha netvā khādati, tasmā tampi tattheva netvā viṭapabbhantare ṭhapetvā āgatamaggaṃ olokesi. Āgatamaggolokanaṃ kira tesaṃ dhammatā. Tasmiṃ khaṇe devī, “idāni imaṃ palāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā ubho hatthe ukkhipitvā pāṇisaddañceva mukhasaddañca katvā taṃ palāpesi. Athassā sūriyatthaṅgamanakāle gabbhe kammajavātā caliṃsu. Sabbadisāsu gajjanto mahāmegho uṭṭhahi. Sukhedhitāya rājamahesiyā “mā bhāyi, ayye”ti vacanamattampi alabhamānāya dukkhaparetāya sabbarattiṃ niddā nāma nāhosi. Vibhātāya pana rattiyā valāhakavigamo ca aruṇuggamanañca tassā gabbhavuṭṭhānañca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Sā meghautuñca pabbatautuñca aruṇautuñca gahetvā jātattā puttassa utenoti nāmaṃ akāsi.

Now at that time, in the region of the Himalayas, there was a great banyan tree that had grown somewhat to stand in the manner of a pavilion. That bird would bring prey such as deer there to eat. Therefore, it brought her there as well, placed her in a fork of the branches, and looked back at the path by which it had come. It is said that looking back at the path one has come by is their nature. At that moment, the queen thought, “Now is the time to make it flee.” Raising both hands, she made the sound of clapping and the sound of shouting, and caused it to flee. Then, at sunset, the kamma-born winds stirred in her womb. A great, thundering cloud rose in all directions. For the chief queen, who had been raised in comfort, not obtaining even a mere word such as, “Do not fear, noble lady,” and being overcome by suffering, there was no sleep at all that night. But when the night had dawned, the dispersal of the clouds, the rising of the dawn, and her delivery from the womb all happened in a single moment. Because he was born taking from the condition of the clouds, the condition of the mountain, and the condition of the dawn, she gave her son the name Utena.

Allakappatāpasassapi kho tato avidūre vasanaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. So pakatiyāva vassadivase sītabhayena phalāphalatthāya vanaṃ na pavisati, taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā sakuṇehi khāditamaṃsānaṃ aṭṭhiṃ āharitvā koṭṭetvā rasaṃ katvā pivati. Tasmā taṃ divasaṃ “aṭṭhiṃ āharissāmī”ti tattha gantvā rukkhamūle aṭṭhiṃ pariyesento [P 1.0166] upari dārakasaddaṃ sutvā ullokento deviṃ disvā “kāsi tva”nti vatvā “mānusitthimhī”ti. “Kathaṃ āgatāsī”ti? “Hatthiliṅgasakuṇenānītāmhī”ti vutte “otarāhī”ti āha[M 1.0106]. “Jātisambhedato bhāyāmi, ayyā”ti. “Kāsi tva”nti? “Khattiyāmhī”ti. “Ahampi khattiyoyevā”ti. “Tena hi khattiyamāyaṃ kathehī”ti. So khattiyamāyaṃ kathesi. “Tena hi āruyha puttaṃ me otārehī”ti. So ekena passena abhiruhanamaggaṃ katvā abhiruhitvā dārakaṃ gaṇhi. “Mā maṃ hatthena chupī”ti ca vutte taṃ achupitvāva dārakaṃ otāresi. Devīpi otari. Atha naṃ assamapadaṃ netvā sīlabhedaṃ akatvāva anukampāya paṭijaggi, nimmakkhikamadhuṃ āharitvā sayaṃjātasāliṃ āharitvā yāguṃ pacitvā adāsi. Evaṃ tasmiṃ paṭijaggante sā aparabhāge cintesi – “ahaṃ neva āgatamaggaṃ jānāmi, na gamanamaggaṃ jānāmi, imināpi me saddhiṃ vissāsamattampi natthi. Sace panāyaṃ amhe pahāya katthaci gamissati, ubhopi idheva maraṇaṃ pāpuṇissāma, yaṃkiñci katvā imassa sīlaṃ bhinditvā yathā maṃ [V 1.0097] na muñcati, tathā taṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Atha naṃ dunnivatthaduppārutadassanena palobhetvā sīlavināsaṃ pāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya dvepi samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu.

The dwelling place of the ascetic Allakappa was also not far from that banyan tree. By nature, on a rainy day, out of fear of the cold, he would not enter the forest for fruits; instead, he would go to the foot of that tree, fetch the bones of the flesh eaten by the great bird, crush them, make a broth, and drink it. Therefore, on that day, thinking, "I will fetch a bone," he went there and, while searching for a bone at the foot of the tree, he heard the sound of a child from above. Looking up, he saw the queen and asked, "Who are you?" She replied, "I am a human woman." "How did you come here?" he asked. When she answered, "I was brought by the Hatthiliṅga bird," he said, "Descend." She replied, "I fear the breaking of my caste, venerable sir." He asked, "Of what caste are you?" She said, "I am of the warrior caste." He said, "I too am of the warrior caste." She said, "If that is so, then speak the secret lore of the warrior caste." He spoke the secret lore of the warrior caste. She said, "If that is so, climb up and bring down my son." He made a path for climbing on one side, climbed up, and took the child. When she said, "Do not touch me with your hand," he brought the child down without touching her. The queen also descended. Then, leading her to his hermitage, without breaking his moral precept, he cared for her out of compassion; he brought honey free from bees, brought naturally grown Sāli rice, cooked gruel, and gave it to her. While he was caring for her in this way, she later thought: "I do not know the path by which I came, nor do I know the path to go. I do not have even the slightest familiarity with this man. If he abandons us and goes somewhere, we both will die right here. I must do something to destroy this man's moral precept so that he will not leave me." Then, tempting him by showing herself improperly dressed and covered, she caused the destruction of his moral precept. From that day on, the two of them lived together in harmony.

Athekadivasaṃ tāpaso nakkhattayogaṃ ullokento pūrantappassa nakkhattamilāyanaṃ disvā “bhadde kosambiyaṃ pūrantapparājā [P 1.0167] mato”ti āha. “Kasmā, ayya, evaṃ vadesi? Kiṃ te tena saddhiṃ āghāto atthī”ti? “Natthi, bhadde, nakkhattamilāyanamassa disvā evaṃ vadāmī”ti, sā parodi. Atha naṃ “kasmā rodasī”ti pucchitvā tāya tassa attano sāmikabhāve akkhāte āha – “mā, bhadde, rodi, jātassa nāma niyato maccū”ti. “Jānāmi, ayyā”ti vutte “atha kasmā rodasī”ti? “Putto me kulasantakassa rajjassa anucchaviko, ‘sace tatra abhavissa, setacchattaṃ ussāpayissa. Idāni mahājāniko vata jāto’ti sokena rodāmi, ayyā”ti. “Hotu, bhadde, mā cintayi, sacassa rajjaṃ patthesi, ahamassa rajjalabhanākāraṃ karissāmī”ti. Athassa hatthikantavīṇañceva hatthikantamante ca adāsi. Tadā anekāni hatthisahassāni āgantvā vaṭarukkhamūle nisīdanti. Atha naṃ āha – “hatthīsu anāgatesuyeva rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā tesu āgatesu imaṃ mantaṃ vatvā imaṃ tantiṃ pahara, sabbe nivattitvā oloketumpi asakkontā palāyissanti, atha otaritvā āgaccheyyāsī”ti. So tathā katvā āgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ dutiyadivase āha – “ajja imaṃ mantaṃ vatvā imaṃ tantiṃ pahareyyāsi[M 1.0107], sabbe nivattitvā olokentā palāyissantī”ti. Tadāpi tathā katvā āgantvā ārocesi[P 1.0168]. Atha naṃ tatiyadivase āha – “ajja imaṃ mantaṃ vatvā imaṃ tantiṃ pahareyyāsi, yūthapati piṭṭhiṃ upanāmento āgamissatī”ti. Tadāpi tathā katvā ārocesi.

Then one day, the ascetic, while observing the conjunction of the stars, saw the fading of Pūrantappa's star and said, 'Good lady, in Kosambī, King Pūrantappa is dead.' 'Why, venerable sir, do you say so? Do you have some grudge against him?' 'No, good lady, I say this after seeing the fading of his star,' he replied. She wept profusely. Then he asked her, 'Why do you weep?' When she revealed that he was her husband, he said, 'Do not weep, good lady; for a being that is born, death is certain.' When she replied, 'I know, venerable sir,' he asked, 'Then why do you weep?' 'My son is worthy of the kingdom, which is the inheritance of his lineage. If he were there, they would raise the white parasol for him. Now, alas, he has suffered a great loss. It is because of this sorrow, venerable sir, that I weep.' 'Let it be, good lady, do not worry. If you desire the kingdom for him, I will make the arrangements for him to obtain the kingdom.' Then he gave the prince the elephant-charming lute and the elephant-charming mantras. At that time, many thousands of elephants would come and sit at the foot of the banyan tree. Then he said to the prince, 'Before the elephants arrive, climb the tree. When they have arrived, recite this mantra and strike this string. All of them, turning back, will flee, unable even to look. Then, descend and come back.' He did as instructed and, returning, reported the event. Then, on the second day, he said to him, 'Today, recite this mantra and strike this string. All of them will turn back and flee while looking.' On that occasion too, he did as instructed and, returning, reported it. Then, on the third day, he said to him, 'Today, recite this mantra and strike this string. The herd-leader will approach, presenting his back.' On that occasion too, he did as told and reported it.

Athassa mātaraṃ āmantetvā, “bhadde, puttassa te sāsanaṃ vadehi, ettova gantvā rājā bhavissatī”ti āha. Sā puttaṃ āmantetvā, “tāta, tvaṃ kosambiyaṃ pūrantapparañño putto, maṃ sagabbhaṃ hatthiliṅgasakuṇo ānesī”ti vatvā senāpatiādīnaṃ nāmāni ācikkhitvā “asaddahantānaṃ imaṃ pitu pārupanakambalañceva pilandhanamuddikañca dasseyyāsī”ti vatvā uyyojesi. Kumāro tāpasaṃ “idāni kiṃ karomī”ti āha. “Rukkhassa heṭṭhimasākhāya nisīditvā imaṃ mantaṃ vatvā imaṃ tantiṃ pahara, jeṭṭhakahatthī te piṭṭhiṃ upanāpetvā upasaṅkamissati, tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ nisinnova raṭṭhaṃ gantvā rajjaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. So mātāpitaro vanditvā tathā katvā āgatassa hatthino piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīditvā kaṇṇe mantayi – “ahaṃ kosambiyaṃ pūrantapparañño putto, pettikaṃ me rajjaṃ gaṇhitvā dehi sāmī”ti. So taṃ sutvā “anekāni [V 1.0098] hatthisahassāni sannipatantū”ti hatthiravaṃ ravi, anekāni hatthisahassāni sannipatiṃsu. Puna “jiṇṇā hatthī paṭikkamantū”ti hatthiravaṃ ravi, jiṇṇā hatthī paṭikkamiṃsu. Puna “atitaruṇā hatthī nivattantū”ti hatthiravaṃ ravi, tepi nivattiṃsu. So anekehi yūthahatthisahasseheva parivuto paccantagāmaṃ patvā “ahaṃ rañño putto, sampattiṃ [P 1.0169] patthayamānā mayā saddhiṃ āgacchantū”ti āha. “Tato paṭṭhāya manussānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karonto gantvā nagaraṃ parivāretvā ‘yuddhaṃ vā me detu, rajjaṃ vā’”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. Nāgarā āhaṃsu – “mayaṃ dvepi na dassāma. Amhākañhi devī garugabbhā hatthiliṅgasakuṇena nītā, tassā atthibhāvaṃ vā natthibhāvaṃ vā mayaṃ na jānāma. Yāva tassā pavattiṃ na suṇāma. Tāva neva yuddhaṃ dassāma, na rajja”nti. Tadā kira taṃ paveṇirajjaṃ ahosi. Tato kumāro “ahaṃ tassā putto”ti vatvā senāpatiādīnaṃ nāmāni kathetvā tathāpi asaddahantānaṃ kambalañca muddikañca dassesi. Te kambalañca muddikañca sañjānitvā nikkaṅkhā hutvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā taṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Ayaṃ tāva utenassa uppatti.

Then the ascetic, addressing the prince's mother, said, 'Good lady, give this message to your son: "Going from this very place, he will become king."' She called her son and said, 'Dear one, you are the son of King Pūrantappa of Kosambī. A Hatthiliṅga bird brought me here while I was pregnant.' She then told him the names of the commander-in-chief and others, and instructed him, 'To those who do not believe, show them this cloak and signet ring of your father.' Having said this, she sent him off. The prince asked the ascetic, 'What should I do now?' The ascetic replied, 'Sit on the lowest branch of the tree, recite this mantra, and strike this string. The chief elephant will approach and offer its back to you. Seated on its back, go to the country and take the kingdom.' The prince paid homage to his parents, did as instructed, and sat on the back of the elephant that had come. He spoke into its ear, 'I am the son of King Pūrantappa of Kosambī. Take and give me my paternal kingdom, lord.' Hearing this, the elephant roared, 'Let many thousands of elephants assemble!' Many thousands of elephants gathered. Again, it roared, 'Let the old elephants withdraw!' The old elephants withdrew. Again, it roared, 'Let the very young elephants turn back!' They too turned back. Surrounded by many thousands of herd elephants, the prince reached a border village and announced, 'I am the king’s son. Those who desire prosperity, come with me.' From that point on, providing support to the people as he went, he surrounded the city and sent a message: 'Either give me battle or give me the kingdom!' The citizens replied, 'We will give neither. For our queen, while heavily pregnant, was carried off by a Hatthiliṅga bird. We do not know whether she exists or not. As long as we do not hear news of her, we will give neither battle nor the kingdom.' At that time, it is said, the kingdom was hereditary. Then the prince, saying, 'I am her son,' stated the names of the commander-in-chief and others. To those who still did not believe, he showed the cloak and the signet ring. Recognizing the cloak and the signet ring, they became free of doubt, opened the gates, and consecrated him in the kingdom. This, for now, is the origin of Udena.

Allakapparaṭṭhe [M 1.0108] pana dubbhikkhe jīvituṃ asakkonto eko kotuhaliko nāma manusso kāpiṃ nāma taruṇaputtañca kāḷiṃ nāma bhariyañca ādāya “kosambiṃ gantvā jīvissāmī”ti pātheyyaṃ gahetvā nikkhami. “Ahivātarogena mahājane marante disvā nikkhamī”tipi vadantiyeva. Te gacchantā pātheyye parikkhīṇe khudābhibhūtā dārakaṃ vahituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Atha sāmiko pajāpatiṃ āha – “bhadde, mayaṃ jīvantā puna puttaṃ labhissāma, chaḍḍetvā naṃ gacchāmā”ti. Mātu hadayaṃ nāma mudukaṃ hoti. Tasmā sā āha – “nāhaṃ jīvantameva puttaṃ chaḍḍetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. “Atha kiṃ karomā”ti? “Vārena naṃ vahāmā”ti. Mātā attano vāre pupphadāmaṃ viya naṃ ukkhipitvā ure nipajjāpetvā [P 1.0170] aṅkena vahitvā pituno deti. Tassa taṃ gahetvā gamanakāle chātakatopi balavatarā vedanā uppajji. So punappunaṃ āha – “bhadde, mayaṃ jīvantā puttaṃ labhissāma, chaḍḍema na”nti. Sāpi punappunaṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṭivacanaṃ nādāsi. Dārako vārena parivattiyamāno kilanto pitu hatthe niddāyi. So tassa niddāyanabhāvaṃ ñatvā mātaraṃ purato katvā ekassa gacchassa heṭṭhā paṇṇasanthare taṃ nipajjāpetvā pāyāsi. Mātā nivattitvā olokentī puttaṃ adisvā, “sāmi, kuhiṃ me putto”ti pucchi. “Ekassa me gacchassa heṭṭhā nipajjāpito”ti. “Sāmi, mā maṃ nāsayi, puttaṃ vinā jīvituṃ na sakkhissāmi, ānehi me putta”nti uraṃ paharitvā paridevi. Atha naṃ nivattitvā ānesi. Puttopi antarāmagge mato hoti. Iti so ettake ṭhāne puttaṃ chaḍḍetvā tassa nissandena bhavantare satta vāre chaḍḍito. “Pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ appaka”nti na avamaññitabbaṃ.

In the region of Allakappa, during a famine, a man named Kotuhalika, unable to survive, took his young son named Kāpi and his wife named Kāḷī, gathered provisions, and set out, thinking, 'I will go to Kosambī and live.' It is also said that he left after seeing many people dying from a pestilence. As they traveled, their provisions were exhausted, and being overcome by hunger, they were unable to carry the child. Then the husband said to his wife, 'Good lady, if we live, we can have another son. Let us abandon him and go.' A mother’s heart is tender, so she said, 'I cannot abandon my son while he is still alive.' 'Then what shall we do?' 'Let us carry him in turns.' When it was her turn, the mother would lift him like a garland of flowers, lay him on her chest, carry him on her hip, and then give him to the father. When he took him to walk, a pain arose that was even stronger than his hunger. He said again and again, 'Good lady, if we live, we can have another son. Let us abandon him.' But she repeatedly refused and gave no reply. The child, being passed back and forth, became tired and fell asleep in his father’s arms. Knowing that he was asleep, the father had the mother go on ahead, laid him on a bed of leaves beneath a shrub, and departed. The mother, turning to look, did not see her son and asked, 'Husband, where is my son?' 'I laid him down beneath a shrub.' 'Husband, do not destroy me! I cannot live without my son. Bring me my son!' she cried, beating her breast and lamenting. Then he turned back and brought him. The son, however, had died on the path. Thus, having abandoned his son in that place, as a consequence, he was abandoned seven times in a future existence. An evil deed should not be slighted, thinking, 'It is small.'

Te [V 1.0099] gacchantā ekaṃ gopālakulaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Taṃ divasañca gopālakassa dhenumaṅgalaṃ hoti. Gopālakassa gehe nibaddhaṃ eko paccekabuddho bhuñjati. So taṃ bhojetvā maṅgalamakāsi. Bahu pāyāso paṭiyatto hoti. Gopālako te āgate disvā, “kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchitvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ sutvā mudujātiko kulaputto tesu anukampaṃ katvā bahukena sappinā pāyāsaṃ dāpesi. Bhariyā “sāmi, tayi jīvante ahampi jīvāmi nāma, dīgharattaṃ ūnodarosi, yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjāhī”ti sappiñca dadhiñca tadabhimukhaññeva katvā attanā mandasappinā [M 1.0109] thokameva bhuñji. Itaro bahuṃ bhuñjitvā sattaṭṭhadivase chātatāya āhārataṇhaṃ chindituṃ nāsakkhi. Gopālako tesaṃ pāyāsaṃ dāpetvā sayaṃ [P 1.0171] bhuñjituṃ ārabhi. Kotuhaliko taṃ olokento nisīditvā heṭṭhāpīṭhe nipannāya sunakhiyā gopālakena vaḍḍhetvā diyyamānaṃ pāyāsapiṇḍaṃ disvā “puññā vatāyaṃ sunakhī, nibaddhaṃ evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ labhatī”ti cintesi. So rattibhāge taṃ pāyāsaṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto kālaṃ katvā tassā sunakhiyā kucchimhi nibbatti.

As they were traveling, they reached a cowherd's household. On that day, the cowherd was holding a milk-boiling ceremony. A Paccekabuddha regularly took his meal in the cowherd's home. The cowherd, having fed the Paccekabuddha, performed the ceremony. Much milk-rice had been prepared. Seeing them arrive, the cowherd asked, 'Where have you come from?' After hearing their whole story, the cowherd, a kind-hearted man of good family, took pity on them and had a large amount of milk-rice with much ghee given to them. The wife said, 'My husband, as long as you live, I too shall live. You have had an empty stomach for a long time; please eat as much as you desire.' And placing the ghee and curd right before him, she herself ate only a little with a small amount of ghee. The other, having eaten a great deal, was unable to cut off his craving for food, due to having been starved for seven or eight days. The cowherd, having had the milk-rice given to them, began to eat himself. Kotuhalika, while sitting and watching him, saw a lump of milk-rice being served by the cowherd to a female dog lying under the stool. He thought, 'This female dog is truly meritorious! She regularly receives such food.' During the night, being unable to digest that milk-rice, he passed away and was reborn in the womb of that female dog.

Athassa bhariyā sarīrakiccaṃ katvā tasmiṃyeva gehe bhatiṃ katvā taṇḍulanāḷiṃ labhitvā pacitvā paccekabuddhassa patte patiṭṭhāpetvā, “dāsassa vo pāpuṇātū”ti vatvā cintesi – “mayā idheva vasituṃ vaṭṭati, nibaddhaṃ, ayyo, idhāgacchati, deyyadhammo hotu vā, mā vā, devasikaṃ vandantī veyyāvaccaṃ karontī cittaṃ pasādentī bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavissāmī”ti. Sā tattheva bhatiṃ karontī vasi. Sāpi sunakhī chaṭṭhe vā sattame vā māse ekameva kukkuraṃ vijāyi. Gopālako tassa ekadhenuyā khīraṃ dāpesi. So na cirasseva vaḍḍhi. Athassa paccekabuddho bhuñjanto nibaddhaṃ ekaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ deti. So bhattapiṇḍaṃ nissāya paccekabuddhe sinehamakāsi. Gopālakopi nibaddhaṃ dve vāre paccekabuddhassupaṭṭhānaṃ yāti. Gacchantopi antarāmagge vāḷamigaṭṭhāne daṇḍena gacche ca bhūmiñca paharitvā “susū”ti tikkhattuṃ saddaṃ katvā vāḷamige palāpeti. Sunakhopi tena saddhiṃ gacchati.

Then his wife, having performed the funeral rites, worked for wages in that very house. Obtaining a measure of rice, she cooked it, placed it in the Paccekabuddha's bowl, and said, 'May the merit of this reach your servant.' She then thought: 'It is proper for me to live right here. The noble one comes here regularly. Whether there is an offering or not, by daily paying respects, performing services, and gladdening my mind, I will generate much merit.' So she stayed there, working for wages. In the sixth or seventh month, that female dog gave birth to a single puppy. The cowherd had milk from one of his cows given to it. Before long, it grew up. Then the Paccekabuddha, while eating his meal, would regularly give it one lump of rice. On account of that lump of rice, it developed affection for the Paccekabuddha. The cowherd also regularly went to attend upon the Paccekabuddha twice a day. While going, in a place on the path where there were wild beasts, he would strike the bushes and the ground with his stick, making the sound 'susū' three times to make the wild beasts flee. The dog also went with him.

So ekadivasaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ āha – “bhante, yadā me okāso na bhavissati, tadā imaṃ sunakhaṃ pesessāmi, tena saññāṇena āgaccheyyāthā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya anokāsadivase, “gaccha, tāta, ayyaṃ ānehī”ti sunakhaṃ pesesi. So ekavacaneneva pakkhanditvā sāmikassa gacchapothanabhūmipothanaṭṭhāne tikkhattuṃ bhussitvā tena saddena vāḷamigānaṃ palātabhāvaṃ ñatvā [P 1.0172] pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinnassa paccekabuddhassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paṇṇasāladvāre tikkhattuṃ bhussitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā ekamante nipajjati, paccekabuddhe velaṃ sallakkhetvā nikkhante bhussanto purato gacchati. Antarantarā paccekabuddho [V 1.0100] taṃ vīmaṃsanto aññaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjati. Athassa purato [M 1.0110] tiriyaṃ ṭhatvā bhussitvā itaramaggameva naṃ āropeti. Athekadivasaṃ aññaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā tena purato tiriyaṃ ṭhatvā vāriyamānopi anivattitvā sunakhaṃ pādena paharitvā pāyāsi. Sunakho tassa anivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā nivāsanakaṇṇe ḍaṃsitvā ākaḍḍhanto itaramaggameva naṃ āropesi. Evaṃ so tasmiṃ balavasinehaṃ uppādesi.

One day he said to the Paccekabuddha, 'Venerable sir, when I am not free, I will send this dog. By that sign, may you please come.' From then on, on days when he was not free, he would send the dog, saying, 'Go, my dear, and bring the noble one.' With just that one word, the dog would run off. At the place where his master would strike the bushes and the ground, it would bark three times. By that sound, knowing that the wild beasts had fled, it would go to the dwelling place of the Paccekabuddha, who, having already attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, had entered his leaf-hut and was seated. The dog would bark three times at the door of the leaf-hut to announce its arrival and then lie down to one side. When the Paccekabuddha, observing the time, came out, the dog would bark and lead the way. From time to time, the Paccekabuddha, testing it, would take a different path. The dog would then stand crosswise in front of him, bark, and guide him back to the usual path. Then one day, having taken a different path, even though the dog stood crosswise in front and tried to stop him, the Paccekabuddha did not turn back but struck the dog with his foot and went on. The dog, realizing that he would not turn back, bit the corner of his lower robe and, pulling, guided him back to the usual path. In this way, the dog developed a strong affection for him.

Tato aparabhāge paccekabuddhassa cīvaraṃ jīri. Athassa gopālako cīvaravatthāni adāsi. Tamenaṃ paccekabuddho āha – “āvuso, cīvaraṃ nāma ekakena kātuṃ dukkaraṃ, phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā kāressāmī”ti. “Idheva, bhante, karothā”ti. “Na sakkā, āvuso”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, mā ciraṃ bahi vasitthā”ti. Sunakho tesaṃ kathaṃ suṇantova aṭṭhāsi, paccekabuddhopi “tiṭṭha, upāsakā”ti gopālakaṃ nivattāpetvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā gandhamādanābhimukho pāyāsi. Sunakhassa taṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ [P 1.0173] disvā bhukkaritvā ṭhitassa tasmiṃ cakkhupathaṃ vijahante hadayaṃ phalitvā mato. Tiracchānā kira nāmete ujujātikā honti akuṭilā. Manussā pana aññaṃ hadayena cintenti, aññaṃ mukhena kathenti. Tenevāha – “gahanañhetaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ manussā, uttānakañhetaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ pasavo”ti (ma. ni. 2.3).

Subsequently, the Paccekabuddha's robe wore out. Then the cowherd gave him robe-cloth. The Paccekabuddha said to him, 'Friend, it is difficult to make a robe alone; I will go to a suitable place and have it made.' 'Venerable sir, please make it right here.' 'That is not possible, friend.' 'In that case, venerable sir, please do not stay away for long.' The dog stood listening to their conversation. The Paccekabuddha, saying, 'Wait, lay follower,' sent the cowherd back, rose into the air, and departed in the direction of Gandhamādana. The dog, seeing him traveling through the sky, stood there barking. When the Paccekabuddha passed beyond its range of sight, its heart burst, and it died. It is said that these animals are of a straightforward nature, not devious. Humans, however, think one thing in their hearts and say another with their mouths. Therefore it was said: 'This is a thicket, venerable sir, that is to say, humans; this is open country, venerable sir, that is to say, animals.'

Iti so tāya ujucittatāya akuṭilatāya kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatto accharāsahassaparivuto mahāsampattiṃ anubhosi. Tassa kaṇṇamūle mantayantassa saddo soḷasayojanaṭṭhānaṃ pharati, pakatikathāsaddo pana sakalaṃ dasayojanasahassaṃ devanagaraṃ chādeti. Tenevassa “ghosakadevaputto”ti nāmaṃ ahosi. “Kissa panesa nissando”ti. Paccekabuddhe pemena bhukkaraṇassa nissando. So tattha na ciraṃ ṭhatvā cavi. Devalokato hi devaputtā āyukkhayena puññakkhayena āhārakkhayena kopenāti catūhi kāraṇehi cavanti.

Thus, due to that straightforward and uncrooked mind, that dog died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, he enjoyed great celestial fortune. The sound of him whispering at the ear's root pervades a distance of sixteen yojanas, while his ordinary speaking voice covers the entire ten-thousand-yojana celestial city. For this reason, his name became 'Ghosaka the Devaputta.' If it is asked, 'Of what is this the result?' It is the result of barking with affection for the Paccekabuddha. He did not stay there long and passed away. For devaputtas pass away from the deva world for four reasons: due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of merit, the exhaustion of nutriment, and anger.

Tattha yena bahuṃ puññakammaṃ kataṃ hoti, so devaloke uppajjitvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā uparūpari nibbattati. Evaṃ āyukkhayena cavati nāma. Yena parittaṃ puññaṃ kataṃ hoti, tassa rājakoṭṭhāgāre pakkhittaṃ ticatunāḷimattaṃ dhaññaṃ viya antarāva taṃ puññaṃkhīyati, antarāva kālaṃ karoti[M 1.0111]. Evaṃ puññakkhayena cavati nāma. Aparopi kāmaguṇe paribhuñjamāno satisammosena āhāraṃ aparibhuñjitvā kilantakāyo kālaṃ karoti. Evaṃ āhārakkhayena cavati nāma. Aparopi parassa sampattiṃ asahanto [P 1.0174] kujjhitvā kālaṃ karoti. Evaṃ kopena cavati nāma.

In that regard, one who has performed much meritorious kamma is reborn in the deva world and, having lived there for the full lifespan, is reborn in successively higher realms. Thus, it is called passing away due to the exhaustion of lifespan. For one who has performed little merit, like about three or four nāḷis of grain placed in a royal granary, that merit is exhausted in the interim, and they die in the interim. Thus, it is called passing away due to the exhaustion of merit. Another, while enjoying sensual pleasures, through loss of mindfulness, does not partake of nutriment, and with an exhausted body, dies. Thus, it is called passing away due to the exhaustion of nutriment. Yet another, not enduring the fortune of another, becomes angry and dies. Thus, it is called passing away due to anger.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0101] pana kāmaguṇe paribhuñjanto muṭṭhassati hutvā āhārakkhayena cavi, cavitvā ca pana kosambiyaṃ nagarasobhiniyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sāpi jātadivase “kiṃ eta”nti dāsiṃ pucchitvā, “putto, ayye”ti vutte – “handa, je, imaṃ dārakaṃ kattarasuppe āropetvā saṅkārakūṭe chaḍḍehī”ti chaḍḍāpesi. Nagarasobhiniyo hi dhītaraṃ paṭijagganti, na puttaṃ. Dhītarā hi tāsaṃ paveṇī ghaṭīyati. Dārakaṃ kākāpi sunakhāpi parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Paccekabuddhe sinehappabhavassa bhukkaraṇassa nissandena ekopi upagantuṃ na visahi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko manusso bahi nikkhanto taṃ kākasunakhasannipātaṃ disvā, “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti gantvā dārakaṃ disvā puttasinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā “putto me laddho”ti gehaṃ nesi. Tadā kosambakaseṭṭhi rājakulaṃ gacchanto rājanivesanato āgacchantaṃ purohitaṃ disvā, “kiṃ, ācariya, ajja te tithikaraṇanakkhattayogo olokito”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahāseṭṭhi, amhākaṃ kiṃ aññaṃ kiccanti? Janapadassa kiṃ bhavissatī”ti? “Aññaṃ natthi, imasmiṃ pana nagare ajja jātadārako jeṭṭhakaseṭṭhi bhavissatī”ti. Tadā seṭṭhino bhariyā garugabbhā hoti. Tasmā so sīghaṃ gehaṃ purisaṃ pesesi – “gaccha bhaṇe, jānāhi naṃ vijātā vā, no vā”ti. “Na vijāyatī”ti sutvā rājānaṃ disvāva vegena gehaṃ gantvā kāḷiṃ nāma dāsiṃ pakkositvā sahassaṃ datvā, “gaccha [P 1.0175] je, imasmiṃ nagare upadhāretvā sahassaṃ datvā ajja jātadārakaṃ gaṇhitvā ehī”ti. Sā upadhārentī taṃ gehaṃ gantvā dārakaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ dārako kadā jāto”ti gahapatāniṃ pucchitvā “ajja jāto”ti vutte, “imaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti ekakahāpaṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā mūlaṃ vaḍḍhentī sahassaṃ datvā taṃ ānetvā seṭṭhino dassesi. Seṭṭhi “sace me dhītā vijāyissati, tāya naṃ saddhiṃ nivesetvā seṭṭhiṭṭhānassa sāmikaṃ karissāmi. Sace me putto vijāyissati, māressāmi na”nti cintetvā taṃ gehe kāresi.

This devaputta, however, while enjoying sensual pleasures, became one of lapsed mindfulness and passed away due to the exhaustion of nutriment. Having passed away, he took conception in the womb of a city courtesan in Kosambī. On the day of his birth, she asked her female slave, 'What is this?' When it was said, 'A son, my lady,' she had him abandoned, saying, 'Now then, my girl, place this child in a winnowing basket and abandon him on the rubbish heap.' For city courtesans care for a daughter, not a son, as it is by a daughter that their lineage is established. Crows and dogs surrounded the child and sat down. Due to the result of the barking that arose from affection for the Paccekabuddha, not a single one dared to approach. At that moment, a certain man who had gone outside saw that gathering of crows and dogs and, wondering, 'What can this be?', went and saw the child. Gaining a father's affection, he took him home, thinking, 'I have gotten a son!' At that time, the Kosambī merchant, while going to the royal court, saw the purohita coming from the royal residence and asked, 'Teacher, have you observed the conjunction of the lunar day, karaṇa, and constellation today?' 'Yes, great merchant,' he replied. The merchant then asked, 'What will befall us, or the country?' The purohita answered, 'There is nothing else of note, but in this city, a child born today will become the chief merchant.' At that time, the merchant's wife was heavy with child. Therefore, he quickly sent a man to his house, saying, 'Go, my good man, find out whether she has given birth or not.' Hearing, 'She has not given birth,' after seeing the king, he went home with speed, summoned a female slave named Kālī, gave her a thousand, and said, 'Go, my girl, investigate in this city, and having given a thousand, take the child born today and come.' Investigating, she went to that house, saw the child, and asked the housewife, 'When was this child born?' When it was said, 'He was born today,' she said, 'Give this one to me.' Starting with one kahāpaṇa and increasing the price, she gave a thousand, brought him, and showed him to the merchant. The merchant thought, 'If my wife gives birth to a daughter, I will settle him with her and make him master of the merchant's position. If my wife gives birth to a son, I will kill him.' Thinking thus, he had the child cared for in his house.

Athassa [M 1.0112] bhariyā katipāhaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi. Seṭṭhi “imasmiṃ asati mama puttova seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhissati, idāneva taṃ māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā kāḷiṃ āmantetvā, “gaccha, je, vajato gunnaṃ nikkhamanavelāya vajadvāramajjhe imaṃ tiriyaṃ nipajjāpehi, gāviyo naṃ madditvā māressanti, madditāmadditabhāvaṃ panassa ñatvā ehī”ti āha. Sā gantvā gopālakena vajadvāre vivaṭamatteyeva taṃ tathā nipajjāpesi. Gogaṇajeṭṭhako usabho aññasmiṃ kāle sabbapacchā nikkhamantopi taṃ divasaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ nikkhamitvā dārakaṃ catunnaṃ pādānaṃ antare katvā aṭṭhāsi. Anekasatagāviyo usabhassa dve passāni ghaṃsantiyo nikkhamiṃsu. Gopālakopi “ayaṃ usabho pubbe sabbapacchā nikkhamati, ajja pana sabbapaṭhamaṃ nikkhamitvā [V 1.0102] vajadvāramajjhe niccalova ṭhito, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti cintetvā gantvā tassa heṭṭhā nipannaṃ dārakaṃ disvā puttasinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā, “putto me laddho”ti gehaṃ nesi.

Then, after a few days had passed, his wife gave birth to a son. The merchant thought, 'If this one is gone, my own son will obtain the merchant's position. It is right to kill him right now.' Thinking thus, he addressed Kālī and said, 'Go, my girl, at the time the cattle are exiting from the pen, lay this one down crosswise in the middle of the pen gate. The cows will trample and kill him. Come back only after you have learned whether he has been trampled or not.' She went and, just as the cowherd opened the pen gate, she laid him down in that manner. The lead bull of the cattle herd, who at other times would exit last of all, on that day exited first of all. Seeing the child, he stood over him, placing him between his four feet. Many hundreds of cows exited, brushing against the two sides of the bull. The cowherd, too, thought, 'This bull previously would exit last of all, but today he has exited first and stands motionless in the middle of the pen gate. What can this be?' He went and saw the child lying beneath the bull. Feeling a father's affection, he took him home, thinking, 'I have gotten a son!'

Kāḷī gantvā seṭṭhinā pucchitā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā, “gaccha, naṃ puna sahassaṃ datvā ānehī”ti vuttā sahassaṃ datvā puna ānetvā adāsi. Atha [P 1.0176] naṃ āha – “amma, kāḷi imasmiṃ nagare pañca sakaṭasatāni paccūsakāle uṭṭhāya vāṇijjāya gacchanti, tvaṃ imaṃ netvā cakkamagge nipajjāpehi, goṇā vā naṃ maddissanti, cakkā vā chindissanti, pavattiṃ cassa ñatvāva āgaccheyyāsī”ti. Sā taṃ netvā cakkamagge nipajjāpesi. Tadā sākaṭikajeṭṭhako purato ahosi. Athassa goṇā taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā dhuraṃ chaḍḍesuṃ, punappunaṃ āropetvā pājiyamānāpi purato na gacchiṃsu. Evaṃ tassa tehi saddhiṃ vāyamantasseva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahi. So “kiṃ nāmetaṃ goṇā kariṃsū”ti maggaṃ olokento dārakaṃ disvā, “bhāriyaṃ vata me kamma”nti cintetvā, “putto me laddho”ti tuṭṭhamānaso taṃ gehaṃ nesi.

Kāḷī went and, questioned by the merchant, having reported the matter to him, was told, 'Go, give another thousand and bring him back.' Having given the thousand, she brought him back again and handed him over. Then he said to her, 'My dear Kālī, in this city five hundred carts set out for trade at dawn. You take this boy and make him lie down in the cart track. Either the oxen will trample him, or the wheels will cut him to pieces. And only after having ascertained what has become of him should you return.' She took him and made him lie down in the cart track. At that time, the chief of the carters was at the front.
