When his oxen reached that spot, they cast off their yokes. Even though yoked again and again and driven, they did not go forward. While he was thus struggling with them, dawn arose. Wondering, 'What is this the oxen have done?' he looked along the path and saw the boy. Thinking, 'Indeed, my task is a heavy one,' and delighted at heart, thinking, 'I have obtained a son,' he took him home.

Kāḷī gantvā seṭṭhinā pucchitā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā, “gaccha, naṃ puna sahassaṃ datvā ānehī”ti vuttā tathā akāsi. Atha naṃ so āha – “idāni naṃ āmakasusānaṃ netvā gacchantare nipajjāpehi, tattha sunakhādīhi vā khādito, amanussehi vā pahaṭo marissati, mātāmatabhāvañcassa jānitvāva āgaccheyyāsī”ti. Sā taṃ netvā tattha nipajjāpetvā ekamante aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ sunakho vā kāko vā amanusso vā upasaṅkamituṃ [M 1.0113] nāsakkhi. “Nanu cassa neva mātā na pitā na bhātikādīsu koci rakkhitā nāma atthi, ko taṃ rakkhatī”ti? Sunakhakāle paccekabuddhe sinehena pavattitabhukkaraṇamattameva taṃ rakkhati. Atheko ajapālako anekasahassā ajā gocaraṃ nento susānapassena gacchati. Ekā ajā paṇṇāni khādamānā gacchantaraṃ paviṭṭhā dārakaṃ disvā jaṇṇukehi ṭhatvā dārakassa thanaṃ adāsi, ajapālakena “he he”ti sadde katepi na nikkhami. So “yaṭṭhiyā naṃ paharitvā nīharissāmī”ti gacchantaraṃ paviṭṭho jaṇṇukehi [P 1.0177] ṭhatvā dārakaṃ khīraṃ pāyantiṃ ajiṃ disvā dārake puttasinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā, “putto me laddho”ti ādāya pakkāmi.

Kāḷī went and, questioned by the merchant, having related that event to him, was told, 'Go, give another thousand and bring him back.' She did so. Then he said to her, 'Now take him to the charnel ground for uncremated bodies and lay him down in a thicket. There, he will die, either eaten by dogs and other such creatures, or struck by non-humans. And only after having ascertained whether he is dead or not dead should you return.' She took him there, laid him down, and stood at a distance to watch. Neither a dog, nor a crow, nor a non-human was able to approach him. Surely, for him there is no protector—not a mother, not a father, not a brother or anyone else. Who protects him? In his existence as a dog, it was only the kamma of the mere act of barking that arose from affection for a Paccekabuddha that protected him. Then a certain goatherd, leading many thousands of goats to pasture, was passing by the charnel ground. One goat, eating leaves, entered a thicket and saw the child. She stood on her knees and gave the child her udder. Even when the goatherd made the sound, 'Hey, hey!', she did not come out. He, thinking, 'I will drive her out by striking her with a stick,' entered the thicket and saw the she-goat, standing on her knees, giving milk to the child. He conceived a paternal affection for the child, and thinking, 'I have obtained a son,' he took him and departed.

Kāḷī gantvā seṭṭhinā pucchitā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā, “gaccha, taṃ puna sahassaṃ datvā ānehī”ti vuttā tathā akāsi. Atha naṃ āha – “amma kāḷi, imaṃ ādāya corapapātapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā papāte khipa, pabbatakucchiyaṃ paṭihaññamāno khaṇḍākhaṇḍiko hutvā bhūmiyaṃ patissati, matāmatabhāvañcassa ñatvāva āgaccheyyāsī”ti. Sā taṃ tattha netvā pabbatamatthake [V 1.0103] ṭhatvā khipi. Taṃ kho pana pabbatakucchiṃ nissāya mahāveḷugumbo pabbatānusāreneva vaḍḍhi, tassa matthakaṃ ghanajāto jiñjukagumbo avatthari. Dārako patanto kojavake viya tasmiṃ pati. Taṃ divasañca naḷakārajeṭṭhakassa veḷubali patto hoti. So puttena saddhiṃ gantvā taṃ veḷugumbaṃ chindituṃ ārabhi. Tasmiṃ calante dārako saddamakāsi. So “dārakasaddo viyā”ti ekena passena abhiruhitvā taṃ disvā, “putto me laddho”ti tuṭṭhacitto ādāya gato.

Kāḷī went and, questioned by the merchant, having related that event to him, was told, 'Go, give another thousand and bring him back.' She did so. Then he said to her, 'My dear Kālī, take this boy, climb up to the Robbers' Precipice Mountain, and throw him from the precipice. Striking against the mountain hollow, he will be shattered into fragments and fall to the ground. And only after having ascertained whether he is dead or not dead should you return.' She took him there and, standing on the mountain peak, threw him. Now, supported by that mountain hollow, a great bamboo clump had grown along the mountain's slope, and its top was covered by a densely grown jujube bush. The boy, falling, landed on it as if on a woolen rug. On that very day, the bamboo tribute was due for the chief of the reed-workers. He went with his son and began to cut that bamboo clump. As it swayed, the boy made a sound. The man, thinking, 'It is like the sound of a boy,' climbed up from one side and, seeing him, with a delighted mind, thinking, 'I have obtained a son,' took him and went away.

Kāḷī seṭṭhissa santikaṃ gantvā tena pucchitā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā, “gaccha, naṃ puna sahassaṃ datvā ānehī”ti vuttā tathā akāsi. Seṭṭhino idañcidañca karontasseva dārako vaḍḍhito “ghosako”tvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi. So seṭṭhino akkhimhi kaṇṭako viya khāyi, ujukaṃ taṃ oloketumpi na visati. Athassa māraṇūpāyaṃ cintento attano sahāyakassa kumbhakārassa santikaṃ gantvā, “kadā tvaṃ āvāpaṃ ālimpessasī”ti pucchitvā – “sve”ti vutte, “tena [P 1.0178] hi idaṃ sahassaṃ gahetvā mama ekaṃ [M 1.0114] kammaṃ karohī”ti āha. “Kiṃ, sāmī”ti? “Eko me avajātaputto atthi, taṃ tava santikaṃ pesessāmi, atha naṃ gahetvā gabbhaṃ pavesetvā tikhiṇāya vāsiyā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā cāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā āvāpe paceyyāsi, idaṃ te sahassaṃ saccakārasadisaṃ. Uttariṃ pana te kattabbayuttakaṃ pacchā karissāmī”ti. Kumbhakāro “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Seṭṭhi punadivase ghosakaṃ pakkositvā, “hiyyo mayā kumbhakāro ekaṃ kammaṃ āṇatto, ehi, tvaṃ tassa santikaṃ gantvā evaṃ vadehi – ‘hiyyo kira me pitarā āṇattaṃ kammaṃ nipphādehī’”ti pahiṇi. So “sādhū”ti agamāsi. Taṃ tattha gacchantaṃ itaro seṭṭhino putto dārakehi saddhiṃ guḷaṃ kīḷanto disvā taṃ pakkositvā, “kuhiṃ gacchasi bhātikā”ti pucchitvā “pitu sāsanaṃ gahetvā kumbhakārassa santika”nti vutte “ahaṃ tattha gamissāmi. Ime maṃ dārakā bahuṃ lakkhaṃ jiniṃsu, taṃ me paṭijinitvā dehī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ pitu bhāyāmī”ti. “Mā bhāyi, bhātika, ahaṃ taṃ sāsanaṃ harissāmi. Bahūhi jito, yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva me lakkhaṃ paṭijinā”ti.

Kāḷī went to the merchant's presence and, when questioned by him, related that event. Having been told, 'Go, give another thousand and bring him back,' she did so. While the merchant was making these and other attempts, the boy grew up, and his name became Ghosaka. He was like a thorn in the merchant's eye; the merchant did not dare even to look at him directly. Then, contemplating a way to kill him, he went to his friend the potter and asked, 'When will you fire the kiln?' When the potter replied, 'Tomorrow,' the merchant said, 'In that case, take this thousand and do one task for me.' 'What is it, master?' 'I have a degenerate son. I will send him to you. Then, you must take him, lead him into the kiln chamber, cut him into pieces with a sharp adze, put him in a large pot, and bake him in the kiln. This thousand for you is like a pledge. Moreover, I will later give you what is fitting for the task.' The potter agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The next day, the merchant summoned Ghosaka and sent him, saying, 'Yesterday I commanded the potter to do a certain task. Come, go to his presence and say this: "Duly complete the task that my father commanded yesterday."' He said, 'Very well,' and went. As he was going there, the merchant's other son, who was playing a game of marbles with some boys, saw him and called out, 'Where are you going, brother?' When he replied, 'I am taking my father's message to the potter's place,' the other son said, 'I will go there. These boys have won many stakes from me. Win them back for me.' Ghosaka said, 'I am afraid of my father.' 'Do not be afraid, brother. I will carry the message. I have been defeated many times. Until I return, win back my stakes for me.'

Ghosako kira guḷakīḷāya cheko, tena naṃ evaṃ nibandhi. Sopi taṃ “tena hi gantvā kumbhakāraṃ vadehi – ‘pitarā kira me hiyyo ekaṃ kammaṃ āṇattaṃ, taṃ nipphādehī’”ti vatvā uyyojesi. So tassa santikaṃ gantvā tathā avaca. Atha naṃ kumbhakāro seṭṭhinā vuttaniyāmeneva māretvā āvāpe khipi. Ghosakopi divasabhāgaṃ kīḷitvā sāyanhasamaye gehaṃ gantvā [V 1.0104][P 1.0179] “kiṃ, tāta, na gatosī”ti vutte attano agatakāraṇañca kaniṭṭhassa gatakāraṇañca ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhi “ahaṃ dhī”ti mahāviravaṃ viravitvā sakalasarīre pakkuthitalohito viya hutvā, “ambho, kumbhakāra, mā maṃ nāsayi, mā maṃ nāsayī”ti bāhā paggayha kandanto tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Kumbhakāro taṃ tathā āgacchantaṃ disvā, “sāmi, mā saddaṃ kari, kammaṃ te nipphanna”nti āha. So pabbatena viya mahantena sokena avatthaṭo hutvā anappakaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. Yathā taṃ appaduṭṭhassa padussamāno. Tenāha bhagavā –

Ghosaka, it is said, was skilled in playing with marbles, so the other son persistently urged him. Ghosaka, in turn, sent him off, saying, “If that is so, then go and tell the potter: ‘It is said that yesterday my father gave an order for a certain task; please complete it.’” The son went to the potter and spoke thus. Then the potter, following the very method instructed by the merchant, killed him and threw him into the kiln. Ghosaka, having played for part of the day, returned home in the evening. When asked, “Why, my dear son, have you not gone?” he related his own reason for not going and his younger brother’s reason for going. Hearing this, the merchant, blaming himself, cried out, “Fie upon me!” and wailed a great wail. His whole body felt as if it were filled with boiling blood. Raising his arms and weeping, he went to the potter, crying, “Oh, potter, do not destroy me, do not destroy me!” Seeing him approaching in such a state, the potter said, “Master, do not make a sound; your task is completed.” Overwhelmed by great sorrow, as if crushed by a mountain, he experienced immeasurable grief, just as one who harms the harmless does. For this reason, the Blessed One said:

“Yo [M 1.0115] daṇḍena adaṇḍesu, appaduṭṭhesu dussati;

Dasannamaññataraṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippameva nigacchati.

“Whoever with violence harms those who are harmless and innocent, quickly comes to one of ten states:

“Vedanaṃ pharusaṃ jāniṃ, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ;

Garukaṃ vāpi ābādhaṃ, cittakkhepañca pāpuṇe.

He may encounter cruel pain, loss of wealth, destruction of the body, a grievous illness, or else mental derangement.

“Rājato vā upasaggaṃ, abbhakkhānañca dāruṇaṃ;

Parikkhayañca ñātīnaṃ, bhogānañca pabhaṅguraṃ.

Or oppression from the king, or a terrible accusation, the loss of relatives, or the destruction of wealth.

“Atha vāssa agārāni, aggi ḍahati pāvako;

Kāyassa bhedā duppañño, nirayaṃ sopapajjatī”ti. (dha. pa. 137-140);

Or else his houses are burned by fire; upon the dissolution of the body, the one of little wisdom is reborn in hell.”

Evaṃ [P 1.0180] santepi puna naṃ seṭṭhi ujukaṃ oloketuṃ na sakkoti. “Kinti naṃ māreyya”nti cintento, “mama gāmasate āyuttakassa santikaṃ pesetvā māressāmī”ti upāyaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ me avajātaputto, imaṃ māretvā vaccakūpe khipatu, evaṃ kate ahaṃ mātulassa kattabbayuttakaṃ pacchā jānissāmī”ti tassa paṇṇaṃ likhitvā, “tāta ghosaka, amhākaṃ gāmasate āyuttako atthi, imaṃ paṇṇaṃ haritvā tassa dehī”ti vatvā paṇṇaṃ tassa dussante bandhi. So pana akkharasamayaṃ na jānāti. Daharakālato paṭṭhāya hi naṃ mārāpentova seṭṭhi māretuṃ nāsakkhi, kiṃ akkharasamayaṃ sikkhāpessati? Iti so attano mārāpanapaṇṇameva dussante bandhitvā nikkhamanto āha – “pātheyyaṃ me, tāta, natthī”ti. “Pātheyyena te kammaṃ natthi, antarāmagge ‘asukagāme nāma mamasahāyako seṭṭhi atthi, tassa ghare pātarāsaṃ katvā purato gacchāhī’”ti. So “sādhū”ti pitaraṃ vanditvā nikkhanto taṃ gāmaṃ patvā seṭṭhissa gharaṃ [V 1.0105] pucchitvā gantvā seṭṭhijāyaṃ passi. “Tvaṃ kuto āgatosī”ti ca vutte, “antonagarato”ti āha. “Kassa puttosī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ sahāyakaseṭṭhino, ammā”ti. “Tvaṃsi ghosako nāmā”ti? “Āma, ammā”ti. Tassā saha dassaneneva tasmiṃ puttasineho uppajji. Seṭṭhino panekā dhītā atthi pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikā abhirūpā pāsādikā, taṃ rakkhituṃ ekameva pesanakārikaṃ dāsiṃ datvā sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatale sirigabbhe vasāpenti. Seṭṭhidhītā tasmiṃ [P 1.0181] khaṇe taṃ dāsiṃ antarāpaṇaṃ pesesi. Atha naṃ seṭṭhijāyā disvā, “kuhiṃ gacchasī”ti [M 1.0116] pucchitvā, “ayyadhītāya pesanenā”ti vutte “ito tāva ehi, tiṭṭhatu pesanaṃ, puttassa me pīṭhakaṃ attharitvā pāde dhovitvā telaṃ makkhitvā sayanaṃ attharitvā dehi, pacchā pesanaṃ karissasī”ti āha. Sā tathā akāsi.

Even so, the merchant still could not look at him directly. Thinking, “How can I kill him?” he saw a plan: “I will send him to the agent in my hundred villages and have him killed.” So he wrote a letter to the agent: “This is my low-born son. Kill him and throw him into a cesspit. When this is done, I will afterwards know what ought to be done for the uncle.” Having written the letter, he said, “My dear Ghosaka, in our hundred villages there is an agent. Take this letter and give it to him,” and he tied the letter into the hem of Ghosaka's garment. But Ghosaka did not know how to read. For, from a young age, the merchant had only been trying to have him killed and had been unable to do so; how then would he have had him taught to read? Thus, with the very letter ordering his own death tied into his hem, Ghosaka was leaving when he said, “Father, I have no provisions for the journey.” The merchant replied, “You have no need for provisions. On the way, in a certain village, there is a merchant who is a friend of mine. Have your morning meal at his house and then continue on your way.” Saying, “Very well,” Ghosaka paid respects to his father and departed. Reaching that village, he asked for the merchant’s house and went there, where he saw the merchant’s wife. When she asked, “Where have you come from?” he replied, “From the city.” “Whose son are you?” “I am the son of your friend, the merchant, mother.” “Are you the one named Ghosaka?” “Yes, mother.” For her, upon the very sight of him, a mother’s love arose. Now, the merchant had one daughter, about fifteen or sixteen years of age, very beautiful and inspiring. To guard her, they had given her only a single serving maid and had her reside in a splendid chamber on the top floor of a seven-storied palace. At that moment, the merchant’s daughter had sent that maidservant to the market within the town. Then the merchant’s wife saw her and asked, “Where are you going?” When the maid replied, “On an errand for the young mistress,” she said, “Come here first. Let the errand wait. For my son, spread out a seat, wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and prepare a bed for him. Afterwards, you may do your errand.” The maid did so.

Atha naṃ cirenāgataṃ seṭṭhidhītā santajjesi. Atha naṃ sā āha – “mā me kujjhi, seṭṭhiputto ghosako āgato, tassa idañcidañca katvā tattha gantvā āgatāmhī”ti. Seṭṭhidhītāya “seṭṭhiputto ghosako”ti nāmaṃ sutvāva pemaṃ chaviyādīni chinditvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca ṭhitaṃ. Kotuhalakālasmiñhi sā tassa pajāpatī hutvā nāḷikodanaṃ paccekabuddhassa adāsi, tassānubhāvenāgantvā imasmiṃ seṭṭhikule nibbattā. Iti taṃ so pubbasineho avattharitvā gaṇhi. Tenāha bhagavā –

When the maidservant returned after a long time, the merchant’s daughter scolded her. The maidservant then said to her, “My lady, do not be angry with me. The merchant’s son, Ghosaka, has arrived. It was only after doing this and that for him that I went on the errand and have now returned.” For the merchant’s daughter, just upon hearing the name “Ghosaka, the merchant’s son,” a love arose that pierced through her skin and flesh, striking the very marrow of her bones. Indeed, in a past life, she had been his wife when he was Kotūhala, and she had offered a measure of rice to a Paccekabuddha. By the power of that deed, she had been reborn into this merchant’s family. Thus, that love from a former life overwhelmed and seized her. For this reason, the Blessed One said:

“Pubbeva sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake”ti. (jā. 1.2.174);

“Through having lived together in the past, or through a benefit in the present, thus is that love born, just like a lotus in the water.”

Atha naṃ pucchi – “kuhiṃ so, ammā”ti? “Sayane nipanno niddāyatī”ti. “Atthi panassa hatthe kiñcī”ti? “Dussante paṇṇaṃ atthī”ti. Sā “kiṃ paṇṇaṃ nu kho eta”nti tasmiṃ niddāyante mātāpitūnaṃ aññavihitatāya apassantānaṃ otaritvā samīpaṃ gantvā taṃ paṇṇaṃ mocetvā ādāya attano gabbhaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya vātapānaṃ vivaritvā akkharasamaye kusalatāya paṇṇaṃ vācetvā, “aho vata bālo, attano maraṇapaṇṇaṃ dussante bandhitvā [P 1.0182] vicarati, sace mayā na diṭṭhaṃ assa, natthissa jīvita”nti taṃ paṇṇaṃ phāletvā seṭṭhissa vacanena aparaṃ paṇṇaṃ likhi – “ayaṃ mama putto ghosako nāma, gāmasatato paṇṇākāraṃ āharāpetvā imassa janapadaseṭṭhino dhītarā saddhiṃ maṅgalaṃ katvā attano vasanagāmassa majjhe dvibhūmakaṃ gehaṃ kāretvā pākāraparikkhepena ceva purisaguttiyā ca susaṃvihitārakkhaṃ karotu, mayhañca ‘idañcidañca mayā kata’nti sāsanaṃ pesetu, evaṃ kate ahaṃ [V 1.0106] mātulassa kattabbayuttakaṃ pacchā jānissāmī”ti, likhitvā ca pana saṅgharitvā otaritvā dussanteyevassa bandhi.

Then she asked her, “Mother, where is he?” “He is lying on the bed, sleeping.” “Is there anything in his hand?” “There is a letter in the corner of his garment.” She thought, “What kind of letter could this be?” While he was sleeping, and while her parents, being otherwise occupied, were not looking, she descended, untied that letter, took it, and entered her own chamber. Having closed the door and opened the window, being skilled in reading letters, she read the letter: “Alas, what a fool! He wanders about with his own death-letter tied in the corner of his garment. If it had not been seen by me, his life would be no more.” Having torn up that letter, she wrote another letter in the name of the merchant: “This is my son, named Ghosaka. Let him have tribute brought from the hundred villages, perform the wedding ceremony with the daughter of this provincial merchant, have a two-storied house built in the middle of his own residential village, and provide well-arranged protection with a surrounding wall and with a guard of men. And let him send a message to me, saying, ‘This and that have been done by me.’ When this is done, I will afterwards know what is fit to be done for the uncle.” And having written this, she rolled it up, descended, and tied it in the very corner of his garment.

So [M 1.0117] divasabhāgaṃ niddāyitvā uṭṭhāya bhuñjitvā pakkāmi. Punadivase pātova taṃ gāmaṃ gantvā āyuttakaṃ gāmakiccaṃ karontaṃyeva passi. So taṃ disvā, “kiṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. “Pitarā me tumhākaṃ paṇṇaṃ pesita”nti. “Kiṃ paṇṇaṃ, tāta, āharā”ti paṇṇaṃ gahetvā vācetvā tuṭṭhamānaso “passatha, bho, mama sāmino mayi sinehaṃ katvā jeṭṭhaputtassa me maṅgalaṃ karotū”ti mama santikaṃ pahiṇi. “Sīghaṃ dāruādīni āharathā”ti gahapatike vatvā gāmamajjhe vuttapakāraṃ gehaṃ kārāpetvā gāmasatato paṇṇākāraṃ āharāpetvā janapadaseṭṭhino santikā dhītaraṃ ānetvā maṅgalaṃ katvā seṭṭhissa sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “idañcidañca mayā kata”nti.

Having slept for a part of the day, he rose, ate, and departed. Early on the next day, he went to that village and saw the agent still performing his village duties. The agent, seeing him, asked, “For what reason have you come, dear sir?” “My father has sent a letter to you.” “What letter, dear sir? Bring it.” Having taken and read the letter, with a delighted mind, he said, “See, sirs, the affection of my master for me! He has sent him to my presence, saying, ‘Perform the wedding ceremony for his eldest son.’ Quickly, bring wood and other things!” Having said this to the householders, he had a house built in the middle of the village in the manner described, had tribute brought from the hundred villages, brought the daughter from the provincial merchant, performed the wedding ceremony, and sent a message to the merchant, saying, “This and that have been done by me.”

Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhino “yaṃ kāremi, taṃ na hoti; yaṃ na kāremi, tadeva hotī”ti mahantaṃ domanassaṃ uppajji. Puttasokena saddhiṃ so soko ekato hutvā kucchiḍāhaṃ uppādetvā atisāraṃ janesi. Seṭṭhidhītāpi “sace koci seṭṭhino santikā āgacchati, mama akathetvā seṭṭhiputtassa paṭhamataraṃ mā kathayitthā”ti [P 1.0183] jane āṇāpesi. Seṭṭhipi kho “dāni taṃ duṭṭhaputtaṃ mama sāpateyyassa sāmikaṃ na karissāmī”ti cintetvā ekaṃ āyuttakaṃ āha – “mātula, puttaṃ me daṭṭhukāmomhi, ekaṃ pādamūlikaṃ pesetvā mama puttaṃ pakkosāpehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā paṇṇaṃ datvā ekaṃ purisaṃ pesesi. Seṭṭhidhītāpi tassa āgantvā dvāre ṭhitabhāvaṃ sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā, “kiṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. So āha – “seṭṭhi gilāno, puttaṃ passituṃ pakkosāpesi, ayye”ti. “Kiṃ, tāta, balavā, dubbalo”ti? “Balavā tāva, āhāraṃ bhuñjatiyeva, ayye”ti. Sā seṭṭhiputtaṃ ajānāpetvāva tassa nivesanañca paribbayañca dāpetvā “mayā pesitakāle gamissasi, acchassu tāvā”ti āha. Seṭṭhi puna āyuttakaṃ avaca, “kiṃ, mātula, na te mama puttassa santikaṃ pahita”nti? “Pahitaṃ, sāmi, gatapuriso na tāva etī”ti. “Tena hi puna aparaṃ pesehī”ti. So pesesi. Seṭṭhidhītā tasmimpi tatheva paṭipajji. Atha seṭṭhino rogo balavā jāto, ekaṃ bhājanaṃ pavisati, ekaṃ nikkhamati. Puna seṭṭhi āyuttakaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ, mātula, na te mama puttassa santikaṃ pahita”nti? “Pahitaṃ, sāmi, gatapuriso na tāva [M 1.0118] etī”ti. “Tena hi puna aparaṃ pesehī”ti. So pesesi. Seṭṭhidhītā tatiyavāre āgatampi taṃ pavattiṃ pucchi. So “bāḷhagilāno, ayye, seṭṭhi āhāraṃ pacchinditvā maccuparāyaṇo jāto, ekaṃ bhājanaṃ nikkhamati[V 1.0107], ekaṃ pavisatī”ti āha. Seṭṭhidhītā “idāni gantuṃ kālo”ti seṭṭhiputtassa “pitā te kira gilāno”ti ārocetvā “kiṃ vadesi bhadde”ti vutte “aphāsukamassa, sāmī”ti āha. “Idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti. Sāmi? “Gāmasatato vuṭṭhānakapaṇṇākāraṃ [P 1.0184] ādāya gantvā passissāma na”nti. So “sādhū”ti paṇṇākāraṃ āharāpetvā sakaṭehi ādāya pakkāmi.

Hearing that, great displeasure arose in the merchant, thinking, 'What I wish to have done does not happen; what I do not wish to have done, that very thing happens.' That sorrow, together with the sorrow for his son, becoming one, produced a burning in his belly and brought on dysentery. The merchant's daughter also commanded the people, 'If anyone comes from the merchant's presence, do not speak to the merchant's son first without telling me.' The merchant, thinking, 'Now I will not make that wicked son the master of my wealth,' said to an agent, 'Uncle, I am desirous of seeing my son. Send a foot-servant and have my son summoned.' He, saying 'Very well,' gave a letter and sent a man. The merchant's daughter, hearing of his arrival and standing at the gate, had him summoned and asked, 'What is it, dear sir?' He said, 'The merchant is ill; he has had his son summoned to see him, lady.' 'Is he strong or weak, dear sir?' 'For now he is strong, lady; he is still able to eat.' She, without letting the merchant's son know, had lodging and provisions given to him and said, 'You shall go when I send you; for now, please wait.' The merchant again said to the agent, 'Uncle, have you not sent someone to my son?' 'I have sent someone, master, but the man who went has not yet returned.' 'Then send another.' So he sent one. The merchant's daughter acted in the very same way towards him also. Then the merchant's illness became severe; one vessel goes in, one comes out. Again the merchant asked the agent, 'Uncle, have you not sent someone to my son?' 'I have sent someone, master, but the man who went has not yet returned.' 'Then send another.' So he sent one. The merchant's daughter also asked about the situation from the one who came on the third occasion. He said, 'The merchant is gravely ill, lady; having given up food, he is on the verge of death. One vessel comes out, one goes in.' The merchant's daughter, thinking, 'Now is the time to go,' informed the merchant's son, 'It is said your father is ill.' When he said, 'What do you say, my good lady?' she replied, 'He is unwell, master.' 'What is to be done now?' 'Let us take the tribute arising from the hundred villages and go to see him.' He said, 'Very well,' had the tribute brought, and having loaded it onto carts, he departed.

Atha naṃ sā “pitā te dubbalo, ettakaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā gacchantānaṃ papañco bhavissati, etaṃ nivattāpehī”ti vatvā taṃ sabbaṃ attano kulagehaṃ pesetvā puna taṃ āha – “sāmi, tvaṃ attano pitu pādapasse tiṭṭheyyāsi, ahaṃ ussīsakapasse ṭhassāmī”ti. Gehaṃ pavisamānāyeva ca “gehassa purato ca pacchato ca ārakkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti attano purise āṇāpesi. Paviṭṭhakāle pana seṭṭhiputto pitu pādapasse aṭṭhāsi, itarā ussīsakapasse.

Then she said to him, 'Your father is weak. For us, going with so much tribute, there will be a delay. Have it sent back.' Having said this, she sent all of it to her own family home. Again she said to him, 'Master, you should stand at your father's feet; I will stay at the head of the bed.' And just as they were entering the house, she commanded her own men, 'Set a guard at the front and at the back of the house.' When they had entered, the merchant's son stood at his father's feet, while the other sat at the head of the bed.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe seṭṭhi uttānako nipanno hoti. Āyuttako pana tassa pāde parimajjanto “putto te, sāmi, āgato”ti āha. “Kuhiṃ so”ti? “Esa pādamūle ṭhito”ti. Atha naṃ disvā āyakammikaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “mama gehe kittakaṃ dhana”nti pucchi. “Sāmi, dhanasseva cattālīsakoṭiyo, upabhogaparibhogabhaṇḍānaṃ pana vanagāmakkhettadvipadacatuppadayānavāhanānañca ayañca ayañca paricchedo”ti vutte, “ahaṃ ettakaṃ dhanaṃ mama puttassa ghosakassa na demī”ti vattukāmo “demī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhidhītā “ayaṃ puna kathento aññaṃ kiñci katheyyā”ti cintetvā sokāturā viya kese vikiritvā rodamānā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, tāta, vadetha, idampi nāma vo vacanaṃ suṇoma, alakkhikā vatamhā”ti vatvā matthakena naṃ uramajjhe paharantī patitvā yathā puna vattuṃ na sakkoti, tathāssa uramajjhe matthakena ghaṃsentī ārodanaṃ dassesi. Seṭṭhi taṃkhaṇaññeva kālamakāsi. “Seṭṭhi mato”ti gantvā [M 1.0119][P 1.0185] utenassa rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kārāpetvā, “atthi panassa putto vā dhītā vā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, ghosako nāma tassa putto, sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ tassa niyyādetvāva mato, devā”ti.

At that moment, the merchant was lying on his back. The agent, while massaging his feet, said, 'Master, your son has arrived.' 'Where is he?' 'He is standing here at your feet.' Then, seeing him, the merchant summoned the accountant and asked, 'How much wealth is in my house?' When he was told, 'Master, there are forty crores in treasure alone. As for goods for use and enjoyment—forests, villages, fields, bipeds, quadrupeds, and vehicles—such is their extent,' the merchant, wishing to say, 'I will not give this much wealth to my son Ghosaka,' instead said, 'I give it.' Hearing this, the merchant's daughter, thinking, 'Lest he speak again and say something else,' and, as if overcome with grief, she disheveled her hair and wept, exclaiming, 'Father, what is this you say? That we should hear such a word from you! Alas, we are unfortunate!' With that, striking him in the middle of the chest with her head, she fell upon him. Then, so that he could not speak again, she rubbed his chest with her head, displaying great lamentation. The merchant died at that very moment. They went and reported to King Udena, 'The merchant has died.' The king had his funeral rites performed and then asked, 'Does he have a son or a daughter?' 'He does, Your Majesty. He has a son named Ghosaka. He died only after having handed over all his property to him, Your Majesty.'

Rājā aparabhāge seṭṭhiputtaṃ pakkosāpesi. Tasmiñca divase devo vassi. Rājaṅgaṇe tattha tattha udakaṃ saṇṭhāti. Seṭṭhiputto “rājānaṃ passissāmī”ti pāyāsi. Rājā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā taṃ āgacchantaṃ olokento rājaṅgaṇe udakaṃ laṅghitvā āgacchantaṃ disvā āgantvā vanditvā ṭhitaṃ “tvaṃ ghosako nāma, tātā”ti pucchitvā “āma, devā”ti vutte “pitā me [V 1.0108] matoti mā soci, tava pettikaṃ seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ tuyhameva dassāmī”ti taṃ samassāsetvā “gaccha, tātā”ti uyyojesi. Rājā gacchantañca naṃ olokentova aṭṭhāsi. So āgamanakāle laṅghitaṃ udakaṃ gamanakāle otaritvā saṇikaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ rājā tatova pakkosāpetvā, “kiṃ nu kho, tāta, tvaṃ mama santikaṃ āgacchanto udakaṃ laṅghitvā āgamma gacchanto otaritvā saṇikaṃ gacchasī”ti pucchi. “Āma, deva, ahaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe kumārako, kīḷanakālo nāma, so idāni pana me devena ṭhānantaraṃ paṭissutaṃ. Tasmā yathā pure acaritvā idāni sannisinnena hutvā carituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā rājā “dhitimāyaṃ puriso, idānevassa ṭhānantaraṃ dassāmī”ti pitarā bhuttaṃ bhogaṃ datvā sabbasatena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi.

Afterwards, the king had the merchant’s son summoned. On that day, it had rained, and water collected here and there in the royal courtyard. The merchant’s son set out, thinking, 'I will see the king.' The king opened a window and, watching him approach, saw him leap over the water in the courtyard. When the young man had come, paid homage, and was standing there, the king asked, 'Are you Ghosaka, my son?' When he replied, 'Yes, Your Majesty,' the king consoled him, saying, 'Do not grieve that your father has died. I will give you your father’s position as chief merchant.' Then he dismissed him, saying, 'You may go, my son.' The king stood watching as he left. On his way back, the young man stepped down into the water he had earlier leaped over and walked slowly. Then the king called him back from there and asked, 'Why is it, my son, that you leaped over the water when coming to me, but now step down into it and walk slowly on your return?' He replied, 'Yes, Your Majesty. At that time, I was a boy, and it was a time for play. But now, a high position has been promised to me by Your Majesty. Therefore, it is proper for me to conduct myself with composure now, not as before.' Hearing this, the king thought, 'This man is resolute. I will give him the position right now.' He granted him the wealth his father had enjoyed and bestowed upon him the position of chief merchant with all its perquisites.

So rathe ṭhatvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. Olokitolokitaṭṭhānaṃ kampati. Seṭṭhidhītā kāḷidāsiyā saddhiṃ mantayamānā nisinnā [P 1.0186] “amma kāḷi, puttassa te ettikā sampatti maṃ nissāya uppannā”ti āha. “Kiṃ kāraṇā, ammā”ti? “Ayañhi attano maraṇapaṇṇaṃ dussante bandhitvā amhākaṃ gharaṃ āgato, athassa mayā taṃ paṇṇaṃ phāletvā mayā saddhiṃ maṅgalakaraṇatthāya aññaṃ paṇṇaṃ likhitvā ettakaṃ kālaṃ tattha ārakkho kato”ti. “Amma, tvaṃ ettakaṃ passasi, imaṃ pana seṭṭhi daharakālato paṭṭhāya māretukāmo māretuṃ nāsakkhi, kevalaṃ imaṃ nissāya bahuṃ dhanaṃ khīyī”ti. “Amma, atibhāriyaṃ vata seṭṭhinā kata”nti. Nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā gehaṃ pavisantaṃ pana naṃ disvā, “ayaṃ ettikā sampatti maṃ nissāya [M 1.0120] uppannā”ti hasitaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ seṭṭhiputto disvā, “kiṃ kāraṇā hasī”ti pucchi. “Ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ nissāyā”ti. “Kathehi na”nti? “Sā na kathesi”. So “sace na kathessasi, dvidhā taṃ chindissāmī”ti tajjetvā asiṃ nikkaḍḍhi. Sā “ayaṃ ettikā sampatti tayā maṃ nissāya laddhāti cintetvā hasita”nti āha. “Yadi mama pitarā attano santakaṃ mayhaṃ niyyāditaṃ, tvaṃ ettha kiṃ hosī”ti? So kira ettakaṃ kālaṃ kiñci na jānāti, tenassā vacanaṃ na saddahi. Athassa sā “tumhākaṃ pitarā maraṇapaṇṇaṃ datvā pesitā, tumhe mayā idañcidañca katvā rakkhitā”ti sabbaṃ kathesi. “Tvaṃ abhūtaṃ kathesī”ti asaddahanto “mātaraṃ kāḷiṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā “evaṃ kira, ammā”ti. “Āma, tāta, daharakālato paṭṭhāya taṃ māretukāmo māretuṃ asakkonto taṃ nissāya bahuṃ dhanaṃ khīyi, sattasu ṭhānesu tvaṃ maraṇato mutto, idāni bhogagāmato āgamma [P 1.0187] sabbasatena saddhiṃ seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ patto”ti. So taṃ sutvā “bhāriyaṃ vata kammaṃ, evarūpā kho pana maraṇā muttassa mama pamādajīvitaṃ jīvituṃ ayuttaṃ, appamatto bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā devasikaṃ sahassaṃ [V 1.0109] vissajjetvā addhikakapaṇādīnaṃ dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Mitto nāmassa kuṭumbiko dānabyāvaṭo ahosi. Ayaṃ ghosakaseṭṭhino uppatti.

Standing in his chariot, he made a clockwise circumambulation of the city. The places he looked upon trembled. The merchant’s daughter, sitting and conversing with the slave woman Kāḷī, said, “Mother Kāḷī, this great fortune of your son has arisen because of me.” “For what reason, mother?” “Indeed, this one came to our house having tied his own death-letter in the corner of his garment. Then I tore up that letter and wrote another for the purpose of performing the marriage ceremony with me, and for all this time I have kept him under protection there.” “Mother, you see only this much. The merchant, wanting to have him killed from a young age, was unable to do so. Merely on his account, much wealth was wasted.” “Mother, what the merchant has done is very grave indeed.” After circumambulating the city, upon seeing him entering the house, she laughed, thinking, “This great fortune has arisen because of me.” Then the merchant’s son, seeing her, asked her, “For what reason did you laugh?” “On account of a certain reason.” “Then tell me.” She would not tell. He drew his sword, threatening her, “If you do not tell, I will cut you in two.” She said, “I laughed thinking, ‘This great fortune was obtained by you because of me.’” “If my father handed over his own property to me, what did you do in this matter?” Apparently, for all this time he had known nothing, so he did not believe her words. Then she told him everything: “You were sent by your father with a death-letter, but I protected you by doing this and that.” Not believing her, he said, “You are speaking falsehood.” Thinking, “I will ask Mother Kāḷī,” he asked, “Mother, is it really so?” “Yes, my son. From a young age, he wanted to have you killed, but being unable to do so, much wealth was wasted on your account. In seven instances you were freed from death. Now, having come from the village of your inheritance, you have attained the position of merchant with all its appurtenances.” Hearing that, he thought, “This is a grave matter indeed! For me, who has been freed from such a death, it is not proper to live a life of heedlessness. I will be heedful.” Then, giving away a thousand daily, he established alms for travelers, the poor, and others. A householder named Mitta became the manager of his charity. This is the story of Ghosaka the merchant.

Tasmiṃ pana kāle bhaddavatīnagare bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhi nāma ghosakaseṭṭhino adiṭṭhapubbasahāyako ahosi. Bhaddavatīnagarato āgatānaṃ vāṇijānaṃ santike ghosakaseṭṭhi bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhino sampattiñca vayappadesañca sutvā tena saddhiṃ sahāyakabhāvaṃ icchanto paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi. Bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhipi kosambito āgatānaṃ vāṇijānaṃ santike ghosakaseṭṭhino sampattiñca vayappadesañca sutvā tena saddhiṃ sahāyakabhāvaṃ icchanto paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi. Evaṃ te aññamaññaṃ adiṭṭhapubbasahāyakā hutvā vasiṃsu. Aparabhāge bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhino gehe ahivātarogo patito. Tasmiṃ patite paṭhamaṃ makkhikā maranti, tato anukkameneva kīṭā mūsikā kukkuṭā sūkarā gāvo dāsī dāsā sabbapacchā gharamānusakāpi maranti. Tesu ye bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāyanti, te jīvitaṃ labhanti, tadā pana seṭṭhi ca bhariyā ca dhītā cassa tathā palāyitvā [M 1.0121] ghosakaseṭṭhiṃ passituṃ patthentā kosambimaggaṃ [P 1.0188] paṭipajjiṃsu. Te antarāmaggeyeva khīṇapātheyyā vātātapena ceva khuppipāsāhi ca kilantasarīrā kicchena kosambiṃ patvā udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā nhatvā nagaradvāre ekaṃ sālaṃ pavisiṃsu.

At that time, in the city of Bhaddavatī, there was a wealthy merchant named Bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhi, who was a friend of Ghosakaseṭṭhi whom he had not met before. Hearing from merchants who came from Bhaddavatī about the wealth and age of Bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhi, Ghosakaseṭṭhi, desiring friendship with him, sent gifts. Bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhi also, hearing from merchants who came from Kosambī about the wealth and age of Ghosakaseṭṭhi, and desiring friendship with him, sent gifts. Thus, they lived as unseen friends. Later, a pestilence broke out in the house of Bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhi. When it broke out, first the flies died, then in succession the insects, mice, chickens, pigs, cows, female slaves, male slaves, and finally the people of the household also died. Among them, those who broke through the walls and fled survived. At that time, the merchant, his wife, and his daughter, having fled in this way and desiring to see Ghosakaseṭṭhi, took the road to Kosambī. On the way, their provisions exhausted, their bodies weary from the wind, sun, hunger, and thirst, they reached Kosambī with difficulty. Having stopped at a place with convenient water, they bathed and entered a hall at the city gate.

Tato seṭṭhi bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, iminā nīhārena gacchantā vijātamātuyāpi amanāpā honti, sahāyako kira me addhikakapaṇādīnaṃ devasikaṃ sahassaṃ vissajjetvā dānaṃ dāpesi. Tattha dhītaraṃ pesetvā āhāraṃ āharāpetvā ekāhaṃ dvīhaṃ idheva sarīraṃ santappetvā sahāyakaṃ passissāmā”ti. Sā “sādhu, sāmī”ti. Te sālāyameva vasiṃsu. Punadivase kāle ārocite kapaṇaddhikādīsu āhāratthāya gacchantesu mātāpitaro, “amma, gantvā amhākaṃ āhāraṃ āharā”ti dhītaraṃ pesayiṃsu. Mahābhogakulassa dhītā vipattiyā acchinnalajjitāya alajjamānā pātiṃ gahetvā kapaṇajanena saddhiṃ āhāratthāya gantvā “kati paṭivīse gaṇhissasi, ammā”ti puṭṭhā ca pana “tayo”ti āha. Athassā tayo paṭivīse adāsi. Tāya bhatte āhaṭe tayopi ekato bhuñjituṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Then the merchant said to his wife, 'My dear, those who go about in this state are disagreeable even to their own birth mothers. It is said that my friend gives away a thousand daily for travelers, the destitute, and others. Let us send our daughter there to have food brought back. After refreshing our bodies here for a day or two, we shall see our friend.' She replied, 'Very well, my lord.' They stayed in that very hall. The next day, when the time for alms was announced and the destitute, travelers, and others were going for food, the parents sent their daughter, saying, 'Child, go and bring back food for us.' The daughter of a very wealthy family, though her sense of shame was unbroken by her misfortune, could not afford to be ashamed. Taking a bowl, she went with the destitute people for food. When she was asked, 'Child, how many portions will you take?' she replied, 'Three.' Then they gave her three portions. When she brought the food back, all three of them sat down to eat together.

Atha mātādhītaro seṭṭhiṃ āhaṃsu – “sāmi, vipatti nāma mahākulānampi uppajjati, mā amhe oloketvā bhuñja, mā cintayī”ti. Iti naṃ nānappakārehi yācitvā bhojesuṃ. So bhuñjitvā āhāraṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto aruṇe uggacchante kālamakāsi. Mātādhītaro nānappakārehi paridevitvā rodiṃsu. Kumārikā punadivase rodamānā āhāratthāya gantvā, “kati [V 1.0110] paṭivīse gaṇhissasī”ti [P 1.0189] vuttā, “dve”ti vatvā āhāraṃ āharitvā mātaraṃ yācitvā bhojesi. Sāpi tāya yāciyamānā bhuñjitvā āhāraṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkontī taṃ divasameva kālamakāsi. Kumārikā ekikāva roditvā paridevitvā tāya dukkhuppattiyā ativiya sañjātachātakadukkhā punadivase yācakehi saddhiṃ rodantī āhāratthāya gantvā, “kati paṭivīse gaṇhissasi, ammā”ti vuttā “eka”nti āha. Mittakuṭumbiko taṃ tayo divase bhattaṃ gaṇhantiṃ sañjānāti, tena taṃ “apehi nassa, vasali, ajja tava kucchippamāṇaṃ aññāsī”ti āha. Hirottappasampannā kuladhītā [M 1.0122] paccorasmiṃ sattipahāraṃ viya vaṇe khārodakasecanakaṃ viya ca patvā “kiṃ, sāmī”ti āha. “Tayā pure tayo koṭṭhāsā gahitā, hiyyo dve, ajja ekaṃ gaṇhāsi. Ajja te attano kucchippamāṇaṃ ñāta”nti. “Mā maṃ, sāmi, ‘attanova atthāya gaṇhī’ti maññitthā”ti. “Atha kasmā evaṃ gaṇhī”ti? “Pure tayo janā ahumha, sāmi, hiyyo dve, ajja ekikāva jātāmhī”ti. So “kena kāraṇenā”ti pucchitvā ādito paṭṭhāya tāya kathitaṃ sabbaṃ pavattiṃ sutvā assūni sandhāretuṃ asakkonto sañjātabalavadomanasso hutvā, “amma, evaṃ sante mā cintayi, tvaṃ bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhino dhītā ajjakālato paṭṭhāya mama dhītāyeva nāmā”ti vatvā sīse cumbitvā gharaṃ netvā attano jeṭṭhadhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

Then the mother and daughter said to the merchant, 'Master, misfortune befalls even great families. Do not regard us; eat, and do not worry.' Thus, pleading with him in various ways, they fed him. After eating, being unable to digest the food, he passed away at dawn. The mother and daughter lamented in various ways and wept. The next day, the young girl, still weeping, went for food. When asked, 'How many portions will you take?' she replied, 'Two,' and brought back the food. She then pleaded with her mother and fed her. She too, being persuaded by her daughter, ate, and being unable to digest the food, passed away that very day. The young girl, now all alone, wept and lamented. Overwhelmed by this arising of sorrow and exceedingly afflicted by hunger, she went for food the next day with the beggars, weeping. When asked, 'Child, how many portions will you take?' she replied, 'One.' Mitta the householder, who had seen her taking food for three days, recognized her. Therefore, he said to her, 'Go away, perish, you wretched girl! Today you have learned the measure of your own belly.' The noble daughter, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, felt as if struck by a spear in the chest or as if alkaline water were poured on a wound, and said, 'Why do you say this, master?' 'Previously you took three portions, yesterday two, and today you take one. Today you have learned the measure of your own belly!' 'Master, do not think that I took it only for myself.' 'Then why did you take it so?' 'Master, previously we were three people, yesterday we were two, and today I am all alone.' He asked, 'For what reason?' and after hearing from her the whole story from the beginning, he was unable to hold back his tears. Overcome with great sadness, he said, 'Child, if this is so, do not grieve. You are the daughter of the merchant of Bhaddavati; from today onwards, you are my daughter indeed.' Having said this, he kissed her on the head, took her to his home, and established her in the position of his own eldest daughter.

Sā dānagge uccāsaddaṃ mahāsaddaṃ sutvā, “tāta, kasmā etaṃ janaṃ nissaddaṃ katvā dānaṃ na dethā”ti āha. “Na sakkā kātuṃ, ammā”ti. “Sakkā, tātā”ti. “Kathaṃ sakkā, ammā”ti? “Tāta dānaggaṃ parikkhipitvā [P 1.0190] ekekasseva pavesanappamāṇena dve dvārāni yojetvā, ‘ekena dvārena pavisitvā ekena nikkhamathā’ti vadetha, evaṃ nissaddā hutvāva gaṇhissantī”ti. So taṃ sutvā, “bhaddakova, amma, upāyo”ti tathā kāresi. Sāpi pubbe sāmā nāma. Vatiyā pana kāritattā sāmāvatī nāma jātā. Tato paṭṭhāya dānagge kolāhalaṃ pacchindī. Ghosakaseṭṭhi pubbe taṃ saddaṃ suṇanto “mayhaṃ dānagge saddo”ti tussati. Dvīhatīhaṃ pana saddaṃ asuṇanto mittakuṭumbikaṃ attano upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ pucchi – “diyyati kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ dāna”nti? “Āma, sāmī”ti. “Atha kiṃ dvīhatīhaṃ saddo na suyyatī”ti? “Yathā nissaddā hutvā gaṇhanti, tathā me upāyo kato”ti. “Atha pubbeva kasmā nākāsī”ti? “Ajānanatāya, sāmī”ti. “Idāni kathaṃ te ñāto”ti? “Dhītarā me akkhāto, sāmī”ti. Mayhaṃ aviditā “tava dhītā nāma atthī”ti. So ahivātaroguppattito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ bhaddavatiyaseṭṭhino pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā tassā attano jeṭṭhadhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapitabhāvaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi “evaṃ sante mama kasmā na kathesi, mama sahāyakassa [V 1.0111] dhītā mama dhītā nāmā”ti taṃ pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “amma, seṭṭhino dhītāsī”ti? “Āma, tātā”ti. “Tena hi mā cintayi, tvaṃ mama [M 1.0123] dhītāsī”ti taṃ sīse cumbitvā parivāratthāya tassā pañca itthisatāni datvā taṃ attano jeṭṭhadhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

Hearing the loud and great noise at the alms-shed, she said, 'Father, why do you not give alms after making these people silent?' 'It cannot be done, dear.' 'It can, father.' 'How can it be done, dear?' 'Father, enclose the alms-shed and set up two doors, each just wide enough for one person to enter. Then say, "Enter through one door and exit through the other." In this way, they will receive the alms silently.' Hearing this, he thought, 'Dear, your method is indeed good,' and did as she suggested. She was previously named Sāmā. But because she had caused an enclosure (vati) to be made, she became known as Sāmāvatī. From that time on, the uproar at the alms-shed ceased. The merchant Ghosaka, who had previously heard the noise, would rejoice, thinking, 'That is the sound at my alms-shed.' But when he did not hear the noise for two or three days, he asked the householder Mitta who had come to attend on him, 'Is alms being given to the destitute and travelers?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Then why has the sound not been heard for two or three days?' 'I have employed a method so that they receive it silently.' 'Then why did you not do it before?' 'Out of ignorance, sir.' 'How did you come to know of it now?' 'My daughter told me, sir.' 'I did not know you had a daughter!' Then, starting from the arising of the snake-venom-wind disease, he recounted the entire story of the merchant of Bhaddavati and informed him that he had placed her in the position of his eldest daughter. Then the merchant Ghosaka said, 'If that is so, why did you not tell me? The daughter of my friend is my daughter!' He had her summoned and asked, 'Dear, are you the daughter of the merchant of Bhaddavati?' 'Yes, father.' 'Then do not worry, you are my daughter.' Kissing her on the head, he gave her five hundred women for her retinue and placed her in the position of his eldest daughter.

Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ nagare nakkhattaṃ saṅghuṭṭhaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ pana nakkhatte bahi anikkhamanakā kuladhītaropi attano parivārena saddhiṃ padasāva [P 1.0191] nadiṃ gantvā nhāyanti. Tasmā taṃ divasaṃ sāmāvatīpi pañcahi itthisatehi parivāritā rājaṅgaṇeneva nhāyituṃ agamāsi. Uteno sīhapañjare ṭhito taṃ disvā “kassimā nāṭakitthiyo”ti pucchi. “Na kassaci nāṭakitthiyo, devā”ti. “Atha kassa dhītaro”ti? “Ghosakaseṭṭhino dhītā deva, sāmāvatī nāmesā”ti. So disvāva uppannasineho seṭṭhino sāsanaṃ pāhesi – “dhītaraṃ kira me pesetū”ti. “Na pesemi, devā”ti. “Mā kira evaṃ karotu, pesetuyevā”ti. “Mayaṃ gahapatikā nāma kumārikānaṃ pothetvā viheṭhetvā kaḍḍhanabhayena na dema, devā”ti. Rājā kujjhitvā gehaṃ lañchāpetvā seṭṭhiñca bhariyañca hatthe gahetvā bahi kārāpesi. Sāmāvatī, nhāyitvā āgantvā gehaṃ pavisituṃ okāsaṃ alabhantī, “kiṃ etaṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. “Amma, rājā tava kāraṇā pahiṇi. Atha ‘na mayaṃ dassāmā’ti vutte gharaṃ lañchāpetvā amhe bahi kārāpesī”ti. “Tāta, bhāriyaṃ vo kammaṃ kataṃ, raññā nāma pahite ‘na, demā’ti avatvā ‘sace me dhītaraṃ saparivāraṃ gaṇhatha, demā’ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, tātā”ti. “Sādhu, amma, tava ruciyā sati evaṃ karissāmī”ti rañño tathā sāsanaṃ pāhesi. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ saparivāraṃ ānetvā abhisiñcitvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sesā tassāyeva parivāritthiyo ahesuṃ. Ayaṃ sāmāvatiyā uppatti.

Then one day, a festival was proclaimed in that city. During that festival, even daughters of good families, who usually did not go out, went on foot to the river with their retinues to bathe. Therefore, on that day, Sāmāvatī too, surrounded by five hundred women, went through the royal courtyard to bathe. King Utena, standing at the lion-window, saw her and asked, 'Whose dancing girls are these?' 'They are not anyone's dancing girls, Your Majesty.' 'Then whose daughters are they?' 'She is the daughter of the merchant Ghosaka, Your Majesty, named Sāmāvatī.' Upon the very sight of her, affection arose in him, and he sent a message to the merchant: 'Let him send me his daughter.' 'I will not send her, Your Majesty.' 'Let him not act thus; he must indeed send her.' 'We householders do not give our young daughters, fearing they will be beaten, harassed, and dragged away, Your Majesty.' The king, enraged, had the house sealed and had the merchant and his wife seized by the hand and expelled. Sāmāvatī, returning after bathing and finding no opportunity to enter the house, asked, 'What is this, parents?' 'Dear, the king sent a message on your account. When we said, "We will not give her," he had the house sealed and had us expelled.' 'Parents, you have done a grave deed. When a king sends a message, instead of saying "We will not give," you should have said, "If you will take my daughter together with her retinue, we will give her," parents.' 'Very well, dear. If that is your wish, I shall do so.' He then sent such a message to the king. The king, saying 'Good,' accepted it and had her brought with her retinue. He consecrated her and placed her in the position of chief queen. The other women became her attendants. This is the origin of Sāmāvatī.

Utenassa pana aparāpi vāsuladattā nāma devī ahosi [P 1.0192] caṇḍapajjotassa dhītā. Ujjeniyañhi caṇḍapajjoto nāma rājā ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ uyyānato āgacchanto attano sampattiṃ oloketvā, “atthi nu kho aññassapi kassaci evarūpā sampattī”ti vatvā taṃ sutvā manussehi “kiṃ sampatti nāmesā, kosambiyaṃ utenassa rañño atimahatī sampatī”ti vutte rājā āha – “tena hi gaṇhissāma na”nti? “Na sakkā so gahetu”nti. “Kiñci katvā gaṇhissāmayevā”ti? “Na sakkā devā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “So hatthikantaṃ nāma sippaṃ jānāti, mantaṃ [M 1.0124] parivattetvā hatthikantavīṇaṃ vādento nāge palāpetipi gaṇhātipi. Hatthivāhanasampanno tena sadiso nāma natthī”ti. “Na sakkā mayā so gahetu”nti. “Sace te, deva, ekantena ayaṃ nicchayo, tena hi dāruhatthiṃ kāretvā [V 1.0112] tassāsannaṭṭhānaṃ pesehi. So hatthivāhanaṃ vā assavāhanaṃ vā sutvā dūrampi gacchati. Tattha naṃ āgataṃ gahetuṃ sakkā bhavissatī”ti.

Now, Utena had another queen named Vāsuladattā, the daughter of Caṇḍapajjota. Indeed, in Ujjenī there was a king named Caṇḍapajjota. One day, while returning from the park, he observed his own prosperity and said, 'Does any other person have such prosperity?' When his men heard this, they said, 'What is this prosperity of yours? King Utena of Kosambī has exceedingly great prosperity.' The king said, 'Then I shall seize him.' 'It is not possible to seize him,' they said. 'I shall certainly seize him by some means,' he said. 'It is not possible, Your Majesty.' 'For what reason?' 'He knows the art called "elephant-charming." By reciting a mantra and playing the elephant-charming vīṇā, he can both make elephants flee and capture them. He is accomplished in riding elephants; there is no one equal to him.' 'Am I unable to seize him?' said the king. 'If, Your Majesty, this is your absolute resolve, then this is the course of action: have a wooden elephant made and send it to a place near him. When he hears of an elephant mount or a horse mount, he goes even to a distant place. There, once he has arrived, it will be possible to seize him.'

Rājā “attheso upāyo”ti dārumayaṃ yantahatthiṃ kārāpetvā bahi pilotikāhi veṭhetvā katacittakammaṃ katvā tassa vijite āsannaṭṭhāne ekasmiṃ saratīre vissajjāpesi. Hatthino antokucchiyaṃ saṭṭhi purisā aparāparaṃ caṅkamanti, hatthilaṇḍaṃ āharitvā tattha tattha chaḍḍesuṃ. Eko vanacarako hatthiṃ disvā, “amhākaṃ rañño anucchaviko”ti cintetvā, gantvā rañño ārocesi – “deva, mayā sabbaseto kelāsakūṭapaṭibhāgo tumhākaññeva anucchaviko varavāraṇo diṭṭho”ti. Uteno tameva maggadesakaṃ katvā hatthiṃ abhiruyha saparivāro nikkhami. Tassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā [P 1.0193] carapurisā gantvā caṇḍapajjotassa ārocesuṃ. So āgantvā majjhe tucchaṃ katvā ubhosu passesu balakāyaṃ payojesi. Uteno tassāgamanaṃ ajānanto hatthiṃ anubandhi. Anto ṭhitamanussā vegena palāpesuṃ. Kaṭṭhahatthī rañño mantaṃ parivattetvā vīṇaṃ vādentassa tantisaddaṃ asuṇanto viya palāyatiyeva. Rājā hatthināgaṃ pāpuṇituṃ asakkonto assaṃ āruyha anubandhi. Tasmiṃ vegena anubandhante balakāyo ohīyi. Rājā ekakova ahosi. Atha naṃ ubhosu passesu payuttā caṇḍapajjotassa purisā gaṇhitvā attano rañño adaṃsu. Athassa balakāyo amittavasaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā bahinagareva khandhāvāraṃ nivesetvā acchi.

The king, thinking, 'This stratagem is sound,' had a wooden mechanical elephant made, wrapped it externally in rags, had it artistically painted, and had it released on the bank of a certain lake in a nearby place within Utena's territory. Inside the elephant's belly, sixty men could walk back and forth; they brought elephant dung and scattered it here and there. A forest-dweller saw the elephant and thought, 'This is suitable for our king.' He went and reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, I have seen a magnificent elephant, completely white, like a silver mountain peak, suitable only for you.' Utena, making that very man his guide, mounted an elephant and set out with his retinue. Learning of his approach, spies went and informed Caṇḍapajjota. He came, left the center open, and deployed his forces on both flanks. Utena, unaware of his arrival, pursued the elephant. The men inside made it flee with speed. As if not hearing the sound of the strings of the vīṇā of the king who was reciting the mantra and playing, the wooden elephant just kept fleeing. The king, unable to reach the great elephant, mounted a horse and gave chase. As he pursued with great speed, his army was left behind. The king was all alone. Then the men of Caṇḍapajjota, deployed on both flanks, seized him and delivered him to their own king. Then his army, realizing that he had fallen into the enemy's power, established a camp just outside the city and remained there.

Caṇḍapajjotopi utenaṃ jīvaggāhameva gāhāpetvā ekasmiṃ coragehe pakkhipitvā dvāraṃ pidahāpetvā tayo divase jayapānaṃ pivi. Uteno tatiyadivase ārakkhake pucchi – “kahaṃ vo, tāta, rājā”ti? “‘Paccāmitto me gahito’ti jayapānaṃ pivatī”ti. “Kā nāmesā mātugāmassa viya tumhākaṃ rañño kiriyā, nanu paṭirājūnaṃ gahetvā [M 1.0125] vissajjetuṃ vā māretuṃ vā vaṭṭati, amhe dukkhaṃ nisīdāpetvā jayapānaṃ kira pivatī”ti. Te gantvā tamatthaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. So āgantvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ evaṃ vadasī”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu taṃ vissajjessāmi, evarūpo kira te manto atthi, taṃ mayhaṃ dassasī”ti. “Sādhu dassāmi, gahaṇasamaye maṃ vanditvā taṃ gaṇhāhi. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ vandissasī”ti? “Kyāhaṃ taṃ vandissāmi, na vandissāmī”ti? “Ahampi te na dassāmī”ti[P 1.0194]. “Evaṃ sante rājāṇaṃ te karissāmī”ti. “Karohi, sarīrassa me issaro, na pana cittassā”ti. Rājā tassa sūragajjitaṃ sutvā, “kathaṃ nu kho imaṃ mantaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā, “imaṃ mantaṃ aññaṃ jānāpetuṃ na sakkā, mama dhītaraṃ etassa santike [V 1.0113] uggaṇhāpetvā ahaṃ tassā santike gaṇhissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ āha – “aññassa vanditvā gaṇhantassa dassasī”ti. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi amhākaṃ ghare ekā khujjā atthi tassā antosāṇiyaṃ vanditvā nisinnāya tvaṃ bahisāṇiyaṃ ṭhitova mantaṃ vācehī”ti. “Sādhu, mahārāja, khujjā vā hotu pīṭhasappi vā, vandantiyā dassāmī”ti. Tato rājā gantvā dhītaraṃ vāsuladattaṃ āha – “amma, eko saṅkhakuṭṭhī anagghamantaṃ jānāti, taṃ aññaṃ jānāpetuṃ na sakkā. Tvaṃ antosāṇiyaṃ nisīditvā taṃ vanditvā mantaṃ gaṇha, so bahisāṇiyaṃ ṭhatvā tuyhaṃ vācessati. Tava santikā ahaṃ taṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti.

Caṇḍapajjota, for his part, had Utena captured alive, and after confining him in a prison and having the door shut, he drank the victory drink for three days. On the third day, Utena asked the guards, 'My good sirs, where is your king?' 'He is drinking the victory drink, saying, "My enemy has been captured."' 'What kind of conduct is this for your king, like that of a woman? Is it not proper, having captured a rival king, to either release or execute him? Instead, he has me sit here in misery while he, it seems, drinks the victory drink!' They went and reported this matter to the king. He came and asked, 'Is it true that you speak thus?' 'Yes, great king.' 'Very well, I will release you. It is said you possess such a mantra; will you give it to me?' 'Very well, I will give it. At the time of receiving it, you must pay homage to me and then take it. But will you pay homage?' 'Why should I pay homage to you? I will not pay homage!' 'Then I, too, will not give it to you.' 'In that case, I will exercise my royal authority upon you.' 'Do so. You are master of my body, but not of my mind.' The king, hearing his heroic roar, thought, 'How then shall I obtain this mantra? It is not possible to have this mantra taught to another. I will have my daughter learn it from him, and then I will learn it from her.' Then he said to him, 'Will you give it to another who pays homage and receives it?' 'Yes, great king.' 'In that case, in our palace there is a certain hunchbacked woman. While she is seated inside a curtain, having paid homage, you, standing outside the curtain, should teach the mantra.' 'Very well, great king. Be she a hunchback or a cripple, I will give it to one who pays homage.' Then the king went and said to his daughter, Vāsuladattā, 'My dear, a certain man with shell-leprosy knows a priceless mantra. It is not possible to have this mantra taught to another. You are to sit inside a curtain, pay homage to him, and receive the mantra. He will stand outside the curtain and recite it for you. From you, I will then learn it.'

Evaṃ so tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ santhavakaraṇabhayena dhītaraṃ khujjaṃ, itaraṃ saṅkhakuṭṭhiṃ katvā kathesi. So tassā antosāṇiyaṃ vanditvā nisinnāya bahi ṭhito mantaṃ vācesi. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ punappunaṃ vuccamānampi mantapadaṃ vattuṃ asakkontiṃ “are khujje atibahaloṭṭhakapolaṃ te mukhaṃ, evaṃ nāma vadehī”ti āha. “Sā kujjhitvā are duṭṭhasaṅkhakuṭṭhi [P 1.0195] kiṃ vadesi, kiṃ mādisā khujjā nāma hotī”ti? Sāṇikaṇṇaṃ ukkhipitvā “kāsi tva”nti vutte, “rañño dhītā vāsuladattā nāmāha”nti āha. “Pitā te taṃ mayhaṃ kathento ‘khujjā’ti kathesī”ti. “Mayhampi kathento taṃ saṅkhakuṭṭhiṃ katvā kathesī”ti. Te ubhopi “tena hi amhākaṃ santhavakaraṇabhayena kathitaṃ bhavissatī”ti antosāṇiyaññeva santhavaṃ kariṃsu.

Thus, fearing that they would become acquainted with each other, he spoke, making his daughter out to be a hunchback and the other a man with shell-leprosy. While she was seated inside the curtain, having paid homage, he stood outside and taught the mantra. Then one day, when she was unable to say a word of the mantra even as it was being repeated again and again, he said: 'Hey, Hunchback! Your mouth has such thick lips and cheeks! Speak properly!' Enraged, she replied, 'Hey, you wicked man with shell-leprosy, what are you saying? How could one such as I be called a hunchback?' He lifted the edge of the curtain and asked, 'Who are you?' She replied, 'I am the king’s daughter, Vāsuladattā by name.' He said, 'Your father, when speaking to me of you, said you were a hunchback.' She replied, 'And when speaking to me, he made you out to be a man with shell-leprosy.' They both realized, 'In that case, it must have been said out of fear that we would become acquainted.' And so, right there inside the curtain, they became acquainted.

Tato paṭṭhāya mantaggahaṇaṃ vā sippaggahaṇaṃ vā natthi. Rājāpi dhītaraṃ niccaṃ pucchati – “sippaṃ gaṇhasi, ammā”ti? “Gaṇhāmi, tātā”ti. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ uteno [M 1.0126] āha – “bhadde, sāmikena kattabbaṃ nāma neva mātāpitaro na bhātubhaginiyo kātuṃ sakkonti, sace mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dassasi, pañca te itthisatāni parivāraṃ datvā aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ dassāmī”ti. “Sace imasmiṃ vacane patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkhissatha, dassāmi vo jīvita”nti. “Sakkhissāmi, bhadde”ti. Sā “sādhu, sāmī”ti pitu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ so pucchi – “amma, niṭṭhitaṃ sippa”nti? “Na tāva niṭṭhitaṃ, tāta, sippa”nti. Atha naṃ so pucchi – “kiṃ, ammā”ti? “Amhākaṃ ekaṃ dvārañca ekaṃ vāhanañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, tātā”ti. “Idaṃ kiṃ, ammā”ti? “Tāta, rattiṃ kira tārakasaññāya mantassa upacāratthāya ekaṃ osadhaṃ gahetabbaṃ atthi. Tasmā amhākaṃ velāya [P 1.0196] vā avelāya vā nikkhamanakāle ekaṃ dvārañceva ekaṃ vāhanañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Te attano abhirucitaṃ ekaṃ dvāraṃ hatthagataṃ kariṃsu. Rañño pana pañca vāhanāni ahesuṃ. Bhaddavatī nāma kareṇukā [V 1.0114] ekadivasaṃ paññāsa yojanāni gacchati, kāko nāma dāso saṭṭhi yojanāni gacchati, celakaṭṭhi ca muñcakesī cāti dve assā yojanasataṃ gacchanti, nāḷāgiri hatthī vīsati yojanasatanti.

From that time on, there was no learning of mantras or arts. The king would regularly ask his daughter, “Are you learning the art, my dear?” “I am learning, father,” she would reply. Then one day, Utena said to her, “My lady, what ought to be done by a husband, neither parents nor siblings can do. If you will give me my life, I will give you five hundred women as a retinue and give you the position of chief queen.” “If you can stand firm in this word, I will give you your life,” she said. “I will be able, my lady,” he replied. She said, “Very well, my lord,” and went to her father, paid respects, and stood to one side. Then he asked her, “My dear, is the art finished?” “The art is not yet finished, father,” she replied. He then asked her, “What is it, my dear?” “Father, it is proper for us to obtain one gate and one vehicle,” she said. “What is this for, my dear?” he asked. “Father, it is said that at night, by the sign of the stars, a certain medicinal root must be taken for the preliminary practice of the mantra. Therefore, it is proper for us to obtain one gate and one vehicle for leaving at a proper time or an improper time.” The king agreed, saying, “Very well.” They took control of a gate of their own choosing. Now, the king had five vehicles. A female elephant named Bhaddavatī could travel fifty yojanas in a day, a slave named Kāka could travel sixty yojanas, two horses named Celakaṭṭhi and Muñcakesī could travel a hundred yojanas, and the elephant Nāḷāgiri could travel one hundred and twenty yojanas.

So kira rājā anuppanne buddhe ekassa issarassa upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ issare bahinagaraṃ gantvā nhatvā āgacchante eko paccekabuddho nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā sakalanagaravāsīnaṃ mārena āvaṭṭitattā ekaṃ bhikkhāmpi alabhitvā yathādhotena pattena nikkhami. Atha naṃ nagaradvāraṃ pattakāle māro aññātakavesena upasaṅkamitvā, “api, bhante, vo kiñci laddha”nti pucchi. “Kiṃ pana me tvaṃ alabhanākāraṃ karī”ti? “Tena hi nivattitvā puna pavisatha, idāni na karissāmī”ti. “Nāhaṃ puna nivattissāmī”ti. Sace hi nivatteyya, puna so sakalanagaravāsīnaṃ sarīre adhimuñcitvā pāṇiṃ paharitvā hasanakeḷiṃ kareyya. Paccekabuddhe anivattitvā gate māro tattheva antaradhāyi. Atha so issaro yathādhoteneva pattena [P 1.0197] āgacchantaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā vanditvā, “api, bhante, kiñci laddha”nti pucchi. “Caritvā nikkhantamhāvuso”ti. So cintesi – “ayyo, mayā pucchitaṃ akathetvā aññaṃ vadati, na kiñci laddhaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Athassa pattaṃ olokento tucchaṃ disvā gehe bhattassa [M 1.0127] niṭṭhitāniṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ajānanatāya sūro hutvā pattaṃ gahetuṃ avisahanto “thokaṃ, bhante, adhivāsethā”ti vatvā vegena gharaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ bhattaṃ niṭṭhita”nti pucchitvā, “niṭṭhita”nti vutte taṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ āha – “tāta, añño tayā sampannavegataro nāma natthi, sīghena javena bhadantaṃ patvā ‘pattaṃ me, bhante, dethā’ti vatvā pattaṃ gahetvā vegena ehī”ti. So ekavacaneneva pakkhanditvā pattaṃ gahetvā āhari. Issaropi attano bhojanassa pattaṃ pūretvā “imaṃ sīghaṃ gantvā ayyassa sampādehi, ahaṃ te ito pattiṃ dammī”ti āha.

It is said that this king, at a time when no Buddhas had arisen, was an attendant of a certain lord. Then one day, as the lord was returning after having gone outside the city and bathed, a Paccekabuddha entered the city for alms. But because all the city’s residents had been deluded by Māra, he did not receive even a single portion of alms and departed with his bowl just as it had been washed. Then, as he was reaching the city gate, Māra approached him in the guise of an unknown person and asked, “Venerable sir, did you receive anything?” The Paccekabuddha replied, “Why did you cause me to receive nothing?” Māra said, “In that case, turn back and enter again; this time I will not do it.” But the Paccekabuddha said, “I will not turn back.” For if he were to turn back, Māra would again possess the bodies of all the city’s residents, making them clap their hands and engage in laughing and playing. When the Paccekabuddha departed without turning back, Māra vanished right there. Then the lord, seeing the Paccekabuddha coming with his bowl just as it had been washed, paid homage and asked, “Venerable sir, did you receive anything?” The Paccekabuddha replied, “Friend, having wandered for alms, I have departed.” The lord thought, “The noble one, not answering what I asked, says something else. He must have received nothing.” Then, looking at the bowl and seeing it was empty, and not knowing whether the food at home was cooked or not, he was not bold enough to take the bowl, and said, “Venerable sir, please wait a moment.” He went home quickly, asked, “Is our food cooked?” and upon being told, “It is cooked,” he said to that attendant: “Dear one, there is no one faster than you. With great speed, go to the venerable one, say, ‘Venerable sir, please give me the bowl,’ take the bowl, and come back quickly.” With just that one word, the attendant ran, took the bowl, and brought it back. The lord, for his part, having filled the bowl with his own food, said, “Take this quickly and present it to the noble one. I give you a share of the merit from this.”

Sopi taṃ gahetvā javena gantvā paccekabuddhassa pattaṃ datvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, ‘velā upakaṭṭhā’ti ahaṃ atisīghena javena āgato ca gato ca, etassa me javassa phalena yojanānaṃ paṇṇāsasaṭṭhisatavīsasatagamanasamatthāni pañca vāhanāni nibbattantu, āgacchantassa ca me gacchantassa ca sarīraṃ sūriyatejena tatthaṃ, tassa me phalena nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne āṇā sūriyatejasadisā hotu, imasmiṃ me piṇḍapāte sāminā patti dinnā, tassā me nissandena tumhehi diṭṭhadhammassa [P 1.0198] bhāgī homī”ti āha. Paccekabuddho “evaṃ hotū”ti vatvā –

He also, having taken it, went quickly, gave the bowl to the Paccekabuddha, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and said: “Venerable sir, thinking ‘The time is near,’ I came and went with extreme speed. By the fruit of this speed of mine, may five vehicles capable of traveling fifty, sixty, one hundred, and one hundred and twenty yojanas arise. My body, while coming and going, was heated by the sun's radiance. By the fruit of that, in whatever place I am reborn, may my authority be like the radiance of the sun. In this alms-offering, a share of the merit was given to me by my master. By its result, may I become a sharer in the Dhamma seen by you.” The Paccekabuddha said, “May it be so,” and said:

“Icchitaṃ [V 1.0115] patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, sabbameva samijjhatu;

Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95 pubbūpanissayasampattikathā; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1. 192);

“Whatever is wished and longed for by you, may all of it be fulfilled. May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.”

“Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, khippameva samijjhatu;

Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, maṇijotiraso yathā”ti. –

“Whatever is wished and longed for by you, may it be fulfilled for you quickly. May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the wish-fulfilling jewel.”

Anumodanaṃ akāsi. Paccekabuddhānaṃ kira idhāva dve gāthā anumodanagāthā nāma honti. Tattha jotirasoti sabbakāmadadaṃ maṇiratanaṃ vuccati. Idaṃ tassa pubbacaritaṃ. So etarahi caṇḍapajjoto ahosi. Tassa ca kammassa nissandena imāni pañca vāhanāni nibbattiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānakīḷāya nikkhami. Uteno “ajja palāyitabba”nti mahantāmahante cammapasibbake hiraññasuvaṇṇassa pūretvā kareṇukāpiṭṭhe ṭhapetvā vāsuladattaṃ ādāya palāyi. Antepurapālakā palāyantaṃ taṃ disvā gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “sīghaṃ gacchathā”ti balaṃ pahiṇi. Uteno [M 1.0128] balassa pakkhandabhāvaṃ ñatvā kahāpaṇapasibbakaṃ mocetvā pātesi, manussā kahāpaṇe uccinitvā puna pakkhandiṃsu. Itaro suvaṇṇapasibbakaṃ mocetvā pātetvā nesaṃ suvaṇṇalobhena papañcentānaññeva [P 1.0199] bahi nivuṭṭhaṃ attano khandhāvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva attano balakāyo parivāretvā nagaraṃ pavesesi. So patvāva vāsuladattaṃ abhisiñcitvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesīti. Ayaṃ vāsuladattāya uppatti.

He gave his blessing. It is said that for the Paccekabuddhas, only these two verses are called the verses of blessing. Therein, 'jotirasa' is said to be the gem that grants all desires. This was his past meritorious deed. That man has now become King Caṇḍapajjota. And as a result of that meritorious kamma, these five vehicles arose. Then one day, the king went out for sport in the park. Utena, thinking, 'Today I must flee,' filled very large leather bags with silver and gold, placed them on the back of the female elephant, took Vāsuladattā, and fled. The palace guards, seeing him fleeing, went and informed the king. The king dispatched his force, saying, 'Go quickly!' Utena, knowing that the force was in pursuit, untied a bag of coins and dropped it; the men, having picked up the coins, pursued again. The other, having untied a bag of gold and dropped it, while they were delaying out of greed for the gold, reached his own encampment that was stationed outside. Then, upon seeing him coming, his own army surrounded him and led him into the city. Having arrived, he consecrated Vāsuladattā and established her in the position of chief queen. This is the origin of Vāsuladattā.

Aparā pana māgaṇḍiyā nāma rañño santikā aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ labhi. Sā kira kururaṭṭhe māgaṇḍiyabrāhmaṇassa dhītā. Mātāpissā māgaṇḍiyāyeva nāmaṃ. Cūḷapitāpissā māgaṇḍiyova, sā abhirūpā ahosi devaccharapaṭibhāgā. Pitā panassā anucchavikaṃ sāmikaṃ alabhanto mahantehi mahantehi kulehi yācitopi “na mayhaṃ dhītu tumhe anucchavikā”ti tajjetvā uyyojesi. Athekadivasaṃ satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento māgaṇḍiyabrāhmaṇassa sapajāpatikassa anāgāmiphalūpanissayaṃ disvā attano pattacīvaramādāya tassa bahinigame aggiparicaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. So tathāgatassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā, “imasmiṃ loke iminā purisena sadiso añño puriso nāma natthi, ayaṃ mayhaṃ dhītu anucchaviko, imassa posāpanatthāya dhītaraṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā, “samaṇa, ekā me dhītā atthi, ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ tassā anucchavikaṃ purisaṃ na passāmi, tumhe tassā anucchavikā, sā ca tumhākaññeva anucchavikā. Tumhākañhi [P 1.0200] pādaparicārikā, tassā ca bhattā [V 1.0116] laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ vo ahaṃ dassāmi, yāva mamāgamanā idheva tiṭṭhathā”ti āha. Satthā kiñci avatvā tuṇhī ahosi. Brāhmaṇo vegena gharaṃ gantvā, “bhoti, bhoti dhītu me anucchaviko puriso diṭṭho, sīghaṃ sīghaṃ naṃ alaṅkarohī”ti taṃ alaṅkārāpetvā saddhiṃ brāhmaṇiyā ādāya satthu santikaṃ pāyāsi. Sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. Ayaṃ “ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayhaṃ dhītu anucchaviko natthī”ti kassaci adatvā “ajja me dhītu anucchaviko diṭṭho”ti kira vadeti, “kīdiso nu kho so puriso, passissāma na”nti mahājano teneva saddhiṃ nikkhami.

Furthermore, another woman named Māgaṇḍiyā obtained the position of chief queen from the king. It is said that she was the daughter of the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the Kuru country. Her mother's name was also Māgaṇḍiyā, and her paternal uncle's name was also Māgaṇḍiya. She was very beautiful, like a celestial nymph. But her father, not finding a suitable husband for her, even when solicited by very great families, rebuked them, saying, 'You are not suitable for my daughter,' and sent them away. Then one day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the supporting condition for the fruit of non-returning in the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya together with his wife. Taking his bowl and robe, he went to the place of fire-worship outside the Brahmin's town. Seeing the Tathāgata's person, which had attained the pinnacle of beauty and grace, the Brahmin thought, 'In this world there is no other man like this one. This one is suitable for my daughter. I will give my daughter to this man to attend upon him.' He then said, 'Ascetic, I have one daughter. For so long, I have not seen a man suitable for her. You are suitable for her, and she is suitable for you. It is fitting for you to have an attendant at your feet, and it is fitting for her to get a husband. I will give her to you. Wait right here until my return.' The Teacher, saying nothing, remained silent. The Brahmin went home with haste and said, 'Madam, madam, I have seen a suitable man for my daughter! Quickly, quickly, adorn her!' Having had her adorned, he took his daughter along with his wife and proceeded to the Teacher's presence. The whole city was in an uproar. 'It is said that this man, who for so long had not given his daughter to anyone, saying, "There is no one suitable for my daughter," now says, "Today I have seen a man suitable for my daughter!"' 'What kind of man is he? Let us see him!' A great crowd went out with him.

Tasmiṃ [M 1.0129] dhītaraṃ gahetvā āgacchante satthā tena vuttaṭṭhāne aṭṭhatvā tattha padacetiyaṃ dassetvā gantvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Buddhānañhi padacetiyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā akkantaṭṭhāneyeva paññāyati, na aññattha. Yesañcatthāya adhiṭṭhitaṃ hoti, teyeva naṃ passanti. Tesaṃ pana adassanakaraṇatthaṃ hatthiādayo vā akkamantu, mahāmegho vā pavassatu, verambhavātā vā paharantu, na taṃ koci makkhetuṃ sakkoti. Atha brāhmaṇī brāhmaṇaṃ āha – “kuhiṃ so puriso”ti. “‘Imasmiṃ ṭhāne tiṭṭhāhī’ti naṃ avacaṃ, kuhiṃ nu kho so gato”ti ito cito olokento padacetiyaṃ disvā “ayamassa padavalañjo”ti [P 1.0201] āha. Brāhmaṇī salakkhaṇamantānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ paguṇatāya lakkhaṇamante parivattetvā padalakkhaṇaṃ upadhāretvā, “nayidaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pañcakāmaguṇasevino pada”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

While the brahmin was coming with his daughter, the Teacher, not standing in the place he had indicated, showed a footprint shrine there, and having departed, stood in another place. For the footprint shrine of the Buddhas, having been established by their determination, appears only in the place where they have stepped, not elsewhere. And only those for whose benefit it has been established see it. But, should one wish to make it invisible to them, even if elephants or the like should tread on it, or a great cloud should rain, or the Veramba winds should strike, no one is able to obliterate it. Then the Brahmin woman said to the Brahmin, 'Where is that man?' He said, 'I told him, "Stand in this place." Where could he have gone?' Looking here and there, he saw the footprint shrine and said, 'This is his footprint.' The Brahmin woman, due to her proficiency in the three Vedas along with the treatises on characteristics, mentally reviewed the treatise on characteristics, and examining the characteristics of the footprint, said, 'Brahmin, this is not the footprint of one who partakes of the five strands of sensual pleasure,' and spoke this verse:

“Rattassa hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhave,

Duṭṭhassa hoti sahasānupīḷitaṃ;

Mūḷhassa hoti avakaḍḍhitaṃ padaṃ,

Vivaṭṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ pada”nti. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.260-261; visuddhi. 1.45);

“For one with lust, the footprint would be on tiptoe;

for one with hatred, it is pressed down violently;

for one with delusion, the footprint is dragged;

for one whose covering is removed, the footprint is like this.”

Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo evamāha – “bhoti tvaṃ udakapātiyaṃ kumbhīlaṃ, gehamajjhe ca pana coraṃ viya mante passanasīlā, tuṇhī hohī”ti. Brāhmaṇa, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ vadehi, nayidaṃ pañcakāmaguṇasevino padanti. Tato ito cito ca olokento satthāraṃ disvā, “ayaṃ so puriso”ti vatvā brāhmaṇo gantvā, “samaṇa, dhītaraṃ me tava posāpanatthāya demī”ti āha. Satthā “dhītarā te mayhaṃ attho atthi vā natthi vā”ti avatvāva, “brāhmaṇa, ekaṃ te kāraṇaṃ kathemī”ti vatvā, “kathehi samaṇā”ti vutte mahābhinikkhamanato paṭṭhāya yāva ajapālanigrodhamūlā [V 1.0117] mārena anubaddhabhāvaṃ ajapālanigrodhamūle ca pana “atīto dāni me esa visaya”nti tassa sokāturassa sokavūpasamanatthaṃ āgatāhi māradhītāhi kumārikavaṇṇādivasena [P 1.0202] payojitaṃ palobhanaṃ ācikkhitvā, “tadāpi mayhaṃ chando nāhosī”ti vatvā –

Then the brahmin said to her: 'Madam, you are like one who sees a crocodile in a water bowl, or a thief in the middle of the house; in the treatises on signs, you are accustomed to seeing things wrongly. Be silent!' She replied, 'Brahmin, say what you wish, but this is not the footprint of one who indulges in the five strands of sensual pleasure.' Then, looking about, he saw the Teacher and, saying, 'This is that man,' the brahmin went and said, 'Ascetic, I give you my daughter to attend upon you.' Without saying whether he had need of his daughter or not, the Teacher said, 'Brahmin, I will tell you one thing.' When told, 'Speak, ascetic,' he recounted being pursued by Māra from the Great Renunciation up to the Ajapāla banyan tree. And at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he described the temptation employed by Māra’s daughters, who had come to soothe the sorrow of that grief-stricken Māra, after he had thought, 'Now this one is beyond my domain,' appearing in the form of maidens and so forth. 'And even then,' he said, 'I had no desire.'

“Disvāna [M 1.0130] taṇhaṃ aratiṃ ragañca,

Nāhosi chando api methunasmiṃ;

Kimevidaṃ muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ,

Pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na icche”ti. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.260-261; su. ni. 841) –

“Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Raga,

I had no desire even for sexual union;

What is this, filled with urine and feces?

I would not wish to touch it even with my foot.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Gāthāpariyosāne brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Māgaṇḍiyāpi kho “sacassa mayā attho natthi, anatthikabhāvova vattabbo, ayaṃ pana maṃ muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ karoti, pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na iccheti, hotu, attano jātikulapadesabhogayasavayasampattiṃ āgamma tathārūpaṃ bhattāraṃ labhitvā samaṇassa gotamassa kattabbayuttakaṃ jānissāmī”ti satthari āghātaṃ bandhi. “Kiṃ pana satthā tāya attani āghātuppattiṃ jānāti, no”ti? “Jānātiyeva. Jānanto kasmā gāthamāhā”ti? Itaresaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena. Buddhā hi āghātaṃ agaṇetvā maggaphalādhigamārahānaṃ vasena dhammaṃ desentiyeva. Mātāpitaro taṃ netvā cūḷamāgaṇḍiyaṃ kaniṭṭhaṃ paṭicchāpetvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Cūḷamāgaṇḍiyopi [P 1.0203] cintesi – “mama dhītā omakasattassa na anucchavikā, ekassa raññova anucchavikā”ti. Taṃ ādāya kosambiṃ gantvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā, “imaṃ itthiratanaṃ devassa anucchavika”nti utenassa rañño adāsi. So taṃ disvāva uppannabalavasineho abhisekaṃ katvā pañcasatamātugāmaparivāraṃ datvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Ayaṃ māgaṇḍiyāya uppatti.

He spoke this verse. At the end of the verse, both the brahmin and his wife were established in the fruit of non-returning. Māgaṇḍiyā, however, thought: 'If he truly has no need of me, he should have just stated his disinterest. But this one makes me out to be full of urine and excrement, saying he would not wish to touch me even with his foot. So be it! Relying on my own birth, lineage, region, wealth, and youth, I will find a husband of such a kind and then I will know what ought to be done to the ascetic Gotama.' Thus, she harbored a grudge against the Teacher. Now, does the Teacher know that a grudge has arisen in her towards him, or not? He knows indeed. Knowing, why did he speak the verse? For the sake of the other two. For the Buddhas, disregarding any grudge, teach the Dhamma only for the sake of those who are worthy of attaining the path and its fruit. Her parents, taking her and entrusting her to her paternal uncle, Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, went forth and attained Arahantship. Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya also thought: 'My daughter is not suitable for an inferior person; she is suitable only for a king.' Taking her to Kosambi, he adorned her with all ornaments and, saying, 'This jewel of a woman is suitable for Your Majesty,' gave her to King Udena. Upon seeing her, he was overcome with strong affection, performed her consecration, gave her a retinue of five hundred women, and placed her in the position of chief queen. This is the origin story of Māgaṇḍiyā.

Evamassa diyaḍḍhasahassanāṭakitthiparivārā tisso aggamahesiyo ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye ghosakaseṭṭhi kukkuṭaseṭṭhi pāvārikaseṭṭhīti kosambiyaṃ tayo seṭṭhino honti. Te upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya pañcasatatāpase himavantato āgantvā nagare bhikkhāya carante disvā pasīditvā nisīdāpetvā bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā cattāro māse attano santike vasāpetvā puna vassāratte āgamanatthāya paṭijānāpetvā uyyojesuṃ. Tāpasāpi tato paṭṭhāya aṭṭha māse himavante vasitvā cattāro māse tesaṃ santike [M 1.0131] vasiṃsu. Te aparabhāge himavantato āgacchantā [V 1.0118] araññāyatane ekaṃ mahānigrodhaṃ disvā tassa mūle nisīdiṃsu. Tesu jeṭṭhakatāpaso cintesi – “imasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā oramattikā na bhavissati, mahesakkhenevettha devarājena bhavitabbaṃ[P 1.0204], sādhu vata sacāyaṃ isigaṇassa pānīyaṃ dadeyyā”ti. Sopi pānīyaṃ adāsi. Tāpaso nhānodakaṃ cintesi, tampi adāsi. Tato bhojanaṃ cintesi, tampi adāsi. Athassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ devarājā amhehi cintitaṃ cintitaṃ sabbaṃ deti, aho vata naṃ passeyyāmā”ti.
