So rukkhakkhandhaṃ padāletvā attānaṃ dassesi. Atha naṃ tāpasā, “devarāja, mahatī te sampatti, kiṃ nu kho katvā ayaṃ te laddhā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Mā pucchatha, ayyā”ti. “Ācikkha, devarājā”ti. So attanā katakammassa parittakattā lajjamāno kathetuṃ na visahi. Tehi punappunaṃ nippīḷiyamāno pana “tena hi suṇāthā”ti vatvā kathesi.

Thus, he had three chief queens with a retinue of one thousand five hundred female dancers. At that time, there were three wealthy merchants in Kosambi: Ghosaka, Kukkuṭa, and Pāvārika. As the rains-residence was approaching, they saw five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himalayas wandering for alms in the city, and they were filled with confidence. They had them sit down, fed them, and, taking a promise from them, had them stay in their presence for the four months. Then, having made them promise to return for the next rainy season, they sent them away. From then on, the ascetics too, having stayed in the Himalayas for eight months, would spend four months in their presence. On a later occasion, while coming from the Himalayas, they saw a great banyan tree in a forest grove and sat down at its root. The eldest among them thought: 'The deity dwelling in this tree must not be of inferior power; it must be a mighty deva-king. It would be good indeed if this deity were to give drinking water to this group of ascetics.' And the deity gave them drinking water. The ascetic then thought of water for bathing, and that too was given. Next, he thought of food, and that was also provided. Then it occurred to him: 'This deva-king gives whatever we think of. Oh, if only we could see him!' The deity split the tree trunk and revealed himself. The ascetics then asked him, 'O deva-king, great is your prosperity. By what deed did you attain this?' 'Do not ask, venerable sirs,' he replied. 'Tell us, O deva-king,' they insisted. Feeling ashamed due to the smallness of the deed he had done, he did not dare to speak. But being pressed by them repeatedly, he finally said, 'In that case, listen,' and he told his story.

So kireko duggatamanusso hutvā bhatiṃ pariyesanto anāthapiṇḍikassa santike bhatikammaṃ labhitvā taṃ nissāya jīvikaṃ kappesi. Athekasmiṃ uposathadivase sampatte anāthapiṇḍiko vihārato āgantvā pucchi – “tassa bhatikassa ajjuposathadivasabhāvo kenaci kathito”ti? “Na kathito, sāmī”ti. “Tena hissa sāyamāsaṃ pacathā”ti. Athassa patthodanaṃ paciṃsu. So divasaṃ araññe kammaṃ katvā sāyaṃ āgantvā bhatte vaḍḍhetvā dinne “chātomhī”ti sahasā abhuñjitvāva “aññesu divasesu imasmiṃ gehe ‘bhattaṃ detha, sūpaṃ detha, byañjanaṃ dethā’ti mahākolāhalaṃ ahosi, ajja te sabbe nissaddā nipajjiṃsu, mayhameva ekassāhāraṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti cintetvā pucchi – “avasesā bhuñjiṃsu, na bhuñjiṃsū”ti? “Na bhuñjiṃsu, tātā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? Imasmiṃ gehe uposathadivasesu sāyamāsaṃ [P 1.0205] na bhuñjanti, sabbeva uposathikā honti. Antamaso thanapāyinopi dārake mukhaṃ vikkhālāpetvā catumadhuraṃ mukhe pakkhipāpetvā mahāseṭṭhi uposathike kāreti. Gandhatelappadīpe jālante khuddakamahallakadārakā sayanagatā dvattiṃsākāraṃ sajjhāyanti. Tuyhaṃ pana uposathadivasabhāvaṃ kathetuṃ satiṃ na karimhā. Tasmā taveva bhattaṃ pakkaṃ, naṃ bhuñjassūti. Sace idāni uposathikena [M 1.0132] bhavituṃ vaṭṭati, ahampi bhaveyyanti. “Idaṃ seṭṭhi jānātī”ti. “Tena hi naṃ pucchathā”ti. Te gantvā seṭṭhiṃ pucchiṃsu. So evamāha – “idāni pana abhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhahanto upaḍḍhaṃ uposathakammaṃ labhissatī”ti. Itaro taṃ sutvā tathā akāsi.

It is said that he, having once been a poor man, was searching for hire. He obtained work for hire in Anāthapiṇḍika’s household and made his living depending on him. Then, when an Uposatha day arrived, Anāthapiṇḍika came from the monastery and asked, “Has anyone told this hired worker that today is an Uposatha day?” “He has not been told, master,” they replied. “In that case, cook his evening meal.” So they cooked a measure of rice for him. Having worked in the forest all day, he returned in the evening. When the meal was served to him, though he was hungry, he did not eat immediately, thinking, “On other days in this house there was a great commotion—‘Give rice, give soup, give curry!’ But today, they are all silent and have lain down. They have served food only for me. What could be the reason for this?” So he asked, “Have the others eaten or not?” “They have not eaten, dear one.” “For what reason?” “In this house, on Uposatha days, they do not eat an evening meal; all of them are observing the Uposatha. The great merchant has even the nursing infants rinse their mouths, puts the four sweets in their mouths, and has them observe the Uposatha. With fragrant oil lamps burning, the young and old children, having gone to bed, recite the thirty-two parts of the body. We, however, did not remember to tell you that it is an Uposatha day. Therefore, your meal alone was cooked. Eat it.” “If it is permissible to become an observer of the Uposatha now, I too would become one.” “The merchant knows about this.” “In that case, ask him.” They went and asked the merchant. He said this: “Even now, by not eating, rinsing his mouth, and undertaking the Uposatha precepts, he will receive the fruit of half an Uposatha observance.” Hearing that, the other man did so.

Tassa sakaladivasaṃ kammaṃ katvā chātassa sarīre vātā kuppiṃsu. So yottena uraṃ bandhitvā yottakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā parivattati. Seṭṭhi taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā ukkāhi dhāriyamānāhi catumadhuraṃ gāhāpetvā [V 1.0119] tassa santikaṃ āgantvā, “kiṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, vātā me kuppitā”ti. “Tena hi uṭṭhāya idaṃ bhesajjaṃ khādāhī”ti. “Tumhepi khādatha, sāmī”ti. “Amhākaṃ aphāsukaṃ natthi, tvaṃ khādāhī”ti. “Sāmi, ahaṃ uposathakammaṃ karonto [P 1.0206] sakalaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, upaḍḍhakammampi me vikalaṃ mā ahosī”ti na icchi. “Mā evaṃ kari, tātā”ti vuccamānopi anicchitvā aruṇe uṭṭhahante milātamālā viya kālaṃ katvā tasmiṃ nigrodharukkhe devatā hutvā nibbatti. Tasmā imamatthaṃ kathetvā “so seṭṭhi buddhamāmako, dhammamāmako, saṅghamāmako, taṃ nissāya katassa upaḍḍhuposathakammassa nissandenesā sampatti mayā laddhā”ti āha.

Having worked the entire day, being hungry, the winds in his body became agitated. He tied a cord around his chest, held the end of the cord, and tossed about. The merchant, hearing of his condition, had the four-sweet medicine brought by torchlight and came to his side, asking, “What is it, dear one?” “Master, the winds in me are agitated.” “In that case, get up and eat this medicine.” “Do you also eat it, master?” “We have no discomfort; you eat it.” “Master, in undertaking the Uposatha observance, I was not able to do the whole of it. May even the half-observance not be deficient for me,” he said, and did not wish for it. Though he was told, “Do not do so, dear one,” he remained unwilling. As dawn was breaking, he passed away like a withered garland and was reborn as a deity in that banyan tree. Therefore, having related this matter, he said: “That merchant is devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, devoted to the Sangha. It is as a result of the half-Uposatha observance done by relying on him that this prosperity has been obtained by me.”

“Buddho”ti vacanaṃ sutvāva pañcasatā tāpasā uṭṭhāya devatāya añjaliṃ paggayha “buddhoti vadesi, buddhoti vadesī”ti pucchitvā, “buddhoti vadāmi, buddhoti vadāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ paṭijānāpetvā “ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmi”nti udānaṃ udānetvā “devate anekesu kappasatasahassesu asutapubbaṃ saddaṃ tayā suṇāpitamhā”ti āhaṃsu. Atha antevāsino ācariyaṃ etadavocuṃ – “tena hi satthu santikaṃ gacchāmā”ti. “Tātā, tayo seṭṭhino amhākaṃ bahūpakārā, sve tesaṃ nivesane bhikkhaṃ gaṇhitvā tesampi ācikkhitvā gamissāma, adhivāsetha, tātā”ti. Te adhivāsayiṃsu. Punadivase seṭṭhino yāgubhattaṃ sampādetvā āsanāni paññāpetvā “ajja no ayyānaṃ āgamanadivaso”ti ñatvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā te ādāya nivesanaṃ gantvā nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. Te katabhattakiccā mahāseṭṭhino “mayaṃ gamissāmā”ti vadiṃsu. “Nanu, bhante, tumhehi cattāro [P 1.0207] vassike māse amhākaṃ gahitāva paṭiññā, idāni kuhiṃ gacchathā”ti? “Loke [M 1.0133] kira buddho uppanno, dhammo uppanno, saṅgho uppanno, tasmā satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tassa satthuno santikaṃ tumhākaññeva gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Aññesampi avāritaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, āgametha, mayampi gamanaparivacchaṃ katvā gacchāmā”ti. “Tumhesu parivacchaṃ karontesu amhākaṃ papañco hoti, mayaṃ purato gacchāma, tumhe pacchā āgaccheyyāthā”ti vatvā te puretaraṃ gantvā sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā abhitthavitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ satthā anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne sabbepi saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti vacanasamanantaraṃyeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā ehibhikkhū ahesuṃ.

Upon hearing the word “Buddha,” five hundred ascetics arose, raised their hands in reverence to the deity, and asked, “Do you say ‘Buddha’? Do you say ‘Buddha’?” Having made him affirm three times, “I say ‘Buddha,’ I say ‘Buddha’,” they uttered an inspired exclamation: “Indeed, even this sound is rare in the world!” They said, “O deity, you have caused us to hear a sound unheard of before in many hundreds of thousands of eons.” Then the disciples said this to their teacher: “In that case, let us go to the Teacher’s presence.” “Dear ones, the three merchants are our great benefactors. Tomorrow, after receiving alms at their residence and informing them as well, we shall go. Wait, dear ones.” They consented. The next day, the merchants prepared rice-gruel and rice, arranged the seats, and knowing, “Today is the day of our noble sirs’ arrival,” they went out to meet them. Taking them to their residence, they had them seated and gave them alms. When they had finished their meal, they said to the great merchants, “We shall go.” “Venerable sirs, did you not make a promise to us for the four months of the rains? Where are you going now?” “It is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world, the Dhamma has arisen, the Sangha has arisen. Therefore, we shall go to the Teacher’s presence.” “Is it proper for only you to go to that Teacher’s presence?” “It is not barred to others either, friends.” “In that case, venerable sirs, please wait. We too shall make our preparations and go.” “While you are making preparations, it will be a delay for us. We shall go first; you may come afterwards.” Having said this, they went on ahead and, upon seeing the Fully Enlightened One, they praised and venerated him, and sat down to one side. Then the Teacher gave them a progressive discourse and taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the ascetics attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having requested the going forth, immediately after the words, “Come, monks,” they became ‘ehi-bhikkhus,’ bearers of bowls and robes created by psychic power.

Tepi kho tayo seṭṭhino pañcahi pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhattacchādanasappimadhuphāṇitādīni dānūpakaraṇāni ādāya sāvatthiṃ patvā satthāraṃ vanditvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā kathāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale [V 1.0120] patiṭṭhāya addhamāsamattampi dānaṃ dadamānā satthu santike vasitvā kosambiṃ āgamanatthāya satthāraṃ yācitvā satthārā paṭiññaṃ dadantena [P 1.0208] “suññāgāre kho gahapatayo tathāgatā abhiramantī”ti vutte, “aññātaṃ, bhante, amhehi pahitasāsanena āgantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā kosambiṃ gantvā ghosakaseṭṭhi ghositārāmaṃ, kukkuṭaseṭṭhi kukkuṭārāmaṃ, pāvārikaseṭṭhi pāvārikārāmanti tayo mahāvihāre kāretvā satthu āgamanatthāya sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā tattha agamāsi. Te paccuggantvā satthāraṃ vihāraṃ pavesetvā vārena vārena paṭijagganti. Satthā devasikaṃ ekekasmiṃ vihāre vasati. Yassa vihāre vuṭṭho hoti, tasseva gharadvāre piṇḍāya carati. Tesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ seṭṭhīnaṃ upaṭṭhāko sumano nāma mālākāro ahosi. So te seṭṭhino evamāha – “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ upakārako, satthāraṃ bhojetukāmomhi, mayhampi ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ dethā”ti. “Tena hi bhaṇe sve bhojehī”ti. “Sādhu, sāmī”ti so satthāraṃ nimantetvā sakkāraṃ paṭiyādesi.

Those three merchants, each with five hundred carts, brought requisites for offerings—food, clothing, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth—and arrived at Sāvatthī. Having paid homage to the Master and listened to his Dhamma talk, at the end of the discourse they were established in the fruit of stream-entry. They stayed in the Master's presence for about half a month, giving alms, and then requested the Master to come to Kosambī. When the Master, giving his consent, said, 'Householders, Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings,' they replied, 'Venerable sir, it is understood. It is proper that you should come when a message is sent by us.' Having said this, they went to Kosambī. The merchant Ghosaka had the Ghositārāma built, the merchant Kukkuṭa the Kukkuṭārāma, and the merchant Pāvārika the Pāvārikārāma—three great monasteries. They then sent a message for the Master to come. The Master, hearing their message, went there. They went out to welcome him, led the Master into the monastery, and attended to him in turns. The Master stayed one day in each monastery. At whichever merchant's monastery he had stayed, he would go for alms at the door of that very merchant's house. Now, the attendant of these three merchants was a garland-maker named Sumana. He said to those merchants, 'I have been of service to you for a long time. I wish to offer food to the Master. Please grant me the Master for one day as well.' They replied, 'In that case, offer food tomorrow.' 'Very good, sirs,' he said. He then invited the Master and prepared the offerings.

Tadā [M 1.0134] rājā sāmāvatiyā devasikaṃ pupphamūle aṭṭha kahāpaṇe deti. Tassā khujjuttarā nāma dāsī sumanamālākārassa santikaṃ gantvā nibaddhaṃ pupphāni gaṇhāti. Atha naṃ tasmiṃ divase āgataṃ mālākāro āha – “mayā satthā nimantito, ajja pupphehi satthāraṃ pūjessāmi, tiṭṭha tāva, tvaṃ parivesanāya sahāyikā hutvā dhammaṃ sutvā avasesāni pupphāni gahetvā gamissasī”ti[P 1.0209]. Sā “sādhū”ti adhivāsesi. Sumano buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā anumodanakaraṇatthāya pattaṃ aggahesi. Satthā anumodanadhammadesanaṃ ārabhi. Khujjuttarāpi satthu dhammakathaṃ suṇantīyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Sā aññesu divasesu cattāro kahāpaṇe attano gahetvā catūhi pupphāni gahetvā gacchati, taṃ divasaṃ aṭṭhahipi pupphāni gahetvā gatā. Atha naṃ sāmāvatī āha – “kiṃ nu kho, amma, ajja amhākaṃ raññā dviguṇaṃ pupphamūlaṃ dinna”nti? “No, ayye”ti. “Atha kasmā bahūni pupphānī”ti? “Aññesu divasesu ahaṃ cattāro kahāpaṇe attano gahetvā catūhi pupphāni āharāmī”ti. “Ajja kasmā na gaṇhī”ti? “Sammāsambuddhassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā dhammassa adhigatattā”ti. Atha naṃ “are, duṭṭhadāsi ettakaṃ kālaṃ tayā gahitakahāpaṇe me dehī”ti atajjetvā, “amma, tayā pivitaṃ amataṃ amhepi pāyehī”ti vatvā “tena hi maṃ nhāpehī”ti vutte soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhāpetvā dve maṭṭhasāṭake dāpesi. Sā ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ ekaṃsaṃ pārupitvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā ekaṃ bījaniṃ āharāpetvā āsane nisīditvā citrabījaniṃ ādāya pañca mātugāmasatāni āmantetvā tāsaṃ satthārā desitaniyāmeneva dhammaṃ desesi. Tassā dhammakathaṃ sutvā tā sabbāpi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

At that time, the king gave eight kahāpaṇas daily to Sāmāvatī for the price of flowers. Her slave-woman named Khujjuttarā would go to the garland-maker Sumana and regularly buy flowers. On that day, when she arrived, the garland-maker said to her: 'The Master has been invited by me. Today I will honor the Master with flowers. You wait for a while; having become a helper in serving the meal and having listened to the Dhamma, you shall take the remaining flowers and go.' She consented, saying, 'Very well.' Sumana, having served the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, took the bowl for the purpose of giving the discourse of appreciation. The Master began the Dhamma discourse of appreciation. Khujjuttarā, while listening to the Master's Dhamma talk, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. On other days, she would take four kahāpaṇas for herself and bring flowers with the other four, but on that day, she took flowers with all eight kahāpaṇas and went. Then Sāmāvatī said to her: 'My dear, has the king given us double the flower-money today?' 'No, my lady.' 'Then why are there so many flowers?' 'On other days, I take four kahāpaṇas for myself and bring flowers with the other four.' 'Why did you not take any today?' 'Because, having heard the Dhamma talk of the Perfectly Enlightened One, I have attained the Dhamma.' Then Sāmāvatī, instead of threatening her by saying, 'Hey, you wicked slave! Give me the kahāpaṇas you have taken for so long!', said, 'My dear, let us also drink the Deathless that you have drunk.' When Khujjuttarā replied, 'In that case, have me bathed,' Sāmāvatī had her bathed with sixteen pots of scented water and had two fine garments given to her. She, having worn one and draped the other, had a seat prepared, had a fan brought, sat on the seat, and taking up an ornate fan, addressed the five hundred women and taught them the Dhamma in the very same way the Master had taught it. Having heard her Dhamma talk, all those women were also established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tā [V 1.0121] sabbāpi khujjuttaraṃ vanditvā, “amma[P 1.0210], ajjato paṭṭhāya tvaṃ kiliṭṭhakammaṃ mā kari, amhākaṃ mātuṭṭhāne ca ācariyaṭṭhāne ca ṭhatvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthārā desitaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā amhākaṃ kathehī”ti vadiṃsu. Sā tathā karontī aparabhāge tipiṭakadharā jātā. Atha naṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ bahussutānaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ khujjuttarā”ti etadagge ṭhapesi. Tāpi kho pañcasatā itthiyo taṃ evamāhaṃsu – “amma, satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmāmhā, taṃ no dassehi, gandhamālādīhi [M 1.0135] taṃ pūjessāmā”ti. “Ayye, rājakulaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, tumhe gahetvā bahi gantuṃ na sakkā”ti. “Amma, no mā nāsehi, dasseheva amhākaṃ satthāra”nti. “Tena hi tumhākaṃ vasanagabbhānaṃ bhittīsu yattakena oloketuṃ sakkā hoti, tattakaṃ chiddaṃ katvā gandhamālādīni āharāpetvā satthāraṃ tiṇṇaṃ seṭṭhīnaṃ gharadvāraṃ gacchantaṃ tumhe tesu tesu ṭhānesu ṭhatvā oloketha ceva, hatthe ca pasāretvā vandatha, pūjetha cā”ti. Tā tathā katvā satthāraṃ gacchantañca āgacchantañca oloketvā vandiṃsu ceva pūjesuñca.

All of them, having paid homage to Khujjuttarā, said, 'Mother, from today onwards, do not perform menial work. Standing in the position of our mother and teacher, go to the Master's presence, listen to the Dhamma taught by the Master, and then explain it to us.' She did so, and in time became a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. Then the Master placed her in the foremost position, saying, 'Monks, foremost among my female lay disciples who are very learned and are preachers of the Dhamma is this one, that is, Khujjuttarā.' Those five hundred women also spoke to her thus: 'Mother, we wish to see the Master. Show him to us; we will make offerings to him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.' 'Noble ladies, the royal household is a restrictive place; it is not possible to take you and go outside.' 'Mother, do not destroy our hope; just show us the Master.' 'Well then, in the walls of your living quarters, make an opening just large enough to be able to look through. Having had perfumes, garlands, and so forth brought, when the Master is going to the doors of the three merchants' houses, you should stand in those respective places and look at him. And, raising your hands in homage, you should pay reverence and make offerings.' They did so, and watching the Master as he was coming and going, they both paid homage and made offerings.

Athekadivasaṃ māgaṇḍiyā attano pāsādatalato nikkhamitvā caṅkamamānā tāsaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā gabbhesu chiddaṃ disvā, “idaṃ ki”nti pucchitvā, tāhi tassā satthari āghātabaddhabhāvaṃ ajānantīhi “satthā [P 1.0211] imaṃ nagaraṃ āgato, mayaṃ ettha ṭhatvā satthāraṃ vandāma ceva pūjema cā”ti vutte, “āgato nāma imaṃ nagaraṃ samaṇo gotamo, idānissa kattabbaṃ jānissāmi, imāpi tassa upaṭṭhāyikā, imāsampi kattabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti cintetvā gantvā rañño ārocesi – “mahārāja, sāmāvatimissikānaṃ bahiddhā patthanā atthi, katipāheneva te jīvitaṃ māressantī”ti. Rājā “na tā evarūpaṃ karissantī”ti na saddahi. Punappunaṃ vuttepi na saddahi eva. Atha naṃ evaṃ tikkhattuṃ vuttepi asaddahantaṃ “sace me na saddahasi, tāsaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā upacārehi, mahārājā”ti āha. Rājā gantvā gabbhesu chiddaṃ disvā, “idaṃ ki”nti pucchitvā, tasmiṃ atthe ārocite tāsaṃ akujjhitvā, kiñci avatvāva chiddāni pidahāpetvā sabbagabbhesu uddhacchiddakavātapānāni kāresi. Uddhacchiddakavātapānāni kira tasmiṃ kāle uppannāni. Māgaṇḍiyā tāsaṃ kiñci kātuṃ asakkuṇitvā, “samaṇassa gotamasseva kattabbaṃ karissāmī”ti nāgarānaṃ lañjaṃ datvā, “samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ antonagaraṃ pavisitvā vicarantaṃ dāsakammakaraporisehi akkosetvā paribhāsetvā palāpethā”ti āṇāpesi. Micchādiṭṭhikā tīsu ratanesu appasannā antonagaraṃ paviṭṭhaṃ satthāraṃ anubandhitvā[M 1.0136], “corosi[P 1.0212], bālosi, mūḷhosi, oṭṭhosi, goṇosi, gadrabhosi, nerayikosi, tiracchānagatosi, natthi tuyhaṃ sugati, duggatiyeva tuyhaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā”ti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti paribhāsanti.

Then one day, Māgaṇḍiyā, having left her palace roof-terrace and walking about, went to their dwelling place and saw holes in the rooms. Asking, "What is this?" and because they did not know of her deep-seated hatred for the Master, they said, "The Master has come to this city; we stay here to pay homage and make offerings to him." Hearing this, she thought, "So the recluse Gotama has come to this city. Now I will know what must be done concerning him. These women are his supporters; I will also know what must be done concerning them." She went and informed the king: "Great king, Sāmāvatī and her retinue have a desire for a man outside. In just a few days, they will kill you." The king did not believe her, saying, "They would not do such a thing." Even when she repeated it, he still did not believe her. After being told three times without being believed, she said, "If you do not believe me, go to their dwelling place and examine it, great king." The king went and saw the holes in the rooms. Asking, "What is this?" and hearing the explanation, he did not get angry with them. Without saying anything, he had the holes closed up and had upper windows made in all the rooms. It is said that upper windows were first introduced at that time. Unable to do anything to them, Māgaṇḍiyā thought, "I will take action against the recluse Gotama himself." Giving bribes to the citizens, she ordered, "When the recluse Gotama enters the city and walks around, have the slaves, servants, and workers insult, abuse, and chase him away." Holding wrong views and lacking faith in the Triple Gem, they followed the Master as he entered the city, insulting and abusing him with ten kinds of abusive expressions: "You are a thief, a fool, a deluded one, a camel, an ox, a donkey, one bound for hell, one destined for the animal realm. There is no happy destination for you; only an unhappy destination is to be expected for you."

Taṃ [V 1.0122] sutvā āyasmā ānando satthāraṃ etadavoca – “bhante, ime nāgarā amhe akkosanti paribhāsanti, ito aññattha gacchāmā”ti. “Kuhiṃ, ānandoti”? “Aññaṃ nagaraṃ, bhante”ti. “Tattha manussesu akkosantesu puna kattha gamissāma, ānando”ti? “Tatopi aññaṃ nagaraṃ, bhante”ti. “Tatthāpi manussesu akkosantesu kuhiṃ gamissāmā”ti? “Tatopi aññaṃ nagaraṃ, bhante”ti. “Ānanda, evaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yattha adhikaraṇaṃ uppannaṃ, tattheva tasmiṃ vūpasante aññattha gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Ke pana te, ānanda, akkosantī”ti? “Bhante, dāsakammakare upādāya sabbe akkosantī”ti. “Ahaṃ, ānanda, saṅgāmaṃ otiṇṇahatthisadiso, saṅgāmaṃ otiṇṇahatthino hi catūhi disāhi āgate sare sahituṃ bhāro, tatheva bahūhi dussīlehi kathitakathānaṃ sahanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro”ti vatvā attānaṃ ārabbha dhammaṃ desento imā nāgavagge tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Master: "Venerable sir, these townspeople insult and abuse us; let us go elsewhere from here." "Where, Ānanda?" "To another city, venerable sir." "Ānanda, if the people there also revile us, where shall we go then?" "From there also to another city, venerable sir." "If the people there also revile us, where shall we go?" "From there also to another city, venerable sir." "Ānanda, it is not proper to do so. Wherever a dispute has arisen, only there, when that dispute has subsided, is it proper to go elsewhere. But who, Ānanda, reviles you?" "Venerable sir, beginning with the slaves and workmen, everyone reviles us." "Ānanda, I am like a great elephant that has entered into battle. Indeed, for a great elephant that has entered the battlefield, it is its burden to endure the arrows coming from the four directions; just so, to endure the words spoken by many immoral people is my burden." Having said this, the Master, teaching the Dhamma concerning himself, spoke these three verses in the Nāga Vagga:

“Ahaṃ nāgova saṅgāme, cāpato patitaṃ saraṃ;

Ativākyaṃ titikkhissaṃ, dussīlo hi bahujjano.

As a great elephant in battle endures an arrow shot from a bow, so shall I endure abusive speech; for many people are immoral.

“Dantaṃ [P 1.0213] nayanti samitiṃ, dantaṃ rājābhirūhati;

Danto seṭṭho manussesu, yotivākyaṃ titikkhati.

They lead a tamed creature to an assembly; a king mounts a tamed creature. The tamed one is best among humans—he who endures abusive speech.

“Varamassatarā dantā, ājānīyā ca sindhavā;

Kuñjarā ca mahānāgā, attadanto tato vara”nti. (dha. pa. 320-322);

Excellent are tamed mules, and thoroughbreds, and horses of Sindh, and great elephants, the mighty tuskers; but one who is self-tamed is more excellent than they. (dha. pa. 320-322)

Dhammakathā sampattamahājanassa sātthikā ahosi. Evaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā mā cintayi, ānanda, ete sattāhamattameva akkosissanti, aṭṭhame divase tuṇhī bhavissanti, buddhānañhi uppannaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sattāhato uttari na gacchati. Māgaṇḍiyā satthāraṃ akkosāpetvā palāpetuṃ asakkontī, “kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti cintetvā, “imā etassa upatthambhabhūtā, etāsampi byasanaṃ karissāmī”ti ekadivasaṃ rañño surāpānaṭṭhāne upaṭṭhānaṃ karontī cūḷapitu sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “attho me kira kukkuṭehi[M 1.0137], aṭṭha matakukkuṭe, aṭṭha sajīvakukkuṭe ca gahetvā āgacchatu, āgantvā ca sopānamatthake ṭhatvā āgatabhāvaṃ nivedetvā ‘pavisatū’ti vuttepi apavisitvā paṭhamaṃ aṭṭha sajīvakukkuṭe pahiṇatu, ‘pacchā itare’”ti. Cūḷāpaṭṭhākassa ca “mama vacanaṃ kareyyāsī”ti lañjaṃ adāsi. Māgaṇḍiyo āgantvā, rañño nivedāpetvā, “pavisatū”ti vutte, “rañño āpānabhūmiṃ na pavisissāmī”ti āha. Itarā cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ [P 1.0214] pahiṇi [V 1.0123] – “gaccha, tāta, mama cūḷapitu santika”nti. So gantvā tena dinne aṭṭha sajīvakukkuṭe ānetvā, “deva, purohitena paṇṇākāro pahito”ti āha. Rājā “bhaddako vata no uttaribhaṅgo uppanno, ko nu kho paceyyā”ti āha. Māgaṇḍiyā, “mahārāja, sāmāvatippamukhā pañcasatā itthiyo nikkammikā vicaranti, tāsaṃ pesehi, tā pacitvā āharissantī”ti āha. Rājā “gaccha, tāsaṃ datvā aññassa kira hatthe adatvā sayameva māretvā pacantū”ti pesesi. Cūḷupaṭṭhāko “sādhu devā”ti gantvā tathā vatvā tāhi “mayaṃ pāṇātipātaṃ na karomā”ti paṭikkhitto āgantvā tamatthaṃ rañño ārocesi. Māgaṇḍiyā “diṭṭhaṃ te, mahārāja, idāni tāsaṃ pāṇātipātassa karaṇaṃ vā akaraṇaṃ vā jānissasi, ‘samaṇassa gotamassa pacitvā pesentū’ti vadehi devā”ti āha. Rājā tathā vatvā pesesi. Itaro te gahetvā gacchanto viya hutvā gantvā te kukkuṭe purohitassa datvā matakukkuṭe tāsaṃ santikaṃ netvā, “ime kira kukkuṭe pacitvā satthu santikaṃ pahiṇathā”ti āha. Tā, “sāmi, āhara, idaṃ nāma amhākaṃ kicca”nti paccuggantvā gaṇhiṃsu. So rañño santikaṃ gantvā, “kiṃ, tātā”ti puṭṭho, “samaṇassa gotamassa pacitvā pesethāti vuttamatteyeva paṭimaggaṃ āgantvā gaṇhiṃsū”ti ācikkhi. Māgaṇḍiyā “passa, mahārāja, na tā tumhādisānaṃ karonti, bahiddhā patthanā tāsaṃ atthīti vutte na saddahasī”ti āha. Rājā taṃ sutvāpi adhivāsetvā [P 1.0215] tuṇhīyeva ahosi. Māgaṇḍiyā “kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti cintesi.

The discourse on the Dhamma was beneficial to the great multitude that had assembled. Having taught the Dhamma thus, the Blessed One said, “Do not worry, Ānanda. These people will revile me for only seven days. On the eighth day, they will become silent. Indeed, a dispute that has arisen concerning the Buddhas does not last beyond seven days.” Unable to have the Teacher reviled and driven away, Māgaṇḍiyā thought, “What shall I do?” and then, “These women are his support; I will bring about their destruction as well.” One day, while attending at the king’s drinking hall, she sent a message to her uncle: “I have need of chickens. Let him bring eight dead chickens and eight live ones. When he arrives, let him stand at the top of the stairs and announce his arrival. Even if told to enter, he should not enter but first send in the eight live chickens, and then the others afterward.” She also gave a bribe to a junior attendant, saying, “Do as I say.” Her uncle, Māgaṇḍiya, came and, having had his arrival announced to the king, was told, “Let him enter.” But he replied, “I will not enter the king’s drinking hall.” The other one then sent a junior attendant, saying, “Go, dear, to my uncle.” He went and, bringing the eight live chickens given by the uncle, said, “Your Majesty, the chaplain has sent a gift.” The king said, “A fine delicacy has indeed arisen for us! Who, I wonder, should cook it?” Māgaṇḍiyā replied, “Great king, the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī are wandering about without work. Send the chickens to them; they will cook and bring them back.” The king sent the order, saying, “Go, give them to them. But do not give them into anyone else’s hands. Let them kill and cook them themselves.” The junior attendant said, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and went and spoke thus. But being refused by them with the words, “We do not commit the destruction of life,” he returned and reported the matter to the king. Māgaṇḍiyā said, “Have you seen, great king? Now you will know whether they commit the destruction of life or not. Tell them, ‘Cook them and send them to the ascetic Gotama.’” The king spoke thus and sent the order. The attendant, pretending to go, went and gave those chickens to the chaplain, and bringing the dead chickens to the women, said, “It is said you are to cook these chickens and send them to the Teacher.” They said, “Sir, bring them. This, indeed, is our duty,” and went forward to receive them. He went to the king’s presence and, when asked, “What is it, dear?” he reported, “As soon as it was said, ‘Cook and send them for the ascetic Gotama,’ they came to meet me on the way and took them.” Māgaṇḍiyā said, “See, great king, they do not do this for the likes of you. When I said their desire is for an outsider, you did not believe me.” Hearing this, the king endured it and remained silent. Māgaṇḍiyā then thought, “What, I wonder, shall I do?”

Tadā pana rājā “sāmāvatiyā vāsuladattāya māgaṇḍiyāya cā”ti tissannampi etāsaṃ pāsādatale vārena vārena sattāhaṃ sattāhaṃ vītināmeti[M 1.0138]. Atha naṃ “sve vā parasuve vā sāmāvatiyā pāsādatalaṃ gamissatī”ti ñatvā māgaṇḍiyā cūḷapitu sāsanaṃ pahiṇi – “agadena kira dāṭhā dhovitvā ekaṃ sappaṃ pesetū”ti. So tathā katvā pesesi. Rājā attano gamanaṭṭhānaṃ hatthikantavīṇaṃ ādāyayeva gacchati, tassā pokkhare ekaṃ chiddaṃ atthi. Māgaṇḍiyā tena chiddena sappaṃ pavesetvā chiddaṃ mālāguḷena thakesi. Sappo dvīhatīhaṃ antovīṇāyameva ahosi. Māgaṇḍiyā rañño gamanadivase “ajja katarissitthiyā pāsādaṃ gamissasi devā”ti pucchitvā “sāmāvatiyā”ti vutte, “ajja mayā, mahārāja, amanāpo supino diṭṭho. Na sakkā tattha gantuṃ, devā”ti? “Gacchāmevā”ti. Sā yāva tatiyaṃ vāretvā, “evaṃ sante ahampi tumhehi saddhiṃ gamissāmi, devā”ti vatvā nivattiyamānāpi anivattitvā, “na jānāmi, kiṃ bhavissati devā”ti raññā saddhiṃyeva agamāsi.

At that time, the king would spend seven days at a time on the palace terraces of Sāmāvatī, Vāsuladattā, and Māgaṇḍiyā, in turn. Then, knowing that he would go to Sāmāvatī's palace terrace tomorrow or the day after, Māgaṇḍiyā sent a message to her uncle: “It is said you are to send a snake after having washed its fangs with medicine.” He did so and sent it. The king always went to his destination taking the hatthikanta lute, and in its soundbox there was a hole. Māgaṇḍiyā inserted the snake through that hole and plugged the hole with a ball of flowers. The snake remained inside the lute for two or three days. On the day of the king’s departure, Māgaṇḍiyā asked, “Your Majesty, to which lady’s palace will you go today?” When he said, “To Sāmāvatī’s,” she said, “Today, great king, I saw an unpleasant dream. It is not possible to go there, Your Majesty.” He replied, “I will go indeed.” She tried to prevent him up to a third time, and then said, “If that is so, I too will go with you, Your Majesty.” And though he tried to turn her back, she did not turn back, and went right along with the king, saying, “I do not know what will happen, Your Majesty.”

Rājā sāmāvatimissikāhi dinnāni vatthapupphagandhābharaṇāni dhāretvā subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā vīṇaṃ [V 1.0124] ussīsake ṭhapetvā sayane nipajji. Māgaṇḍiyā aparāparaṃ vicarantī viya hutvā vīṇāchiddato pupphaguḷaṃ apanesi. Sappo dvīhatīhaṃ nirāhāro tena chiddena nikkhamitvā passasanto phaṇaṃ katvā sayanapiṭṭhe nipajji[P 1.0216]. Māgaṇḍiyā taṃ disvā, “dhī dhī, deva, sappo”ti mahāsaddaṃ katvā rājānañca tā ca akkosantī, “ayaṃ andhabālarājā alakkhiko mayhaṃ vacanaṃ na suṇāti, imāpi nissirīkā dubbinītā, kiṃ nāma rañño santikā na labhanti, kiṃ nu tumhe imasmiṃ mateyeva sukhaṃ jīvissatha, jīvante dukkhaṃ jīvatha, ‘ajja mayā pāpasupino diṭṭho, sāmāvatiyā pāsādaṃ gantuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti vārentiyāpi me vacanaṃ na suṇasi, devā”ti āha. Rājā sappaṃ disvā maraṇabhayatajjito “evarūpampi nāma imā karissanti, aho pāpā, ahaṃ imāsaṃ pāpabhāvaṃ ācikkhantiyāpi imissā vacanaṃ na saddahiṃ, paṭhamaṃ attano gabbhesu chiddāni katvā nisinnā, puna mayā pesite kukkuṭe paṭipahiṇiṃsu, ajja sayane sappaṃ vissajjiṃsū”ti kodhena sampajjalito viya ahosi.

The king, adorned with the clothes, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments given by the women of whom Sāmāvatī was the chief, ate a fine meal, placed the lute at the head of the bed, and lay down. Māgaṇḍiyā, pretending to wander about, removed the flower-ball from the lute’s hole. The snake, having been without food for two or three days, emerged from that hole, hissing and spreading its hood, and lay on the surface of the bed. Seeing it, Māgaṇḍiyā cried out loudly, “Fie, fie, Your Majesty, a snake!” and reviled the king and those women, saying: “This blind, foolish king is heedless and does not listen to my word. These women, too, are unfortunate and ill-disciplined. What is it that they do not get from the king? Will you live happily only when he is dead? While he lives, you live in misery. Even when I was preventing you, saying, ‘Today I saw a bad dream; it is not proper to go to Sāmāvatī’s palace,’ you did not listen to my word, Your Majesty!” The king, seeing the snake and terrified by the fear of death, thought, “Indeed, these women would do such a thing! Oh, how wicked! Even when this one was explaining their evil nature, I did not believe her word. First, they sat having made holes in their own chambers. Then, they sent back the chickens sent by me. Today, they have released a snake on the bed!” He became as if ablaze with anger.

Sāmāvatīpi [M 1.0139] pañcannaṃ itthisatānaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi – “ammā, amhākaṃ aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, narinde ca deviyā ca attani ca samameva mettacittaṃ pavattetha, mā kassaci kopaṃ karitthā”ti. Rājā sahassathāmaṃ siṅgadhanuṃ ādāya jiyaṃ pothetvā visapītaṃ saraṃ sannayhitvā sāmāvatiṃ dhure katvā sabbā [P 1.0217] tā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapāpetvā sāmāvatiyā ure saraṃ vissajjesi. So tassā mettānubhāvena paṭinivattitvā āgatamaggābhimukhova hutvā rañño hadayaṃ pavisanto viya aṭṭhāsi. Rājā cintesi – “mayā khitto saro silampi vinivijjhitvā gacchati, ākāse paṭihananakaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, atha ca panesa nivattitvā mama hadayābhimukho jāto, ayañhi nāma nissatto nijjīvo saropi etissā guṇaṃ jānāti, ahaṃ manussabhūtopi na jānāmī”ti, so dhanuṃ chaḍḍetvā añjaliṃ paggayha sāmāvatiyā pādamūle ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Sāmāvatī also gave advice to the five hundred women: “Dear ones, we have no other refuge. Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness equally toward the king, the queen, and yourselves. Do not harbor anger toward anyone.” The king, taking his horn bow of a thousand-fold strength, drew the bowstring, fitted a poison-imbued arrow, and placing Sāmāvatī at the front, had all those women stand in a row and released the arrow at Sāmāvatī’s breast. That arrow, by the power of her loving-kindness, turned back, and facing the path it had come, stood as if about to enter the king’s heart. The king thought: “The arrow shot by me pierces even a solid rock and goes through; in the sky, there is no place of obstruction. And yet this arrow, having turned back, now faces my heart. Indeed, even this non-sentient, lifeless arrow knows her virtue, but I, though a human being, do not know it.” He threw down the bow, raised his hands in reverence, and squatting down at Sāmāvatī’s feet, spoke this verse:

“Sammuyhāmi pamuyhāmi, sabbā muyhanti me disā;

Sāmāvati maṃ tāyassu, tvañca me saraṇaṃ bhavā”ti.

“I am bewildered, utterly bewildered; all directions are bewildering to me. Sāmāvatī, protect me, and be my refuge.”

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “sādhu, deva, maṃ saraṇaṃ gacchā”ti avatvā, “yamahaṃ, mahārāja, saraṇaṃ gatā, tameva tvampi saraṇaṃ gacchāhī”ti idaṃ vatvā sāmāvatī sammāsambuddhasāvikā –

Hearing his words, she did not say, “Very well, Your Majesty, go to me for refuge,” but instead said this: “Great King, you too should go for refuge to the very one to whom I have gone for refuge.” Having said this, Sāmāvatī, a female disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One—

“Mā [V 1.0125] maṃ tvaṃ saraṇaṃ gaccha, yamahaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā;

Esa buddho mahārāja, esa buddho anuttaro;

Saraṇaṃ gaccha taṃ buddhaṃ, tvañca me saraṇaṃ bhavā”ti. –

“Do not go to me for refuge; go to the one to whom I have gone for refuge. This is the Buddha, Great King; this is the unsurpassed Buddha. Go for refuge to that Buddha, and you, be a refuge for me.”

Āha[P 1.0218]. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “idānāhaṃ atirekataraṃ bhāyāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, hearing her words, said, “Now I am even more exceedingly afraid,” and spoke this verse:

“Esa bhiyyo pamuyhāmi, sabbā muyhanti me disā;

Sāmāvati maṃ tāyassu, tvañca me saraṇaṃ bhavā”ti.

“Because of this, I am even more bewildered; all directions are bewildering to me. Sāmāvatī, protect me! You be my refuge.”

Atha naṃ sā purimanayeneva puna paṭikkhipitvā, “tena hi tvañca saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, satthārañca saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, varañca te dammī”ti vutte, “varo gahito hotu, mahārājā”ti āha. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā saraṇaṃ gantvā nimantetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā [M 1.0140] sāmāvatiṃ āmantetvā, “uṭṭhehi, varaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha. “Mahārāja, mayhaṃ hiraññādīhi attho natthi, imaṃ pana me varaṃ dehi, tathā karohi, yathā satthā nibaddhaṃ pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ idhāgacchati, dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti. Rājā satthāraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nibaddhaṃ idhāgacchatha, sāmāvatimissikā ‘dhammaṃ suṇissāmā’ti vadantī”ti āha. “Mahārāja, buddhānaṃ nāma ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nibaddhaṃ gantuṃ na vaṭṭati, mahājano satthāraṃ āgamanatthāya paccāsīsatī”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpethā”ti. Satthā ānandattheraṃ āṇāpesi. So tato paṭṭhāya pañca bhikkhusatāni ādāya nibaddhaṃ rājakulaṃ gacchati. Tāpi deviyo nibaddhaṃ theraṃ saparivāraṃ bhojenti, dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tā ekadivasaṃ therassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasīditvā, pañcahi uttarāsaṅgasatehi dhammapūjaṃ akaṃsu[P 1.0219]. Ekeko uttarāsaṅgo pañca satāni pañca satāni agghati.

Then, when she had rejected him again in the same way as before, and he said, “In that case, I go to you for refuge, and I go to the Teacher for refuge, and I give you a boon,” she replied, “Let the boon be taken, Great King.” He approached the Teacher, went for refuge, invited him, and for seven days gave a great offering of alms to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. Then he addressed Sāmāvatī and said, “Arise, take the boon.” She replied, “Great King, I have no need for gold and such things. But grant me this boon: arrange it so that the Teacher comes here regularly with five hundred monks, that we may listen to the Dhamma.” The king paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, please come here regularly with five hundred monks. The women of whom Sāmāvatī is the chief say, ‘We will listen to the Dhamma.’” The Teacher replied, “Great King, it is not proper for Buddhas to go regularly to one place. The great populace hopes for the Teacher's arrival.” “In that case, Venerable Sir, please appoint one monk.” The Teacher appointed the Elder Ānanda. From then on, he took five hundred monks and went regularly to the royal household. Those queens also regularly fed the Elder and his retinue and listened to the Dhamma. One day, having heard the Elder's Dhamma talk and being pleased, they made a Dhamma-offering of five hundred upper robes. Each upper robe was worth five hundred.

Tā ekavatthā disvā rājā pucchi – “kuhiṃ vo uttarāsaṅgo”ti. “Ayyassa no dinnā”ti. “Tena sabbe gahitā”ti? “Āma, gahitā”ti. Rājā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tāhi uttarāsaṅgānaṃ dinnabhāvaṃ pucchitvā tāhi dinnabhāvañca therena gahitabhāvañca sutvā, “nanu, bhante, atibahūni vatthāni, ettakehi kiṃ karissathā”ti pucchi. “Amhākaṃ pahonakāni vatthāni gaṇhitvā sesāni jiṇṇacīvarikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dassāmi, mahārājā”ti. “Te attano jiṇṇacīvarāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Jiṇṇataracīvarikānaṃ dassantī”ti. “Te [V 1.0126] attano jiṇṇataracīvarāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Paccattharaṇāni karissantī”ti. “Purāṇapaccattharaṇāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Bhūmattharaṇāni karissantī”ti. “Purāṇabhūmattharaṇāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Pādapuñchanāni karissanti, mahārājā”ti. “Purāṇapādapuñchanāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ koṭṭetvā mattikāya madditvā bhittiṃ limpissantī”ti. “Bhante, ettakāni katvāpi ayyānaṃ dinnāni na nassantī”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. Rājā pasanno aparānipi pañca vatthasatāni āharāpetvā therassa pādamūle ṭhapāpesi. Thero kira pañcasatagghanakāneva vatthāni pañcasatabhāgena [P 1.0220] pādamūle ṭhapetvā dinnāni pañcasatakkhattuṃ labhi, sahassagghanakāni sahassabhāgena pādamūle ṭhapetvā dinnāni [M 1.0141] sahassakkhattuṃ labhi, satasahassagghanakāni satasahassabhāgena pādamūle ṭhapetvā dinnāni satasahassakkhattuṃ labhi. Ekaṃ dve tīṇi cattāri pañca dasātiādinā nayena laddhānaṃ pana gaṇanā nāma natthi. Tathāgate kira parinibbute thero sakalajambudīpaṃ vicaritvā sabbavihāresu bhikkhūnaṃ attano santakāneva pattacīvarāni adāsi.

Not seeing even a single upper robe with them, the king asked, “Where are your upper robes?” “They were given to our lord.” “Did he take them all?” “Yes, he took them.” The king approached the elder, paid homage, and inquired about the giving of the upper robes. Upon hearing that they had been given by them and accepted by the elder, he asked, “Venerable sir, are these not very many cloths? What will you do with so many?” “Great King, I will take the cloths that are sufficient for us and give the rest to the bhikkhus with worn-out robes.” “What will they do with their own worn-out robes?” “They will give them to those with more worn-out robes.” “And what will they do with their more worn-out robes?” “They will make them into bedspreads.” “And what will they do with the old bedspreads?” “They will make them into ground coverings.” “And what will they do with the old ground coverings?” “They will make them into foot-wipes, Great King.” “And what will they do with the old foot-wipes?” “They will chop them into small pieces, knead them with clay, and plaster the walls.” “Venerable sir, even after being used in so many ways, do the things given to the noble ones not perish?” “Indeed, they do not, Great King.” Pleased, the king had another five hundred cloths brought and placed at the elder’s feet. It is said that for cloths worth five hundred that were given to him, the elder received them five hundred times over; for those worth a thousand, he received them a thousand times over; for those worth a hundred thousand, he received them a hundred thousand times over. As for those received in quantities of one, two, three, four, five, ten, and so on, there was no counting them. It is said that after the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, the elder traveled throughout all of Jambudīpa, giving his own bowls and robes to the bhikkhus in all the monasteries.

Tadā māgaṇḍiyāpi “yamahaṃ karomi. Taṃ tathā ahutvā aññathāva hoti, idāni kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti cintetvā, “attheso upāyo”ti raññe uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchante cūḷapitu sāsanaṃ pahiṇi – “sāmāvatiyā pāsādaṃ gantvā, dussakoṭṭhāgārāni ca telakoṭṭhāgārāni ca vivarāpetvā, dussāni telacāṭīsu temetvā temetvā thambhe veṭhetvā tā sabbāpi ekato katvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā bahi yantakaṃ datvā daṇḍadīpikāhi gehe aggiṃ dadamāno otaritvā gacchatū”ti. So pāsādaṃ abhiruyha koṭṭhāgārāni [P 1.0221] vivaritvā vatthāni telacāṭīsu temetvā temetvā thambhe veṭhetuṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ sāmāvatippamukhā itthiyo “kiṃ etaṃ cūḷapitā”ti vadantiyo upasaṅkamiṃsu. “Ammā, rājā daḷhikammatthāya ime thambhe telapilotikāhi veṭhāpeti, rājagehe nāma suyuttaṃ duyuttaṃ dujjānaṃ, mā me santike hotha, ammā”ti evaṃ vatvā tā āgatā gabbhe pavesetvā dvārāni pidahitvā bahi yantakaṃ datvā ādito paṭṭhāya aggiṃ dento otari. Sāmāvatī tāsaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi – “amhākaṃ anamatagge saṃsāre vicarantīnaṃ evameva agginā jhāyamānānaṃ attabhāvānaṃ paricchedo buddhañāṇenapi na sukaro, appamattā hothā”ti. Tā gehe jhāyante vedanāpariggahakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontiyo kāci dutiyaphalaṃ, kāci tatiyaphalaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘idha, bhante, rañño utenassa uyyānagatassa antepuraṃ daḍḍhaṃ, pañca ca itthisatāni kālakatāni [V 1.0127] sāmāvatippamukhāni. Tāsaṃ, bhante, upāsikānaṃ kā gati, ko abhisamparāyo’ti? Santettha, bhikkhave, upāsikāyo sotāpannā[P 1.0222], santi sakadāgāmiyo, santi anāgāmiyo, sabbā tā, bhikkhave[M 1.0142], upāsikāyo anipphalā kālakatā”ti. Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Then Māgaṇḍiyā, thinking, 'What I do does not turn out as intended—now what shall I do?' and deciding, 'This is the way,' sent a message to her paternal uncle when the king went to the pleasure garden: 'Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, open the storerooms of cloth and oil, soak the cloths in oil, wrap them around the pillars, gather all the women together, close the doors, set a locking device outside, and then set the house on fire with torches before descending and leaving.' He climbed the palace, opened the storerooms, soaked the cloths in oil, and began wrapping them around the pillars. Then the women, led by Sāmāvatī, approached him, asking, 'What is this, uncle?' He replied, 'My dears, the king has ordered these pillars to be wrapped with oil-soaked cloth for strengthening. In a king's palace, what is proper or improper is hard to know—do not be near me, my dears.' Having said this, he led the women who had come into an inner chamber, closed the doors, set a locking device outside, and starting from the beginning, set the house ablaze before descending. Sāmāvatī advised them: 'For us who are wandering in this beginningless saṃsāra, the limit of our existences that have been burned by fire just like this is not easy to determine even with a Buddha's knowledge—be heedful!' As the house burned, they attended to the meditation subject of the comprehension of feeling. Some attained the second fruition, and some the third. Therefore it was said: 'Then, in the afternoon, after returning from their alms-round, a number of bhikkhus went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. So seated, they said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, while King Udena was away in the park, the inner palace was burned down, and five hundred women, with Sāmāvatī at their head, have died. What is the destination of those female lay-followers, venerable sir, what is their future course?” “Among them, bhikkhus, are female lay-followers who are stream-enterers, some are once-returners, and some are non-returners. Not one of those female lay-followers, bhikkhus, has died without fruit.”' Then the Blessed One, understanding the meaning of this, at that time uttered this inspired utterance:

“Mohasambandhano loko, bhabbarūpova dissati;

Upadhībandhano bālo, tamasā parivārito;

Sassatoriva khāyati, passato natthi kiñcana”nti. (udā. 70);

The world is bound by delusion; it appears splendid. The fool, bound by attachments, is enveloped in darkness. He seems to be eternal, but for one who sees, there is no impediment.

Evañca pana vatvā, “bhikkhave, sattā nāma vaṭṭe vicarantā niccakālaṃ appamattā hutvā puññakammameva na karonti, pamādino hutvā pāpakammampi karonti. Tasmā vaṭṭe vicarantā sukhampi dukkhampi anubhavantī”ti dhammaṃ desesi.

Having said this, he taught the Dhamma: 'Bhikkhus, beings wandering in the cycle of existence do not always perform only meritorious deeds by being heedful; being negligent, they also commit evil deeds. Therefore, wandering in the cycle, they experience both pleasure and pain.'

Rājā “sāmāvatiyā gehaṃ kira jhāyatī”ti sutvā vegenāgacchantopi adaḍḍhe sampāpuṇituṃ nāsakkhi. Āgantvā pana gehaṃ nibbāpento uppannabalavadomanasso amaccagaṇaparivuto nisīditvā sāmāvatiyā guṇe anussaranto, “kassa nu kho idaṃ kamma”nti cintetvā – “māgaṇḍiyāya kāritaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā, “tāsetvā pucchiyamānā na kathessati, saṇikaṃ upāyena pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā amacce [P 1.0223] āha – “ambho, ahaṃ ito pubbe uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya āsaṅkitaparisaṅkitova homi, sāmāvatī me niccaṃ otārameva gavesati, idāni pana me cittaṃ nibbutaṃ bhavissati, sukhena ca vasituṃ labhissāmī”ti, te “kena nu kho, deva, idaṃ kata”nti āhaṃsu. “Mayi sinehena kenaci kataṃ bhavissatī”ti. Māgaṇḍiyāpi samīpe ṭhitā taṃ sutvā, “nāñño koci kātuṃ sakkhissati, mayā kataṃ, deva, ahaṃ cūḷapitaraṃ āṇāpetvā kāresi”nti āha. “Taṃ ṭhapetvā añño mayi sineho satto nāma natthi, pasannosmi, varaṃ te dammi, attano ñātigaṇaṃ pakkosāpehī”ti. Sā ñātakānaṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇi – “rājā me pasanno varaṃ deti, sīghaṃ āgacchantū”ti. Rājā āgatāgatānaṃ mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ kāresi. Taṃ disvā tassā aññātakāpi lañjaṃ datvā “mayaṃ māgaṇḍiyāya ñātakā”ti āgacchiṃsu. Rājā te sabbe gāhāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe nābhippamāṇe āvāṭe khaṇāpetvā te tattha nisīdāpetvā paṃsūhi pūretvā upari palāle vikirāpetvā aggiṃ dāpesi. Cammassa daḍḍhakāle ayanaṅgalena [P 1.0224] kasāpetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hīrāhīraṃ kāresi. Māgaṇḍiyāya [M 1.0143] sarīratopi tikhiṇena [V 1.0128] satthena ghanaghanaṭṭhānesu maṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā telakapālaṃ uddhanaṃ āropetvā pūve viya pacāpetvā tameva khādāpesi.

The king, hearing, “Queen Sāmāvatī’s palace is burning, it is said,” though coming with speed, was not able to arrive before it was burnt. Having arrived, while extinguishing the fire of the palace, he sat down surrounded by his retinue of ministers, with great displeasure having arisen, and recollected Sāmāvatī’s virtues. Thinking, “Whose deed, indeed, is this?” and knowing, “It must have been caused by Māgaṇḍiyā,” he thought, “If questioned after being threatened, she will not confess. I will question her gently, with a stratagem.” He then addressed his ministers: “Sirs, before this, having arisen and exerted myself, I was ever anxious and suspicious, for Sāmāvatī constantly sought only my ruin. But now, my mind will be at peace, and I shall get to live in happiness.” They asked, “By whom indeed, Your Majesty, was this done?” He replied, “It must have been done by someone out of affection for me.” Māgaṇḍiyā, standing nearby, heard this and said, “No one else would be able to do it. It was done by me, Your Majesty. I commanded my uncle and had it done.” The king said, “Besides you, there is no other being who has affection for me. I am pleased. I shall give you a boon—have your kinsfolk summoned.” She sent a message to her relatives: “The king is pleased with me and gives a boon. Let them come quickly.” The king had great honor shown to each and every one who came. Seeing that, even those who were not her relatives gave a bribe and came, saying, “We are Māgaṇḍiyā’s relatives.” The king had them all seized, and in the royal courtyard, had pits the depth of a navel dug. He had them all sit there, had the pits filled with earth, had straw scattered on top, and had a fire set. When their skin was burning, he had them plowed with an iron plowshare, causing them to be cut into pieces and fragments. From Māgaṇḍiyā’s own body, with a sharp sword, he had flesh carved out from the thickest parts, and having placed an oil pan on a stove, had it fried like cakes, and made her herself eat it.

Dhammasabhāyampi bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “ananucchavikaṃ vata, āvuso, evarūpāya saddhāya pasannāya upāsikāya evarūpaṃ maraṇa”nti. Satthā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ attabhāve sāmāvatippamukhānaṃ itthīnaṃ etaṃ ayuttaṃ sampattaṃ. Pubbe katakammassa pana yuttameva etāhi laddha”nti vatvā, “kiṃ, bhante, etāhi pubbe kataṃ, taṃ ācikkhathā”ti tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari –

In the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: “Friends, for a female lay disciple of such faith and devotion, such a death is indeed unfitting!” The Teacher, having approached, asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When it was said, “For this very discussion,” he replied, “Monks, in this existence, this death that has befallen the women headed by Sāmāvatī is unfitting. But in regard to the deed done in the past, what was fitting is just what has been received by them.” Being requested by them, “Venerable Sir, what was done by them in the past? Please declare that to us,” he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente rājagehe nibaddhaṃ aṭṭha paccekabuddhā bhuñjanti. Pañcasatā itthiyo te upaṭṭhahanti. Tesu satta paccekabuddhā himavantaṃ gacchanti, eko nadītīre ekaṃ tiṇagahanaṃ atthi, tattha jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā paccekabuddhesu gatesu tā itthiyo ādāya nadiyaṃ udakakīḷaṃ [P 1.0225] kīḷituṃ gato. Tattha tā itthiyo divasabhāgaṃ udake kīḷitvā uttaritvā sītapīḷitā aggiṃ visibbetukāmā “amhākaṃ aggikaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ olokethā”ti aparāparaṃ vicarantiyo taṃ tiṇagahanaṃ disvā, “tiṇarāsī”ti saññāya taṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā aggiṃ adaṃsu. Tiṇesu jhāyitvā patantesu paccekabuddhaṃ disvā, “naṭṭhāmhā, amhākaṃ rañño paccekabuddho jhāyati, rājā ñatvā amhe nāsessati, sudaḍḍhaṃ naṃ karissāmā”ti sabbā tā itthiyo ito cito ca dārūni āharitvā tassa upari dārurāsiṃ kariṃsu. Mahādārurāsi ahosi. Atha naṃ ālimpetvā, “idāni jhāyissatī”ti pakkamiṃsu. Tā paṭhamaṃ asañcetanikā hutvā kammunā na bajjhiṃsu, idāni pacchā sañcetanāya kammunā bajjhiṃsu. Paccekabuddhaṃ pana antosamāpattiyaṃ sakaṭasahassehi dārūni āharitvā ālimpentāpi usmākāramattampi gahetuṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā so sattame divase uṭṭhāya yathāsukhaṃ agamāsi. Tā tassa kammassa katattā bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccitvā tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena attabhāvasate imināva niyāmena gehe jhāyamāne jhāyiṃsu. Idaṃ etāsaṃ pubbakammanti.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, while King Brahmadatta was ruling, eight Paccekabuddhas regularly took their meal in the royal palace. Five hundred women attended upon them. Among them, seven Paccekabuddhas went to the Himavanta. One sat down on the riverbank in a grass thicket there, having entered into jhāna. Then one day, when the Paccekabuddhas had gone, the king, taking those women, went to play the water-sport in the river. There, those women, having played in the water for a part of the day and having come out, were afflicted by the cold and desired to warm themselves by a fire. Wandering about here and there looking for a place to make a fire, they saw that grass thicket and, with the perception that it was a heap of grass, they stood surrounding it and set fire to it. When the grass, having burned, fell away, they saw the Paccekabuddha and thought, “We are ruined! We have burned the king’s Paccekabuddha! The king, upon knowing, will destroy us. Let us make him thoroughly burnt!” All those women, bringing firewood from here and there, made a pile of wood on top of him. It became a great pile of wood. Then, having set fire to it, they departed, thinking, “Now he will be completely burnt.” Those women, at first being without intention, were not bound by the kamma. But afterwards, with intention, they were bound by the kamma. As for the Paccekabuddha, however, while he was within the attainment, even though they brought firewood with a thousand carts and set it on fire, it was not able to produce even the slightest amount of heat. Therefore, on the seventh day, he arose and went as he pleased. Those women, because of having done that kamma, after being tormented in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remaining result of that very kamma, for a hundred existences, were burned in this very way when their house was burning. This was their past kamma.

Evaṃ [M 1.0144] vutte bhikkhū satthāraṃ paṭipucchiṃsu – “khujjuttarā pana, bhante, kena kammena khujjā jātā, kena kammena mahāpaññā, kena kammena sotāpattiphalaṃ adhigatā, kena kammena paresaṃ pesanakāritā [P 1.0226] jātā”ti? Bhikkhave, tasseva rañño bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ karaṇakāle sveva [V 1.0129] paccekabuddho thokaṃ khujjadhātuko ahosi. Athekā upaṭṭhāyikā itthī kambalaṃ pārupitvā suvaṇṇasaraṇaṃ gahetvā, “amhākaṃ paccekabuddho evañca evañca vicaratī”ti khujjā hutvā tassa vicaraṇākāraṃ dassesi. Tassa nissandena khujjā jātā. Te pana paccekabuddhe paṭhamadivase rājagehe nisīdāpetvā patte gāhāpetvā pāyāsassa pūretvā dāpesi. Uṇhapāyāsassa pūre patte paccekabuddhā parivattetvā parivattetvā gaṇhanti. Sā itthī te tathā karonte disvā attano santakāni aṭṭha dantavalayāni datvā, “idha ṭhapetvā gaṇhathā”ti āha. Tesu tathā katvā taṃ oloketvā ṭhitesu tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ ñatvā, “natthi, bhante, amhākaṃ etehi attho. Tumhākaññeva etāni pariccattāni, gahetvā gacchathā”ti āha. Te gahetvā nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamaṃsu. Ajjatanāpi tāni valayāni arogāneva. Sā tassa kammassa nissandena idāni tipiṭakadharā mahāpaññā jātā. Paccekabuddhānaṃ kataupaṭṭhānassa nissandena pana sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Idamassā buddhantare pubbakammaṃ.

When this was said, the monks again questioned the Teacher: 'But, Venerable Sir, by what kamma was Khujjuttarā born hunchbacked? By what kamma was she of great wisdom? By what kamma did she attain the fruit of stream-entry? By what kamma was she born a servant to others?' 'Monks, during the reign of that very king in Bārāṇasī, one of the Paccekabuddhas was slightly hunchbacked by nature. Then one of the female attendants, wrapping herself in a blanket and taking a golden bowl, made herself hunchbacked and demonstrated his manner of walking, saying, "Our Paccekabuddha walks just so." As a consequence of that kamma, she was born hunchbacked. On the first day, she had those Paccekabuddhas seated in the royal palace, had their bowls taken, and had them filled with milk-rice to be given. When the bowls were filled with hot milk-rice, the Paccekabuddhas kept turning them over and over as they received them. Seeing them do this, that woman gave her own eight ivory bracelets and said, "Place the bowls upon these and accept the offering." When they had done so and stood looking at her, she, understanding their intention, said, "Venerable sirs, we have no need for these. They are relinquished to you alone—take them and go." They took them and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain slope. Even to this day, those bracelets remain undamaged. As a consequence of that kamma, she is now a bearer of the Tipiṭaka and of great wisdom. And as a consequence of her service rendered to the Paccekabuddhas, she attained the fruit of stream-entry. This was her past kamma performed in the interval between Buddhas.'

Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle pana ekā bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dhītā vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya ādāsaṃ gahetvā attānaṃ alaṅkarontī nisīdi. Athassā vissāsikā ekā khīṇāsavā [P 1.0227] bhikkhunī taṃ daṭṭhuṃ agamāsi. Bhikkhuniyo hi khīṇāsavāpi sāyanhasamaye upaṭṭhākakulāni daṭṭhukāmā honti. Tasmiṃ pana khaṇe seṭṭhidhītāya santike kāci pesanakārikā natthi, sā “vandāmi, ayye, etaṃ tāva me pasādhanapeḷakaṃ gahetvā dethā”ti āha. Therī cintesi – “sacassā imaṃ gaṇhitvā na dassāmi, mayi āghātaṃ katvā niraye nibbattissati. Sace pana dassāmi, parassa pesanakārikā hutvā nibbattissati. Nirayasantāpato kho pana parassa pesanabhāvova seyyo”ti. “Sā anudayaṃ paṭicca taṃ gahetvā tassā adāsi. Tassa kammassa nissandena paresaṃ pesanakārikā jātā”ti.

During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa, a daughter of a wealthy merchant in Bārāṇasī sat adorning herself in the afternoon, holding a mirror. At that moment, a trusted Arahant bhikkhunī, who was an acquaintance of hers, came to see her. For indeed, even Arahant bhikkhunīs are desirous of seeing their supporter families in the evening. At that moment, the merchant's daughter had no servant nearby. She said, "Venerable lady, I pay homage. Please first take this ornament box of mine and give it to me." The elder bhikkhunī thought: "If I take this and do not give it to her, she will, having conceived hatred for me, be reborn in hell. But if I do give it to her, she will be reborn as a servant to another. Surely, the state of being a servant to another is better than the torment of hell." So, motivated by compassion, she took it and gave it to her. As a consequence of that kamma, she was born a servant to others.

Atha [M 1.0145] punekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “sāmāvatippamukhā pañcasatā itthiyo gehe agginā jhāyiṃsu, māgaṇḍiyāya ñātakā upari palālaggiṃ datvā ayanaṅgalehi bhinnā, māgaṇḍiyā pakkuthitatele pakkā, ke nu kho ettha jīvanti nāma, ke matā nāmā”ti. Satthā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, ye keci pamattā, te vassasataṃ jīvantāpi matāyeva nāma. Ye appamattā, te matāpi jīvantiyeva. Tasmā māgaṇḍiyā jīvantīpi matāyeva nāma, sāmāvatippamukhā pañcasatā itthiyo matāpi jīvantiyeva nāma. Na hi, bhikkhave, appamattā maranti nāmā”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then on another day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "The five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī were burned by fire in the palace; Māgaṇḍiyā's relatives were split apart with iron ploughshares after a straw fire was set above them; Māgaṇḍiyā was cooked in boiling oil. Among these, who, it may be asked, are truly living, and who are truly dead?" The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?" When it was said, "For this one," he replied, "Monks, whoever are heedless, though they live for a hundred years, are indeed called dead. Those who are heedful, though they may be dead, are indeed living. Therefore, Māgaṇḍiyā, though living, is indeed called dead, while the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī, though dead, are indeed called living. For indeed, monks, the heedful do not die." Having said this, he spoke these verses:

21.

21.

“Appamādo [V 1.0130][P 1.0228] amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ;

Appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā.

Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.

22.

22.

“Evaṃ visesato ñatvā, appamādamhi paṇḍitā;

Appamāde pamodanti, ariyānaṃ gocare ratā.

Having understood this distinction, the wise in heedfulness delight in heedfulness, rejoicing in the domain of the Noble Ones.

23.

23.

“Te jhāyino sātatikā, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā;

Phusanti dhīrā nibbānaṃ, yogakkhemaṃ anuttara”nti.

Those meditative ones, ever persevering, constantly firm in their effort—the wise attain Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Tattha appamādoti padaṃ mahantaṃ atthaṃ dīpeti, mahantaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Sakalampi hi tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āharitvā kathiyamānaṃ appamādapadameva otarati. Tena vuttaṃ –

Therein, the term 'heedfulness' reveals a great meaning; it stands, having encompassed a great meaning. For indeed, when the entire Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, is brought forth and taught, it all converges upon this single principle of heedfulness. Therefore it is said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici jaṅgalānaṃ pāṇānaṃ padajātāni, sabbāni tāni hatthipade samodhānaṃ gacchanti, hatthipadaṃ tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati yadidaṃ mahantattena. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbete appamādamūlakā appamādasamosaraṇā, appamādo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.140).

Just as, monks, the footprints of any land-dwelling creatures whatsoever are all encompassed by the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared chief among them in terms of size; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, they all have heedfulness as their root, they converge on heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared chief among those states.

So panesa atthato satiyā avippavāso nāma. Niccaṃ upaṭṭhitāya satiyā cetaṃ nāmaṃ. Amatapadanti amataṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ. Tañhi ajātattā nu jīyati na mīyati, tasmā amatanti vuccati. Pajjanti imināti padaṃ, amataṃ [M 1.0146] pāpuṇantīti attho. Amatassa padaṃ amatapadaṃ, amatassa adhigamūpāyoti vuttaṃ hoti, pamādoti pamajjanabhāvo, muṭṭhassatisaṅkhātassa satiyā vosaggassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Maccunoti [P 1.0229] maraṇassa. Padanti upāyo maggo. Pamatto hi jātiṃ nātivattati, jāto jīyati ceva mīyati cāti pamādo maccuno padaṃ nāma hoti, maraṇaṃ upeti. Appamattā na mīyantīti satiyā samannāgatā hi appamattā na maranti. Ajarā amarā hontīti na sallakkhetabbaṃ. Na hi koci satto ajaro amaro nāma atthi, pamattassa pana vaṭṭaṃ nāma aparicchinnaṃ, appamattassa paricchinnaṃ. Tasmā pamattā jātiādīhi aparimuttattā jīvantāpi matāyeva nāma. Appamattā pana appamādalakkhaṇaṃ vaḍḍhetvā khippaṃ maggaphalāni sacchikatvā dutiyatatiyaattabhāvesu na nibbattanti. Tasmā te jīvantāpi matāpi na mīyantiyeva nāma. Ye pamattā yathā matāti ye pana sattā pamattā, te pamādamaraṇena matattā, yathā hi jīvitindriyupacchedena matā dārukkhandhasadisā apagataviññāṇā[V 1.0131], tatheva honti. Tesampi hi matānaṃ viya gahaṭṭhānaṃ tāva “dānaṃ dassāma, sīlaṃ rakkhissāma, uposathakammaṃ karissāmā”ti ekacittampi na uppajjati, pabbajitānampi “ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni pūressāma, dhutaṅgāni samādiyissāma, bhāvanaṃ vaḍḍhessāmā”ti na uppajjatīti matena te kiṃ nānākaraṇāva honti. Tena vuttaṃ – “ye pamattā yathā matā”ti.

This, in meaning, is called non-separation from mindfulness. It is a name for mindfulness that is constantly present. Regarding 'amatapadaṃ' (the path to the Deathless), Nibbāna is called 'amata' (the Deathless). Indeed, since it is unborn, it does not age or die; therefore, it is called the Deathless. 'Pada' is so called because by this one attains; the meaning is that they attain the Deathless. The path to the Deathless is 'amatapadaṃ'; it is said to be the means for the attainment of the Deathless. 'Pamāda' (heedlessness) is the state of negligence; it is the name for the abandonment of mindfulness, which is known as lost mindfulness. 'Maccuno' means 'of death'. 'Padaṃ' means the cause, the path. Indeed, the heedless person does not overcome birth; one who is born both ages and dies. Therefore, heedlessness is called the path of death; one reaches death. Regarding 'the heedful do not die': indeed, the heedful, being endowed with mindfulness, do not die. 'They become ageless and deathless'—this should not be understood literally. For indeed, no being whatsoever is called ageless and deathless. But for the heedless, the round of existence is uninterrupted, while for the heedful, it is interrupted. Therefore, the heedless, because they are not freed from birth and so on, are called as if dead even while living. The heedful, however, having developed the characteristic of heedfulness, quickly realize the paths and fruits and are not reborn in second and third existences. Therefore, they, whether living or dead, are called as if they do not die. Regarding 'those who are heedless are as if dead': whatever beings are heedless, they, being dead through the death of heedfulness, are just like those who are dead by the cutting off of the life faculty—like a block of wood, devoid of consciousness. Indeed, for them, just like for the dead, in the case of householders, not even a single wholesome thought arises, such as, "We will give alms, we will observe the precepts, we will perform the Uposatha observance." For the ordained ones too, not even a single wholesome thought arises, such as, "We will fulfill our duties towards teachers, preceptors, and so on; we will undertake the ascetic practices; we will develop meditation." Therefore, how are they different from the dead? Therefore, it is said: "Those who are heedless are as if dead."

Evaṃ visesato ñatvāti pamattassa vaṭṭato nissaraṇaṃ natthi, appamattassa atthīti evaṃ [P 1.0230] visesatova jānitvā. Ke panetaṃ visesaṃ jānantīti? Appamādamhi paṇḍitāti ye paṇḍitā medhāvino sappaññā attano appamāde ṭhatvā appamādaṃ vaḍḍhenti, te evaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ jānanti. Appamāde pamodantīti te evaṃ ñatvā tasmiṃ attano appamāde pamodanti, pahaṃsitamukhā tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā honti. Ariyānaṃ gocare ratāti te evaṃ appamāde pamodantā taṃ appamādaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyānaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ gocarasaṅkhāte catusatipaṭṭhānādibhede sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme navavidhalokuttaradhamme ca ratā niratā, abhiratā hontīti attho.

Regarding 'having thus known the distinction': having thus known this very distinction—that for the heedless there is no escape from the round of suffering, while for the heedful there is. If it is asked, "But who knows this distinction?" Regarding 'the wise in heedfulness': those wise ones who are intelligent and discerning, who, established in their own heedfulness, develop heedfulness—they know this distinctive reason. Regarding 'they rejoice in heedfulness': having known thus, they rejoice in that heedfulness of their own; they have joyful faces and are pleased and delighted. Regarding 'delighting in the domain of the Noble Ones': those noble ones, thus rejoicing in heedfulness, having developed that heedfulness, greatly delight in the domain of the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—which is known as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment with their divisions such as the four foundations of mindfulness, and also in the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. This is the meaning.

Te [M 1.0147] jhāyinoti te appamattā paṇḍitā aṭṭhasamāpattisaṅkhātena ārammaṇūpanijjhānena vipassanāmaggaphalasaṅkhātena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena cāti duvidhenapi jhānena jhāyino. Sātatikāti abhinikkhamanakālato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā satataṃ pavattakāyikacetasikavīriyā. Niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamāti yaṃ taṃ purisathāmena purisavīriyena purisaparakkamena pattabbaṃ, na taṃ apāpuṇitvā vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti evarūpena vīriyena antarā anosakkitvā niccappavattena daḷhaparakkamena samannāgatā. Phusantīti ettha dve phusanā ñāṇaphusanā ca, vipākaphusanā ca. Tattha cattāro maggā ñāṇaphusanā nāma, cattāri phalāni vipākaphusanā nāma. Tesu idha vipākaphusanā adhippetā. Ariyaphalena nibbānaṃ sacchikaronto [P 1.0231] dhīrā paṇḍitā tāya vipākaphusanāya phusanti, nibbānaṃ sacchikaronti. Yogakkhemaṃ anuttaranti ye cattāro yogā mahājanaṃ vaṭṭe osīdāpenti, tehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ sabbehi lokiyalokuttaradhammehi seṭṭhattā anuttaranti.

Regarding 'they are meditative': those heedful, wise ones are meditative—that is, they burn up the hindrances—through both kinds of jhāna: namely, through the absorption on an object, known as the eight attainments, and through the absorption on characteristics, known as insight, path, and fruition. Regarding 'constantly persevering': from the time of the great renunciation up until the path of Arahantship, they have constantly active bodily and mental energy. Regarding 'ever firm in effort': they are endowed with firm effort that is constantly active, not slackening in between, with energy of this sort: "Whatever is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human effort—without attaining that, there will be no cessation of energy." Regarding 'they touch': here, there are two kinds of touching: touching by knowledge and touching by result. Therein, the four paths are called touching by knowledge; the four fruits are called touching by result. Of these two, touching by result is intended here. The steadfast wise ones, realizing Nibbāna through the noble fruit, touch by means of that touching by result; they realize Nibbāna. Regarding 'the unsurpassed security from bondage': it is secure and fearless from those four bonds that cause the great mass of people to sink in the round of existence. It is unsurpassed because it is supreme among all worldly and supramundane dhammas.

Desanāpariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, many became Stream-enterers and so on. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly.

Sāmāvatīvatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The Story of Sāmāvatī: The First.

2. Kumbhaghosakaseṭṭhivatthu

2. The Story of the Merchant Kumbhaghosaka

Uṭṭhānavatoti [V 1.0132] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto kumbhaghosakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Rājagahanagarasmiñhi rājagahaseṭṭhino gehe ahivātarogo uppajji, tasmiṃ uppanne makkhikā ādiṃ katvā yāva gāvā paṭhamaṃ tiracchānagatā maranti, tato dāsakammakaro, sabbapacchā gehasāmikā, tasmā so rogo sabbapacchā seṭṭhiñca jāyañca gaṇhi. Te rogena phuṭṭhā puttaṃ santike ṭhitaṃ oloketvā assupuṇṇehi nettehi taṃ āhaṃsu – “tāta, imasmiṃ kira roge uppanne bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāyantāva jīvitaṃ labhanti, tvaṃ amhe anoloketvā palāyitvā jīvanto punāgantvā amhākaṃ asukaṭṭhāne nāma cattālīsa dhanakoṭiyo [M 1.0148] nidahitvā ṭhapitā, tā uddharitvā jīvikaṃ kappeyyāsī”ti. So [P 1.0232] tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā rudamāno mātāpitaro vanditvā maraṇabhayabhīto bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāyitvā pabbatagahanaṃ gantvā dvādasa vassāni tattha vasitvā mātāpituvasanaṭṭhānaṃ paccāgañchi.

The Teacher delivered this discourse, which begins with 'Uṭṭhānavato,' while residing in the Veḷuvana, concerning Kumbhaghosaka. Indeed, in the city of Rājagaha, a plague arose in the house of the Rājagaha merchant. When it arose, beginning with flies up to cattle, first the animals died. After that, the slaves and workers died, and last of all, the masters of the house died. Therefore, that disease last of all afflicted the merchant and his wife. They, being afflicted by the plague, looked at their son who was standing nearby, and with eyes full of tears, they said to him: “Dear son, it is said that when this plague arises, only those who break through the wall and flee obtain life. You, without looking at us, should flee. While living, return again and unearth the forty crores of wealth that have been buried and placed in such-and-such a place, and you should make your living.” Hearing their words, he, weeping, paid homage to his parents, and fearing the danger of death, broke through the wall and fled. Having gone to a mountain wilderness and lived there for twelve years, he returned to the place where his parents had lived.

Atha naṃ daharakāle gantvā parūḷhakesamassukāle āgatattā na koci sañjāni. So mātāpitūhi dinnasaññāvasena dhanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā dhanassa arogabhāvaṃ ñatvā cintesi – “maṃ na koci sañjānāti, sacāhaṃ dhanaṃ uddharitvā valañjissāmi, ‘ekena duggatena nidhi uddhaṭo’ti maṃ gahetvā viheṭheyyuṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīveyya”nti. Athekaṃ pilotikaṃ nivāsetvā, “atthi koci bhatakena atthiko”ti pucchanto bhatakavīthiṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ bhatakā disvā, “sace amhākaṃ ekaṃ kammaṃ karissasi, bhattavetanaṃ te dassāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Kiṃ kammaṃ nāmā”ti? “Pabodhanacodanakammaṃ. Sace ussahasi, pātova uṭṭhāya ‘tātā, uṭṭhahatha, sakaṭāni sannayhatha, goṇe yojetha, hatthiassānaṃ tiṇatthāya gamanavelā; ammā, tumhepi uṭṭhahatha, yāguṃ pacatha, bhattaṃ pacathā’ti vicaritvā ārocehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Athassa vasanatthāya ekaṃ gharaṃ adaṃsu. So devasikaṃ taṃ kammaṃ akāsi.

Then, because he had gone away at a young age and returned when his hair and beard were grown, no one recognized him. He, by means of the sign given by his parents, went to the place of the wealth, and knowing the wealth was unharmed, he thought: “No one recognizes me. If I were to unearth the wealth and use it, they would seize me and harass me, saying, ‘A treasure has been unearthed by a poor man.’ What if I were to make a living by working for wages?” Then, having put on a single worn-out cloth, he reached the street of hired workers, asking, “Is there anyone in need of a hired worker?” Then the hirers, seeing him, said: “If you will do one job for us, we will give you food and wages.” “What is this job?” “The job of waking and urging. If you are able, rise early in the morning and go around announcing: ‘Fathers, arise! Prepare the carts, yoke the oxen, it is time to go for grass for the elephants and horses. Mothers, you too arise! Cook the gruel, cook the rice!’” He agreed, saying, “Good.” Then they gave him a house to live in. He did that job daily.

Athassa ekadivasaṃ rājā bimbisāro saddamassosi. So pana sabbaravaññū ahosi. Tasmā “mahādhanassa purisassesa saddo”ti āha. Athassa santike ṭhitā ekā paricārikā “rājā yaṃ vā [P 1.0233] taṃ vā na kathessati, idaṃ mayā ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā – “gaccha, tāta, etaṃ jānāhī”ti ekaṃ purisaṃ pahiṇi. So vegena gantvā taṃ disvā āgantvā, “eko bhatakānaṃ bhatikārako kapaṇamanusso eso”ti ārocesi. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṇhī hutvā dutiyadivasepi tatiyadivasepi taṃ tassa saddaṃ sutvā tatheva āha. Sāpi paricārikā [V 1.0133] tatheva cintetvā punappunaṃ pesetvā, “kapaṇamanusso eso”ti vutte cintesi – “rājā ‘kapaṇamanusso eso’ti vacanaṃ sutvāpi na saddahati, punappunaṃ ‘mahādhanassa purisassesa saddo’ti vadati, bhavitabbamettha kāraṇena, yathāsabhāvato etaṃ ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā rājānaṃ āha, “deva[M 1.0149], ahaṃ sahassaṃ labhamānā dhītaraṃ ādāya gantvā etaṃ dhanaṃ rājakulaṃ pavesessāmī”ti. Rājā tassā sahassaṃ dāpesi.

One day, King Bimbisāra heard his voice. Now, he was a knower of all sounds. Therefore, he said, “This is the voice of a man of great wealth.” Then a female attendant standing near him thought, “The king would not say just anything; it is proper for me to find this out,” and she sent a man, saying, “Go, good man, and find this out.” He went with speed, saw him, returned, and reported, “He is a poor man, a hired laborer.” Hearing his words, the king became silent. On the second and third days, hearing his voice, he said the very same thing. That female attendant, thinking in the same way, sent someone again and again, and when it was said, “He is a poor man,” she thought: “Even after hearing the words, ‘He is a poor man,’ the king does not believe it, but says again and again, ‘This is the voice of a man of great wealth.’ There must be a reason for this; it is proper to know this in its true nature.” She said to the king, “Your Majesty, if I obtain a thousand, I will take my daughter and cause this wealth to enter the royal household.” The king had a thousand given to her.

Sā taṃ gahetvā dhītaraṃ ekaṃ malinadhātukaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsāpetvā tāya saddhiṃ rājagehato nikkhamitvā maggapaṭipannā viya bhatakavīthiṃ gantvā ekaṃ gharaṃ pavisitvā, “amma, mayaṃ maggapaṭipannā, ekāhadvīhaṃ idha vissamitvā gamissāmā”ti āha. “Amma, bahūni gharamānusakāni, na sakkā idha vasituṃ, etaṃ kumbhaghosakassa gehaṃ tucchaṃ, tattha gacchathā”ti. Sā tattha gantvā, “sāmi, mayaṃ maggapaṭipannakā, ekāhadvīhaṃ idha vasissāmā”ti vatvā tena punappunaṃ paṭikkhittāpi, “sāmi, ajjekadivasamattaṃ vasitvā pātova gamissāmā”ti nikkhamituṃ na icchi.
