Sā tattheva vasitvā punadivase tassa araññagamanavelāya, “sāmi, tava nivāpaṃ datvā yāhi[P 1.0234], āhāraṃ te pacissāmī”ti vatvā, “alaṃ, amma, ahameva pacitvā bhuñjissāmī”ti vutte punappunaṃ nibandhitvā tena dinne gahitamattakeyeva katvā antarāpaṇato bhājanāni ceva parisuddhataṇḍulādīni ca āharāpetvā rājakule pacananiyāmena suparisuddhaṃ odanaṃ, sādhurasāni ca dve tīṇi sūpabyañjanāni pacitvā tassa araññato āgatassa adāsi. Atha naṃ bhuñjitvā muducittataṃ āpannaṃ ñatvā, “sāmi, kilantamha, ekāhadvīhaṃ idheva homā”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

She, taking that, had her daughter put on a single soiled garment and, leaving the royal palace with her, went to the street of hired workers as if they were travelers on a journey. Entering a house, she said, “Mother, we are travelers on a journey; we will rest here for a day or two and then go.” “Dear daughter, the people of this house are many; it is not possible to stay here. Kumbhaghosaka’s house is empty, go there.” She went there and said, “Master, we are travelers on a journey; we will stay here for a day or two.” Although she was repeatedly refused by him, she was unwilling to leave, saying, “Master, we will stay for just one day today and go early in the morning.” Staying right there, on the next day, at the time of his departure for the forest, she said, “Master, give your provisions and go; I will cook your food.” When he said, “Enough, mother, I myself will cook and eat,” she insisted again and again. When he gave them, making it seem as if she had only taken that much, she had vessels and very pure rice and other things brought from the market. Then, in the manner of cooking in the royal palace, she cooked very pure rice and two or three curries with delicious flavors and gave them to him when he had returned from the forest. Then, knowing that his mind had become softened after he ate, she said, “Master, we are tired; let us be here for another day or two.” He agreed, saying, “Good.”

Athassa sāyampi punadivasepi madhurabhattaṃ pacitvā adāsi. Atha muducittataṃ tassa ñatvā “sāmi, katipāhaṃ idheva vasissāmā”ti. Tattha vasamānā tikhiṇena satthena tassa mañcavāṇaṃ heṭṭhāaṭaniyaṃ tahaṃ tahaṃ chindi. Mañco tasmiṃ āgantvā nisinnamatteyeva heṭṭhā olambi. So “kasmā ayaṃ mañco evaṃ chijjitvā gato”ti āha. “Sāmi, daharadārake vāretuṃ na sakkomi, ettheva sannipatantī”ti. “Amma, idaṃ me dukkhaṃ tumhe nissāya jātaṃ. Ahañhi pubbe katthaci gacchanto dvāraṃ pidahitvā gacchāmī”ti. “Kiṃ karomi, tāta, vāretuṃ na sakkomī”ti. Sā imināva niyāmena dve tayo divase chinditvā tena ujjhāyitvā khīyitvā vuccamānāpi tatheva vatvā puna ekaṃ dve rajjuke ṭhapetvā sese chindi. Taṃ divasaṃ [P 1.0235] tasmiṃ nisinnamatteyeva sabbaṃ vāṇaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pati, sīsaṃ jaṇṇukehi saddhiṃ ekato ahosi, so uṭṭhāya, “kiṃ karomi, idāni kuhiṃ gamissāmi[M 1.0150], nipajjanamañcassapi tumhehi asāmiko [V 1.0134] viya katomhī”ti āha. “Tāta, kiṃ karomi, paṭivissakadārake vāretuṃ na sakkomi, hotu, mā cintayi, imāya nāma velāya kuhiṃ gamissasī”ti dhītaraṃ āmantetvā, “amma, tava bhātikassa nipajjanokāsaṃ karohī”ti āha. Sā ekapasse sayitvā “idhāgaccha, sāmī”ti āha. Itaropi naṃ “gaccha, tāta, bhaginiyā saddhiṃ nipajjā”ti vadesi. So tāya saddhiṃ ekamañce nipajjitvā taṃ divasaññeva santhavaṃ akāsi, kumārikā parodi. Atha naṃ mātā pucchi – “kiṃ, amma, rodasī”ti? “Amma, idaṃ nāma jāta”nti. “Hotu, amma, kiṃ sakkā kātuṃ, tayāpi ekaṃ bhattāraṃ imināpekaṃ pādaparicārikaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ jāmātaraṃ akāsi. Te samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu.

Then she cooked delicious rice for him that evening and on the next day as well. Then, knowing his gentle nature, she said, "Master, let us stay here for a few days." While staying there, she cut the webbing of his bed here and there at the lower frame with a sharp knife. When he came and sat on the bed, it sagged beneath him. He asked, "Why has this bed broken like this?" "Master, I cannot stop the young children; they gather right here," she replied. "Mother, this suffering of mine has arisen on account of you. For previously, whenever I went anywhere, I would go only after closing the door." "What can I do, dear son? I cannot stop them." By this very method, she cut it for two or three days, and though he grumbled and complained at her, she kept saying the same thing. Then, leaving one or two cords, she cut the rest. That day, as soon as he sat on it, all the webbing fell to the ground, and his head became one with his knees. Getting up, he said, "What shall I do? Where shall I go now? You have made me as if without ownership even of my sleeping bed." "Dear son, what can I do? I cannot stop the neighbor's children. Let it be, do not worry. Where will you go at this hour?" Then, calling her daughter, she said, "Child, make a sleeping space for your brother." She lay down on one side and said, "Come here, master." The mother also said to him, "Go, dear son, lie down with your sister." He lay down on the same bed with her, and on that very day, they became intimate. The young girl wept. Then her mother asked her, "Why do you weep, child?" "Mother, this certain thing has happened." "Let it be, child. What can be done? It is fitting for you to get a husband, and for him also to have a foot-servant." Thus, she made him her son-in-law. They lived together in harmony.

Sā katipāhaccayena rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi – “bhatakavīthiyaṃ chaṇaṃ karontu. Yassa pana ghare chaṇo na karīyati, tassa ettako nāma daṇḍoti ghosanaṃ kāretū”ti. Rājā tathā kāresi. Atha naṃ sassu āha – “tāta, bhatakavīthiyaṃ rājāṇāya chaṇo kattabbo jāto, kiṃ karomā”ti? “Amma, ahaṃ bhatiṃ karontopi jīvituṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ karissāmī”ti? “Tāta, gharāvāsaṃ vasantā nāma iṇampi gaṇhanti, rañño [P 1.0236] āṇā akātuṃ na labbhā. Iṇato nāma yena kenaci upāyena muccituṃ sakkā, gaccha, kutoci ekaṃ vā dve vā kahāpaṇe āharā”ti āha. So ujjhāyanto khīyanto gantvā cattālīsakoṭidhanaṭṭhānato ekameva kahāpaṇaṃ āhari. Sā taṃ kahāpaṇaṃ rañño pesetvā attano kahāpaṇena chaṇaṃ katvā puna katipāhaccayena tatheva sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Puna rājā tatheva “chaṇaṃ karontu, akarontānaṃ ettako daṇḍo”ti āṇāpesi. Punapi so tāya tatheva vatvā nippīḷiyamāno gantvā tayo kahāpaṇe āhari. Sā tepi kahāpaṇe rañño pesetvā puna katipāhaccayena tatheva sāsanaṃ pahiṇi – “idāni purise pesetvā imaṃ pakkosāpetū”ti. Rājā pesesi. Purisā gantvā, “kumbhaghosako nāma kataro”ti pucchitvā pariyesantā taṃ disvā “ehi, bho rājā, taṃ pakkosatī”ti āhaṃsu. So bhīto “na maṃ rājā jānātī”tiādīni vatvā gantuṃ na icchi. Atha naṃ balakkārena hatthādīsu gahetvā [M 1.0151] ākaḍḍhiṃsu. Sā itthī te disvā, “are, dubbinītā, tumhe mama jāmātaraṃ hatthādīsu gahetuṃ ananucchavikā”ti tajjetvā, “ehi, tāta, mā bhāyi, rājānaṃ disvā tava hatthādigāhakānaṃ hattheyeva chindāpessāmī”ti dhītaraṃ ādāya purato hutvā rājagehaṃ patvā vesaṃ parivattetvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Itarampi parikaḍḍhitvā ānayiṃsuyeva.

After a few days, she sent a message to the king: “Let them hold a festival in the street of the wage-earners. And let it be proclaimed that for the house of whomever a festival is not held, there will be such-and-such a fine.” The king had it done so. Then his mother-in-law said to him, “Dear son, by the king’s order, a festival must be held in the street of the wage-earners. What shall we do?” “Mother, even while working for wages I am not able to make a living—what shall I do?” “Dear son, those who live the household life even take on debt. The king’s command cannot be left undone. From debt, it is possible to be freed by some means or other. Go, bring one or two kahāpaṇas from somewhere,” she said. Grumbling and complaining, he went and brought just one kahāpaṇa from the place of the forty crores of wealth. She sent that kahāpaṇa to the king and held the festival with her own kahāpaṇa. Then after a few days, she sent a message in the very same way. Again the king commanded, “Let them hold the festival; for those who do not, there will be such-and-such a fine.” Again, being pressed by her in the same way, he went and brought three kahāpaṇas. She sent those kahāpaṇas to the king and after a few days sent a message in the very same way: “Now, send men and have this man summoned.” The king sent them. The men went and asked, “Who is the one named Kumbhaghosaka?” Searching, they saw him and said, “Come, sir, the king summons you.” Frightened, he said, “The king does not know me,” and so on, and did not wish to go. Then they seized him by his hands and such and dragged him by force. Seeing them, the woman scolded them, saying, “Hey, you ill-mannered ones, it is not proper for you to seize my son-in-law by his hands and such!” Then she reassured him, “Come, dear son, do not fear. After seeing the king, I will have the very hands of those who seized you cut off.” Taking her daughter, she went ahead, reached the royal palace, changed her attire, adorned herself with all ornaments, and stood to one side. They also dragged the other one and brought him.

Atha naṃ vanditvā ṭhitaṃ rājā āha – “tvaṃ kumbhaghosako nāmā”ti? “Āma, devā”ti[V 1.0135]. “Kiṃ kāraṇā mahādhanaṃ vañcetvā khādasī”ti[P 1.0237]? “Kuto me, deva, dhanaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvantassā”ti? “Mā evaṃ kari, kiṃ amhe vañcesī”ti? “Na vañcemi, deva, natthi me dhana”nti. Athassa rājā te kahāpaṇe dassetvā, “ime kassa kahāpaṇā”ti āha. So sañjānitvā, “aho bālomhi, kathaṃ nu kho ime rañño hatthaṃ pattā”ti ito cito ca olokento tā dvepi paṭimaṇḍitapasādhanā gabbhadvāramūle ṭhitā disvā, “bhāriyaṃ vatidaṃ kammaṃ, imāhi raññā payojitāhi bhavitabba”nti cintesi. Atha naṃ rājā “vadehi, bho, kasmā evaṃ karosī”ti āha. “Nissayo me natthi, devā”ti. “Mādiso nissayo bhavituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. “Kalyāṇaṃ, deva, sace me devo avassayo hotī”ti. “Homi, bho, kittakaṃ te dhana”nti? “Cattālīsakoṭiyo, devā”ti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Sakaṭāni devā”ti? Rājā anekasatāni sakaṭāni yojāpetvā pahiṇitvā taṃ dhanaṃ āharāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe rāsiṃ kārāpetvā rājagahavāsino sannipātāpetvā, “atthi kassaci imasmiṃ nagare “ettakaṃ dhana”nti pucchitvā “natthi, devā”ti. “Kiṃ panassa kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Sakkāraṃ, devā”ti vutte mahantena sakkārena taṃ seṭṭhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā dhītaraṃ tasseva datvā tena saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, passathimaṃ purisaṃ, evarūpo dhitimā nāma natthi, cattālīsakoṭivibhavo hontopi uppilāvitākāraṃ vā asmimānamattaṃ vā na karoti, kapaṇo viya pilotikaṃ [P 1.0238] nivāsetvā bhatakavīthiyaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvanto mayā iminā nāma upāyena ñāto. Jānitvā ca pana pakkosāpetvā sadhanabhāvaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā taṃ dhanaṃ āharāpetvā [M 1.0152] seṭṭhiṭṭhāne ṭhapito, dhītā cassa mayā dinnā. Bhante, mayā ca evarūpo dhitimā na diṭṭhapubbo”ti āha.

Then the king said to him, who stood having paid homage, “Are you the one named Kumbhaghosaka?” “Yes, Your Majesty.” “For what reason do you conceal your great wealth and not enjoy it?” “From where would I have wealth, Your Majesty, I who live by working for wages?” “Do not act thus; why do you deceive us?” “I do not deceive you, Your Majesty; I have no wealth.” Then the king showed him those kahāpaṇas and said, “Whose kahāpaṇas are these?” Recognizing them, he thought, “Alas, I have been foolish. How indeed have these reached the king’s hand?” Looking here and there, he saw those two, adorned with ornaments, standing at the door of the chamber and thought, “This is a grave matter; they must have been employed by the king.” Then the king said to him, “Speak, sir; why do you act thus?” “I have no protector, Your Majesty.” “Is one like me not suitable to be your protector?” “It would be excellent, Your Majesty, if you would be my refuge.” “I shall be, sir. How much is your wealth?” “Forty crores, Your Majesty.” “What is needed to get it?” “Carts, Your Majesty.” The king had many hundreds of carts prepared and sent, had that wealth brought, had it heaped in the royal courtyard, assembled the inhabitants of Rājagaha, and asked, “Does anyone in this city have this much wealth?” When they replied, “No, Your Majesty,” he asked, “What then should be done for him?” When it was said, “He should be honored, Your Majesty,” with great honor he established him in the position of a Seṭṭhi and gave his own daughter to him. Together with him, he went to the Teacher’s presence, paid homage, and said, “Venerable Sir, behold this man. There is no one so steadfast. Though possessing a fortune of forty crores, he shows no frivolity or even a trace of the conceit ‘I am.’ Like a poor man, wearing a worn-out cloth, he lived by working for wages in the laborers' street. By this very means was he discovered by me. And having discovered him, I had him summoned, made him acknowledge his possession of wealth, had that wealth brought, and have established him in the position of a Seṭṭhi. My daughter has also been given to him by me. Venerable Sir, I have never before seen such a steadfast man.”

Taṃ sutvā satthā “evaṃ jīvantassa jīvikaṃ dhammikajīvikaṃ nāma, mahārāja, corikādikammaṃ pana idhaloke ceva pīḷeti hiṃseti, paraloke ca, tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ nāma natthi. Purisassa hi dhanapārijuññakāle kasiṃ vā bhatiṃ vā katvā jīvikameva dhammikajīvikaṃ nāma. Evarūpassa hi vīriyasampannassa satisampannassa kāyavācāhi parisuddhakammassa paññāya nisammakārino kāyādīhi saññatassa dhammajīvikaṃ jīvantassa satiavippavāse ṭhitassa issariyaṃ vaḍḍhatiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Teacher said: “Great King, the livelihood of one who lives thus is called a righteous livelihood. But deeds such as theft oppress and harm one in this world and also in the next; from that cause, there is no happiness whatsoever. For a man, when his wealth is depleted, making a living by farming or by working for wages is indeed called a righteous livelihood. For one of such a nature who is endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, of pure action in body and speech, who acts with wise consideration, is restrained in body and so on, lives a righteous livelihood, and is established in unremitting mindfulness—his sovereignty indeed grows.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

24.

24.

“Uṭṭhānavato satīmato,

Sucikammassa nisammakārino;

Saññatassa [V 1.0136] dhammajīvino,

Appamattassa yasobhivaḍḍhatī”ti.

For one who is energetic and mindful,

Of pure action, acting with consideration,

Restrained, living righteously,

And heedful—his fame ever increases.

Tattha uṭṭhānavatoti uṭṭhānavīriyavantassa. Satimatoti satisampannassa. Sucikammassāti niddosehi niraparādhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgatassa. Nisammakārinoti evañce bhavissati, evaṃ karissāmīti vā, imasmiṃ kamme evaṃ kate idaṃ nāma bhavissatīti vā evaṃ nidānaṃ sallakkhetvā rogatikicchanaṃ [P 1.0239] viya sabbakammāni nisāmetvā upadhāretvā karontassa. Saññatassāti kāyādīhi saññatassa nicchiddassa. Dhammajīvinoti agārikassa tulākūṭādīni vajjetvā kasigorakkhādīhi, anagārikassa vejjakammadūtakammādīni vajjetvā dhammena samena bhikkhācariyāya jīvikaṃ kappentassa. Appamattassāti avippavutthasatino. Yasobhivaḍḍhatīti issariyabhogasampannasaṅkhāto ceva kittivaṇṇabhaṇanasaṅkhāto ca yaso abhivaḍḍhatīti.

Therein, ‘energetic’ means one endowed with energy and effort. ‘Mindful’ means one endowed with mindfulness. ‘Of pure action’ means one endowed with blameless and faultless bodily actions and so on. ‘Acting with consideration’ means one who, after marking the cause—thinking, “Thus it will be,” or “Thus I will do,” or “When this deed is done thus, this result will occur”—acts by investigating and examining all deeds like a physician treating a disease. ‘Restrained’ means restrained in body and so on, flawless. ‘Living righteously’ means, for a householder, avoiding false scales and so on and living by agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so on; for one who has gone forth, avoiding the practice of medicine, acting as a messenger, and so on, and making a living righteously and justly by the practice of alms-gathering. ‘Heedful’ means one of unremitting mindfulness. ‘Fame ever increases’ means that both the status known as sovereignty and wealth, and the fame known as praise and good report, greatly increase.

Gāthāpariyosāne kumbhaghosako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. Evaṃ mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, Kumbhaghosaka was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so on. Thus, a beneficial Dhamma discourse occurred for the great assembly.

Kumbhaghosakaseṭṭhivatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Second Story: Kumbhaghosaka the Seṭṭhi.

3. Cūḷapanthakattheravatthu

3. The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka

Uṭṭhānenappamādenāti [M 1.0153] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto cūḷapanthakattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'By exertion, by heedfulness,' while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery, with reference to the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.

Rājagahe kira dhanaseṭṭhikulassa dhītā vayappattakāle mātāpitūhi sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatale ativiya rakkhiyamānā yobbanamadamattatāya purisalolā hutvā attano [P 1.0240] dāseneva saddhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā, “aññepi me idaṃ kammaṃ jāneyyu”nti bhītā evamāha – “amhehi imasmiṃ ṭhāne na sakkā vasituṃ. Sace me mātāpitaro imaṃ dosaṃ jānissanti, khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ maṃ karissanti. Videsaṃ gantvā vasissāmā”ti. Te hatthasāraṃ gahetvā aggadvārena nikkhamitvā, “yattha vā tattha vā aññehi ajānanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vasissāmā”ti ubhopi agamaṃsu. Tesaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya tassā kucchismiṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā gabbhaparipākaṃ āgamma tena saddhiṃ mantesi, “gabbho me paripākaṃ gato, ñātibandhuvirahite [V 1.0137] ṭhāne gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ubhinnampi amhākaṃ dukkhāvahaṃ, kulagehameva gacchāmā”ti. So “sacāhaṃ tattha gamissāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthī”ti bhayena “ajja gacchāma, sve gacchāmā”ti divase atikkāmesi. Sā cintesi – “ayaṃ bālo attano dosamahantatāya gantuṃ na ussahati, mātāpitaro nāma ekantahitāva, ayaṃ gacchatu vā, mā vā, ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Sā tasmiṃ gehā nikkhante gehaparikkhāraṃ paṭisāmetvā attano kulagharaṃ gatabhāvaṃ anantaragehavāsīnaṃ ārocetvā maggaṃ paṭipajji.

It is said that in Rājagaha, the daughter of a wealthy merchant's family, upon coming of age, was guarded with extreme care by her parents on the upper floor of a seven-storied mansion. However, intoxicated by the pride of youth and becoming wanton towards men, she formed an illicit intimacy with her own slave. Fearing, 'Others too might learn of this deed of mine,' she spoke thus: 'It is not possible for us to live in this place. If my parents find out about this fault, they will cut me into pieces. Let us go to another country and live there.' Taking their valuables, they left by the main gate, thinking, 'We will go to some place or other, a place unknown to others, and live there.' Thus, both of them departed. While they were living in a certain place, as a result of their cohabitation, a conception took place in her womb. When her pregnancy came to term, she consulted with him, saying, 'My pregnancy has reached its full term. To give birth in a place devoid of relatives and kin will bring suffering to both of us. Let us go to my family home.' But he, fearing, 'If I go there, my life is forfeit,' let the days pass, saying, 'Let us go today, let us go tomorrow.' She thought: 'This fool, due to the greatness of his own fault, does not dare to go. Parents, however, are always entirely well-wishers. Whether he goes or not, I shall go.' When he had gone out of the house, she put the household belongings in order, informed the neighbors of her departure for her family home, and set out on the road.

Sopi gharaṃ āgantvā taṃ adisvā paṭivissake pucchitvā, “sā kulagharaṃ gatā”ti sutvā vegena anubandhitvā antarāmagge sampāpuṇi. Tassāpi tattheva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. So “kiṃ idaṃ, bhadde”ti [P 1.0241] pucchi. “Sāmi, me eko putto jāto”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karissāmā”ti? “Yassatthāya mayaṃ kulagharaṃ gaccheyyāma, taṃ kammaṃ antarāmaggeva nipphannaṃ, tattha gantvā kiṃ karissāma, nivattissāmā”ti dvepi ekacittā hutvā nivattiṃsu. Tassa ca dārakassa panthe jātattā panthakoti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassā nacirasseva aparopi gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sabbaṃ [M 1.0154] purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Tassapi dārakassa panthe jātattā paṭhamajātassa mahāpanthakoti nāmaṃ katvā itarassa cūḷapanthakoti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te dvepi dārake gahetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gatā. Tesaṃ tattha vasantānaṃ mahāpanthakadārako aññe dārake “cūḷapitā mahāpitāti, ayyako ayyikā”ti ca vadante sutvā mātaraṃ pucchi – “amma, aññe dārakā ‘ayyako ayyikā’tipi, ‘mahāpitā cūḷapitā’tipi vadanti, kacci amhākaññeva ñātakā natthī”ti? “Āma, tāta, amhākaṃ ettha ñātakā natthi. Rājagahanagare pana vo dhanaseṭṭhi nāma ayyako, tattha amhākaṃ bahū ñātakā”ti. “Kasmā tattha na gacchatha, ammā”ti? Sā attano agamanakāraṇaṃ puttassa akathetvā puttesu punappunaṃ kathentesu sāmikaṃ āha – “ime dārakā [P 1.0242] maṃ ativiya kilamenti, kiṃ no mātāpitaro disvā maṃsaṃ khādissanti, ehi, dārakānaṃ ayyakakulaṃ dassessāmā”ti? “Ahaṃ sammukhā bhavituṃ na sakkhissāmi, te pana nayissāmī”ti. “Sādhu yena kenaci upāyena dārakānaṃ ayyakakulameva daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Dvepi janā dārake ādāya anupubbena rājagahaṃ patvā nagaradvāre ekissā sālāya pavisitvā dārakamātā dve dārake gahetvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ārocāpesi. Te taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā, “saṃsāre vicarantānaṃ na putto na dhītā bhūtapubbā nāma natthi, te amhākaṃ mahāparādhikā, na sakkā tehi amhākaṃ cakkhupathe ṭhātuṃ, ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ gahetvā dvepi janā phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jīvantu, dārake pana idha pesentū”ti dhanaṃ datvā dūtaṃ pāhesuṃ.

He, too, returning home and not seeing her, asked the neighbors. Hearing that she had gone to her family's home, he followed swiftly and caught up with her on the way. There, on the road, her childbirth also occurred. He asked, 'What is this, my dear?' 'My lord, a son has been born to me.' 'What shall we do now?' 'The purpose for which we were going to my family's home has been accomplished right here on the road. What would we do by going there? Let us turn back.' Both being of one mind, they turned back. And because the child was born on the path, they gave him the name Panthaka. Before long, she conceived another child. The entire account should be elaborated as before. Because this child was also born on the path, they named the firstborn Mahāpanthaka, and the other Cūḷapanthaka. Taking the two children, they returned to their own dwelling place. While they were living there, the boy Mahāpanthaka, hearing other children call out 'younger uncle,' 'elder uncle,' 'grandfather,' and 'grandmother,' asked his mother: 'Mother, other children speak of grandfathers and grandmothers, and of elder and younger uncles. Is it that we alone have no relatives?' 'It is so, my son. Here we have no relatives. But in the city of Rājagaha, you have a grandfather named Dhanaseṭṭhi; there we have many relatives.' 'Why do you not go there, Mother?' Not telling her son the reason for not going, as her sons asked her again and again, she said to her husband: 'These children trouble me greatly. Surely my parents will not eat my flesh upon seeing me? Come, let us show the children their grandfather's family.' He replied, 'I will not be able to face them, but I will take you there.' 'Good. By some means or other, it is right for the children to see their grandfather's family.' The two of them, taking the children, traveled by stages and reached Rājagaha. Having entered a public hall at the city gate, the children's mother had a message sent to her parents announcing her arrival. Hearing the message, they said: 'For those wandering in saṃsāra, there is no one who has not formerly been a son or a daughter. They have greatly wronged us; it is not possible for them to stand in our sight. Let the two of them take this much wealth, go to a comfortable place, and live. But let them send the children here.' Having given the wealth, they sent a messenger.

Tehi [V 1.0138] pesitaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā dārake āgatadūtānaññeva hatthe datvā pahiṇiṃsu. Dārakā ayyakakule vaḍḍhanti. Tesu cūḷapanthako atidaharo, mahāpanthako pana ayyakena saddhiṃ dasabalassa dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ gacchati. Tassa niccaṃ satthu santikaṃ gacchantassa pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami. So ayyakaṃ āha – “sace maṃ anujāneyyātha, ahaṃ pabbajeyya”nti[P 1.0243]. “Kiṃ vadesi, tāta, sakalassa lokassapi me pabbajjāto tava pabbajjā bhaddikā. Sace sakkosi pabbajāhī”ti. Taṃ [M 1.0155] satthu santikaṃ netvā, “kiṃ, gahapati, dārako te laddho”ti vutte, “āma, bhante, ayaṃ me nattā tumhākaṃ santike pabbajitukāmo”ti āha. Satthā aññataraṃ piṇḍapātacārikaṃ bhikkhuṃ “imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājehī”ti āṇāpesi. Thero tassa tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbājesi. So bahuṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā paripuṇṇavasso upasampadaṃ labhitvā yonisomanasikārena kammaṭṭhānaṃ karonto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So jhānasukhena phalasukhena vītināmento cintesi – “sakkā nu kho idaṃ sukhaṃ cūḷapanthakassa dātu”nti! Tato ayyakaseṭṭhissa santikaṃ gantvā evamāha – “mahāseṭṭhi, sace anujāneyyātha, ahaṃ cūḷapanthakaṃ pabbājeyya”nti. “Pabbājetha, bhante”ti. Seṭṭhi kira sāsane ca suppasanno, “kataradhītāya vo ete puttā”ti pucchiyamāno ca “palātadhītāyā”ti vattuṃ lajjati, tasmā sukheneva tesaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujāni. Thero cūḷapanthakaṃ pabbājetvā [P 1.0244] sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. So pabbajitvāva dandho ahosi.

They took the money sent by the parents and, giving the boys into the hands of the very messengers who had come, sent them away. The boys grew up in their grandfather's household. Of the two, Cūḷapanthaka was very young, while Mahāpanthaka would go with his grandfather to listen to the Dhamma talk of the One with Ten Powers. Constantly going into the Teacher's presence, his mind inclined toward going forth. He said to his grandfather, 'If you would permit me, I would go forth.' 'What are you saying, dear grandson? For me, the going forth of the entire world is welcome; your going forth is excellent. If you are able, go forth.' He took him into the Teacher's presence. When asked, 'Householder, from where did you get this boy?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, this is my grandson. He wishes to go forth in your presence.' The Teacher instructed a certain alms-faring monk, 'Give this boy the going forth.' The elder taught him the meditation subject of the five parts ending with the skin and gave him the going forth. He learned much of the Buddha's word and, upon reaching twenty years of age, he received the higher ordination. By practicing the meditation subject with wise attention, he attained arahantship. While passing the time with the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition, he thought, 'Might it be possible to give this bliss to Cūḷapanthaka?' Then, going to his grandfather the setthi, he said, 'Great setthi, if you would permit, I would give Cūḷapanthaka the going forth.' 'Give him the going forth, venerable sir.' It is said that the setthi was very devout toward the Dispensation, and also, when asked, 'Whose daughter's sons are these?' he was ashamed to say, 'They are the sons of the daughter who ran away.' Therefore, he very easily permitted their going forth. The elder gave Cūḷapanthaka the going forth and established him in the moral precepts. Upon going forth, he was dull-witted.

“Padmaṃ yathā kokanadaṃ sugandhaṃ,

Pāto siyā phullamavītagandhaṃ;

Aṅgīrasaṃ passa virocamānaṃ,

Tapantamādiccamivantalikkhe”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.123; a. ni. 5.195) –

Just as a fragrant red lotus blooms at dawn, its scent not yet faded; Behold Aṅgīrasa, shining forth, like the sun blazing in the sky.

Imaṃ ekaṃ gāthaṃ catūhi māsehi uggaṇhituṃ nāsakkhi. So kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle pabbajitvā paññavā hutvā aññatarassa dandhabhikkhuno uddesaggahaṇakāle parihāsakeḷiṃ akāsi. So bhikkhu tena parihāsena lajjito neva uddesaṃ gaṇhi, na sajjhāyamakāsi. Tena kammena ayaṃ pabbajitvāva dandho jāto, gahitagahitaṃ padaṃ uparūparipadaṃ gaṇhantassa nassati. Tassa imameva gāthaṃ uggahetuṃ vāyamantassa cattāro māsā atikkantā. Atha naṃ mahāpanthako, “cūḷapanthaka, tvaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane abhabbo, catūhi māsehi ekaṃ gāthampi gaṇhituṃ [V 1.0139] na sakkosi, pabbajitakiccaṃ pana kathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpessasi, nikkhama ito”ti vihārā nikkaḍḍhi. Cūḷapanthako buddhasāsane sinehena gihibhāvaṃ na pattheti.

He was not able to learn this single verse in four months. It is said that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, he had gone forth and, being intelligent, had made a mocking jest at a certain dull monk who was receiving instruction. That monk, being shamed by the mockery, neither took up the instruction nor made recitation. By that kamma, he became dull upon going forth; as he was learning the next phrase, the phrase he had just learned was lost. While he was striving to learn this very verse, four months passed by. Then Mahāpanthaka expelled him from the monastery, saying, 'Cūḷapanthaka, you are unfit for this Dispensation. In four months you are not able to learn even a single verse; how then will you bring the duties of one gone forth to completion? Get out of here!' But Cūḷapanthaka, out of affection for the Buddha’s Dispensation, did not desire the state of a householder.

Tasmiñca kāle mahāpanthako bhattuddesako ahosi. Jīvako komārabhacco bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ ādāya attano ambavanaṃ [M 1.0156] gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā dhammaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā dasabalaṃ vanditvā mahāpanthakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “kittakā[P 1.0245], bhante, satthu santike bhikkhū”ti pucchi. “Pañcamattāni bhikkhusatānī”ti. “Sve, bhante, buddhappamukhāni pañca bhikkhusatāni ādāya amhākaṃ nivesane bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. “Upāsaka, cūḷapanthako nāma bhikkhu dandho aviruḷhidhammo, taṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ nimantanaṃ sampaṭicchāmī”ti thero āha. Taṃ sutvā cūḷapanthako cintesi – “thero ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nimantanaṃ sampaṭicchanto maṃ bāhiraṃ katvā sampaṭicchati, nissaṃsayaṃ mayhaṃ bhātikassa mayi cittaṃ bhinnaṃ bhavissati, kiṃ dāni mayhaṃ iminā sāsanena, gihī hutvā dānādīni puññāni karonto jīvissāmī”ti? So punadivase pātova vibbhamituṃ pāyāsi.

At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the allocator of meal invitations. Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, went to his own mango grove. Having paid homage to the Teacher and listened to the Dhamma, he rose from his seat, venerated the One with Ten Powers, approached Mahāpanthaka, and asked, 'Venerable sir, how many monks are in the Teacher's presence?' 'About five hundred monks.' 'Venerable sir, tomorrow, taking the five hundred monks headed by the Buddha, please accept a meal at our residence.' The elder replied, 'Lay follower, there is a monk named Cūḷapanthaka who is dull and whose understanding of the Dhamma does not grow. Setting him aside, I accept the invitation for the rest.' Hearing that, Cūḷapanthaka thought: 'The elder, while accepting the invitation for so many monks, accepts it having made me an outsider. Without a doubt, my brother has turned against me. What use is this Dispensation to me now? I will become a householder and live by making merit, such as giving alms.' So on the next day, early in the morning, he set out to leave the monastic life.

Satthā paccūsakāleyeva lokaṃ volokento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā paṭhamataraṃ gantvā cūḷapanthakassa gamanamagge dvārakoṭṭhake caṅkamanto aṭṭhāsi. Cūḷapanthako gacchanto satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “kuhiṃ pana tvaṃ, cūḷapanthaka, imāya velāya gacchasī”ti āha. “Bhātā maṃ, bhante, nikkaḍḍhati, tenāhaṃ vibbhamituṃ gacchāmī”ti. “Cūḷapanthaka, tava pabbajjā nāma mama santakā, bhātarā nikkaḍḍhito kasmā mama santikaṃ nāgañchi, ehi, kiṃ te gihibhāvena, mama santike bhavissasī”ti cakkaṅkitatalena pāṇinā taṃ sirasi parāmasitvā ādāya gantvā gandhakuṭippamukhe nisīdāpetvā, “cūḷapanthaka, puratthābhimukho hutvā imaṃ pilotikaṃ ‘rajoharaṇaṃ rajoharaṇa’nti parimajjanto idheva hohī”ti iddhiyā abhisaṅkhataṃ parisuddhaṃ [P 1.0246] pilotikaṃ datvā kāle ārocite bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto jīvakassa gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Cūḷapanthakopi sūriyaṃ olokento taṃ pilotikaṃ “rajoharaṇaṃ rajoharaṇa”nti parimajjanto nisīdi. Tassa taṃ pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ parimajjantassa kiliṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Tato cintesi – “idaṃ pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ ativiya parisuddhaṃ, imaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ nissāya purimapakatiṃ vijahitvā evaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ jātaṃ, aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapento vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhesi. Satthā “cūḷapanthakassa cittaṃ vipassanaṃ āruḷha”nti ñatvā, “cūḷapanthaka, tvaṃ pilotikakhaṇḍameva saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ ‘rajaṃ raja’nti [V 1.0140] mā saññaṃ kari, abbhantare pana te rāgarajādayo atthi, te harāhī”ti [M 1.0157] vatvā obhāsaṃ vissajjetvā purato nisinno viya paññāyamānarūpo hutvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

At the very break of dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw this reason and went ahead, pacing at the gateway on the path Cūḷapanthaka was taking. Cūḷapanthaka, on his way, saw the Teacher, approached, paid homage, and stood there. Then the Teacher said to him, "Where are you going at this early hour, Cūḷapanthaka?" "Venerable sir, my brother has expelled me, so I am going to disrobe." "Cūḷapanthaka, your ordination belongs to me. When expelled by your brother, why did you not come to me? Come, what use is the household life to you? You shall remain in my presence." With his hand marked by the wheel, he stroked his head and led him away. Seating him near the Perfumed Chamber, he said, "Cūḷapanthaka, face the east and stay right here, rubbing this cloth and repeating, 'Remover of dust, remover of dust.'" He gave him a perfectly pure cloth created by psychic power, and when the time was announced, surrounded by the community of monks, he went to Jīvaka’s house and sat on the prepared seat. Cūḷapanthaka, too, looking at the sun, sat rubbing the cloth and repeating, 'Remover of dust, remover of dust.' As he rubbed that piece of cloth, it became soiled. Then he reflected, "This piece of cloth is extremely pure, yet because of this body, having abandoned its former nature, it has become so soiled. Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned phenomena!" Contemplating decay and cessation, he developed insight. The Teacher, knowing that Cūḷapanthaka’s mind had ascended to insight, said, "Cūḷapanthaka, do not think that it is only this piece of cloth that is soiled, and that this is dust. Rather, within you there are dusts such as lust; remove them!" Then, sending forth a radiance, appearing as if seated before him, he spoke these verses:

“Rāgo rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati,

Rāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajjaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo,

Viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane.

Lust is called dust, but it is not called mere powder; 'dust' is a term for lust. Having abandoned this dust, those monks dwell in the Dispensation of the one free from dust.

“Doso rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati,

Dosassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo,

Viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane.

Hatred is called dust, but it is not called mere powder; 'dust' is a term for hatred. Having abandoned this dust, those monks dwell in the Dispensation of the one free from dust.

“Moho rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati,

Mohassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo,

Viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane”ti. (mahāni. 209);

Delusion is called dust, but it is not called mere powder; 'dust' is a term for delusion. Having abandoned this dust, those monks dwell in the Dispensation of the one free from dust.

Gāthāpariyosāne [P 1.0247] cūḷapanthako saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Saha paṭisambhidāhiyevassa tīṇi piṭakāni āgamiṃsu.

At the conclusion of the verses, Cūḷapanthaka attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Along with the analytical knowledges, the three Piṭakas came to him.

So kira pubbe rājā hutvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto nalāṭato sede muccante parisuddhena sāṭakena nalāṭantaṃ puñchi, sāṭako kiliṭṭho ahosi. So “imaṃ sarīraṃ nissāya evarūpo parisuddho sāṭako pakatiṃ jahitvā kiliṭṭho jāto, aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Te kāraṇenassa rajoharaṇameva paccayo jāto.

It is said that in a past life, when he was a king circumambulating the city, sweat was released from his forehead. He wiped his forehead with a pure cloth, and the cloth became soiled. He thought, "Because of this body, such a pure cloth has abandoned its original nature and become soiled. Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned phenomena!" and he obtained the perception of impermanence. For that reason, the 'remover of dust' itself became a supporting condition for him.

Jīvakopi kho komārabhacco dasabalassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ upanāmesi. Satthā “nanu, jīvaka, vihāre bhikkhū atthī”ti hatthena pattaṃ pidahi. Mahāpanthako “nanu, bhante, vihāre bhikkhū natthī”ti āha. Satthā “atthi, jīvakā”ti āha. Jīvako “tena hi bhaṇe gaccha, vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ vā natthibhāvaṃ vā tvaññeva jānāhī”ti purisaṃ pesesi. Tasmiṃ [V 1.0141] khaṇe cūḷapanthako “mayhaṃ bhātiko ‘vihāre bhikkhū natthī’ti bhaṇati[M 1.0158], vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvamassa pakāsessāmī”ti sakalaṃ ambavanaṃ bhikkhūnaññeva pūresi. Ekacce bhikkhū cīvarakammaṃ karonti, ekacce rajanakammaṃ karonti, ekacce sajjhāyaṃ karonti. Evaṃ aññamaññaasadisaṃ bhikkhusahassaṃ māpesi. So puriso vihāre bahū bhikkhū disvā nivattitvā, “ayya, sakalaṃ ambavanaṃ bhikkhūhi paripuṇṇa”nti jīvakassa ārocesi. Theropi kho tattheva –

Jīvaka Komārabhacca also offered the dedication water to the Ten-Powered One. The Teacher, saying, "Jīvaka, are there not monks in the monastery?" covered the bowl with his hand. Mahāpanthaka said, "But venerable sir, there are no monks in the monastery." The Teacher said, "There are, Jīvaka." Jīvaka then sent a man, saying, "Go and see for yourself whether there are monks in the monastery or not." At that moment, Cūḷapanthaka thought, "My brother says there are no monks in the monastery—I will reveal the presence of monks to this man," and he filled the entire mango grove with monks. Some monks were doing robe-making, some were doing dyeing, and some were reciting. Thus, he created a thousand monks, each unlike the other. The man, seeing many monks in the monastery, returned and reported to Jīvaka, "Sir, the entire mango grove is filled with monks." The Elder, too, was right there—

“Sahassakkhattumattānaṃ[P 1.0248], nimminitvāna panthako;

Nisīdambavane ramme, yāva kālappavedanā”ti.

Panthaka, having created a thousand forms of himself, sat in the delightful mango grove until the time was announced.

Atha satthā taṃ purisaṃ āha – “vihāraṃ gantvā ‘satthā cūḷapanthakaṃ nāma pakkosatī’ti vadehī”ti. Tena gantvā tathā vutte, “ahaṃ cūḷapanthako, ahaṃ cūḷapanthako”ti mukhasahassaṃ uṭṭhahi. So puriso puna gantvā, “sabbepi kira, bhante, cūḷapanthakāyeva nāmā”ti āha. “Tena hi gantvā yo ‘ahaṃ cūḷapanthako’ti paṭhamaṃ vadati, taṃ hatthe gaṇha, avasesā antaradhāyissantī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Tāvadeva sahassamattā bhikkhū antaradhāyiṃsu. Theropi tena purisena saddhiṃ agamāsi. Satthā bhattakiccapariyosāne jīvakaṃ āmantesi – “jīvaka, cūḷapanthakassa pattaṃ gaṇhāhi, ayaṃ te anumodanaṃ karissatī”ti. Jīvako tathā akāsi. Thero sīhanādaṃ nadanto taruṇasīho viya tīhi piṭakehi saṅkhobhetvā anumodanamakāsi. Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhūhi vatte dassite gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghassa sugatovādaṃ datvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ uyyojetvā surabhigandhavāsitaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ upagato. Atha sāyanhasamaye bhikkhū ito cito ca samosaritvā rattakambalasāṇiyā parikkhittā viya [P 1.0249] nisīditvā satthu guṇakathaṃ ārabhiṃsu, “āvuso, mahāpanthako cūḷapanthakassa ajjhāsayaṃ ajānanto catūhi māsehi ekaṃ gāthaṃ uggaṇhāpetuṃ na sakkoti, ‘dandho aya’nti vihārā nikkaḍḍhi, sammāsambuddho pana attano anuttaradhammarājatāya ekasmiṃyevassa antarabhatte saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ adāsi, tīṇi piṭakāni saha paṭisambhidāhiyeva āgatāni, aho buddhānaṃ balaṃ nāma mahanta”nti.

Then the Teacher said to that man, 'Go to the monastery and say, "The Teacher is calling for the monk named Cūḷapanthaka."' When that man went and said so, a thousand mouths responded, saying, 'I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka.' That man went back and said, 'Venerable sir, it seems they are all named Cūḷapanthaka.' 'In that case, go and take by the hand the one who first says, "I am Cūḷapanthaka"; the rest will disappear.' He did so. At that very moment, the thousand monks vanished. The Elder also went with that man. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher addressed Jīvaka, 'Jīvaka, take Cūḷapanthaka's bowl; this monk will deliver the anumodanā discourse for you.' Jīvaka did so. The Elder, roaring a lion's roar like a young lion, delivered the anumodanā, stirring up the three Piṭakas. The Teacher rose from his seat, and surrounded by the assembly of monks, went to the monastery. When the monks had performed their duties, he stood at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber, gave the Sugata's exhortation to the assembly of monks, taught the meditation subject, dismissed the assembly of monks, and having entered the Perfumed Chamber, fragrant with sweet scents, he lay down on his right side in the lion's posture. Then, in the evening, the monks gathered from here and there, and sitting as if enclosed by a red woolen curtain, they began a discussion on the Teacher's virtues: 'Friends, Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka's disposition, was unable to make him learn a single verse in four months and expelled him from the monastery, saying, "This one is dull." The Fully Enlightened One, however, by his supreme kingship of the Dhamma, bestowed upon him Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges within a single interval between meals. The three Piṭakas, along with the analytical knowledges, came to him. Ah, how great indeed is the power of the Buddhas!'

Atha [M 1.0159] bhagavā dhammasabhāyaṃ imaṃ kathāpavattiṃ ñatvā, “ajja mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti buddhaseyyāya uṭṭhāya surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā vijjulataṃ viya kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā rattakambalasadisaṃ sugatamahācīvaraṃ pārupitvā surabhigandhakuṭito nikkhamma mattavaravāraṇasīhavijambhitavilāsena [V 1.0142] anantāya buddhalīḷāya dhammasabhaṃ gantvā alaṅkatamaṇḍalamāḷamajjhe supaññattavarabuddhāsanaṃ abhiruyha chabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo vissajjento aṇṇavakucchiṃ khobhayamāno yugandharamatthake bālasūriyo viya āsanamajjhe nisīdi. Sammāsambuddhe pana āgatamatte bhikkhusaṅgho kathaṃ pacchinditvā tuṇhī ahosi. Satthā mudukena mettacittena [P 1.0250] parisaṃ oloketvā, “ayaṃ parisā ativiya sobhati, ekassapi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā ukkāsitasaddo vā khipitasaddo vā natthi, sabbepi ime buddhagāravena sagāravā, buddhatejena tajjitā. Mayi āyukappampi akathetvā nisinne paṭhamaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā na kathessanti. Kathāsamuṭṭhāpanavattaṃ nāma mayāva jānitabbaṃ, ahameva paṭhamaṃ kathessāmī”ti madhurena brahmassarena bhikkhū āmantetvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “na, bhikkhave, cūḷapanthako idāneva dandho, pubbepi dandhoyeva. Na kevalañcassāhaṃ idāneva avassayo jāto, pubbepi avassayo ahosimeva. Pubbe panāhaṃ imaṃ lokiyakuṭumbassa sāmikaṃ akāsiṃ, idāni lokuttarakuṭumbassā”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ vitthārato sotukāmehi bhikkhūhi āyācito atītaṃ āhari –

Then the Blessed One, knowing this discussion was taking place in the Dhamma hall, thought, 'Today it is fitting for me to go.' Rising from the Buddha-couch, he put on his deep-red, double-layered undergarment, fastened his girdle like a flash of lightning, wrapped himself in the Sugata's great outer robe, which was like a red blanket, and went forth from his fragrant Perfumed Chamber. With the graceful bearing of a stretching lion and a fine, intoxicated elephant, and with infinite Buddha-grace, he went to the Dhamma hall. He ascended the well-prepared, excellent Buddha-seat in the middle of the adorned circular hall. Radiating the six-colored Buddha-rays, he sat in the middle of the seat like the morning sun on the peak of Mount Yugandhara, as if stirring the very belly of the ocean. As soon as the Fully Enlightened One arrived, the assembly of monks cut short their talk and became silent. The Teacher, with a gentle and loving mind, surveyed the assembly and thought: 'This assembly is exceedingly splendid. For not a single one is there fidgeting of the hands or feet, nor the sound of coughing or sneezing. All these monks are reverent out of respect for the Buddha; they are awed by the Buddha’s majesty. If I were to sit for an entire life-eon without speaking, they would not be the first to raise a topic of conversation. The proper way to initiate a talk is to be known by me alone. I myself shall be the first to speak.' With a sweet, Brahma-like voice, he addressed the monks: 'Monks, for what topic of discussion are you now gathered? And what was your unfinished talk that was interrupted?' When they replied, 'It was about this matter,' he said: 'Monks, it is not only now that Cūḷapanthaka is dull; he was dull in the past as well. And it is not only now that I have become his refuge; I was his refuge in the past as well. In the past, however, I made him the master of worldly wealth; now, I have made him the master of supramundane wealth.' Having said this, being requested by the monks who desired to hear the matter in detail, he related a story of the past.

“Atīte, bhikkhave, bārāṇasinagaravāsī eko māṇavo takkasilaṃ gantvā sippuggahaṇatthāya disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa dhammantevāsiko hutvā pañcannaṃ māṇavakasatānaṃ antare ativiya ācariyassa upakārako ahosi, pādaparikammādīni sabbakiccāni karoti. Dandhatāya pana kiñci uggaṇhituṃ na sakko”ti. Ācariyo “ayaṃ mama bahūpakāro, sikkhāpessāmi na”nti vāyamantopi kiñci sikkhāpetuṃ [P 1.0251] na sakkoti. So ciraṃ vasitvā ekagāthampi uggaṇhituṃ asakkonto ukkaṇṭhitvā “gamissāmī”ti ācariyaṃ āpucchi. Ācariyo cintesi – “ayaṃ mayhaṃ upakārako, paṇḍitabhāvamassa paccāsīsāmi, na naṃ kātuṃ sakkomi[M 1.0160], avassaṃ mayā imassa paccupakāro kātabbo, ekamassa mantaṃ bandhitvā dassāmī”ti so taṃ araññaṃ netvā “ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā ghaṭṭesi? Ahampi taṃ jānāmi jānāmī”ti imaṃ mantaṃ bandhitvā uggaṇhāpento anekasatakkhattuṃ parivattāpetvā, “paññāyati te”ti pucchitvā, “āma, paññāyatī”ti vutte “dandhena nāma vāyāmaṃ katvā paguṇaṃ kataṃ sippaṃ na palāyatī”ti cintetvā maggaparibbayaṃ datvā, “gaccha, imaṃ mantaṃ nissāya jīvissasi, apalāyanatthāya panassa niccaṃ sajjhāyaṃ kareyyāsī”ti vatvā taṃ uyyojesi. Athassa mātā bārāṇasiyaṃ sampattakāle “putto me sippaṃ sikkhitvā āgato”ti mahāsakkārasammānaṃ akāsi.

“Monks, in the past, a certain young man, a resident of the city of Bārāṇasī, went to Takkasilā to learn a skill. He became a close disciple of the world-renowned teacher and, among five hundred young men, was exceedingly helpful to the teacher, performing all duties such as massaging his feet. But due to his dullness, he was unable to learn anything. The teacher, thinking, 'This one is of great service to me; I will teach him,' strove, yet was unable to teach him anything. After staying for a long time, unable to learn even a single stanza, he became disheartened and, saying, 'I will go,' asked the teacher for permission to leave. The teacher reflected: 'This one is of great service to me. I hoped for him to become learned, but I was not able to make it so. I must certainly repay his service. I will compose a mantra for him and give it.' So, leading him to the forest, he composed this mantra and made him learn it: 'You strive, you strive! For what reason do you strive? I too know that, I know!' After making him repeat it more than a hundred times, he asked, 'Is it clear to you?' When the young man replied, 'Yes, it is clear,' the teacher thought, 'A skill made proficient with effort by a dull person does not vanish.' Giving him provisions for the road, he said, 'Go. You will make a living by relying on this mantra. And so that it is not forgotten, you should constantly recite it.' Having said this, he sent him off. Then, when he arrived in Bārāṇasī, his mother, thinking, 'My son has returned after learning a skill,' accorded him great honor and respect.”

Tadā [V 1.0143] bārāṇasirājā “atthi nu kho me kāyakammādīsu koci doso”ti paccavekkhanto attano aruccanakaṃ kiñci kammaṃ adisvā “attano vajjaṃ nāma attano na paññāyati, paresaṃ paññāyati, nāgarānaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā sāyaṃ aññātakavesena nikkhamitvā, “sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā nisinnamanussānaṃ kathāsallāpo nāma nānappakārako hoti, ‘sacāhaṃ adhammena rajjaṃ kāremi, pāpena adhammikena raññā daṇḍabaliādīhi hatamhā’ti vakkhanti. ‘Sace dhammena rajjaṃ kāremi, dīghāyuko hotu no rājā’tiādīni [P 1.0252] vatvā mama guṇaṃ kathessantī”ti tesaṃ tesaṃ gehānaṃ bhittianusāreneva vicarati.

At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī, while reflecting, 'Is there any fault of mine in my bodily actions and so forth?' and not seeing any unsuitable action of his own, thought: 'One's own fault is not apparent to oneself; it is apparent to others. I will investigate the citizens.' Having thought thus, he went out in the evening in disguise, thinking: 'The conversation of people sitting after having eaten their evening meal is of various kinds. If I should rule the kingdom unrighteously, they will say, "We are ruined by the wicked, unrighteous king through punishments, taxes, and so on." If I rule the kingdom righteously, they will speak of my virtues, saying such things as, "May our king be long-lived!"' Thus, he wandered along by the very walls of those various houses.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe umaṅgacorā dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare umaṅgaṃ bhindanti ekaumaṅgeneva dve gehāni pavisanatthāya. Rājā te disvā gehacchāyāya aṭṭhāsi. Tesaṃ umaṅgaṃ bhinditvā gehaṃ pavisitvā bhaṇḍakaṃ olokitakāle māṇavo pabujjhitvā taṃ mantaṃ sajjhāyanto “ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā ghaṭṭesi? Ahampi taṃ jānāmi jānāmī”ti āha. Te taṃ sutvā, “iminā kiramhā ñātā, idāni no nāsessatī”ti nivatthavatthānipi chaḍḍetvā bhītā sammukhasammukhaṭṭhāneneva palāyiṃsu. Rājā te palāyante disvā itarassa ca mantasajjhāyanasaddaṃ sutvā gehaññeva vavatthapetvā nāgarānaṃ pariggaṇhitvā nivesanaṃ pāvisi. So vibhātāya pana rattiyā pātovekaṃ purisaṃ pakkositvā āha – “gaccha bhaṇe, asukavīthiyaṃ nāma yasmiṃ gehe umaṅgo bhinno, tattha takkasilato sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgatamāṇavo atthi, taṃ ānehī”ti. So [M 1.0161] gantvā “rājā taṃ pakkosatī”ti vatvā māṇavaṃ ānesi. Atha naṃ rājā āha – “tvaṃ, tāta, takkasilato sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgatamāṇavo”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Amhākampi taṃ sippaṃ dehī”ti. “Sādhu, deva, samānāsane nisīditvā gaṇhāhī”ti. Rājāpi tathā katvā mantaṃ gahetvā “ayaṃ te [P 1.0253] ācariyabhāgo”ti sahassaṃ adāsi.

At that moment, tunnel thieves were breaking a tunnel between two houses in order to enter both houses with just one tunnel. The king, seeing them, stood in the shadow of a house. At the time when they, having broken through the tunnel and entered the house, were looking at the goods, the young man woke up and, reciting that mantra, said: 'You grind, you grind! For what reason do you grind? I too know that, I know!' Hearing that, they thought, 'It seems we are known by this one! Now he will destroy us!' Terrified, they abandoned even the clothes they were wearing and fled just in the direction they were facing. The king, seeing them fleeing and hearing the sound of the other's mantra recitation, took note of that very house and, having finished investigating the citizens, entered the palace. Then, when the night had dawned, early in the morning he summoned a certain man and said: 'Go, friend, to such-and-such a street. In the house where a tunnel was broken, there is a young man who has come after learning a skill from Takkasilā. Bring him.' That man went and, saying, 'The king summons you,' brought the young man. Then the king said to him: 'My dear son, are you the young man who has come after learning a skill from Takkasilā?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'Give that skill to us also.' 'Very well, Your Majesty. Sit on an equal seat and learn it.' The king also, having done so, learned the mantra and, saying, 'This is your teacher's portion,' gave him a thousand.

Tadā senāpati rañño kappakaṃ āha – “kadā rañño massuṃ karissasī”ti? “Sve vā parasuve vā”ti. So tassa sahassaṃ datvā “kiccaṃ me atthī”ti vatvā, “kiṃ, sāmī”ti vutte “rañño massukammaṃ karonto viya hutvā khuraṃ ativiya pahaṃsitvā galanāḷiṃ chinda, tvaṃ senāpati bhavissasi, ahaṃ rājā”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rañño massukammakaraṇadivase gandhodakena massuṃ temetvā khuraṃ pahaṃsitvā nalāṭante gahetvā, “khuro thokaṃ kuṇṭhadhāro, ekappahāreneva galanāḷiṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti puna ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā khuraṃ pahaṃsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā attano mantaṃ saritvā sajjhāyaṃ karonto “ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā [V 1.0144] ghaṭṭesi? Ahampi taṃ jānāmi jānāmī”ti āha. Nhāpitassa nalāṭato sedā mucciṃsu. So “jānāti mama kāraṇaṃ rājā”ti bhīto khuraṃ bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā pādamūle urena nipajji. Rājāno nāma chekā honti, tena taṃ evamāha – “are, duṭṭha, nhāpita, ‘na maṃ rājā jānātī’ti saññaṃ karosī”ti. “Abhayaṃ me dehi, devā”ti. “Hotu, mā bhāyi, kathehī”ti. Senāpati me, deva, sahassaṃ datvā, “rañño massuṃ karonto viya galanāḷiṃ chinda, ahaṃ rājā hutvā taṃ senāpatiṃ karissāmī”ti āhāti. Rājā taṃ sutvā “ācariyaṃ me nissāya jīvitaṃ laddha”nti cintetvā senāpatiṃ [P 1.0254] pakkosāpetvā, “ambho, senāpati, kiṃ nāma tayā mama santikā na laddhaṃ, idāni taṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkomi, mama raṭṭhā nikkhamāhī”ti taṃ raṭṭhā pabbājetvā ācariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “ācariya, taṃ nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddha”nti vatvā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ karitvā tassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. “So tadā cūḷapanthako ahosi, satthā disāpāmokkho ācariyo”ti.

Then the general said to the king’s barber: “When will you perform the king's shave?” “Tomorrow or the day after,” he replied. The general gave him a thousand and said, “I have a task for you.” When asked, “What is it, master?” he replied, “Pretending to perform the king's shave, sharpen the razor exceedingly and cut his throat. You will become the general, and I will be king.” The barber agreed, saying, “Very well.” On the day of the king’s shave, he moistened the beard with scented water, sharpened the razor, and holding it at the king’s forehead, thought, “The razor is a bit dull-edged; it is proper to cut the throat with a single stroke.” Then, having stood aside, he sharpened the razor again. At that moment, the king remembered his mantra and, reciting it, said: “You grind, you grind! For what reason do you grind? I too know that, I know!” Sweat poured from the barber’s forehead. Terrified, he thought, “The king knows my purpose!” He threw the razor to the ground and fell at the king’s feet, prostrating himself with his chest. Kings are indeed clever; therefore, the king said to him, “Hey, wicked barber, do you hold the perception, ‘The king does not know me’?” The barber pleaded, “Grant me safety, Your Majesty!” The king replied, “So be it. Do not fear. Speak.” The barber confessed, “Your Majesty, the general gave me a thousand and said, ‘Pretending to shave the king’s beard, cut his throat. I, having become king, will make you the general.’” Hearing this, the king reflected, “My life was obtained by relying on my teacher.” He had the general summoned and said, “O general, what have you not received from me? Now I cannot bear to see you; depart from my kingdom!” He banished him from the kingdom. Then he had the teacher summoned and said, “Teacher, my life was obtained because of you.” He accorded him great honor and appointed him to the position of general. He at that time was Cūḷapanthaka, and the Teacher was the world-renowned teacher.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā, “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi cūḷapanthako dandhoyeva ahosi, tadāpissāhaṃ avassayo hutvā taṃ lokiyakuṭumbe [M 1.0162] patiṭṭhāpesi”nti vatvā puna ekadivasaṃ “aho satthā cūḷapanthakassa avassayo jāto”ti kathāya samuṭṭhitāya cūḷaseṭṭhijātake atītavatthuṃ kathetvā –

The Teacher, having brought forth this past event, said: “Monks, thus in the past too Cūḷapanthaka was indeed slow-witted. At that time too, I, having become his refuge, established him in worldly prosperity.” Then, one day, when a discussion arose, “Oh, the Teacher has become a refuge for Cūḷapanthaka,” he related the past story from the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka:

“Appakenāpi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti. (jā. 1.1.4) –

“A wise and discerning person, even with little capital, establishes himself, just as one blowing on a small fire makes it great.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā, “na, bhikkhave, idānevāhaṃ imassa avassayo jāto, pubbepi avassayo ahosimeva. Pubbe panāhaṃ imaṃ lokiyakuṭumbassa sāmikaṃ akāsiṃ, idāni lokuttarakuṭumbassa. Tadā hi cūḷantevāsiko cūḷapanthako ahosi, cūḷaseṭṭhi pana paṇḍito byatto nakkhattakovido ahamevā”ti jātakaṃ samodhānesi.

Having spoken the verse, he said: “Monks, it is not only now that I have become his refuge; in the past too I was indeed his refuge. In the past, I made him the master of worldly wealth; now, I have made him the master of supramundane wealth. At that time, the young apprentice was Cūḷapanthaka, whereas I myself was the junior treasurer, wise, accomplished, and skilled in astrology.” Thus he connected the Jātaka.

Punekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “āvuso, cūḷapanthako catūhi māsehi catuppadaṃ gāthaṃ gahetuṃ asakkontopi vīriyaṃ anossajjitvāva arahatte patiṭṭhito[P 1.0255], idāni lokuttaradhammakuṭumbassa sāmiko jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, mama sāsane āraddhavīriyo bhikkhu lokuttaradhammassa sāmiko hotiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

On another occasion, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, although Cūḷapanthaka could not grasp a four-line verse in four months, by not abandoning his effort he became established in Arahantship. Now he has become the master of the wealth of the supramundane Dhamma.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what topic of discussion are you assembled here now?” and when they replied, “For this topic,” he said, “Monks, in my dispensation, a monk who has aroused his effort certainly becomes the master of the supramundane Dhamma.” Then he spoke this verse:

25.

25.

“Uṭṭhānenappamādena[V 1.0145], saṃyamena damena ca;

Dīpaṃ kayirātha medhāvī, yaṃ ogho nābhikīratī”ti.

“By exertion and heedfulness, by restraint and self-control, let the wise one make an island that no flood can overwhelm.”

Tattha dīpaṃ kayirāthāti vīriyasaṅkhātena uṭṭhānena, satiyā avippavāsākārasaṅkhātena appamādena, catupārisuddhisīlasaṅkhātena saṃyamena, indriyadamena cāti imehi kāraṇabhūtehi catūhi dhammehi dhammojapaññāya samannāgato medhāvī imasmiṃ ativiya dullabhapatiṭṭhatāya atigambhīre saṃsārasāgare attano patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ dīpaṃ kayirātha kareyya, kātuṃ sakkuṇeyyāti attho. Kīdisaṃ? Yaṃ ogho nābhikīratīti yaṃ catubbidhopi kilesogho abhikirituṃ viddhaṃsetuṃ na sakkoti. Na hi sakkā arahattaṃ oghena abhikiritunti.

Herein, ‘let the wise one make an island’ means this: a wise person, endowed with wisdom born of the Dhamma, should, by means of these four causal principles—exertion (that is, effort), heedfulness (that is, the state of not departing from mindfulness), restraint (that is, the fourfold purity of virtue), and the taming of the senses—create for himself an island, which is the fruit of Arahantship and serves as his foundation in this exceedingly deep ocean of saṃsāra where a footing is so difficult to find. What kind of island? ‘That no flood can overwhelm’ means an island that the fourfold flood of defilements cannot overwhelm or destroy. For indeed, it is not possible for Arahantship to be overwhelmed by the flood.

Gāthāpariyosāne [M 1.0163] bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Evaṃ desanā sampattaparisāya sātthikā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and so forth. Thus, the teaching became beneficial for the assembled congregation.

Cūḷapanthakattheravatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, the Third.

4. Bālanakkhattasaṅghuṭṭhavatthu

4. The Story of the Proclamation of the Fool's Festival

Pamādamanuyuñjantīti [P 1.0256] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bālanakkhattaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, “They pursue heedlessness,” concerning the Fool's Festival.

Ekasmiñhi samaye sāvatthiyaṃ bālanakkhattaṃ nāma saṅghuṭṭhaṃ. Tasmiṃ nakkhatte bālā dummedhino janā chārikāya ceva gomayena ca sarīraṃ makkhetvā sattāhaṃ asabbhaṃ bhaṇantā vicaranti. Kiñci ñāti suhajjaṃ vā pabbajitaṃ vā disvā lajjantā nāma natthi. Dvāre dvāre ṭhatvā asabbhaṃ bhaṇanti. Manussā tesaṃ asabbhaṃ sotuṃ asakkontā yathābalaṃ aḍḍhaṃ vā pādaṃ vā kahāpaṇaṃ vā pesenti. Te tesaṃ dvāre laddhaṃ laddhaṃ gahetvā pakkamanti. Tadā pana sāvatthiyaṃ pañca koṭimattā ariyasāvakā vasanti, te satthu santikaṃ sāsanaṃ pesayiṃsu – “bhagavā, bhante, sattāhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ nagaraṃ appavisitvā vihāreyeva hotū”ti. Tañca pana sattāhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa vihāreyeva yāgubhattādīni sampādetvā pahiṇiṃsu, sayampi gehā na nikkhamiṃsu. Te nakkhatte pana pariyosite aṭṭhame divase buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā nagaraṃ pavesetvā mahādānaṃ datvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā, “bhante, atidukkhena no satta divasāni atikkantāni, bālānaṃ asabbhāni suṇantānaṃ [P 1.0257] kaṇṇā bhijjanākārappattā honti, koci kassaci [V 1.0146] na lajjati, tena mayaṃ tumhākaṃ antonagaraṃ pavisituṃ nādamha, mayampi gehato na nikkhamimhā”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “bālānaṃ dummedhānaṃ kiriyā nāma evarūpā hoti, medhāvino pana dhanasāraṃ viya appamādaṃ rakkhitvā amatamahānibbānasampattiṃ pāpuṇantī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Indeed, at one time in Sāvatthī, a festival called the Fool's Festival was proclaimed. During this festival, foolish and witless people would smear their bodies with ashes and cow dung, and for seven days they would wander about speaking unseemly words. There was no one who felt shame upon seeing any relative, friend, or renunciate. Standing at every door, they would utter unseemly words. Unable to bear their unseemly speech, people would send them a half, a quarter, or a kahāpaṇa, according to their means. Taking whatever they received at each door, they would then depart. At that time, fifty million noble disciples lived in Sāvatthī. They sent a message to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, along with the community of monks, refrain from entering the city for seven days and remain in the monastery.” For those seven days, they prepared and sent rice gruel, meals, and other provisions to the monastic community at the monastery, and they themselves did not leave their homes. When the festival ended, on the eighth day, they invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, had them enter the city, gave a great offering, and sat to one side. They said: “Venerable Sir, these seven days have passed for us with great difficulty. Listening to the unseemly words of the fools, our ears felt as if they would break. No one felt shame toward anyone else. That is why we did not allow you to enter the city, and we ourselves did not leave our homes.” Hearing their words, the Teacher said: “Such is the conduct of foolish and witless people. The wise, however, guarding heedfulness like a precious treasure, attain the accomplishment of the deathless, the great Nibbāna.” Then he spoke these verses:

26.

26.

“Pamādamanuyuñjanti, bālā dummedhino janā;

Appamādañca medhāvī, dhanaṃ seṭṭhaṃva rakkhati.

Fools, witless people, pursue heedlessness; but the wise one guards heedfulness as the greatest treasure.

27.

27.

“Mā [M 1.0164] pamādamanuyuñjetha, mā kāmaratisanthavaṃ;

Appamatto hi jhāyanto, pappoti vipulaṃ sukha”nti.

Do not pursue heedlessness, nor intimacy with sensual delight. For the heedful one, meditating, attains abundant happiness.

Tattha bālāti bālyena samannāgatā idhalokaparalokatthaṃ ajānantā. Dummedhinoti nippaññā. Te pamāde ādīnavaṃ apassantā pamādaṃ anuyuñjanti pavattenti, pamādena kālaṃ vītināmenti. Medhāvīti dhammojapaññāya samannāgato pana paṇḍito kulavaṃsāgataṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ sattaratanadhanaṃ viya appamādaṃ rakkhati. Yathā hi uttamaṃ dhanaṃ nissāya “kāmaguṇasampattiṃ pāpuṇissāma, puttadāraṃ posessāma, paralokagamanamaggaṃ sodhessāmā”ti dhane ānisaṃsaṃ passantā taṃ rakkhanti, evaṃ paṇḍitopi appamatto “paṭhamajjhānādīni [P 1.0258] paṭilabhissāmi, maggaphalādīni pāpuṇissāmi, tisso vijjā, cha abhiññā sampādessāmī”ti appamāde ānisaṃsaṃ passanto dhanaṃ seṭṭhaṃva appamādaṃ rakkhatīti attho. Mā pamādanti tasmā tumhe mā pamādamanuyuñjetha mā pamādena kālaṃ vītināmayittha. Mā kāmaratisanthavanti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu ratisaṅkhātaṃ taṇhāsanthavampi mā anuyuñjetha mā cintayittha mā paṭilabhittha. Appamatto hīti upaṭṭhitassatitāya hi appamatto jhāyanto puggalo vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ nibbānasukhaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Herein, “fools” are those endowed with foolishness, not knowing the welfare of this world and the next. “Witless” means lacking wisdom. Not seeing the danger in heedlessness, they engage in heedlessness, cause it to arise, and pass their time in heedlessness. “The wise one,” however, being a wise person endowed with the wisdom that knows the Dhamma, guards heedfulness like the excellent, supreme treasure of the seven gems that has come down through the family line. Just as those who rely on excellent wealth see its benefits—“We will attain the fulfillment of sensual pleasures, support our children and wife, and clear the path to the next world”—and thus protect it, so too does the wise person, being heedful, see the benefits of heedfulness: “I will attain the first jhāna and so on, I will reach the paths and fruits, I will accomplish the three knowledges and the six direct knowledges.” Seeing thus, they guard heedfulness as the greatest treasure. This is the meaning. “Do not pursue heedlessness” means: Therefore, do not engage in heedlessness, do not let time pass by in heedlessness. “Nor intimacy with sensual delight” means: Do not engage in, think upon, or re-obtain the association of craving, which is called delight in sensual objects and defilements. “For the heedful one” means: Indeed, a person who is heedful through established mindfulness, meditating, attains the vast, sublime bliss of Nibbāna.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verses, many became stream-enterers and so on. The Dhamma discourse became beneficial for the great assembly.

Bālanakkhattasaṅghuṭṭhavatthu catutthaṃ.

The Fourth Story: The Proclaimed Fool's Festival.

5. Mahākassapattheravatthu

5. The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa

Pamādaṃ [V 1.0147] appamādenāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahākassapattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Jetavana monastery, spoke this Dhamma discourse, which begins with 'Pamādaṃ appamādena,' concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.

Ekasmiñhi divase thero pipphaliguhāyaṃ viharanto rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pamatte ca appamatte ca udakapathavīpabbatādīsu cavanake upapajjanake ca satte [M 1.0165] dibbena cakkhunā olokento nisīdi. Satthā jetavane nisinnakova [P 1.0259] “kena nu kho vihārena ajja mama putto kassapo viharatī”ti dibbena cakkhunā upadhārento “sattānaṃ cutūpapātaṃ olokento viharatī”ti ñatvā “sattānaṃ cutūpapāto nāma buddhañāṇenapi aparicchinno, mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro ajānāpetvā cavanasattānaṃ paricchedo kātuṃ na sakkā, te jānituṃ tava avisayo, kassapa, appamattako tava visayo, sabbaso pana cavante ca upapajjante ca jānituṃ passituṃ buddhānameva visayo”ti vatvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā sammukhe nisinno viya hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, one day, the Elder, while dwelling in the Pipphali Cave, having gone for alms in Rājagaha and returned from the alms-round after the meal, developed the light kasina and sat observing with the divine eye beings in places such as water, earth, and mountains who were heedful and heedless, and those who were passing away and being reborn. The Teacher, seated in the Jetavana monastery, investigated with his divine eye, 'In what state does my son Kassapa dwell today?' Knowing, 'He dwells observing the passing away and rebirth of beings,' he thought, 'The passing away and rebirth of beings is indeed unlimitable even by a Buddha's knowledge. It is not possible to determine the limit of beings who, having taken conception in a mother's womb, pass away without their parents' knowledge. To know them is not your domain, Kassapa. Your scope is but a small one. However, to know and see in all aspects those who are passing away and being reborn is the domain of Buddhas alone.' Having said this, he suffused his radiance, and becoming as if seated in his presence, spoke this verse:

28.

28.

“Pamādaṃ appamādena, yadā nudati paṇḍito;

Paññāpāsādamāruyha, asoko sokiniṃ pajaṃ;

Pabbataṭṭhova bhūmaṭṭhe, dhīro bāle avekkhatī”ti.

When the wise one dispels heedlessness with heedfulness, having ascended the palace of wisdom, being sorrowless, he surveys the sorrowing folk. As one standing on a mountain beholds those on the ground, so the steadfast one looks upon fools.

Tattha nudatīti yathā nāma pokkharaṇiṃ pavisantaṃ navodakaṃ purāṇodakaṃ khobhetvā tassokāsaṃ adatvā taṃ attano matthakamatthakena palāyantaṃ nudati nīharati, evameva paṇḍito appamādalakkhaṇaṃ brūhento pamādassokāsaṃ adatvā yadā appamādavegena taṃ nudati nīharati, atha so panunnapamādo accuggatatthena parisuddhaṃ dibbacakkhusaṅkhātaṃ paññāpāsādaṃ tassa anucchavikaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrento tāya paṭipadāya nisseṇiyā pāsādaṃ viya āruyha pahīnasokasallatāya asoko, appahīnasokasallatāya sokiniṃ pajaṃ sattanikāyaṃ cavamānañceva upapajjamānañca dibbacakkhunā avekkhati passati. Yathā kiṃ? Pabbataṭṭhova [P 1.0260] bhūmaṭṭheti pabbatamuddhani ṭhito bhūmiyaṃ ṭhite, uparipāsāde vā pana ṭhito pāsādapariveṇe ṭhite akicchena avekkhati, tathā sopi dhīro paṇḍito mahākhīṇāsavo asamucchinnavaṭṭabīje bāle cavante ca upapajjante ca akicchena avekkhatīti.

Therein, 'nudati' means: just as fresh water entering a pond, having agitated the old water and giving it no space, dispels and expels that fleeing water with its own force; in the same way, when the wise one, developing the characteristic of heedfulness and giving no space to heedlessness, dispels and expels it with the force of heedfulness, then he, with heedlessness dispelled, ascends the palace of wisdom—which is pure, extremely lofty, and known as the divine eye—by means of that practice suitable for it, just as one might ascend a palace with a ladder. Being sorrowless due to having abandoned the dart of sorrow, he observes and sees with the divine eye the sorrowing folk, the assembly of beings who are passing away and being reborn, who are sorrowful due to not having abandoned the dart of sorrow. How so? 'As one standing on a mountain peak looks upon those on the ground' means as one looks without difficulty upon those standing on the ground, or as one standing on the upper floor of a palace looks upon those in the palace compound. In the same way, that steadfast wise one, the great one whose cankers are destroyed, looks without difficulty upon the foolish ones whose seed of the round of existence is not cut off, as they are passing away and being reborn.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0148] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni sacchikariṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many realized the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Mahākassapattheravatthu pañcamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa, the Fifth.

6. Pamattāpamattadvesahāyakavatthu

6. The Story of the Two Friends, the Heedless and the Heedful

Appamatto [M 1.0166] pamattesūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve sahāyake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse, beginning with the words 'The heedful among the heedless,' concerning two monks who were friends.

Te kira satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā āraññakavihāraṃ pavisiṃsu. Tesu eko kira kālasseva dārūni āharitvā aṅgārakapallaṃ sajjetvā daharasāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamayāmaṃ visibbamāno nisīdati. Eko appamatto samaṇadhammaṃ karonto itaraṃ ovadati, “āvuso, mā evaṃ kari, pamattassa hi cattāro apāyā sakagharasadisā. Buddhā nāma sāṭheyyena ārādhetuṃ na sakkā”ti so tassovādaṃ na suṇāti. Itaro “nāyaṃ vacanakkhamo”ti taṃ avatvā appamattova samaṇadhammamakāsi. Alasattheropi [P 1.0261] paṭhamayāme visibbetvā itarassa caṅkamitvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhakāle pavisitvā, “mahākusīta, tvaṃ nipajjitvā sayanatthāya araññaṃ paviṭṭhosi, kiṃ buddhānaṃ santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā uṭṭhāya samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nipajjitvā supati. Itaropi majjhimayāme vissamitvā pacchimayāme paccuṭṭhāya samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. So evaṃ appamatto viharanto na cirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Itaro pamādeneva kālaṃ vītināmesi. Te vuṭṭhavassā satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā, “kacci, bhikkhave, appamattā samaṇadhammaṃ karittha, kacci vo pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta”nti pucchi. Paṭhamaṃ pamatto bhikkhu āha – “kuto, bhante, etassa appamādo, gatakālato paṭṭhāya nipajjitvā niddāyanto kālaṃ vītināmesī”ti. “Tvaṃ pana bhikkhū”ti. “Ahaṃ, bhante, kālasseva dārūni āharitvā aṅgārakapallaṃ sajjetvā paṭhamayāme visibbento nisīditvā aniddāyantova kālaṃ vītināmesi”nti. Atha naṃ satthā “tvaṃ pamatto kālaṃ vītināmetvā ‘appamattomhī’ti vadasi, appamattaṃ pana pamattaṃ karosī”ti āha. Puna pamāde dose, appamāde ānisaṃse pakāsetuṃ, “tvaṃ mama puttassa [P 1.0262] santike javacchinno dubbalasso viya, esa pana tava santike sīghajavasso viyā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, they entered a forest monastery. Among them, one, having brought firewood early in the morning and prepared a brazier, would sit warming himself by the fire during the first watch, chatting with the young novices. The other, being heedful and practicing the ascetic's duties, admonished him, saying: 'Friend, do not act thus. For the heedless, the four woeful states are like their own home. The Buddhas, it should be known, cannot be pleased by deceit.' But he did not listen to his advice. The other, thinking, 'This one is not amenable to advice,' said nothing more to him and heedfully practiced the ascetic's duties. The lazy elder, after warming himself by the fire in the first watch, went in when the other, having finished his walking meditation, had entered his cell, and said: 'You great sluggard! Have you entered the forest just to lie down and sleep? Having taken a meditation subject from the Buddhas, is it not proper to rise and practice the ascetic's duties?' Having said this, he entered his own dwelling place, lay down, and slept. The other, however, having rested in the middle watch, would rise in the last watch and practice the ascetic's duties. Dwelling thus heedfully, he before long attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The other passed his time in heedlessness. When the rains retreat was over, they went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Teacher, having exchanged friendly greetings with them, asked: 'Bhikkhus, I trust you have practiced the ascetic's duties heedfully? I trust your task of the homeless life has reached its culmination?' The one who had been heedless spoke: 'Venerable Sir, how could there be heedfulness for this one? From the time he left, he has passed the time lying down and dozing.' 'And what about you, bhikkhu?' 'Venerable Sir, I, having brought firewood early in the morning and prepared a brazier, sat warming myself by the fire during the first watch and passed the time without sleeping.' Then the Teacher said to him: 'You, being heedless, have passed the time, yet you say, "I am heedful." You, however, make the heedful one out to be heedless.' Then, to make clear the fault in heedlessness and the benefit in heedfulness, he said: 'You, in the presence of my son, are like a weak horse whose speed is spent; but this one, in your presence, is like a swift horse.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

29.

29.

“Appamatto [V 1.0149][M 1.0167] pamattesu, suttesu bahujāgaro;

Abalassaṃva sīghasso, hitvā yāti sumedhaso”ti.

Heedful among the heedless, wide awake among those who sleep, the wise one advances, leaving them behind, like a swift horse leaving behind a weak one.

Tattha appamattoti sativepullappattatāya appamādasampanne khīṇāsavo. Pamattesūti sativosagge ṭhitesu sattesu. Suttesūti satijāgariyābhāvena sabbiriyāpathesu niddāyantesu. Bahujāgaroti mahante sativepulle jāgariye ṭhito. Abalassaṃvāti kuṇṭhapādaṃ chinnajavaṃ dubbalassaṃ sīghajavo sindhavājānīyo viya. Sumedhasoti uttamapañño. Tathārūpaṃ puggalaṃ āgamenapi adhigamenapi hitvā yāti. Mandapaññasmiñhi ekaṃ suttaṃ gahetuṃ vāyamanteyeva sumedhaso ekaṃ vaggaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ tāva āgamena hitvā yāti. Mandapaññe pana rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni kātuṃ vāyamanteyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā sajjhāyanteyeva ca sumedhaso pubbabhāgepi parena kataṃ rattiṭṭhānaṃ vā divāṭṭhānaṃ vā pavisitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasanto sabbakilese khepetvā neva lokuttaradhamme hatthagate [P 1.0263] karoti, evaṃ adhigamenapi hitvā yāti. Vaṭṭe pana naṃ hitvā chaḍḍetvā vaṭṭato nissaranto yātiyevāti.

Herein, 'heedful' refers to one whose cankers are destroyed, who is endowed with heedfulness by having attained an abundance of mindfulness. 'Among the heedless' means among beings who are established in the lapse of mindfulness. 'Among those who sleep' means among those who are sleeping in all postures due to the absence of the wakefulness of mindfulness. 'Wide awake' means one who is established in great wakefulness that has reached an abundance of mindfulness. 'Like a swift horse a weak one' means like a swift thoroughbred Sindh horse surpassing a weak horse with lame feet and spent speed. 'The wise' means a person of supreme wisdom. He surpasses and leaves behind such a person both in learning and in attainment. Indeed, while a person of dull wisdom is still striving to learn one discourse, the wise person grasps a whole chapter; thus, firstly, he surpasses and leaves him behind by way of learning. Furthermore, while the person of dull wisdom is still striving to prepare places for day and night solitude, and is just learning and reciting the meditation subject, the wise person, even beforehand entering a place for day or night solitude already prepared by another, and contemplating the meditation subject, eradicates all defilements and brings the nine supramundane states into his grasp. Thus he surpasses and leaves him behind by way of attainment. As for the round of existence, having abandoned and discarded him, he escapes from the round of existence and indeed goes forth to Nibbāna.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the verse, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Pamattāpamattadvesahāyakavatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of the Two Companions, the Heedless and the Heedful, the Sixth.

7. Maghavatthu

7. The Story of Magha

Appamādena maghavāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā vesāliyaṃ upanissāya kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharanto sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling near Vesālī in the Hall with the Peaked Roof, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Appamādena maghavā,' with reference to Sakka, the king of the devas.

Vesāliyañhi mahāli nāma licchavī vasati, so tathāgatassa sakkapañhasuttantadesanaṃ (dī. ni. 2.344 ādayo) sutvā “sammāsambuddho sakkasampattiṃ mahatiṃ katvā kathesi, ‘disvā nu kho kathesi, udāhu adisvā. Jānāti nu kho sakkaṃ, udāhu no’ti pucchissāmi na”nti cintesi. Atha kho, mahāli, licchavī yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, ekamantaṃ nisinno kho, mahāli, licchavī bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “diṭṭho [M 1.0168] kho, bhante, bhagavatā sakko devānamindo”ti? “Diṭṭho kho me[P 1.0264], mahāli, sakko devānamindo”ti. “So hi nuna, bhante, sakkapatirūpako bhavissati[V 1.0150]. Duddaso hi, bhante, sakko devānamindo”ti. “Sakkañca khvāhaṃ, mahāli, pajānāmi sakkakaraṇe ca dhamme, yesaṃ dhammānaṃ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṃ ajjhagā, tañca pajānāmi”.
