For in Vesālī, it is said, there lived a Licchavi named Mahāli. Having heard the Tathāgata's discourse on the Sakkapañha Sutta, he thought: 'The Fully Enlightened One spoke, making much of the fortune of Sakka. Did he speak having seen him, or without having seen him? Does he know Sakka, or not? I shall ask him.' Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One, paid homage, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, has the Blessed One seen Sakka, the lord of the devas?' 'I have indeed seen Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas.' 'Then, venerable sir, that must surely have been a likeness of Sakka. For Sakka, the lord of the devas, is hard to see.' 'I, Mahāli, know Sakka, and I know the qualities that make one Sakka. And I know those qualities by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of being Sakka.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno magho nāma māṇavo ahosi, tasmā “maghavā”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, was a young man named Magha. Therefore, he is called 'Maghavā.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno pure dānaṃ adāsi, tasmā “purindado”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave gifts previously. Therefore, he is called 'Purindada.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsi, tasmā “sakko”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave gifts respectfully. Therefore, he is called 'Sakka.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno āvasathaṃ adāsi, tasmā “vāsavo”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave a lodging place. Therefore, he is called 'Vāsava.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo sahassampi atthaṃ muhuttena cinteti, tasmā “sahassakkho”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, considers a thousand matters in a moment. Therefore, he is called 'Sahassakkha.'

Sakkassa, mahāli, devānamindassa sujā nāma asurakaññā, pajāpati, tasmā “sujampatī”ti vuccati.

Mahāli, the consort of Sakka, the lord of the devas, is an Asura maiden named Sujā. Therefore, he is called 'Sujampati.'

Sakko, mahāli, devānamindo devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ issariyādhipaccaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti, tasmā “devānamindo”ti vuccati.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, exercises rulership and sovereignty over the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Therefore, he is called 'the Lord of the Devas.'

Sakkassa, mahāli, devānamindassa pubbe manussabhūtassa satta vatapadāni samattāni samādinnāni ahesuṃ, yesaṃ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṃ [P 1.0265] ajjhagā. Katamāni satta vatapadāni? Yāvajīvaṃ mātāpettibharo assaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī assaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ saṇhavāco assaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ apisuṇavāco assaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvaseyyaṃ, muttacāgo payatapāṇi vosaggarato yācayogo dānasaṃvibhāgarato assaṃ. Yāvajīvaṃ [V 1.0151] saccavāco assaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ akkodhano assaṃ, “sacepi me kodho uppajjeyya, khippameva na paṭivineyya”nti. Sakkassa, mahāli, devānamindassa pubbe manussabhūtassa imāni [M 1.0169] satta vatapadāni samattāni samādinnāni ahesuṃ, yesaṃ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṃ ajjhagāti.

Mahāli, when Sakka, the lord of the devas, was formerly a human being, he undertook and completed seven vows, by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of being Sakka. What were the seven vows? 'For as long as I live, may I support my parents. For as long as I live, may I respect the elders in my clan. For as long as I live, may I be of gentle speech. For as long as I live, may I be of non-slanderous speech. For as long as I live, may I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, responsive to requests, and delighting in giving and sharing. For as long as I live, may I be of truthful speech. For as long as I live, may I be without anger; and if anger should arise in me, may I quickly dispel it.' Mahāli, when Sakka, the lord of the devas, was formerly a human being, these seven vows were undertaken and completed by him, by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of being Sakka.

“Mātāpettibharaṃ jantuṃ, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyinaṃ;

Saṇhaṃ sakhilasambhāsaṃ, pesuṇeyyappahāyinaṃ.

A person who supports his mother and father, who respects the elders in his clan, who is gentle and courteous in speech, and who has abandoned slander;

“Maccheravinaye yuttaṃ, saccaṃ kodhābhibhuṃ naraṃ;

Taṃ ve devā tāvatiṃsā, āhu sappuriso itī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.257) –

one who is engaged in dispelling stinginess, is truthful, and has overcome anger—that person, the Tāvatiṃsa devas indeed call a virtuous person.

Idaṃ, mahāli, sakkena maghamāṇavakāle katakammanti vatvā puna tena “kathaṃ, bhante, maghamāṇavo paṭipajjī”ti? Tassa paṭipattiṃ vitthārato sotukāmena puṭṭho “tena hi, mahāli, suṇāhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari –

Having said, 'This, Mahāli, is the deed done by Sakka when he was the young man Magha,' and being asked again by Mahāli, who wished to hear of his conduct in detail, 'Venerable sir, how did the young man Magha conduct himself?' the Blessed One said, 'Well then, Mahāli, listen,' and recounted a story from the past.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe macalagāme magho nāma māṇavo [P 1.0266] gāmakammakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā attano ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ pādantena paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā ramaṇīyaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi. Aparo taṃ bāhunā paharitvā tato apanetvā sayaṃ tattha aṭṭhāsi. So tassa akujjhitvāva aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ katvā ṭhito. Tatopi naṃ añño āgantvā bāhunā paharitvā apanetvā sayaṃ aṭṭhāsi. So tassapi akujjhitvāva aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ katvā ṭhito, iti taṃ gehato nikkhantā nikkhantā purisā bāhunā paharitvā ṭhitaṭhitaṭṭhānato apanesuṃ. So “sabbepete maṃ nissāya sukhitā jātā, iminā kammena mayhaṃ sukhadāyakena puññakammena bhavitabba”nti cintetvā, punadivase kudālaṃ ādāya khalamaṇḍalamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ akāsi. Sabbe gantvā tattheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ sītasamaye aggiṃ katvā adāsi, gimhakāle udakaṃ. Tato “ramaṇīyaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāma sabbesaṃ piyaṃ, kassaci appiyaṃ nāma natthi, ito paṭṭhāya mayā maggaṃ samaṃ karontena vicarituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā, pātova nikkhamitvā, maggaṃ samaṃ karonto chinditvā, haritabbayuttakā rukkhasākhā haranto vicarati. Atha naṃ aparo disvā āha – “samma, kiṃ karosī”ti? “Mayhaṃ saggagāminaṃ maggaṃ karomi, sammā”ti. “Tena hi ahampi te sahāyo homī”ti. “Hohi, samma, saggo nāma bahūnampi manāpo sukhabahulo”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya dve janā [V 1.0152] ahesuṃ. Te disvā [P 1.0267] tatheva pucchitvā ca sutvā ca aparopi [M 1.0170] tesaṃ sahāyo jāto, evaṃ aparopi aparopīti sabbepi tettiṃsa janā jātā. Te sabbepi kudālādihatthā maggaṃ samaṃ karontā ekayojanadviyojanamattaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti.

In the past, in the country of Magadha, in the village of Macala, a young man named Magha went to the place where the villagers worked. Having cleared the dust from his standing spot with the tip of his foot, he made it pleasant and stood there. Another man struck him with his arm, removed him from that place, and stood there himself. Without getting angry at him, he made another spot pleasant and stood there. From that spot also, another man came, struck him with his arm, removed him, and stood there himself. Again, without getting angry at him, he made another spot pleasant and stood there. In this way, the men who came out from their houses, one after another, struck him with their arms and removed him from each and every place he stood. He thought, “All these people have become happy because of me. This deed of mine must be a meritorious deed that brings happiness.” The next day, taking a hoe, he made a place the size of a threshing floor pleasant. Everyone went and stood right there. Then, during the cold season, he made a fire and gave it to them. After that, he thought, “A pleasant place is dear to all; it is disliked by no one. From now on, it is proper for me to go about leveling the road.” Having set out early in the morning, he went about leveling the road, cutting and carrying away tree branches that should be removed. Then another man saw him and asked, “Friend, what are you doing?” “I am making my road that leads to heaven, friend.” “In that case, I too shall be your companion.” “Be so, friend. Heaven is delightful to many and abounds in happiness.” From then on, there were two people. Seeing them, and having asked and heard in the same way, another also became their companion. Thus, another and yet another, until all thirty-three people had come to be. All of them, with hoes and other tools in hand, went about leveling the road for a distance of about one or two yojanas.

Te disvā gāmabhojako cintesi – “ime manussā ayoge yuttā, sace ime araññato macchamaṃsādīni vā āhareyyuṃ. Suraṃ vā katvā piveyyuṃ, aññaṃ vā tādisaṃ kammaṃ kareyyuṃ, ahampi kiñci kiñci labheyya”nti. Atha ne pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “kiṃ karontā vicarathā”ti? “Saggamaggaṃ, sāmī”ti. “Gharāvāsaṃ vasantehi nāma evaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, araññato macchamaṃsādīni āharituṃ, suraṃ katvā pātuṃ, nānappakāre ca kammante kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Te tassa vacanaṃ paṭikkhipiṃsu, evaṃ punappunaṃ vuccamānāpi paṭikkhipiṃsuyeva. So kujjhitvā “nāsessāmi ne”ti rañño santikaṃ gantvā, “core te, deva, vaggabandhanena vicarante passāmī”ti vatvā, “gaccha, te gahetvā ānehī”ti vutte tathā katvā sabbe te bandhitvā ānetvā rañño dassesi. Rājā avīmaṃsitvāva “hatthinā maddāpethā”ti āṇāpesi. Magho sesānaṃ ovādamadāsi – “sammā, ṭhapetvā mettaṃ añño amhākaṃ avassayo natthi, tumhe katthaci kopaṃ akatvā raññe ca gāmabhojake ca maddanahatthimhi ca attani ca mettacittena samacittāva hothā”ti. Te tathā kariṃsu. Atha nesaṃ mettānubhāvena hatthī uppasaṅkamitumpi na visahi. Rājā tamatthaṃ sutvā bahū [P 1.0268] manusse disvā maddituṃ na visahissati? “Gacchatha, ne kilañjena paṭicchādetvā maddāpethā”ti āha. Te kilañjena paṭicchādetvā maddituṃ pesiyamānopi hatthī dūratova paṭikkami.

Seeing them, the village headman thought, “These men are engaged in an improper undertaking. If they were to bring fish, meat, and so on from the forest, or make and drink liquor, or do other such work, I too might get something.” Then, having summoned them, he asked, “What are you doing, going about?” “We are making the path to heaven, sir.” “For those living the household life, it is not proper to do thus. It is proper to bring fish, meat, and so on from the forest, to make and drink liquor, and to do various kinds of work.” They rejected his words. Even when told again and again, they just rejected them. He became angry and, thinking, “I will destroy them,” went to the king and said, “Your Majesty, I see thieves wandering about, having formed a gang.” When told, “Go, seize them and bring them here,” he did so, and having bound them all and brought them, he presented them to the king. The king, without investigating, commanded, “Have them crushed by an elephant.” Magha gave this advice to the others: “Friends, besides loving-kindness, there is no other refuge for us. Without getting angry at anyone, be of equal mind with a mind of loving-kindness toward the king, the village headman, the crushing elephant, and yourselves.” They did so. Then, by the power of their loving-kindness, the elephant did not even dare to approach. The king, hearing of this, thought, “Will it not dare to crush them, seeing so many people?” He said, “Go, cover them with a mat and have them crushed.” Even when he was sent to crush them after they were covered with a mat, the elephant retreated from afar.

Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “kāraṇenettha bhavitabba”nti te pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “tātā, maṃ nissāya tumhe kiṃ na labhathā”ti? “Kiṃ nāmetaṃ, devā”ti? “Tumhe kira vaggabandhanena corā hutvā araññe vicarathā”ti? “Ko evamāha, devā”ti? “Gāmabhojako, tātā”ti. “Na mayaṃ, deva, corā, mayaṃ pana attano saggamaggaṃ sodhentā idañcidañca karoma, gāmabhojako amhe akusalakiriyāya niyojetvā attano vacanaṃ akaronte nāsetukāmo kujjhitvā evamāhā”ti. Atha rājā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā somanassappatto hutvā, “tātā, ayaṃ tiracchāno tumhākaṃ [M 1.0171] guṇe jānāti, ahaṃ manussabhūto jānituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, khamatha me”ti. Evañca pana vatvā saputtadāraṃ gāmabhojakaṃ tesaṃ dāsaṃ, hatthiṃ ārohaniyaṃ, tañca gāmaṃ yathāsukhaṃ paribhogaṃ katvā adāsi. Te “idheva no katapuññassānisaṃso diṭṭho”ti bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānasā hutvā taṃ hatthiṃ vārena vārena abhiruyha gacchantā mantayiṃsu [V 1.0153] “idāni amhehi [P 1.0269] atirekataraṃ puññaṃ kātabbaṃ, kiṃ karoma? Catumahāpathe thāvaraṃ katvā mahājanassa vissamanasālaṃ karissāmā”ti. Te vaḍḍhakiṃ pakkosāpetvā sālaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. Mātugāmesu pana vigatacchandatāya tassā sālāya mātugāmānaṃ pattiṃ nādaṃsu.

The king, hearing this account, thought, “There must be a reason for this.” Having summoned them, he asked, “Dears, what do you not receive from me?” “What is this, Your Majesty?” “It is said that you wander in the forest as thieves, having formed a gang.” “Who said so, Your Majesty?” “The village headman, dears.” “We are not thieves, Your Majesty. We, however, are clearing our own path to heaven and doing this and that. The village headman, having urged us toward unwholesome actions, became angry when we did not follow his word and, wishing to destroy us, spoke thus.” Then the king, hearing their account, became pleased and said, “Dears, this animal knows your virtues, while I, though a human being, was not able to know them. Forgive me.” And having spoken thus, he gave them the village headman with his wife and children as their slaves, the elephant for riding, and that village for their enjoyment as they pleased. They thought, “The result of the merit we have done is seen right here in this very life,” and with even greater joy and pleased minds, mounting the elephant in turns as they went, they consulted, “Now, even more merit should be done by us. What shall we do? We shall build a permanent rest hall for the populace at the great crossroads.” They summoned a carpenter and had the hall established. But, due to their lack of desire concerning women, they did not give a share of the merit from that hall to women.

Maghassa pana gehe nandā, cittā, sudhammā, sujāti catasso itthiyo honti. Tāsu sudhammā vaḍḍhakinā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā, “bhātika, imissā sālāya maṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ karohī”ti vatvā lañjaṃ adāsi. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā paṭhamameva kaṇṇikatthāya rukkhaṃ sukkhāpetvā tacchetvā vijjhitvā kaṇṇikaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā, “sudhammā nāma ayaṃ sālā”ti akkharāni chinditvā vatthena paliveṭhetvā ṭhapesi. Atha ne vaḍḍhakī sālaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā kaṇṇikāropanadivase “aho, ayyā, ekaṃ karaṇīyaṃ na sarimhā”ti āha. “Kiṃ nāma, bho”ti? “Kaṇṇika”nti. “Hotu taṃ āharissāmā”ti. “Idāni chinnarukkhena kātuṃ na sakkā, pubbeyeva taṃ chinditvā tacchetvā vijjhitvā ṭhapitakaṇṇikā laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Sace kassaci gehe niṭṭhāpetvā ṭhapitā vikkāyikakaṇṇikā [P 1.0270] atthi, sā pariyesitabbā”ti. Te pariyesantā sudhammāya gehe disvā sahassaṃ datvāpi mūlena na labhiṃsu. “Sace maṃ sālāya pattiṃ karotha, dassāmī”ti vutte pana “mayaṃ mātugāmānaṃ pattiṃ na dammā”ti āhaṃsu.

Now, in the house of the young man Magha, there were four wives: Nandā, Cittā, Sudhammā, and Sujātā. Among them, Sudhammā, having conspired with the carpenter, said, 'Brother, make me the chief in this hall,' and gave him a bribe. He, accepting with 'Very well,' first had a tree dried for the finial, and having shaped and bored it, completed the finial. Then, having carved the letters, 'This hall is named Sudhammā,' he wrapped it in cloth and set it aside. Then, the carpenter, having completed the hall, on the day for raising the finial, said to them, 'Sirs, we did not remember one task.' 'What is that, sir?' 'The finial.' 'Let it be, we will bring it.' 'Now it is not possible to make it with a recently cut tree. It is proper to obtain a finial that was previously cut, shaped, bored, and set aside.' 'What is to be done now?' 'If there is a finial for sale in anyone's house, which has been completed and set aside, it should be sought out.' Searching, they saw one in Sudhammā's house, but even offering a thousand as the price, they could not obtain it. But when she said, 'If you give me a share in the hall, I will give it,' they replied, 'We do not give a share to women.'

Atha ne vaḍḍhakī āha – “ayyā, tumhe kiṃ kathetha, ṭhapetvā brahmalokaṃ aññaṃ mātugāmarahitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, gaṇhatha kaṇṇikaṃ. Evaṃ sante amhākaṃ kammaṃ niṭṭhaṃ gamissatī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti kaṇṇikaṃ gahetvā sālaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā tidhā vibhajiṃsu. Ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse issarānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kariṃsu, ekasmiṃ duggatānaṃ, ekasmiṃ gilānānaṃ. Tettiṃsa janā tettiṃsa phalakāni paññapetvā hatthissa saññaṃ adaṃsu – “āgantuko āgantvā yassa atthataphalake nisīdati, taṃ gahetvā phalakasāmikasseva [M 1.0172] gehe patiṭṭhapehi, tassa pādaparikammapiṭṭhiparikammapānīyakhādanīyabhojanīyasayanāni sabbāni phalakasāmikasseva bhāro bhavissatī”ti. Hatthī āgatāgataṃ gahetvā phalakasāmikasseva gharaṃ neti. So tassa taṃ divasaṃ kattabbaṃ karoti. Magho sālāya avidūre koviḷārarukkhaṃ ropetvā tassa mūle pāsāṇaphalakaṃ atthari. Sālaṃ paviṭṭhapaviṭṭhā janā kaṇṇikaṃ oloketvā akkharāni vācetvā, “sudhammā nāmesā sālā”ti vadanti. Tettiṃsajanānaṃ nāmaṃ na paññāyati. Nandā cintesi – “ime sālaṃ karontā amhe apattikā kariṃsu, sudhammā [P 1.0271] pana attano byattatāya kaṇṇikaṃ katvā pattikā jātā, mayāpi kiñci kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti? Athassā etadahosi [V 1.0154] – “sālaṃ āgatāgatānaṃ pānīyañceva nhānodakañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpessāmī”ti. Sā pokkharaṇiṃ kāresi. Cittā cintesi – “sudhammāya kaṇṇikā dinnā, nandāya pokkharaṇī kāritā, mayāpi kiñci kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti? Athassā etadahosi – “sālaṃ āgatāgatehi pānīyaṃ pivitvā nhatvā gamanakālepi mālaṃ pilandhitvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati, pupphārāmaṃ kārāpessāmī”ti. Sā ramaṇīyaṃ pupphārāmaṃ kāresi. Yebhuyyena tasmiṃ ārāme “asuko nāma pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkho natthī”ti nāhosi.

Then the carpenter said to them, 'Sirs, what are you saying? Except for the Brahma world, there is no place devoid of women. Take the finial. This being so, our work will be completed.' They, saying 'Very well,' took the finial, completed the hall, and divided it into three parts. In one section, they made a place for rulers to stay; in another, a place for the poor; and in another, a place for the sick. The thirty-three men, having prepared thirty-three planks, gave a sign to the elephant: 'When a traveler arrives and sits on a plank laid out by someone, take that person and establish them in the house of the plank's owner. All the services for that traveler—massaging the feet, rubbing the back, drinkables, edibles, and bedding—will be the burden of the plank's owner.' The elephant would take each person who arrived and lead them to the house of the plank's owner. That owner would perform the necessary duties for that person for that day. Magha planted a coral tree not far from the hall and laid out a stone slab at its base. People who entered the hall would look up at the finial, read the letters, and say, 'This hall is named Sudhammā.' The names of the thirty-three men were not apparent. Nandā thought: 'These men, while building the hall, made us without a share. Sudhammā, however, through her own cleverness, has obtained a share. It is fitting that I too should do something. What, I wonder, shall I do?' Then this thought occurred to her: 'It is fitting for those who come to the hall to get drinking water and bathing water. I will have a lotus pond dug.' She had a lotus pond made. Cittā thought: 'The finial was given by Sudhammā; a lotus pond was caused to be made by Nandā. It is fitting that I too should do something. What, I wonder, shall I do?' Then this thought occurred to her: 'It is fitting that those who come to the hall, after drinking water and bathing, should be able to wear a garland when they leave. I will have a flower park made.' She had a delightful flower park made. For the most part, in that park, there was no flowering or fruit-bearing tree of which it could be said, 'This one is not here.'

Sujā pana “ahaṃ maghassa mātuladhītā ceva pādaparicārikā ca, etena kataṃ kammaṃ mayhameva, mayā kataṃ etassevā”ti cintetvā, kiñci akatvā attabhāvameva maṇḍayamānā kālaṃ vītināmesi. Maghopi mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ kule jeṭṭhāpacāyanakammaṃ saccavācaṃ apharusavācaṃ api, suṇavācaṃ maccheravinayaṃ akkodhananti imāni satta vatapadāni pūretvā –

Sujātā, however, thinking, 'I am both Magha's maternal uncle's daughter and his attendant at his feet. The deed done by him is mine, and the deed done by me is his,' did nothing, and passed her time just adorning her own person. Magha, too, lived fulfilling these seven vows: attending to his mother and father, respecting the elders in his clan, truthful speech, gentle speech, absence of slanderous speech, the disciplining of stinginess, and freedom from anger—

“Mātāpettibharaṃ [P 1.0272] jantuṃ, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyinaṃ;

Saṇhaṃ sakhilasambhāsaṃ, pesuṇeyyappahāyinaṃ.

A person who supports his mother and father, who honors the elders in the clan, whose speech is gentle and friendly, who has abandoned slanderous talk,

“Maccheravinaye yuttaṃ, saccaṃ kodhābhibhuṃ naraṃ;

Taṃ ve devā tāvatiṃsā, āhu ‘sappuriso’itī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.257) –

The man who is devoted to the subduing of stinginess, who is truthful, and who has overcome anger—him the Tāvatiṃsa gods indeed call a 'virtuous person.'

Evaṃ pasaṃsiyabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā jīvitapariyosāne tāvatiṃsabhavane sakko devarājā hutvā nibbatti, tepissa sahāyakā tattheva [M 1.0173] nibbattiṃsu, vaḍḍhakī vissakammadevaputto hutvā nibbatti. Tadā tāvatiṃsabhavane asurā vasanti. Te “abhinavā devaputtā nibbattā”ti dibbapānaṃ sajjayiṃsu. Sakko attano parisāya kassaci apivanatthāya saññamadāsi. Asurā dibbapānaṃ pivitvā majjiṃsu. Sakko “kiṃ me imehi sādhāraṇena rajjenā”ti attano parisāya saññaṃ datvā te pādesu gāhāpetvā mahāsamudde khipāpesi. Te avaṃsirā samudde patiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ puññānubhāvena sineruno heṭṭhimatale asuravimānaṃ nāma nibbatti, cittapāṭali nāma nibbatti.

Having thus attained a praiseworthy state, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, having become Sakka, king of the devas. His thirty-three companions were also reborn right there. The carpenter was reborn, having become the deva-son Vissakamma. At that time, the asuras were dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Thinking, 'New deva-sons have been born,' they prepared a divine beverage. Sakka gave a sign for no one in his own retinue to drink. The asuras drank the divine beverage and became intoxicated. Sakka, thinking, 'What use to me is a kingdom shared with these beings?', gave a sign to his retinue and had the asuras seized by the feet and thrown into the great ocean. They fell head-downwards into the ocean. Then, through the power of their merit, at the base of Mount Sineru, a realm named the Asura Abode arose, and a trumpet-flower tree named Cittapāṭali arose.

Devāsurasaṅgāme pana asuresu parājitesu dasayojanasahassaṃ tāvatiṃsadevanagaraṃ nāma nibbatti. Tassa pana nagarassa pācīnapacchimadvārānaṃ antarā dasayojanasahassaṃ hoti, tathā dakkhiṇuttaradvārānaṃ. Taṃ kho pana nagaraṃ dvārasahassayuttaṃ ahosi ārāmapokkharaṇipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ. Tassa [V 1.0155] majjhe sālāya [P 1.0273] nissandena tiyojanasatubbedhehi dhajehi paṭimaṇḍito sattaratanamayo sattayojanasatubbedho vejayanto nāma pāsādo uggañchi. Suvaṇṇayaṭṭhīsu maṇidhajā ahesuṃ, maṇiyaṭṭhīsu suvaṇṇadhajā; pavāḷayaṭṭhīsu muttadhajā, muttayaṭṭhīsu pavāḷadhajā; sattaratanamayāsu yaṭṭhīsu sattaratanadhajā, majjhe ṭhito dhajo tiyojanasatubbedho ahosi. Iti sālāya nissandena yojanasahassubbedho pāsādo sattaratanamayova hutvā nibbatti, koviḷārarukkhassa nissandena samantā tiyojanasataparimaṇḍalo pāricchattako nibbatti, pāsāṇaphalakassa nissandena pāricchattakamūle dīghato saṭṭhiyojanā puthulato paṇṇāsayojanā bahalato pañcadasayojanā jayasumanarattakambalavaṇṇā paṇḍukambalasilā nibbatti. Tattha nisinnakāle upaḍḍhakāyo pavisati, uṭṭhitakāle ūnaṃ paripūrati.

In the battle between the devas and asuras, when the asuras were defeated, the celestial city named Tāvatiṃsa, ten thousand yojanas in extent, came into being. The distance between the eastern and western gates of that city is ten thousand yojanas, and likewise between the southern and northern gates. That city was endowed with a thousand gates and adorned with parks and ponds. In its center, as a result of the rest-house, the palace named Vejayanta, seven hundred yojanas high and made of the seven precious gems, arose, adorned with banners three hundred yojanas high. On golden flagstaffs were jeweled banners, and on jeweled flagstaffs were golden banners; on coral flagstaffs were pearl banners, and on pearl flagstaffs were coral banners; on flagstaffs made of the seven precious gems were banners of the seven precious gems. The banner standing in the middle was three hundred yojanas high. Thus, as a result of the rest-house, the palace, one thousand yojanas high, arose, made entirely of the seven precious gems. As a result of the koviḷāra tree, the Pāricchattaka tree, three hundred yojanas in circumference, arose. As a result of the stone slab, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat arose, sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifteen yojanas in thickness, with a color like a red blanket of jayasumana flowers. When one sits upon it, half of one's body sinks in, and when one stands up, the indentation fills up again.

Hatthī pana erāvaṇo nāma devaputto hutvā nibbatti. Devalokasmiñhi tiracchānagatā na honti. Tasmā so uyyānakīḷāya nikkhamanakāle attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko erāvaṇo nāma hatthī ahosi. So tettiṃsajanānaṃ atthāya tettiṃsa kumbhe māpesi [M 1.0174] āvaṭṭena tigāvutaaḍḍhayojanappamāṇe, sabbesaṃ majjhe sakkassa atthāya sudassanaṃ nāma tiṃsayojanikaṃ kumbhaṃ māpesi. Tassa upari dvādasayojaniko ratanamaṇḍapo [P 1.0274] hoti. Tattha antarantarā sattaratanamayā yojanubbedhā dhajā uṭṭhahanti. Pariyante kiṅkiṇikajālaṃ olambati. Yassa mandavāteritassa pañcaṅgikatūriyasaddasaṃmisso dibbagītasaddo viya ravo niccharati. Maṇḍapamajjhe sakkassatthāya yojaniko maṇipallaṅko paññatto hoti, tattha sakko nisīdi. Tettiṃsa devaputtā attano kumbhe ratanapallaṅke nisīdiṃsu. Tettiṃsāya kumbhānaṃ ekekasmiṃ kumbhe satta satta dante māpesi. Tesu ekeko paṇṇāsayojanāyāmo, ekekasmiñcettha dante satta satta pokkharaṇiyo honti, ekekāya pokkharaṇiyā satta satta paduminīgacchāni, ekekasmiṃ gacche satta satta pupphāni honti, ekekasmiṃ pupphe satta satta pattāni, ekekasmiṃ patte satta satta devadhītaro naccanti. Evaṃ samantā paṇṇāsayojanaṭhānesu hatthidantesuyeva naṭasamajjā honti. Evaṃ mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavanto sakko devarājā vicarati.

The elephant, named Erāvaṇa, came into being as a devaputta. Indeed, in the world of the devas, there are no animals. Therefore, when going out for sport in the park, he would abandon his own form and become the elephant named Erāvaṇa, one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. For the sake of the thirty-three devas, he created thirty-three heads all around, each measuring three gāvutas and half a yojana. In the center of them all, for Sakka's sake, he created a head named Sudassana, thirty yojanas in size. Above it is a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas high. There, at intervals, banners made of the seven precious gems, each a yojana high, arise. Along the edges hangs a net of tinkling bells. When stirred by a gentle breeze, a sound issues forth from it, like a divine song mixed with the sound of the five-part celestial orchestra. In the middle of the pavilion, a jeweled throne one yojana in size is prepared for Sakka, and there Sakka sits. On each of the thirty-three heads, he created seven tusks. Each of these tusks is fifty yojanas long. On each tusk, there are seven ponds. In each pond, there are seven thickets of lotus plants. In each thicket, there are seven flowers. In each flower, there are seven petals. On each petal, seven devadhītās dance. Thus, on the elephant's tusks themselves, all around over a space of fifty yojanas, there are gatherings of dancers. Experiencing such great glory, Sakka, king of the devas, goes about.

Sudhammāpi kālaṃ katvā gantvā tattheva nibbatti. Tassā sudhammā nāma nava yojanasatikā devasabhā nibbatti. Tato ramaṇīyataraṃ kira aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāma natthi[P 1.0275], māsassa aṭṭha divase dhammassavanaṃ tattheva hoti. Yāvajjatanā aññataraṃ ramaṇīyaṃ ṭhānaṃ disvā, “sudhammā devasabhā viyā”ti vadanti. Nandāpi kālaṃ katvā gantvā tattheva nibbatti, tassā pañcayojanasatikā nandā nāma pokkharaṇī nibbatti. Cittāpi kālaṃ katvā gantvā tattheva nibbatti[V 1.0156], tassāpi pañcayojanasatikaṃ cittalatāvanaṃ nāma nibbatti, tattha uppannapubbanimitte devaputte netvā mohayamānā vicaranti. Sujā pana kālaṃ katvā ekissā girikandarāya ekā bakasakuṇikā hutvā nibbatti. Sakko attano paricārikā olokento “sudhammā idheva nibbattā, tathā nandā ca cittā ca, sujā nu kho kuhiṃ nibbattā”ti cintento taṃ tattha nibbattaṃ disvā, “bālā kiñci puññaṃ akatvā idāni tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattā, idāni pana taṃ puññaṃ kāretvā idhānetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā aññātakavesena tassā [M 1.0175] santikaṃ gantvā, “kiṃ karontī idha vicarasī”ti pucchi. “Ko pana tvaṃ, sāmī”ti? “Ahaṃ te sāmiko magho”ti. “Kuhiṃ nibbattosi, sāmī”ti? “Ahaṃ tāvatiṃsadevaloke nibbatto”. “Tava sahāyikānaṃ pana nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānāsī”ti? “Na jānāmi, sāmī”ti. “Tāpi mameva santike nibbattā, passissasi tā sahāyikā”ti. “Kathāhaṃ tattha gamissāmī”ti? Sakko “ahaṃ taṃ tattha nessāmī”ti vatvā hatthatale ṭhapetvā devalokaṃ netvā nandāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre vissajjetvā itarāsaṃ tissannaṃ ārocesi – “tumhākaṃ sahāyikaṃ sujaṃ passissathā”ti. “Kuhiṃ sā, devā”ti[P 1.0276]? “Nandāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre ṭhitā”ti āha. Tā tissopi gantvā, “aho ayyāya evarūpaṃ attabhāvamaṇḍanassa phalaṃ, idānissā tuṇḍaṃ passatha, pāde passatha, jaṅghā passatha, sobhati vatassā attabhāvo”ti keḷiṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu.

Sudhammā too, after passing away, went and was reborn right there. For her, the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, nine hundred yojanas in size, came into being. It is said that there is no other place more delightful than it; on the eighth day of the month, the hearing of the Dhamma takes place right there. Even to this day, upon seeing any delightful place, people say, 'It is like the Sudhammā divine assembly hall.' Nandā too, after passing away, went and was reborn right there; for her, the pond named Nandā, five hundred yojanas in size, came into being. Cittā too, after passing away, went and was reborn right there; for her, the grove named Cittalatāvana, five hundred yojanas in size, came into being. There they go about, bringing devaputtas for whom the preliminary signs of death have arisen and causing them to rejoice. Sujā, however, after passing away, was reborn as a female heron in a certain mountain ravine. Sakka, looking for his consorts and thinking, 'Sudhammā was reborn right here, as were Nandā and Cittā. But where, I wonder, was Sujā reborn?', saw that she had been reborn there. He thought, 'The foolish one, having done no merit, has now been reborn in the animal realm. It is now fitting to have her perform a meritorious deed and bring her here.' Abandoning his own form, he went to her in the guise of a stranger and asked, 'What are you doing, wandering about here?' 'But who are you, lord?' 'I am your husband, Magha.' 'Where were you reborn, lord?' 'I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva world.' 'But do you know the place of rebirth of your companions?' 'I do not know, lord.' 'They too were reborn in my presence. Would you like to see your companions?' 'How shall I get there?' Sakka said, 'I will take you there,' and placing her on the palm of his hand, he brought her to the deva world. He released her on the bank of the Nandā pond and informed the other three, 'Go and see your companion, Sujā.' 'Where is she, Lord?' 'She is standing on the bank of the Nandā pond,' he said. Those three also went and, making sport of her, said, 'Oh, what a result of our lady's self-adornment! Now look at her beak, look at her feet, look at her shanks! How truly splendid her form is!' Then they departed.

Puna sakko tassā santikaṃ gantvā, “diṭṭhā te sahāyikā”ti vatvā “diṭṭhā maṃ uppaṇḍetvā gatā, tattheva maṃ nehī”ti vutte taṃ tattheva netvā udake vissajjetvā, “diṭṭhā te tāsaṃ sampattī”ti pucchi. “Diṭṭhā, devā”ti? “Tayāpi tattha nibbattanūpāyaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Kiṃ karomi, devā”ti? “Mayā dinnaṃ ovādaṃ rakkhissasī”ti. “Rakkhissāmi, devā”ti. Athassā pañca sīlāni datvā, “appamattā rakkhāhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya sayaṃmatamacchakeyeva pariyesitvā khādati. Sakko katipāhaccayena tassā vīmaṃsanatthāya gantvā, vālukāpiṭṭhe matamacchako viya hutvā uttāno nipajji. Sā taṃ disvā “matamacchako”ti saññāya aggahesi. Maccho gilanakāle naṅguṭṭhaṃ cālesi. Sā “sajīvamacchako”ti udake vissajjesi. So thokaṃ vītināmetvā puna tassā purato uttāno hutvā nipajji. Puna sā “matamacchako”ti saññāya gahetvā gilanakāle agganaṅguṭṭhaṃ cālesi. Taṃ disvā “sajīvamaccho”ti vissajjesi. Evaṃ tikkhattuṃ vīmaṃsitvā “sādhukaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhatī”ti attānaṃ jānāpetvā “ahaṃ tava vīmaṃsanatthāya āgato, sādhukaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhasi, evaṃ rakkhamānā [P 1.0277] na cirasseva mama santike nibbattissasi, appamattā hohī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

Again, Sakka went to her and said, “Have you seen your companions?” When she replied, “I have seen them. They ridiculed me and left. Take me back to that very place,” he took her there, released her into the water, and then asked, “Have you seen their prosperity?” “I have seen it, lord.” “It is fitting for you, too, to make the cause for rebirth there.” “What shall I do, lord?” “Will you guard the instruction given by me?” “I will guard it, lord.” Then, having given her the five precepts and said, “Guard them with heedfulness,” he departed. From that time on, she searched for and ate only fish that had died of themselves. After a few days, Sakka went for the purpose of testing her and lay on his back on a sandbank, as if he were a dead fish. Seeing him, with the perception “this is a dead fish,” she seized him. At the moment of swallowing, the fish moved its tail. Realizing, “This is a live fish,” she released it into the water. After a short while, he again lay on his back before her. Again, with the perception “this is a dead fish,” she took him, and at the moment of swallowing, he moved the tip of his tail. Seeing that, she released him, thinking, “This is a live fish.” Having tested her thus three times, and concluding, “She guards her virtue well,” he made himself known and said, “I came for the purpose of testing your virtue. You guard your virtue well. Guarding it thus, you will before long be reborn in my presence. Be heedful.” Having said this, he departed.

Sā [V 1.0157][M 1.0176] tato paṭṭhāya pana sayaṃmatamacchaṃ labhati vā, na vā. Alabhamānā katipāhaccayeneva sussitvā kālaṃ katvā tassa sīlassa phalena bārāṇasiyaṃ kumbhakārassa dhītā hutvā nibbatti. Athassā pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikakāle sakko “kuhiṃ nu kho sā nibbattā”ti āvajjento disvā, “idāni mayā tattha gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti eḷālukavaṇṇena paññāyamānehi sattahi ratanehi yānakaṃ pūretvā taṃ pājento bārāṇasiṃ pavisitvā, “ammatātā, eḷālukāni gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti ugghosento vīthiṃ paṭipajji. Muggamāsādīni gahetvā āgate pana “mūlena na demī”ti vatvā, “kathaṃ desī”ti vutte, “sīlarakkhikāya itthiyā dammī”ti āha. “Sīlaṃ nāma, sāmi, kīdisaṃ, kiṃ kāḷaṃ, udāhu nīlādivaṇṇa”nti? “Tumhe ‘sīlaṃ kīdisa’ntipi na jānātha, kimeva naṃ rakkhissatha, sīlarakkhikāya pana dassāmī”ti. “Sāmi, esā kumbhakārassa dhītā ‘sīlaṃ rakkhāmī’ti vicarati, etissā dehī”ti. Sāpi naṃ “tena hi mayhaṃ dehi, sāmī”ti āha. “Kāsi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ avijahitapañcasīlā”ti. “Tuyhamevetāni [P 1.0278] mayā ānītānī”ti yānakaṃ pājento tassā gharaṃ gantvā aññehi anāhariyaṃ katvā eḷālukavaṇṇena devadattiyaṃ dhanaṃ datvā attānaṃ jānāpetvā, “idaṃ te jīvitavuttiyā dhanaṃ, pañcasīlāni akhaṇḍādīni katvā rakkhāhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

From that time onward, she sometimes obtained fish that had died of themselves, and sometimes not. When she could not obtain any, after just a few days she withered away and died. By the fruit of that virtue, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the daughter of a potter. Then, when she was about fifteen or sixteen years old, Sakka, reflecting, “Where, I wonder, has she been reborn?” saw her and thought, “Now it is right for me to go there.” Filling a small cart with seven kinds of jewels that appeared in the form of cucumbers, he drove it into Bārāṇasī and proceeded down the street, crying out, “Mothers and fathers, take these cucumbers, take these cucumbers!” When people came bringing mung beans and other goods, he said, “I will not give them for a price.” When asked, “How then will you give them?” he replied, “I will give them to a woman who guards her virtue.” They asked, “Lord, what is this thing called virtue like? Is it black, or is it blue or some other color?” “You do not even know what virtue is like; how then could you guard it? I will give these to a woman who guards her virtue.” Then people said, “Lord, this potter’s daughter goes about saying, ‘I guard my virtue.’ Give them to her.” She too said to him, “In that case, lord, give them to me.” He asked, “Who are you?” She replied, “I am one who has not abandoned the five precepts.” “It is for you alone that I have brought these,” he said. Driving the cart to her house and making the wealth unable to be taken by others, he gave her the divinely given wealth that was in the form of cucumbers. He then made himself known and said, “This wealth is for your livelihood. Make the five precepts unbroken and guard them.” Having said this, he departed.

Sāpi tato cavitvā asurabhavane asurajeṭṭhakassa dhītā hutvā sakkassa verighare nibbatti. Dvīsu pana attabhāvesu sīlassa surakkhitattā abhirūpā ahosi suvaṇṇavaṇṇā asādhāraṇāya rūpasiriyā samannāgatā. Vepacittiasurindo āgatāgatānaṃ asurānaṃ “tumhe mama dhītu anucchavikā na hothā”ti taṃ kassaci adatvā, “mama dhītā attanāva attano anucchavikaṃ sāmikaṃ gahessatī”ti asurabalaṃ sannipātāpetvā, “tuyhaṃ anucchavikaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhā”ti tassā, hatthe pupphadāmaṃ adāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko tassā nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ olokento taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā, “idāni mayā gantvā taṃ ānetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti mahallakaasuravaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā gantvā parisapariyante aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi ito cito ca olokentī taṃ diṭṭhamattāva pubbasannivāsavasena uppannena pemena mahogheneva ajjhotthaṭahadayā hutvā, “eso me sāmiko”ti tassa upari pupphadāmaṃ khipi[M 1.0177]. Asurā “amhākaṃ rājā ettakaṃ kālaṃ dhītu anucchavikaṃ alabhitvā idāni labhi, ayamevassa dhītu pitāmahato mahallako anucchaviko”ti lajjamānā [P 1.0279] apakkamiṃsu. Sakkopi taṃ hatthe gahetvā “sakkohamasmī”ti naditvā ākāse pakkhandi. Asurā “vañcitamhā jarasakkenā”ti taṃ anubandhiṃsu. Mātali, saṅgāhako vejayantarathaṃ āharitvā antarāmagge aṭṭhāsi. Sakko taṃ tattha āropetvā devanagarābhimukho pāyāsi. Athassa sippalivanaṃ sampattakāle rathasaddaṃ sutvā bhītā garuḷapotakā [V 1.0158] viraviṃsu. Tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā sakko mātaliṃ pucchi – “ke ete viravantī”ti? “Garuḷapotakā, devā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Rathasaddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayenā”ti. “Maṃ ekaṃ nissāya ettako dijo rathavegena vicuṇṇito mā nassi, nivattehi ratha”nti. Sopi sindhavasahassassa daṇḍakasaññaṃ datvā rathaṃ nivattesi. Taṃ disvā asurā “jarasakko asurapurato paṭṭhāya palāyanto idāni rathaṃ nivattesi, addhā tena upatthambho laddho bhavissatī”ti nivattetvā āgamanamaggeneva asurapuraṃ pavisitvā puna sīsaṃ na ukkhipiṃsu.

She too, having passed away from that existence, was reborn in the Asura realm as the daughter of the chief of the Asuras, in the house of Sakka's enemy. In these two existences, because her virtue was well-guarded, she was exceedingly beautiful, of golden complexion, and endowed with uncommon splendor of form. The Asura king Vepacitti, saying to the Asuras who came one after another, “You are not suitable for my daughter,” did not give her to anyone. Thinking, “My daughter will choose a suitable husband for herself by herself,” he had the Asura host assembled and, giving a flower garland into her hand, said, “Choose a suitable husband for yourself.” At that moment, Sakka, observing her place of rebirth and learning of this event, thought, “It is now fitting for me to go and bring her here.” He created the form of an elderly Asura, went, and stood at the edge of the assembly. She too, looking here and there, the very moment she saw him, her heart was overwhelmed by a love that arose due to their past association, as if by a great flood. Thinking, “This is my husband,” she threw the flower garland upon him. The Asuras, feeling ashamed, departed, saying, “For so long our king could not find a suitable match for his daughter, and now he has found one! This very old man, older than her grandfather, is a suitable match for his daughter!” Sakka, taking her by the hand, roared, “I am Sakka!” and leapt into the sky. The Asuras, thinking, “We have been deceived by the old Sakka,” pursued him. Mātali the charioteer, having brought the Vejayanta chariot, stood waiting on the way. Sakka, placing her in it, proceeded toward the city of the devas. Then, as he reached the silk-cotton tree forest, young Garuḍa birds, frightened by the sound of the chariot, cried out. Hearing their sound, Sakka asked Mātali, “Who are these who are crying out?” “They are young Garuḍa birds, Lord.” “For what reason?” “Having heard the sound of the chariot, they cry out from fear of death.” “On account of me alone, let not so great a number of birds be crushed to powder and destroyed by the speed of the chariot. Turn the chariot back!” He too, giving the goad-signal to the thousand Sindhava horses, turned the chariot back. Seeing this, the Asuras thought, “The old Sakka, who was fleeing from the Asura city, has now turned his chariot back. Surely he must have obtained support!” Turning back, they entered the Asura city by the very path they had come and did not raise their heads again.

Sakkopi sujaṃ asurakaññaṃ devanagaraṃ netvā aḍḍhateyyānaṃ accharākoṭīnaṃ jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā sakkaṃ varaṃ yāci – “mahārāja, mama imasmiṃ devaloke mātāpitaro vā bhātikabhaginiyo vā natthi, yattha yattha gacchasi, tattha tattha maṃ gahetvāva [P 1.0280] gaccheyyāsī”ti. So “sādhū”ti tassā paṭiññaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya cittapāṭaliyā pupphitāya asurā “amhākaṃ nibbattaṭṭhāne dibbapāricchattakassa pupphanakālo”ti yuddhatthāya saggaṃ abhiruhanti. Sakko heṭṭhāsamudde nāgānaṃ ārakkhaṃ adāsi, tato supaṇṇānaṃ, tato kumbhaṇḍānaṃ, tato yakkhānaṃ. Tato catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ. Sabbūpari pana upaddavanivattanatthāya devanagaradvāresu vajirahatthā indapaṭimā ṭhapesi. Asurā nāgādayo jinitvā āgatāpi indapaṭimā dūrato disvā “sakko nikkhanto”ti palāyanti. Evaṃ, mahāli, magho māṇavo appamādapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajji. Evaṃ appamatto panesa evarūpaṃ issariyaṃ patvā dvīsu devalokesu rajjaṃ kāresi. Appamādo nāmesa buddhādīhi pasattho. Appamādañhi nissāya sabbesampi lokiyalokuttarānaṃ visesānaṃ adhigamo hotīti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka also took Sujā, the Asura maiden, to the city of the devas and established her in the position of chief over twenty-five million celestial nymphs. She requested a boon from Sakka: “Great King, in this deva world I have no mother or father, nor brothers or sisters. Wherever you go, may you take me with you.” Saying, “It is well,” he gave her his promise. From that time on, when the Cittapāṭali tree blossomed, the Asuras, thinking, “It is the time for the divine Pāricchattaka tree in our place of rebirth to blossom,” would ascend to heaven for the purpose of war. Sakka appointed the Nāgas as guards in the ocean below, then the Supaṇṇas, then the Kumbhaṇḍas, then the Yakkhas. Then, he appointed the Four Great Kings. But above all, for the purpose of warding off calamities, he placed at the gates of the city of the devas images of Indra holding a vajra. The Asuras, even when they came having conquered the Nāgas and others, would see the images of Indra from afar and flee, thinking, “Sakka has come forth!” Thus, Mahāli, the youth Magha undertook the practice of diligence. Being thus diligent, he attained such sovereignty and exercised rulership in two deva worlds. This quality called diligence is praised by the Buddhas and others. For, by relying on diligence, the attainment of all special worldly and supramundane benefits occurs. Having said this, he spoke this verse:

30.

30.

“Appamādena [M 1.0178] maghavā, devānaṃ seṭṭhataṃ gato;

Appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, pamādo garahito sadā”ti.

By diligence, Maghavā attained supremacy among the devas; diligence is praised, negligence is always censured.

Tattha appamādenāti macalagāme bhūmippadesasodhanaṃ ādiṃ katvā katena appamādena. Maghavāti idāni “maghavā”tipaññāto magho māṇavo dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ rājabhāvena devānaṃ seṭṭhataṃ gato. Pasaṃsantīti buddhādayo paṇḍitā appamādameva thomenti [P 1.0281] vaṇṇayanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Sabbesaṃ lokiyalokuttarānaṃ visesānaṃ paṭilābhakāraṇattā. Pamādo garahito sadāti pamādo pana tehi ariyehi niccaṃ garahito nindito. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Sabbavipattīnaṃ mūlabhāvato. Manussadobhaggaṃ vā hi apāyuppatti vā sabbā pamādamūlikāyevāti.

Therein, 'by diligence' means by the diligence that was performed, beginning with the clearing of the ground in the village of Macala. 'Maghavā' means the youth Magha, now known as 'Maghavā', who, through the state of being king of the two deva worlds, has attained supremacy among the devas. 'They praise' means that the wise, beginning with the Buddhas, praise and extol diligence alone. For what reason? Because it is the cause for the attainment of all special worldly and supramundane benefits. 'Negligence is always censured' means that negligence, however, is always blamed and censured by those noble ones. For what reason? Because of its being the root of all calamities. Indeed, human misfortune or rebirth in the woeful states—all have negligence as their root.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0159] mahāli licchavī sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, sampattaparisāyapi bahū sotāpannādayo jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, Mahāli the Licchavi was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and among the assembled company also, many became stream-enterers and so on.

Maghavatthu sattamaṃ.

The Seventh Story: Magha.

8. Aññatarabhikkhuvatthu

8. The Story of a Certain Monk

Appamādarato bhikkhūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Jetavana monastery, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'A monk delighting in diligence,' concerning a certain monk.

So kira satthu santike yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ nāsakkhi. So “visesetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpessāmī”ti tato nikkhamitvā satthu santikaṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge mahantaṃ dāvaggiṃ uṭṭhitaṃ disvā vegena ekaṃ muṇḍapabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruyha nisinno araññaṃ [P 1.0282] ḍayhamānaṃ aggiṃ disvā ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhi – “yathā ayaṃ aggi mahantāni ca khuddakāni ca upādānāni ḍahanto gacchati, evaṃ ariyamaggañāṇaggināpi mahantāni ca khuddakāni ca saṃyojanāni ḍahantena gantabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova tassa cittācāraṃ ñatvā, “evameva, bhikkhu, mahantānipi khuddakānipi upādānāni viya imesaṃ sattānaṃ abbhantare uppajjamānāni aṇuṃthūlāni saṃyojanāni, tāni [M 1.0179] ñāṇagginā jhāpetvā abhabbuppattikāni kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā obhāsaṃ vissajjetvā tassa bhikkhuno abhimukhe nisinno viya paññāyamāno imaṃ obhāsagāthamāha –

Indeed, that monk, having had a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship explained in the Teacher's presence, entered a forest. Though he strove and made an effort, he was not able to attain Arahantship. Thinking, 'I will have a meditation subject explained in greater detail,' he departed from there. While coming to the Teacher's presence, on the way he saw a great forest fire that had arisen. Quickly ascending to the peak of a bare mountain and sitting down, he saw the fire burning the forest and took it as his object of meditation: 'Just as this fire proceeds, burning up both great and small fuel, in the same way, one must proceed with the fire of the knowledge of the Noble Path, burning up both great and small fetters.' The Teacher, seated in the Perfumed Chamber, knowing the state of his mind, said, 'It is just so, monk. Like this great and small fuel, the subtle and gross fetters that arise within these beings should be completely burned up by the fire of knowledge, rendering them incapable of arising again.' Having said this, he emitted a radiance, and appearing as if seated in the presence of that monk, he spoke this radiant verse:

31.

31.

“Appamādarato bhikkhu, pamāde bhayadassi vā;

Saṃyojanaṃ aṇuṃ thūlaṃ, ḍahaṃ aggīva gacchatī”ti.

A monk who delights in heedfulness, or one who sees danger in heedlessness, advances like a fire, burning the fetters, both subtle and gross.

Tattha appamādaratoti appamāde rato abhirato, appamādena vītināmentoti attho. Pamāde bhayadassi vāti nirayuppattiādikaṃ pamāde bhayaṃ bhayato passanto, tāsaṃ vā uppattīnaṃ mūlattā pamādaṃ bhayato passanto. Saṃyojananti vaṭṭadukkhena saddhiṃ yojanaṃ bandhanaṃ pajānaṃ vaṭṭe osīdāpanasamatthaṃ dasavidhaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Aṇuṃ thūlanti mahantañca khuddakañca. Ḍahaṃ aggīva gacchatīti yathā ayaṃ aggī etaṃ mahantañca [P 1.0283] khuddakañca upādānaṃ ḍahantova gacchati. Evameso [V 1.0160] appamādarato bhikkhu appamādādhigatena ñāṇagginā etaṃ saṃyojanaṃ ḍahanto abhabbuppattikaṃ karonto gacchatīti attho.

Therein, 'delighting in heedfulness' means one who delights and takes great delight in heedfulness; the meaning is one who passes the time with heedfulness. 'Or one who sees danger in heedlessness' means one who sees the danger in heedlessness, beginning with birth in hell; or, because it is the root of those rebirths, one who sees heedlessness as a danger. 'Fetter' means the ten kinds of fetters, which are a bond, a binding together with the suffering of the round of existence, and are capable of causing beings to sink in that round. 'Subtle and gross' means great and small. 'Advances like a fire, burning' means: just as this fire proceeds, burning up this great and small fuel, in the same way, that monk who delights in heedfulness proceeds with the fire of knowledge well-attained through heedfulness, burning up this fetter and rendering it incapable of arising again. This is the meaning.

Gāthāpariyosāne so bhikkhu yathānisinnova sabbasaṃyojanāni jhāpetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā ākāsenāgantvā tathāgatassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ thometvā vaṇṇetvā vandamānova pakkāmīti.

At the conclusion of the verse, that monk, just as he was seated, burned up all the fetters and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having come through the air, he praised and extolled the Tathāgata's body, which was the color of pure gold, and only after paying homage did he depart.

Aññatarabhikkhuvatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Eighth Story: The Story of a Certain Monk.

9. Nigamavāsitissattheravatthu

9. The Story of the Elder Nigamavāsitissa

Appamādaratoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto nigamavāsitissattheraṃ nāma ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Appamādarato,' concerning the Elder named Nigamavāsitissa.

Ekasmiñhi sāvatthito avidūre nigamagāme jātasaṃvaḍḍho eko kulaputto satthu sāsane pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado “nigamavāsitissatthero nāma appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto āraddhavīriyo”ti paññāyi. So nibaddhaṃ ñātigāmeyeva piṇḍāya vicarati. Anāthapiṇḍikādīsu mahādānāni karontesu, pasenadikosale asadisadānaṃ karontepi [M 1.0180] sāvatthiṃ nāgacchati. Bhikkhū “ayaṃ nigamavāsitissatthero uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya ñātisaṃsaṭṭho viharati, anāthapiṇḍikādīsu mahādānādīni karontesu, pasenadikosale asadisadānaṃ karontepi neva āgacchatī”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā [P 1.0284] satthu ārocayiṃsu. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā, “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, evaṃ karosī”ti pucchitvā, “natthi, bhante, mayhaṃ ñātisaṃsaggo, ahaṃ ete manusse nissāya ajjhoharaṇīyamattaṃ āhāraṃ labhāmi lūkhe vā paṇīte vā. Yāpanamatte laddhe puna kiṃ āhārapariyesanenāti na gacchāmi, ñātīhi pana me saṃsaggo nāma natthi, bhante”ti vutte satthā pakatiyāpi tassa ajjhāsayaṃ vijānanto – “sādhu sādhu, bhikkhū”ti tassa sādhukāraṃ datvā, “anacchariyaṃ kho panetaṃ bhikkhu, yaṃ tvaṃ mādisaṃ ācariyaṃ labhitvā appiccho ahosi. Ayañhi appicchatā nāma mama tanti, mama paveṇī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari –

Indeed, in a certain market town not far from Sāvatthī, a certain man of good family, born and raised there, having gone forth in the Teacher's Dispensation and received the higher ordination, became known as 'the Elder Nigamavāsitissa, one of few wants, content, secluded, and of aroused effort.' He consistently went for alms only in his relatives’ village. Even when great offerings were being made by Anāthapiṇḍika and others, or when King Pasenadi of Kosala was giving the incomparable offering, he did not go to Sāvatthī. The monks raised a discussion, saying, 'This Elder Nigamavāsitissa, being diligent and active, dwells associated with his relatives. Even when great offerings are being made by Anāthapiṇḍika and others, or when King Pasenadi is giving the incomparable offering, he still does not come.' They reported this matter to the Teacher. The Teacher had him summoned and asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you act in this way?' When he replied, 'Venerable Sir, I have no association with my relatives. I depend on these people merely for just enough food to consume, whether it be coarse or fine. Once I have received just enough to sustain myself, what is the use of searching for more food? That is why I do not go. But, Venerable Sir, I have no association whatsoever with my relatives,' the Teacher, knowing his noble disposition even by nature, gave him approval, saying, 'Good, good, monk!' Then he declared, 'It is no wonder, monk, that having found a teacher like me, you became one of few wants. For this quality of having few wants is my tradition, my lineage.' Requested by the monks, he then related a story of the past:

Atīte himavante gaṅgātīre ekasmiṃ udumbaravane anekasahassā suvā vasiṃsu. Tatreko suvarājā [V 1.0161] attano nivāsarukkhassa phalesu khīṇesu yaṃ yadeva avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti aṅkuro vā pattaṃ vā taco vā, taṃ taṃ khāditvā gaṅgāyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivitvā paramappiccho santuṭṭho hutvā aññattha na gacchati. Tassa appicchasantuṭṭhabhāvaguṇena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjamāno taṃ disvā tassa vīmaṃsanatthaṃ attano ānubhāvena taṃ rukkhaṃ sukkhāpesi. Rukkho obhaggo khāṇumatto chiddāvachiddova hutvā vāte paharante ākoṭito viya saddaṃ nicchārento aṭṭhāsi. Tassa chiddehi cuṇṇāni nikkhamanti. Suvarājā [P 1.0285] tāni khāditvā gaṅgāyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivitvā aññattha agantvā vātātapaṃ agaṇetvā udumbarakhāṇumatthake nisīdati. Sakko tassa paramappicchabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “mittadhammaguṇaṃ kathāpetvā varamassa datvā udumbaraṃ amataphalaṃ katvā āgamissāmī”ti eko haṃsarājā hutvā sujaṃ asurakaññaṃ purato katvā udumbaravanaṃ gantvā avidūre ekassa rukkhassa sākhāya nisīditvā tena saddhiṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, on the banks of the Ganges in the Himalayan region, in a certain fig forest, many thousands of parrots lived. Among them was a parrot king who, when the fruits of his dwelling tree were exhausted, would eat whatever remained—be it a sprout, a leaf, or bark—and drink water from the Ganges. Being extremely of few wants and content, he would not go elsewhere. The virtue of his state of few wants and contentment shook the abode of Sakka. Sakka, reflecting upon this, saw him and, to test him, dried up that tree by his own power. The tree broke, becoming a mere stump full of holes, and when the wind struck it, it stood emitting a sound as if being beaten. Powdered wood came out from its holes. The parrot king ate that powder, drank water from the Ganges, and without going elsewhere, disregarding wind and sun, sat upon the fig tree stump. Sakka, recognizing his state of extreme fewness of wants, thought, 'Having had him speak on the virtue of friendship, having given him a boon, and having made the fig tree bear ambrosial fruit, I will return.' Becoming a goose king and placing Sujā, the asura maiden, before him, he went to the fig forest. Sitting on a branch of a nearby tree and wishing to converse with him, he spoke this verse:

“Santi rukkhā haripattā, dumānekaphalā bahū;

Kasmā nu sukkhe koḷāpe, suvassa nirato mano”ti. (jā. 1.9.30);

There are trees with green leaves, many trees with abundant fruit; why, then, does the parrot's mind delight in a dry stump?

Sabbaṃ [M 1.0181] suvajātakaṃ navakanipāte āgatanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Aṭṭhuppattiyeva hi tattha ca idha ca nānā, sesaṃ tādisameva. Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā, “tadā sakko ānando ahosi, suvarājā ahamevā”ti vatvā, “evaṃ, bhikkhave, appicchatā nāmesā mama tanti, mama paveṇī, anacchariyā mama puttassa nigamavāsitissassa mādisaṃ ācariyaṃ labhitvā appicchatā, bhikkhunā nāma nigamavāsitissena viya appiccheneva bhavitabbaṃ. Evarūpo hi bhikkhu abhabbo samathavipassanādhammehi vā maggaphalehi vā parihānāya, aññadatthu nibbānasseva santike hotī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The entire Suva Jātaka should be elaborated in the same manner as it appears in the Nipāta of Nines. Indeed, only the occasion for the story differs there and here; the rest is just the same. Having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher declared: 'At that time, Sakka was Ānanda, and the parrot king was I myself.' Then he said: 'Thus, monks, this quality of having few wants is my tradition, my lineage. It is no wonder that my son, Nigamavāsitissa, having found a teacher like me, is of few wants. Indeed, a monk should be of few wants, just like Nigamavāsitissa. Such a monk is incapable of falling away from the states of serenity and insight, or from the path and its fruits; on the contrary, he is in the very presence of Nibbāna itself.' Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:

32.

32.

“Appamādarato bhikkhu, pamāde bhayadassi vā;

Abhabbo parihānāya, nibbānasseva santike”ti.

A monk delighting in heedfulness, or seeing danger in heedlessness, is incapable of falling away; he is in the very presence of Nibbāna.

Tattha abhabbo parihānāyāti so evarūpo bhikkhu samathavipassanādhammehi vā maggaphalehi vā parihānāya [P 1.0286] abhabbo, nāpi pattehi parihāyati, na appattāni na pāpuṇāti. Nibbānasseva santiketi kilesaparinibbānassapi anupādāparinibbānassāpi santikeyevāti.

Herein, 'incapable of falling away' means that such a monk is incapable of falling away from the states of serenity and insight, or from the path and its fruits. He does not fall away from what he has attained, and he attains what he has not yet attained. 'In the very presence of Nibbāna' means that he is in the very presence of both the Nibbāna of the extinction of defilements and the Nibbāna without residue of aggregates.

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0162] nigamavāsitissatthero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verse, the Elder Nigamavāsitissa, together with the analytical knowledges, attained Arahantship. Many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great assembly.

Nigamavāsitissattheravatthu navamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Nigamavāsitissa, the Ninth.

Appamādavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā. Dutiyo vaggo.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Heedfulness is concluded. The Second Chapter is finished.

3. Cittavaggo

3. 3. The Chapter on the Mind

1. Meghiyattheravatthu

1. The Story of the Elder Meghiya

Phandanaṃ [M 1.0182][V 1.0163][P 1.0287] capalaṃ cittanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā cālikāya pabbate viharanto āyasmantaṃ meghiyaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling on Cālikā Mountain, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Flickering and unsteady is the mind,' concerning the Venerable Meghiya.

Tassa vatthuṃ vibhāvanatthaṃ sabbaṃ meghiyasuttantaṃ (udā. 31) vitthāretabbaṃ. Satthā pana tīhi vitakkehi anvāsattatāya tasmiṃ ambavane padhānaṃ anuyuñjituṃ asakkuṇitvā āgataṃ meghiyattheraṃ āmantetvā, “atibhāriyaṃ te, meghiya, kataṃ ‘āgamehi tāva, meghiya, ekakomhi yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchatī’ti maṃ yācantaṃ ekakaṃ pahāya gacchantena bhikkhunā nāma evaṃ cittavasikena bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, cittaṃ nāmetaṃ lahukaṃ, taṃ attano vase vattetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imā dve gāthā abhāsi –

To make this story clear, the entire Meghiya Sutta should be elaborated upon. The Teacher addressed the Elder Meghiya, who had returned, being unable to apply himself to the practice in that mango grove due to being assailed by three kinds of thoughts, saying: 'Meghiya, what you have done is a very grave thing. It is not proper for a monk, having abandoned me who was alone while I was requesting, "Wait for a while, Meghiya, I am alone until some other monk arrives," to go and thus be under the sway of the mind. This thing called mind is quick; it is proper to bring it under one's own control.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

33.

33.

“Phandanaṃ capalaṃ cittaṃ, dūrakkhaṃ dunnivārayaṃ;

Ujuṃ karoti medhāvī, usukārova tejanaṃ.

Flickering and unsteady is the mind, difficult to guard, difficult to restrain; the wise one makes it straight, as a fletcher an arrow shaft.

34.

34.

“Vārijova thale khitto, okamokataubbhato;

Paripphandatidaṃ cittaṃ, māradheyyaṃ pahātave”ti.

Like a fish pulled from its watery abode and cast upon dry land, this mind thrashes about, in order to abandon the domain of Māra.

Tattha [P 1.0288] phandananti rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu vipphandamānaṃ. Capalanti ekairiyāpathena asaṇṭhahanto gāmadārako viya ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato capalaṃ. Cittanti viññāṇaṃ, bhūmivatthuārammaṇakiriyādivicittatāya panetaṃ “citta”nti vuttaṃ. Dūrakkhanti kiṭṭhasambādhe ṭhāne kiṭṭhakhādakagoṇaṃ viya ekekasmiṃ sappāyārammaṇeyeva duṭṭhapanato dūrakkhaṃ. Dunnivārayanti visabhāgārammaṇaṃ gacchantaṃ paṭisedhetuṃ dukkhattā dunnivārayaṃ. Usukārova tejananti yathā nāma usukāro araññato ekaṃ vaṅkadaṇḍakaṃ āharitvā nittacaṃ katvā kañjiyatelena makkhetvā aṅgārakapalle tāpetvā rukkhālake uppīḷetvā nivaṅkaṃ ujuṃ vālavijjhanayoggaṃ karoti, katvā ca [V 1.0164] pana rājarājamahāmattānaṃ sippaṃ dassetvā mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ labhati, evameva [M 1.0183] medhāvī paṇḍito viññū puriso phandanādisabhāvametaṃ cittaṃ dhutaṅgāraññāvāsavasena, nittacaṃ apagataoḷārikakilesaṃ katvā saddhāsinehena temetvā kāyikacetasikavīriyena tāpetvā samathavipassanālake uppīḷetvā ujuṃ akuṭilaṃ nibbisevanaṃ karoti, katvā ca pana saṅkhāre sammasitvā mahantaṃ avijjakkhandhaṃ padāletvā, “tisso vijjā, cha abhiññā, nava lokuttaradhamme”ti imaṃ visesaṃ hatthagatameva katvā aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ [P 1.0289] labhati.

Herein, 'flickering' means trembling among objects such as forms. 'Unsteady' means fickle, like a village boy who does not stay still in one posture and does not settle on one object. 'Mind' refers to consciousness; it is called 'citta' because it is variegated by plane, basis, object, function, and so on. 'Difficult to guard' means it is hard to guard, like a crop-eating bull in a confined, overgrown place, because it is difficult to place on a single suitable object. 'Difficult to restrain' means it is difficult to prevent it from going to an unsuitable object. 'As a fletcher an arrow shaft': Just as a fletcher, having brought a crooked shaft from the forest, makes it barkless, soaks it in sour rice-gruel oil, heats it in a charcoal pan, presses it in a straightening tool, and makes it straight, uncrooked, and fit for piercing an animal; and having done so, by showing his skill to kings and royal ministers, he receives great honor and esteem; even so, a wise, intelligent person takes this mind which has the nature of flickering and so on, and by means of undertaking ascetic practices and dwelling in the forest, makes it 'barkless' by removing coarse defilements, moistens it with the adhesive of faith, heats it with bodily and mental energy, presses it in the straightening tool of serenity and insight, and makes it straight, uncrooked, and free from poison. And having done so, by contemplating the conditioned formations, splitting open the great mass of ignorance, and bringing into his hands this distinction—namely, the three true knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the nine supramundane Dhammas—he attains the state of being a foremost recipient of offerings.

Vārijovāti maccho viya, thale khittoti hatthena vā pādena vā jālādīnaṃ vā aññatarena thale chaḍḍito. Okamokataubbhatoti “okapuṇṇehi cīvarehī”ti ettha (mahāva. 306) udakaṃ okaṃ, “okaṃ pahāya aniketasārī”ti ettha (su. ni. 850) ālayo, ettha ubhayampi labbhati. “Okamokataubbhato”ti hi ettha okamokatoti udakasaṅkhātā ālayāti ayamattho. Ubbhatoti uddhaṭo. Paripphandatidaṃ cittanti yathā so udakālayato ubbhato thale khitto maccho udakaṃ alabhanto paripphandati, evamidaṃ pañcakāmaguṇālayābhirataṃ cittaṃ tato uddharitvā māradheyyasaṅkhātaṃ vaṭṭaṃ pahātuṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhāne khittaṃ kāyikacetasikavīriyena santāpiyamānaṃ paripphandati, saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Evaṃ santepi dhuraṃ anikkhipitvā medhāvī puggalo taṃ vuttanayeneva ujuṃ kammaniyaṃ karotīti attho. Aparo nayo – idaṃ māradheyyaṃ kilesavaṭṭaṃ avijahitvā ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ so vārijo viya paripphandati, tasmā māradheyyaṃ pahātave, yena kilesavaṭṭasaṅkhātena māradheyyeneva paripphandati, taṃ pahātabbanti.

'Like a fish' (vārijo'va): like a fish. 'Cast upon the land' (thale khitto): thrown onto dry land by hand, by foot, or by some other means such as a net. 'Pulled from its watery abode' (okamokata-ubbhato): In the phrase 'with robes full of water,' oka means water. In the phrase 'having abandoned home, wandering without a home,' oka means abode. Here, both meanings are obtained. In the phrase okamokata-ubbhato, okamokata means 'from the abode which is designated as water'; ubbhato means 'pulled out.' 'This mind thrashes about': Just as that fish, pulled from its watery abode and cast upon the land, thrashes about because it cannot get water, even so this mind, which delights in the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure, when it is pulled out from there and applied to the meditation subject of insight in order to abandon the round of existence known as Māra's domain, being tormented by bodily and mental energy, it thrashes about and is unable to become steady. Even so, a wise person, without laying down the burden, makes that mind straight and workable in the manner already described. This is the meaning. Another method: This mind, which remains without having abandoned this domain of Māra, the round of defilements, thrashes about like that fish. Therefore, the domain of Māra is to be abandoned. That domain of Māra, designated as the round of defilements, by which the mind thrashes about—that is what should be abandoned.

Gāthāpariyosāne meghiyatthero sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito, aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo jātāti.

At the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Meghiya was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also became stream-enterers and so forth.

Meghiyattheravatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Meghiya, the First.

2. Aññatarabhikkhuvatthu

2. The Story of a Certain Monk

Dunniggahassa [P 1.0290] lahunoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, which begins 'Hard to check, swift,' concerning a certain monk.

Kosalarañño [M 1.0184] kira vijite pabbatapāde mātikagāmo nāma eko ghanavāso gāmo ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ saṭṭhimattā bhikkhū satthu santike yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā taṃ [V 1.0165] gāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Atha ne yo tassa gāmassa sāmiko mātiko nāma, tassa mātā disvā gehe nisīdāpetvā nānaggarasena yāgubhattena parivisitvā, “bhante, kattha gantukāmā”ti pucchi. “Yathā phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ mahāupāsike”ti. Sā “vassāvāsaṭṭhānaṃ, ayyā, pariyesanti maññe”ti ñatvā pādamūle nipajjitvā, “sace, ayyā, imaṃ temāsaṃ idha vasissanti, ahaṃ tīṇi saraṇāni, pañca sīlāni gahetvā uposathakammaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Bhikkhū “mayaṃ imaṃ nissāya bhikkhāya akilamantā bhavanissaraṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissāmā”ti adhivāsayiṃsu. Sā tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vihāraṃ paṭijaggitvā adāsi.

It is said that in the kingdom of the Kosala king, at the foot of a mountain, there was a densely populated village named Mātikagāma. One day, about sixty monks, having received from the Teacher a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship, went to that village and entered it for alms-food. Then, the mother of the headman of that village, who was named Mātika, saw them, had them seated in her house, and served them with gruel and rice of various excellent flavors. She then asked, 'Venerable sirs, where do you intend to go?' 'To a place that is comfortable, great laywoman.' Realizing, 'I think the noble ones are searching for a place for the rains-residence,' she prostrated at their feet and said, 'Venerable sirs, if you will stay here for these three months of the rains, I will take the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts and perform the Uposatha observance.' The monks consented, thinking, 'Relying on this laywoman, we will be able to bring about release from existence without becoming weary for alms-food.' She prepared the monastery as a dwelling place for them and gave it.

Te tattheva vasantā ekadivasaṃ sannipatitvā aññamaññaṃ ovadiṃsu, “āvuso, amhehi pamādacāraṃ carituṃ na vaṭṭati. Amhākañhi sakagehaṃ viya aṭṭha mahānirayā vivaṭadvārāyeva, dharamānakabuddhassa kho pana santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā mayaṃ āgatā, buddhā ca nāma padānupadikaṃ vicarantenāpi saṭhena ārādhetuṃ na sakkā, yathājjhāsayeneva ārādhetuṃ sakkā, appamattā hotha, dvīhi ekaṭṭhāne na ṭhātabbaṃ, na nisīditabbaṃ, sāyaṃ kho pana therūpaṭṭhānakāle pātova bhikkhācārakāle ekato bhavissāma, sesakāle dve ekato na bhavissāma, apica kho pana aphāsukena bhikkhunā [P 1.0291] āgantvā vihāramajjhe ghaṇḍiyā pahatāya ghaṇḍisaññāya āgantvā tassa bhesajjaṃ karissāmā”ti.

While they were dwelling there, they assembled one day and admonished one another, saying: 'Friends, it is not proper for us to live negligently. For us, the eight great hells are indeed with doors open, just like our own dwelling places. We have come here after receiving a meditation subject from the living Buddha. And Buddhas cannot be pleased by a deceitful person, even one following step by step; they can be pleased only by noble intention. Be heedful! Two persons should not stand in one place, nor should they sit. However, in the evening at the time of attending to the elder monks, and early in the morning at the time of the alms-round, we will be together. At other times, two of us will not be together. Furthermore, should the gong in the middle of the monastery be struck by a monk who is unwell, we will come at the signal of the gong and prepare medicine for him.'

Tesu evaṃ katikaṃ katvā viharantesu ekadivasaṃ sā upāsikā sappitelaphāṇitādīni gāhāpetvā dāsadāsikammakarādīhi parivutā sāyanhasamaye taṃ vihāraṃ gantvā vihāramajjhe bhikkhū adisvā, “kahaṃ nu kho, ayyā, gatā”ti purise pucchitvā, “attano attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu nisinnā bhavissanti, ayye”ti vutte, “kiṃ nu kho katvā daṭṭhuṃ [M 1.0185] sakkhissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa katikavattaṃ jānanamanussā āhaṃsu – “ghaṇḍiyā pahatāya sannipatissanti, ayye”ti. Sā ca ghaṇḍiṃ paharāpesi. Bhikkhū ghaṇḍisaddaṃ sutvā, “kassaci aphāsukaṃ bhavissatī”ti sakasakaṭṭhānehi nikkhamitvā vihāramajjhe sannipatiṃsu. Dvepi janā ekamaggenāgatā nāma natthi. Upāsikā ekekaṭṭhānato ekekameva āgacchantaṃ disvā, “mama puttehi aññamaññaṃ kalaho kato bhavissatī”ti cintetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vanditvā pucchi – “kalahaṃ nu kho, bhante, karitthā”ti? “Na karoma, mahāupāsike”ti. “Sace vo, bhante, kalaho natthi, atha kasmā yathā amhākaṃ gehaṃ āgacchantā sabbe ekatova āgacchatha, evaṃ anāgantvā ekekaṭṭhānato ekekāva āgatā”ti? “Mahāupāsike, ekekasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditvā samaṇadhammaṃ karimhā”ti. “Ko esa[V 1.0166], bhante, samaṇadhammo nāmā”ti? “Dvattiṃsākāre sajjhāyaṃ karoma, attabhāve ca khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapema, mahāupāsike”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, dvattiṃsākāre sajjhāyaṃ kātuṃ, attabhāve ca khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetuṃ tumhākameva vaṭṭati, udāhu amhākampīti, kassacipi [P 1.0292] avārito esa dhammo, mahāupāsike”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, mayhampi dvattiṃsākāraṃ detha, attabhāve ca khayavayapaṭṭhapanaṃ ācikkhathā”ti. “Tena hi uggaṇha, mahāupāsike”ti sabbaṃ uggaṇhāpesuṃ.

While they were dwelling thus, having made this agreement, one day that laywoman had ghee, oil, molasses, and other items brought, and surrounded by male and female servants, workers, and others, she went to the monastery in the evening. Not seeing the monks in the middle of the monastery, she asked the men, 'Where, indeed, have the noble ones gone?' When they replied, 'Madam, they must be seated in their respective places for the night and for the day,' she said, 'How, indeed, can I get to see them?' Then, some people who knew the agreement of the community of monks told her, 'Madam, they will assemble when the gong is struck.' And she had the gong struck. Hearing the sound of the gong, the monks thought, 'Someone must be unwell,' and coming out from their own places, they assembled in the middle of the monastery. Not even two persons came by the same path. Seeing them coming one by one from separate places, the laywoman thought, 'My sons must have had a quarrel with one another.' After paying homage to the community of monks, she asked, 'Venerable sirs, have you perhaps quarreled?' 'We have not quarreled, great laywoman.' 'Venerable sirs, if you have not quarreled, then why did you not come all together, as you do when coming to our house, but instead came one by one from separate places?' 'Great laywoman, seated in our individual places, we were practicing the duty of a recluse.' 'Venerable sirs, what is this duty of a recluse?' 'Great laywoman, we recite the thirty-two parts of the body and establish the contemplation of decay and dissolution in this personality.' 'But, venerable sirs, is it proper only for you to recite the thirty-two parts and to establish the contemplation of decay and dissolution in this personality, or is it also proper for us?' 'Great laywoman, this Dhamma is not forbidden to anyone.' 'In that case, venerable sirs, please give me the teaching on the thirty-two parts and explain the establishing of the contemplation of decay and dissolution in this personality.' 'In that case, great laywoman, learn it.' And they had her learn it all.

Sā tato paṭṭhāya dvattiṃsākāre sajjhāyaṃ katvā attani khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā tehi bhikkhūhi puretarameva tayo magge, tīṇi ca phalāni pāpuṇi. Maggeneva cassā catasso paṭisambhidā lokiyaabhiññā ca āgamiṃsu. Sā maggaphalasukhato vuṭṭhāya dibbacakkhunā oloketvā, “kadā nu kho mama puttehi ayaṃ dhammo adhigato”ti upadhārentī sabbepime sarāgā sadosā samohā jhānavipassanāmattampi tesaṃ natthi, “kiṃ nu kho mayhaṃ puttānaṃ arahattassa upanissayo atthi, natthī”ti āvajjetvā, “atthī”ti disvā, “senāsanasappāyaṃ nu kho atthi, natthī”ti āvajjetvā tampi disvā, “puggalasappāyaṃ nu kho labhanti, na labhantī”ti āvajjesi, puggalasappāyampi disvā, “āhārasappāyaṃ nu kho labhanti, na labhantī”ti upadhārentī “āhārasappāyaṃ nesaṃ natthī”ti disvā tato paṭṭhāya nānāvidhaṃ yāguṃ, anekappakāraṃ khajjakaṃ, nānaggarasañca bhojanaṃ sampādetvā gehe bhikkhū nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā, “bhante[M 1.0186], tumhākaṃ yaṃ yaṃ ruccati, taṃ taṃ gahetvā paribhuñjathā”ti niyyādesi. Te yathāruci yāguādīni gahetvā paribhuñjanti. Tesaṃ sappāyāhāraṃ labhantānaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi.

From that time onward, she recited the thirty-two parts of the body, established in herself the contemplation of decay and dissolution, and even before those monks, she herself attained the three paths and the three fruits. Along with the path, the four analytical knowledges and mundane higher knowledges also arose in her. Having emerged from the bliss of the path and fruit, she looked with the divine eye and reflected, "When will my sons attain this Dhamma?" Observing them, she saw that they were all still full of lust, hatred, and delusion—they did not even have a trace of jhāna or insight. She then considered, "Is there or is there not a support for my sons to attain arahantship?" Reflecting, she saw that there was. Next, she considered, "Is there suitable lodging for them or not?" Seeing that there was, she further reflected, "Are they obtaining suitable companionship or not?" Observing, she saw that they were. Then she reflected, "Are they obtaining suitable food or not?" Realizing, "They are not obtaining suitable food," from that time onward, she prepared various kinds of gruel, many types of snacks, and food with diverse excellent flavors. She invited the monks to sit in her house, offered them water of dedication, and offered, saying, "Venerable sirs, please take whatever you like and enjoy it." They took the gruel and other foods according to their preference and partook. As they obtained suitable food, their minds became concentrated.

Te ekaggena cittena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā na cirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā cintayiṃsu – “aho mahāupāsikā amhākaṃ patiṭṭhā jātā, sace mayaṃ sappāyāhāraṃ na labhimha, na no maggaphalapaṭivedho abhavissa, idāni vuṭṭhavassā pavāretvā satthu [P 1.0293] santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti. Te “satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmamhā”ti mahāupāsikaṃ āpucchiṃsu. “Mahāupāsikā sādhu, ayyā”ti. Te anugantvā punapi, “bhante, amhe olokeyyāthā”ti bahūni piyavacanāni vatvā paṭinivatti. Tepi kho bhikkhū sāvatthiṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā “kacci, bhikkhave, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, na ca piṇḍakena kilamitthā”ti vutte “khamanīyaṃ, bhante, yāpanīyaṃ, bhante, piṇḍakena pana neva kilamimha. Amhākañhi mātikamātā nāmekā upāsikā cittācāraṃ ñatvā, ‘aho vata no evarūpaṃ nāma [V 1.0167] āhāraṃ paṭiyādeyyā’ti cintite yathācintitaṃ āhāraṃ paṭiyādetvā adāsī”ti tassā guṇakathaṃ kathayiṃsu.

With one-pointed minds, they developed insight and soon attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then they reflected: "Ah, the great laywoman has been our support. If we had not obtained suitable food, we would not have penetrated the path and fruit. Now that the rains retreat is over, we shall perform the Pavāraṇā and go to the Teacher's presence." They took leave of the great laywoman, saying, "We wish to see the Teacher." She replied, "Very well, venerable sirs." After accompanying them for a distance, she turned back, saying many affectionate words such as, "Venerable sirs, please look upon us again." Those monks went to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. When asked, "I hope, monks, you are keeping well, I hope you are comfortable? And you were not wearied by the alms-round?" they replied, "We are keeping well, venerable sir, we are comfortable, venerable sir. And we were not at all wearied by the alms-round. For a laywoman named Mātikamātā, knowing the inclination of our minds, when we thought, ‘Oh, if only she would prepare such and such food for us,’ she prepared the food exactly as we had thought and gave it to us." Then they spoke in praise of her virtues.

Aññataro bhikkhu tassā guṇakathaṃ sutvā tattha gantukāmo hutvā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā, “bhante, taṃ gāmaṃ gamissāmī”ti satthāraṃ āpucchitvā jetavanato nikkhamitvā anupubbena taṃ gāmaṃ patvā vihāraṃ pavisanadivaseyeva cintesi – “ayaṃ kira upāsikā cintitacintitaṃ jānāti, ahañca maggakilanto vihāraṃ paṭijaggituṃ na sakkhissāmi, aho vata me vihārapaṭijaggakaṃ manussaṃ peseyyā”ti. Upāsikā gehe nisinnāva āvajjentī tamatthaṃ ñatvā, “gaccha, vihāraṃ paṭijaggitvā ehī”ti manussaṃ pesesi. Itaropi pānīyaṃ pivitukāmo “aho vata me sakkharapānakaṃ katvā peseyyā”ti cintesi. Upāsikā tampi pesesi. So punadivase “pātova siniddhayāguṃ me sauttaribhaṅgaṃ pesetū”ti cintesi. Upāsikā tathā akāsi[P 1.0294]. So yāguṃ pivitvā, “aho vata me evarūpaṃ khajjakaṃ peseyyā”ti cintesi.
