Upāsikā tampi pesesi. So cintesi – “ayaṃ upāsikā mayā sabbaṃ cintitacintitaṃ pesesi, ahaṃ [M 1.0187] etaṃ daṭṭhukāmo, aho vata me nānaggarasabhojanaṃ gāhāpetvā sayameva āgaccheyyā”ti. Upāsikā “mama putto maṃ daṭṭhukāmo, āgamanaṃ me paccāsīsatī”ti bhojanaṃ gāhāpetvā vihāraṃ gantvā tassa adāsi. So katabhattakicco “mātikamātā nāma tvaṃ, mahāupāsike”ti pucchi. “Āma, tātā”ti. “Tvaṃ paracittaṃ jānāsī”ti? “Kiṃ maṃ pucchasi, tātā”ti? “Mayā cintitacintitaṃ sabbamakāsi, tena taṃ pucchāmī”ti. “Paracittajānanakabhikkhū bahū, tātā”ti? “Nāhaṃ aññe pucchāmi, tuvaṃ pucchāmi, upāsike”ti. Evaṃ santepi upāsikā “paracittaṃ jānāmī”ti avatvā “paracittaṃ jānantā nāma evaṃ karonti puttā”ti āha. So “bhāriyaṃ vatidaṃ kammaṃ, puthujjanā nāma sobhanampi asobhanampi cintenti, sacāhaṃ kiñci ayuttaṃ cintayissāmi, saha bhaṇḍakena coraṃ cūḷāya gaṇhantī viya maṃ vippakāraṃ pāpeyya, mayā ito palāyituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā, “upāsike, ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti āha. “Kahaṃ, ayyā”ti? “Satthu santikaṃ, upāsike”ti. “Vasatha tāva, bhante, idhā”ti. “Na vasissāmi, upāsike, gamissāmevā”ti nikkhamitvā satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ bhikkhu na tvaṃ tattha vasasī”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante, na sakkā tattha vasitu”nti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā bhikkhū”ti? “Bhante, sā upāsikā cintitacintitaṃ sabbaṃ jānāti, puthujjanā ca nāma sobhanampi asobhanampi cintenti, sacāhaṃ kiñci ayuttaṃ cintessāmi, saha bhaṇḍakena coraṃ cūḷāya gaṇhantī viya maṃ vippakāraṃ pāpessatī”ti cintetvā [V 1.0168] āgatomhīti. “Bhikkhu, tattheva tayā vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti[P 1.0295], “na sakkomi, bhante, nāhaṃ tattha vasissāmī”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ekameva rakkhituṃ sakkhissasī”ti. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti? “Tava cittameva rakkha, cittaṃ nāmetaṃ durakkhaṃ, tvaṃ attano cittameva niggaṇha, mā aññaṃ kiñci cintayi, cittaṃ nāmetaṃ dunniggaha”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

A certain monk, having heard of her virtues, wished to go there. After receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he took leave of the Teacher, saying, 'Venerable sir, I will go to that village.' Leaving Jetavana, he gradually reached that village. On the very day he entered the monastery, he thought, 'This lay follower, it seems, knows whatever is thought. And I, weary from the journey, will not be able to tend to the monastery. Oh, if only she would send a person to tend to the monastery for me.' The lay follower, sitting in her house and reflecting, knew of this matter and sent a person, saying, 'Go, tend to the monastery and come back.' The monk, wishing for a drink, thought, 'Oh, if only she would have a sugar drink prepared and sent to me.' The lay follower sent that too. The next day, he thought, 'Early in the morning, may she send me smooth gruel with a side dish.' The lay follower did so. After drinking the gruel, he thought, 'Oh, if only she would send me such a hard food.' The lay follower sent that too. He thought, 'This lay follower has sent everything I have thought. I wish to see her. Oh, if only she would have a meal with various excellent flavors brought and come herself.' The lay follower thought, 'My son wishes to see me; he is expecting my arrival.' Having had the meal brought, she went to the monastery and gave it to him. Having finished his meal, he asked, 'Great lay follower, are you the one named Mātikamātā?' 'Yes, dear son.' 'Do you know the minds of others?' 'Why do you ask me, dear son?' 'You did everything I thought; that is why I ask you.' 'Dear son, there are many monks who know the minds of others.' 'I am not asking about others; I am asking you, lay follower.' Even so, the lay follower did not say, 'I know the minds of others,' but said, 'Son, those who know the minds of others act in this way.' He thought, 'This is a serious matter. Ordinary people think of both beautiful and unbeautiful things. If I should think anything improper, she would bring me to ruin, just as one might seize a thief with the stolen goods by his top-knot. It is proper for me to flee from here.' Having thought thus, he said, 'Lay follower, I will go.' 'Where, venerable sir?' 'To the Teacher’s presence, lay follower.' 'Venerable sir, please stay here for a while.' 'I will not stay, lay follower, I will surely go.' Having departed, he went to the Teacher’s presence. Then the Teacher asked him, 'Monk, why do you not stay there?' 'Indeed, venerable sir, it is not possible to stay there.' 'For what reason, monk?' 'Venerable sir, that lay follower knows everything that is thought. And ordinary people think of both beautiful and unbeautiful things. If I should think anything improper, she will bring me to ruin, just as one might seize a thief with the stolen goods by his top-knot. Having thought thus, I have come.' 'Monk, it is proper for you to stay right there.' 'I cannot, venerable sir, I will not stay there.' 'In that case, monk, can you guard just one thing?' 'What, venerable sir?' 'Guard your own mind. This thing called mind is hard to guard. Restrain your own mind; do not think of anything else. This thing called mind is hard to restrain.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

35.

35.

“Dunniggahassa lahuno, yatthakāmanipātino;

Cittassa damatho sādhu, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvaha”nti.

Hard to restrain, swift, alighting wherever it wishes; taming the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.

Tattha cittaṃ nāmetaṃ dukkhena niggayhatīti dunniggahaṃ. Lahuṃ uppajjati ca nirujjhati cāti lahu. Tassa dunniggahassa lahuno. Yatthakāmanipātinoti yattha katthacideva nipatanasīlassa. Etañhi labhitabbaṭṭhānaṃ vā alabhitabbaṭṭhānaṃ vā yuttaṭṭhānaṃ vā ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ vā na jānāti, neva jātiṃ [M 1.0188] oloketi, na gottaṃ, na vayaṃ. Yattha yattha icchati, tattha tattheva nipatatīti “yatthakāmanipātī”ti vuccati. Tassa evarūpassa cittassa damatho sādhu catūhi ariyamaggehi dantabhāvo yathā nibbisevanaṃ hoti, tathā katabhāvo sādhu. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Idañhi cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvahaṃ nibbisevanaṃ kataṃ maggaphalasukhaṃ paramatthanibbānasukhañca āvahatīti.

In that verse, this thing called 'mind' is 'hard to restrain' (dunniggahaṃ) because it is restrained with difficulty. It is 'swift' (lahu) because it arises and ceases swiftly. Of that hard-to-restrain, swift mind. 'Alighting wherever it wishes' (yatthakāmanipātinoti) means it has the nature of alighting on any object whatsoever. For this mind does not know whether a place is attainable or unattainable, suitable or unsuitable; it does not consider birth, lineage, or age. Wherever it desires, right there it alights—thus it is called 'alighting wherever it wishes.' For such a mind, taming is good; its state of being tamed by the four noble paths, and its being made free from the poison of defilements, is good. For what reason? For this tamed mind, made free from poison, brings happiness; it brings the happiness of the path and fruit, and the supreme happiness of Nibbāna.

Desanāpariyosāne sampattaparisāya bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ, mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many in the assembled congregation became stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great multitude.

Satthā tassa [P 1.0296] bhikkhuno imaṃ ovādaṃ datvā, “gaccha, bhikkhu, aññaṃ kiñci acintayitvā tattheva vasāhī”ti pahiṇi. So bhikkhu satthu santikā ovādaṃ labhitvā tattha agamāsi. Kiñci bahiddhā cintanaṃ nāma na cintesi. Mahāupāsikāpi dibbena cakkhunā olokentī theraṃ disvā, “idāni ovādadāyakaṃ ācariyaṃ labhitvā punāgato mama putto”ti attano ñāṇeneva paricchinditvā tassa sappāyāhāraṃ paṭiyādetvā adāsi. So sappāyabhojanaṃ sevitvā katipāheneva arahattaṃ patvā maggaphalasukhena vītināmento “aho mahāupāsikā mayhaṃ patiṭṭhā jātā, ahaṃ imaṃ nissāya bhavanissaraṇaṃ pattomhī”ti cintetvā, “imasmiṃ tāva me attabhāve patiṭṭhā jātā, saṃsāre pana me saṃsarantassa aññesupi attabhāvesu ayaṃ patiṭṭhā bhūtapubbā, no”ti upadhārento ekūnaattabhāvasataṃ anussari. Sāpi ekūnaattabhāvasate tassa pādaparicārikā aññesu paṭibaddhacittā hutvā taṃ jīvitā voropesi. Thero [V 1.0169] tassā ettakaṃ aguṇaṃ disvā, “aho mayaṃ mahāupāsikā bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ akāsī”ti cintesi.

The Teacher gave this instruction to that monk and sent him away, saying, 'Go, monk, without thinking of anything else, dwell right there.' Having received the Teacher’s instruction, the monk went there. He did not think any thought whatsoever of external objects. The great lay follower, looking with the divine eye, saw the Elder and, discerning with her own knowledge, thought, 'Now, having found a teacher who can give instruction, my son has come again.' She prepared suitable food for him and gave it. Having partaken of the suitable food, in just a few days he reached Arahantship. Passing the time with the bliss of the path and fruit, he thought, 'Oh, the great lay follower has become my support. Relying on her, I have reached the escape from existence.' Then, investigating, he thought, 'In this very existence, she has become my support. But in saṃsāra, while I was wandering, has this support for me existed before in other existences, or not?' Thus, he recollected ninety-nine existences. In those ninety-nine existences, she too, having been his wife who served at his feet, became attached to others and deprived him of life. The Elder, seeing this great mass of demerit in her, thought, 'Oh, this great lay follower has done a weighty deed.'

Mahāupāsikāpi gehe nisinnāva “kiṃ nu kho mayhaṃ puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ mattakaṃ pattaṃ, no”ti upadhārayamānā tassa arahattapattiṃ ñatvā uttari upadhāriyamānā, “mama putto arahattaṃ patvā aho vata me ayaṃ upāsikā mahatī patiṭṭhā jātā”ti cintetvā, “atītepi nu kho me ayaṃ patiṭṭhā bhūtapubbā, no”ti upadhārento ekūnaattabhāvasataṃ anussari, “ahaṃ kho pana ekūnaattabhāvasate aññehi saddhiṃ ekato [M 1.0189] hutvā etaṃ jīvitā voropesiṃ, ayaṃ me ettakaṃ aguṇaṃ [P 1.0297] disvā ‘aho bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ upāsikāyā”ti cintesi. “Atthi nu kho evaṃ saṃsāre saṃsarantiyā mama puttassa upakāro katapubbo”ti upadhārayamānā tato uttariṃ satamaṃ attabhāvaṃ anussaritvā satame attabhāve mayā etassa pādaparicārikāya hutvā etasmiṃ jīvitā voropanaṭṭhāne jīvitadānaṃ dinnaṃ, aho mayā mama puttassa mahāupakāro katapubbo”ti gehe nisinnāva uttariṃ visesetvā “upadhārethā”ti āha. So dibbāya sotadhātuyā saddaṃ sutvā visesetvā satamaṃ attabhāvaṃ anussaritvā tattha tāya attano jīvitassa dinnabhāvaṃ disvā, “aho mama imāya mahāupāsikāya upakāro katapubbo”ti attamano hutvā tassā tattheva catūsu maggaphalesu pañhaṃ kathetvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyīti.

The great female lay disciple, while sitting in her house, investigated, 'I wonder, has my son's duty as a monk reached its culmination, or not?' Knowing his attainment of Arahantship and investigating further, she perceived his train of thought: 'My son, having reached Arahantship, thought, "Oh, this female lay disciple has become a great support for me." Then, investigating, "I wonder if this support for me has existed before in the past, or not?" he recollected ninety-nine existences. He then saw my demerit: "In ninety-nine existences, I, together with others, deprived him of life," and he thought, "Oh, a weighty deed was done by the female lay disciple."' Then she herself thought, 'While wandering thus in saṃsāra, have I ever done a good deed for my son?' Investigating, she recollected the hundredth existence beyond that and realized, 'In the hundredth existence, I, having been his wife who served at his feet, gave the gift of my own life at the very place where he was to be deprived of life. Oh, a great good deed was done by me for my son!' While still sitting in her house, she investigated this in greater detail and said aloud, 'Please investigate further!' He, having heard the sound with the divine ear-element, investigated in greater detail and recollected the hundredth existence. Seeing there the fact that she had given her own life for him, he became delighted and thought, 'Oh, what a good deed was done for me by this great female lay disciple!' Then, right there in her monastery, he expounded on the subject of the four paths and fruits and attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

Aññatarabhikkhuvatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Second Story of a Certain Monk.

3. Aññataraukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuvatthu

3. The Story of a Certain Discontented Monk

Sududdasanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto aññataraṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Sududdasaṃ,' concerning a certain discontented monk.

Satthari kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante eko seṭṭhiputto attano kulūpagattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, ahaṃ dukkhā muccitukāmo, ekaṃ me dukkhato muccanakāraṇaṃ kathethā”ti [P 1.0298] āha. “Sādhāvuso, sacesi dukkhā muccitukāmo, salākabhattaṃ dehi, pakkhikabhattaṃ dehi, vassāvāsikaṃ dehi, cīvarādayo paccaye dehi, attano sāpateyyaṃ tayo koṭṭhāse katvā ekena kammantaṃ payojehi, ekena puttadāraṃ posehi, ekaṃ buddhasāsane dehī”ti āha. So “sādhu, bhante”ti [V 1.0170] vuttapaṭipāṭiyā sabbaṃ katvā puna theraṃ pucchi – “tato uttariṃ aññaṃ kiṃ karomi, bhante”ti? “Āvuso, tīṇi saraṇāni gaṇha, pañca sīlāni gaṇhāhī”ti. Tānipi paṭiggahetvā tato uttariṃ pucchi. “Tena hi dasa sīlāni gaṇhāhī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti gaṇhi. So evaṃ anupubbena puññakammassa katattā anupubbaseṭṭhiputto nāma jāto. Tato “uttarimpi kattabbaṃ atthi, bhante”ti puna pucchitvā, “tena hi pabbajāhī”ti vutto nikkhamitvā [M 1.0190] pabbaji. Tasseko ābhidhammikabhikkhu ācariyo ahosi. Eko vinayadharo upajjhāyo. Tassa laddhūpasampadassa ācariyo attano santikaṃ āgatakāle abhidhamme pañhaṃ kathesi – “buddhasāsane nāma idaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, idaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Upajjhāyopissa attano santikaṃ āgatakāle vinaye pañhaṃ kathesi – “buddhasāsane nāma idaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, idaṃ na vaṭṭati, idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti. So cintesi – “aho bhāriyaṃ idaṃ kammaṃ, ahaṃ dukkhā muccitukāmo pabbajito, idha ca mama hatthapasāraṇaṭṭhānampi na paññāyati, gehe [P 1.0299] ṭhatvāva dukkhā muccituṃ sakkā, mayā gihinā bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya ukkaṇṭhito anabhirato dvattiṃsākāre sajjhāyaṃ na karoti, uddesaṃ na gaṇhāti, kiso lūkho dhamanisanthatagatto ālassiyābhibhūto kacchuparikiṇṇo ahosi.

It is said that when the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain wealthy man's son approached the Elder who frequented his family's home and said, 'Venerable sir, I desire to be freed from suffering. Please teach me one way to be freed from suffering.' 'Good, layman. If you desire to be freed from suffering, give ticket-food, give fortnightly food, and give rains-residence requisites. Divide your wealth into three portions: with one, conduct your business; with one, support your wife and children; and one, give to the Buddha's Dispensation.' He said, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and did everything according to the instructions. Then he asked the Elder again, 'Venerable sir, what more should I do beyond that?' 'Layman, take the Three Refuges and undertake the five precepts.' Having accepted those as well, he asked what was beyond that. 'In that case, undertake the ten precepts.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' he said, and undertook them. Because he had performed meritorious deeds in this gradual way, he became known as the 'Gradual Wealthy Man's Son.' Then, asking again, 'Venerable sir, is there anything further to be done?' he was told, 'In that case, go forth.' Leaving home, he went forth. An Abhidhamma monk became his teacher, and a Vinaya expert became his preceptor. After he had received the higher ordination, whenever he went to his teacher's presence, the teacher would instruct him on the subject of the Abhidhamma, saying: 'In the Buddha's Dispensation, this is proper to do, this is not proper.' His preceptor also, whenever he came to his presence, would instruct him on the subject of the Vinaya, saying: 'In the Buddha's Dispensation, this is proper to do, this is not proper; this is allowable, this is not allowable.' He thought: 'Oh, how burdensome is this task! I went forth because I desired to be freed from suffering, but here not even a place to stretch my hand is apparent. It is possible to be freed from suffering even while staying at home. It is right for me to become a layman.' From then on, he became discontented and dissatisfied. He did not recite the thirty-two parts of the body, nor did he take up the textual recitation. He became thin, rough, his body covered with protruding veins, overcome by laziness, and covered with scabies.

Atha naṃ daharasāmaṇerā, “āvuso, kiṃ tvaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne ṭhitova nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnova ahosi, paṇḍurogābhibhūto kiso lūkho dhamanisanthatagatto ālassiyābhibhūto kacchuparikiṇṇo, kiṃ te kata”nti pucchiṃsu. “Ukkaṇṭhitomhi, āvuso”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Te tassa ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Ācariyupajjhāyā taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, āgatatthā”ti āha. “Bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu tumhākaṃ sāsane ukkaṇṭhito”ti. “Evaṃ kira bhikkhū”ti. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, dukkhā muccitukāmova pabbajito, tassa me ācariyo abhidhammakathaṃ kathesi, upajjhāyo vinayakathaṃ kathesi, svāhaṃ ‘idha me hatthapasāraṇaṭṭhānampi natthi, gihinā hutvā sakkā dukkhā muccituṃ, gihi bhavissāmī’ti sanniṭṭhānamakāsiṃ, bhante”ti. “Sace tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ekameva rakkhituṃ sakkhissasi, avasesānaṃ rakkhanakiccaṃ natthī”ti. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti? “Tava cittameva rakkhituṃ sakkhissasī”ti. “Sakkhissāmi, bhante”ti. “Tena hi attano cittameva rakkhāhi, sakkā dukkhā muccitu”nti imaṃ ovādaṃ datvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the young novices asked him, 'Friend, why is it that you are just standing in the place of standing and just sitting in the place of sitting, overcome by a wasting disease, thin, rough, with veins standing out on your body, overcome by sloth, and covered with scabs? What have you done?' 'I am discontented, friends.' 'For what reason?' He told them the matter. They informed his teachers and preceptors. The teachers and preceptors took him and went to the Teacher’s presence. The Teacher asked, 'Monks, why have you come?' 'Venerable Sir, this monk is discontented with your dispensation.' 'Is it so, monk?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' 'For what reason?' 'Venerable Sir, I went forth desiring to be freed from suffering. My teacher gave a discourse on the Abhidhamma, and my preceptor gave a discourse on the Vinaya. I then thought: "Here, there is not even a place for me to stretch my hand. It is possible to be freed from suffering by being a layman. I shall become a layman." Thus, Venerable Sir, I made this resolution.' 'Monk, if you are able to guard just one thing, there is no need to guard the rest.' 'What is that, Venerable Sir?' 'Will you be able to guard your own mind?' 'I will be able, Venerable Sir.' 'In that case, guard your own mind. It is possible to be freed from suffering.' Having given this instruction, he spoke this verse:

36.

36.

“Sududdasaṃ [V 1.0171] sunipuṇaṃ, yatthakāmanipātinaṃ;

Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī, cittaṃ guttaṃ sukhāvaha”nti.

“Very hard to see, extremely subtle, flitting wherever it pleases—the mind. The wise one should guard the mind; a guarded mind brings happiness.”

Tattha [M 1.0191] sududdasanti [P 1.0300] suṭṭhu duddasaṃ. Sunipuṇanti suṭṭhu nipuṇaṃ paramasaṇhaṃ. Yatthakāmanipātinanti jātiādīni anoloketvā labhitabbālabhitabbayuttāyuttaṭṭhānesu yattha katthaci nipatanasīlaṃ. Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvīti andhabālo dummedho attano cittaṃ rakkhituṃ samattho nāma natthi, cittavasiko hutvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Medhāvī pana paṇḍitova cittaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkoti, tasmā tvampi cittameva gopehi. Idañhi cittaṃ guttaṃ sukhāvahaṃ maggaphalanibbānasukhāni āvahatīti.

Herein, “very hard to see” means exceedingly difficult to see. “Extremely subtle” means exceedingly subtle, supremely fine. “Flitting wherever it pleases” means having the nature of alighting wherever it may be, without regard for birth and other factors, in places that are obtainable or unobtainable, suitable or unsuitable. As for “The wise one should guard the mind”: a blind fool, one without wisdom, is by no means able to guard his own mind; being under the sway of the mind, he reaches misfortune and ruin. But indeed, only a wise person with penetrating insight is able to guard the mind. Therefore, you too should secure the mind. For this guarded mind brings happiness—it brings the happiness of the path, fruition, and Nibbāna.

Desanāpariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi, aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ, desanā mahājanassa sātthikā ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, that monk attained the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also became stream-enterers and so on. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly.

Aññataraukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuvatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Third Story of a Certain Discontented Monk.

4. Saṅgharakkhitabhāgineyyattheravatthu

4. The Story of the Elder, the Nephew of Saṅgharakkhita

Dūraṅgamanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto saṅgharakkhitaṃ nāma bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Dūraṅgamaṃ,' concerning a monk named Saṅgharakkhita.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nikkhamitvā pabbajito laddhūpasampado saṅgharakkhitatthero nāma hutvā katipāheneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa [P 1.0301] kaniṭṭhabhaginī puttaṃ labhitvā therassa nāmaṃ akāsi. So bhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhito nāma hutvā vayappatto therasseva santike pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado aññatarasmiṃ gāmakārāme vassaṃ upagantvā, “ekaṃ sattahatthaṃ, ekaṃ aṭṭhahattha”nti dve vassāvāsikasāṭake labhitvā aṭṭhahatthaṃ “upajjhāyassa me bhavissatī”ti sallakkhetvā “sattahatthaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā vuṭṭhavasso “upajjhāyaṃ passissāmī”ti āgacchanto antarāmagge piṇḍāya caranto āgantvā there vihāraṃ anāgateyeva vihāraṃ pavisitvā therassa divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā pādodakaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā āgamanamaggaṃ olokento nisīdi. Athassāgamanabhāvaṃ disvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā pattacīvaraṃ [M 1.0192] paṭiggahetvā, “nisīdatha, bhante”ti theraṃ nisīdāpetvā tālavaṇṭaṃ ādāya [V 1.0172] bījitvā pānīyaṃ datvā pāde dhovitvā taṃ sāṭakaṃ ānetvā pādamūle ṭhapetvā, “bhante, imaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti vatvā bījayamāno aṭṭhāsi.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain man of good family, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, went forth and was ordained. Having received the higher ordination, he became known as the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, and in just a few days, he reached Arahantship. His younger sister, having had a son, gave him the Elder's name. That nephew, named Saṅgharakkhita, having come of age, was ordained in the presence of that very Elder and, having received the higher ordination, entered the rains-residence in a certain village monastery. There, having received two rains-residence cloths, “one of seven cubits, one of eight cubits,” he designated the eight-cubit one, thinking, “It will be for my preceptor,” and thought, “The seven-cubit one will be for me.” Having completed the rains-residence, coming with the thought, “I will see my preceptor,” while wandering for alms on the way, he arrived. Even before the Elder arrived at the monastery, he entered the monastery, swept the Elder's day-quarters, set out water for the feet, prepared a seat, and sat watching the path of his arrival. Then, seeing his arrival, he went out to meet him, received his bowl and robe, and having seated the Elder, said, “Please be seated, venerable sir.” Taking a palm-leaf fan and fanning him, he offered drinking water, washed his feet, and brought that cloth. Placing it at the Elder's feet, he said, “Venerable sir, please use this,” and stood there fanning him.

Atha naṃ thero āha – “saṅgharakkhita, mayhaṃ cīvaraṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, tvameva paribhuñjā”ti. “Bhante, mayā laddhakālato paṭṭhāya ayaṃ tumhākameva sallakkhito, paribhogaṃ karothā”ti. “Hotu, saṅgharakkhita, paripuṇṇaṃ me cīvaraṃ, tvameva paribhuñjā”ti. “Bhante, mā evaṃ karotha, tumhehi paribhutte mayhaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Atha naṃ tassa punappunaṃ kathentassapi [P 1.0302] thero na icchiyeva.

Then the Elder said to him, “Saṅgharakkhita, my robes are sufficient; you yourself should use it.” “Venerable sir, from the time I received it, this has been intended only for you. Please make use of it.” “Be that as it may, Saṅgharakkhita, my robes are sufficient; you yourself should use it.” “Venerable sir, please do not do so. If it is used by you, it will be of great fruit to me.” Yet, although the nephew spoke to him again and again, the Elder would not consent.

Evaṃ so bījayamāno ṭhitova cintesi – “ahaṃ therassa gihikāle bhāgineyyo, pabbajitakāle saddhivihāriko, evampi mayā saddhiṃ upajjhāyo paribhogaṃ na kattukāmo. Imasmiṃ mayā saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ akaronte kiṃ me samaṇabhāvena, gihi bhavissāmī”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “dussaṇṭhāpito gharāvāso, kiṃ nu kho katvā gihibhūto jīvissāmī”ti. Tato cintesi – “aṭṭhahatthasāṭakaṃ vikkiṇitvā ekaṃ eḷikaṃ gaṇhissāmi, eḷikā nāma khippaṃ vijāyati, svāhaṃ vijātaṃ vijātaṃ vikkiṇitvā mūlaṃ karissāmi, mūle bahū katvā ekaṃ pajāpatiṃ ānessāmi, sā ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyissati. Athassa mama mātulassa nāmaṃ katvā cūḷayānake nisīdāpetvā mama puttañca bhariyañca ādāya mātulaṃ vandituṃ āgamissāmi, āgacchante antarāmagge mama bhariyaṃ evaṃ vakkhāmi – ‘ānehi tāva me puttaṃ vahissāmina’nti. Sā ‘kiṃ te puttena, ehi, imaṃ yānakaṃ pājehī’ti vatvā puttaṃ gahetvā, ‘ahaṃ nessāmi na’nti netvā sandhāretuṃ asakkontī cakkapathe chaḍḍessati. Athassa sarīraṃ abhiruhitvā cakkaṃ gamissati, atha naṃ ‘tvaṃ mama puttaṃ neva mayhaṃ adāsi, naṃ sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhi nāsitosmi tayā’ti vatvā patodayaṭṭhiyā piṭṭhiyaṃ paharissāmī”ti.

Thus, while standing there fanning, he thought: “In the Elder’s household life, I was his nephew; after ordination, I am his co-resident disciple. Even so, my preceptor does not wish to share its use with me. If he does not share its use with me, what is the use of my monkhood? I will become a layman.” Then this thought occurred to him: “The household life is difficult to establish. Having become a layman, what shall I do to make a living?” Then he thought: “I will sell the eight-cubit cloth and buy a she-goat. A she-goat gives birth quickly. I will sell each young one that is born and make capital. Having made much capital, I will take a wife. She will give birth to a son. Then, giving him my uncle's name, I will seat him in a small cart and, taking my son and wife, I will come to pay respects to my uncle. While coming on the way, I will say to my wife, ‘Bring my son first; I will carry him.’ She will say, ‘What is to be done with your son? Come, drive this cart.’ And taking the son, saying, ‘I will carry him,’ while carrying him, being unable to hold him firmly, she will drop him on the wheel-track. Then the wheel will run over his body. Then I will say to her, ‘You did not give me my son, nor were you able to hold him firmly; I am ruined by you,’ and I will strike her on the back with a goad-stick.”

So evaṃ cintentova ṭhatvā [P 1.0303] bījayamāno therassa sīse tālavaṇṭena pahari. Thero “kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ saṅgharakkhitena sīse pahato”ti [M 1.0193] upadhārento tena cintitacintitaṃ sabbaṃ ñatvā, “saṅgharakkhita, mātugāmassa pahāraṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhi, ko ettha mahallakattherassa doso”ti āha. So “aho naṭṭhomhi, ñātaṃ kira me upajjhāyena cintitacintitaṃ, kiṃ me samaṇabhāvenā”ti tālavaṇṭaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyituṃ āraddho.

Standing there and thinking thus, while fanning, he struck the Elder on the head with the palm-leaf fan. The Elder, investigating, “Why have I been struck on the head by Saṅgharakkhita?” and knowing all that had been thought by him, said, “Saṅgharakkhita, you were not able to give the woman a blow; in that, what fault is there of a great elder?” He thought, “Alas, I am ruined! It seems my preceptor has known my every thought! What use is my monkhood to me?” Then, throwing away the palm-leaf fan, he began to flee.

Atha naṃ daharā ca sāmaṇerā ca anubandhitvā ādāya satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā te [V 1.0173] bhikkhū disvāva “kiṃ, bhikkhave, āgatattha, eko vo bhikkhu laddho”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante, imaṃ daharaṃ ukkaṇṭhitvā palāyantaṃ gahetvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgatamhā”ti. “Evaṃ kira bhikkhū”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kimatthaṃ te bhikkhu evaṃ bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, nanu tvaṃ āraddhavīriyassa ekassa buddhassa putto, mādisassa nāma buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā attānaṃ dametvā sotāpannoti vā sakadāgāmīti vā anāgāmīti vā arahāti vā vadāpetuṃ nāsakkhi, kimatthaṃ evaṃ bhāriyaṃ kammamakāsī”ti? “Ukkaṇṭhitosmi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti? So evaṃ vassāvāsikasāṭakānaṃ laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva therassa tālavaṇṭena pahārā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā, “iminā kāraṇena palātosmi, bhante”ti [P 1.0304] āha. Atha naṃ satthā “ehi bhikkhu, mā cintayi cittaṃ nāmetaṃ dūre hontampi ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchanakajātikaṃ, rāgadosamohabandhanā muccanatthāya vāyamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then young monks and novices followed him, seized him, and went to the Teacher. As soon as the Teacher saw those monks, he asked, “Why, monks, have you come? Have you obtained a monk?” “Yes, venerable sir. We caught this young monk who was discontented and fleeing, and have brought him to your presence.” “Is that so, monk?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Why, monk, have you done such a weighty deed? Are you not the son of the one Buddha who has aroused effort? Having gone forth in the dispensation of a Buddha such as I, and having tamed yourself, were you not able to have yourself declared a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arahant? Why have you done such a weighty deed?” “I was discontented, venerable sir.” “For what reason were you discontented?” He then recounted the entire affair, starting from the day he received the rains-residence robes up to his striking the Elder with the palm-leaf fan, and said, “For this reason, venerable sir, I fled.” Then the Teacher said to him, “Come, monk, do not worry. This which is called 'mind' is of a nature to receive an object even when it is far away. It is fitting to strive for liberation from the bonds of greed, hatred, and delusion.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

37.

37.

“Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ, asarīraṃ guhāsayaṃ;

Ye cittaṃ saṃyamessanti, mokkhanti mārabandhanā”ti.

“Far-ranging, solitary, formless, dwelling in a cave—those who restrain this mind will be liberated from the bonds of Māra.”

Tattha dūraṅgamanti cittassa hi makkaṭasuttamattakampi puratthimādidisābhāgena gamanāgamanaṃ nāma natthi, dūre santampi pana ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchatīti dūraṅgamaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Sattaṭṭhacittāni pana ekato kaṇṇikabaddhāni ekakkhaṇe uppajjituṃ samatthāni nāma natthi. Uppattikāle ekekameva cittaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ niruddhe puna ekekameva uppajjatīti ekacaraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Cittassa sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ vā nīlādippakāro vaṇṇabhedo vā natthīti asarīraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Guhā nāma catumahābhūtaguhā, idañca hadayarūpaṃ nissāya pavattatīti guhāsayaṃ [M 1.0194] nāma jātaṃ. Ye cittanti ye keci purisā vā itthiyo vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā anuppajjanakakilesassa uppajjituṃ adentā satisammosena uppannakilesaṃ pajahantā cittaṃ saṃyamessanti saṃyataṃ avikkhittaṃ karissanti. Mokkhanti mārabandhanāti [P 1.0305] sabbete kilesabandhanābhāvena mārabandhanasaṅkhātā tebhūmakavaṭṭā muccissantīti.

Herein, as to 'far-ranging': for the mind, there is no such thing as coming and going to regions in the eastern direction and so on, even for the duration of a monkey's sleep. But it receives an object that exists even when it is far away; therefore, it comes to be called 'far-ranging'. Furthermore, seven or eight minds are not able to arise together in a single moment, bound like the pericarp of a lotus. At the time of arising, only one mind arises at a time; when that has ceased, again only one arises. Therefore, it comes to be called 'solitary'. The mind has no bodily form or distinction of color, such as blue, etc.; therefore, it comes to be called 'formless'. The 'cave' means the cave of the four great elements, and this mind occurs depending on the heart-basis; therefore, it comes to be called 'dwelling in a cave'. As to 'those who... the mind': whoever—whether men or women, householders or renunciants—not giving an opportunity for an unarisen defilement to arise and abandoning defilements that have arisen due to a lapse of mindfulness, will restrain the mind, that is, they will make it restrained and undistracted. As to 'they are liberated from the bonds of Māra': all of them will be liberated from the round of the three planes, which is designated as the bonds of Māra, through the absence of the bonds of defilements.

Desanāpariyosāne bhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitatthero sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi, aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo jātā, mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also became stream-enterers and so on. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial to the great multitude.

Saṅgharakkhitabhāgineyyattheravatthu catutthaṃ.

The fourth story, concerning the Elder who was the nephew of Saṅgharakkhita, is concluded.

5. Cittahatthattheravatthu

5. The Story of the Elder Cittahattha

Anavaṭṭhitacittassāti [V 1.0174] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto cittahatthattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in Sāvatthī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words 'Anavaṭṭhitacittassa,' concerning the Elder Cittahattha.

Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto naṭṭhagoṇaṃ pariyesanto araññaṃ pavisitvā majjhanhike kāle goṇaṃ disvā goyūthe vissajjetvā, “avassaṃ ayyānaṃ santike āhāramattaṃ labhissāmī”ti khuppipāsāpīḷito vihāraṃ pavisitvā bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye bhikkhūnaṃ avakkārapātiyaṃ bhuttāvasesakaṃ bhattaṃ hoti, te taṃ chātakapīḷitaṃ disvā, “ito bhattaṃ gahetvā bhuñjāhī”ti vadiṃsu. Buddhakāle ca pana anekasūpabyañjanaṃ bhattaṃ uppajjati, so tato yāpanamattaṃ [P 1.0306] gahetvā bhuñjitvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā hatthe dhovitvā bhikkhū vanditvā, “kiṃ, bhante, ajja, ayyā, nimantanaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsū”ti pucchi. “Natthi, upāsaka, bhikkhū imināva nīhārena nibaddhaṃ labhantī”ti. So “mayaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya rattindivaṃ nibaddhaṃ kammaṃ karontāpi evaṃ madhurabyañjanaṃ bhattaṃ na labhāma, ime kira nibaddhaṃ bhuñjanti, kiṃ me gihibhāvena, bhikkhu bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Atha naṃ bhikkhū “sādhu upāsakā”ti pabbājesuṃ.

It is said that a certain man of good family, a resident of Sāvatthī, while searching for a lost ox, entered the forest. At midday, having seen the ox, he released it into the herd of cattle. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, and thinking, 'Surely, I might get at least some leftover food in the presence of the noble ones,' he entered the monastery, approached the monks, paid homage, and sat down at a suitable place. Now at that time, there was leftover rice in the monks' refuse bowl. Seeing him afflicted by hunger, they said, 'Take rice from here and eat.' Now, during the time of a Buddha, food with many curries and condiments arises. He took just enough from there to sustain himself, ate, drank water, washed his hands, paid homage to the monks, and asked, 'Venerable sirs, did the noble ones go to a place of invitation today?' 'No, lay supporter. The monks regularly receive alms in this very manner.' He thought, 'We, having arisen and striven, working constantly day and night, do not get such food with delicious curries, but it seems these monks eat it regularly. What is the use to me of the household life? I will become a monk.' Having thought thus, he approached the monks and requested the going forth. Then the monks, saying, 'It is good, lay supporter,' gave him the going forth.

So [M 1.0195] laddhūpasampado sabbappakāraṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ akāsi. So buddhānaṃ uppannena lābhasakkārena katipāhaccayena thūlasarīro ahosi. Tato cintesi – “kiṃ me bhikkhāya caritvā jīvitena, gihī bhavissāmī”ti. So vibbhamitvā gehaṃ pāvisi. Tassa gehe kammaṃ karontassa katipāheneva sarīraṃ milāyi. Tato “kiṃ me iminā dukkhena, samaṇo bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā puna gantvā pabbaji. So katipāhaṃ vītināmetvā puna ukkaṇṭhitvā vibbhami, pabbajitakāle pana bhikkhūnaṃ upakārako hoti. So katipāheneva punapi ukkaṇṭhitvā, “kiṃ me gihibhāvena, pabbajissāmī”ti gantvā bhikkhū vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Atha naṃ bhikkhū upakāravasena puna pabbājayiṃsu. Evaṃ so iminā niyāmeneva chakkhattuṃ pabbajitvā uppabbajito. Tassa bhikkhū “esa cittavasiko hutvā vicaratī”ti cittahatthattheroti nāmaṃ kariṃsu.

Having received the higher ordination, he performed all kinds of major and minor duties. Due to the gain and honor that arose for the Buddhas, after only a few days, his body became stout. Then he thought, 'What is the use to me of this life of wandering for alms? I will become a householder.' He disrobed and entered his house. While he was working at home, in just a few days his body withered. Then, thinking, 'What is the use to me of this suffering? I will become a recluse,' he went again and went forth. After passing a few days, he again became dissatisfied and disrobed. However, when he was ordained, he was helpful to the monks. After just a few days, he again became dissatisfied and, thinking, 'What is the use to me of the household life? I will go forth,' he went, paid homage to the monks, and requested the going forth. Then the monks, on account of his helpfulness, gave him the going forth again. Thus, in this very way, he went forth and disrobed six times. The monks, thinking, 'This one wanders, being under the control of his mind,' gave him the name Cittahatthatthera.

Tassevaṃ aparāparaṃ vicarantasseva bhariyā gabbhinī ahosi. So sattame vāre araññato kasibhaṇḍamādāya [P 1.0307] gehaṃ gantvā bhaṇḍakaṃ ṭhapetvā “attano kāsāvaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti gabbhaṃ pāvisi[V 1.0175]. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tassa bhariyā nipajjitvā niddāyati. Tassā nivatthasāṭako apagato hoti, mukhato ca lālā paggharati, nāsā ghuraghurāyati, mukhaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ, dantaṃ ghaṃsati, sā tassa uddhumātakasarīraṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi. So “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ ida”nti saññaṃ labhitvā, “ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ pabbajitvā imaṃ nissāya bhikkhubhāve saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi”nti kāsāyakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā udare bandhitvā gehā nikkhami.

While he was thus repeatedly wandering back and forth, his wife became pregnant. On the seventh occasion, taking a farming implement from the field and going to the house, he put down the tool and, thinking, 'I will take my ochre robe,' entered the inner room. At that moment, his wife was lying down and sleeping. Her lower garment had slipped off, saliva was flowing from her mouth, her nose was snoring, her mouth was open, and she was grinding her teeth. She appeared to him like a bloated corpse. Gaining the perception, 'This is impermanent, this is suffering,' he thought, 'Having gone forth for so long, because of this woman I have been unable to establish myself in the state of a monk.' Taking the edge of his ochre robe and tying it around his belly, he left the house.

Athassa anantaragehe ṭhitā sassu taṃ tathā gacchantaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ paṭiukkaṇṭhito bhavissati, idāneva araññato āgantvā kāsāvaṃ udare bandhitvāva gehā nikkhanto vihārābhimukho gacchati, kiṃ nu kho”ti gehaṃ pavisitvā niddāyamānaṃ dhītaraṃ passitvā “imaṃ disvā so vippaṭisārī hutvā gato”ti ñatvā dhītaraṃ paharitvā “uṭṭhehi kāḷakaṇṇi, sāmiko te taṃ niddāyamānaṃ disvā vippaṭisārī hutvā gato, natthi so ito paṭṭhāya tuyha”nti āha. “Apehi apehi, amma, kuto tassa gamanaṃ atthi, katipāheneva punāgamissatī”ti āha. Sopi “aniccaṃ dukkha”nti vatvā [P 1.0308] gacchanto gacchantova sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. So [M 1.0196] gantvā bhikkhū vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. “Na sakkhissāma maṃyaṃ taṃ pabbājetuṃ, kuto tuyhaṃ samaṇabhāvo, satthakanisānapāsāṇasadisaṃ tava sīsa”nti. “Bhante, idāni maṃ anukampāya ekavāraṃ pabbājethā”ti. Te taṃ upakāravasena pabbājayiṃsu. So katipāheneva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then his mother-in-law, who was in the next house, seeing him going in that manner, thought, 'This one must be disaffected again. Just now he came from the field, and having tied the ochre robe around his belly, he has left the house and is going facing the monastery. What could be the reason?' Entering the house and seeing her daughter sleeping, and knowing, 'Seeing her, he has become remorseful and has gone,' she struck her daughter and said, 'Get up, you wretched one! Your husband, seeing you sleeping, became remorseful and has gone. From this day on, he is no longer yours.' She replied, 'Go away, go away, mother! How long will his going last? In just a few days, he will come again.' He too, saying, 'Impermanent, suffering,' attained the fruit of stream-entry even as he was walking along. He went, paid homage to the monks, and requested the going forth. 'We will not be able to give you the going forth,' they said. 'How could there be the state of a recluse for you? Your head is like a whetstone for razors.' He pleaded, 'Venerable sirs, now, out of compassion, please give me the going forth just this one time.' They, on account of his helpfulness, gave him the going forth. In just a few days, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Tepi naṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso cittahattha, tava gamanasamayaṃ tvameva jāneyyāsi, imasmiṃ vāre te cirāyita”nti. “Bhante, saṃsaggassa atthibhāvakāle gatamhā, so no saṃsaggo chinno, idāni agamanadhammā jātamhā”ti. Bhikkhū satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu amhehi evaṃ vutto evaṃ nāma kathesi, aññaṃ byākaroti, abhūtaṃ vadatī”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā “āma, bhikkhave, mama putto attano anavaṭṭhitacittakāle saddhammaṃ ajānanakāle gamanāgamanaṃ akāsi, idānissa puññañca pāpañca pahīna”nti vatvā imā dve gāthā āha –

They too said to him, 'Friend Cittahattha, you yourself would know the time for your departure. This time you have delayed long.' 'Venerable sirs, I went when there was a state of association. That association of ours is now cut off. Now I have become one whose nature is not to go.' The monks went to the Teacher and said, 'Venerable sir, this monk, when spoken to by us in this way, said such-and-such. He declares the final knowledge. He speaks what is not true.' The Teacher said, 'Yes, monks. My son, during the time when his mind was unestablished and he did not know the true Dhamma, he did his coming and going. Now for him both merit and demerit are abandoned.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

38.

38.

“Anavaṭṭhitacittassa, saddhammaṃ avijānato;

Pariplavapasādassa, paññā na paripūrati.

For one with an unestablished mind, who does not know the true Dhamma, whose confidence is wavering, wisdom is not fulfilled.

39.

39.

“Anavassutacittassa, ananvāhatacetaso;

Puññapāpapahīnassa, natthi jāgarato bhaya”nti.

For one whose mind is not drenched by lust, whose mind is not struck by aversion, who has abandoned merit and demerit, there is no fear for one who is awake.

Tattha [V 1.0176] anavaṭṭhitacittassāti cittaṃ nāmetaṃ kassaci nibaddhaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā natthi. Yo pana puggalo assapiṭṭhe [P 1.0309] ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍaṃ viya ca thusarāsimhi koṭṭitakhāṇuko viya ca khallāṭasīse ṭhapitakadambapupphaṃ viya ca na katthaci saṇṭhāti, kadāci buddhasāvako hoti, kadāci ājīvako, kadāci nigaṇṭho, kadāci tāpaso. Evarūpo puggalo anavaṭṭhitacitto nāma. Tassa anavaṭṭhitacittassa. Saddhammaṃ avijānatoti sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammabhedaṃ imaṃ saddhammaṃ avijānantassa parittasaddhatāya vā uplavasaddhatāya vā pariplavapasādassa kāmāvacararūpāvacarādibhedā paññā na paripūrati. Kāmāvacarāyapi aparipūrayamānāya kutova rūpāvacarārūpāvacaralokuttarapaññā paripūrissatīti dīpeti. Anavassutacittassāti rāgena atintacittassa. Ananvāhatacetasoti “āhatacitto khilajāto”ti [M 1.0197] (dī. ni. 3.319; vibha. 941; ma. ni. 1.185) āgataṭṭhāne dosena cittassa pahatabhāvo vutto, idha pana dosena appaṭihatacittassāti attho. Puññapāpapahīnassāti catutthamaggena pahīnapuññassa ceva pahīnapāpassa ca khīṇāsavassa. Natthi jāgarato bhayanti khīṇāsavassa jāgarantasseva abhayabhāvo kathito viya. So pana saddhādīhi pañcahi jāgaradhammehi samannāgatattā jāgaro [P 1.0310] nāma. Tasmā tassa jāgarantassāpi ajāgarantassāpi kilesabhayaṃ natthi kilesānaṃ apacchāvattanato. Na hi taṃ kilesā anubandhanti tena tena maggena pahīnānaṃ kilesānaṃ puna anupagamanato. Tenevāha – “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchati, sakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattamaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatī”ti (cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 27).

Here, 'one with an unsteady mind' means that the mind is not fixed or stable for anyone. A person whose mind does not settle anywhere—like a pot placed on a horse’s back, a pestle pounded into a heap of chaff, or a kadamba flower placed on a bald head—sometimes becomes a disciple of the Buddha, sometimes an Ājīvaka, sometimes a Jain, sometimes a hermit. Such a person is called one with an unsteady mind. For one with an unsteady mind, 'not understanding the true Dhamma' means that due to weak faith or wavering conviction, their wisdom does not fully develop regarding this true Dhamma, which consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. If wisdom does not mature even in the sense-sphere, how much less so will wisdom in the form-sphere, formless-sphere, or supramundane realms mature? 'One with an unmoistened mind' means a mind not moistened by lust. 'One whose mind is unassailed': in the passage where it says, 'a mind struck, hardened,' the state of the mind being struck by aversion is spoken of; here, however, the meaning is a mind not struck by aversion. 'One who has abandoned merit and demerit' refers to an Arahant who has abandoned both merit and demerit through the fourth path. 'There is no fear for one who is wakeful': it is as if the absence of fear for an Arahant who is indeed awake is spoken of. That one, however, is called 'awake' because they are endowed with the five qualities of wakefulness beginning with faith. Therefore, for that one, whether awake or not, there is no fear of defilements, because the defilements do not return. Indeed, the defilements do not pursue that one, because the defilements abandoned by the respective paths do not approach again. For this reason, it is said: 'The defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry do not return, do not come back. The defilements abandoned by the paths of once-returning, non-returning, and Arahantship do not return, do not come back.'

Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā saphalā ahosi.

The teaching was beneficial and fruitful for the great multitude.

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “bhāriyā vatime, āvuso, kilesā nāma, evarūpassa arahattassa upanissāyasampanno kulaputto kilesehi āloḷito sattavāre gihī hutvā sattavāre pabbajito”ti. Satthā tesaṃ taṃ kathāpavattiṃ sutvā taṅkhaṇānurūpena gamanena dhammasabhaṃ gantvā buddhāsane nisinno “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte evameva, bhikkhave, kilesā nāma bhāriyā, sace ete rūpino hutvā katthaci pakkhipituṃ sakkā bhaveyyuṃ, cakkavāḷaṃ atisambādhaṃ, brahmaloko atinīcakoti okāso nesaṃ na bhaveyya, mādisampi nāmete paññāsampannaṃ purisājāneyyaṃ āloḷenti, avasesesu kā kathā? “Ahañhi aḍḍhanāḷimattaṃ varakacorakaṃ [P 1.0311] kuṇṭhakudālañca nissāya [V 1.0177] cha vāre pabbajitvā uppabbajitapubbo”ti. “Kadā, bhante, kadā sugatā”ti? “Suṇissatha, bhikkhave”ti. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Tena hi suṇāthā”ti atītaṃ āhari –

Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Truly, friends, these defilements are burdensome. A clansman endowed with strong supporting conditions for Arahantship, agitated by defilements, has been a householder seven times and gone forth seven times." The Teacher, hearing of their discussion, went to the Dhamma hall in a manner appropriate to that moment. Seated on the Buddha’s seat, he asked, "Monks, what discussion were you engaged in just now?" When they told him, he said, "Indeed, monks, defilements are burdensome. If these defilements had material form and could be placed somewhere, the cosmos would be too constricted, the Brahma-world too low—there would be no space for them. They agitate even one like me, a thoroughbred man endowed with wisdom. What need be said of others? For my part, relying on a mere half-nāḷi measure of varaka grain and a blunt hoe, I went forth and relapsed six times." "Venerable sir, when was this, O Well-gone One?" "Will you listen, monks?" "Yes, Venerable sir." "Then listen," and he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kudālapaṇḍito nāma bāhirakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭha māse himavante vasitvā vassārattasamaye bhūmiyā tintāya “gehe me aḍḍhanāḷimatto varakacorako ca kuṇṭhakudālako [M 1.0198] ca atthi, varakacorakabījaṃ mā nassī”ti uppabbajitvā ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ kudālena kasitvā taṃ bījaṃ vapitvā vatiṃ katvā pakkakāle uddharitvā nāḷimattabījaṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ khādi. So “kiṃ me dāni gehena, puna aṭṭha māse pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā nikkhamitvā pabbaji. Imināva nīhārena nāḷimattaṃ varakacorakañca kuṇṭhakudālañca nissāya sattavāre gihī hutvā sattavāre pabbajitvā sattame pana vāre cintesi – “ahaṃ cha vāre imaṃ kuṇṭhakudālaṃ nissāya gihī hutvā pabbajito, katthacideva naṃ chaḍḍessāmī”ti. So gaṅgāya tīraṃ gantvā, “patitaṭṭhānaṃ passanto otaritvā gaṇheyyaṃ, yathāssa patitaṭṭhānaṃ na passāmi, tathā naṃ chaḍḍessāmī”ti cintetvā nāḷimattaṃ bījaṃ pilotikāya bandhitvā pilotikaṃ kudālaphalake bandhitvā kudālaṃ aggadaṇḍake gahetvā gaṅgāya tīre ṭhito akkhīni nimīletvā uparisīse tikkhattuṃ āvijjhitvā gaṅgāyaṃ khipitvā [P 1.0312] nivattitvā olokento patitaṭṭhānaṃ adisvā “jitaṃ me, jitaṃ me”ti tikkhattuṃ saddamakāsi.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a wise man named Kudālapaṇḍita took up the life of an external ascetic. After living in the Himalayas for eight months, when the ground was soaked during the rainy season, he thought, "In my house, I have half a nāḷi measure of varaka grain and a blunt hoe. May the varaka grain seeds not perish!" So he relapsed from the ascetic life, dug a spot with the hoe, sowed the seeds, fenced it off, and when the time came, he harvested them. He kept a nāḷi measure of seeds and ate the rest. He thought, "What use is a household life to me now? I will go forth again for eight months," and so he left and became an ascetic again. By this very means, relying on the nāḷi measure of varaka grain and the blunt hoe, he became a householder seven times and went forth seven times. But on the seventh occasion, he thought, "I have relied on this blunt hoe to become a householder and go forth six times. Now I must discard it somewhere." He went to the bank of the Ganges and thought, "If I see where it falls, I might go down and retrieve it. I will discard it in such a way that I do not see where it falls." So he tied the nāḷi measure of seeds in a piece of cloth, tied the cloth to the hoe's blade, held the hoe by the end of the handle, stood on the riverbank, closed his eyes, whirled it three times above his head, and threw it into the Ganges. Turning back to look, he did not see where it had fallen. Then he shouted three times, "I have won! I have won!"

Tasmiṃ khaṇe bārāṇasirājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā āgantvā nadītīre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsetvā nhānatthāya nadiṃ otiṇṇo taṃ saddaṃ assosi. Rājūnañca nāma “jitaṃ me”ti saddo amanāpo hoti, so tassa santikaṃ gantvā, “ahaṃ idāni amittamaddanaṃ katvā ‘jitaṃ me’ti āgato, tvaṃ pana ‘jitaṃ me, jitaṃ me’ti viravasi, kiṃ nāmeta”nti pucchi. Kudālapaṇḍito “tvaṃ bāhirakacore jini, tayā jitaṃ puna avajitameva hoti, mayā pana ajjhattiko lobhacoro jito, so puna maṃ na jinissati, tasseva jayo sādhū”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the king of Benares, having pacified the frontier and returned, set up camp on the riverbank and entered the river to bathe when he heard that sound. Now, for kings, the sound “Victory is mine!” is unpleasant. So he approached him and asked, “I have just returned after crushing my enemies, proclaiming ‘Victory is mine!’ But you shout ‘Victory is mine, victory is mine!’—what is this?” Kudālapaṇḍita replied, “You conquer external thieves, but what is conquered by you becomes unconquered again. I, however, have conquered the inner thief of greed, and he will not conquer me again. That victory alone is excellent.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

“Na taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ avajīyati;

Taṃ kho jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ nāvajīyatī”ti. (jā. 1.1.70);

“That victory is not well won which can be won back again; but that victory is well won which, once won, cannot be won back again.”

Taṃ khaṇaṃyeva ca gaṅgaṃ olokento āpokasiṇaṃ nibbattetvā adhigataviseso ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdi. Rājā mahāpurisassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā saddhiṃ balakāyena [V 1.0178] pabbaji. Yojanamattā parisā ahosi. Aparopi sāmantarājā tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā, “tassa rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āgantvā tathā samiddhaṃ nagaraṃ [M 1.0199] suññaṃ disvā, “evarūpaṃ nagaraṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajito rājā orake ṭhāne na pabbajissati, mayāpi pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā tattha gantvā mahāpurisaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā saparivāro pabbaji. Eteneva nīhārena satta rājāno pabbajiṃsu. Sattayojaniko assamo ahosi. Satta rājāno bhoge [P 1.0313] chaḍḍetvā ettakaṃ janaṃ gahetvā pabbajiṃsu. Mahāpuriso brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasitvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

At that very moment, gazing at the Ganges, he developed the water-kasiṇa and, having attained a special distinction, sat cross-legged in the sky. The king, having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, paid homage and requested ordination, then went forth along with his army. The assembly was about a yojana in extent. Another neighboring king, hearing of his renunciation and thinking, “I shall seize his kingdom,” came and saw the prosperous city was now empty. He reflected, “Having abandoned such a city, the king would not have renounced for some inferior state. It is fitting for me to renounce as well.” So he went there, approached the Great Being, requested ordination, and went forth with his retinue. In this same way, seven kings went forth. The hermitage was seven yojanas in extent. The seven kings, having abandoned their wealth, took this many people and went forth. The Great Being, having lived the holy life, became one destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā, “ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tadā kudālapaṇḍito ahosiṃ, kilesā nāmete evaṃ bhāriyā”ti āha.

The Teacher, having presented this Dhamma discourse, said: 'Bhikkhus, at that time I was Kudālapaṇḍita. These defilements were indeed so burdensome.'

Cittahatthattheravatthu pañcamaṃ.

The fifth story: that of the Elder Cittahattha.

6. Pañcasatabhikkhuvatthu

6. The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus

Kumbhūpamanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto āraddhavipassake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Kumbhūpamaṃ' in reference to monks who had commenced insight meditation.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira pañcasatā bhikkhū satthu santike yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā, “samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmā”ti yojanasatamaggaṃ gantvā ekaṃ mahāvāsagāmaṃ agamaṃsu. Atha te manussā disvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā paṇītehi yāgubhattādīhi parivisitvā, “kahaṃ, bhante, gacchathā”ti pucchitvā, “yathāphāsukaṭṭhāna”nti vutte, “bhante, imaṃ temāsaṃ idheva vasatha, mayampi tumhākaṃ santike saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya pañca sīlāni rakkhissāmā”ti yācitvā tesaṃ adhivāsanaṃ viditvā, “avidūre ṭhāne mahanto vanasaṇḍo atthi, ettha vasatha, bhante”ti vatvā uyyojesuṃ. Bhikkhū taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe adhivatthā devatā “sīlavanto, ayyā, imaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ [P 1.0314] anuppattā, ayuttaṃ kho pana asmākaṃ ayyesu idha vasantesu puttadāre gahetvā rukkhe abhiruyha vasitu”nti rukkhato otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ nisīditvā cintayiṃsu, “ayyā, imasmiṃ ṭhāne ajjekarattiṃ vasitvā addhā sve gamissantī”ti. Bhikkhūpi punadivase antogāme piṇḍāya caritvā puna tameva vanasaṇḍaṃ āgamiṃsu. Devatā “bhikkhusaṅgho [V 1.0179] svātanāya kenaci nimantito bhavissati, tasmā punāgacchati[M 1.0200], ajja gamanaṃ na bhavissati, sve gamissati maññe”ti iminā upāyena aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ bhūmiyameva acchiṃsu.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, five hundred bhikkhus received a meditation subject from the Teacher leading up to Arahantship. Thinking, 'We will practice the recluse's duty,' they traveled a distance of one hundred yojanas and arrived at a large village. Then the people, seeing them, had them sit on prepared seats and served them with excellent rice-gruel, boiled rice, and other foods. Having asked, 'Venerable sirs, where are you going?' and being told, 'To a suitable place,' they requested, 'Venerable sirs, please dwell right here for this three-month rains retreat. We too, in your presence, will establish ourselves in the refuges and observe the five precepts.' Knowing their consent, they said, 'There is a large forest grove in a place not far from here. Venerable sirs, please dwell there,' and sent them on their way. The bhikkhus entered that forest grove. The deities dwelling in that forest grove thought, 'Virtuous noble ones have arrived in this forest grove. While the noble ones are dwelling here, it is indeed not proper for us to take our sons and wives, climb the trees, and dwell there.' Descending from the trees and sitting on the ground, they thought, 'The noble ones, having dwelt in this place for one night today, will surely depart tomorrow.' The bhikkhus, on the next day, after going for alms in the village, returned again to that very forest grove. The deities thought, 'The community of bhikkhus has likely been invited by someone for tomorrow; therefore, they have returned. Their departure will not happen today. We think they will depart tomorrow.' By this reasoning, they remained on the ground for about half a month.

Tato cintayiṃsu – “bhadantā imaṃ temāsaṃ idheva maññe vasissanti, idheva kho pana imesu vasantesu amhākaṃ rukkhe abhiruhitvā nisīditumpi na yuttaṃ, temāsaṃ puttadāre gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ nisīdanaṭṭhānānipi dukkhāni, kiñci katvā ime bhikkhū palāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tā tesu tesu rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu ceva caṅkamanakoṭīsu ca chinnasīsāni kabandhāni dassetuṃ amanussasaddañca bhāvetuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Bhikkhūnaṃ khipitakāsādayo rogā pavattiṃsu. Te aññamaññaṃ “tuyhaṃ, āvuso, kiṃ rujjatī”ti pucchantā, “mayhaṃ khipitarogo, mayhaṃ kāso”ti vatvā, “āvuso, ahaṃ ajja caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ chinnasīsaṃ addasaṃ, ahaṃ rattiṭṭhāne kabandhaṃ addasaṃ[P 1.0315], ahaṃ divāṭṭhāne amanussasaddaṃ assosiṃ, parivajjetabbayuttakamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ, amhākaṃ idha aphāsukaṃ ahosi, satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti nikkhamitvā anupubbena satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Then they thought: 'We think the venerable sirs will dwell right here for this three-month rains retreat. Indeed, while they are dwelling right here, it is not proper for us to climb the trees and sit. For three months, taking our sons and wives, the places to sit on the ground are also uncomfortable. It is right to do something to make these bhikkhus flee.' Those deities began to show severed heads and headless trunks in the various places for relieving oneself by night and day and at the ends of the walking paths, and to cause inhuman sounds to be heard. Illnesses such as sneezing and coughing arose for the bhikkhus. Asking one another, 'Friend, what afflicts you?' and saying, 'I have an illness of sneezing,' 'I have a cough,' they also said: 'Friend, today at the end of the walking path I saw a severed head. I saw a headless trunk at the place for relieving oneself by night. I heard an inhuman sound at the place for relieving oneself by day. This place is one that should be avoided. It has become uncomfortable for us here. Let us go to the Teacher’s presence.' Having departed, they went in due course to the Teacher’s presence, paid homage, and sat down to one side.

Atha ne satthā āha – “kiṃ, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkhissathā”ti? “Āma, bhante, amhākaṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ evarūpāni bheravārammaṇāni upaṭṭhahanti, evarūpaṃ aphāsukaṃ hoti, tena mayaṃ ‘vajjetabbayuttakamidaṃ ṭhāna’nti taṃ chaḍḍetvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgatā”ti. “Bhikkhave, tattheva tumhākaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Na sakkā, bhante”ti. “Bhikkhave, tumhe āvudhaṃ aggahetvā gatā, idāni āvudhaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti. “Katarāvudhaṃ, bhante”ti? Satthā “ahaṃ āvudhaṃ vo dassāmi, mayā dinnaṃ āvudhaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti vatvā –

Then the Teacher said to them: 'Why, bhikkhus, were you not able to dwell in that place?' 'Yes, venerable sir. For us dwelling in that place, such terrifying objects appear, and such discomfort occurs. Therefore, thinking, "This place is one that should be avoided," we abandoned it and have come to your presence.' 'Bhikkhus, it is right for you to go to that very place.' 'It is not possible, venerable sir.' 'Bhikkhus, you went without taking a weapon. Now, taking a weapon, go.' 'What weapon, venerable sir?' The Teacher said, 'I will give you a weapon. Taking the weapon given by me, go'—

“Karaṇīyamatthakusalena, yanta santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca;

Sakko ujū ca suhujū ca, suvaco cassa mudu anatimānī”ti. (khu. pā. 9.1; su. ni. 143) –

This is what should be done by one skilled in the good, having comprehended the state of peace: one should be capable, upright, and exceedingly upright, amenable to correction, gentle, and not arrogant.

Sakalaṃ mettasuttaṃ kathetvā, “bhikkhave, imaṃ tumhe bahi vihārassa vanasaṇḍato paṭṭhāya sajjhāyantā antovihāraṃ paviseyyāthā”ti uyyojesi. Te satthāraṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā anupubbena taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā bahivihāre gaṇasajjhāyaṃ katvā sajjhāyamānā vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisiṃsu. Sakalavanasaṇḍe devatā mettacittaṃ paṭilabhitvā tesaṃ paccuggamanaṃ katvā pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇaṃ [M 1.0201] āpucchiṃsu, hatthapādasambāhanaṃ [P 1.0316] āpucchiṃsu, tesaṃ tattha tattha ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu, pakkadhūpanatelaṃ [V 1.0180] viya sannisinnā ahesuṃ. Katthaci amanussasaddo nāma nāhosi. Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi. Te rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu nisinnā vipassanāya cittaṃ otāretvā attani khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā, “ayaṃ attabhāvo nāma bhijjanakaṭṭhena athāvaraṭṭhena kulālabhājanasadiso”ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu. Sammāsambuddho gandhakuṭiyā nisinnova tesaṃ vipassanāya āraddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā te bhikkhū āmantetvā, “evameva, bhikkhave, ayaṃ attabhāvo nāma bhijjanakaṭṭhena athāvaraṭṭhena kulālabhājanasadiso evā”ti vatvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā yojanasate ṭhitopi abhimukhe nisinno viya chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjetvā dissamānena rūpena imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having taught the entire Metta Sutta, he sent them off, saying, 'Bhikkhus, starting from the forest grove outside the monastery, you should enter the monastery while reciting this.' They paid homage to the Teacher, departed, and in due course arrived at that place. Having performed a group recitation outside the monastery, they entered the forest grove while reciting. The deities in the entire forest grove, having gained minds of loving-kindness, went out to meet them, asked to take their bowls and robes, asked to massage their hands and feet, and arranged protection for them in various places. They became still, like oil that has been boiled and settled. Nowhere was there any sound of non-humans. The minds of those bhikkhus became concentrated. They, sitting in the places for relieving oneself by night and day, directed their minds to insight, established within themselves the contemplation of decay and dissolution, and developed insight, thinking, 'This individual existence, by its nature of breaking up and its instability, is like an unbaked potter's vessel.' The Fully Enlightened One, while sitting in the perfumed chamber, knowing that their practice of insight had commenced, addressed those bhikkhus. Having said, 'Even so, bhikkhus, this individual existence, by its nature of breaking up and its instability, is indeed like an unbaked potter's vessel,' he suffused the area with an effulgence. Though he was a hundred yojanas away, appearing as if sitting before them, he emitted the six-colored rays, and with his visible form, he spoke this verse:

40.

40.

“Kumbhūpamaṃ kāyamiṃma viditvā, nagarūpamaṃ cittamidaṃ ṭhapetvā;

Yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena, jitañca rakkhe anivesano siyā”ti.

Knowing this body to be like an earthen pot, establishing this mind like a fortified city, one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom. One should guard what has been conquered and be without attachment.

Tattha kumbhūpamanti abaladubbalaṭṭhena anaddhaniyatāvakālikaṭṭhena imaṃ kesādisamūhasaṅkhātaṃ [P 1.0317] kāyaṃ kumbhūpamaṃ kulālabhājanasadisaṃ viditvā. Nagarūpamaṃ cittamidaṃ ṭhapetvāti nagaraṃ nāma bahiddhā thiraṃ hoti, gambhīraparikhaṃ pākāraparikkhittaṃ dvāraṭṭālakayuttaṃ, antosuvibhattavīthicatukkasiṅghāṭakasampannaṃ antarāpaṇaṃ, taṃ “vilumpissāmā”ti bahiddhā corā āgantvā pavisituṃ asakkontā pabbataṃ āsajja paṭihatā viya gacchanti, evameva paṇḍito kulaputto attano vipassanācittaṃ thiraṃ nagarasadisaṃ katvā ṭhapetvā nagare ṭhito ekatodhārādinānappakārāvudhena coragaṇaṃ viya vipassanāmayena ca ariyamaggamayena ca paññāvudhena taṃtaṃmaggavajjhaṃ kilesamāraṃ paṭibāhanto taṃ taṃ kilesamāraṃ yodhetha, pahareyyāthāti attho. Jitañca rakkheti jitañca uppāditaṃ taruṇavipassanaṃ āvāsasappāyautusappāyabhojanasappāyapuggalasappāyadhammassavanasappāyādīni āsevanto antarantarā samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya suddhacittena saṅkhāre sammasanto rakkheyya.

Herein, 'like a pot' means: having understood this body—designated as a collection of hair and the like—to be like an unfired potter's vessel, on account of its being powerless and weak, and on account of its being not long-lasting and temporary. 'Having established this mind like a city' means: a city is sturdy on the outside, has a deep moat, is surrounded by a rampart, and is endowed with gate-towers; inside, it is complete with well-divided streets, crossroads, and an inner market. When robbers from the outside, thinking, 'We will plunder it,' come but are unable to enter, they depart as if repulsed after approaching a mountain. In just this way, a wise son of good family, having made and established his own insight-mind to be firm like a city, should fight that Māra of defilements. Just as a single warrior standing in the city would strike a band of robbers with various kinds of weapons, such as single-edged swords, so too, with the weapon of wisdom consisting of insight and the Noble Path, while dispelling the defilements to be destroyed by each respective path, one should strike that Māra of defilements. This is the meaning. 'And guard what is conquered' means: one should guard the nascent insight that has been generated by frequenting suitable dwellings, seasons, food, persons, and opportunities for listening to the Dhamma. From time to time, having entered into an attainment and having arisen from it, one should guard it by contemplating formations with a pure mind.

Anivesano [M 1.0202] siyāti anālayo bhaveyya. Yathā nāma yodho saṅgāmasīse balakoṭṭhakaṃ katvā amittehi saddhiṃ yujjhanto chāto vā pipāsito [P 1.0318] vā hutvā sannāhe vā sithile āvudhe vā patite balakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā vissamitvā bhuñjitvā pivitvā sannahitvā āvudhaṃ gahetvā puna nikkhamitvā yujjhanto parasenaṃ maddati, ajitaṃ jināti, jitaṃ rakkhati. So hi sace balakoṭṭhake ṭhito evaṃ vissamanto taṃ assādento accheyya, rajjaṃ parahatthagataṃ kareyya, evameva, bhikkhu, paṭiladdhaṃ taruṇavipassanaṃ punappunaṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya [V 1.0181] suddhacittena saṅkhāre sammasanto rakkhituṃ sakkoti, uttarimaggaphalapaṭilābhena kilesamāraṃ jināti. Sace pana so samāpattimeva assādeti, suddhacittena punappunaṃ saṅkhāre na sammasati, maggaphalapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā rakkhitabbayuttakaṃ rakkhanto anivesano siyā, samāpattiṃ nivesanaṃ katvā tattha na niveseyya, ālayaṃ na kareyyāti attho. “Addhā tumhepi evaṃ karothā”ti evaṃ satthā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desesi.

‘One should be without a dwelling’ (anivesano siyā) means one should be without clinging. Just as a warrior, having established a stronghold at the forefront of battle, fights with his enemies, and when he becomes hungry or thirsty, or his armor becomes loose, or his weapon is dropped, he enters the stronghold, rests, eats, drinks, fastens his armor, takes up his weapon, and then goes out again to fight, crushing the enemy forces, conquering the unconquered, and protecting what has been conquered. For if he were to remain in the stronghold, resting and delighting in it, he would cause the kingdom to fall into the hands of others. In the same way, a monk is able to guard the nascent insight he has obtained by repeatedly entering into a meditative attainment, and upon emerging from it, contemplating formations with a pure mind; through the attainment of higher paths and fruits, he conquers the Māra of defilements. But if he only delights in the attainment and does not repeatedly contemplate formations with a pure mind, he is unable to realize the higher paths and fruits. Therefore, while guarding what ought to be guarded, one should be without a dwelling. Having made the attainment a dwelling, one should not settle there; one should not create clinging to it. This is the meaning. “You too should certainly act in this way.” Thus the Teacher taught the Dhamma to those monks.

Desanāvasāne pañcasatā bhikkhū nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnāyeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā tathāgatassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ vaṇṇayantā thomentā vandantāva āgacchiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, the five hundred monks, while still seated in their places, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Praising, extolling, and venerating the Tathāgata's golden-hued body, they approached him.

Pañcasatabhikkhuvatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth story, the Story of the Five Hundred Monks, is finished.

7. Pūtigattatissattheravatthu

7. The Story of the Elder Pūtigatta Tissa

Aciraṃ [P 1.0319] vatayaṃ kāyoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto pūtigattatissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Not long, indeed, will this body last”—the Teacher gave this Dhamma discourse while dwelling at Sāvatthī, concerning the elder Pūtigatta Tissa.

Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito, so laddhūpasampado tissatthero nāma ahosi. Gacchante gacchante kāle tassa sarīre rogo udapādi. Sāsapamattiyo piḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Tā anupubbena muggamattā kalāyamattā kolaṭṭhimattā āmalakamattā beḷuvasalāṭumattā beḷuvamattā hutvā pabhijjiṃsu, sakalasarīraṃ chiddāvachiddaṃ ahosi. Pūtigattatissattherotvevassa nāmaṃ udapādi. Athassa aparabhāge aṭṭhīni bhijjiṃsu. So appaṭijaggiyo [M 1.0203] ahosi. Nivāsanapārupanaṃ pubbalohitamakkhitaṃ jālapūvasadisaṃ ahosi. Saddhivihārikādayo paṭijaggituṃ asakkontā chaḍḍayiṃsu. So anātho hutvā nipajji.

It is said that a certain clansman residing in Sāvatthī, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, placed his confidence in the Dispensation and went forth. After receiving full ordination, he was known as the elder Tissa. As time went on, a disease arose in his body. Mustard-seed-sized boils appeared. Gradually, they grew to the size of mung beans, kidney beans, jujube stones, Emblic myrobalan fruits, unripe wood-apples, and then wood-apples, and then burst open. His entire body became riddled with holes. Thus, the name Pūtigatta Tissa (Tissa with the rotten body) arose for him. Later, his bones began to break. He became one who could not be tended to. His lower and upper robes, smeared with pus and blood, became like a net-like cake. His co-residents and disciples, unable to care for him, abandoned him. He, being without a protector, lay down.

Buddhānañca nāma dve vāre lokavolokanaṃ avijahitaṃ hoti. Paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokentā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭito paṭṭhāya gandhakuṭiabhimukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ katvā olokenti, sāyaṃ olokentā gandhakuṭito paṭṭhāya bāhirābhimukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ katvā olokenti. Tasmiṃ pana samaye bhagavato ñāṇajālassa anto pūtigattatissatthero paññāyi. Satthā tassa bhikkhuno arahattassa upanissayaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ saddhivihārikādīhi chaḍḍito, idānissa maṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ [V 1.0182] natthī”ti gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā vihāracārikaṃ caramāno viya aggisālaṃ gantvā ukkhaliṃ dhovitvā udakaṃ datvā uddhanaṃ āropetvā udakassa tattabhāvaṃ āgamayamāno aggisālāyameva aṭṭhāsi. Tattabhāvaṃ jānitvā gantvā tassa bhikkhuno nipannamañcakoṭiyaṃ [P 1.0320] gaṇhi, tadā bhikkhū “apetha, bhante, mayaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti mañcakaṃ gahetvā aggisālaṃ ānayiṃsu. Satthā ambaṇaṃ āharāpetvā uṇhodakaṃ āsiñcitvā tehi bhikkhūhi tassa pārupanaṃ gāhāpetvā uṇhodake maddāpetvā mandātape vissajjāpesi. Athassa santike ṭhatvā sarīraṃ uṇhodakena temetvā ghaṃsitvā nhāpesi, tassa nahānapariyosāne pārupanaṃ sukkhi. Atha naṃ taṃ nivāsāpetvā nivatthakāsāvaṃ udake maddāpetvā ātape vissajjāpesi. Athassa gatte udake chinnamatte tampi sukkhi. So ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā sallahukasarīro ekaggacitto mañcake nipajji. Satthā tassa ussīsake ṭhatvā, “bhikkhu ayaṃ tava kāyo apetaviññāṇo nirupakāro hutvā kaliṅgaraṃ viya pathaviyaṃ sessatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The surveying of the world by the Buddhas is never abandoned, occurring twice. At dawn, surveying the world, they direct their knowledge from the edge of the universe-sphere toward the perfumed chamber. In the evening, surveying, they direct their knowledge from the perfumed chamber outward. At that time, within the Blessed One’s net of knowledge, the elder Pūtigatta Tissa appeared. The Teacher, seeing that this monk had the supporting condition for Arahantship, thought, “This one has been abandoned by his co-residents and disciples. Now, apart from me, he has no other refuge.” Leaving the perfumed chamber as if going on a tour of the monastery, the Teacher went to the fire-hall. There, he washed a pot, filled it with water, placed it on the hearth, and, waiting for the water to become hot, stood right in the fire-hall. Knowing it was hot, he went and took hold of the edge of the cot on which the monk was lying. Then the monks said, “Step aside, venerable sir, we will take it.” Taking the cot, they brought it to the fire-hall. The Teacher had a trough brought, poured warm water into it, and had those monks take the monk’s outer robe, had it kneaded in warm water, and then had it spread out in the gentle sun. Then, standing near him, he moistened the monk’s body with warm water, rubbed it, and bathed him. At the end of his bath, the outer robe was dry. Then, having him wear that robe, he had the lower robe that had been worn kneaded in water and spread in the sun. Then, as soon as the water on his body was gone, that robe also dried. He, wearing one robe and wrapping another, with a light body and a concentrated mind, lay down on the cot. The Teacher, standing at his head-side, said, “Monk, this body of yours, having become devoid of consciousness and useless, will lie on the earth like a log.” Then he spoke this verse:

41.

41.

“Aciraṃ vatayaṃ kāyo, pathaviṃ adhisessati;

Chuddho apetaviññāṇo, niratthaṃva kaliṅgara”nti.

“Indeed, soon, alas, this body will lie upon the earth, discarded, devoid of consciousness, like a useless log.”

Tattha aciraṃ vatāti bhikkhu na cirasseva ayaṃ kāyo pathaviṃ adhisessati, imissā pakatisayanena sayitāya pathaviyā upari sayissati[M 1.0204]. Chuddhoti apaviddho, apagataviññāṇatāya [P 1.0321] tuccho hutvā sessatīti dasseti. Yathā kiṃ? Niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ nirupakāraṃ niratthakaṃ kaṭṭhakhaṇḍaṃ viya. Dabbasambhāratthikā hi manussā araññaṃ pavisitvā ujukaṃ ujukasaṇṭhānena vaṅkaṃ vaṅkasaṇṭhānena chinditvā dabbasambhāraṃ gaṇhanti, avasesaṃ pana susirañca pūtikañca asārakañca gaṇṭhijātañca chinditvā tattheva chaḍḍenti. Aññe dabbasambhāratthikā āgantvā taṃ gahetāro nāma natthi, oloketvā attano upakārakameva gaṇhanti, itaraṃ pathavīgatameva hoti. Taṃ pana tena tena upāyena mañcapaṭipādakaṃ vā pādakathalikaṃ vā phalakapīṭhaṃ vā kātuṃ sakkāpi bhaveyya. Imasmiṃ pana attabhāve dvattiṃsāya koṭṭhāsesu ekakoṭṭhāsopi mañcapaṭipādakādivasena aññena vā upakāramukhena gayhūpago nāma natthi, kevalaṃ niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ ayaṃ kāyo apagataviññāṇo katipāheneva pathaviyaṃ sessatīti.

Herein, 'soon, alas' means: O monk, not long hence this body will lie upon the earth; by this is meant it will lie upon the earth, which is its natural bed. 'Discarded' means cast away; it shows that, being devoid of consciousness, it will lie there empty. How so? Like a useless log, an unbeneficial, worthless piece of wood. For people needing building materials enter the forest, and cutting a straight tree for a straight form and a crooked tree for a crooked form, they take the building materials. But the remainder—what is hollow, rotten, without heartwood, and knotted—they cut and discard right there. Other people needing building materials who come do not take it; looking it over, they take only what is useful to them. The other part becomes just like the ground. But that wood, by some means or other, might be able to be made into a cot-leg, or a foot-stool, or a plank-seat. In this individual existence, however, among the thirty-two parts, not even one part is fit to be taken for the purpose of a cot-leg or for any other beneficial use. Simply like a useless log, this body, devoid of consciousness, will in just a few days lie upon the earth.

Desanāvasāne pūtigattatissatthero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo [V 1.0183] ahesuṃ. Theropi arahattaṃ patvāva parinibbāyi. Satthā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kārāpetvā dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ kārāpesi. Bhikkhū satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu – “bhante, pūtigattatissatthero kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti. “Parinibbuto, bhikkhave”ti. “Bhante, evarūpassa pana arahattūpanissayasampannassa bhikkhuno kiṃ kāraṇā gattaṃ putikaṃ jātaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇā aṭṭhīni bhinnāni, kimassa kāraṇaṃ arahattassa upanissayabhāvaṃ patta”nti? “Bhikkhave, sabbametaṃ etassa attanā katakammeneva nibbatta”nti. “Kiṃ pana tena, bhante, kata”nti? “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇāthā”ti atītaṃ āhari –

At the end of the discourse, the elder Pūtigatta Tissa, together with the analytical knowledges, attained Arahantship, and many others became Stream-enterers and so on. The elder also, having attained Arahantship, attained Parinibbāna. The Teacher had his funeral rites performed, and taking the relics, had a cetiya built. The monks asked the Teacher, “Venerable sir, where has the elder Pūtigatta Tissa been reborn?” “He has attained Parinibbāna, O monks.” “But, venerable sir, for a monk such as this, endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship, for what reason did his body become rotten and his bones broken? And what was the cause that became the supporting condition for his Arahantship?” “Monks, all this was produced by the kamma done by himself.” “But what, venerable sir, was done by him?” “In that case, monks, listen,” and he related a story of the past.

Ayaṃ [P 1.0322] kassapasammāsambuddhakāle sākuṇiko hutvā bahū sakuṇe vadhitvā issarajanaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Tesaṃ dinnāvasese vikkiṇāti, “vikkitāvasesā māretvā ṭhapitā pūtikā bhavissantī”ti yathā uppatituṃ na sakkonti, tathā tesaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhīni ca pakkhaṭṭhīni ca bhinditvā rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapeti, te punadivase vikkiṇāti. Atibahūnaṃ pana laddhakāle attanopi atthāya pacāpeti. Tassekadivasaṃ rasabhojane pakke eko khīṇāsavo piṇḍāya caranto gehadvāre aṭṭhāsi. So theraṃ disvā [M 1.0205] cittaṃ pasādetvā, “mayā bahū pāṇā māretvā khāditā, ayyo ca me gehadvāre ṭhito, antogehe ca rasabhojanaṃ saṃvijjati, piṇḍapātamassa dassāmī”ti tassa pattaṃ ādāya pūretvā rasapiṇḍapātaṃ datvā theraṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, tumhehi diṭṭhadhammassa matthakaṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti āha. Thero “evaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ akāsi. “Bhikkhave, tadā katakammavasenetaṃ tissassa nipphannaṃ, sakuṇānaṃ aṭṭhibhedananissandena tissassa gattañca pūtikaṃ jātaṃ, aṭṭhīni ca bhinnāni, khīṇāsavassa rasapiṇḍapātadānanissandena arahattaṃ patto”ti.

In the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, this person was a bird-catcher. Having killed many birds, he served the king. He would sell what remained after presenting them to the king. Thinking, 'If those remaining after selling are killed and kept, they will become putrid,' he would break their leg-bones and wing-bones so they could not fly, and keep them in a pile.
