He would sell them the next day. When he obtained a great many, however, he would have them cooked for his own benefit as well. One day, when a savory meal was cooked for him, an Arahant, while wandering for alms, stood at the door of his house. Seeing the Elder, he made his mind serene and thought, 'I have killed and eaten many living beings, and this noble one stands at my door. Inside the house, there is a savory meal. I will give alms-food to him.' Taking the Elder's bowl, he filled it with the savory alms-food and offered it. Having venerated the Elder with the five-point prostration, he said, 'Venerable sir, may I attain the pinnacle of the Dhamma seen by you.' The Elder gave his blessing, saying, 'So be it.' The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, at that time, all this happened to Tissa by the power of the kamma he had done. As a consequence of breaking the birds' bones, Tissa's body became putrid and his bones were broken. As a consequence of the gift of savory alms-food to the Arahant, he attained Arahantship.'

Pūtigattatissattheravatthu sattamaṃ.

The seventh story, the Story of Elder Tissa of the Putrid Body, is finished.

8. Nandagopālakavatthu

8. The Story of Nanda the Cowherd

Diso disanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā kosalajanapade nandagopālakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Diso disaṃ' in the country of Kosala, concerning Nanda the cowherd.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatino nando nāma [P 1.0323] gopālako goyūthaṃ rakkhati aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo. So kira yathā keṇiyo jaṭilo pabbajjāvesena, evaṃ gopālakattena rājabaliṃ pariharanto attano kuṭumbaṃ rakkhati. So kālena kālaṃ pañca gorase ādāya [V 1.0184] anāthapiṇḍikassa santikaṃ āgantvā satthāraṃ passati, dhammaṃ suṇāti, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgamanatthāya satthāraṃ yācati. Satthā tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno āgantvā paripakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā ekadivasaṃ mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ caranto maggā okkamma tassa vasanaṭṭhānāsanne aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Nando satthu santikaṃ agantvā vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā satthāraṃ nimantetvā satthāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa paṇītaṃ pañcagorasadānaṃ adāsi. Sattame divase satthā anumodanaṃ katvā dānakathādibhedaṃ anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne nandagopālako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya satthu pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ anugacchanto dūraṃ gantvā, “tiṭṭha, upāsakā”ti nivattiyamāno vanditvā nivatti. Atha naṃ eko luddako vijjhitvā māresi. Pacchato āgacchantā bhikkhū naṃ disvā gantvā satthāraṃ [M 1.0206] āhaṃsu – “nando, bhante, gopālako tumhākaṃ idhāgatattā mahādānaṃ datvā anugantvā nivattento mārito, sace tumhe nāgacchissatha, nāssa maraṇaṃ abhavissā”ti. Satthā[P 1.0324], “bhikkhave, mayi āgatepi anāgatepi tassa catasso disā catasso anudisā ca gacchantassāpi maraṇato muccanūpāyo nāma natthi. Yañhi neva corā, na verino karonti, taṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ antopaduṭṭhaṃ micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittameva karotī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a cowherd named Nanda, who was affluent, of great wealth, and of great possessions, tended the herd of cattle belonging to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. Just as the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya did in the guise of a renunciant, so he, in his capacity as a cowherd, protected his own wealth by avoiding the royal tax. From time to time, taking the five products of the cow, he would go to Anāthapiṇḍika, see the Teacher, and listen to the Dhamma. He would request the Teacher to come to his dwelling place. The Teacher, waiting for the ripening of his knowledge, one day, knowing that it had matured, while wandering on tour accompanied by a great assembly of bhikkhus, stepped off the road and sat at the foot of a certain tree near Nanda’s dwelling place. Nanda approached the Teacher, paid respects, exchanged friendly greetings, and invited the Teacher. For seven days, he offered excellent alms of the five products of the cow to the assembly of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. On the seventh day, the Teacher expressed his appreciation and delivered a gradual discourse, with its divisions such as the talk on giving. At the end of the discourse, Nanda the cowherd was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Taking the Teacher's bowl, he followed the Teacher. Having gone a long way, he was sent back with the words, 'Stay, lay follower.' He paid homage and turned back. Then a certain hunter shot and killed him. The bhikkhus who were coming along behind saw him, went to the Teacher, and said: 'Venerable sir, the cowherd Nanda, having given a great offering on account of your coming here and having followed you, was killed as he was returning. If you had not come, his death would not have occurred.' The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, whether I come or not, even if he were to go in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions, there is no means of escape from death for him. For what neither thieves nor enemies do, that their own internally corrupt, wrongly directed mind does to these beings.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

42.

42.

“Diso disaṃ yaṃ taṃ kayirā, verī vā pana verinaṃ;

Micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, pāpiyo naṃ tato kare”ti.

Whatever a foe may do to a foe, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly directed mind can do one a far greater harm.

Tattha diso disanti coro coraṃ. “Disvā”ti pāṭhaseso. Yaṃ taṃ kayirāti yaṃ taṃ tassa anayabyasanaṃ kareyya. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – eko ekassa mittadubbhī coro puttadārakhettavatthu gomahiṃsādīsu aparajjhanto yassa aparajjhati, tampi tatheva attani aparajjhantaṃ coraṃ disvā, veri vā pana kenacideva kāraṇena baddhaveraṃ veriṃ disvā attano kakkhaḷatāya dāruṇatāya yaṃ taṃ tassa anayabyasanaṃ kareyya, puttadāraṃ vā pīḷeyya, khettādīni vā nāseyya, jīvitā vā pana naṃ voropeyya, dasasu akusalakammapathesu micchāṭhapitattā micchāpahiṇitaṃ cittaṃ pāpiyo naṃ tato kare taṃ purisaṃ tato pāpataraṃ kareyya. Vuttappakārehi, diso disassa vā verī verino vā imasmiṃyeva [P 1.0325] attabhāve dukkhaṃ vā uppādeyya, jīvitakkhayaṃ vā kareyya. Idaṃ pana akusalakammapathesu micchāṭhapitaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme anayabyasanaṃ pāpeti, attabhāvasatasahassesupi catūsu apāyesu khipitvā sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na detīti.

Herein, 'a foe to a foe' means a thief to a thief. The reading is supplemented with 'having seen.' 'Whatever he might do' means whatever misfortune and ruin he might inflict upon him. The same method applies to the second line. This is what is meant: One thief, being a thief who betrays a friend, transgresses against another's son, wife, field, property, cattle, buffalo, and so on. When he sees that very person against whom he transgresses also transgressing against himself in the same way; or an enemy, having seen an enemy with whom he has a binding enmity for some reason—then, due to his own harshness and cruelty, whatever misfortune and ruin he might inflict upon that person, whether he oppresses his son and wife, or destroys his fields and other things, or even deprives him of life—a mind wrongly directed, because it is established in the ten unwholesome courses of action, would do him a far greater harm than that. By the means mentioned, a foe might cause suffering to a foe, or an enemy to an enemy, in this very existence, or might bring about the destruction of life. But this mind, wrongly established in the unwholesome courses of action, leads to misfortune and ruin in this very life; and for hundreds of thousands of existences, having thrown one into the four woeful states, it does not allow one to lift one's head.

Desanāpariyosāne [V 1.0185] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Mahājanassa sātthikā desanā jātā. Upāsakena pana bhavantare katakammaṃ bhikkhūhi na pucchitaṃ, tasmā satthārā na kathitanti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other such states. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly of people. However, the kamma done by the lay follower in another existence was not asked about by the bhikkhus; therefore, it was not spoken of by the Teacher.

Nandagopālakavatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Eighth Story: Nanda the Cowherd.

9. Soreyyattheravatthu

9. The Story of the Elder Soreyya

Na [M 1.0207] taṃ mātā pitā kayirāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ jetavane viharanto soreyyattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana in Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, which begins with the words 'Na taṃ mātā pitā kayirā,' concerning the Elder Soreyya.

Vatthu soreyyanagare samuṭṭhitaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Sammāsambuddhe sāvatthiyaṃ viharante soreyyanagare soreyyaseṭṭhiputto ekena sahāyakena saddhiṃ sukhayānake nisīditvā mahantena parivārena nhānatthāya nagarā nikkhami. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahākaccāyanatthero soreyyanagaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisitukāmo hutvā bahinagare saṅghāṭiṃ pārupati. Therassa ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ. Soreyyaseṭṭhiputto taṃ disvā cintesi – “aho vata ayaṃ vā thero mama bhariyā bhaveyya, mama vā bhariyāya sarīravaṇṇo etassa sarīravaṇṇo [P 1.0326] viya bhaveyyā”ti. Tassa cintitamatteyeva purisaliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, itthiliṅgaṃ pāturahosi. So lajjamāno yānakā oruyha palāyi. Parijano taṃ asañjānanto “kimeta”nti āha. Sāpi takkasilamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Sahāyakopissā ito cito ca vicaritvāpi nāddasa. Sabbe nhāyitvā gehaṃ agamiṃsu. “Kahaṃ seṭṭhiputto”ti ca vutte, “nhatvā āgato bhavissatīti maññimhā”ti vadiṃsu. Athassa mātāpitaro tattha tattha pariyesitvā apassantā roditvā paridevitvā, “mato bhavissatī”ti matakabhattaṃ adaṃsu. Sā ekaṃ takkasilagāmiṃ satthavāhaṃ disvā yānakassa pacchato pacchato anubandhi.

The story arose in the city of Soreyya and concluded in Sāvatthī. While the Perfectly Enlightened One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, the son of a merchant from Soreyya, accompanied by a friend, set out from the city in a comfortable carriage with a large retinue to bathe. At that moment, the Elder Mahākaccāyana, wishing to enter Soreyya for alms-food, was putting on his outer robe outside the city. The Elder's body was of a golden color. Upon seeing him, the merchant's son thought, 'Ah, if only this elder were my wife, or if my wife's complexion were like his!' No sooner had he thought this than his male characteristics disappeared and female characteristics appeared. Ashamed, he descended from the carriage and fled. His attendants, not recognizing her, asked, 'What is this?' She then took the road to Takkasilā. His friend searched here and there but could not find him. Everyone bathed and returned home. When asked, 'Where is the merchant's son?' they replied, 'We assumed he had bathed and returned.' His parents, searching everywhere and not finding him, wept and lamented; thinking, 'He must be dead,' they offered a funeral meal. She, seeing a caravan heading to Takkasilā, followed behind its vehicle.

Atha naṃ manussā disvā, “amhākaṃ yānakassa pacchato pacchato anugacchati, mayaṃ ‘kassesā dārikā’ti taṃ na jānāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Sāpi “tumhe attano yānakaṃ pājetha, ahaṃ padasā gamissāmī”ti gacchantī aṅgulimuddikaṃ datvā ekasmiṃ yānake okāsaṃ kāresi. Manussā cintayiṃsu – “takkasilanagare amhākaṃ seṭṭhiputtassa bhariyā natthi, tassa ācikkhissāma, mahāpaṇṇākāro no bhavissatī”ti. Te gehaṃ gantvā, “sāmi, amhehi tumhākaṃ [P 1.0327] ekaṃ itthiratanaṃ ānīta”nti āhaṃsu. So taṃ sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā attano vayānurūpaṃ [V 1.0186] abhirūpaṃ pāsādikaṃ disvā uppannasineho gehe akāsi. Purisā hi itthiyo, itthiyo [M 1.0208] vā purisā abhūtapubbā nāma natthi. Purisā hi parassa dāresu aticaritvā kālaṃ katvā bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccitvā manussajātiṃ āgacchantā attabhāvasate itthibhāvaṃ āpajjanti.

Then the people, seeing her, said: 'She is following behind our vehicle; we do not know whose daughter she is.' She said, 'You drive your own vehicle; I will go on foot.' As she was walking, her feet became sore, so she gave a finger-ring and had a space made for herself in one of the vehicles. The people thought: 'In the city of Takkasilā, our merchant's son has no wife. We will inform him, and a great gift will be ours.' Having gone to his house, they said: 'Master, we have brought a jewel of a woman for you.' Hearing this, he had her summoned, and seeing her beautiful and pleasing form, suitable for his own age, affection arose in him and he established her in his house. For indeed, there are no men who have not formerly been women, nor women who have not formerly been men. Men, having transgressed with the wives of others and died, after being tormented in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, upon returning to a human birth, attain a female state for a hundred existences.

Ānandattheropi kappasatasahassaṃ pūritapāramī ariyasāvako saṃsāre saṃsaranto ekasmiṃ attabhāve kammārakule nibbatto. Paradārakammaṃ katvā niraye paccitvā pakkāvasesena cuddasasu attabhāvesu purisassa pādaparicārikā itthī ahosi, sattasu attabhāvesu bījuddharaṇaṃ pāpuṇi. Itthiyo pana dānādīni puññāni katvā itthibhāve chandaṃ virājetvā, “idaṃ no puññaṃ purisattabhāvapaṭilābhāya saṃvattatū”ti cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā kālaṃ katvā purisattabhāvaṃ paṭilabhanti, patidevatā hutvā sāmike sammāpaṭipattivasenāpi purisattabhāvaṃ paṭilabhanteva.

Even the Elder Ānanda, a noble disciple who had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons, while wandering in saṃsāra, was in one existence born into a blacksmith's family. Having committed adultery and having been tormented in hell, by the remainder of that kamma, in fourteen existences he was a woman serving at a man’s feet, and in seven existences he underwent castration. Women, however, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and having become dispassionate towards the female state, after resolving in their minds, 'May this merit of ours lead to the attainment of a male state!' and then dying, attain a male state. By becoming devoted to their husbands and through right conduct towards them, they also certainly attain a male state.

Ayaṃ pana seṭṭhiputto there ayoniso cittaṃ uppādetvā imasmiṃyeva attabhāve itthibhāvaṃ paṭilabhi. Takkasilāyaṃ seṭṭhiputtena saddhiṃ saṃvāsamanvāya pana tassā kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ labhitvā tassa padasā gamanakāle aparampi puttaṃ paṭilabhi. Evamassā kucchiyaṃ vutthā dve, soreyyanagare taṃ paṭicca nibbattā dveti cattāro puttā ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kāle soreyyanagarato tassā sahāyako seṭṭhiputto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi takkasilaṃ [P 1.0328] gantvā sukhayānake nisinno nagaraṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ sā uparipāsādatale vātapānaṃ vivaritvā antaravīthiṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā disvā sañjānitvā dāsiṃ pesetvā pakkosāpetvā mahātale nisīdāpetvā mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ so āha – “bhadde, tvaṃ ito pubbe amhehi na diṭṭhapubbā, atha ca pana no mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ karosi, jānāsi tvaṃ amhe”ti. “Āma, sāmi, jānāmi, nanu tumhe soreyyanagaravāsino”ti? “Āma, bhadde”ti. Sā mātāpitūnañca bhariyāya ca puttānañca arogabhāvaṃ pucchi. Itaro “āma, bhadde, arogā”ti vatvā “jānāsi tvaṃ ete”ti āha. “Āma sāmi, jānāmi. Tesaṃ eko putto atthi, so kahaṃ, sāmī”ti? “Bhadde, mā etaṃ kathehi, mayaṃ tena saddhiṃ ekadivasaṃ sukhayānake nisīditvā nhāyituṃ nikkhantā nevassa gatiṃ jānāma, ito cito ca vicaritvā taṃ adisvā mātāpitūnaṃ [M 1.0209] ārocayimhā, tepissa roditvā kanditvā petakiccaṃ kiriṃsū”ti. “Ahaṃ so, sāmī”ti. “Apehi, bhadde, kiṃ kathesi mayhaṃ sahāyo devakumāro viya eko puriso”ti? “Hotu, sāmi, ahaṃ so”ti. “Atha idaṃ kiṃ nāmā”ti? “Taṃ divasaṃ te ayyo mahākaccāyanatthero diṭṭho”ti? “Āma, diṭṭho”ti. Ahaṃ ayyaṃ [P 1.0329] mahākaccāyanattheraṃ oloketvā, “aho vata ayaṃ vā thero mama bhariyā bhaveyya[V 1.0187], etassa vā sarīravaṇṇo viya mama bhariyāya sarīravaṇṇo bhaveyyā”ti cintesiṃ. Cintitakkhaṇeyeva me purisaliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavi. Athāhaṃ lajjamānā kassaci kiñci vattuṃ asakkuṇitvā tato palāyitvā idhāgatā, sāmīti.

Now, this merchant's son, having given rise to an improper thought concerning the Elder, attained the state of a woman in this very existence. In Takkasilā, due to cohabitation with a merchant's son, a fetus was established in her womb. After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son, and at the time when he was able to walk, she obtained another son. Thus, there were two sons born from her womb, and two who had been born in Soreyya on account of him, making four sons in total. At that time, her friend, the merchant's son from Soreyya, went to Takkasilā with five hundred carts and entered the city seated in a comfortable carriage. Then she, standing on the upper floor of the palace, opened a window and, while looking at the main street, saw and recognized him. She sent a maidservant to have him summoned, had him seated in the great hall, and paid him great honor and respect. Then he said to her, 'Good lady, we have not seen you before, yet you pay us great honor. Do you know us?' 'Yes, master, I know you. Are you not residents of Soreyya?' 'Yes, good lady.' She asked about the health of his parents, wife, and sons. The other replied, 'Yes, good lady, they are well,' and then said, 'Do you know them?' 'Yes, master, I know them. They have one son; where is he, master?' 'Good lady, do not speak of that. One day, we set out to bathe, having sat together in a comfortable carriage, but we do not know where he went. After searching here and there and not seeing him, we informed his parents. They too, after weeping and lamenting, performed the rites for the deceased.' 'I am he, master.' 'Away with you, good lady! What are you saying? My friend was a man like a divine youth!' 'Let it be, master, I am he.' 'Then what is the meaning of this?' 'On that day, did you see the venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana?' 'Yes, I saw him.' 'Having looked at the venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana, I thought, “Oh, if only this Elder were my wife!” or “Oh, if only my wife's complexion were like the complexion of this Elder!” In the very moment of thinking, my male form disappeared, and the female form appeared. Then I, being ashamed and unable to say anything to anyone, fled from there and came here, master.'

“Aho vata te bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, kasmā mayhaṃ nācikkhi, apica pana te thero khamāpito”ti? “Na khamāpito, sāmi. Jānāsi pana tvaṃ kahaṃ thero”ti? “Imameva nagaraṃ upanissāya viharatī”ti. “Sace piṇḍāya caranto idhāgaccheyya, ahaṃ mama ayyassa bhikkhāhāraṃ dadeyyaṃ, sāmī”ti. “Tena hi sīghaṃ sakkāraṃ karohi, amhākaṃ ayyaṃ khamāpessāmā”ti so therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno, “bhante, sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. “Nanu tvaṃ, seṭṭhiputta, āgantukosī”ti. “Bhante, mā amhākaṃ āgantukabhāvaṃ pucchatha, sve me bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Thero adhivāsesi, gehepi therassa mahāsakkāro paṭiyatto. Thero punadivase taṃ gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ nisīdāpetvā paṇītenāhārena parivisitvā seṭṭhiputto taṃ itthiṃ gahetvā therassa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā, “bhante, mayhaṃ sahāyikāya khamathā”ti āha. “Kimeta”nti? “Ayaṃ, bhante, pubbe mayhaṃ piyasahāyako hutvā tumhe oloketvā evaṃ nāma cintesi, athassa purisaliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavi, khamatha, bhante”ti. “Tena hi uṭṭhahatha, khamāmi vo aha”nti. Therena [P 1.0330] “khamāmī”ti vuttamatteyeva itthiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, purisaliṅgaṃ pātubhavi.

'Alas, what a grave deed you have done! Why did you not tell me? Moreover, have you asked the Elder for forgiveness?' 'I have not asked for his forgiveness, master. But do you know where the Elder is?' 'He dwells in dependence on this very city.' 'If he should come here while wandering for alms, I would give alms-food to my venerable one, master.' 'In that case, quickly prepare the offerings. We shall ask our venerable one for forgiveness.' So he went to the Elder's dwelling place, paid his respects, and sat to one side. He said, 'Venerable sir, tomorrow, please accept my alms-food.' 'Merchant's son, are you not a visitor?' 'Venerable sir, do not ask about my status as a visitor. Tomorrow, please accept my alms-food.' The Elder consented. In the house, a great offering was prepared for the Elder. The next day, the Elder went to the door of that house. Then, having had him seated and having served him with excellent food, the merchant's son took that woman, made her prostrate at the Elder's feet, and said, 'Venerable sir, please forgive my female companion.' 'What is this?' 'Venerable sir, this person was formerly my dear companion. Having looked at you, he thought in such a way. Then his male form disappeared, and the female form appeared. Please forgive, venerable sir.' 'In that case, arise. I forgive you.' The very moment the Elder said, 'I forgive,' the female form disappeared, and the male form appeared.

Purisaliṅge pātubhūtamatteyeva taṃ takkasilāya seṭṭhiputto āha – “samma sahāyaka, ime dve dārakā tava kucchiyaṃ vutthattā maṃ paṭicca nibbattattā ubhinnampino puttā eva, idheva vasissāma, mā ukkaṇṭhī”ti. “Samma, ahaṃ ekenattabhāvena paṭhamaṃ puriso hutvā itthibhāvaṃ patvā puna [M 1.0210] puriso jātoti vippakārappatto, paṭhamaṃ maṃ paṭicca dve puttā nibbattā, idāni me kucchito dve puttā nikkhantā, svāhaṃ ekenattabhāvena vippakārappatto, puna ‘gehe vasissatī’ti saññaṃ mā kari, ahaṃ mama ayyassa santike pabbajissāmi. Ime dve dārakā tava bhārāti, imesu mā pamajjī”ti vatvā putte sīse paricumbitvā parimajjitvā ure nipajjāpetvā pitu niyyādetvā nikkhamitvā therassa santike pabbajjaṃ yāci. Theropi naṃ pabbājetvā upasampādetvā gaṇhitvāva cārikaṃ caramāno anupubbena sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Tassa soreyyattheroti nāmaṃ ahosi. Janapadavāsino taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā saṅkhubhitvā kotūhalajātā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchiṃsu [P 1.0331] – “evaṃ kira, bhante”ti? “Āma, āvuso”ti. “Bhante, evarūpampi kāraṇaṃ nāma hoti”? “Tumhākaṃ kucchiyaṃ kira dve puttā nibbattā, tumhe paṭicca [V 1.0188] dve jātā, tesaṃ vo kataresu balavasineho hotī”ti? “Kucchiyaṃ vutthakesu, āvuso”ti. Āgatāgatā nibaddhaṃ tatheva pucchiṃsu.

As soon as the male form appeared, the merchant's son of Takkasilā said to him: 'Dear friend, these two boys, having been born from your womb and having come into being on account of me, are indeed the sons of both of us. Let us live right here; do not be distressed.' 'Friend,' he replied, 'I, in a single existence, having first been a man, then having reached the state of a woman, and now having become a man again, have thus undergone a transformation. First, two sons came into being on account of me, and now two sons have come forth from my womb. I, having undergone such a transformation in a single existence, do not wish to entertain the thought, “I will live in the household life again.” I will go forth in the presence of my master. These two boys are your responsibility; do not be heedless regarding them.' Having said this, he kissed the sons on their heads, stroked them, had them lie on his chest, entrusted them to their father, and departed. He went to the Elder and requested the going forth. The Elder too, having given him the going forth and the higher ordination, took him along and, while wandering on tour, in due course arrived at Sāvatthī. His name became the Elder Soreyya. The country-dwellers, having learned of this event, became agitated and filled with curiosity. They approached him and asked, 'Venerable sir, is it true?' 'Yes, friends.' 'Venerable sir, can such a thing indeed happen? It is said that two sons were born from your womb, and two were born on account of you. Among them, for which do you have stronger affection?' 'For those born from the womb, friends.' Those who came and came constantly asked in just the same way.

Thero “kucchiyaṃ vuttakesu eva sineho balavā”ti punappunaṃ kathento harāyamāno ekova nisīdati, ekova tiṭṭhati. So evaṃ ekattūpagato attabhāve khayavayaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ āgatāgatā pucchanti – “bhante, evaṃ kira nāma ahosī”ti? “Āmāvuso”ti. “Kataresu sineho balavā”ti? “Mayhaṃ katthaci sineho nāma natthī”ti. Bhikkhū “ayaṃ abhūtaṃ kathesi, purimadivasesu ‘kucchiyaṃ vutthaputtesu sineho balavā’ti vatvā idāni ‘mayhaṃ katthaci sineho natthī’ti vadati, aññaṃ byākaroti, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, mama putto aññaṃ byākaroti, mama puttassa sammāpaṇihitena cittena maggassa diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya na katthaci sineho jāto, yaṃ sampattiṃ neva mātā, na pitā kātuṃ sakkoti, taṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ abbhantare pavattaṃ sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittameva detī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Elder, feeling ashamed while repeatedly saying, 'Affection is strong only for those born from the womb,' would sit alone and stand alone. Thus, having resorted to solitude, he established mindfulness on the decay and dissolution in his own being and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then, those who came and came asked him, 'Venerable sir, is it true that this happened?' 'Yes, friends.' 'For which was the affection stronger?' 'For me, there is no affection for anything whatsoever.' The monks said, 'This one speaks what is not true. In former days he said, “Affection is strong for the sons born from the womb,” but now he says, “For me, there is no affection for anything.” He is declaring the highest knowledge, venerable sir.' The Teacher said, 'No, monks, my son is not making a false declaration. For my son, with his mind well-directed, from the very moment he saw the path, no affection has arisen for anything whatsoever. That attainment which neither a mother nor a father can bring about, that very well-directed mind, arisen within these beings, gives.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

43.

43.

“Na [P 1.0332] taṃ mātā pitā kayirā, aññe vāpi ca ñātakā;

Sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti.

That which neither a mother nor a father nor any other relative can do, a well-directed mind can do for one, making one far better.

Tatthana tanti taṃ kāraṇaṃ neva mātā kareyya, na pitā, na aññe ñātakā. Sammāpaṇihitanti dasasu kusalakammapathesu sammā ṭhapitaṃ. Seyyaso [M 1.0211] naṃ tato kareti tato kāraṇato seyyaso naṃ varataraṃ uttaritaraṃ kareyya, karotīti attho. Mātāpitaro hi puttānaṃ dhanaṃ dadamānā ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve kammaṃ akatvā sukhena jīvikakappanaṃ dhanaṃ dātuṃ sakkonti. Visākhāya mātāpitaropi tāva mahaddhanā mahābhogā, tassā ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve sukhena jīvikakappanaṃ dhanaṃ adaṃsu. Catūsu pana dīpesu cakkavattisiriṃ dātuṃ samatthā mātāpitaropi nāma puttānaṃ natthi, pageva dibbasampattiṃ vā paṭhamajjhānādisampattiṃ vā, lokuttarasampattidāne kathāva natthi, sammāpaṇihitaṃ pana cittaṃ sabbampetaṃ sampattiṃ dātuṃ sakkoti. Tena vuttaṃ “seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti.

Herein, `na taṃ` means: that deed, neither a mother, nor a father, nor other relatives could do. `Sammāpaṇihitaṃ` means well-established in the ten wholesome courses of action. `Seyyaso naṃ tato kare` means: than that deed, it makes that person better, more excellent, more superior; this is the meaning. Indeed, parents, when giving wealth to their children, are able to give enough wealth for them to live comfortably without working in that single existence. Visākhā's parents, for instance, were of great wealth and great possessions; they gave her wealth sufficient for a comfortable livelihood in just one existence. But there are no parents capable of giving their children the glory of a universal monarch over the four continents, let alone divine attainment, or the attainment of the first jhāna and so on. As for giving supramundane attainment, there is no question of it. A well-directed mind, however, is able to give all these attainments. Therefore it was said, 'it makes one far better.'

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Soreyyattheravatthu navamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Soreyya, the Ninth.

Cittavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Mind is concluded.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Pupphavaggo

4. 4. The Chapter on Flowers

1. Pathavikathāpasutapañcasatabhikkhuvatthu

1. The Story of the Five Hundred Monks Engaged in Talk about the Earth

Ko [M 1.0212][V 1.0189][P 1.0333] imaṃ pathaviṃ vicessatīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto pathavikathāpasute pañcasate bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Who will investigate this earth?' concerning five hundred monks who were engaged in talk about the earth.

Te kira bhagavatā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ caritvā jetavanaṃ āgantvā sāyanhasamaye upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ sannisinnā attanā gatagataṭṭhānesu “asukagāmato asukagāmagamanaṭṭhāne samaṃ visamaṃ kaddamabahulaṃ sakkharabahulaṃ kāḷamattikaṃ tambamattika”nti pathavikathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “bhante, amhehi vicaritaṭṭhāne pathavikathāyā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, esā bāhirapathavī nāma, tumhehi ajjhuttikapathaviyaṃ parikammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imā dve gāthā abhāsi –

It is said that those monks, having traveled through the countryside with the Blessed One and returned to Jetavana, were seated together in the assembly hall in the evening. They spoke about the earth in the places they had gone, saying, 'On the way from such-and-such village to such-and-such village, the ground was level, uneven, very muddy, very gravelly, of black soil, or of red soil.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what talk are you now assembled?' When they replied, 'Venerable Sir, we are assembled for talk about the earth in the places we have traveled,' he said, 'Monks, this is called the external earth. It is fitting for you to do the preliminary work on the internal earth.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

44.

44.

“Ko imaṃ pathaviṃ vicessati,

Yamalokañca imaṃ sadevakaṃ;

Ko dhammapadaṃ sudesitaṃ,

Kusalo pupphamiva pacessati.

Who will investigate this earth, and this world of Yama together with the world of devas? Who will discern the well-taught path of the Dhamma, as a skilled person selects a flower?

45.

45.

“Sekho [P 1.0334] pathaviṃ vicessati,

Yamalokañca imaṃ sadevakaṃ;

Sekho dhammapadaṃ sudesitaṃ,

Kusalo pupphamiva pacessatī”ti.

The trainee will investigate this earth, and this world of Yama together with the world of devas. The trainee will discern the well-taught path of the Dhamma, as a skilled person selects a flower.

Tattha ko imanti ko imaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ pathaviṃ. Vicessatīti attano ñāṇena vicinissati vijānissati, paṭivijjhissati, sacchikarissatīti attho. Yamalokañcāti catubbidhaṃ apāyalokañca. Imaṃ sadevakanti imaṃ manussalokañca devalokena saddhiṃ ko vicessati [V 1.0190] vicinissati vijānissati paṭivijjhissati sacchikarissatīti pucchi. Ko dhammapadaṃ sudesitanti yathāsabhāvato kathitattā sudesitaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhātaṃ dhammapadaṃ kusalo mālākāro pupphaṃ vicinanto viya ko [M 1.0213] pacessati vicinissati vijānissati upaparikkhissati paṭivijjhissati, sacchikarissatīti attho. Sekhoti adhisīlasikkhā, adhicittasikkhā, adhipaññāsikkhāti imā tisso sikkhā sikkhanato sotāpattimaggaṭṭhaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattamaggaṭṭhā sattavidho sekho imaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ pathaviṃ arahattamaggena tato chandarāgaṃ apakaḍḍhanto vicessati vicinissati vijānissati [P 1.0335] paṭivijjhissati sacchikarissati. Yamalokañcāti taṃ yathāvuttapakāraṃ yamalokañca imaṃ manussalokañca saha devehi sadevakaṃ sveva vicessati vicinissati vijānissati paṭivijjhissati sacchikarissati. Sekhoti sveva sattavidho sekho, yathā nāma kusalo mālākāro pupphārāmaṃ pavisitvā taruṇamakuḷāni ca pāṇakaviddhāni ca milātāni ca gaṇṭhikajātāni ca pupphāni vajjetvā sobhanāni sujātasujātāneva pupphāni vicināti, evameva imaṃ sukathitaṃ suniddiṭṭhaṃ bodhipakkhiyadhammapadampi paññāya pacessati vicinissati upaparikkhissati paṭivijjhissati sacchikarissatīti satthā sayameva pañhaṃ vissajjesi.

Therein, as to 'Who this earth?': Who will, with their own knowledge, investigate, know, penetrate, and realize this earth which is called the personal existence? This is the meaning. As to 'and the world of Yama': the fourfold world of woe. As to 'this with the world of devas': Who will investigate, know, penetrate, and realize this human world together with the world of devas? Thus he asked. As to 'Who the well-taught path of the Dhamma?': Who will select, investigate, know, scrutinize, penetrate, and realize the path of the Dhamma—called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which is well-taught because it was spoken according to its true nature—like a skilled garland-maker selecting a flower? This is the meaning. As to 'the trainee': because of training in these three trainings—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—the seven kinds of persons, beginning with the one established in the stream-entry path up to the one established in the Arahant path, are called the trainee. That trainee will investigate, know, penetrate, and realize this earth which is called the personal existence by means of the Arahant path, while removing desire and lust from it. As to 'and the world of Yama': that very person will investigate, know, penetrate, and realize that world of Yama of the aforesaid kind, this human world, and the world together with the devas. As to 'the trainee': that same sevenfold trainee, just as a skilled garland-maker, having entered a flower garden and having avoided young buds, insect-bitten flowers, withered flowers, and knotted flowers, selects only the beautiful and well-formed flowers, in the very same way, will with wisdom select, investigate, scrutinize, penetrate, and realize this well-spoken and well-expounded path of the Dhamma of the factors of enlightenment. Thus, the Teacher himself answered the question.

Desanāvasāne pañcasatāpi bhikkhū saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sampattaparisāyapi sātthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, all five hundred monks attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. For the assembled congregation also, the Dhamma discourse was fruitful.

Pathavikathāpasutapañcasatabhikkhuvatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The First: The Story of the Five Hundred Monks Engaged in Talk about the Earth.

2. Marīcikammaṭṭhānikattheravatthu

2. The Story of the Elder Who Practiced the Mirage as a Meditation Subject

Pheṇūpamanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto aññataraṃ marīcikammaṭṭhānikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma discourse, which begins 'Like foam,' concerning a certain monk who practiced the mirage as a meditation subject.

So [P 1.0336] kira bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā, “samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭetvā vāyamitvā arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkonto “visesetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpessāmī”ti satthu santikaṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge marīciṃ disvā, “yathā ayaṃ gimhasamaye uṭṭhitā marīci dūre ṭhitānaṃ rūpagatā viya paññāyati, santikaṃ āgacchantānaṃ neva paññāyati, ayaṃ attabhāvopi uppādavayaṭṭhena evarūpo”ti marīcikammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvento āgantvā [V 1.0191] maggakilanto aciravatiyaṃ nhāyitvā ekasmiṃ [M 1.0214] caṇḍasotatīre rukkhachāyāya nisinno udakavegābhighātena uṭṭhahitvā mahante mahante pheṇapiṇḍe bhijjamāne disvā, “ayaṃ attabhāvopi uppajjitvā bhijjanaṭṭhena evarūpoyevā”ti ārammaṇaṃ aggahesi. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ ṭhitova taṃ theraṃ disvā, “evameva, bhikkhu, evarūpovāyaṃ attabhāvo pheṇapiṇḍo viya marīci viya uppajjanabhijjanasabhāvoyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

That monk, it is said, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered the forest thinking, 'I will practice the ascetic's duty.' Striving and exerting himself, but unable to attain Arahantship, he thought, 'I will have the meditation subject explained in detail,' and while coming to the Teacher, he saw a mirage on the way. He thought: 'Just as this mirage, arising in the hot season, appears like a form to those standing at a distance but is not perceived by those approaching, so too this personal existence is of such a nature, due to its arising and passing away.' Developing the mirage as his meditation subject, he came along, and weary from the journey, bathed in the Aciravatī River. While sitting in the shade of a tree on a bank with a swift current, he saw very large masses of foam arising and breaking apart as they were struck by the force of the water. He took this as his object of meditation, thinking: 'This personal existence, too, is of just such a nature—arising and then breaking apart.' The Teacher, while standing in his perfumed chamber, saw that elder and said, 'Just so, monk, this personal existence is indeed of such a nature; like a mass of foam, like a mirage, its nature is only to arise and break apart.' Then he spoke this verse:

46.

46.

“Pheṇūpamaṃ kāyamimaṃ viditvā,

Marīcidhammaṃ abhisambudhāno;

Chetvāna mārassa papupphakāni,

Adassanaṃ maccurājassa gacche”ti.

Having known this body to be like foam, comprehending its nature to be like a mirage, and cutting off Māra's flowers, one goes unseen by the King of Death.

Tattha pheṇūpamanti imaṃ kesādisamūhasaṅkhātaṃ kāyaṃ abaladubbalaṭṭhena anaddhaniyatāvakālikaṭṭhena pheṇapiṇḍasarikkhakoti [P 1.0337] viditvā. Marīcidhammanti yathā marīci dūre ṭhitānaṃ rūpagatā viya gayhūpagā viya hoti, santike upagacchantānaṃ rittā tucchā agayhūpagā sampajjati, evameva khaṇikaittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ayaṃ kāyopi marīcidhammoti abhisambudhāno bujjhanto, jānantoti attho. Mārassa papupphakānīti mārassa papupphakasaṅkhātāni tebhūmakāni vaṭṭāni ariyamaggena chinditvā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu maccurājassa adassanaṃ avisayaṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ gaccheyyāti.

Herein, 'like foam' means having known this body, which is called the aggregate of hair and so on, to be like a mass of foam, being powerless due to its weakness and not long-lasting due to its temporary nature. 'Having the nature of a mirage' means fully awakening, understanding, and knowing that just as a mirage appears to those standing far away as if it has form and can be grasped, but to those approaching it becomes empty, hollow, and unfit to be grasped, so too this body has the nature of a mirage due to its momentary and brief appearance. 'Māra's flowers' means the rounds of the three planes of existence, which are called Māra's flowers; a monk with taints destroyed, having cut them off with the noble path, should go to the deathless great Nibbāna, which is beyond the sight and domain of the King of Death.

Gāthāpariyosāne thero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā satthu suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ thomento vaṇṇento vandantova āgatoti.

At the end of the verse, the elder, having attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, returned praising, extolling, and paying homage to the Teacher's golden-hued body.

Marīcikammaṭṭhānikattheravatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Who Practiced Mirage Meditation, the Second.

3. Viṭaṭūbhavatthu

3. The Story of Viṭaṭūbha

Pupphāniheva pacinantanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto saparisaṃ mahoghena ajjhottharitvā māritaṃ viṭaṭūbhaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma discourse, which begins 'Just as one gathers flowers,' concerning Viṭaṭūbha, who, along with his retinue, was overwhelmed and killed by a great flood.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 1.0215] anupubbikathā – sāvatthiyañhi mahākosalarañño putto pasenadikumāro nāma. Vesāliyaṃ [V 1.0192] licchavirañño putto licchavikumāro [P 1.0338] mahāli nāma, kusinārāyaṃ mallarājaputto bandhulo nāmāti ime tayo disāpāmokkhassācariyassa santike sippuggahaṇatthaṃ takkasilaṃ gantvā bahinagare sālāya samāgatā aññamaññassa āgatakāraṇañca kulañca nāmañca pucchitvā sahāyakā hutvā ekatova ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā sippaṃ sikkhantā na cirasseva uggahitasippā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā ekatova nikkhamitvā sakasakaṭṭhānāni agamaṃsu. Tesu pasenadikumāro pitu sippaṃ dassetvā pasannena pitarā rajje abhisitto. Mahālikumāro licchavīnaṃ sippaṃ dassento mahantena ussāhena dassesi, tassa akkhīni bhijjitvā agamaṃsu. Licchavirājāno “aho vata amhākaṃ ācariyo akkhivināsaṃ patto, na naṃ pariccajissāma, upaṭṭhahissāma na”nti tassa satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ ekaṃ dvāraṃ adaṃsu. So taṃ nissāya pañcasate licchavirājaputte sippaṃ sikkhāpento vasi. Bandhulakumāro saṭṭhiṃ saṭṭhiṃ veḷū gahetvā majjhe ayasalākaṃ pakkhipitvā saṭṭhikalāpe ussāpetvā ṭhapite mallarājakulehi “ime kappetū”ti vutto asītihatthaṃ ākāsaṃ ullaṅghitvā asinā kappento agamāsi. So osānakalāpe [P 1.0339] ayasalākāya “kirī”ti saddaṃ sutvā, “kiṃ eta”nti pucchitvā sabbakalāpesu ayasalākānaṃ ṭhapitabhāvaṃ ñatvā asiṃ chaḍḍetvā rodamāno “mayhaṃ ettakesu ñātisuhajjesu ekopi sasineho hutvā imaṃ kāraṇaṃ nācikkhi. Sace hi ahaṃ jāneyyaṃ, ayasalākāya saddaṃ anuṭṭhāpentova chindeyya”nti vatvā, “sabbepime māretvā rajjaṃ kareyya”nti mātāpitūnaṃ kathesi. Tehi “paveṇirajjaṃ nāma, tāta, idaṃ na labbhā evaṃ kātu”nti nānappakārena vārito “tena hi mama sahāyakassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti sāvatthiṃ agamāsi.

Here is the sequential account: In Sāvatthī, there was a prince named Pasenadi, the son of the great Kosalan king. In Vesālī, there was a Licchavi prince named Mahāli, the son of the Licchavi king. In Kusinārā, there was a Malla prince named Bandhula. These three went to Takkasilā to learn skills under the renowned teacher Disāpāmokkha. Meeting in a hall outside the city, they inquired about each other’s reason for coming, family, and name, and became friends. Together, they approached the teacher and studied their skills. Before long, having mastered their skills, they took leave of the teacher and departed together, each returning to his own place. Among them, Prince Pasenadi demonstrated his skills to his father, and being pleased, his father consecrated him as king. Prince Mahāli, while displaying his skills to the Licchavis, exerted himself greatly, and his eyes were destroyed. The Licchavi kings lamented, 'Alas, our teacher has lost his sight! We will not abandon him; we will care for him.' They granted him a gate that yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand. Relying on this, he lived teaching his craft to five hundred Licchavi princes. Prince Bandhula had sixty bundles of bamboos set up, each containing sixty bamboos with an iron spike inserted in the middle. When told by the Malla princes, 'Cut these,' he leaped eighty cubits into the air and went along cutting them with his sword. In the last bundle, hearing the 'kirī' sound of the iron spike, he asked, 'What is that?' Learning that iron spikes had been placed in all the bundles, he threw down his sword and wept, saying, 'Among so many of my relatives and friends, not even one, out of affection, told me of this matter. Indeed, if I had known, I would have cut them without letting the iron spike make a sound!' Then he said to his parents, 'I will kill all of these Mallas and take the kingdom!' He was dissuaded by them in various ways, saying, 'Dear son, this which is called hereditary kingship cannot be obtained by acting in such a way.' Being thus prevented, he said, 'In that case, I will go to my friend,' and he went to Sāvatthī.

Pasenadi kosalo rājā tassāgamanaṃ sutvā paccuggantvā mahantena sakkārena taṃ nagaraṃ pavesetvā senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So mātāpitaro pakkosāpetvā tattheva vāsaṃ kappesi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā [M 1.0216] uparipāsāde ṭhito antaravīthiṃ olokayamāno “anāthapiṇḍikassa cūḷaanāthapiṇḍikassa visākhāya suppavāsāyā”ti etesaṃ gehe niccaṃ bhattakiccatthāya gacchante anekasahasse bhikkhū disvā, “kahaṃ, ayyā, gacchantī”ti pucchitvā, “deva, anāthapiṇḍikassa gehe niccabhattasalākabhattagilānabhattādīnaṃ atthāya devasikaṃ dve bhikkhusahassāni gacchanti, cūḷaanāthapiṇḍikassa gehe pañcasatāni, tathā visākhāya tathā suppavāsāyā”ti vutte sayampi bhikkhusaṅghaṃ upaṭṭhahitukāmo vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ [P 1.0340] satthāraṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ sahatthā dānaṃ datvā sattame divase satthāraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, pañcahi me bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nibaddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. “Mahārāja buddhā [V 1.0193] nāma ekaṭṭhāne nibaddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhanti, bahū janā buddhānaṃ āgamanaṃ paccāsīsantī”ti. “Tena hi ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ nibaddhaṃ pesethā”ti āha. Satthā ānandattherassa bhāraṃ akāsi. Rājā bhikkhusaṅghe āgate pattaṃ gahetvā, “ime nāma parivisantū”ti avicāretvāva sattāhaṃ sayameva parivisitvā aṭṭhame divase vikkhittacitto pamajjamakāsi. Rājakule nāma anāṇattā āsanāni paññāpetvā bhikkhū nisīdāpetvā parivisituṃ na labhanti “na mayaṃ idha ṭhātuṃ sakkhissāmā”ti bahū bhikkhū pakkamiṃsu. Rājā dutiyadivasepi pamajji, dutiyadivasepi bahū bhikkhū pakkamiṃsu. Tatiyadivasepi pamajji, tadā ānandattheraṃ ekakameva ṭhapetvā avasesā pakkamiṃsu. Puññavantā nāma kāraṇavasikā honti, kulānaṃ pasādaṃ rakkhanti. Tathāgatassa ca sāriputtatthero mahāmoggallānattheroti dve aggasāvakā, khemā uppalavaṇṇāti dve aggasāvikā, upāsakesu citto, gahapati, hatthako āḷavakoti dve aggaupāsakā, upāsikāsu veḷukaṇṭhakī nandamātā, khujjuttarāti dve aggaupāsikā, iti ime aṭṭha jane ādiṃ katvā ṭhānantarapattā sabbepi sāvakā ekadesena dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ pūritattā mahāpuññā abhinīhārasampannā. Ānandattheropi [P 1.0341] kappasatasahassaṃ pūritapāramī abhinīhārasampanno mahāpuñño attano kāraṇavasikatāya kulassa pasādaṃ rakkhanto aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ ekakameva nisīdāpetvā parivisiṃsu.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, upon hearing of his arrival, went out to meet him and, with great honor, led him into the city and appointed him to the position of commander-in-chief. He had his parents summoned and made them live right there. Then one day, the king, while standing on the upper terrace of his palace and looking down at the street, saw many thousands of monks going to the houses of Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and Suppavāsā for the purpose of their meal. He asked, 'Venerable sirs, where are you going?' When told, 'Your Majesty, two thousand monks go daily to Anāthapiṇḍika’s house for the sake of regular meals, ticket-meals, meals for the sick, and so on; five hundred to Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika’s house; likewise to Visākhā’s; and likewise to Suppavāsā’s,' he himself, desiring to support the Saṅgha of monks, went to the monastery. He invited the Teacher along with a thousand monks and for seven days gave alms with his own hands. On the seventh day, after paying homage to the Teacher, he said, 'Venerable sir, please accept a regular meal in my house for five hundred monks.' The Teacher replied, 'Great King, Buddhas do not accept a regular meal in one place; many people long for the arrival of the Buddhas.' 'In that case, venerable sir, please send one monk regularly,' he said. The Teacher assigned this duty to the Elder Ānanda. When the Saṅgha of monks arrived, the king took their bowls and, without assigning others by saying, 'Let these ones serve,' he himself served for seven days. On the eighth day, his mind was distracted, and he became negligent. In a royal household, they do not get to prepare seats, have the monks sit, and serve them without being ordered. Therefore, many monks departed, thinking, 'We will not be able to stay here.' The king was negligent on the second day as well, and many monks departed. He was negligent on the third day as well; then, leaving only the Elder Ānanda, the remaining monks departed. Those of great merit act in accordance with the situation; they protect the faith of families. The Tathāgata’s two chief disciples were the Elder Sāriputta and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; the two chief female disciples were Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā; among the male lay disciples, the two chief ones were Citta the householder and Hatthaka of Āḷavaka; and among the female lay disciples, the two chief ones were Veḷukaṇṭhakī Nandamātā and Khujjuttarā. Beginning with these eight people, all the disciples who had attained special status were of great merit and endowed with aspiration, having fulfilled the ten perfections in part. The Elder Ānanda, too, having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons, was of great merit and endowed with aspiration. Due to his own practice of acting in accordance with the situation, he remained, protecting the faith of the family. Seating him alone, they served him.

Rājā [M 1.0217] bhikkhūnaṃ gatakāle āgantvā khādanīyabhojanīyāni tatheva ṭhitāni disvā, “kiṃ, ayyā, nāgamiṃsū”ti pucchitvā, “ānandatthero ekakova āgato devā”ti sutvā, “addhā ettakaṃ me bhattacchedanamakaṃsū”ti bhikkhūnaṃ kuddho satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, mayā pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ bhikkhā paṭiyattā, ānandatthero kira ekakovāgato, paṭiyattā bhikkhā tatheva ṭhitā, pañcasatā bhikkhū mama gehe saññaṃ na kariṃsu, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āha. Satthā bhikkhūnaṃ dosaṃ avatvā, “mahārāja, mama sāvakānaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ vissāso natthi, tena na gatā bhavissantī”ti vatvā kulānaṃ anupagamanakāraṇañca upagamanakāraṇañca pakāsento bhikkhū āmantetvā imaṃ suttamāha –

After the monks had departed, the king arrived and, seeing the hard and soft foods still standing as they were, asked, “Sirs, did they not come?” Hearing, “Your Majesty, it is said that only the Elder Ānanda came,” he became angry with the monks, thinking, “Indeed, they have caused me this much loss of alms-food!” Then he went to the Teacher’s presence and said, “Venerable Sir, I had prepared alms for five hundred monks, but it seems only the Elder Ānanda came. The prepared alms remain just as they were. The five hundred monks did not resolve to take their meal in my house. What, indeed, could be the reason?” Without speaking of the monks’ fault, the Teacher said, “Great King, my disciples have no intimacy with you; for that reason, they probably did not come.” Then, explaining the reason for not approaching families and the reason for approaching them, he addressed the monks and spoke this sutta:

“Navahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ kulaṃ anupagantvā vā nālaṃ upagantuṃ, upagantvā vā nālaṃ upanisīdituṃ. Katamehi navahi? Na manāpena paccuṭṭhenti, na manāpena abhivādenti, na manāpena āsanaṃ denti, santamassa pariguhanti, bahukampi thokaṃ denti, paṇītampi lūkhaṃ denti, asakkaccaṃ denti no sakkaccaṃ, na upanisīdanti dhammassavanāya, bhāsitamassa na sussūsanti[P 1.0342]. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, navahaṅgehi [V 1.0194] samannāgataṃ kulaṃ anupagantvā vā nālaṃ upagantuṃ, upagantvā vā nālaṃ upanisīdituṃ.

“Monks, a family endowed with nine factors is unfit to be approached if unvisited, and unfit to be sat near if visited. What are the nine? They do not rise up pleasantly; they do not pay homage pleasantly; they do not offer a seat pleasantly; they conceal what is present; though there is much, they give little; though it is fine, they give what is coarse; they give disrespectfully, not respectfully; they do not sit near to listen to the Dhamma; and they do not listen attentively to what is spoken. Monks, a family endowed with these nine factors is unfit to be approached if unvisited, and unfit to be sat near if visited.”

“Navahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ kulaṃ anupagantvā vā alaṃ upagantuṃ, upagantvā vā alaṃ upanisīdituṃ. Katamehi navahi? Manāpena paccuṭṭhenti, manāpena abhivādenti, manāpena āsanaṃ denti, santamassa na pariguhanti, bahukampi bahukaṃ denti, paṇītampi paṇītaṃ denti, sakkaccaṃ denti no asakkaccaṃ, upanisīdanti dhammassavanāya, bhāsitamassa sussūsanti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, navahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ kulaṃ anupagantvā vā alaṃ upagantuṃ, upagantvā vā alaṃ upanisīditu”nti (a. ni. 9.17).

“Monks, a family endowed with nine factors is fit to be approached if unvisited, and fit to be sat near if visited. What are the nine? They rise up pleasantly; they pay homage pleasantly; they offer a seat pleasantly; they do not conceal what is present; though there is much, they give much; though it is fine, they give what is fine; they give respectfully, not disrespectfully; they sit near to listen to the Dhamma; and they listen attentively to what is spoken. Monks, a family endowed with these nine factors is fit to be approached if unvisited, and fit to be sat near if visited.”

Iti kho, mahārāja, mama sāvakā tumhākaṃ santikā vissāsaṃ alabhantā na gatā bhavissantīti. Porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi hi avissāsikaṭṭhāne sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhiyamānāpi māraṇantikaṃ vedanaṃ patvā vissāsikaṭṭhānameva agamiṃsūti. “Kadā, bhante”ti raññā puṭṭho atītaṃ āhari –

“Thus, indeed, Great King, my disciples, not obtaining intimacy from you, probably did not go. For indeed, even the wise ones of old, though being respectfully attended to in a place without intimacy, having reached a suffering that ends in death, went only to a place of intimacy.” When asked by the king, “When, Venerable Sir?” he brought forth the past:

Atīte [M 1.0218] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kesavo nāma rājā rajjaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Taṃ pañca purisasatāni anupabbajiṃsu. So kesavatāpaso nāma ahosi. Pasādhanakappako panassa anupabbajitvā kappako nāma antevāsiko ahosi. Kesavatāpaso parisāya saddhiṃ aṭṭha māse himavante vasitvā vassārattasamaye loṇambilasevanatthāya [P 1.0343] bārāṇasiṃ patvā bhikkhāya pāvisi. Atha naṃ rājā disvā pasīditvā catumāsaṃ attano santike vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gahetvā uyyāneva vasāpento sayaṃ sāyaṃpātaṃ assa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Avasesā tāpasā katipāhaṃ vasitvā hatthisaddādīhi ubbāḷhā hutvā ukkaṇṭhitvā, “ācariya, ukkaṇṭhitamhā, gacchāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Kahaṃ, tātā”ti? “Himavantaṃ, ācariyā”ti. Rājā amhākaṃ āgatadivaseyeva catumāsaṃ idha vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhi. “Kathaṃ gamissatha, tātā”ti? “Tumhehi amhākaṃ anācikkhitvāva paṭiññā dinnā, mayaṃ idha na sakkoma vasituṃ, ito avidūre tumhākaṃ pavattissavanaṭṭhāne vasissāmā”ti vanditvā pakkamiṃsu. Kappantevāsikena saddhiṃ ācariyo ohīyi.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a king named Kesava, having abandoned his kingdom, went forth into the ascetic life. Five hundred men went forth after him. He became known as the ascetic Kesava. His barber, having also gone forth, became his resident pupil named Kappaka. The ascetic Kesava, together with his retinue, having lived in the Himalayas for eight months, arrived in Bārāṇasī during the rainy season for the sake of partaking of salt and sour things, and entered the city for alms. Then the king, seeing him and being pleased, took a promise for him to stay in his presence for four months, and making him dwell in the park, he himself would go to attend on him in the evening and morning. The remaining ascetics, having stayed for a few days, being oppressed by the sounds of elephants and so on, became discontented and said, “Teacher, we are discontented; let us go.” He asked, “Where to, dear ones?” “To the Himalayas, Teacher.” “The king took a promise from us on the very day we arrived to stay here for four months. How will you go, dear ones?” “The promise was given by you without informing us; we are not able to stay here. We will dwell not far from here, in a place where news of you can be heard.” Having paid homage, they departed. The teacher was left behind with his pupil Kappaka.

Rājā upaṭṭhānaṃ āgato, “kahaṃ, ayyā”ti pucchi. “Sabbe ukkaṇṭhitamhāti vatvā himavantaṃ [V 1.0195] gatā, mahārājā”ti āha. Kappakopi na cirasseva ukkaṇṭhitvā ācariyena punappunaṃ vāriyamānopi “na sakkomī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Itaresaṃ pana santikaṃ agantvā ācariyassa pavattiṃ suṇanto avidūre ṭhāne vasi. Aparabhāge ācariyassa antevāsike anussarantassa kucchirogo uppajji. Rājā vejjehi tikicchāpesi, rogo na vūpasammati. Tāpaso āha – “kiṃ, mahārāja, icchasi me rogavūpasama”nti? “Bhante, sacāhaṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ, idāneva vo phāsukaṃ kareyya”nti. “Mahārāja, sace me phāsukaṃ icchasi, maṃ antevāsikānaṃ santikaṃ pesehī”ti. Rājā “sādhu[P 1.0344], bhante”ti taṃ mañcake nipajjāpetvā nāradaamaccappamukhe cattāro amacce “mama ayyassa pavattiṃ ñatvā, mayhaṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇeyyāthā”ti uyyojesi. Kappantevāsiko ācariyassa āgamanaṃ sutvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā itare “kaha”nti vutte, “asukaṭṭhāne kira vasantī”ti āha. Tepi ācariyassāgamanabhāvaṃ sutvā tattheva samosaritvā ācariyassa uṇhodakaṃ datvā phalāphalaṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ [M 1.0219] khaṇaññeva rogo vūpasammati. So katipāheneva suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi. Atha naṃ nārado pucchi –

The king came to attend on him and asked, “Where are the venerable ones?” He replied, “Great King, they all said, ‘We are discontented,’ and went to the Himalayas.” Kappaka too, not long after, became discontented, and though repeatedly restrained by the teacher, he said, “I am not able,” and departed. However, not going to the others, he dwelt in a place not far away, listening for news of his teacher. In time, while the teacher was remembering his pupils, a stomach disease arose in him. The king had him treated by physicians, but the disease did not subside. The ascetic said, “Great King, do you wish for my disease to subside?” “Venerable Sir, if I were able, I would make you comfortable right now.” “Great King, if you wish for my comfort, send me to my pupils.” The king said, “Very well, Venerable Sir,” and having had him lie down on a couch, he dispatched four ministers headed by Nārada, saying, “Learn of my venerable one’s condition and send a message to me.” The pupil Kappaka, hearing of the teacher’s arrival, went out to meet him. When asked, “Where are the others?” he said, “It is said they are dwelling in such-and-such a place.” They too, hearing of the teacher’s arrival, assembled right there, gave the teacher warm water, and offered him various fruits. At that very moment, the disease subsided. In just a few days, his complexion became golden. Then Nārada asked him:

“Manussindaṃ jahitvāna, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Kathaṃ nu bhagavā kesī, kappassa ramati assame.

“Having abandoned the lord of men, the provider of all desires, how then does the Blessed One, Kesī, delight in the hermitage of Kappa?”

“Sādūni ramaṇīyāni, santi vakkhā manoramā;

Subhāsitāni kappassa, nārada ramayanti maṃ.

“There are trees here, Nārada, that are sweet, delightful, and pleasing to the mind; and the well-spoken words of Kappa delight me.”

“Sālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Kathaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ, aloṇaṃ chādayanti taṃ.

“Having eaten pure Sāli rice with meat sauce, how can unsalted millet and wild rice now satisfy you?”

“Sāduṃ vā yadi vāsāduṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Vissattho yattha bhuñjeyya, vissāsaparamā rasā”ti. (jā. 1.4.181-184);

“Whether it be tasty or not, whether it be little or much, where one eats with trust—that is where the taste is. Trust is the supreme flavor.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānento “tadā rājā moggallāno ahosi, nārado sāriputto, kappantevāsiko [P 1.0345] ānando, kesavatāpaso ahamevā”ti vatvā, “evaṃ, mahārāja, pubbepi paṇḍitā māraṇantikaṃ vedanaṃ patvā vissāsikaṭṭhānaṃ gamiṃsu, mama sāvakā [V 1.0196] tumhākaṃ santike vissāsaṃ na labhanti maññe”ti āha. Rājā “bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ mayā vissāsaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kathaṃ nu kho karissāmīti sammāsambuddhassa ñātidhītaraṃ mama gehe kātuṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ sante ‘daharā ca sāmaṇerā ca sammāsambuddhassa ñātirājā’ti mama santikaṃ vissatthā nibaddhaṃ āgamissantī”ti cintetvā – “ekaṃ me dhītaraṃ dentū”ti sākiyānaṃ santikaṃ sāsanaṃ pesesi. “Katarassa sakyassa dhītā”ti ca pucchitvā, “ñatvā āgaccheyyāthā”ti vatvā dūte āṇāpesi. Dūtā gantvā sākiye dārikaṃ yāciṃsu. Te sannipatitvā, “pakkhantariko rājā, sace na dassāma, vināsessati no, na kho pana amhehi kulena sadiso, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti mantayiṃsu. Mahānāmo “mama dāsiyā kucchimhi jātā vāsabhakhattiyā nāma dhītā rūpasobhaggappattā atthi, taṃ dassāmā”ti vatvā dūte āha – “sādhu, rañño dārikaṃ dassāmā”ti. “Sā kassa, dhītā”ti? “Sammāsambuddhassa cūḷapituputtassa mahānāmassa sakkassa dhītā vāsabhakhattiyā nāmā”ti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and connecting the Jātaka, said: 'At that time, the king was Moggallāna, Nārada was Sāriputta, Kappa's disciple was Ānanda, and Kesava the ascetic was myself.' Then he said, 'Thus, great king, in the past, the wise, having experienced mortal pain, went to a place of trust. It seems my disciples do not find trust in your presence.' The king thought, 'It is fitting for me to establish trust with the community of monks. How shall I do it? It is proper to have a kinswoman of the Fully Enlightened One in my home. In this way, young monks and novices, thinking, "He is a kinsman-king of the Fully Enlightened One," will come to my presence trustingly and continually.' Having thought thus, he sent a message to the Sākiyans: 'Give me a daughter.' And he commanded the messengers, saying, 'Ask, "Whose daughter is she, of which Sākiyan?" and having found out, return.' The messengers went and requested a girl from the Sākiyans. They assembled and deliberated, 'The king has many allies. If we do not give her, he will destroy us. But he is not our equal in clan. What is to be done?' Mahānāma said, 'I have a daughter named Vāsabhakhattiyā, born in the womb of my slave woman, who has attained beauty and grace. We will give her.' And he said to the messengers, 'Good, we will give a girl to the king.' When asked, 'Whose daughter is she?' they replied, 'She is Vāsabhakhattiyā, the daughter of Mahānāma the Sākiyan, the son of the Fully Enlightened One’s paternal younger uncle.'

Te [M 1.0220] gantvā rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā “yadi evaṃ, sādhu, sīghaṃ ānetha, khattiyā ca nāma bahumāyā, dāsidhītarampi pahiṇeyyuṃ, pitarā saddhiṃ ekabhājane bhuñjantiṃ āneyyāthā”ti [P 1.0346] pesesi. Te gantvā, “deva, tumhehi saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjantiṃ rājā icchatī”ti āhaṃsu. Mahānāmo “sādhu, tātā”ti taṃ alaṅkārāpetvā attano bhojanakāle pakkosāpetvā tāya saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjanākāraṃ dassetvā dūtānaṃ niyyādesi. Te taṃ ādāya sāvatthiṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā tuṭṭhamānaso taṃ pañcannaṃ itthisatānaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ katvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne abhisiñci. Sā na cirasseva suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi.

They went and informed the king. The king said, 'If that is so, good. Bring her quickly. For nobles are indeed full of deceit; they might even send a slave girl. Bring the girl who is eating from the same dish with her father.' He sent them. They went and said, 'O Deva, the king wishes for the girl who eats together with you.' Mahānāma replied, 'Good, my dears,' and having had her adorned, he had her summoned at his mealtime. Having shown the manner of eating together with her, he entrusted her to the messengers. Taking her, they went to Sāvatthī and reported the matter to the king. The king, with a pleased mind, made her the chief among five hundred women and consecrated her in the position of chief queen. Not long after, she gave birth to a son with a golden complexion.

Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase rājā dārakassa ayyakassa santikaṃ pesesi “sakyarājadhītā vāsabhakhattiyā puttaṃ vijātā, kimassa nāmaṃ karomā”ti? Taṃ pana sāsanaṃ gahetvā gato amacco thokaṃ badhiradhātuko, so gantvā rañño ayyakassa ārocesi, so taṃ sutvā “vāsabhakhattiyā puttaṃ avijāyitvāpi sabbajanaṃ abhibhavi, idāni pana rañño ativiya vallabhā bhavissatī”ti āha. Badhiro amacco “vallabhā”ti vacanaṃ dussutaṃ sutvā “viṭaṭūbho”ti sallakkhetvā rājānaṃ upagantvā, “deva, kumārassa kira ‘viṭaṭūbho’ti nāmaṃ karothā”ti āha. Rājā “porāṇakaṃ no kulasantakaṃ nāmaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā taṃ nāmaṃ akāsi. Athassa daharakāleyeva rājā “satthu piyaṃ karomī”ti senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi.

Then, on the day for the naming of the child, the king sent a message to the boy's grandfather, saying: 'The Sākiyan princess Vāsabhakhattiyā has given birth to a son. What name shall we give him?' Now, the minister who took the message was somewhat hard of hearing. He went and reported to the boy's grandfather, the king. Hearing this, he said: 'Even before giving birth to a son, Vāsabhakhattiyā held sway over everyone; now she will become exceedingly beloved to the king.' The deaf minister, mishearing the word 'vallabhā,' took it to be 'Viṭaṭūbha,' and approaching the king, he said: 'Deva, they say you should give the prince the name "Viṭaṭūbha."' The king, thinking, 'This must be an ancient name belonging to our clan,' gave him that name. Then, while he was still a boy, the king, thinking, 'I will do what is pleasing to the Teacher,' gave him the position of general.

So kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhanto sattavassikakāle aññesaṃ kumārānaṃ mātāmahakulato hatthirūpakaassarūpakādīni [V 1.0197] āhariyamānāni disvā mātaraṃ pucchi – “amma, aññesaṃ mātāmahakulato [P 1.0347] paṇṇākāro āharīyati, mayhaṃ koci kiñci na pesesi, kiṃ tvaṃ nimātā nipitā”ti? Atha naṃ sā, “tāta, tava sakyarājāno mātāmahā dūre pana vasanti, tena te kiñci na pesentī”ti vañcesi. Soḷasavassikakāle, “amma, tava mātāmahakulaṃ passitukāmomhī”ti vatvā, “alaṃ, tāta, kiṃ tattha gantvā karissatī”ti vāriyamānopi punappunaṃ yāci. Athassa mātā “tena hi gacchā”ti sampaṭicchi. So pitu ārocetvā mahantena parivārena nikkhami. Vāsabhakhattiyā puretaraṃ paṇṇaṃ pesesi – “ahaṃ [M 1.0221] idha sukhaṃ vasāmi, māssa kiñci sāmino antaraṃ dassayiṃsū”ti. Sākiyā viṭaṭūbhassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā, “vandituṃ na sakkomā”ti tassa daharadahare kumāre janapadaṃ pahiṇitvā tasmiṃ kapilapuraṃ sampatte santhāgāre sannipatiṃsu. Kumāro tattha gantvā aṭṭhāsi.

He, growing up with the attendance befitting a prince, at the age of seven, saw that other princes were brought toy elephants, toy horses, and the like from their maternal relatives, and he asked his mother: 'Mother, gifts are brought to other princes from their maternal relatives, but no one sends me anything. Do you have no mother, no father?' Then she deceived him, saying: 'My dear, your maternal relatives, the Sākiyan kings, live far away; that is why they do not send you anything.' At the age of sixteen, he said, 'Mother, I wish to see your maternal family.' Though he was restrained by her saying, 'Enough, my dear, what will you do by going there?' he asked again and again. Then his mother consented, 'In that case, go.' He informed his father and set out with a great retinue. Vāsabhakhattiyā sent a message ahead: 'I am living happily here. Let them not reveal any inferiority concerning my son.' The Sākiyans, learning of Viṭaṭūbha's arrival, thought, 'We cannot pay him homage,' and sent their very youngest princes to the countryside. When he arrived at Kapilapura, they assembled in the council hall. The prince went there and stood.

Atha naṃ “ayaṃ te, tāta, mātāmaho, ayaṃ mātulo”ti vatvā vandāpesuṃ. So sabbe vandamāno vicaritvā ekampi attānaṃ vandantaṃ adisvā “kiṃ nu kho maṃ vandantā natthī”ti pucchi. Sākiyā, “tāta, te kaniṭṭhakumārā janapadaṃ gatā”ti vatvā tassa mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ [P 1.0348] kariṃsu. So katipāhaṃ vasitvā mahantena parivārena nikkhami. Athekā dāsī santhāgāre tena nisinnaphalakaṃ “idaṃ vāsabhakhattiyāya dāsiyā puttassa nisinnaphalaka”nti akkositvā paribhāsitvā khīrodakena dhovi. Eko puriso attano āvudhaṃ pamussitvā nivatto taṃ gaṇhanto viṭaṭūbhakumārassa akkosanasaddaṃ sutvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchitvā, “vāsabhakhattiyā dāsiyā kucchimhi mahānāmasakkaṃ paṭicca jātā”ti ñatvā balakāyassa kathesi. “Vāsabhakhattiyā kira dāsidhītā”ti mahākolāhalaṃ ahosi. Taṃ sutvā viṭaṭūbho “ete tāva mama nisinnaphalakaṃ khīrodakena dhovantu, ahaṃ pana rajje patiṭṭhitakāle etesaṃ galalohitaṃ gahetvā mama nisinnaphalakaṃ dhovissāmī”ti cittaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ sāvatthiṃ gate amaccā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā “mayhaṃ dāsidhītaraṃ adaṃsū”ti sākiyānaṃ kujjhitvā vāsabhakhattiyāya ca puttassa ca dinnaparihāraṃ acchinditvā dāsadāsīhi laddhabbamattameva dāpesi.

Then they said to him, 'My dear, this is your maternal grandfather, this is your maternal uncle,' and had him pay homage. He paid homage to all, but after looking around and not seeing even one person paying homage to him, he asked, 'Is there truly no one to pay homage to me?' The Sākiyans replied, 'My dear, the younger princes have gone to the countryside,' and they showed him great honor. After staying for some days, he departed with a large retinue. Then a certain female slave in the assembly hall reviled and scolded the seat he had sat upon, saying, 'This is the seat of the son of Vāsabhakhattiyā, the slave woman,' and washed it with milk-water. A certain man, having forgotten his weapon, returned to retrieve it and heard Prince Viṭaṭūbha being reviled. Inquiring into the matter, he learned, 'Vāsabhakhattiyā was born in the womb of a slave woman through Mahānāma the Sākiyan,' and told it to the army. A great uproar arose: 'It seems Vāsabhakhattiyā is a slave's daughter!' Hearing this, Viṭaṭūbha made a resolution, 'For now, let them wash the seat I sat on with milk-water. But when I am established in the kingdom, I will take the blood from their throats and wash the seat I sat on.' When he arrived in Sāvatthī, the ministers reported the matter to the king. The king, angered that 'They gave me a slave's daughter!', revoked the provisions granted to Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son, and had them given only what is fit to be received by male and female slaves.

Tato katipāhaccayena satthā rājanivesanaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Rājā āgantvā vanditvā, “bhante, tumhākaṃ kira ñātakehi dāsidhītā mayhaṃ [P 1.0349] dinnā, tenassā ahaṃ saputtāya parihāraṃ acchinditvā dāsadāsīhi laddhabbamattameva dāpesi”nti āha. Satthā “ayuttaṃ, mahārāja, sākiyehi kataṃ, dadantehi nāma samānajātikā dātabbā assa, taṃ pana[V 1.0198], mahārāja, vadāmi, vāsabhakhattiyā khattiyarājadhītā khattiyarañño gehe abhisekaṃ labhi. Viṭaṭūbhopi khattiyarājānameva paṭicca jāto, mātugottaṃ [M 1.0222] nāma kiṃ karissati, pitugottameva pamāṇanti. Porāṇakapaṇḍitā dalidditthiyā kaṭṭhahārikāya aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ adaṃsu, tassā ca kucchimhi jātakumāro dvādasayojanikāya bārāṇasiyā rajjaṃ patvā kaṭṭhavāhanarājā nāma jāto”ti kaṭṭhahārijātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.7) kathesi. Rājā dhammakathaṃ sutvā “pitugottameva kira pamāṇa”nti tussitvā vāsabhakhattiyāya ca puttassa ca pakatiparihārameva dāpesi.

Then, after some days had passed, the Teacher went to the king’s residence and sat down on the prepared seat. The king approached, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, it seems your kinsmen gave me a slave's daughter. For that reason, I revoked the provisions for her and her son, and had them given only what is appropriate for male and female slaves.' The Teacher replied, 'Great King, what the Sakyans have done is improper. When giving in marriage, one of equal birth should be given. However, Great King, I say this: Vāsabhakhattiyā is a king's daughter and received the royal consecration in the house of a Khattiya king. Viṭaṭūbha, too, was born through a Khattiya king. What can the mother’s lineage do? The father’s lineage is the standard.' Then he related the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka: 'The wise men of old gave the position of chief queen to a poor wood-gathering woman. The prince born from her womb attained the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent, and became King Kaṭṭhavāhana.' Hearing the Dhamma discourse, the king was pleased and thought, 'Indeed, the father’s lineage is the standard,' and he had the normal provisions restored to Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son.

Bandhulasenāpatissapi kho kusinārāyaṃ mallarājadhītā mallikā nāma bhariyā dīgharattaṃ puttaṃ na vijāyi. Atha naṃ bandhulo “attano kulagharameva gacchā”ti uyyojesi. Sā “satthāraṃ disvāva gamissāmī”ti jetavanaṃ pavisitvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā ṭhitā, “kahaṃ gacchasī”ti vuttā “sāmiko maṃ [P 1.0350] bhante, kulagharaṃ pesetī” āha. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Vañjhā kirasmi aputtikā”ti. “Yadi evaṃ, gamanakiccaṃ natthi, nivattassū”ti. Sā tuṭṭhamānasā satthāraṃ vanditvā nivesanaṃ gantvā “kasmā nivattāsī”ti vuttā “dasabalena nivattitāmhī”ti āha bandhulo “diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati dīghadassinā kāraṇa”nti sampaṭicchi. Sā na cirasseva gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā uppannadāhaḷā “dohaḷo me uppanno”ti ārocesi. “Kiṃ dohaḷo”ti? “Vesālinagare gaṇarājakulānaṃ abhisekamaṅgalapokkharaṇiyaṃ otaritvā nhatvā pānīyaṃ pātukāmāmhi, sāmī”ti. Bandhulo “sādhū”ti vatvā sahassathāmadhanuṃ gahetvā taṃ rathaṃ āropetvā sāvatthito nikkhamitvā rathaṃ pājento mahālilicchavino dinnadvārena vesāliṃ pāvisi. Mahālilicchavino ca dvārasamīpe eva nivesanaṃ hoti. So rathassa ummāre panighātasaddaṃ sutvāva “bandhulassa rathasaddo eso, ajja licchavīnaṃ bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti āha.

Now, the wife of General Bandhula was named Mallikā, the daughter of a Malla king in Kusinārā. For a long time, she did not bear a son. Then Bandhula urged her, saying, 'Go to your own family home.' She, thinking, 'I will go only after seeing the Teacher,' entered Jetavana, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and stood there. When asked, 'Where are you going?' she said, 'Venerable sir, my husband is sending me to my family home.' 'For what reason?' 'It seems I am barren and childless.' 'If that is so, there is no need to go; turn back.' With a delighted mind, she paid homage to the Teacher and went home. When asked, 'Why have you returned?' she said, 'I was turned back by the One with Ten Powers.' Bandhula accepted this, saying, 'A reason must have been seen by the Far-Seeing One.' Not long after, she conceived, and when a pregnancy craving arose, she announced, 'A craving has arisen in me.' 'What is the craving?' 'My lord, I wish to descend into the auspicious consecration pond of the ruling clans in Vesālī, bathe, and drink the water.' Bandhula said, 'Very well,' and taking a bow with the strength of a thousand men, he placed her in a chariot and set out from Sāvatthī. Driving the chariot, he entered Vesālī through the gate assigned to Mahāli the Licchavi. Mahāli the Licchavi's residence was right near the gate. As soon as he heard the sound of the chariot striking the gate's threshold, he said, 'That is the sound of Bandhula’s chariot. Today, a danger will arise for the Licchavis.'

Pokkharaṇiyā anto ca bahi ca ārakkhā balavatī, upari lohajālaṃ patthaṭaṃ, sakuṇānampi okāso natthi. Bandhulasenāpati [P 1.0351] pana rathā otaritvā ārakkhake manusse vettena paharanto palāpetvā lohajālaṃ chinditvā antopokkharaṇīyaṃ bhariyaṃ nhāpetvā sayampi nhatvā puna taṃ rathaṃ āropetvā nagarā nikkhamitvā āgatamaggeneva pāyāsi. Te ārakkhamanussā licchavirājūnaṃ ārocesuṃ. Licchavirājāno kujjhitvā pañca rathasatāni āruyha “bandhulamallaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti nikkhamiṃsu. Taṃ pavattiṃ [M 1.0223] mahālissa ārocesuṃ. Mahāli, “mā gamittha, so hi vo sabbe ghotessatī”ti āha. Tepi “mayaṃ gamissāma evā”ti vadiṃsu. “Tena hi tassa rathacakkassa yāva nābhito pathaviṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ disvā nivatteyyātha, tato [V 1.0199] anivattantā purato asanisaddaṃ viya suṇissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha. Tato anivattantā tumhākaṃ rathadhuresu chiddaṃ passissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha, purato mā gamitthā”ti. Te tassa vacanena anivattitvā taṃ anubandhiṃsu [P 1.0352] eva. Mallikā disvā, “rathā, sāmi, paññāyantī”ti āha. “Tena hi ekasseva rathassa paññāyanakāle maṃ āroceyyāsī”ti. Sā yadā sabbe rathā eko viya hutvā paññāyiṃsu, tadā “ekameva, sāmi, rathasīsaṃ paññāyatī”ti āha. Bandhulo “tena hi imā rasmiyo gaṇhāhī”ti tassā rasmiyo datvā rathe ṭhitova dhanuṃ āropesi, rathacakkaṃ yāva nābhito pathaviṃ pāvisi.

Inside and outside the pond, the guards were strong, and above, an iron net was spread; there was no opening even for birds. But General Bandhula, descending from his chariot, struck the guards with his sword, causing them to flee. He cut through the iron net, entered the pond, had his wife bathe and drink, and after bathing himself, he again placed her on the chariot, departed from the city, and proceeded by the very same road he had come. Those guards informed the Licchavi kings. The Licchavi kings, having become enraged, mounted five hundred chariots and set out, saying, 'We will capture Bandhula and Mallikā!' They informed Mahāli of this matter. Mahāli said, 'Do not go, for he will kill all of you.' But they said, 'We will go nonetheless.' 'In that case, when you see the place where his chariot wheel has sunk into the ground up to the hub, you should turn back. If you do not turn back from there, you will hear a sound ahead like thunder; you should turn back from that place. If you do not turn back from there, you will see a hole in the yokes of your chariots; you should turn back from that place. After that, do not go any further.' Not turning back at his word, they pursued him indeed. Mallikā, seeing them, said, 'My lord, chariots are visible.' 'In that case, inform me when only a single chariot appears.' When all the chariots appeared as if they were one, she then said, 'My lord, only a single chariot-front is visible.' Bandhula said, 'In that case, take these reins.' Giving her the reins, while standing on the chariot, he strung his bow. The chariot wheel sank into the ground up to the hub.

Licchavino taṃ ṭhānaṃ disvāpi na nivattiṃsu. Itaro thokaṃ gantvā jiyaṃ pothesi, asanisaddo viya ahosi. Te tatopi na nivattiṃsu, anubandhantā gacchanteva. Bandhulo rathe ṭhitakova ekasaraṃ khipi, so pañcannaṃ rathasatānaṃ rathasīse chiddaṃ katvā pañca rājasatāni parikarabandhanaṭṭhāne vinivijjhitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Te attano paviddhabhāvaṃ ajānitvā, “tiṭṭha, re, tiṭṭha, re”ti vadantā anubandhiṃsu eva. Bandhulo rathaṃ ṭhapetvā “tumhe matakā, matakehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ yuddhaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. “Matakā nāma amhādisā na hontī”ti. “Tena hi sabbapacchimassa parikaraṃ mocethā”ti. Te mocayiṃsu. So muttamatte eva maritvā patito. Atha te sabbepi “tumhe evarūpā, attano gharāni gantvā saṃvidhātabbaṃ saṃvidahitvā puttadāraṃ anusāsitvā sannāhaṃ [P 1.0353] mocethā”ti āha. Te tathā katvā sabbepi jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā. Bandhulopi mallikaṃ sāvatthiṃ ānesi. Sā soḷasakkhattuṃ yamake yamake putte vijāyi. Sabbepi sūrā thāmasampannā ahesuṃ, sabbasippānaṃ nipphattiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Ekekassa purisasahassaṃ parivāro ahosi. Pitarā saddhiṃ rājanivesanaṃ gacchantehi teheva rājaṅgaṇaṃ paripūri.

The Licchavis, though seeing that place, did not turn back. The other, having gone a short distance, twanged his bowstring; it was like the sound of thunder. They did not turn back from there either, but continued their pursuit. Bandhula, while standing on his chariot, shot a single arrow. That arrow, having made a hole in the fronts of the five hundred chariots, pierced through the five hundred kings at the place where their armor was fastened and entered the earth. They, not knowing that they had been pierced, continued to pursue, shouting, 'Stop, fellow! Stop, fellow!' Bandhula, having stopped his chariot, said, 'You are dead men. I do not battle with the dead.' They said, 'Dead men are not like us.' 'In that case, have the armor of the very last man loosened.' They had it loosened. As soon as it was loosened, he died and fell. Then he said to all of them, 'You are also in the same state. Go to your own homes, arrange what must be arranged, instruct your sons and wives, and then remove your armor.' They did so, and all of them reached the end of their lives. Bandhula also brought Mallikā to Sāvatthī. She gave birth to sons in pairs sixteen times. All of them were brave and endowed with strength; they reached the completion of all skills. Each one had a retinue of a thousand men. When they went with their father to the royal palace, the royal courtyard was filled by them alone.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0224] vinicchaye kūṭaṭṭaparājitā manussā bandhulaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā mahāviravaṃ viravantā vinicchayaamaccānaṃ kūṭaṭṭakaraṇaṃ tassa ārocesuṃ. So vinicchayaṃ gantvā taṃ aṭṭaṃ vicāretvā sāmikameva sāmikaṃ akāsi. Mahājano mahāsaddena sādhukāraṃ pavatteti. Rājā “kiṃ ida”nti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā tussitvā sabbepi te amacce hāretvā bandhulasseva vinicchayaṃ niyyādesi. So tato paṭṭhāya sammā vinicchayi. Tato te porāṇakavinicchayikā amaccā kiñci lañjaṃ alabhantā appalābhā hutvā “bandhulo rajjaṃ patthetī”ti rājakule paribhindiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ kathaṃ saddahitvā cittaṃ niggahetuṃ nāsakkhi. “Imasmiṃ idheva ghātiyamāne garahā me uppajjissatī”ti puna cintetvā payuttapurisehi paccantaṃ pahārāpetvā bandhulaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “paccanto kira kupito, tava puttehi saddhiṃ gantvā[P 1.0354], core gaṇhāhī”ti [V 1.0200] pahiṇitvā, “etthevassa dvattiṃsāya puttehi saddhiṃ sīsaṃ chinditvā āharathā”ti tehi saddhiṃ aññepi samatthe mahāyodhe pesesi. Tasmiṃ paccantaṃ gacchanteyeva “senāpati kira āgacchatī”ti payuttacorā palāyiṃsu. So taṃ padesaṃ āvāsāpetvā saṇṭhāpetvā nivatti.

Then one day, at the hall of justice, people who had been defeated by a fraudulent judgment, seeing Bandhula coming, made a great lamentation and reported to him the fraudulent actions of the judicial ministers. He went to the hall of justice, investigated that case, and made the rightful owner the owner indeed. The great crowd raised a great shout of approval.
