The king, having asked, 'What is this?' and having heard the matter, was pleased. He had all those ministers removed and entrusted the administration of justice to Bandhula alone. From that time on, he judged righteously. Then those former judicial ministers, not receiving any bribes and thus having little gain, sowed discord among the royal family, saying, 'Bandhula desires the kingdom.' The king, believing their words, was unable to control his mind. Thinking again, 'If this one is killed right here, blame will arise for me,' he had the border region attacked by dispatched men. Then, having had Bandhula summoned, he sent him, saying, 'The border region, it is said, is in revolt. Go with your sons and seize the thieves.' And with them, he also sent other capable, great warriors, saying, 'Right there, cut off his head along with his thirty-two sons and bring it here.' Just as he was going to the border region, the dispatched thieves fled, thinking, 'The general, it is said, is coming!' He, having had that region inhabited and pacified, returned.

Athassa nagarato avidūre ṭhāne te yodhā puttehi saddhiṃ sīsaṃ chindiṃsu. Taṃ divasaṃ mallikāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ dve aggasāvakā nimantitā honti. Athassā pubbaṇhe eva “sāmikassa te saddhiṃ puttehi sīsaṃ chinna”nti paṇṇaṃ āharitvā adaṃsu. Sā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā kassaci kiñci avatvā paṇṇaṃ ucchaṅge ṭhapetvā bhikkhusaṅghameva parivisi. Athassā paricārikāyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhattaṃ datvā sappicāṭiṃ āharantiyo therānaṃ purato sappicāṭiṃ bhindiṃsu. Dhammasenāpati “bhedanadhammaṃ bhinnaṃ, na cintitabba”nti āha. Sā ucchaṅgato paṇṇaṃ nīharitvā “dvattiṃsāya puttehi saddhiṃ pitusīsaṃ chinnanti me imaṃ paṇṇaṃ āhariṃsu, ahaṃ idaṃ sutvāpi na cintemi, sappicāṭiyā bhinnāya kiṃ cintayissāmi, bhante”ti āha. Dhammasenāpati “animittamanaññātaṃ[P 1.0355], maccānaṃ idha jīvita”ntiādīni (su. ni. 579) vatvā dhammaṃ desetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāpi dvattiṃsa suṇisāyo pakkosāpetvā, “tumhākaṃ sāmikā niraparādhā attano purimakammaphalaṃ labhiṃsu[M 1.0225], tumhe mā socayittha, mā paridevittha, rañño upari manopadosaṃ mā karitthā”ti ovadi.

Then, at a place not far from the city, those warriors cut off his head along with his sons. On that day, Mallikā had invited the two chief disciples together with five hundred monks. Then, in the early morning, they brought and gave her a letter stating: “Your husband’s head has been cut off along with his sons.” Knowing this news, she, without saying anything to anyone, placed the letter in her lap and served only the community of monks. Then, as her female attendants, having given food to the monks, were bringing a pot of ghee, they broke the ghee pot in front of the elders. The General of the Dhamma said, “That which is of a nature to break has broken; it should not be worried about.” She, taking the letter from her lap, said, “They brought me this letter stating that the father’s head has been cut off along with his thirty-two sons. Even having heard this, I do not worry. Why, venerable sir, should I worry about a broken ghee pot?” The General of the Dhamma, having spoken the verses beginning with “Unsignified and unknown is the life of mortals here,” and having taught the Dhamma, rose from his seat and went to the monastery. She too, having had her thirty-two daughters-in-law summoned, advised them: “Your husbands were innocent; they have received the fruit of their own past kamma. Do not sorrow, do not lament, and do not bear ill will towards the king.”

Rañño carapurisā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā gantvā tesaṃ niddosabhāvaṃ rañño kathayiṃsu. Rājā saṃvegappatto tassā nivesanaṃ gantvā mallikañca suṇisāyo cassā khamāpetvā mallikāya varaṃ adāsi. Sā “varo gahito me hotū”ti vatvā tasmiṃ gate matakabhattaṃ datvā nhatvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā, “deva, tumhehi mayhaṃ varo dinno, mayhañca aññena attho natthi, dvattiṃsāya me suṇisānaṃ mamañca kulagharagamanaṃ anujānāthā”ti āha. Rājā sampaṭicchi. Sā dvattiṃsa suṇisāyo yathāsakāni kulāni pesesi, sayampi kusinārānagare attano kulagharaṃ agamāsi.

The king’s spies, having heard that conversation, went and reported their state of blamelessness to the king. The king, stricken with remorse, went to her residence, asked for forgiveness from Mallikā and her daughters-in-law, and gave a boon to Mallikā. She said, “Let the boon be accepted by me.” After he had gone, she gave food for the dead, bathed, approached the king, paid homage, and said, “Your Majesty, a boon was given to me by you, and I have no need for anything else. Please permit my thirty-two daughters-in-law and me to return to our family homes.” The king agreed. She sent the thirty-two daughters-in-law to their own respective family homes, and she herself went to her own family home in the city of Kusinārā.

Rājāpi bandhulasenāpatino bhāgineyyassa dīghakārāyanassa nāma senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So pana “mātulo me iminā mārito”ti rañño otāraṃ gavesanto vicarati. Rājāpi niraparādhassa [P 1.0356] bandhulassa māritakālato paṭṭhāya vippaṭisārī hutvā cittassādaṃ na labhati, rajjasukhaṃ nānubhoti. Tadā satthā sakyānaṃ medāḷupaṃ nāma nigamaṃ upanissāya viharati. Rājā tattha gantvā ārāmato avidūre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsetvā, “mandena parivārena satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti [V 1.0201] vihāraṃ gantvā pañcarājākakudhabhaṇḍāni dīghakārāyanassa datvā ekakova gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Sabbaṃ dhammacetiyasuttaniyāmena (ma. ni. 2.364 ādayo) dīpetabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe dīghakārāyano tāni pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni gahetvā viṭaṭūbhaṃ rājānaṃ katvā rañño ekaṃ assaṃ ekañca upaṭṭhānakārikaṃ mātugāmaṃ ṭhapetvā nivattetvā sāvatthiṃ agamāsi.

The king also gave the position of commander-in-chief to Dīghakārāyana, the nephew of Bandhula the commander-in-chief. But he, thinking, “My maternal uncle was killed by this one,” went about seeking an opportunity against the king. The king, too, from the time of the killing of the innocent Bandhula, being remorseful, found no peace of mind and did not enjoy the pleasure of kingship. At that time, the Teacher was dwelling near a Sakyan market town named Medāḷupa. The king went there and, setting up camp not far from the monastery, went to the monastery thinking, “I will pay homage to the Teacher with a small retinue.” He gave the five royal insignia to Dīghakārāyana and entered the perfumed chamber all alone. Everything should be explained according to the method of the Dhammacetiya Sutta. When he had entered the perfumed chamber, Dīghakārāyana, taking those five royal insignia, made Viṭaṭūbha king, and having left one horse and one attendant woman for the king, he turned back and went to Sāvatthī.

Rājā satthārā saddhiṃ piyakathaṃ kathetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nikkhanto senaṃ adisvā taṃ mātugāmaṃ pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā, “ahaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ ādāya gantvā, viṭaṭūbhaṃ gahessāmī”ti rājagahanagaraṃ gacchanto vikāle dvāresu pidahitesu nagaraṃ patvā ekissā sālāya nipajjitvā vātātapehi kilanto rattibhāge tattheva kālamakāsi. Vibhātāya rattiyā, “deva, kosalanarinda anātho jātosī”ti vippalapantiyā [M 1.0226] tassā itthiyā saddaṃ sutvā rañño ārocesuṃ. So mātulassa mahantena sakkārena sarīrakiccaṃ kāresi.

The king, having had a pleasant conversation with the Teacher and having paid homage to the Teacher, came out. Not seeing his army, he questioned that woman, and having heard the news, he thought, “Taking my nephew, I will go and seize Viṭaṭūbha.” As he was going to the city of Rājagaha, he arrived at the city at the wrong time when the gates were closed. Lying down in a certain hall, exhausted by wind and sun, he passed away in that very place during the night. At dawn, having heard the sound of that woman wailing, “O Lord, King of Kosala, you have become without a protector!” they informed the king. He had the funeral rites for his maternal uncle performed with great honor.

Viṭaṭūbhopi [P 1.0357] rajjaṃ labhitvā taṃ veraṃ saritvā “sabbepi sākiye māressāmī”ti mahatiyā senāya nikkhami. Taṃ divasaṃ satthā paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento ñātisaṅghassa vināsaṃ disvā, “ñātisaṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā pubbaṇhasamaye piṇḍāya caritvā, piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiyaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā, sāyanhasamaye ākāsena gantvā, kapilavatthusāmante ekasmiṃ kabaracchāye rukkhamūle nisīdi. Tato viṭaṭūbhassa rajjasīmāya mahanto sandacchāyo nigrodho atthi. Viṭaṭūbho satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā, “bhante, kiṃ kāraṇā evarūpāya uṇhavelāya imasmiṃ kabaracchāye rukkhamūle nisīdatha, etasmiṃ sandacchāye nigrodhamūle nisīdatha, bhante”ti vatvā, “hotu, mahārāja, ñātakānaṃ chāyā nāma sītalā”ti vutte, “ñātakānurakkhanatthāya satthā āgato bhavissatī”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nivattitvā sāvatthiṃyeva paccāgami. Satthāpi uppatitvā jetavanameva gato.

Viṭaṭūbha, too, having obtained the kingdom and remembering that enmity, set out with a great army, thinking, “I will kill all the Sakyans.” That day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the impending destruction of the community of his kinsmen and thought, “It is proper to render assistance to my kinsmen.” In the morning, having gone for alms and returned from the alms-round, he lay down on the lion’s couch in the perfumed chamber. In the evening, he went through the air and sat down at the foot of a certain tree with sparse shade near Kapilavatthu. Nearby, on the border of Viṭaṭūbha’s kingdom, there was a great banyan tree with dense shade. Viṭaṭūbha, seeing the Teacher, approached, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, for what reason do you sit at the foot of this tree with sparse shade at such a hot time? Please sit, venerable sir, at the foot of this banyan tree with dense shade.” When the Teacher replied, “Let it be, great king. The shade of kinsmen is indeed cool,” Viṭaṭūbha thought, “The Teacher must have come for the purpose of protecting his kinsmen.” He paid homage to the Teacher, turned back, and returned to Sāvatthī. The Teacher, too, having risen into the air, went back to Jetavana.

Rājā sākiyānaṃ dosaṃ saritvā dutiyampi nikkhamitvā tatheva satthāraṃ passitvā puna nivatti. Tatiyavārepi nikkhamitvā tatheva satthāraṃ passitvā puna nivatti. Catutthavāre pana tasmiṃ nikkhante satthā sākiyānaṃ pubbakammaṃ oloketvā tesaṃ ekadivasaṃ nadiyaṃ visapakkhipanapāpakammassa appaṭibāhiyabhāvaṃ ñatvā catutthavāre nāgamāsi. Viṭaṭūbho “sākiye ghātessāmī”ti mahantena balakāyena [P 1.0358] nikkhami. Sammāsambuddhassa pana ñātakā asattaghātakā nāma, attanā marantāpi paresaṃ jīvitaṃ na voropenti. Te cintayiṃsu – “mayaṃ susikkhitā [V 1.0202] katahatthā katūpāsanā mahissāsā, na kho pana sakkā amhehi paraṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ, attano kammaṃ dassetvā palāpessāmā”ti te katasannāhā nikkhamitvā yuddhaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Tehi khittā sarā viṭaṭūbhassa purisānaṃ antarantarena gacchanti, phalakantarakaṇṇachiddantarādīhi nikkhamanti. Viṭaṭūbho disvā nanu bhaṇe “sākiyā asattaghātakāmhā”ti vadanti, atha ca pana me purise nāsentīti.

The king, remembering the offense of the Sākiyas, went out a second time and, seeing the Teacher in that very place, turned back again. A third time he went out and, seeing the Teacher in that very place, turned back again. But when he went out the fourth time, the Teacher, observing the past kamma of the Sākiyas, knew that their evil deed of one day putting poison in the river was unpreventable, and so he did not go the fourth time. Viṭaṭūbha went forth with a great army, thinking, “I will kill the Sākiyas.” Now, the kinsmen of the Perfectly Enlightened One were not killers; even while dying themselves, they would not deprive others of life. They thought, “We are well-trained, skilled, armored, and great archers, but it is not possible for us to deprive another of life. Let us show our skill and make them flee.” Having put on their armor, they went out and began the battle. The arrows shot by them passed between Viṭaṭūbha’s men and exited through the gaps between shields, the holes in their ears, and so on. Seeing this, Viṭaṭūbha said, “Sirs, do not the Sākiyas say, ‘We are not killers’? And yet they are destroying my men!”

Atha [M 1.0227] naṃ eko puriso āha – “kiṃ sāmi, nivattitvā olokesī”ti? “Sākiyā me purise nāsentī”ti. “Tumhākaṃ koci puriso mato nāma natthi. Iṅgha te gaṇāpethā”ti. Gaṇāpento ekassapi khayaṃ na passi. So tato nivattitvā “ye ye pana bhaṇe ‘sākiyamhā’ti bhaṇanti, sabbe māretha, mātāmahassa pana mahānāmasakkassa santike ṭhitānaṃ jīvitaṃ dethā”ti āha. Sākiyā gahetabbagahaṇaṃ apassantā ekacce tiṇaṃ ḍaṃsitvā, ekacce naḷaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. “Tumhe sākiyā, no”ti pucchitā yasmā te marantāpi musāvādaṃ na bhaṇanti, tasmā tiṇaṃ ḍaṃsitvā ṭhitā “no sāko, tiṇa”nti [P 1.0359] vadanti. Naḷaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā “no sāko, naḷo”ti vadanti. Ye ca mahānāmassa santike ṭhitā, te ca jīvitaṃ labhiṃsu. Tesu tiṇaṃ ḍaṃsitvā ṭhitā tiṇasākiyā nāma, naḷaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā naḷasākiyā nāma jātāti, viṭaṭūbho avasese khīrapakepi dārake avissajjetvā ghātāpento lohitanadiṃ pavattetvā tesaṃ galalohitena phalakaṃ dhovāpesi. Evaṃ sākiyavaṃso viṭaṭūbhena upacchinno.

Then a man said to him, “What is it, master? Turn back and look!” “The Sākiyas are destroying my men,” he replied. “Not a single one of your men is dead. Come now, have them seized!” While having them seized, he did not see the destruction of even one person. So he turned back from there and said, “Sirs, whoever says, ‘I am a Sākiya,’ kill them all, but grant life to those who are standing in the presence of my maternal grandfather, Mahānāma the Sākiya.” The Sākiyas, seeing no other recourse, some stood biting grass, and others stood holding reeds. When asked, “Are you Sākiyas or not?,” because they would not speak falsely even while dying, those who stood biting grass said, “Not a Sākiya, but grass.” Those who stood holding reeds said, “Not a Sākiya, but a reed.” And those who stood in the presence of Mahānāma also received their lives. Among them, those who stood biting grass became known as the Tiṇa-sākiyā, and those who stood holding reeds became known as the Naḷa-sākiyā. Viṭaṭūbha, not sparing even the remaining milk-drinking children, had them killed, causing a river of blood to flow, and had his sitting-plank washed with the blood from their throats. Thus was the Sākiyan lineage cut off by Viṭaṭūbha.

So mahānāmasakkaṃ gāhāpetvā nivatto “pātarāsavelāya pātarāsaṃ karissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne otaritvā bhojane upanīte “ekatova bhuñjissāmā”ti ayyakaṃ pakkosāpesi. Khattiyā pana jīvitaṃ cajantāpi dāsiputtehi saddhiṃ na bhuñjanti. Tasmā mahānāmo ekaṃ saraṃ oloketvā “kiliṭṭhagattomhi, nhāyissāmi, tātā”ti āha. “Sādhu, ayyaka, nhāyathā”ti. So “ayaṃ maṃ ekato abhuñjantaṃ ghātessati, sayameva me mataṃ seyyo”ti kese muñcitvā agge gaṇṭhiṃ katvā kesesu pādaṅguṭṭhake pavesetvā udake nimujji. Tassa guṇatejena nāgabhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Nāgarājā “kiṃ nu kho”ti upadhārento taṃ ñatvā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā taṃ attano phaṇe nisīdāpetvā nāgabhavanaṃ pavesesi. So dvādassa vassāni tattheva vasi. Viṭaṭūbhopi “mayhaṃ ayyako idāni āgamissati, idāni āgamissatī”ti āgamayamānova nisīdi. Tasmiṃ aticirāyante saraṃ vicināpetvā dīpālokena purisabbhantarānipi oloketvā adisvā “gato bhavissatī”ti pakkāmi. So [M 1.0228] rattibhāge aciravatiṃ [P 1.0360] patvā khandhāvāraṃ nivāsesi. Ekacce antonadiyaṃ vālukāpuline nipajjiṃsu[V 1.0203], ekacce bahithale, antonipannesupi pubbe akatapāpakammā atthi, bahinipannesupi pubbe katapāpakammā atthi, tesaṃ nipannaṭṭhānesu kipillikā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Te “mayhaṃ nipannaṭṭhāne kipillikā, mayhaṃ nipannaṭṭhāne kipillikā”ti uṭṭhahitvā akatapāpakammā uttaritvā thale nipajjiṃsu, katapāpakammā otaritvā vālukāpuline nipajjiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā ghanavassaṃ vassi. Nadiyā ogho āgantvā viṭaṭūbhaṃ saddhiṃ parisāya samuddameva pāpesi. Sabbe tattha macchakacchapabhakkhā ahesuṃ.

Having had Mahānāma the Sākiya taken, he turned back. At breakfast time, thinking, “I will have breakfast,” he dismounted at a certain place. When the food was brought, he had his grandfather summoned, thinking, “We will eat together.” Khattiyas, however, do not eat with the sons of slave women, even if they must give up their lives. Therefore, Mahānāma, looking at a lake, said, “My dear, my body is soiled; I will bathe.” “Very well, grandfather, you may bathe.” Thinking, “This man will kill me if I do not eat with him; it is better for me to die by my own accord,” he loosened his hair, made a knot at the end, inserted his big toes into his hair, and submerged himself in the water. By the power of his virtue, the nāga-abode showed signs of heat. The nāga king, investigating, “What can this be?,” understood the cause, came to him, seated him on his hood, and had him enter the nāga-abode. He lived there for twelve years. Viṭaṭūbha also sat waiting, thinking, “My grandfather will come now, he will come now.” When he was very late, he had the lake searched. Having looked even with the light of lamps in the spaces between the men and not seeing him, he departed, thinking, “He must have gone.” In the night, he reached the Aciravatī river and set up camp. Some lay down on a sandbank within the river, others on the high ground outside. Among those lying within the river were some who had not done evil kamma in the past, and among those lying outside were some who had done evil kamma in the past. In the places where they lay, ants arose. Saying, “There are ants in my sleeping place, there are ants in my sleeping place,” they got up. Those who had not done evil kamma went up and lay down on the high ground. Those who had done evil kamma went down and lay on the sandbank. At that moment, a great cloud arose and rained a solid sheet of water. A flood came down the river and swept Viṭaṭūbha, together with his retinue, into the ocean itself. There, they all became food for fish and turtles.

Mahājano kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “sākiyānaṃ maraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, ‘evaṃ nāma koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā sākiyā māretabbā’ti ananucchavikameta”nti. Satthā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ attabhāve kiñcāpi sākiyānaṃ evaṃ maraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, pubbe katapāpakammavasena pana yuttamevetehi laddha”nti āha. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, ete pubbe akaṃsū”ti? Sabbe ekato hutvā nadiyaṃ visaṃ pakkhipiṃsūti. Punekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “viṭaṭūbho ettake sākiye māretvā āgacchanto attano manorathe matthakaṃ appatteyeva ettakaṃ janaṃ ādāya mahāsamudde macchakacchapabhakkho jāto”ti[P 1.0361]. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “imesaṃ sattānaṃ manorathe matthakaṃ appatteyeva maccurājā suttaṃ gāmaṃ ajjhottharanto mahogho viya jīvitindriyaṃ chinditvā catūsu apāyasamuddesu nimujjāpetī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The great multitude raised a discussion: “The death of the Sākiyas is unsuitable. ‘That the Sākiyas should be killed in this way, having been beaten again and again’—this is inappropriate.” The Teacher, having heard that talk, said: “Monks, in this existence, although such a death for the Sākiyas is indeed unsuitable, it was nevertheless obtained by them as a fitting result, by the power of an evil deed done previously.” “But, Venerable Sir, what did they do previously?” “They all, having come together, put poison in a river.” Again, on another day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Viṭaṭūbha, having killed so many Sākiyas, while returning, even before his heart’s desire reached its culmination, taking so many people with him, became food for fish and turtles in the great ocean.” The Teacher, having approached, asked: “Monks, for what talk are you now assembled together?” When it was said, “For this one,” he said: “Even before the heart’s desire of these beings reaches its culmination, the King of Death, like a great flood overwhelming a sleeping village, cuts off the life faculty and causes them to sink in the four oceans of the woeful states.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

47.

47.

“Pupphāni heva pacinantaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ;

Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahoghova, maccu ādāya gacchatī”ti.

Death carries away the person whose mind is attached, who is gathering only flowers, just as a great flood carries away a sleeping village.

Tattha byāsattamanasaṃ naranti sampatte vā asampatte vā laggamānasaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā mālākāro pupphārāmaṃ pavisitvā “pupphāni pacinissāmī”ti tato pupphāni gahetvā aññamaññaṃ vā gacchaṃ patthento sakale pupphārāme manaṃ peseti, “ito cito ca pupphāni pacinissāmī”ti tato pupphāni aggahetvā aññattha manaṃ pesesi, tameva gacchaṃ pacinanto [M 1.0229] pamādamāpajjati, evameva ekacco pupphārāmasadisaṃ pañcakāmaguṇamajjhaṃ otaritvā manoramaṃ rūpaṃ labhitvā manoramānaṃ saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbānaṃ aññataraṃ pattheti. Añño tesu vā aññataraṃ labhitvā aññataraṃ pattheti[P 1.0362], rūpameva vā labhitvā aññaṃ apatthento tameva assādeti, saddādīsu vā aññataraṃ. Eseva nayo gomahiṃsadāsidāsakhettavatthugāmanigamajanapadādīsu, pabbajitānampi pariveṇavihārapattacīvarādīsūti evaṃ pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātāni pupphāni eva pacinantaṃ [V 1.0204] sampatte vā asampatte vā kāmaguṇe byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ. Suttaṃ gāmanti gāmassa gehabhittiādīnaṃ pana supanavasena supanaṃ nāma natthi, sattānaṃ pana suttapamattataṃ upādāya sutto nāma hoti. Evaṃ suttaṃ gāmaṃ dve tīṇi yojanāni āyatagambhīro mahoghova maccu ādāya gacchati. Yathā so mahogho itthipurisagomahiṃsakukkuṭādīsu kiñci anavasesetvā sabbaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ samuddaṃ pāpetvā macchakacchapabhakkhaṃ karoti, evameva byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ maccu ādāya jīvitindriyamassa chinditvā catūsu apāyasamuddesu nimujjāpetīti.

Therein, "a person with a deeply attached mind" means a mind that is clinging, whether to sensual pleasures that have been attained or to those that have not been attained. This is what is meant: just as a garland-maker, having entered a flower garden thinking, “I will gather flowers,” then, without taking flowers from there, but desiring one or another branch, sends his mind throughout the entire flower garden, thinking, “I will gather flowers from here and there,” and not having taken flowers from there, sends his mind elsewhere, and while gathering from that very branch, he falls into negligence; in the very same way, a certain person, having descended into the midst of the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are like a flower garden, and having obtained a pleasing form, longs for one of the other pleasing things among sounds, scents, tastes, and tangible objects. Another, having obtained one among them, longs for another; or having obtained only a form and not longing for another, he delights in that very one; or among sounds and the others, he longs for one or another. This is the same method with regard to cattle, buffaloes, female and male slaves, fields, properties, villages, towns, provinces, and so on. For the ordained as well, one longs for one or another among monastic cells, monasteries, bowls, robes, and so on. Thus, for such a person who is gathering only the flowers called the five strands of sensual pleasure, whose mind is deeply attached to sensual pleasures, whether attained or unattained—death carries away that person just as a great flood, two or three leagues long and deep, carries away a sleeping village. As for "a sleeping village," for the houses, walls, and so forth of a village, there is no such thing as "sleeping" by way of the act of sleeping; but on account of the sleep-like negligence of the beings, it is called "sleeping." Just as that great flood, leaving nothing behind among women, men, cattle, buffaloes, chickens, and so on, having caused that entire village of beings to reach the ocean and making them food for fish and turtles; in the very same way, death, having seized the person with a deeply attached mind and having cut off their life faculty, causes them to sink in the four oceans of the woeful states.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Mahājanassa sātthikā desanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on. The discourse was beneficial to the great multitude.

Viṭaṭūbhavatthu tatiyaṃ.

The third, the Story of Viṭaṭūbha.

4. Patipūjikakumārivatthu

4. The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā

Pupphāni hevāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto patipūjikaṃ nāma kumārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu [P 1.0363] tāvatiṃsadevaloke samuṭṭhitaṃ.

While dwelling at Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Pupphāni heva,' concerning a maiden named Patipūjikā. The story originated in the Tāvatiṃsa deva world.

Tattha kira mālabhārī nāma devaputto accharāsahassaparivuto uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Pañcasatā devadhītaro rukkhaṃ āruyha pupphāni pātenti, pañcasatā patitāni pupphāni gahetvā devaputtaṃ alaṅkaronti. Tāsu ekā devadhītā rukkhasākhāyameva cutā, sarīraṃ dīpasikhā viya nibbāyi. Sā sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kulagehe paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā jātakāle [M 1.0230] jātissarā hutvā “mālabhārīdevaputtassa bhariyāmhī”ti anussarantī vuḍḍhimanvāya gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ katvā sāmikassa santike abhinibbattiṃ patthesi. Sā soḷasavassakāle parakulaṃ gatāpi salākabhattapakkhikabhattavassāvāsikādīni datvā, “ayaṃ me sāmikassa santike nibbattanatthāya paccayo hotū”ti vadati. Athassā bhikkhū “ayaṃ kumārikā uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya patimeva patthetīti patipūjikā”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Sāpi nibaddhaṃ āsanasālaṃ paṭijaggati, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapeti, āsanāni paññapeti. Aññepi manussā salākabhattādīni dātukāmā, “amma, imānipi bhikkhusaṅghassa paṭipādeyyāsī”ti vatvā āharitvā denti. Sāpi etena niyāmena āgacchantī gacchantī ekapadavāre chapaññāsa kusaladhamme (dha. sa. 1; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 yevāpanakavaṇṇanā) paṭilabhati. Tassā kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassa padasā gamanakāle aññampi aññampīti cattāro putte paṭilabhi.

It is said that there, a deva named Mālabhārī, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, entered a park. Five hundred of the celestial maidens climbed a flower tree and caused flowers to fall, while another five hundred gathered the fallen flowers to adorn the deva. Among them, one celestial maiden passed away while on a tree branch, and her body was extinguished like the flame of a lamp. She was conceived in a certain family household in Sāvatthī. At the time of her birth, she became one who could remember past lives and, recalling, “I was the wife of the deva Mālabhārī,” upon growing up, she made offerings of perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and prayed for rebirth in the presence of her husband. Even after going to her husband's family at the age of sixteen, she gave alms such as ticket-meals, fortnightly meals, and rains-residence robes, and would say, “May this be a condition for my rebirth in the presence of my husband.” Then the bhikkhus, noting, “This maiden, having arisen and striven diligently, prays only for her husband,” gave her the name “Patipūjikā.” She also regularly maintained the assembly hall, prepared drinking water, and arranged the seats. When other people, wishing to give ticket-meals and the like, would say, “Mother, please provide these to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,” they would bring them and give them to her. In this way, while coming and going, with every single footstep she acquired fifty-six wholesome states. A conception was established in her womb. After ten months, she gave birth to a son. When he was able to walk, she had another son, and then another, until she had four sons.

Sā [V 1.0205] ekadivasaṃ dānaṃ datvā pūjaṃ katvā dhammaṃ sutvā [P 1.0364] sikkhāpadāni rakkhitvā divasapariyosāne taṃ khaṇaṃ nibbattena kenaci rogena kālaṃ katvā attano sāmikasseva santike nibbatti. Itarāpi ettakaṃ kālaṃ devaputtaṃ alaṅkaronti eva. Devaputto taṃ disvā “tvaṃ pātova paṭṭhāya na dissasi, kuhiṃ gatāsī”ti āha. “Cutāmhi sāmī”ti. “Kiṃ vadesī”ti? “Evametaṃ, sāmī”ti. “Kuhiṃ nibbattāsī”ti? “Sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe”ti. “Kittakaṃ kālaṃ tattha ṭhitāsī”ti? “Dasamāsaccayena mātu kucchito nikkhamitvā soḷasavassakāle parakulaṃ gantvā cattāro putte vijāyitvā dānādīni puññāni katvā tumhe patthetvā āgantvā tumhākameva santike nibbattāmhi, sāmī”ti. “Manussānaṃ kittakaṃ āyū”ti? “Vassasatamatta”nti. “Ettakamevā”ti? “Āma, sāmī”ti. “Ettakaṃ āyuṃ gahetvā nibbattamanussā kiṃ nu kho suttapamattā kālaṃ atikkāmenti, udāhu dānādīni puññāni karontī”ti. “Kiṃ vadetha, sāmi”? “Asaṅkhyeyyaṃ āyuṃ gahetvā nibbattā viya ajarāmarā viya ca niccaṃ pamattā, manussā”ti. Mālabhārīdevaputtassa mahāsaṃvego udapādi “vassasatamattamāyuṃ gahetvā nibbattamanussā kira pamattā nipajjitvā niddāyanti, kadā nu kho dukkhā muccissantī”ti? Manussānaṃ [M 1.0231] pana vassasataṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ eko rattindivo, tāya rattiyā tiṃsarattiyo māso, tena māsena dvādasamāsiko saṃvaccharo, tena saṃvaccharena dibbavassasahassaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ[P 1.0365], taṃ manussagaṇanāya tisso vassakoṭiyo, saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassāni honti. Tasmā tassa devaputtassa ekadivasopi nātikkanto muhuttasadisova kālo ahosi. Evaṃ appāyukamanussānaṃ pamādo nāma ativiya ayuttoti.

One day, after giving alms, making offerings, listening to the Dhamma, and observing the precepts, at the end of the day, she passed away due to some illness that arose at that moment and was reborn in the very presence of her own husband. The other celestial maidens, for all this time, were still adorning the deva. Seeing her, the deva said, “You were not seen since morning; where have you gone?” “I passed away, my lord.” “What are you saying?” “It is so, my lord.” “Where were you reborn?” “In a family household in Sāvatthī.” “How long did you stay there?” “After ten months, having come forth from my mother’s womb, at the age of sixteen I went to my husband's family, gave birth to four sons, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and having aspired for you, I returned and was reborn right in your presence, my lord.” “What is the lifespan of humans?” “About one hundred years.” “Only that much?” “Yes, my lord.” “Having obtained such a lifespan, do humans spend their time asleep and heedless, or do they perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms?” “My lord, what is there to say? Humans are always heedless, as if born with an incalculable lifespan, as if ageless and immortal.” Great spiritual urgency arose in the deva Mālabhārī: “It seems that humans, born with a lifespan of a mere hundred years, are heedless, lie down, and sleep! When indeed will they be freed from suffering?” Now, one hundred years for humans is but a single day and night for the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Thirty of those day-and-nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. By that measure, a thousand divine years is their lifespan, which, by human calculation, is thirty-six million years. Therefore, for that deva, not even one day had passed; the time was just like a moment. Thus, heedlessness is extremely inappropriate for short-lived humans.

Punadivase bhikkhū gāmaṃ paviṭṭhā āsanasālaṃ apaṭijaggitaṃ, āsanāni apaññattāni, pānīyaṃ anuṭṭhapitaṃ disvā, “kahaṃ patipūjikā”ti āhaṃsu. “Bhante, kahaṃ tumhe taṃ dakkhissatha, hiyyo ayyesu bhuñjitvā gatesu sāyanhasamaye matā”ti. Taṃ sutvā puthujjanā bhikkhū tassā upakāraṃ sarantā assūni sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Khīṇāsavānaṃ dhammasaṃvego udapādi. Te bhattakiccaṃ katvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pucchiṃsu – “bhante, patipūjikā nāma upāsikā uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya nānappakārāni puññāni katvā sāmikameva patthesi, sā idāni matā, kahaṃ nu kho nibbattā”ti? “Attano sāmikasseva santike, bhikkhave”ti. “Natthi, bhante, sāmikassa santike”ti. “Na sā, bhikkhave, etaṃ sāmikaṃ pattheti, tāvatiṃsabhavane tassā mālabhārīdevaputto nāma sāmiko, sā tassa pupphapilandhanaṭṭhānato cavitvā puna gantvā tasseva santike nibbattā”ti. “Evaṃ kira, bhante”ti. “Āma, bhikkhave”ti. “Aho parittaṃ, bhante, sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ, pātova amhe parivisitvā [V 1.0206] sāyaṃ uppannabyādhinā matā”ti. Satthā “āma, bhikkhave, parittaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ nāma, teneva ime satte vatthukāmehi ceva kilesakāmehi ca atitte eva antako attano vase [P 1.0366] vattetvā kandante paridevante gahetvā gacchatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

On the next day, the bhikkhus entered the village and, seeing the dining hall unswept, the seats unprepared, and the drinking water not set out, they asked, “Where is Patipūjikā?” “Venerable sirs, how would you see her? Yesterday, after the noble ones had eaten and departed, she died in the evening.” Hearing this, the ordinary bhikkhus, remembering her helpfulness, could not hold back their tears. For the Arahants, a sense of spiritual urgency arose. After completing their meal, they went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked: “Venerable sir, the laywoman named Patipūjikā, having arisen and striven to perform various kinds of meritorious deeds, aspired only for her husband. She has now died—where, indeed, has she been reborn?” “Near her own husband, bhikkhus.” “But, venerable sir, she is not near her husband.” “Bhikkhus, she did not aspire for this husband. In the Tāvatiṃsa realm, her husband is a deva named Mālabhārī. Having passed away from the place where she adorned him with flowers, she has gone and been reborn near him once again.” “Is it truly so, venerable sir?” “Yes, bhikkhus.” “Alas, venerable sir, how brief is the life of beings! Having served us in the morning, she died in the evening from an illness that had arisen.” The Teacher said, “Yes, bhikkhus, the life of beings is indeed brief. For that very reason, while these beings are still insatiable in sensual pleasures—both of objects and of defilements—the Ender brings them under his control and carries them away as they weep and lament.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

48.

48.

“Pupphāni heva pacinantaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ;

Atittaṃyeva kāmesu, antako kurute vasa”nti.

The man gathering flowers, his mind attached, insatiable in sensual pleasures—him the Ender brings under his control.

Tattha pupphāni heva pacinantanti pupphārāme mālākāro nānāpupphāni viya attabhāvapaṭibaddhāni ceva upakaraṇapaṭibaddhāni ca kāmaguṇapupphāni ocinantameva[M 1.0232]. Byāsattamanasaṃ naranti asampattesu patthanāvasena, sampattesu gedhavasena vividhenākārena āsattacittaṃ. Atittaṃyeva kāmesūti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu pariyesanenapi paṭilābhenapi paribhogenapi nidhānenapi atittaṃ eva samānaṃ. Antako kurute vasanti maraṇasaṅkhāto antako kandantaṃ paridevantaṃ gahetvā gacchanto attano vasaṃ pāpetīti attho.

Therein, 'gathering only flowers' means this: just as a garland-maker in a flower garden picks various flowers, it refers to one gathering the flowers of sensual pleasures connected both to one's own being and to one's possessions. 'A man with an attached mind' means a mind attached in various ways, through longing for what is unattained and through greed for what is attained. 'Insatiable in sensual pleasures' means being unsatisfied with sensual pleasures of objects and defilements, whether in seeking, obtaining, enjoying, or hoarding them. 'The Ender brings under his control' means the Ender, known as Death, seizes one who is weeping and lamenting and brings them under his power. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā, desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the like. The discourse was of benefit to the great assembly.

Patipūjikakumārivatthu catutthaṃ.

The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā, the Fourth.

5. Macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhivatthu

5. The Story of the Miserly Treasurer Kosiya

Yathāpi bhamaro pupphanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu rājagahe samuṭṭhitaṃ.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, 'Yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ,' concerning the miserly treasurer Kosiya. The story of this treasurer originated in Rājagaha.

Rājagahanagarassa [P 1.0367] kira avidūre sakkāraṃ nāma nigamo ahosi. Tattheko macchariyakosiyo nāma seṭṭhi asītikoṭivibhavo paṭivasati. So tiṇaggena telabindumpi paresaṃ na deti, na attanā paribhuñjati. Itissa taṃ vibhavajātaṃ neva puttadārādīnaṃ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ atthaṃ anubhoti, rakkhasapariggahitā pokkharaṇī viya aparibhogaṃ tiṭṭhati. Satthā ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya sakalalokadhātuyaṃ bodhaneyyabandhave olokento pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake vasantassa seṭṭhino sapajāpatikassa sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ addasa. Tato purimadivase pana so rājānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ rājagehaṃ gantvā rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ katvā [V 1.0207] āgacchanto ekaṃ chātajjhattaṃ janapadamanussaṃ kummāsapūraṃ kapallakapūvaṃ khādantaṃ disvā tattha pipāsaṃ uppādetvā attano gharaṃ gantvā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ kapallakapūvaṃ khāditukāmomhīti vakkhāmi, bahū manussā mayā saddhiṃ khāditukāmā bhavissanti, evaṃ me bahūni tilataṇḍulasappiphāṇitādīni parikkhayaṃ gamissanti, na [M 1.0233] kassaci kathessāmī”ti taṇhaṃ adhivāsento carati. So gacchante gacchante kāle uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto jāto. Tato taṇhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto gabbhaṃ pavisitvā mañcake upagūhitvā nipajji. Evaṃ gatopi [P 1.0368] dhanahānibhayena na kassaci kiñci kathesi.

It is said that not far from the city of Rājagaha, there was a market town named Sakkāra. There lived a treasurer named Macchariya Kosiya, who possessed eighty crores of wealth. He would not give to others even a drop of oil taken with the tip of a blade of grass, nor did he use it himself. Thus, the wealth he had amassed served neither the well-being of his wife, children, and others, nor that of ascetics and brahmins; it remained unused, like a pond possessed by a rākṣasa. One day, at dawn, the Teacher, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion and surveying the entire world-system for beings suitable for awakening, saw the supporting condition for the fruit of stream-entry in the treasurer and his wife, who were dwelling forty-five yojanas away. On the previous day, that treasurer had gone to the royal palace to attend upon the king. Having performed his service to the king and while returning, he saw a starving man from the countryside eating a barley-cake and a pan-cake. Seeing this, he conceived a craving for it. Going to his own house, he thought: 'If I say that I desire to eat a pan-cake, many people will desire to eat with me. In that case, much of my sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, and so on will be depleted. I will not tell anyone.' Thinking thus, he went about suppressing his craving. As time went on, he became pale and yellowish, and his body became covered with a network of prominent veins. Then, unable to suppress his craving, he entered an inner room, clung to his bed, and lay down. Even so, out of fear of his wealth diminishing, he said nothing to anyone.

Atha naṃ bhariyā upasaṅkamitvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā, “kiṃ te, sāmi, aphāsukaṃ jāta”nti pucchi. “Na me kiñci aphāsukaṃ atthī”ti. “Kiṃ nu kho te rājā kupito”ti? “Rājāpi me na kuppatī”ti. “Atha kiṃ te puttadhītāhi vā dāsakammakarādīhi vā kiñci amanāpaṃ kataṃ atthī”ti? “Evarūpampi natthī”ti. “Kismiñci pana te taṇhā atthī”ti? Evaṃ vuttepi dhanahānibhayena kiñci avatvā nissaddova nipajji, atha naṃ bhariyā “kathehi, sāmi kismiñci te taṇhā atthī”ti āha. So vacanaṃ parigilanto viya “atthi me taṇhā”ti āha. “Kiṃ taṇhā, sāmī”ti? “Kapallakapūvaṃ khāditukāmomhī”ti. “Atha kimatthaṃ me na kathesi, kiṃ tvaṃ daliddosi, idāni sakalanigamavāsīnaṃ pahonake kapallakapūve pacissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ te etehi, attano kammaṃ katvā khādissantī”ti? “Tena hi ekaracchavāsīnaṃ pahonake pacissāmī”ti. “Jānāmahaṃ tava mahaddhanabhāva”nti. “Imasmiṃ gehasāmante sabbesaṃ pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Jānāmahaṃ tava mahajjhāsayabhāva”nti. “Tena hi te puttadāramattasseva pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Kiṃ te etehī”ti? “Kiṃ pana tuyhañca mayhañca pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti? “Tvaṃ kiṃ karissasī”ti[P 1.0369]? “Tena hi ekakasseva te pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne pacamāne bahū paccāsīsanti. Sakalataṇḍule ṭhapetvā bhinnataṇḍule ca uddhanakapallāni ca ādāya thokaṃ khīrasappimadhuphāṇitañca gahetvā sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatalaṃ āruyha paca, tatthāhaṃ ekakova nisīditvā khādissāmī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā gahetabbaṃ gāhāpetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha dāsiyo vissajjetvā seṭṭhiṃ pakkosāpesi, so ādito paṭṭhāya dvārāni pidahanto sabbadvāresu sūcighaṭikaṃ datvā sattamatalaṃ abhiruhitvā tatthapi dvāraṃ pidahitvā nisīdi. Bhariyāpissa uddhane aggiṃ jāletvā kapallaṃ āropetvā pūve pacituṃ ārabhi.

Then his wife approached him, stroked his back, and asked, 'My lord, what discomfort has befallen you?' 'I have no discomfort,' he said. 'Then is the king perhaps angry with you?' 'The king is not angry with me.' 'Then have your sons and daughters, or your servants and workers, done anything to displease you?' 'It is nothing of that sort.' 'Do you, then, have a craving for something?' Even when asked this, out of fear of his wealth diminishing, he said nothing and lay down in silence. Then his wife said, 'Tell me, my lord, do you have a craving for something?' As if exhausted by her words, he said, 'I have a craving.' 'What is your craving, my lord?' 'I desire to eat a pan-cake.' 'Then why did you not tell me? Are you a poor man? I will now cook enough pan-cakes for all the inhabitants of this town.' 'What are they to you? They can do their own work and then eat.' 'In that case, I will cook enough for the residents of one street.' 'I know how wealthy you are,' he said sarcastically. 'Then I will prepare enough for all those living in the vicinity of this house.' 'I know how generous your intentions are,' he retorted. 'In that case, I will prepare enough just for your wife and children.' 'What are they to you?' 'Well then, shall I prepare enough for you and me?' 'And what will you do?' 'In that case, I will prepare enough for you alone.' 'If you cook in this place, many will expect some. Put aside the whole rice grains and take some broken rice, a stove and a pan, and a little milk, ghee, honey, and molasses. Climb to the top floor of the seven-storied mansion and cook there. There I will sit all alone and eat.' She agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Having had the necessary items brought, she ascended to the mansion, dismissed the female servants, and had the treasurer summoned. He, starting from the ground floor, went up closing the doors, placing a bolt on every door. He ascended to the seventh floor, and there too he closed the door and sat down. His wife then lit a fire in the stove, placed the pan upon it, and began to cook the cakes.

Atha [M 1.0234][V 1.0208] satthā pātova mahāmoggallānattheraṃ āmantesi – “eso, moggallāna, rājagahassa avidūre sakkāranigame macchariyaseṭṭhi ‘kapallakapūve khādissāmī’ti aññesaṃ dassanabhayena sattabhūmike pāsāde kapallakapūve pacāpeti, tvaṃ tattha gantvā seṭṭhiṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā ubhopi jāyampatike pūve ca khīrasappimadhuphāṇitāni ca gāhāpetvā attano balena jetavanaṃ ānehi, ajjāhaṃ pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vihāre eva nisīdissāmi, pūveheva bhattakiccaṃ karissāmī”ti.

Then the Teacher, early in the morning, addressed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, saying: 'Moggallāna, in the market town of Sakkāra, not far from Rājagaha, that miserly merchant, thinking, "I will eat griddle-cakes," is having griddle-cakes cooked in a seven-storied mansion out of fear of being seen by others. You are to go there, subdue that merchant, and make him free from the poison of his stinginess. Then, have them take both the husband and wife, the griddle-cakes, and the milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, and bring them to Jetavana by your own power. Today, I, together with five hundred monks, will remain right here in the monastery, and we will make our meal with those very griddle-cakes.'

Thero “sādhu, bhante”ti satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā [P 1.0370] tāvadeva iddhibalena taṃ nigamaṃ gantvā tassa pāsādassa sīhapañjaradvāre sunivattho supāruto ākāse eva maṇirūpakaṃ viya aṭṭhāsi. Mahāseṭṭhino theraṃ disvāva hadayamaṃsaṃ kampi. So ahaṃ evarūpānaṃyeva dassanabhayena imaṃ ṭhānamāgato, ayañca bhikkhu ākāsenāgantvā vātapānadvāre ṭhitoti. So gahetabbagahaṇaṃ apassanto aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya dosena taṭataṭāyanto evamāha – “samaṇa, ākāse ṭhatvāpi kiṃ labhissasi, ākāse apade padaṃ dassetvā caṅkamantopi neva labhissasī”ti. Thero tasmiṃ eva ṭhāne aparāparaṃ caṅkami. Seṭṭhi “caṅkamanto kiṃ labhissasi, ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdantopi na labhissasiyevā”ti āha. Thero pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ “ākāse nisinno kiṃ labhissasi, āgantvā vātapānassa ummāre ṭhitopi na labhissasī”ti āha. Thero ummāre ṭhito. “Ummāre ṭhitopi kiṃ labhissasi, dhūmāyantopi na labhissasi evā”ti āha. Theropi dhūmāyi. Sakalapāsādo ekadhūmo ahosi. Seṭṭhino akkhīnaṃ sūciyā vijjhanakālo viya ahosi, gehajjhāyanabhayena pana “tvaṃ pajjalantopi na labhissasī”ti avatvā “ayaṃ samaṇo suṭṭhu laggo, aladdhā na gamissati[P 1.0371], ekamassa pūvaṃ dāpessāmī”ti bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde ekaṃ khuddakapūvaṃ pacitvā samaṇassa datvā uyyojehi na”nti. Sā thokaṃ eva piṭṭhaṃ kapallapātiyaṃ pakkhipi, mahāpūvo hutvā sakalapātiṃ pūretvā uddhumāto hutvā aṭṭhāsi.

The Elder, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," accepted the Teacher's words and immediately went to that market town by his psychic power. Well-dressed and well-robed, he stood in the sky at the lion-window of the mansion like a jeweled statue. Upon seeing the Elder, the great merchant's heart trembled. He thought, "I came to this place fearing to see such beings, and now this monk has come through the sky and stands at the window." Not seeing any way to seize him, the merchant, sputtering with anger like salt and gravel thrown into a fire, said, "Ascetic, even if you stand in the sky, what will you get? Even if you show a footstep in the trackless sky while walking, you will get nothing!" The Elder then walked back and forth in that very place. The merchant said, "What will you get by walking? Even if you sit cross-legged in the sky, you will get nothing at all!" The Elder sat cross-legged. Then the merchant said, "What will you get by sitting in the sky? Even if you come and stand on the threshold of the window, you will get nothing!" The Elder stood on the threshold. "What will you get by standing on the threshold? Even if you emit smoke, you will get nothing at all!" he said. The Elder then emitted smoke. The entire mansion became filled with smoke. It was as if needles were piercing the merchant's eyes. Fearing the house might burn down, he did not say, "Even if you blaze up, you will get nothing!" Instead, he thought, "This ascetic is very persistent; he will not leave without getting something. I will have one griddle-cake given to him." He told his wife, "Dear, prepare a small griddle-cake, give it to the ascetic, and send him away." She put a little flour into the griddle-pan, but it became a large griddle-cake, filling the entire pan and swelling up as it stood.

Seṭṭhi taṃ disvā “bahuṃ tayā piṭṭhaṃ gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti sayameva dabbikaṇṇena thokaṃ piṭṭhaṃ gahetvā pakkhipi, pūvo purimapūvato mahantataro jāto[M 1.0235]. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ pacati, so so mahantamahantova hoti. So nibbinno bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, imassa ekaṃ pūvaṃ dehī”ti. Tassā pacchito ekaṃ pūvaṃ gaṇhantiyā sabbe ekābaddhā allīyiṃsu. Sā seṭṭhiṃ āha – “sāmi, sabbe pūvā ekato laggā, visuṃ kātuṃ na sakkomī”ti. “Ahaṃ karissāmī”ti sopi kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Ubhopi janā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā kaḍḍhantāpi viyojetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu eva[V 1.0209]. Athassa pūvehi saddhiṃ vāyamantasseva sarīrato sedā mucciṃsu, pipāsā upacchijji. Tato bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, na me pūvehi attho, pacchiyā saddhiṃyeva imassa dehī”ti. Sā pacchiṃ ādāya theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā adāsi. Thero ubhinnampi dhammaṃ desesi, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ kathesi, “atthi [P 1.0372] dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭha”nti dinnadānādīnaṃ phalaṃ gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ viya dassesi.

Seeing this, the merchant said, "You must have taken a lot of flour," and he himself took a little flour with the tip of a ladle and put it in; the griddle-cake became even larger than the previous one. In this way, whatever he cooked became larger and larger. Disgusted, he said to his wife, "Dear, give this monk one of the griddle-cakes." When she was taking one griddle-cake from the basket, all of them stuck together as one. She said to the merchant, "Master, all the griddle-cakes are stuck together; I cannot separate them." "I will do it," he said, but he too was unable to do it. Both of them, grasping an edge and pulling, were still unable to separate them. Then, as he was struggling with the griddle-cakes, sweat poured from his body, and his craving for them was cut off. Then he said to his wife, "Dear, I have no use for the griddle-cakes; give them to this monk, basket and all." She took the basket, approached the Elder, and gave it to him. The Elder taught the Dhamma to both of them and spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels. Saying, "There is fruit in what is given, there is fruit in what is offered," he showed the result of the gift that had been given, as if displaying the full moon in the expanse of the sky.

Taṃ sutvā pasannacitto hutvā seṭṭhi “bhante, āgantvā imasmiṃ pallaṅke nisīditvā paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Thero, “mahāseṭṭhi, sammāsambuddho ‘pūve khādissāmī’ti pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vihāre nisinno, tumhākaṃ ruciyā sati ahaṃ vo nessāmi, seṭṭhibhariyaṃ pūve ca khīrādīni ca gaṇhāpetha, satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. “Kahaṃ pana, bhante, etarahi satthā”ti? “Ito pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake jetavanavihāre, mahāseṭṭhī”ti. “Bhante, kālaṃ anatikkamitvā ettakaṃ addhānaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmā”ti. “Mahāseṭṭhi, tumhākaṃ ruciyā sati ahaṃ vo attano iddhibalena nessāmi, tumhākaṃ pāsāde sopānasīsaṃ attano ṭhāne eva bhavissati, sopānapariyosānaṃ pana vo jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake bhavissati, uparipāsādā heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ otaraṇakālamatteneva jetavanaṃ nessāmī”ti. So “sādhu, bhante”ti sampaṭicchi.

Hearing that, the merchant, with a confident heart, said, "Venerable sir, please come, sit on this couch, and partake." The Elder said, "Great merchant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is seated in the monastery with five hundred monks, intending to eat the griddle-cakes. If it is your wish, I will take you. Have your wife take the griddle-cakes and milk products, and we shall go to the Teacher's presence." The merchant then asked, "But where, venerable sir, is the Teacher now?" "Forty-five yojanas from here, in the Jetavana monastery, great merchant." "Venerable sir, how can we travel such a distance without passing the time for the meal?" "Great merchant, if it is your wish, I will take you by my own psychic power. The head of your mansion's staircase will remain in its own place, but the foot of your staircase will be at the gatehouse of Jetavana. I will take you to Jetavana in only the time it takes to descend from the upper mansion to the lower mansion." He agreed, saying, "Very well, venerable sir."

Thero sopānasīsaṃ tattheva katvā “sopānapādamūlaṃ jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Tatheva ahosi. Iti thero seṭṭhiñca seṭṭhibhariyañca uparipāsādā heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ otaraṇakālato khippataraṃ jetavanaṃ sampāpesi. Te ubhopi satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā kālaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā bhattaggaṃ pavisitvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Mahāseṭṭhi buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ [P 1.0373] adāsi. Bhariyāpissa tathāgatassa patte pūvaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Satthā attano [M 1.0236] yāpanamattaṃ gaṇhi, pañcasatā bhikkhūpi yāpanamattaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Seṭṭhi khīrasappimadhusakkharādīni dadamāno na khayaṃ agamāsi. Satthā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Mahāseṭṭhipi saddhiṃ bhariyāya yāvadatthaṃ khādi. Pūvānaṃ pariyosānameva na paññāyati. Sakalavihāre bhikkhūnañca vighāsādānañca dinnesupi pariyanto na paññāyateva. “Bhante, pūvā parikkhayaṃ na gacchantī”ti bhagavato ārocesuṃ. “Tena hi jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake chaḍḍethā”ti. Atha ne dvārakoṭṭhakassa avidūre pabbhāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍayiṃsu. Yāvajjatanāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ kapallakapūvapabbhāranteva paññāyati. Mahāseṭṭhi saha bhariyāya bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā anumodanamakāsi. Anumodanāvasāne ubhopi [V 1.0210] sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya satthāraṃ vanditvā dvārakoṭṭhake sopānaṃ āruyha attano pāsādeyeva patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

The Elder, having made the head of the staircase remain right there, resolved, 'Let the foot of the staircase be at the gatehouse of Jetavana.' And so it was. Thus, the Elder brought the merchant and his wife to Jetavana more swiftly than the time it takes to descend from the upper to the lower mansion. Both of them approached the Teacher and announced the time. The Teacher entered the dining hall and sat on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat, together with the community of monks. The great merchant gave the water of dedication to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. His wife also placed a griddle-cake in the Tathāgata's bowl. The Teacher took just enough for his sustenance, and the five hundred monks also took just enough. As the merchant gave milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, they did not run out. The Teacher, together with the five hundred monks, finished the meal with only the griddle-cakes. Afterwards, the great merchant, together with his wife, ate as much as they desired. No end to the griddle-cakes was apparent. Even when given to the monks in the entire monastery and to those who eat leftovers, no end was apparent at all. They reported to the Blessed One, 'Venerable Sir, the griddle-cakes are not running out.' He said, 'In that case, discard them at the gatehouse of Jetavana.' Then they discarded them in a low-lying place not far from the gatehouse. To this day, that place is known as 'The Chasm of the Discarded Griddle-Cakes.' The great merchant, together with his wife, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Blessed One gave a discourse of appreciation. At the conclusion of the discourse, both of them, having become established in the fruit of stream-entry, paid homage to the Teacher, ascended the staircase at the gatehouse, and were established back in their own mansion.

Tato paṭṭhāya seṭṭhi asītikoṭidhanaṃ buddhasāsaneyeva vikkiri. Punadivase sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā bhikkhū “passathāvuso, mahāmoggallānattherassa ānubhāvaṃ, anupahacca nāma saddhaṃ, anupahacca bhoge macchariyaseṭṭhiṃ [P 1.0374] muhutteneva dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā pūve gāhāpetvā jetavanaṃ ānetvā satthu sammukhaṃ katvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesi, aho mahānubhāvo thero”ti therassa guṇaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā dibbāya sotadhātuyā kathaṃ sutvā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, kuladamakena nāma bhikkhunā anupahacca saddhaṃ, anupahacca bhoge, kulaṃ akilametvā aviheṭhetvā pupphato reṇuṃ gaṇhantena bhamarena viya upasaṅkamitvā buddhaguṇaṃ jānāpetabbaṃ, tādiso mama putto moggallāno”ti theraṃ pasaṃsitvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

From that day onward, the merchant dispersed his eighty crores of wealth for the Buddha’s Dispensation. The next day, in the evening, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and sat discussing: "Friends, behold the power of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna! Without harming faith, without harming wealth, he subdued the miserly merchant in an instant, made him free from the poison of stinginess, had him take cakes, brought him to Jetavana, placed him in the presence of the Teacher, and established him in the fruit of stream-entry. Ah, the great power of the Elder!" While they were thus recounting the Elder’s virtues, the Teacher, hearing their conversation with his divine ear element, arrived and asked, "Monks, for what topic of discussion are you assembled here now?" When they replied, "For this topic," he said, "Monks, a monk who is a tamer of families should approach without harming faith, without harming wealth, without causing the family to be weary, and without vexing them, just like a bee gathering pollen from a flower. He should make known the virtues of the Buddha. Such a one is my son, Moggallāna." Having praised the Elder, he spoke this verse:

49.

49.

“Yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ, vaṇṇagandhamaheṭhayaṃ;

Paleti rasamādāya, evaṃ gāme munī care”ti.

Just as a bee, without harming the flower, its color, or its scent, flies away, having taken its nectar, so should a sage wander in a village.

Tattha bhamaroti yā kāci madhukarajāti. Pupphanti pupphārāme caranto pupphañca vaṇṇañca gandhañca aheṭhayanto avināsento vicaratīti attho. Paletīti evaṃ caritvā yāvadatthaṃ rasaṃ pivitvā aparampi madhukaraṇatthāya [P 1.0375] ādāya [M 1.0237] paleti, so evaṃ vanagahanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā ekasmiṃ rukkhasusire taṃ rajamissakaṃ rasaṃ ṭhapetvā anupubbena madhurarasaṃ madhuṃ karoti, na tassa pupphārāme vicaritapaccayā pupphaṃ vā vaṇṇagandhaṃ vāssa vigacchati, atha kho sabbaṃ pākatikameva hoti. Evaṃ gāme munī careti evaṃ sekhāsekhabhedo anāgāriyamuni kulapaṭipāṭiyā gāme bhikkhaṃ gaṇhanto vicaratīti attho. Na hi tassa gāme caraṇapaccayā kulānaṃ saddhāhāni vā bhogahāni vā honti. Saddhāpi bhogāpi pākatikāva honti. Evaṃ caritvā ca pana nikkhamitvā sekhamuni tāva bahigāme udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā nisinno akkhabhañjanavaṇapaṭicchādanaputtamaṃsūpamādivasena paccavekkhanto piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā tathārūpaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ anupavisitvā ajjhattikakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasanto cattāro magge, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni hatthagatāneva karoti. Asekhamuni pana diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāramanuyuñjati[P 1.0376]. Ayamassa bhamarena saddhiṃ madhukaraṇasarikkhatā veditabbā. Idha pana khīṇāsavova adhippeto.

Therein, "bee" (bhamara) refers to any species of honey-maker. "Flower" (pupphaṃ) means that, while roaming in a flower garden, it moves about without harming or destroying the flower, its color, or its fragrance. "Flies away" (paleti) means that after roaming thus and drinking as much nectar as it desires, it takes more for the purpose of making honey and flies away. In this way, having entered a forest thicket and having placed that nectar mixed with pollen in a tree hollow, it gradually makes sweet honey. Due to its roaming in the flower garden, neither the flower nor its color and fragrance are lost; rather, everything remains just as it was. "So should a sage wander in a village" means that in the same way, a sage—whether a trainee or one who has finished training, having gone forth—wanders in the village receiving alms by following the sequence of houses. Indeed, due to his wandering in the village for alms, there is no loss of faith or loss of wealth for the families. Both faith and wealth remain just as they were. Having wandered thus and departed, a trainee sage first sits down outside the village in a comfortable place near water, spreads his outer robe, and consumes the almsfood while reflecting on it by way of the similes of greasing an axle, dressing a wound, or eating the flesh of one's son. Then, having entered a suitable forest grove and contemplating the internal meditation subject, he makes the four paths and the four fruits of recluseship as if they were in his very hand. A sage beyond training, however, devotes himself to the blissful dwelling in this very life. This should be understood as his similarity to the bee in the making of honey. In this verse, however, only one whose cankers are destroyed is intended.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0211] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ vatvā uttaripi therassa guṇaṃ pakāsetuṃ “na, bhikkhave, idāneva moggallānena macchariyaseṭṭhi damito, pubbepi naṃ dametvā kammaphalasambandhaṃ jānāpesi evā”ti vatvā imamatthaṃ pakāsento atītaṃ āharitvā –

Having given this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher, to further reveal the Elder's virtue, said: "Monks, it is not only now that Moggallāna has tamed the miserly merchant; in the past, too, he tamed him and made him understand the connection between kamma and its result." Revealing this matter, he brought forth the past:

“Ubho khañjā ubho kuṇī, ubho visamacakkhukā;

Ubhinnaṃ piḷakā jātā, nāhaṃ passāmi illisa”nti. (jā. 1.1.78) –

Both are lame, both are crippled, both have uneven eyes; moles have appeared on both of them. I do not see Illisa.

Imaṃ illisajātakaṃ kathesīti.

He related this Illisa Jātaka.

Macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhivatthu pañcamaṃ.

The fifth story is that of the miserly merchant Kosiya.

6. Pāveyyakājīvakavatthu

6. The Story of the Ājīvaka Pāveyyaka

Na paresaṃ vilomānīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto pāveyyaṃ nāma ājīvakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Not the transgressions of others,' concerning a certain Ājīvaka named Pāveyya.

Sāvatthiyaṃ [M 1.0238] kirekā gahapatānī puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā pāveyyaṃ nāma ājīvakaṃ paṭijaggi. Tassānantaragharesu manussā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā āgantvā, “aho acchariyā buddhānaṃ dhammadesanā”ti nānappakārehi buddhaguṇe vaṇṇenti. Sā buddhānaṃ guṇakathaṃ sutvā vihāraṃ [P 1.0377] gantvā dhammaṃ sotukāmā ājīvakassa etamatthaṃ kathetvā, “gacchissāmi ahaṃ buddhasantikaṃ, ayyā”ti āha. So “mā gacchāhī”ti nivāretvā taṃ punappunaṃ yācamānampi nivāresi eva. Sā “ayaṃ mama vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sotuṃ na deti, satthāraṃ nimantetvā idheva dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti sāyanhasamaye puttaṃ pakkositvā, “gaccha, tāta, svātanāya satthāraṃ nimantehī”ti pesesi. So gacchanto paṭhamataraṃ ājīvakassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ so “kahaṃ gacchasī”ti āha. “Mātu vacanena satthāraṃ nimantetuṃ gacchāmī”ti āha. “Mā tassa santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti. “Alaṃ, ayya, mama mātu bhāyāmi, gacchissāmaha”nti. “Etassa katasakkāraṃ ubhopi khādissāma, mā gacchāhī”ti. “Alaṃ, ayya, mātā me tajjessatī”ti. Tena hi gaccha, gantvā pana nimantetvā, “amhākaṃ gehaṃ asukaṭṭhāne [V 1.0212] vā asukavīthiyaṃ vā asukamaggena vā gantabba”nti mā ācikkhi. “Santike ṭhito viya aññena maggena gacchanto viya palāyitvā ehī”ti. So ājīvakassa vacanaṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā nimantetvā ājīvakena vuttaniyāmeneva sabbaṃ katvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā, “kiṃ te kata”nti puṭṭho, “sabbaṃ kataṃ, ayyā”ti āha. “Bhaddakaṃ te kataṃ, tassa sakkāraṃ ubhopi khādissāmā”ti vatvā punadivase ājīvako pātova taṃ gehaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ gahetvā pacchāgabbhe nisīdāpesuṃ.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain householder-woman supported an Ājīvaka named Pāveyya, having established him in the position of a son. In the neighboring houses, people who had heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse would come and praise the virtues of the Buddha in various ways, saying, 'Ah, how wonderful is the Dhamma discourse of the Buddhas!' Hearing this talk of the Buddha's virtues, she became desirous of going to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. She told this matter to the Ājīvaka, saying, 'Venerable sir, I will go to the presence of the Buddha.' He prevented her, saying, 'Do not go,' and though she entreated him again and again, he still prevented her. She thought, 'This man does not allow me to go to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. I will invite the Teacher here and listen to the Dhamma in this very place.' In the evening, she had her adopted son summoned and sent him, saying, 'Go, dear, and invite the Teacher for tomorrow.' As he was going, he first went to the dwelling place of his teacher, the Ājīvaka, paid homage to him, and sat down. Then his teacher asked him, 'Where are you going?' He replied, 'By my mother's word, I am going to invite the Teacher.' The teacher said, 'Do not go to his presence.' 'Enough, venerable sir, I fear my mother; I will go.' 'We both shall eat the offerings made for this one. Do not go.' 'Enough, venerable sir, my mother will scold me.' 'In that case, go. But having gone and invited him, do not tell him, "Our house is to be reached in such-and-such a place, or on such-and-such a street, or by such-and-such a path." As if standing near him, and as if going by another path, flee and come back.' He, having heard the Ājīvaka's words, went to the Teacher's presence, invited him, and having done everything according to the method told by the Ājīvaka, went to his teacher's presence. When asked, 'What have you done?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, everything has been done.' 'What you have done is good. We both shall eat the offerings made for him.' Having said this, on the next day, the Ājīvaka went to that house early in the morning. They took him and had him sit in the back of the inner chamber.

Paṭivissakamanussā taṃ gehaṃ allagomayena upalimpitvā lājapañcamāni [P 1.0378] pupphāni vikiritvā satthu nisīdanatthāya mahārahaṃ āsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Buddhehi saddhiṃ aparicitamanussā hi āsanapaññattiṃ na jānanti, buddhānañca maggadesakena kiccaṃ nāma natthi, bodhimūle dasasahassisokadhātuṃ kampetvā sambodhiṃ pattadivaseyeva hi nesaṃ “ayaṃ maggo nirayaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ tiracchānayoniṃ, ayaṃ pettivisayaṃ, ayaṃ manussalokaṃ, ayaṃ devalokaṃ, ayaṃ amatamahānibbāna”nti sabbe maggā āvibhūtā. Gāmanigamādīnaṃ pana magge vattabbameva natthi. Tasmā satthā pātova pattacīvaramādāya mahāupāsikāya gehadvāraṃ gato. Sā gehā nikkhamitvā satthāraṃ [M 1.0239] pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā antonivesanaṃ pavesetvā āsane nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisi. Upāsikā katabhattakiccassa satthuno anumodanaṃ kāretukāmā pattaṃ gaṇhi. Satthā madhurassarena anumodanadhammakathaṃ ārabhi. Upāsikā “sādhu, sādhū”ti sādhukāraṃ dadamānā dhammaṃ suṇi. Ājīvakopi pacchāgabbhe nisinnova tassā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇantiyā saddaṃ sutvā sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhi. “Na idānesā mayha”nti nikkhamitvā “naṭṭhāsi kāḷakaṇṇi, etassa evaṃ sakkāraṃ karotī”ti nānappakārena upāsikañca satthārañca akkosanto palāyi. Upāsikā tassa kathāya lajjitā aññathattaṃ gataṃ cittaṃ desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ upāsike cittaṃ desanānugataṃ kātuṃ na sakkosī”ti? “Bhante, etassa me kathāya cittaṃ aññathattaṃ upagata”nti[P 1.0379]. Satthā “evarūpassa visabhāgajanassa kathitaṃ kathaṃ nāma āvajjituṃ na vaṭṭati, evarūpaṃ asamannāharitvā attano katākatameva oloketuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The neighboring people smeared that house with fresh cow-dung, scattered flowers with parched rice as the fifth, and prepared a seat of great value for the Teacher to sit upon. Indeed, people unacquainted with the Buddhas do not know how to prepare a seat, and for the Buddhas, there is no need for a guide. For at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having shaken the ten-thousandfold world-system, on the very day of attaining perfect enlightenment, all paths became manifest to them: 'This path leads to hell, this to the animal realm, this to the realm of ghosts, this to the human world, this to the heavenly world, this to the great, deathless Nibbāna.' As for the paths to villages, towns, and so on, there is nothing that needs to be said. Therefore, the Teacher, taking his bowl and robe early in the morning, went to the door of the great laywoman's house. She came out of the house, paid homage to the Teacher with the five-point prostration, led him into the inner dwelling, seated him on the prepared seat, and having given the water of dedication, served him with excellent hard and soft food. The laywoman, wishing to have the Teacher give the discourse of appreciation after he had finished his meal, took his bowl. The Teacher began the Dhamma talk of appreciation with a sweet voice. The laywoman, giving cries of 'Sādhu, sādhu!', listened to the Dhamma. The Ājīvaka, sitting in the back of the inner chamber, heard her voice giving cries of approval as she listened to the Dhamma and was unable to contain himself. Thinking, 'Now she is no longer mine,' he came out and, reviling both the laywoman and the Teacher in various ways, saying, 'You are ruined, you wretched woman! You pay such honor to this one!', he fled. The laywoman, shamed by his words, found her mind disturbed and was unable to direct her understanding in accordance with the teaching. Then the Teacher asked her, 'Laywoman, why are you unable to make your mind follow the teaching?' 'Venerable sir, my mind has become disturbed by his words.' The Teacher said, 'It is not proper to pay attention to the words spoken by such a vile and dissimilar person. Without giving mind to such things, one should look only at one's own deeds done and undone.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

50.

50.

“Na paresaṃ vilomāni, na paresaṃ katākataṃ;

Attanova avekkheyya, katāni akatāni cā”ti.

Not the transgressions of others, not their done and undone; one should observe only one's own deeds, done and undone.

Tattha [V 1.0213] na paresaṃ vilomānīti paresaṃ vilomāni pharusāni mammacchedakavacanāni na manasikātabbāni. Na paresaṃ katākatanti “asuko upāsako assaddho appasanno, nāpissa gehe kaṭacchubhikkhādīni diyyanti, na salākabhattādīni, na cīvarādipaccayadānaṃ etassa atthi, tathā asukā upāsikā assaddhā appasannā, nāpissā gehe kaṭacchubhikkhādīni diyyanti, na salākabhattādīni, na cīvarādipaccayadānaṃ etissā atthi, tathā asuko bhikkhu assaddho appasanno, nāpi upajjhāyavattaṃ karoti, na ācariyavattaṃ, na āgantukavattaṃ, na gamikavattaṃ, na cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ, na uposathāgāravattaṃ, na bhojanasālāvattaṃ, na jantāgharavattādīni, nāpissa kiñci dhutaṅgaṃ atthi, na bhāvanārāmatāya ussāhamattampī”ti evaṃ paresaṃ katākataṃ nāma na oloketabbaṃ. Attanova avekkheyyāti “kathaṃ bhūtassa me rattindivā vītivattantīti pabbajitena abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabba”nti (a. ni. 10.48) imaṃ ovādaṃ anussaranto saddhāpabbajito kulaputto “kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ ‘aniccaṃ [M 1.0240] dukkhaṃ anattā’ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā yoge kammaṃ kātuṃ sakkhiṃ[P 1.0380], nāsakkhi”nti evaṃ attano katākatāni olokeyyāti.

Therein, "not the contrary things of others" (na paresaṃ vilomāni) means that one should not pay attention to the contrary, harsh, and heart-rending words of others. "Not what is done and undone by others" (na paresaṃ katākatant) means one should not observe the deeds done or left undone by others, thinking: "Such and such a layman is faithless and not devoted; in his house, not even a spoonful of alms-food is given, nor ticket-food, nor is there the giving of requisites such as robes for him. Likewise, such and such a laywoman is faithless and not devoted; in her house, not even a spoonful of alms-food is given, nor ticket-food, nor is there the giving of requisites such as robes for her. Likewise, such and such a monk is faithless and not devoted; he does not perform his duties toward his preceptor, nor his duties toward his teacher, nor his duties toward guests, nor his duties toward those departing, nor his duties at the stupa courtyard, nor his duties at the Uposatha hall, nor his duties at the dining hall, nor his duties at the steam-bath house and so on. He has not undertaken any ascetic practice, nor does he have even the slightest exertion in the delight of meditation." In this way, the "done and undone" of others should not be observed. "One should look at one's own" means: remembering this instruction, "A renunciant should constantly reflect: 'How do my days and nights pass?'" (AN 10.48), a son of good family who has gone forth in faith should look at his own deeds done and undone thus: "Was I able to apply the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self and to work toward [deliverance from] the yokes, or was I not able?"

Desanāvasāne sā upāsikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā, desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, that laywoman was established in the fruition of stream-entry, and the teaching became beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Pāveyyakājīvakavatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of the Ājīvaka from Pāveyyaka is the sixth.

7. Chattapāṇiupāsakavatthu

7. The Story of the Lay Follower Chattapāṇi

Yathāpi ruciraṃ pupphanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto chattapāṇiupāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While the Teacher was dwelling in Sāvatthī, he delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning the lay follower Chattapāṇi, which begins, 'Just as a beautiful flower...'

Sāvatthiyañhi chattapāṇi nāma upāsako tipiṭakadharo anāgāmī. So pātova uposathiko hutvā satthu upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Anāgāmiariyasāvakānañhi samādānavasena uposathakammaṃ nāma natthi, maggeneva tesaṃ brahmacariyañca ekabhattikañca āgataṃ. Tenevāha – “ghaṭikāro kho, mahārāja, kumbhakāro ekabhattiko brahmacārī sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo”ti (ma. ni. 2.288). Evaṃ anāgāmino pakatiyāva ekabhattikā ca brahmacārino ca honti. Sopi tatheva uposathiko hutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā dhammakathaṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye rājā pasenadi kosalo satthu upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Chattapāṇi upāsako [V 1.0214] taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “uṭṭhātabbaṃ nu kho, no”ti cintetvā – “ahaṃ aggarājassa santike nisinno, tassa me padesarājānaṃ disvā uṭṭhātuṃ na yuttaṃ, rājā kho pana me anuṭṭhahantassa kujjhissati, etasmiṃ kujjhantepi neva uṭṭhahissāmi[P 1.0381]. Rājānaṃ disvā uṭṭhahantena hi rājā garukato hoti, no satthā, tasmā neva uṭṭhahissāmī”ti na uṭṭhahi. Paṇḍitapurisā nāma garutarānaṃ santike nisīditvā anuṭṭhahantaṃ disvā na kujjhanti. Rājā pana taṃ anuṭṭhahantaṃ disvā kupitamānaso satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā kupitabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “mahārāja, ayaṃ chattapāṇi upāsako paṇḍito diṭṭhadhammo tipiṭakadharo atthānatthakusalo”ti upāsakassa guṇaṃ kathesi. Rañño tassa guṇakathaṃ suṇantasseva cittaṃ mudukaṃ jātaṃ.

Indeed, in Sāvatthī there was a lay follower named Chattapāṇi, a master of the Tipiṭaka and a non-returner. Early in the morning, observing the Uposatha, he went to attend upon the Teacher. For non-returner noble disciples, there is no act of Uposatha by way of formal undertaking; for them, the holy life and eating only one meal come about through the path itself. Therefore it was said: 'Indeed, great king, Ghaṭīkāra the potter ate only one meal, was a celibate, virtuous, and of noble character' (MN 82). Thus, non-returners are by nature eaters of one meal and celibate. He too, in the same way, observing the Uposatha, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down listening to the Dhamma talk. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala came to attend upon the Teacher. The lay follower Chattapāṇi, seeing him approaching, considered, 'Should I rise, or should I not?' He then reflected: 'I am seated in the presence of the supreme king; it is not proper for me to rise upon seeing a provincial king. The king, however, will be angry with me for not rising. Even if he becomes angry, I will not rise. For by rising upon seeing the king, the king is honored, not the Teacher. Therefore, I will not rise.' And so he did not rise. Wise people do not become angry when they see someone not rising while seated in the presence of one who is more venerable. The king, however, seeing him not rising, became angry-minded. After paying homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side. The Teacher, knowing his state of anger, spoke of the lay follower's virtues: 'Great king, this lay follower Chattapāṇi is wise, one who has seen the Dhamma, a master of the Tipiṭaka, and skilled in what is beneficial and not beneficial.' Just as the king was listening to this account of his virtues, his mind softened.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0241] rājā uparipāsāde ṭhito chattapāṇiṃ upāsakaṃ katabhattakiccaṃ chattamādāya upāhanamāruyha rājaṅgaṇena gacchantaṃ disvā pakkosāpesi. So chattupāhanaṃ apanetvā rājānamupasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ rājā āha – “bho upāsaka, kinte chattupāhanaṃ apanīta”nti. “‘Rājā pakkosatī’ti sutvā apanetvā āgatomhī”ti. “Ajja amhākaṃ rājabhāvo tumhehi ñāto bhavissatī”ti. “Sadāpi mayaṃ, deva, tumhākaṃ rājabhāvaṃ jānāmā”ti. “Yadi evaṃ kasmā purimadivase satthu santike nisinno maṃ disvā na uṭṭhahī”ti? “Mahārāja, ahaṃ aggarājassa santike nisinno, padesarājānaṃ disvā uṭṭhahanto satthari agāravaṃ pavedeyyaṃ, tasmā na uṭṭhahi”nti. “Hotu, bho, tiṭṭhatetaṃ”. “Tumhe kira diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ [P 1.0382] atthānatthānaṃ kusalā tipiṭakadharā amhākaṃ antepure dhammaṃ vācethā”ti. “Na sakkomi, devā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Rājagehaṃ nāma mahāsāvajjaṃ, duyuttasuyuttakāni garukānettha, devā”ti. “Mā evaṃ vadetha, ‘purimadivase maṃ disvā na uṭṭhitomhī’ti mā kukkuccaṃ karothā”ti. “Deva, gihīnaṃ vicaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ nāma mahāsāvajjaṃ, ekaṃ pabbajitaṃ pakkosāpetvā dhammaṃ vācāpethā”ti. Rājā “sādhu, bho, gacchatha tumhe”ti taṃ uyyojetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ yāci, “bhante, mallikā ca devī vāsabhakhattiyā ca dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇissāmāti vadanti, pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nibaddhaṃ mama gehaṃ gantvā tāsaṃ dhammaṃ uddisathā”ti. “Buddhānaṃ nibaddhaṃ ekaṭṭhānagamanaṃ nāma natthi, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, aññaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ dethā”ti. Satthā ānandattherassa bhāramakāsi. Thero nibaddhaṃ gantvā tāsaṃ uddesaṃ uddisati. Tāsu mallikā sakkaccaṃ gahetvā sajjhāyitvā uddesaṃ paṭicchāpesi. Vāsabhakhattiyā pana neva sakkaccaṃ gaṇhāti, na sajjhāyati, na uddesaṃ paṭicchāpetuṃ sakkoti.

Then, one day, the king, standing on the upper terrace of the palace, saw the lay follower Chattapāṇi, who had finished his morning meal, taking up an umbrella, putting on his sandals, and walking through the royal courtyard, and had him summoned. That man, having removed his umbrella and sandals, approached the king, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then the king said to him: “O lay follower, why were your umbrella and sandals removed?” “Having heard, ‘The king summons,’ I removed them and came.” “Is it only today that our kingship has become known to you?” “Your Majesty, we always know your kingship.” “If so, why, on a previous day, while seated in the Teacher's presence, did you not rise upon seeing me?” “Great King, I was seated in the presence of the supreme king. If I were to rise upon seeing a provincial king, I would be showing disrespect to the Teacher. Therefore, I did not rise.” “Let it be, good sir, let that matter rest. It is said that you are skilled in what is beneficial and not beneficial for the present life and for future lives, and are a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. Recite the Dhamma in our inner palace.” “I am not able, Your Majesty.” “For what reason?” “The royal household, Your Majesty, is a place of great fault; matters are wrongly and rightly conjoined, and the responsibilities here are heavy.” “Do not speak thus. Do not feel remorse, thinking, ‘On a previous day, I did not rise upon seeing him.’” “Your Majesty, the sphere of activity for householders is a place of great fault. Having had one who has gone forth summoned, have him recite the Dhamma.” The king said, “Very well, good sir, you may go.” Having dismissed him, the king went to the Teacher's presence and requested of the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, Queen Mallikā and Vāsabhakhattiyā say, ‘We will learn the Dhamma.’ Please, together with five hundred monks, come regularly to my house and teach them the Dhamma.” “For Buddhas, Great King, there is no such thing as regularly going to one place.” “In that case, Venerable Sir, please provide another monk.” The Teacher assigned the duty to the Elder Ānanda. The Elder went regularly and taught them the recitation. Among them, Mallikā learned it carefully, rehearsed it, and was able to recite it back. Vāsabhakhattiyā, however, neither learned carefully, nor rehearsed, nor was she able to recite it back.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0215] satthā theraṃ pucchi – “kimānanda, upāsikā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantī”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kā sakkaccaṃ gaṇhātī”ti? “Mallikā, bhante, sakkaccaṃ gaṇhāti, sakkaccaṃ sajjhāyati, sakkaccaṃ uddesaṃ paṭicchāpetuṃ sakkoti. Tumhākaṃ pana ñātidhītā neva sakkaccaṃ gaṇhāti, na sajjhāyati, na uddesaṃ paṭicchāpetuṃ sakkotī”ti. Satthā therassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “ānanda, mayā kathitadhammo nāma sakkaccamasuṇantassa aggaṇhantassa asajjhāyantassa [P 1.0383] adesentassa vaṇṇasampannaṃ agandhakapupphaṃ viya aphalo hoti, sakkaccaṃ pana [M 1.0242] savanādīni karontassa mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso”ti vatvā imā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then, one day, the Teacher asked the Elder, “Ānanda, are the female lay followers learning the Dhamma?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “Which female lay follower is learning carefully?” “Mallikā, Venerable Sir, learns carefully, rehearses carefully, and is able to recite it back carefully. Your kinswoman, however, neither learns carefully, nor rehearses, nor is she able to recite it back.” The Teacher, having heard the Elder's words, said, “Ānanda, the Dhamma spoken by me, for one who does not listen carefully, does not learn it, does not rehearse it, and does not teach it, is fruitless, like a flower endowed with color but without fragrance.
