But for one who carefully engages in listening and so on, it is of great fruit and great benefit.” Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

51.

51.

“Yathāpi ruciraṃ pupphaṃ, vaṇṇavantaṃ agandhakaṃ;

Evaṃ subhāsitā vācā, aphalā hoti akubbato.

Just as a lovely flower, endowed with color but scentless, so is a well-spoken word fruitless for one who does not act upon it.

52.

52.

“Yathāpi ruciraṃ pupphaṃ, vaṇṇavantaṃ sagandhakaṃ;

Evaṃ subhāsitā vācā, saphalā hoti kubbato”ti.

Just as a lovely flower, endowed with color and fragrant, so is a well-spoken word fruitful for one who acts upon it.

Tattha ruciranti sobhanaṃ. Vaṇṇavantanti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānasampannaṃ, agandhakanti gandhavirahitaṃ pālibhaddakagirikaṇṇikajayasumanādibhedaṃ. Evaṃ subhāsitā vācāti subhāsitā vācā nāma tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānasampannaṃ agandhakapupphasadisaṃ. Yathā pana agandhakapupphaṃ yo naṃ dhāreti, tassa sarīre gandhaṃ na pharati, evaṃ etampi yo naṃ sakkaccaṃ savanādīhi na samācarati, tassa sakkaccaṃ asamācarantassa yaṃ tattha kattabbaṃ, taṃ akubbato sutagandhañca vācāgandhañca paṭipattigandhañca na āvahati aphalā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ [P 1.0384] subhāsitā vācā, aphalā hoti akubbato”ti. Sagandhakanti campakanīluppalādibhedaṃ. Evanti yathā taṃ pupphaṃ dhārentassa sarīre gandho pharati, evaṃ tepiṭakabuddhavacanasaṅkhātā subhāsitā vācāpi. Kubbatoti yo sakkaccaṃ savanādīhi tattha kattabbaṃ karoti, sā assa puggalassa saphalā hoti, sutagandhavācāgandhapaṭipattigandhānaṃ āvahanato mahapphalā hoti, mahānisaṃsāti attho.

Therein, `ruciraṃ` means beautiful. `Vaṇṇavantaṃ` means endowed with color and form. `Agandhakaṃ` means devoid of fragrance, of varieties such as the coral tree, butterfly pea, and jayasumanā flowers. As for 'so is a well-spoken word,' a 'well-spoken word' means the word of the Buddha, the Tipiṭaka. It is like a flower endowed with color and form but without fragrance. Just as a scentless flower, for one who wears it, does not pervade his body with fragrance, so too, for one who does not properly practice this with careful listening and so on, not doing what should be done in that regard, it does not bring forth the fragrance of learning, the fragrance of speech, and the fragrance of practice; it is fruitless. Therefore it was said: 'so is a well-spoken word fruitless for one who does not act upon it.' `Sagandhakaṃ` means of varieties such as the campaka and blue lotus flowers. As for 'so': just as the fragrance of that flower pervades the body of one who wears it, so too the well-spoken word, known as the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka. As for 'for one who acts': for that person who carefully does what should be done in that regard, with listening and so on, it is fruitful. Because it brings forth the fragrance of learning, the fragrance of speech, and the fragrance of practice, it is of great fruit and great benefit. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly.

Chattapāṇiupāsakavatthu sattamaṃ.

The Story of the Lay Follower Chattapāṇi is the seventh.

8. Visākhāvatthu

8. The Story of Visākhā

Yathāpi [V 1.0216] puppharāsimhāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ upanissāya pubbārāme viharanto visākhaṃ upāsikaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, relying on Sāvatthī and dwelling in the Pubbārāma, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Yathāpi puppharāsimhā,' concerning the laywoman Visākhā.

Sā [M 1.0243] kira aṅgaraṭṭhe bhaddiyanagare meṇḍakaseṭṭhiputtassa dhanañcayaseṭṭhino aggamahesiyā sumanadeviyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Tassā sattavassikakāle satthā selabrāhmaṇādīnaṃ bodhaneyyabandhavānaṃ upanissayasampadaṃ disvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro cārikaṃ caramāno taṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇi.

It is said that she was born in the womb of Sumanadevī, the chief consort of the seṭṭhi Dhanañcaya, son of the seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka, in the city of Bhaddiya in the country of Aṅga. When she was seven years old, the Teacher, seeing the perfection of supporting conditions for the enlightenment of kinsmen to be guided, such as Sela the brahmin and others, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of monks and wandering on tour, arrived at that city.

Tasmiñca samaye meṇḍako, gahapati, tasmiṃ nagare pañcannaṃ mahāpuññānaṃ jeṭṭhako [P 1.0385] hutvā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ karoti. Pañca mahāpuññā nāma meṇḍako seṭṭhi, candapadumā nāma tasseva jeṭṭhakabhariyā, tasseva jeṭṭhakaputto dhanañcayo nāma, tassa bhariyā sumanadevī nāma, meṇḍakaseṭṭhino dāso puṇṇo nāmāti. Na kevalañca meṇḍakaseṭṭhiyeva, bimbisārarañño pana vijite pañca amitabhogā nāma ahesuṃ – jotiko, jaṭilo, meṇḍako, puṇṇako, kākavaliyoti. Tesu ayaṃ meṇḍakaseṭṭhi dasabalassa attano nagaraṃ sampattabhāvaṃ ñatvā puttassa dhanañcayaseṭṭhino dhītaraṃ visākhaṃ dārikaṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “amma, tuyhampi maṅgalaṃ, amhākampi maṅgalaṃ, tava parivārehi pañcahi dārikāsatehi saddhiṃ pañca rathasatāni āruyha pañcahi dāsisatehi parivutā dasabalassa paccuggamanaṃ karohī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā tathā akāsi. Kāraṇākāraṇesu pana kusalattā yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi, yānena gantvā yānā paccorohitvā pattikāva satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Athassā cariyāvasena satthā dhammaṃ desesi. Sā desanāvasāne pañcahi dārikāsatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Meṇḍakaseṭṭhipi kho satthāramupasaṅkamitvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya svātanāya nimantetvā punadivase attano nivesane paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā eteneva upāyena aḍḍhamāsaṃ mahādānamadāsi. Satthā bhaddiyanagare yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā pakkāmi.

And at that time, Meṇḍaka the householder, being the foremost of the five greatly meritorious persons in that city, held the position of seṭṭhi. The five greatly meritorious persons were: the seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka; his chief wife named Candapadumā; his eldest son named Dhanañcaya; his wife named Sumanadevī; and the seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka’s slave named Puṇṇa. And not only the seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka, but in King Bimbisāra’s kingdom there were five of immeasurable wealth: Jotika, Jaṭila, Meṇḍaka, Puṇṇaka, and Kālavaliya. Among them, this seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka, knowing that the One of Ten Powers had arrived in his city, had his son the seṭṭhi Dhanañcaya’s daughter, the maiden Visākhā, summoned and said: 'Dear daughter, it will be an auspicious thing for you and for us. With your retinue of five hundred maidens, mount five hundred chariots, and surrounded by five hundred female servants, go and welcome the One of Ten Powers.' She, having consented with 'Very well,' did so. And being skilled in what was proper and improper, she went by vehicle as far as the ground was suitable for a vehicle, then dismounted from the vehicle, and on foot approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then, by the power of her previously practiced conduct, the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, she, together with the five hundred maidens, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka also approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma talk, and having been established in the fruit of stream-entry, invited him for the next day. On the following day, in his own residence, he served the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at its head with excellent hard and soft food, and in this very way, gave a great offering for half a month. The Teacher, having dwelt in the city of Bhaddiya for as long as he pleased, departed.

Tena kho pana samayena bimbisāro ca pasenadi kosalo ca aññamaññaṃ bhaginipatikā honti. Athekadivasaṃ kosalarājā [P 1.0386] cintesi – “bimbisārassa vijite pañca amitabhogā mahāpuññā vasanti, mayhaṃ vijite ekopi tādiso natthi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bimbisārassa santikaṃ gantvā [V 1.0217] ekaṃ mahāpuññaṃ yāceyya”nti. So tattha gantvā raññā katapaṭisanthāro “kiṃ kāraṇā āgatosī”ti [M 1.0244] puṭṭho “‘tumhākaṃ vijite pañca amitabhogā mahāpuññā vasanti, tato ekaṃ gahetvā gamissāmī’ti āgatomhi, tesu me ekaṃ dethā”ti āha. “Mahākulāni amhehi cāletuṃ na sakkā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ aladdhā na gamissāmī”ti āha. Rājā amaccehi saddhiṃ mantetvā “jotikādīnaṃ mahākulānaṃ cālanaṃ nāma mahāpathaviyā cālanasadisaṃ, meṇḍakamahāseṭṭhissa putto dhanañcayaseṭṭhi nāma atthi, tena saddhiṃ mantetvā paṭivacanaṃ te dassāmī”ti vatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā, tāta, kosalarājā “‘ekaṃ dhanaseṭṭhiṃ gahetvā gamissāmī’ti vadati, tvaṃ tena saddhiṃ gacchāhī”ti. “Tumhesu pahiṇantesu gamissāmi, devā”ti. “Tena hi parivacchaṃ katvā gaccha, tātā”ti. So attano kattabbayuttakamakāsi. Rājāpissa mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā, “imaṃ ādāya gacchathā”ti pasenadirājānaṃ uyyojesi. So taṃ ādāya sabbattha ekarattivāsena gacchanto ekaṃ phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ patvā nivāsaṃ gaṇhi, atha naṃ dhanañcayaseṭṭhi pucchi – “idaṃ kassa vijita”nti? “Mayhaṃ, seṭṭhī”ti. “Kīva dūro ito sāvatthī”ti[P 1.0387]? “Sattayojanamatthake”ti. “Antonagaraṃ sambādhaṃ, amhākaṃ parijano mahanto, sace rocetha, idheva vaseyyāma, devā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne nagaraṃ māpetvā tassa datvā agamāsi. Tasmiṃ padese sayaṃ vasanaṭṭhānassa gahitattā nagarassa sāketantveva nāmaṃ ahosi.

At that time, King Bimbisāra and King Pasenadi of Kosala were brothers-in-law to each other. Then one day, the King of Kosala thought: 'In King Bimbisāra's kingdom dwell five greatly meritorious persons of immeasurable wealth. In my kingdom, there is not even one such person. What if I were to go to King Bimbisāra and ask for one greatly meritorious person?' So he went there, and having been greeted hospitably by the king, was asked, 'For what reason have you come?' He replied, 'In your kingdom dwell five greatly meritorious persons of immeasurable wealth. I have come to take one of them and go. Give me one of them.' The king said, 'It is not possible for us to move the great families.' The other said, 'I will not go without getting one.' The king, having consulted with his ministers, said, 'To move the great families of Jotika and others is like shaking the great earth. There is the seṭṭhi named Dhanañcaya, son of the great seṭṭhi Meṇḍaka. After consulting with him, I will give you a reply.' Having said this, he had Dhanañcaya summoned and said, 'My dear, the King of Kosala says, "I will take one wealthy seṭṭhi and go." You should go with him.' Dhanañcaya replied, 'If you send me, Your Majesty, I will go.' 'In that case,' said the king, 'make your preparations and go, my dear.' So he made the arrangements that were his duty. The king also, having paid him great honor, sent King Pasenadi off, saying, 'Take this one and go.' He, taking Dhanañcaya, traveled, staying one night at each place. Reaching a pleasant place, he took up residence. Then the seṭṭhi Dhanañcaya asked him, 'Whose kingdom is this?' 'Mine, seṭṭhi.' 'How far is Sāvatthī from here?' 'It is seven yojanas from here.' 'Your Majesty, the inner city is crowded, and our retinue is large. If it pleases you, we would stay right here.' The king, accepting with 'Very well,' had a city created in that place, gave it to him, and departed. Because in that region a place of residence was taken by himself, the city's name became Sāketa.

Sāvatthiyampi kho migāraseṭṭhino putto puṇṇavaḍḍhanakumāro nāma vayappatto ahosi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro vadiṃsu – “tāta, tava ruccanaṭṭhāne ekaṃ dārikaṃ upadhārehī”ti. “‘Mayhaṃ evarūpāya bhariyāya kiccaṃ natthī’ti, putta, mā evaṃ kari, kulaṃ nāma aputtakaṃ na tiṭṭhatī”ti. So punappunaṃ vuccamāno “tena hi pañcakalyāṇasamannāgataṃ dārikaṃ labhamāno tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. “Kāni panetāni pañca kalyāṇāni nāma, tātā”ti. Kesakalyāṇaṃ, maṃsakalyāṇaṃ, aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ, chavikalyāṇaṃ, vayakalyāṇanti. Mahāpuññāya hi itthiyā kesā morakalāpasadisā hutvā muñcitvā vissaṭṭhā nivāsanantaṃ paharitvā nivattitvā uddhaggā tiṭṭhanti, idaṃ kesakalyāṇaṃ nāma, dantāvaraṇaṃ bimbaphalasadisaṃ vaṇṇasampannaṃ samaṃ suphusitaṃ hoti[M 1.0245], idaṃ maṃsakalyāṇaṃ nāma, dantā sukkā samā aviraḷā ussāpetvā ṭhapitavajirapanti viya samacchinnasaṅkhapanti viya ca sobhanti, idaṃ aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ nāma, kāḷiyā cuṇṇakādīhi avilitto eva [P 1.0388] chavivaṇṇo siniddho nīluppaladāmasadiso hoti, odātāya ca kaṇikārapupphadāmasadiso hoti, idaṃ chavikalyāṇaṃ nāma, dasakkhattuṃ vijātāpi kho pana sakiṃ vijātā viya avigatayobbanāyeva hoti, idaṃ vayakalyāṇaṃ nāma hoti. Athassa [V 1.0218] mātāpitaro aṭṭhuttarasatabrāhmaṇe nimantetvā bhojetvā “pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā itthiyo nāma hontī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Āma, hontī”ti. “Tena hi evarūpaṃ dārikaṃ pariyesituṃ aṭṭha janā gacchantū”ti bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā “āgatakāle vo kattabbaṃ jānissāma, gacchatha, evarūpaṃ dārikaṃ pariyesatha, diṭṭhakāle ca imaṃ pilandhanaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇamālaṃ datvā uyyojesuṃ.

In Sāvatthī also, the son of the merchant Migāra, a young man named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, had come of age. Then his parents said to him: 'Dear son, seek out a maiden for yourself in a place that pleases you.' 'I have no need for such a wife.' 'Son, do not speak thus; a family without a son does not endure.' Being told this repeatedly, he said: 'Very well, if I find a maiden endowed with the five beauties, I will do as you say.' 'But what, dear son, are these five beauties?' 'Beauty of hair, beauty of flesh, beauty of bones, beauty of skin, and beauty of youth. For a woman of great merit, her hair is like a peacock's tail-plume; when unbound and let down, it strikes the hem of her lower garment, turns back, and stands with its tips pointing upwards. This is called beauty of hair. The lips are like a ripe Bimba fruit, perfect in color, even, and well-formed. This is called beauty of flesh. The teeth are white, even, and without gaps; they shine like a row of set diamonds or like a smoothly cut conch shell. This is called beauty of bones. For a dark woman, her skin complexion, as if unmarred by powders and the like, is smooth and like a garland of blue lotuses; and for a fair woman, it is like a garland of Kaṇikāra flowers. This is called beauty of skin. Even after having given birth ten times, she is indeed like one who has given birth only once, with her youth undiminished. This is called beauty of youth.' Then his parents invited eight brahmins, fed them, and asked: 'Do women endowed with the five beauties exist?' 'Yes, they do.' 'Then let eight men go to search for such a maiden.' Giving them much wealth, they said: 'When you return, we will know what reward is to be given to you. Go, search for such a maiden, and when you see her, give her this ornament.' They gave them a golden garland worth a hundred thousand and sent them off.

Te mahantamahantāni nagarāni gantvā pariyesamānā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgataṃ dārikaṃ adisvā nivattitvā āgacchantā vivaṭanakkhattadivase sāketaṃ anuppattā – “ajja amhākaṃ kammaṃ nipphajjissatī”ti cintayiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pana nagare anusaṃvaccharaṃ vivaṭanakkhattaṃ nāma hoti. Tadā bahi anikkhamanakulānipi parivārena saddhiṃ gehā nikkhamitvā appaṭicchannena sarīrena padasāva nadītīraṃ gacchanti. Tasmiṃ divase khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ puttāpi “attano samānajātikaṃ manāpaṃ kuladārikaṃ disvā mālāguḷena parikkhipissāmā”ti taṃ taṃ maggaṃ nissāya tiṭṭhanti. Tepi kho brāhmaṇā nadītīre ekaṃ sālaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. “Tasmiṃ khaṇe visākhā pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikā hutvā sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā pañcahi kumārikāsatehi parivutā nadiṃ gantvā nhāyissāmī”ti taṃ padesaṃ pattā, atha kho megho [P 1.0389] uṭṭhahitvā pāvassi. Pañcasatā kumārikāyo vegena gantvā sālaṃ pavisiṃsu. Brāhmaṇā olokentā tāsu ekampi pañcakalyāṇasamannāgataṃ na passiṃsu. Atha visākhā pakatigamaneneva sālaṃ pāvisi, vatthābharaṇāni temiṃsu. Brāhmaṇā tassā cattāri kalyāṇāni disvā dante passitukāmā “alasajātikā amhākaṃ dhītā, etissā sāmiko kañjikamattampi na labhissati maññe”ti aññamaññaṃ kathayiṃsu. Atha ne visākhā āha – “kaṃ vadetha tumhe”ti? “Taṃ kathema, ammā”ti. Madhuro hi tassā saddo kaṃsatāḷasaro viya niccharati. Atha ne [M 1.0246] puna madhurasaddena “kiṃ kāraṇā bhaṇathā”ti pucchi. “Tava parivāritthiyo vatthālaṅkāre atemetvā vegena sālaṃ paviṭṭhā, tuyhaṃ ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ vegena āgamanamattampi natthi, vatthābharaṇāni temetvā āgatāsi. Tasmā kathema, ammā”ti.

They went to very great cities searching, but not seeing a maiden endowed with the five beauties, they turned back. As they were returning, they arrived in Sāketa on the day of the open-door festival and thought, 'Today our task will be accomplished.' In that city, a festival called the open-door festival was held annually. At that time, even those from families who did not usually go outside came forth from their homes with their retinues and went on foot to the riverbank with their bodies unconcealed. On that day, the sons of nobles, wealthy men, and the like also stood along the various roads, thinking, 'When we see a pleasing maiden from a suitable family, we will cast a garland upon her.' Those brahmins, too, entered a hall by the riverbank and stayed there. At that moment, Visākhā, who was about fifteen or sixteen years of age, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by five hundred maidens, arrived at that place, intending to go to the river and bathe. Then a cloud arose and it rained. The five hundred maidens went quickly and entered the hall. The brahmins, looking at them, did not see even one among them endowed with the five beauties. Then Visākhā entered the hall at her normal gait, and her clothes and ornaments became wet. The brahmins, seeing four of her beauties and wishing to see her teeth, said to one another, 'Our daughter is of a lazy nature; I think her husband will not get even rice-gruel.' Then Visākhā asked them, 'Whom are you speaking about?' 'We are speaking of you, mother,' they replied. For her voice issued forth sweetly, like the sound of a bronze cymbal. Then, again with her sweet voice, she asked, 'For what reason do you say this?' They answered, 'Your attendant women entered the hall quickly without getting their clothes and ornaments wet, but you did not come quickly to this place at all; you arrived having let your clothes and ornaments get wet. That is why we speak thus, mother.'

“Tātā, evaṃ mā vadetha, ahaṃ etāhi balavatarā, kāraṇaṃ pana sallakkhetvā javena nāgatāmhī”ti. “Kiṃ, ammā”ti? “Tātā, cattāro janā javamānā na sobhanti, aparampi kāraṇaṃ atthī”ti. “Katame cattāro janā javamānā na sobhanti, ammā”ti? Tātā, abhisittarājā tāva sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍito kacchaṃ bandhitvā rājaṅgaṇe javamāno na sobhati, “kiṃ ayaṃ rājā gahapatiko viya dhāvatī”ti aññadatthu garahaṃ labhati, saṇikaṃ gacchantova [V 1.0219] sobhati. Rañño maṅgalahatthīpi alaṅkato javamāno na sobhati, vāraṇalīḷāya gacchantova sobhati. Pabbajito javamāno na sobhati, “kiṃ ayaṃ samaṇo gihī viya dhāvatī”ti kevalaṃ garahameva [P 1.0390] labhati, samitagamanena pana sobhati. Itthī javamānā na sobhati, “kiṃ esā itthī puriso viya dhāvatī”ti garahitabbāva hoti, “ime cattāro janā javamānā na sobhanti, tātā”ti. “Katamaṃ pana aparaṃ kāraṇaṃ, ammā”ti? “Tātā, mātāpitaro nāma dhītaraṃ aṅgapaccaṅgāni saṇṭhāpetvā posenti. Mayañhi vikkiṇeyyabhaṇḍaṃ nāma, amhe parakulapesanatthāya posenti. Sace javamānānaṃ nivatthadussakaṇṇe vā akkamitvā bhūmiyaṃ vā pakkhalitvā patitakāle hattho vā pādo vā bhijjeyya, kulasseva bhāro bhaveyya, pasādhanabhaṇḍaṃ pana me temetvā sussissati. Imaṃ kāraṇaṃ sallakkhetvā na dhāvitāmhi, tātā”ti.

“Fathers, do not speak thus. I am stronger than they are; however, having considered a reason, I did not come swiftly.” “What is the reason, Mother?” “Fathers, four persons are not graceful when running, and there is another reason as well.” “Which four persons are not graceful when running, Mother?” “Fathers, firstly, an anointed king, adorned with all ornaments and with his lower garment fastened, is not graceful when running in the royal courtyard. He receives only blame, as people say, ‘Why does this king run like a householder?’ He is graceful only when walking slowly. The king’s auspicious elephant, too, though adorned, is not graceful when running; it is graceful only when moving with the majestic gait of an elephant. A renunciant is not graceful when running. He receives only blame, as people say, ‘Why does this ascetic run like a layman?’ He is graceful, however, when walking with tranquility. A woman is not graceful when running. She is only to be blamed, as people say, ‘Why does this woman run like a man?’ These, Fathers, are the four persons who are not graceful when running.” “But what is the other reason, Mother?” “Fathers, parents raise a daughter, having well-formed her major and minor limbs. Indeed, we are called goods to be sold; they raise us for the purpose of sending us to another family. If, while running, I were to step on the corner of my lower garment or stumble on the ground, and at the time of falling, a hand or a foot were to break, it would become a burden to the family. My adornments, on the other hand, having become wet, will dry. Having considered this reason, Fathers, I did not run.”

Brāhmaṇā tassā kathanakāle dantasampattiṃ disvā “evarūpā no dantasampatti diṭṭhapubbā”ti tassā sādhukāraṃ datvā, “amma, tuyhamevesā anucchavikā”ti vatvā taṃ suvaṇṇamālaṃ pilandhayiṃsu. Atha ne pucchi – “kataranagarato āgatāttha, tātā”ti? “Sāvatthito, ammā”ti. “Seṭṭhikulaṃ kataraṃ nāmā”ti? “Migāraseṭṭhi nāma, ammā”ti. “Ayyaputto ko [M 1.0247] nāmā”ti? “Puṇṇavaḍḍhanakumāro nāma, ammā”ti. Sā “samānajātikaṃ no kula”nti adhivāsetvā pitu sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “amhākaṃ rathaṃ pesetū”ti[P 1.0391]. Kiñcāpi hi sā āgamanakāle padasā āgatā, suvaṇṇamālāya pana pilandhanakālato paṭṭhāya tathā gantuṃ na labhati, issaradārikā rathādīhi gacchanti, itarā pakatiyānakaṃ vā abhiruhanti, chattaṃ vā tālapaṇṇaṃ vā upari karonti, tasmimpi asati nivatthasāṭakassa dasantaṃ ukkhipitvā aṃse khipantā gacchanti eva. Tassā pana pitā pañca rathasatāni pesesi. Sā saparivārā rathaṃ āruyha gatā. Brāhmaṇāpi ekatova agamaṃsu. Atha ne seṭṭhi pucchi – “kuto āgatātthā”ti? “Sāvatthito mahāseṭṭhī”ti. “Seṭṭhi kataro nāmā”ti? “Migāraseṭṭhi nāmā”ti. “Putto ko nāmā”ti? “Puṇṇavaḍḍhanakumāro nāma mahāseṭṭhī”ti. “Dhanaṃ kittaka”nti? “Cattālīsakoṭiyo mahāseṭṭhī”ti. “Dhanaṃ tāva amhākaṃ dhanaṃ upādāya kākaṇikamattaṃ, dārikāya pana ārakkhamattāya laddhakālato paṭṭhāya kiṃ aññena kāraṇenā”ti adhivāsesi. So tesaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā ekāhadvīhaṃ vasāpetvā uyyojesi.

At the time of her speaking, the brahmins saw the perfection of her teeth and, giving her praise, said, “We have never before seen such perfection of teeth. Mother, this is truly fitting for you,” and they adorned her with the golden garland. Then she asked them, “From which city have you come, Fathers?” “From Sāvatthī, Mother.” “What is the name of the merchant family?” “The merchant named Migāra, Mother.” “What is the name of the young master?” “The young man named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, Mother.” She, thinking, “The family is of equal birth to ours,” consented and sent a message to her father: “Let him send a chariot for us.” Indeed, although she had come on foot, from the moment she was adorned with the golden garland, she could no longer travel in that manner. Daughters of the wealthy travel by chariot and other such vehicles; others ride on ordinary conveyances or hold an umbrella or a palm leaf above them. If even these are not available, they lift the edge of their lower garment and throw it over their shoulders as they walk. Her father, however, sent five hundred chariots. She, along with her retinue, mounted a chariot and departed. The brahmins also went together. Then the merchant asked them, “From where have you come?” “From Sāvatthī, great merchant.” “What is the name of the merchant?” “The merchant named Migāra.” “What is the name of his son?” “The young man named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, great merchant.” “How much is his wealth?” “Forty crores, great merchant.” “As for the wealth, compared to our wealth, it is a mere trifle. However, regarding the maiden, now that the time has come to ensure her protection, what need is there for any other reason?” Thus he consented. He honored them, had them stay for a day or two, and then sent them off.

Te sāvatthiṃ gantvā migāraseṭṭhissa “laddhā no dārikā”ti ārocayiṃsu. “Kassa dhītā”ti? “Dhanañcayaseṭṭhino”ti. So “mahākulassa me dārikā laddhā, khippameva naṃ ānetuṃ [V 1.0220] vaṭṭatī”ti tattha gamanatthaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “‘mahākulaṃ etaṃ mayā bimbisārassa santikā ānetvā sākete nivesitaṃ, tassa [P 1.0392] sammānaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti ahampi āgamissāmī”ti āha, so “sādhu, devā”ti vatvā dhanañcayaseṭṭhino sāsanaṃ pesesi – “mayi āgacchante rājāpi āgamissati, mahantaṃ rājabalaṃ ettakassa janassa kattabbayuttakaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasi, na sakkhissasī”ti? Itaropi “sacepi dasa rājāno āgacchanti, āgacchantū”ti paṭisāsanaṃ pesesi. Migāraseṭṭhi tāva mahante nagare gehagopakamattaṃ ṭhapetvā sesajanaṃ ādāya gantvā aḍḍhayojanamatte ṭhāne ṭhatvā “āgatāmhā”ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Dhanañcayaseṭṭhi bahupaṇṇākāraṃ pesetvā dhītarā saddhiṃ mantesi, “amma, sasuro kira te kosalaraññā saddhiṃ āgato, tassa kataraṃ gehaṃ paṭijaggitabbaṃ, rañño kataraṃ[M 1.0248], uparājādīnaṃ katarānī”ti? Paṇḍitā seṭṭhidhītā vajiraggatikhiṇañāṇā kappasatasahassaṃ patthitapatthanā abhinīhārasampannā “sasurassa me asukagehaṃ paṭijaggatha, rañño asukagehaṃ, uparājādīnaṃ asukānī”ti saṃvidahitvā dāsakammakare pakkosāpetvā “ettakā rañño kattabbakiccaṃ karotha, ettakā uparājādīnaṃ, hatthiassādayopi tumheyeva paṭijaggatha, assabandhādayopi āgantvā maṅgalachaṇaṃ anubhavissantī”ti saṃvidahi. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”? “‘Mayaṃ visākhāya maṅgalaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā na kiñci labhimha, assarakkhaṇādīni karontā sukhaṃ na vicarimhā’ti keci vattuṃ mā labhiṃsū”ti.

They went to Sāvatthī and informed Migāra the financier, "We have obtained a girl." "Whose daughter?" "Dhanañjaya the financier's." He thought, "A girl from a great family has been obtained for me; it is proper that she be brought quickly," and informed the King of his intention to go there. The King said, "This is a great family that I brought from near King Bimbisāra and settled in Sāketa. It is proper to honor them. I too will come." He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and sent a message to Dhanañjaya the financier: "When I come, the King will also come. Will you be able to make the suitable provisions for such a large royal retinue, or not?" The other also sent a reply: "Even if ten kings come, let them come." First, Migāra the financier left behind only enough people to guard the houses in the great city and set out with the rest of the people. He stopped at a place half a yojana away and sent a message: "We have arrived." Dhanañjaya the financier sent many gifts and consulted with his daughter: "Dear, your father-in-law has come, they say, together with the King of Kosala. Which house should be prepared for him, which for the King, and which for the viceroy and others?" The financier's daughter was wise, with intelligence as sharp as a diamond's edge, having made an aspiration for a hundred thousand eons and being endowed with its fulfillment. She arranged: "Prepare such and such a house for my father-in-law, such and such for the King, and such and such for the viceroy and others." She summoned the servants and workers and instructed them: "So many of you perform the duties for the King, so many for the viceroy and others. You yourselves must attend to the elephants, horses, and so on. The horse-grooms and others will also come and enjoy the auspicious celebrations." "For what reason?" "Lest some should say, 'We went to Visākhā's auspicious place and obtained nothing. While we were busy attending to the horses and so on, we did not get to move about freely.'"

Taṃ divasameva visākhāya pitā pañcasate suvaṇṇakāre pakkosāpetvā “dhītu me mahālatāpasādhanaṃ nāma [P 1.0393] karothā”ti rattasuvaṇṇassa nikkhasahassaṃ, tadanurūpāni ca rajatamaṇimuttāpavāḷavajirādīni dāpesi. Rājā katipāhaṃ vasitvāva dhanañcayaseṭṭhissa sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “na sakkā seṭṭhinā amhākaṃ ciraṃ posanaṃ nāma kātuṃ, dāni dārikāya gamanakālaṃ jānātū”ti. Sopi rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi – “idāni vassakālo āgato, na sakkā catumāsaṃ vicarituṃ, tumhākaṃ balakāyassa yaṃ yaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, sabbaṃ taṃ mama bhāro, mayā pesitakāle devo gamissatī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya sāketanagaraṃ niccanakkhattaṃ viya ahosi. Rājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbesaṃ mālāgandhavatthādīni paṭiyattāneva honti. Tato te janā cintayiṃsu – “seṭṭhi amhākameva sakkāraṃ karotī”ti, evaṃ tayo māsā atikkantā, pasādhanaṃ pana tāva na niṭṭhāti. Kammantādhiṭṭhāyakā āgantvā seṭṭhino ārocesuṃ – “aññaṃ asantaṃ nāma natthi, balakāyassa pana bhattapacanadārūni nappahontī”ti. “Gacchatha, tātā, imasmiṃ nagare parijiṇṇā hatthisālādayo ceva parijiṇṇakāni ca gehāni gahetvā pacathā”ti. Evaṃ pacantānampi aḍḍhamāso atikkanto. Tato punapi “dārūni natthī”ti ārocayiṃsu[V 1.0221]. “Imasmiṃ kāle na sakkā dārūni laddhuṃ, dussakoṭṭhāgārāni vivaritvā thūlasāṭakehi vaṭṭiyo katvā telacāṭīsu [P 1.0394] temetvā bhattaṃ pacathā”ti. Te aḍḍhamāsaṃ tathā akaṃsu. Evaṃ cattāro māsā atikkantā, pasādhanampi niṭṭhitaṃ.

On that very day, Visākhā's father summoned five hundred goldsmiths and said, "Make for my daughter an ornament called Mahālatāpasādhana." He gave them a thousand nikkhas of red gold and an appropriate amount of silver, gems, pearls, corals, diamonds, and so on. After staying a few days, the King sent a message to the financier Dhanañjaya: "It is not possible for the financier to support us for long. Now let him know the time for the maiden's departure." He also sent a message to the King: "Now the rainy season has come; it is not possible to travel for four months. Whatever is needed for your army, all that is my responsibility. Your Majesty shall depart when I send word." From then on, the city of Sāketa was like a perpetual festival. Starting with the King, garlands, perfumes, and clothes were always being prepared for everyone. Then the people thought, "The financier is honoring only us," and so three months passed, but the ornament was still not finished. The overseers of the work came and informed the financier: "There is nothing else lacking, but the firewood for cooking rice for the army is insufficient." "Go, my dears, take the dilapidated elephant stables and dilapidated buildings in this city and cook with them." Even as they cooked thus, half a month passed. Then again they reported, "There is no firewood." "At this time, it is not possible to obtain firewood. Open the cloth storehouses, make wicks with the coarse cloth, soak them in oil jars, and cook the rice with them." They did so for half a month. Thus four months passed, and the ornament was also completed.

Tasmiṃ pasādhane catasso vajiranāḷiyo upayogaṃ agamaṃsu, muttānaṃ ekādasa nāḷiyo, pavāḷassa bāvīsati nāḷiyo, maṇīnaṃ tettiṃsa [M 1.0249] nāḷiyo. Iti etehi ca aññehi ca ratanehi niṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Asuttamayaṃ pasādhanaṃ rajatena suttakiccaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ sīse paṭimukkaṃ pādapiṭṭhiṃ gacchati. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne muddikā yojetvā katā suvaṇṇamayā gaṇṭhikā honti, rajatamayā pāsakā, matthakamajjhe ekā muddikā, dvīsu kaṇṇapiṭṭhīsu dve, galavāṭake ekā, dvīsu jattūsu dve, dvīsu kapparesu dve, dvīsu kaṭipassesu dveti. Tasmiṃ kho pana pasādhane ekaṃ moraṃ kariṃsu, tassa dakkhiṇapakkhe rattasuvaṇṇamayāni pañca pattasatāni ahesuṃ, vāmapakkhe pañca pattasatāni, tuṇḍaṃ pavāḷamayaṃ, akkhīni maṇimayāni, tathā gīvā ca piñchāni ca, pattanāḷiyo rajatamayā, tathā jaṅghāyo. So visākhāya matthakamajjhe pabbatakūṭe ṭhatvā naccanamayūro viya khāyati. Pattanāḷisahassassa saddo dibbasaṅgītaṃ viya pañcaṅgikatūriyaghoso viya ca pavattati. Santikaṃ upagatāyeva tassā amorabhāvaṃ jānanti. Pasādhanaṃ [P 1.0395] navakoṭiagghanakaṃ ahosi, satasahassaṃ hatthakammamūlaṃ dīyittha.

In that ornament, four measures of diamonds were employed, eleven measures of pearls, twenty-two measures of coral, and thirty-three measures of gems. Thus, with these and other jewels, it was brought to completion. The ornament was made without thread; the work of thread was done with silver. Placed on the head, it reached the instep of the foot. At various places, rings were joined to make golden knots, with silver clasps. One ring was placed at the center of the head, two on the backs of the ears, one at the neck, two on the collarbones, two on the elbows, and two on the hips. Moreover, in that ornament, they made a peacock. On its right wing, there were five hundred feathers of red gold; on the left wing, five hundred feathers. Its beak was made of coral, its eyes of gems, and likewise its neck and tail feathers. The feather-quills were made of silver, as were its legs. It appeared like a dancing peacock standing on a mountain peak in the center of Visākhā's head. The sound of the thousand feather-quills was like divine music and like the sound of a five-part orchestra. Only those who came close knew that it was not a real peacock. The ornament was worth nine crores, and a hundred thousand was given as the wage for the handiwork.

“Kissa pana nissandena tāyetaṃ pasādhanaṃ laddha”nti? Sā kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ cīvarasāṭakaṃ datvā suttampi sūciyopi rajanampi attano santakameva adāsi. Tassa cīvaradānassa nissandena imaṃ mahālatāpasādhanaṃ labhi. Itthīnañhi cīvaradānaṃ mahālatāpasādhanabhaṇḍena matthakaṃ pappoti, purisānaṃ iddhimayapattacīvarenāti. Evaṃ mahāseṭṭhi catūhi māsehi dhītu parivacchaṃ katvā tassā deyyadhammaṃ dadamāno kahāpaṇapūrāni pañca sakaṭasatāni adāsi, suvaṇṇabhājanapūrāni pañca, rajatabhājanapūrāni pañca, tambabhājanapūrāni pañca, pattuṇṇavatthakoseyyavatthapūrāni pañca, sappipūrāni pañca, telapūrāni pañca, sālitaṇḍulapūrāni pañca, naṅgalaphālādiupakaraṇapūrāni pañcasakaṭasatāni adāsi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “mama dhītu gataṭṭhāne ‘asukena nāma me attho’ti mā parassa gehadvāraṃ pahiṇī”ti. Tasmā sabbūpakaraṇāni dāpesi. Ekekasmiṃ rathe sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā tisso tisso vaṇṇadāsiyo ṭhapetvā pañca rathasatāni adāsi. “Etaṃ nhāpentiyo bhojentiyo alaṅkarontiyo vicarathā”ti diyaḍḍhasahassaparicārikāyo [M 1.0250] adāsi. Athassa etadahosi – “mama dhītu gāvo dassāmī”ti. So purise [P 1.0396] āṇāpesi – “gacchatha [V 1.0222] bhaṇe cūḷavajassa dvāraṃ vivaritvā tīsu gāvutesu tisso bheriyo gahetvā tiṭṭhatha, puthulato usabhamatte ṭhāne ubhosu passesu tiṭṭhatha. Gāvīnaṃ tato paraṃ gantuṃ mā adattha. Evaṃ ṭhitakāle bherisaññaṃ kareyyāthā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Te gāvīnaṃ vajato nikkhamitvā gāvutaṃ gatakāle bherisaññaṃ akaṃsu, puna aḍḍhayojanaṃ gatakāle akaṃsu. Punapi tigāvutaṃ gatakāle bherisaññaṃ akaṃsu, puthulato gamanañca nivāresuṃ. Evaṃ dīghato tigāvute, puthulato usabhamatte ṭhāne gāviyo aññamaññaṃ nighaṃsantiyo aṭṭhaṃsu.

“By the result of what kamma did she obtain that ornament?” It is said that during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One, she gave robe-cloth to twenty thousand bhikkhus, and also gave thread, needles, and dye that were her own property. As a result of that gift of robes, she obtained this Mahālatā ornament. Indeed, for women, the gift of robes culminates in obtaining the Mahālatā ornament, while for men, it culminates in obtaining a bowl and robes created by psychic power. Thus the great merchant, having made preparations for his daughter over four months, gave her these wedding gifts: five hundred cartloads filled with kahāpaṇas, five hundred filled with golden vessels, five hundred with silver vessels, five hundred with copper vessels, five hundred with fine woolen and silk garments, five hundred with ghee, five hundred with oil, five hundred with fine rice, and five hundred cartloads filled with farming implements such as plows and plowshares. It is said this thought occurred to him: “In the place where my daughter has gone, may she not have to send a messenger to another's house, saying, ‘I have need of such-and-such a thing.’” Therefore, he had all the necessary equipment given. Having placed in each of the five hundred chariots three maidservants of high birth, adorned with all ornaments, he gave them. He also gave fifteen hundred female attendants, saying, “You are to attend to her by bathing, feeding, and adorning her.” Then this thought occurred to him: “I will give my daughter cows.” He commanded his men: “Go, open the gate of the small cattle pen, and taking three large drums, stand at a distance of three gāvutas. Stand on both sides in a space of one usabha in width. Do not let the cows go beyond that. When they are thus positioned, make a signal with the drums.” They did so. When the cows, having come out of the pen, had gone one gāvuta, they made a signal with the drums. Again, when they had gone half a yojana, they made the signal. And again, when they had gone three gāvutas, they made the signal with the drums and also blocked their movement sideways. Thus, in a space three gāvutas in length and one usabha in width, the cows stood pressing against one another.

Mahāseṭṭhi “mama dhītu ettakā gāvo alaṃ, dvāraṃ pidahathā”ti vajadvāraṃ pidahāpesi. Dvārasmiṃ pidahite visākhāya puññabalena balavagāvo ca dhenuyo ca uppatitvā uppatitvā nikkhamiṃsu. Manussānaṃ vārentānaṃ vārentānameva saṭṭhisahassā balavagāvo ca saṭṭhisahassā dhenuyo ca nikkhantā, tattakā balavavacchā tāsaṃ dhenūnaṃ usabhā uppatitvā anubandhā ahesuṃ. “Kissa pana nissandena evaṃ gāvo gatā”ti? Nivārentānaṃ nivārentānaṃ dinnadānassa. Sā kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kikissa rañño sattannaṃ dhītānaṃ kaniṭṭhā saṅghadāsī nāma hutvā vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ pañcagorasadānaṃ [P 1.0397] dadamānā therānañca daharānañca sāmaṇerānañca pattaṃ pidahitvā, “alaṃ, ala”nti nivārentānampi “idaṃ madhuraṃ, idaṃ manāpa”nti adāsi. Evaṃ tassa nissandena vāriyamānāpi gāvo nikkhamiṃsu. Seṭṭhinā ettakassa dhanassa dinnakāle seṭṭhibhariyā āha – “tumhehi mayhaṃ dhītu sabbaṃ saṃvidahitaṃ, veyyāvaccakarā pana dāsadāsiyo na saṃvidahitā, kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Mama dhītari sasinehanissinehānaṃ jānanatthaṃ. Ahañhi tāya saddhiṃ āgacchamānake gīvāya gahetvā na pahiṇāmi, yānaṃ āruyha gamanakāleyeva etāya saddhiṃ gantukāmā gacchantu, mā agantukāmāti vakkhāmī”ti āha.

The great merchant, saying, “This many cows are enough for my daughter; close the gate,” had the gate of the pen closed. When the gate was closed, by the power of Visākhā’s merit, strong bulls and cows leaped out again and again. Even while the men were trying to stop them, sixty thousand strong bulls and sixty thousand cows went out; and an equal number of strong bulls followed them, leaping up behind those cows. By the result of what kamma, then, did the cows go forth in this way? It was the result of a gift given to those who were repeatedly refusing it. It is said that during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One, she had been the one named Saṅghadāsī, the youngest of the seven daughters of King Kiki. While giving the five dairy products to twenty thousand bhikkhus, even when the elder monks, the junior monks, and the novices covered their bowls and refused, saying, “Enough, enough,” she gave it to them, saying, “This is sweet, this is delicious.” Thus, as a result of that kamma, the cows went out even though they were being stopped. When the merchant had given this much wealth, the merchant's wife said: “You have provided everything for my daughter, but you have not provided male and female servants to attend to her. What is the reason?” He replied: “It is for the purpose of knowing those who have affection for my daughter and those who do not. Indeed, I will not seize by the neck and send those who are unwilling to go with her. Only at the time of departure, when she has mounted the vehicle, will I say: ‘Let those who wish to go with her, go. Let those who do not wish to go, not go.’”

Atha “sve mama dhītā gamissatī”ti gabbhe nisinno dhītaraṃ samīpe nisīdāpetvā, “amma, patikule vasantiyā nāma imañca imañca ācāraṃ rakkhituṃ [M 1.0251] vaṭṭatī”ti ovādamadāsi. Ayampi migāraseṭṭhi anantaragabbhe nisinno dhanañcayaseṭṭhino ovādaṃ assosi. Sopi seṭṭhi dhītaraṃ evaṃ ovadi –

Then, thinking, “Tomorrow my daughter will depart,” he sat in his private chamber, and having had his daughter sit nearby, he gave her this advice: “Dear daughter, a woman living in her husband’s family ought to observe this and that conduct.” This Migāra the merchant, sitting in an adjacent chamber, also heard the advice of Dhanañjaya the merchant. That merchant advised his daughter thus:

“Amma, sasurakule vasantiyā nāma antoaggi bahi na nīharitabbo, bahiaggi anto na pavesetabbo, dadantasseva dātabbaṃ, adadantassa na dātabbaṃ, dadantassāpi [P 1.0398] adadantassāpi dātabbaṃ, sukhaṃ nisīditabbaṃ, sukhaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ, sukhaṃ nipajjitabbaṃ, aggi paricaritabbo, antodevatā namassitabbā”ti.

“Dear daughter, while living in your father-in-law's household, the inner fire should not be taken outside; the outer fire should not be brought inside. One should give only to those who give; one should not give to those who do not give. One should give both to those who give and to those who do not give. One should sit comfortably; one should eat comfortably; one should lie down comfortably. The fire should be attended to, and the household deities should be revered.”

Imaṃ [V 1.0223] dasavidhaṃ ovādaṃ datvā punadivase sabbā seniyo sannipātetvā rājasenāya majjhe aṭṭha kuṭumbike pāṭibhoge gahetvā, “sace me gataṭṭhāne dhītu doso uppajjati, tumhehi sodhetabbo”ti vatvā navakoṭiagghanakena mahālatāpasādhanena dhītaraṃ pasādhetvā nhānacuṇṇamūlakaṃ catupaṇṇāsakoṭidhanaṃ datvā yānaṃ āropetvā sāketassa sāmantā attano santakesu anurādhapuramattesu cuddasasu bhattagāmesu bheriṃ carāpesi – “mama dhītarā saddhiṃ gantukāmā gacchantū”ti. Te saddaṃ sutvāva – “amhākaṃ ayyāya gamanakāle kiṃ amhākaṃ idhā”ti cuddasa gāmakā kiñci asesetvā nikkhamiṃsu? Dhanañcayaseṭṭhipi rañño ca migāraseṭṭhino ca sakkāraṃ katvā thokaṃ anugantvā tehi saddhiṃ dhītaraṃ uyyojesi.

Having given this tenfold advice, on the following day he assembled all the armies, and in the midst of the royal army, having taken eight householders as sureties, he said, “If a fault arises in my daughter at the place she has gone, it must be rectified by you.” Then, having adorned his daughter with the Mahālatā ornament worth nine crores, he gave wealth of fifty-four crores as the price for bath powder, had her mount a vehicle, and had a drum beaten in the fourteen sustenance villages—which were his own property in the vicinity of Sāketa and were the size of Anurādhapura—proclaiming, “Let those who wish to go with my daughter, go.” Upon hearing the sound, the people of the fourteen villages departed, leaving not a single person behind, thinking, “When our lady is going, what is there for us here?” The treasurer Dhanañjaya also, having paid respects to the king and to the treasurer Migāra, followed for a short distance and sent his daughter off with them.

Migāraseṭṭhipi sabbapacchato yānake nisīditvā gacchanto balakāyaṃ disvā, “ke nāmete”ti pucchi. “Suṇisāya vo veyyāvaccakarā dāsidāsā”ti. “Ettake ko posessa”ti? “Pothetvā te palāpetha, apalāyante ito daṇḍaṃ karothā”ti. Visākhā pana “apetha, mā vāretha, balameva balassa bhattaṃ dassatī”ti āha. Seṭṭhi evaṃ [P 1.0399] vuttepi, “amma, natthi amhākaṃ etehi attho, ko ete posessatī”ti leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi pothetvā palāpetvā sesake “alaṃ amhākaṃ ettakehī”ti gahetvā pāyāsi. Atha visākhā sāvatthinagaradvāraṃ sampattakāle cintesi – “paṭicchannayānasmiṃ nu kho nisīditvā pavisissāmi, udāhu rathe ṭhatvā”ti. Athassā etadahosi – “paṭicchannayānena me pavisantiyā mahālatāpasādhanassa viseso na paññāyissatī”ti. Sā [M 1.0252] sakalanagarassa attānaṃ dassentī rathe ṭhatvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Sāvatthivāsino visākhāya sampattiṃ disvā, “esā kira visākhā nāma, evarūpā ayaṃ sampatti etissāva anucchavikā”ti āhaṃsu. Iti sā mahāsampattiyā seṭṭhino gehaṃ pāvisi. Gatadivase cassā sakalanagaravāsino “amhākaṃ dhanañcayaseṭṭhi attano nagaraṃ sampattānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ akāsī”ti yathāsatti yathābalaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Visākhā pahitapahitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ tasmiṃyeva nagare aññamaññesu kulesu sabbatthakameva dāpesi. Iti sā “idaṃ mayhaṃ mātu detha, idaṃ mayhaṃ pitu detha, idaṃ mayhaṃ bhātu detha, idaṃ mayhaṃ bhaginiyā dethā”ti tesaṃ tesaṃ vayānurūpaṃ piyavacanaṃ vatvā paṇṇākāraṃ pesentī sakalanagaravāsino ñātake viya akāsi. Athassā rattibhāgasamanantare ājaññavaḷavāya gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Sā dāsīhi daṇḍadīpikā gāhāpetvā tattha gantvā vaḷavaṃ uṇhodakena nhāpetvā telena [P 1.0400] makkhāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi.

The treasurer Migāra also, while going, sitting in a vehicle at the very rear, saw the retinue and asked, “Who are these?” “They are the male and female slaves, the attendants of your daughter-in-law.” “Who will support so many?” he asked. “Beat them and make them flee. For those who do not flee, inflict punishment.” Visākhā, however, said, “Move aside, do not obstruct them. The retinue itself will provide food for the retinue.” Even when this was said, the treasurer said, “My dear, we have no need for them. Who will support them?” and having had them beaten with clods of earth, sticks, and so on, and made them flee, he took the remaining ones, saying, “This many is enough for us,” and departed. Then, when Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she thought: “Should I enter sitting in a covered vehicle, or standing in a chariot?” Then this occurred to her: “If I enter in a covered vehicle, the splendor of the Mahālatā ornament will not be apparent.” So, showing herself to the entire city, she stood in the chariot and entered the city. The inhabitants of Sāvatthī, seeing Visākhā’s fortune, said, “So this, it seems, is the one named Visākhā. Such fortune as this is suitable only for her.” Thus, with great fortune, she entered the treasurer’s house. On the day of her arrival, all the city’s inhabitants, thinking, “Our treasurer Dhanañjaya showed great honor to those who arrived in his city,” sent gifts according to their ability and means. Visākhā had the gifts that were sent distributed right there in that city among the various families. Thus she, sending the gifts with affectionate words suited to their age, saying, “Give this to my mother, give this to my father, give this to my brother, give this to my sister,” made all the city’s inhabitants like her own relatives. Then, soon after night began, a thoroughbred mare gave birth. Having had the female slaves take torches, she went there, had the mare bathed with warm water, had it anointed with oil, and returned to her own dwelling place.

Migāraseṭṭhipi puttassa āvāhamaṅgalaṃ karonto dhuravihāre vasantampi tathāgataṃ amanasikaritvā [V 1.0224] dīgharattaṃ naggasamaṇakesu patiṭṭhitena pemena codiyamāno “mayhaṃ ayyānampi sakkāraṃ karissāmī”ti ekadivasaṃ anekasatesu navabhājanesu nirudakapāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā pañcasate acelake nimantāpetvā antogehaṃ pavesetvā, “āgacchatu me suṇisā, arahante vandatū”ti visākhāya sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Sā “arahanto”ti vacanaṃ sutvā sotāpannā ariyasāvikā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā tesaṃ bhojanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā te oloketvā, “evarūpā hirottappavirahitā arahantā nāma na honti, kasmā maṃ sasuro pakkosāpesī”ti, “dhī, dhī”ti seṭṭhiṃ garahitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gatā. Acelakā taṃ disvā sabbe ekappahāreneva seṭṭhiṃ garahiṃsu – “kiṃ tvaṃ, gahapati, aññaṃ nālattha, samaṇassa gotamassa sāvikaṃ mahākāḷakaṇṇiṃ idha pavesesi, vegena naṃ imasmā gehā nikkaḍḍhāpehī”ti. So “na sakkā mayā imesaṃ vacanamatteneva nikkaḍḍhāpetuṃ, mahākulassa sā dhītā”ti cintetvā, “ayyā, daharā nāma jānitvā vā ajānitvā vā kareyyuṃ, tumhe tuṇhī hothā”ti te uyyojetvā [M 1.0253] sayaṃ mahārahe āsane nisīditvā suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ nirudakaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ paribhuñji.

The treasurer Migāra, while performing the marriage ceremony for his son, did not pay attention to the Tathāgata, even though he was dwelling in the principal monastery. Urged by an affection for the naked ascetics that was long-established, he thought, “I will pay respect to my masters as well.” One day, he had milk-rice without water cooked in many hundreds of new vessels, invited five hundred naked ascetics, and had them enter his house. He then sent a message to Visākhā: “Let my daughter-in-law come and pay homage to the Arahants.” She, a stream-enterer and noble female disciple, hearing the word “Arahants,” became joyful and delighted. She came to their dining place and, looking at them, thought, “Such ones, devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing, are not called Arahants. Why did my father-in-law have me summoned?” Reproaching the treasurer, saying, “Shame, shame!” she returned to her own dwelling place. The naked ascetics, seeing her, all at once reproached the treasurer: “Why, householder, did you not get another? You have brought the female disciple of the ascetic Gotama, a great bringer of misfortune, in here. Quickly have her driven out from this house!” He, thinking, “It is not possible for me to have her driven out merely on their word; she is the daughter of a great family,” dismissed them, saying, “Sirs, the young may act knowingly or unknowingly. You be silent.” Then he himself, sitting on a costly seat, ate the honey-sweetened milk-rice without water from a golden bowl.

Tasmiṃ samaye eko piṇḍapātikatthero piṇḍāya [P 1.0401] caranto taṃ nivesanaṃ pāvisi. Visākhā sasuraṃ bījayamānā ṭhitā taṃ disvā “sasurassa ācikkhituṃ ayutta”nti yathā so theraṃ passati, evaṃ apagantvā aṭṭhāsi. So pana bālo theraṃ disvāpi apassanto viya hutvā adhomukho bhuñjateva. Visākhā “theraṃ disvāpi me sasuro saññaṃ na karotī”ti ñatvā, “aticchatha, bhante, mayhaṃ sasuro purāṇaṃ khādatī”ti āha. So nigaṇṭhehi kathitakāle adhivāsetvāpi “purāṇaṃ khādatī”ti vuttakkhaṇeyeva hatthaṃ apanetvā, “imaṃ pāyāsaṃ ito nīharatha, etaṃ imasmā gehā nikkaḍḍhatha, ayaṃ maṃ evarūpe maṅgalakāle asucikhādakaṃ nāma karotī”ti āha. Tasmiṃ kho pana nivesane sabbepi dāsakammakarā visākhāya santakāva, ko naṃ hatthe vā pāde vā gaṇhissati, mukhena kathetuṃ samatthopi natthi. Visākhā sasurassa kathaṃ sutvā āha – “tāta, na ettakeneva mayaṃ nikkhamāma, nāhaṃ tumhehi udakatitthato kumbhadāsī viya ānītā, dharamānakamātāpitūnaṃ dhītaro nāma na ettakeneva nikkhamanti, eteneva me kāraṇena pitā idhāgamanakāle aṭṭha kuṭumbike pakkosāpetvā ‘sace me dhītu doso uppajjati, sodheyyāthā’ti vatvā maṃ tesaṃ hatthe ṭhapesi, te pakkosāpetvā mayhaṃ dosādosaṃ sodhāpethā”ti.

At that time, a certain elder who observed the practice of going for alms-food entered that residence while wandering for alms. Visākhā, who was standing fanning her father-in-law, saw him and, thinking, 'It is not proper to inform my father-in-law,' she stepped aside in such a way that her father-in-law would see the elder. But that foolish man, even though he saw the elder, acted as if he did not see him and continued eating with his head down. Visākhā, realizing, 'Even after seeing the elder, my father-in-law takes no notice,' said, 'Please pass by, venerable sir. My father-in-law is eating what is old.' Though he had tolerated it when the Nigaṇṭhas spoke, at the very moment he heard 'eating what is old,' he withdrew his hand and said, 'Take this milk-rice away from here! Drive this woman out of this house! On such an auspicious occasion, she calls me an eater of filth!' Now, in that residence, all the servants and workers belonged to Visākhā. Who would seize her by the hand or by the foot? There was no one who was even capable of speaking against her. Hearing her father-in-law's words, Visākhā said, 'Father, I will not leave for such a trifle. I was not brought by you from the water-ford like a slave girl with a water pot. Daughters of prominent parents do not leave for such a small matter. For this very reason, when my father came here, he had eight householders summoned and, saying, "If any fault should arise in my daughter, you are to investigate it," he placed me in their hands. Have them summoned and let them investigate my fault or lack of fault.'

Seṭṭhi “kalyāṇaṃ esā kathetī”ti aṭṭha kuṭumbike pakkosāpetvā, “ayaṃ dārikā maṅgalakāle nisīditvā suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ nirudakapāyāsaṃ paribhuñjantaṃ maṃ ‘asucikhādako’ti vadatī”ti [V 1.0225][P 1.0402] āha, “imissā dosaṃ āropetvā imaṃ gehato nikkaḍḍhathā”ti. “Evaṃ kira, ammā”ti. Nāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi, ekasmiṃ pana piṇḍapātikatthere gharadvāre ṭhite sasuro me appodakaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ paribhuñjanto taṃ na manasikaroti, ahaṃ “mayhaṃ sasuro imasmiṃ attabhāve puññaṃ na karoti, purāṇapuññameva khādatī”ti cintetvā, “aticchatha, bhante, mayhaṃ sasuro purāṇaṃ khādatī”ti avacaṃ, “ettha me ko doso”ti? “Ayya, idha doso natthi, amhākaṃ dhītā yuttaṃ katheti, tvaṃ kasmā kujjhasī”ti? “Ayyā, esa tāva doso [M 1.0254] mā hotu, ayaṃ pana ekadivasaṃ majjhimayāme dāsīparivutā pacchāgehaṃ agamāsī”ti. “Evaṃ kira, ammā”ti. “Tātā, nāhaṃ aññena kāraṇena gatā, imasmiṃ pana gehe ājāneyyavaḷavāya vijātāya saññampi akatvā nisīdituṃ nāma ayutta”nti daṇḍadīpikā gāhāpetvā uṇhodakādīnipi gāhāpetvā dāsīhi saddhiṃ gantvā vaḷavāya vijātaparihāraṃ kārāpesiṃ, “ettha me ko doso”ti? “Ayya, idha doso natthi, amhākaṃ dhītā tava gehe dāsīhipi akattabbayuttakaṃ kammaṃ karoti, tvaṃ kiṃ ettha dosaṃ passasī”ti?

The merchant, having summoned the eight householders, said: “This Visākhā speaks a fine word! This girl calls me, who am partaking of thick milk-rice from a golden bowl during an auspicious meal, an ‘eater of filth.’ Having accused her of this fault, drive her from the house.” They asked, “Is this so, dear lady?” “I did not speak in that way. But when a certain elder who lives on alms-food was standing at the house door, my father-in-law, while partaking of honeyed milk-rice with little water, did not pay him any mind. I, thinking, ‘My father-in-law is not making merit in this present existence; he is only eating his old merit,’ then said, ‘Please pass by, venerable sir, my father-in-law is eating what is old.’ What fault of mine is there in this?” “Sir, there is no fault in this. Our daughter speaks what is proper. Why are you angry?” “Sirs, let that not be a fault for now. But this one, on a certain day, in the middle watch of the night, surrounded by her female slaves, went to the back of the house.” They asked, “Is this so, dear lady?” “Fathers, I did not go for any other reason. But in this house, a thoroughbred mare was giving birth, and it is indeed improper to sit without taking any notice. So, having had torches and hot water and so on brought, I went with the female slaves and had the care for the birthing mare performed. What fault of mine is there in this?” “Sir, there is no fault in this. Our daughter performs work in your house that ought not even be done by female slaves. What fault do you see in this?”

Ayyā, idhāpi tāva doso mā hotu, imissā pana pitā idhāgamanakāle imaṃ ovadanto guyhe paṭicchanne dasa ovāde adāsi, tesaṃ atthaṃ na jānāmi, tesaṃ me atthaṃ kathetu. Imissā pana [P 1.0403] pitā “antoaggi bahi na nīharitabbo”ti āha, “sakkā nu kho amhehi ubhato paṭivissakagehānaṃ aggiṃ adatvā vasitu”nti? “Evaṃ kira, ammā”ti. “Tātā, mayhaṃ pitā na etaṃ sandhāya kathesi. Idaṃ pana sandhāya kathesi – ‘amma, tava sassusasurasāmikānaṃ aguṇaṃ disvā bahi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ gehe ṭhatvā mā kathesi. Evarūpo hi aggisadiso aggi nāma natthī’”ti.

“Sirs, here too let there not be a fault for now. However, this one's father, at the time of her coming here, while admonishing her, gave ten secret and concealed instructions. I do not know their meaning; let her tell me their meaning. This one's father said, ‘The inside fire is not to be carried outside.’ Is it really possible for us to live without giving fire to the neighboring houses on both sides?” They asked, “Is this so, dear lady?” “Fathers, my father did not speak with reference to that. Rather, he spoke with reference to this: ‘My dear, having seen a fault in your mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband, do not speak of it while standing outside in this or that house. For there is truly no fire like that kind of fire.’”

Ayyā, etaṃ tāva evaṃ hotu, imissā pana pitā “bāhirato aggi na anto pavesetabbo”ti āha, “kiṃ sakkā amhehi anto aggimhi nibbute bāhirato aggiṃ anāharitu”nti? “Evaṃ kira, ammā”ti. Tātā, mayhaṃ pitā na etaṃ sandhāya kathesi, idaṃ pana sandhāya kathesi – sace paṭivissakagehesu itthiyo vā purisā vā sassusasurasāmikānaṃ aguṇaṃ kathenti, tehi kathitaṃ āharitvā “asuko nāma tumhākaṃ evañca evañca aguṇaṃ kathetī”ti puna mā katheyyāsi. “Etena hi agginā sadiso aggi nāma natthī”ti. Evaṃ imasmimpi kāraṇe sā niddosāva ahosi. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ sesesupi.

“Sirs, let that be so for now. But this one's father said, ‘Fire from outside is not to be brought inside.’ Is it possible for us not to bring in fire from outside when the fire inside has been extinguished?” They asked, “Is this so, dear lady?” “Fathers, my father did not speak with reference to that. Rather, he spoke with reference to this: ‘If in the neighboring houses women or men speak of the faults of their mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband, do not bring what was said by them and repeat it, saying, “So-and-so says such-and-such a fault about you.” For there is truly no fire like this fire.’ Thus, in this matter too, she was blameless. And as in these matters, so too was she in the remaining ones.

Tesu pana ayamadhippāyo – yampi hi tassā pitarā “ye dadanti, tesaṃyeva dātabba”nti [V 1.0226] vuttaṃ. Taṃ “yācitakaṃ upakaraṇaṃ gahetvā ye paṭidenti, tesaññeva dātabba”nti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Now, this is the meaning of those instructions: That which was said by her father, ‘One should give only to those who give back,’ was said with reference to this: ‘One should give only to those who, having taken a borrowed utensil, return it.’”

“Ye na denti, tesaṃ na dātabba”nti idampi ye yācitakaṃ gahetvā na paṭidenti, tesaṃ na dātabbanti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

This too, ‘To those who do not give back, one should not give,’ was said with reference to this: ‘To those who, having taken something borrowed, do not return it, one should not give.’”

“Dadantassāpi [M 1.0255] adadantassāpi dātabba”nti idaṃ pana daliddesu ñātimittesu [P 1.0404] sampattesu te paṭidātuṃ sakkontu vā mā vā, tesaṃ dātumeva vaṭṭatīti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“‘One should give both to one who returns and to one who does not return.’ This, however, was said with reference to poor relatives and friends who have come: whether they are able to give back or not, it is proper to give to them.”

“Sukhaṃ nisīditabba”nti idampi sassusasurasāmike disvā vuṭṭhātabbaṭṭhāne nisīdituṃ na vaṭṭatīti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“‘One should sit comfortably.’ This too was said with reference to this: ‘It is not proper to sit in a place where one ought to stand up upon seeing one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband.’”

“Sukhaṃ bhuñjitabba”nti idaṃ pana sassusasurasāmikehi puretaraṃ abhuñjitvā te parivisitvā sabbehi laddhāladdhaṃ ñatvā pacchā sayaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“‘One should eat happily.’ This, however, was said with reference to this: it is proper for her to eat herself only after having served her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband, not eating before them, and after having ascertained what is available and what is not among all the provisions.”

“Sukhaṃ nipajjitabba”nti idampi sassusasurasāmikehi puretaraṃ sayanaṃ āruyha na nipajjitabbaṃ, tesaṃ kattabbayuttakaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā pacchā sayaṃ nipajjituṃ yuttanti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“‘One should lie down comfortably.’ This too was said with reference to this: one should not ascend the bed and lie down before one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband. It is fitting for her to lie down herself only after having performed for them the duties and services that ought to be done.”

“Aggi paricaritabbo”ti idaṃ pana sassumpi sasurampi sāmikampi aggikkhandhaṃ viya uragarājānaṃ viya ca katvā passituṃ vaṭṭatīti sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“‘The fire is to be attended to.’ This, however, was said with reference to this: it is proper to regard one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as one would a great mass of fire or a Nāga king.”

“Antodevatā namassitabbā”ti idampi sassuñca sasurañca sāmikañca devatā viya katvā daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatīti sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evaṃ seṭṭhi imesaṃ dasaovādānaṃ atthaṃ sutvā paṭivacanaṃ apassanto adhomukho nisīdi.

“‘The household deities are to be revered.’ This was said with reference to this: it is proper to regard one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as deities. Thus, the merchant, having heard the meaning of these ten admonitions and seeing no reply to make, sat with his face cast down.

Atha naṃ kuṭumbikā “kiṃ seṭṭhi aññopi amhākaṃ dhītu doso atthī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Natthi, ayyā”ti. “Atha kasmā naṃ niddosaṃ akāraṇena gehā nikkaḍḍhāpesī”ti evaṃ vutte visākhā āha – “tātā, kiñcāpi mayhaṃ sasurassa vacanena paṭhamameva gamanaṃ na yuttaṃ, pitā pana me āgamanakāle mama dosasodhanatthāya maṃ tumhākaṃ hatthe ṭhapesi, tumhehi ca me niddosabhāvo [V 1.0227] ñāto, idāni ca mayhaṃ gantuṃ yutta”nti dāsidāse “yānādīhi sajjāpethā”ti āṇāpesi. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi kuṭumbike gahetvā “amma, mayā [P 1.0405] ajānitvāva kathitaṃ, khamāhi me”ti āha. “Tāta, tumhākaṃ khamitabbaṃ tāva khamāmi, ahaṃ pana buddhasāsane aveccappasannassa kulassa dhītā, na mayaṃ vinā bhikkhusaṅghena vattāma, sace mama ruciyā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṭijaggituṃ labhāmi, vasissāmī”ti. “Amma, tvaṃ yathāruciyā tava samaṇe paṭijaggā”ti āha.

Then the householders asked him, “Merchant, is there any other fault in our daughter?” “There is none, sirs.” “Then why did you have her, who is faultless, driven from the house for no reason?” When this was said, Visākhā spoke: “Fathers, although it was not proper for me to depart at the very first word of my father-in-law, my father, at the time of my arrival, placed me in your hands for the purpose of clearing my faults. My state of faultlessness has been known by you, and now it is proper for me to go.” She then commanded her male and female servants, “Prepare the vehicles and so forth.” Then the merchant, taking the householders with him, said to her, “Mother, I spoke without knowing. Forgive me.” “Father, as for what is to be forgiven on your part, I do forgive it. However, I am the daughter of a family with unwavering faith in the Buddha's Dispensation. We cannot live without the community of monks. If I may be allowed to attend upon the community of monks according to my own liking, I will stay.” “Mother,” he said, “attend upon your ascetics as you wish.”

Visākhā [M 1.0256] dasabalaṃ nimantāpetvā punadivase nivesanaṃ pavesesi. Naggasamaṇāpi satthu migāraseṭṭhino gehaṃ gamanabhāvaṃ sutvā gantvā gehaṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Visākhā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā “sabbo sakkāro paṭiyādito, sasuro me āgantvā dasabalaṃ parivisatū”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. Atha naṃ gantukāmaṃ ājīvakā “mā kho tvaṃ, gahapati, samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gacchā”ti nivāresuṃ. So “suṇhā me sayameva parivisatū”ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Sā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā niṭṭhite bhattakicce puna sāsanaṃ pesesi – “sasuro me āgantvā dhammakathaṃ suṇātū”ti. Atha naṃ “idāni agamanaṃ nāma ativiya ayutta”nti dhammaṃ sotukāmatāya gacchantaṃ puna te āhaṃsu – “tena hi samaṇassa gotamassa dhammaṃ suṇanto bahisāṇiyā nisīditvā suṇāhī”ti. Puretaramevassa gantvā sāṇiṃ parikkhipiṃsu. So gantvā bahisāṇiyaṃ nisīdi. Satthā “tvaṃ bahisāṇiyaṃ vā nisīda, parakuṭṭe vā parasele vā paracakkavāḷe vā pana nisīda, ahaṃ buddho nāma sakkomi taṃ mama saddaṃ sāvetu”nti [P 1.0406] mahājambuṃ khandhe gahetvā cālento viya amatavassaṃ vassento viya ca dhammaṃ desetuṃ anupubbiṃ kathaṃ ārabhi.

Visākhā had the One with Ten Powers invited, and on the following day, had him enter the residence. The naked ascetics, hearing that the Teacher was going to the house of the merchant Migāra, also went, surrounded the house, and sat down. Visākhā, having given the water of dedication, sent a message, saying: “All the honorific offerings have been prepared. Let my father-in-law come and serve the One with Ten Powers.” Then, when he was desirous of going, the Ājīvakas prevented him, saying, “Householder, do not go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” So he sent a message: “Let my daughter-in-law serve by herself.” After she had served the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, and when the meal was finished, she sent another message: “Let my father-in-law come and listen to the Dhamma discourse.” Then, thinking, “Not to go now would be extremely improper,” he was proceeding with the desire to hear the Dhamma when those ascetics again spoke to him: “In that case, while listening to the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama, sit outside the curtain and listen.” Even before he arrived, they had gone and enclosed the area with a curtain. He went and sat outside the curtain. The Teacher proclaimed: “Whether you sit outside the curtain, or beyond a wall, or beyond a mountain, or beyond a world-system, I, who am the Buddha, am able to make you hear my voice.” Then, as if grasping the trunk of a great Jambu tree and shaking it, or as if raining down a shower of the deathless, he began the graduated discourse.

Sammāsambuddhe ca pana dhammaṃ desente purato ṭhitāpi pacchato ṭhitāpi cakkavāḷasataṃ cakkavāḷasahassaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāpi akaniṭṭhabhavane ṭhitāpi “satthā mamaññeva oloketi, mayhameva dhammaṃ desetī”ti vadanti. Satthā hi taṃ taṃ olokento viya tena tena saddhiṃ sallapanto viya ca ahosi. Candasamā kira buddhā. Yathā cando gaganamajjhe ṭhito “mayhaṃ upari cando, mayhaṃ upari cando”ti sabbasattānaṃ khāyati, evameva yattha katthaci ṭhitānaṃ abhimukhe ṭhitā viya khāyanti. Idaṃ kira tesaṃ alaṅkatasīsaṃ chinditvā añjitaakkhīni uppāṭetvā hadayamaṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā parassa dāsatthāya jālisadise putte kaṇhājināsadisā dhītaro maddisadisā pajāpatiyo pariccajitvā dinnadānassa phalaṃ. Migāraseṭṭhipi kho tathāgate dhammadesanaṃ vinivattente bahisāṇiyaṃ nisinnova sahassa nayapaṭimaṇḍite [V 1.0228] sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya acalāya saddhāya samannāgato tīsu ratanesu nikkaṅkho hutvā sāṇikaṇṇaṃ ukkhipitvā āgantvā suṇhāya thanaṃ mukhena gahetvā, “tvaṃ me ajjato paṭṭhāya mātā”ti [M 1.0257] taṃ mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tato paṭṭhāya migāramātā nāma jātā. Pacchābhāge [P 1.0407] puttaṃ labhitvāpi migārotissa nāmamakāsi.

Indeed, when a Perfectly Enlightened One is teaching the Dhamma, those standing in front, those standing behind, those standing beyond a hundred or a thousand world-systems, and even those in the Akaniṭṭha celestial realm declare, “The Teacher is looking only at me; he is teaching the Dhamma only for me.” For the Teacher would appear as if looking at each and every one, as if conversing with each and every one. Buddhas, it is said, are like the moon. Just as the moon, situated in the middle of the sky, appears to all beings as if it were directly above them, so too do the Buddhas appear as if standing face-to-face with beings wherever they may be. This, it is said, is the fruit of gifts given after having cut off one's own adorned head, plucked out one's kohl-lined eyes, torn out the flesh of one's heart, and renounced sons like Jāli, daughters like Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Maddī for the sake of servitude to another. As the Tathāgata was concluding his Dhamma discourse, the merchant Migāra, while still seated outside the curtain, became established in the fruit of stream-entry, which is adorned with a thousand methods. Endowed with unshakable faith and having become free from doubt regarding the Three Jewels, he lifted the corner of the curtain, came forward, took his daughter-in-law’s breast in his mouth, and declared, “From this day forward, you are my mother.” Thus he established her in the position of his mother. From that time on, she came to be known as Migāramātā. Later, upon gaining a son, she gave him the name Migāra.

Mahāseṭṭhi suṇhāya thanaṃ vissajjetvā gantvā bhagavato dvīsu pādesu sirasā nipatitvā pāde pāṇīhi ca parisambāhanto mukhena ca paricumbanto “migāro ahaṃ, bhante, migāro ahaṃ, bhante”ti tikkhattuṃ nāmaṃ sāvetvā, “ahaṃ, bhante, ettakaṃ kālaṃ yattha nāma dvinnaṃ mahapphalanti na jānāmi, idāni ca me suṇisaṃ nissāya ñātaṃ, sabbā apāyadukkhā muttomhi, suṇisā me imaṃ gehaṃ āgacchantī mama atthāya hitāya sukhāya āgatā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The great merchant, having released his daughter-in-law's breast, went and fell at the Blessed One's two feet with his head. Then, stroking the feet with his hands and kissing them with his mouth, he announced his name three times, saying, 'Venerable sir, I am Migāra. Venerable sir, I am Migāra.' He then said, 'Venerable sir, for all this time I did not know where giving bears great fruit. Now, on account of my daughter-in-law, it is known to me. I am freed from all the suffering of the planes of misery. My daughter-in-law, in coming to this house, has come for my benefit, welfare, and happiness.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

“Sohaṃ ajja pajānāmi, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ;

Atthāya vata me bhaddā, suṇisā gharamāgatā”ti.

“Today I understand where giving is of great fruit. Indeed, for my welfare has my virtuous daughter-in-law come to my home.”

Visākhā punadivasatthāyapi satthāraṃ nimantesi. Athassā punadivasepi sassu sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ gehaṃ sāsanassa vivaṭadvāraṃ ahosi. Tato seṭṭhi cintesi – “bahūpakārā me suṇisā pasannākāramassā karissāmi, etissā bhāriyaṃ pasādhanaṃ niccakālaṃ pasādhetuṃ na sakkā, sallahukamassā divā ca ratto ca sabbairiyāpathesu pasādhanayoggaṃ pasādhanaṃ kāressāmī”ti satasahassagghanakaṃ ghanamaṭṭhakaṃ nāma pasādhanaṃ kāretvā tasmiṃ niṭṭhite buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā sakkaccaṃ bhojetvā visākhaṃ soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhāpetvā satthu sammukhe ṭhapetvā pasādhetvā satthāraṃ vandāpesi. Satthā anumodanaṃ [P 1.0408] katvā vihārameva gato. Visākhāpi tato paṭṭhāya dānādīni puññāni karontī satthu santikā aṭṭha vare (mahāva. 350) labhitvā gaganatale candalekhā viya paññāyamānā puttadhītāhi vuḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇi. Tassā kira dasa puttā dasa dhītaro ca ahesuṃ. Tesu ekekassa dasa dasa puttā dasa dasa dhītaro ahesuṃ. Tesu tesupi ekekassa dasa dasa puttā dasa dasa dhītaro cāti evamassā puttanattapanattasantānavasena pavattāni vīsādhikāni cattāri satāni aṭṭha ca pāṇasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Visākhā invited the Teacher again for the next day. On the following day, her mother-in-law also attained the fruit of stream-entry. From that time onwards, that house became one with its doors open to the Dispensation. Then the merchant thought: 'My daughter-in-law has been of great help to me; I shall make a gesture of my appreciation to her. It is not possible for her to wear this heavy ornament at all times. I shall have a light ornament made for her, suitable for wearing day and night, in all postures.' He had an ornament called Ghanamaṭṭhaka made, worth one hundred thousand. When it was finished, he invited the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, fed them respectfully, had Visākhā bathed with sixteen pots of scented water, had her adorned in the Teacher's presence, and had her pay homage to the Teacher. The Teacher, after giving a discourse of appreciation, went back to the monastery. Visākhā, too, from that time onwards, performing meritorious deeds such as giving, received eight boons from the Teacher. Becoming renowned like the crescent moon in the sky, she prospered with sons and daughters. It is said she had ten sons and ten daughters. Among them, each one had ten sons and ten daughters. And among those grandchildren as well, each one had ten sons and ten daughters. Thus, through the lineage of her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, there came to be four hundred and twenty children and grandchildren, and eight thousand great-grandchildren. Therefore the ancients said:

“Visākhā [V 1.0229][M 1.0258] vīsati puttā, nattā ca caturo satā;

Panattā aṭṭhasahassā, jambudīpe supākaṭā”ti.

“Visākhā had twenty children, four hundred grandchildren, and eight thousand great-grandchildren; she was very famous in Jambudīpa.”

Āyu vīsavassasataṃ ahosi, sīse ekampi palitaṃ nāma nāhosi, niccaṃ soḷasavassuddesikā viya ahosi. Taṃ puttanattapanattaparivāraṃ vihāraṃ gacchantiṃ disvā, “katamā ettha visākhā”ti paripucchitāro honti? Ye naṃ gacchantiṃ passanti, “idāni thokaṃ gacchatu, gacchamānāva no, ayyā sobhatī”ti, cintenti. Ye naṃ ṭhitaṃ nisinnaṃ nipannaṃ passanti, “idāni thokaṃ nipajjatu, nipannāva no, ayyā, sobhatī”ti cintenti. Iti sā “catūsu iriyāpathesu asukairiyāpathena nāma na sobhatī”ti vattabbā na hoti. Pañcannaṃ kho pana hatthīnaṃ [P 1.0409] balaṃ dhāreti. Rājā “visākhā kira pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāretī”ti sutvā tassā vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā āgamanavelāya thāmaṃ vīmaṃsitukāmo hatthiṃ vissajjāpesi, so soṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā visākhābhimukho agamāsi. Tassā parivāritthiyo pañcasatā ekaccā palāyiṃsu, ekaccā na parissajjitvā “kiṃ ida”nti vutte – “rājā kira te, ayye, balaṃ vīmaṃsitukāmo hatthiṃ vissajjāpesī”ti vadiṃsu. Visākhā imaṃ disvā, “kiṃ palāyitena, kathaṃ nu kho taṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā, “sace taṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhissāmi, vinasseyyā”ti dvīhi aṅgulīhi soṇḍāya gahetvā paṭipaṇāmesi. Hatthī attānaṃ sandhāretvā ṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, rājaṅgaṇe ukkuṭiko hutvā patito. Mahājano sādhukāraṃ adāsi. Sāpi saparivārā sotthinā gehaṃ agamāsi.

Her lifespan was one hundred and twenty years, and not a single grey hair appeared on her head; she always looked like a sixteen-year-old girl. When people saw her going to the monastery surrounded by her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, they would ask, 'Which one among these is Visākhā?' Those who saw her walking would think, 'Let her walk a little; our lady is beautiful even as she is walking.' Those who saw her standing, sitting, or lying down would think, 'Let her lie down a little; our lady is beautiful even as she is lying down.' Thus, it could not be said of her, 'She is not beautiful in such-and-such a posture,' among the four postures. Indeed, she possessed the strength of five elephants. The king, having heard, 'It is said that Visākhā possesses the strength of five elephants,' went to the monastery, listened to the Dhamma, and on the way back, wishing to test her strength, had an elephant released. The elephant, raising its trunk, advanced towards Visākhā. Of her five hundred attendant women, some fled. Some, having surrounded her to protect her, asked, 'What is this?' When it was said, 'Lady, it seems the king, wishing to test your strength, has had an elephant released,' Visākhā, seeing it, thought, 'What is the use of fleeing? How shall I seize it?' Reflecting, 'If I seize it too firmly, it will perish,' she took hold of its trunk with two fingers and pushed it back. The elephant was unable to steady itself and stand; it fell into a squatting position in the royal courtyard. The great crowd gave a shout of approval. She too, with her retinue, returned home safely.

Tena kho pana samayena sāvatthiyaṃ visākhā migāramātā bahuputtā hoti bahunattā arogaputtā aroganattā abhimaṅgalasammatā, tāvatakesu puttanattesu ekopi antarā maraṇaṃ patto nāma nāhosi. Sāvatthivāsino maṅgalesu chaṇesu visākhaṃ paṭhamaṃ nimantetvā bhojenti. Athekasmiṃ ussavadivase mahājane maṇḍitapasādhite dhammassavanāya vihāraṃ gacchante visākhāpi [P 1.0410] nimantitaṭṭhāne bhuñjitvā mahālatāpasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā mahājanena saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅgena bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā dāsiyā adāsi. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Now at that time in Sāvatthī, Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, had many children and many grandchildren; her children were healthy and her grandchildren were healthy, and she was considered highly auspicious. Among so many children and grandchildren, not even one had died in the interim. The people of Sāvatthī would invite Visākhā first to auspicious festivals and feed her. Then, on one festival day, when the great crowd, adorned and decorated, was going to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma, Visākhā too, having eaten at the place where she was invited, adorned herself with the Mahālatā ornament and went with the great crowd to the monastery. She took off her ornaments, tied them into a bundle with her upper robe, and gave it to her female attendant. It is in reference to this that it was said:

“Tena [M 1.0259] kho pana samayena sāvatthiyaṃ ussavo hoti, manussā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā ārāmaṃ gacchanti, visākhāpi migāramātā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā vihāraṃ gacchati. Atha kho [V 1.0230] visākhā migāramātā ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅgena bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā dāsiyā adāsi ‘handa je imaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ gaṇhāhī’”ti (pāci. 503).

“Now at that time, there was a festival in Sāvatthī. The people, adorned and arrayed, went to the monastery. Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, also adorned and arrayed, went to the monastery. Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, took off her ornaments, tied them into a bundle with her upper robe, and gave it to her female servant, saying, ‘Here now, girl, take this bundle.’”

Sā kira vihāraṃ gacchantī cintesi – “evarūpaṃ mahagghaṃ pasādhanaṃ sīse paṭimukkaṃ yāva pādapiṭṭhiṃ alaṅkāraṃ alaṅkaritvā vihāraṃ pavisituṃ ayutta”nti naṃ omuñcitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā attano puññeneva nibbattāya pañcahatthithāmadharāya dāsiyā hatthe adāsi. Sā eva kira taṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkoti. Tena naṃ āha – “amma, imaṃ pasādhanaṃ gaṇha, satthusantikā nivattanakāle pasādhessāmi na”nti. Taṃ pana datvā ghanamaṭṭhakaṃ pasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ assosi, dhammassavanāvasāne bhagavantaṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāya pakkāmi. Sāpissā dāsī taṃ pasādhanaṃ pamuṭṭhā. Dhammaṃ sutvā pana pakkantāya parisāya sace kiñci pamuṭṭhaṃ hoti, taṃ ānandatthero paṭisāmeti. Iti so taṃ divasaṃ mahālatāpasādhanaṃ disvā satthu ārocesi – “bhante, visākhā pasādhanaṃ pamussitvā gatā”ti. “Ekamantaṃ ṭhapehi, ānandā”ti. Thero taṃ ukkhipitvā sopānapasse laggetvā [P 1.0411] ṭhapesi.

It is said that while going to the monastery, she thought: 'It is not proper to enter the monastery wearing such a valuable ornament, adorning myself with it from head to the top of the foot.' So she removed it, made it into a bundle, and gave it into the hand of her maidservant, who possessed the strength of five elephants and was born of Visākhā's own merit. It is said that only she was able to carry it. Therefore, she said to her: 'Dear, take this ornament; I will adorn myself with it when returning from the Teacher’s presence.' Having given it to her, she adorned herself with the ghanamaṭṭhaka ornament, approached the Teacher, and listened to the Dhamma. At the end of the Dhamma discourse, she paid homage to the Blessed One, rose, and departed. But that maidservant of hers forgot the ornament. Now, after the assembly had listened to the Dhamma and departed, if anything was left behind, it was the Venerable Ānanda who would put it away. Thus, on that day, seeing the Mahālatā ornament, he informed the Teacher: 'Venerable Sir, Visākhā has forgotten her ornament and left.' 'Place it in a suitable spot, Ānanda.' The Elder then picked it up and hung it by the side of the stairs.

Visākhāpi suppiyāya saddhiṃ “āgantukagamikagilānādīnaṃ kattabbayuttakaṃ jānissāmī”ti antovihāre vicari. Tā pana upāsikāyo antovihāre disvā sappimadhutelādīhi atthikā pakatiyāva daharā ca sāmaṇerā ca thālakādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamanti. Tasmimpi divase tatheva kariṃsu. Athekaṃ gilānaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā suppiyā (mahāva. 280) “kenattho ayyassā”ti pucchitvā “paṭicchādanīyenā”ti vutte hotu, ayya, pesessāmīti dutiyadivase kappiyamaṃsaṃ alabhantī attano ūrumaṃsena kattabbakiccaṃ katvā puna satthari pasādena pākatikasarīrāva ahosi. Visākhāpi gilāne ca dahare ca sāmaṇere ca oloketvā aññena dvārena nikkhamitvā vihārūpacāre ṭhitā, “amma, pasādhanaṃ āhara pasādhessāmī”ti āha. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sā dāsī pamussitvā nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “ayye, pamuṭṭhāmhī”ti āha. “Tena hi gantvā gaṇhitvā ehi, sace pana [M 1.0260] mayhaṃ ayyena ānandattherena ukkhipitvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapitaṃ hoti, mā āhareyyāsi, ayyasseva taṃ mayā pariccatta”nti. Jānāti kira sā “kulamanussānaṃ pamuṭṭhabhaṇḍakaṃ thero paṭisāmetī”ti; tasmā evamāha. Theropi taṃ dāsiṃ disvāva “kimatthaṃ āgatāsī”ti pucchitvā, “ayyāya me pasādhanaṃ pamussitvā āgatāmhī”ti vutte, “etasmiṃ me sopānapasse ṭhapitaṃ, gaccha naṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. Sā, “ayya, tumhākaṃ hatthena āmaṭṭhabhaṇḍakaṃ mayhaṃ ayyāya [P 1.0412] anāhāriyaṃ kata”nti vatvā tucchahatthāva gantvā, “kiṃ, ammā”ti visākhāya puṭṭhā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. “Amma[V 1.0231], nāhaṃ mama ayyena āmaṭṭhabhaṇḍaṃ pilandhissāmi, pariccattaṃ mayā. Ayyānaṃ pana paṭijaggituṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ vissajjetvā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ upanessāmi, gaccha, taṃ āharāhī”ti. Sā gantvā āhari. Visākhā taṃ apilandhitvāva kammāre pakkosāpetvā agghāpesi.
