Tehi “nava koṭiyo agghati, hatthakārāpaṇiyaṃ panassa satasahassa”nti vutte pasādhanaṃ yāne ṭhapāpetvā “tena hi taṃ vikkiṇathā”ti āha. Bhattakaṃ dhanaṃ datvā gaṇhiṃtu na koci sakkhissati. Tañhi pasādhanaṃ pasādhetuṃ anucchavikā itthiyo nāma dullabhā. Pathavimaṇḍalasmiñhi tissova itthiyo mahālatāpasādhanaṃ labhiṃsu visākhā mahāupāsikā, bandhulamallasenāpatissa bhariyā, mallikā, bārāṇasīseṭṭhino dhītāti.

Visākhā, together with Suppiyā, went about inside the monastery, thinking: 'I will find out what ought to be done for visitors, travelers, the sick, and others.' Seeing those laywomen inside the monastery, the young monks and novices, who were naturally in need of ghee, honey, oil, and so forth, approached them carrying bowls and other such things. On that day, too, they did just so. Then, seeing a certain sick monk, Suppiyā asked, 'What does the venerable one need?' When he replied, 'Meat broth,' she said, 'So be it, Venerable Sir, I will send it.' The next day, being unable to obtain allowable meat, she performed the necessary task with flesh from her own thigh, and through her faith in the Teacher, her body became whole as before. Visākhā too, having attended to the sick, the young monks, and the novices, exited through another gate and stood in the monastery precincts. 'Dear,' she said, 'bring the ornament; I will put it on.' At that moment, the maidservant, realizing she had forgotten it and left, said, 'My lady, I have forgotten it.' 'In that case, go and fetch it. But if my lord, the Venerable Ānanda, has picked it up and placed it elsewhere, do not bring it. It has been given up by me to my lord.' For she knew, it is said, that 'the Elder puts away the forgotten belongings of people of good family'; therefore she spoke thus. The Elder, too, upon seeing the maidservant, asked, 'For what reason have you come?' When she replied, 'I have come because my lady forgot her ornament,' he said, 'I have placed it by the side of these stairs; go and get it.' She said, 'Venerable Sir, my lady has made it so that any item touched by your hand is not to be brought back.' Saying this, she returned empty-handed, and when asked by Visākhā, 'What is it, dear?' she related the matter. 'Dear, I will not wear an item touched by my lord; it has been given up by me. But it is difficult for the venerable ones to look after it. I will sell it and offer an allowable item. Go and bring it.' She went and brought it. Visākhā, without wearing it, had smiths summoned and asked them to appraise it. When they said, 'It is worth nine crores, and the craftsmanship is worth a hundred thousand,' she had the ornament placed on a cart and said, 'In that case, sell it.' No one would be able to buy it by giving that much wealth. For indeed, women suitable to wear that ornament are rare. On the face of the earth, only three women obtained the Mahālatā ornament: Visākhā, the great lay supporter; Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula of the Mallas; and the daughter of the merchant of Bārāṇasī.

Tasmā visākhā sayameva tassa mūlaṃ datvā satasahassādhikā nava koṭiyo sakaṭe āropetvā vihāraṃ netvā satthāraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, mayhaṃ ayyena ānandattherena mama pasādhanaṃ hatthena āmaṭṭhaṃ, tena āmaṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya na sakkā taṃ mayā pilandhituṃ. Taṃ pana vissajjetvā kappiyaṃ upanessāmīti vikkiṇāpentī aññaṃ taṃ gaṇhituṃ samatthaṃ adisvā ahameva tassa mūlaṃ gāhāpetvā āgatā, catūsu paccayesu katarapaccayena upanessāmi, bhante”ti. Pācīnadvāre saṅghassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0413] kātuṃ te yuttaṃ visākheti “yuttaṃ, bhante”ti visākhā tuṭṭhamānasā navakoṭīhi bhūmimeva gaṇhi. Aparāhi navakoṭīhi vihāraṃ kātuṃ ārabhi.

Therefore, Visākhā herself provided its value, and having loaded nine crores and one hundred thousand onto carts, she brought the sum to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and said, 'Venerable Sir, my ornament was touched by the hand of my lord, the Venerable Ānanda. From the time it was touched, it is not possible for me to wear it. Thinking, "I will sell it and offer something allowable," I had it put up for sale, but seeing no one else capable of buying it, I myself provided its value and have come. With which of the four requisites should I offer this, Venerable Sir?' The Teacher said, 'Visākhā, it is fitting for you to build a dwelling place for the Saṅgha at the eastern gate.' 'It is fitting, Venerable Sir,' said Visākhā, with a delighted mind. With nine crores, she purchased the land itself. With another nine crores, she began to build the monastery.

Athekadivasaṃ satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento devalokā cavitvā bhaddiyanagare seṭṭhikule nibbattassa bhaddiyassa nāma seṭṭhiputtassa upanissayasampattiṃ disvā anāthapiṇḍikassa gehe bhattakiccaṃ [M 1.0261] katvā uttaradvārābhimukho ahosi. Pakatiyā hi satthā visākhāya gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhitvā dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā jetavane vasati. Anāthapiṇḍikassa gehe bhikkhaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā pubbārāme vasati. Uttaradvāraṃ sandhāya gacchantaṃyeva bhagavantaṃ disvā, “cārikaṃ pakkamissatī”ti jānanti. Visākhāpi taṃ divasaṃ “satthā uttaradvārābhimukho gato”ti sutvā vegena gantvā vanditvā āha – “cārikaṃ gantukāmattha, bhante”ti? “Āma, visākhe”ti. “Bhante, ettakaṃ dhanaṃ pariccajitvā tumhākaṃ vihāraṃ kāremi, nivattatha, bhante”ti. “Anivattagamanaṃ idaṃ visākhe”ti. Sā “addhā hetusampannaṃ kañci passissati bhagavā”ti cintetvā, “tena hi, bhante, mayhaṃ katākatavijānanakaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ nivattetvā gacchathā”ti āha. “Yaṃ ruccasi, tassa pattaṃ [P 1.0414] gaṇha visākhe”ti āha. Sā kiñcāpi ānandattheraṃ piyāyati, “mahāmoggallānatthero iddhimā, etaṃ me nissāya kammaṃ lahuṃ [V 1.0232] nipphajjissatī”ti pana cintetvā therassa pattaṃ gaṇhi. Thero satthāraṃ olokesi. Satthā “tava parivāre pañcasate bhikkhū gahetvā nivatta moggallānā”ti āha. So tathā akāsi. Tassānubhāvena paññāsasaṭṭhiyojanānipi rukkhatthāya ca pāsāṇatthāya ca gatā manussā mahante mahante rukkhe ca pāsāṇe ca gahetvā taṃ divasameva āgacchanti, neva sakaṭe rukkhapāsāṇe āropentā kilamanti, na akkho bhijjati. Na cirasseva dvebhūmikaṃ pāsādaṃ kariṃsu. Heṭṭhābhūmiyaṃ pañca gabbhasatāni, uparibhūmiyaṃ pañca gabbhasatānīti gabbhasahassapaṭimaṇḍito pāsādo ahosi. Aṭṭhakarīse parisuddhe bhūmibhāge pāsādaṃ kārāpesi, “suddhapāsādo pana na sobhatī”ti taṃ parivāretvā pañca padhānavettagehasatāni, pañca cūḷapāsādasatāni, pañca dīghamāḷakasatāni kārāpesi.

Then one day, at dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw the supporting conditions for attainment of Bhaddiya, the merchant’s son, who had been reborn in the household of a wealthy merchant in the city of Bhaddiya after passing away from the deva realm. After the meal in Anāthapiṇḍika’s residence, he faced the northern gate. For it is the Teacher's custom to receive alms in Visākhā’s residence and depart through the southern gate to reside in Jetavana. After receiving alms in Anāthapiṇḍika’s residence, he would leave through the eastern gate to dwell in the Pubbārāma. Seeing the Blessed One heading toward the northern gate, they knew, “He will set out on a journey.” That day, Visākhā also, hearing, “The Teacher has gone toward the northern gate,” hurried to him, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sir, do you wish to go on a journey?” “Yes, Visākhā.” “Venerable sir, having given up so much wealth, I am having a monastery built for you; please turn back, venerable sir!” “This is a journey from which there is no turning back, Visākhā.” She thought, “Surely, the Blessed One sees someone endowed with the right conditions.” So she said, “In that case, venerable sir, please have one monk who knows what has and has not been done for me turn back, and then you may depart.” He replied, “Take the bowl of whomever you please, Visākhā.” Although she held the Venerable Ānanda dear, she thought, “The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is powerful; relying on him, this work of mine will be quickly accomplished,” and so she took the elder’s bowl. The elder looked to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Moggallāna, taking the five hundred monks of your retinue, turn back.” He did so. By his power, people who had gone fifty or sixty yojanas for wood and stone returned that very day, bringing great trees and stones. They did not tire while loading the trees and stones onto carts, nor did the axles break. Before long, they had built a two-storied mansion. With five hundred chambers on the lower floor and five hundred chambers on the upper floor, the mansion was thus adorned with a thousand chambers. She had the mansion built on a purified plot of land of eight karīsas. Thinking, “A plain mansion is not splendid,” she had it surrounded with five hundred meditation halls, five hundred smaller mansions, and five hundred long pavilions.

Atha satthā navahi māsehi cārikaṃ caritvā puna sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Visākhāyapi pāsāde kammaṃ navahi māsehi niṭṭhitaṃ. Pāsādakūṭaṃ ghanakoṭṭitarattasuvaṇṇeneva saṭṭhiudakaghaṭagaṇhanakaṃ [P 1.0415] kārāpesi. “Satthā jetavanavihāraṃ gacchatī”ti ca sutvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā satthāraṃ attano vihāraṃ netvā paṭiññaṃ gaṇhi, “bhante, imaṃ catumāsaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā idheva vasatha, pāsādamahaṃ karissāmī”ti. Satthā adhivāsesi. Sā [M 1.0262] tato paṭṭhāya buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa vihāre eva dānaṃ deti. Athassā ekā sahāyikā satasahassagghanakaṃ ekaṃ vatthaṃ ādāya āgantvā, “sahāyike ahaṃ imaṃ vatthaṃ tava pāsāde bhūmattharaṇasaṅkhepena attharitukāmā, attharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ me ācikkhathā”ti āha. “Sādhu sahāyike, sace tyāhaṃ ‘okāso natthī’ti vakkhāmi, tvaṃ ‘me okāsaṃ adātukāmā’ti maññissasi, sayameva pāsādassa dve bhūmiyo gabbhasahassañca oloketvā attharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ jānāhī”ti āha. Sā satasahassagghanakaṃ vatthaṃ gahetvā tattha tattha vicarantī tato appataramūlaṃ vatthaṃ adisvā “nāhaṃ imasmiṃ pāsāde puññabhāgaṃ labhāmī”ti domanassappattā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne rodantī aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ ānandatthero disvā, “kasmā rodasī”ti pucchi. Sā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Thero “mā cintayi, ahaṃ te attharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti vatvā, “sopānapādamūle pādadhovanaṭṭhāne imaṃ pādapuñchanakaṃ katvā attharāhi, bhikkhū pāde dhovitvā paṭhamaṃ ettha pādaṃ puñchitvā [P 1.0416] anto pavisissanti, evaṃ te mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti āha. Visākhāya kiretaṃ asallakkhitaṭṭhānaṃ.

Then, after wandering for nine months, the Teacher returned to Sāvatthī. The work on Visākhā’s mansion was also completed in nine months. She had the pinnacle of the mansion made of solid, beaten red gold, large enough to hold sixty water pots. Hearing that “the Teacher is going to the Jetavana Monastery,” she went out to meet him and, bringing the Teacher to her own monastery, secured his promise: “Venerable Sir, please stay here with the community of monks for these four months, and I will hold a festival for the mansion.” The Teacher consented. From then on, she offered alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha right there in the monastery. Then, one of her friends, bringing a cloth worth a hundred thousand, came and said, “Friend, I wish to spread this cloth as a floor covering in your mansion. Please show me a place to spread it.” “Very well, friend. If I were to say to you, ‘There is no space,’ you might think, ‘She does not wish to give me an opportunity.’ So, go and look around the two floors and thousand chambers of the mansion yourself and find a place to spread it,” she replied. Taking the cloth worth a hundred thousand, her friend wandered here and there but, not seeing any cloth of lesser value than it, she became distressed, thinking, “I will not obtain a share of merit in this mansion,” and stood weeping in one spot. Then, the Venerable Ānanda saw her and asked, “Why are you crying?” She explained the matter. The elder said, “Do not worry, I will show you a place to spread it.” Then he said, “At the foot of the stairs, in the foot-washing area, make this into a foot-wiping cloth and spread it. The monks, after washing their feet, will first wipe their feet on it before entering. Thus, it will be of great fruit for you.” Indeed, this was a spot Visākhā had not considered.

Visākhā cattāro māse antovihāre buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ adāsi, avasānadivase bhikkhusaṅghassa cīvarasāṭake adāsi. Saṅghanavakena laddhacīvarasāṭakā sahassagghanakā [V 1.0233] honti. Sabbesaṃ pattāni pūretvā bhesajjaṃ adāsi. Dānapariccāge nava koṭiyo agamaṃsu. Iti vihārassa bhūmiggahaṇe nava koṭiyo, vihārassa kārāpane nava, vihāramahe navāti sabbāpi sattavīsati koṭiyo sā buddhasāsane pariccaji. Itthibhāve ṭhatvā micchādiṭṭhikassa gehe vasamānāya evarūpo mahāpariccāgo nāma aññissā natthi. Sā vihāramahassa niṭṭhitadivase vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya puttanattapanattaparivutā “yaṃ yaṃ mayā pubbe patthitaṃ, sabbameva matthakaṃ patta”nti pāsādaṃ anupariyāyantī pañcahi gāthāhi madhurasaddena imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

For four months, Visākhā offered alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha inside the monastery. On the final day, she gave robe-cloths to the community of monks. The robe-cloths received by the most junior monk were worth a thousand. Filling all their bowls, she also gave medicines. In this offering of gifts, nine crores were spent. Thus: nine crores for acquiring the land for the monastery, nine for its construction, and nine for the monastery festival—in all, she relinquished twenty-seven crores for the Buddha's Dispensation. For a woman, while dwelling in the house of one with wrong views, to make such a great offering is something unheard of for any other. On the day the monastery festival was completed, in the afternoon, surrounded by her sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, she joyfully thought, “Whatever I have previously wished for, all of it has reached its culmination.” Circling the mansion, she uttered this inspired utterance in a sweet voice with five verses:

“Kadāhaṃ pāsādaṃ rammaṃ, sudhāmattikalepanaṃ;

Vihāradānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.

“When shall I give the gift of a monastery—a delightful mansion, plastered with pure lime and clay? Today, my aspiration is fulfilled.”

“Kadāhaṃ [M 1.0263] mañcapīṭhañca, bhisibimbohanāni ca;

Senāsanabhaṇḍaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.

“When shall I give the requisites for lodging—beds and benches, mattresses and pillows? Today, my aspiration is fulfilled.”

“Kadāhaṃ [P 1.0417] salākabhattaṃ, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Bhojanadānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.

“When shall I give the gift of food—pure ticket-food with savory meat curries? Today, my aspiration is fulfilled.”

“Kadāhaṃ kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ, khomakappāsikāni ca;

Cīvaradānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.

“When shall I give the gift of robes—cloth from Kasi, and garments of linen and cotton? Today, my aspiration is fulfilled.”

“Kadāhaṃ sappinavanītaṃ, madhutelañca phāṇitaṃ;

Bhesajjadānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito”ti.

“When shall I give ghee and fresh butter, honey, oil, and molasses, the gift of medicine? My aspiration is fulfilled.”

Bhikkhū tassā saddaṃ sutvā satthu ārocayiṃsu – “bhante, amhehi ettake addhāne visākhāya gāyanaṃ nāma na diṭṭhapubbaṃ, sā ajja puttanattapanattaparivutā gāyamānā pāsādaṃ anupariyāyati, kiṃ nu khvassā pittaṃ vā kupitaṃ, udāhu ummattikā jātā”ti? Satthā “na, bhikkhave, mayhaṃ dhītā gāyati, attano panassā ajjhāsayo paripuṇṇo, sā ‘patthitapatthanā me matthakaṃ pattā’ti tuṭṭhamānasā udānaṃ udānentī vicaratī”ti vatvā “kadā pana, bhante, tāya patthanā patthitā”ti? “Suṇissatha, bhikkhave”ti. “Suṇissāma, bhante”ti vutte atītaṃ āhari –

The monks, hearing her voice, reported to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, in all this long time, we have never before witnessed Visākhā singing. Today, surrounded by her sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, she is singing as she circles the mansion. Can it be that her bile is agitated, or has she gone mad?” The Teacher replied, “No, monks, my daughter is not singing; rather, her own noble aspiration has been fulfilled. With a delighted mind, thinking, ‘The aspiration I have sought has reached its culmination,’ she goes about uttering a joyous exclamation.” They asked, “But when, venerable sir, was that aspiration made by her?” “Listen, monks.” When they replied, “We will listen, venerable sir,” he brought forth the past.

“Atīte[V 1.0234], bhikkhave, ito kappasatasahassamatthake padumuttaro nāma buddho loke nibbatti. Tassa vassasatasahassaṃ āyu ahosi, khīṇāsavānaṃ satasahassaparivāro, nagaraṃ haṃsavatī nāma, pitā sunando nāma rājā, mātā sujātā nāma devī, tassa aggaupaṭṭhāyikā ekā upāsikā aṭṭha vare yācitvā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhatvā satthāraṃ catūhi paccayehi paṭijaggantī sāyaṃpātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Tassā ekā sahāyikā tāya saddhiṃ vihāraṃ nibaddhaṃ gacchati. Sā tassā satthārā saddhiṃ vissāsena kathanañca vallabhabhāvañca disvā, ‘kiṃ nu kho katvā evaṃ buddhānaṃ vallatā hotī’ti cintetvā satthāraṃ pucchi – ‘bhante, esā itthī tumhākaṃ kiṃ hotī’”ti? “Upaṭṭhāyikānaṃ [P 1.0418] aggā”ti. “Bhante, kiṃ katvā upaṭṭhāyikānaṃ aggā hotī”ti? “Kappasatasahassaṃ patthanaṃ patthetvā”ti. “Idāni patthetvā laddhuṃ sakkā, bhante”ti. “Āma, sakkā”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, bhikkhusatasahassena saddhiṃ sattāhaṃ mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Satthā adhivāsesi. Sā sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā osānadivase cīvarasāṭake datvā satthāraṃ [M 1.0264] vanditvā pādamūle nipajjitvā, “bhante, nāhaṃ imassa dānassa phalena devissariyādīnaṃ aññataraṃ patthemi, tumhādisassa panekassa buddhassa santike aṭṭha vare labhitvā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhatvā catūhi paccayehi paṭijaggituṃ samatthānaṃ aggā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Satthā “samijjhissati nu kho imissā patthanā”ti anāgataṃ āvajjento kappasatasahassaṃ oloketvā “kappasatasahassapariyosāne gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tadā tvaṃ visākhā nāma upāsikā hutvā tassa santike aṭṭha vare labhitvā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhatvā catūhi paccayehi paṭijaggantīnaṃ upaṭṭhāyikānaṃ aggā bhavissasī”ti āha. Tassā sā sampatti sveva laddhabbā viya ahosi.

“Monks, in the past, a hundred thousand eons from this one, a Buddha named Padumuttara arose in the world. His lifespan was a hundred thousand years, and he was attended by a hundred thousand of those whose corruptions were destroyed. His city was named Haṃsāvatī, his father was King Sunanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā. His chief female lay supporter, having requested eight boons and established herself in the position of a mother, served the Teacher with the four requisites, attending upon him in the evening and the morning. A friend of hers regularly went with her to the monastery. Seeing her familiar conversation with the Teacher and her dearness to him, she thought, ‘By doing what, indeed, does one become so dear to the Buddhas?’ and asked the Teacher, ‘Venerable sir, what is this woman to you?’ ‘She is the foremost of my female lay supporters who serve me.’ ‘Venerable sir, by doing what does one become the foremost of female lay supporters who serve?’ ‘By making an aspiration for a hundred thousand eons.’ ‘Venerable sir, is it possible to make that aspiration now and attain it?’ ‘Yes, it is possible.’ ‘In that case, venerable sir, please accept my offering of alms for seven days, together with a hundred thousand monks.’ The Teacher consented. She gave alms for seven days, and on the final day, having given cloth for robes, she paid homage to the Teacher, prostrated at his feet, and established her aspiration, saying: ‘Venerable sir, by the fruit of this gift, I do not aspire for any divine sovereignty or the like; but rather, in the presence of a Buddha such as yourself, having received eight boons and established myself in the position of a mother, may I be the foremost among those who are able to serve with the four requisites.’ The Teacher, reflecting on the future, ‘Will this woman’s aspiration be fulfilled or not?’, looked forward a hundred thousand eons and said: ‘At the end of a hundred thousand eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. At that time, you, having become a female lay supporter named Visākhā, will receive eight boons in his presence, establish yourself in the position of a mother, and become the foremost among the female lay supporters who serve with the four requisites.’ For her, that attainment seemed as if it were to be received the very next day.”

Sā yāvatāyukaṃ puññaṃ katvā tato cutā devaloke nibbattitvā devamanussesu saṃsarantī kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kikissa kāsirañño sattannaṃ dhītānaṃ kaniṭṭhā saṅghadāsī nāma hutvā parakulaṃ agantvā tāhi jeṭṭhabhaginīhi saddhiṃ dīgharattaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā kassapasammāsambuddhassa pādamūlepi “anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa mātuṭṭhāne ṭhatvā catupaccayadāyikānaṃ aggā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya pana devamanussesu saṃsarantī imasmiṃ attabhāve meṇḍakaseṭṭhiputtassa [P 1.0419] dhanañcayaseṭṭhino dhītā hutvā nibbattā. Mayhaṃ sāsane bahūni puññāni akāsi. Iti kho, bhikkhave, “na mayhaṃ dhītā gāyati, patthitapatthanāya pana nipphattiṃ disvā udānaṃ udānetī”ti vatvā satthā dhammaṃ desento, “bhikkhave, yathā nāma cheko mālākāro nānāpupphānaṃ mahantaṃ rāsiṃ katvā nānappakāre mālāguṇe karoti, evameva visākhāya nānappakārāni puññāni kātuṃ cittaṃ namatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

“She, having performed meritorious deeds for her entire lifespan, passed away from there and was reborn in a celestial world. Wandering among gods and humans, during the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, she was born as the youngest of the seven daughters of Kiki, the king of Kasi, and was named Saṅghadāsī. Without going to a husband's family, she, together with her elder sisters, performed meritorious deeds such as giving for a long time. At the feet of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, she also made the aspiration: ‘In the future, having established myself in the position of a mother to a Buddha like you, may I be the foremost among the female donors of the four requisites.’ From that time onwards, wandering among gods and humans, in this very existence she was reborn as the daughter of the wealthy merchant Dhanañjaya, son of the wealthy merchant Meṇḍaka. In my Dispensation, she has performed many meritorious deeds. Therefore, monks, my daughter is not singing; rather, seeing the fulfillment of the aspiration she had made, she utters a joyous exclamation.” Having said this, the Teacher, while teaching the Dhamma, said: “Monks, just as a skilled garland-maker, from a great heap of various flowers, makes many kinds of garlands, even so does Visākhā’s mind incline to perform various kinds of meritorious deeds.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

53.

53.

“Yathāpi [V 1.0235] puppharāsimhā, kayirā mālāguṇe bahū;

Evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti.

“Just as from a heap of flowers one might make many garlands, so by one born a mortal much that is wholesome should be done.”

Tattha puppharāsimhāti nānappakārānaṃ pupphānaṃ rāsimhā. Kayirāti kareyya. Mālāguṇe bahūti ekato vaṇṭikamālādibhedā nānappakārā mālāvikatiyo. Maccenāti maritabbasabhāvatāya “macco”ti laddhanāmena sattena cīvaradānādibhedaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ kattabbaṃ. Tattha puppharāsiggahaṇaṃ bahupupphadassanatthaṃ. Sace hi appāni pupphāni honti, mālākāro ca cheko [M 1.0265] neva bahū mālāguṇe kātuṃ sakkoti, acheko pana appesu bahūsupi pupphesu na sakkotiyeva. Bahūsu pana pupphesu sati cheko mālākāro dakkho kusalo bahū mālāguṇe karoti, evameva sace ekaccassa saddhā mandā hoti, bhogā ca bahū saṃvijjanti, neva sakkoti bahūni kusalāni kātuṃ, mandāya ca [P 1.0420] pana saddhāya mandesu ca pana bhogesu na sakkoti. Uḷārāya ca pana saddhāya mandesu ca bhogesu na sakkotiyeva. Uḷārāya ca pana saddhāya uḷāresu ca bhogesu sati sakkoti. Tathārūpā ca visākhā upāsikā. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “yathāpi…pe… kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti.

Herein, 'from a heap of flowers' means from a collection of various kinds of flowers. 'One might make' (kayirā) means one should make. 'Many garlands' refers to various types of floral arrangements, such as garlands with stems tied on one side. 'By a mortal' means by a being who has received the name 'mortal' due to their nature of being subject to death. Much that is wholesome, such as the offering of robes and so forth, should be done. Here, the mention of a 'heap of flowers' is for the purpose of showing an abundance of flowers. For if there are few flowers, even a skilled garland-maker is unable to make many garlands; and an unskilled one, however, is unable whether the flowers are few or many. But when there are many flowers, a skilled, discerning, and expert garland-maker makes many garlands. In the very same way, if a person has weak faith, even if they have abundant possessions, they are not able to perform many wholesome deeds. With weak faith and meager possessions, they are not able. With strong faith but meager possessions, they are certainly not able. But when there is strong faith and abundant possessions, they are able. The female lay follower Visākhā was such a person. With reference to her, this was said: 'Just as... much that is wholesome should be done.'

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, many became stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great assembly of people.

Visākhāvatthu aṭṭhamaṃ

The Story of Visākhā, the Eighth.

9. Ānandattherapañhāvatthu

9. The Story of the Elder Ānanda's Question

Na pupphagandho paṭivātametīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto ānandattherassa pañhaṃ vissajjento kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'The fragrance of a flower does not travel against the wind,' while answering a question from the Elder Ānanda.

Thero kira sāyanhasamaye paṭisallīno cintesi – “bhagavatā mūlagandho, sāragandho, pupphagandhoti tayo uttamagandhā vuttā, tesaṃ anuvātameva gandho gacchati, no paṭivātaṃ. Atthi nu kho taṃ gandhajātaṃ, yassa paṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “kiṃ mayhaṃ attanā vinicchitena, satthāraṃyeva pucchissāmī”ti. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ –

It is said that the Elder, while in seclusion in the evening, thought: 'The Blessed One has spoken of three supreme fragrances: root fragrance, heartwood fragrance, and flower fragrance. Their scent travels only downwind; it does not go upwind. Might there be a kind of fragrance whose scent travels upwind as well?' Then this thought occurred to him: 'What is the use of my deciding this by myself? I shall ask the Teacher himself.' So he approached the Teacher and asked. Therefore, it was said:

“Atha kho āyasmā ānando sāyanhasamaye paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami[V 1.0236], upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ [P 1.0421] etadavoca –

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having arisen from seclusion in the evening, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated thus to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“Tīṇimāni, bhante, gandhajātāni, yesaṃ anuvātameva gandho gacchati, no paṭivātaṃ. Katamāni tīṇi? Mūlagandho, sāragandho, pupphagandho[M 1.0266], imāni kho, bhante, tīṇi gandhajātāni. Yesaṃ anuvātameva gandho gacchati, no paṭivātaṃ. Atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci gandhajātaṃ yassa anuvātampi gandho gacchati, paṭivātampi gandho gacchati, anuvātapaṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti? (A. ni. 3.80)

“Venerable sir, there are these three kinds of fragrances whose scent travels only downwind, not upwind. What are the three? The fragrance of roots, the fragrance of heartwood, and the fragrance of flowers. These, venerable sir, are the three kinds of fragrances whose scent travels only downwind, not upwind. Is there, venerable sir, any kind of fragrance whose scent travels downwind, travels upwind, and travels both downwind and upwind?”

Athassa bhagavā pañhaṃ vissajjento –

Then the Blessed One, answering his question, said:

“Atthānanda, kiñci gandhajātaṃ, yassa anuvātampi gandho gacchati, paṭivātampi gandho gacchati, anuvātapaṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti. “Katamaṃ pana taṃ, bhante, gandhajātaṃ”? “Yassa anuvātampi gandho gacchati, paṭivātampi gandho gacchati, anuvātapaṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti?

“There is, Ānanda, a kind of fragrance whose scent travels downwind, travels upwind, and travels both downwind and upwind.” “But what, venerable sir, is that kind of fragrance whose scent travels downwind, travels upwind, and travels both downwind and upwind?”

“Idhānanda, yasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā itthī vā puriso vā buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti, kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, musāvādā paṭivirato hoti, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti, sīlavā hoti kalyāṇadhammo, vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato yācayogo dānasaṃvibhāgarato.

“Here, Ānanda, in whatever village or town a woman or a man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge; abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from intoxicants—liquor and spirits—which are a cause of heedlessness; is virtuous, of good character; dwells at home with a mind devoid of the stain of stinginess, is freely generous, open-handed, delights in relinquishment, is amenable to requests, and delights in giving and sharing.

“Tassa disāsu samaṇabrāhmaṇā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, ‘amukasmiṃ nāma gāme vā nigame vā itthī vā puriso vā buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti…pe… dānasaṃvibhāgarato’”ti.

“Ascetics and brahmins in all directions speak in praise of that person, saying: ‘In such-and-such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge… and delights in giving and sharing.’”

“Devatāpissa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, ‘amukasmiṃ nāma [P 1.0422] gāme vā nigame vā itthī vā puriso vā buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti…pe… dānasaṃvibhāgarato’”ti. “Idaṃ kho taṃ, ānanda, gandhajātaṃ, yassa anuvātampi [V 1.0237] gandho gacchati, paṭivātampi gandho gacchati[M 1.0267], anuvātapaṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti (a. ni. 3.80) vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

“The devas also speak in praise of that person, saying: ‘In such-and-such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge… and delights in giving and sharing.’ This, Ānanda, is that kind of fragrance whose scent travels downwind, travels upwind, and travels both downwind and upwind.” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

54.

54.

“Na pupphagandho paṭivātameti,

Na candanaṃ tagaramallikā vā;

Satañca gandho paṭivātameti,

Sabbā disā sappuriso pavāyati. (a. ni. 3.80);

“The fragrance of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine; but the fragrance of the virtuous travels against the wind; a good person pervades all directions.

55.

55.

“Candanaṃ tagaraṃ vāpi, uppalaṃ atha vassikī;

Etesaṃ gandhajātānaṃ, sīlagandho anuttaro”ti.

“Sandalwood, tagara, lotus, or jasmine—among these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is supreme.”

Tattha na pupphagandhoti tāvatiṃsabhavane paricchattakarukkho āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanasatiko, tassa pupphānaṃ ābhā paññāsa yojanāni gacchati, gandho yojanasataṃ, sopi anuvātameva gacchati, paṭivātaṃ pana aṭṭhaṅgulamattampi gantuṃ na sakkoti, evarūpopi na pupphagandho paṭivātameti. Candananti candanagandho. Tagaramallikā vāti imesampi gandho eva adhippeto. Sāragandhānaṃ aggassa hi lohitacandanassāpi tagarassapi mallikāyapi anuvātameva vāyati, no paṭivātaṃ. Satañca gandhoti sappurisānaṃ pana buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ sīlagandho paṭivātameti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Sabbā disā sappuriso pavāyati yasmā pana sappuriso sīlagandhena sabbāpi disā ajjhottharitvāva gacchati, tasmā “tassa gandho na paṭivātametī”ti na vattabbo[P 1.0423]. Tena vuttaṃ “paṭivātametī”ti. Vassikīti jātisumanā. Etesanti imesaṃ candanādīnaṃ gandhajātānaṃ gandhato sīlavantānaṃ sappurisānaṃ sīlagandhova anuttaro asadiso apaṭibhāgoti.

Therein, 'not the fragrance of flowers' refers to the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, which is a hundred yojanas in height and in breadth. The radiance of its flowers travels for fifty yojanas, and their fragrance for a hundred yojanas. That fragrance, too, travels only downwind; against the wind, it is not able to travel even as much as eight finger-breadths. Even such a fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind. 'Sandalwood' means the fragrance of sandalwood. 'Tagara or jasmine' means the fragrance of these is also intended. For the fragrance of the best of heartwood-scents, of red sandalwood, of tagara, and of jasmine wafts only downwind, not against the wind. 'But the fragrance of the virtuous' means the fragrance of virtue of good persons—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—travels against the wind. For what reason? Does it waft in all directions? Because a good person, with the fragrance of virtue, travels pervading all directions, therefore it should not be said, 'his fragrance does not go against the wind.' For that reason, it is said, 'It travels against the wind.' 'Vassikī' means the great jasmine. 'Among these' means: compared to the fragrance of these kinds of scents, such as sandalwood, the fragrance of virtue of virtuous, good persons is supreme, without equal, and incomparable.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth. The discourse became beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Ānandattherapañhāvatthu navamaṃ.

The Ninth: The Story of the Elder Ānanda’s Question.

10. Mahākassapattherapiṇḍapātadinnavatthu

10. The Story of the Alms-food Given to the Elder Mahākassapa

Appamatto [M 1.0268][V 1.0238] ayaṃ gandhoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto mahākassapattherassa piṇḍapātadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, spoke this Dhamma discourse, beginning with “This fragrance is of little measure,” concerning the offering of alms-food to the Elder Mahākassapa.

Ekasmiñhi divase thero sattāhaccayena nirodhā vuṭṭhāya “rājagahe sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti nikkhami. Tasmiṃ pana samaye sakkassa devarañño paricārikā kakuṭapādiniyo pañcasatā accharāyo “therassa piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmā”ti ussāhajātā pañca piṇḍapātasatāni sajjetvā ādāya antarāmagge ṭhatvā, “bhante, imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ gaṇhatha, saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti vadiṃsu. “Gacchatha tumhe, ahaṃ duggatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Bhante, mā no nāsetha, saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti. Thero ñatvā puna paṭikkhipitvā punapi apagantuṃ anicchamānā [P 1.0424] yācantiyo “attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātha, apagacchathā”ti accharaṃ pahari. Tā therassa accharasaddaṃ sutvā santhambhitvā sammukhā ṭhātuṃ asakkontiyo palāyitvā devalokameva gantvā, sakkena “kahaṃ gatātthā”ti puṭṭhā, “‘samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa therassa piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmā’ti gatāmhā, devā”ti. “Dinno pana vā”ti? “Gaṇhituṃ na icchatī”ti. “Kiṃ kathesī”ti? “‘Duggatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī’ti āha, devā”ti. “Tumhe kenākārena gatā”ti. “Imināva, devā”ti. Sakko “tumhādisiyo therassa piṇḍapātaṃ kiṃ dassantī”ti sayaṃ dātukāmo hutvā, jarājiṇṇo mahallako khaṇḍadanto palitakeso otaggasarīro mahallakatanta vāyo hutvā sujampi devadhītaraṃ tathārūpameva mahallikaṃ katvā ekaṃ pesakāravīthiṃ māpetvā tantaṃ pasārento acchi.

For on one day, the Elder, having arisen from the attainment of cessation after seven days, set out, thinking, “I will walk for alms from house to house in Rājagaha.” But at that time, five hundred celestial nymphs named Kakuṭapādinī, attendants of Sakka, king of the devas, became eager, thinking, “We will give alms-food to the Elder.” Having prepared and taken five hundred portions of alms-food, they stood in the middle of the road and said, “Venerable sir, accept this alms-food. Do us a favor.” “You go. I will do a favor for the poor.” “Venerable sir, do not ruin this for us. Do us a favor.” The Elder, knowing, rejected them again. As they were still unwilling to depart and kept pleading, he said, “You do not know your own measure. Depart!” and snapped his fingers. They, hearing the sound of the Elder’s finger-snap, were stunned, and unable to stand in his presence, fled and went to the deva world. When asked by Sakka, “Where have you been?” they said, “Lord, we went to give alms-food to the Elder who had arisen from attainment.” “But was it given?” “He did not wish to accept it.” “What did he say?” “Lord, he said, ‘I will do a favor for the poor.’” “In what form did you go?” “Lord, in this very form.” Sakka, thinking, “How can women like you give alms-food to the Elder?” became desirous of giving himself. He became an old weaver who was aged and decrepit, old, with broken teeth, with white hair, and with a stooped body. He also made the deva-daughter Sujā into a similarly-formed old woman, and having created a weaver’s lane, he sat stretching the warp.

Theropi “duggatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti nagarābhimukho gacchanto bahinagare eva taṃ vīthiṃ disvā olokento dve jane addasa. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko tantaṃ pasāreti, sujā tasaraṃ vaṭṭeti. Thero cintesi – “ime mahallakakālepi kammaṃ karontiyeva imasmiṃ nagare imehi duggatatarā natthi maññe, imehi [P 1.0425] dinnaṃ uḷuṅkamattampi sākamattampi gahetvā imesaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti. So tesaṃ gehābhimukho ahosi. Sakko taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā sujaṃ āha – “bhadde, mayhaṃ ayyo ito āgacchati, tvaṃ apassantī viya tuṇhī hutvā nisīda, khaṇena theraṃ vañcetvā piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmā”ti. Thero āgantvā gehadvāre [M 1.0269] aṭṭhāsi. Tepi apassantā viya attano kammameva karontā thokaṃ āgamiṃsu.

The Elder, too, thinking, 'I shall render assistance to the poor,' was proceeding towards the city when, just outside the city, he saw that lane. As he looked, he saw two people. At that moment, Sakka was stretching the warp, and Sujā was plying the shuttle. The Elder thought: 'These people are still working even in their old age. In this city, I think there are none poorer than they. Having accepted even just a ladleful or a measure of greens given by them, I shall render them assistance.' Thus, he went towards their house. Sakka, seeing him approaching, said to Sujā: 'Good lady, my noble lord is coming this way. You, as if not seeing him, sit silently. In a moment, having deceived the Elder, we shall give the alms-food.' The Elder arrived and stood at the door of the house. They too, as if not seeing him, continued with their own work and waited for a short while.

Atha [V 1.0239] sakko “gehadvāre eko thero viya ṭhito, upadhārehi tāvā”ti āha. “Gantvā upadhāretha, sāmī”ti. So gehā nikkhamitvā theraṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā ubhohi hatthehi jaṇṇukāni olambitvā nitthunanto uṭṭhāya “kataro thero nu kho ayyo”ti thokaṃ osakkitvā “akkhīni me dhūmāyantī”ti vatvā nalāṭe hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā uddhaṃ oloketvā “aho dukkhaṃ, ayyo no mahākassapatthero cirassaṃ me kuṭidvāraṃ āgato, atthi nu kho kiñci gehe”ti āha. Sujā thokaṃ ākulaṃ viya hutvā “atthi, sāmī”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. Sakko, “bhante, lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vāti acintetvā saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti pattaṃ gaṇhi. Thero “etehi dinnaṃ sākaṃ vā hotu kuṇḍakamuṭṭhi vā, saṅgahaṃ [P 1.0426] nesaṃ karissāmī”ti pattaṃ adāsi. So antogharaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭiodanaṃ nāma ghaṭiyā uddharitvā pattaṃ pūretvā therassa hatthe ṭhapesi. So ahosi piṇḍapāto anekasūpabyañjano, sakalaṃ rājagahanagaraṃ gandhena ajjhotthari.

Then Sakka said, 'It seems an elder is standing at the door of the house; do investigate.' 'Lord, you go and investigate,' she replied. He went out from the house and, having venerated the Elder with the five-point prostration, he stood up, pressing his knees with both hands and groaning. 'Which elder might the noble one be?' he said, stepping back a little. Then, saying, 'My eyes are dim,' he placed his hand on his forehead, looked up, and exclaimed, 'Oh, what sorrow! Our noble lord, the Elder Mahākassapa, has come to the door of my hut after a long time. Is there anything at all in the house?' Sujā, acting as if a little flustered, replied, 'There is, lord.' Sakka took the bowl, saying, 'Venerable sir, without considering whether it is coarse or fine, please render us assistance.' The Elder, thinking, 'Be it greens or a handful of broken rice given by them, I shall render them assistance,' gave his bowl. He entered the inner part of the house and, taking out ghee-rice from the pot, filled the bowl and placed it in the Elder's hands. That alms-food was complete with many kinds of curries and sauces, and it pervaded the entire city of Rājagaha with its fragrance.

Tadā thero cintesi – “ayaṃ puriso appesakkho, piṇḍapāto mahesakkho, sakkassa bhojanasadiso, ko nu kho eso”ti. Atha naṃ “sakko”ti ñatvā āha – “bhāriyaṃ te kammaṃ kataṃ duggatānaṃ sampattiṃ vilumpantena, ajja mayhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kocideva duggato senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ vā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ vā labheyyā”ti. “Mayā duggatataro natthi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā tvaṃ duggato devaloke rajjasiriṃ anubhavanto”ti? “Bhante, evaṃ nāmetaṃ, mayā pana anuppanne buddhe kalyāṇakammaṃ kataṃ, buddhuppāde vattamāne kalyāṇakammaṃ katvā cūḷarathadevaputto mahārathadevaputto anekavaṇṇadevaputtoti ime tayo samānadevaputtā mama āsannaṭṭhāne nibbattā, mayā tejavantatarā. Ahañhi tesu devaputtesu ‘nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā’ti paricārikāyo gahetvā [P 1.0427] antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇesu palāyitvā gehaṃ pavisāmi. Tesañhi sarīrato tejo mama sarīraṃ ottharati, mama sarīrato tejo tesaṃ sarīraṃ na ottharati, ‘ko mayā duggatataro, bhante’ti. ‘Evaṃ santepi ito paṭṭhāya [M 1.0270] mayhaṃ mā evaṃ vañcetvā dānamadāsī’”ti. “Vañcetvā tumhākaṃ dāne dinne mayhaṃ kusalaṃ atthi, na atthī”ti? “Atthāvuso”ti. “Evaṃ sante kusalakammakaraṇaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro, bhante”ti. So evaṃ vatvā theraṃ vanditvā sujaṃ gahetvā theraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā “aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhita”nti udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the Elder thought: 'This man is of little power, but the alms-food is of great power, like the food of Sakka. Who could this be?' Then, recognizing him to be Sakka, he said: 'A grave deed has been done by you, plundering the good fortune of the poor. Today, by giving alms to me, some poor person could have obtained the position of a general or the position of a great merchant.' 'Venerable sir, there is no one poorer than I.' 'For what reason are you poor, while enjoying the splendor of kingship in the deva world?' 'Venerable sir, that is indeed so. However, I performed wholesome kamma when a Buddha had not arisen. But now, during the time of a Buddha's appearance, having performed wholesome kamma, these three devaputtas of equal standing—namely Cūḷaratha-devaputta, Mahāratha-devaputta, and Anekavaṇṇa-devaputta—have been reborn near my place, and they are more powerful than I. Indeed, when those devaputtas, thinking, ‘We shall play at the festival,’ take their female attendants and descend into the main street, I flee and enter my house. For the radiance from their bodies overwhelms my body, but the radiance from my body does not overwhelm their bodies. Venerable sir, who is poorer than I?' 'Even so, from this day forward, do not give alms to me by deceiving me thus.' 'When alms are given to you through deception, is there merit for me, or is there not?' 'There is, friend.' 'If that is so, venerable sir, the performance of wholesome kamma is my responsibility.' Having said this, he paid homage to the Elder, took Sujā, circumambulated the Elder, rose up into the sky, and uttered this inspired utterance: 'Oh, the gift, the supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa!' Therefore it was said:

“Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākassapo pippaliguhāyaṃ viharati, sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno [V 1.0240] hoti aññataraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjitvā. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo tassa sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhāsi. Atha kho āyasmato mahākassapassa tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhitassa etadahosi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya paviseyya”nti.

On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pipphali Cave; having attained a certain concentration, he remained seated for seven days in a single posture. Then, at the end of those seven days, the Venerable Mahākassapa arose from that concentration. Then, having arisen from that concentration, this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘What if I were to enter Rājagaha for alms?’

“Tena kho pana samayena pañcamattāni devatāsatāni ussukkaṃ āpannāni honti āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātapaṭilābhāya. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo tāni pañcamattāni devatāsatāni [P 1.0428] paṭikkhipitvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Now at that time, five hundred deities had become eager to provide alms-food for the Venerable Mahākassapa. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having refused those five hundred deities, dressed himself in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.

“Tena kho pana samayena sakko devānamindo āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātaṃ dātukāmo hoti. Pesakāravaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā tantaṃ vināti, sujā asurakaññā tasaraṃ pūreti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo rājagahe sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno yena sakkassa devānamindassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami, addasā kho sakko devānamindo āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ, disvā gharā nikkhamitvā paccuggantvā hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā gharaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭiyā odanaṃ uddharitvā pattaṃ pūretvā āyasmato mahākassapassa adāsi. So ahosi piṇḍapāto anekasūpo anekabyañjano anekarasabyañjano. Atha kho āyasmato mahākassapassa etadahosi – ‘ko nu kho ayaṃ satto, yassāyaṃ evarūpo iddhānubhāvo’ti. Atha kho āyasmato [M 1.0271] mahākassapassa etadahosi – ‘sakko kho ayaṃ devānamindo’ti viditvā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ etadavoca – ‘kataṃ kho [P 1.0429] te idaṃ, kosiya, mā punapi evarūpamakāsī’”ti. “Amhākampi, bhante kassapa, puññena attho, amhākampi puññena karaṇīya”nti.

Now at that time, Sakka, the lord of the devas, was desirous of giving alms-food to the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having created the appearance of a weaver, he was weaving at the loom, while Sujā, the Asura maiden, was filling the shuttle. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, while going for alms from house to house in Rājagaha, approached the dwelling of Sakka, the lord of the devas. Sakka, the lord of the devas, saw the Venerable Mahākassapa coming from afar. Having seen him, he came out of the house, went to meet him, took the bowl from his hand, entered the house, took out rice from the pot, filled the bowl, and gave it to the Venerable Mahākassapa. That alms-food had many curries, many condiments, and many sauces. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘Who can this being be, who has such psychic power?’ Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘This is surely Sakka, the lord of the devas.’ Knowing this, he said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas: ‘This deed was done by you, Kosiya. Do not do such a thing again!’ ‘Venerable Kassapa, we too have need of merit; we too have meritorious deeds to perform.’

“Atha kho sakko devānamindo āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā ākāse antalikkhe tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi – ‘aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhitaṃ, aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhitaṃ, aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhita’”nti (udā. 27).

Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, having paid homage to the Venerable Mahākassapa and circumambulated him, rose up into the sky and in mid-air uttered this inspired utterance three times: ‘Oh, what a gift, a supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa! Oh, what a gift, a supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa! Oh, what a gift, a supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa!’

Atha kho bhagavā vihāre ṭhito eva tassa taṃ saddaṃ sutvā bhikkhū āmantetvā – “passatha[V 1.0241], bhikkhave, sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā ākāsena gacchanta”nti āha. “Kiṃ pana tena kataṃ, bhante”ti? “Vañcetvā tena mayhaṃ puttassa kassapassa piṇḍapāto dinno, taṃ datvā tuṭṭhamānaso udānaṃ udānento gacchatī”ti. “Therassa piṇḍapātaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kathaṃ, bhante, tena ñātanti. “Bhikkhave, mama puttena sadisaṃ nāma piṇḍapātikaṃ devāpi manussāpi pihayantīti vatvā sayampi udānaṃ udāne”si. Sutte pana etthakameva āgataṃ –

Then the Blessed One, while still in the monastery, heard that sound and addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see Sakka, lord of the devas, going through the sky after uttering an inspired utterance?” “But what has been done by him, venerable sir?” “Having deceived, he gave almsfood to my son Kassapa. Having given it, with a pleased mind, he goes along uttering an inspired utterance.” “Venerable sir, how did he know that it was proper to give almsfood to the Elder?” “Bhikkhus, both devas and humans cherish an alms-goer such as my son.” Having said this, he himself also uttered an inspired utterance. In the Sutta, however, only this much has come down:

“Assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya sakkassa devānamindassa vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā ākāse antalikkhe tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānentassa “aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhitaṃ, aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhitaṃ, aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhita”nti (udā. 27).

The Blessed One, with his divine ear element, purified and surpassing that of humans, heard the sound of Sakka, lord of the devas, who, having risen up into the sky, was uttering an inspired utterance three times in the sky, in space: “Oh, the gift! The supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa! Oh, the gift! The supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa! Oh, the gift! The supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa!”

Atha [P 1.0430] kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

“Piṇḍapātikassa [M 1.0272] bhikkhuno,

Attabharassa anaññaposino;

Devā pihayanti tādino,

Upasantassa sadā satīmato”ti. (udā. 27);

“Even the devas cherish such a one: the monk who goes for alms, who supports himself and is not supported by others, who is steadfast, with defilements calmed, and ever mindful.”

Imañca pana udānaṃ udānetvā, “bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo mama puttassa sīlagandhena āgantvā piṇḍapātaṃ adāsī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

And having uttered this inspired utterance, he said: “Bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, came because of the fragrance of my son's virtue and gave him almsfood,” and then spoke this verse:

56.

56.

“Appamatto ayaṃ gandho, yvāyaṃ tagaracandanaṃ;

Yo ca sīlavataṃ gandho, vāti devesu uttamo”ti.

“This fragrance of tagara and sandalwood is of little measure; but the fragrance of the virtuous wafts supreme among the devas.”

Tattha appamattoti parittappamāṇo. Yo ca sīlavatanti yo pana sīlavantānaṃ sīlagandho, so tagaraṃ viya lohitacandanaṃ viya ca parittako na hoti, ativiya uḷāro vipphārito. Teneva kāraṇena vāti devesu uttamoti pavaro seṭṭho hutvā devesu ca manussesu ca sabbatthameva vāyati, ottharanto gacchatīti.

Therein, 'of little measure' means small in extent. 'And the fragrance of the virtuous' means that the fragrance of virtue of the virtuous is not small like that of tagara or red sandalwood; it is exceedingly grand and widespread. For that very reason, it is said, 'it wafts supreme among the devas.' 'It wafts supreme among the devas' means that, being excellent and noble, it wafts everywhere among both devas and humans, reaching them by pervading all directions.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0242] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth. The discourse became beneficial for the great assembly of people.

Mahākassapattherapiṇḍapātadinnavatthu dasamaṃ.

The Story of the Almsfood Given to the Elder Mahākassapa is the Tenth.

11. Godhikattheraparinibbānavatthu

11. The Story of the Elder Godhika's Parinibbāna.

Tesaṃ [P 1.0431] sampannasīlānanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharanto godhikattherassa parinibbānaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Of those accomplished in virtue…”—this Dhamma discourse was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery near Rājagaha, concerning the Parinibbāna of the Elder Godhika.

So hi āyasmā isigilipasse kāḷasilāyaṃ viharanto appamatto ātāpī pahitatto sāmāyikaṃ cetovimuttiṃ phusitvā ekassa anussāyikassa rogassa vasena tato parihāyi. So dutiyampi tatiyampi chakkhattuṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvā parihīno, sattame vāre uppādetvā cintesi – “ahaṃ chakkhattuṃ jhānā parihīno, parihīnajjhānassa kho [M 1.0273] pana aniyatā gati, idāneva satthaṃ āharissāmī”ti kesoropanasatthakaṃ gahetvā galanāḷiṃ chindituṃ pañcake nipajji. Māro tassa cittaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ bhikkhu satthaṃ āharitukāmo, satthaṃ āharantā kho pana jīvite nirapekkhā honti, te vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattampi pāpuṇanti, sacāhaṃ etaṃ vāressāmi, na me vacanaṃ karissati, satthāraṃ vārāpessāmī”ti aññātakavesena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha –

Indeed, that venerable one, while dwelling on the Black Rock at the side of Mount Isigili, being diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained temporary liberation of mind but fell away from it due to a certain recurrent disease. A second time, a third time, up to six times, he produced jhāna but fell away from it. On the seventh occasion, having produced it, he thought: “I have fallen away from jhāna six times. For one who has fallen from jhāna, the future destination is indeed uncertain. Right now I shall take a knife.” Taking a razor for shaving hair, he lay down on his couch to cut his throat. Māra, knowing his thought, thought: “This monk wishes to take a knife. Those who take a knife are indifferent to life. Having established insight, they may even attain Arahantship. If I were to stop him, he would not do as I say. I will have the Teacher stop him.” Assuming an unknown guise, he approached the Teacher and said this:

“Mahāvīra [P 1.0432] mahāpañña, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Sabbaverabhayātīta, pāde vandāmi cakkhuma.

“Great Hero, great in wisdom, blazing with psychic power and renown, you who have overcome all enmity and fear, O Visionary, I pay homage to your feet.”

“Sāvako te mahāvīra, maraṇaṃ maraṇābhibhū;

Ākaṅkhati cetayati, taṃ nisedha jutindhara.

“O Great Hero, your disciple, overcome by death, desires death, he intends it. O Bearer of Radiance, prevent him.”

“Kathañhi bhagavā tuyhaṃ, sāvako sāsane rato;

Appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃ kayirā jane sutā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

“How indeed, O Blessed One, renowned among people, could your disciple, delighting in the teaching, a learner whose mind has not yet attained its goal, pass away?”

Tasmiṃ [V 1.0243] khaṇe therena satthaṃ āharitaṃ hoti. Satthā “māro aya”nti viditvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the knife had been taken by the elder. The Teacher, knowing, “This is Māra,” spoke this verse:

“Evañhi dhīrā kubbanti, nāvakaṅkhanti jīvitaṃ;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, godhiko parinibbuto”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

“Thus indeed do the wise act; they do not long for life. Having uprooted craving with its root, Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.”

Atha kho bhagavā sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ therassa satthaṃ āharitvā nipannaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe māro pāpimā “kattha nu kho imassa paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhita”nti dhūmarāsi viya timirapuñjo viya ca hutvā sabbadisāsu therassa viññāṇaṃ samanvesati. Bhagavā taṃ dhūmatimirabhāvaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dassetvā “eso kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā godhikassa kulaputtassa viññāṇaṃ samanvesati ‘kattha godhikassa kulaputtassa viññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhita’nti. Apatiṭṭhitena ca, bhikkhave, viññāṇena godhiko kulaputto parinibbuto”ti āha. Māropi tassa viññāṇaṭṭhānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asakkonto kumārakavaṇṇo hutvā [P 1.0433] beluvapaṇḍuvīṇaṃ ādāya satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi –

Then the Blessed One, together with many monks, went to the place where the elder who had taken the knife lay. At that moment, Māra the evil one, thinking, “Where indeed is the relinking consciousness of this one established?” became like a mass of smoke and a heap of darkness and searched in all directions for the elder’s consciousness. The Blessed One, showing that state of smoke and darkness to the monks, said, “Bhikkhus, this is Māra the evil one searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, wondering, ‘Where is the consciousness of the clansman Godhika established?’ Bhikkhus, with consciousness unestablished, the clansman Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.” Māra, too, being unable to see the place of his consciousness, taking the form of a young boy and carrying a lute the color of a ripe beluva fruit, approached the Teacher and asked:

“Uddhaṃ [M 1.0274] adho ca tiriyaṃ, disā anudisā svahaṃ;

Anvesaṃ nādhigacchāmi, godhiko so kuhiṃ gato”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

“Above, below, and across, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, I have searched but do not find him. Where has that Godhika gone?”

Atha naṃ satthā āha –

Then the Teacher said to him:

“Yo dhīro dhitisampanno, jhāyī jhānarato sadā;

Ahorattaṃ anuyuñjaṃ, jīvitaṃ anikāmayaṃ.

“That wise one, endowed with fortitude, a meditator ever delighting in jhāna, striving day and night, not desiring life,

“Jetvāna maccuno senaṃ, anāgantvā punabbhavaṃ;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, godhiko parinibbuto”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

having conquered the army of Death, not returning to a future existence, having uprooted craving with its root, Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.”

Evaṃ vutte māro pāpimā bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

When this was said, Māra the evil one addressed the Blessed One with a verse:

“Tassa [V 1.0244] sokaparetassa, vīṇā kacchā abhassatha;

Tato so dummano yakkho, tatthevantaradhāyathā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

“From him, who was overcome with sorrow, the lute slipped from his armpit. Then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.”

Satthāpi “kiṃ te, pāpima, godhikassa kulaputtassa nibbattaṭṭhānena? Tassa hi nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ satampi sahassampi daṭṭhuṃ na sakkotī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher also said, “What use is the place of rebirth of the clansman Godhika to you, evil one? Indeed, a hundred or even a thousand of those like you are not able to see his place of rebirth.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

57.

57.

“Tesaṃ sampannasīlānaṃ, appamādavihārinaṃ;

Sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ, māro maggaṃ na vindatī”ti.

“Māra does not find the path of those who are accomplished in virtue, who dwell in heedfulness, and are liberated through right understanding.”

Tattha [P 1.0434] tesanti yathā appatiṭṭhitena viññāṇena godhiko kulaputto parinibbuto, ye ca evaṃ parinibbāyanti, tesaṃ sampannasīlānanti paripuṇṇasīlānaṃ. Appamādavihārinanti satiavippavāsasaṅkhātena appamādena viharantānaṃ. Sammadaññā vimuttānanti hetunā ñāyena kāraṇena jānitvā “tadaṅgavimuttiyā, vikkhambhanavimuttiyā, samucchedavimuttiyā, paṭippassaddhivimuttiyā, nissaraṇavimuttiyā”ti imāhi pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuttānaṃ. Māro maggaṃ na vindatīti evarūpānaṃ mahākhīṇāsavānaṃ sabbathāmena maggantopi māro gatamaggaṃ na vindati na labhati na passatīti.

Herein, `tesaṃ` (of those) refers to the clansman Godhika, who attained Parinibbāna with unestablished consciousness, and to those who attain Parinibbāna in the same way. `Sampannasīlānaṃ` (of those accomplished in virtue) means of those perfected in virtue. `Appamādavihārinaṃ` (of those dwelling heedfully) means of those dwelling with heedfulness, which is characterized by the non-absence of mindfulness. `Sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ` (of those liberated through right understanding) means of those who, knowing by cause, method, and reason, are liberated by these five liberations: liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by suppression, liberation by eradication, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape. `Māro maggaṃ na vindati` (Māra does not find the path) means that Māra, though searching with all his might, does not find, obtain, or see the path taken by such great destroyers of the taints.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā jātāti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth. The discourse became beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Godhikattheraparinibbānavatthu ekādasamaṃ.

The Story of the Parinibbāna of the Elder Godhika is the Eleventh.

12. Garahadinnavatthu

12. The Story of Garahadinna

Yathā [M 1.0275] saṅkāraṭṭhānasminti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto garahadinnaṃ nāma nigaṇṭhasāvakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, beginning with `Yathā saṅkāraṭṭhānasmiṃ`, concerning a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas named Garahadinna.

Sāvatthiyañhi sirigutto ca garahadinno cāti dve sahāyakā ahesuṃ. Tesu sirigutto upāsako buddhasāvako, garahadinno nigaṇṭhasāvako[P 1.0435]. Taṃ nigaṇṭhā abhikkhaṇaṃ evaṃ vadanti – “tava sahāyakaṃ siriguttaṃ ‘kiṃ tvaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamasi, tassa santike kiṃ labhissasī’ti [V 1.0245] vatvā yathā amhe upasaṅkamitvā amhākañca deyyadhammaṃ dassati, kiṃ evaṃ ovadituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Garahadinno tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā abhikkhaṇaṃ gantvā ṭhitanisinnaṭṭhānādīsu siriguttaṃ evaṃ ovadati – “samma, kiṃ te samaṇena gotamena, taṃ upasaṅkamitvā kiṃ labhissasi, kiṃ te mama, ayye, upasaṅkamitvā tesaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? Sirigutto tassa kathaṃ sutvāpi bahū divase tuṇhī hutvā nibbijjitvā ekadivasaṃ, “samma, tvaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ āgantvā maṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānādīsu evaṃ vadesi, ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā kiṃ labhissasi, mama, ayye, upasaṅkamitvā tesaṃ dānaṃ dehī’ti, kathehi tāva me, tava, ayyā, kiṃ jānantī”ti? “‘Aho, sāmi, mā evaṃ vada, mama ayyānaṃ aññātaṃ nāma natthi, sabbaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ kāyavacīmanokammaṃ idaṃ bhavissati, idaṃ na bhavissatī’ti sabbaṃ bhabbābhabbaṃ jānantī”ti? “Evaṃ vadesī”ti. “Āma, vademī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ, atibhāriyaṃ te kataṃ, ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayhaṃ etamatthaṃ anācikkhantena, ajja mayā [P 1.0436] ayyānaṃ ñāṇānubhāvo ñāto, gaccha, samma, ayye, mama vacanena nimantehī”ti. So nigaṇṭhānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā te vanditvā “mayhaṃ sahāyako sirigutto svātanāya tumhe nimantetī”ti āha. “Siriguttena sāmaṃ tvaṃ vutto”ti? “Āma, ayyā”ti. Te haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā “nipphannaṃ no kiccaṃ, siriguttassa amhesu pasannakālato paṭṭhāya kā nāma sampatti amhākaṃ na bhavissatī”ti vadiṃsu.

Indeed, in Sāvatthī, there were two friends, Sirigutta and Garahadinna. Of them, Sirigutta was a lay disciple, a follower of the Buddha, while Garahadinna was a follower of the Nigaṇṭhas. The Nigaṇṭhas would repeatedly say to him: 'Why do you not speak to your friend Sirigutta, saying, “Why do you approach the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain from him?” and advise him in such a way that he will approach us and give us offerings?' Hearing their words, Garahadinna would frequently go and advise Sirigutta in various situations, whether standing or sitting, saying: 'Friend, what use is the ascetic Gotama to you? What will you gain by approaching him? Why is it not proper for you to approach my masters and give them an offering?' Having heard his words, Sirigutta remained silent for many days. Then, becoming weary of it, one day he said: 'Friend, you repeatedly come to me in various situations and say, “What will you gain by approaching the ascetic Gotama? Approach my masters and give them an offering.” First, tell me, what do your masters know?' 'Ah, sir, do not say such a thing! There is nothing my masters do not know. They know everything—past, future, and present; all bodily, verbal, and mental actions; what will be and what will not be. They know everything that is possible and impossible.' 'Is that what you say?' 'Yes, that is what I say.' 'If that is so, you have done a very grave thing by not telling me of this matter for so long. Today I have come to know the power of your masters' knowledge. Go, friend, invite your masters in my name.' So he went to the Nigaṇṭhas, paid homage to them, and said, 'My friend Sirigutta invites you for tomorrow.' 'Did Sirigutta tell you himself?' 'Yes, masters.' Delighted and overjoyed, they said, 'Our work is accomplished! From the time Sirigutta has faith in us, what prosperity will not be ours?'

Siriguttassāpi mahantaṃ nivesanaṃ. So tasmiṃ dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare ubhato dīghaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpetvā gūthakalalassa pūrāpesi. Bahiāvāṭe dvīsu pariyantesu khāṇuke koṭṭāpetvā tesu rajjuyo bandhāpetvā āsanānaṃ purimapāde āvāṭassa purimapasse ṭhapāpetvā pacchimapāde rajjukesu ṭhapāpesi. “Evaṃ nisinnakāle evaṃ avaṃsirā patissantī”ti [M 1.0276] maññamāno yathā āvāṭo na paññāyati, evaṃ āsanānaṃ upari paccattharaṇāni dāpesi. Mahantā mahantā cāṭiyo ṭhapāpetvā kadalipaṇṇehi ca setapilotikāhi ca mukhāni bandhāpetvā tā tucchā eva gehassa pacchimabhāge bahi yāgubhattasitthasappitelamadhuphāṇitapūvacuṇṇamakkhitā katvā ṭhapāpesi. Garahadinno pātova tassa gharaṃ vegena gantvā, “ayyānaṃ sakkāro sajjito”ti pucchi. “Āma, samma, sajjito”ti. “Kahaṃ pana eso”ti. “Etāsu ettikāsu cāṭīsu yāgu, ettikāsu bhattaṃ, ettikāsu sappiphāṇitapūvādīni [P 1.0437] pūritāni, āsanāni paññattānī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā gato tassa gatakāle pañcasatā nigaṇṭhā āgamiṃsu. Sirigutto gehā nikkhamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena nigaṇṭhe vanditvā tesaṃ purato añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhito evaṃ cintesi – “tumhe kira atītādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ jānātha, evaṃ tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhākena mayhaṃ [V 1.0246] kathitaṃ. Sace sabbaṃ tumhe jānātha, mayhaṃ gehaṃ mā pavisittha. Mama gehaṃ paviṭṭhānañhi vo neva yāgu atthi, na bhattādīni. Sace ajānitvā pavisissatha, gūthaāvāṭe vo pātetvā pothessāmī”ti evaṃ cintetvā purisānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi. Evaṃ tesaṃ nisīdanabhāvaṃ ñatvā pacchimapasse ṭhatvā āsanānaṃ upari paccattharaṇāni apaneyyātha, mā tāni asucinā makkhayiṃsūti.

Sirigutta also had a large residence. Between two of his houses, he had a long pit dug and had it filled with excrement and mire. At the outer edges of the pit, he had stakes driven in and ropes tied to them. He had the front legs of the seats placed on the near edge of the pit and the back legs placed on the ropes. He had them set up thinking, 'Thus, at the very moment of sitting, they will fall headfirst.' So that the pit would not be apparent, he had coverings placed over the seats. He had very large jars set up, and having had their mouths covered with banana leaves and white cloths, he had them placed, empty, outside in the back part of the house, after having them smeared with remnants of rice-gruel, cooked rice, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and cake-flour. Garahadinna went quickly to his house early in the morning and asked, 'Is the offering for the masters prepared?' 'Yes, friend, it is prepared.' 'And where is it?' 'In so many of these jars is rice-gruel, in so many is cooked rice, and in so many are ghee, molasses, cakes, and so on, all filled up. The seats are prepared.' Saying, 'Excellent,' he departed. When he had gone, five hundred Nigaṇṭhas arrived. Sirigutta came out of the house, paid homage to the Nigaṇṭhas with the five-point prostration, and stood before them with his hands raised in reverence, thinking: 'It is said that you know everything, of the past and so on; thus was I told by your attendant. If you know everything, do not enter my house. For those who enter my house, there is neither rice-gruel nor food and so on. If you enter without knowing, I will have you thrown into the pit of excrement and have you beaten.' Having thought thus, he gave a signal to his men: 'Thus, knowing that they are about to sit, stand at the back and remove the coverings from the seats, lest they be smeared with filth.'

Atha nigaṇṭhe “ito etha, bhante”ti āha. Nigaṇṭhā pavisitvā paññattāsanesu nisīdituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Atha ne manussā vadiṃsu – “āgametha, bhante, mā tāva nisīdathā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Amhākaṃ gehaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ ayyānaṃ vattaṃ ñatvā nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, āvuso”ti? “Attano attano pattāsanamūlesu ṭhatvā sabbepi ekappahāreneva nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Idaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – “ekasmiṃ āvāṭe patite ‘mā, āvuso, avasesā āsane nisīdantū’ti [P 1.0438] vattuṃ mā labhatū”ti. Te “sādhū”ti vatvā “imehi kathitakathaṃ amhehi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintayiṃsu. Atha sabbe attano attano pattāsanamūle paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha ne, “bhante, khippaṃ ekappahāreneva nisīdathā”ti vatvā tesaṃ nisinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā āsanānaṃ upari paccattharaṇāni nīhariṃsu. Nigaṇṭhā ekappahāreneva nisinnā, rajjūnaṃ upari ṭhapitā āsanapādā bhaṭṭhā, nigaṇṭhā avaṃsirā āvāṭe patiṃsu. Sirigutto tesu patitesu dvāraṃ pidahitvā [M 1.0277] te uttiṇṇuttiṇṇe “atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ kasmā na jānāthā”ti daṇḍehi pāthetvā “ettakaṃ etesaṃ vaṭṭissatī”ti dvāraṃ vivarāpesi. Te nikkhamitvā palāyituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Gamanamagge pana tesaṃ sudhāparikammakataṃ bhūmiṃ picchilaṃ kārāpesi. Te tattha asaṇṭhahitvā patite patite puna pothāpetvā “alaṃ ettakaṃ tumhāka”nti uyyojesi. Te “nāsitamhā tayā, nāsitamhā tayā”ti kandantā upaṭṭhākassa gehadvāraṃ agamaṃsu.

Then he said to the Nigaṇṭhas, "Venerable sirs, come here." The Nigaṇṭhas entered and began to sit on the prepared seats. Then the men said to them, "Wait, venerable sirs, do not sit down yet." "For what reason?" "It is proper for the venerable ones who have entered our house to sit down after knowing the custom." "What is proper to do, friends?" "It is proper for all to stand at the base of their respective seats and sit down all together at once." This, it seems, was his intention: "When one falls into the pit, let him not be able to say, 'Friends, let the others not sit on the seats.'" They said, "Good," and thought, "It is proper for us to do as these men have said." Then all stood in order at the base of their respective seats. Then, saying, "Venerable sirs, sit down quickly all at once," and knowing that they had sat down, they removed the coverings from above the seats. The Nigaṇṭhas sat down all at once; the legs of the seats placed on the ropes slipped, and the Nigaṇṭhas fell headfirst into the pit. When they had fallen, Sirigutta closed the door and, as they climbed out one by one, had them beaten with sticks, saying, "Why do you not know the past, future, and present?" Then, thinking, "This much will suffice for them," he had the door opened. They came out and began to flee. On their path of departure, however, he had the plastered ground made slippery. There, unable to stand firm, he had them beaten again as they fell, and sent them away, saying, "This much is enough for you." Crying, "We have been ruined by you, we have been ruined by you," they went to the door of their supporter's house.

Garahadinno taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā kuddho “nāsitamhi siriguttena, hatthaṃ pasāretvā vandantānaṃ sadevake loke yathāruciyā dātuṃ samatthe nāma puññakkhettabhūte mama, ayye[P 1.0439], pothāpetvā byasanaṃ pāpesī”ti rājakulaṃ gantvā tassa kahāpaṇasahassaṃ daṇḍaṃ kāresi. Athassa rājā sāsanaṃ pesesi. So gantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā, “deva, upaparikkhitvā daṇḍaṃ gaṇhatha, mā anupaparikkhitvā”ti āha. “Upaparikkhitvā gaṇhissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, devā”ti. “Tena hi gaṇhāhī”ti. Deva, mayhaṃ sahāyako nigaṇṭhasāvako maṃ upasaṅkamitvā ṭhitanisinnaṭṭhānādīsu abhiṇhaṃ evaṃ vadesi – “samma, kiṃ te samaṇena gotamena, taṃ upasaṅkamitvā kiṃ labhissasī”ti idaṃ [V 1.0247] ādiṃ katvā sirigutto sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “deva, sace imasmiṃ kāraṇe daṇḍaṃ gahetuṃ yuttaṃ, gaṇhathā”ti. Rājā garahadinnaṃ oloketvā “saccaṃ kira te evaṃ vutta”nti āha. “Saccaṃ, devā”ti. Tvaṃ ettakampi ajānante satthāroti gahetvā vicaranto “sabbaṃ jānantī”ti kiṃ kāraṇā tathāgatasāvakassa kathesi. “Tayā āropitadaṇḍo tuyhameva hotū”ti evaṃ sveva daṇḍaṃ pāpito, tasseva kulūpakā pothetvā nīhaṭā.

Seeing that injurious act, Garahadinna became enraged and went to the royal court, saying, "I have been ruined by Sirigutta! He has had my venerable ones—who are a field of merit, capable of giving as they please in this world with its devas to those who pay homage with outstretched hands—beaten and brought to ruin!" And he had a fine of a thousand kahāpaṇas imposed on him. Then the king sent a summons to Sirigutta. He went, paid homage to the king, and said, "Your Majesty, impose the fine after investigating; do not impose it without investigating." "I will investigate before imposing," replied the king. "Very well, Your Majesty." "Then state your case." "Your Majesty, my friend is a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas. He would approach me and, in places of standing, sitting, and so on, repeatedly say this: 'Friend, what use is the ascetic Gotama to you? What will you gain by approaching him?'" Starting with this, Sirigutta related the entire event and said, "Your Majesty, if it is proper to impose a fine in this matter, then impose it." The king looked at Garahadinna and asked, "Is it true that you spoke thus?" "It is true, Your Majesty." "You wander about taking as teachers those who do not know even this much; for what reason did you say 'they know everything' to a disciple of the Tathāgata? Let the fine you imposed be upon you alone." Thus, the fine was imposed upon that very person, and his own family preceptors were beaten and driven out.

So taṃ kujjhitvā tato paṭṭhāya aḍḍhamāsamattampi siriguttena saddhiṃ akathetvā cintesi – “evaṃ vicarituṃ mayhaṃ ayuttaṃ, etassa kulūpakānampi mayā byasanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti siriguttaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “sahāya siriguttā”ti. “Kiṃ, sammā”ti? “Ñātisuhajjānaṃ [P 1.0440] nāma kalahopi hoti vivādopi, kiṃ tvaṃ kiñci na kathesi, kasmā evaṃ karosī”ti? “Samma, tava mayā saddhiṃ akathanato na kathemī”ti. “Yaṃ, samma, kataṃ, katameva taṃ na mayaṃ mettiṃ bhindissāmā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya ubhopi ekaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti nisīdanti[M 1.0278]. Athekadivasaṃ sirigutto garahadinnaṃ āha – “kiṃ te nigaṇṭhehi, te upasaṅkamitvā kiṃ labhissasi, mama satthāraṃ upasaṅkamituṃ vā ayyānaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ vā kiṃ te na vaṭṭatī”ti? Sopi etameva paccāsīsati, tenassa kaṇḍuvanaṭṭhāne nakhena vilekhitaṃ viya ahosi. So, “sirigutta, tava satthā kiṃ jānātī”ti pucchi. “Ambho, mā evaṃ vada, satthu me ajānitabbaṃ nāma natthi, atītādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ jānāti, soḷasahākārehi sattānaṃ cittaṃ paricchindatī”ti. “Ahaṃ evaṃ na jānāmi, kasmā mayhaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ na kathesi, tena hi tvaṃ gaccha, tava satthāraṃ svātanāya nimantehi, bhojessāmi, pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mama bhikkhaṃ gaṇhituṃ vadehī”ti.

He, being angered at him, from then on did not speak with Sirigutta for half a month. Then he thought, "It is not proper for me to behave like this. It is proper for me to bring ruin even upon his family preceptors." He approached Sirigutta and said, "Friend Sirigutta." "What is it, friend?" "Among relatives and friends, quarrels and disputes do arise. Why do you not say anything? Why do you act like this?" "Friend, I do not speak because you do not speak with me." "Friend, what has been done is done. We shall not break our friendship." From then on, both of them stood and sat in the same place. Then one day, Sirigutta said to Garahadinna, "What use are the Nigaṇṭhas to you? What will you gain by approaching them? Why is it not proper for you to approach my Teacher or to give alms to the venerable ones?" He too was hoping for just this, so for him it was like scratching an itchy spot with a fingernail. He asked, "Sirigutta, what does your Teacher know?" "Friend, do not speak thus. There is nothing that is unknowable to my Teacher. He knows everything, distinguished as past, future, and present. He discerns the minds of beings in sixteen ways." "I did not know this. Why did you not tell me for so long? In that case, you go and invite your Teacher for tomorrow's meal. I will provide food. Tell him to accept my alms-food together with five hundred monks."

Sirigutto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā evamāha – “bhante, mama sahāyako garahadinno tumhe nimantāpeti, pañcahi kira bhikkhusatehi [P 1.0441] saddhiṃ sve tassa bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatha, purimadivase kho pana tassa kulūpakānaṃ mayā idaṃ nāma kataṃ, mayā katassa paṭikaraṇampi na jānāmi, tumhākaṃ suddhacittena bhikkhaṃ dātukāmatampi na jānāmi, āvajjetvā yuttaṃ ce, adhivāsetha. No ce, mā adhivāsayitthā”ti. Satthā “kiṃ nu kho so amhākaṃ kātu kāmo”ti āvajjetvā addasa “dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare mahantaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpetvā asītisakaṭamattāni khadiradārūni āharāpetvā pūrāpetvā aggiṃ datvā amhe aṅgāraāvāṭe pātetvā niggaṇhitukāmo”ti. Puna āvajjesi – “kiṃ nu kho tattha gatapaccayā attho atthi, natthī”ti. Tato idaṃ addasa – “ahaṃ aṅgāraāvāṭe pādaṃ pasāressāmi, taṃ paṭicchādetvā [V 1.0248] ṭhapitakilañjaṃ antaradhāyissati, aṅgārakāsuṃ bhinditvā cakkamattaṃ mahāpadumaṃ uṭṭhahissati, athāhaṃ padumakaṇṇikā akkamanto āsane nisīdissāmi, pañcasatā bhikkhūpi tatheva gantvā nisīdissanti, mahājano sannipatissati, ahaṃ tasmiṃ samāgame dvīhi gāthāhi anumodanaṃ karissāmi, anumodanapariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo bhavissati, sirigutto ca garahadinno ca sotāpannā bhavissanti, attano ca dhanarāsiṃ sāsane vikirissanti, imaṃ kulaputtaṃ nissāya mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti [P 1.0442] bhikkhaṃ adhivāsesi.

Sirigutta approached the Teacher, paid homage, and said thus: "Venerable Sir, my friend Garahadinna has you invited. Please accept his alms-meal tomorrow, together with five hundred monks. However, on a previous day, a certain thing was done by me to his family preceptors. I do not know what amends to make for what I have done, nor do I know if he desires to give you an alms-meal with a pure mind. Having reflected, if it is suitable, please consent. If it is not, please do not consent." The Teacher, reflecting, "What now does he wish to do to us?" saw this: "He wishes to have a great pit dug between the two houses, have it filled with eighty cartloads of acacia wood, set it on fire, and, having caused us to fall into the pit of embers, to subdue us." He reflected again: "Is there benefit on account of going there, or is there not?" Then he saw this: "I will extend my foot over the pit of embers. The mat placed to cover it will disappear. Splitting the pit of embers, a great lotus the size of a wheel will arise. Then I, stepping on the lotus pericarp, will sit on the seat. The five hundred monks will also go there and sit in the same way. A great crowd of people will assemble. In that assembly, I will give a blessing with two verses. At the conclusion of the blessing, there will be the realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings. Both Sirigutta and Garahadinna will become stream-enterers, and they will distribute their wealth in the Dispensation. On account of this son of good family, it is fitting for me to go." Thus, he consented to the alms-meal.

Sirigutto gantvā satthu adhivāsanaṃ garahadinnassa ārocetvā “lokajeṭṭhassa sakkāraṃ karohī”ti āha. Garahadinno “idānissa [M 1.0279] kattabbayuttakaṃ jānissāmī”ti dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare mahantaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpetvā asītisakaṭamattāni khadiradārūni āharāpetvā pūrāpetvā aggiṃ datvā khadiraṅgārarāsīnaṃ yojāpetvā sabbarattiṃ dhamāpetvā khadiraṅgārarāsiṃ kārāpetvā āvāṭamatthake rukkhapadarāni ṭhapāpetvā kilañjena paṭicchādetvā gomayena limpāpetvā ekena passena dubbaladaṇḍake attharitvā gamanamaggaṃ kāresi, “evaṃ akkantaakkantakāle daṇḍakesu bhaggesu parivaṭṭetvā aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patissantī”ti maññamāno gehapacchābhāge siriguttena ṭhapitaniyāmeneva cāṭiyo ṭhapāpesi, āsanānipi tatheva paññāpesi. Sirigutto pātova tassa gehaṃ gantvā “kato te, samma, sakkāro”ti āha. “Āma, sammā”ti. “Kahaṃ pana so”ti? “Ehi, passāmā”ti sabbaṃ siriguttena dassitanayeneva dassesi. Sirigutto “sādhu, sammā”ti āha. Mahājano sannipati. Micchādiṭṭhikena hi nimantite mahanto sannipāto ahosi. Micchādiṭṭhikāpi “samaṇassa gotamassa vippakāraṃ [P 1.0443] passissāmā”ti sannipatanti, sammādiṭṭhikāpi “ajja satthā mahādhammadesanaṃ desessati, buddhavisayaṃ buddhalīlaṃ upadhāressāmā”ti sannipatanti.

Sirigutta went and, having informed Garahadinna of the Teacher's consent, said, 'Prepare an offering for the Elder of the World.'
