Garahadinna, thinking, 'Now I shall know what is fitting to be done to him,' had a great pit dug between the two houses, had eighty cartloads of acacia wood brought and the pit filled, set it on fire, had the heaps of acacia embers arranged, and, having kept them smouldering all night, had a heap of acacia embers made. On top of the pit, he had wooden planks placed, had it covered with a mat, had it smeared with cow-dung, and, having spread weak bamboo slats on one side, he had a walking path made. Thinking, 'Thus, at the very time of stepping, when the slats are broken, they will turn over and fall into the pit of embers,' he had pots placed in the back part of thehouse in the very same manner arranged by Sirigutta; he also had the seats prepared in the same way. Sirigutta, early in the morning, went to his house and said, 'Friend, is the offering prepared by you?' 'Yes, friend.' 'But where is it?' 'Come, let us see.' He showed everything in the very manner shown by Sirigutta. Sirigutta said, 'Good, friend.' A great crowd of people assembled. For when an invitation is made by one with wrong view, a great assembly occurs. Those with wrong view also assemble, thinking, 'We shall see the ruin of the ascetic Gotama.' Those with right view also assemble, thinking, 'Today the Teacher will deliver a great Dhamma discourse; we shall observe the Buddha's range and the Buddha's majestic bearing.'

Punadivase satthā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ garahadinnassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. So gehā nikkhamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā purato añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhito cintesi – “bhante, ‘tumhe kira atītādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ jānātha, sattānaṃ soḷasahākārehi cittaṃ paricchindathā’ti evaṃ tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhākena mayhaṃ kathitaṃ. Sace jānātha, mayhaṃ gehaṃ mā pavisittha. Paviṭṭhānañhi vo neva yāgu atthi, na bhattādīni, sabbe kho pana tumhe aṅgārakāsuyaṃ pātetvā niggaṇhissāmī”ti. Evaṃ cintetvā satthu pattaṃ gahetvā “ito etha bhagavā”ti vatvā, “bhante, amhākaṃ gehaṃ āgatānaṃ vattaṃ ñatvā āgantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, āvuso”ti? “Ekekassa pavisitvā purato gantvā nisinnakāle pacchā aññena [V 1.0249] āgantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “purato gacchantaṃ aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patitaṃ disvā avasesā na āgacchissanti, ekekameva pātetvā niggaṇhissāmī”ti. Satthā “sādhū”ti vatvā ekakova pāyāsi. Garahadinno aṅgārakāsuṃ patvā apasakkitvā ṭhito [M 1.0280] “purato yātha, bhante”ti āha. Atha satthā aṅgārakāsumatthake pādaṃ pasāresi, kilañjaṃ antaradhāyi, aṅgārakāsuṃ bhinditvā cakkamattāni padumāni uṭṭhahiṃsu[P 1.0444]. Satthā padumakaṇṇikā akkamanto gantvā paññatte buddhāsane nisīdi, bhikkhūpi tatheva gantvā nisīdiṃsu. Garahadinnassa kāyato ḍāho uṭṭhahi.

On the next day, the Teacher, together with five hundred monks, went to the door of Garahadinna’s house. He, having come out from the house, having paid homage with the five-point prostration, stood in front with hands raised in reverence and thought: 'Venerable Sir, it was told to me by your attendant thus: "It is said that you know everything, distinguished as past and so on; it is said that you discern the minds of beings by sixteen modes." If you know this, do not enter my house. For, for those of you who have entered, there is neither gruel nor rice and so on. Indeed, I will subdue all of you by throwing you into the pit of embers.' Having thought thus, he took the Teacher’s bowl and, saying, 'Come this way, Blessed One,' he said, 'Venerable Sir, it is proper to come having known the custom for those who come to our house.' 'What is proper to do, friend?' 'It is proper for each one to enter, go forward, and be seated, and only then for another to come afterwards.' It is said this was his thought: 'Seeing the one going in front fallen into the pit of embers, the remaining ones will not come. I will subdue them, having thrown them in just one by one.' The Teacher, saying, 'Good,' proceeded all alone. Garahadinna, having reached the pit of embers, stepped back and stood, saying, 'Go forward, Venerable Sir.' Then the Teacher extended his foot over the pit of embers; the mat vanished. Splitting the pit of embers, lotuses the size of wheels arose. The Teacher, stepping on the lotus pericarps, went and sat down on the prepared Buddha-seat. The monks also went and sat down in the same way. From Garahadinna’s body, a burning arose.

So vegena gantvā siriguttaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “sāmi, me tāṇaṃ hohī”ti āha. “Kiṃ eta”nti? “Pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ gehe yāgu vā bhattādīni vā natthi, kiṃ nu kho karomī”ti? “Kiṃ pana tayā kata”nti āha. Ahaṃ dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare mahantaṃ āvāṭaṃ aṅgārassa pūraṃ kāresiṃ – “tattha pātetvā niggaṇhissāmī”ti. “Atha naṃ bhinditvā mahāpadumāni uṭṭhahiṃsu. Sabbe padumakaṇṇikā akkamitvā gantvā paññattāsanesu nisinnā, idāni kiṃ karomi, sāmī”ti? Nanu tvaṃ idāneva mayhaṃ “‘ettikā cāṭiyo, ettikā yāgu, ettakāni sattādīnī’ti dassesī”ti. “Musā taṃ, sāmi, tucchāva cāṭiyo”ti. Hotu, “gaccha, tāsu cāṭīsu yāguādīni olokehī”ti. Taṃ khaṇaññeva tena yāsu cāṭīsu “yāgū”ti vuttaṃ, tā yāguyā pūrayiṃsu, yāsu “bhattādīnī”ti vuttaṃ, tā bhattādīnaṃ paripuṇṇāva [P 1.0445] ahesuṃ. Taṃ sampattiṃ disvāva garahadinnassa sarīraṃ pītipāmojjena paripūritaṃ, cittaṃ pasannaṃ. So sakkaccaṃ buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā katabhattakiccassa satthuno anumodanaṃ kāretukāmo pattaṃ gaṇhi. Satthā anumodanaṃ karonto “ime sattā paññācakkhuno abhāveneva mama sāvakānaṃ buddhasāsanassa guṇaṃ na jānanti. Paññācakkhuvirahitā hi andhā nāma, paññavanto sacakkhukā nāmā”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

He quickly went to Sirigutta, approached him, and said, 'Master, be my refuge!' 'What is this matter?' 'In the house, there is no rice gruel or food for five hundred monks. What am I to do?' 'But what have you done?' he asked. 'Between the two houses, I had a large pit made full of embers, thinking, "Having made them fall in there, I will suppress them." Then, breaking through it, great lotuses arose. All the monks, having stepped on the lotus pericarps, went and sat on the prepared seats. Now what am I to do, master?' 'Did you not just now show me, saying, "There are this many pots of gruel, and this much food and other things"?' 'That was false, master; the pots are just empty.' 'Let it be. Go and look in those pots for gruel and other things.' In that very moment, those pots which were called 'gruel' filled with gruel, and those which were called 'food and other things' became completely full of food and other things. Upon seeing that success, Garahadinna's body was filled with rapture and joy, and his mind became serene. He respectfully served the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. When the Teacher had finished the business of the meal, wishing to have him give the thanksgiving, Garahadinna took the bowl. The Teacher, while giving the thanksgiving, said: 'These beings, only because of the absence of the eye of wisdom, do not know the quality of my disciples and of the Buddha's Dispensation. Indeed, those devoid of the eye of wisdom are called blind, while those with wisdom are called "those with eyes."' Having said this, he spoke these verses:

58.

58.

“Yathā saṅkāradhānasmiṃ, ujjhitasmiṃ mahāpathe;

Padumaṃ tattha jāyetha, sucigandhaṃ manoramaṃ.

Just as upon a rubbish heap, discarded on the highway, a lotus might arise there, of pure fragrance and delighting the mind.

59.

59.

“Evaṃ saṅkārabhūtesu, andhabhūte puthujjane;

Atirocati paññāya, sammāsambuddhasāvako”ti.

Even so, among the common folk who are like rubbish, who have become blind, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One outshines them with wisdom.

Tattha saṅkāradhānasminti saṅkāraṭhānasmiṃ, kacavararāsimhīti attho. Ujjhitasmiṃ mahāpatheti mahāmagge [V 1.0250] chaḍḍitasmiṃ. Sucigandhanti surabhigandhaṃ. Mano ettha ramatīti manoramaṃ. Saṅkārabhūtesūti saṅkāramiva bhūtesu. Puthujjaneti [M 1.0281] puthūnaṃ kilesānaṃ jananato evaṃladdhanāme [P 1.0446] lokiyamahājane. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma mahāpathe chaḍḍite saṅkārarāsimhi asucijegucchiyapaṭikūlepi sucigandhaṃ padumaṃ jāyetha, taṃ rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ manoramaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ uparimatthake patiṭṭhānārahameva bhaveyya, evameva saṅkārabhūtesupi puthujjanesu jāto nippaññassa mahājanassa acakkhukassa antare nibbattopi attano paññābalena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ, nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā pabbajito pabbajjāmattenapi, kato uttariṃ sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanāni ārādhetvāpi atirocati. Sammāsambuddhasāvako hi khīṇāsavo bhikkhu andhabhūte puthujjane atikkamitvā rocati virocati sobhatīti.

Therein, 'upon a rubbish heap' means in a place for rubbish, that is, on a heap of refuse. 'Discarded on the great path' means cast away on the main road. 'Of pure fragrance' means of sweet scent. 'The mind delights in it' is why it is called 'mind-delighting'. 'Among those who are like rubbish' means among those who are like rubbish. 'A common person' refers to the worldly masses, who are so-named because of their generating numerous defilements. This is what is meant: Just as on a great path, in a discarded rubbish heap, though it is impure, loathsome, and repulsive, a lotus of pure fragrance might be born, which would be mind-delighting, dear, and pleasing to kings, great ministers, and others, and worthy of being placed upon their heads; even so, one born among the common folk who are like rubbish, though arisen in the midst of the great populace that is without wisdom and without sight, through the power of his own wisdom sees the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, and having gone forth, becomes a monk. Not content with the mere act of going forth, but having further fulfilled virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he shines exceedingly. Indeed, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One, a monk whose cankers are destroyed, having surpassed the blind common folk, shines, shines brightly, and is beautiful.

Desanāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Garahadinno ca sirigutto ca sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Te sabbaṃ attano dhanaṃ buddhasāsane vippakiriṃsu. Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāramagamāsi. Bhikkhū sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “aho acchariyā buddhaguṇā nāma, tathārūpaṃ nāma khadiraṅgārarāsiṃ bhinditvā padumāni uṭṭhahiṃsū”ti. Satthā [P 1.0447] āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā, “imāya nāmā”ti vutte – “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ mama etarahi buddhabhūtassa aṅgārarāsimhā padumāni uṭṭhitāni, aparipakke ñāṇe vattamānassa bodhisattabhūtassapi me uṭṭhahiṃsū”ti vatvā, “kadā, bhante, ācikkhatha no”ti yācito atītaṃ āharitvā –

At the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings realized the Dhamma. Garahadinna and Sirigutta attained the fruit of stream-entry. They distributed all their wealth in the Buddha’s Dispensation. The Teacher, rising from his seat, went to the monastery. In the evening, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! From such a heap of acacia-wood embers, lotuses arose!' The Teacher approached and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not wonderful that for me, who am now a Buddha, lotuses arose from a heap of embers. They arose for me even when I was a Bodhisatta, while my knowledge was still immature.' Having been requested, 'When, venerable sir? Please tell us,' he brought forth the past:

“Kāmaṃ patāmi nirayaṃ, uddhaṃpādo avaṃsiro;

Nānariyaṃ karissāmi, handa piṇḍaṃ paṭiggahā”ti. (jā. 1.1.40) –

Willingly would I fall into hell, feet up and head down; I will not do an ignoble act. Come, accept the alms-food.

Idaṃ khadiraṅgārajātakaṃ vitthāretvā kathesīti.

He related this Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka in detail.

Garahadinnavatthu dvādasamaṃ.

The Story of Garahadinna, the twelfth.

Pupphavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of Flowers is finished.

Catuttho vaggo.

The Fourth Chapter.

5. Bālavaggo

5. 5. The Chapter on the Fool

1. Aññatarapurisavatthu

1. The Story of a Certain Man

Dīghā [V 1.0251][M 1.0282][P 2.0001] jāgarato rattīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto pasenadikosalañceva aññatarañca purisaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

“Long is the night to the wakeful…” This teaching on the Dhamma was given by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala and a certain man.

Rājā kira pasenadi kosalo ekasmiṃ chaṇadivase alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sabbasetaṃ ekaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ nāma hatthiṃ abhiruyha mahantena rājānubhāvena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. Ussāraṇāya vattamānāya leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi pothiyamāno mahājano palāyanto gīvaṃ parivaṭṭetvāpi oloketiyeva. Rājūnaṃ kira sudinnadānassetaṃ phalaṃ. Aññatarassāpi duggatapurisassa bhariyā sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparitale ṭhitā ekaṃ vātapānakavāṭaṃ vivaritvā rājānaṃ oloketvāva apagacchi. Rañño puṇṇacando valāhakantaraṃ paviṭṭho viya upaṭṭhāsi. So tassā paṭibaddhacitto hatthikkhandhato patanākārappatto viya hutvā khippaṃ [P 2.0002] nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā antepuraṃ pavisitvā ekaṃ vissāsakaṃ amaccaṃ āha – “asukaṭṭhāne te mayā olokitapāsādo diṭṭho”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Tatthekaṃ itthiṃ addasā”ti? “Addasaṃ, devā”ti. “Gaccha, tassā sasāmikaasāmikabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti. So gantvā tassā sasāmikabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgantvā rañño “sasāmikā”ti ārocesi. Atha raññā “tena hi tassā sāmikaṃ pakkosāhī”ti vutte so gantvā, “ehi, bho, rājā taṃ pakkosatī”ti āha. So “bhariyaṃ me nissāya bhayena uppannena bhavitabba”nti cintetvā rañño āṇaṃ paṭibāhituṃ asakkonto gantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ rājā “maṃ ito paṭṭhāya upaṭṭhāhī”ti āha. “Alaṃ, deva, ahaṃ attano kammaṃ katvā tumhākaṃ suṅkaṃ dadāmi, ghareyeva me jīvikā hotū”ti. “Tava suṅkena mayhaṃ attho natthi, ajjato paṭṭhāya maṃ upaṭṭhāhī”ti tassa phalakañca āvudhañca dāpesi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “kañcidevassa dosaṃ āropetvā ghātetvā bhariyaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ so maraṇabhayabhīto appamatto hutvā upaṭṭhāsi.

It is said that King Pasenadi of Kosala, on a certain festival day, mounted a fully adorned, all-white elephant named Puṇḍarīka and, with great royal splendor, circumambulated the city. As the procession was underway, the great crowd, though pushed back with clods and sticks, would flee and yet still turn their necks to look. This, it is said, is the fruit of a well-given gift for kings. The wife of a certain poor man, standing on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace, opened a window shutter, looked at the king, and then withdrew. To the king, she appeared like the full moon entering into the clouds. His mind became bound to her, and feeling as though he might fall from the elephant's back, he quickly finished circumambulating the city and entered the inner palace. He summoned a trusted minister and said: “At such-and-such a place, did you see the palace I was looking at?” “Yes, Your Majesty.” “Did you see a woman there?” “I saw her, Your Majesty.” “Go, find out whether she has a husband or not.” The minister went, and having learned that she had a husband, returned and informed the king, “She has a husband.” Then, when the king said, “In that case, summon her husband,” the minister went and said, “Come, good sir, the king summons you.” The man thought, “A danger must have arisen on account of my wife.” Unable to refuse the king’s command, he went, paid homage to the king, and stood there. Then the king said to him, “From this day forward, attend upon me.” “That is not necessary, Your Majesty. I do my own work and pay you taxes. Let my livelihood remain at home.” “I have no need for your taxes. From today onward, you must attend upon me.” And he had a shield and a weapon given to him. It is said the king's thought was this: “Having accused him of some fault, I will have him killed and take his wife.” Then the man, fearful of death, attended upon the king with diligence.

Rājā [V 1.0252][M 1.0283] tassa dosaṃ apassanto kāmapariḷāhe vaḍḍhante “ekamassa [P 2.0003] dosaṃ āropetvā rājāṇaṃ karissāmī”ti pakkosāpetvā evamāha – “ambho ito yojanamatthake nadiyā asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gantvā sāyaṃ mama nhānavelāya kumuduppalāni ceva aruṇavatīmattikañca āhara. Sace tasmiṃ khaṇe nāgacchasi, āṇaṃ te karissāmī”ti. Sevako kira catūhipi dāsehi patikiṭṭhataro. Dhanakkītādayo hi dāsā “sīsaṃ me rujjati, piṭṭhi me rujjatī”ti vatvā acchituṃ labhantiyeva. Sevakassetaṃ natthi, āṇattakammaṃ kātumeva vaṭṭati. Tasmā so “avassaṃ mayā gantabbaṃ, kumuduppalehi saddhiṃ aruṇavatīmattikā nāma nāgabhavane uppajjati, ahaṃ kuhiṃ labhissāmī”ti cintento maraṇabhayabhīto vegena gehaṃ gantvā, “bhadde, niṭṭhitaṃ me bhatta”nti āha. “Uddhanamatthake, sāmī”ti. So yāva bhattaṃ otarati, tāva sandhāretuṃ asakkonto uḷuṅkena kañjikaṃ harāpetvā yathāladdhena byañjanena saddhiṃ allameva bhattaṃ pacchiyaṃ opīḷetvā ādāya yojanikaṃ maggaṃ pakkhando, tassa gacchantasseva bhattaṃ pakkaṃ ahosi. So anucchiṭṭhaṃ katvāva thokaṃ bhattaṃ apanetvā bhuñjanto ekaṃ addhikaṃ disvā mayā apanetvā ṭhapitaṃ thokaṃ anucchiṭṭhaṃ bhattameva atthi gahetvā bhuñja sāmīti. So gaṇhitvā bhuñji. Itaropi bhuñjitvā ekaṃ bhattamuṭṭhiṃ [P 2.0004] udake khipitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā mahantena saddena “imasmiṃ nadīpadese adhivatthā nāgā supaṇṇā devatā ca vacanaṃ me suṇantu, rājā mayhaṃ āṇaṃ kātukāmo ‘kumuduppalehi saddhiṃ aruṇavatīmattikaṃ āharā’ti maṃ āṇāpesi, addhikamanussassa ca me bhattaṃ dinnaṃ, taṃ sahassānisaṃsaṃ, udake macchānaṃ dinnaṃ, taṃ satānisaṃsaṃ. Ettakaṃ puññaphalaṃ tumhākaṃ pattiṃ katvā dammi, mayhaṃ kumuduppalehi saddhiṃ aruṇavatīmattikaṃ āharathā”ti tikkhattuṃ anussāvesi. Tattha adhivattho nāgarājā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā mahallakavesena tassa santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ vadesī”ti āha. So punapi tatheva vatvā “mayhaṃ taṃ pattiṃ dehī”ti vutte, “demī”ti āha. Punapi “dehī”ti vutte, “demi, sāmī”ti āha. Evaṃ so dve tayo vāre pattiṃ āharāpetvā kumuduppalehi saddhiṃ aruṇavatīmattikaṃ adāsi.

The king, seeing no fault in him, but with the burning of his sensual passion increasing, thought, “I will accuse him of some fault and impose the king's authority upon him.” Having had the man summoned, he said this: “Sir, go to a place named so-and-so in the river, a yojana from here, and in the evening, at the time of my bath, bring me white and blue water lilies, and also Aruṇavatī earth. If you do not return at that moment, I will execute my authority upon you.” A royal servant, it is said, is more wretched than even the four kinds of slaves. For slaves bought with money and so on, by saying, “My head hurts, my back hurts,” are able to rest. For a servant, this is not possible; he must do the commanded work. Therefore, the man thought, “I must certainly go. Aruṇavatī earth, along with white and blue water lilies, is found in the realm of the nāgas. Where will I get it?” Fearing death, he went home quickly and asked, “My dear, is my meal ready?” “It is on the hearth, master.” Unable to wait until the rice was taken down, he had some rice-gruel ladled out, and then, pressing the still-moist rice together with whatever curry was available into a basket, he took it and set off running on the yojana-long road. As he was going, the rice became fully cooked. Setting aside a small portion so it would not be a leftover, he was eating when he saw a traveler and said, “Master, I have a little rice here that I have set aside and is not a leftover. Take it and eat.” The traveler took it and ate. The other man also, having eaten, threw a handful of rice into the water, rinsed his mouth, and proclaimed with a loud voice: “May the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and devas dwelling in this river region hear my words! The king, wishing to execute his authority on me, commanded me, ‘Bring Aruṇavatī earth along with white and blue water lilies.’ I have given food to a traveler; may that have a thousandfold benefit. I have given food to the fish in the water; may that have a hundredfold benefit. I give this much fruit of merit to you as a share. Bring me Aruṇavatī earth along with white and blue water lilies!” He announced this three times. The nāga king dwelling there heard that sound and, approaching him in the guise of an old man, asked, “What are you saying?” The man repeated what he had said. When the nāga king said, “Give me that share of merit,” the man replied, “I give it.” When he said again, “Give it,” the man replied, “I give it, master.” Thus, having had the share of merit offered two or three times, the nāga king gave him the Aruṇavatī earth along with the white and blue water lilies.

Rājā [M 1.0284] pana cintesi – “manussā nāma bahumāyā, sace so kenaci upāyena labheyya, kiccaṃ me na nipphajjeyyā”ti. So kālasseva dvāraṃ pidahāpetvā muddikaṃ attano santikaṃ āharāpesi. Itaropi puriso rañño nhānavelāyamevāgantvā dvāraṃ alabhanto dvārapālaṃ pakkosetvā “dvāraṃ vivarā”ti āha. “Na sakkā vivarituṃ, rājā kālasseva muddikaṃ datvā rājagehaṃ āharāpesī”ti. So “rājadūto ahaṃ, dvāraṃ vivarā”ti vatvāpi “dvāraṃ alabhanto natthi me idāni jīvitaṃ. Kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti cintetvā dvārassa upariummāre [P 2.0005] mattikāpiṇḍaṃ [V 1.0253] khipitvā tassūpari pupphāni laggetvā mahāsaddaṃ karonto, “ambho, nagaravāsino rañño mayā āṇattiyā gatabhāvaṃ jānātha, rājā maṃ akāraṇena vināsetukāmo”ti tikkhattuṃ viravitvā “kattha nu kho gacchissāmī”ti cintetvā “bhikkhū nāma muduhadayā, vihāraṃ gantvā nipajjissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānamakāsi. Ime hi nāma sattā sukhitakāle bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvampi ajānitvā dukkhābhibhūtakāle vihāraṃ gantukāmā honti, tasmā sopi “me aññaṃ tāṇaṃ natthī”ti vihāraṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ phāsukaṭṭhāne nipajji. Atha raññopi taṃ rattiṃ niddaṃ alabhantassa taṃ itthiṃ anussarantassa kāmapariḷāho uppajji. So cintesi – “vibhātakkhaṇeyeva taṃ purisaṃ ghātāpetvā taṃ itthiṃ ānessāmī”ti.

The king thought, “Men are indeed very deceitful; if he were to obtain her by any means, my purpose would not be fulfilled.” So, very early, he had the door closed and the key brought to his presence. The other man also arrived at the king's bathing time but, unable to gain entry, summoned the gatekeeper and said, “Open the door!” “It cannot be opened. The king locked it very early and had the key brought to the royal residence,” replied the gatekeeper. “I am the king’s messenger, open the door!” he said. But still not gaining entry, he thought, “Now my life is over. What shall I do?” Then, throwing a lump of clay above the door's lintel and attaching flowers to it, he made a loud noise and cried out three times, “Ho, citizens! Know that I have gone by the king’s command. The king wishes to destroy me without cause!” Having lamented thus, he pondered, “Where indeed shall I go?” and decided, “Monks are gentle-hearted; I will go to the monastery and lie down.” Indeed, these beings, in times of happiness, do not even acknowledge the existence of monks, but when overwhelmed by suffering, they wish to go to the monastery. Therefore, he too, thinking, “I have no other refuge,” went to the monastery and lay down in a comfortable place. Then, for the king, who could not get to sleep that night while remembering that woman, the fever of lust arose. He thought, “At the very break of dawn, I will have that man killed and bring that woman here.”

Tasmiṃ khaṇeyeva saṭṭhiyojanikāya lohakumbhiyā nibbattā cattāro purisā pakkuthitāya ukkhaliyā taṇḍulā viya samparivattakaṃ paccamānā tiṃsāya vassasahassehi heṭṭhimatalaṃ patvā aparehi tiṃsāya vassasahassehi puna mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Te sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā aññamaññaṃ oloketvā ekekaṃ gāthaṃ vattukāmā vattuṃ asakkontā ekekaṃ akkharaṃ vatvā parivattitvā lohakumbhimeva paviṭṭhā. Rājā niddaṃ alabhanto majjhimayāmasamanantare taṃ saddaṃ sutvā [P 2.0006] bhīto utrastamānaso “kiṃ nu kho mayhaṃ jīvitantarāyo bhavissati, udāhu me aggamahesiyā, udāhu me rajjaṃ vinassissatī”ti cintento sakalarattiṃ akkhīni nimīletuṃ nāsakkhi. So aruṇuggamanavelāya eva purohitaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “ācariya, mayā majjhimayāmasamanantare mahantā bheravasaddā sutā, ‘rajjassa vā aggamahesiyā vā mayhaṃ vā kassa antarāyo [M 1.0285] bhavissatī’ti na jānāmi, tena me tvaṃ pakkosāpito”ti āha. Mahārāja, kiṃ te saddā sutāti? “Ācariya, du-iti sa-iti na-iti so-itīti ime sadde assosiṃ, imesaṃ nipphattiṃ upadhārehī”ti. Brāhmaṇassa mahāandhakāraṃ paviṭṭhassa viya na kiñci paññāyati, “na jānāmī”ti vutte “pana lābhasakkāro me parihāyissatī”ti bhāyitvā “bhāriyaṃ, mahārājā”ti āha. “Kiṃ, ācariyā”ti? “Jīvitantarāyo te paññāyatī”ti. So dviguṇaṃ bhīto, “ācariya, atthi kiñci pana paṭighātakāraṇa”nti āha. “Atthi, mahārāja, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ tayo vede jānāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Sabbasatayaññaṃ yajitvā jīvitaṃ labhissasi, devā”ti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? Hatthisataṃ assasataṃ usabhasataṃ dhenusataṃ ajasataṃ urabbhasataṃ kukkuṭasataṃ sūkarasataṃ dārakasataṃ dārikāsatanti evaṃ ekekaṃ pāṇajātiṃ sataṃ sataṃ katvā [P 2.0007] gaṇhāpento “sace migajātimeva gaṇhāpessāmi, ‘attano khādanīyameva gaṇhāpetī’ti vakkhantī”ti hatthiassamanussepi gaṇhāpeti. Rājā “mama jīvitameva mayhaṃ lābho”ti cintetvā “sabbapāṇe [V 1.0254] sīghaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Āṇattamanussā adhikataraṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ kosalasaṃyutte –

At that very moment, four men who had arisen in a sixty-yojana-wide iron cauldron hell, being cooked and turning over and over like rice grains in a boiling pot, reached the bottom after thirty thousand years, and after another thirty thousand years, they rose again to the rim. Raising their heads and looking at one another, they wished to recite a verse each, but being unable to speak, they uttered one syllable each before turning back and entering the iron cauldron itself. The king, unable to sleep, heard that sound just after the middle watch of the night. Frightened and with a terrified mind, he wondered, “Will there be a danger to my life? Or to my chief queen? Or will my kingdom be destroyed?” He spent the entire night unable to close his eyes. At the very time of sunrise, he had the royal chaplain summoned and said, “Teacher, just after the middle watch of the night, I heard great, frightful sounds. I do not know whether it will be a danger to the kingdom, to the chief queen, or to myself—that is why you were summoned by me.” “Great king, what sounds did you hear?” “Teacher, I heard these sounds: ‘du,’ ‘sa,’ ‘na,’ and ‘so.’ Investigate their meaning.” For the brahmin, it was as if he had entered a great darkness; nothing appeared to him. But fearing that his gain and honor would diminish if he were to say, “I do not know,” he said, “This is a serious matter, great king.” “What is it, teacher?” “A danger to your life appears.” The king, now doubly afraid, asked, “Teacher, is there any means of prevention?” “There is, great king, do not be afraid. I know the three Vedas.” “What then must be obtained?” “By performing the sacrifice of a hundred of everything, you will obtain your life, O deva.” “What must be obtained?” He had them take a hundred of each species of living being: a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, a hundred milk-cows, a hundred goats, a hundred rams, a hundred chickens, a hundred pigs, a hundred boys, and a hundred girls. Fearing that if he had only animal species taken, people would say, ‘He is only having his own food taken,’ he also had elephants, horses, and humans taken. The king, thinking, “My life itself is my gain,” commanded, “Take all living beings quickly.” The men who were commanded took even more. And this was also said in the Kosala Saṃyutta:

“Tena kho pana samayena rañño pasenadissa kosalassa mahāyañño paccupaṭṭhito hoti, pañca ca usabhasatāni pañca ca vacchatarasatāni pañca ca vacchatarisatāni pañca ca ajasatāni pañca ca urabbhasatāni thūṇūpanītāni honti yaññatthāya. Yepissa te honti dāsāti vā pessāti vā kammakarāti vā, tepi daṇḍatajjitā bhayatajjitā assumukhā rudamānā parikammāni karontī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.120).

At that time, a great sacrifice for King Pasenadi of Kosala had been prepared. Five hundred bulls, five hundred young bulls, five hundred young cows, five hundred goats, and five hundred rams had been brought to the sacrificial post for the sake of the sacrifice. And those who were his slaves, messengers, or workers—they too, threatened by punishment and threatened by fear, with tearful faces and weeping, were performing the preparatory tasks.

Mahājano attano attano puttadhītuñātīnaṃ atthāya paridevamāno mahāsaddamakāsi, mahāpathavīundriyanasaddo viya ahosi. Atha mallikā devī taṃ saddaṃ sutvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ nu kho te, mahārāja, indriyāni apākatikāni, kilantarūpāni viya paññāyantī”ti pucchi. “Kiṃ tuyhaṃ[P 2.0008], mallike, tvaṃ mama kaṇṇamūlena āsivisampi gacchantaṃ na jānāsī”ti? “Kiṃ panetaṃ, devā”ti? “Rattibhāge me evarūpo nāma saddo suto[M 1.0286], svāhaṃ purohitaṃ pucchitvā jīvitantarāyo te paññāyati, sabbasatayaññaṃ yajitvā jīvitaṃ labhissasī”ti sutvā “mama jīvitameva mayhaṃ lābho”ti ime pāṇe gaṇhāpesinti. Mallikā devī, “andhabālosi, mahārāja, kiñcāpi mahābhakkhosi, anekasūpabyañjanavikatikaṃ doṇapākaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjasi, dvīsu raṭṭhesu rajjaṃ kāresi, paññā pana te mandā”ti āha. “Kasmā evaṃ vadesi, devī”ti? “Kahaṃ tayā aññassa maraṇena aññassa jīvitalābho diṭṭhapubbo, andhabālassa brāhmaṇassa kathaṃ gahetvā kasmā mahājanassa upari dukkhaṃ khipasi, dhuravihāre sadevakassa lokassa aggapuggalo atītādīsu appaṭihatañāṇo satthā vasati, taṃ pucchitvā tassovādaṃ karohī”ti vutte rājā sallahukehi yānehi mallikāya saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā maraṇabhayatajjito kiñci vattuṃ asakkonto satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

The great crowd, lamenting for the sake of their own sons, daughters, and relatives, made a great uproar; it was like the roaring sound of an earthquake. Then Queen Mallikā, hearing that sound, went to the king and asked, 'Why, great king, do your faculties seem unnatural, as if you are exhausted?' 'Mallikā, why do you not know of the venomous snake passing by my ear?' 'What is this, lord?' 'In the night, I heard a sound of this kind. When I asked the royal chaplain, I was told, “A danger to your life is apparent. By performing a sacrifice of one hundred of every kind of creature, you will obtain life.” Having heard this, thinking, “My life is my only gain,” I had these creatures seized.' Queen Mallikā said, 'You are utterly foolish, great king. Although you are a great eater, consuming meals of a doṇa measure with many kinds of curries and sauces, and although you rule over two kingdoms, your wisdom is indeed scant.' 'Why do you speak thus, queen?' 'Where have you ever seen the life of one person gained by the death of another? Having accepted the word of an utterly foolish brahmin, why do you cast suffering upon the great crowd? In the nearby monastery, the Teacher resides—the foremost person in the world with its gods, whose knowledge of the past and so on is unobstructed. Go and ask him, and then act on his advice.' When this was said, the king, terrified by the fear of death, went with Mallikā in light carriages to the monastery. Unable to say anything, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side.

Atha naṃ satthā “handa kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti paṭhamataraṃ ālapi. So tuṇhīyeva nisīdi. Tato mallikā bhagavato ārocesi – “bhante, raññā kira majjhimayāmasamanantare saddo suto. Atha naṃ purohitassa ārocesi. Purohito ‘jīvitantarāyo te bhavissati, tassa paṭighātatthāya sabbasate [P 2.0009] pāṇe gahetvā tesaṃ galalohitena yaññe yajite jīvitaṃ labhissasī’ti āha. Rājā pāṇe gaṇhāpesi, tenāyaṃ mayā [V 1.0255] idhānīto”ti. “Evaṃ kira, mahārājā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kinti te saddo suto”ti? So attanā sutaniyāmeneva ācikkhi. Tathāgatassa taṃ sutvāva ekobhāso ahosi. Atha naṃ sattā āha – “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, tava antarāyo natthi, pāpakammino satthā attano dukkhaṃ āvīkarontā evamāhaṃsū”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, tehi kata”nti? Atha kho bhagavā tesaṃ kammaṃ ācikkhituṃ “tena hi, mahārāja, suṇāhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari –

Then the Teacher first addressed him, saying, 'Well now, great king, from where do you come in the middle of the day?' He just sat in silence. Then Mallikā reported to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, it seems the king heard a sound right after the middle watch of the night. He then reported this to the royal chaplain. The chaplain said, “There will be a danger to your life. To avert it, if you seize one hundred of every kind of creature and perform a sacrifice with the blood from their throats, you will gain life.” The king had the creatures seized, and for that reason I brought him here.' 'Is it so, great king?' 'It is so, venerable sir.' 'What kind of sound did you hear?' He described it exactly as he had heard it. Upon hearing it, the matter became instantly clear to the Tathāgata. He then said to him, 'Do not be afraid, great king, there is no danger to you. It was beings who had committed evil who spoke thus, unable to endure their own suffering.' 'But what, venerable sir, had they done?' Then the Blessed One, in order to explain their kamma, said, 'In that case, great king, listen,' and he related a story of the past:

Atīte vīsativassasahassāyukesu manussesu kassapo bhagavā loke uppajjitvā vīsatiyā khīṇāsavasahassehi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasimagamāsi. Bārāṇasivāsino dvepi tayopi bahutarāpi [M 1.0287] ekato hutvā āgantukadānaṃ pavattayiṃsu. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ cattālīsakoṭivibhavā cattāro seṭṭhiputtā sahāyakā ahesuṃ. Te mantayiṃsu – “amhākaṃ gehe bahudhanaṃ, tena kiṃ karomā”ti? “Evarūpe buddhe cārikaṃ caramāne dānaṃ dassāma, sīlaṃ rakkhissāma, pūjaṃ karissāmā”ti ekopi avatvā tesu eko tāva evamāha – “tikhiṇasuraṃ pivantā madhuramaṃsaṃ khādantā vicarissāma, idaṃ amhākaṃ jīvitaphala”nti. Aparopi evamāha – “devasikaṃ tivassikagandhasālibhattaṃ [P 2.0010] nānaggarasehi bhuñjantā vicarissāmā”ti. Aparopi evamāha – “nānappakāraṃ pūvakhajjakavikatiṃ pacāpetvā khādantā vicarissāmā”ti. Aparopi evamāha – “sammā mayaṃ aññaṃ kiñci na karissāma, ‘dhanaṃ dassāmā’ti vutte anicchamānā itthī nāma natthi, tasmā dhanena palobhetvā pāradārikakammaṃ karissāmā”ti. “Sādhu, sādhū”ti sabbeva tassa kathāya aṭṭhaṃsu.

In the past, when the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years, the Blessed One Kassapa arose in the world. While wandering on tour with twenty thousand who had destroyed the cankers, he arrived in Bārāṇasī. The residents of Bārāṇasī—in groups of two, three, or even more—came together and established the practice of giving to visitors. At that time in Bārāṇasī, there were four sons of treasurers who were friends, each possessing forty crores of wealth. They conferred, saying, 'There is much wealth in our homes. What shall we do with it?' Not a single one of them said, 'While a Buddha such as this is wandering on tour, let us give alms, keep the precepts, and make offerings.' Instead, one of them first said this: 'Let us spend our time drinking strong liquor and eating sweet meat. This is the fruit of our life.' Another said: 'Let us spend our time eating daily meals of three-year-old fragrant rice with various excellent flavors.' Yet another said: 'Let us spend our time having various kinds of cakes and sweetmeats prepared and then eating them.' And the last one said: 'Friends, we shall do nothing else. When one says, “We will give you wealth,” there is no such thing as an unwilling woman. Therefore, by tempting them with wealth, let us commit adultery.' 'Excellent, excellent!' they all stood by his words.

Te tato paṭṭhāya abhirūpānaṃ itthīnaṃ dhanaṃ pesetvā vīsativassasahassāni pāradārikakammaṃ katvā kālaṃ katvā avīciniraye nibbattā. Te ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā tattha kālaṃ katvā pakkāvasesena saṭṭhiyojanikāya lohakumbhiyā nibbattitvā tiṃsāya vassasahassehi heṭṭhimatalaṃ patvā punapi tiṃsāya vassasahassehi lohakumbhimukhaṃ patvā ekekaṃ gāthaṃ vattukāmā hutvā vattuṃ asakkontā ekekaṃ akkharaṃ vatvā puna parivattitvā, lohakumbhimeva paviṭṭhā. “Vadehi, mahārāja, paṭhamaṃ te kiṃ saddo nāma suto”ti? “Du-iti, bhante”ti. Satthā tena aparipuṇṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ gāthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā dassento evamāha –

From that time on, for twenty thousand years, they sent wealth to exceedingly beautiful women and committed adultery. After doing so, they died and were reborn in the great Avīci hell. Having been tormented in hell for one Buddha-interval, they died there and, by the remainder of their kamma, were reborn in a sixty-yojana iron cauldron. After taking thirty thousand years to reach the bottom, and another thirty thousand years to reach the mouth of the iron cauldron, they wished to utter one verse each. But being unable to speak, they uttered one syllable each and then, turning back around, plunged once more into that same iron cauldron. 'Tell me, great king, what was the first sound you heard?' 'It was “Du—”, venerable sir.' The Teacher, completing the verse that had been spoken incompletely by that being, showed it in its complete form and said:

“Dujjīvitamajīvimha[V 1.0256], ye sante na dadamhase;

Vijjamānesu bhogesu, dīpaṃ nākamha attano”ti. (jā. 1.4.53; pe. va. 804);

A wretched life we lived, we who did not give, though we had the means; while our wealth existed, we made no island for ourselves.

Atha [P 2.0011] rañño imissā gāthāya atthaṃ pakāsetvā, “kiṃ te, mahārāja, dutiyasaddo tatiyasaddo catutthasaddo suto”ti pucchitvā “evaṃ nāmā”ti vutte avasesaṃ paripūrento –

Then, having explained the meaning of this verse to the king, he asked, 'Great king, what was the second sound, the third sound, and the fourth sound that you heard?' When the king told him, the Teacher completed the remaining verses, saying:

“Saṭṭhivassasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Niraye paccamānānaṃ, kadā anto bhavissati.

Sixty thousand years have been completed in full for us who are being tormented in hell. When will there be an end?

“Natthi [M 1.0288] anto kuto anto, na anto paṭidissati;

Tadā hi pakataṃ pāpaṃ, mama tuyhañca mārisā.

O sirs, there is no end. From where could there be an end? No end is seen. For then, evil was done by me and by you.

“Sohaṃ nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ;

Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahu”nti. (jā. 1.4.54-56; pe. va. 802, 803, 805) –

Having gone from here and obtained a human birth, I, being generous and accomplished in virtue, will surely perform much that is wholesome.

Paṭipāṭiyā imā gāthā vatvā tāsaṃ atthaṃ pakāsetvā “iti kho, mahārāja, te cattāro janā ekekaṃ gāthaṃ vattukāmāpi vattuṃ asakkontā ekakameva akkharaṃ vatvā puna lohakumbhimeva paviṭṭhā”ti āha.

Having spoken these verses in sequence and explained their meaning, he said: 'Thus, O great king, those four people, although wishing to speak one verse each, being unable to speak it, uttered only a single syllable each and entered the iron cauldron again.'

Raññā kira pasenadikosalena tassa saddassa sutakālato paṭṭhāya te heṭṭhā bhassanti eva, ajjāpi ekaṃ vassasahassaṃ nātikkamanti. Rañño taṃ desanaṃ sutvā mahāsaṃvego uppajji. So “bhāriyaṃ vatidaṃ pāradārikakammaṃ nāma, ekaṃ kira buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā tato cutā saṭṭhiyojanikāya lohakumbhiyā nibbattitvā tattha saṭṭhivassasahassāni paccitvā evampi nesaṃ dukkhā muccanakālo na paññāyati, ahampi paradāre sinehaṃ katvā sabbarattiṃ [P 2.0012] niddaṃ na labhiṃ, idāni ito paṭṭhāya paradāre mānasaṃ na bandhissāmī”ti cintetvā tathāgataṃ āha – “bhante, ajja me rattiyā dīghabhāvo ñāto”ti. Sopi puriso tattheva nisinno taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “laddho me balavappaccayo”ti satthāraṃ āha – “bhante, raññā tāva ajja rattiyā dīghabhāvo ñāto, ahaṃ pana hiyyo sayameva yojanassa dīghabhāvaṃ aññāsi”nti. Satthā dvinnampi [V 1.0257] kathaṃ saṃsanditvā “ekaccassa ratti dīghā hoti, ekaccassa yojanaṃ dīghaṃ hoti, bālassa pana saṃsāro dīgho hotī”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that from the time King Pasenadi of Kosala heard that sound, those beings have been sinking downwards, and even today a thousand years have not yet passed. Upon hearing that teaching, great spiritual urgency arose in the king. He thought: 'Indeed, this deed called adultery is a heavy burden. It is said that after being tormented in hell for one Buddha-interval, and having passed away from there, they are reborn in a sixty-yojana iron cauldron. There they are tormented for sixty thousand years, and even so, a time for their release from suffering is not apparent. I, too, having felt affection for another's wife, did not get any sleep the whole night. From this day forward, I will not bind my heart to another's wife.' Reflecting thus, he said to the Tathāgata: 'Venerable Sir, today the length of the night has been known by me.' That man, sitting right there, upon hearing that conversation, thought, 'A strong support has been obtained by me,' and said to the Teacher: 'Venerable Sir, the king has just now known the length of the night, but I, for my part, knew the length of a yojana yesterday.' The Teacher, connecting the statements of both, said: 'For one, the night is long; for another, a yojana is long; but for the fool, saṃsāra is long.' And teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

60.

60.

“Dīghā jāgarato ratti, dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ;

Dīgho bālāna saṃsāro, saddhammaṃ avijānata”nti.

Long is the night for one who is awake; long is a league for one who is weary; long is saṃsāra for fools who do not know the true Dhamma.

Tattha dīghāti ratti nāmesā tiyāmamattāva, jāgarantassa pana dīghā hoti, dviguṇatiguṇā viya hutvā khāyati. Tassā dīghabhāvaṃ attānaṃ maṅkuṇasaṅghassa bhattaṃ katvā yāva sūriyuggamanā samparivattakaṃ semāno [M 1.0289] mahākusītopi, subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā sirisayane sayamāno kāmabhogīpi na jānāti, sabbarattiṃ pana padhānaṃ padahanto yogāvacaro ca, dhammakathaṃ kathento [P 2.0013] dhammakathiko ca, āsanasamīpe ṭhatvā dhammaṃ suṇanto ca, sīsarogādiphuṭṭho vā hatthapādacchedanādiṃ patto vā vedanābhibhūto ca, rattiṃ maggapaṭipanno addhiko ca jānāti. Yojananti yojanampi catugāvutamattameva, santassa pana kilantassa dīghaṃ hoti, dviguṇatiguṇaṃ viya khāyati. Sakaladivasañhi maggaṃ gantvā kilanto paṭipathaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “purato gāmo kīvadūro”ti pucchitvā “yojana”nti vutte thokaṃ gantvā aparampi pucchitvā tenāpi “yojana”nti vutte puna thokaṃ gantvā aparampi pucchati. Sopi “yojana”nti vadati. So pucchitapucchitā yojananteva vadanti, dīghaṃ vatidaṃ yojanaṃ, ekayojanaṃ dve tīṇi yojanāni viya maññeti. Bālānanti idhalokaparalokatthaṃ pana ajānantānaṃ bālānaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭassa pariyantaṃ kātuṃ asakkontānaṃ yaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyabhedaṃ saddhammaṃ ñatvā saṃsārassa antaṃ karonti, taṃ saddhammaṃ avijānataṃ saṃsāro dīgho nāma hoti. So hi attano dhammatāya eva dīgho nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro, pubbā koṭi na paññāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.124). Bālānaṃ pana pariyantaṃ kātuṃ asakkontānaṃ atidīghoyevāti.

Therein, as to 'long': this thing called night is only three watches long, but for one who is awake, it is long; it appears as if doubled or tripled. Its length is not known by the very lazy person who, making himself a meal for a community of bedbugs, lies tossing and turning until sunrise; nor is it known by the pleasure-seeker who, having eaten a fine meal, sleeps on a luxurious bed. However, the practitioner of yoga striving all night, the Dhamma-teacher giving a discourse, one who stands near the seat listening to the Dhamma, one afflicted with a headache or the like, one who has suffered the cutting off of hands and feet or the like and is overwhelmed by pain, and the traveler journeying on the road at night—they know it. As to 'yojana': a yojana is merely four gāvutas, but for one who is weary and exhausted, it is long; it appears as if doubled or tripled. Indeed, one who is exhausted from walking the road the entire day, seeing someone coming along the path, asks, 'How far is the village ahead?' Having been told 'a yojana,' he goes a little way and asks another. When told by that one also 'a yojana,' he goes a little way again and asks another. That one also says 'a yojana.' He thinks, 'Those I ask all say a yojana. This yojana is indeed long!' and considers one yojana to be like two or three yojanas. As to 'for fools': for fools who do not know what is for their welfare in this world and the next, who are unable to make an end to the round of saṃsāra, saṃsāra is called long, as they do not know that good Dhamma—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—by knowing which beings make an end of saṃsāra. For, by its very nature, it is called long. And this was said: 'Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned.' But for fools who are unable to make an end, it is exceedingly long.

Desanāvasāne [P 2.0014] so puriso sotāpattiphalaṃ patto, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pattā. Mahājanassa sātthikā dhammadesanā jātāti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, that man attained the fruit of stream-entry, and many others attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages of awakening. The Dhamma discourse was of benefit to the great assembly of people.

Rājā satthāraṃ vanditvā gacchantoyeva te satte bandhanā mocesi. Tattha itthipurisā bandhanā muttā sīsaṃ nhatvā sakāni gehāni gacchantā “ciraṃ jīvatu no, ayyā, mallikā devī, taṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhimhā”ti mallikāya guṇakathaṃ kathayiṃsu. Sāyanhasamaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “aho paṇḍitā vatāyaṃ, mallikā, attano paññaṃ nissāya ettakassa [V 1.0258] janassa jīvitadānaṃ adāsī”ti. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā dhammasabhaṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya [M 1.0290] sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “na, bhikkhave, mallikā, idāneva attano paññaṃ nissāya mahājanassa jīvitadānaṃ deti, pubbepi adāsiyevā”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ pakāsanto atītaṃ āhari –

The king, having paid homage to the Teacher, freed those beings from their bonds as he was leaving. The men and women, freed from their bonds, bathed their heads and, while going to their own homes, spoke in praise of Mallikā's virtue, saying: 'May our noble lady, Queen Mallikā, live long! It is by relying on her that we have received our lives.' In the evening, the monks raised a topic of discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Oh, how wise is this Mallikā! Relying on her own wisdom, she gave the gift of life to so many people.' The Teacher, while seated in the perfumed chamber, heard the conversation of those monks. Coming out from the perfumed chamber, he entered the Dhamma hall, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked: 'Monks, for what topic of discussion are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'Regarding this, namely...,' he said: 'Monks, it is not only now that Mallikā, relying on her own wisdom, gives the gift of life to a great number of people; she gave it in the past as well.' And to make that matter clear, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ rañño putto ekaṃ nigrodharukkhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tattha nibbattāya devatāya āyāci – “sāmi devarāja, imasmiṃ jambudīpe ekasatarājāno ekasataaggamahesiyo, sacāhaṃ pitu accayena rajjaṃ labhissāmī, etesaṃ galalohitena baliṃ karissāmī”ti. So pitari kālakate rajjaṃ patvā “devatāya me ānubhāvena rajjaṃ pattaṃ, balimassā karissāmī”ti mahatiyā senāya nikkhamitvā ekaṃ rājānaṃ attano vase vattetvā tena saddhiṃ aparampi [P 2.0015] aparampīti sabbe rājāno attano vase katvā saddhiṃ aggamahesīhi ādāya gacchanto uggasenassa nāma sabbakaniṭṭhassa rañño dhammadinnā nāma aggamahesī garugabbhā, taṃ ohāya āgantvā “ettakajanaṃ visapānakaṃ pāyetvā māressāmī”ti rukkhamūlaṃ sodhāpesi. Devatā cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā ettake rājāno gaṇhanto ‘maṃ nissāya gahitā ime’ti cintetvā tesaṃ galalohitena mayhaṃ baliṃ kātukāmo, sace panāyaṃ ete ghātessati, jambudīpe rājavaṃso upacchijjissati, rukkhamūlepi, me asuci bhavissati, sakkhissāmi nu kho etaṃ nivāretu”nti. Sā upadhārentī “nāhaṃ sakkhissāmī”ti ñatvā aññampi devataṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā “tvaṃ sakkhissasī”ti āha. Tāyapi paṭikkhittā aññampi aññampīti evaṃ sakalacakkavāḷadevatāyo upasaṅkamitvā tāhipi paṭikkhittā catunnaṃ mahārājūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “mayaṃ na sakkoma, amhākaṃ pana rājā amhehi puññena ca paññāya ca visiṭṭho, taṃ pucchā”ti tehipi paṭikkhittakāle sakkaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā, “deva, tumhesu appossukkataṃ āpannesu khattiyavaṃso upacchijjissati, tassa paṭisaraṇaṃ hothā”ti [P 2.0016] āha. Sakko “ahampi naṃ paṭibāhituṃ na sakkhissāmi, upāyaṃ pana te vakkhāmī”ti vatvā upāyaṃ ācikkhi – “gaccha, tvaṃ rañño passantasseva rattavatthaṃ nivāsetvā attano rukkhato nikkhamitvā gamanākāraṃ dassehi. Atha taṃ rājā ‘devatā gacchati, nivattāpessāmi na’nti nānappakārena yācissati. Atha naṃ vadeyyāsi ‘tvaṃ ekasatarājāno [M 1.0291] saddhiṃ aggamahesīhi ānetvā tesaṃ galalohitena baliṃ karissāmī’ti mayhaṃ āyācitvā uggasenassa rañño deviṃ ohāya āgato, nāhaṃ tādisassa musāvādassa baliṃ sampaṭicchāmī”ti, “evaṃ kira vutte rājā taṃ āṇāpessati, sā rañño dhammaṃ desetvā ettakassa [V 1.0259] janassa jīvitadānaṃ dassatī”ti. Iminā kāraṇena sakko devatāya imaṃ upāyaṃ ācikkhi. Devatā tathā akāsi.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king's son approached a banyan tree and made a request to the deity dwelling there: 'Lord divine king, in this Jambudīpa there are one hundred and one kings and one hundred and one chief queens. If I should obtain the kingdom after my father's passing, I will make a sacrificial offering with the blood from their throats.' When his father passed away, he obtained the kingdom and thought, 'I have attained the kingdom through the deity's power; I will make a sacrificial offering to her.' He set out with a great army, subdued one king, and with him subdued another and another, and thus having brought all the kings and their chief queens under his control, he was proceeding. The chief queen of King Uggasena, the youngest of all the kings, named Dhammadinnā, was heavily pregnant. Leaving her behind, he came and ordered, 'I will make this many people drink a poisoned beverage and kill them,' and had the base of the tree cleared. The deity thought: 'This king, capturing so many kings, thinks, "They were captured because of me," and wishes to make a sacrificial offering to me with the blood from their throats. But if he kills them, the royal lineage in Jambudīpa will be cut off, and the base of my tree will become impure. Can I prevent this?' Reflecting, she realized, 'I cannot.' She then approached another deity and explained the matter, saying, 'Can you?' But that deity also refused. One after another, she approached all the deities of the entire Cakkavāḷa, but they all declined. She then went to the presence of the Four Great Kings. When they too refused, saying, 'We are not able, but our king is superior to us in merit and wisdom; ask him,' she approached Sakka and explained the situation, saying, 'Lord, if you become unconcerned, the Khattiya lineage will be destroyed. Be a protection for them.' Sakka replied, 'I too cannot stop him, but I will tell you a stratagem.' He instructed her: 'Go, and in full view of the king, dress in red garments and emerge from your tree as if about to leave. Then the king, thinking, "The deity is leaving; I must make her return," will implore you in various ways. Then you should say to him, "You made a vow to me, saying, ‘I will bring one hundred and one kings with their chief queens and make a sacrificial offering with the blood from their throats,’ yet you came having left behind King Uggasena’s queen. I do not accept the offering of such a liar." When this is said, the king will surely send for her. She will then teach the king the Dhamma and give the gift of life to all these people.' For this reason, Sakka instructed the deity in this stratagem. The deity did so.

Rājāpi taṃ āṇāpesi. Sā āgantvā tesaṃ rājūnaṃ pariyante nisinnampi attano rājānameva vandi. Rājā “mayi sabbarājajeṭṭhake ṭhite sabbakaniṭṭhaṃ attano sāmikaṃ vandatī”ti tassā kujjhi. Atha naṃ sā āha – “kiṃ mayhaṃ tayi paṭibaddhaṃ, ayaṃ pana me sāmiko issariyassa dāyako, imaṃ avanditvā kasmā taṃ vandissāmī”ti? Rukkhadevatā passantasseva mahājanassa “evaṃ, bhadde, evaṃ, bhadde”ti vatvā taṃ pupphamuṭṭhinā pūjesi[P 2.0017]. Puna rājā āha – “sace maṃ na vandasi, mayhaṃ rajjasiridāyikaṃ evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ devataṃ kasmā na vandasī”ti? “Mahārāja, tayā attano puññe ṭhatvā rājāno gahitā, na devatāya gahetvā dinnā”ti. Punapi taṃ devatā “evaṃ, bhadde, evaṃ, bhadde”ti vatvā tatheva pūjesi. Puna sā rājānaṃ āha – “tvaṃ ‘devatāya me ettakā rājāno gahetvā dinnā’ti vadesi, idāni te devatāya upari vāmapasse rukkho agginā daḍḍho, sā taṃ aggiṃ nibbāpetuṃ kasmā nāsakkhi, yadi evaṃ mahānubhāvā”ti. Punapi taṃ devatā “evaṃ, bhadde, evaṃ, bhadde”ti vatvā tatheva pūjesi.

The king also sent for her. She came and paid homage only to her own king, who was seated at the very end among those kings. The king became angry with her, thinking, 'While I, the most senior of all kings, am present, she pays homage to her own husband, the most junior.' Then she said to him: 'What connection have I with you? This husband of mine, however, is the giver of sovereignty. Without paying homage to him, why should I pay homage to you?' The tree-deity, in full view of the great assembly, said, 'It is so, good lady! It is so, good lady!' and honored her with a handful of flowers. Again the king said: 'If you do not pay homage to me, why do you not pay homage to the deity of such great power, the giver of my royal fortune?' 'Great King, it is by standing on your own merit that you have captured the kings; they were not captured and given by the deity.' Once more, the deity said, 'It is so, good lady! It is so, good lady!' and honored her in the same way. Again, she said to the king: 'You say, "The deity captured and gave me this many kings." Now, the tree on the left side above your deity was burnt by fire. Why was she unable to extinguish that fire, if she is of such great power?' Once more, the deity said, 'It is so, good lady! It is so, good lady!' and honored her in the same way.

Sā kathayamānā ṭhitā rodi ceva hasi ca. Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ ummattikāsī”ti āha. “Kasmā deva evaṃ vadesi”? “Na mādisiyo ummattikā hontī”ti. Atha “naṃ kiṃ kāraṇā rodasi ceva hasasi cā”ti? “Suṇāhi, mahārāja, ahañhi atīte kuladhītā hutvā patikule vasantī sāmikassa sahāyakaṃ pāhunakaṃ āgataṃ disvā tassa bhattaṃ pacitukāmā ‘maṃsaṃ āharā’ti dāsiyā kahāpaṇaṃ datvā tāya maṃsaṃ alabhitvā āgatāya ‘natthi maṃsa’nti vutte gehassa pacchimabhāge sayitāya eḷikāya sīsaṃ chinditvā bhattaṃ sampādesiṃ. Sāhaṃ ekissāya eḷikāya sīsaṃ chinditvā niraye paccitvā pakkāvasesena tassā lomagaṇanāya sīsacchedaṃ pāpuṇiṃ, ‘tvaṃ ettakaṃ janaṃ vadhitvā kadā dukkhā [M 1.0292] muccissasī’ti [P 2.0018] evamahaṃ tava dukkhaṃ anussarantī rodi”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

As she stood there speaking, she both wept and laughed. Then the king said to her, 'Are you mad?' 'Why, lord, do you speak thus? Women such as I are not mad.' Then he asked her, 'For what reason do you both weep and laugh?' 'Listen, great king. In the past, I was a clan-daughter living in my husband's family home. Seeing that a guest, a friend of my husband, had arrived, and wishing to cook a meal for him, I gave a kahāpaṇa to a female servant, saying, "Bring meat." When she returned, having been unable to get meat, and said, "There is no meat," I cut off the head of a she-goat that was sleeping in the back part of the house and prepared the meal. I, for having cut off the head of that one she-goat, was cooked in hell, and by the remainder of that kamma, I have undergone decapitation for a number of times equal to the count of its hairs. Thinking, "You, having killed so many kings, when will you be freed from suffering?"—thus, recollecting your suffering, I wept.' Having said this, she spoke this verse:

“Ekissā kaṇṭhaṃ chetvāna, lomagaṇanāya paccisaṃ;

Bahūnaṃ kaṇṭhe chetvāna, kathaṃ kāhasi khattiyā”ti.

“Having cut the neck of one, I was cooked according to the number of its hairs; having cut the necks of many, what will you do, O Khattiya?”

Atha “kasmā tvaṃ hasasī”ti? “‘Etasmā dukkhā muttāmhī’ti tussitvā, mahārājā”ti[V 1.0260]. Punapi taṃ devatā “evaṃ, bhadde, evaṃ, bhadde”ti vatvā pupphamuṭṭhinā pūjesi. Rājā “aho me bhāriyaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ, ayaṃ kira ekaṃ eḷikaṃ vadhitvā niraye pakkāvasesena tassā lomagaṇanāya sīsacchedaṃ pāpuṇi, ahaṃ ettakaṃ janaṃ vadhitvā kadā sotthiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti sabbe rājāno mocetvā attano mahallakatare vanditvā daharadaharānaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha sabbe khamāpetvā sakasakaṭṭhānameva pahiṇi.

Then she was asked, 'Why do you laugh?' 'Great king, I laughed, rejoicing that I am freed from this suffering.' Again, the deity, saying, 'It is so, good lady! It is so, good lady!' honored her with a handful of flowers. The king thought, 'Alas, a grave deed I have done! This woman, it is said, having killed a single she-goat, by the residual effect of that kamma after being cooked in hell, underwent decapitation equal to the number of hairs on that goat. I, having killed so many kings, when shall I ever find safety?' Having released all the kings, he paid homage to those older than himself and, raising his hands in añjali to the younger ones, sought forgiveness from all and sent them back to their own respective places.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, na idāneva, mallikā devī, attano paññaṃ nissāya mahājanassa jīvitadānaṃ deti, pubbepi adāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā pasenadi kosalo ahosi, dhammadinnā, devī mallikā, rukkhadevatā ahamevā”ti. Evaṃ atītaṃ samodhānetvā puna dhammaṃ desento, “bhikkhave, pāṇātipāto [P 2.0019] nāma na kattabbayuttako. Pāṇātipātino hi dīgharattaṃ socantī”ti vatvā imā gāthā āha –

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, 'Thus, monks, it is not only now that Queen Mallikā gives the gift of life to many people through her wisdom—she did so in the past as well.' Having connected the past, he said, 'At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was King Pasenadi of Kosala, Dhammadinnā was Queen Mallikā, and the tree deity was none other than myself.' Having thus connected the past, he continued teaching the Dhamma: 'Monks, the destruction of life should not be done. Indeed, those who destroy life grieve for a long time.' Then he spoke these verses:

“Idha socati pecca socati,

Pāpakārī ubhayattha socati;

So socati so vihaññati,

Disvā kammakiliṭṭhamattano”ti. (dha. pa. 15);

“Here he grieves, hereafter he grieves; the evil-doer grieves in both states. He grieves, he is afflicted, seeing the defilement of his own deeds.”

“Evaṃ ce sattā jāneyyuṃ, dukkhāyaṃ jātisambhavo;

Na pāṇo pāṇinaṃ haññe, pāṇaghātī hi socatī”ti. (jā. 1.1.18);

“If beings were to know thus: ‘This arising of birth is suffering,’ then a living being would not kill another living being, for one who kills living beings surely grieves.”

Aññatarapurisavatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The first story, concerning a certain man, is concluded.

2. Mahākassapattherasaddhivihārikavatthu

2. The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa's Resident Pupil

Carañce [M 1.0293] nādhigaccheyyāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ jetavane viharanto mahākassapattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Desanā rājagahe samuṭṭhitā.

The Teacher delivered this discourse beginning with 'Carañce nādhigaccheyya' while dwelling at Jetavana in Sāvatthī, concerning a resident pupil of the Elder Mahākassapa. The story originated in Rājagaha.

Theraṃ kira rājagahaṃ nissāya pippaliguhāyaṃ vasantaṃ dve saddhivihārikā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Tesu eko sakkaccaṃ vattaṃ karoti, eko tena kataṃ kataṃ attanā kataṃ viya dassento mukhodakadantakaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0261] paṭiyāditabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “bhante, mukhodakadantakaṭṭhāni me paṭiyāditāni, mukhaṃ dhovathā”ti vadati, pādadhovananhānādikālepi evameva vadati. Itaro cintesi – “ayaṃ niccakālaṃ mayā kataṃ kataṃ attanā kataṃ viya katvā dasseti, hotu, kattabbayuttakamassa karissāmī”ti. Tassa bhuñjitvā supantasseva nhānodakaṃ tāpetvā ekasmiṃ ghaṭe katvā piṭṭhikoṭṭhake ṭhapesi, udakatāpanabhājane pana nāḷimattaṃ udakaṃ [P 2.0020] sesetvā usumaṃ muñcantaṃ ṭhapesi. Taṃ itaro sāyanhasamaye pabujjhitvā usumaṃ nikkhantaṃ disvā “udakaṃ tāpetvā koṭṭhake ṭhapitaṃ bhavissatī”ti vegena gantvā theraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, koṭṭhake udakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, nhāyathā”ti vatvā therena saddhiṃyeva koṭṭhakaṃ pāvisi. Thero udakaṃ apassanto “kahaṃ udakaṃ, āvuso”ti āha. Daharo aggisālaṃ gantvā bhājane uḷuṅkaṃ otāretvā tucchabhāvaṃ ñatvā “passatha duṭṭhassa kammaṃ tucchabhājanaṃ uddhane āropetvā kuhiṃ gato, ahaṃ ‘koṭṭhake udaka’nti saññāya ārocesi”nti ujjhāyanto ghaṭaṃ ādāya titthaṃ agamāsi. Itaropi piṭṭhikoṭṭhakato udakaṃ āharitvā koṭṭhake ṭhapesi.

It is said that two resident pupils attended upon the Elder, who was dwelling near Rājagaha in the Pipphali Cave. One of them performed his duties diligently. The other, presenting what had been done by the first as if he himself had done it, knowing that water for washing the face and a tooth-stick had been prepared, would say, 'Venerable sir, I have prepared water for washing the face and a tooth-stick; please wash your face.' He would say the same at the time for washing feet, bathing, and so on. The other pupil thought, 'This one always presents what I have done as if he himself had done it. Let it be, I will do to him what ought to be done.' After that monk had eaten and was sleeping, he heated water for bathing, put it into one pot, and placed it at the back of the bathing chamber. In the water-heating vessel, however, he left about a nāḷi-measure of water, placing it so that it would release steam. In the evening, the other pupil awoke, and seeing the steam being emitted, thought, 'The water must have been heated and placed in the bathing chamber.' Going quickly, he paid homage to the Elder and said, 'Venerable sir, water has been placed in the bathing chamber; please bathe,' and entered the bathing chamber together with the Elder. The Elder, not seeing the water, said, 'Friend, where is the water?' The young monk went to the fire hall, lowered a ladle into the vessel, and realizing it was empty, grumbled, 'Look at the work of this wicked one! Having placed an empty vessel on the hearth, where has he gone? I announced it, thinking there was water in the bathing chamber!' Grumbling thus, he took a pot and went to the water-front. The other pupil then brought the water from the back of the bathing chamber and placed it in the bathing chamber.

Thero cintesi – “ayaṃ daharo ‘udakaṃ me tāpetvā koṭṭhake ṭhapitaṃ, etha, bhante, nhāyathā’ti vatvā idāni ujjhāyanto ghaṭaṃ ādāya titthaṃ gacchati, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti upadhārento “ettakaṃ kālaṃ esa daharo iminā kataṃ vattaṃ attanāva kataṃ viya pakāsetī”ti ñatvā sāyaṃ āgantvā nisinnassa ovādamadāsi, “āvuso, bhikkhunā nāma ‘attanā katameva kata’nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, no akataṃ, tvaṃ idāneva ‘koṭṭhake udakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, nhāyatha, bhante’ti vatvā mayi pavisitvā ṭhite ghaṭaṃ [M 1.0294] ādāya ujjhāyanto gacchasi, pabbajitassa nāma evaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. So “passatha therassa kammaṃ, udakamattakaṃ nāma nissāya maṃ evaṃ vadesī”ti kujjhitvā punadivase therena saddhiṃ piṇḍāya na pāvisi. Thero itarena saddhiṃ ekaṃ padesaṃ agamāsi. So tasmiṃ gate therassa upaṭṭhākakulaṃ gantvā “thero kahaṃ, bhante”ti puṭṭho [P 2.0021] “therassa aphāsukaṃ jātaṃ, vihāreyeva nisinno”ti āha. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Evarūpaṃ kira nāma āhāraṃ dethā”ti vutte tena vuttaniyāmeneva sampādetvā adaṃsu. So antarāmaggeva taṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gato. Theropi gataṭṭhāne mahantaṃ sukhumavatthaṃ labhitvā attanā saddhiṃ gatadaharassa adāsi. So taṃ rajitvā attano nivāsanapārupanaṃ akāsi.

The Elder thought: 'This young monk, after saying, "I have heated water and placed it in the bathing chamber for you; come, venerable sir, and bathe," now goes to the water-front grumbling while carrying a pot. What could this be?' Investigating, he realized, 'For all this time, this young monk has been presenting the duties done by the other as if done by himself.' In the evening, he came and gave this admonition to the seated pupil: 'Friend, a monk should say that he has done only what he himself has done; it is not proper to say one has done what one has not. Just now, you said, "Water has been placed in the bathing chamber; please bathe, venerable sir," and when I had entered and was standing there, you went off grumbling, carrying a pot. It is not proper for one who has gone forth to act in this way.' That monk became angry, thinking, 'Look at the Elder's action! He speaks to me this way just because of a little water!' The next day, he did not go for alms with the Elder. The Elder went to a certain place with the other monk. When the Elder had gone, that monk went to the Elder's supporter family and, when asked, 'Venerable sir, where is the Elder?' he replied, 'The Elder has become unwell; he is resting in the monastery.' They asked, 'Venerable sir, what would be suitable for him to receive?' When he said, 'You should give such-and-such food,' they prepared it exactly as he had instructed and gave it to him. He ate that food on the way back and went to the monastery. The Elder, for his part, received a large, fine cloth at the place he had gone and gave it to the young monk who had accompanied him. That monk dyed it and made it his lower and upper robe.

Thero punadivase taṃ upaṭṭhākakulaṃ gantvā, “bhante, ‘tumhākaṃ kira aphāsukaṃ jāta’nti amhehi daharena vuttaniyāmeneva paṭiyādetvā āhāro pesito, paribhuñjitvā vo phāsukaṃ jāta”nti [V 1.0262] vutte tuṇhī ahosi. Vihāraṃ pana gantvā taṃ daharaṃ vanditvā nisinnaṃ evamāha – “āvuso, tayā kira hiyyo, idaṃ nāma kataṃ, idaṃ pabbajitānaṃ na anucchavikaṃ, viññattiṃ katvā bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. So kujjhitvā there āghātaṃ bandhitvā “purimadivase udakamattaṃ nissāya maṃ musāvādiṃ katvā ajja attano upaṭṭhākakule bhattamuṭṭhiyā bhuttakāraṇā maṃ ‘viññattiṃ katvā bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti vadati, vatthampi tena attano upaṭṭhākasseva dinnaṃ, aho therassa bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ, jānissāmissa kattabbayuttaka”nti punadivase there gāmaṃ pavisante sayaṃ vihāre ohīyitvā daṇḍaṃ gahetvā paribhogabhājanāni bhinditvā therassa paṇṇasālāya aggiṃ datvā yaṃ na jhāyati, taṃ muggarena paharanto bhinditvā nikkhamitvā palāto. So kālaṃ katvā avīcimahāniraye nibbatti.

On the next day, the Elder went to that supporter's family. When they said, “Venerable sir, hearing that you were unwell, we sent food prepared exactly according to the young monk's instructions. Having partaken of it, are you now well?” he remained silent. However, having gone to the monastery, he spoke thus to that young monk who was sitting there after paying homage: “Friend, it is said that yesterday you did such-and-such a thing. This is not suitable for the ordained. It is not proper to eat after having made a solicitation.” That young monk, becoming angry and bearing a grudge against the Elder, thought: “On a previous day, on account of mere water, he made me out to be a liar. Today, because of eating a mouthful of rice at his own supporter's family, he tells me, ‘It is not proper to eat after having made a solicitation.’ The robe-cloth, too, was given by him only to his own attendant. Oh, the Elder's deed is grave! I will know what ought to be done to him.” On the next day, when the Elder was entering the village, he himself, staying behind in the monastery, took a staff, broke the vessels for use, set fire to the Elder's leaf hut, and that which did not burn, he struck with a mallet and broke it. Then, having departed, he fled. After he passed away, he arose in the great Avīci hell.

Mahājano [P 2.0022] kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi – “therassa kira saddhivihāriko ovādamattaṃ asahanto kujjhitvā paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpetvā palāto”ti. Atheko bhikkhu aparabhāge rājagahā nikkhamitvā satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmo jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā satthārā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kuto āgatosī”ti puṭṭho “rājagahato, bhante”ti āha. “Mama puttassa mahākassapassa khamanīya”nti? “Khamanīyaṃ, bhante, eko pana saddhivihāriko ovādamattena [M 1.0295] kujjhitvā paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpetvā palāto”ti. Satthā “na so idāneva ovādaṃ sutvā kujjhati, pubbepi kujjhiyeva. Na idāneva kuṭiṃ dūseti, pubbepi dūsesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari –

The people started a rumor: “It is said that the Elder's co-resident disciple, unable to endure a mere admonition, became angry, set fire to the leaf hut, and fled.” Then, at a later time, a certain monk, having departed from Rājagaha, desiring to see the Teacher, went to Jetavana. After paying homage to the Teacher, he was greeted with a friendly conversation and asked, “From where have you come?” He replied, “From Rājagaha, Venerable Sir.” “Is my son Mahākassapa well?” “He is well, Venerable Sir. But a certain co-resident disciple of his, angered by a mere admonition, set fire to the leaf hut and fled.” The Teacher said, “It is not only now that he becomes angry upon hearing an admonition; he became angry in the past as well. It is not only now that he destroys the hut; he destroyed it in the past as well,” and he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente himavantapadese eko siṅgilasakuṇo kulāvakaṃ katvā vasi. Athekadivasaṃ deve vassante eko makkaṭo sītena kampamāno taṃ padesaṃ agamāsi. Siṅgilo taṃ disvā gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a certain siṅgila bird lived in the Himavanta region, having made a nest. Then one day, while it was raining, a certain monkey, shivering with cold, came to that place. The siṅgila bird, seeing him, spoke a verse:

“Manussasseva te sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca vānara;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, agāraṃ te na vijjatī”ti. (jā. 1.4.81);

“O monkey, your head is like a human's, and your hands and feet are also like a human's. That being so, for what reason do you have no house?”

Makkaṭo “kiñcāpi me hatthapādā atthi, yāya pana paññāya vicāretvā agāraṃ kareyyaṃ, sā me paññā natthī”ti cintetvā tamatthaṃ viññāpetukāmo imaṃ gāthamāha –

The monkey, thinking, “Although I do have hands and feet, I do not have the wisdom by which I might reflect and build a house,” and wishing to make that matter known, spoke this verse:

“Manussasseva me sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca siṅgila;

Yāhu seṭṭhā manussesu, sā me paññā na vijjatī”ti. (jā. 1.4.82);

“O siṅgila, my head is like a human's, and my hands and feet are like a human's. That wisdom which is said to be excellent among humans, that wisdom I do not possess.”

Atha [V 1.0263] naṃ “evarūpassa tava kathaṃ gharāvāso ijjhissatī”ti garahanto siṅgilo imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

Then the siṅgila bird, reproaching him, “For one such as you, how will the household life succeed?” spoke this pair of verses:

“Anavaṭṭhitacittassa[P 2.0023], lahucittassa dubbhino;

Niccaṃ addhuvasīlassa, sukhabhāvo na vijjati.

“For one of unsteady mind, of fickle mind, who is treacherous to friends, and of ever-unstable conduct, there is no state of happiness.

“So karassu ānubhāvaṃ, vītivattassu sīliyaṃ;

Sītavātaparittāṇaṃ, karassu kuṭavaṃ kapī”ti. (jā. 1.4.83-84);

“Therefore, exert your power, overcome this ruinous tendency. Make a hut, O monkey, a protection from the cold and wind.”

Makkaṭo “ayaṃ maṃ anavaṭṭhitacittaṃ lahucittaṃ mittadubbhiṃ addhuvasīlaṃ karoti, idānissa mittadubbhibhāvaṃ dassessāmī”ti kulāvakaṃ viddhaṃsetvā vippakiri. Sakuṇo tasmiṃ kulāvakaṃ gaṇhante eva ekena passena nikkhamitvā palāyi.

The monkey thought: “This bird makes me out to be of unsteady mind, of fickle mind, a treacherous friend, and of unstable conduct. Now I will show it what being a treacherous friend is!” Having torn apart the nest, he scattered it. Just as the monkey was seizing the nest, the bird escaped by one side and fled.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo kuṭidūsakabhikkhu ahosi, siṅgilasakuṇo kassapo ahosī”ti[M 1.0296]. Jātakaṃ samodhānetvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, na idāneva, pubbepi so ovādakkhaṇe kujjhitvā kuṭiṃ dūsesi, mama puttassa kassapassa evarūpena bālena saddhiṃ vasanato ekakasseva nivāso seyyo”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the monkey was the hut-destroying monk; the siṅgila bird was Kassapa.” Having connected the Jātaka, he said: “Thus, monks, it is not only now. In the past also, that monk, becoming angry at the moment of admonition, destroyed the hut. For my son Kassapa, dwelling all alone is better than living together with such a fool.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

61.

61.

“Carañce nādhigaccheyya, seyyaṃ sadisamattano;

Ekacariyaṃ daḷhaṃ kayirā, natthi bāle sahāyatā”ti.

“If, while wandering, one should not find a companion better than or equal to oneself, let one resolutely maintain a solitary course; there is no companionship with a fool.”

Tattha caranti iriyāpathacāraṃ aggahetvā manasācāro veditabbo, kalyāṇamittaṃ pariyesantoti attho. Seyyaṃ sadisamattanoti attano sīlasamādhipaññāguṇehi adhikataraṃ [P 2.0024] vā sadisaṃ vā na labheyya ce. Ekacariyanti etesu hi seyyaṃ labhamāno sīlādīhi vaḍḍhati, sadisaṃ labhamāno na parihāyati, hīnena pana saddhiṃ ekato vasanto ekato saṃbhogaparibhogaṃ karonto sīlādīhi parihāyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “evarūpo puggalo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo aññatra anuddayā aññatra anukampā”ti (pu. pa. 121; a. ni. 3.26). Tasmā sace kāruññaṃ paṭicca “ayaṃ maṃ nissāya sīlādīhi vaḍḍhissatī”ti tamhā puggalā kiñci apaccāsīsanto taṃ saṅgaṇhituṃ sakkoti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ[V 1.0264]. No ce sakkoti, ekacariyaṃ daḷhaṃ kayirā ekībhāvameva thiraṃ katvā sabbairiyāpathesu ekakova vihareyya. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Natthi bāle sahāyatāti sahāyatā nāma cūḷasīlaṃ majjhimasīlaṃ mahāsīlaṃ dasa kathāvatthūni terasa dhutaṅgaguṇā vipassanāguṇā cattāro maggā cattāri phalāni tisso vijjā cha abhiññā. Ayaṃ sahāyatāguṇo bālaṃ nissāya natthīti.

Herein, 'wandering' (caranti) should be understood as mental conduct, not as movement in the physical postures; the meaning is 'seeking a virtuous friend with the mind.' 'Better or equal to oneself' means if one does not find one who is superior to or equal to oneself in the qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. As for 'a solitary life' (ekacariyaṃ): for among these, one who finds a superior person grows in virtue and so forth; one who finds an equal does not decline. But one who lives together with an inferior, sharing their company and association, declines in virtue and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'Such a person should not be served, should not be frequented, should not be attended upon, unless it is out of compassion.' Therefore, if, on account of compassion, thinking, 'This person, by relying on me, will grow in virtue and so forth,' and without expecting anything in return from that person, one is able to support them, this is wholesome. If one is not able, one should firmly lead a solitary life. Having made the state of being alone firm, one should dwell alone in all physical postures. For what reason? 'There is no companionship with a fool.' 'Companionship' refers to the minor, middle, and major categories of virtue, the ten topics of talk, the thirteen ascetic qualities, the qualities of insight, the four paths, the four fruits, the three knowledges, and the six super-knowledges. This quality of companionship does not exist in reliance on a fool; for this reason, one should dwell alone.

Desanāvasāne āgantuko bhikkhu sotāpattiphalaṃ patto, aññepi [P 2.0025] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu, desanā mahājanassa sātthikā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the visiting monk attained the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. The discourse was beneficial to the great assembly of people.

Mahākassapattherasaddhivihārikavatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Second Story: The Co-resident Disciple of the Elder Mahākassapa.

3. Ānandaseṭṭhivatthu

3. The Story of Ānanda the Treasurer

Puttā [M 1.0297] matthīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto ānandaseṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in Sāvatthī, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Sons are mine,' concerning Ānanda the Treasurer.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira ānandaseṭṭhi nāma cattālīsakoṭivibhavo mahāmaccharī ahosi. So anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ ñātake sannipātetvā puttaṃ mūlasiriṃ nāma tīsu velāsu evaṃ ovadati – “idaṃ cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ ‘bahū’”ti mā saññaṃ kari, vijjamānaṃ dhanaṃ na dātabbaṃ, navaṃ dhanaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Ekekampi hi kahāpaṇaṃ vayaṃ karontassa pana khīyateva. Tasmā –

In Sāvatthī, it is said, there was a treasurer named Ānanda, who possessed a fortune of forty crores and was extremely miserly. Every half-month, he would assemble his kinsmen and admonish his son, named Mūlasiri, at three times, thus: 'Do not hold the perception that this fortune of forty crores is 'much.' Existing wealth should not be given away; new wealth must be produced. Indeed, for one who spends even a single kahāpaṇa, wealth is simply exhausted. Therefore—'

“Añjanānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, upacikānañca ācayaṃ;

Madhūnañca samāhāraṃ, paṇḍito gharamāvase”ti.

'Seeing the depletion of eye-salve, and the accumulation by termites, and the gathering of nectar by bees, a wise person should dwell in the household life.'

So aparena samayena attano pañca mahānidhiyo puttassa anācikkhitvā dhananissito maccheramalamalino kālaṃ katvā tasseva nagarassa ekasmiṃ dvāragāmake caṇḍālānaṃ kulasahassaṃ paṭivasati. Tatthekissā caṇḍāliyā kucchismiṃ [P 2.0026] paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Rājā tassa kālakiriyaṃ sutvā puttamassa mūlasiriṃ pakkosāpetvā seṭṭhiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tampi caṇḍālakulasahassaṃ ekatova bhatiyā kammaṃ katvā jīvamānaṃ tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya neva bhatiṃ labhati, na yāpanamattato paraṃ bhattapiṇḍampi. Te “mayaṃ etarahi kammaṃ karontāpi piṇḍabhattampi na labhāma, amhākaṃ antare kāḷakaṇṇiyā bhavitabba”nti dve koṭṭhāsā hutvā yāva tassa mātāpitaro [V 1.0265] visuṃ honti, tāva vibhajitvā “imasmiṃ kule kāḷakaṇṇī uppannā”ti tassa mātaraṃ nīhariṃsu.

At a later time, without having revealed his five great treasure-troves to his son, attached to his wealth and defiled by the stain of miserliness, he died and took conception in the womb of a certain outcaste woman in a village near a gate of that very city, where a thousand families of outcastes resided. The king, hearing of his death, had his son Mūlasiri summoned and established him in the position of treasurer. And that thousand-family clan of outcastes, who lived by working together for wages, from the time he took conception, received no wages, not even enough for bare subsistence. They thought, 'Now, even when we work, we do not receive even a morsel of food. There must be an unlucky person among us.' Becoming two groups, they divided themselves until his mother and father were separate, and then, saying, 'An unlucky one has arisen in this family,' they drove out his mother.

Sāpi yāvassā so kucchigato, tāva yāpanamattampi kicchena labhitvā puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassa hatthā ca pādā ca akkhīni ca kaṇṇā ca nāsā ca mukhañca yathāṭhāne na ahesuṃ. So evarūpena aṅgavekallena samannāgato paṃsupisācako viya ativirūpo ahosi. Evaṃ santepi taṃ mātā na pariccaji. Kucchiyaṃ vasitaputtasmiñhi sineho balavā hoti. Sā taṃ kicchena posayamānā taṃ ādāya gatadivase kiñci alabhitvā gehe katvā sayameva gatadivase bhatiṃ labhati. Atha naṃ piṇḍāya caritvā jīvituṃ samatthakāle sā kapālakaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā, “tāta[M 1.0298], mayaṃ taṃ nissāya mahādukkhaṃ pattā, idāni na sakkomi taṃ posetuṃ, imasmiṃ nagare kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ [P 2.0027] paṭiyattabhattāni atthi, tattha bhikkhāya caritvā jīvāhī”ti taṃ vissajjesi. So gharapaṭipāṭiyā caranto ānandaseṭṭhikāle nivuttaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jātissaro hutvā attano gehaṃ pāvisi. Tīsu pana dvārakoṭṭhakesu na koci sallakkhesi. Catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake mūlasiriseṭṭhino puttakā disvā ubbiggahadayā parodiṃsu. Atha naṃ seṭṭhipurisā “nikkhama kāḷakaṇṇī”ti pothetvā nīharitvā saṅkāraṭṭhāne khipiṃsu. Satthā ānandattherena pacchāsamaṇena piṇḍāya caranto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patto theraṃ oloketvā tena puṭṭho taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Thero mūlasiriṃ pakkosāpesi. Atha mahājanakāyo sannipati. Satthā mūlasiriṃ āmantetvā “jānāsi eta”nti pucchitvā “na jānāmī”ti vutte, “pitā te ānandaseṭṭhī”ti vatvā asaddahantaṃ “ānandaseṭṭhi puttassa te pañca mahānidhiyo ācikkhāhī”ti ācikkhāpetvā saddahāpesi. So satthāraṃ saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Tassa dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

And she, for as long as he was in her womb, obtained with difficulty even enough for bare subsistence, and then gave birth to her son.
