His hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth were not in their proper places. Possessed of such physical deformities, he was extremely ugly, like a dust-demon. Even so, his mother did not abandon him, for the affection for a son who has dwelt in the womb is indeed strong. Nurturing him with difficulty, on days she went out taking him with her, she would obtain nothing; leaving him at home, on days she went out by herself, she would receive wages. Then, when he was old enough to live by wandering for alms, she placed a potsherd in his hand and said, 'Dear son, because of you, we have come to great suffering. Now I am not able to support you. In this city, there is food provided for the destitute and for travelers. Go and live by wandering for alms there,' and sent him away. He, wandering from house to house in order, went to the place of his former existence during his time as Ānanda the Treasurer, and, remembering his past birth, entered his own house. In the first three gate-houses, no one noticed him. At the fourth gate-house, the sons of Mūlasiri the Treasurer saw him and, with terrified hearts, began to wail. Then the treasurer's men, beating him and shouting, 'Get out, you unlucky creature!', dragged him out and threw him on a rubbish heap. The Teacher, while wandering for alms with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk, arrived at that place. Looking at the Elder, and being questioned by him, the Teacher explained the matter. The Elder had Mūlasiri summoned. Then a great crowd of people assembled. The Teacher addressed Mūlasiri and asked, 'Do you know this one?' When he replied, 'I do not know,' the Teacher said, 'He is your father, Ānanda the Treasurer.' When Mūlasiri did not believe, the Teacher had the boy who was Ānanda the Treasurer tell his son of the five great treasure-troves, and thus made him believe. Mūlasiri then went for refuge to the Teacher. Teaching him the Dhamma, the Teacher spoke this verse:

62.

62.

“Puttā matthi dhanammatthi, iti bālo vihaññati;

Attā hi attano natthi, kuto puttā kuto dhana”nti.

"I have sons, I have wealth," thus the fool is tormented. Indeed, one's own self is not one's own; whence sons, whence wealth?

Tassattho [P 2.0028] – puttā me atthi, dhanaṃ me atthi, iti bālo puttataṇhāya ceva dhanataṇhāya ca haññati vihaññati dukkhayati, “puttā me nassiṃsū”ti vihaññati, “nassantī”ti vihaññati, “nassissantī”ti vihaññati. Dhanepi eseva nayo. Iti chahākārehi vihaññati. “Putte posessāmī”ti rattiñca divā ca thalajalapathādīsu nānappakārato vāyamantopi vihaññati, “dhanaṃ uppādessāmī”ti kasivāṇijjādīni karontopi vihaññateva. Evaṃ [V 1.0266] vihaññassa ca attā hi attano natthi tena vighātena dukkhitaṃ attānaṃ sukhitaṃ kātuṃ asakkontassa pavattiyampissa attā hi attano natthi, maraṇamañce nipannassa māraṇantikāhi vedanāhi aggijālāhi viya pariḍayhamānassa chijjamānesu sandhibandhanesu, bhijjamānesu aṭṭhisaṅghāṭesu nimīletvā paralokaṃ ummīletvā idhalokaṃ passantassāpi divase divase dvikkhattuṃ nhāpetvā tikkhattuṃ bhojetvā gandhamālādīhi alaṅkaritvā yāvajīvaṃ positopi sahāyabhāvena [M 1.0299] dukkhaparittāṇaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya attā hi attano natthi. Kuto [P 2.0029] puttā kuto dhanaṃ puttā vā dhanaṃ vā tasmiṃ samaye kimeva karissanti, ānandaseṭṭhinopi kassaci kiñci adatvā puttassatthāya dhanaṃ saṇṭhapetvā pubbe vā maraṇamañce nipannassa, idāni vā imaṃ dukkhaṃ pattassa kuto puttā kuto dhanaṃ. Puttā vā dhanaṃ vā tasmiṃ samaye kiṃ dukkhaṃ hariṃsu, kiṃ vā sukhaṃ uppādayiṃsūti.

The meaning of that verse is this: 'I have sons, I have wealth'—thus the fool is tormented, afflicted, and made to suffer due to craving for sons and craving for wealth. He is afflicted thinking, 'My sons have perished'; he is afflicted thinking, 'They are perishing'; he is afflicted thinking, 'They will perish.' The same method applies to wealth. Thus, he is afflicted in six ways. Striving day and night in various ways on land-routes, water-routes, and so on, thinking, 'I will support my sons,' he is afflicted. Striving to generate wealth through farming, trade, and other means, he is also afflicted. For one who is thus afflicted, one's own self cannot be a refuge for oneself. For one who is unable to make the suffering self happy due to that affliction, even in the course of life, one's own self cannot be a refuge for oneself. When lying on the deathbed, burning as if by blazing flames with the pains that end in death, as the joints and ligaments are being severed and the bone structures are breaking apart, even for one who, having closed his eyes to the next world and opened his eyes to see this world—though he may have been bathed twice a day, fed three times a day, adorned with perfumes and garlands, and nourished for his entire life—one's own self cannot be a refuge for oneself due to the inability to act as a companion and provide protection from suffering. Whence sons? Whence wealth? What indeed will sons or wealth do at that time? Even in the case of the wealthy merchant Ānanda, who, without giving anything to anyone, established a treasure for his son's sake—whether before or while lying on his deathbed, or now, having encountered this suffering—whence sons? Whence wealth? What suffering did his sons or wealth remove at that time? Or what happiness did they produce? This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Desanā mahājanassa sātthikā ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings attained the comprehension of the Dhamma. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

Ānandaseṭṭhivatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Third Story of the Merchant Ānanda.

4. Gaṇṭhibhedakacoravatthu

4. The Story of the Cutpurses

Yo bāloti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto gaṇṭhibhedakacore ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Yo bālo,' concerning some cutpurses.

Te kira dve sahāyakā dhammassavanatthāya gacchantena mahājanena saddhiṃ jetavanaṃ gantvā eko dhammakathaṃ assosi, eko attano gayhūpagaṃ olokesi. Tesu eko dhammaṃ suṇamāno sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi, itaro ekassa dussante baddhaṃ pañcamāsakamattaṃ labhi. Tassa taṃ gehe pākabhattaṃ jātaṃ, itarassa gehe na paccati. Atha naṃ sahāyakacoro attano bhariyāya saddhiṃ uppaṇḍayamāno “tvaṃ atipaṇḍitatāya attano gehe pākabhattamūlampi na nipphādesī”ti āha. Itaro pana “bālabhāveneva vatāyaṃ attano paṇḍitabhāvaṃ maññatī”ti taṃ pavattiṃ satthu ārocetuṃ [P 2.0030] ñātīhi saddhiṃ jetavanaṃ gantvā ārocesi. Satthā tassa dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that two companions went to Jetavana together with a great crowd that was going to listen to the Dhamma. One listened to the Dhamma talk, while the other looked for something to take. Of these two, the one who listened to the Dhamma attained the fruit of stream-entry, while the other obtained about five māsakas that were tied in the end of a garment. With this, a meal was cooked in his home, but in the other's home, nothing was cooked. Then the thieving companion, together with his wife, ridiculed him, saying: 'Because of your excessive cleverness, you could not even produce the means for a cooked meal in your own home!' But the other thought, 'Truly, it is only out of foolishness that this one considers himself wise,' and he went with his relatives to Jetavana to report the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher, while teaching him the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

63.

63.

“Yo [V 1.0267] bālo maññati bālyaṃ, paṇḍito vāpi tena so;

Bālo ca paṇḍitamānī, sa ve ‘bālo’ti vuccatī”ti.

The fool who recognizes his folly is wise at least to that extent; but the fool who thinks himself wise is truly called a 'fool'.

Tattha yo bāloti yo andhabālo apaṇḍito samāno “bālo aha”nti attano bālyaṃ bālabhāvaṃ maññati jānāti. Tena soti [M 1.0300] tena kāraṇena so puggalo paṇḍito vāpi hoti paṇḍitasadiso vā. So hi “bālo aha”nti jānamāno aññaṃ paṇḍitaṃ upasaṅkamanto payirupāsanto tena paṇḍitabhāvatthāya ovadiyamāno anusāsiyamāno taṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhitvā paṇḍito vā hoti paṇḍitataro vā. Sa ve bāloti yo ca bālo samāno “ko añño mayā sadiso bahussuto vā dhammakathiko vā vinayadharo vā dhutaṅgadharo vā atthī”ti evaṃ paṇḍitamānī hoti. So aññaṃ paṇḍitaṃ anupasaṅkamanto apayirupāsanto neva pariyattiṃ uggaṇhāti, na paṭipattiṃ pūreti, ekantabālabhāvameva pāpuṇāti. So gaṇṭhibhedakacoro viya. Tena vuttaṃ “sa ve ‘bālo’ti vuccatī”ti.

Herein, 'a fool who...': one who, being a blind fool, an unwise person, knows his own folly, his state of foolishness, thinking, 'I am a fool.' 'Is wise... to that extent': for that reason that person becomes wise or at least like a wise person. For, knowing, 'I am a fool,' he approaches and attends upon another wise person; being advised and instructed by him for the sake of becoming wise, he accepts that advice and becomes wise or even wiser. 'But the fool... is truly called a fool': this is one who, being a fool, is conceited about his wisdom, thinking: 'Who else is like me—so learned, a preacher of the Dhamma, an expert in the Vinaya, an observer of the ascetic practices?' Not approaching or attending upon another wise person, he neither learns the scriptural teaching nor fulfills the practice; he attains a state of utter foolishness. He is like the cutpurse thief. Therefore it is said: 'he is truly called a fool.'

Desanāpariyosāne itarassa ñātakehi saddhiṃ mahājano sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the great crowd, along with the relatives of the other man, attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Gaṇṭhibhedakacoravatthu catutthaṃ.

The Fourth Story of the Cutpurses.

5. Udāyittheravatthu

5. 5. The Story of the Elder Udāyī

Yāvajīvampi ce bāloti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto udāyittheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, 'Yāvajīvampi ce bālo,' concerning the Elder Udāyī.

So [P 2.0031] kira mahātheresu paṭikkantesu dhammasabhaṃ gantvā dhammāsane nisīdi. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ āgantukā bhikkhū disvā “ayaṃ bahussuto mahāthero bhavissatī”ti maññamānā khandhādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ pañhaṃ pucchitvā kiñci ajānamānaṃ “ko eso, buddhehi saddhiṃ ekavihāre vasamāno khandhadhātuāyatanamattampi na jānātī”ti garahitvā taṃ pavattiṃ tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ. Satthā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that after the great elders had departed, he would go to the Dhamma hall and sit on the seat of the Dhamma preachers. Then one day, some visiting monks saw him and, thinking, 'This must be a great elder of great learning,' they asked him a question connected with the aggregates and other topics. When they found that he knew nothing, they reproached him, saying: 'Who is this one? Though living in the same monastery as the Buddha, he does not know even about the aggregates, elements, and sense bases!' Having reproached him thus, they reported that matter to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, intending to teach them the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

64.

64.

“Yāvajīvampi ce bālo, paṇḍitaṃ payirupāsati;

Na so dhammaṃ vijānāti, dabbī sūparasaṃ yathā”ti.

Even if a fool attends upon a wise person all his life, he does not know the Dhamma, just as a ladle does not know the taste of soup.

Tassattho [V 1.0268] – bālo nāmesa yāvajīvampi paṇḍitaṃ upasaṅkamanto payirupāsanto “idaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, ettakaṃ buddhavacana”nti evaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ vā “ayaṃ [M 1.0301] cāro, ayaṃ vihāro, ayaṃ ācāro, ayaṃ gocaro, idaṃ sāvajjaṃ, idaṃ anavajjaṃ, idaṃ sevitabbaṃ, idaṃ na sevitabbaṃ, idaṃ paṭivijjhitabbaṃ, idaṃ sacchikātabba”nti evaṃ paṭipattipaṭivedhadhammaṃ vā na jānāti. Yathā kiṃ? Dabbī sūparasaṃ yathāti. Yathā hi dabbī yāva parikkhayā nānappakārāya sūpavikatiyā samparivattamānāpi “idaṃ loṇikaṃ, idaṃ aloṇikaṃ, idaṃ tittakaṃ, idaṃ khārikaṃ, idaṃ kaṭukaṃ, idaṃ ambilaṃ, idaṃ anambilaṃ, idaṃ kasāva”nti [P 2.0032] sūparasaṃ na jānāti, evameva bālo yāvajīvampi paṇḍitaṃ payirupāsamāno vuttappakāraṃ dhammaṃ na jānātīti.

The meaning of that verse is this: This one called a fool, though he may approach and attend upon a wise person for his entire life, does not know either the scriptural Dhamma—such as, 'This is the word of the Buddha; the word of the Buddha has such and such qualities'—or the Dhamma of practice and penetration—such as, 'This is right conduct, this is the right dwelling, this is disciplined behavior, this is the right resort; this is blameworthy, this is blameless; this should be cultivated, this should not be cultivated; this is to be penetrated, this is to be realized.' How is this so? Just as a ladle does not know the taste of soup. Indeed, just as a ladle, though it is stirred back and forth in various kinds of special curries until it is worn out, does not know the taste of the soup—'this is salty, this is not salty, this is bitter, this is alkaline, this is pungent, this is sour, this is not sour, this is astringent'—even so, a fool, though he attends upon a wise person for his entire life, does not know the Dhamma of the kinds described.

Desanāvasāne āgantukā bhikkhū āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the minds of the visiting monks were liberated from the taints.

Udāyittheravatthu pañcamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Udāyī, the Fifth.

6. Tiṃsamattapāveyyakabhikkhuvatthu

6. 6. The Story of the Thirty Monks from Pāveyyaka

Muhuttamapi ce viññūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto tiṃsamatte pāveyyake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, 'Muhuttamapi ce viññū,' concerning about thirty monks from Pāveyyaka.

Tesañhi bhagavā itthiṃ pariyesantānaṃ kappāsikavanasaṇḍe paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Tadā te sabbeva ehibhikkhubhāvaṃ patvā iddhimayapattacīvaradharā hutvā terasa dhutaṅgāni samādāya vattamānā punapi dīghassa addhuno accayena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā anamataggadhammadesanaṃ sutvā tasmiṃyeva āsane arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Bhikkhū “aho vatimehi bhikkhūhi khippameva dhammo viññāto”ti dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā taṃ sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ime tiṃsamattā sahāyakā dhuttā hutvā tuṇḍilajātake (jā. 1.6.88 ādayo) mahātuṇḍilassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvāpi khippameva [P 2.0033] dhammaṃ viññāya pañca sīlāni samādiyiṃsu, te teneva upanissayena etarahi nisinnāsaneyeva arahattaṃ pattā”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, the Blessed One first taught the Dhamma to them in the cotton-wood forest grove while they were searching for a woman. Then, all of them, having attained the state of an 'ehi bhikkhu,' became bearers of bowls and robes created by psychic power. Having undertaken and been practicing the thirteen ascetic practices, after a long period of time had passed, they again approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma discourse on the unknowable beginning, and right on that seat attained Arahantship. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma assembly, saying, “Ah, how quickly the Dhamma was understood by these monks!” Hearing that talk, the Teacher said, “Not only now, O monks. In the past too, these thirty companions, having been drunkards, also heard the Dhamma discourse of Mahātuṇḍila in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka and, quickly understanding the Dhamma, undertook the five precepts. By that very supportive condition, they have now attained Arahantship while still seated.” Having said this, and desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

65.

65.

“Muhuttamapi ce viññū, paṇḍitaṃ payirupāsati;

Khippaṃ dhammaṃ vijānāti, jivhā sūparasaṃ yathā”ti.

Even if a discerning person associates with a wise person for only a moment, they quickly understand the Dhamma, just as the tongue knows the taste of soup.

Tassattho [V 1.0269][M 1.0302] – viññū paṇḍitapuriso muhuttamapi ce aññaṃ paṇḍitaṃ payirupāsati, so tassa santike uggaṇhanto paripucchanto khippameva pariyattidhammaṃ vijānāti. Tato kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā paṭipattiyaṃ ghaṭento vāyamanto yathā nāma anupahatajivhāpasādo puriso rasavijānanatthaṃ jivhagge ṭhapetvā eva loṇikādibhedaṃ rasaṃ vijānāti, evaṃ paṇḍito khippameva lokuttaradhammampi vijānātīti.

The meaning of that verse is this: If a discerning, wise person attends upon another wise person even for a moment, that person, while learning and questioning in the presence of that wise one, quickly knows the scriptural Dhamma. After that, having had a meditation subject explained, while striving and making effort in the practice, just as a person whose faculty of taste is unimpaired knows the taste with its distinctions of salty and so on just by placing it on the tip of the tongue for the sake of knowing the taste, even so, a wise person quickly knows even the supramundane Dhamma.

Desanāvasāne bahū bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many monks attained Arahantship.

Tiṃsamattapāveyyakabhikkhuvatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of the Thirty Monks from Pāveyyaka, the Sixth.

7. Suppabuddhakuṭṭhivatthu

7. The Story of Suppabuddha the Leper

Caranti bālā dummedhāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto suppabuddhakuṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Suppabuddhakuṭṭhivatthu udāne (udā. 43) āgatameva.

This Dhamma teaching beginning with, 'Fools of little wisdom wander,' the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery concerning Suppabuddha the leper. The story of Suppabuddha the leper is indeed found in the Udāna.

Tadā hi suppabuddhakuṭṭhi parisapariyante nisinno bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ [P 2.0034] satthu ārocetukāmo parisamajjhe ogāhituṃ avisahanto mahājanassa satthāraṃ vanditvā anugantvā nivattanakāle vihāraṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko devarājā “ayaṃ suppabuddhakuṭṭhi attano satthu sāsane paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātukāmo”ti ñatvā “vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti gantvā ākāse ṭhitova etadavoca – “suppabuddha, tvaṃ manussadaliddo manussavarāko, ahaṃ te apariyantaṃ dhanaṃ dassāmi, ‘buddho na buddho, dhammo na dhammo, saṅgho na saṅgho, alaṃ me buddhena, alaṃ me dhammena, alaṃ me saṅghenā’ti vadehī”ti. Atha naṃ so āha – “kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ sakko”ti. Andhabāla, ahirika tvaṃ mayā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ na yuttarūpo, tvaṃ maṃ “duggato daliddo kapaṇo”ti vadesi, nevāhaṃ duggato, na daliddo, sukhappatto ahamasmi mahaddhano –

Indeed, at that time, Suppabuddha the leper, sitting at the edge of the assembly, having heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Wishing to announce to the Teacher the quality he had attained, but not daring to enter into the midst of the assembly, he went to the monastery at the time of returning, after the great crowd had paid homage to the Teacher and followed him. At that moment, Sakka, the king of the devas, knowing, 'This Suppabuddha the leper wishes to make manifest the quality he has attained in the Teacher's Dispensation,' went to test him and, standing in the air, said this: 'Suppabuddha, you are a poor human, a wretched human. I will give you limitless wealth. Say: "The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Sangha is not the Sangha. I have no need of the Buddha, I have no need of the Dhamma, I have no need of the Sangha."' Then that one said to him, 'Who are you?' 'I am Sakka.' 'Blind fool, shameless one, you are not fit to speak with me. You call me wretched, poor, and miserable, but I am not wretched, nor am I poor. I have attained happiness; I am of great wealth.'

“Saddhādhanaṃ sīladhanaṃ, hirī ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ;

Sutadhanañca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhanaṃ.

The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of shame and fear of wrongdoing; and the wealth of learning, and generosity, and indeed, wisdom is the seventh wealth.

“Yassa [M 1.0303][V 1.0270] ete dhanā atthi, itthiyā purisassa vā;

‘Adaliddo’ti taṃ āhu, amoghaṃ tassa jīvita”nti. (a. ni. 7.5-6) –

For whomever, be it a woman or a man, these treasures exist, that one they call 'not poor'; their life is not in vain.

Imāni me sattavidhaariyadhanāni santi, yesañhi imāni satta dhanāni santi, na te buddhehi vā paccekabuddhehi vā “daliddā”ti [P 2.0035] vuccantīti. Sakko tassa kathaṃ sutvā taṃ antarāmagge ohāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ vacanapaṭivacanaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ bhagavā āha – “na kho, sakka, sakkā tādisānaṃ satenapi sahassenapi suppabuddhakuṭṭhiṃ ‘buddho na buddho’ti vā, ‘dhammo na dhammo’ti vā, ‘saṅgho na saṅgho’ti vā kathāpetu”nti. Suppabuddhopi kho kuṭṭhi satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthārā katapaṭisanthāro sammodamāno attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocetvā vuṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Atha naṃ acirapakkantaṃ gāvī taruṇavacchā jīvitā voropesi.

These seven kinds of noble wealth are mine. Indeed, those who possess these seven treasures are not called 'poor' by Buddhas or by Paccekabuddhas.” Having heard his speech, Sakka, leaving him on the path, went to the Teacher's presence and reported that entire speech and reply. Then the Blessed One said to him: “Indeed, Sakka, it is not possible for a hundred or even a thousand such as you to make Suppabuddha the leper say, 'The Buddha is not the Buddha,' or 'The Dhamma is not the Dhamma,' or 'The Sangha is not the Sangha.'” Suppabuddha the leper also, having gone to the Teacher's presence and having been given a friendly greeting by the Teacher, rejoicing, announced the quality he had attained, rose from his seat, and departed. Then, not long after he had departed, a cow with a young calf deprived him of life.

Sā kira ekā yakkhinī pukkusātikulaputtaṃ, bāhiyaṃ dārucīriyaṃ, tambadāṭhikacoraghātakaṃ, suppabuddhakuṭṭhinti imesaṃ catunnaṃ janānaṃ anekasate attabhāve gāvī hutvā jīvitā voropesi. Te kira atīte cattāro seṭṭhiputtā hutvā ekaṃ nagarasobhiniṃ gaṇikaṃ uyyānaṃ netvā divasaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavitvā sāyanhasamaye evaṃ sammantayiṃsu – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne añño natthi, imissā amhehi dinnaṃ kahāpaṇasahassañca sabbañca pasādhanabhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā imaṃ māretvā gacchāmā”ti. Sā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “ime nillajjā, mayā saddhiṃ abhiramitvā idāni maṃ māretukāmā, jānissāmi nesaṃ kattabbayuttaka”nti tehi māriyamānā [P 2.0036] “ahaṃ yakkhinī hutvā yathā maṃ ete mārenti, evameva te māretuṃ samatthā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Tassa nissandena ime māresi. Sambahulā bhikkhū tassa kālakiriyaṃ bhagavato ārocetvā “tassa kā gati, kena ca kāraṇena kuṭṭhibhāvaṃ patto”ti pucchiṃsu. Satthā sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā tassa tāvatiṃsabhavane uppannabhāvañca tagarasikhipaccekabuddhaṃ disvā niṭṭhubhitvā apasabyaṃ katvā dīgharattaṃ niraye paccitvā vipākāvasesena idāni kuṭṭhibhāvappattiñca byākaritvā, “bhikkhave, ime sattā attanāva [M 1.0304] attano kaṭukavipākakammaṃ karontā vicarantī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā uttari dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that she was a certain yakkhinī who, having become a cow in many hundreds of existences, deprived these four persons of life: Pukkusāti the clansman, Bāhiya Dārucīriya, Tambadāṭhika the thief-killer, and Suppabuddha the leper. It is said that in the past, they were four sons of merchants. Having taken a city-beautifying courtesan to a park and having experienced pleasure for the day, in the evening they conspired thus: 'There is no one else in this place. Let us take the thousand kahāpaṇas and all the ornaments given by us to her, kill her, and go.' Hearing their words, she thought, 'These shameless men, having delighted with me, now wish to kill me. I shall know what is fitting for their deed.' As she was being killed by them, she made this aspiration: 'Having become a yakkhinī, may I be able to kill them in the very same way that they are killing me.' As a result of that, she killed them. Many bhikkhus, having informed the Blessed One of his death, asked: 'What is his destination, and for what reason did he attain the state of a leper?' The Teacher then declared his attainment of the fruit of stream-entry and his arising in the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm, and also that, having seen the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhi, spat, and performed a disrespectful act, he was tormented in hell for a long time, and by the remainder of that result, he now attained the state of a leper. Having said, 'Bhikkhus, these beings wander about, performing for themselves kamma that has a bitter result,' and connecting the narrative, he taught the Dhamma further and spoke this verse:

66.

66.

“Caranti bālā dummedhā, amitteneva attanā;

Karontā pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, yaṃ hoti kaṭukapphala”nti.

Fools of little wisdom wander, with themselves as their own enemy, performing evil kamma which has a bitter fruit.

Tattha [V 1.0271] carantīti catūhi iriyāpathehi akusalameva karontā vicaranti. Bālāti idhalokatthañca paralokatthañca ajānantā idha bālā nāma. Dummedhāti duppaññā. Amitteneva [P 2.0037] attanāti attanā amittabhūtena viya verinā hutvā. Kaṭukapphalanti tikhiṇaphalaṃ dukkhaphalanti.

Therein, `caranti` (they wander) means: they move about in the four postures performing only unwholesome kamma. `Bālā` (fools) means: those who do not know what is for their welfare in this world and the next are called 'fools' here. `Dummedhā` (of little wisdom) means: of deficient wisdom. `Amitteneva attanā` (with themselves as their own enemy) means: by oneself, as if having become an enemy, a foe. `Kaṭukapphalaṃ` (which has a bitter fruit) means: having a pungent result, a painful result.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Suppabuddhakuṭṭhivatthu sattamaṃ.

The Seventh Story: Suppabuddha the Leper.

8. Kassakavatthu

8. The Story of the Farmer

Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kassakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this discourse on the Dhamma beginning with, 'That deed is not well done,' concerning a certain farmer.

So kira sāvatthito avidūre ekaṃ khettaṃ kasati. Corā udakaniddhamanena nagaraṃ pavisitvā ekasmiṃ aḍḍhakule umaṅgaṃ bhinditvā bahuṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā udakaniddhamaneneva nikkhamiṃsu. Eko coro te vañcetvā ekaṃ sahassatthavikaṃ ovaṭṭikāya katvā taṃ khettaṃ gantvā tehi saddhiṃ bhaṇḍaṃ bhājetvā ādāya gacchanto ovaṭṭikato patamānaṃ sahassatthavikaṃ na sallakkhesi. Taṃ divasaṃ satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento taṃ kassakaṃ attano ñāṇajālassa antopaviṭṭhaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti upadhārayamāno idaṃ addasa – “ayaṃ kassako pātova kasituṃ gamissati, bhaṇḍasāmikā corānaṃ anupadaṃ gantvā ovaṭṭikato patamānaṃ sahassatthavikaṃ disvā etaṃ gaṇhissanti, maṃ ṭhapetvā tassa añño sakkhī nāma [P 2.0038] na bhavissati, sotāpattimaggassa upanissayopissa atthi, tattha mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sopi kassako pātova kasituṃ gato. Satthā ānandattherena pacchāsamaṇena tattha agamāsi. Kassako satthāraṃ disvā gantvā bhagavantaṃ [M 1.0305] vanditvā puna kasituṃ ārabhi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ kiñci avatvāva sahassatthavikāya patitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ disvā ānandattheraṃ āha – “passa, ānanda, āsīviso”ti. “Passāmi, bhante, ghoraviso”ti.

It is said that he tilled a field not far from Sāvatthī. Thieves, having entered the city by a water conduit, broke a tunnel into a wealthy household, took much silver and gold, and exited by that same water conduit. One thief, having deceived them, placed a bag containing one thousand in his loincloth, went to that field, divided the goods with them, and as he was leaving, did not notice the bag of one thousand falling from his loincloth. That day, at dawn, the Teacher, while surveying the world, saw that farmer enter the net of His knowledge. Investigating, 'What, I wonder, will happen?' He perceived this: 'This farmer will go to plow early in the morning. The owners of the goods, following the thieves' tracks, will see the bag of one thousand that fell from the loincloth and will seize him. Apart from me, there will be no other witness for him. He also has the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry. It is proper for me to go there.' That farmer also went to plow early in the morning. The Teacher went there with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk. Seeing the Teacher, the farmer approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, and resumed plowing. Without saying anything to him, the Teacher went to the spot where the bag of one thousand had fallen and, seeing it, said to the Venerable Ānanda, 'Ānanda, see the venomous serpent.' 'I see, Venerable Sir, the deadly venomous serpent.'

Kassako taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “mama velāya vā avelāya vā vicaraṇaṭṭhānametaṃ, āsīviso kirettha atthī”ti cintetvā satthari ettakaṃ vatvā pakkante “māressāmi na”nti patodalaṭṭhiṃ ādāya gato sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ disvā “imaṃ sandhāya satthārā kathitaṃ bhavissatī”ti taṃ ādāya [V 1.0272] nivatto, abyattatāya ekamante ṭhapetvā paṃsunā paṭicchādetvā puna kasituṃ ārabhi. Manussā ca vibhātāya rattiyā gehe corehi katakammaṃ disvā padānupadaṃ gacchantā taṃ khettaṃ gantvā tattha corehi bhaṇḍassa bhājitaṭṭhānaṃ disvā kassakassa padavalañjaṃ addasaṃsu. Te tassa padānusārena gantvā thavikāya ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ disvā paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā thavikaṃ ādāya “tvaṃ gehaṃ vilumpitvā khettaṃ kasamāno viya vicarasī”ti tajjetvā pothetvā netvā rañño dassayiṃsu. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā [P 2.0039] tassa vadhaṃ āṇāpesi. Rājapurisā taṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā kasāhi tāḷentā āghātanaṃ nayiṃsu. So kasāhi tāḷiyamāno aññaṃ kiñci avatvā “passānanda, āsīvisoti, passāmi bhagavā ghoraviso”ti vadanto gacchati. Atha naṃ rājapurisā “tvaṃ satthu ceva ānandattherassa ca kathaṃ kathesi, kiṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā – “rājānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhamāno kathessāmī”ti vutte rañño santikaṃ netvā rañño taṃ pavattiṃ kathayiṃsu. Atha naṃ rājā “kasmā evaṃ kathesī”ti pucchi. So “nāhaṃ, deva, coro”ti vatvā kasanatthāya nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ācikkhi. Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ bhaṇe loke aggapuggalaṃ satthāraṃ sakkhiṃ apadisati, na yuttaṃ etassa dosaṃ āropetuṃ, ahamettha kattabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti taṃ ādāya sāyanhasamaye satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pucchi – “bhagavā kacci tumhe ānandattherena saddhiṃ etassa kassakassa kasanaṭṭhānaṃ gatā”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃ vo tattha diṭṭha”nti? “Sahassatthavikā, mahārājā”ti. “Disvā kiṃ avocutthā”ti? “Idaṃ nāma, mahārājā”ti. “Bhante, sacāyaṃ puriso tumhādisaṃ apadisaṃ nākarissa, na jīvitaṃ alabhissa, tumhehi pana kathitakathaṃ [M 1.0306] kathetvā tena jīvitaṃ laddha”nti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “āma, mahārāja, ahampi ettakameva vatvā gato, paṇḍitena nāma yaṃ kammaṃ katvā pacchānutappaṃ [P 2.0040] hoti, taṃ na kattabba”nti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing these words, the farmer thought, 'This is a place where I wander, whether at the proper time or not; it seems a venomous serpent is here.' After the Teacher had said that much and departed, he thought, 'I will kill it.' Taking a goad, he went and saw the bag of one thousand. Thinking, 'The Teacher must have been referring to this,' he took it and returned. Due to his foolishness, he placed it aside in a secluded spot, covered it with dust, and resumed plowing. When the night had dawned, the townspeople saw the deed done by the thieves in the house and, following the tracks step-by-step, they went to that field. There they saw the place where the thieves had divided the goods and noticed the farmer's footprints. Following his tracks, they went and saw the spot where the bag was placed. They brushed aside the dust, took the bag, and threatened him, saying, 'You plunder a house and then wander about as if plowing a field!' They beat him, took him away, and presented him to the king. The king, hearing the account, ordered his execution. The king's men bound his hands behind his back and, beating him with whips, led him to the execution ground. As he was being beaten with whips, he said nothing else, but went along muttering the words, 'Ānanda, see the venomous serpent,' and 'Blessed One, I see the deadly venomous serpent.' Then the king's men asked him, 'You speak the words of the Teacher and the Elder Ānanda. What does this mean?' When he replied, 'If I am able to see the king, I will explain,' they took him to the king's presence and related the account to the king. Then the king asked him, 'Why did you speak thus?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, I am not a thief,' and explained the entire account to the king, starting from the time he went out to plow. Hearing his words, the king said to his ministers, 'Sirs, this man points to the Teacher, the foremost person in the world, as his witness. It is not right to attribute fault to him. I myself will find out what should be done in this matter.' Taking him, he went to the Teacher's presence in the evening and asked the Teacher, 'Venerable Sir, did you and the Venerable Ānanda go to this farmer's plowing place?' 'Yes, great king.' 'What did you see there?' 'A bag of one thousand, great king.' 'Having seen it, what did you say?' 'We said just that, great king.' 'Venerable Sir, if this man had not made one such as you his witness, he would not have saved his life. But by repeating the words spoken by you, he has obtained his life.' Hearing this, the Teacher said, 'Yes, great king. I too departed after saying just that much. A wise person, indeed, should not do a deed which, having been done, is regretted afterwards.' And connecting the theme, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

67.

67.

“Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā anutappati;

Yassa assumukho rodaṃ, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti.

That deed is not well done which, having done it, one regrets, and whose result one experiences with a tearful face, weeping.

Tattha na taṃ kammanti yaṃ nirayādīsu nibbattanasamatthaṃ dukkhudrayaṃ kammaṃ katvā anussaranto anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe anutappati anusocati, taṃ kataṃ na sādhu na sundaraṃ niratthakaṃ. Yassa assumukhoti yassa assūhi tintamukho rodanto vipākaṃ anubhotīti.

Therein, 'that deed is not well done' means: having done a deed that is capable of causing rebirth in hell and so forth, a basis for painful feeling, one recollects it and, at every moment of recollection, one repeatedly regrets and sorrows; that deed is not good, not beautiful, and fruitless. 'Whose tearful face' means: one who experiences the result with a face wet with tears, weeping.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0273] kassako upāsako sotāpattiphalaṃ patto, sampattabhikkhūpi sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the farmer, a lay follower, attained the fruit of stream-entry, and the monks who had assembled also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Kassakavatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Eighth Story: The Farmer.

9. Sumanamālākāravatthu

9. The Story of Sumana the Garland-Maker

Tañca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto sumanaṃ nāma mālākāraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

This teaching, beginning with ‘That deed is well done,’ was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, concerning a garland-maker named Sumana.

So [P 2.0041] kira devasikaṃ bimbisārarājānaṃ pātova aṭṭhahi sumanapupphanāḷīhi upaṭṭhahanto aṭṭha kahāpaṇe labhati. Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ pupphāni gahetvā nagaraṃ paviṭṭhamatte bhagavā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjetvā mahatā buddhānubhāvena mahatiyā buddhalīḷāya nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Bhagavā hi ekadā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo cīvarena paṭicchādetvā aññataro piṇḍapātiko viya carati tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ aṅgulimālassa paccuggamanaṃ gacchanto viya, ekadā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjetvā kapilavatthuppavesanādīsu viya. Tasmimpi divase sarīrato chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjento mahantena buddhānubhāvena mahatiyā buddhalīḷāya rājagahaṃ pāvisi. Mālākāro bhagavato ratanagghiyasadisaṃ attabhāvaṃ disvā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītānubyañjanasarīrasobhaggaṃ [M 1.0307] oloketvā pasannacitto “kiṃ nu kho satthu adhikāraṃ karomī”ti cintetvā aññaṃ apassanto “imehi pupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjessāmī”ti cintetvā puna cintesi – “imāni rañño nibaddhaṃ upaṭṭhānapupphāni, rājā imāni alabhanto maṃ bandhāpeyya vā ghātāpeyya vā raṭṭhato vā pabbājeyya, kiṃ nu kho karomī”ti? Athassa etadahosi “rājā maṃ ghātetu vā bandhāpetu vā raṭṭhato pabbājetu vā, so hi mayhaṃ dadamānopi imasmiṃ attabhāve jīvitamattaṃ dhanaṃ dadeyya, satthupūjā pana me anekāsu kappakoṭīsu alaṃ hitāya ceva sukhāya cā”ti attano [P 2.0042] jīvitaṃ tathāgatassa pariccaji.

It is said that daily, presenting King Bimbisāra with eight measures of jasmine flowers early in the morning, he would receive eight kahāpaṇas. Then one day, just as he had taken those flowers and entered the city, the Blessed One, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, emitted six-colored rays. With great Buddha-power and with great Buddha-majesty, he entered the city for alms. For sometimes the Blessed One would conceal the six-colored rays with his robe and travel like an ordinary alms-gatherer, as when he went a distance of thirty yojanas to meet Aṅgulimāla. At other times, he would emit the six-colored rays, as when entering Kapilavatthu and on other such occasions. On that day too, emitting the six-colored rays from his body with great Buddha-power and with great Buddha-majesty, he entered Rājagaha. The garland-maker, seeing the Blessed One’s person, which was like a priceless gem, and beholding the splendor of his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics, with a mind of faith, thought, “What offering can I make to the Teacher?” Seeing nothing else, he thought, “I will worship the Blessed One with these flowers.” Then he thought again: “These are the flowers for the king’s constant attendance. If the king does not receive these, he might have me imprisoned, or killed, or banished from the kingdom. What should I do?” Then this occurred to him: “Let the king have me killed, or imprisoned, or banished from the kingdom. For he, even when giving to me, would only give wealth sufficient for a livelihood in this present existence. But this worship of the Teacher will be sufficient for my welfare and happiness for many crores of eons.” Thus, he surrendered his own life to the Tathāgata.

So “yāva me pasannaṃ cittaṃ na patikuṭati, taṃ tāvadeva pūjaṃ karissāmī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho udaggudaggo satthāraṃ pūjesi. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ tāva dveva pupphamuṭṭhiyo tathāgatassa upari khipi, tā uparimatthake vitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Aparā dve muṭṭhiyo khipi, tā dakkhiṇahatthapassena mālāpaṭacchannena [V 1.0274] otaritvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Aparā dve muṭṭhiyo khipi, tā piṭṭhipassena otaritvā tatheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Aparā dve muṭṭhiyo khipi, tā vāmahatthapassena otaritvā tatheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ aṭṭha nāḷiyo aṭṭha muṭṭhiyo hutvā catūsu ṭhānesu tathāgataṃ parikkhipiṃsu. Purato gamanadvāramattameva ahosi. Pupphānaṃ vaṇṭāni anto ahesuṃ, pattāni bahimukhāni. Bhagavā rajatapattaparikkhitto viya hutvā pāyāsi. Pupphāni acittakānipi sacittakaṃ nissāya sacittakāni viya abhijjitvā apatitvā satthārā saddhiṃyeva gacchanti, ṭhitaṭhitaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti. Satthu sarīrato satasahassavijjulatā viya raṃsiyo nikkhamiṃsu. Purato ca pacchato ca dakkhiṇato ca vāmato ca sīsamatthakato ca nirantaraṃ nikkhantaraṃsīsu ekāpi sammukhasammukhaṭṭhāneneva apalāyitvā sabbāpi satthāraṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā taruṇatālakkhandhappamāṇā [P 2.0043] hutvā purato eva dhāvanti. Sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. Antonagare nava koṭiyo, bahinagare nava koṭiyoti aṭṭhārasasu koṭīsu ekopi puriso vā itthī vā bhikkhaṃ gahetvā anikkhanto nāma natthi. Mahājano sīhanādaṃ nadanto celukkhepasahassāni karonto satthu puratova gacchati. Satthāpi mālākārassa guṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ tigāvutappamāṇe nagare bhericaraṇamaggeneva [M 1.0308] acari. Mālākārassa sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā paripūri.

He thought, “As long as my faithful mind does not shrink, I will make this offering.” Greatly delighted and overjoyed, he worshipped the Teacher. How? First, he tossed two handfuls of flowers above the Tathāgata; they formed a canopy above his head and remained there. He tossed another two handfuls; they descended along his right side, hanging like a covering of garlands, and remained there. He tossed another two handfuls; they descended along his back and remained there in the same way. He tossed another two handfuls; they descended along his left side and remained there in the same way. Thus, the eight measures, being eight handfuls of flowers, encircled the Tathāgata in four places. In front, only an opening for passage remained. The stems of the flowers faced inward, while the petals faced outward. The Blessed One proceeded as if surrounded by a silver screen. The flowers, though without consciousness, by dependence on him who has consciousness, acted as if conscious themselves; without scattering or falling, they went along with the Teacher and stopped wherever he stopped. From the Teacher’s body, rays emerged like a hundred thousand flashes of lightning. From the front, the back, the right, the left, and from above his head, the rays issued forth continuously. Not a single ray shot straight out; rather, all of them, having circumambulated the Teacher three times to the right, became the size of a young palm trunk and then rushed forward. The entire city was in an uproar. Inside the city were nine crores of people and outside the city nine crores; among these eighteen crores, there was not a single man or woman who did not take alms and go out. The great crowd, roaring a lion’s roar and making thousands of cloth-tossings, went before the Teacher. The Teacher, to make the garland-maker’s virtue manifest, proceeded through the city, which was three gāvutas in extent, only by the main thoroughfare where the drum is beaten. The garland-maker’s entire body was filled with fivefold joy.

So thokaññeva tathāgatena saddhiṃ caritvā manosilārase nimuggo viya buddharasmīnaṃ anto paviṭṭho satthāraṃ thometvā vanditvā tucchapacchimeva gahetvā gehaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ bhariyā pucchi “kahaṃ pupphānī”ti? “Satthā me pūjito”ti. “Rañño dāni kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Rājā maṃ ghātetu vā raṭṭhato vā nīharatu, ahaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā satthāraṃ pūjesiṃ, sabbapupphāni aṭṭha muṭṭhiyova ahesuṃ, evarūpā nāma pūjā jātā. Mahājano ukkuṭṭhisahassāni karonto satthārā saddhiṃ carati, yo esa mahājanassa ukkuṭṭhisaddo, tasmiṃ ṭhāne eso”ti. Athassa bhariyā andhabālatāya evarūpe pāṭihāriye [P 2.0044] pasādaṃ nāma ajanetvā taṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā “rājāno nāma caṇḍā, sakiṃ kuddhā hatthapādādicchedanena bahumpi anatthaṃ karonti, tayā katakammena mayhampi anattho siyā”ti putte ādāya rājakulaṃ gantvā raññā pakkositvā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchitā āha – “mama sāmiko tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhānapupphehi satthāraṃ pūjetvā tucchahattho gharaṃ āgantvā ‘kahaṃ pupphānī’ti mayā puṭṭho idaṃ nāma vadesi, ahaṃ taṃ paribhāsitvā ‘rājāno nāma caṇḍā, sakiṃ kuddhā hatthapādādicchedanena bahumpi anatthaṃ karonti, tayā katakammena mayhampi anattho siyā’ti taṃ chaḍḍetvā idhāgatā, tena kataṃ kammaṃ sukataṃ vā hotu, dukkaṭaṃ vā, tassevetaṃ, mayā tassa chaḍḍitabhāvaṃ jānāhi, devā”ti. Rājā paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpattiphalaṃ patto saddho pasanno ariyasāvako cintesi [V 1.0275] – “aho ayaṃ itthī andhabālā, evarūpe guṇe pasādaṃ na uppādesī”ti. So kuddho viya hutvā, “amma, kiṃ vadesi, mayhaṃ upaṭṭhānapupphehi tena pūjā katā”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Bhaddakaṃ te kataṃ taṃ chaḍḍentiyā, mama pupphehi pūjākārassa ahaṃ kattabbayuttakaṃ jānissāmī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā vegena satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā satthārā [P 2.0045] saddhiṃyeva vicari.

Having walked just a short distance with the Tathāgata, he entered into the Buddha's radiance as if submerged on a plane of realgar. Having praised and paid homage to the Teacher, he took the empty basket and went home. Then his wife asked him, “Where are the flowers?” “I have made an offering to the Teacher,” he replied. “What will you do now regarding the king?” she asked. “Let the king execute me or banish me from the kingdom—I have given up my life to make an offering to the Teacher. All the flowers were just eight handfuls, and such an offering was made. The great crowd walks with the Teacher, making thousands of shouts of acclamation. That sound is the great crowd's shout of acclamation in that place.” Then his wife, due to her blind foolishness, did not give rise to faith in such a marvel. Having scolded and reviled him, she said, “Kings are cruel; once angered, they inflict great harm by severing hands and feet. Because of the deed you have done, harm may come to me as well.” Taking her children, she went to the royal court. Having been summoned by the king and asked, “What is this?” she said: “My husband made an offering to the Teacher with the flowers meant for your service and came home empty-handed. When asked by me, ‘Where are the flowers?’ he said such-and-such. I reviled him, saying, ‘Kings are cruel; once angered, they inflict great harm by severing hands and feet. Because of the deed you have done, harm may come to me as well.’ Therefore, having abandoned him, I have come here. Whether the deed he has done is good or bad, it is his alone. Know, Your Majesty, that he has been abandoned by me.” The king, who had attained the fruit of stream-entry at his very first sight of the Buddha, being a faithful, devoted noble disciple, thought: “Alas, this woman is blind and foolish; she did not give rise to faith in such a virtue!” Becoming as if angry, he said, “Mother, what are you saying? Was an offering made by him with my service-flowers?” “Yes, Your Majesty.” “It was a good thing done by you in abandoning him. For the one who made an offering with my flowers, I will know what is fitting to be done.” Having dismissed her, he went quickly to the Teacher's presence, paid homage, and walked together with the Teacher.

Satthā rañño cittappasādaṃ ñatvā bhericaraṇavīthiyā nagaraṃ caritvā rañño gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ gehaṃ pavesetukāmo ahosi. Satthā pana rājaṅgaṇeyeva nisīdanākāraṃ dassesi[M 1.0309]. Rājā taṃ ñatvā “sīghaṃ maṇḍapaṃ karothā”ti taṅkhaṇaññeva maṇḍapaṃ kārāpesi. Nisīdi satthā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Kasmā pana satthā rājagehaṃ na pāvisi?

The Teacher, knowing the serene faith of the king's mind, walked through the city by way of the street of the proclamation drum and came to the king's house-door. The king, taking the alms-bowl, was desirous of having the Teacher enter the house. The Teacher, however, showed the manner of one who would sit right in the royal courtyard. The king, knowing that, said, “Quickly, make a pavilion,” and at that very moment had a pavilion made. The Teacher sat down together with the community of monks. But why did the Teacher not enter the king's house?

Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “sacāhaṃ anto pavisitvā nisīdeyyaṃ, mahājano maṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labheyya, mālākārassa guṇo pākaṭo na bhaveyya, rājaṅgaṇe pana maṃ nisinnaṃ mahājano daṭṭhuṃ labhissati, mālākārassa guṇo pākaṭo bhavissatī”ti. Guṇavantānañhi guṇaṃ buddhā eva pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti, avasesajano guṇavantānaṃ guṇaṃ kathento maccharāyati. Cattāro pupphapaṭā catuddisaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahājano satthāraṃ parivāresi. Rājā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītenāhārena parivisi. Satthā bhattakiccāvasāne anumodanaṃ katvā purimanayeneva catūhi pupphapaṭehi parikkhitto sīhanādaṃ nadanto mahājanena parivuto vihāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā satthāraṃ anugantvā nivatto mālākāraṃ pakkosāpetvā “mama āharitapupphehi kinti katvā satthāraṃ pūjesī”ti pucchi. Mālākāro “rājā maṃ ghātetu vā raṭṭhato vā pabbājetūti jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā pūjesiṃ devā”ti āha. Rājā “tvaṃ mahāpuriso nāmā”ti vatvā aṭṭha hatthī ca asse ca dāse ca dāsiyo [P 2.0046] ca mahāpasādhanāni ca aṭṭha kahāpaṇasahassāni ca rājakulato nīharitvā sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍitā aṭṭha nāriyo ca aṭṭha gāmavare cāti idaṃ sabbaṭṭhakaṃ nāma dānaṃ adāsi.

It is said that this occurred to him: 'If I were to enter inside and sit down, the great crowd would not get to see me, and the garland-maker's virtue would not become manifest. But if I sit in the royal courtyard, the great crowd will get to see me, and the garland-maker's virtue will become manifest.' For indeed, only Buddhas are able to make manifest the virtue of the virtuous; other people, when speaking of the virtue of the virtuous, become envious. Four flower canopies stood in the four directions. The great crowd surrounded the Teacher. The king served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent food. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher gave a discourse of appreciation and, surrounded by the four flower canopies as before, uttering a lion's roar and encircled by the great crowd, went to the monastery. The king, having accompanied the Teacher and turned back, had the garland-maker summoned and asked, 'With what intention did you make an offering to the Teacher with the flowers brought for me?' The garland-maker replied, 'Your Majesty, I made the offering having given up my life, thinking, “Let the king kill me or banish me from the kingdom.”' The king said, 'You are a great man,' and gave him eight elephants, eight horses, eight male slaves, eight female slaves, eight great ornaments, eight thousand kahāpaṇas brought from the royal treasury, eight women adorned with all ornaments, and eight excellent villages—this gift called the 'All-Eights'.

Ānandatthero cintesi – “ajja pātova paṭṭhāya sīhanādasahassāni ceva celukkhepasahassāni ca pavattanti, ko nu kho mālākārassa vipāko”ti? So satthāraṃ pucchi. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “ānanda, iminā mālākārena appamattakaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti mā sallakkhesi, ayañhi mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā pūjaṃ akāsi. So evaṃ mayi cittaṃ pasādetvā –

The Elder Ānanda thought: 'From early this morning, thousands of shouts of acclamation and thousands of tossings of cloths have been occurring. What, indeed, will be the result for this garland-maker?' He asked the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to him: 'Ānanda, do not consider that this garland-maker has done an insignificant deed. For he made this offering to me, having given up his life. He, having thus made his mind serene towards me—

“Kappānaṃ [V 1.0276] satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ na gamissati;

Ṭhatvā devamanussesu, phalaṃ etassa kammuno;

Pacchā paccekasambuddho, sumano nāma bhavissatī”ti. –

For a hundred thousand aeons, he will not go to a woeful state. As the fruit of this kamma, having been established among devas and humans, he will afterwards become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana.

Āha. Satthu pana vihāraṃ gantvā gandhakuṭipavisanakāle tāni pupphāni dvārakoṭṭhake patiṃsu. Sāyanhasamaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ [M 1.0310] – “aho acchariyaṃ mālākārassa kammaṃ, dharamānakabuddhassa jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā pupphapūjaṃ katvā taṅkhaṇaññeva sabbaṭṭhakaṃ nāma labhatī”ti. Satthā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā tiṇṇaṃ gamanānaṃ aññatarena gamanena dhammasabhaṃ [P 2.0047] gantvā buddhāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “āma, bhikkhave, yassa kammassa katattā pacchānutappaṃ na hoti, anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe somanassameva uppajjati, evarūpaṃ kammaṃ kattabbamevā”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus he spoke. Now, when the Teacher had gone to the monastery, at the time of his entering the Perfumed Chamber, those flowers fell at the doorframe. In the evening, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Oh, how wonderful is the deed of the garland-maker! Having given up his life for the living Buddha and made a flower offering, in that very moment he obtains the gift called the 'All-Eights'.' The Teacher, having emerged from the Perfumed Chamber and gone to the Hall of Dhamma by one of the three modes of deportment, sat down on the Buddha-seat and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'For this one,' he replied, 'Yes, monks. A deed should be done which, having been done, does not cause subsequent remorse. At every moment of recollection, only gladness arises. Such a deed should indeed be done.' Having made this connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

68.

68.

“Tañca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā nānutappati;

Yassa patīto sumano, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti.

That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not regret; whose result one experiences pleased and gladdened.

Tattha yaṃ katvāti yaṃ devamanussasampattīnañceva nibbānasampattiyā ca nibbattanasamatthaṃ sukhudrayaṃ kammaṃ katvā nānutappati, atha kho diṭṭhadhammeyeva anussaritānussaritakkhaṇeyeva pītivegena patīto somanassavegena ca sumano hutvā āyatiṃ pītisomanassajāto hutvā vipākaṃ paṭisevati, taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu bhaddakanti.

Herein, 'having done which' refers to having done a deed which is a basis for pleasant feeling and is capable of bringing about the attainments in the human and deva realms, as well as the attainment of Nibbāna, one does not have remorse. But rather, in this very life, at the very moment of repeated recollection, being pleased with the force of rapture and gladdened with the force of joy, in the future, being one in whom rapture and gladness have arisen, one experiences its result. That deed is well done, it is excellent.

Desanāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings.

Sumanamālākāravatthu navamaṃ.

The Story of Sumana the Garland-maker is the ninth.

10. Uppalavaṇṇattherīvatthu

10. The Story of the Therī Uppalavaṇṇā

Madhuvā [P 2.0048] maññatīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uppalavaṇṇattheriṃ ārabbha kathesi.

'The fool thinks it is like honey'—this Dhamma discourse the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana with reference to the Therī Uppalavaṇṇā.

Sā [V 1.0277] kira padumuttarabuddhassa pādamūle patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā kappasatasahassaṃ puññāni kurumānā devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsarantī imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devalokato cavitvā sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhikule paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Nīluppalagabbhasamānavaṇṇatāya cassā uppalavaṇṇātveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Athassā vayappattakāle sakalajambudīpe rājāno ca seṭṭhino ca seṭṭhissa santikaṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu – “dhītaraṃ amhākaṃ detū”ti[M 1.0311]. Apahiṇanto nāma nāhosi. Tato seṭṭhi cintesi – “ahaṃ sabbesaṃ manaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, upāyaṃ panekaṃ karissāmī”ti dhītaraṃ pakkosāpetvā, “amma, pabbajituṃ sakkhissasī”ti āha. Tassā pacchimabhavikattā taṃ vacanaṃ sīse āsittaṃ satapākatelaṃ viya ahosi. Tasmā pitaraṃ “pabbajissāmi, tātā”ti āha. So tassā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā bhikkhunīupassayaṃ netvā pabbājesi[P 2.0049]. Tassā acirapabbajitāya eva uposathāgāre kālavāro pāpuṇi. Sā dīpaṃ jāletvā uposathāgāraṃ sammajjitvā dīpasikhāya nimittaṃ gaṇhitvā ṭhitāva punappunaṃ olokayamānā tejokasiṇārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvā tameva pādakaṃ katvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi saddhiṃ paṭisambhidāhi ceva abhiññāhi ca.

It is said that she, having made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara, for a hundred thousand aeons performed meritorious deeds, wandering among devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, she passed away from the deva world and took conception in a wealthy merchant's family in Sāvatthī. When she came of age, kings and wealthy men from all over Jambudīpa sent messengers to the merchant, saying, 'Give us your daughter.' There was no one who did not send such a request. Then the merchant thought, 'I cannot please everyone, so I will devise a plan.' He summoned his daughter and said, 'My dear, will you be able to go forth?' Because it was her final existence, that word was like oil refined a hundred times poured on her head. Therefore, she replied to her father, 'I will go forth, dear father.' He then paid her great honor, took her to the nunnery, and had her ordained. Not long after her ordination, her turn to tend to the Uposatha hall arrived. She lit a lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and, taking the flame of the lamp as her object of meditation, stood repeatedly gazing at it. She developed the absorption with the fire-kasiṇa as its object and, making that its foundation, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges and the supernormal powers.

Sā aparena samayena janapadacārikaṃ caritvā paccāgantvā andhavanaṃ pāvisi. Tadā bhikkhunīnaṃ araññavāso appaṭikkhitto hoti. Athassā tattha kuṭikaṃ katvā mañcakaṃ paññāpetvā sāṇiyā parikkhipiṃsu. Sā sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā nikkhami. Mātulaputto panassā nandamāṇavo nāma gihikālato paṭṭhāya paṭibaddhacitto. So tassā āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā theriyā āgamanato puretarameva andhavanaṃ gantvā taṃ kuṭikaṃ pavisitvā heṭṭhāmañcake nilīno theriyā āgantvā kuṭikaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya mañcake nisinnamattāya bahi ātapato āgatattā cakkhupathe andhakāre avigateyeva heṭṭhāmañcakato nikkhamitvā mañcakaṃ abhiruyha “mā nassi bāla, mā nassi bālā”ti theriyā vāriyamānoyeva abhibhavitvā attanā patthitakammaṃ katvā pāyāsi. Athassa aguṇaṃ dhāretuṃ asakkontī [P 2.0050] viya mahāpathavī dvedhā bhijji. So pathaviṃ paviṭṭho gantvā mahāavīcimhi eva nibbatti. Therīpi tamatthaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhuniyo bhikkhūnaṃ etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocayiṃsu. Taṃ sutvā satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā, “bhikkhave, bhikkhubhikkhūnī upāsakaupāsikāsu yo koci bālo pāpakammaṃ karonto madhusakkharādīsu kiñci deva madhurarasaṃ khādamāno puriso viya tuṭṭhahaṭṭho udaggudaggo viya karotī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

At a later time, she went wandering in the countryside and, upon returning, entered the Andhavana. At that time, dwelling in the wilderness was not forbidden for nuns. There they built a hut for her, prepared a couch, and surrounded it with a curtain. She entered Sāvatthī for alms-food and then left. Now, her maternal cousin, a young man named Nanda, had been infatuated with her since her days as a layperson. Hearing of her return, he went to the Andhavana even before the Therī arrived. Entering her hut, he hid beneath the couch. When the Therī arrived, she entered the hut, closed the door, and as soon as she sat on the couch—since she had come from the heat outside and the darkness had not yet cleared from her vision—he emerged from under the couch and climbed onto it. Despite the Therī's protests—'Do not be ruined, you fool! Do not be ruined, you fool!'—he overpowered her, did what he desired, and then left. Then, as if unable to bear his wicked deed, the great earth split in two. He, having entered the earth, was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell. The Therī reported the matter to the other nuns. The nuns informed the monks of this matter. The monks told the Blessed One. Hearing this, the Teacher addressed the monks: 'Monks, among monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, any fool who commits an evil deed does so pleased and delighted, as if a person tasting some sweet flavor like honey or sugar.' Having made this connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

69.

69.

“Madhuvā [V 1.0278][M 1.0312] maññati bālo, yāva pāpaṃ na paccati;

Yadā ca paccati pāpaṃ, bālo dukkhaṃ nigacchatī”ti.

The fool thinks it is like honey, so long as the evil has not ripened; but when the evil ripens, then the fool comes to grief.

Tattha madhuvāti bālassa hi pāpaṃ akusalakammaṃ karontassa taṃ kammaṃ madhu viya madhurarasaṃ viya iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. Iti naṃ so madhuṃva maññati. Yāvāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Pāpaṃ na paccatīti diṭṭhadhamme vā samparāye vā vipākaṃ na deti, tāva naṃ evaṃ maññati. Yadā cāti yadā panassa diṭṭhadhamme vā vividhā kammakāraṇā kayiramānassa, samparāye vā nirayādīsu mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantassa taṃ pāpaṃ paccati, atha so bālo dukkhaṃ nigacchati vindati paṭilabhatīti.

In that verse, 'madhuvā' means: for the fool who performs an evil, unwholesome action, that action appears like honey, like a sweet taste, like a desirable, pleasing, and delightful object. Thus, he regards it as honey. 'Yāva' means for as long a time. 'Pāpaṃ na paccati' means as long as it does not give its result in the present life or in a future existence, for that long he regards it thus. 'Yadā ca' means but when that evil action ripens—either in the present life as he undergoes various punishments, or in a future existence as he experiences great suffering in hell and other states—then that fool undergoes, finds, and obtains suffering. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the like.

Aparena [P 2.0051] pana samayena dhammasabhāyaṃ mahājano kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “khīṇāsavāpi maññe kāmasukhaṃ sādiyanti, kāmaṃ sevanti, kiṃ na sevissanti, na hi ete koḷāparukkhā, na ca vammikā allamaṃsasarīrāva, tasmā etepi kāmasukhaṃ sādiyanti, kāmaṃ sevantī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “na, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavā kāmasukhaṃ sādiyanti, na kāmaṃ sevanti. Yathā hi padumapatte patitaṃ udakabindu, na vilimpati, na saṇṭhāti, vinivattetvā patateva, yathā ca āragge sāsapo na vilimpati, na saṇṭhāti, vinivattetvā patateva, evaṃ khīṇāsavassa citte duvidhopi kāmo na vilimpati, na saṇṭhātī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ brāhmaṇavagge gāthamāha –

Furthermore, at another time, in the Dhamma hall, a great crowd of people raised a topic of discussion: 'Even the Arahants, it seems, enjoy sensual pleasure and indulge in sensual desire. Why would they not indulge? Indeed, they are not hollow trees, nor are they anthills; they just have bodies of moist flesh. Therefore, these Arahants also enjoy sensual pleasure and indulge in sensual desire.' The Teacher, having come, asked, 'Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'For this particular discussion,' he replied, 'Bhikkhus, Arahants do not enjoy sensual pleasure, nor do they indulge in sensual desire. For example, just as a drop of water that has fallen on a lotus leaf does not smear or stay, but rolls off and falls away; and just as a mustard seed on the point of an awl does not smear or stay, but rolls off and falls away; in the same way, in the mind of an Arahant, both kinds of sensual pleasure—sensual objects and sensual defilements—do not smear or stay.' Thus, the Teacher, having connected the sequence and wishing to teach the Dhamma, spoke this verse in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga:

“Vāri pokkharapatteva, āraggeriva sāsapo;

Yo na limpati kāmesu, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 401);

As water on a lotus leaf, as a mustard seed on the point of an awl; he who does not cling to sensual pleasures—him I call a brāhmaṇa.

Imissā attho brāhmaṇavaggeyeva āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana rājānaṃ pasenadikosalaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “mahārāja, imasmiṃ sāsane yatheva kulaputtā, evaṃ kuladhītaropi mahantaṃ ñātigaṇañca bhogakkhandhañca [P 2.0052] pahāya pabbajitvā araññe viharanti. Tā evaṃ viharamānā rāgarattā pāpapuggalā omānātimānavasena viheṭhentipi, brahmacariyantarāyampi pāpenti, tasmā bhikkhunisaṅghassa antonagare vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kātuṃ [M 1.0313] vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā nagarassa [V 1.0279] ekapasse bhikkhunisaṅghassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kārāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhuniyo antogāmeyeva vasantīti.

The meaning of this verse will become clear in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga itself. The Teacher then had King Pasenadi of Kosala summoned and said, 'Great King, in this Dispensation, just as sons of good family, so too daughters of good family, having abandoned a great retinue of relatives and a mass of wealth, go forth and dwell in the forest. While they are dwelling thus, evil persons inflamed with lust may harass them through contempt and excessive conceit, and may even cause an obstacle to their holy life. Therefore, it is proper to make a dwelling place for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs within the city.' The king, having accepted, saying, 'Very well,' had a dwelling place for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs built on one side of the city. From that time onwards, the bhikkhunīs have dwelt only within a village.

Uppalavaṇṇattherīvatthu dasamaṃ.

The tenth, the Story of the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā, is concluded.

11. Jambukattheravatthu

11. The Story of the Elder Jambuka

Māse māseti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto jambukaṃ ājīvakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with the words 'Māse māse' concerning the Ājīvaka Jambuka.

Atīte kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle gāmavāsī eko kuṭumbiko ekassa therassa vihāraṃ katvā taṃ tattha viharantaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahi. Thero tassa gehe nibaddhaṃ bhuñjati. Atheko khīṇāsavo bhikkhu divā piṇḍāya caranto tassa gehadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Kuṭumbiko taṃ disvā tassa iriyāpathe pasanno gehaṃ pavesetvā sakkaccaṃ paṇītena bhojanena parivisitvā, “bhante, imaṃ sāṭakaṃ rajitvā nivāseyyāthā”ti mahantaṃ sāṭakaṃ datvā, “bhante, kesā [P 2.0053] vo dīghā, tumhākaṃ kesoropanatthāya nhāpitaṃ ānessāmi, sayanatthāya ca vo mañcakaṃ gāhāpetvā āgamissāmī”ti āha. Nibaddhaṃ gehe bhuñjanto kulūpako bhikkhu taṃ tassa sakkāraṃ disvā cittaṃ pasādetuṃ nāsakkhi, “ayaṃ taṃ muhuttaṃ diṭṭhakassa evarūpaṃ sakkāraṃ karoti, nibaddhaṃ gehe bhuñjantassa pana mayhaṃ na karotī”ti cintetvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Itaropi teneva saddhiṃ gantvā kuṭumbikena dinnasāṭakaṃ rajitvā nivāsesi. Kuṭambikopi nhāpitaṃ ādāya gantvā therassa kese ohārāpetvā mañcakaṃ attharāpetvā, “bhante, imasmiṃyeva mañcake sayathā”ti vatvā dvepi there svātanāya nimantetvā pakkāmi.

It is said that in the past, during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, a certain householder living in a village, having built a monastery for a certain elder, supported him who was dwelling there with the four requisites. The elder regularly ate at his house. Then, a certain bhikkhu who was an Arahant, while wandering for alms during the day, arrived at the householder’s door. The householder, seeing him and being pleased with his deportment, invited him into the house. Having respectfully served him with choice food and given him a large cloth, he said, 'Venerable sir, having dyed this cloth, please wear it.' He also said, 'Venerable sir, your hair is long. For the purpose of having your hair shorn, I will bring a barber. And for you to lie down, I will have a couch brought and will come.' The family's patron monk, who regularly ate at the house, seeing that honor being shown to the other, was not able to gladden his mind. Thinking, 'This man shows such honor to one seen for just a moment, but for me, who regularly eats at his house, he does not do so,' he went to the monastery. The other monk also, having gone together with him, dyed the cloth given by the householder and wore it. The householder too, having brought a barber and gone there, had the elder’s hair shorn, had a couch spread out, and said, 'Venerable sir, please lie down on this very couch.' Then, having invited both elders for the next day, he departed.

Nevāsiko tassa taṃ sakkāraṃ kayiramānaṃ adhivāsetuṃ nāsakkhi. Athassa so sāyaṃ therassa nipannaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā catūhākārehi theraṃ akkosi, “āvuso, āgantuka kuṭumbikassa te gehe bhattaṃ bhuñjanato varataraṃ mīḷhaṃ khādituṃ, kuṭumbikena ānītanhāpitena kesohārāpanato varataraṃ tālaṭṭhikena kese luñcāpetuṃ. Kuṭumbikena dinnasāṭakanivāsanato varataraṃ naggena vicarituṃ, kuṭumbikena ābhatamañcake nipajjanato varataraṃ [M 1.0314] bhūmiyaṃ nipajjitu”nti. Theropi “mā esa bālo maṃ nissāya nassī”ti nimantanaṃ anādiyitvā pātova uṭṭhāya yathāsukhaṃ agamāsi[P 2.0054]. Nevāsikopi pātova vihāre kattabbavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāravelāya [V 1.0280] “idānipi āgantuko niddāyati, ghaṇḍikasaddena pabujjheyyā”ti saññāya nakhapiṭṭheneva ghaṇḍiṃ paharitvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Kuṭumbikopi sakkāraṃ katvā therānaṃ āgamanamaggaṃ olokento nevāsikaṃ disvā, “bhante, thero kuhi”nti pucchi. Atha naṃ nevāsiko “mā, āvuso, kiñci avaca, tuyhaṃ kulūpako hiyyo, tava nikkhantavelāya ovarakaṃ pavisitvā niddaṃ okkanto pātova uṭṭhāya mama vihārasammajjanasaddampi pānīyaghaṭaparibhojanīyaghaṭesu udakasiñcanasaddampi ghaṇḍikasaddampi karontassa na jānātī”ti āha. Kuṭumbiko cintesi – “tādisāya iriyāpathasampattiyā samannāgatassa me ayyassa yāva imamhā kālā niddāyanaṃ nāma natthi, maṃ pana tassa sakkāraṃ karontaṃ disvā addhā iminā bhadantena kiñci vuttaṃ bhavissatī”ti. So attano paṇḍitabhāvena taṃ sakkaccaṃ bhojetvā tassa pattaṃ sādhukaṃ dhovitvā nānaggarasabhojanassa pūretvā, “bhante, sace me ayyaṃ passeyyātha, imamassa piṇḍapātaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti āha.

The resident monk was not able to endure that honor being shown to the other. Then, in the evening, he went to the elder's resting place and reviled the elder in four ways: 'Friend, visiting monk, it is better to eat excrement than to eat a meal in the householder's home. It is better to have one's hair plucked out with tongs made from a palm-seed husk than to have one's hair cut by a barber brought by the householder. It is better to wander naked than to wear a cloth given by the householder. It is better to lie on the ground than to lie on a couch brought by the householder.' The elder, thinking, 'May this fool not be destroyed on account of me,' did not accept the invitation, and rising early in the morning, went as he pleased. The resident monk also, having risen early and performed his duties in the monastery, at the time for the alms-round, with the thought, 'Even now the visiting monk is sleeping; he might be awakened by the sound of the gong,' struck the gong with just the back of his fingernail and entered the village for alms. The householder, having prepared offerings and watching the path for the elders' arrival, saw the resident monk and asked, 'Venerable sir, where is the elder?' Then the resident monk said to him, 'Friend, do not say anything. Your patron monk, having entered the inner room when you left yesterday, fell into a deep sleep. Though I rose early and made the sound of sweeping my monastery, the sound of pouring water into the drinking and utility water pots, and the sound of the gong, he did not know it.' The householder thought: 'For my noble one, who is endowed with such perfect deportment, there is no such thing as sleeping until this time. Seeing me showing honor to that elder, surely something unpleasant must have been said by this venerable one.' He, through his own wisdom, respectfully fed the monk, washed his bowl well, filled it with food of various excellent flavors, and said, 'Venerable sir, if you should see my noble one, please give this almsfood to him.'

Itaro taṃ gahetvāva cintesi – “sace so evarūpaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjissati, imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne paluddho bhavissatī”ti antarāmagge taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ chaḍḍetvā therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ tattha olokento na addasa. Atha naṃ ettakassa kammassa katattā vīsativassasahassāni [P 2.0055] katopi samaṇadhammo rakkhituṃ nāsakkhi. Āyupariyosāne pana kālaṃ katvā avīcimhi nibbattitvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahanagare ekasmiṃ bahvannapāne kulaghare nibbatti. So padasā gamanakālato paṭṭhāya neva sayane sayituṃ, na bhattaṃ bhuñjituṃ icchati, attano sarīravalañjameva khādati. “Bālatāya ajānanto karotī”ti taṃ posayiṃsu. Mahallakakālepi vatthaṃ nivāsetuṃ na icchati, naggova vicarati, bhūmiyaṃ sayati, attano sarīravalañjameva khādati. Athassa mātāpitaro “nāyaṃ kulagharassa anucchaviko, kevalaṃ alajjanako ājīvakānaṃ esa anucchaviko”ti tesaṃ santikaṃ netvā “imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājethā”ti adaṃsu. Atha naṃ te pabbājesuṃ. Pabbājentā ca [M 1.0315] pana galappamāṇe āvāṭe ṭhapetvā dvinnaṃ aṃsakūṭānaṃ upariṃ padarāni datvā tesaṃ upari nisīditvā tālaṭṭhikhaṇḍena kese luñciṃsu. Atha ne tassa mātāpitaro svātanāya nimantetvā pakkamiṃsu.

The other monk, taking the almsfood, thought: 'If he eats such almsfood, he will become attached to this very place.' Thinking thus, he discarded that almsfood on the way. Having gone to the elder's dwelling place and looking for him there, he did not see him. Then, because he had done such a deed, even the ascetic practice he had performed for twenty thousand years was not able to protect him. At the end of his lifespan, he passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. Having experienced great suffering for one Buddha-interval, during this present Buddha-era, he was reborn in a wealthy household with abundant food and drink in the city of Rājagaha. From the time he was able to walk on foot, he did not wish to sleep on a bed, nor to eat a meal; he ate only his own excrement. Thinking, 'He does this out of ignorance due to his youth,' they raised him. Even when he was older, he did not wish to wear clothes, wandered naked, slept on the ground, and ate only his own excrement. Then his parents, thinking, 'This one is not suitable for a family home; he is simply shameless. He is suitable for the Ājīvakas,' took him to them and said, 'Ordain this boy,' and gave him to them. Then they ordained him. And while ordaining him, having placed him in a pit the depth of his neck and having placed planks over his two shoulders, they, sitting on top of those planks, plucked out his hair with a piece of a palm-seed husk. Then his parents, having invited them for the next day, departed.

Punadivase ājīvakā “ehi, gāmaṃ pavisissāmā”ti taṃ vadiṃsu. So “gacchatha tumhe, ahaṃ idheva bhavissāmī”ti na icchi. Atha naṃ punappunaṃ vatvā anicchamānaṃ ohāya agamaṃsu. Sopi tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā vaccakuṭiyā padaraṃ vivaritvā oruyha ubhohi hatthehi ālopaṃ [V 1.0281] ālopaṃ katvā gūthaṃ khādi[P 2.0056]. Ājīvakā tassa antogāmato āhāraṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Tampi na icchi. Punappunaṃ vuccamānopi “na me iminā attho. Laddho me āhāro”ti āha. “Kahaṃ laddho”ti? “Idheva laddho”ti. Evaṃ dutiye tatiye catutthepi divase tehi bahumpi vuccamāno “ahaṃ idheva bhavissāmī”ti gāmaṃ gantuṃ na icchi. Ājīvakā “ayaṃ divase divase neva gāmaṃ pavisituṃ icchati, na amhehi pahitāhāraṃ āharituṃ icchati, ‘idheva me laddho’ti vadati, kiṃ nu kho karoti, pariggaṇhissāma na”nti gāmaṃ pavisantā ekaṃ dve jane tassa pariggaṇhanatthaṃ ohāya gamiṃsu. Te pacchato gacchantā viya hutvā nilīyiṃsu. Sopi tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā purimanayeneva vaccakuṭiṃ oruyha gūthaṃ khādi.

On the next day, the Ājīvakas said to him, “Come, let us enter the village.” He replied, “You go, I will stay right here,” and did not wish to. Then, after repeatedly telling him, since he was unwilling, they left him behind and departed. He also, knowing that they had gone, opened the plank of the latrine and descended, and with both hands, making mouthful after mouthful, ate the excrement. The Ājīvakas sent food to him from within the village. He did not want that either. Even when told repeatedly, he said, “I have no need for this. Food has been obtained by me.” “Where was it obtained?” “It was obtained right here.” Similarly, on the second, third, and also on the fourth day, though he was told much by them, saying, “I will obtain it right here,” he did not wish to go to the village. The Ājīvakas thought, “Day after day, he does not wish to enter the village, nor does he wish to take the food sent by us. He says, ‘It has been obtained by me right here.’ What indeed is he doing? Let us observe him.” As they were entering the village, they left behind one or two people to observe him. They, acting as if they were following along behind, hid themselves. He also, knowing that they had gone, in the same way as before, descended into the latrine and ate the excrement.

Itare tassa kiriyaṃ disvā ājīvakānaṃ ārocayiṃsu. Taṃ sutvā ājīvakā “aho bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ, sace samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā jāneyyuṃ, ‘ājīvakā gūthaṃ khādamānā vicarantī’ti amhākaṃ akittiṃ pakāseyyuṃ, nāyaṃ amhākaṃ anucchaviko”ti taṃ attano santikā nīhariṃsu. So tehi nīharito mahājanassa uccārakaraṇaṭṭhāne pattharito eko piṭṭhipāsāṇo atthi. Tasmiṃ mahantaṃ soṇḍi, piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ nissāya mahājanassa uccārakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. So tattha gantvā rattiṃ gūthaṃ khāditvā mahājanassa sarīravalañjanatthāya āgamanakāle ekena hatthena pāsāṇassa ekaṃ antaṃ olubbha [P 2.0057] ekaṃ pādaṃ ukkhipitvā jaṇṇuke ṭhapetvā uddhaṃvātābhimukho mukhaṃ vivaritvā tiṭṭhati. Mahājano taṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā, “bhante, kasmā ayyo mukhaṃ vivaritvā ṭhito”ti pucchati. “Ahaṃ vātabhakkho, añño me āhāro natthī”ti. Atha “kasmā ekaṃ pādaṃ jaṇṇuke katvā ṭhitosi, bhante”ti? “Ahaṃ uggatapo [M 1.0316] ghoratapo, mayā dvīhi pādehi akkantā pathavī kampati, tasmā ekaṃ pādaṃ ukkhipitvā jaṇṇuke ṭhapetvā ṭhitomhi. Ahañhi rattindivaṃ ṭhitakova vītināmemi, na nisīdāmi, na nipajjāmī”ti. Manussā nāma yebhuyyena vacanamattameva saddahanti, tasmā “aho acchariyaṃ, evarūpāpi nāma tapassino honti, na no evarūpā diṭṭhapubbā”ti yebhuyyena aṅgamagadhavāsino saṅkhubhitvā upasaṅkamitvā māse māse mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ abhiharanti. So “ahaṃ vātameva bhakkhāmi, na aññaṃ āhāraṃ. Aññañhi me khādantassa tapo nassatī”ti tehi abhihaṭaṃ na kiñci icchati. Manussā “mā no, bhante, nāsetha, tumhādisena ghoratapena paribhoge kate amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattatī”ti punappunaṃ yācanti. Tassa añño āhāro na ruccati. Mahājanassa pana yācanāya pīḷito tehi ābhatāni sappiphāṇitādīni kusaggena jivhagge ṭhapetvā “gacchatha, alaṃ [V 1.0282] vo ettakaṃ hitāya sukhāya cā”ti uyyojesi. Evaṃ so pañcapaññāsa vassāni naggo gūthaṃ khādanto kese luñcanto bhūmiyaṃ sayamāno vītināmesi.

The others, seeing his action, informed the Ājīvakas. Hearing this, the Ājīvakas thought: 'Oh, what a grave deed! If the disciples of the ascetic Gotama were to find out, they would proclaim our ill repute, saying, "The Ājīvakas wander about eating excrement." This one is not suitable for us.' Thus, they expelled him from their presence. Having been expelled by them, he went to the place where the populace relieves themselves. A single flat stone slab had been laid out there. Near that great stone slab, which served as a support, was the place where the populace relieved themselves. Having gone there, after eating excrement at night, he would stand there at the time when the populace came to cleanse their bodies, holding on to one edge of the stone slab with one hand, lifting one foot and placing it on his knee, with his mouth open, facing upwind. The populace, seeing him, approached, paid homage, and asked: 'Venerable sir, why does the noble one stand with his mouth open?' He replied: 'I am a wind-eater; I have no other food.' Then they asked: 'Venerable sir, why do you stand with one foot placed on your knee?' He answered: 'I am one of renowned austerity, of fierce austerity. The earth, when trodden upon by me with both feet, trembles. That is why I stand having lifted one foot and placed it on my knee. Indeed, I pass the time day and night only standing; I do not sit, I do not lie down.' People, for the most part, believe mere words. Therefore, the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha, greatly stirred, exclaimed: 'Oh, how wonderful! Such ascetics exist! We have never seen such a one before!' They would approach and bring him great offerings month after month. He would not accept anything they brought, saying: 'I consume only wind, no other food. For if I were to eat anything else, my austerity would be destroyed.' The people pleaded again and again: 'Venerable sir, do not cause us loss! When something is partaken of by one of fierce austerity like you, it leads to our long-term welfare and happiness.' No other food was pleasing to him. But, being pressed by the pleading of the populace, he would take the ghee, molasses, and so on, that they brought, touch it to the tip of his tongue with the tip of a kusa grass blade, and dismiss them, saying: 'Go. This much is sufficient for your welfare and happiness.' Thus for fifty-five years he passed his time naked, eating excrement, pulling out his hair, and sleeping on the ground.

Buddhānampi [P 2.0058] kho paccūsakāle lokavolokanaṃ avijahitameva hoti. Tasmā ekadivasaṃ bhagavato paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokentassa ayaṃ jambukājīvako ñāṇajālassa anto paññāyi. Satthā “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti āvajjetvā tassa saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattassūpanissayaṃ disvā “ahaṃ etaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsissāmi, gāthāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo bhavissati. Imaṃ kulaputtaṃ nissāya mahājano sotthibhāvaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti ñatvā punadivase rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “ānanda, jambukājīvakassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti. “Bhante, kiṃ tumheyeva gamissathā”ti? “Āma, ahamevā”ti evaṃ vatvā satthā vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya tassa santikaṃ pāyāsi.

Indeed, for the Buddhas as well, the surveying of the world at dawn is never abandoned. Therefore, one day at dawn, as the Blessed One was surveying the world, this Ājīvaka Jambuka appeared within the net of His knowledge.
