The Teacher, having reflected, 'What indeed will come of this?' and seeing his supporting condition for Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, knew: 'Taking him as the subject, I will speak one verse. At the conclusion of the verse, there will be a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings. On account of this clansman, the great populace will attain a state of well-being.' Knowing this, on the next day, after walking for alms in Rājagaha and having returned from the alms round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, I will go to the Ājīvaka Jambuka.' 'Venerable sir, will you go alone?' 'Yes, I alone will.' Having said this, the Teacher set out toward him in the afternoon when the shadow was growing.

Devatā cintayiṃsu – “satthā sāyaṃ jambukājīvakassa santikaṃ gacchati, so ca jegucche uccārapassāvadantakaṭṭhakiliṭṭhe piṭṭhipāsāṇe vasati, devaṃ vassāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti attano ānubhāvena taṃ muhuttaṃyeva devaṃ vassāpesuṃ. Piṭṭhipāsāṇo suci nimmalo ahosi. Athassa upari [M 1.0317] pañcavaṇṇaṃ pupphavassaṃ vassāpesuṃ. Satthā sāyaṃ jambukājīvakassa santikaṃ gantvā “jambukā”ti saddamakāsi. Jambuko “ko nu kho esa, dujjano maṃ jambukavādena vadatī”ti cintetvā “ko eso”ti āha. “Ahaṃ samaṇo”ti. “Kiṃ mahāsamaṇā”ti? “Ajja me ekarattiṃ idha vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dehī”ti. “Natthi, mahāsamaṇa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasanaṭṭhāna”nti[P 2.0059]. “Jambuka, mā evaṃ kari, ekarattiṃ me vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dehi, pabbajitā nāma pabbajitaṃ patthenti, manussā manussaṃ, pasavo pasava”nti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ pabbajito”ti? “Āma, pabbajitomhī”ti. “Sace tvaṃ pabbajito, kahaṃ te lābukaṃ, kahaṃ dhūmakaṭacchuko, kahaṃ yaññasuttaka”nti? “‘Atthetaṃ mayhaṃ, visuṃ visuṃ pana gahetvā vicaraṇaṃ dukkha’nti abbhantareneva gahetvā carāmī”ti. So “carissasi tvaṃ etaṃ aggaṇhitvā”ti kujjhi. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “hotu, jambuka, mā kujjha, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ me ācikkhā”ti. “Natthi, mahāsamaṇa, ettha vasanaṭṭhāna”nti.

The devas thought: 'The Teacher is going to the Ājīvaka Jambuka this evening. He lives on a stone slab in a disgusting place, soiled with excrement, urine, and tooth-sticks. It is proper to make it rain.' By their own power, they made it rain at that very moment. The stone slab became clean and spotless. Then they rained down a shower of five-colored flowers upon it. In the evening, the Teacher went to the Ājīvaka Jambuka and called out: 'Jambuka!' Jambuka thought, 'Who is this wicked person calling me by the name Jambuka?' and asked, 'Who is this?' 'I am an ascetic.' 'Why have you come, great ascetic?' 'Give me a place to stay here for one night.' 'There is no place to stay in this spot, great ascetic.' 'Jambuka, do not act like that. Give me a place to stay for one night. Ascetics seek out ascetics, humans seek out humans, and beasts seek out beasts.' 'But are you an ascetic?' 'Yes, I am an ascetic.' 'If you are an ascetic, where is your water-pot, where is your smoke-ladle, where is your sacrificial thread?' 'I have them, but it is troublesome to carry them around separately, so I carry them internally.' He became angry, saying: 'So you wander about without carrying them?' Then the Teacher said to him: 'Let it be, Jambuka, do not be angry. Just show me a place to stay.' 'There is no place to stay here, great ascetic.'

Satthā tassa vasanaṭṭhānato avidūre ekaṃ pabbhāraṃ atthi, taṃ niddisanto “etasmiṃ pabbhāre ko vasatī”ti āha. “Natthi koci, mahāsamaṇā”ti. “Tena hi etaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti[V 1.0283]. “Tvaññeva jāna, mahāsamaṇā”ti. Satthā pabbhāre nisīdanaṃ paññāpetvā nisīdi. Paṭhamayāme cattāro mahārājāno catuddisaṃ ekobhāsaṃ karontā satthu upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamiṃsu. Jambuko obhāsaṃ disvā “ko obhāso nāmeso”ti cintesi. Majjhimayāme sakko devarājā āgami. Jambuko tampi disvā “ko nāmeso”ti cintesi. Pacchimayāme ekāya aṅguliyā ekaṃ, dvīhi dve, dasahi dasa cakkavāḷāni obhāsetuṃ samattho mahābrahmā sakalaṃ araññaṃ ekobhāsaṃ karonto āgami. Jambuko tampi [P 2.0060] disvā “ko nu kho eso”ti cintetvā pātova satthu santikaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito satthāraṃ pucchi – “mahāsamaṇa, tumhākaṃ santikaṃ catasso disā obhāsento ke āgatā”ti? “Cattāro mahārājāno”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Maṃ upaṭṭhātu”nti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ catūhi mahārājehi uttaritaro”ti? “Āma, jambuka, mahārājūnampi atirājā”ti. “Majjhimayāme pana ko āgato”ti? “Sakko devarājā, jambukā”ti[M 1.0318]. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Maṃ upaṭṭhātumevā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ sakkadevarājatopi uttaritaro”ti? “Āma, jambuka, sakkatopi uttaritaromhi, eso pana mayhaṃ gilānupaṭṭhāko kappiyakārakasāmaṇerasadiso”ti. “Pacchimayāme sakalaṃ araññaṃ obhāsetvā ko āgato”ti? “Yaṃ loke brāhmaṇādayo khipitvā pakkhalitvā ‘namo mahābrahmuno’ti vadanti, so eva mahābrahmā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ mahābrahmatopi uttaritaro”ti? “Āma, jambuka, ahañhi brahmunāpi atibrahmā”ti. “Acchariyosi tvaṃ, mahāsamaṇa, mayhaṃ pana pañca paññāsa vassāni idha vasantassa etesu ekopi maṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ nāgatapubbo. Ahañhi ettakaṃ addhānaṃ vātabhakkho hutvā ṭhitakova vītināmesiṃ, na tāva te mayhaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatapubbā”ti.

The Teacher pointed to a cave not far from Jambuka's dwelling place and asked: 'Who lives in this cave?' 'No one, great ascetic.' 'Then give it to me.' 'As you wish, great ascetic.' The Teacher prepared a seat in the cave and sat down. In the first watch, the Four Great Kings came to attend on the Teacher, making the four directions a single blaze of light. Jambuka saw the radiance and thought, 'What is this radiance?' In the middle watch, Sakka, king of the devas, arrived. Jambuka saw him too and thought, 'Who is this?' In the last watch, Mahābrahmā, who was capable of illuminating one world system with one finger, two with two, and ten with ten fingers, came, making the entire forest a single blaze of light. Jambuka saw him too and thought, 'Who could this be?' In the morning he went to the Teacher, and after an exchange of friendly greetings, he stood to one side and asked the Teacher: 'Great ascetic, who were they who came to you, illuminating the four directions?' 'The Four Great Kings.' 'For what reason?' 'To attend on me.' 'Are you then superior to the Four Great Kings?' 'Yes, Jambuka, I am a king beyond the great kings.' 'And who came in the middle watch?' 'Sakka, king of the devas, Jambuka.' 'For what reason?' 'To attend on me.' 'Are you then superior to Sakka, king of the devas?' 'Yes, Jambuka, I am superior even to Sakka. He is like a novice attendant who serves me and provides what is allowable when I am sick.' 'And who came in the last watch, illuminating the entire forest?' 'He is that very Mahābrahmā to whom the brahmins and others in the world pay homage, saying, "Homage to Mahābrahmā!" when they sneeze or stumble.' 'Are you then superior even to Mahābrahmā?' 'Yes, Jambuka, for I am a Brahmā beyond Brahmā.' 'You are wonderful, great ascetic! While I have been living here for fifty-five years, not even one of these has ever come to attend on me. For all this time I have passed my days as a wind-eater, only standing, yet they have never come to attend on me.'

Atha naṃ satthā āha – jambuka, tvaṃ lokasmiṃ andhabālaṃ mahājanaṃ vañcayamāno mampi vañcetukāmo jāto, nanu tvaṃ pañcapaññāsa vassāni gūthameva khādi, bhūmiyaṃyeva nipajji, naggo hutvā vicari, tālaṭṭhikhaṇḍena kese luñci. Atha [P 2.0061] ca pana lokaṃ vañcento “ahaṃ vātabhakkho, ekapādena tiṭṭhāmi, na nisīdāmi, na nipajjāmī”ti vadesi, “mamampi vañcetukāmosi pubbepi tvaṃ pāpikaṃ lāmikaṃ diṭṭhiṃ nissāya ettakaṃ kālaṃ gūthabhakkho bhūmisayo naggo vicaranto tālaṭṭhikhaṇḍena kesaluñcanaṃ patto, idānipi pāpikaṃ lāmikaṃ diṭṭhimeva gaṇhāsī”ti. “Kiṃ pana mayā kataṃ, mahāsamaṇā”ti? Athassa satthā pubbe katakammaṃ ācikkhi. Tassa satthari kathenteyeva saṃvego uppajji, hirottappaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ, so ukkuṭiko nisīdi. Athassa satthā udakasāṭikaṃ khipitvā adāsi. So taṃ nivāsetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthāpissa anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathetvā dhammaṃ desesi. So desanāvasāne [V 1.0284] saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā satthāraṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pabbajjañca upasampadañca yāci. Ettāvatā tassa purimakammaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ. Ayañhi khīṇāsavamahātheraṃ catūhi akkosehi akkositvā yāvāyaṃ mahāpathavī tigāvutādhikaṃ yojanaṃ ussannā, tāva avīcimhi paccitvā tattha pakkāvasesena pañcapaññāsa vassāni imaṃ vippakāraṃ patto. Tenassa taṃ kammaṃ khīṇaṃ. Vīsati pana vassasahassāni iminā katassa samaṇadhammassa phalaṃ nāsetuṃ na sakkā. Tasmā satthā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā “ehi, bhikkhu, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa [M 1.0319] antakiriyāyā”ti āha. Tāvadevassa gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi aṭṭhaparikkhāradharo saṭṭhivassikamahāthero [P 2.0062] viya ahosi.

Then the Teacher said to him: "Jambuka, you who have been deceiving the blind and foolish populace in the world, now seek to deceive me as well. Have you not for fifty-five years eaten only excrement, lain only on the ground, wandered about naked, and plucked out your hair with a piece of a palm seed? And yet, while deceiving the world, you say, 'I live on air, I stand on one foot, I do not sit, I do not lie down.' You seek to deceive me too. In the past, by relying on an evil, base view, for so long a time you came to eat excrement, lie on the ground, wander naked, and pluck out your hair with a piece of a palm seed. Now, too, you take up that same evil, base view." "But what have I done, great ascetic?" Then the Teacher told him of the deed he had done in the past. As the Teacher was speaking, agitation arose in him, and shame and fear of wrongdoing were established. He sat down squatting on his heels. Then the Teacher threw him a bathing cloth and gave it to him. Having put it on, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. The Teacher, having given him a gradual discourse, taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, having attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, he paid homage to the Teacher, rose from his seat, and requested the going forth and full ordination. With that, his former kamma was exhausted. Indeed, having reviled an Arahant great elder with four terms of abuse, for as long as this great earth, a yojana and three gāvutas, rose up, for that long he was tormented in Avīci, and with the remainder of that kamma's result, he experienced this perversion for fifty-five years. By that, his kamma was exhausted. However, the fruit of the ascetic's practice he had performed for twenty thousand years could not be destroyed. Therefore, the Teacher extended his right hand and said, "Come, bhikkhu, live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering." At that very moment, his lay appearance vanished, and he became a bearer of the eight requisites, like a great elder of sixty years' standing.

Aṅgamagadhavāsīnaṃ tassa sakkāraṃ gahetvā āgatadivaso kiresa, tasmā ubhayaraṭṭhavāsino sakkāraṃ gahetvā āgatā tathāgataṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho amhākaṃ ayyo jambuko mahā, udāhu samaṇo gotamo”ti cintetvā “sace samaṇo gotamo mahā bhaveyya, ayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gaccheyya, jambukājīvakassa pana mahantatāya samaṇo gotamo imassa santikaṃ āgato”ti cintayiṃsu. Satthā mahājanassa parivitakkaṃ ñatvā, “jambuka, tava upaṭṭhākānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindāhī”ti āha, so “ahampi, bhante, ettakameva paccāsīsāmī”ti vatvā catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā uṭṭhāya tālappamāṇaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā “satthā me, bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmī”ti vatvā oruyha vanditvā puna dvitālamattaṃ titālamattanti evaṃ sattatālamattaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā oruyha attano sāvakabhāvaṃ jānāpesi. Taṃ disvā mahājano “aho buddhā nāma acchariyā anopamaguṇā”ti cintesi. Satthā mahājanena saddhiṃ kathento evamāha – “ayaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ tumhehi ābhataṃ sakkāraṃ kusaggena jivhagge ṭhapetvā ‘tapacaraṇaṃ pūremī’ti idha nivuṭṭho, sacepi iminā upāyena vassasataṃ tapacaraṇaṃ pūreyya, yā cassa idāni kālaṃ vā bhattaṃ vā kukkuccāyitvā abhuñjantassa bhattacchedanakusalacetanā, tassā taṃ tapacaraṇaṃ soḷasiṃ kalampi na agghatī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that this was the day the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha came, bringing offerings for him. Therefore, the inhabitants of both countries, having brought offerings, came and saw the Tathāgata. They thought, "Who, I wonder, is greater? Our noble Jambuka, or the ascetic Gotama?" Then they considered, "If the ascetic Gotama were the greater one, this Jambuka would go to the ascetic Gotama's presence. But it is due to the greatness of Jambuka the Ājīvaka that the ascetic Gotama has come to his presence." The Teacher, knowing the great crowd's deliberation, said, "Jambuka, cut off the doubt of your attendants." He replied, "Venerable sir, this is all that I myself was hoping for." Having said this, he entered the fourth jhāna, rose from it, and ascended into the sky to the height of a palm tree. He declared, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple!" Then he descended, paid homage, and again ascended into the sky to the height of two palm trees, three palm trees, and so on up to seven palm trees, descending and making known his status as a disciple. Seeing this, the great crowd thought, "Oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas, of incomparable virtue!" The Teacher, speaking with the great crowd, said this: "For so long, this man has lived here, placing the offerings brought by you on the tip of his tongue with a blade of kusa grass, thinking, 'I will fulfill the ascetic practice.' Even if he were to fulfill the ascetic practice in this way for a hundred years, that ascetic practice would not be worth a sixteenth part of the wholesome volition of one who, being scrupulous about the time or the food, now abstains from a meal." Connecting the narrative, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

70.

70.

“Māse māse kusaggena, bālo bhuñjeyya bhojanaṃ;

Na so saṅkhātadhammānaṃ, kalaṃ agghati soḷasi”nti.

Month after month, a fool may eat food with a kusa-grass tip; he is not worth a sixteenth part of those who have comprehended the Dhamma.

Tassattho [P 2.0063] – sace bālo apariññātadhammo sīlādiguṇā paribāhiro titthāyatane pabbajito “tapacaraṇaṃ pūressāmī”ti māse māse patte kusaggena bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto vassasataṃ bhuñjeyya [V 1.0285] bhojanaṃ. Na so saṅkhātadhammānaṃ, kalaṃ agghati soḷasinti saṅkhātadhammā vuccanti ñātadhammā tulitadhammā. Tesu heṭṭhimakoṭiyā sotāpanno saṅkhātadhammo, uparimakoṭiyā khīṇāsavo. Imesaṃ saṅkhātadhammānaṃ so bālo kalaṃ na [M 1.0320] agghati soḷasinti puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā. Ayaṃ panettha attho – yā cassa tathā tapacaraṇaṃ pūrentassa vassasataṃ cetanā yā ca saṅkhātadhammānaṃ kālaṃ vā bhattaṃ vā kukkuccāyitvā abhuñjantānaṃ ekā bhattacchedanakusalacetanā, tassā cetanāya sā tāva dīgharattaṃ pavattacetanā soḷasiṃ kalaṃ na agghati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tassā saṅkhātadhammānaṃ cetanāya phalaṃ, taṃ soḷasa koṭṭhāse katvā tato ekekaṃ puna soḷasa soḷasa koṭṭhāse katvā tato ekassa koṭṭhāsassa yaṃ phalaṃ, tadeva tassa bālassa tapacaraṇato mahapphalataranti.

Its meaning: If a fool, for whom the Dhamma is not comprehended, who is devoid of virtues such as morality, having gone forth in a sectarian institution, thinking, 'I will fulfill the ascetic practice,' should eat food from a bowl with the tip of a kusa grass blade month after month for a hundred years, he is not worth a sixteenth part of those who have comprehended the Dhamma. 'Those who have comprehended the Dhamma' (saṅkhātadhammā) are said to be those who have known the Dhamma, those who have weighed the Dhamma. Among them, at the lowest level, a stream-enterer is one who has comprehended the Dhamma; at the highest level, an Arahant. That fool is not worth a sixteenth part of these who have comprehended the Dhamma. This is the discourse based on the individual. This, however, is the meaning here in principle: There is the volition of one fulfilling the ascetic practice in such a way for a hundred years, and there is the single wholesome volition of abstaining from a meal of those who have comprehended the Dhamma, who do not eat, being scrupulous about the time or the food. That long-sustained volition is not worth a sixteenth part of that latter volition. This is what is meant: The fruit of that volition of those who have comprehended the Dhamma, if it were made into sixteen portions, and then each of those portions were again made into sixteen portions, the fruit of even one of those portions would be of far greater fruit than that fool's ascetic practice.

Desanāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, the comprehension of the Dhamma occurred for eighty-four thousand beings.

Jambukattheravatthu ekādasamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Jambuka, the Eleventh.

12. Ahipetavatthu

12. The Story of the Snake-Peta

Na hi pāpaṃ kataṃ kammanti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto aññataraṃ ahipetaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, 'Na hi pāpaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ,' concerning a certain snake-peta.

Ekasmiñhi [P 2.0064] divase jaṭilasahassassa abbhantaro āyasmā lakkhaṇatthero ca mahāmoggallānatthero ca “rājagahe piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti gijjhakūṭato otaranti. Tesu āyasmā mahāmoggallānatthero ekaṃ ahipetaṃ disvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Atha naṃ lakkhaṇatthero “kasmā, āvuso, sitaṃ pātukarosī”ti sitakāraṇaṃ pucchi. “Akālo, āvuso lakkhaṇa, imassa pañhassa, bhagavato santike maṃ puccheyyāsī”ti thero āha. Tesu rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā nisinnesu lakkhaṇatthero pucchi, “āvuso, moggallānaṃ tvaṃ gijjhakūṭā otaranto sitaṃ pātukaritvā mayā sitakāraṇaṃ puṭṭho ‘bhagavato santike maṃ puccheyyāsī’ti avaca, kathehi idāni taṃ kāraṇa”nti. Thero āha – “ahaṃ, āvuso, ekaṃ petaṃ disvā sitaṃ pātvākāsiṃ. Tassa evarūpo attabhāvo – manussasīsaṃ viya assa sīsaṃ, ahissa viya [M 1.0321] seso attabhāvo, ahipeto nāmesa pamāṇato pañcavīsatiyojaniko, tassa sīsato uṭṭhitā aggijālā yāva naṅguṭṭhā gacchanti, naṅguṭṭhato uṭṭhitā aggijālā yāva sīsā, majjhesīsato uṭṭhitā dve passāni gacchanti, dvīhi passehi uṭṭhitā majjhe otarantī”ti[V 1.0286]. Dvinnaṃyeva kira petānaṃ attabhāvo pañcavīsatiyojaniko, avasesānaṃ tigāvutappamāṇo. Imassa ceva ahipetassa kākapetassa ca pañcavīsatiyojaniko. Tesu ayaṃ tāva ahipeto. Kākapetampi mahāmoggallāno gijjhakūṭamatthake paccamānaṃ disvā tassa pubbakammaṃ pucchanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, on a certain day, from among a thousand matted-hair ascetics, the Venerable Lakkhaṇatthera and the Venerable Mahāmoggallānatthera were descending from Gijjhakūṭa Peak, thinking, 'We will go for alms in Rājagaha.' Among them, the Venerable Mahāmoggallānatthera saw a certain snake-peta and made a smile manifest. Then, the Venerable Lakkhaṇatthera asked him the reason for smiling, saying, 'Friend, why do you make a smile manifest?' The elder replied, 'Friend Lakkhaṇa, it is not the time for this question. You should ask me in the presence of the Blessed One.' After they had gone for alms in Rājagaha, gone to the Blessed One, and were seated, the Venerable Lakkhaṇatthera asked, 'Friend Moggallāna, as you were descending from Gijjhakūṭa, you made a smile manifest. When asked by me for the reason for smiling, you said, "You should ask me in the presence of the Blessed One." Now, tell that reason.' The elder said: 'Friend, I saw a certain peta and made a smile manifest. Its bodily form was of this nature: its head was like a human head, and the rest of its body was like a snake's. This being, named Ahipeta, was twenty-five yojanas in size. Flames rising from its head travel as far as its tail; flames rising from its tail travel as far as its head; flames rising from the middle of its head go to the two sides; and flames rising from the two sides descend into the middle.' It is said that the bodily form of only two petas is twenty-five yojanas; that of the remaining ones is three gāvutas in size. The bodily form of both this snake-peta and the crow-peta was twenty-five yojanas. Of these two, this one, for now, is the snake-peta. As for the crow-peta, Mahāmoggallāna saw it being tormented on the summit of Gijjhakūṭa Peak and, wishing to ask about its past kamma, spoke this verse:

“Pañcayojanikā [P 2.0065] jivhā, sīsaṃ te navayojanaṃ;

Kāyo accuggato tuyhaṃ, pañcavīsatiyojanaṃ;

Kiṃ nu kammaṃ karitvāna, pattosi dukkhamīdisa”nti.

Your tongue is five yojanas, your head nine yojanas; Your body towers, twenty-five yojanas high. What kamma, now, having done, have you attained such suffering?

Athassa peto ācikkhanto –

Then the peta, wishing to inform him, said:

“Ahaṃ bhante moggallāna, kassapassa mahesino;

Saṅghassa ābhataṃ bhattaṃ, āhāresiṃ yadicchaka”nti. –

Venerable Moggallāna, I partook as I wished of the meal brought for the Sangha of Kassapa, the great sage.

Gāthaṃ vatvā āha – “bhante, kassapabuddhakāle sambahulā bhikkhū gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu,. Manussā there disvā sampiyāyamānā āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā pāde dhovitvā telaṃ makkhetvā yāguṃ pāyetvā khajjakaṃ datvā piṇḍapātakālaṃ āgamayamānā dhammaṃ suṇantā nisīdiṃsu. Dhammakathāvasāne therānaṃ patte ādāya attano attano gehā nānaggarasabhojanassa pūretvā āhariṃsu. Tadā ahaṃ kāko hutvā āsanasālāya chadanapiṭṭhe nilīno taṃ disvā ekena gahitapattato tikkhattuṃ mukhaṃ pūrento tayo kabaḷe aggahesiṃ. Taṃ pana bhattaṃ neva saṅghassa santakaṃ, na saṅghassa niyametvā dinnaṃ, na bhikkhūhi gahitāvasesakaṃ. Attano attano gehaṃ netvā manussehi bhuñjitabbakaṃ, kevalaṃ saṅghaṃ uddissa abhihaṭamattameva. Tato mayā tayo kabaḷā gahitā, ettakaṃ me pubbakammaṃ. Svāhaṃ kālaṃ katvā tassa kammassa vipākena avīcimhi [P 2.0066] paccitvā tattha pakkāvasesena idāni gijjhakūṭe kākapeto hutvā nibbatto imaṃ dukkhaṃ paccānubhomī”ti. Idaṃ kākapetassa vatthu.

Having spoken the verse, he said: 'Venerable sir, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, many bhikkhus entered a village for alms. The people, seeing the elders and feeling affectionate, had them sit in the assembly hall, washed their feet, anointed them with oil, had them drink gruel, gave them hard food, and, while waiting for the time of the alms-meal, sat listening to the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, taking the elders' bowls, they filled them with various choice and delicious foods from their own homes and brought them. At that time, having become a crow and hiding on the roof-ridge of the assembly hall, I saw that food. From a bowl held by one person, I took three morsels, filling my mouth three times. Now, that food was not yet the property of the Sangha; it had not been dedicated and given to the Sangha; nor was it the remainder after the bhikkhus had taken their portion. It was to be taken to their respective homes to be eaten by the people; it was merely brought forth with the Sangha as the object. From that, three morsels were taken by me. This much was my past kamma. I, having passed away, as a result of that kamma, was tormented in Avīci, and now, by the remainder of that kamma, I have been reborn on Gijjhakūṭa Peak as a crow-peta and am experiencing this suffering.' This is the story of the crow-peta.

Idha [M 1.0322] pana thero “ahipetaṃ disvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi”nti āha. Athassa satthā sakkhī hutvāpi uṭṭhāya “saccaṃ, bhikkhave, moggallāno āha. Mayāpesa sambodhipattadivaseyeva diṭṭho, apicāhaṃ ‘ye me vacanaṃ na saddaheyyuṃ, tesaṃ ahitāya bhaveyyā’ti parānuddayāya na kathesi”nti āha. Lakkhaṇasaṃyuttepi (saṃ. ni. 2.202 ādayo) hi mahāmoggallānena diṭṭhakāleyeva [V 1.0287] satthā tassa sakkhī hutvā vinītavatthūni kathesi, idampi tena tatheva kathitaṃ. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū tassa pubbakammaṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthāpi tesaṃ kathesi –

Here, however, the elder said, 'Having seen the snake-peta, I made a smile manifest.' Then the Teacher, rising up to bear witness for him, said: 'Bhikkhus, Moggallāna speaks the truth. This peta was also seen by me on the very day I attained full enlightenment. However, out of compassion for others, I did not speak of it, thinking, "It would be to the detriment of those who might not believe my word."' Indeed, in the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta, at the very time Mahāmoggallāna saw them, the Teacher, acting as his witness, related the settled accounts. This account, too, was related by him in the same way. Hearing that, the bhikkhus asked about the peta's past kamma. The Teacher then told them:

Atīte kira bārāṇasiṃ nissāya nadītīre paccekabuddhassa paṇṇasālaṃ kariṃsu. So tattha viharanto nibaddhaṃ nagare piṇḍāya carati. Nāgarāpi sāyaṃpātaṃ gandhapupphādihatthā paccekabuddhassūpaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Eko bārāṇasivāsī puriso taṃ maggaṃ nissāya khettaṃ kasi. Mahājano sāyaṃpātaṃ paccekabuddhassūpaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto taṃ khettaṃ maddanto gacchati. Kassako ca “mā me khettaṃ maddathā”ti vārentopi vāretuṃ nāsakkhi. Athassa etadahosi – “sace imasmiṃ ṭhāne paccekabuddhassa paṇṇasālā na bhaveyya, na me khettaṃ maddeyyu”nti. So paccekabuddhassa piṇḍāya paviṭṭhakāle paribhogabhājanāni bhinditvā paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpesi. Paccekabuddho [P 2.0067] taṃ jhāmaṃ disvā yathāsukhaṃ pakkāmi. Mahājano gandhamālaṃ ādāya āgato jhāmapaṇṇasālaṃ disvā “kahaṃ nu kho no ayyo gato”ti āha. Sopi mahājaneneva saddhiṃ gato mahājanamajjhe ṭhitakova evamāha – “mayā tassa paṇṇasālā jhāpitā”ti. Atha naṃ “gaṇhatha, imaṃ pāpimaṃ nissāya mayaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhimhā”ti daṇḍādīhi pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ. So avīcimhi nibbattitvā yāvāyaṃ mahāpathavī yojanamattaṃ ussannā, tāva niraye paccitvā pakkāvasesena gijjhakūṭe ahipeto hutvā nibbatti. Satthā idaṃ tassa pubbakammaṃ kathetvā, “bhikkhave, pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ khīrasadisaṃ, yathā khīraṃ duyhamānameva na pariṇamati. Tathā kammaṃ kayiramānameva na vipaccati. Yadā pana vipaccati, tadā evarūpena dukkhena socatī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, it is said, near Varanasi, on a riverbank, people built a leaf-hut for a Paccekabuddha. Dwelling there, he would regularly go into the city for alms-food. The city-dwellers, with perfumes, flowers, and the like in hand, would go to attend upon the Paccekabuddha in the evening and morning. A certain man who lived in Varanasi cultivated a field near that path. The great crowd, going to attend upon the Paccekabuddha in the evening and morning, would pass by, trampling his field. Though the farmer tried to prevent them, saying, 'Do not trample my field,' he was unable to stop them. Then this thought occurred to him: 'If the Paccekabuddha’s leaf-hut were not in this place, they would not trample my field.' So, when the Paccekabuddha had entered the city for alms-food, he broke the utensils and set fire to the leaf-hut. The Paccekabuddha, seeing it burnt, departed to a place of ease. The great crowd, having arrived with perfumes and garlands, saw the burnt leaf-hut and said, 'Where indeed has our noble one gone?' That farmer, who had gone along with the great crowd, stood in their midst and said, 'I set fire to his leaf-hut.' Then, saying, 'Seize him! On account of this wicked man, we do not get to see the Paccekabuddha,' they beat him with sticks and the like and brought him to the end of his life. He was reborn in the Avīci hell and was tormented there for as long as this great earth is a yojana in height. With the remainder of the ripening of that kamma, he was reborn as a snake-peta on Gijjhakūṭa mountain. The Teacher, having related this past kamma of his, said: 'Bhikkhus, an evil deed is like milk. Just as milk does not curdle at the very moment it is milked, so too, a deed does not ripen at the very moment it is done. But when it does ripen, one grieves with such suffering.' Having made this connection while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

71.

71.

“Na [M 1.0323] hi pāpaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ, sajjukhīraṃva muccati;

Ḍahantaṃ bālamanveti, bhasmacchannova pāvako”ti.

Indeed, an evil deed that has been done does not immediately curdle, like freshly drawn milk; burning, it follows the fool, like a fire covered by ashes.

Tattha sajjukhīraṃ vāti taṃ khaṇaṃyeva dhenuyā thanehi nikkhantaṃ abbhuṇhaṃ khīraṃ na muccati na pariṇamati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā idaṃ sajjukhīraṃ taṃ khaṇaññeva na muccati na pariṇamati na pakatiṃ vijahati. Yasmiṃ pana bhājane duhitvā gahitaṃ yāva tattha [P 2.0068] takkādiambilaṃ na pakkhipati, yāva dadhibhājanādikaṃ ambilabhājanaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva pakatiṃ avijahitvā pacchā jahati, evameva pāpakammampi kariyamānameva na vipaccati. Yadi vipacceyya, na koci pāpakammaṃ kātuṃ visaheyya. Yāva pana kusalābhinibbattā khandhā dharanti, tāva naṃ te rakkhanti. Tesaṃ bhedā apāye nibbattakkhandhesu vipaccati, vipaccamānañca [V 1.0288] ḍahantaṃ bālamanveti.“Kiṃ viyā”ti? “Bhasmacchannova pāvako”ti. Yathā hi chārikāya paṭicchanno vītaccitaṅgāro akkantopi chārikāya paṭicchannattā na tāva ḍahati, chārikaṃ pana tāpetvā cammādīnaṃ ḍahanavasena yāva matthaluṅgā ḍahanto gacchati, evameva pāpakammampi yena kataṃ hoti, taṃ bālaṃ dutiye vā tatiye vā attabhāve nirayādīsu nibbattaṃ ḍahantaṃ anugacchatīti.

Therein, 'like freshly drawn milk' means that milk which is still warm, having come from a cow’s udders at that very moment, does not turn or change. This is what is meant: just as this freshly drawn milk does not immediately turn, change, or abandon its natural state. But when it has been milked and taken in a vessel, for as long as a souring agent like buttermilk is not put into it, or for as long as it does not reach a souring vessel like a yogurt pot, for that long it does not abandon its natural state, but does so afterwards. In the very same way, an evil deed also does not ripen at the very moment it is being done. If it were to ripen immediately, no one would dare to do an evil deed. For as long as the aggregates produced by wholesome kamma endure, they protect that person. At the breaking up of those aggregates, when new aggregates have arisen in a state of woe, it ripens. And while ripening, it follows the fool, burning him. 'Like what?' 'Like a fire covered by ashes.' For just as a flameless ember covered by ash, even when stepped on, does not burn at first because it is covered by ash, but having heated the ash, it goes on burning through skin and the like right up to the brain-marrow; in the very same way, an evil deed, done by a fool, follows that fool in the second or third existence, burning him when he is reborn in hell and other such states.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesunti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many became stream-enterers and so on.

Ahipetavatthu dvādasamaṃ.

The Story of the Snake-Peta, the Twelfth.

13. Saṭṭhikūṭapetavatthu

13. The Story of the Peta of the Sixty Hammers

Yāvadeva anatthāyāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto saṭṭhikūṭapetaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, beginning with the words 'Yāvadeva anatthāya,' concerning the Peta of the Sixty Hammers.

Purimanayeneva hi mahāmoggallānatthero lakkhaṇattherena saddhiṃ gijjhakūṭā orohanto aññatarasmiṃ padese sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Therena sitakāraṇaṃ puṭṭho “bhagavato santike [P 2.0069] maṃ puccheyyāsī”ti vatvā piṇḍāya caritvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā nisinnakāle puna puṭṭho āha – “ahaṃ, āvuso, ekaṃ petaṃ addasaṃ tigāvutappamāṇena attabhāvena, tassa saṭṭhi ayakūṭasahassāni ādittāni sampajjalitāni uparimatthake patitvā patitvā uṭṭhahanti sīsaṃ bhindanti, bhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ puna samuṭṭhahati[M 1.0324], iminā attabhāvena mayā evarūpo attabhāvo na diṭṭhapubbo, ahaṃ taṃ disvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi”nti. Petavatthusmiñhi –

Indeed, in the same way as before, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, while descending from Gijjhakūṭa mountain with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, made a smile manifest at a certain place. When asked by the Elder the reason for his smile, he said, 'Ask me in the presence of the Blessed One.' Having said this, and after going for alms, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and at the time of being seated, when asked again, he said: 'Friend, I saw a certain peta with a body three gāvutas in size. Upon its head, sixty thousand iron hammers, burning and blazing, were falling again and again and rising up. They split the head. Having been split again and again, it forms anew. In this existence, I have never before seen such a form of existence. Having seen that peta, I made a smile manifest.' Indeed, in the Petavatthu:

“Saṭṭhi kūṭasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Sīse tuyhaṃ nipatanti, vobhindanteva matthaka”nti. (pe. va. 808, 810, 813) ādi –

'Sixty thousand hammers, completely full in every way, fall upon your head, splitting your crown.' (Petavatthu, verses 808, 810, 813), and so on.

Imameva petaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Satthā therassa kathaṃ sutvāva, “bhikkhave, mayāpesa satto bodhimaṇḍe nisinneneva diṭṭho ‘ye ca pana me vacanaṃ na saddaheyyuṃ, tesaṃ ahitāya bhaveyyā’ti paresaṃ anukampāya [V 1.0289] na kathesiṃ, idāni pana moggallānassa sakkhī hutvā kathemī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū tassa pubbakammaṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthāpi nesaṃ kathesi –

It was said with reference to this very peta. Having heard the elder’s words, the Teacher said: 'Monks, I too saw this being while seated at the Bodhimaṇḍa. But thinking, "Whoever would not believe my word, it would be for their harm," out of compassion for others, I did not speak of it. Now, however, having Moggallāna as a witness, I will speak.' Hearing this, the monks asked about the peta's past kamma. The Teacher then told it to them:

Atīte kira bārāṇasiyaṃ sāḷittakasippe nipphattiṃ patto eko pīṭhasappi ahosi. So nagaradvāre ekassa vaṭarukkhassa heṭṭhā nisinno sakkharāni khipitvā tassa paṇṇāni chindanto “hatthirūpakaṃ no dassehi, assarūpakaṃ no dassehī”ti gāmadārakehi [P 2.0070] vuccamāno icchiticchitāni rūpāni dassetvā tesaṃ santikā khādanīyādīni labhati. Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānaṃ gacchanto taṃ padesaṃ pāpuṇi. Dārakā pīṭhasappiṃ pārohantare katvā palāyiṃsu. Rañño ṭhitamajjhanhike rukkhamūlaṃ paviṭṭhassa chiddāvachiddacchāyā sarīraṃ phari. So “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti uddhaṃ olokento rukkhapaṇṇesu hatthirūpakādīni disvā “kassetaṃ kamma”nti pucchitvā “pīṭhasappino”ti sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “mayhaṃ purohito atimukharo appamattakepi vutte bahuṃ bhaṇanto maṃ upaddaveti, sakkhissasi tassa mukhe nāḷimattā ajalaṇḍikā khipitu”nti? “Sakkhissāmi, deva. Ajalaṇḍikā āharāpetvā purohitena saddhiṃ tumhe antosāṇiyaṃ nisīdatha, ahamettha kattabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti. Atha rājā tathā kāresi. Itaro kattariyaggena sāṇiyā chiddaṃ katvā purohitassa raññā saddhiṃ kathentassa mukhe vivaṭamatte ekekaṃ ajalaṇḍikaṃ khipi. Purohito mukhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ gili. Pīṭhasappī khīṇāsu ajalaṇḍikāsu sāṇiṃ cālesi. Rājā tāya saññāya ajalaṇḍikānaṃ khīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “ācariya, ahaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ kathento kathaṃ [M 1.0325] nittharituṃ na sakkhissāmi, tumhe atimukharatāya nāḷimattā ajalaṇḍikā gilantāpi tuṇhībhāvaṃ nāpajjathā”ti. Brāhmaṇo [P 2.0071] maṅguubhāvaṃ āpajjitvā tato paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ vivaritvā raññā saddhiṃ sallapituṃ nasakkhi. Rājā pīṭhasappiguṇaṃ anussaritvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “taṃ nissāya me sukhaṃ laddha”nti tuṭṭho tassa sabbaṭṭhakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ datvā nagarassa catūsu disāsu cattāro varagāme adāsi. Tamatthaṃ viditvā rañño atthadhammānusāsako amacco imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, it is said, in Bārāṇasī, there was a certain cripple who had attained perfection in the art of pebble-throwing. While sitting at the city gate beneath a banyan tree, he would cut the leaves of that tree by throwing pebbles. When the village children would say, 'Show us the form of an elephant! Show us the form of a horse!' he would show them whatever forms they desired and would receive from them snacks and other items. Then one day, the king, while going to the park, arrived at that place. The children, placing the cripple between the buttress roots, ran away. When the king entered the shade of the tree at midday, its perforated shadow fell upon his body. Wondering, 'What could this be?' he looked up and saw the forms of elephants and other creatures on the tree's leaves. He asked, 'Whose work is this?' and upon hearing it was the cripple's, he had him summoned and said: 'My purohita is extremely garrulous. When even a small thing is said, he speaks at length, harassing me. Will you be able to throw a nāḷi-measure of goat-dung pellets into his mouth?' 'I will be able, Your Majesty. Have the goat-dung pellets brought, and you sit with the purohita inside a curtain. I will know what needs to be done in this matter.' Then the king had it done so. The other, making a hole in the curtain with the tip of a pair of scissors, threw one goat-dung pellet at a time into the purohita's mouth just as it opened while he was speaking with the king. The purohita swallowed each pellet as it entered his mouth. When the goat-dung pellets were finished, the cripple shook the curtain. The king, knowing by that sign that the goat-dung pellets were finished, said: 'Ācariya, when I am speaking with you, I cannot bring the conversation to a conclusion. Due to your extreme garrulousness, even while swallowing a nāḷi-measure of goat-dung pellets, you do not fall silent!' The brahmin, becoming discomfited, was from then on unable to open his mouth to converse with the king. The king, recalling the cripple's good deed, had him summoned and, pleased, said, 'Through you, I have obtained happiness.' He gave him the wealth named 'Sabbaṭṭhaka' and granted him four choice villages in the four directions of the city. An advisor, a minister who instructed the king on matters of welfare and Dhamma, knowing of this matter, spoke this verse:

“Sādhu kho sippakaṃ nāma, api yādisa kīdisaṃ;

Passa khañjappahārena, laddhā gāmā catuddisā”ti. (jā. 1.1.107);

'A skill, indeed, is a good thing, of whatever kind it may be. See, by the throw of the cripple, villages in the four directions were obtained.'

So pana amacco tena samayena ayameva bhagavā ahosi. Atheko puriso pīṭhasappinā laddhasampattiṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ nāma pīṭhasappī hutvā imaṃ sippaṃ nissāya mahāsampattiṃ patto, mayāpetaṃ sikkhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “idaṃ me[V 1.0290], ācariya, sippaṃ dethā”ti āha. “Na sakkā, tāta, dātu”nti. So tena paṭikkhitto “hotu, ārādhessāmi na”nti tassa hatthapādaparikammādīni karonto cirassaṃ taṃ ārādhetvā punappunaṃ yāci, pīṭhasappī “ayaṃ me ativiya upakāro”ti taṃ paṭibāhituṃ asakkonto sippaṃ sikkhāpetvā “nipphannaṃ te, tāta, sippaṃ, idāni kiṃ karissasī”ti āha. “Bahi gantvā sippaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Gāviṃ vā manussaṃ vā paharitvā māressāmī”ti. “Tātā, gāviṃ mārentassa sataṃ daṇḍo hoti manussaṃ mārentassa sahassaṃ, tvaṃ saputtadāropi taṃ nittharituṃ na sakkhissasi, mā vinassa, yamhi [P 2.0072] pahaṭe daṇḍo natthi, tādisaṃ nimātāpitikaṃ kañci upadhārehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sakkharā ucchaṅge katvā tādisaṃ upadhārayamāno vicaranto gāviṃ disvā “ayaṃ sasāmikā”ti paharituṃ na visahi, manussaṃ disvā “ayaṃ samātāpitiko”ti paharituṃ na visati.

That minister, at that time, was I, the Blessed One. Then a certain man, seeing the prosperity gained by the cripple, thought: 'This person, being a cripple, has attained great prosperity by relying on this skill. It is fitting for me to learn it too.' He approached him, paid homage, and said, 'Master, give me this skill.' 'It cannot be given, dear one,' he replied. Having been rejected by him, the man thought, 'So be it, I will please him.' He began to serve him by massaging his hands and feet and so on. After a long time, having pleased him, he repeatedly requested. The cripple, thinking, 'This man is extremely helpful to me,' and being unable to refuse him, had him learn the skill and then said, 'Dear one, your skill is perfected. What will you do now?' 'I will go out and test my skill,' he replied. 'What will you do?' 'I will strike and kill a cow or a person.' 'Dear one, for killing a cow, the fine is a hundred; for killing a person, a thousand. You, even with your wife and children, will not be able to get out of it. Do not be ruined. Search for someone without mother or father, who, when struck, incurs no penalty.' He said, 'Very well,' and putting pebbles in his waist-cloth, he wandered about searching for such a person. Seeing a cow, he thought, 'This one has an owner,' and did not dare to strike it. Seeing a person, he thought, 'This one has a mother and father,' and did not dare to strike.

Tena samayena sunetto nāma paccekabuddho taṃ nagaraṃ nissāya paṇṇasālāya viharati. So taṃ piṇḍāya pavisantaṃ nagaradvārantare disvā “ayaṃ nimātāpitiko, imasmiṃ pahaṭe daṇḍo natthi, imaṃ paharitvā sippaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti paccekabuddhassa dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotaṃ sandhāya sakkharaṃ [M 1.0326] khipi. Sā dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotena pavisitvā vāmena nikkhami, dukkhā vedanā uppajji. Paccekabuddho bhikkhāya carituṃ nāsakkhi, ākāsena paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā parinibbāyi. Manussā paccekabuddhe anāgacchante “kiñci aphāsukaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā tattha gantvā taṃ parinibbutaṃ disvā rodiṃsu parideviṃsu. Sopi mahājanaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā tattha gantvā paccekabuddhaṃ sañjānitvā “ayaṃ piṇḍāya pavisanto dvārantare mama sammukhībhūto, ahaṃ attano sippaṃ vīmaṃsanto imaṃ pahari”nti āha. Manussā “iminā kira pāpakena paccekabuddho pahaṭo, gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti pothetvā tattheva naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ. So avīcimhi nibbattitvā yāvāyaṃ mahāpathavī yojanamattaṃ ussannā, tāva paccitvā vipākāvasesena gijjhakūṭamatthake saṭṭhikūṭapeto hutvā nibbatti. Satthā tassa imaṃ pubbakammaṃ kathetvā, “bhikkhave, bālassa [P 2.0073] nāma sippaṃ vā issariyaṃ vā uppajjamānaṃ anatthāya uppajjati. Bālo hi sippaṃ vā issariyaṃ vā labhitvā attano anatthameva karotī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha.

At that time, a paccekabuddha named Sunetta was dwelling in a leaf-hut, relying on that city. Seeing him entering for alms near the city gate, that man thought, 'This one is without mother or father. If he is struck, there is no penalty. I will test my skill by striking him.' Aiming for the paccekabuddha’s right ear-opening, he threw a pebble. It entered through the right ear-opening and exited through the left, and a painful sensation arose. The paccekabuddha was unable to go for alms; he went to his leaf-hut through the sky and attained parinibbāna. When the paccekabuddha did not come, the people thought, 'Some misfortune must have occurred,' and went there. Seeing that he had attained parinibbāna, they wept and lamented. That man, too, seeing the great crowd going there, went and recognized the paccekabuddha. He said, 'As this one was entering for alms, he came face-to-face with me near the gate. While testing my own skill, I struck him.' The people cried, 'It seems this wicked man has struck the paccekabuddha! Seize him, seize him!' They beat him and right there brought him to the end of his life. He was reborn in Avīci and was tormented there for as long as this great earth is a yojana in depth. Then, by the remainder of that result, he was reborn as a sixty-spiked peta on the peak of Gijjhakūṭa. The Teacher, having related this past kamma of his, said, 'Monks, for a fool, any skill or power that arises, arises for his harm. For a fool, having gained skill or power, brings about only his own harm.' Connecting the narrative, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma.

72.

72.

“Yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyati;

Hanti bālassa sukkaṃsaṃ, muddhamassa vipātaya”nti.

A fool's skill arises only for his own harm; it destroys the fool's portion of merit, shattering his wisdom.

Tattha yāvadevāti avadhiparicchedanatthe nipāto. Ñattanti jānanasabhāvo. Yaṃ sippaṃ jānāti[V 1.0291], yamhi vā issariye yase sampattiyañca ṭhito janena ñāyati, pākaṭo paññāto hoti, tassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sippaṃ vā hi issariyādibhāvo vā bālassa anatthāyeva jāyati. Taṃ nissāya so attano anatthameva karoti. Hantīti vināseti. Sukkaṃsanti kusalakoṭṭhāsaṃ, bālassa hi sippaṃ vā issariyaṃ vā uppajjamānaṃ kusalakoṭṭhāsaṃ ghātentameva uppajjati. Muddhanti paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vipātayanti viddhaṃsayamānaṃ. Tassa hi taṃ sukkaṃsaṃ hanantaṃ paññāsaṅkhātaṃ muddhaṃ vipātentaṃ viddhaṃsentameva hantīti.

Herein, 'yāvadeva' is a particle in the sense of limitation. 'Ñattaṃ' is the state of being known. It is the name for whatever skill one knows, or whatever power, fame, or prosperity in which one is established and thereby becomes known, manifest, and renowned among people. Indeed, skill or a state of power and the like arises only for the harm of a fool. Relying on it, he brings about only his own harm. 'Hanti' means it destroys. 'Sukkaṃsaṃ' is the portion of merit; for a fool's skill or power, when it arises, arises only while destroying the portion of merit. 'Muddhaṃ' is a name for wisdom. 'Vipātayaṃ' means shattering. For that skill of his, while destroying his portion of merit and shattering his wisdom, which is called 'muddhaṃ', indeed destroys him.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Saṭṭhikūṭapetavatthu terasamaṃ.

The Story of the Sixty-Spiked Peta is the thirteenth.

14. Cittagahapativatthu

14. The Story of Citta the Householder

Asantaṃ [M 1.0327][P 2.0074] bhāvanamiccheyyāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sudhammattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Desanā macchikāsaṇḍe samuṭṭhāya sāvatthiyaṃ niṭṭhitā.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this discourse, which begins with the words Asantaṃ bhāvanamiccheyya, concerning the Elder Sudhamma. The discourse arose in Macchikāsaṇḍa and concluded in Sāvatthī.

Macchikāsaṇḍanagarasmiñhi citto nāma gahapati pañcavaggiyānaṃ abbhantaraṃ mahānāmattheraṃ nāma piṇḍāya caramānaṃ disvā tassa iriyāpathe pasīditvā pattaṃ ādāya gehaṃ pavesetvā bhojetvā bhattakiccāvasāne dhammakathaṃ suṇanto sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā acalasaddho hutvā ambāṭakavanaṃ nāma attano uyyānaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kattukāmo therassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā niyyādesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe “patiṭṭhitaṃ buddhasāsana”nti udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī kampi. Mahāseṭṭhi uyyāne mahāvihāraṃ kāretvā sabbadisāhi āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vivaṭadvāro ahosi. Macchikāsaṇḍe sudhammatthero nāma nevāsiko ahosi.

Indeed, in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa, a householder named Citta, seeing the Elder named Mahānāma, who was one of the group of five, walking for alms, was pleased with his deportment. Taking the Elder's bowl, he led him into his house and served him a meal. At the conclusion of the meal, while listening to a Dhamma talk, he attained the fruit of stream-entry and became one of unshakable faith. Wishing to make his own park, named Ambāṭakavana, into a monastery for the Sangha, he poured water into the Elder's hands and dedicated it. At that moment, the donation being sealed by the pouring of water, the great earth trembled, as if to say, 'The Buddha's dispensation is established.' The great merchant had a large monastery built in the park, and its doors were open to monks coming from all directions. In Macchikāsaṇḍa, there was a resident monk named Elder Sudhamma.

Aparena samayena cittassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā dve aggasāvakā tassa saṅgahaṃ kattukāmā macchikāsaṇḍaṃ agamaṃsu. Citto gahapati tesaṃ āgamanaṃ sutvā aḍḍhayojanamaggaṃ paccuggantvā te ādāya attano vihāraṃ pavesetvā āgantukavattaṃ katvā, “bhante, thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sotukāmomhī”ti dhammasenāpatiṃ yāci. Atha naṃ thero, “upāsaka, addhānena āgatāmhā kilantarūpā. Apica thokaṃ suṇāhī”ti tassa dhammaṃ kathesi. So therassa dhammaṃ suṇantova anāgāmiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. So dve aggasāvake vanditvā, “bhante, sve bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ mama [V 1.0292] gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantetvā [P 2.0075] pacchā nevāsikaṃ sudhammattheraṃ “tumhepi, bhante, sve therehi saddhiṃ āgaccheyyāthā”ti nimantesi. So “ayaṃ maṃ pacchā nimantetī”ti kuddho paṭikkhipitvā punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi paṭikkhipi eva. Upāsako “paññāyissatha, bhante”ti pakkamitvā punadivase attano nivesane mahādānaṃ sajjesi. Sudhammattheropi paccūsakāleyeva “kīdiso nu kho gahapatinā aggasāvakānaṃ sakkāro sajjito, sve gantvā passissāmī”ti cintetvā pātova pattacīvaraṃ ādāya tassa gehaṃ agamāsi.

At a later time, having heard talk of Citta's virtues, the two chief disciples, wishing to support him, went to Macchikāsaṇḍa. Hearing of their arrival, the householder Citta went half a yojana to meet them. Bringing them to his monastery and performing the duties for arriving guests, he requested the General of the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, I wish to hear a little of the Dhamma." Then the Elder said to him, "Householder, we have come by a long road and our bodies are weary. Nevertheless, listen for a little while," and he taught him the Dhamma. Even while listening to the Elder's Dhamma, he attained the fruit of non-returning. He paid homage to the two chief disciples and invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, tomorrow please accept alms in my house along with a thousand monks." Afterwards, he invited the resident Elder Sudhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, you too should come tomorrow with the Elders." That Elder, becoming angry thinking, "He invites me last," refused. Though repeatedly requested, he just kept refusing. The householder said, "You will see, venerable sir," and departed. The next day, he prepared a great offering in his home. The Elder Sudhamma, too, at the very time of dawn, thought, "What kind of offerings has the householder prepared for the chief disciples? I will go and see," and taking his bowl and robe early in the morning, he went to the householder's home.

So gahapatinā “nisīdatha, bhante”ti vuccamānopi “nāhaṃ nisīdāmi, piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti vatvā aggasāvakānaṃ paṭiyāditaṃ sakkāraṃ oloketvā [M 1.0328] gahapatiṃ jātiyā ghaṭṭetukāmo “uḷāro te, gahapati, sakkāro, apicettha ekaññeva natthī”ti āha. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti? “Tilasaṃguḷikā, gahapatī”ti vatvā gahapatinā kākopamāya apasādito kujjhitvā “eso te, gahapati, āvāso, pakkamissāmaha”nti vatvā yāvatatiyaṃ vāriyamānopi pakkamitvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā cittena ca attanā ca vuttavacanaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “tayā upāsako saddho pasanno hīnena khuṃsito”ti tasseva dosaṃ āropetvā paṭisāraṇīyakammaṃ kārāpetvā “gaccha, cittagahapatiṃ khamāpehī”ti pesesi. So tattha gantvā, “gahapati, mayhameva so doso, khamāhi me”ti vatvāpi “nāhaṃ khamāmī”ti [P 2.0076] tena paṭikkhitto maṅkubhūto taṃ khamāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. Punadeva satthu santikaṃ paccāgamāsi. Satthā “nāssa upāsako khamissatī”ti jānantopi “mānathaddho esa, tiṃsayojanaṃ tāva maggaṃ gantvā paccāgacchatū”ti khamanūpāyaṃ anācikkhitvāva uyyojesi. Athassa punāgatakāle nihatamānassa anudūtaṃ datvā “gaccha, iminā saddhiṃ gantvā upāsakaṃ khamāpehī”ti vatvā “samaṇena nāma ‘mayhaṃ vihāro, mayhaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ, mayhaṃ upāsako, mayhaṃ upāsikā’ti mānaṃ vā issaṃ vā kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ karontassa hi icchāmānādayo kilesā vaḍḍhantī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Although the householder said, "Please sit down, venerable sir," he replied, "I will not sit; I will go for alms." Having observed the offerings prepared for the chief disciples, and wishing to disparage the householder regarding his lineage, he said, "Householder, your offering is grand, but one thing is missing." "What is that, venerable sir?" "Sesame cakes, householder." Having been disparaged by the householder with the crow simile, he became angry and said, "This is your monastery, householder; I am leaving." Though he was restrained up to the third time, he departed and went to the Teacher’s presence. There, he reported the words spoken by Citta and by himself. The Teacher, placing the blame on him alone, said, "You have reviled a faithful and devoted lay follower with a base thing." He had him perform the act of reconciliation and sent him away, saying, "Go, and have the householder Citta forgive you." He went there and said, "Householder, that was my fault alone. Forgive me." But he was rebuffed by him, who said, "I will not forgive." Dispirited, he was unable to get him to grant forgiveness. He returned once more to the Teacher’s presence. The Teacher, though knowing that the lay follower would not forgive him, did not explain the means for gaining forgiveness, but sent him away, thinking, "This one is stiff with pride. Let him go the thirty-yojana road and return." Then, when he returned with his pride subdued, the Teacher gave him an accompanying monk and said, "Go, and with this monk, have the lay follower forgive you." Then he said, "A monk should not give rise to pride or envy, thinking, ‘This is my monastery, this is my dwelling place, this is my lay supporter, this is my female lay supporter.’ For one who acts thus, defilements such as desire and pride increase." Connecting this to the underlying principle, he taught the Dhamma by speaking these verses:

73.

73.

“Asantaṃ bhāvanamiccheyya, purekkhārañca bhikkhusu;

Āvāsesu issariyaṃ, pūjā parakulesu ca.

One might desire undeserved esteem, and precedence among monks, lordship in the monasteries, and veneration from other families.

74.

74.

“Mameva kata maññantu, gihī pabbajitā ubho.

Let both householders and the ordained think that this was done by me alone.

Mamevātivasā assu, kiccākiccesu kismici;

Iti bālassa saṅkappo, icchā māno ca vaḍḍhatī”ti.

In any matter, great or small, let them be subject to my will alone. Such are the thoughts of a fool; his desire and pride increase.

Tattha [V 1.0293] asantanti yo bālo bhikkhu avijjamānaṃ sambhāvanaṃ iccheyya, “assaddhova samāno ‘saddhoti maṃ jano [P 2.0077] jānātū’ti icchatī”ti. Pāpicchatāniddese (vibha. 851) vuttanayeneva bālo “asaddho dussīlo appassuto appavivitto kusīto anupaṭṭhitassati asamāhito duppañño akhīṇāsavova samāno ‘aho vata maṃ jano ayaṃ saddho, sīlavā, bahussuto, pavivitto, āraddhavīriyo, upaṭṭhitassati, samāhito, paññavā[M 1.0329], khīṇāsavo’ti jāneyyā”ti idaṃ asantasambhāvanaṃ icchati. Purekkhāranti parivāraṃ. “Aho vata maṃ sakalavihāre bhikkhū parivāretvā pañhaṃ pucchantā vihareyyu”nti evaṃ icchācāre ṭhatvā purekkhārañca bhikkhūsu icchati. Āvāsesūti saṅghikesu ca āvāsesu yāni vihāramajjhe paṇītasenāsanāni, tāni attano sandiṭṭhasambhattādīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “tumhe idha vasathā”ti vicārento sayampi varataraṃ senāsanaṃ palibodhento, sesānaṃ āgantukabhikkhūnaṃ paccantimāni lāmakasenāsanāni ceva amanussapariggahitāni ca “tumhe idha vasathā”ti vicārento āvāsesu issariyaṃ icchati. Pūjā parakulesu cāti neva mātāpitūnaṃ na ñātakānaṃ paresuyeva kulesu “aho vatime mayhameva dadeyyuṃ, na aññesa”nti evaṃ catuppaccayehi pūjaṃ icchati.

Herein, as for asantaṃ (the non-existent): it is when a foolish monk desires praise that does not exist. Being without faith, he desires, 'Let the people know me as faithful.' As stated in the exposition on evil desires, the foolish one—being faithless, immoral, of little learning, not delighting in seclusion, lazy, with unestablished mindfulness, unconcentrated, unwise, and not an Arahant—desires this praise for what does not exist, thinking: 'Oh, may the people know me as faithful, virtuous, learned, delighting in seclusion, of aroused energy, with established mindfulness, concentrated, wise, and an Arahant!' As for purekkhāraṃ (pre-eminence): it means an entourage. Standing in such evil desire, he thinks, 'Oh, if only the monks in the entire monastery would surround me, asking questions, and dwell thus!' and he desires pre-eminence among the monks. As for āvāsesu (in dwellings): desiring authority in the communal dwellings, he arranges the excellent lodgings in the middle of the monastery for the monks who are his acquaintances and associates, saying, 'You all stay here,' while he himself takes possession of a more excellent lodging. For the remaining visiting monks, he arranges the remote, inferior lodgings and those possessed by non-humans, saying, 'You all stay here.' As for pūjā parakulesu ca (and offerings from other families): not from his parents or relatives, but only in the families of others, he desires offerings of the four requisites, thinking, 'Oh, may these people give only to me, and not to others!'

Mameva kata maññantūti yassa ca bālassa [P 2.0078] “yaṃkiñci vihāre uposathāgārādikaraṇavasena kataṃ navakammaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ amhākaṃ therena katanti evaṃ gihī ca pabbajitā ca ubhopi mameva nissāya kataṃ parikammaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ maññantū”ti saṅkappo uppajjati. Mamevātivasā assūti “gihī ca pabbajitā ca sabbepi mameva vase vattantu, sakaṭagoṇavāsipharasuādīni vā laddhabbāni hontu, antamaso yāgumattampi tāpetvā pivanādīni vā, evarūpesu kiccākiccesu khuddakamahantesu karaṇīyesu kismiñci ekakiccepi mameva vase vattantu, mameva āpucchitvā karontū”ti saṅkappo uppajjati. Iti bālassāti yassa bālassa sā ca icchā ayañca evarūpo saṅkappo uppajjati, tassa neva vipassanā, na maggaphalāni vaḍḍhanti. Kevalaṃ panassa candodaye samuddassa udakaṃ viya chasu dvāresu uppajjamānā taṇhā ceva navavidhamāno ca vaḍḍhatīti.

As for 'Let them think it was done by me': it is when this intention arises in a foolish monk: 'Whatever new work has been done in the monastery, such as the construction of the Uposatha hall, let both householders and the ordained think, "All of it was done by our Elder," and "The preparatory work was completed by relying only on me."' As for 'Let them be under my sway': it is when this intention arises: 'Let all, both householders and the ordained, act under my power. Whether it be obtaining things like carts, oxen, adzes, or axes, or at the very least, acts like heating and drinking even gruel—in all such duties and non-duties, small and great, in any single task to be done, let them act under my power. Let them do it only after asking me.' Thus, for the foolish monk in whom such an evil desire and this kind of intention arise, neither insight nor the paths and fruits grow. For him, merely, just as the water of the ocean rises with the moon, so too, arising at the six doors, do craving and the ninefold conceit increase.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Sudhammattheropi imaṃ ovādaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tena anudūtena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ gantvā upāsakassa cakkhupathe āpattiṃ paṭikaritvā upāsakaṃ khamāpesi. So upāsakena “khamāmahaṃ, bhante, sace mayhaṃ doso atthi, khamatha me”ti paṭikhamāpito [V 1.0294] satthārā dinne ovāde ṭhatvā katipāheneva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ [M 1.0330] pāpuṇi. Upāsakopi [P 2.0079] cintesi – “mayā satthāraṃ adisvāva sotāpattiphalaṃ pattaṃ, adisvā eva anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhito, satthāraṃ me daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tilataṇḍulasappiphāṇitavatthacchādanādīhi paripūrāni pañca sakaṭasatāni yojāpetvā “satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmā āgacchantu, piṇḍapātādīhi na kilamissantī”ti bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocāpetvā bhikkhunīsaṅghassāpi upāsakānampi upāsikānampi ārocāpesi. Tena saddhiṃ pañcasatā pañcasatā bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo ca upāsakā ca upāsikāyo ca nikkhamiṃsu. So tesañceva attano parisāya cāti tiṇṇaṃ janasahassānaṃ yathā tiṃsayojane magge yāgubhattādīhi kiñci vekallaṃ na hoti, tathā saṃvidahi. Tassa pana nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā yojane yojane devatā khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā dibbehi yāgukhajjakabhattapānakādīhi taṃ mahājanaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu, kassaci kenaci vekallaṃ na hoti. Evaṃ devatāhi upaṭṭhiyamāno devasikaṃ yojanaṃ gacchanto māsena sāvatthiṃ pāpuṇi, pañca sakaṭasatāni yathāpūritāneva ahesuṃ. Devatāhi ceva manussehi ca abhihaṭaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ vissajjentova agamāsi.

The Elder Sudhamma, having heard this instruction, paid homage to the Teacher, rose from his seat, circumambulated him to the right, and went with that accompanying monk. Within sight of the lay devotee, he remedied the offense and had the lay devotee forgive him. Having been asked for forgiveness in turn by the lay devotee, who said, 'I forgive you, venerable sir. If there is any fault in me, please forgive me,' he stood in the instruction given by the Teacher and in just a few days attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The lay devotee also reflected: 'Without having seen the Teacher, I attained the fruit of stream-entry; without having seen him, I became established in the fruit of non-returning. It is proper for me to see the Teacher.' He had five hundred carts yoked, filled with sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, cloth, coverings, and so on, and had it announced to the community of monks, and also to the community of nuns, the male lay devotees, and the female lay devotees: 'Let those who wish to see the Teacher come; they will not be wearied by lack of almsfood and so on.' Together with him, five hundred monks, five hundred nuns, five hundred male lay devotees, and five hundred female lay devotees set out. For those four assemblies and for his own retinue—thus for three thousand people—he arranged it so that on the thirty-yojana journey, there would be no deficiency of anything like rice porridge, meals, and so on. But the deities, knowing of his departure, set up a camp at every yojana and served that great crowd of people with divine rice porridge, snacks, meals, drinks, and so on. For no one was there any deficiency of anything. Thus, being served by the deities and traveling a yojana each day, he reached Sāvatthī in a month. The five hundred carts were just as full as before. He proceeded while distributing the gifts brought forth by both deities and humans.

Satthā ānandattheraṃ āha – “ānanda, ajja vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya citto gahapati pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto āgantvā maṃ vandissatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, tassa tumhākaṃ [P 2.0080] vandanakāle kiñci pāṭihāriyaṃ bhavissatī”ti? “Bhavissati, ānandā”ti. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti? Tassa āgantvā “maṃ vandanakāle rājamānena aṭṭhakarīsamatte padese jaṇṇukamattena odhinā pañcavaṇṇānaṃ dibbapupphānaṃ ghanavassaṃ vassissatī”ti. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā nagaravāsino “evaṃ mahāpuñño kira citto nāma gahapati āgantvā ajja satthāraṃ vandissati, evarūpaṃ kira pāṭihāriyaṃ bhavissati, mayampi taṃ mahāpuññaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhissāmā”ti paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya maggassa ubhosu passesu aṭṭhaṃsu. Vihārasamīpe āgatakāle pañca bhikkhusatāni paṭhamaṃ āgamiṃsu. Citto gahapati, “ammā, tumhe pacchato āgacchathā”ti mahāupāsikāyo ṭhapetvā pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Buddhānaṃ sammukhaṭṭhāne pana ṭhitā vā nisinnā vā ito vā etto vā na honti, buddhavīthiyā dvīsu passesu niccalāva tiṭṭhanti. Citto gahapati mahantaṃ buddhavīthiṃ okkami. Tīṇi phalāni pattena ariyasāvakena olokitolokitaṭṭhānaṃ kampi. “Eso kira citto gahapatī”ti mahājano olokesi[M 1.0331]. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā chabbaṇṇānaṃ buddharasmīnaṃ anto pavisitvā dvīsu gopphakesu satthu pāde gahetvā vandi. Taṃ khaṇaññeva vuttappakāraṃ pupphavassaṃ vassi, sādhukārasahassāni pavattayiṃsu. So ekamāsaṃ satthu santike vasi, vasamāno ca sakalaṃ buddhappamukhaṃ [V 1.0295] bhikkhusaṅghaṃ [P 2.0081] vihāreyeva nisīdāpetvā mahādānaṃ adāsi, attanā saddhiṃ āgatepi antovihāreyeva katvā paṭijaggi. Ekadivasampi attano sakaṭesu kiñci gahetabbaṃ nāhosi, devamanussehi ābhatapaṇṇākāreneva dānaṃ adāsi, sabbakiccāni akāsi. So satthāraṃ vanditvā āha – “bhante, ahaṃ ‘tumhākaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī’ti āgacchanto māsaṃ antarāmagge ahosiṃ. Idheva me māso vītivatto, mayā ābhataṃ paṇṇākāraṃ kiñci gahetuṃ na labhāmi, ettakaṃ kālaṃ devamanussehi ābhatapaṇṇākāreneva dānaṃ adāsiṃ, sohaṃ sacepi idha saṃvaccharaṃ vasissāmi, neva mama deyyadhammaṃ dātuṃ labhissāmi. Ahaṃ sakaṭāni otāretvā gantuṃ icchāmi, paṭisāmanaṭṭhānaṃ me ārocāpethā”ti.

The Teacher said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, today, when the afternoon shadow lengthens, the householder Citta, accompanied by five hundred carts, will come and pay homage to me.” “But, Venerable Sir, will any marvel occur at the time he pays homage to you?” “It will, Ānanda.” “What, Venerable Sir?” “When he comes and pays homage to me, in a place measuring eight karīsas by the royal measure, a thick rain of divine flowers of five colors will fall to a depth of one's knee.” Hearing this, the townspeople thought, “It seems the householder named Citta, a man of great merit, will come today and pay homage to the Teacher. It seems such a marvel will occur. We too shall get to see that man of great merit.” Taking offerings, they stood on both sides of the road. When he arrived near the monastery, five hundred monks came first. The householder Citta, saying, “Mothers, you come later,” left the great female lay devotees behind and, surrounded by five hundred male lay followers, approached the Teacher. Now, in the presence of Buddhas, people are neither standing nor sitting, neither here nor there; they stand motionless on both sides of the Buddha’s path. The householder Citta entered the great Buddha’s path. Wherever the noble disciple, who had attained the three fruits, looked, that place trembled. “This must be Citta the householder,” the great crowd of people watched. He approached the Teacher, entered into the midst of the six-colored Buddha-rays, took hold of the Teacher’s feet at the two ankles, and paid homage. At that very moment, the rain of flowers of the kind foretold fell, and thousands of cries of ‘Sādhu’ arose. He stayed in the presence of the Teacher for one month. While staying, he had the entire community of monks headed by the Buddha seated in the monastery itself and gave a great offering. He also had those who came with him stay within the monastery and attended to them. Not even for a single day was there any need to take anything from his own carts; he gave alms and performed all duties only with the offerings brought by devas and humans. He paid homage to the Teacher and said: “Venerable Sir, while coming with the intention, ‘I will give an offering to you,’ I was on the road for a month. Here, too, a month has passed. I do not get to take any of the offerings I brought. For this long, I have given alms only with the offerings brought by devas and humans. If I were to stay here for a year, I would not get to give my own goods for donation. I wish to unload the carts and go. Please inform me of a place to store them.”

Satthā ānandattheraṃ āha – “ānanda, upāsakassa ekaṃ padesaṃ tucchaṃ kāretvā dehī”ti. Thero tathā akāsi. Kappiyabhūmi (mahāva. 295) kira cittassa gahapatino anuññātā. Upāsakopi attanā saddhiṃ āgatehi tīhi janasahassehi saddhiṃ tucchasakaṭehi puna maggaṃ paṭipajji. Devamanussā uṭṭhāya, “ayya, tayā tucchasakaṭehi gamanakammaṃ kata”nti sattahi ratanehi sakaṭāni pūrayiṃsu. So attano ābhatapaṇṇākāreneva mahājanaṃ paṭijagganto agamāsi. Ānandatthero satthāraṃ vanditvā āha – “bhante, tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchantopi māsena āgato, idhāpi māsameva vuṭṭho, ettakaṃ kālaṃ devamanussehi abhihaṭapaṇṇākāreneva mahāvadānaṃ adāsi, idāni pañca sakaṭasatāni tucchāni katvā māseneva kira gamissati, devamanussā panassa uṭṭhāya, ‘ayya[P 2.0082], tayā tucchasakaṭehi gamanakammaṃ kata’nti pañca sakaṭasatāni sattaratanehi pūrayiṃsu. So puna attano ābhatapaṇṇākāreneva kira mahājanaṃ paṭijagganto gamissatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, etassa tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchantassevāyaṃ sakkāro uppajjati, udāhu aññattha gacchantassāpi uppajjatī”ti? “Ānanda, mama santikaṃ āgacchantassāpi aññattha gacchantassāpi etassa [M 1.0332] uppajjateva. Ayañhi upāsako saddho pasanno sampannasīlo, evarūpo puggalo yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tatthevassa lābhasakkāro nibbattatī”ti vatvā satthā imaṃ pakiṇṇakavagge gāthamāha –

The Teacher said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, having made a place empty for the lay follower, give it to him.” The Elder did so. It is said that a suitable storeroom was permitted for the householder Citta. The lay follower, together with the three thousand people who had come with him, again set out on the road with empty carts. Devas and humans arose and, saying, “Noble sir, you have undertaken a journey with empty carts,” filled the carts with the seven kinds of gems. He departed, attending to the great crowd of people only with the offerings that had been brought. The Venerable Ānanda paid homage to the Teacher and said: “Venerable Sir, even when coming to your presence, he arrived in a month. Here, too, he has stayed for a month. For this long, he gave a great offering only with the provisions brought forth by devas and humans. Now, having made the five hundred carts empty, it is said he will depart in a month. But devas and humans arose and, saying, ‘Noble sir, you have undertaken a journey with empty carts,’ filled the five hundred carts with the seven gems. It is said he will again depart, attending to the great crowd of people only with the offerings that had been brought. But, Venerable Sir, does this honor arise for him only when he is coming to your presence, or does it arise also when he is going elsewhere?” “Ānanda, it arises for him both when he is coming to my presence and when he is going elsewhere. For this lay follower has faith, is devout, and is endowed with virtue. Whatever place such a person resorts to, right there gain and honor accrue to him.” Having said this, the Teacher spoke this verse in the Pakiṇṇaka Vagga:

“Saddho sīlena sampanno, yaso bhogasamappito;

Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tattheva pūjito”ti. (dha. pa. 303);

“One who has faith, is endowed with virtue, possessed of renown and wealth; whatever place he resorts to, right there he is honored.”

Attho panassā tattheva āvibhavissati.

But the meaning of this verse will become clear in that very section (the Pakiṇṇaka Vagga).

Evaṃ [V 1.0296] vutte ānandatthero cittassa pubbakammaṃ pucchi. Athassa satthā ācikkhanto āha –

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked about Citta's past kamma. Then the Teacher, wishing to explain it to him, said:

Ānanda, ayaṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle katābhinīhāro kappasatasahassaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā kassapabuddhakāle migaluddakakule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya ekadivasaṃ deve vassante migānaṃ māraṇattāya sattiṃ ādāya araññaṃ gantvā mige olokento ekasmiṃ akaṭapabbhāre sasīsaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ nisinnaṃ disvā “eko, ayyo, samaṇadhammaṃ karonto nisinno bhavissati, bhattamassa āharissāmī”ti vegena gehaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ uddhane hiyyo, ābhatamaṃsaṃ, ekasmiṃ bhattaṃ pacāpetvā aññe piṇḍapātacārike bhikkhū disvā tesampi patte ādāya paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ sampādetvā, “ayye, parivisathā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpetvā taṃ bhattaṃ puṭake pakkhipitvā ādāya [P 2.0083] gacchanto antarāmagge nānāpupphāni ocinitvā pattapuṭe katvā therassa nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, saṅgahaṃ karothā”ti vatvā pattaṃ ādāya pūretvā therassa hatthe ṭhapetvā tehi pupphehi pūjaṃ katvā “yathā me ayaṃ rasapiṇḍapāto pupphapūjāya saddhiṃ cittaṃ tosesi, evaṃ nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne paṇṇākārasahassāni ādāya āgantvā mayhaṃ cittaṃ tosentu, pañcavaṇṇakusumavassañca vassatū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatti, nibbattaṭṭhāne jaṇṇukamattena odhinā dibbapupphavassaṃ vassi. Idānipissa jātadivase ceva idha ca āgatassa pupphavassavassanañca paṇṇākārābhihāro ca sattahi ratanehi sakaṭapūraṇañca tasseva kammassa nissandoti.

“Ānanda, this householder made an aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara. After wandering among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he was reborn in a family of deer hunters. Having reached maturity, one day when it was raining, he took a spear and went into the forest to kill deer. While searching for deer, he saw a monk sitting in a natural mountain cave, covered including his head. Thinking, ‘A noble one must be sitting, practicing the ascetic’s duties. I will bring him almsfood,’ he hurried home. He had rice cooked on one hearth and meat obtained the day before on another. Seeing other monks on their alms round, he took their bowls as well, seated them on prepared seats, and prepared the almsfood. Then, ordering another person, ‘Venerable sirs, please serve!’, he had that meal packed in a wrapper and set out. Along the way, he gathered various flowers and placed them on the food packet. Reaching the elder’s seated place, he said, ‘Venerable sir, please grant me your support.’ Taking the bowl, he filled it and placed it in the elder’s hands, then made an offering with those flowers. He made this aspiration: ‘Just as this tasty almsfood, along with the flower offering, has pleased my mind, so too, in each and every existence, may thousands of gifts come and delight my mind, and may a rain of five-colored flowers fall.’ Having performed meritorious deeds for his entire life, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. In his place of rebirth, a rain of divine flowers fell knee-deep. Even now, on the day of his birth and when he came here, the showering of flowers, the bringing of presents, and the filling of the carts with the seven kinds of jewels—all are the result of that very deed.”

Cittagahapativatthu cuddasamaṃ.

The fourteenth story, the Story of the Householder Citta.

15. Vanavāsītissasāmaṇeravatthu

15. The Story of the Novice Tissa, the Forest-Dweller

Aññā [M 1.0333][P 2.0084] hi lābhūpanisāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto vanavāsikatissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Desanā rājagahe samuṭṭhitā.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with “Different indeed is the means to gain” concerning the Elder Tissa, the forest-dweller. The discourse arose in Rājagaha.

Sāriputtattherasa kira pitu vaṅgantabrāhmaṇassa sahāyako mahāsenabrāhmaṇo nāma rājagahe vasati. Sāriputtatthero ekadivasaṃ piṇḍāya caranto tasmiṃ anukampāya tassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. So pana parikkhīṇavibhavo daliddo. So “mama putto mayhaṃ gehadvāraṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ āgato bhavissati, ahañcamhi duggato, mayhaṃ duggatabhāvaṃ na jānāti maññe, natthi me koci deyyadhammo”ti therassa sammukhā bhavituṃ asakkonto nilīyi. Thero aparampi divasaṃ [V 1.0297] agamāsi, brāhmaṇo tatheva nilīyi. “Kiñcideva labhitvā dassāmī”ti cintentopi nālabhi. Athekadivasaṃ ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇavācake thūlasāṭakena saddhiṃ pāyasapātiṃ labhitvā ādāya gehaṃ gantvāva theraṃ anussari, “imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ mayā therassa dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Theropi taṃ khaṇaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā “brāhmaṇo deyyadhammaṃ labhitvā mama āgamanaṃ paccāsīsati, mayā tattha gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ ādāya tassa gehadvāre ṭhitameva attānaṃ dassesi.

It is said that a friend of the brahmin Vaṅganta, the father of the Elder Sāriputta, a brahmin named Mahāsena, lived in Rājagaha. One day, while wandering for alms, the Elder Sāriputta, out of compassion for him, went to his house door. But he, his wealth having been exhausted, was poor. Thinking, ‘My son must have come to my door to go for alms, but I am destitute. I think he does not know of my destitute state. I have no gift whatsoever,’ he hid, unable to be in the presence of the elder. The elder went on another day as well, and the brahmin hid just as before. Even though he thought, ‘Having obtained anything at all, I will give it,’ he did not obtain anything. Then one day, at a recitation of the brahmins' lore, he received a bowl of milk-rice along with a coarse cloth. Taking it and going home, he then remembered the elder, thinking: ‘It is proper for me to give this almsfood to the elder.’ At that very moment, the elder entered a meditative absorption and, emerging from that attainment, saw the brahmin. Thinking, ‘The brahmin has obtained something to give and is hoping for my arrival; it is proper for me to go there,’ he draped his outer robe, took his bowl, and showed himself standing at the brahmin's house door.

Brāhmaṇo theraṃ disvāva cittaṃ pasīdi. Atha naṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā antogehe nisīdāpetvā pāyasapātiṃ gahetvā therassa patte ākiri[P 2.0085]. Thero upaḍḍhaṃ sampaṭicchitvā hatthena pattaṃ pidahi. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo āha – “bhante, ekapaṭivīsamattova ayaṃ pāyaso, paralokasaṅgahaṃ me karotha, mā idhalokasaṅgahaṃ, niravasesameva dātukāmomhī”ti sabbaṃ ākiri. Thero tattheva paribhuñji. Athassa bhattakiccapariyosāne tampi sāṭakaṃ datvā vanditvā evamāha – “bhante, ahampi tumhehi diṭṭhadhammameva pāpuṇeyya”nti. Thero “evaṃ hotu brāhmaṇā”ti tassa anumodanaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamanto anupubbena cārikaṃ caranto jetavanaṃ agamāsi. “Duggatakāle dinnadānaṃ pana ativiya tosetī”ti brāhmaṇopi taṃ dānaṃ datvā pasannacitto somanassajāto there adhimattaṃ sinehamakāsi. So there sineheneva kālaṃ katvā sāvatthiyaṃ therassūpaṭṭhākakule paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi[M 1.0334]. Taṃkhaṇeyeva panassa mātā “kucchiyaṃ me gabbho patiṭṭhito”ti ñatvā sāmikassa ārocesi. So tassā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi.

Upon seeing the elder, the brahmin's mind became serene. Then, approaching him, he paid homage, welcomed him respectfully, and seated him inside the house. Taking the bowl of milk-rice, he poured it into the elder's bowl. The elder accepted half and covered the bowl with his hand. Then the brahmin said to him, ‘Venerable sir, this milk-rice is only a single portion. Please grant me support for the next world; do not grant me support for this world. I wish to give it all without remainder,’ and so he poured in all of it. The elder consumed it right there. When his meal was finished, the brahmin gave him that cloth as well, paid homage, and said, ‘Venerable sir, may I too attain the very Dhamma that has been seen by you.’ The elder, saying, ‘So be it, brahmin,’ gave his blessing, rose from his seat, and departing, he gradually wandered until he arrived at Jetavana. A gift given in a time of poverty, indeed, is exceedingly pleasing. The brahmin, having given that gift with a serene mind and being filled with joy, developed an intense affection for the elder. Through that very affection for the elder, he passed away and was reborn in Sāvatthī in the family of the elder's attendant. At that very moment, his mother knew, ‘A conception has been established in my womb,’ and informed her husband. He provided her with care during her pregnancy.

Tassā accuṇhaatisītaatiambilādiparibhogaṃ vajjetvā sukhena gabbhaṃ parihariyamānāya evarūpo dohaḷo uppajji “aho vatāhaṃ sāriputtattherappamukhāni pañca bhikkhusatāni nimantetvā gehe nisīdāpetvā asambhinnakhīrapāyasaṃ datvā sayampi kāsāyavatthāni paridahitvā suvaṇṇasarakaṃ ādāya āsanapariyante nisīditvā ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ucchiṭṭhapāyasaṃ paribhuñjeyya”nti. Tassā kira so kāsāyavatthaparidahane dohaḷo kucchiyaṃ puttassa buddhasāsane pabbajjāya pubbanimittaṃ ahosi. Athassā ñātakā [P 2.0086] “dhammiko no dhītāya dohaḷo”ti sāriputtattheraṃ saṅghattheraṃ katvā pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ asambhinnakhīrapāyasaṃ adaṃsu. Sāpi ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā suvaṇṇasarakaṃ gahetvā āsanapariyante nisinnā ucchiṭṭhapāyasaṃ paribhuñji, dohaḷo paṭippassambhi. Tassā yāva gabbhavuṭṭhānā antarantarā katamaṅgalesupi, dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijātāya katamaṅgalesupi sāriputtattherappamukhānaṃ [V 1.0298] pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ appodakamadhupāyasameva adaṃsu. Pubbe kiresa dārakena brāhmaṇakāle dinnapāyasassa nissando.

For her, avoiding consumables that were too hot, too cold, too sour, and so on, while she was carrying the pregnancy with ease, a craving of this sort arose: 'Oh, that I might invite the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta, have them seated in the house, give them milk-rice undiluted with water, and having myself put on ochre-colored robes, taking a golden bowl, and sitting at the edge of the seats, I might partake of the leftover milk-rice of so many bhikkhus!' It is said that this craving of hers to wear ochre-colored robes was a prior sign of her son's ordination in the Buddha's Dispensation while he was in the womb. Then her relatives, thinking, 'Our daughter's craving is righteous,' made the Elder Sāriputta the Elder of the Sangha and gave milk-rice undiluted with water to the five hundred bhikkhus. She too, having put on one ochre-colored robe as a lower garment and draped another, taking a golden bowl, and sitting at the edge of the seats, partook of the leftover milk-rice; the craving was pacified. For her, up until the delivery from the womb, during the auspicious ceremonies performed in between, and also during the auspicious ceremonies performed after giving birth to a son at the end of ten months, they gave only waterless honey-rice to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta. It is said this was the result of the milk-rice given by the boy when he was a brahmin.

Jātamaṅgaladivase pana taṃ dārakaṃ pātova nhāpetvā maṇḍetvā sirisayane satasahassagghanikassa kambalassa upari nipajjāpesuṃ. So tattha nipannakova theraṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ me pubbācariyo, mayā theraṃ nissāya ayaṃ sampatti laddhā, mayā imassa ekaṃ pariccāgaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sikkhāpadagahaṇatthāya ānīyamāno taṃ kambalaṃ cūḷaṅguliyā veṭhetvā aggahesi.
