Athassa “aṅguliyaṃ kambalo laggo”ti te taṃ harituṃ ārabhiṃsu. So parodi. Ñātakā “apetha, mā dārakaṃ rodāpethā”ti kambaleneva saddhiṃ ānayiṃsu. So theraṃ vandanakāle kambalato aṅguliṃ apakaḍḍhitvā kambalaṃ therassa pādamūle pātesi. Ñātakā “daharakumārena ajānitvā kata”nti avatvā “puttena no dinnaṃ, pariccattameva hotu, bhante”ti vatvā, “bhante, satasahassagghanikena kambalena pūjākārakassa tumhākaṃ dāsassa sikkhāpadāni dethā”ti [P 2.0087] āhaṃsu. “Ko nāmo ayaṃ dārako”ti? “Bhante, ayyena samānanāmako[M 1.0335], tisso nāmesa bhavissatī”ti. Thero kira gihikāle upatissamāṇavo nāma ahosi. Mātāpissa cintesi – “na mayā puttassa ajjhāsayo bhinditabbo”ti. Evaṃ dārakassa nāmakaraṇamaṅgalaṃ katvā puna tassa āhāraparibhogamaṅgalepi puna tassa kaṇṇavijjhanamaṅgalepi dussagahaṇamaṅgalepi cūḷākappanamaṅgalepi sāriputtattherappamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ appodakamadhupāyasameva adaṃsu.

On the day of the birth ceremony, they bathed the boy early in the morning, adorned him, and laid him on a splendid bed, upon a blanket worth one hundred thousand. Lying there, he looked at the Elder and thought, 'This is my former teacher. It is by relying on the Elder that I have obtained this prosperity. It is fitting for me to make a single offering to him.' As he was being brought for the purpose of taking the precepts, he wrapped the blanket with his little finger and grasped it. Then, as they began to remove it, thinking, 'The blanket is stuck on his finger,' he cried. The relatives said, 'Stand aside, do not make the boy cry,' and brought him along with the blanket. At the time of paying homage to the Elder, he pulled his finger from the blanket and caused the blanket to fall at the Elder's feet. The relatives, not saying, 'It was done by the young boy unknowingly,' said, 'It has been given by our son; let it be a complete relinquishment, venerable sir.' And they said, 'Venerable sir, please give the precepts to your servant who makes this offering with a blanket worth one hundred thousand.' The Elder asked, 'What is this boy's name?' They replied, 'Venerable sir, he has the same name as the noble one.' The Elder then said, 'He shall be named Tissa.' It is said that the Elder, in his lay life, was the young man named Upatissa. The boy's mother also thought, 'My son's inclination should not be thwarted by me.' Thus, having performed the boy's naming ceremony, and again at his first-meal ceremony, and again at his ear-piercing ceremony, cloth-wearing ceremony, and top-knot ceremony, they gave only waterless honey-rice to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta.

Dārako vuddhimanvāya sattavassikakāle mātaraṃ āha – “amma, therassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, tāta, pubbevāhaṃ ‘na mayā puttassa ajjhāsayo bhinditabbo’ti manaṃ akāsiṃ, pabbaja, puttā”ti theraṃ nimantāpetvā tassa āgatassa bhikkhañca datvā, “bhante, tumhākaṃ dāso ‘pabbajissāmī’ti vadati, imaṃ ādāya sāyaṃ vihāraṃ āgamissāmā”ti theraṃ uyyojetvā sāyanhasamaye mahantena sakkārasammānena puttaṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā therassa niyyādesi. Thero tena saddhiṃ kathesi – “tissa, pabbajjā nāma dukkarā, uṇhena atthe sati sītaṃ labhati, sītena atthe sati uṇhaṃ labhati, pabbajitā kicchena jīvanti, tvañca sukhedhito”ti. “Bhante, ahaṃ tumhehi vuttaniyāmeneva sabbaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. Thero “sādhū”ti vatvā tassa paṭikūlamanasikāravasena tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ [P 2.0088] ācikkhitvā taṃ pabbājesi. Sakalampi hi dvattiṃsākāraṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Sabbaṃ kathetuṃ asakkontena pana tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetabbameva. Idañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0299] sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitameva. Kesādīsu ekekakoṭṭhāsesu arahattaṃ pattānaṃ bhikkhūnampi bhikkhunīnampi upāsakānampi upāsikānampi paricchedo natthi. Abyattā bhikkhū pana pabbajentā arahattassūpanissayaṃ nāsenti. Tasmā thero kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbājetvā dasasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi.

The boy, having grown up, at the age of seven said to his mother: 'Mother, I will go forth in the presence of the Elder.' 'Good, dear son. Even before, I made up my mind, "My son's inclination should not be thwarted by me." Go forth, my son.' Having had the Elder invited, and having given him alms-food when he arrived, she said, 'Venerable sir, your servant says, "I will go forth." Taking him, I will come to the monastery in the evening.' Having sent the Elder off, in the evening, with great honor and respect, she took her son to the monastery and entrusted him to the Elder. The Elder spoke with him: 'Tissa, the ordained life is difficult. When there is need for heat, one gets cold; when there is need for cold, one gets heat. The ordained live with hardship, and you are accustomed to comfort.' 'Venerable sir, I will be able to do everything just as instructed by you.' The Elder said, 'Good,' and having taught him the meditation subject of the five parts ending with the skin by way of attention to repulsiveness, he ordained him. For it is indeed fitting to explain all thirty-two parts. But by one who is unable to explain all, the meditation subject of the five parts ending with the skin should certainly be explained. For this meditation subject is indeed never abandoned by any of the Buddhas. There is no limit to the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen who have attained Arahantship through any one of the parts beginning with the hair of the head. Incompetent bhikkhus, however, when ordaining others, destroy the supporting condition for Arahantship. Therefore, the Elder, having taught the meditation subject, ordained him and established him in the ten precepts.

Mātāpitaro puttassa pabbajitasakkāraṃ karontā sattāhaṃ vihāreyeva buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa appodakamadhupāyasameva adaṃsu. Bhikkhūpi “nibaddhaṃ appodakamadhupāyasaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na sakkomā”ti ujjhāyiṃsu. Tassapi mātāpitaro sattame divase sāyaṃ gehaṃ agamaṃsu. Sāmaṇero aṭṭhame divase bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sāvatthivāsino “sāmaṇero kira ajja piṇḍāya pavisissati, sakkāramassa [M 1.0336] karissāmā”ti pañcahi sāṭakasatehi cumbaṭakāni katvā pañca piṇḍapātasatāni sajjetvā ādāya paṭipathe ṭhatvā adaṃsu, punadivase vihārassa upavanaṃ āgantvā adaṃsu. Evaṃ sāmaṇero dvīheva divasehi sāṭakasahassehi saddhiṃ piṇḍapātasahassaṃ labhitvā bhikkhusaṅghassa dāpesi. Brāhmaṇakāle dinnathūlasāṭakassa kiresa nissando. Athassa bhikkhū “piṇḍapātadāyakatisso”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu.

The mother and father, honoring their son's going forth, for seven days offered only waterless honey-rice to the community of monks headed by the Buddha in the monastery itself. The monks also complained, saying, 'We are unable to constantly consume waterless honey-rice.' On the seventh day, his parents returned home in the evening. On the eighth day, the novice went for alms-food together with the monks. The residents of Sāvatthī thought, 'It seems the novice will go for alms-food today; let us make an offering to him.' Having made rolls from five hundred cloths and prepared five hundred portions of alms-food, they took them, stood along the path, and gave. On the next day, they came to the monastery's vicinity and gave. Thus, in just two days, the novice received a thousand portions of alms-food along with a thousand cloths and had them given to the community of monks. This, it is said, was the result of the coarse cloth given when he was a brahmin. Then the monks gave him the name 'Tissa the Giver of Alms-food'.

Punekadivasaṃ sāmaṇero sītakāle vihāracārikaṃ caranto bhikkhū tattha tattha aggisālādīsu [P 2.0089] visibbente disvā āha – “kiṃ, bhante, visibbentā nisinnātthā”ti? “Sītaṃ no pīḷeti sāmaṇero”ti. “Bhante, sītakāle nāma kambalaṃ pārupituṃ vaṭṭati. So hi sītaṃ paṭibāhituṃ samattho”ti. Sāmaṇera “tvaṃ mahāpuñño kambalaṃ labheyyāsi, amhākaṃ kuto kambalo”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, kambalatthikā mayā saddhiṃ āgacchantū”ti sakalavihāre ārocāpesi. Atha bhikkhū “sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ gantvā kambalaṃ āharissāmā”ti sattavassikasāmaṇeraṃ nissāya sahassamattā bhikkhū nikkhamiṃsu. So “ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kuto kambalaṃ labhissāmī”ti cittampi anuppādetvā te ādāya nagarābhimukho pāyāsi. Sudinnassa hi dānassa evarūpo ānubhāvo hoti. So bahinagareyeva gharapaṭipāṭiyā caranto pañca kambalasatāni labhitvā antonagaraṃ pāvisi. Manussā ito cito ca kambale āharanti.

Again, on a certain day during the cold season, the novice, while on his monastic rounds, saw monks here and there in the fire-halls and other such places warming themselves and asked, 'Venerable sirs, why are you sitting warming yourselves?' 'The cold afflicts us, novice.' 'Venerable sirs, in the cold season it is proper to wear a blanket, for it is able to ward off the cold.' 'Novice, you are of great merit; you might obtain a blanket. But from where would a blanket come for us?' 'In that case, venerable sirs, let those who need a blanket come with me,' he had announced throughout the entire monastery. Then the monks, thinking, 'Going with the novice, we shall bring back blankets,' set out in reliance upon the seven-year-old novice, about a thousand monks in all. He, without even letting the thought arise, 'From where shall I get blankets for so many monks?', took them with him and set out towards the city. For such is the power of a well-given gift. Going from house to house just outside the city, he received five hundred blankets and then entered the city proper. People brought blankets from here and there.

Eko pana puriso āpaṇadvārena āgacchanto pañca kambalasatāni pasāretvā nisinnaṃ ekaṃ āpaṇikaṃ disvā āha – “ambho, eko sāmaṇero kambale saṃharanto āgacchati, tava kambale paṭicchādehī”ti? “Kiṃ pana so dinnake gaṇhāti, udāhu adinnake”ti? “Dinnake gaṇhātī”ti[V 1.0300]. “Evaṃ sante sace icchāmi, dassāmi, no ce, na dassāmi, gaccha tva”nti uyyojesi. Maccharino hi andhabālā evarūpesu dānaṃ dadamānesu maccharāyitvā asadisadānaṃ disvā maccharāyanto kāḷo (dha. pa. 177) viya niraye nibbattanti. Āpaṇiko cintesi – “ayaṃ puriso attano dhammatāya āgacchamāno ‘tava kambale paṭicchādehī’ti maṃ āha. ‘Sacepi so dinnakaṃ [P 2.0090] gaṇhā’ti, ahaṃ pana ‘mama santakaṃ sace icchāmi, dassāmi, no ce, na [M 1.0337] dassāmī’ti avacaṃ, diṭṭhakaṃ pana adentassa lajjā uppajjati, attano santakaṃ paṭicchādentassa doso natthi, imesu pañcakambalasatesu dve kambalāni satasahassagghanikāni, imāneva paṭicchādetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Dvepi kambale dasāya dasaṃ sambandhitvā tesaṃ antare pakkhipitvā paṭicchādesi. Sāmaṇeropi bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ taṃ padesaṃ pāpuṇi. Āpaṇikassa sāmaṇeraṃ disvāva puttasineho uppajji, sakalasarīraṃ sinehena paripuṇṇaṃ ahosi. So cintesi – “tiṭṭhatu kambalāni, imaṃ disvā hadayamaṃsampi dātuṃ yutta”nti. Te dvepi kambale nīharitvā sāmaṇerassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā vanditvā, “bhante, tayā diṭṭhadhammassa bhāgī assa”nti avaca. Sopissa “evaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ akāsi.

Now a certain man, coming through the market gate, saw a shopkeeper seated with five hundred blankets spread out, and said, 'Friend, a novice is coming collecting blankets—cover up your blankets!' The shopkeeper asked, 'Does he take what is given, or what is not given?' 'He takes what is given.' 'That being so, if I wish, I shall give; if not, I shall not give. You may go,' he said, dismissing him. For the miserly and blind fools, being envious when such gifts are being given, are reborn in hell like Kāḷa who was envious upon seeing the incomparable gift. The shopkeeper thought: 'This man, coming here on his own accord, told me, "Cover up your blankets." And I replied, "If he takes only what is given, then if I wish, I shall give what is mine; if not, I shall not give." But for one who does not give to a person seen right before them, shame arises. There is no fault, however, for one who covers up his own property. Among these five hundred blankets, two are worth a hundred thousand each. It is proper to cover up just these.' Tying the two blankets together fringe to fringe, he placed them inside the others and covered them. The novice, too, together with a thousand monks, reached that place. Upon the very sight of the novice, affection as for a son arose in the shopkeeper; his whole body was filled with affection. He thought: 'Let the blankets be! Seeing him, it would be fitting even to give the flesh of my heart.' Taking out both those blankets, placing them at the novice's feet, and paying homage, he said, 'Venerable sir, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma you have realized.' The novice, in turn, gave his blessing, saying, 'So be it.'

Sāmaṇero antonagarepi pañca kambalasatāni labhi. Evaṃ ekadivasaṃyeva kambalasahassaṃ labhitvā bhikkhusahassassa adāsi. Athassa kambaladāyakatissattheroti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Evaṃ nāmakaraṇadivase dinnakambalo sattavassikakāle kambalasahassabhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Buddhasāsanañhi ṭhapetvā natthaññaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ, yattha appaṃ dinnaṃ bahuṃ hoti, bahuṃ dinnaṃ bahutaraṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

The novice received five hundred blankets in the city proper as well. Thus, in a single day, having received a thousand blankets, he gave them to the thousand monks. Then they gave him the name 'Kambaladāyaka-Tissatthera,' meaning 'Tissa the Elder, the Giver of Blankets.' Thus, the blanket given on his naming day resulted in a thousand blankets when he was seven years old. For, setting aside the Buddha's Dispensation, there is no other place where a little that is given becomes much, and much that is given becomes very much more. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Tathārūpoyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhusaṅgho, yathārūpe bhikkhusaṅghe appaṃ dinnaṃ bahuṃ hoti, bahuṃ dinnaṃ bahutara”nti [P 2.0091] (ma. ni. 3.146) –

“Monks, of such a nature is this community of monks, a community wherein a little that is given becomes much, and much that is given becomes exceedingly more.”

Evaṃ sāmaṇero ekakambalassa nissandena sattavassikova kambalasahassaṃ labhi. Tassa jetavane viharantassa abhikkhaṇaṃ ñātidāyakā santikaṃ āgantvā kathāsallāpaṃ karonti. So cintesi – “mayā idha vasantena ñātidāyakesu āgantvā kathentesu akathetumpi na sakkā, etehi saddhiṃ kathāpapañcena attano patiṭṭhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā araññaṃ paviseyya”nti. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā upajjhāyaṃ vanditvā pattacīvaramādāya vihārā nikkhamitvā “sace āsannaṭṭhāne vasissāmi, ñātakā maṃ pakkosissantī”ti vīsati yojanasataṃ maggaṃ agamāsi. Athekena gāmadvārena gacchanto ekaṃ mahallakapurisaṃ disvā pucchi – “kiṃ nu kho, mahāupāsaka[V 1.0301], imasmiṃ padese vasantānaṃ [M 1.0338] āraññakavihāro atthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Tena hi me maggaṃ ācikkhāhī”ti. Mahallakaupāsakassa pana taṃ disvāva puttasineho udapādi. Athassa tattheva ṭhito anācikkhitvā “ehi, bhante, ācikkhissāmi [P 2.0092] te”ti gahetvā agamāsi. Sāmaṇero tena saddhiṃ gacchanto antarāmagge nānāpupphaphalapaṭimaṇḍite rukkhapabbatapadese disvā “ayaṃ, upāsaka, kiṃ padeso nāma, ayaṃ upāsaka kiṃ padeso nāmā”ti pucchi. Sopissa tesaṃ nāmāni ācikkhanto āraññakavihāraṃ patvā “idaṃ, bhante, phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ, idheva vasāhī”ti vatvā, “bhante, ko nāmo tva”nti nāmaṃ pucchitvā “ahaṃ vanavāsītisso nāma upāsakā”ti vutte, “sve amhākaṃ gāme bhikkhāya carituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā nivattitvā antogāmameva gato. “Vanavāsītisso nāma vihāraṃ āgato, tassa yāgubhattādīni paṭiyādethā”ti manussānaṃ ārocesi.

Thus the novice, as the fruit of a single blanket, obtained a thousand blankets when he was seven years of age. While he was dwelling in Jetavana, his relatives and lay supporters frequently came to him and engaged in conversation. He thought: 'While I am dwelling here, when my relatives and lay supporters come and speak, it is not possible to refrain from speaking; and through this proliferation of talk with them, it is not possible to establish a spiritual refuge for myself. What if I were to learn a meditation subject in the Teacher's presence and enter the forest?' He approached the Teacher, paid homage, and had a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship taught to him. After paying homage to his preceptor and taking his bowl and robes, he departed from the monastery. Thinking, 'If I dwell in a nearby place, my relatives will summon me,' he traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas. Then, while passing through a certain village gate, he saw an old man and asked, 'Good lay follower, is there in this region a forest monastery suitable for residence?' 'There is, venerable sir.' 'In that case, show me the way.' Upon seeing the novice, affection as for a son arose in the old lay follower. Then, instead of showing him the way while standing there, he took him along, saying, 'Come, venerable sir, I will show you.' As the novice was going with him, he saw along the way regions of trees and mountains adorned with various flowers and fruits and asked, 'Lay follower, what is this region called? Lay follower, what is this region called?' The man told him their names, and having reached the forest monastery, said, 'Venerable sir, this is a pleasant place; please dwell right here.' Then, having asked his name, 'Venerable sir, what is your name?' When the novice replied, 'Lay follower, I am named Vanavāsī Tissa,' the man said, 'Tomorrow it would be proper to go for alms in our village,' and then turned back and went right into the village. He announced to the people, 'A venerable one named Vanavāsī Tissa has come to the monastery; prepare gruel, rice, and so forth for him.'

Sāmaṇero paṭhamameva tisso nāma hutvā tato piṇḍapātadāyakatisso kambaladāyakatisso vanavāsītissoti tīṇi nāmāni labhitvā sattavassabbhantare cattāri nāmāni labhi. So punadivase pātova taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Manussā bhikkhaṃ datvā vandiṃsu. Sāmaṇero “sukhitā hotha, dukkhā muccathā”ti āha. Ekamanussopi tassa bhikkhaṃ datvā puna gehaṃ gantuṃ nāsakkhi, sabbeva olokentā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sopi attano yāpanamattameva gaṇhi. Sakalagāmavāsino tassa pādamūle urena nipajjitvā, “bhante, tumhesu imaṃ temāsaṃ idha vasantesu mayaṃ tīṇi saraṇāni gahetvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāya māsassa aṭṭha uposathakammāni [P 2.0093] upavasissāma, idha vasanatthāya no paṭiññaṃ dethā”ti. So upakāraṃ sallakkhetvā tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ datvā nibaddhaṃ tattheva piṇḍapātacāraṃ cari. Vanditavanditakkhaṇe ca “sukhitā hotha, dukkhā muccathā”ti padadvayameva kathetvā pakkāmi. So tatthevapaṭhamamāsañca dutiyamāsañca vītināmetvā tatiyamāse gacchante saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The novice, having first been named Tissa, thereafter received three names—Piṇḍapātadāyaka Tissa, Kambaladāyaka Tissa, and Vanavāsī Tissa—thus obtaining four names within seven years. On the next day, early in the morning, he entered that village for alms. The people, having given alms, paid homage. The novice said, 'May you be happy; may you be freed from suffering.' Not even one person, having given him alms, was able to go home again; all of them just stood watching. He too accepted only what was sufficient for his sustenance. All the villagers, having prostrated with their chests at his feet, said, 'Venerable sir, while you are dwelling here for these three months of the rains retreat, we, having taken the three refuges and being established in the five precepts, will observe the eight Uposatha days of the month. Give us a promise to dwell here.' He, considering their support, gave them a promise and regularly went on the alms-round in that very place. And at the very moment of being paid homage, having spoken only the two phrases, 'May you be happy; may you be freed from suffering,' he departed. He, having passed the first month and the second month right there, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges as the third month was passing.

Athassa pavāretvā vuṭṭhavassakāle upajjhāyo satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, tissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ gacchāmī”ti. “Gaccha, sāriputtā”ti. So attano parivāre pañcasate bhikkhū [M 1.0339] ādāya pakkanto, “āvuso moggallāna, ahaṃ tissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ gacchāmī”ti āha. Mahāmoggallānatthero “ahampi, āvuso, gacchāmī”ti pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nikkhami. Etenupāyena mahākassapatthero anuruddhatthero upālitthero puṇṇattheroti sabbe mahāsāvakā pañcahi pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nikkhamiṃsu. Sabbepi mahāsāvakānaṃ parivārā cattālīsa bhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Te vīsatiyojanasataṃ maggaṃ gantvā [V 1.0302] gocaragāmaṃ sampattā. Sāmaṇerassa nibaddhūpaṭṭhāko upāsako dvāreyeva [P 2.0094] disvā paccuggantvā vandi.

Then, when the novice had concluded the rains retreat with the Pavāraṇā ceremony, his preceptor approached the Teacher, paid homage, and said: 'Venerable sir, I will go to the presence of the novice Tissa.' 'Go, Sāriputta,' he replied. He departed, taking his own retinue of five hundred monks, and said, 'Friend Moggallāna, I am going to the presence of the novice Tissa.' The Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, 'I too, friend, will go,' and departed with five hundred monks. In this way, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Anuruddha, the Elder Upāli, and the Elder Puṇṇa—all the great disciples departed with five hundred monks each. Altogether, the retinues of all the great disciples were four thousand monks. They traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas and arrived at the alms-resort village. The lay follower who was the constant attendant of the novice saw them right at the gate, went out to meet them, and paid homage.

Atha naṃ sāriputtatthero pucchi – “atthi nu kho, upāsaka, imasmiṃ padese āraññakavihāro”ti? “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Sabhikkhuko, abhikkhuko”ti? “Sabhikkhuko, bhante”ti. “Ko nāmo tattha vasatī”ti? “Vanavāsītisso, bhante”ti. “Tena hi maggaṃ no ācikkhā”ti. “Ke tumhe, bhante”ti? “Mayaṃ sāmaṇerassa santikaṃ āgatā”ti. Upāsako oloketvā dhammasenāpatiṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbepi mahāsāvake sañjānitvā nirantaraṃ pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīro hutvā “tiṭṭhatha tāva, bhante”ti vegena gāmaṃ pavisitvā “ete, ayyā, sāriputtattheraṃ ādiṃ katvā asīti mahāsāvakā attano attano parivārehi saddhiṃ sāmaṇerassa santikaṃ āgatā, mañcapīṭhapaccattharaṇadīpatelādīni gahetvā vegena nikkhamathā”ti ugghosesi. Manussā “tāvadeva mañcādīni gahetvā therānaṃ padānupadikā hutvā therehi saddhiṃyeva vihāraṃ pavisiṃsu. Sāmaṇero bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sañjānitvā katipayānaṃ mahātherānaṃ pattacīvarāni paṭiggahetvā vattamakāsi. Tassa therānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahantassa pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmentasseva andhakāro jātā”ti. Sāriputtatthero upāsake āha – “gacchatha, upāsakā, tumhākaṃ andhakāro jāto”ti. “Bhante, ajja dhammassavanadivaso, na mayaṃ gamissāma, dhammaṃ suṇissāma, ito pubbe dhammassavanampi natthī”ti. “Tena hi, sāmaṇera, dīpaṃ jāletvā dhammassavanassa kālaṃ ghosehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Atha naṃ thero āha – “tissa tava upaṭṭhākā ‘dhammaṃ sotukāmāmhā’ti vadanti[P 2.0095], kathehi tesaṃ dhamma”nti. Upāsakā ekappahāreneva uṭṭhāya, “bhante, amhākaṃ ayyo ‘sukhitā hotha, dukkhā muccathā’ti imāni dve padāni ṭhapetvā aññaṃ dhammakathaṃ na jānāti[M 1.0340], amhākaṃ aññaṃ dhammakathikaṃ dethā”ti vadiṃsu. “Sāmaṇero pana arahattaṃ patvāpi neva tesaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathesī”ti.

Then the Elder Sāriputta asked him, 'Is there, lay follower, a forest monastery in this area?' 'There is, venerable sir,' he replied. 'Is it with a monk or without a monk?' 'It is with a monk, venerable sir.' 'What is the name of the one who dwells there?' 'Vanavāsī Tissa, venerable sir.' 'In that case, show us the path.' 'Who are you, venerable sirs?' 'We have come to the novice.' The lay follower looked and, recognizing the General of the Dhamma and all the great disciples, his body was pervaded with continuous joy. He said, 'Wait a moment, venerable sirs,' and quickly entered the village. He announced, 'Good people, these eighty great disciples, led by the Elder Sāriputta, have come to the novice, each with his own retinue. Taking beds, seats, coverings, lamps, oil, and so on, come out quickly!' The people immediately took the beds and other items, followed in the footsteps of the elders, and entered the monastery together with them. The novice, recognizing the community of monks, received the bowls and robes of some of the great elders and performed his duties. While he was arranging dwelling places for the elders and putting away their bowls and robes, darkness fell. The Elder Sāriputta said to the lay followers, 'Go, lay followers, it has become dark for you.' 'Venerable sir, today is a day for hearing the Dhamma. We will not go; we will listen to the Dhamma. Before this, there has not even been a hearing of the Dhamma.' 'In that case, novice, light a lamp and announce the time for hearing the Dhamma.' He did so. Then the elder said to him, 'Tissa, your supporters say they wish to hear the Dhamma. Preach the Dhamma to them.' The lay followers rose up at once and said, 'Venerable sirs, our master knows no other Dhamma talk besides these two phrases: "May you be happy; may you be freed from suffering." Please give us another Dhamma speaker.' For the novice, even though he had attained Arahantship, had not yet preached a Dhamma talk to them.

Tadā pana naṃ upajjhāyo, “sāmaṇera, kathaṃ pana sukhitā honti, ‘kathaṃ pana dukkhā muccantī’ti imesaṃ no dvinnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ kathehī”ti āha. So “sādhu, bhante”ti cittabījaniṃ gahetvā dhammāsanaṃ āruyha pañcahi nikāyehi atthañca kāraṇañca ākaḍḍhitvā ghanavassaṃ vassanto cātuddīpakamahāmegho viya khandhadhātuāyatanabodhipakkhiyadhamme vibhajanto arahattakūṭena dhammakathaṃ kathetvā, “bhante, evaṃ arahattappattassa sukhaṃ hoti, arahattaṃ pattoyeva dukkhā muccati, sesajanā jātidukkhādīhi ceva nirayadukkhādīhi ca na parimuccantī”ti āha. “Sādhu, sāmaṇera, sukathito te paṭibhāṇo, idāni sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti. So sarabhaññampi [V 1.0303] bhaṇi. Aruṇe uggacchante sāmaṇerassa upaṭṭhākamanussā dve bhāgā ahesuṃ. Ekacce “na vata no ito pubbe evarūpo kakkhaḷo diṭṭhapubbo. Kathañhi nāma evarūpaṃ dhammakathaṃ jānanto ettakaṃ kālaṃ mātāpituṭṭhāne ṭhatvā upaṭṭhahantānaṃ manussānaṃ ekampi dhammapadaṃ na kathesī”ti kujjhiṃsu. Ekacce “lābhā vata no, ye mayaṃ evarūpaṃ bhadantaṃ guṇaṃ vā aguṇaṃ vā ajānantāpi upaṭṭhahimha[P 2.0096], idāni ca panassa santike dhammaṃ sotuṃ labhimhā”ti tussiṃsu.

Then his preceptor said to him, 'Novice, explain to us the meaning of these two phrases: "How, then, are they happy?" and "How, then, are they freed from suffering?"' He replied, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and taking an ornate fan, he ascended the Dhamma seat. Drawing out the meaning and the reason from the five Nikāyas, like a great cloud over the four continents raining down a heavy rain, he analyzed the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the qualities pertaining to enlightenment, and delivered a Dhamma talk with Arahantship as its culmination. He then said, 'Venerable sir, in this way, happiness comes to one who has attained Arahantship. Only one who has attained Arahantship is freed from suffering. The remaining people are not freed from the sufferings of birth and so on, nor from the sufferings of the hells and so on.' 'Well said, novice! Your inspired speech is excellent. Now recite the Sarabhañña.' So he recited the Sarabhañña as well. As dawn was breaking, the people who attended on the novice were divided into two groups. Some became angry, saying, 'Indeed, we have never before seen such a harsh person. How could one who knows such a Dhamma talk, having stayed so long in the position of a mother and father, not speak even a single word of the Dhamma to the people who attended on him?' Others were pleased, saying, 'It is truly our gain! We who attended on such a venerable one, even without knowing his virtue or lack thereof, have now had the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in his presence.'

Sammāsambuddhopi taṃ divasaṃ paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento vanavāsītissassa upaṭṭhāke attano ñāṇajālassa anto paviṭṭhe disvā “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti āvajjento imamatthaṃ upadhāresi “vanavāsītissasāmaṇerassa upaṭṭhākā ekacce tuṭṭhā, ekacce kuddhā, mayhaṃ puttassa pana sāmaṇerassa kuddhā nirayabhāgino bhavissanti, gantabbameva tattha mayā, mayi gate sabbepi te sāmaṇere mettacittaṃ katvā dukkhā muccissantī”ti. Tepi manussā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā gāmaṃ gantvā maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā yāgubhattādīni sampādetvā āsanāni paññāpetvā saṅghassa āgamanamaggaṃ olokentā nisīdiṃsu. Bhikkhūpi sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhācāravelāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisantā sāmaṇeraṃ pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ, tissa, tvaṃ amhehi saddhiṃ gamissasi, udāhu pacchā”ti? “Mama gamanavelāyameva gamissāmi, gacchatha tumhe, bhante”ti. Bhikkhū pattacīvaramādāya pavisiṃsu.

On that day, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, surveying the world at dawn, saw that the attendants of Tissa the forest-dweller had entered into the net of his knowledge. Reflecting, “What will happen now?” he considered the matter thus: “Some of the attendants of the novice Tissa the forest-dweller are pleased, while others are angry. Those who are angry towards my son, the novice, will be destined for hell. I must go there. When I go, all of them will develop loving-kindness towards the novice and be freed from suffering.” Those people, having invited the community of bhikkhus, went to the village, had a pavilion made, arranged rice porridge and other food, set out seats, and sat watching the road for the Sangha’s arrival. The bhikkhus, having attended to their bodily needs, entered the village for alms at the time for the alms round and asked the novice, “Well, Tissa, will you come with us or later?” “I will come at my own time of departure. Go ahead, venerable sirs.” The bhikkhus, taking their bowls and robes, entered.

Satthā [M 1.0341] jetavanasmiṃyeva cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattamādāya ekacittakkhaṇeneva gantvā bhikkhūnaṃ purato ṭhitameva attānaṃ dassesi. “Sammāsambuddho āgato”ti sakalagāmo saṅkhubhitvā ekakolāhalo ahosi. Manussā udaggacittā buddhappamukhaṃ [P 2.0097] bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ datvā khajjakaṃ adaṃsu. Sāmaṇero bhatte aniṭṭhiteyeva antogāmaṃ pāvisi. Gāmavāsino nīharitvā tassa sakkaccaṃ bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. So yāpanamattaṃ gahetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā pattaṃ upanāmesi. Satthā “āhara, tissā”ti hatthaṃ pasāretvā pattaṃ gahetvā “passa, sāriputta, tava sāmaṇerassa patta”nti therassa dassesi. Thero satthu hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā sāmaṇerassa datvā “gaccha, attano pattaṭṭhāne nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ karohī”ti āha.

The Teacher, having donned His robe in Jetavana itself and taken His bowl, in just a single mind-moment went and showed Himself standing right in front of the bhikkhus. “The Perfectly Enlightened One has come!” Thus the entire village was stirred up and became a single uproar. The people, with joyful minds, had the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head seated, and having offered gruel, gave them solid food. The novice entered the village even before the meal was finished. The villagers, having brought forth food, respectfully gave him alms. He, having taken just enough to sustain himself, went to the Teacher's presence and offered the bowl. The Teacher, saying, “Bring it, Tissa,” stretched out His hand, took the bowl, and showed it to the Elder, saying, “See, Sāriputta, the bowl of your novice.” The Elder took the bowl from the Teacher’s hand, gave it to the novice, and said, “Go, and having sat down in your own allotted place, perform the duty of the meal.”

Gāmavāsino buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā anumodanaṃ yāciṃsu. Satthā anumodanaṃ karonto evamāha – “lābhā vata vo upāsakā, ye tumhe attano kulūpakaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ nissāya sāriputtaṃ moggallānaṃ kassapaṃ anuruddhanti asītimahāsāvake [V 1.0304] dassanāya labhatha, ahampi tumhākaṃ kulūpakameva nissāya āgato, buddhadassanampi vo imaṃ nissāyeva laddhaṃ, lābhā vo, suladdhaṃ vo”ti. Manussā cintayiṃsu – “aho amhākaṃ lābhā, buddhānañceva bhikkhusaṅghassa ca ārādhanasamatthaṃ amhākaṃ ayyaṃ dassanāya labhāma, deyyadhammañcassa dātuṃ labhāmā”ti sāmaṇerassa kuddhā manussā tussiṃsu. Tuṭṭhā manussā bhiyyosomattāya pasīdiṃsu. Anumodanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Manussā satthāraṃ anugantvā vanditvā nivattiṃsu. Satthā sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ samadhurena gacchanto[P 2.0098], “sāmaṇera, ayaṃ padeso konāmo, ayaṃ padeso konāmo”ti pubbe tassa upāsakena dassitapadese pucchanto agamāsi. Sāmaṇeropi, “bhante, ayaṃ itthannāmo, ayaṃ itthannāmo”ti ācikkhamānova agamāsi. Satthā tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhi. Tattha ṭhitānaṃ pana mahāsamuddo paññāyati. Satthā sāmaṇeraṃ pucchi – “tissa, pabbatamatthake ṭhito ito cito ca oloketvā kiṃ passasī”ti? “Mahāsamuddaṃ, bhante”ti. “Mahāsamuddaṃ disvā kiṃ cintesī”ti? “Mama dukkhitakāle rodantassa catūhi mahāsamuddehi atirekatarena [M 1.0342] assunā bhavitabbanti idaṃ, bhante, cintesi”nti. “Sādhu sādhu, tissa, evametaṃ. Ekekassa hi sattassa dukkhitakāle paggharitaassūni catūhi mahāsamuddehi atirekatarānevā”ti. Idañca pana vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The villagers, having served the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head, paid homage to the Teacher and requested a blessing. The Teacher, while giving the blessing, spoke thus: “Fortunate indeed are you, lay devotees, you who, relying on your family's preceptor, the novice, get to see Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Anuruddha, and so on, the eighty great disciples. I too have come relying only on your preceptor. Even the sight of the Buddha has been obtained by you relying only on this one. Fortunate are you, well-obtained is it for you.” The people thought: “Oh, what a gain for us! We get to see our noble one, who is capable of pleasing the Buddhas and the community of bhikkhus, and we get to give him requisites.” Thus, the people who had been angry with the novice were pleased. The pleased people gained even greater faith. At the conclusion of the blessing, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so on. The Teacher, rising from His seat, departed. The people, having followed the Teacher and paid homage, turned back. The Teacher, going together with the novice, went along asking, “Novice, what is this region called? What is this region called?” about the regions previously pointed out to him by the lay supporter. The novice also went along, explaining, “Venerable Sir, this is called such-and-such; this is called such-and-such.” The Teacher, having gone to his dwelling place, ascended the mountain peak. Now, for those standing there, the great ocean is visible. The Teacher asked the novice: “Tissa, standing on the mountain peak and looking here and there, what do you see?” “The great ocean, Venerable Sir.” “Having seen the great ocean, what do you think?” “Venerable Sir, I think this: ‘For me, weeping in times of suffering, the tears must have been more abundant than the four great oceans.’” “Good, good, Tissa. It is just so. Indeed, for each and every being, the tears shed in times of suffering are indeed more abundant than the four great oceans.” And having said this, He spoke this verse:

“Catūsu samuddesu jalaṃ parittakaṃ,

Tato bahuṃ assujalaṃ anappakaṃ;

Dukkhena phuṭṭhassa narassa socanā,

Kiṃkāraṇā samma tuvaṃ pamajjasī”ti.

The water in the four oceans is but little; far more than that, immeasurable, is the water of tears from the sorrow of a person touched by suffering. For what reason, my good man, are you heedless?

Atha naṃ puna pucchi – “tissa, kahaṃ vasasī”ti? “Imasmiṃ pabbhāre, bhante”ti. “Tattha pana vasanto kiṃ cintesī”ti? “Mayā marantena imasmiṃ ṭhāne katassa sarīranikkhepassa paricchedo ‘natthī’ti cintesiṃ, bhante”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, tissa, evametaṃ. Imesañhi sattānaṃ pathaviyaṃ [P 2.0099] nipajjitvā amataṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā –

Then He asked him again: “Tissa, where do you dwell?” “In this mountain slope, Venerable Sir.” “And while dwelling there, what do you contemplate?” “Venerable Sir, I contemplated thus: ‘For me, dying in this place, there is no limit to the casting off of the body that has been done.’” “Good, good, Tissa. It is just so. Indeed, for these beings, having lain down on the earth, there is no such thing as a place where one has not died.” Having said this:

“Upasāḷakanāmāni, sahassāni catuddasa;

Asmiṃ padese daḍḍhāni, natthi loke anāmataṃ.

Fourteen thousand beings named Upasāḷaka have been cremated in this very region. In the world, there is no place where one has not died.

“Yamhi [V 1.0305] saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Etaṃ ariyā sevanti, etaṃ loke anāmata”nti. (jā.1.2.31-32) –

That wherein exist truth, Dhamma, non-harming, restraint, and self-control—that the noble ones resort to. That, in the world, is the deathless.

Imaṃ dukanipāte upasāḷakajātakaṃ kathesi. Iti pathaviyaṃ sarīranikkhepaṃ katvā marantesu sattesu amatapubbapadese marantā nāma natthi, ānandattherasadisā pana amatapubbapadese parinibbāyanti.

He related this Upasāḷaka Jātaka from the Book of Twos. Thus, among beings who die having cast off their bodies on the earth, there is no one who dies in a place where they have not died before. However, those like the Elder Ānanda attain Parinibbāna in a place where they have not died before.

Ānandatthero kira vīsavassasatikakāle āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokento parikkhīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ito sattame divase parinibbāyissāmī”ti ārocesi. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rohiṇīnadiyā ubhayatīravāsikesu manussesu orimatīravāsikā “mayaṃ therassa bahūpakārā, amhākaṃ santike parinibbāyissatī”ti vadiṃsu. Paratīravāsikāpi “mayaṃ therassa bahūpakārā, amhākaṃ santike parinibbāyissatī”ti vadiṃsu. Thero tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “ubhayatīravāsino mayhaṃ upakārā, ime nāma anupakārāti na sakkā vattuṃ, sacāhaṃ orimatīre [M 1.0343] parinibbāyissāmi, paratīravāsino dhātugahaṇatthaṃ tehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karissanti. Sace paratīre parinibbāyissāmi, orimatīravāsinopi tathā karissanti, kalaho uppajjamānopi maṃ nissāyeva uppajjissati, vūpasamamānopi maṃ nissāyeva [P 2.0100] vūpasamissatī”ti cintetvā “orimatīravāsinopi mayhaṃ upakārā, paratīravāsinopi mayhaṃ upakārā, anupakārāpi nāma natthi, orimatīravāsino orimatīreyeva sannipatantu, paratīravāsinopi paratīreyevā”ti āha. Tato sattame divase majjhenadiyā sattatālappamāṇe ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ kathetvā “mama sarīraṃ majjhe bhijjitvā eko bhāgo orimatīre patatu, eko bhāgo paratīre”ti adhiṭṭhāya yathānisinnova tejodhātuṃ samāpajji, jālā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Sarīraṃ majjhe bhijjitvā eko bhāgo orimatīre pati, eko bhāgo paratīre. Tato mahājano paridevi, pathaviundriyanasaddo viya ārodanasaddo ahosi. Satthu parinibbāne ārodanasaddatopi kāruññataro ahosi. Manussā cattāro māse rodantā paridevantā “satthu pattacīvaraggāhake tiṭṭhante satthu ṭhitakālo viya no ahosi, idāni no satthā parinibbuto”ti vippalapantā viravantā vicariṃsūti.

It is said that the Elder Ānanda, while observing his life-formation at the age of one hundred and twenty, knew it was exhausted and announced, 'On the seventh day from today, I shall attain Parinibbāna.' Hearing this news, among the people living on both banks of the Rohiṇī River, those on the near bank said, 'We have been of great service to the Elder; he will attain Parinibbāna in our presence.' Those on the far bank also said, 'We have been of great service to the Elder; he will attain Parinibbāna in our presence.' Hearing their words, the Elder thought, 'The dwellers on both banks have been of service to me; it is not possible to say that these have not been of service. If I were to attain Parinibbāna on the near bank, the dwellers on the far bank would quarrel with them to take the relics. If I were to attain Parinibbāna on the far bank, the dwellers on the near bank would do likewise. A quarrel, if it arises, will arise on account of me, and if it is pacified, it will be pacified on account of me.' Having thought thus, he said, 'The dwellers on the near bank have been of service to me, and the dwellers on the far bank have also been of service to me; there are none who have not been of service. Let the dwellers on the near bank assemble on the near bank, and let the dwellers on the far bank assemble on the far bank.' Then, on the seventh day, having sat cross-legged in the sky at a height of seven palm trees over the middle of the river and having taught the Dhamma to the great assembly, he made a resolution, 'May my body, having split in the middle, have one part fall on the near bank and one part fall on the far bank.' Just as he was seated, he entered the fire-element meditation, and flames arose. His body, having split in the middle, one part fell on the near bank, and one part fell on the far bank. Then the great assembly lamented; the sound of wailing was like the roaring of an earthquake. It was more pitiful than the sound of wailing at the Teacher's Parinibbāna. For four months, the people wept and lamented, wandering about, wailing and crying out, 'While the holder of the Teacher's bowl and robe was present, it was for us as if the Teacher were present. Now our teacher has attained Parinibbāna!'

Puna satthā sāmaṇeraṃ pucchi – “tissa, imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe dīpiādīnaṃ saddena bhāyasi, na bhāyasī”ti? “Na bhāyāmi bhagavā, apica kho pana me etesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā vanarati nāma uppajjatī”ti vatvā saṭṭhimattāhi gāthāhi vanavaṇṇanaṃ nāma kathesi. Atha naṃ satthā “tissā”ti āmantesi. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti? “Mayaṃ gacchāma, tvaṃ gamissasi, nivattissasī”ti. “Mayhaṃ upajjhāye maṃ ādāya gacchante gamissāmi, nivattente nivattissāmi[V 1.0306], bhante”ti[P 2.0101]. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pakkāmi. Sāmaṇerassa pana nivattitumeva ajjhāsayo, thero taṃ ñatvā “tissa, sace nivattitukāmo, nivattā”ti āha. So satthārañca bhikkhusaṅghañca vanditvā nivatti. Satthā jetavanameva agamāsi.

Again, the Teacher asked the novice, "Tissa, in this forest grove, are you afraid of the sounds of leopards and so forth, or not afraid?" "I am not afraid, Blessed One. Moreover, when I hear these sounds, a delight in the forest arises in me," he said, and then spoke in praise of the forest with about sixty verses. Then the Teacher addressed him, "Tissa." "What is it, Bhante?" "We are going; will you go, or will you turn back?" "Bhante, if my preceptor takes me and goes, I will go; if he has me turn back, I will turn back." The Teacher departed with the community of monks. The novice, however, had the inclination to turn back. The elder, knowing this, said, "Tissa, if you wish to turn back, then turn back." He paid homage to the Teacher and the community of monks and turned back. The Teacher went to Jetavana itself.

Bhikkhūnaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathā udapādi – “aho vata vanavāsītissasāmaṇero dukkaraṃ karoti, paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāyassa ñātakā sattasu maṅgalesu pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ appodakamadhupāyasameva adaṃsu, pabbajitakāle antovihāre buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa satta divasāni appodakamadhupāyasameva [M 1.0344] adaṃsu. Pabbajitvā aṭṭhame divase antogāmaṃ pavisanto dvīheva divasehi sāṭakasahassena saddhiṃ piṇḍapātasahassaṃ labhi, punekadivasaṃ kambalasahassaṃ labhi. Itissa idha vasanakāle mahālābhasakkāro uppajji, idāni evarūpaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ chaḍḍetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā missakāhārena yāpeti, dukkarakārako vata tissasāmaṇero”ti. Satthā āgantvā, “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “āma, bhikkhave, lābhūpanisā nāmesā aññā, nibbānagāminī paṭipadā aññā. ‘Evaṃ lābhaṃ labhissāmī’ti hi āraññikādidhutaṅgasamādānavasena lābhūpanisaṃ rakkhantassa bhikkhuno cattāro apāyā vivaṭadvārā eva tiṭṭhanti, nibbānagāminiyā pana paṭipadāya uppannaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto arahattaṃ gaṇhātī”ti anusandhiṃ [P 2.0102] ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the Dhamma hall, a discussion arose among the monks: "Oh, indeed, the novice Tissa, the forest-dweller, performs a difficult task! From the moment of his conception, his relatives gave only thick honey-rice-porridge on seven auspicious occasions to five hundred monks. At the time of his ordination, inside the monastery, they gave only thick honey-rice-porridge for seven days to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. After going forth, on the eighth day, when he entered the village, he received a thousand portions of alms-food along with a thousand cloths in just two days. Then, on another day, he received a thousand blankets. Thus, great gain and honor arose for him while living here. Now, having abandoned such gain and honor, he has entered the forest and subsists on mixed food. Truly, the novice Tissa is one who performs a difficult task." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?" When they replied, "This one," he said, "Yes, monks. One thing is the pursuit of gain, and another is the path leading to Nibbāna. For a monk who guards the pursuit of gain by undertaking ascetic practices like forest-dwelling, thinking, 'Thus I will gain,' the four states of woe stand with wide-open doors. But on the path leading to Nibbāna, by abandoning arisen gain and honor, one enters the forest, strives, exerts, and attains Arahantship." Connecting the discourse, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

75.

75.

“Aññā hi lābhūpanisā, aññā nibbānagāminī;

Evametaṃ abhiññāya, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Sakkāraṃ nābhinandeyya, vivekamanubrūhaye”ti.

One is the pursuit of gain, another leads to Nibbāna. Having directly known this, the monk, a disciple of the Buddha, should not rejoice in offerings, but develop seclusion.

Tattha aññā hi lābhūpanisā, aññā nibbānagāminīti lābhūpanisā nāmesā aññā eva, aññā nibbānagāminī paṭipadā. Lābhuppādakena hi bhikkhunā thokaṃ akusalakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kāyavaṅkādīni kātabbāni honti. Yasmiñhi kāle kāyavaṅkādīsu kiñci karoti, tadā lābho uppajjati. Pāyasapātiyañhi vaṅkaṃ akatvā ujukameva hatthaṃ otāretvā ukkhipantassa hattho makkhitamattakova hoti, vaṅkaṃ katvā otāretvā ukkhipantassa pana pāyasapiṇḍaṃ uddharantova nikkhamati, evaṃ kāyavaṅkādīni karaṇakāleyeva lābho uppajjati. Ayaṃ adhammikā lābhūpanissā nāma. Upadhisampadā cīvaradhāraṇaṃ bāhusaccaṃ parivāro araññavāsoti evarūpehi pana kāraṇehi uppanno lābho dhammiko nāma hoti. Nibbānagāminiṃ [V 1.0307] paṭipadaṃ pūrentena pana bhikkhunā kāyavaṅkādīni pahātabbāni. Anandheneva andhena viya, amūgeneva mūgena viya, abadhireneva badhirena viya bhavituṃ vaṭṭati. Asaṭhena amāyena bhavituṃ vaṭṭati. Evametanti etaṃ lābhuppādanaṃ paṭipadañca nibbānagāminiṃ paṭipadañca [P 2.0103] evaṃ ñatvā sabbesaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammānaṃ bujjhanaṭṭhena [M 1.0345] buddhassa savanante jātaṭṭhena ovādānusāsaniṃ vā savanaṭṭhena sāvako bhikkhu adhammikaṃ catupaccayasakkāraṃ nābhinandeyya, na ceva dhammikaṃ paṭikkoseyya, kāyavivekādikaṃ vivekaṃ anubrūhaye. Tattha kāyavivekoti kāyassa ekībhāvo. Cittavivekoti aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Upadhivivekoti nibbānaṃ. Tesu kāyaviveko gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodeti, cittaviveko kilesasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodeti, upadhiviveko saṅkhārasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodeti. Kāyaviveko cittavivekassa paccayo hoti, cittaviveko upadhivivekassa paccayo hoti. Vuttampihetaṃ –

Herein, the pursuit of gain is one thing, and the path leading to Nibbāna is another. This pursuit of gain is indeed different; the path leading to Nibbāna is a different path. For a monk who produces gain, it is permissible to do a little unwholesome kamma; crooked bodily actions and so forth are to be done. For at whatever time he does something among crooked bodily actions and so forth, then gain arises. Indeed, for one who lowers his hand straight into a bowl of milk-rice and lifts it without bending it, his hand is only smeared. But for one who, having bent his hand, lowers it and lifts it, it comes out taking a lump of milk-rice. Thus, gain arises only at the time of performing crooked bodily actions and so forth. This is called the unrighteous pursuit of gain. However, gain that has arisen from such causes as accomplishment in the requisites, the wearing of the robe, great learning, having a retinue, or dwelling in the forest, is called righteous. But a monk who is fulfilling the path leading to Nibbāna must abandon crooked bodily actions and so forth. Though not blind, he should be as if blind; though not mute, he should be as if mute; though not deaf, he should be as if deaf. He should be without deceit, without guile. Knowing this thus—knowing thus this path of producing gain and the path leading to Nibbāna—a disciple monk, so called because he understands all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, or because he is born in the presence of the Buddha, or because he hears his advice and instruction, should not delight in unrighteous honor through the four requisites, nor should he reject that which is righteous. He should cultivate seclusion, beginning with bodily seclusion. Therein, bodily seclusion is the solitude of the body. Mental seclusion is the eight attainments. Seclusion from the substrates is Nibbāna. Among these, bodily seclusion dispels delight in company; mental seclusion dispels delight in the company of defilements; seclusion from the substrates dispels delight in the company of formations. Bodily seclusion is a condition for mental seclusion; mental seclusion is a condition for seclusion from the substrates. And this has been said:

“Kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ, cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ, upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna”nti (mahāni. 150). –

“Bodily seclusion is for those who desire seclusion of the body, who delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those with purified minds, who have attained the highest purity. Seclusion from the substrates is for those persons without substrates, who have gone beyond formations.” (Mahāni. 150).

Imaṃ tividhampi vivekaṃ brūheyya vaḍḍheyya, upasampajja vihareyyāti attho.

This threefold seclusion should be developed and cultivated; having undertaken it, one should dwell therein—this is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Vanavāsītissasāmaṇeravatthu pannarasamaṃ.

The fifteenth story, that of the novice Tissa the Forest-Dweller, is concluded.

Bālavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Fool is concluded.

Pañcamo vaggo.

The Fifth Chapter.

6. Paṇḍitavaggo

6. The Chapter on the Wise

1. Rādhattheravatthu

1. The Story of the Elder Rādha

Nidhīnaṃva [V 1.0308][M 1.0346][P 2.0104] pavattāranti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmantaṃ rādhattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this discourse on the Dhamma concerning the Venerable Elder Rādha, which begins, 'Like a revealer of treasures...'

So kira gihikāle sāvatthiyaṃ duggatabrāhmaṇo ahosi. So “bhikkhūnaṃ santike jīvissāmī”ti cintetvā vihāraṃ gantvā appaharitakaṃ karonto pariveṇaṃ sammajjanto mukhadhovanādīni dadanto antovihāreyeva vasi. Bhikkhūpi naṃ saṅgaṇhiṃsu, pabbājetuṃ pana na icchanti. So pabbajjaṃ alabhamāno kiso ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ satthā paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho”ti upadhārento “arahā bhavissatī”ti ñatvā sāyanhasamaye vihāracārikaṃ caranto viya brāhmaṇassa santikaṃ gantvā, “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ karonto vicarasī”ti āha. “Bhikkhūnaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ karonto, bhante”ti[P 2.0105]. “Labhasi nesaṃ santikā saṅgaha”nti? “Āma, bhante, āhāramattaṃ labhāmi, na pana maṃ pabbājentī”ti. Satthā etasmiṃ nidāne bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā tamatthaṃ pucchitvā, “bhikkhave, atthi koci imassa brāhmaṇassa adhikāraṃ saratī”ti pucchi. Sāriputtatthero “ahaṃ, bhante, sarāmi, ayaṃ me rājagahe piṇḍāya carantassa attano abhihaṭaṃ kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ dāpesi, imamassāhaṃ adhikāraṃ sarāmī”ti āha. So satthārā “kiṃ pana te, sāriputta, evaṃ katūpakāraṃ dukkhato mocetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vutte, “sādhu, bhante, pabbājessāmī”ti taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pabbājesi. Tassa bhattagge āsanapariyante āsanaṃ pāpuṇāti, yāgubhattādīhipi kilamati. Thero taṃ ādāya cārikaṃ pakkāmi, abhikkhaṇañca naṃ “idaṃ te kattabbaṃ, idaṃ te na kattabba”nti ovadi anusāsi. So suvaco ahosi padakkhiṇaggāhī. Tasmā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāno katipāheneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

It is said that in his time as a layman, he was a poor brahmin in Sāvatthī. Thinking, 'I will make a living in the presence of the monks,' he went to the monastery. There he performed services, sweeping the monastery grounds and providing water for washing the face and so on, and he lived right inside the monastery. The monks supported him, but they did not wish to ordain him. Unable to gain ordination, he grew thin. Then one day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw that brahmin. Reflecting, 'What could this be?' He knew, 'He will become an Arahant.' In the evening, as if on his regular walk through the monastery, He went to the brahmin and asked, 'Brahmin, what are you doing, wandering about?' 'Venerable Sir, I am performing the major and minor duties for the monks.' 'Do you receive support from them?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir, I receive just enough food, but they do not ordain me.' On this occasion, the Teacher had the community of monks assembled, and having asked about the matter, He inquired, 'Monks, is there anyone who remembers a service done by this brahmin?' The Elder Sāriputta said, 'I remember, Venerable Sir. In Rājagaha, while I was on my alms round, he had a ladleful of his own alms-food given to me. I remember this service of his.' When the Teacher said to him, 'Sāriputta, is it not proper for you to free from suffering one who has done you such a service?' he replied, 'Very well, Venerable Sir, I will ordain him,' and he ordained that brahmin. In the dining hall, he would get a seat at the very end of the row, and he struggled even for gruel and rice. The Elder took him and departed on an alms tour. He repeatedly admonished and instructed him, saying, 'This you should do; this you should not do.' He was easy to admonish and receptive to instruction. Therefore, practicing as he was instructed, in just a few days he attained Arahantship.

Thero taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā āha – “suvaco nu kho, sāriputta, te antevāsiko”ti[M 1.0347]. “Āma, bhante, ativiya [V 1.0309] suvaco, kismiñci dose vuccamāne na kuddhapubbo”ti. “Sāriputta[P 2.0106], evarūpe saddhivihārike labhanto kittake gaṇheyyāsī”ti? “Bhante, bahukepi gaṇheyyamevā”ti. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāya kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “sāriputtatthero kira kataññū katavedī, kaṭacchubhikkhāmattaṃ upakāraṃ saritvā duggatabrāhmaṇaṃ pabbājesi. Theropi ovādakkhamo ovādakkhamameva labhī”ti. Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi sāriputto kataññū katavedīyevā”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ –

The Elder, taking him along, went to the Teacher's presence, paid homage, and sat down. Then the Teacher, after exchanging pleasantries, said, 'Sāriputta, is your pupil easy to admonish?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir, he is very easy to admonish. He has never been angry when any fault is pointed out.' 'Sāriputta, if you could get co-resident pupils of such a nature, how many would you take?' 'Venerable Sir, I would take even many.' Then one day, a conversation arose in the Dhamma hall: 'The Elder Sāriputta, it seems, is grateful and appreciative. Remembering the service of a mere ladleful of alms-food, he ordained a poor brahmin. The Elder, being one who is open to admonishment, has found a pupil who is also open to it.' Hearing their conversation, the Teacher said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Sāriputta was grateful and appreciative.' And to clarify that matter, He said:

“Alīnacittaṃ nissāya, pahaṭṭhā mahatī camū;

Kosalaṃ senāsantuṭṭhaṃ, jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayi.

Relying on King Alīnacitta, the great and joyful army seized the King of Kosala, who was complacent with his own forces, and took him alive.

“Evaṃ nissayasampanno, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo;

Bhāvayaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, yogakkhemassa pattiyā;

Pāpuṇe anupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya”nti. (jā. 1.2.11-12) –

Thus, a monk endowed with such a support, with energy aroused, cultivating wholesome states for the attainment of security from the yokes, would gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.

Imaṃ dukanipāte alīnacittajātakaṃ vitthāretvā kathesi. Tadā kira vaḍḍhakīhi pādassa arogakaraṇabhāvena kahaṃ attano upakāraṃ ñatvā sabbasetassa hatthipotakassa dāyako ekacāriko hatthī sāriputtatthero ahosīti evaṃ theraṃ ārabbha jātakaṃ kathetvā rādhattheraṃ ārabbha, “bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma rādhena viya suvacena bhavitabbaṃ, dosaṃ dassetvā ovadiyamānenapi na kujjhitabbaṃ, ovādadāyako pana nidhiācikkhaṇako viya daṭṭhabbo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ [P 2.0107] ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

He taught this Alīnacitta Jātaka from the Book of Twos in detail. At that time, it is said, the elephant that wandered alone was the Elder Sāriputta. In gratitude for the service done for him by the carpenters—who had cured his foot by removing a splinter—he gave them an all-white young elephant. Thus, having told the Jātaka concerning the Elder, and then turning to the matter of Elder Rādha, He said: 'Monks, a monk should be easy to admonish, like Rādha. Even when being admonished and having one's faults pointed out, one should not become angry. Moreover, one who gives admonishment should be regarded like one who points out a treasure.' Having thus connected the narrative, He taught the Dhamma by speaking this verse:

76.

76.

“Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ, yaṃ passe vajjadassinaṃ;

Niggayhavādiṃ medhāviṃ, tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje;

Tādisaṃ bhajamānassa, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo”ti.

One should follow a wise person who points out faults and speaks reprovingly, an intelligent sage, as one would a revealer of hidden treasure. For one who follows such a person, it is better, never worse.

Tattha nidhīnanti tattha tattha nidahitvā ṭhapitānaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādipūrānaṃ nidhikumbhīnaṃ. Pavattāranti kicchajīvike duggatamanusse anukampaṃ katvā “ehi, sukhena jīvanūpāyaṃ dassessāmī”ti nidhiṭṭhānaṃ netvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā “imaṃ gahetvā sukhena jīvā”ti ācikkhitāraṃ viya. Vajjadassinanti dve vajjadassino “iminā naṃ asāruppena vā khalitena vā saṅghamajjhe niggaṇhissāmī”ti randhagavesako [M 1.0348] ca, aññātaṃ ñāpanatthāya ñātaṃ anuggahaṇatthāya [V 1.0310] sīlādīnamassa vuddhikāmatāya taṃ taṃ vajjaṃ olokanena ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhito ca. Ayaṃ idha adhippeto. Yathā hi duggatamanusso “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti tajjetvāpi pothetvāpi nidhiṃ dassente kopaṃ na karoti, pamudito eva hoti, evameva evarūpe puggale asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā ācikkhante kopo na kātabbo, tuṭṭheneva bhavitabbaṃ, “bhante, mahantaṃ vo kammaṃ kataṃ[P 2.0108], mayhaṃ ācariyupajjhāyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā ovadantehi punapi maṃ vadeyyāthā”ti pavāretabbameva. Niggayhavādinti ekacco hi saddhivihārikādīnaṃ asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā “ayaṃ me mukhodakadānādīhi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahati, sace naṃ vakkhāmi, na maṃ upaṭṭhahissati, evaṃ me parihāni bhavissatī”ti vatthuṃ avisahanto na niggayhavādī nāma hoti. So imasmiṃ sāsane kacavaraṃ ākirati. Yo pana tathārūpaṃ vajjaṃ disvā vajjānurūpaṃ tajjento paṇāmento daṇḍakammaṃ karonto vihārā taṃ nīharanto sikkhāpeti, ayaṃ niggayhavādī nāma seyyathāpi sammāsambuddho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “niggayha niggayhāhaṃ, ānanda, vakkhāmi, pavayha pavayha, ānanda, vakkhāmi, yo sāro so ṭhassatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.196). Medhāvinti dhammojapaññāya samannāgataṃ. Tādisanti evarūpaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhajeyya payirupāseyya. Tādisañhi ācariyaṃ bhajamānassa antevāsikassa seyyo hoti, na pāpiyo vaḍḍhiyeva hoti, no parihānīti.

Therein, `nidhīnaṃ` refers to treasure pots filled with gold, silver, and so on, which have been buried and placed in various places. `Pavattāraṃ` is like one who, out of compassion for poor people living with difficulty, leads them to the place of the treasure, saying, “Come, I will show you a means to live comfortably,” and extending a hand, says, “Take this and live comfortably,” thus pointing it out. `Vajjadassinaṃ` refers to two kinds of fault-seers: one who seeks for faults with the intention, “I will suppress him in the midst of the Sangha for this impropriety or this mistake,” and another who is established in the nature of uplifting, who looks at this and that fault for the sake of making known what is unknown, for the sake of supporting what is known, and out of a desire for the growth of that person's virtues such as morality. This latter one is intended here. For just as a poor person does not get angry but is only delighted when someone, even after threatening or striking them, points out a treasure, saying, “Take this,” in the very same way, when one sees an impropriety or a mistake in such a person and points it out, one should not get angry but should be pleased, and one should indeed invite them, saying, “Venerable sir, a great deed has been done by you. Standing in the place of my teacher and preceptor, you advise me. Please speak to me again.” `Niggayhavādī` means: indeed, a certain person, having seen an impropriety or a mistake in their co-residents and so on, being unable to speak, thinking, “This person attends to me respectfully with the giving of water for the face, etc. If I were to speak to him, he will not attend to me, and thus there will be a loss for me,” is not called one who speaks reprovingly. That person scatters rubbish in this Dispensation. But whoever, having seen such a fault, trains that person according to the fault by threatening, rebuking, imposing a penalty, and expelling them from the monastery—this one is called one who speaks reprovingly, just like the Fully Enlightened One. For it is said: “Reprovingly, reprovingly, Ānanda, I will speak; encouragingly, encouragingly, Ānanda, I will speak. Whoever is of substance will stand fast” (MN 3.196). `Medhāvī` means endowed with the wisdom that penetrates the Dhamma. `Tādisaṃ` means one should associate with and attend upon such a wise person. Indeed, for a disciple who attends upon such a teacher, there is improvement, not decline; there is only growth, not deterioration.

Desanāpariyosāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Rādhattheravatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Rādha (First).

2. Assajipunabbasukavatthu

2. The Story of Assaji and Punabbasu

Ovadeyyānusāseyyāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto assajipunabbasukabhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Desanā [P 2.0109] pana kīṭāgirismiṃ samuṭṭhitā.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse on the Dhamma concerning the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, beginning with 'One should advise and instruct.' The teaching, however, originated at Kīṭāgiri.

Te kira dve bhikkhū kiñcāpi aggasāvakānaṃ saddhivihārikā, alajjino pana ahesuṃ pāpabhikkhū. Te pāpakehi attano parivārehi pañcahi bhikkhusatehi [M 1.0349] saddhiṃ kīṭāgirismiṃ viharantā “mālāvacchaṃ ropentipi ropāpentipī”tiādikaṃ (pārā. 431; cūḷava. 21) nānappakāraṃ anācāraṃ karontā kuladūsakakammaṃ katvā tato uppannehi paccayehi jīvikaṃ kappentā taṃ āvāsaṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anāvāsaṃ akaṃsu. Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ [V 1.0311] sutvā tesaṃ pabbājanīyakammakaraṇatthāya saparivāre dve aggasāvake āmantetvā “gacchatha, sāriputtā, tesu ye tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ na karonti, tesaṃ pabbājanīyakammaṃ karotha, ye pana karonti, te ovadatha anusāsatha. Ovadanto hi anusāsanto apaṇḍitānaṃyeva appiyo hoti amanāpo, paṇḍitānaṃ pana piyo hoti manāpo”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that those two monks, although they were pupils of the chief disciples, were shameless, wicked monks. Residing at Kīṭāgiri with their own wicked following of five hundred monks, they engaged in various kinds of misconduct, such as "planting small flowering plants and having them planted," and having committed acts that corrupt families, they made a living with the requisites that arose from that, and they made that monastery unsuitable for virtuous monks. The Teacher, having heard that account, summoned the two chief disciples with their following in order to have the act of banishment performed on them, and said, 'Go, Sāriputtas. Among them, perform the act of banishment on those who do not follow your word. But those who do, advise and instruct them. Indeed, one who advises and instructs is unloved and disagreeable only to the unwise, but to the wise, they are loved and agreeable.' Thus, making a connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

77.

77.

“Ovadeyyānusāseyya, asabbhā ca nivāraye;

Satañhi so piyo hoti, asataṃ hoti appiyo”ti.

“One should advise and instruct, and from impropriety restrain; for such a one is dear to the good, but is disliked by the bad.”

Tattha ovadeyyāti uppanne vatthusmiṃ vadanto ovadati nāma, anuppanne vatthusmiṃ “ayasopi te siyā”tiādivasena anāgataṃ dassento anusāsati nāma. Sammukhā vadanto ovadati nāma, parammukhā dūtaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā pesento anusāsati nāma. Sakiṃ vadanto ovadati nāma, punappunaṃ [P 2.0110] vadanto anusāsati nāma. Ovadanto eva vā anusāsati nāmāti evaṃ ovadeyya anusāseyya. Asabbhā cāti akusaladhammā ca nivāreyya, kusaladhamme patiṭṭhāpeyyāti attho. Satañhi so piyo hotīti so evarūpo puggalo buddhādīnaṃ sappurisānaṃ piyo hoti. Ye pana adiṭṭhadhammā avitiṇṇaparalokā āmisacakkhukā jīvikatthāya pabbajitā, tesaṃ asataṃ so ovādako anusāsako, “‘na tvaṃ amhākaṃ upajjhāyo, na ācariyo, kasmā amhe ovadasī’ti evaṃ mukhasattīhi vijjhantānaṃ appiyo hotī”ti.

Herein, `ovadeyya` means advising when a matter has arisen; `anusāseyya` means instructing before a matter has arisen by showing what is to come, by way of saying, 'Disrepute may come to you.' Advising is speaking face-to-face; instructing is sending a messenger or a message in one's absence. Advising is speaking once; instructing is speaking repeatedly. Or, advising itself is also called instructing. Thus, one should advise and instruct. 'And from impropriety' means one should restrain from unwholesome states and establish one in wholesome states; this is the meaning. 'For such a one is dear to the good' means such a person is dear to the good people, such as the Buddha and others. But to those bad people who have not seen the Dhamma, who have gone forth for the sake of livelihood with eyes only for material gain, that advisor and instructor is not dear. To them, who pierce with the spears of their mouths, saying, 'You are not our preceptor or teacher, why do you advise us?', he is not dear.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti. Sāriputtamoggallānāpi tattha gantvā te bhikkhū ovadiṃsu anusāsiṃsu. Tesu ekacce ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sammā vattiṃsu, ekacce vibbhamiṃsu, ekacce pabbājanīyakammaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the teaching, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. Sāriputta and Moggallāna also went there and advised and instructed those monks. Among them, some accepted the advice and conducted themselves rightly, some disrobed, and some were subjected to the act of banishment.

Assajipunabbasukavatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Story of Assaji and Punabbasu (Second).

3. Channattheravatthu

3. The Story of the Elder Channa

Na [M 1.0350] bhaje pāpake mitteti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto channattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Channa, beginning with 'Do not associate with evil friends.'

So [V 1.0312] kira āyasmā “ahaṃ amhākaṃ ayyaputtena saddhiṃ mahābhinikkhamanaṃ [P 2.0111] nikkhanto tadā aññaṃ ekampi na passāmi, idāni pana ‘ahaṃ sāriputto nāma, ahaṃ moggallāno nāma, mayaṃ aggasāvakamhā’ti vatvā ime vicarantī”ti dve aggasāvake akkosati. Satthā bhikkhūnaṃ santikā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā channattheraṃ pakkosāpetvā ovadati. So taṅkhaṇeyeva tuṇhī hutvā puna gantvā there akkosatiyeva. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ akkosantaṃ pakkosāpetvā satthā ovaditvā “channa, dve aggasāvakā nāma tuyhaṃ kalyāṇamittā uttamapurisā, evarūpe kalyāṇamitte sevassu bhajassū”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that the venerable one reviled the two chief disciples, saying: 'I went forth on the Great Renunciation together with our master's son. At that time, I did not see any other single person. But now, these ones wander about, declaring, "I am Sāriputta, I am Moggallāna, we are the chief disciples."' The Teacher, hearing of this matter from the monks, had the Elder Channa summoned and admonished him. He became silent at that very moment, but later went and reviled the elders again. The Teacher had him summoned as he was reviling up to the third time, and after admonishing him, said: 'Channa, the two chief disciples are your good friends, excellent men. Associate with and attend upon such good friends.' Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

78.

78.

“Na bhaje pāpake mitte, na bhaje purisādhame;

Bhajetha mitte kalyāṇe, bhajetha purisuttame”ti.

“Do not associate with evil friends, do not associate with inferior men. Associate with good friends, associate with excellent men.”

Tassattho – kāyaduccaritādiakusalakammābhiratā pāpamittā nāma. Sandhicchedanādike vā ekavīsatianesanādibhede vā aṭṭhāne niyojakā purisādhamā nāma. Ubhopi vā ete pāpamittā ceva purisādhamā ca, te na bhajeyya na payirupāseyya, viparītā pana kalyāṇamittā ceva sappurisā ca, te bhajetha payirupāsethāti.

The meaning of that verse is: Those who delight in unwholesome actions such as bodily misconduct and so on are called evil friends. Those who engage others in improper things, such as breaking into houses or the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, are called inferior men. Both of these are indeed evil friends and inferior men; one should not associate with nor attend upon them. But those who are the opposite are called good friends and virtuous men; one should associate with and attend upon them. This is the meaning of the verse.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Channatthero pana taṃ ovādaṃ sutvāpi purimanayeneva bhikkhū akkosati paribhāsati. Punapi satthu ārocesuṃ[P 2.0112]. Satthā, “bhikkhave, mayi dharante channaṃ sikkhāpetuṃ na sakkhissatha, mayi pana parinibbute sakkhissathā”ti vatvā parinibbānakāle āyasmatā ānandena, “bhante, kathaṃ channatthere amhehi paṭipajjitabba”nti vutte, “ānanda, channassa bhikkhuno brahmadaṇḍo dātabbo”ti āṇāpesi. So satthari parinibbute ānandattherena ārocitaṃ brahmadaṇḍaṃ sutvā dukkhī dummano tikkhattuṃ mucchito patitvā “mā [M 1.0351] maṃ, bhante, nāsayitthā”ti yācitvā sammā vattaṃ pūrento na cirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti.

But the Elder Channa, even after hearing that admonition, reviled and abused the monks in the same way as before. They informed the Teacher again. The Teacher said: 'Monks, while I am present, you will not be able to train Channa. But when I have attained Parinibbāna, you will be able to.' Having said this, at the time of the Parinibbāna, when the venerable Ānanda asked, 'Venerable Sir, how should we act towards the Elder Channa?' he commanded, 'Ānanda, the brahmadanda should be imposed on the monk Channa.' When the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, Channa, having heard the brahmadanda announced by the Elder Ānanda, became sorrowful and dejected. Fainting and falling three times, he pleaded, 'Venerable sirs, do not destroy me!' Then, while fulfilling his duties properly, before long he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Channattheravatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Channa, the third.

4. Mahākappinattheravatthu

4. The Story of the Elder Mahākappina

Dhammapīti [V 1.0313] sukhaṃ setīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahākappinattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning the Elder Mahākappina, which begins: 'One who delights in the Dhamma sleeps happily.'

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbī kathā – atīte kira āyasmā mahākappino padumuttarabuddhassa pādamūle katābhinīhāro saṃsāre saṃsaranto bārāṇasito avidūre ekasmiṃ pesakāragāme jeṭṭhakapesakāro hutvā nibbatti. Tadā sahassamattā paccekabuddhā aṭṭha māse himavante vasitvā vassike cattāro māse janapade vasanti. Te ekavāraṃ bārāṇasiyā avidūre otaritvā “senāsanakaraṇatthāya hatthakammaṃ yācathā”ti [P 2.0113] rañño santikaṃ aṭṭha paccekabuddhe pahiṇiṃsu. Tadā pana rañño vappamaṅgalakālo hoti. So “paccekabuddhā kira āgatā”ti sutvā tasmiṃ khaṇe nikkhamitvā āgatakāraṇaṃ pucchitvā “ajja, bhante, okāso natthi, sve amhākaṃ vappamaṅgalaṃ, tatiyadivase karissāmī”ti vatvā paccekabuddhe animantetvāva pāvisi. Paccekabuddhā “aññattha gamissāmā”ti pakkamiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe jeṭṭhapesakārassa bhariyā kenacideva karaṇīyena bārāṇasiṃ gacchantī te paccekabuddhe disvā vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, avelāya, ayyā, āgatā”ti pucchitvā ādito paṭṭhāya kathesuṃ. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā saddhāsampannā ñāṇasampannā itthī “sve, bhante, amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantesi. “Bahukā mayaṃ bhaginī”ti. “Kittakā, bhante”ti? “Sahassamattā”ti. “Bhante, imasmiṃ gāme sahassapesakārā vasimha. Ekeko ekekassa bhikkhaṃ dassati, bhikkhaṃ adhivāsetha, ahameva vo vasanaṭṭhānampi kāressāmī”ti āha. Paccekabuddhā adhivāsayiṃsu.

Here is the story in sequence: In the past, it is said, the Venerable Mahākappina made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara and, wandering through saṃsāra, was reborn as the chief weaver in a weavers’ village not far from Bārāṇasī. At that time, a thousand Paccekabuddhas, having spent eight months in the Himalayas, would dwell in the inhabited lands for the four months of the rainy season. Once, they descended near Bārāṇasī and sent eight Paccekabuddhas to the king to request manual labor for preparing lodgings. Now at that time it was the king's sowing festival. Hearing that Paccekabuddhas had arrived, he came out at that moment, asked the reason for their visit, and said: 'Today, venerable sirs, there is no opportunity. Tomorrow is our sowing festival; I will attend to it on the third day.' Having said this, he entered without inviting the Paccekabuddhas. The Paccekabuddhas departed, thinking: 'We will go elsewhere.' At that moment, the wife of the chief weaver was going to Bārāṇasī on some business. Seeing the Paccekabuddhas, she paid homage and asked: 'Venerable sirs, why have you come at this untimely hour?' They told her the whole story from the beginning. Hearing the account, the woman, who was endowed with faith and wisdom, invited them, saying: 'Tomorrow, venerable sirs, please accept our almsfood.' 'We are many, sister.' 'How many, venerable sirs?' 'About a thousand.' 'Venerable sirs, in this village live a thousand weavers. Each one will give almsfood to one of you. Please consent to the almsfood, and I myself will also have your lodgings arranged.' The Paccekabuddhas consented.

Sā gāmaṃ pavisitvā ugghosesi – “ahaṃ sahassamatte paccekabuddhe disvā nimantayiṃ, ayyānaṃ nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahatha[P 2.0114], yāgubhattādīni sampādethā”ti[M 1.0352]. Gāmamajjhe maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā āsanāni paññāpetvā punadivase paccekabuddhe nisīdāpetvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisitvā bhattakiccāvasāne tasmiṃ gāme sabbā itthiyo ādāya tāhi saddhiṃ paccekabuddhe vanditvā, “bhante, temāsaṃ vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ dethā”ti tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā puna gāme ugghosesi – “ammatātā, ekekakulato ekeko puriso pharasuvāsiādīni gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā dabbasambhāre āharitvā ayyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ karotū”ti. Gāmavāsino tassāyeva vacanaṃ sutvā ekeko ekekaṃ katvā saddhiṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānehi paṇṇasālasahassaṃ kāretvā attano attano paṇṇasālāyaṃ vassūpagate paccekabuddhe “ahaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmi, ahaṃ sakkaccaṃ [V 1.0314] upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Vassaṃvuṭṭhakāle “attano attano paṇṇasālāya vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ cīvarasāṭake sajjethā”ti samādapetvā ekekassa sahassasahassamūlaṃ cīvaraṃ dāpesi. Paccekabuddhā vuṭṭhavassā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu.

She entered the village and announced: 'I have seen and invited about a thousand Paccekabuddhas. Prepare seating for the noble sirs and provide gruel, rice, and other foods.' In the middle of the village, she had a pavilion built and seats arranged. The next day, she had the Paccekabuddhas seated and served them with fine hard and soft food. When the meal was over, she gathered all the women of the village and together with them paid homage to the Paccekabuddhas and requested: 'Venerable sirs, please give your promise to stay for the three months.' Having obtained their promise, she again announced in the village: 'Dear mothers and fathers, let one man from each household take an axe, adze, and other tools, enter the forest, gather materials, and build dwellings for the noble sirs.' Hearing her words, the villagers, each doing his part, had a thousand leaf-huts built, complete with places for resting by day and by night. When the Paccekabuddhas entered the rains-residence, each in his own leaf-hut, the villagers attended to them diligently, each saying, 'I will attend carefully, I will attend carefully.' At the end of the rains-residence, she encouraged them, saying: 'Prepare robe-cloths for the Paccekabuddhas who have completed the rains in your respective leaf-huts.' She had robes worth a thousand each given to every one of them. The Paccekabuddhas, having completed the rains-residence, gave their blessings and departed.

Gāmavāsinopi idaṃ puññakammaṃ katvā ito cutā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattitvā gaṇadevaputtā nāma ahesuṃ. Te tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā kassapasammāsambuddhakāle [P 2.0115] bārāṇasiyaṃ kuṭumbikagehesu nibbattiṃsu. Jeṭṭhakapesakāro jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa putto ahosi. Bhariyāpissa jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikasseva dhītā ahosi. Tā sabbāpi vayappattā parakulaṃ gacchantiyo tesaṃ tesaṃyeva gehāni agamiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ vihāre dhammassavanaṃ saṅghuṭṭhaṃ. “Satthā dhammaṃ desessatī”ti sutvā sabbepi te kuṭumbikā “dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti bhariyāhi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ agamiṃsu. Tesaṃ vihāramajjhaṃ paviṭṭhakkhaṇe vassaṃ uṭṭhahi. Yesaṃ kulūpakā vā ñātisāmaṇerādayo vā atthi, te tesaṃ pariveṇāni pavisiṃsu. Te pana tathārūpānaṃ natthitāya katthaci, pavisituṃ avisahantā vihāramajjheyeva aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha ne jeṭṭhakakuṭumbiko āha – “passatha amhākaṃ vippakāraṃ, kulaputtehi nāma ettakena lajjituṃ yutta”nti. “Ayya, kiṃ pana karomā”ti? “Mayaṃ vissāsikaṭṭhānassa abhāvena imaṃ vippakāraṃ pattā, sabbe [M 1.0353] dhanaṃ saṃharitvā pariveṇaṃ karomā”ti. “Sādhu, ayyā”ti jeṭṭhako sahassaṃ adāsi, sesā pañca pañca satāni. Itthiyo aḍḍhateyyāni aḍḍhateyyāni satāni. Te taṃ dhanaṃ saṃharitvā sahassakūṭāgāraparivāraṃ [P 2.0116] satthu vasanatthāya mahāpariveṇaṃ nāma ārabhiṃsu. Navakammassa mahantatāya dhane appahonte pubbe dinnadhanato puna upaḍḍhūpaḍḍhaṃ adaṃsu. Niṭṭhite pariveṇe vihāramahaṃ karontā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ cīvarāni sajjiṃsu.

The villagers too, having performed this meritorious deed, passed away from there and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where they became devas named the Gaṇadevaputtas. Having enjoyed divine bliss there, during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, they were reborn in the households of prominent families in Bārāṇasī. The chief weaver became the son of the chief householder. His wife, too, became the daughter of that same chief householder. When all the women came of age and went to other families in marriage, they went to the very homes of those men. Then one day, it was announced that there would be a Dhamma talk at the monastery. Hearing, 'The Teacher will give a Dhamma talk,' all those householders went to the monastery with their wives to hear the Dhamma. At the very moment they entered the monastery grounds, it began to rain. Those who had patron monks or novice-relatives entered their cells. But these people, having no such connections, were unable to enter anywhere and remained standing in the middle of the monastery grounds. Then the chief householder said to them: 'See our predicament! It is right for those of good family to be shamed by such a thing.' 'Sir, what should we do?' 'It is because we lack a familiar place that we have met with this predicament. Let us all pool our funds and build a residence complex.' 'Very well, sirs,' they agreed. The chief gave a thousand, the others five hundred each. The women gave two hundred and fifty each. Pooling their funds, they began to build a great residence complex for the Teacher to dwell in, called the Mahāpariveṇa, which was surrounded by a thousand gabled chambers. As the construction work was vast and the funds were insufficient, they again contributed half of their original donations.
