When the residence complex was completed, they held a festival for the monastery. For seven days they gave a great offering of alms to the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and provided robes for twenty thousand bhikkhus.

Jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa pana bhariyā sabbehi samānaṃ akatvā attano paññāya ṭhitā “atirekataraṃ katvā satthāraṃ pūjessāmī”ti anojapupphavaṇṇena sahassamūlena sāṭakena saddhiṃ anojapupphacaṅkoṭakaṃ gahetvā anumodanakāle satthāraṃ anojapupphehi pūjetvā taṃ sāṭakaṃ satthu pādamūle ṭhapetvā, “bhante, nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne anojapupphavaṇṇaṃyeva me sarīraṃ hotu, anojā eva ca me nāmaṃ hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Satthā “evaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ akāsi. Te sabbepi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cutā devaloke nibbattitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devalokā cavitvā jeṭṭhakakuṭumbiko kukkuṭavatīnagare rājakule nibbattitvā vayappatto mahākappinarājā nāma ahosi, sesā amaccakule nibbattiṃsu. Jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa bhariyā maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagare rājakule [V 1.0315] nibbatti, anojapupphavaṇṇamevassā sarīraṃ ahosi, anojātvevassā nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Sā [P 2.0117] vayappattā mahākappinarañño gehaṃ gantvā anojādevī nāma ahosi. Sesitthiyopi amaccakulesu nibbattitvā vayappattā tesaṃyeva amaccaputtānaṃ gehāni agamaṃsu. Te sabbe rañño sampattisadisaṃ sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu. Yadā rājā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā vicari, tadā tepi tatheva vicaranti. Tasmiṃ assena vā rathena vā vicarante tepi tatheva vicaranti? Evaṃ te ekato hutvā katānaṃ puññānaṃ ānubhāvena ekatova sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu. Rañño pana balo, balavāhano, puppho, pupphavāhano, supattoti pañca assā honti. Rājā tesu supattaṃ assaṃ sayaṃ ārohati, itare cattāro assārohānaṃ sāsanāharaṇatthāya adāsi. Rājā te pātova bhojetvā “gacchatha [M 1.0354] dve vā tīṇi vā yojanāni āhiṇḍitvā buddhassa vā dhammassa vā saṅghassa vā uppannabhāvaṃ ñatvā mayhaṃ sukhasāsanaṃ āharathā”ti pesesi. Te catūhi dvārehi nikkhamitvā tīṇi yojanāni āhiṇḍitvā sāsanaṃ alabhitvā paccāgacchanti.

The chief householder’s wife, however, not acting in the same manner as the others but relying on her own wisdom, resolved: 'I will honor the Teacher with an extraordinary gift.' She took a basket of anojā flowers and a cloth of the color of anojā flowers worth a thousand, and at the time of the blessings, she honored the Teacher with the anojā flowers, placed the cloth at the Teacher’s feet, and made this aspiration: 'Venerable sir, in whatever state of existence I am reborn, may my body be the color of anojā flowers, and may my name be Anojā.' The Teacher gave his blessing, saying, 'So be it.' They all lived out their lifespans and, after passing away, were reborn in a deva world. At the time of this Buddha's arising, they passed away from the deva world. The chief householder was reborn into the royal family in the city of Kukkuṭavatī and, on coming of age, became King Mahākappina. The others were reborn in the families of ministers. The chief householder’s wife was reborn into the royal family in the city of Sāgala in the Madda country. Her body was the color of anojā flowers, and they gave her the name Anojā. When she came of age, she went to the household of King Mahākappina and became Queen Anojā. The other women were also reborn in the families of ministers and, on coming of age, went to the households of those same ministers' sons. All of them enjoyed a fortune equal to the king’s. When the king, adorned with all his ornaments, rode about on his elephant, they too would ride about in the same way. When he traveled by horse or by chariot, they too would travel in the same way. Thus, through the power of the merit they had made together, they enjoyed their good fortune together. The king had five horses: Bala, Balavāhana, Puppha, Pupphavāhana, and Supatta. The king himself rode the horse Supatta; the other four he gave to his horsemen for carrying messages. The king would feed them early in the morning and send them out, saying: 'Go, wander for two or three yojanas, and if you learn of the arising of a Buddha, a Dhamma, or a Sangha, bring me the happy news.' They would leave by the four gates, wander for two or three yojanas, and return without having found any such news.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā supattaṃ assaṃ āruyha amaccasahassaparivuto uyyānaṃ gacchanto kilantarūpe pañcasatavāṇijake nagaraṃ pavisante disvā “ime addhānakilantā, addhā imesaṃ santikā ekaṃ bhaddakaṃ sāsanaṃ sossāmī”ti [P 2.0118] te pakkosāpetvā “kuto āgacchathā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, ito vīsatiyojanasatamatthake sāvatthi nāma nagaraṃ, tato āgacchāmā”ti. “Atthi pana vo padese kiñci sāsanaṃ uppanna”nti. “Deva, aññaṃ kiñci natthi, sammāsambuddho pana uppanno”ti. Rājā tāvadeva pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīro kiñci sallakkhetuṃ asakkonto muhuttaṃ vītināmetvā, “tātā, kiṃ vadethā”ti pucchi. “Buddho, deva, uppanno”ti. Rājā dutiyampi tatiyampi tatheva vītināmetvā catutthe vāre “kiṃ vadetha, tātā”ti pucchitvā “buddho, deva, uppanno”ti vutte, “tātā, vo satasahassaṃ dadāmī”ti vatvā “aññampi kiñci sāsanaṃ atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, dhammo uppanno”ti. Rājā tampi sutvā purimanayeneva tayo vāre vītināmetvā catutthe vāre “dhammo uppanno”ti vutte “idhāpi vo satasahassaṃ dammī”ti vatvā “aparampi sāsanaṃ atthi, tātā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, saṅgharatanaṃ uppanna”nti. Rājā tampi sutvā tayo vāre vītināmetvā catutthe vāre “saṅgho”ti pade vutte “idhāpi vo satasahassaṃ dammī”ti vatvā amaccasahassaṃ oloketvā, “tātā, kiṃ karissathā”ti pucchi. “Deva, tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Ahaṃ, tātā, ‘buddho uppanno, dhammo uppanno, saṅgho uppanno’ti sutvā na puna nivattissāmi, satthāraṃ uddissa gantvā tassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi, deva[V 1.0316], tumhehi saddhiṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. Rājā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe akkharāni likhāpetvā vāṇijake āha [P 2.0119] – “anojā nāma devī tumhākaṃ tīṇi satasahassāni dassati, evañca pana naṃ vadeyyātha ‘rañño kira te issariyaṃ vissaṭṭhaṃ, yathāsukhaṃ sampattiṃ paribhuñjāhī’ti, sace pana vo ‘rājā kaha’nti pucchati, ‘satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajissāmīti vatvā gato’ti āroceyyāthā”ti. Amaccāpi attano attano bhariyānaṃ tatheva sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu[M 1.0355]. Rājā vāṇijake uyyojetvā assaṃ abhiruyha amaccasahassaparivuto taṃ khaṇaṃyeva nikkhami.

Then one day, the king, mounted on the horse Supatta and surrounded by a thousand ministers, was going to the park when he saw five hundred merchants entering the city, who appeared weary. Thinking, 'These are weary from a long journey; surely I will hear some good news from them,' he had them summoned and asked, 'From where have you come?' 'Your Majesty, one hundred and twenty yojanas from here, there is a city named Sāvatthī. We come from there.' 'But has any news arisen in your region?' 'Your Majesty, there is nothing else, but a Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen.' The king, at that very moment, his body suffused with fivefold joy, was unable to comprehend anything. After letting a moment pass, he asked, 'Sirs, what did you say?' 'A Buddha, Your Majesty, has arisen.' The king let a second and a third time pass in the same way. On the fourth occasion, having asked, 'Sirs, what did you say?' and when it was said, 'A Buddha, Your Majesty, has arisen,' he said, 'Sirs, I give you a hundred thousand.' Then he asked, 'Is there any other news?' 'Yes, Your Majesty, the Dhamma has arisen.' Hearing this, the king, in the same manner as before, let three times pass. On the fourth occasion, when it was said, 'The Dhamma has arisen,' he declared, 'For this too, I give you a hundred thousand.' Then he asked, 'Sirs, is there any further news?' 'Yes, Your Majesty, the Sangha-jewel has arisen.' The king, hearing this as well, let three times pass. On the fourth occasion, when the word 'Sangha' was uttered, he said, 'For this too, I give you a hundred thousand.' Then, looking at his thousand ministers, he asked, 'Sirs, what will you do?' 'Your Majesty, what will you do?' 'Sirs, I, having heard that "a Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Sangha has arisen," will not turn back. I will go with the Teacher as my destination and go forth in his presence.' 'Your Majesty, we too will go forth with you.' The king had letters inscribed on a golden leaf and said to the merchants, 'The queen named Anojā will give you three hundred thousand. And you should tell her this: "It seems the king has relinquished his sovereignty to you. Enjoy your fortune as you please." But if she asks, "Where is the king?" you should inform her, "He has departed, saying, ‘I will go forth with the Teacher as my destination.’"' The ministers likewise sent a similar message to their own wives. The king dismissed the merchants, mounted his horse, and surrounded by his thousand ministers, departed at that very moment.

Satthāpi taṃ divasaṃ paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento mahākappinarājānaṃ saparivāraṃ disvā “ayaṃ mahākappino vāṇijakānaṃ santikā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ uppannabhāvaṃ sutvā tesaṃ vacanaṃ tīhi satasahassehi pūjetvā rajjaṃ pahāya amaccasahassehi parivuto maṃ uddissa pabbajitukāmo sve nikkhamissati. So saparivāro saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati, paccuggamanamassa karissāmī”ti punadivase cakkavattī viya khuddakagāmabhojakaṃ paccuggacchanto sayameva pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vīsayojanasataṃ maggaṃ paccuggantvā candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre nigrodharukkhamūle chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjento nisīdi. “Rājāpi āgacchanto ekaṃ nadiṃ patvā “kā nāmesā”ti pucchi. “Aparacchā nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇaṃ, tātā”ti? “Gambhīrato [P 2.0120] gāvutaṃ, puthulato dve gāvutāni, devā”ti. “Atthi panettha nāvā vā uḷumpo vā”ti? “Natthi, devā”ti. “Nāvādīni olokente amhe jāti jaraṃ upaneti, jarā maraṇaṃ. Ahaṃ nibbematiko hutvā tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhanto, tesaṃ me ānubhāvena imaṃ udakaṃ udakaṃ viya mā ahosī”ti tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ āvajjetvā “itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti buddhānussatiṃ anussaranto saparivāro assasahassena udakapiṭṭhiṃ pakkhandi. Sindhavā piṭṭhipāsāṇe viya pakkhandiṃsu. Khurānaṃ aggā neva temiṃsu.

The Teacher also, on that day at dawn, surveying the world, saw King Mahākappina with his retinue and thought: 'This King Mahākappina, having heard from merchants of the arising of the Three Jewels, honored their words with three hundred thousand, renounced his kingdom, and, surrounded by a thousand ministers, desires to go forth for my sake and will depart tomorrow. He and his retinue will attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. I shall go out to meet him.' The next day, like a universal monarch going to meet a minor village headman, the Teacher himself took his bowl and robe, traveled one hundred and twenty yojanas to meet them, and sat at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, emitting the six-colored rays. The king also, while approaching, came to a river and asked, 'What is this river's name?' 'It is named Aparacchā, lord.' 'What are its dimensions, sirs?' 'In depth, a gāvuta; in width, two gāvutas, lord.' 'Is there a boat or a raft here?' 'There is not, lord.' 'While we look for boats and the like, birth leads us to old age, and old age to death. I have gone forth, free from doubt, for the sake of the Three Jewels. By their power, may this water not be like water!' Reflecting on the virtues of the Three Jewels and recollecting the Buddha with the words, 'Indeed, the Blessed One is the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,' he and his retinue rode forth onto the surface of the water with a thousand horses. The Sindhu horses advanced as if on a stone slab. The tips of their hooves did not get wet.

So taṃ uttaritvā purato gacchanto aparampi nadiṃ disvā “ayaṃ kā nāmā”ti pucchi. “Nīlavāhinī nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇa”nti? “Gambhīratopi puthulatopi aḍḍhayojanaṃ, devā”ti. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Taṃ pana nadiṃ disvā “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”ti dhammānussatiṃ anussaranto pakkhandi. Tampi atikkamitvā gacchanto aparampi nadiṃ disvā “ayaṃ kā nāmā”ti pucchi. “Candabhāgā nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇa”nti? “Gambhīratopi puthulatopi yojanaṃ, devā”ti. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Imaṃ [M 1.0356] pana nadiṃ disvā “suppaṭipanno [P 2.0121] bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”ti saṅghānussatiṃ anussaranto [V 1.0317] pakkhandi. Taṃ pana nadiṃ atikkamitvā gacchanto satthu sarīrato nikkhantā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo addasa. Nigrodharukkhassa sākhāviṭapapalāsāni sovaṇṇamayāni viya ahesuṃ. Rājā cintesi – “ayaṃ pana obhāso neva candassa, na sūriyassa, na devamārabrahmanāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ aññatarassa, addhā ahaṃ satthāraṃ uddissa āgacchanto mahāgotamabuddhena diṭṭho bhavissāmī”ti. So tāvadeva assapiṭṭhito otaritvā onatasarīro rasmianusārena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā manosilārase nimujjanto viya buddharasmīnaṃ anto pavisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi saddhiṃ amaccasahassena, satthā tassa anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Desanāvasāne rājā saparivāro sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Atha sabbeva uṭṭhahitvā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Satthā “āgamissati nu kho imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ iddhimayapattacīvara”nti upadhārento “ime kulaputtā paccekabuddhasahassassa cīvarasahassaṃ adaṃsu, kassapasammāsambuddhakāle vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānampi vīsaticīvarasahassānipi adaṃsu. Anacchariyaṃ imesaṃ iddhimayapattacīvarāgamana”nti ñatvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā [P 2.0122] “etha, bhikkhavo, caratha brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti āha. Te tāvadeva aṭṭhaparikkhāradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya hutvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā paccorohitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu.

Having crossed it, as he proceeded forward, he saw another river and asked, 'What is this river called?' 'It is called the Nīlavāhinī, Your Majesty.' 'What is its extent?' 'In depth and breadth, half a yojana, Your Majesty.' The rest was similar to the previous account. Upon seeing this river, recollecting the Dhamma with the words, 'Well-expounded is the Blessed One’s Dhamma,' he crossed over. Having crossed that river and proceeding further, he saw yet another river and asked, 'What is this river called?' 'It is called the Candabhāgā, Your Majesty.' 'What is its extent?' 'In depth and breadth, one yojana, Your Majesty.' The rest was similar to the previous account. Upon seeing this river, recollecting the Saṅgha with the words, 'Well-practiced is the Blessed One’s community of disciples,' he crossed over. Having crossed that river and proceeding further, he saw the six-colored rays emanating from the Teacher’s body. The branches, twigs, and leaves of the banyan tree appeared as if made of gold. The king reflected, 'This radiance is neither that of the moon nor the sun, nor of any deva, Māra, Brahmā, nāga, or supaṇṇa. Surely, as I approach intending to see the Teacher, I must have been seen by the great Gotama Buddha.' At once, he dismounted from his horse, bowed his body, and approached the Teacher following the rays, as if diving into a pool of red arsenic pigment, entering the Buddha’s radiance. He paid homage to the Teacher and sat to one side with his thousand ministers. The Teacher gave him a progressive discourse. At the end of the teaching, the king and his retinue were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, they all rose and requested ordination. The Teacher, considering whether psychically created robes and bowls would come to these clansmen, discerned, 'These clansmen once gave a thousand robes to a thousand paccekabuddhas, and in the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, they also gave twenty thousand robes to twenty thousand monks. It is no wonder that psychically created robes and bowls should come to them.' Knowing this, he stretched out his right hand and said, 'Come, monks, practice the holy life well for the complete ending of suffering.' Instantly, they became monks possessing the eight requisites, appearing like elders of sixty years’ standing. They rose into the air, descended, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.

Tepi vāṇijakā rājakulaṃ gantvā raññā pahitabhāvaṃ ārocāpetvā deviyā “āgacchantū”ti vutte pavisitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha ne devī pucchi – “tātā, kiṃ kāraṇā āgatātthā”ti? “Mayaṃ raññā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pahitā, tīṇi kira no satasahassāni dethā”ti. “Tātā, atibahuṃ bhaṇatha, kiṃ tumhehi rañño kataṃ, kismiṃ vo rājā pasanno ettakaṃ dhanaṃ dāpesī”ti? “Devi, na aññaṃ kiñci kataṃ, rañño pana ekaṃ sāsanaṃ ārocayimhā”ti? “Sakkā pana, tātā, mayhaṃ ārocetu”nti. “Sakkā, devī”ti. “Tena hi, tātā, vadethā”ti. “Devi buddho loke uppanno”ti. Sāpi “taṃ sutvā purimanayeneva pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīrā tikkhattuṃ kiñci asallakkhetvā catutthe vāre ‘buddho’ti padaṃ sutvā, tātā, imasmiṃ pade raññā kiṃ dinna”nti? “Satasahassaṃ, devī”ti. “Tātā[M 1.0357], ananucchavikaṃ raññā kataṃ evarūpaṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā tumhākaṃ satasahassaṃ dadamānena. Ahañhi vo mama duggatapaṇṇākāre tīṇi satasahassāni dammi, aparampi tumhehi rañño kiṃ ārocita”nti? Te idañcidañcāti [P 2.0123] itarānipi dve sāsanāni ārocayiṃsu. Devī purimanayeneva pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīrā tikkhattuṃ kiñci asallakkhetvā catutthe vāre tatheva sutvā tīṇi tīṇi satasahassāni dāpesi, evaṃ te sabbānipi dvādasa satasahassāni labhiṃsu.

Those merchants went to the royal court and, having announced that they had been sent by the king, when the queen said, “Let them come,” they entered, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then the queen asked them: “Sirs, for what reason have you come?” “We have been sent to you by the king; he says to give us three hundred thousand.” “Sirs, you speak of a very large amount. What have you done for the king? In what way was the king so pleased with you that he would have such a sum of wealth given?” “Your Majesty, we have done nothing else, but we delivered a single message to the king.” “Is it possible, sirs, to tell it to me?” “It is possible, Your Majesty.” “Then, sirs, speak.” “Your Majesty, a Buddha has arisen in the world.” On hearing this, her body was pervaded with joy just as before. Three times she did not grasp anything, but on the fourth occasion, having heard the word “Buddha,” she asked: “Sirs, for this word, what did the king give?” “A hundred thousand, Your Majesty.” “Sirs, the king has acted unworthily in giving you only a hundred thousand on hearing such a message. I myself will give you three hundred thousand as my humble gift. What else did you report to the king?” They told her the other two messages as well. The queen, her body pervaded with joy just as before, three times did not grasp anything, but on the fourth occasion, having heard them in the same way, she had three hundred thousand given for each. Thus they received twelve hundred thousand in all.

Atha [V 1.0318] ne devī pucchi – “rājā kahaṃ, tātā”ti? Devi, “satthāraṃ uddissa ‘pabbajissāmī’ti gato”ti. “Mayhaṃ tena kiṃ sāsanaṃ dinna”nti? “Sabbaṃ kira tena tumhākaṃ issariyaṃ vissaṭṭhaṃ, tumhe kira yathāruciyā sampattiṃ anubhavathā”ti. “Amaccā pana kahaṃ, tātā”ti? Tepi “‘raññā saddhiṃyeva pabbajissāmā’ti gatā, devī”ti. Sā tesaṃ bhariyāyo pakkosāpetvā, ammā, tumhākaṃ sāmikā “raññā saddhiṃ pabbajissāmā”ti gatā, “tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Kiṃ pana tehi amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ pahitaṃ, devī”ti? “Tehi kira attano sampatti tumhākaṃ vissaṭṭhā, tumhe kira taṃ sampattiṃ yathāruci paribhuñjathā”ti. “Tumhe pana, devi, kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Ammā, so tāva rājā sāsanaṃ sutvā magge ṭhitakova tīhi satasahassehi tīṇi ratanāni pūjetvā kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya sampattiṃ pahāya ‘pabbajissāmī’ti nikkhanto, mayā pana tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā tīṇi ratanāni navahi satasahassehi pūjitāni, na kho panesā sampatti nāma raññoyeva dukkhā, mayhampi dukkhāyeva. Ko raññā chaḍḍitakheḷapiṇḍaṃ jāṇukehi patiṭṭhahitvā mukhena gaṇhissati, na mayhaṃ sampattiyā attho, ahampi satthāraṃ uddissa gantvā pabbajissāmī”ti. “Devi, mayampi tumheheva saddhiṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Sace sakkotha, sādhu, ammā”ti? “Sakkoma, devī”ti. “Sādhu, ammā, tena [P 2.0124] hi ethā”ti rathasahassaṃ yojāpetvā rathaṃ āruyha tāhi saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā antarāmagge paṭhamaṃ nadiṃ disvā yathā raññā puṭṭhaṃ, tatheva pucchitvā sabbapavattiṃ sutvā “rañño gatamaggaṃ olokethā”ti vatvā “sindhavānaṃ padavalañjaṃ na passāma, devī”ti vutte “rājā tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhanto saccakiriyaṃ katvā gato bhavissati. Ahampi tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhantā, tesameva anubhāvena idaṃ udakaṃ viya mā ahosī”ti [M 1.0358] tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ anussaritvā rathasahassaṃ pesesi. Udakaṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇasadisaṃ ahosi. Cakkānaṃ aggagganemivaṭṭiyo neva temiṃsu. Eteneva upāyena itarā dve nadiyo uttari.

Then the queen asked them: “Sirs, where is the king?” “Your Majesty, he has gone for the sake of the Teacher, declaring, ‘I will go forth.’” “What message did he give for me?” “He has, it seems, relinquished all sovereignty to you; you may enjoy your fortune as you wish.” “But where are the ministers, sirs?” “Your Majesty, they too have gone, saying, ‘We will go forth with the king.’” She had their wives summoned and said: “Ladies, your husbands have gone, declaring, ‘We will go forth with the king.’ What will you do?” “Your Majesty, what message did they send for us?” “They have, it seems, relinquished their own fortune to you; you may enjoy that fortune as you wish.” “But what will you do, Your Majesty?” “Ladies, that king, on hearing the message, while still on the road, worshipped the Three Jewels with three hundred thousand, and abandoning his fortune like a lump of spittle, he departed, saying, ‘I will go forth.’ But I, on hearing the message of the Three Jewels, have worshipped the Three Jewels with nine hundred thousand. This fortune is not a source of suffering for the king alone; it is so for me too. Who would receive on their knees a lump of spittle discarded by the king and take it with their mouth? I have no use for this fortune. I too will go for the sake of the Teacher and go forth.” “Your Majesty, we too will go forth with you.” “If you are able, that is good, ladies.” “We are able, Your Majesty.” “Good, ladies. In that case, come.” She had a thousand chariots yoked, mounted a chariot, and set out with them. On the way, seeing the first river, she inquired just as the king had done and heard the whole story. She said, “Look for the king’s path.” When they replied, “Your Majesty, we do not see the hoofprints of the Sindhava horses,” she thought: “The king set out for the sake of the Three Jewels; he must have gone by making an act of truth. I too have set out for the sake of the Three Jewels. By their power, may this not be like water!” Recalling the virtues of the Three Jewels, she sent the thousand chariots across. The water became like a stone slab. Only the very rims of the wheels got wet. By this same method, she crossed the other two rivers.

Atha satthā tassāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā yathā attano santike nisinnā bhikkhū na paññāyanti, evamakāsi. Sāpi gacchantī gacchantī satthu sarīrato nikkhantā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo disvā tatheva cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā pucchi – “bhante, mahākappino tumhākaṃ uddissa nikkhanto āgatettha maññe, kahaṃ so, amhākampi naṃ dassethā”ti? “Nisīdatha tāva, idheva naṃ passissathā”ti[P 2.0125]. Tā sabbāpi tuṭṭhacittā “idheva kira nisinnā sāmike passissāmā”ti nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tāsaṃ anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi, anojādevī desanāvasāne saparivārā sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Mahākappinatthero tāsaṃ vaḍḍhitadhammadesanaṃ [V 1.0319] suṇanto saparivāro saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā tāsaṃ te bhikkhū arahattappatte dassesi. Tāsaṃ kira āgatakkhaṇeyeva attano sāmike kāsāvadhare muṇḍakasīse disvā cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na bhaveyya, tena maggaphalāni pattuṃ na sakkuṇeyyuṃ. Tasmā acalasaddhāya patiṭṭhitakāle tāsaṃ te bhikkhū arahattappatteyeva dassesi.

Then the Teacher, knowing of her approach, made it so that the monks sitting near him were not visible. As she was proceeding, she saw the six-colored rays issuing from the Teacher’s body. Thinking in the same way as before, she approached the Teacher, paid homage, stood to one side, and asked: “Venerable sir, I believe Mahākappina has come here, having set out on your account. Where is he? Please show him to us too.” “First sit down; you will see him right here.” All of them, with delighted minds, sat down, thinking, “Indeed, we will see our husbands while sitting right here.” The Teacher gave them a gradual discourse. At the conclusion of the discourse, Queen Anojā and her retinue attained the fruit of stream-entry. While listening to the Dhamma discourse being elaborated for them, the Venerable Mahākappina and his retinue attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. At that moment, the Teacher revealed to the women those monks who had attained arahantship. For if they had seen their husbands with shaven heads and wearing ochre robes at the very moment of their arrival, their minds would not have become concentrated, and thus they would have been unable to attain the paths and fruits. Therefore, only when their faith was firmly established did he reveal to them those monks, who had by then attained arahantship.

Tāpi te disvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, tumhākaṃ tāva pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta”nti vatvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Evaṃ kira vutte “satthā uppalavaṇṇāya āgamanaṃ cintesī”ti ekacce vadanti. Satthā pana tā upāsikāyo āha – “sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhikkhunīupassaye pabbajethā”ti. Tā anupubbena janapadacārikaṃ caramānā antarāmagge mahājanena abhihaṭasakkārasammānā padasāva vīsayojanasatikaṃ gantvā bhikkhunīupassaye pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthāpi bhikkhusahassaṃ ādāya ākāseneva jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā mahākappino rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīsu “aho sukhaṃ[P 2.0126], aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānento vicarati. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ – “bhante, mahākappino ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti udānaṃ udānento vicarati, attano kāmasukhaṃ rajjasukhaṃ ārabbha kathesi maññe”ti. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, kappina, kāmasukhaṃ rajjasukhaṃ [M 1.0359] ārabbha udānaṃ udānesī”ti. “Bhagavā me, bhante, taṃ ārabbha udānabhāvaṃ vā anudānabhāvaṃ vā jānātī”ti? Satthā “na, bhikkhave, mama putto kāmasukhaṃ rajjasukhaṃ ārabbha udānaṃ udāneti, puttassa pana me dhammapīti nāma dhammarati nāma uppajjati, so amatamahānibbānaṃ ārabbha eva udānaṃ udānesī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing them, they paid homage with the five-point prostration and said, “Venerable sirs, your task of the going forth has reached its consummation.” Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side and requested the going forth. (Some say that when this was said, the Teacher was thinking of the arrival of Uppalavaṇṇā.) The Teacher, however, said to those laywomen: “Go to Sāvatthī and go forth at the nunnery.” Traveling by stages through the country, honored and revered by the populace along the way, they went on foot for one hundred and twenty yojanas, went forth at the nunnery, and attained arahantship. The Teacher, too, taking the thousand monks, went through the air to the Jeta Grove. There, it seems, the Venerable Mahākappina was spending his time in places of seclusion for the night and day, uttering the inspired utterance: “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” The monks reported this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, Mahākappina is spending his time uttering the inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’ We think he is speaking with reference to his former sensual happiness and royal happiness.” The Teacher had him summoned and asked, “Is it true, Kappina, that you utter this inspired utterance with reference to sensual happiness and royal happiness?” He replied, “Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows whether I uttered it with reference to that or not.” The Teacher said: “No, monks, my son does not utter this inspired utterance with reference to sensual happiness or royal happiness. Rather, for my son, delight in the Dhamma and joy in the Dhamma have arisen. He utters this inspired utterance with reference to the deathless, great Nibbāna.” Then, connecting the incidents, he taught the Dhamma by speaking this verse:

79.

79.

“Dhammapīti sukhaṃ seti, vippasannena cetasā;

Ariyappavedite dhamme, sadā ramati paṇḍito”ti.

He who drinks the Dhamma lives in happiness with a serene mind; the wise one ever delights in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.

Tattha dhammapītīti dhammapāyako, dhammaṃ pivantoti attho. Dhammo ca nāmesa na sakkā bhājanena yāguādīni viya pātuṃ? Navavidhaṃ pana lokuttaradhammaṃ nāmakāyena phusanto ārammaṇato sacchikaronto pariññābhisamayādīhi dukkhādīni ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhanto [P 2.0127] dhammaṃ pivati nāma. Sukhaṃ setīti desanāmattamevetaṃ, catūhipi iriyāpathehi sukhaṃ viharatīti attho. Vippasannenāti anāvilena nirupakkilesena. Ariyappavediteti buddhādīhi ariyehi pavedite [V 1.0320] satipaṭṭhānādibhede bodhipakkhiyadhamme. Sadā ramatīti evarūpo dhammapīti vippasannena cetasā viharanto paṇḍiccena samannāgato sadā ramati abhiramatīti.

Herein, 'he who drinks the Dhamma' means a drinker of the Dhamma, one who imbibes the Dhamma. This is the meaning. This Dhamma, however, cannot be drunk from a vessel like gruel and other things. But one who, with the mental body, makes contact with the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, who realizes it as an object, who penetrates the Noble Truths of suffering and so on by means of full understanding, breakthrough, and so on—such a one is said to ‘drink the Dhamma.’ 'Lives in happiness': this is just a figure of speech; the meaning is that one dwells happily in all four postures. 'With a serene mind': with a mind that is untroubled and undefiled. 'In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones': in the aids to enlightenment, with their divisions into the foundations of mindfulness and so on, proclaimed by the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas. 'Ever delights': such a drinker of the Dhamma, endowed with wisdom and dwelling with a mind serene with delight, always delights and takes great joy.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesunti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many became stream-enterers and so on.

Mahākappinattheravatthu catutthaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Mahākappina, the Fourth.

5. Paṇḍitasāmaṇeravatthu

5. The Story of the Wise Novice

Udakañhi nayantīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paṇḍitasāmaṇeraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Udakañhi nayanti,' concerning the wise novice.

Atīte kira kassapasammāsambuddho vīsatikhīṇāsavasahassaparivāro bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Manussā attano balaṃ sallakkhetvā aṭṭhapi dasapi ekato hutvā agantukadānādīni adaṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ satthā bhattakiccapariyosāne evaṃ anumodanamakāsi –

In the past, it is said, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand arahants, went to Bārāṇasī. The people, assessing their own capacity, gathered in groups of eight or ten and gave alms to the visitors and so forth. Then one day, at the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher gave this expression of appreciation:

“Upāsakā idha ekacco ‘attano santakameva dātuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ parena samādapitenā’ti attanāva dānaṃ deti, paraṃ na samādapeti[M 1.0360]. So [P 2.0128] nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne bhogasampadaṃ labhati, no parivārasampadaṃ. Ekacco paraṃ samādapeti, attanā na deti. So nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne parivārasampadaṃ labhati, no bhogasampadaṃ ekacco attanāpi na deti, parampi na samādapeti. So nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne neva bhogasampadaṃ labhati, na parivārasampadaṃ, vighāsādova hutvā jīvati. Ekacco attanā ca deti, parañca samādapeti. So nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne bhogasampadampi labhati parivārasampadampī”ti.

“Lay followers, here a certain person thinks, ‘It is proper to give only from my own possessions; what is the use of having encouraged another?’ Thus, he himself gives alms but does not encourage others. That person, in whatever place he is reborn, obtains the perfection of wealth, but not the perfection of a retinue. A certain person encourages others but does not give himself. That person, in whatever place he is reborn, obtains the perfection of a retinue, but not the perfection of wealth. A certain person neither gives himself nor encourages others. That person, in whatever place he is reborn, obtains neither the perfection of wealth nor the perfection of a retinue; he lives by eating leftovers. A certain person both gives himself and encourages others. That person, in whatever place he is reborn, obtains both the perfection of wealth and the perfection of a retinue.”

Taṃ sutvā samīpe ṭhito eko paṇḍitapuriso cintesi – “ahaṃ dāni tathā karissāmi, yathā me dvepi sampattiyo bhavissantī”ti. So satthāraṃ vanditvā āha – “bhante, svātanāya mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. “Kittakehi te bhikkhūhi attho”ti? “Kittako pana vo, bhante, parivāro”ti? “Vīsati bhikkhusahassānī”ti. “Bhante, sabbehi saddhiṃ svātanāya mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Satthā adhivāsesi. So gāmaṃ pavisitvā, “ammatātā, svātanāya mayā buddhappamukho bhikkhusaṅgho nimantito, tumhe yattakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dātuṃ [V 1.0321] sakkhissatha, tattakānaṃ dānaṃ dethā”ti ārocetvā vicaranto attano attano balaṃ sallakkhetvā “mayaṃ dasannaṃ dassāma, mayaṃ vīsatiyā, mayaṃ satassa, mayaṃ pañcasatāna”nti vutte sabbesaṃ vacanaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya paṇṇe āropesi.

Hearing that, a wise man standing nearby thought, 'Now I will act in such a way that both perfections will be mine.' Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said, 'Venerable Sir, please accept my alms-food for tomorrow.' 'With how many monks do you have need?' 'Venerable Sir, how large is your retinue?' 'Twenty thousand monks.' 'Venerable Sir, together with all of them, please accept my alms-food for tomorrow.' The Teacher consented. Having entered the village, he went about announcing, 'O mothers and fathers, for tomorrow I have invited the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. Please give alms to as many monks as you are able to.' When, after each had assessed their own capacity, they said, 'We will give to ten,' 'We to twenty,' 'We to a hundred,' 'We to five hundred,' he recorded the words of all from the beginning in a register.

Tena ca samayena tasmiṃ nagare atiduggatabhāveneva “mahāduggato”ti [P 2.0129] paññāto eko puriso atthi. So tampi sammukhāgataṃ disvā, samma mahāduggata, mayā svātanāya buddhappamukho bhikkhusaṅgho nimantito, sve nagaravāsino dānaṃ dassanti, “tvaṃ kati bhikkhū bhojessasī”ti? “Sāmi, mayhaṃ kiṃ bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūhi nāma sadhanānaṃ attho, mayhaṃ pana sve yāguatthāya taṇḍulanāḷimattampi natthi, ahaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvāmi, kiṃ me bhikkhūhī”ti? Samādapakena nāma byattena bhavitabbaṃ. Tasmā so tena “natthī”ti vuttepi tuṇhībhūto ahutvā evamāha – “samma mahāduggata, imasmiṃ nagare subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā sukhumavatthaṃ nivāsetvā nānābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā sirisayane sayamānā bahū janā sampattiṃ anubhavanti, tvaṃ pana divasaṃ bhatiṃ katvā kucchipūraṇamattampi na labhasi, evaṃ [M 1.0361] santepi ‘ahaṃ pubbe puññaṃ akatattā kiñci na labhāmī’ti na jānāsī”ti? “Jānāmi, sāmī”ti. “Atha kasmā idāni puññaṃ na karosi, tvaṃ yuvā balasampanno, kiṃ tayā bhatiṃ katvāpi yathābalaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? So tasmiṃ kathenteyeva saṃvegappatto hutvā “mayhampi ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṇṇe āropehi, kiñcideva bhatiṃ katvā ekassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Itaro “kiṃ ekena bhikkhunā paṇṇe āropitenā”ti na āropesi? Mahāduggatopi [P 2.0130] gehaṃ gantvā bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, nagaravāsino sve saṅghabhattaṃ karissanti, ahampi samādapakena ‘ekassa bhikkhaṃ dehī’ti vutto, mayampi sve ekassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā”ti. Athassa bhariyā “mayaṃ daliddā, kasmā tayā sampaṭicchita”nti avatvāva, “sāmi, bhaddakaṃ te kataṃ, mayaṃ pubbepi kiñci adatvā idāni duggatā jātā, mayaṃ ubhopi bhatiṃ katvā ekassa bhikkhaṃ dassāma, sāmī”ti vatvā ubhopi gehā nikkhamitvā bhatiṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu.

At that time, in that city, there was a man known as 'Mahāduggata' precisely because of his extreme poverty. The organizer, seeing him in his presence, said, 'Friend Mahāduggata, for tomorrow I have invited the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. Tomorrow the city-dwellers will give alms. How many monks will you feed?' 'Sir, what need have I of monks? Monks are for those who have wealth. As for me, tomorrow I do not even have a measure of rice for gruel. I live by working for wages. What use are monks to me?' One who encourages should indeed be skilled. Therefore, that organizer, even when told 'I have nothing,' did not remain silent but spoke thus: 'Friend Mahāduggata, in this city many people enjoy prosperity, eating fine food, wearing fine clothes, adorned with various ornaments, and sleeping on splendid beds. But you, working for wages by day, do not get even enough to fill your stomach. This being so, do you not know, "Because I did not make merit in the past, I get nothing"?' 'I know, sir.' 'Then why do you not make merit now? You are young and endowed with strength. Why is it not proper for you, even having worked for wages, to give alms according to your ability?' While the other was still speaking, he became stirred with emotion and said, 'Put down one monk for me too on the list. Having done some work for wages, I will give alms-food to one monk.' The other, thinking, 'What is the use of putting one monk on the list?', did not put him down. Mahāduggata, however, went home and said to his wife, 'Dear, tomorrow the city-dwellers will make an offering of food to the Sangha. I too was told by the organizer, "Give alms-food to one monk." We too will give alms-food to one monk tomorrow.' Then his wife, without saying, 'We are poor, why did you accept?', said, 'Husband, you have done a good thing. Because in the past we gave nothing, we have now become poor. Husband, let us both work for wages and give alms-food to one monk.' Having said this, both left the house and went to a place of work.

Mahāseṭṭhi taṃ disvā “kiṃ, samma mahāduggata, bhatiṃ karissasī”ti pucchi. “Āma, ayyā”ti. “Kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Yaṃ tumhe kāressatha, taṃ karissāmī”ti. “Tena hi mayaṃ sve dve tīṇi bhikkhusatāni bhojessāma, ehi, dārūni phālehī”ti vāsipharasuṃ nīharitvā dāpesi. Mahāduggato daḷhaṃ kacchaṃ bandhitvā mahussāhappatto vāsiṃ pahāya pharasuṃ gaṇhanto, pharasuṃ pahāya vāsiṃ gaṇhanto dārūni phāleti. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi āha – “samma, tvaṃ ajja ativiya ussāhappatto kammaṃ karosi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Sāmi, ahaṃ sve [V 1.0322] ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhojessāmī”ti. Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhi pasannamānaso cintesi – “aho iminā dukkaraṃ kataṃ, ‘ahaṃ duggato’ti tuṇhībhāvaṃ anāpajjitvā ‘bhatiṃ katvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhojessāmī’ti vadatī”ti. Seṭṭhibhariyāpi tassa bhariyaṃ disvā, “amma, kiṃ kammaṃ karissasī”ti pucchitvā “yaṃ tumhe [P 2.0131] kāressatha, taṃ karomī”ti vutte udukkhalasālaṃ pavesetvā suppamusalādīni dāpesi. Sā naccantī viya tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā vīhiṃ koṭṭeti ceva ophuṇāti ca. Atha naṃ seṭṭhibhariyā pucchi – “amma, tvaṃ ativiya tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā kammaṃ karosi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Ayye, imaṃ bhatiṃ katvā mayampi ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhojessāmā”ti. Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhibhariyāpi tassaṃ “aho vatāyaṃ dukkarakārikā”ti pasīdi. Seṭṭhi mahāduggatassa dārūnaṃ [M 1.0362] phālitakāle “ayaṃ te bhatī”ti sālīnaṃ catasso nāḷiyo dāpetvā “ayaṃ te tuṭṭhidāyo”ti aparāpi catasso nāḷiyo dāpesi.

Seeing him, the great merchant asked, “Friend Mahāduggata, will you work for wages?” “Yes, master,” he replied. “What work will you do?” “Whatever you have me do, that I will do.” “Well then, tomorrow we will feed two or three hundred monks. Come, split the firewood.” He had an adze and an axe brought out and given to him. Mahāduggata, having tightly fastened his loincloth and filled with great energy, split the firewood, switching back and forth between the adze and the axe. Then the merchant said to him, “Friend, today you are working with extraordinary energy—what, indeed, is the reason?” “Master, tomorrow I will feed one monk.” Hearing this, the merchant, his mind pleased, thought, “Ah, what a difficult thing this man has done! Without resorting to silence thinking ‘I am poor,’ he declares, ‘Having worked for wages, I will feed one monk!’” The merchant’s wife, too, seeing his wife, asked, “Mother, what work will you do?” When she replied, “Whatever you have me do, that I will do,” she had her enter the rice-husking shed and gave her winnowing fans, pestles, and so on. As if dancing, greatly delighted, she both pounded and winnowed the paddy. Then the merchant’s wife asked her, “Mother, you are working with extraordinary delight and joy—what, indeed, is the reason?” “Noble lady, by doing this wage-work, we too will feed one monk.” Hearing this, the merchant’s wife was also pleased with her, thinking, “Ah, what a doer of difficult deeds this woman is!” When Mahāduggata had split the firewood, the merchant said, “This is your wage,” and had four nāḷis of Sāli rice given to him. Then he added, “This is a gift of appreciation,” and had another four nāḷis given to him.

So gehaṃ gantvā bhariyaṃ āha – “mayā bhatiṃ katvā sāli laddho, ayaṃ nivāpo bhavissati, tayā laddhāya bhatiyā dadhitelakaṭukabhaṇḍāni gaṇhāhī”ti. Seṭṭhibhariyāpi puna tassā ekaṃ sappikaroṭikañceva dadhibhājanañca kaṭukabhaṇḍañca suddhataṇḍuḷināḷiñca dāpesi. Iti ca ubhinnampi nava taṇḍulanāḷiyo ahesuṃ. Te “deyyadhammo no laddho”ti tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā pātova uṭṭhahiṃsu. Bhariyā mahāduggataṃ āha – “gaccha, sāmi, paṇṇaṃ pariyesitvā āharā”ti. So antarāpaṇe paṇṇaṃ adisvā nadītīraṃ gantvā “ajja ayyānaṃ bhojanaṃ dātuṃ labhissāmī”ti pahaṭṭhamānaso gāyanto paṇṇaṃ uccinati. Mahājālaṃ khipitvā ṭhito kevaṭṭo [P 2.0132] “mahāduggatassa saddena bhavitabba”nti taṃ pakkositvā pucchi – “ativiya tuṭṭhacitto gāyasi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Paṇṇaṃ uccināmi, sammā”ti. “Kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhojessāmī”ti. “Aho sukhito, bhikkhu, so tava kiṃ paṇṇaṃ khādissatī”ti? “Kiṃ karomi, samma, attanā laddhapaṇṇena bhojessāmī”ti? “Tena hi ehī”ti. “Kiṃ karomi, sammā”ti? “Ime macche gahetvā pādagghanakāni aḍḍhagghanakāni kahāpaṇagghanakāni ca uddānāni karohī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Baddhabaddhe macche nagaravāsino nimantitanimantitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya hariṃsu. Tassa macchuddānāni karontasseva bhikkhācāravelā pāpuṇi. So velaṃ sallakkhetvā “gamissāmahaṃ, samma, ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āgamanavelā”ti āha. “Atthi pana kiñci macchuddāna”nti? “Natthi, samma, sabbāni khīṇānī”ti. “Tena hi mayā attano atthāya vālukāya nikhaṇitvā cattāro rohitamacchā ṭhapitā, sace bhikkhuṃ bhojetukāmosi, ime gahetvā gacchā”ti te macche tassa adāsi.

Having gone home, he said to his wife: “I have obtained Sāli rice by working for wages. This will be our provision. With the wages you have earned, buy curds, oil, and spices.” The merchant's wife also had a pot of ghee, a pot of curds, some spices, and a nāḷi of pure husked rice given to her. Thus, between the two of them, there were nine nāḷis of husked rice. Delighted and joyful, they rose very early, thinking: “We have obtained a gift for offering.” The wife said to Mahāduggata: “Go, husband, search for leafy greens and bring them back.” Not finding any leafy greens in the market, he went to the riverbank. With an elated mind, singing and thinking, “Today I will be able to give a meal to the noble ones,” he began gathering leafy greens. A fisherman, standing there after casting a large net, thought, “This must be the voice of Mahāduggata,” and calling him over, asked: “You are singing with great joy; what is the reason?” “I am gathering leafy greens, friend.” “What will you do with them?” “I will feed a monk.” “Ah, what a fortunate monk! Will he eat your leafy greens?” “What can I do, friend? I will feed him with the leafy greens I have obtained.” “Well then, come here.” “What should I do, friend?” “Take these fish and make them into strings worth a quarter-kahāpaṇa, a half-kahāpaṇa, and a kahāpaṇa.” He did so. The townspeople took each string of fish as it was made for the monks they had respectively invited. While he was still making the strings of fish, the time for the alms-round arrived. Noticing the time, he said: “Friend, I must go now; this is the time for the monks to arrive.” “Are there any strings of fish left?” “No, friend, they are all gone.” “Well then, I have buried four rohita fish in the sand for myself; if you wish to feed a monk, take these and go.” And he gave him those fish.

Taṃ [V 1.0323] divasaṃ pana satthā paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento mahāduggataṃ attano ñāṇajālassa anto paviṭṭhaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti āvajjento “mahāduggato ‘ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhojessāmī’ti bhariyāya [M 1.0363] saddhiṃ hiyyo bhatiṃ akāsi, kataraṃ nu kho bhikkhuṃ labhissatī”ti cintetvā “manussā [P 2.0133] paṇṇe āropitasaññāya bhikkhū gahetvā attano attano gehesu nisīdāpessanti, mahāduggato maṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ na labhissatī”ti upadhāresi. Buddhā kira duggatesu anukampaṃ karonti. Tasmā satthā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā “mahāduggataṃ saṅgaṇhissāmī”ti gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Mahāduggatepi macche gahetvā gehaṃ pavisante sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti olokento “hiyyo, mahāduggato ‘ekassa bhikkhuno bhikkhaṃ dassāmī’ti attano bhariyāya saddhiṃ bhatiṃ akāsi, kataraṃ nu kho bhikkhuṃ labhissatī”ti cintetvā “natthetassa añño bhikkhu, satthā pana mahāduggatassa saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinno. Mahāduggato attano upakappanakaṃ yāgubhattaṃ paṇṇasūpeyyampi tathāgatassa dadeyya, “yaṃnūnāhaṃ mahāduggatassa gehaṃ gantvā bhattakārakakammaṃ kareyya”nti aññātakavesena tassa gehasamīpaṃ gantvā “atthi nu kho kassaci kiñci bhatiyā kātabba”nti pucchi. Mahāduggato taṃ disvā āha – “samma, kiṃ kammaṃ karissasī”ti? “Ahaṃ, sāmi, sabbasippiko, mayhaṃ ajānanasippaṃ nāma natthi, yāgubhattādīnipi sampādetuṃ jānāmī”ti. “Samma, mayaṃ tava kammena atthikā, tuyhaṃ pana kiñci dātabbaṃ bhatiṃ na passāmā”ti. “Kiṃ pana te kattabba”nti? “Ekassa [P 2.0134] bhikkhussa bhikkhaṃ dātukāmomhi, tassa yāgubhattasaṃvidhānaṃ icchāmī”ti. “Sace bhikkhussa bhikkhaṃ dassasi, na me bhatiyā attho, kiṃ mama puññaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? “Evaṃ sante sādhu, samma, pavisā”ti. So tassa gehaṃ pavisitvā telataṇḍulādīni āharāpetvā “gaccha, attano pattabhikkhuṃ ānehī”ti taṃ uyyojesi. Dānaveyyāvaṭikopi paṇṇe āropitaniyāmeneva tesaṃ tesaṃ gehāni bhikkhū pahiṇi.

On that day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the very poor man who had entered the net of His knowledge. Adverting to it, He thought: 'What will come of this?' He reflected: 'Yesterday the very poor man worked for wages with his wife, thinking, “I will feed a monk.” Which monk will he get?' Then He considered: 'People, by the sign of the assigned leaves, will take monks and have them sit in their respective homes. The very poor man will not get any monk other than me.' For Buddhas, it is said, have compassion for the poor. Therefore, having attended to His bodily needs early in the morning, the Teacher entered the fragrant chamber and sat down, thinking, 'I will extend my support to the very poor man.' As the very poor man was entering his house with the fish, Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed signs of heat. Looking to see the reason, he thought: 'Yesterday the very poor man worked for wages with his wife, thinking, “I will give alms to one monk.” Which monk will he get?' He reflected: 'There is no other monk for him; the Teacher Himself is seated in the fragrant chamber, intending to extend His support to the very poor man. The very poor man might give his own suitable portion of gruel, rice, and leaf-curry to the Tathāgata. What if I were to go to the very poor man’s house and do the work of preparing the meal?' In the guise of a stranger, he went near his house and asked: 'Is there any work to be done for wages?' The very poor man saw him and said: 'Friend, what kind of work can you do?' 'Master, I am an expert in all crafts; there is no craft I do not know. I also know how to prepare things like gruel and rice.' 'Friend, we have need of your work, but we see nothing to give you as wages.' 'What is it that you need to have done?' 'I wish to give alms to one monk, and I desire the preparation of gruel and rice for him.' 'If you are giving alms to a monk, I have no need for wages. Does merit not also accrue to me?' 'In that case, it is good, friend. Come in.' He entered his house, had oil, rice, and other things brought, and then sent the man off, saying: 'Go and bring the monk who has been allotted to you.' The one in charge of the donations, following the very rule of the assigned leaves, sent the monks to their respective houses.

Mahāduggato tassa santikaṃ gantvā “mayhaṃ pattabhikkhuṃ dehī”ti āha. So tasmiṃ khaṇe satiṃ labhitvā “ahaṃ tava bhikkhuṃ pamuṭṭho”ti āha. Mahāduggato tikhiṇāya sattiyā kucchiyaṃ pahaṭo viya, “sāmi, kasmā maṃ nāsesi, ahaṃ tayā hiyyo samādapito bhariyāya saddhiṃ divasaṃ bhatiṃ katvā ajja pātova paṇṇatthāya nadītīre āhiṇḍitvā āgato, dehi me ekaṃ bhikkhu”nti bāhā paggayha paridevi. Manussā sannipatitvā [M 1.0364] “kimetaṃ, mahāduggatā”ti pucchiṃsu. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Te veyyāvaṭikaṃ pucchiṃsu – “saccaṃ kira, samma, tayā esa ‘bhatiṃ katvā ekassa bhikkhussa bhikkhaṃ dehī’ti samādapito”ti? “Āma[V 1.0324], ayyā”ti. “Bhāriyaṃ te kammaṃ kataṃ, yo tvaṃ ettake bhikkhū saṃvidahanto etassa ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ nādāsī”ti. So tesaṃ vacanena maṅkubhūto taṃ āha – “samma mahāduggata, mā maṃ nāsayi, ahaṃ [P 2.0135] tava kāraṇā mahāvihesaṃ patto, manussā paṇṇe āropitaniyāmena attano attano pattabhikkhū nayiṃsu, attano gehe nisinnabhikkhuṃ nīharitvā dento nāma natthi, satthā pana mukhaṃ dhovitvā gandhakuṭiyameva nisinno, rājayuvarājasenāpatiādayo satthu gandhakuṭito nikkhamanaṃ olokentā nisinnā satthu pattaṃ gahetvā ‘gamissāmā’ti. Buddhā nāma duggate anukampaṃ karonti, tvaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā ‘duggatomhi, bhante, mama saṅgahaṃ karothā’ti satthāraṃ vanda, sace te puññaṃ atthi, addhā lacchasī”ti.

The very poor man went to him and said, 'Give me my allotted monk.' At that moment, the man, recollecting himself, said, 'I have forgotten your monk.' The very poor man felt as if he had been struck in the belly with a sharp spear. Raising his arms, he lamented: 'Master, why do you ruin me? Yesterday I was instructed by you, and after working for wages all day with my wife, I came here this morning after wandering along the riverbank for greens. Give me one monk!' People gathered and asked, 'What is this, Mahāduggata?' He told them the matter. They questioned the one in charge of donations: 'Is it true, friend, that you instructed this man, saying, “Work for wages and give alms to one monk”?' 'Yes, sirs.' 'You have done a grave thing! While arranging for so many monks, you did not give a single one to this man.' Disconcerted by their words, he said to him: 'Friend Mahāduggata, do not ruin me. I have gotten into great trouble on your account. People have taken their own allotted monks according to the rule of the assigned leaves. There is no one who would take out a monk already seated in their home and give him away. However, the Teacher, having washed His face, is seated in the fragrant chamber. The king, the crown prince, the general, and others are sitting, watching for the Teacher to come out of the fragrant chamber, intending to take His bowl and go. Buddhas, by their nature, have compassion for the poor. Go to the monastery, pay homage to the Teacher, and say: “Venerable Sir, I am a poor man. Please grant me your support.” If you have merit, you will surely obtain Him.'

So vihāraṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ aññesu divasesu vihāre vighāsādabhāvena diṭṭhattā rājayuvarājādayo, “mahāduggata, na tāva bhattakālo, kasmā tvaṃ āgacchasī”ti āhaṃsu. So “jānāmi, sāmi, ‘na tāva bhattakālo’ti. Satthāraṃ pana vandituṃ āgacchāmī”ti vadanto gantvā gandhakuṭiyā ummāre sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, imasmiṃ nagare mayā duggatataro natthi, avassayo me hotha, karotha me saṅgaha”nti āha. Satthā gandhakuṭidvāraṃ vivaritvā pattaṃ nīharitvā tassa hatthe ṭhapesi. So cakkavattisiriṃ patto viya ahosi, rājayuvarājādayo aññamaññassa mukhāni olokayiṃsu. Satthārā dinnapattañhi [P 2.0136] koci issariyavasena gahetuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Evaṃ pana vadiṃsu, “samma mahāduggata, satthu pattaṃ amhākaṃ dehi ettakaṃ nāma te dhanaṃ dassāma, tvaṃ duggato dhanaṃ gaṇhāhi, kiṃ te pattenā”ti? Mahāduggato “na kassaci dassāmi, na me dhanena attho, satthāraṃyeva bhojessāmī”ti āha. Avasesā taṃ yācitvā pattaṃ alabhitvā nivattiṃsu. Rājā pana “mahāduggato dhanena palobhiyamānopi satthu pattaṃ na deti, satthārā ca sayaṃ dinnapattaṃ koci gahetuṃ na sakkoti, imassa deyyadhammo nāma kittako bhavissati, iminā deyyadhammassa dinnakāle satthāraṃ ādāya gehaṃ netvā mayhaṃ sampāditaṃ āhāraṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā satthārā saddhiṃyeva [M 1.0365] agamāsi. Sakkopi devarājā yāgukhajjakabhattasūpeyyapaṇṇādīni sampādetvā satthu nisīdanārahaṃ āsanaṃ paññapetvā nisīdi.

He went to the monastery. Then, because the king, crown prince, and others had seen him in the monastery on other days as a scrap-eater, they said: “Mahāduggata, it is not yet mealtime. Why have you come?” He replied: “Sirs, I know it is not yet mealtime. But I have come to pay homage to the Teacher.” So saying, he went and, placing his head on the threshold of the Fragrant Chamber, he paid homage with the five-point prostration and said: “Venerable sir, in this city there is no one more destitute than I. Be my refuge, grant me your support.” The Teacher opened the door of the Fragrant Chamber, brought out his bowl, and placed it in his hands. He became as if he had attained the glory of a universal monarch. The king, crown prince, and others looked at one another’s faces. Indeed, no one is able to take by force of authority a bowl given by the Teacher. But they said this: “Friend Mahāduggata, give us the Teacher’s bowl and we will give you so much wealth. You are destitute, so take the wealth. What will you do with the bowl?” Mahāduggata said: “I will not give it to anyone. I have no need for wealth. I will feed only the Teacher.” The others, having requested the bowl from him and not received it, turned back. The king, however, thought: “Mahāduggata does not give up the Teacher’s bowl even when tempted with wealth, and no one can take a bowl given by the Teacher himself. How much of an offering can he have? When he has given his offering, I will take the Teacher to my palace and give him the food I have prepared.” Thinking thus, he went along with the Teacher. Sakka, king of the devas, also prepared rice gruel, hard food, boiled rice, curries, and vegetables, and having prepared a seat suitable for the Teacher to sit on, he sat down.

Mahāduggato satthāraṃ netvā “pavisatha, bhante”ti āha. Vasanagehañcassa nīcaṃ hoti, anonatena pavisituṃ na sakkā. Buddhā ca nāma gehaṃ pavisantā na onamitvā pavisanti. Gehañhi pavisanakāle mahāpathavī vā heṭṭhā ogacchati, gehaṃ vā uddhaṃ gacchati. Idaṃ tesaṃ sudinnadānassa phalaṃ. Puna nikkhamitvā gatakāle sabbaṃ pākatikameva hoti. Tasmā satthā ṭhitakova [V 1.0325][P 2.0137] gehaṃ pavisitvā sakkena paññattāsane nisīdi. Satthari nisinne rājā āha – “samma mahāduggata, tayā amhākaṃ yācantānampi satthu patto na dinno, passāma tāva, kīdiso te satthu sakkāro kato”ti? Athassa sakko yāgukhajjakādīni vivaritvā dassesi. Tesaṃ vāsagandho sakalanagaraṃ chādetvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā yāguādīni oloketvā bhagavantaṃ āha – “bhante, ‘ahaṃ mahāduggatassa deyyadhammo kittako bhavissati, iminā deyyadhamme dinne satthāraṃ gehaṃ netvā attano sampāditaṃ āhāraṃ dassāmī’ti cintetvā āgato, mayā evarūpo āhāro na diṭṭhapubbo, mayi idha ṭhite mahāduggato kilameyya, gacchāmaha”nti satthāraṃ vanditvā pakkāmi. Sakkopi satthāraṃ yāguādīni datvā sakkaccaṃ parivisi. Satthāpi katabhattakicco anumodanaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.

Mahāduggata led the Teacher and said: “Please enter, venerable sir.” His dwelling was low, and it was not possible to enter without stooping. But Buddhas do not stoop when they enter a house. Indeed, when they enter a house, either the great earth sinks down or the house rises up. This is the fruit of their well-given gifts. Again, when they have departed and gone, everything becomes normal. Therefore the Teacher entered the house standing upright and sat down on the seat prepared by Sakka. When the Teacher was seated, the king said: “Friend Mahāduggata, you did not give us the Teacher’s bowl even when we requested it. Let us first see what kind of honor you have prepared for the Teacher.” Then Sakka uncovered his rice gruel, hard food, and other items and showed them. Their fragrant scent pervaded the entire city. The king, seeing the rice gruel and other things, said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I came here thinking: ‘How much of an offering will Mahāduggata have? When he has given his offering, I will take the Teacher to my home and give him the food I have prepared.’ But I have never before seen such food. If I stay here, Mahāduggata might be troubled, so I will go.” Having paid homage to the Teacher, he departed. Sakka also served the Teacher respectfully, giving him the rice gruel and other items. The Teacher also, having finished his meal, gave a discourse of appreciation, rose from his seat, and departed.

Sakko mahāduggatassa saññaṃ adāsi. So pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ anugacchi. Sakko nivattitvā mahāduggatassa gehadvāre ṭhito ākāsaṃ olokesi. Tāvadeva ākāsato sattaratanavassaṃ vassitvā tassa gehe sabbabhājanāni pūretvā sakalaṃ gehaṃ pūresi. Tassa gehe okāso nāhosi. Tassa bhariyā dārake hatthesu gahetvā nīharitvā bahi aṭṭhāsi. So satthāraṃ anugantvā nivatto dārake bahi disvā “kiṃ ida”nti pucchi. “Sāmi, sakalaṃ no gehaṃ sattahi ratanehi puṇṇaṃ, pavisituṃ okāso natthī”ti. So “ajjeva me dānena vipāko dinno”ti cintetvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā [P 2.0138] vanditvā, “kasmā āgatosī”ti vutte āha –“deva, gehaṃ me sattahi ratanehi puṇṇaṃ, taṃ dhanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Rājā “aho buddhānaṃ [M 1.0366] dinnadānaṃ, ajjeva matthakaṃ patta”nti cintetvā taṃ āha – “kiṃ te laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Dhanaharaṇatthāya sakaṭasahassaṃ, devā”ti. Rājā sakaṭasahassaṃ pesetvā dhanaṃ āharāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe okirāpesi. Tālappamāṇo rāsi ahosi. Rājā nagare sannipātāpetvā “imasmiṃ nagare atthi kassaci ettakaṃ dhana”nti pucchi. “Natthi, devā”ti. “Evaṃ mahādhanassa kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati, devā”ti. Rājā tassa mahāsakkāraṃ katvā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ dāpesi.

Sakka gave a sign to Mahāduggata. Taking the bowl, he accompanied the Teacher. Sakka turned back, stood at the door of Mahāduggata’s house, and looked up at the sky. Instantly, a rain of the seven treasures poured from the sky, filling all the vessels in his house and then the entire house. There was no space left in his house. His wife, taking the children by their hands, brought them out and stood outside. When he returned after accompanying the Teacher, he saw the children outside and asked: “What is this?” “Master,” she replied, “our entire house is filled with the seven treasures; there is no space to enter.” He thought, “The result of my gift has been given this very day,” and went to the king's presence. Having paid homage, he was asked by the king, “Why have you come?” He said: “Your Majesty, my house is filled with the seven treasures. Please take this wealth.” The king thought, “Oh, a gift given to the Buddhas has reached its culmination this very day,” and he asked him: “What is it proper for you to receive?” “A thousand carts to carry the wealth, Your Majesty.” The king sent a thousand carts, had the wealth brought, and had it piled up in the royal courtyard. The heap was the size of a palmyra palm. The king had the townspeople assembled and asked: “Does anyone in this city have this much wealth?” “No, Your Majesty.” “This being so, what is it proper to do for one with such great wealth?” “It is proper to give him the position of treasurer, Your Majesty.” The king, having paid him great honor, had the position of treasurer bestowed upon him.

Athassa pubbe ekassa seṭṭhino gehaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā “ettha jāte gacche harāpetvā gehaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā vasāhī”ti āha. Tassa taṃ ṭhānaṃ sodhetvā samaṃ katvā bhūmiyā khaññamānāya aññamaññaṃ āhacca nidhikumbhiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu. Tena rañño ārocite “tava puññena nibbattā, tvameva gaṇhāhī”ti āha. So gehaṃ kāretvā sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Tato parampi yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhanto puññāni karitvā āyupariyosāne devaloke nibbatto.

Then the king pointed out to him the site of a former treasurer’s house and said: “Have the thickets that have grown here cleared away, build a house, and live here.” When that site was being cleared and leveled for him, and the ground was being dug, treasure jars rose up, striking against one another. When he reported this to the king, the king said: “They have arisen through your merit; you yourself take them.” He had the house built and for seven days gave a great offering of alms to the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Thereafter, for as long as he lived, he performed meritorious deeds, and at the end of his life, he was reborn in a deva world.

Ekaṃ [V 1.0326] buddhantaraṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde tato cuto [P 2.0139] sāvatthiyaṃ sāriputtattherassūpaṭṭhākakule seṭṭhidhītu kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Athassā mātāpitaro gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā gabbhaparihāraṃ adaṃsu. Tassā aparena samayena evarūpo dohaḷo uppajji – “aho vatāhaṃ dhammadesanāpatiṃ ādiṃ katvā pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ rohitamaccharasena dānaṃ datvā kāsāyāni vatthāni nivāsetvā āsanapariyante nisinnā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ucchiṭṭhabhattaṃ paribhuñjeyya”nti. Sā mātāpitūnaṃ ārocetvā tathā akāsi, dohaḷo paṭipassambhi. Athassā tato aparesupi sattasu maṅgalesu rohitamaccharaseneva dhammasenāpatittherappamukhāni pañca bhikkhusatāni bhojesuṃ. Sabbaṃ tissakumārassa vatthumhi vuttaniyāmeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayamassa pana mahāduggatakāle dinnassa rohitamaccharasadānasseva nissando. Nāmaggahaṇadivase panassa, “bhante, dāsassa vo sikkhāpadāni dethā”ti mātarā vutte thero āha – “konāmo ayaṃ dārako”ti? “Bhante, imassa dārakassa kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya imasmiṃ gehe jaḷā eḷamūgāpi paṇḍitā [M 1.0367] jātā, tasmā me puttassa paṇḍitotveva nāmaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Thero sikkhāpadāni adāsi. Jātadivasato paṭṭhāya panassa “nāhaṃ mama puttassa ajjhāsayaṃ bhindissāmī”ti mātu cittaṃ uppajji. So sattavassikakāle mātaraṃ [P 2.0140] āha – “amma, therassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, tāta, ‘ahaṃ tava ajjhāsayaṃ na bhindissāmicceva manaṃ uppādesi’”nti vatvā theraṃ nimantetvā bhojetvā, “bhante, dāso vo pabbajitukāmo, ahaṃ imaṃ sāyanhasamaye vihāraṃ ānessāmī”ti theraṃ uyyojetvā ñātake sannipātāpetvā “mama puttassa gihikāle kattabbasakkāraṃ ajjeva karissāmā”ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ kāretvā taṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā “imaṃ, bhante, pabbājethā”ti therassa adāsi.

Having enjoyed celestial fortune for one Buddha-interval, he passed away from there and, during the dispensation of the present Buddha, took conception in Sāvatthī in the womb of a treasurer’s daughter from a family that supported the Elder Sāriputta. Then her parents, knowing that conception had been established, provided the protective care for the embryo. Later, a pregnancy craving of this sort arose in her: “Oh, that I might give an offering of red fish curry to five hundred bhikkhus headed by the General of the Dhamma, and then, having put on saffron robes and sat down at the end of the row of seats, I might eat the leftover rice of those bhikkhus!” She told her parents and did so, and the craving subsided. Then, on seven other auspicious occasions, they fed the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder, the General of the Dhamma, with red fish curry. All this should be understood in the same way as described in the story of the youth Tissa. This was the result of the offering of red fish curry given during his time as Mahāduggata. On the day of his naming, his mother said: “Venerable sir, please give the training precepts to your servant.” The elder asked: “What is this boy’s name?” “Venerable sir, from the time this boy took conception in my womb, even the foolish, stammering, and mute in this house have become wise. Therefore, my son’s name shall be Paṇḍita.” The elder gave him the training precepts. From the day of his birth, the thought arose in his mother: “I will not obstruct my son’s inclination.” When he was seven years old, he said to his mother: “Mother, I want to go forth under the elder.” “Good, my dear son. The thought had already arisen in me, ‘I will not obstruct your inclination.’” So saying, she invited the elder, offered him a meal, and said: “Venerable sir, your servant wishes to go forth. I will bring him to the monastery this evening.” After sending the elder off, she had her relatives assembled and said: “Let us today perform the honors for my son that should be done while he is a layman.” Having arranged a great display of honor, she took him to the monastery and gave him to the elder, saying: “Venerable sir, please give him the going forth.”

Thero pabbajjāya dukkarabhāvaṃ ācikkhitvā “karissāmahaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ ovāda”nti vutte “tena hi ehī”ti kese temetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbājesi. Mātāpitaropissa sattāhaṃ vihāreyeva vasantā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa rohitamaccharaseneva dānaṃ datvā sattame divase sāyaṃ gehaṃ agamaṃsu. Thero aṭṭhame divase antogāmaṃ gacchanto taṃ ādāya gacchati, bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ nāgamāsi. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Na tāvassa pattacīvaraggahaṇāni vā iriyāpatho vā pāsādiko hoti, apica vihāre therassa kattabbavattaṃ atthi. Thero hi bhikkhusaṅghe antogāmaṃ paviṭṭhe sakalavihāraṃ vicaranto asammajjanaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā tucchabhājanesu pānīyaparibhojanīyāni upaṭṭhapetvā dunnikkhittāni mañcapīṭhādīni paṭisāmetvā pacchā gāmaṃ pavisati. Apica “aññatitthiyā [P 2.0141] tucchavihāraṃ pavisitvā ‘passatha [V 1.0327] samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakānaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānānī’ti vattuṃ mā labhiṃsū”ti sakalavihāraṃ paṭijaggitvā pacchā gāmaṃ pavisati. Tasmā taṃ divasampi sāmaṇerena pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā divātaraṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi.

The elder explained the difficulty of the going forth. When the boy said, “Venerable sir, I shall follow your instruction,” the elder replied, “Well then, come.” He then wet the boy's hair, explained the meditation subject of the five constituents ending with the skin, and gave him the going forth. His parents stayed in the monastery for seven days, giving alms with the flavor of rohita fish to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, they returned home in the evening. On the eighth day, as the elder was going into the village, he took the novice along with him, but he did not go with the Sangha of bhikkhus. For what reason? Because the novice's handling of the bowl and robes and his deportment were not yet graceful. Moreover, the elder had duties to perform in the monastery. For when the Sangha of bhikkhus had entered the village, the elder would walk around the entire monastery, sweeping unswept areas, setting up drinking water and water for use in empty vessels, putting away improperly placed beds and chairs, and only then would he enter the village. Furthermore, thinking, “Let not the adherents of other sects, upon entering the empty monastery, be able to say, ‘Look at the sitting places of the recluse Gotama’s disciples!’” he would take care of the entire monastery before entering the village. Therefore, on that day too, having had the novice take his bowl and robes, he entered for alms later in the day.

Sāmaṇero upajjhāyena saddhiṃ gacchanto antarāmagge mātikaṃ disvā, “bhante, idaṃ kiṃ nāmā”ti pucchi. “Mātikā nāma, sāmaṇerā”ti. “Imāya kiṃ karontī”ti? “Ito cito ca udakaṃ āharitvā attano sassakammaṃ sampādentī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhante, udakassa cittaṃ atthī”ti[M 1.0368]? “Natthāvuso”ti. “Evarūpaṃ acittakaṃ attano icchitaṭṭhānaṃ haranti, bhante”ti? “Āmāvuso”ti. So cintesi – “sace evarūpampi acittakaṃ attano icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ haritvā kammaṃ karonti, kasmā sacittakāpi cittaṃ attano vase vattetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti. Atheso purato gacchanto usukāre saradaṇḍakaṃ aggimhi tāpetvā akkhikoṭiyā oloketvā ujukaṃ karonte disvā, “ime, bhante, ke nāmā”ti pucchi. “Usukārā nāmāvuso”ti. “Kiṃ panete karontī”ti? “Aggimhi tāpetvā saradaṇḍakaṃ ujuṃ karontī”ti. “Sacittako, bhante, eso”ti? “Acittako, āvuso”ti[P 2.0142]. So cintesi – “sace acittakaṃ gahetvā aggimhi tāpetvā ujuṃ karonti, kasmā sacittakāpi attano cittaṃ vase vattetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti. Atheso purato gacchanto dārūni araneminābhiādīni tacchante disvā, “bhante, ime ke nāmā”ti pucchi. “Tacchakā nāmāvuso”ti. “Kiṃ panete karontī”ti? “Dārūni gahetvā yānakādīnaṃ cakkādīni karonti, āvuso”ti. “Etāni pana sacittakāni, bhante”ti? “Acittakāni, āvuso”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “sace acittakāni kaṭṭhakaliṅgarāni gahetvā cakkādīni karonti, kasmā sacittakā attano cittaṃ vase vattetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti. So imāni kāraṇāni disvā, “bhante, sace tumhākaṃ pattacīvare tumhe gaṇheyyātha, ahaṃ nivatteyya”nti. Thero “ayaṃ adhunā pabbajito daharasāmaṇero maṃ anubandhamāno evaṃ vadetī”ti cittaṃ anuppādetvāva “āhara, sāmaṇerā”ti vatvā attano pattacīvaraṃ aggahesi.

The novice, while walking with his preceptor, saw an irrigation channel along the way and asked, “Venerable sir, what is this called?” “It is called a watercourse, novice.” “What do they do with this?” “They channel water from here and there to accomplish their farm work.” “But, venerable sir, does water have a mind?” “No, friend.” “Venerable sir, do they lead such a mindless thing to any place they wish?” “Yes, friend.” He thought: “If they can lead even such a mindless thing to any place they wish to do work, why can’t those with a mind bring their own minds under control and practice the duties of a recluse?” Then, as he walked on, he saw fletchers heating arrow-shafts over a fire and straightening them by sighting along them. He asked, “Venerable sir, who are these?” “They are fletchers, friend.” “What are they doing?” “They heat the arrow-shafts over a fire and straighten them.” “Venerable sir, does this arrow-shaft have a mind?” “It is mindless, friend.” He thought: “If they take a mindless arrow-shaft, heat it over a fire, and straighten it, why can’t those with a mind bring their own minds under control and practice the duties of a recluse?” Then, as he walked on, he saw carpenters shaping wood for things like the felloes, spokes, and hubs of wheels. He asked, “Venerable sir, who are these?” “They are carpenters, friend.” “What are they doing?” “They take wood and make wheels and other parts for vehicles, friend.” “But, venerable sir, does this wood have a mind?” “It is mindless, friend.” Then it occurred to him: “If they take mindless pieces of wood and make wheels and other things, why can’t those with a mind bring their own minds under control and practice the duties of a recluse?” Having seen these examples, he said, “Venerable sir, if you would take your bowl and robes, I would turn back.” The elder, without giving rise to the thought, “This young novice, so recently gone forth, speaks thus while following me,” simply said, “Bring them, novice,” and took his own bowl and robes.

Sāmaṇeropi upajjhāyaṃ vanditvā nivattanto, “bhante, mayhaṃ āhāraṃ āharanto rohitamaccharaseneva āhareyyāthā”ti āha. “Kathaṃ labhissāmāvuso”ti? “Bhante, attano puññena alabhantā mama puññena labhissathā”ti āha. Thero “daharasāmaṇerassa bahi nisinnakassa paripanthopi [P 2.0143] bhaveyyā”ti kuñjikaṃ datvā “mayhaṃ vasanagabbhassa dvāraṃ vivaritvā anto [V 1.0328] pavisitvā nisīdeyyāsī”ti āha. So tathā katvā attano karajakāye ñāṇaṃ otāretvā attabhāvaṃ sammasanto nisīdi. Athassa guṇatejena sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti [M 1.0369] upadhārento “paṇḍitasāmaṇero upajjhāyassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā ‘samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti nivatto, mayāpi tattha gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā cattāro mahārāje āmantetvā “vihārassa upavane vasante sakuṇe palāpetvā samantato ārakkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā candadevaputtaṃ “candamaṇḍalaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhāhī”ti, sūriyadevaputtaṃ “sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā sayaṃ gantvā āviñchanarajjuṭṭhāne ārakkhaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi, vihāre purāṇapaṇṇassa patantassapi saddo nāhosi, sāmaṇerassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi. So antarābhatteyeva attabhāvaṃ sammasitvā tīṇi phalāni pāpuṇi.

The novice, having paid homage to his preceptor and turned back, said, “Venerable sir, when you bring my food, please bring it with the flavor of rohita fish.” “How shall we obtain that, friend?” “Venerable sir, if you do not obtain it by your own merit, you will obtain it by my merit,” he said. The elder, thinking, “Danger might befall this young novice sitting outside,” gave him a key and said, “Open the door of my living quarters, go inside, and sit down.” He did so, and directing his knowledge to his own kamma-born body, he sat contemplating his personal existence. Then, by the power of his virtue, Sakka’s throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, wondering, “What can be the reason?” reflected: “The wise novice, having given his preceptor his bowl and robes, has turned back thinking, ‘I shall perform the duties of a recluse.’ It is proper for me to go there too.” Summoning the Four Great Kings, he instructed them: “Drive away the birds dwelling in the grove near the monastery and stand guard on all sides.” He told the deva Canda, “Draw back and hold the lunar disk,” and the deva Sūriya, “Draw back and hold the solar disk.” Then he himself went and stood guard at the post of the door-bolt rope. In the monastery, not even the sound of an old leaf falling was heard; the novice’s mind became one-pointed. Before the meal, while contemplating his personal existence, he attained the three fruits.

Theropi “sāmaṇero vihāre nisinno, tassa upakappanakaṃ bhojanaṃ asukakule nāma sakkā laddhu”nti ekaṃ pemagāravayuttaṃ upaṭṭhākakulaṃ agamāsi. Tattha ca manussā taṃ divasaṃ rohitamacche labhitvā therasseva āgamanaṃ olokento nisīdiṃsu. Te theraṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā[P 2.0144], “bhante, bhaddakaṃ vo kataṃ idhāgacchantehī”ti antogehe pavesetvā yāgukhajjakādīni datvā rohitamaccharasenassa piṇḍapātaṃ adaṃsu. Thero haraṇākāraṃ dassesi. Manussā “paribhuñjatha, bhante, haraṇakabhattampi labhissathā”ti vatvā therassa bhattakiccāvasāne pattaṃ rohitamaccharasabhojanassa pūretvā adaṃsu. Thero “sāmaṇero me chāto”ti sīghaṃ agamāsi. Satthāpi taṃ divasaṃ kālasseva bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā evaṃ āvajjesi – “paṇḍitasāmaṇero upajjhāyassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā ‘samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti nivatto, nipphajjissati nu kho assa pabbajitakicca”nti upadhārento tiṇṇaṃ phalānaṃ pattabhāvaṃ ñatvā “arahattassa upanissayo atthi, natthī”ti āvajjento “atthī”ti disvā “purebhattameva arahattaṃ pattuṃ sakkhissati, na sakkhissatī”ti upadhārento “sakkhissatī”ti aññāsi. Athassa etadahosi – “sāriputto sāmaṇerassa bhattaṃ ādāya sīghaṃ āgacchati, antarāyampissa kareyya dvārakoṭṭhake ārakkhaṃ gahetvā nisīdissāmi, atha naṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, tasmiṃ pañhe vissajjiyamāne sāmaṇero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti. Tato gantvā [M 1.0370] dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā sampattaṃ theraṃ cattāro pañhe pucchi, puṭṭhaṃ puṭṭhaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjesi.

The elder, too, thought: "The novice is sitting in the monastery. It should be possible to get some suitable food for him from such and such a family." He went to a family of supporters who were full of affection and respect for him. The people there had obtained rohita fish that day and were sitting looking out for the elder’s arrival. Seeing the elder coming, they said, "Venerable sir, it is good that you have come here." They led him into the house, gave him gruel and hard food, and then offered him almsfood with rohita fish curry. The elder indicated that he wished to take some away. The people said, "Please eat, venerable sir; you will also get food to take away." When the elder had finished his meal, they filled his bowl with the meal of rohita fish curry and gave it to him. The elder, thinking, "My novice is hungry," hurried back. The Teacher, too, having eaten early that day and gone to the monastery, reflected thus: "The wise novice, having given his preceptor his bowl and robes, has turned back thinking, ‘I will perform the duties of a recluse.’ Will his task as one gone forth be accomplished?" Investigating, he knew that the novice had attained the three fruits. Reflecting further, "Is there a supporting condition for arahantship or not?" he saw that there was. Then he considered, "Will he be able to attain arahantship before the meal or not?" and he knew that he would be able to. Then it occurred to him: "Sāriputta is coming quickly, bringing the novice’s food. An obstacle might arise for him. I will sit guarding the gatehouse and ask him questions. While the questions are being answered, the novice will attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges." Then he went and stood at the gatehouse, and when the elder arrived, he asked him four questions. The elder answered each question as it was asked.

Tatridaṃ pucchāvissajjanaṃ – satthā kira naṃ [P 2.0145] āha – “sāriputta, kiṃ te laddha”nti? “Āhāro, bhante”ti. “Āhāro nāma kiṃ āharati, sāriputtā”ti? “Vedanaṃ, bhante”ti. “Vedanaṃ kiṃ āharati, sāriputtā”ti? “Rūpaṃ, bhante”ti. “Rūpaṃ pana kiṃ āharati, sāriputtā”ti[V 1.0329]? “Phassaṃ, bhante”ti. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – “jighacchitena hi paribhutto āhāro tassa khuddaṃ pariharitvā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ āharati. Āhāraparibhogena sukhitassa sukhāya vedanāya uppajjamānāya sarīre vaṇṇasampatti hoti. Evaṃ vedanā rūpaṃ āharati. Sukhito pana āhārajarūpavasena uppannasukhasomanasso ‘idāni me assādo jāto’ti nippajjanto vā nisīdanto vā sukhasamphassaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti.

Here is the questioning and answering: The Teacher, it is said, asked him: "Sāriputta, what have you obtained?" "Food, Venerable Sir." "Sāriputta, what does food bring?" "Feeling, Venerable Sir." "Sāriputta, what does feeling bring?" "Form, Venerable Sir." "And Sāriputta, what does form bring?" "Contact, Venerable Sir." Herein is the meaning: "For food consumed by a hungry person removes his hunger and brings pleasant feeling. When one is happy from consuming food, with the arising of pleasant feeling, perfection of complexion occurs in the body. Thus feeling brings form. Then one who is happy, with happiness and joy having arisen on account of matter derived from nutriment, obtains pleasant contact whether lying down or sitting, thinking, ‘Now gratification has arisen for me.’"

Evaṃ imesu catūsu pañhesu vissajjikesu sāmaṇero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patto. Satthāpi theraṃ āha – “gaccha, sāriputta, tava sāmaṇerassa bhattaṃ dehī”ti. Thero gantvā dvāraṃ ākoṭesi. Sāmaṇero nikkhamitvā therassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhapetvā tālavaṇṭena theraṃ bīji. Atha naṃ thero āha – “sāmaṇera, bhattakiccaṃ karohī”ti. “Tumhe pana, bhante”ti. “Kataṃ mayā bhattakiccaṃ, tvaṃ karohī”ti. Sattavassikadārako pabbajitvā aṭṭhame divase taṃ khaṇaṃ vikasitapadumuppalasadiso arahattaṃ patto, paccavekkhitaṭṭhānaṃ pana paccavekkhanto nisīditvā [P 2.0146] bhattakiccamakāsi. Tena pattaṃ dhovitvā paṭisāmitakāle candadevaputto candamaṇḍalaṃ vissajjesi, sūriyadevaputto sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ. Cattāro mahārājāno catuddisaṃ ārakkhaṃ vissajjesuṃ, sakko devarājā āviñchanake ārakkhaṃ vissajjesi. Sūriyo majjhaṭṭhānato galitvā gato.

Thus, while these four questions were being answered, the novice attained arahantship along with the analytical knowledges. The Teacher also said to the elder, “Go, Sāriputta, give the food to your novice.” The elder went and knocked on the door. The novice came out, took the bowl from the elder's hand, set it aside in a suitable place, and fanned the elder with a palm-leaf fan. Then the elder said to him, “Novice, perform the task of eating.” “And you, venerable sir?” “I have performed the task of eating; you do so.” The seven-year-old boy, having gone forth, attained arahantship on the eighth day—at that moment he was like a newly blossomed lotus. But, reviewing the ground for reflection, he sat down and performed the task of eating. When he had washed the bowl and put it away, the deva’s son Canda released the moon’s orb, and the deva’s son Suriya, the sun’s orb. The Four Great Kings released their guards in the four directions. Sakka, king of the devas, released his guard at the place for pulling the door-cord. The sun, having slipped from its zenith, was gone.

Bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu, “chāyā adhikappamāṇā jātā, sūriyo majjhaṭṭhānato galitvā gato, sāmaṇerena ca idāneva bhuttaṃ, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti.
