Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā āgantvā pucchi – “bhikkhave, kiṃ kathethā”ti? “Idaṃ nāma, bhante”ti? “Āma, bhikkhave, puññavato samaṇadhammaṃ karaṇakāle [M 1.0371] candadevaputto candamaṇḍalaṃ, sūriyadevaputto sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhi, cattāro mahārājāno vihāropavane catuddisaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, sakko devarājā āviñchanake ārakkhaṃ gaṇhi, ahampi ‘buddhomhī’ti appossukko nisīdituṃ nālatthaṃ, gantvā dvārakoṭṭhake mama puttassa ārakkhaṃ aggahesiṃ, nettike ca mātikāya udakaṃ harante, usukāre ca usuṃ ujuṃ karonte, tacchake ca dārūni tacchante disvā ettakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā paṇḍitā attānaṃ dametvā arahattaṃ gaṇhantiyevā”ti [P 2.0147] vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The monks complained, “The shadow has grown to an excessive length, the sun has slipped from its zenith and is gone, and the novice has only just now eaten. What indeed can this be?” The Teacher, knowing of this event, came and asked, “Bhikkhus, what are you discussing?” “This very matter, venerable sir.” “Yes, bhikkhus, when a meritorious one performs the duties of a recluse, the deva’s son Canda draws and holds the moon’s orb, the deva’s son Suriya draws and holds the sun’s orb, the Four Great Kings take up guard in the monastery grove in the four directions, Sakka, king of the devas, takes up guard at the place for pulling the door-cord, and even I, though I am the Buddha, could not sit unconcerned. I went and took up guard at the gateway for my son. For that novice, having seen irrigators leading water by a channel, fletchers straightening an arrow, and carpenters shaping wood—by taking just this as an object, the wise tame themselves and attain arahantship.” Having said this, he made the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, recited this verse:

80.

80.

“Udakañhi nayanti nettikā, usukārā namayanti tejanaṃ;

Dāruṃ namayanti tacchakā, attānaṃ damayanti paṇḍitā”ti.

Irrigators indeed guide the water, fletchers shape the arrow-shaft; carpenters shape the wood; the wise tame themselves.

Tattha [V 1.0330] udakanti pathaviyā thalaṭṭhānaṃ khaṇitvā āvāṭaṭṭhānaṃ pūretvā mātikaṃ vā katvā rukkhadoṇiṃ vā ṭhapetvā attanā icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ. Nentīti nettikā. Tejananti kaṇḍaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nettikā attano ruciyā udakaṃ nayanti, usukārāpi tāpetvā tejanaṃ namayanti usuṃ ujuṃ karonti. Tacchakāpi nemiādīnaṃ atthāya tacchantā dāruṃ namayanti attano ruciyā ujuṃ vā vaṅkaṃ vā karonti. Evaṃ ettakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paṇḍitā sotāpattimaggādīni uppādentā attānaṃ damayanti, arahattappattā pana ekantadantā nāma hontīti.

In that verse: By digging a high place on the earth, filling a low place, making a channel, or placing a wooden trough, they lead water to whatever place they desire. Therefore, they are called irrigators (nettikā). 'Tejana' means an arrow. This is what is meant: Irrigators lead water according to their own desire. Fletchers, too, by heating an arrow-shaft, straighten it; they make the arrow straight. Carpenters, too, while shaping wood for the purpose of wheel-rims and so on, straighten the wood; according to their liking, they make it straight or crooked. In the same way, by making this much their object, the wise, while giving rise to the paths of stream-entry and so on, tame themselves. But those who have attained arahantship are indeed the completely tamed. This is the meaning of the verse.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Paṇḍitasāmaṇeravatthu pañcamaṃ.

The Story of the Novice Paṇḍita: The Fifth.

6. Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheravatthu

6. The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

Selo [P 2.0148] yathāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, which begins with the words, 'Just as a rock.'

Puthujjanā [M 1.0372] kira sāmaṇerādayo theraṃ disvā sīsepi kaṇṇesupi nāsāyapi gahetvā “kiṃ, cūḷapita, sāsanasmiṃ na ukkaṇṭhasi, abhiramasī”ti vadanti. Thero tesu neva kujjhati, na dussati. Dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “passathāvuso, lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheraṃ disvā sāmaṇerādayo evañcevañca viheṭhenti, so tesu neva kujjhati, na dussatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kiṃ kathetha, bhikkhave”ti pucchitvā “imaṃ nāma, bhante”ti vutte “āma, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavā nāma neva kujjhanti, na dussanti. Ghanaselasadisā hete acalā akampiyā”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that some worldlings, novices and the like, upon seeing the elder, would grab him by the head, ears, and nose, and say: 'What, little father, are you not dissatisfied with this Dispensation? Do you still delight in it?' The elder never got angry at them nor bore any resentment. In the Dhamma-hall a discussion arose: 'Friends, look how novices and the like harass the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya in this and that way, yet he never gets angry at them nor bears any resentment.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, what are you discussing?' When they told him, 'This very matter, venerable sir,' he said: 'Yes, bhikkhus, those whose taints are destroyed never get angry and never bear resentment. They are like a solid rock, stable and unshakable.' Then, making the connection, he taught the Dhamma by speaking this verse:

81.

81.

“Selo yathā ekaghano, vātena na samīrati;

Evaṃ nindāpasaṃsāsu, na samiñjanti paṇḍitā”ti.

Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by blame and praise.

Tattha nindāpasaṃsāsūti kiñcāpi idha dve lokadhammā vuttā, attho pana aṭṭhannampi vasena veditabbo. Yathā hi ekaghano asusiro selo puratthimādibhedena [P 2.0149] vātena na samīrati na iñjati [V 1.0331] na calati, evaṃ aṭṭhasupi lokadhammesu ajjhottharantesu paṇḍitā na samiñjanti, paṭighavasena vā anunayavasena vā na calanti na kampanti.

In that verse, regarding 'in blame and praise': although only two worldly conditions are mentioned here, the meaning should be understood in terms of all eight. For just as a solid, non-hollow rock is not stirred, shaken, or moved by winds from the east and so on, so too the wise do not waver when assailed by the eight worldly conditions; they are not moved through either aversion or attraction.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheravatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya: The Sixth.

7. Kāṇamātuvatthu

7. The Story of Kāṇā’s Mother

Yathāpi rahadoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kāṇamātaraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu vinaye (pāci. 230) āgatameva.

“As a deep lake…”: The Teacher spoke this discourse on the Dhamma while dwelling in the Jetavana, concerning Kāṇā’s mother. The story is indeed found in the Vinaya.

Tadā pana kāṇamātarā atucchahatthaṃ dhītaraṃ patikulaṃ pesetuṃ pakkesu pūvesu catukkhattuṃ catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dinnakāle satthārā tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ sikkhāpade paññatte kāṇāya sāmikena aññāya pajāpatiyā ānītāya kāṇā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “imehi me gharāvāso nāsito”ti diṭṭhadiṭṭhe bhikkhū akkosati paribhāsati. Bhikkhū [M 1.0373] taṃ vīthiṃ paṭipajjituṃ na visahiṃsu. Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā tattha agamāsi. Kāṇamātā satthāraṃ vanditvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakaṃ adāsi. Satthā katapātarāso “kahaṃ kāṇā”ti pucchi. “Esā, bhante, tumhe disvā maṅkubhūtā rodantī ṭhitā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Esā, bhante, bhikkhū [P 2.0150] akkosati paribhāsati, tasmā tumhe disvā maṅkubhūtā rodamānā ṭhitā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā pakkosāpetvā – “kāṇe, kasmā maṃ disvā maṅkubhūtā nilīyitvā rodasī”ti. Athassā mātā tāya katakiriyaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “kiṃ pana kāṇamāte mama sāvakā tayā dinnakaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, adinnaka”nti? “Dinnakaṃ, bhante”ti. “Sace mama sāvakā piṇḍāya carantā tava gehadvāraṃ pattā tayā dinnakaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, ko tesaṃ doso”ti? “Natthi, bhante, ayyānaṃ doso”. “Etissāyeva doso”ti. Satthā kāṇaṃ āha – “kāṇe, mayhaṃ kira sāvakā piṇḍāya caramānā gehadvāraṃ āgatā, atha nesaṃ tava mātarā pūvā dinnā, ko nāmettha mama sāvakānaṃ doso”ti? “Natthi, bhante, ayyānaṃ doso, mayhameva doso”ti satthāraṃ vanditvā khamāpesi.

At that time, Kāṇā’s mother, in order to send her daughter to her husband’s family not empty-handed, had fried some cakes. When, on four occasions, these were given to four bhikkhus, and the Teacher had laid down a training rule concerning this matter, Kāṇā’s husband brought another wife. Hearing this news, Kāṇā thought, “My household life has been destroyed by these bhikkhus,” and she abused and reviled whatever bhikkhus she saw. The bhikkhus did not dare to take that street. The Teacher, learning of the incident, went there. Kāṇā’s mother paid homage to the Teacher, had him sit on the prepared seat, and gave him gruel and solid food. After he had finished his morning meal, the Teacher asked, “Where is Kāṇā?” “Here she is, venerable sir, standing and weeping, abashed at seeing you.” “For what reason?” “Venerable sir, she abuses and reviles the bhikkhus; that is why, upon seeing you, she is abashed and stands weeping.” Then the Teacher had her summoned and said: “Kāṇā, why, upon seeing me, are you abashed, and hide and weep?” Her mother then told him what she had done. Then the Teacher said to her: “Kāṇā’s mother, did my disciples take what was given by you, or what was not given?” “What was given, venerable sir.” “If my disciples, wandering for alms, arrived at your house door and took what was given by you, what fault is it of theirs?” “There is no fault of the venerables, venerable sir. The fault is hers alone.” The Teacher said to Kāṇā: “Kāṇā, it seems my disciples, wandering for alms, came to your house door, and then your mother gave them cakes. What fault is there in this for my disciples?” “There is no fault of the venerables, venerable sir. The fault is mine alone.” She then paid homage to the Teacher and asked for his forgiveness.

Athassā satthā anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi, sā sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā [V 1.0332] vihāraṃ gacchanto rājaṅgaṇena pāyāsi. Rājā disvā “satthā viya bhaṇe”ti pucchitvā “āma, devā”ti vutte “gacchatha, mama āgantvā vandanabhāvaṃ ārocethā”ti pesetvā rājaṅgaṇe ṭhitaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “kahaṃ, bhante, gatātthā”ti pucchi. “Kāṇamātāya gehaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā, bhante”ti? “Kāṇā kira bhikkhū akkosati paribhāsati, taṃkāraṇā gatomhī”ti. “Kiṃ pana vo, bhante, tassā anakkosanabhāvo kato”ti? “Āma, mahārāja, bhikkhūnañca anakkosikā katā, lokuttarakuṭumbasāminī cā”ti[P 2.0151]. “Hotu, bhante, tumhehi sā lokuttarakuṭumbasāminī katā, ahaṃ pana naṃ lokiyakuṭumbasāminiṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā rājā satthāraṃ vanditvā paṭinivatto paṭicchannamahāyoggaṃ pahiṇitvā kāṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā sabbābharaṇehi alaṅkaritvā jeṭṭhadhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā “mama dhītaraṃ posetuṃ [M 1.0374] samatthā gaṇhantū”ti āha. Atheko sabbatthakamahāmatto “ahaṃ devassa dhītaraṃ posessāmī”ti taṃ attano gehaṃ netvā sabbaṃ issariyaṃ paṭicchāpetvā “yathāruci puññāni karohī”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya kāṇā catūsu dvāresu purise ṭhapetvā attanā upaṭṭhātabbe bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo ca pariyesamānāpi na labhati. Kāṇāya gehadvāre paṭiyādetvā ṭhapitaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ mahogho viya pavattati. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “pubbe, āvuso, cattāro mahallakattherā kāṇāya vippaṭisāraṃ kariṃsu, sā evaṃ vippaṭisārinī hutvāpi satthāraṃ āgamma saddhāsampadaṃ labhi. Satthārā puna tassā gehadvāraṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upasaṅkamanārahaṃ kataṃ. Idāni upaṭṭhātabbe bhikkhū vā bhikkhuniyo vā pariyesamānāpi na labhati, aho buddhā nāma acchariyaguṇā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti [P 2.0152] vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva tehi mahallakabhikkhūhi kāṇāya vippaṭisāro kato, pubbepi kariṃsuyeva. Na ca idāneva mayā kāṇā mama vacanakārikā katā, pubbepi katāyevā”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ sotukāmehi bhikkhūhi yācito –

Then the Teacher gave her a graduated discourse, and she attained the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher rose from his seat and, while going to the monastery, passed through the royal courtyard. The king saw him and asked, “Sirs, is that not the Teacher?” When it was said, “Yes, your majesty,” he sent them, saying, “Go and announce that I am coming to pay homage.” He then approached the Teacher, who was standing in the royal courtyard, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sir, where have you been?” “To the house of Kāṇā’s mother, great king.” “For what reason, venerable sir?” “It seems Kāṇā abuses and reviles the bhikkhus; for that reason I went.” “But, venerable sir, have you brought about for her a state of not abusing?” “Yes, great king. She has been made one who does not abuse the bhikkhus, and also a mistress of a supramundane household.” “So be it, venerable sir. You have made her mistress of a supramundane household; I, for my part, will make her mistress of a worldly household.” Having said this, the king paid homage to the Teacher, returned, sent a great covered carriage, had Kāṇā summoned, adorned her with all ornaments, established her in the position of his eldest daughter, and announced: “Let those who are able to support my daughter take her.” Then a chief minister for all affairs said, “I will support the king’s daughter.” He took her to his own home, handed over all authority to her, and said, “Make merit as you wish.” From then on, Kāṇā stationed men at the four gates and, though she herself searched for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who should be attended on, she could not find any. The edible and soft food prepared and placed at Kāṇā’s house door flowed on like a great flood. The bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the hall of Dhamma: “Friends, previously four elder theras caused Kāṇā to feel remorse. Though she was so remorseful, by approaching the Teacher she obtained the accomplishment of faith. The Teacher then made her house door a suitable place for bhikkhus to approach. Now, though she searches for bhikkhus or bhikkhunīs to attend on, she cannot find any. Ah, wonderful indeed are the qualities of the Buddhas!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what topic of discussion, bhikkhus, are you now gathered together?” When they told him it was this one, he said: “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that those elder bhikkhus caused Kāṇā to feel remorse; they did so in the past as well. And it is not only now that I have made Kāṇā do my bidding; I did so in the past as well.” Then, being requested by the bhikkhus who were eager to hear that matter, he related a story of the past.

“Yattheko labhate babbu, dutiyo tattha jāyati;

Tatiyo ca catuttho ca, idaṃ te babbukā bila”nti. (jā. 1.1.137) –

“Where one cat gets a mouse, a second one appears there; a third and a fourth as well. This, O cats, is your hole!”

Idaṃ babbujātakaṃ vitthārena kathetvā “tadā cattāro mahallakabhikkhū cattāro biḷārā ahesuṃ, mūsikā kāṇā, maṇikāro ahamevā”ti jātakaṃ samodhānetvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, atītepi kāṇā dummanā āvilacittā vikkhittacittā hutvā mama vacanena pasannaudakarahado viya vippasannacittā ahosī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having related this Babbujātaka in full, he connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time, the four elder bhikkhus were the four cats, the mouse was Kāṇā, and the gem-cutter was I myself.” Then he said: “Thus, bhikkhus, in the past too, Kāṇā, being dejected, with a turbid mind and a distracted mind, through my words became one with a perfectly serene mind, like a clear pool of water.” Having said this, connecting the theme, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

82.

82.

“Yathāpi [V 1.0333] rahado gambhīro, vippasanno anāvilo;

Evaṃ dhammāni sutvāna, vippasīdanti paṇḍitā”ti.

Just as a deep ocean is clear and untroubled, so too, having heard the teachings, the wise become perfectly serene.

Tattha [M 1.0375] rahadoti yo caturaṅginiyāpi senāya ogāhantiyā nakhubhati evarūpo udakaṇṇavo, sabbākārena pana caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro nīlamahāsamuddo rahado nāma. Tassa hi heṭṭhā cattālīsayojanasahassamatte ṭhāne [P 2.0153] udakaṃ macchehi calati, upari tāvattakeyeva ṭhāne udakaṃ vātena calati, majjhe catuyojanasahassamatte ṭhāne udakaṃ niccalaṃ tiṭṭhati. Ayaṃ gambhīro rahado nāma. Evaṃ dhammānīti desanādhammāni. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma rahado anākulatāya vippasanno, acalatāya anāvilo, evaṃ mama desanādhammaṃ sutvā sotāpattimaggādivasena nirupakkilesacittataṃ āpajjantā vippasīdanti paṇḍitā, arahattappattā pana ekantavippasannāva hontīti.

Herein, `rahado` means an ocean of such a kind that it is not agitated even by a four-limbed army plunging into it. In all aspects, however, the great blue ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, is called a `rahado`. Indeed, in its lower part, for a distance of about forty thousand yojanas, the water is moved by fish; in the upper part, for just that same distance, the water is moved by the wind; and in the middle, for a distance of about four thousand yojanas, the water stands motionless. This is called a deep `rahado`. The phrase `evaṃ dhammāni` means the teachings that have been taught. This is the intended meaning: Just as an ocean is especially clear due to being unagitated and is untroubled due to being motionless, so too, having heard my teaching of the Dhamma, the wise who attain a state of mind without defilements by way of the path of stream-entry and so on become especially serene. But having attained Arahantship, they become completely and especially serene indeed.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Kāṇamātuvatthu sattamaṃ.

The Story of Kāṇā's Mother, the Seventh.

8. Pañcasatabhikkhuvatthu

8. The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus

Sabbattha ve sappurisā cajantīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto pañcasate bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Desanā verañjāyaṃ samuṭṭhitā.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with `Sabbattha ve sappurisā cajanti`, with reference to five hundred bhikkhus. The discourse originated in Verañjā.

Paṭhamabodhiyañhi bhagavā verañjaṃ gantvā verañjena brāhmaṇena nimantito pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vassaṃ upagañchi. Verañjo brāhmaṇo mārāvaṭṭanena āvaṭṭo ekadivasampi satthāraṃ ārabbha satiṃ na uppādesi. Verañjāpi dubbhikkhā ahosi, bhikkhū santarabāhiraṃ [P 2.0154] verañjaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātaṃ alabhantā kilamiṃsu. Tesaṃ assavāṇijakā patthapatthapulakaṃ bhikkhaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Te kilamante disvā mahāmoggallānatthero pathavojaṃ bhojetukāmo, uttarakuruñca piṇḍāya pavesetukāmo ahosi, satthā taṃ paṭikkhipi. Bhikkhūnaṃ ekadivasampi piṇḍapātaṃ ārabbha parittāso nāhosi[M 1.0376], icchācāraṃ vajjetvā eva vihariṃsu. Satthā tattha temāsaṃ vasitvā verañjaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ apaloketvā tena katasakkārasammāno taṃ saraṇesu patiṭṭhāpetvā tato nikkhanto anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno ekasmiṃ samaye sāvatthiṃ patvā [V 1.0334] jetavane vihāsi, sāvatthivāsino satthu āgantukabhattāni kariṃsu. Tadā pana pañcasatamattā vighāsādā bhikkhū nissāya antovihāreyeva vasanti. Te bhikkhūnaṃ bhuttāvasesāni paṇītabhojanāni bhuñjitvā niddāyitvā uṭṭhāya nadītīraṃ gantvā nadantā vaggantā mallamuṭṭhiyuddhaṃ yujjhantā kīḷantā antovihārepi bahivihārepi anācārameva carantā vicaranti. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “passathāvuso[P 2.0155], ime vighāsādā dubbhikkhakāle verañjāyaṃ kañci vikāraṃ na dassesuṃ, idāni pana evarūpāni paṇītabhojanāni bhuñjitvā anekappakāraṃ vikāraṃ dassentā vicaranti. Bhikkhū pana verañjāyampi upasantarūpā viharitvā idānipi upasantupasantāva viharantī”ti. Satthā dhammasabhaṃ gantvā, “bhikkhave, kiṃ kathethā”ti pucchitvā “idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “pubbepete gadrabhayoniyaṃ nibbattā pañcasatā gadrabhā hutvā pañcasatānaṃ ājānīyasindhavānaṃ allarasamuddikapānakapītāvasesaṃ ucchiṭṭhakasaṭaṃ udakena madditvā makacipilotikāhi parissāvitattā ‘volodaka’nti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ pivitvā madhumattā viya nadantā vicariṃsūti vatvā –

Indeed, in the first period after his Enlightenment, the Blessed One went to Verañjā and, having been invited by the brahmin Verañja, entered upon the rains-residence there with five hundred bhikkhus. The brahmin Verañja, being overcome by Māra's influence, did not bring the Teacher to mind even for a single day. There was also a famine in Verañjā, and the bhikkhus, wandering inside and outside Verañjā for alms, grew weary when they did not obtain almsfood. Horse traders provided them with an allowance of barley meal. Seeing their exhaustion, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna wished to feed them with the nutritive essence of the earth and to send them to Uttarakuru for alms, but the Teacher rejected this. The bhikkhus had no anxiety about almsfood even for a single day; they lived avoiding improper conduct. After spending three months there, the Teacher took leave of the brahmin Verañja and, having been honored and revered by him, established him in the refuges before departing. Traveling in stages, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī and stayed in Jetavana. The residents of Sāvatthī prepared arrival meals for the Teacher. At that time, about five hundred eaters of leftovers were living right inside the monastery, dependent on the bhikkhus. They ate the fine food left over by the bhikkhus, slept, rose, went to the riverbank, and wandered about shouting, jumping, engaging in wrestling and boxing, playing, and behaving improperly both inside and outside the monastery. The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, look, these eaters of leftovers showed no misconduct during the famine in Verañjā, but now, having eaten such fine food, they wander about displaying various kinds of misconduct. The bhikkhus, on the other hand, having lived peacefully even in Verañjā, now also live very peacefully indeed.' The Teacher went to the Dhamma hall and asked, 'Bhikkhus, what are you discussing?' When they told him, he said: 'In the past, these ones were also reborn in the donkey womb. Having become five hundred donkeys, they drank the tasteless and inferior leftover dregs of a fresh grape juice drink of five hundred thoroughbred Sindh horses—which, having been mixed with water and strained through worn-out hemp cloths, came to be known as `vālodaka`. As if intoxicated by honey-liquor, they wandered about braying.' And having said this:

“Vālodakaṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ,

Pitvā mado jāyati gadrabhānaṃ;

Imañca pitvāna rasaṃ paṇītaṃ,

Mado na sañjāyati sindhavānaṃ.

Having drunk `vālodaka`, a tasteless and inferior liquid, intoxication arises in donkeys; but having drunk this excellent, flavorful drink, intoxication does not arise in the Sindh horses.

“Appaṃ [P 2.0156] pivitvāna nihīnajacco,

So majjatī tena janinda puṭṭho;

Dhorayhasīlī ca kulamhi jāto,

Na majjatī aggarasaṃ pivitvā”ti. (jā. 1.2.65);

O great king, that one of low birth, having drunk even a little, becomes intoxicated, being affected by it. But one born of a noble line, capable of bearing burdens, does not become intoxicated even after drinking the finest liquid.

Idaṃ vālodakajātakaṃ vitthārena kathetvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, sappurisā lokadhammaṃ vivajjetvā sukhitakālepi dukkhitakālepi nibbikārāva [M 1.0377] hontī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having related the Vālodaka Jātaka in detail, the Teacher made the connection, saying, 'Thus, bhikkhus, good persons, by avoiding worldly conditions, remain unchanged both in times of happiness and in times of sorrow.' Then, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

83.

83.

“Sabbattha ve sappurisā cajanti,

Na kāmakāmā lapayanti santo;

Sukhena [V 1.0335] phuṭṭhā atha vā dukhena,

Na uccāvacaṃ paṇḍitā dassayantī”ti.

Everywhere, indeed, the good renounce; the peaceful do not prattle out of desire for sensual pleasures. Touched by happiness or by sorrow, the wise show neither elation nor depression.

Tattha sabbatthāti pañcakkhandhādibhedesu sabbadhammesu. Sappurisāti supurisā. Cajantīti arahattamaggañāṇena apakaḍḍhantā chandarāgaṃ vijahanti. Kāmakāmāti kāme kāmayantā kāmahetu kāmakāraṇā. Na lapayanti santoti buddhādayo santo kāmahetu neva attanā [P 2.0157] lapayanti, na paraṃ lapāpenti. Ye hi bhikkhāya paviṭṭhā icchācāre ṭhitā “kiṃ, upāsaka, sukhaṃ te puttadārassa, rājacorādīnaṃ vasena dvipadacatuppadesu natthi koci upaddavo”tiādīni vadanti, tāva te lapayanti nāma. Tathā pana vatvā “āma, bhante, sabbesaṃ no sukhaṃ, natthi koci upaddavo, idāni no gehaṃ pahūtaannapānaṃ, idheva vasathā”ti attānaṃ nimantāpentā lapāpenti nāma. Santo pana idaṃ ubhayampi na karonti. Sukhena phuṭṭhā atha vā dukhenāti desanāmattametaṃ, aṭṭhahi pana lokadhammehi phuṭṭhā tuṭṭhibhāvamaṅkubhāvavasena vā vaṇṇabhaṇanaavaṇṇabhaṇanavasena vā uccāvacaṃ ākāraṃ paṇḍitā na dassayantīti.

Herein, `sabbattha` means in all phenomena, such as those divided into the five aggregates and so on. `Sappurisā` means virtuous persons. `Cajanti` means they abandon desire and lust, pulling them away with the knowledge of the path to Arahantship. `Kāmakāmā` means desiring sensual objects for the sake of sensual objects. `Na lapayanti santo` means that the peaceful, such as the Buddhas, do not themselves prattle for the sake of sensual objects, nor do they cause others to prattle. For those who, having entered for alms, stand in base conduct and say such things as, 'Well, lay follower, are your wife and children well? Is there no danger to your bipeds and quadrupeds from kings, thieves, and so on?'—they are said to be prattling. And by speaking thus and causing themselves to be invited with words like, 'Yes, venerable sir, we are all well, there is no danger. Our house now has abundant food and drink, please stay right here,' they are said to be causing others to prattle. But the peaceful ones do neither of these two things. `Sukhena phuṭṭhā atha vā dukhena` is an illustrative statement; for when touched by the eight worldly conditions, the wise do not display a high or low demeanor—either by way of satisfaction and dejection, or by way of speaking praise and blame.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Pañcasatabhikkhuvatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus, the Eighth.

9. Dhammikattheravatthu

9. The Story of the Elder Dhammika

Na attahetūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammikattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with `Na attahetu`, with reference to the Elder Dhammika.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko upāsako dhammena samena agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. So pabbajitukāmo hutvā ekadivasaṃ bhariyāya saddhiṃ nisīditvā [M 1.0378] sukhakathaṃ kathento āha – “bhadde, icchāmahaṃ pabbajitu”nti. “Tena hi, sāmi, āgamehi tāva[P 2.0158], yāvāhaṃ kucchigataṃ dārakaṃ vijāyāmī”ti. So āgametvā dārakassa padasā gamanakāle puna taṃ āpucchitvā “āgamehi tāva, sāmi, yāvāyaṃ vayappatto hotī”ti vutte “kiṃ me imāya apalokitāya vā anapalokitāya vā, attano dukkhanissaraṇaṃ karissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā pabbaji. So kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto attano pabbajitakiccaṃ niṭṭhapetvā tesaṃ dassanatthāya puna sāvatthiṃ gantvā puttassa dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Sopi nikkhamitvā pabbaji, pabbajitvā ca pana na [V 1.0336] cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Purāṇadutiyikāpissa “yesaṃ atthāya ahaṃ gharāvāse vaseyyaṃ, te ubhopi pabbajitā, idāni me kiṃ gharāvāsena, pabbajissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā pabbaji, pabbajitvā ca pana na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, dhammikaupāsako attano dhamme patiṭṭhitattā nikkhamitvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto puttadārassāpi patiṭṭhā jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā ‘imāya nāmā’”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, paṇḍitena nāma neva attahetu, na parahetu samiddhi icchitabbā, dhammikeneva [P 2.0159] pana dhammapaṭisaraṇena bhavitabba”nti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower lived a righteous and just household life. Wishing to go forth, one day, while sitting together with his wife and having a pleasant conversation, he said, 'Dear lady, I wish to go forth.' She replied, 'In that case, my lord, please wait until I give birth to the child in my womb.' He waited, and when the child was able to walk, he asked her again. When she said, 'My lord, wait a little longer, until he comes of age,' he thought, 'What use is it to me whether she gives permission or not? I will bring about my own escape from suffering.' He then went forth and became a monk. Having taken a meditation subject, he strove and made an effort, and having completed his duties as a monk, he went again to Sāvatthī to see his family and gave a Dhamma talk to his son. The son also went forth and became a monk, and not long after going forth, he attained Arahantship. His former wife also thought, 'Those for whose sake I would remain in the household life have both gone forth. Now, what use is the household life to me? I shall go forth.' She went forth and became a nun, and not long after going forth, she attained Arahantship. Then one day in the Dhamma hall, a discussion arose: 'Friends, the lay follower Dhammika, because he himself was established in the Dhamma, went forth, became a monk, and attained Arahantship. He also became a refuge for his son and wife.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?' When they replied that it was about this matter, he said, 'Monks, a wise person should desire success neither for his own sake nor for another’s. One should be righteous and have the Dhamma as one's refuge.' Then, connecting the theme, he taught the Dhamma by speaking this verse:

84.

84.

“Na attahetu na parassa hetu,

Na puttamicche na dhanaṃ na raṭṭhaṃ;

Na iccheyya adhammena samiddhimattano,

Sa sīlavā paññavā dhammiko siyā”ti.

Not for one's own sake, nor for the sake of another, should one desire a son, wealth, or a kingdom. One should not desire one's own success by unrighteous means. Such a one is virtuous, wise, and righteous.

Tattha na attahetūti paṇḍito nāma attahetu vā parahetu vā pāpaṃ na karoti. Na puttamiccheti puttaṃ vā dhanaṃ vā raṭṭhaṃ vā pāpakammena na iccheyya, etānipi icchato pāpakammaṃ na karotiyevāti attho. Samiddhimattanoti yā attano samiddhi, tampi adhammena na iccheyya,samiddhikāraṇāpi pāpaṃ na karotīti attho. Sa sīlavāti yo evarūpo puggalo[M 1.0379], so eva sīlavā ca paññavā ca dhammikoca siyā, na aññoti attho.

Herein, 'not for one's own sake' means that a wise person does not do evil for his own sake or for another's. 'Should not desire a son' means one should not desire a son, wealth, or a kingdom by means of an evil deed; the meaning is that even while desiring these things, one does not commit an evil deed at all. 'One's own success' means one should not desire one's own success by unrighteous means; the meaning is that one does not do evil even for the sake of success. 'Such a one is virtuous' means that a person of this sort is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous, and no other—this is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Dhammikattheravatthu navamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Dhammika, the Ninth.

10. Dhammassavanavatthu

10. The Story of Listening to the Dhamma

Appakā te manussesūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammassavanaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Few are they among humans,' concerning the listening to the Dhamma.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira ekavīthivāsino manussā samaggā hutvā [P 2.0160] gaṇabandhena dānaṃ datvā sabbarattiṃ [V 1.0337] dhammassavanaṃ kāresuṃ, sabbarattiṃ pana dhammaṃ sotuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Ekacce kāmaratinissitā hutvā, puna gehameva gatā, ekacce dosanissitā hutvā, ekacce mānanissitā hutvā, ekacce thinamiddhasamaṅgino hutvā tattheva nisīditvā pacalāyantā sotuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Punadivase bhikkhū taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, imā sattā nāma yebhuyyena bhavanissitā, bhavesu eva laggā viharanti, pāragāmino nāma appakā”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā āha –

It is said that in Sāvatthī, the people living on one street, having come together, gave alms as a group and arranged for a listening to the Dhamma throughout the whole night. However, they were not able to listen to the Dhamma throughout the whole night. Some, being dependent on sensual pleasure, went back home again; some were dependent on aversion; some were dependent on conceit; and some, being possessed of sloth and torpor, sat right there drowsing and were unable to listen. On the next day, the monks, having learned of this event, raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, these beings for the most part are dependent on existence; they dwell clinging only to states of existence. Those who go to the far shore are indeed few.' Having made this connection, he taught the Dhamma by speaking these verses:

85.

85.

“Appakā te manussesu, ye janā pāragāmino;

Athāyaṃ itarā pajā, tīramevānudhāvati.

Few are they among humans, the people who go to the far shore. The rest of this populace just runs along this shore.

86.

86.

“Ye ca kho sammadakkhāte, dhamme dhammānuvattino;

Te janā pāramessanti, maccudheyyaṃ suduttara”nti.

But those who practice in accordance with the well-expounded Dhamma, those people will cross over Death’s domain, so very hard to surmount.

Tattha appakāti thokā na bahū. Pāragāminoti nibbānapāragāmino. Athāyaṃ itarā pajāti yā panāyaṃ avasesā pajā sakkāyadiṭṭhitīrameva anudhāvati, ayameva bahutarāti [P 2.0161] attho. Sammadakkhāteti sammā akkhāte sukathite. Dhammeti desanādhamme. Dhammānuvattinoti taṃ dhammaṃ [M 1.0380] sutvā tadanucchavikaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretvā maggaphalasacchikaraṇena dhammānuvattino. Pāramessantīti te evarūpā janā nibbānapāraṃ gamissanti. Maccudheyyanti kilesamārasaṅkhātassa maccussa nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ tebhūmikavaṭṭaṃ. Suduttaranti ye janā dhammānuvattino, te etaṃ suduttaraṃ duratikkamaṃ māradheyyaṃ taritvā atikkamitvā nibbānapāraṃ gamissantīti attho.

Herein, `appakā` means few, not many. `Pāragāmino` means those who go to the far shore of Nibbāna. `Athāyaṃ itarā pajā` means this remaining populace runs along this very hither shore of identity view; this populace is far more numerous—this is the meaning. `Sammadakkhāte` means well-expounded, well-spoken. `Dhamme` means in the teaching of the Dhamma. `Dhammānuvattino` means those who, having heard that Dhamma, fulfill the practice suitable to it and by means of realizing the path and fruit, live in accordance with the Dhamma. `Pāramessanti` means those people of such a nature will reach the far shore of Nibbāna. `Maccudheyyaṃ` means the round of the three planes which is the abode of Death, who is called the Māra of the defilements. `Suduttaraṃ` means: those people who live in accordance with the Dhamma, only they, having crossed over and gone beyond this domain of Māra, which is very difficult to cross and difficult to transcend, will reach the far shore of Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Dhammassavanavatthu dasamaṃ.

The Story of Listening to the Dhamma, the Tenth.

11. Pañcasataāgantukabhikkhuvatthu

11. The Story of the Five Hundred Visiting Monks

Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ vippahāyāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto pañcasate āgantuke bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, “Having abandoned the dark state,” concerning five hundred visiting monks.

Kosalaraṭṭhe [V 1.0338] kira pañcasatā bhikkhū vassaṃ vasitvā vuṭṭhavassā “satthāraṃ passissāmā”ti jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ cariyapaṭipakkhaṃ nisāmetvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

It is said that in the Kosala country, five hundred monks, having spent the rains-residence and completed it, thought, “We will see the Teacher.” They went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. The Teacher, having discerned what was contrary to their temperament, and wishing to teach the Dhamma, spoke these verses:

87.

87.

“Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ vippahāya, sukkaṃ bhāvetha paṇḍito;

Okā anokamāgamma, viveke yattha dūramaṃ.

Having abandoned the dark state, a wise person should develop the bright. Having gone from home to homelessness, one should seek delight in seclusion, where delight is hard to find.

88.

88.

“Tatrābhiratimiccheyya[P 2.0162], hitvā kāme akiñcano;

Pariyodapeyya attānaṃ, cittaklesehi paṇḍito.

Therein one should seek delight, having abandoned sensual pleasures, a person of no attachments. The wise one should cleanse himself of the defilements of the mind.

89.

89.

“Yesaṃ sambodhiyaṅgesu, sammā cittaṃ subhāvitaṃ;

Ādānapaṭinissagge, anupādāya ye ratā;

Khīṇāsavā jutimanto, te loke parinibbutā”ti.

Those whose minds are rightly well developed in the factors of enlightenment, who delight in non-clinging through the relinquishing of grasping—they, with taints destroyed, luminous, are fully extinguished in the world.

Tattha kaṇhaṃ dhammanti kāyaducaritādibhedaṃ akusalaṃ dhammaṃ vippahāya jahitvā. Sukkaṃ bhāvethāti paṇḍito bhikkhu abhinikkhamanato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā kāyasucaritādibhedaṃ sukkaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveyya. Kathaṃ? Okā [M 1.0381] anokamāgammāti okaṃ vuccati ālayo, anokaṃ vuccati anālayo, ālayato nikkhamitvā anālayasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ paṭicca ārabbha taṃ patthayamāno bhāveyyāti attho. Tatrābhiratimiccheyyāti yasmiṃ anālayasaṅkhāte viveke nibbāne imehi sattehi durabhiramaṃ, tatra abhiratiṃ iccheyya. Hitvā kāmeti vatthukāmakilesakāme hitvā akiñcano hutvā viveke abhiratiṃ iccheyyāti attho. Cittaklesehīti pañcahi nīvaraṇehi, attānaṃ pariyodapeyya vodāpeyya, parisodheyyāti attho. Sambodhiyaṅgesūti sambojjhaṅgesu. Sammā cittaṃ subhāvitanti hetunā nayena cittaṃ suṭṭhu bhāvitaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Ādānapaṭinissaggeti [P 2.0163] ādānaṃ vuccati gahaṇaṃ, tassa paṭinissaggasaṅkhāte aggahaṇe catūhi upādānehi kiñci anupādiyitvā ye ratāti attho. Jutimantoti ānubhāvavanto, arahattamaggañāṇajutiyā khandhādibhede dhamme jotetvā ṭhitāti attho. Te loketi imasmiṃ khandhādiloke parinibbutā nāma arahattapattito paṭṭhāya kilesavaṭṭassa khepitattā saupādisesena, carimacittanirodhena khandhavaṭṭassa khepitattā anupādisesena cāti dvīhi parinibbānehi parinibbutā, anupādāno viya padīpo apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gatāti attho.

Herein, the dark state means the unwholesome state comprising bodily misconduct and so on; having abandoned means having forsaken it. A wise person should develop the bright: a wise monk, from the time of his renunciation up to the path of arahantship, should develop the bright state comprising bodily good conduct and so on. How? Having gone from home to homelessness: home is said to be attachment; homelessness is said to be non-attachment. The meaning is that having gone forth from attachment, with reference to Nibbāna, which is designated as non-attachment, one should develop it while aspiring for it. Therein one should seek delight: in that seclusion, Nibbāna, designated as non-attachment, in which it is hard for these beings to find delight, therein one should wish for delight. Having abandoned sensual pleasures: the meaning is that having abandoned sensual pleasures of the object-bases and sensual pleasures of the defilements, and having become a person with nothing, one should wish for delight in seclusion. Of the defilements of the mind: from the five hindrances. The meaning is that one should cleanse, purify, and thoroughly purify oneself. In the factors of enlightenment: in the enlightenment factors. Whose minds are rightly well developed: the mind is well developed and augmented by cause and method. In the relinquishing of grasping: grasping is called taking. The meaning is that they delight in the non-taking designated as the relinquishment of that, not clinging to anything by means of the four kinds of clinging. Luminous: possessed of splendor. The meaning is that they stand illuminating phenomena such as the aggregates with the radiance of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. They are fully extinguished in the world: in this world of aggregates and so on, they are said to be fully extinguished. From the attainment of arahantship, because the round of defilements has been destroyed, this is full extinguishment with residue remaining; with the cessation of the final consciousness, because the round of aggregates has been destroyed, this is full extinguishment without residue remaining. Thus they are fully extinguished by two kinds of full extinguishment. The meaning is that, like a lamp without fuel, they have gone to a state beyond designation.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0339] bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Pañcasataāgantukabhikkhuvatthu ekādasamaṃ.

The Eleventh Story: The Five Hundred Visiting Monks.

Paṇḍitavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on the Wise is concluded.

Chaṭṭho vaggo.

The Sixth Chapter.

7. Arahantavaggo

7. The Chapter on the Arahant

1. Jīvakapañhavatthu

1. The Story Concerning Jīvaka’s Question.

Gataddhinoti [V 1.0340][M 1.0382][P 2.0164] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jīvakambavane viharanto jīvakena puṭṭhapañhaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Jīvakavatthu khandhake (mahāva. 326 ādayo) vitthāritameva.

While dwelling in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with Gataddhino, concerning a question asked by Jīvaka. The story of Jīvaka has been set forth in detail in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 326, etc.).

Ekasmiṃ pana samaye devadatto ajātasattunā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā gijjhakūṭaṃ abhiruhitvā paduṭṭhacitto “satthāraṃ vadhissāmī”ti silaṃ pavijjhi. Taṃ dve pabbatakūṭāni sampaṭicchiṃsu. Tato bhijjitvā gatā papaṭikā bhagavato pādaṃ paharitvā lohitaṃ uppādesi, bhusā vedanā pavattiṃsu. Bhikkhū satthāraṃ maddakucchiṃ nayiṃsu. Satthā tatopi jīvakambavanaṃ gantukāmo “tattha maṃ nethā”ti āha. Bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ ādāya jīvakambavanaṃ agamaṃsu. Jīvako taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vaṇapaṭikammatthāya tikhiṇabhesajjaṃ [P 2.0165] datvā vaṇaṃ bandhitvā satthāraṃ etadavoca – “bhante, mayā antonagare ekassa manussassa bhesajjaṃ kataṃ, tassa santikaṃ gantvā puna āgamissāmi, idaṃ bhesajjaṃ yāva mamāgamanā baddhaniyāmeneva tiṭṭhatū”ti. So gantvā tassa purisassa kattabbakiccaṃ katvā dvārapidahanavelāya āgacchanto dvāraṃ na sampāpuṇi. Athassa etadahosi – “aho mayā bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, yvāhaṃ aññatarassa purisassa viya tathāgatassa pāde tikhiṇabhesajjaṃ datvā vaṇaṃ bandhiṃ, ayaṃ tassa mocanavelā, tasmiṃ amuccamāne sabbarattiṃ bhagavato sarīre pariḷāho uppajjissatī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “ānanda, jīvako sāyaṃ āgacchanto dvāraṃ na sampāpuṇi, ‘ayaṃ vaṇassa mocanavelā’ti pana cintesi, mocesi na”nti. Thero mocesi, vaṇo rukkhato challi viya apagato. Jīvako antoaruṇeyeva satthu santikaṃ vegena āgantvā “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, sarīre vo pariḷāho uppanno”ti pucchi. Satthā “tathāgatassa kho, jīvaka, bodhimaṇḍeyeva sabbapariḷāho vūpasanto”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Now on one occasion, Devadatta, having joined with Ajātasattu, climbed Vulture Peak and with a malevolent mind, thinking, “I will kill the Teacher,” he hurled a rock. Two mountain peaks intercepted it, but a splinter that broke off from it struck the Blessed One’s foot and drew blood. Severe pains arose. The monks took the Teacher to Maddakucchi. From there, the Teacher, wishing to go to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, said, “Take me there.” The monks took the Blessed One and went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Hearing of this, Jīvaka went to the Teacher and, to treat the wound, applied a potent medicine and bandaged it. He then said to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, I have to apply medicine to a man in the city. I will go to him and then return. Until I come back, let this bandage remain just as it is tied.” Having gone and done what was needed for that man, he was returning at the time the city gates were being closed and could not get through. Then it occurred to him: “Alas, I have done a grave thing! I applied a potent medicine to the Tathāgata’s foot and bandaged the wound, just as I would for any other man. Now is the time for its removal. If it is not removed, a burning will arise in the Blessed One’s body all night long.” At that moment, the Teacher addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, Jīvaka was returning in the evening but could not get through the gate. He is thinking, ‘Now is the time for the bandage to be removed.’ Remove it.” The elder removed it, and the wound came away like bark from a tree. At early dawn, Jīvaka came quickly to the Teacher and asked: “Venerable sir, did any burning arise in your body?” The Teacher, connecting the sequence, said: “Jīvaka, for the Tathāgata, all burning was allayed at the very site of enlightenment,” and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

90.

90.

“Gataddhino [M 1.0383][V 1.0341] visokassa, vippamuttassa sabbadhi;

Sabbaganthappahīnassa, pariḷāho na vijjatī”ti.

For one who has finished the journey, who is sorrowless, liberated in every way, and has abandoned all bonds, no burning is found.

Tattha [P 2.0166] gataddhinoti gatamaggassa kantāraddhā vaṭṭaddhāti dve addhā nāma. Tesu kantārapaṭipanno yāva icchitaṭṭhānaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva addhikoyeva, etasmiṃ pana patte gataddhi nāma hoti. Vaṭṭasannissitāpi sattā yāva vaṭṭe vasanti, tāva addhikā eva. Kasmā? Vaṭṭassa akhepitattā. Sotāpannādayopi addhikā eva, vaṭṭaṃ pana khepetvā ṭhito khīṇāsavo gataddhi nāma hoti. Tassa gataddhino. Visokassāti vaṭṭamūlakassa sokassa vigatattā visokassa. Vippamuttassa sabbadhīti sabbesu khandhādidhammesu vippamuttassa, sabbaganthappahīnassāti catunnampi ganthānaṃ pahīnattā sabbāganthappahīnassa. Pariḷāho na vijjatīti duvidho pariḷāho kāyiko cetasiko cāti. Tesu khīṇāsavassa sītuṇhādivasena uppannattā kāyikapariḷāho anibbutova, taṃ sandhāya jīvako pucchati. Satthā pana dhammarājatāya desanāvidhikusalatāya cetasikapariḷāhavasena desanaṃ vinivattento, “jīvaka, paramatthena evarūpassa khīṇāsavassa pariḷāho na vijjatī”ti āha.

Herein, for one who has finished the journey: for one who has traversed the path. There are two journeys: the journey through the wilderness and the journey through the round of existence. Of these, one who has entered upon the path through the wilderness is a traveler until he reaches his desired destination; only when he has reached it is he called one who has finished the journey. Similarly, beings dependent on the round of existence are travelers as long as they dwell in the round. Why? Because the round has not been exhausted. Even stream-enterers and others are travelers. But the one with taints destroyed, who stands having exhausted the round, is called one who has finished the journey. For such a one who has finished the journey. Who is sorrowless: because sorrow rooted in the round has departed, he is sorrowless. Liberated in every way: liberated from all things, such as the aggregates. And has abandoned all bonds: because he has abandoned all four bonds, he has abandoned all bonds. No burning is found: there are two kinds of burning, bodily and mental. Of these, for one whose taints are destroyed, the bodily burning that arises on account of cold, heat, and so on is not allayed; it is with reference to this that Jīvaka asks. But the Teacher, in his capacity as King of the Dhamma and because of his skill in the method of teaching, directs the discourse by way of the mental burning and says: “Jīvaka, in the ultimate sense, for such a one whose taints are destroyed no burning is found.”

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Jīvakapañhavatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The Story of Jīvaka’s Question: The First.

2. Mahākassapattheravatthu

2. The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa.

Uyyuñjantīti [P 2.0167] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto mahākassapattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in the Veḷuvana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with Uyyuñjanti, concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.

Ekasmiñhi samaye satthā rājagahe vuṭṭhavasso “addhamāsaccayena cārikaṃ pakkamissāmī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ ārocāpesi. Vattaṃ kiretaṃ buddhānaṃ bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ caritukāmānaṃ “evaṃ bhikkhū attano pattapacanacīvararajanādīni katvā sukhaṃ gamissantī”ti “idāni addhamāsaccayena cārikaṃ pakkamissāmī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ ārocāpanaṃ. Bhikkhūsu pana attano pattacīvarādīni karontesu [M 1.0384] mahākassapattheropi cīvarāni dhovi. Bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu “thero kasmā cīvarāni dhovati, imasmiṃ nagare anto ca bahi ca aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo vasanti[V 1.0342]. Tattha ye therassa na ñātakā, te upaṭṭhākā, ye na upaṭṭhākā, te ñātakā. Te therassa catūhi paccayehi sammānasakkāraṃ karonti. Ettakaṃ upakāraṃ pahāya esa kahaṃ gamissati? Sacepi gaccheyya, māpamādakandarato paraṃ na gamissatī”ti. Satthā kira yaṃ kandaraṃ patvā nivattetabbayuttake bhikkhū “tumhe ito nivattatha, mā pamajjitthā”ti vadati. Taṃ “māpamādakandara”nti vuccati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Indeed, on one occasion, the Teacher, having passed the rains retreat in Rājagaha, announced to the bhikkhus, 'In half a month, I will set out on a journey.' It is said that this is the custom of the Buddhas who wish to travel with the bhikkhus: 'Thus the bhikkhus, having done things such as baking their bowls and dyeing their robes, will depart comfortably.' Therefore, the announcement is made to the bhikkhus, 'Now, in half a month, I will set out on a journey.' While the bhikkhus were preparing their bowls, robes, and other requisites, the Elder Mahākassapa also washed his robes. The bhikkhus complained, 'Why does the elder wash his robes? In this city, inside and outside, live eighteen crores of people. Among them, those who are not the elder’s relatives are his supporters, and those who are not his supporters are his relatives. They offer honor and respect to the elder with the four requisites. Having abandoned such great support, where will he go? Even if he were to go, he will not go beyond the Māpamāda Gorge.' It is said that the Teacher, having reached the gorge where it is suitable for certain bhikkhus to turn back, tells them, 'You turn back from here; do not be negligent.' That gorge is called the 'Māpamāda Gorge.' This was said with reference to that.

Satthāpi cārikaṃ pakkamanto [P 2.0168] cintesi – “imasmiṃ nagare anto ca bahi ca aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo vasanti. Manussānaṃ maṅgalāmaṅgalaṭṭhānesu bhikkhūhi gantabbaṃ hoti, na sakkā vihāraṃ tucchaṃ kātuṃ, kaṃ nu kho nivattessāmī”ti? Athassa etadahosi –“kassapassa hete manussā ñātakā ca upaṭṭhākā ca, kassapaṃ nivattetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So theraṃ āha – “kassapa, na sakkā vihāraṃ tucchaṃ kātuṃ, manussānaṃ maṅgalāmaṅgalaṭṭhānesu bhikkhūhi attho hoti, tvaṃ attano parisāya saddhiṃ nivattassū”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero parisaṃ ādāya nivatti. Bhikkhū upajjhāyiṃsu “diṭṭhaṃ vo, āvuso, nanu idāneva amhehi vuttaṃ ‘mahākassapo kasmā cīvarāni dhovati, na eso satthārā saddhiṃ gamissatī’ti, yaṃ amhehi vuttaṃ, tadeva jāta”nti. Satthā bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā nivattitvā ṭhito āha – “bhikkhave, kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathethā”ti? “Mahākassapattheraṃ ārabbha kathema, bhante”ti attanā kathitaniyāmeneva sabbaṃ ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā satthā “na, bhikkhave, tumhe kassapaṃ ‘kulesu ca paccayesu ca laggo’ti vadetha, so ‘mama vacanaṃ karissāmī’ti nivatto. Eso hi pubbe patthanaṃ karontoyeva ‘catūsu paccayesu alaggo candūpamo hutvā kulāni upasaṅkamituṃ samattho bhaveyya’nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Natthetassa [P 2.0169] kule vā paccaye vā laggo, ahaṃ candopamappaṭipadañceva (saṃ. ni. 2.146) ariyavaṃsappaṭipadañca kathento mama puttaṃ kassapaṃ ādiṃ katvā kathesi”nti āha.

The Teacher, while setting out on his journey, thought: 'In this city, inside and outside, there are eighteen crores of people. Bhikkhus have to go to places of auspicious and inauspicious rites; it is not possible to leave the monastery empty. Whom shall I have turn back?' Then it occurred to him: 'These people are relatives and supporters of Kassapa; it is fitting to have Kassapa turn back.' He said to the elder: 'Kassapa, it is not possible to leave the monastery empty. People have need of bhikkhus at places of auspicious and inauspicious rites. You should turn back with your retinue.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' the elder replied and turned back with his retinue. The bhikkhus grumbled: 'Have you seen, friends? Did we not just say, “Why is Mahākassapa washing his robes? He will not go with the Teacher.” What we said has come true.' Hearing the bhikkhus’ conversation, the Teacher turned back, stood, and said: 'Bhikkhus, what is this you are talking about?' 'We are talking about the Elder Mahākassapa, venerable sir,' they replied, and told him everything exactly as they had spoken it. Hearing this, the Teacher said: 'Bhikkhus, do not say that Kassapa is attached to families and requisites. He turned back, thinking, “I will carry out my word.” Indeed, in the past, when making his aspiration, he aspired: “May I, being unattached to the four requisites and like the moon, be capable of approaching families.” He has no attachment to families or requisites. When I taught the practice similar to the moon and the practice of the noble lineages, I taught it taking my son Kassapa as the foremost example.'

Bhikkhū [M 1.0385] satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu – “bhante, kadā pana therena patthanā ṭhapitā”ti? “Sotukāmāttha, bhikkhave”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. Satthā tesaṃ, “bhikkhave, ito kappasatasahassamatthake padumuttaro nāma buddho loke udapādī”ti vatvā padumuttarapādamūle tena ṭhapitapatthanaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ therassa pubbacaritaṃ kathesi. Taṃ therapāḷiyaṃ (theragā. 1054 ādayo) vitthāritameva. Satthā pana imaṃ therassa pubbacaritaṃ vitthāretvā “iti kho, bhikkhave, ahaṃ candopamappaṭipadañceva ariyavaṃsappaṭipadañca mama puttaṃ kassapaṃ ādiṃ katvā kathesiṃ, mama puttassa kassapassa paccayesu vā kulesu vā vihāresu vā pariveṇesu vā laggo nāma natthi[V 1.0343], pallale otaritvā tattha caritvā gacchanto rājahaṃso viya katthaci alaggoyeva mama putto”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The bhikkhus asked the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, when was the aspiration made by the Elder?' 'Bhikkhus, do you wish to hear?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' The Teacher said to them, 'Bhikkhus, a hundred thousand aeons ago, a Buddha named Padumuttara arose in the world.' Having spoken thus, he began with the aspiration made at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara and recounted the Elder’s entire past history. This is detailed in the Thera-pāḷi. Then, after elaborating on this past history of the Elder, the Teacher connected the themes, saying: 'Thus, bhikkhus, I have taught both the practice similar to the moon and the practice of the noble lineages, taking my son Kassapa as the foremost example. My son Kassapa has no attachment whatsoever to requisites, families, monasteries, or cells. Like a royal swan that descends into a pond, moves about there, and departs, my son remains unattached anywhere.' Having thus connected the themes, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

91.

91.

“Uyyuñjanti satīmanto, na nikete ramanti te;

Haṃsāva pallalaṃ hitvā, okamokaṃ jahanti te”ti.

The mindful exert themselves; they do not delight in dwellings. Like swans that have left their lake, they abandon home after home.

Tattha [P 2.0170] uyyuñjanti satīmantoti sativepullappattā khīṇāsavā attanā paṭividdhaguṇesu jhānavipassanādīsu āvajjanasamāpajjanavuṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇāhi yuñjanti ghaṭenti. Na nikete ramanti teti tesaṃ ālaye rati nāma natthi. Haṃsāvāti desanāsīsametaṃ, ayaṃ panettha attho – yathā gocarasampanne pallale sakuṇā attano gocaraṃ gahetvā gamanakāle “mama udakaṃ, mama padumaṃ, mama uppalaṃ, mama kaṇṇikā”ti tasmiṃ ṭhāne kañci ālayaṃ akatvā anapekkhāva taṃ ṭhānaṃ pahāya uppatitvā ākāse kīḷamānā gacchanti; evamevaṃ khīṇāsavā yattha katthaci viharantāpi kulādīsu alaggā eva viharitvā gamanasamayepi taṃ ṭhānaṃ pahāya gacchantā “mama vihāro, mama pariveṇaṃ, mamūpaṭṭhākā”ti anālayā anupekkhāva gacchanti. Okamokanti ālayālayaṃ, sabbālaye pariccajantīti attho.

Therein, The mindful exert themselves means that the Arahants, who have attained fullness of mindfulness, exert themselves and strive in the qualities they have penetrated by themselves—such as jhāna and insight—through adverting, attaining, emerging, resolving, and reviewing. They do not delight in a dwelling means they have no delight whatsoever in attachment. Like swans is the head of the teaching, but this is the meaning here: Just as birds in a pond rich with feeding grounds, having taken their food, at the time of departure, do not form any attachment to that place, thinking, 'This is my water, my lotus, my water lily, my pericarp,' but instead, without longing, abandon that place, fly up, and go, sporting in the sky; even so, the Arahants, though dwelling anywhere, having dwelt unattached to families and so on, at the time of departure, abandon that place and go without attachment and without longing, not thinking, 'This is my monastery, my monastic cell, my supporters.' They abandon home after home means they abandon intense attachment; the meaning is that they abandon all attachments.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Mahākassapattheravatthu dutiyaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa, the Second.

3. Belaṭṭhasīsattheravatthu

3. The Story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa

Yesaṃ [M 1.0386] sannicayo natthīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmantaṃ belaṭṭhasīsaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning the Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa, which begins with the verse: 'For whom there is no accumulation.'

So [P 2.0171] kirāyasmā antogāme ekaṃ vīthiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā puna aparaṃ vīthiṃ caritvā sukkhaṃ kūraṃ ādāya vihāraṃ haritvā paṭisāmetvā “nibaddhaṃ piṇḍapātapariyesanaṃ nāma dukkha”nti katipāhaṃ jhānasukhena vītināmetvā āhārena atthe sati taṃ paribhuñjati. Bhikkhū ñatvā ujjhāyitvā tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Satthā etasmiṃ nidāne āyatiṃ sannidhikāraparivajjanatthāya bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetvāpi therena pana apaññatte sikkhāpade [V 1.0344] appicchataṃ nissāya katattā tassa dosābhāvaṃ pakāsento anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Reportedly, that venerable one, having walked one street in the village for alms and having finished his meal, walked another street, collected dry rice, brought it back to the monastery, and stored it away. Then, thinking, 'The constant search for alms is suffering,' he spent a few days in the bliss of jhāna, consuming it when he needed food. The monks, learning of this, complained and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher, on this occasion, laid down a training rule for the monks for the future avoidance of storing provisions; but since the elder had acted out of fewness of wishes before the training rule was laid down, the Teacher, revealing his faultlessness, connected the narrative and, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

92.

92.

“Yesaṃ sannicayo natthi, ye pariññātabhojanā;

Suññato animitto ca, vimokkho yesaṃ gocaro;

Ākāseva sakuntānaṃ, gati tesaṃ durannayā”ti.

For whom there is no accumulation, who have fully understood their food; whose resort is the liberation that is void and signless; their track is hard to trace, like that of birds in the sky.

Tattha sannicayoti dve sannicayā – kammasannicayo ca, paccayasannicayo ca. Tesu kusalākusalakammaṃ kammasannicayo nāma, cattāro paccayā paccayasannicayo nāma. Tattha vihāre vasantassa bhikkhuno ekaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ, catubhāgamattaṃ sappiṃ, ekañca taṇḍulanāḷiṃ ṭhapentassa paccayasannicayo natthi, tato uttari hoti. Yesaṃ ayaṃ duvidhopi sannicayo natthi. Pariññātabhojanāti [P 2.0172] tīhi pariññāhi pariññātabhojanā. Yāguādīnañhi yāgubhāvādijānanaṃ ñātapariññā, āhāre paṭikūlasaññāvasena pana bhojanassa parijānanaṃ tīraṇapariññā, kabaḷīkārāhāre chandarāgaapakaḍḍhanañāṇaṃ pahānapariññā. Imāhi tīhi pariññāhi ye pariññātabhojanā. Suññato animitto cāti ettha appaṇihitavimokkhopi gahitoyeva. Tīṇipi cetāni nibbānasseva nāmāni. Nibbānañhi rāgadosamohānaṃ abhāvena suññato, tehi ca vimuttanti suññato vimokkho, tathā rāgādinimittānaṃ abhāvena animittaṃ, tehi ca vimuttanti animitto vimokkho, rāgādipaṇidhīnaṃ pana abhāvena appaṇihitaṃ[M 1.0387], tehi ca vimuttanti appaṇihito vimokkhoti vuccati. Phalasamāpattivasena taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā viharantānaṃ ayaṃ tividho vimokkho yesaṃ gocaro. Gati tesaṃ durannayāti yathā nāma ākāsena gatānaṃ sakuṇānaṃ padanikkhepassa adassanena gati durannayā na sakkā jānituṃ, evameva yesaṃ ayaṃ duvidho sannicayo natthi, imāhi ca tīhi pariññāhi pariññātabhojanā, yesañca [P 2.0173] ayaṃ vuttappakāro vimokkho gocaro, tesaṃ tayo bhavā, catasso yoniyo, pañca gatiyo, satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, nava sattāvāsāti imesu pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu iminā nāma gatāti gamanassa apaññāyanato gati durannayā na sakkā paññāpetunti.

Herein, 'accumulation' is of two kinds: accumulation of kamma and accumulation of requisites. Among these, wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called the accumulation of kamma; the four requisites are called the accumulation of requisites. In this regard, for a monk dwelling in a monastery, there is no accumulation of requisites when he keeps one lump of molasses, a quarter-measure of ghee, and one nāḷi of rice; beyond that, it becomes an accumulation. This is said of those for whom neither of these two kinds of accumulation exists. 'Fully understood their food' means that their food is fully understood by three kinds of full understanding. The knowing of gruel and so on as merely gruel is full understanding as the known. The full understanding of food by means of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is full understanding by scrutiny. The knowledge that removes sensual desire for physical food is full understanding by abandoning. By these three kinds of full understanding, they are ones who have 'fully understood their food.' By 'void and signless,' the desireless liberation is also included. All three are names for Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called 'void' because of the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and because it is liberated from them, it is called the 'void liberation.' Likewise, because of the absence of the signs of greed, etc., it is called 'signless,' and because it is liberated from them, it is called the 'signless liberation.' And because of the absence of the longing of greed, etc., it is called 'desireless,' and because it is liberated from them, it is called the 'desireless liberation.' For those who dwell making this their object through the attainment of fruition, this threefold liberation is their domain. 'Their track is hard to trace': just as the track of birds that have gone through the sky is hard to trace because their footprints are not seen, so too for those for whom this twofold accumulation does not exist, who have fully understood their food by these three kinds of full understanding, and for whom this liberation just described is their domain—their track among these five divisions (the three planes of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings) cannot be designated as 'gone by this path,' and thus their track is hard to trace and cannot be designated.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Belaṭṭhasīsattheravatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa, the Third.

4. Anuruddhattheravatthu

4. The Story of the Elder Anuruddha

Yassāsavāti [V 1.0345] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto anuruddhattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in the Veḷuvana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning the Elder Anuruddha, which begins with the verse: 'He whose taints...'

Ekasmiñhi divase thero jiṇṇacīvaro saṅkārakūṭādīsu cīvaraṃ pariyesati. Tassa ito tatiye attabhāve purāṇadutiyikā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattitvā jālinī nāma devadhītā ahosi. Sā theraṃ coḷakāni pariyesamānaṃ disvā therassa atthāya terasahatthāyatāni catuhatthavitthatāni tīṇi dibbadussāni gahetvā “sacāhaṃ imāni iminā nīhārena dassāmi, thero na gaṇhissatī”ti cintetvā tassa coḷakāni pariyesamānassa purato ekasmiṃ saṅkārakūṭe yathā nesaṃ dasantamattameva paññāyati, tathā ṭhapesi. Thero tena maggena [P 2.0174] coḷakapariyesamānaṃ caranto nesaṃ dasantaṃ disvā tattheva gahetvā ākaḍḍhamāno vuttappamāṇāni dibbadussāni disvā “ukkaṭṭhapaṃsukūlaṃ vata ida”nti ādāya pakkāmi. Athassa cīvarakaraṇadivase satthā pañcasatabhikkhuparivāro vihāraṃ gantvā nisīdi, asītimahātherāpi tattheva nisīdiṃsu, cīvaraṃ sibbetuṃ mahākassapatthero mūle nisīdi, sāriputtatthero majjhe, ānandatthero agge, bhikkhusaṅgho suttaṃ vaṭṭesi, satthā sūcipāsake [M 1.0388] āvuṇi, mahāmoggallānatthero yena yena attho, taṃ taṃ upanento vicari.

Indeed, on one day, the elder, his robes being worn out, was searching for robe-cloth on refuse heaps and so on. His former wife from his third existence from this one had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm and became a devadhītā named Jālinī. Seeing the elder searching for cloths, she took three divine cloths, each thirteen cubits long and four cubits wide, for the elder's sake. Thinking, 'If I give these in this manner, the elder will not accept them,' she placed them on a refuse heap before him as he was searching for cloths, in such a way that only the very edge of them was visible. As the elder was walking along that path searching for cloth, he saw their edge, took hold of them right there, and upon pulling them out, he saw the divine cloths of the aforementioned dimensions. Thinking, 'This is truly excellent rag-robe cloth!' he took them and departed. Then, on the day of making the robe for him, the Teacher, with a retinue of five hundred monks, went to the monastery and sat down. The eighty great elders also sat there. To sew the robe, the Elder Mahākassapa sat at the base, the Elder Sāriputta in the middle, and the Elder Ānanda at the end. The Saṅgha of monks twisted the thread, the Teacher threaded the eye of the needle, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna moved about, supplying whatever was needed.

Devadhītāpi antogāmaṃ pavisitvā “bhontā ayyassa no anuruddhattherassa cīvaraṃ karonto satthā asītimahāsāvakaparivuto pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vihāre nisīdi, yāguādīni ādāya vihāraṃ gacchathā”ti bhikkhaṃ samādapesi. Mahāmoggallānattheropi antarābhatte mahājambupesiṃ āhari, pañcasatā bhikkhū parikkhīṇaṃ khādituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Sakko cīvarakaraṇaṭṭhāne bhūmiparibhaṇḍamakāsi, bhūmi alattakarasarañjitā viya ahosi. Bhikkhūhi paribhuttāvasesānaṃ yāgukhajjakabhattānaṃ mahārāsi ahosi. Bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu “ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [P 2.0175] kiṃ evaṃbahukehi yāguādīhi, nanu nāma pamāṇaṃ sallakkhetvā ettakaṃ nāma āharathā”ti ñātakā ca upaṭṭhākā ca vattabbā siyuṃ, anuruddhatthero attano ñātiupaṭṭhākānaṃ bahubhāvaṃ ñāpetukāmo maññe”ti, atha ne satthā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, kathethā”ti pucchitvā, “bhante, idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “kiṃ pana tumhe, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ anuruddhena āharāpita’nti maññathā”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, mama putto anuruddho evarūpaṃ vadeti. Na hi khīṇāsavā paccayapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ kathenti, ayaṃ pana piṇḍapāto devatānubhāvena nibbatto”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The devadhītā also entered the village and prompted the people, saying: 'Sirs, while making a robe for our master, the Elder Anuruddha, the Teacher is seated in the monastery, surrounded by the eighty great disciples and with five hundred monks. Take gruel and other foods and go to the monastery!' Thus she had the almsfood provided. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna also brought a large jambu fruit during the mealtime; five hundred monks were unable to eat it all. Sakka prepared the ground at the robe-making place; the ground became as if dyed with lac-dye. There was a great heap of gruel, hard food, and rice left over after the monks had eaten. The monks complained: 'For so many monks, what is the use of so much gruel and other food? Should not the relatives and supporters be told, "After considering the right amount, bring only that much"? We think the Elder Anuruddha wants to make known how many relatives and supporters he has.' Then the Teacher asked them, 'Monks, what are you talking about?' When they replied, 'It is this matter, venerable sir,' he asked, 'But monks, do you think, "This was brought at Anuruddha’s request"?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'No, monks, my son Anuruddha does not say such a thing. Indeed, those whose taints are destroyed do not engage in talk connected with requisites. This almsfood, however, was produced by the power of a devatā.' Connecting the narrative, he taught the Dhamma by speaking this verse:

93.

93.

“Yassāsavā [V 1.0346] parikkhīṇā, āhāre ca anissito;

Suññato animitto ca, vimokkho yassa gocaro;

Ākāseva sakuntānaṃ, padaṃ tassa durannaya”nti.

He whose taints are destroyed, who is not dependent on nutriment; whose resort is the liberation that is void and signless; his track is hard to trace, like that of birds in the sky.

Tattha yassāsavāti yassa cattāro āsavā parikkhīṇā. Āhāre ca anissitoti āhārasmiñca taṇhādiṭṭhinissayehi anissito. Padaṃ tassa durannayanti yathā ākāse gacchantānaṃ sakuṇānaṃ “imasmiṃ ṭhāne pādehi akkamitvā gatā, idaṃ ṭhānaṃ urena paharitvā gatā, idaṃ sīsena, idaṃ pakkhehī”ti na sakkā ñātuṃ, evameva evarūpassa bhikkhuno “nirayapadena vā gato, tiracchānayonipadena vā”tiādinā nayena padaṃ paññāpetuṃ nāma na sakkoti.

Therein, 'he whose taints' means one for whom the four taints are destroyed. 'And not dependent on nutriment' means not dependent on nutriment through the dependencies of craving and views. 'His track is hard to trace': just as it is not possible to know of birds flying in the sky, 'They went having stepped in this place with their feet, they went having struck this place with their chest, this with their head, this with their wings,' even so, it is not possible to make known the track of such a monk by saying, 'He has gone by the track to hell, or by the track to the animal realm,' and so on.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpatti phalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Anuruddhattheravatthu catutthaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Anuruddha, the Fourth.

5. Mahākaccāyanattheravatthu

5. The Story of the Elder Mahākaccāyana

Yassindriyānīti [M 1.0389][P 2.0176] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā pubbārāme viharanto mahākaccāyanattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at the Pubbārāma monastery, spoke this Dhamma discourse, which begins with the words 'Whose faculties,' concerning the Elder Mahākaccāyana.

Ekasmiñhi samaye bhagavā mahāpavāraṇāya migāramātuyā pāsādassa heṭṭhā mahāsāvakaparivuto nisīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye mahākaccāyanatthero avantīsu viharati. So panāyasmā dūratopi āgantvā dhammassavanaṃ paggaṇhātiyeva. Tasmā mahātherā nisīdantā mahākaccāyanattherassa āsanaṃ ṭhapetvā nisīdiṃsu. Sakko devarājā dvīhi devalokehi devaparisāya saddhiṃ āgantvā dibbagandhamālādīhi satthāraṃ pūjetvā ṭhito mahākaccāyanattheraṃ adisvā kiṃ nu kho mama, ayyo, na dissati, sādhu kho panassa sace āgaccheyyāti. Theropi taṃ khaṇaññeva āgantvā attano āsane nisinnameva attānaṃ dassesi. Sakko theraṃ disvā gopphakesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā “sādhu vata me, ayyo, āgato, ahaṃ ayyassa āgamanameva paccāsīsāmī”ti vatvā ubhohi hatthehi pāde sambāhitvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu. “Sakko mukhaṃ [P 2.0177] oloketvā sakkāraṃ karoti, avasesamahāsāvakānaṃ evarūpaṃ sakkāraṃ akaritvā mahākaccāyanaṃ disvā vegena gopphakesu [V 1.0347] gahetvā ‘sādhu vata me, ayyo, āgato, ahaṃ ayyassa āgamanameva paccāsīsāmī’ti vatvā ubhohi hatthehi pāde sambāhitvā pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito”ti. Satthā tesaṃ taṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “bhikkhave, mama puttena mahākaccāyanena sadisā indriyesu guttadvārā bhikkhū devānampi manussānampi piyāyevā”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

On one occasion, at the time of the great Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Blessed One was seated below the palace of Migāramātā, surrounded by a great retinue of disciples. At that time, the Elder Mahākaccāyana was dwelling in the Avantī country. That venerable one, however, would always come, even from afar, to honor the hearing of the Dhamma. Therefore, when the great elders were taking their seats, they set aside a seat for the Elder Mahākaccāyana before sitting down. Sakka, the king of the devas, arrived with an assembly of devas from two deva worlds. After honoring the Teacher with divine perfumes, garlands, and so on, he stood there. Not seeing the Elder Mahākaccāyana, he thought: “Why is my venerable lord not to be seen? It would be truly good if he were to come.” At that very moment, the elder arrived and revealed himself already seated in his own seat. Seeing the elder, Sakka firmly grasped his ankles and said: “It is truly good that my venerable lord has come! I was hoping for the venerable one’s arrival.” Then, with both hands, he massaged the elder’s feet, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and so on, paid homage, and stood to one side. The monks became indignant, saying: “Sakka shows favoritism when he pays respect. He does not show such respect to the other great disciples, but upon seeing Mahākaccāyana, he quickly grasps his ankles, says, ‘It is truly good that my venerable lord has come! I was hoping for the venerable one’s arrival,’ massages his feet with both hands, honors him, pays homage, and stands aside.” Hearing their talk, the Teacher said: “Monks, monks like my son Mahākaccāyana, who have the doors of their sense faculties guarded, are dear to both devas and humans.” Then, connecting the sequence of events, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:

94.

94.

“Yassindriyāni samathaṅgatāni,

Assā yathā sārathinā sudantā;

Pahīnamānassa anāsavassa,

Devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino”ti.

Whose faculties are becalmed, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer; who has abandoned conceit and is free from taints—even the devas hold dear such a steadfast one.

Tassattho [M 1.0390] – yassa bhikkhuno chekena sārathinā sudantā assā viya cha indriyāni samathaṃ dantabhāvaṃ nibbisevanabhāvaṃ gatāni, tassa navavidhaṃ mānaṃ pahāya ṭhitattā pahīnamānassa catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ abhāvena anāsavassa. Tādinoti tādibhāvasaṇṭhitassa tathārūpassa devāpi pihayanti, manussāpi dassanañca āgamanañca patthentiyevāti.

The meaning is this: The six faculties of that monk have reached a state of calmness, tameness, and being without venom, like horses well-tamed by a skilled charioteer. Having abandoned the ninefold conceit, he is one with conceit abandoned. Through the absence of the four taints, he is one without taints. Of such a one, established in that steadfast state, even the devas hold him dear, and humans too long for the sight of him and for his arrival.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Mahākaccāyanattheravatthu pañcamaṃ.

The Fifth Story: The Elder Mahākaccāyana.

6. Sāriputtattheravatthu

6. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta

Pathavisamoti [P 2.0178] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Jeta Grove, delivered this Dhamma discourse, which begins with the words “Like the earth,” concerning the Elder Sāriputta.

Ekasmiñhi samaye āyasmā sāriputto vuṭṭhavasso cārikaṃ pakkamitukāmo bhagavantaṃ āpucchitvā vanditvā attano parivārena saddhiṃ nikkhami. Aññepi bahū bhikkhū theraṃ anugacchiṃsu. Thero ca nāmagottavasena paññāyamāne bhikkhū nāmagottavasena kathetvā nivattāpesi. Aññataro nāmagottavasena apākaṭo bhikkhu cintesi – “aho vata mampi nāmagottavasena paggaṇhanto kathetvā nivattāpeyyā”ti thero mahābhikkhusaṅghassa antare taṃ na sallakkhesi. So “aññe viya bhikkhū na maṃ paggaṇhātī”ti there āghātaṃ bandhi. Therassapi saṅghāṭikaṇṇo [V 1.0348] tassa bhikkhuno sarīraṃ phusi, tenāpi āghātaṃ bandhiyeva. So “dāni thero vihārūpacāraṃ atikkanto bhavissatī”ti ñatvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “āyasmā maṃ, bhante, sāriputto tumhākaṃ aggasāvakomhīti kaṇṇasakkhaliṃ bhindanto viya paharitvā akhamāpetvāva cārikaṃ pakkanto”ti āha. Satthā theraṃ pakkosāpesi.

On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta, having completed the rains-residence and wishing to set out on a wandering tour, took leave of the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and departed with his retinue. Many other monks also followed the elder. The elder, however, addressed by name and clan those monks who were known by their name and clan and sent them back. A certain monk who was not well-known by name or clan thought: “Oh, if only the elder would single me out by name and clan, speak to me, and send me back!” But amidst the great community of monks, the elder did not notice him. So the monk conceived a grudge against the elder, thinking, “He does not single me out like the other monks.” Then the corner of the elder’s outer robe brushed against that monk’s body, and for this reason too he conceived a grudge. When he knew, “Now the elder must have passed beyond the monastery precincts,” he approached the Teacher and said: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta, thinking ‘I am your chief disciple,’ struck me as if to shatter my ear and then departed on his tour without obtaining my pardon.” The Teacher had the elder summoned.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāmoggallānatthero ca ānandatthero ca cintesuṃ – “amhākaṃ aggajeṭṭhabhātarā imassa bhikkhuno apahaṭabhāvaṃ satthā no na jānāti, sīhanādaṃ pana [P 2.0179] nadāpetukāmo bhavissatīti parisaṃ sannipātāpessāmā”ti. Te kuñcikahatthā pariveṇadvārāni vivaritvā “abhikkamathāyasmanto[M 1.0391], abhikkamathāyasmanto, idānāyasmā sāriputto bhagavato sammukhā sīhanādaṃ nadissatī”ti (a. ni. 9.11) mahābhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātesuṃ. Theropi āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā tamatthaṃ pucchi. Thero “nāyaṃ bhikkhu mayā pahaṭo”ti avatvāva attano guṇakathaṃ kathento “yassa nūna, bhante, kāye kāyagatāsati anupaṭṭhitā assa, so idha aññataraṃ sabrahmacāriṃ āsajja appaṭinissajja cārikaṃ pakkameyyā”ti vatvā “seyyathāpi, bhante, pathaviyaṃ sucimpi nikkhipanti, asucimpi nikkhipantī”tiādinā nayena attano pathavīsamacittatañca āpotejovāyo rajoharaṇacaṇḍālakumārakausabhachinnavisāṇasamacittatañca ahikuṇapādīhi viya attano kāyena aṭṭiyanañca medakathālikā viya attano kāyapariharaṇañca pakāsesi. Imāhi ca pana navahi upamāhi there attano guṇe kathente navasupi ṭhānesu udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī kampi. Rajoharaṇacaṇḍālakumārakamedakathāliko pamānaṃ pana āharaṇakāle puthujjanā bhikkhū assūni sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, khīṇāsavānaṃ dhammasaṃvego udapādi.

At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Ānanda thought: “It is not that our Teacher does not know that our chief elder brother struck this monk; rather, he must wish to have him roar a lion’s roar. Therefore, we will assemble the community.” Taking keys in hand, they opened the doors of the monastic cells and called out: “Come forth, venerable sirs, come forth! Now the Venerable Sāriputta will roar a lion’s roar in the presence of the Blessed One!” Thus they assembled the great community of monks. The elder, too, arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. Then the Teacher questioned him about the matter.
