Without saying, “This monk was not struck by me,” the elder began to speak of his own qualities: “Venerable sir, it is surely one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is unestablished who might, in this Teaching, offend a fellow spiritual practitioner and depart on a tour without having made amends.” Then, beginning with, “Just as, venerable sir, people throw both clean and unclean things on the earth,” he explained his own mind’s equanimity, like the earth, water, fire, and air; like a cleaning rag; like an outcaste boy; and like a bull with broken horns. He also explained his disgust with his own body, as if with a snake’s carcass, and how he bears his body about like a pot of fat. As the elder was explaining his own qualities with these nine similes, the great earth quaked on all nine occasions, down to its water-boundary. When he brought up the similes of the cleaning rag, the outcaste boy, and the pot of fat, the ordinary monks could not hold back their tears, and a sense of spiritual urgency arose in the arahants.

There attano guṇaṃ kathenteyeva abbhācikkhanakassa [P 2.0180] bhikkhuno sakalasarīre ḍāho uppajji, so tāvadeva bhagavato pādesu patitvā attano abbhācikkhanadosaṃ pakāsetvā accayaṃ desesi. Satthā theraṃ āmantetvā, “sāriputta, khama imassa moghapurisassa, yāvassa sattadhā muddhā na phalatī”ti āha. Thero ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggayha “khamāmahaṃ, bhante, tassa āyasmato, khamatu ca me so āyasmā, sace mayhaṃ doso atthī”ti āha. Bhikkhū kathayiṃsu “passatha dānāvuso, therassa anopamaguṇaṃ, evarūpassa nāma musāvādena abbhācikkhanakassa bhikkhuno upari appamattakampi kopaṃ vā dosaṃ vā akatvā sayameva ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggayha khamāpetī”ti. “Satthā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā, bhikkhave, kiṃ kathethā”ti pucchitvā “idaṃ nāma, bhante”ti vutte, “na bhikkhave, sakkā sāriputtasadisānaṃ kopaṃ vā dosaṃ vā uppādetuṃ[V 1.0349], mahāpathavīsadisaṃ, bhikkhave, indakhīlasadisaṃ pasannaudakarahadasadisañca [M 1.0392] sāriputtassa citta”nti vatvā anusandhiṃ [P 2.0181] ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Just as the elder was speaking of his own virtues, a burning sensation arose all over the body of the accusing monk. He immediately fell at the Blessed One’s feet, revealed his fault of slander, and confessed his transgression. The Teacher addressed the elder: “Sāriputta, forgive this foolish man, before his head splits into seven pieces.” The elder sat on his heels, raised his hands in reverence, and said: “Venerable sir, I forgive that venerable one. And may that venerable one forgive me, if there is any fault in me.” The monks remarked to one another: “See, friends, the elder’s incomparable virtue! Toward the monk who slandered him with a lie, he showed not the slightest anger or ill will, but instead sat on his heels, raised his hands, and asked for forgiveness himself!” The Teacher, hearing their talk, asked: “Monks, what are you discussing?” When they told him, he said: “Monks, it is not possible to arouse anger or ill will in one like Sāriputta. Monks, Sāriputta’s mind is like the great earth, like a city-pillar, and like a lake of clear water.” Then, connecting the sequence of events, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:

95.

95.

“Pathavisamo no virujjhati,

Indakhilupamo tādi subbato;

Rahadova apetakaddamo,

Saṃsārā na bhavanti tādino”ti.

Like the earth, he is not resentful; like a city-pillar, he is steadfast, a man of good vows. Like a lake free of mud, for such a steadfast one there are no more wanderings in saṃsāra.

Tassattho – bhikkhave, yathā nāma pathaviyaṃ sucīni gandhamālādīnipi nikkhipanti, asucīni muttakarīsādīnipi nikkhipanti, yathā nāma nagaradvāre nikhātaṃ indakhīlaṃ dārakādayo omuttentipi ūhadantipi, apare pana taṃ gandhamālādīhi sakkaronti. Tattha pathaviyā indakhīlassa ca neva anurodho uppajjati, na virodho; evameva yvāyaṃ khīṇāsavo bhikkhu aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi akampiyabhāvena tādi, vatānaṃ sundaratāya subbato. So “ime maṃ catūhi paccayehi sakkaronti, ime pana na sakkarontī”ti sakkārañca asakkārañca karontesu neva anurujjhati, no virujjhati, atha kho pathavisamo ca indakhilupamo eva ca hoti. Yathā [P 2.0182] ca apagatakaddamo rahado pasannodako hoti, evaṃ apagatakilesatāya rāgakaddamādīhi akaddamo vippasannova hoti. Tādinoti tassa pana evarūpassa sugatiduggatīsu saṃsaraṇavasena saṃsārā nāma na hontīti.

The meaning of that verse is this, bhikkhus: Just as on the earth people deposit both clean things like fragrances and garlands and unclean things like urine and excrement; and just as at a city gate, a post is urinated and defecated upon by boys and others, while still others honor it with fragrances and garlands; yet for the earth and the post no attraction or repulsion arises; so too, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is steadfast, being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions, and is of good practice because of the beauty of his observances. Toward those who offer him honor with the four requisites and those who do not, he feels neither attraction nor repulsion, but is just like the earth and the post. And just as a lake free from mud has clear water, so too, with the departure of the defilements, he is free from the mud of lust and the like, and is perfectly serene. As to ‘steadfast’: for such a one, there are no more wanderings in saṃsāra by way of faring on to good and bad destinations.

Desanāvasāne nava bhikkhusahassāni saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, nine thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Sāriputtattheravatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Sāriputta is the sixth.

7. Kosambivāsītissattherasāmaṇeravatthu

7. The Story of the Novice of the Elder Tissa of Kosambī

Santaṃ tassa manaṃ hotīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto tissattherassa sāmaṇeraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher gave this Dhamma talk with reference to the novice of the Elder Tissa, beginning with the verse, 'Peaceful is his mind.'

Eko kira kosambivāsī kulaputto satthu sāsane pabbajitvā laddhupasampado “kosambivāsītissatthero”ti paññāyi. Tassa kosambiyaṃ vuṭṭhavassassa [M 1.0393] upaṭṭhāko ticīvarañceva [V 1.0350] sappiphāṇitañca āharitvā pādamūle ṭhapesi. Atha naṃ thero āha – “kiṃ idaṃ upāsakā”ti. “Nanu mayā, bhante, tumhe vassaṃ vāsitā, amhākañca vihāre vuṭṭhavassā imaṃ lābhaṃ labhanti, gaṇhatha, bhante”ti. “Hotu, upāsaka, na mayhaṃ iminā attho”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā, bhante”ti? “Mama santike kappiyakārako sāmaṇeropi natthi, āvuso”ti. “Sace, bhante, kappiyakārako natthi, mama putto ayyassa santike sāmaṇero bhavissatī”ti. Thero adhivāsesi. Upāsako sattavassikaṃ attano puttaṃ therassa santikaṃ netvā “imaṃ pabbājethā”ti adāsi. Athassa thero kese temetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā pabbājesi[P 2.0183]. So khuraggeyeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

A certain clansman from Kosambī, it is said, went forth in the Teacher’s Dispensation, and after receiving the higher ordination, he became known as the Elder Tissa of Kosambī. When he had completed the rains residence in Kosambī, his supporter brought the three robes, along with ghee and jaggery, and placed them at his feet. The elder asked him, “What is this, lay follower?” “Venerable sir, did I not have you spend the rains here? Those who have completed the rains residence in our monastery receive this gift. Please accept it, venerable sir.” “Let it be, lay follower, I have no use for this.” “For what reason, venerable sir?” “Friend, I do not have a novice or an attendant to make things allowable for me.” “If, venerable sir, you do not have an attendant to make things allowable, my son will become a novice under you.” The elder consented. The lay follower brought his seven-year-old son to the elder and gave him over, saying, “Please give him the going forth.” The elder moistened the boy’s hair, gave him the meditation subject of the five constituents ending with the skin, and gave him the going forth. At the very tip of the razor, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Thero taṃ pabbājetvā aḍḍhamāsaṃ tattha vasitvā “satthāraṃ passissāmī”ti sāmaṇeraṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ gāhāpetvā gacchanto antarāmagge ekaṃ vihāraṃ pāvisi. Sāmaṇero upajjhāyassa senāsanaṃ gahetvā paṭijaggi. Tassa taṃ paṭijaggantasseva vikālo jāto, tena attano senāsanaṃ paṭijaggituṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ upaṭṭhānavelāyaṃ āgantvā nisinnaṃ thero pucchi – “sāmaṇera, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggita”nti? “Bhante, paṭijaggituṃ okāsaṃ nālattha”nti. “Tena hi mama vasanaṭṭhāneyeva vasa, dukkhaṃ te āgantukaṭṭhāne bahi vasitu”nti taṃ gahetvāva senāsanaṃ pāvisi. Thero pana puthujjano nipannamattova niddaṃ okkami. Sāmaṇero cintesi – “ajja me upajjhāyena saddhiṃ tatiyo divaso ekasenāsane vasantassa, ‘sace nipajjitvā niddāyissāmi, thero sahaseyyaṃ āpajjeyyā’ti nisinnakova vītināmessāmī”ti upajjhāyassa mañcakasamīpe pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnakova rattiṃ vītināmesi. Thero paccūsakāle paccuṭṭhāya “sāmaṇeraṃ nikkhamāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti mañcakapasse ṭhapitabījaniṃ gahetvā bījanipattassa aggena sāmaṇerassa kaṭasārakaṃ paharitvā bījaniṃ uddhaṃ ukkhipanto [P 2.0184] “sāmaṇera, bahi nikkhamā”ti āha, bījanipattadaṇḍako akkhimhi paṭihaññi, tāvadeva akkhi bhijji. So “kiṃ, bhante”ti vatvā uṭṭhāya “bahi nikkhamā”ti vutte “akkhi me, bhante, bhinna”nti avatvā ekena hatthena paṭicchādetvā nikkhami. Vattakaraṇakāle ca pana “akkhi me bhinna”nti tuṇhī anisīditvā ekena hatthena akkhiṃ gahetvā ekena hatthena [M 1.0394] muṭṭhisammuñjaniṃ ādāya vaccakuṭiñca mukhadhovanaṭṭhānañca sammajjitvā mukhadhovanodakañca ṭhapetvā pariveṇaṃ sammajji. So upajjhāyassa dantakaṭṭhaṃ dadamāno ekeneva hatthena adāsi.

Having given him the going forth, the elder dwelt there for half a month. Then, thinking, “I will see the Teacher,” he had the novice take his requisites and set out. On the way, he entered a certain monastery. The novice took and prepared the lodging for his preceptor. While he was preparing it, it grew late, so he was unable to prepare his own lodging. Then, at the time for personal attendance, the elder saw him sitting there and asked: “Novice, have you prepared your own dwelling place?” “Venerable sir, I did not get an opportunity to prepare it.” “In that case, stay in my own dwelling place. It would be difficult for you, a visitor, to stay outside.” Taking the novice with him, he entered the lodging. The elder, being a worldling, fell asleep as soon as he lay down. The novice thought: “This is the third day I am staying in the same lodging with my preceptor. If I lie down and sleep, the elder might incur the offense of sleeping together. I will pass the night sitting up.” He sat down cross-legged near his preceptor’s bed and passed the night sitting. At dawn, the elder got up and thought, “It is time to send the novice out.” He took a fan that was placed by the side of the bed, struck the novice’s rush mat with the tip of the fan handle, and while lifting the fan, said, “Novice, get out!” The fan handle struck the novice in the eye, and his eye immediately burst. The novice said, “What is it, venerable sir?” and got up. When told, “Get out!” he did not say, “Venerable sir, my eye has burst,” but covered it with one hand and went out. At the time for performing his duties, instead of sitting silently thinking, “My eye has burst,” he held his eye with one hand, took a hand-broom with the other, swept the latrine and the place for washing the face, set out water for washing the face, and swept the compound. When giving the tooth-stick to his preceptor, he gave it with only one hand.

Atha naṃ upajjhāyo āha – “asikkhito vatāyaṃ sāmaṇero, ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ ekena [V 1.0351] hatthena dantakaṭṭhaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Jānāmahaṃ, bhante, “na evaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti, eko pana me hattho na tucchoti. “Kiṃ sāmaṇerā”ti? So ādito paṭṭhāya taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Thero sutvāva saṃviggamānaso “aho vata mayā bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti vatvā “khamāhi me, sappurisa, nāhametaṃ jānāmi, avassayo me hohī”ti añjaliṃ paggayha sattavassikadārakassa pādamūle ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ sāmaṇero āha – “nāhaṃ, bhante, etadatthāya kathesiṃ, tumhākaṃ cittaṃ [P 2.0185] anurakkhantena mayā evaṃ vuttaṃ nevettha tumhākaṃ doso atthi, na mayhaṃ. Vaṭṭasseveso doso, mā cintayittha, mayā tumhākaṃ vippaṭisāraṃ rakkhanteneva nārocita”nti. Thero sāmaṇerena assāsiyamānopi anassāsitvā uppannasaṃvego sāmaṇerassa bhaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā satthu santikaṃ pāyāsi. Satthāpissa āgamanaṃ olokentova nisīdi. So gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā satthārā saddhiṃ paṭisammodanaṃ katvā “khamanīyaṃ te bhikkhu, kiñci atirekaṃ aphāsukaṃ atthī”ti pucchito āha – “khamanīyaṃ, bhante, natthi me kiñci atirekaṃ aphāsukaṃ, apica kho pana me ayaṃ daharasāmaṇero viya añño atirekaguṇo na diṭṭhapubbo”ti. “Kiṃ pana iminā kataṃ bhikkhū”ti. So ādito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ bhagavato ārocento āha – “evaṃ, bhante, mayā khamāpiyamāno maṃ evaṃ vadesi ‘nevettha tumhākaṃ doso atthi, na mayhaṃ. Vaṭṭasseveso doso, tumhe mā cintayitthā’ti, iti maṃ assāsesiyeva, mayi neva kopaṃ, na dosamakāsi, na me, bhante, evarūpo guṇasampanno diṭṭhapubbo”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “bhikkhu khīṇāsavā nāma na kassaci kuppanti, na dussanti, santindriyā santamānasāva hontī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his preceptor said to him: “Alas, this novice is like one who has not learned the training rules! It is not proper to give a tooth-stick to one’s teachers and preceptors with only one hand.” “I know, venerable sir, that it is not proper to do so, but one of my hands is not empty.” “What is it, novice?” The novice then related the incident from the beginning. Upon hearing it, the elder, his mind stirred with alarm, exclaimed, “Alas, what a grave deed I have done!” and said, “Forgive me, good man. I did not know this. Be my refuge!” Then, raising his hands in reverence, he squatted down at the feet of the seven-year-old boy. Then the novice said to him: “Venerable sir, I did not speak for that purpose. I spoke thus while wishing to guard your mind. There is no fault of yours in this, nor is there any fault of mine. This is the fault of the round of existence itself. Do not worry. It was only while protecting you from remorse that I did not inform you.” Although being consoled by the novice, the elder was not consoled. With a sense of urgency having arisen, he took the novice’s requisites and departed for the Teacher’s presence. The Teacher, too, was sitting, watching for his arrival. Having gone and paid homage to the Teacher, and after exchanging friendly greetings with the Teacher, he was asked, “Is it tolerable for you, bhikkhu? Is there any particular discomfort?” He replied: “It is tolerable, venerable sir. I have no particular discomfort. However, I have never before seen another with such extraordinary qualities as this young novice.” “But what, bhikkhu, was done by this one?” Then, relating the entire incident from the beginning to the Blessed One, he said: “Thus, venerable sir, when I was asking for his forgiveness, he said to me: ‘There is no fault of yours in this, nor is there any fault of mine. This is the fault of the round of existence itself. You should not worry.’ Thus he only consoled me; he showed neither anger nor ill will toward me. Venerable sir, I have never before seen one so endowed with virtue.” Then the Teacher said to him: “Bhikkhu, those whose taints are destroyed are not angry toward anyone, nor do they harbor ill will; they are of peaceful faculties and peaceful mind.” Having said this, he made the connection and, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

96.

96.

“Santaṃ [M 1.0395] tassa manaṃ hoti, santā vācā ca kamma ca;

Sammadaññā vimuttassa, upasantassa tādino”ti.

Peaceful is his mind, peaceful his speech and action, of one who is liberated by perfect knowledge, pacified and steadfast.

Tattha santaṃ tassāti tassa khīṇāsavasāmaṇerassa abhijjhādīnaṃ abhāvena manaṃ santameva hoti upasantaṃ nibbutaṃ[P 2.0186]. Tathā musāvādādīnaṃ abhāvena vācā ca pāṇātipātādīnaṃ abhāvena kāyakammañca santameva hoti. Sammadaññā vimuttassāti nayena hetunā jānitvā pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuttassa. Upasantassāti abbhantare rāgādīnaṃ upasamena upasantassa. Tādinoti tathārūpassa guṇasampannassāti.

Herein, 'peaceful is his': the mind of that novice whose taints are destroyed is indeed peaceful, pacified, and quenched through the absence of covetousness and so on. Likewise, his speech is peaceful through the absence of false speech and so on, and his bodily action is peaceful through the absence of destroying living beings and so on. 'Of one who is liberated by perfect knowledge': of one liberated by the five kinds of liberation, having known by way of method and cause. 'Pacified': inwardly pacified by the subsidence of lust and so on. 'Steadfast': of one of such a nature, endowed with virtue.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0352] kosambivāsītissatthero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Sesamahājanassāpi sātthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder Tissa of Kosambī attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The Dhamma talk was also beneficial to the rest of the great assembly.

Kosambivāsītissattherasāmaṇeravatthu sattamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Tissa of Kosambī and the Novice is the seventh.

8. Sāriputtattheravatthu

8. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta

Assaddhoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, which begins with the word 'Assaddho,' concerning the Elder Sāriputta.

Ekasmiñhi samaye tiṃsamattā āraññakā bhikkhū satthu santikaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattassūpanissayaṃ disvā sāriputtattheraṃ āmantetvā “saddahasi tvaṃ, sāriputta, saddhindriyaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulīkataṃ amatogadhaṃ hoti amatapariyosāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.514) evaṃ pañcindriyāni ārabbha pañhaṃ pucchi. Thero “na khvāhaṃ, bhante, ettha bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmi, saddhindriyaṃ…pe… amatapariyosānaṃ. Yesañhetaṃ, bhante, aññātaṃ assa adiṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ asacchikataṃ aphassitaṃ paññāya, te tattha paresaṃ [P 2.0187] saddhāya gaccheyyuṃ. Saddhindriyaṃ…pe… amatapariyosāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.514) evaṃ taṃ pañhaṃ byākāsi. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “sāriputtatthero micchāgahaṇaṃ neva vissajjesi, ajjāpi sammāsambuddhassa na saddahatiyevā”ti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, bhikkhave, vadetha. Ahañhi ‘pañcindriyāni abhāvetvā samathavipassanaṃ avaḍḍhetvā [M 1.0396] maggaphalāni sacchikātuṃ samattho nāma atthīti saddahasi tvaṃ sāriputto’ti pucchiṃ. So ‘evaṃ sacchikaronto atthi nāmāti na saddahāmi, bhante’ti kathesi. Na dinnassa vā katassa vā phalaṃ vipākaṃ na saddahati, nāpi buddhādīnaṃ guṇaṃ na saddahati. Eso pana attanā paṭividdhesu jhānavipassanāmaggaphaladhammesu paresaṃ saddhāya na gacchati. Tasmā anupavajjo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, on one occasion, about thirty forest-dwelling monks approached the Teacher, paid homage to him, and sat down. The Teacher, seeing their supporting condition for attaining Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, addressed the Elder Sāriputta and asked him a question concerning the five faculties: “Sāriputta, do you believe that the faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless and has the Deathless as its final goal?” Thus he asked a question concerning the five faculties. The Elder replied: “Venerable sir, in this matter I do not go by faith in the Blessed One that the faculty of faith has the Deathless as its final goal. Those for whom this is unknown, unseen, uncomprehended, unrealized, and uncontacted by wisdom—it is they who would go by faith in others that the faculty of faith has the Deathless as its final goal.” Thus he answered the question. Hearing this, the monks raised a talk among themselves: “The Elder Sāriputta has not given up his wrong view; even today he does not believe in the Perfectly Enlightened One!” Hearing this, the Teacher said: “What is this you are saying, monks? For I asked him: ‘Sāriputta, do you believe that there is anyone who is able to realize the paths and fruits without having developed the five faculties and without having cultivated serenity and insight?’ And he replied: ‘Venerable sir, I do not believe that there is anyone who realizes them in such a way.’ It is not that he does not believe in the fruit and result of what is given or done, nor that he does not believe in the qualities of the Buddha and so on. Rather, in regard to the states of jhāna, insight, path, and fruit that he has penetrated for himself, he does not go by faith in others. Therefore, he is blameless.” Having said this and established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma he spoke this verse:

97.

97.

“Assaddho akataññū ca, sandhicchedo ca yo naro,

Hatāvakāso vantāso, sa ve uttamaporiso”ti.

The man who is faithless, a knower of the Uncreated, a breaker of connections, who has destroyed all opportunity and abandoned all longing—he is truly the supreme person.

Tassatho – attano paṭividdhaguṇaṃ paresaṃ kathāya na saddahatīti assaddho. Akataṃ nibbānaṃ [V 1.0353] jānātīti akataññū[P 2.0188], sacchikatanibbānoti attho. Vaṭṭasandhiṃ, saṃsārasandhiṃ chinditvā ṭhitoti sandhicchedo. Kusalākusalakammabījassa khīṇattā nibbattanāvakāso hato assāti hatāvakāso. Catūhi maggehi kattabbakiccassa katattā,sabbā āsā iminā vantāti vantāso. So evarūpo naro. Paṭividdhalokuttaradhammatāya purisesu uttamabhāvaṃ pattoti purisuttamoti.

The meaning of this is as follows: Because he does not believe in the qualities he has penetrated for himself based on the word of others, he is 'faithless' (assaddho). Because he knows the Unconditioned, Nibbāna, he is a 'knower of the uncreated' (akataññū); the meaning is that he has realized Nibbāna. Because he stands having cut the connection of the round of existence, the connection of saṃsāra, he is a 'breaker of connections' (sandhicchedo). Because the seed of wholesome and unwholesome kamma is exhausted, the opportunity for his rebirth is destroyed; thus he is one who has 'destroyed opportunity' (hatāvakāso). Because the task to be done by means of the four paths has been done, all longing has been vomited by him; thus he is one who has 'vomited longing' (vantāso). Such a man, having attained the supreme state among persons by having penetrated the supramundane Dhamma, is a 'supreme person' (purisuttamo).

Gāthāvasāne te āraññakā tiṃsamattā bhikkhū saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sesajanassāpi satthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the verse, those thirty forest-dwelling monks attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The Dhamma discourse was also beneficial to the rest of the assembly.

Sāriputtattheravatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Eighth Story: The Elder Sāriputta.

9. Khadiravaniyarevatattheravatthu

9. The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Wood

Gāme vāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto khadiravaniyarevatattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, which begins with the words 'Gāme vā,' concerning the Elder Revata of the Acacia Wood.

Āyasmā hi sāriputto sattāsītikoṭidhanaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā cālā, upacālā, sīsūpacālāti tisso bhaginiyo, cundo upasenoti ime dve ca bhātaro pabbājesi. Revatakumāro ekova gehe avasiṭṭho. Athassa mātā cintesi – “mama putto [P 2.0189] upatisso ettakaṃ [M 1.0397] dhanaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā tisso ca bhaginiyo dve ca bhātaro pabbājesi, revato ekova avaseso. Sace imampi pabbājessati, ettakaṃ no dhanaṃ nassissati, kulavaṃso pacchijjissati, daharakāleyeva naṃ gharāvāsena bandhissāmī”ti. Sāriputtattheropi paṭikacceva bhikkhū āṇāpesi “sace, āvuso, revato pabbajitukāmo āgacchati, āgatamattameva naṃ pabbājeyyātha, mama mātāpitaro micchādiṭṭhikā, kiṃ tehi āpucchitehi, ahameva tassa mātā ca pitā cā”ti. Mātāpissa revatakumāraṃ sattavassikameva gharabandhanena bandhitukāmā samānajātike kule dārikaṃ vāretvā divasaṃ vavatthapetvā kumāraṃ maṇḍetvā pasādhetvā mahatā parivārena saddhiṃ ādāya kumārikāya ñātigharaṃ agamāsi. Atha nesaṃ katamaṅgalānaṃ dvinnampi ñātakesu sannipatitesu udakapātiyaṃ hatthe otāretvā maṅgalāni vatvā kumārikāya vuḍḍhiṃ ākaṅkhamānā ñātakā “tava ayyikāya diṭṭhadhammaṃ passa, ayyikā viya ciraṃ jīva, ammā”ti āhaṃsu. Revatakumāro “ko nu kho imissā ayyikāya diṭṭhadhammo”ti cintetvā “katarā [V 1.0354] imissā ayyikā”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ āhaṃsu, “tāta, kiṃ na passasi imaṃ vīsavassasatikaṃ khaṇḍadantaṃ palitakesaṃ [P 2.0190] valittacaṃ tilakāhatagattaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ, esā etissā ayyikā”ti. “Kiṃ pana ayampi evarūpā bhavissatī”ti? “Sace jīvissati, bhavissati, tātā”ti. So cintesi – “evarūpampi nāma sarīraṃ jarāya imaṃ vippakāraṃ pāpuṇissati, imaṃ me bhātarā upatissena diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati, ajjeva mayā palāyitvā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Atha naṃ ñātakā kumārikāya saddhiṃ ekayānaṃ āropetvā ādāya pakkamiṃsu.

Indeed, the Venerable Sāriputta, having gone forth after renouncing wealth of eighty-seven crores, also had his three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—and his two brothers—Cunda and Upasena—go forth. Only the young Revata remained at home. Then his mother thought: “My son Upatissa renounced so much wealth to go forth and also ordained his three sisters and two brothers. Only Revata is left. If he ordains this one too, our great wealth will be lost and our family line will be cut off. I must bind him with the ties of household life while he is still young.” The Elder Sāriputta, anticipating this, instructed the monks beforehand: “Friends, if Revata comes wishing to go forth, ordain him as soon as he arrives. My parents hold wrong views; what is the point of asking them? I myself am his mother and father.” His mother, wishing to bind the seven-year-old boy Revata with the bond of the household, arranged for a girl from a family of equal status, fixed the day, and having adorned and prepared the boy, went with a large retinue to the girl's relatives' home. When the relatives of both had assembled for the auspicious rites, they poured water over their hands from a ceremonial pitcher, recited the blessings, and wishing for the girl's prosperity, the relatives said: “Dear girl, behold the present condition of your grandmother, and live long like her!” The young Revata thought, “What is this present condition of her grandmother?” and asked, “Which one is her grandmother?” They told him: “Son, do you not see this one who is a hundred and twenty years old, with broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkled skin, a body covered with spots, and bent over like a roof-rafter? That is her grandmother.” “Will this girl also become like that?” “If she lives long enough, son, she will.” He thought: “So a body like this will come to such a state of ruin through old age! This must be what my brother Upatissa saw. I must run away and go forth this very day!” Then the relatives, having placed him in the same vehicle with the girl, departed with them.

So thokaṃ gantvā sarīrakiccaṃ apadisitvā “ṭhapetha tāva yānaṃ, otaritvā āgamissāmī”ti yānā otaritvā ekasmiṃ gumbe thokaṃ papañcaṃ katvā agamāsi. Punapi thokaṃ gantvā teneva apadesena otaritvā abhiruhi, punapi tatheva akāsi. Athassa ñātakā “addhā imassa uṭṭhānāni vattantī”ti sallakkhetvā nātidaḷhaṃ ārakkhaṃ kariṃsu. So punapi thokaṃ gantvā teneva apadesena otaritvā “tumhe pājento purato gacchatha, mayaṃ pacchato saṇikaṃ āgamissāmā”ti vatvā otaritvā gumbābhimukho ahosi. Ñātakāpissa “pacchato āgamissatī”ti saññāya yānaṃ pājentā [P 2.0191] gamiṃsu. Sopi [M 1.0398] tato palāyitvā ekasmiṃ padese tiṃsamattā bhikkhū vasanti, tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā āha – “pabbājetha maṃ, bhante”ti. “Āvuso, tvaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito, mayaṃ te rājaputtabhāvaṃ vā amaccaputtabhāvaṃ vā na jānāma, kathaṃ pabbājessāmā”ti? “Tumhe maṃ, bhante, na jānāthā”ti? “Na jānāmāvuso”ti. “Ahaṃ upatissassa kaniṭṭhabhātiko”ti. “Ko esa upatisso nāmā”ti? “Bhante, bhaddantā mama bhātaraṃ ‘sāriputto’ti vadanti, tasmā mayā ‘upatisso’ti vutte na jānantī”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ sāriputtattherassa kaniṭṭhabhātiko”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Tena hi ehi, bhātarā te anuññātamevā”ti vatvā bhikkhū tassa ābharaṇāni omuñcāpetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhapetvā taṃ pabbājetvā therassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Thero taṃ sutvā bhagavato ārocesi – “bhante, ‘āraññikabhikkhūhi kira revato pabbājito’ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu, gantvā taṃ passitvā āgamissāmī”ti. Satthā “adhivāsehi tāva, sāriputtā”ti gantuṃ na adāsi. Thero puna katipāhaccayena satthāraṃ āpucchi. Satthā “adhivāsehi tāva, sāriputta, mayampi āgamissāmā”ti neva gantuṃ adāsi.

Having gone a short distance, he made an excuse about a bodily need, saying, “Stop the vehicle for a moment; I will get down and come back.” He got down from the vehicle, delayed for a short while in a thicket, and then went on. After going a little further, he got down with the same excuse and got back in. He did this yet again. His relatives, thinking, “Surely he has to relieve himself frequently,” did not guard him very closely. Again, after going a short distance, he got down with the same excuse and said, “You drive on ahead; we will come slowly behind.” Having gotten down, he headed towards a thicket. His relatives, thinking, “He will come along behind,” drove the vehicle onward. He, however, fled from there and went to a place where some thirty monks were dwelling. Approaching them, he paid homage and said, “Venerable sirs, please ordain me.” “Friend, you are adorned with all kinds of ornaments. We do not know if you are a prince or a minister's son. How can we ordain you?” “Venerable sirs, do you not know me?” “No, friend, we do not.” “I am the younger brother of Upatissa.” “Who is this Upatissa?” “Venerable sirs, the venerable ones call my brother ‘Sāriputta,’ so you did not recognize him when I said ‘Upatissa.’” “What? Are you the younger brother of the Elder Sāriputta?” “Yes, venerable sirs.” “In that case, come. Your brother has already given his permission.” Having said this, the monks had him remove his ornaments, set them aside in a suitable place, and ordained him. Then they sent a message to the Elder. The Elder, on hearing this, informed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the forest-dwelling monks have sent a message that Revata has been ordained. I will go to see him and return.” The Teacher said, “Be patient for a while, Sāriputta,” and did not give him permission to go. After a few days had passed, the Elder again asked the Teacher for permission. The Teacher said, “Be patient for a while, Sāriputta. We too shall go,” and still did not give him permission to go.

Sāmaṇeropi “sacāhaṃ idha vasissāmi[P 2.0192], ñātakā maṃ anubandhitvā pakkosissantī”ti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā pattacīvaramādāya cārikaṃ caramāno [V 1.0355] tato tiṃsayojanike ṭhāne khadiravanaṃ gantvā antovasseyeva temāsabbhantare saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Theropi pavāretvā satthāraṃ puna tattha gamanatthāya āpucchi. Satthā “mayampi gamissāma, sāriputtā”ti pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ nikkhami. Thokaṃ gatakāle ānandatthero dvedhāpathe ṭhatvā satthāraṃ āha – “bhante, revatassa santikaṃ gamanamaggesu ayaṃ parihārapatho saṭṭhiyojaniko manussāvāso, ayaṃ ujumaggo tiṃsayojaniko amanussapariggahito, katarena gacchāmā”ti. “Sīvali, pana, ānanda, amhehi saddhiṃ āgato”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Sace, sīvali, āgato, ujumaggameva gaṇhāhī”ti. Satthā kira “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ yāgubhattaṃ uppādessāmi, ujumaggaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti avatvā “tesaṃ tesaṃ janānaṃ puññassa vipākadānaṭṭhānaṃ eta”nti ñatvā “sace, sīvali, āgato, ujumaggaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti [M 1.0399] āha. Satthari pana taṃ maggaṃ paṭipanne devatā “amhākaṃ ayyassa sīvalittherassa sakkāraṃ karissāmā”ti cintetvā ekekayojane vihāre kāretvā ekayojanato uddhaṃ gantuṃ adatvā pāto vuṭṭhāya dibbayāguādīni [P 2.0193] gahetvā, “ayyo, no sīvalitthero kahaṃ nisinno”ti vicaranti. Thero attano abhihaṭaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dāpesi. Evaṃ satthā saparivāro tiṃsayojanikaṃ kantāraṃ sīvalittherassa puññaṃ anubhavamānova āgamāsi. Revatattheropi satthu āgamanaṃ ñatvā bhagavato gandhakuṭiṃ māpetvā pañca kūṭāgārasatāni, pañca caṅkamanasatāni, pañcarattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānasatāni ca māpesi. Satthā tassa santike māsamattameva vasi. Tasmiṃ vasamānopi sīvalittherasseva puññaṃ anubhavi.

The novice, thinking, 'If I remain here, my relatives will follow me and call for me,' learned a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship from those monks. Taking his bowl and robe and wandering on tour, he went from there to the Khadira forest, a place thirty yojanas away. Within the three months of the rains retreat itself, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The Elder, having performed the Pavāraṇā, asked the Teacher for permission to go there again. The Teacher said, 'We too will go, Sāriputta,' and he set out with five hundred monks. When they had gone a short way, the Elder Ānanda, standing at a fork in the road, said to the Teacher: 'Venerable sir, of the paths to the Elder Revata’s presence, this circuitous route is sixty yojanas long and is a human settlement, while this direct route is thirty yojanas long and is possessed by non-human beings. By which shall we go?' 'Ānanda, has Sīvali come with us?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'If Sīvali has come, take the direct route.' It is said that the Teacher, knowing, 'This is the occasion for the merit of those various people to yield its fruit,' did not say, 'I will produce rice gruel and food for you; take the direct route,' but said, 'If Sīvali has come, take the direct route.' When the Teacher had entered upon that path, the deities, thinking, 'We will pay homage to our noble Elder Sīvali,' had monasteries created at every yojana and did not allow them to proceed more than a yojana. Rising early, they would take divine rice gruel and other items and go about asking, 'Where is our noble Elder Sīvali seated?' The Elder had what was brought to him given to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. In this way, the Teacher and his retinue proceeded through the thirty-yojana wilderness, sustained by the Elder Sīvali's merit. The Elder Revata, learning of the Teacher's arrival, had a perfumed chamber created for the Blessed One, as well as five hundred gabled halls, five hundred walking paths, and five hundred places for staying at night and by day. The Teacher dwelt in his presence for about a month. While dwelling there, he was sustained by the merit of the Elder Sīvali alone.

Tattha pana dve mahallakabhikkhū satthu khadiravanaṃ pavisanakāle evaṃ cintayiṃsu – “ayaṃ bhikkhu ettakaṃ navakammaṃ karonto kiṃ sakkhissati samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ, satthā ‘sāriputtassa kaniṭṭho’ti mukholokanakiccaṃ karonto evarūpassa navakammikassa bhikkhussa santikaṃ āgato”ti. Satthāpi taṃ divasaṃ paccūsakāle lokaṃ voloketvā te bhikkhū disvā tesaṃ cittācāraṃ aññāsi. Tasmā tattha māsamattaṃ vasitvā nikkhamanadivase yathā te bhikkhū attano telanāḷiñca udakatumbañca upāhanāni ca pamussanti, tathā adhiṭṭhahitvā nikkhamanto vihārūpacārato bahi nikkhantakāle iddhiṃ vissajjesi. Atha te bhikkhū “mayā idañcidañca pamuṭṭhaṃ[P 2.0194], mayāpi pamuṭṭha”nti ubhopi nivattitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ asallakkhetvā khadirarukkhakaṇṭakehi vijjhamānā vicaritvā ekasmiṃ khadirarukkhe olambantaṃ attano bhaṇḍakaṃ disvā ādāya pakkamiṃsu. Satthāpi bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ādāya puna māsamatteneva sīvalittherassa puññaṃ anubhavamāno paṭigantvā pubbārāmaṃ pāvisi.

Now, in that place, two elderly monks, at the time of the Teacher's entering the Khadira forest, thought thus: 'This monk is doing so much new work; how will he be able to fulfill the duties of a recluse? The Teacher, showing favoritism because he is Sāriputta's younger brother, has come to the presence of such a monk who undertakes new work.' The Teacher, on that day at dawn, while surveying the world, saw those monks and knew the course of their thoughts. Therefore, after dwelling there for about a month, on the day of his departure he made a determination that those monks would forget their oil tube, water gourd, and sandals. As he was leaving, just after he had gone beyond the monastery precincts, he withdrew his psychic power. Then those monks, thinking, 'I have forgotten this and that,' and 'I too have forgotten,' both turned back. But not recognizing the place, they wandered about, being pierced by the thorns of the khadira trees. Seeing their belongings hanging on a khadira tree, they took them and departed. The Teacher, taking the Saṅgha of monks and again being sustained by the Elder Sīvali's merit, returned in about a month and entered the Eastern Monastery.

Atha [V 1.0356] te mahallakabhikkhū pātova mukhaṃ dhovitvā “āgantukabhattadāyikāya visākhāya gharaṃ yāguṃ pivissāmā”ti gantvā yāguṃ pivitvā khajjakaṃ khāditvā nisīdiṃsu. Atha ne visākhā pucchi – “tumhepi, bhante, satthārā saddhiṃ revatattherassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamitthā”ti. “Āma, upāsiketi, ramaṇīyaṃ, bhante, therassa vasanaṭṭhāna”nti. “Kuto tassa ramaṇīyatā setakaṇṭakakhadirarukkhagahanaṃ petānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānasadisaṃ upāsike”ti. Athaññe dve daharabhikkhū āgamiṃsu. Upāsikā tesampi yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā tatheva paṭipucchi[M 1.0400]. Te āhaṃsu – “na sakkā upāsike vaṇṇetuṃ, sudhammadevasabhāsadisaṃ iddhiyā abhisaṅkhataṃ viya therassa vasanaṭṭhāna”nti. Upāsikā cintesi – “paṭhamaṃ āgatā bhikkhū aññathā vadiṃsu, ime aññathā vadanti, paṭhamaṃ āgatā bhikkhū kiñcideva pamussitvā iddhiyā vissaṭṭhakāle paṭinivattitvā gatā bhavissanti, ime pana iddhiyā [P 2.0195] abhisaṅkharitvā nimmitakāle gatā bhavissantī”ti attano paṇḍitabhāvena etamatthaṃ ñatvā “satthāraṃ āgatakāle pucchissāmī”ti aṭṭhāsi. Tato muhuttaṃyeva satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto visākhāya gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Sā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sakkaccaṃ parivisitvā bhattakiccāvasāne satthāraṃ vanditvā paṭipucchi – “bhante, tumhehi saddhiṃ gatabhikkhūsu ekacce revatattherassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ‘khadiragahanaṃ arañña’nti vadanti, ekacce ‘ramaṇīya’nti, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti? Taṃ sutvā satthā “upāsike gāmo vā hotu araññaṃ vā, yasmiṃ ṭhāne arahanto viharanti, taṃ ramaṇīyamevā”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then those elderly monks, having washed their faces early in the morning, went to the house of the lay follower Visākhā, who provides almsfood for visiting monks, thinking, 'We will drink rice gruel.' Having drunk the gruel and eaten the hard food, they sat down. Then Visākhā asked them: 'Venerable sirs, did you also go with the Teacher to the Elder Revata’s dwelling place?' 'Yes, lay follower.' 'Venerable sirs, is the Elder's dwelling place delightful?' 'Lay follower, how could that place be delightful? It is a thicket of thorny khadira trees, like a dwelling place for petas.' Then two other young monks arrived. The lay follower gave them rice gruel and hard food as well and asked them the same question. They said: 'It is beyond description, lay follower. The Elder’s dwelling place is as if fashioned by psychic power, like the Sudhammā assembly hall of the devas.' The lay follower thought: 'The monks who came first spoke in one way, these speak in another. The first monks must have forgotten something and gone back after the psychic power was withdrawn, while these must have gone when it had been fashioned and created by psychic power.' Knowing this matter through her own wisdom, she decided, 'I will ask the Teacher when he comes,' and waited. A moment later, the Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to Visākhā’s house and sat down on the prepared seat. She respectfully served the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. When the meal was over, she paid homage to the Teacher and asked: 'Venerable sir, among the monks who went with you, some say the Elder Revata’s dwelling place is "a wilderness thicket of khadira trees," while others say it is "delightful." What, indeed, is the case?' Hearing this, the Teacher said: 'Lay follower, whether it be a village or a wilderness, any place where arahants dwell is itself delightful.' Then, making the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:

98.

98.

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyaka”nti.

Whether in a village or in the wilderness, in a valley or on high ground, wherever arahants dwell, that spot of earth is delightful.

Tattha kiñcāpi arahanto gāmante kāyavivekaṃ na labhanti, cittavivekaṃ pana labhanteva. Tesañhi dibbapaṭibhāgānipi ārammaṇāni cittaṃ cāletuṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā gāmo vā hotu araññādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ, yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakanti so bhūmipadeso ramaṇīyo evāti attho.

In that verse, although arahants do not obtain physical seclusion in the vicinity of a village, they certainly obtain mental seclusion. For even objects that are counterparts to the divine are unable to stir their minds. Therefore, whether it be a village or one of the forests and so on, wherever arahants dwell, 'that ground is delightful' means that very piece of land is pleasant. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Aparena [P 2.0196] samayena bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, kena nu kho kāraṇena āyasmā sīvalitthero sattadivasasattamāsādhikāni satta vassāni mātu kucchiyaṃ vasi, kena niraye [V 1.0357] pacci, kena nissandena lābhaggayasaggappatto jāto”ti? Satthā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “bhikkhave, kiṃ kathethā”ti pucchitvā, “bhante, idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte tassāyasmato pubbakammaṃ kathento āha –

On a later occasion, the monks raised a topic of discussion: 'Friends, for what reason did the Venerable Sīvali dwell in his mother's womb for seven years, seven months, and seven days? For what deed was he tormented in hell? And as a result of what did he become one who attained the peak of gains and glory?' Having heard their discussion, the Teacher asked, 'Monks, what are you discussing?' When they replied, 'Venerable sir, it is about this particular matter,' the Teacher, relating the past kamma of that venerable one, said:

Bhikkhave[M 1.0401], ito ekanavutikappe vipassī bhagavā loke uppajjitvā ekasmiṃ samaye janapadacārikaṃ caritvā pitu nagaraṃ paccāgamāsi. Rājā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa āgantukadānaṃ sajjetvā nāgarānaṃ sāsanaṃ pesesi “āgantvā mayhaṃ dāne sahāyakā hontū”ti. Te tathā katvā “raññā dinnadānato atirekataraṃ dassāmā”ti satthāraṃ nimantetvā punadivase dānaṃ paṭiyādetvā rañño sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Rājā āgantvā tesaṃ dānaṃ disvā “ito adhikataraṃ dassāmī”ti punadivasatthāya satthāraṃ nimantesi, neva rājā nāgare parājetuṃ sakkhi, na nāgarā rājānaṃ. Nāgarā chaṭṭhe vāre “sve dāni yathā ‘imasmiṃ dāne idaṃ nāma natthī’ti na sakkā hoti vattuṃ, evaṃ dānaṃ dassāmā”ti cintetvā punadivase dānaṃ paṭiyādetvā “kiṃ nu kho ettha natthī”ti olokentā allamadhumeva [P 2.0197] na addasaṃsu. Pakkamadhu pana bahuṃ atthi. Te allamadhussatthāya catūsu nagaradvāresu cattāri kahāpaṇasahassāni gāhāpetvā pahiṇiṃsu. Atheko janapadamanusso gāmabhojakaṃ passituṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge madhupaṭalaṃ disvā makkhikā palāpetvā sākhaṃ chinditvā sākhādaṇḍakeneva saddhiṃ madhupaṭalaṃ ādāya “gāmabhojakassa dassāmī”ti nagaraṃ pāvisi. Madhuatthāya gato taṃ disvā, “ambho, vikkiṇiyaṃ madhu”nti pucchi. “Na vikkiṇiyaṃ, sāmī”ti. “Handa, imaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gahetvā dehī”ti. So cintesi – “imaṃ madhupaṭalaṃ pādamattampi na agghati, ayaṃ pana kahāpaṇaṃ deti. Bahukahāpaṇako maññe, mayā vaḍḍhetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Atha naṃ “na demī”ti āha, “tena hi dve kahāpaṇe gaṇhāhī”ti. “Dvīhipi na demī”ti. Evaṃ tāva vaḍḍhesi, yāva so “tena hi idaṃ sahassaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti bhaṇḍikaṃ upanesi.

Bhikkhus, ninety-one aeons ago, the Blessed One Vipassī arose in the world. On one occasion, while wandering on tour through the country, he returned to his father’s city. The king, having prepared an offering for guests for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, sent a message to the townspeople: 'Come and assist me in my almsgiving.' They did so, and thinking, 'We will give an offering even more magnificent than the king’s,' they invited the Teacher for the next day. Having prepared the alms, they sent a message to the king. The king came, saw their alms, and thinking, 'I will give an even more abundant offering than this,' he invited the Teacher for the following day. Neither could the king defeat the townspeople, nor could the townspeople defeat the king. On the sixth occasion, the townspeople thought: 'Tomorrow we will give such an alms that it will not be possible to say, "Such and such is lacking in this offering."' Having prepared the alms for the next day, they looked it over, wondering, 'What could be missing here?' and they saw only that fresh honey was not there. There was, however, much stored honey. For the sake of fresh honey, they sent men out from the four city gates, having them take four thousand kahāpaṇas. Now a certain man from the countryside, who was coming to see the village headman, saw a honeycomb on the way. Shooing away the bees, he cut the branch and, taking the honeycomb together with the branch it was on, he entered the city, thinking, 'I will give this to the village headman.' A man who had gone out for honey saw him and asked: 'Friend, is this honey for sale?' 'It is not for sale, sir.' 'Come now, take this kahāpaṇa and give it to me.' The man thought: 'This honeycomb is not worth even a quarter, yet this man offers a kahāpaṇa. He must have many kahāpaṇas; I should raise the price.' Then he told him: 'I will not give it.' 'In that case, take two kahāpaṇas.' 'I will not give it for two either.' In this way he kept raising the price until the other said, 'In that case, take this thousand,' and brought forward the purse.

Atha naṃ so āha – “kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ ummattako[P 2.0198], udāhu kahāpaṇānaṃ ṭhapanokāsaṃ na labhasi, pādampi na agghanakaṃ madhuṃ ‘sahassaṃ gahetvā dehī’ti vadasi, ‘kiṃ nāmeta’”nti? ‘Jānāmahaṃ, bho, iminā pana me kammaṃ atthi, tenevaṃ vadāmī’ti. “Kiṃ kammaṃ, sāmī”ti? “Amhehi vipassībuddhassa aṭṭhasaṭṭhisamaṇasahassaparivārassa mahādānaṃ sajjitaṃ, tatrekaṃ allamadhumeva natthi, tasmā evaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti. Evaṃ, sante, nāhaṃ mūlena dassāmi, sace “ahampi dāne pattiṃ labhissāmi, dassāmī”ti. So gantvā nāgarānaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Nāgarā tassa saddhāya balavabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “sādhu, pattiko hotū”ti [M 1.0402] paṭijāniṃsu, te buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ [V 1.0358] nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā mahatiṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ āharāpetvā madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷāpesuṃ. Teneva manussena paṇṇākāratthāya dadhivārakopi āhaṭo atthi, so tampi dadhiṃ pātiyaṃ ākiritvā tena madhunā saṃsanditvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa ādito paṭṭhāya adāsi. Taṃ yāvadatthaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ sabbesaṃ pāpuṇi uttarimpi avasiṭṭhaṃ ahosiyeva. “Evaṃ thokaṃ madhu kathaṃ tāva bahūnaṃ [P 2.0199] pāpuṇī”ti na cintetabbaṃ. Tañhi buddhānubhāvena pāpuṇi. Buddhavisayo na cintetabbo. Cattāri hi “acinteyyānī”ti (a. ni. 4.77) vuttāni. Tāni cintento ummādasseva bhāgī hotīti. So puriso ettakaṃ kammaṃ katvā āyupariyosāne devaloke nibbattitvā ettakaṃ kālaṃ saṃsaranto ekasmiṃ samaye devalokā cavitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ rājakule nibbatto pitu accayena rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. So “ekaṃ nagaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti gantvā parivāresi, nāgarānañca sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “rajjaṃ vā me dentu yuddhaṃ vā”ti. Te “neva rajjaṃ dassāma, na yuddha”nti vatvā cūḷadvārehi nikkhamitvā dārūdakādīni āharanti, sabbakiccāni karonti.

Then the honey-seller said to him: 'Are you mad, or can you not find a place to store your kahāpaṇas, that you say, "Take a thousand and give me this honey," which is not worth even a quarter? What is this?' 'I know, sir, but I have a task to perform with this; that is why I speak so.' 'What task, master?' 'We have prepared a great almsgiving for the Buddha Vipassī and his retinue of sixty-eight thousand ascetics, and in it only fresh honey is lacking. That is why I am acquiring it thus.' 'If that is so, I will not give it for a price. But if I too may receive a share of the merit from the alms, I will give it.' The man went and reported this to the townspeople. Recognizing the strength of his faith, the townspeople agreed, saying, 'Good, let him be a sharer of the merit.' They had the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head take their seats, gave them rice gruel and solid food, and then had a large golden bowl brought and had the honeycomb squeezed. That same man had also brought a pot of curds as a gift; he poured the curds into the bowl, mixed it with the honey, and gave it to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, starting from the beginning. As they took as much as they needed, it was sufficient for all, and there was even some left over. One should not think: 'How could so little honey be sufficient for so many?' For it was sufficient through the Buddha’s power. The range of a Buddha is not to be pondered. For four things are said to be 'inconceivables' (AN 4.77). One who ponders them becomes a partaker of madness. Having done this deed, at the end of his life that man was reborn in the deva world. Having wandered in saṃsāra for so long, on one occasion he passed away from the deva world and was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī. After his father’s passing, he attained the kingship. Thinking, 'I will take a certain city,' he went and besieged it. He sent a message to the townspeople: 'Either give me the kingdom or give battle.' They replied, 'We will give neither the kingdom nor battle,' and, exiting through the small gates, they brought in firewood, water, and so on, and did all their tasks.

Itaropi cattāri mahādvārāni rakkhanto sattamāsādhikāni satta vassāni nagaraṃ uparundhi. Athassa mātā “kiṃ me putto karotī”ti pucchitvā “idaṃ nāma devī”ti taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “bālo mama putto, gacchatha, tassa ‘cūḷadvārānipi pidhāya nagaraṃ uparundhatū’ti vadethā”ti. So mātu sāsanaṃ sutvā tathā akāsi. Nāgarāpi bahi nikkhamituṃ alabhantā sattame divase attano rājānaṃ māretvā tassa rajjaṃ adaṃsu. So imaṃ kammaṃ katvā āyupariyosāne avīcimhi nibbattitvā yāvāyaṃ pathavī yojanamattaṃ [P 2.0200] ussannā, tāva niraye paccitvā catunnaṃ cūḷadvārānaṃ pidahitattā tato cuto tassā eva mātu kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā sattamāsādhikāni satta vassāni antokucchismiṃ vasitvā satta divasāni yonimukhe tiriyaṃ nipajji. Evaṃ, bhikkhave, sīvali, tadā nagaraṃ uparundhitvā gahitakammena ettakaṃ kālaṃ niraye paccitvā catunnaṃ cūḷadvārānaṃ pidahitattā tato cuto tassā eva mātu kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā ettakaṃ kālaṃ kucchiyaṃ vasi. Navamadhuno dinnattā lābhaggayasaggappatto jātoti.

The other king, guarding the four great gates, besieged the city for seven years and seven months. Then his mother asked, 'What is my son doing?' and when she heard the report, 'This is what he is doing, Your Majesty,' she said: 'My son is a fool. Go, tell him to besiege the city after closing the small gates as well.' Hearing his mother’s message, he did so. The townspeople, unable to go outside, on the seventh day killed their own king and gave him the kingdom. Having done this deed, at the end of his life he was reborn in Avīci. He was boiled in hell for as long as this earth has risen by a yojana. Because he had closed the four small gates, when he passed away from there, he took conception in the womb of that very same mother. He dwelled in her womb for seven years and seven months and for seven days lay crosswise at the mouth of the womb. Thus, bhikkhus, it was Sīvali who, as a result of the kamma of having besieged and taken the city at that time, was boiled in hell for so long. Because he had closed the four small gates, when he passed away from there, he took conception in that very mother’s womb and dwelled in the womb for so long. Because he had given the fresh honey, he was born having attained the peak of gain and the peak of glory.

Punekadivasaṃ [M 1.0403] bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “aho sāmaṇerassa lābho, aho puññaṃ, yena ekakena pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañcakūṭāgārasatādīni katānī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, mayhaṃ puttassa neva puññaṃ atthi, na pāpaṃ, ubhayamassa pahīna”nti vatvā brāhmaṇavagge imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then one day the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion: 'Oh, the gain of the novice! Oh, his merit! By himself he has had five hundred gabled chambers and so on made for five hundred bhikkhus.' The Teacher came and asked: 'For what topic of conversation, bhikkhus, are you now gathered together?' When they said, 'For this one,' he said: 'Bhikkhus, for my son there is neither merit nor evil; he has abandoned both.' Then, in the Brāhmaṇa Chapter, he spoke this verse:

“Yodha [V 1.0359] puññañca pāpañca, ubho saṅgamupaccagā;

Asokaṃ virajaṃ suddhaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 412);

One who here has transcended both merit and evil, and the bond of both, who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure—him I call a brahmin.

Khadiravaniyarevatattheravatthu navamaṃ.

The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Wood is the ninth.

10. Aññataraitthivatthu

10. The Story of a Certain Woman

Ramaṇīyānīti [P 2.0201] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ itthiṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Ramaṇīyāni” concerning a certain woman.

Eko kira piṇḍapātiko bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ jiṇṇauyyānaṃ pavisitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Ekā nagarasobhinī itthī purisena saddhiṃ “ahaṃ asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gamissāmi, tvaṃ tattha āgaccheyyāsī”ti saṅketaṃ katvā agamāsi. So puriso nāgacchi. Sā tassa āgamanamaggaṃ olokentī taṃ adisvā ukkaṇṭhitvā ito cito ca vicaramānā taṃ uyyānaṃ pavisitvā theraṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnaṃ disvā ito cito ca olokayamānā aññaṃ kañci adisvā “ayañca puriso eva, imassa cittaṃ pamohessāmī”ti tassa purato ṭhatvā punappunaṃ nivatthasāṭakaṃ mocetvā nivāseti, kese muñcitvā bandhati, pāṇiṃ paharitvā hasati. Therassa saṃvego uppajjitvā sakalasarīraṃ phari. So “kiṃ nu kho ida”nti cintesi. Satthāpi “mama santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ‘samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti gatassa bhikkhuno kā nu kho pavattī”ti upadhārento taṃ itthiṃ disvā tassā anācārakiriyaṃ, therassa ca saṃveguppattiṃ ñatvā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova tena saddhiṃ kathesi [P 2.0202] – “bhikkhu, kāmagavesakānaṃ aramaṇaṭṭhānameva vītarāgānaṃ ramaṇaṭṭhānaṃ hotī”ti[M 1.0404]. Evañca pana vatvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā tassa dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that a certain monk who lived on alms-food received a meditation subject from the Teacher and entered an old park to practice the ascetic discipline. A certain city beauty made an appointment with a man, saying, “I will go to such and such a place; you should come there,” and went. That man did not come. She, looking for his arrival along the path and not seeing him, became distressed. Wandering here and there, she entered that park and saw the elder sitting cross-legged. Looking around here and there and not seeing anyone else, she thought, “This is also a man; I will bewilder his mind.” Standing before him, she repeatedly loosened and put on her lower garment, let down her hair and tied it up, clapped her hands and laughed. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in the elder and pervaded his entire body. He thought, “What, indeed, is this?” The Teacher, reflecting, “What is happening to the monk who took a meditation subject from me and went to practice the ascetic discipline?” saw that woman and her improper behavior. Knowing that the elder's sense of spiritual urgency had arisen, he spoke to him while seated in the perfumed chamber: “Bhikkhu, what is a place of non-delight for those seeking sensual pleasures is a place of delight for those free from lust.” Having said this, he radiated light and, desiring to teach the Dhamma to him, spoke this verse:

99.

99.

“Ramaṇīyāni araññāni, yattha na ramatī jano;

Vītarāgā ramissanti, na te kāmagavesino”ti.

“Delightful are the forests where the common person does not delight; those free from lust will delight there, for they are not seekers of sensual pleasures.”

Tattha araññānīti supupphitataruvanasaṇḍapaṭimaṇḍitāni vimalasalilasampannāni araññāni nāma ramaṇīyāni. Yatthāti yesu araññesu vikasitesu padumavanesu gāmamakkhikā viya kāmagavesako jano na ramati. Vītarāgāti vigatarāgā pana khīṇāsavā nāma bhamaramadhukarā viya padumavanesu [V 1.0360] tathārūpesu araññesu ramissanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Na te kāmapavesino, yasmā te kāmagavesino na hontīti attho.

Herein, `forests` means great forests that are delightful, adorned with groves of well-blossomed young trees and endowed with clear water. `Where` refers to those forests in which the populace that seeks sensual pleasures does not delight, just as village flies do not delight in blossoming lotus groves. `Those free from lust` means those free from lust, namely the Arahants, will delight in such forests, just as bees and honey-makers delight in lotus groves. Why? Because `they are not seekers of sensual pleasures`; the meaning is that because they are not those who seek sensual pleasures.

Desanāvasāne so thero yathānisinnova saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā ākāsenāgantvā thutiṃ karonto tathāgatassa pāde vanditvā agamāsīti.

At the end of the discourse, that elder, just as he was seated, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then, having come through the air, while praising the Tathāgata, he paid homage at his feet and departed.

Aññataraitthivatthu dasamaṃ.

The Story of a Certain Woman is the tenth.

Arahantavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on the Arahant is concluded.

Sattamo vaggo.

The Seventh Chapter.

8. Sahassavaggo

8. The Chapter on Thousands

1. Tambadāṭhikacoraghātakavatthu

1. The Story of Tambadāṭhika, the Executioner of Thieves

Sahassamapi [M 1.0405][V 1.0361][P 2.0203] ce vācāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto tambadāṭhikacoraghātakaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery, delivered this Dhamma teaching, which begins with the words 'Sahassamapi ce vācā,' concerning Tambadāṭhika, the executioner of thieves.

Ekūnapañcasatā kira corā gāmaghātakādīni karontā jīvikaṃ kappesuṃ. Atheko puriso nibbiddhapiṅgalo tambadāṭhiko tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “ahampi tumhehi saddhiṃ jīvissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ corajeṭṭhakassa dassetvā “ayampi amhākaṃ santike vasituṃ icchatī”ti āhaṃsu. Atha naṃ corajeṭṭhako oloketvā “ayaṃ mātu thanaṃ chinditvā pitu vā galalohitaṃ nīharitvā khādanasamattho atikakkhaḷo”ti cintetvā “natthetassa amhākaṃ santike vasanakicca”nti paṭikkhipi. So evaṃ paṭikkhittopi āgantvā ekaṃ tasseva antevāsikaṃ upaṭṭhahanto ārādhesi. So taṃ ādāya corajeṭṭhakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “sāmi, bhaddako esa, amhākaṃ upakārako, saṅgaṇhatha na”nti yācitvā corajeṭṭhakaṃ paṭicchāpesi. Athekadivasaṃ [P 2.0204] nāgarā rājapurisehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā te core gahetvā vinicchayamahāmaccānaṃ santikaṃ nayiṃsu. Amaccā tesaṃ pharasunā sīsacchedaṃ āṇāpesuṃ. Tato “ko nu kho ime māressatī”ti pariyesantā te māretuṃ icchantaṃ kañci adisvā corajeṭṭhakaṃ āhaṃsu – “tvaṃ ime māretvā jīvitañceva labhissasi sammānañca, mārehi ne”ti. Sopi attānaṃ nissāya vasitattā te māretuṃ na icchi. Etenūpāyena ekūnapañcasate pucchiṃsu, sabbepi na icchiṃsu. Sabbapacchā taṃ nibbiddhapiṅgalaṃ tambadāṭhikaṃ pucchiṃsu. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā te sabbepi māretvā jīvitañceva sammānañca labhi. Etenūpāyena nagarassa dakkhiṇatopi pañca corasatāni ānetvā amaccānaṃ dassetvā tehi tesampi sīsacchede āṇatte corajeṭṭhakaṃ ādiṃ katvā pucchantā kañci māretuṃ icchantaṃ adisvā “purimadivase eko puriso pañcasate core māresi, kahaṃ nu kho so”ti. “Asukaṭṭhāne amheti diṭṭho”ti vutte taṃ pakkosāpetvā “ime mārehi, sammānaṃ lacchasī”ti āṇāpesuṃ. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā te sabbepi māretvā sammānaṃ labhi. Atha naṃ “bhaddako ayaṃ [M 1.0406] puriso, nibaddhaṃ coraghātakameva etaṃ karissāmā”ti [V 1.0362] mantetvā tassa taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ datvāva [P 2.0205] sammānaṃ kariṃsu. So pacchimadisatopi uttaradisatopi ānīte pañcasate pañcasate core ghātesiyeva. Evaṃ catūhi disāhi ānītāni dve sahassāni māretvā tato paṭṭhāya devasikaṃ ekaṃ dveti ānīte te manusse māretvā pañcapaṇṇāsa saṃvaccharāni coraghātakakammaṃ akāsi.

It is said that four hundred and ninety-nine thieves made their living by committing acts such as the destruction of villages. Then a certain man, who was one-eyed and had a copper-colored beard, approached them and said, 'I too will make a living with you.' Then, showing him to the chief of the thieves, they said, 'This man also wishes to live with us.' The chief of the thieves, looking at him, thought, 'This one is capable of cutting off his mother's breast or drawing out his father's throat-blood to eat; he is extremely cruel.' Thinking thus, he rejected him, saying, 'There is no reason for this one to live with us.' Though rejected thus, he returned and, by attending upon one of that very chief's disciples, pleased him. That disciple, taking him, approached the chief of thieves and, having requested, 'Master, this one is of good character and will be of service to us; please accept him,' he caused the chief of thieves to consent. Then one day, the townspeople, together with the king's men, captured those thieves and brought them to the judicial ministers. The ministers ordered their beheading with an axe. Then, searching, 'Who now will kill these men?' and not seeing anyone willing to kill them, they spoke to the chief of thieves: 'If you kill these men, you will receive both your life and a reward. Kill them!' But he, because they lived depending on him, did not wish to kill them. In this way, they asked the four hundred and ninety-nine thieves, and all of them did not wish to do it. Last of all, they asked that one-eyed man with the copper-colored beard. He, agreeing, 'Very well,' killed all of them and received both his life and a reward. In this same way, when five hundred thieves were brought from the south of the city and presented to the ministers, and when they ordered their beheading, they began by asking the chief of thieves, but seeing no one who wished to kill them, they said, 'On a previous day, a certain man killed five hundred thieves. Where is he now?' When it was said, 'He was seen by us in such-and-such a place,' they had him summoned and ordered, 'Kill these men; you will receive a reward.' He, agreeing, 'Very well,' killed all of them and received the reward. Then, having conferred, 'This man is excellent for the task; we shall make him the permanent executioner of thieves,' they gave him that very position and bestowed the reward upon him. He then executed the five hundred thieves brought from the west and the five hundred thieves brought from the north. In this way, having killed two thousand thieves brought from the four directions, from then on, he killed the men brought daily—one, two, or three—and for fifty-five years, he performed the work of an executioner of thieves.

So mahallakakāle ekappahāreneva sīsaṃ chindituṃ na sakkoti, dve tayo vāre paharanto manusse kilameti. Nāgarā cintayiṃsu – “aññopi coraghātako uppajjissati, ayaṃ ativiya manusse kilameti, kiṃ iminā”ti tassa taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ hariṃsu. So pubbe coraghātakakammaṃ karonto “ahatasāṭake nivāsetuṃ, navasappinā saṅkhataṃ khīrayāguṃ pivituṃ, sumanapupphāni pilandhituṃ, gandhe vilimpitu”nti imāni cattāri na labhi. So ṭhānā cāvitadivase “khīrayāguṃ me pacathā”ti vatvā ahatavatthasumanamālāvilepanāni gāhāpetvā nadiṃ gantvā nhatvā ahatavatthāni nivāsetvā mālā pilandhitvā gandhehi anulittagatto gehaṃ āgantvā nisīdi. Athassa navasappinā saṅkhataṃ [P 2.0206] khīrayāguṃ purato ṭhapetvā hatthadhovanodakaṃ āhariṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sāriputtatthero samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “kattha nu kho ajja mayā gantabba”nti attano bhikkhācāraṃ olokento tassa gehe khīrayāguṃ disvā “karissati nu kho me puriso saṅgaha”nti upadhārento “maṃ disvā mama saṅgahaṃ karissati, karitvā ca pana mahāsampattiṃ labhissati ayaṃ kulaputto”ti ñatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ ādāya tassa gehadvāre ṭhitameva attānaṃ dassesi.

In his old age, he was not able to cut off a head with a single blow; striking two or three times, he caused the men to suffer. The townspeople thought: 'Another executioner of thieves will arise. This one greatly torments people. What is the use of him?' And so they removed him from that position. Previously, while performing the work of an executioner, he did not obtain these four things: to wear new clothes, to drink milk-gruel prepared with fresh ghee, to wear jasmine flowers, and to anoint himself with perfumes. On the day he was removed from his position, he said, 'Cook milk-gruel for me.' Having procured new clothes, garlands, and perfumes, he went to the river, bathed, put on the new clothes, wore the garlands, and, with his body anointed with perfumes, returned to his house and sat down. Then, having placed the milk-gruel prepared with fresh ghee before him, they brought water for washing his hands. At that moment, the Elder Sāriputta, having arisen from meditative attainment and surveying his alms-round, thought, 'Where indeed should I go today?' Seeing the milk-gruel in that man's house, he investigated, 'Will this man indeed make an offering to me?' Knowing, 'Seeing me, he will make an offering to me, and having done so, this man of good family will obtain great good fortune,' he put on his robe, took his bowl, and showed himself standing right at the door of the man's house.

So theraṃ disvā pasannacitto cintesi – “mayā ciraṃ coraghātakakammaṃ kataṃ, bahū manussā māritā, idāni me gehe khīrayāgu paṭiyattā, thero āgantvā mama gehadvāre ṭhito, idāni mayā ayyassa deyyadhammaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti purato ṭhapitayāguṃ apanetvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā antogehe nisīdāpetvā patte khīrayāguṃ ākiritvā navasappiṃ āsiñcitvā theraṃ bījamāno aṭṭhāsi. Athassa ca dīgharattaṃ aladdhapubbatāya khīrayāguṃ pātuṃ balavaajjhāsayo ahosi. Thero tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā “tvaṃ, upāsaka, attano yāguṃ pivā”ti [M 1.0407] āha. So aññassa hatthe bījaniṃ datvā yāguṃ pivi. Thero bījamānaṃ purisaṃ “gaccha, upāsakameva bījāhī”ti āha. So bījiyamāno kucchipūraṃ yāguṃ pivitvā āgantvā theraṃ bījamāno ṭhatvā katāhārakiccassa therassa [P 2.0207] pattaṃ aggahesi. Thero tassa anumodanaṃ ārabhi. So attano cittaṃ therassa dhammadesanānugaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Thero sallakkhetvā, “upāsaka, kasmā cittaṃ desanānugaṃ kātuṃ na sakkosī”ti pucchi. “Bhante, mayā dīgharattaṃ kakkhaḷakammaṃ kataṃ, bahū manussā māritā, tamahaṃ attano kammaṃ anussaranto cittaṃ [V 1.0363] ayyassa desanānugaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi”nti. Thero “vañcessāmi na”nti cintetvā “kiṃ pana tvaṃ attano ruciyā akāsi, aññehi kāritosī”ti? “Rājā maṃ kāresi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ nu kho te, upāsaka, evaṃ sante akusalaṃ hotī”ti? Mandadhātuko upāsako therenevaṃ vutte “natthi mayhaṃ akusala”nti saññī hutvā tena hi, “bhante, dhammaṃ kathethā”ti. So there anumodanaṃ karonte ekaggacitto hutvā dhammaṃ suṇanto sotāpattimaggassa orato anulomikaṃ khantiṃ nibbattesi. Theropi anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Seeing the elder, with a devout mind, he thought: 'For a long time I have done the work of an executioner of thieves; many people have been killed. Now in my house, milk-gruel has been prepared. The elder has come and stands at my door. Now it is fitting for me to give a suitable offering to the venerable one.' He removed the gruel set before him, approached the elder, paid homage, seated him inside the house, poured milk-gruel into his bowl, poured fresh ghee over it, and stood fanning him. Now, because he had not obtained it for a long time, a strong desire to drink the milk-gruel arose in him. The elder, knowing his desire, said, 'Lay devotee, drink your own gruel.' Giving the fan into another's hand, he drank the gruel. The elder said to the man who was fanning, 'Go; do not fan me.' He, while being fanned, drank the gruel until his belly was full, then returned and stood fanning the elder. When the elder had finished his meal, he took the elder's bowl. The elder began the discourse of appreciation. He was unable to make his mind follow the elder’s Dhamma discourse. The elder, observing this, asked, 'Lay devotee, why are you unable to make your mind follow the discourse?' 'Venerable sir, for a long time I have done a harsh deed; many people have been killed. Remembering that, my own deed, I was unable to make my mind follow the venerable one's discourse.' The elder, thinking, 'I shall win him over,' asked, 'Did you do it of your own preference, or were you caused to do it by others?' 'The king caused me to do it, venerable sir.' 'In that case, lay devotee, what unwholesomeness could there be for you?' The lay devotee, being of a dull nature, upon hearing the elder’s words, perceived, 'There is no unwholesomeness for me,' and said, 'In that case, venerable sir, please teach the Dhamma.' While the elder was giving the discourse of appreciation, he, with a one-pointed mind, listened to the Dhamma and produced conformity-receptivity, which is on this side of the path of stream-entry. The elder, having given the discourse of appreciation, departed.

Upāsakaṃ theraṃ anugantvā nivattamānaṃ ekā yakkhinī dhenuvesena āgantvā ure paharitvā māresi. So kālaṃ katvā tusitapure nibbatti. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “coraghātako pañcapaṇṇāsa vassāni kakkhaḷakammaṃ katvā ajjeva tato mutto, ajjeva therassa bhikkhaṃ datvā ajjeva kālaṃ kato, kahaṃ nu kho nibbatto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte[P 2.0208], “bhikkhave, tusitapure nibbatto”ti āha. “Kiṃ, bhante, vadetha, ettakaṃ kālaṃ ettake manusse ghātetvā tusitavimāne nibbatto”ti. “Āma, bhikkhave, mahanto tena kalyāṇamitto laddho, so sāriputtassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā anulomañāṇaṃ nibbattetvā ito cuto tusitavimāne nibbatto”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

As the lay devotee was returning after accompanying the elder, a certain yakkhinī, having come in the form of a cow, struck him on the chest and killed him. After his death, he arose in the Tusita celestial realm. The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “The executioner of thieves, having done a harsh deed for fifty-five years, was freed from it only today. Only today he gave alms-food to the elder, and only today he died. Where could he have arisen?” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, he has arisen in the Tusita celestial realm.” “Venerable sir, what are you saying? After killing so many people for so long, has he arisen in the Tusita celestial abode?” “Yes, monks. A great good friend was obtained by him. He, having heard Sāriputta’s Dhamma discourse and produced conformity-knowledge, passed away from here and arose in the Tusita celestial abode.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

“Subhāsitaṃ suṇitvāna, nagare coraghātako;

Anulomakhantiṃ laddhāna, modatī tidivaṃ gato”ti.

“Having heard the well-spoken word, the executioner in the city, having gained conformity-receptivity, rejoices, having gone to the heavenly realm.”

“Bhante[M 1.0408], anumodanakathā nāma na balavā, tena kataṃ akusalakammaṃ mahantaṃ, kathaṃ ettakena visesaṃ nibbattesī”ti. Satthā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, ‘mayā desitadhammassa appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā’ti mā pamāṇaṃ gaṇhatha. Ekavācāpi hi atthanissitā seyyāvā”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

“Venerable sir, the discourse of appreciation is not powerful; the unwholesome deed done by him was great. How could he produce such a special attainment with so little?” The Teacher said, “Monks, do not take the measure of the Dhamma taught by me as ‘little’ or ‘much.’ For even a single word connected with the goal is better.” Having made the connection, he then taught the Dhamma, reciting this verse:

100.

100.

“Sahassamapi ce vācā, anatthapadasaṃhitā;

Ekaṃ atthapadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammatī”ti.

“Though a thousand speeches be spoken, composed of words without benefit, better is one beneficial word, which, having heard, one is pacified.”

Tattha sahassamapīti paricchedavacanaṃ, ekaṃ sahassaṃ dve sahassānīti evaṃ sahassena cepi paricchinnavācā honti, tā ca pana anatthapadasaṃhitā ākāsavaṇṇanāpabbatavaṇṇanāvanavaṇṇanādīni [V 1.0364][P 2.0209] pakāsakehi aniyyānadīpakehi anatthakehi padehi saṃhitā yāva bahukā hoti, tāva pāpikā evāti attho. Ekaṃ atthapadanti yaṃ pana “ayaṃ kāyo, ayaṃ kāyagatāsati, tisso vijjā anuppatto, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti evarūpaṃ ekaṃ atthapadaṃ sutvā rāgādivūpasamena upasammati, taṃ atthasādhakaṃ nibbānappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgasatipaṭṭhānaparidīpakaṃ ekampi padaṃ seyyoyevāti attho.

Herein, 'even a thousand' is a word of limitation. Even if there are speeches limited by a thousand—one thousand or two thousand—if they are connected with words without benefit, such as those that describe praise of the sky, praise of mountains, or praise of forests, and are connected with words that are without benefit and do not illuminate the path of escape, then the more there are, the more evil they are. This is the meaning. As for 'a single beneficial phrase': having heard one such beneficial phrase as, “This is the body; this is mindfulness directed to the body; the three true knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled,” one becomes pacified through the calming of lust and so on. That phrase, which accomplishes the goal, is connected with Nibbāna, and illuminates the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and foundations of mindfulness—even a single such phrase is far better. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Tambadāṭhikacoraghātakavatthu paṭhamaṃ.

The Story of Tambadāṭhika, the Executioner of Thieves (First).

2. Bāhiyadārucīriyattheravatthu

2. The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya

Sahassamapi ce gāthāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dārucīriyattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, which begins with the verse 'Though a thousand verses...', concerning the Elder Dārucīriya.

Ekasmiñhi kāle bahū manussā nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhanditvā antomahāsamudde bhinnāya nāvāya macchakacchapabhakkhā [P 2.0210] ahesuṃ. Ekovettha ekaṃ phalakaṃ gahetvā vāyamanto suppārakapaṭṭanatīraṃ okkami, tassa nivāsanapārupanaṃ natthi. So aññaṃ kiñci apassanto sukkhakaṭṭhadaṇḍake vākehi paliveṭhetvā nivāsanapārupanaṃ katvā devakulato kapālaṃ [M 1.0409] gahetvā suppārakapaṭṭanaṃ agamāsi, manussā taṃ disvā yāgubhattādīni datvā “ayaṃ eko arahā”ti sambhāvesuṃ. So vatthesu upanītesu “sacāhaṃ nivāsessāmi vā pārupissāmi vā, lābhasakkāro me parihāyissatī”ti tāni vatthāni paṭikkhipitvā dārucīrāneva paridahi. Athassa bahūhi “arahā arahā”ti vuccamānassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “ye kho keci loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā, ahaṃ tesaṃ aññataro”ti. Athassa purāṇasālohitā devatā evaṃ cintesi.

Indeed, at one time, many people, having set out on the great ocean by ship, became food for fish and turtles when the ship broke apart in the middle of the great ocean. One among them, taking a plank and striving, reached the shore of the port of Suppāraka. He had no lower or upper garment. Seeing nothing else, he bound together dry firewood and bamboo with bark fibers, made it into a lower and upper garment, took a bowl from a spirit shrine, and went to the port of Suppāraka. When people saw him, they gave him rice-gruel, cooked rice, and other things, honoring him and saying, 'This is an Arahant.' When clothes were offered to him, he thought, 'If I were to wear a lower garment or put on an upper garment, my gain and honor would diminish.' Thus, he rejected those clothes and wore only the garments of wood-bark. Then, as he was being called 'Arahant, Arahant' by many, this thought arose in his mind: 'Whoever in the world are Arahants or have attained the path to Arahantship, I am one of them.' Then a deity, who had been his companion in a former life, thought thus.

Purāṇasālohitāti pubbe ekato katasamaṇadhammā. Pubbe kira kassapadasabalassa sāsane osakkamāne sāmaṇerādīnaṃ vippakāraṃ disvā satta bhikkhū saṃvegappattā “yāva sāsanassa antaradhānaṃ na hoti, tāva attano patiṭṭhaṃ karissāmā”ti suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ vanditvā araññaṃ paviṭṭhā ekaṃ pabbataṃ disvā “jīvite sālayā [P 2.0211] nivattantu. Nirālayā imaṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhantū”ti [V 1.0365] vatvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā sabbepi taṃ abhiruyha nisseṇiṃ pātetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu saṅghatthero ekarattātikkameneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So anotattadahe nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā uttarakuruto piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā te bhikkhū āha – “āvuso, imaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti. Kiṃ pana, bhante, amhehi evaṃ katikā katā “yo paṭhamaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tenābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ avasesā paribhuñjissantī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Tena hi sace mayampi tumhe viya visesaṃ nibbattessāma, sayaṃ āharitvā paribhuñjissāmā”ti na icchiṃsu. Dutiyadivase dutiyatthero anāgāmiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Sopi tatheva piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā itare nimantesi. Te evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ pana, bhante, amhehi evaṃ katikā katā ‘mahātherena ābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhuñjitvā anutherena ābhataṃ bhuñjissāmā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Evaṃ sante tumhe viya mayampi visesaṃ nibbattetvā attano purisakārena bhuñjituṃ sakkontā bhuñjissāmā”ti na icchiṃsu. Tesu arahattaṃ patto bhikkhu parinibbāyi, anāgāmī brahmaloke nibbatti. Itare [P 2.0212] pañca therā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkontā sussitvā sattame divase kālaṃ katvā [M 1.0410] devaloke nibbattitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde tato cavitvā tattha tattha kulagharesu nibbattiṃsu. Tesu eko pukkusāti rājā (ma. ni. 3.342) ahosi, eko kumārakassapo (ma. ni. 1.249), eko dārucīriyo (udā. 10), eko dabbo mallaputto (pārā. 380; udā. 79) eko sabhiyo paribbājakoti (su. ni. sabhiyasuttaṃ). Tattha yo brahmaloke nibbatto bhikkhu taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “purāṇasālohitā devatā”ti.

As for 'former companion,' it means one who formerly practiced the monk's duties together. It is said that formerly, during the decline of the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, seven monks, having become spiritually stirred upon seeing the corrupt conduct of novices and others, resolved, 'As long as the dispensation has not disappeared, we shall establish a refuge for ourselves.' Having paid homage to the golden cetiya, they entered the forest, and upon seeing a mountain, said, 'Let those who have attachment to life turn back. Let those without attachment ascend this mountain.' Having fashioned a ladder, all of them ascended it, pushed down the ladder, and practiced the monk's duties. Among them, the Saṅghatthera attained Arahantship in the passing of just one night. He, having chewed a nāgalatā tooth-stick at Lake Anotatta and brought almsfood from Uttarakuru, said to the other monks, 'Friends, having chewed this tooth-stick and washed your faces, partake of this almsfood.' 'But, venerable sir, did we make such an agreement: “Whoever first attains Arahantship, the others will partake of the almsfood brought by him”?' 'No, friends, that is not so.' 'In that case, if we too, like you, can bring about a special attainment, we will bring our own and eat.' Thus they did not desire it. On the second day, the second elder attained the fruit of non-returning. He too, in the same way, brought almsfood and invited the others. They said thus: 'But, venerable sir, did we make such an agreement: “Having not eaten the almsfood brought by the great elder, we will eat that brought by the next elder”?' 'No, friends, that is not so.' 'That being the case, if we too, like you, can bring about a special attainment and are able to eat through our own manly effort, we shall eat.' Thus they did not desire it. Among them, the monk who had attained Arahantship attained parinibbāna; the non-returner was reborn in the Brahma-world. The other five elders, being unable to bring about a special attainment, withered away and on the seventh day passed away and were reborn in the deva-world. In this Buddha-era, having passed away from there, they were reborn in various family homes.
