Among them, one became King Pukkusāti, one became Kumārakassapa, one became Dārucīriya, one became Dabba the Mallian, and one became the wanderer Sabhiya. Therein, with reference to the monk who was reborn in the Brahma-world, this was said: 'a deity who was a former companion.'

Tassa hi brahmuno etadahosi – “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi, idāni imaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā vicaranto vinasseyya, saṃvejessāmi na”nti. Atha naṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – “neva kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, arahā, napi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpanno, sāpi te paṭipadā natthi, yāya tvaṃ arahā vā assa arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpanno”ti. Bāhiyo ākāse ṭhatvā kathentaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ oloketvā cintesi – “aho bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, ahaṃ ‘arahantomhī’ti cintesiṃ, ayañca maṃ ‘na tvaṃ arahā, napi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannosī’ti vadati, atthi nu kho [P 2.0213] loke añño arahā”ti. Atha naṃ pucchi – “atthi nu kho etarahi devate loke arahā vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpanno”ti. Athassa devatā ācikkhi – “atthi, bāhiya, uttaresu janapadesu sāvatthi nāma nagaraṃ, tattha so bhagavā etarahi viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. So hi, bāhiya, bhagavā arahā ceva arahattatthāya ca dhammaṃ desetī”ti.

Indeed, this thought occurred to that Brahmā: 'This one fashioned a ladder with me, ascended the mountain, and practiced the ascetic's duties. Now, wandering about holding this view, he might be ruined. I shall stir him.' Then, having approached him, he said thus: 'You, Bāhiya, are certainly not an Arahant, nor have you entered upon the path to Arahantship. You do not even have that practice by which you might be an Arahant or one who has entered upon the path to Arahantship.' Bāhiya, looking at the great Brahmā speaking while standing in the sky, thought: 'Oh, what a grave matter I have undertaken! I thought, “I am an Arahant,” and this one tells me, “You are not an Arahant, nor have you entered upon the path to Arahantship.” Could there be another Arahant in the world?' Then he asked him: 'O deity, is there now in the world an Arahant or one who has entered upon the path to Arahantship?' Then the deity told him: 'There is, Bāhiya. In the northern districts there is a city named Sāvatthī. There that Blessed One is now dwelling, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Indeed, Bāhiya, that Blessed One is himself an Arahant and he also teaches the Dhamma for the sake of attaining Arahantship.'

Bāhiyo [V 1.0366] rattibhāge devatāya kathaṃ sutvā saṃviggamānaso taṃ khaṇaṃyeva suppārakā nikkhamitvā ekarattivāsena sāvatthiṃ agamāsi, sabbaṃ vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ ekarattivāseneva agamāsi. Gacchanto ca pana devatānubhāvena gato. “Buddhānubhāvenā”tipi vadantiyeva. Tasmiṃ pana khaṇe satthā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho hoti. So bhuttapātarāse kāyaālasiyavimocanatthaṃ abbhokāse caṅkamante sambahule bhikkhū “kahaṃ etarahi satthā”ti pucchi. Bhikkhū “bhagavā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti vatvā taṃ pucchiṃsu – “tvaṃ pana kuto āgatosī”ti? “Suppārakā āgatomhī”ti. “Kadā [M 1.0411] nikkhantosī”ti? “Hiyyo sāyaṃ [P 2.0214] nikkhantomhī”ti. “Dūratosi āgato, nisīda, tava pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā thokaṃ vissamāhi, āgatakāle satthāraṃ dakkhissasī”ti. “Ahaṃ, bhante, satthu vā attano vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, ekarattenevamhi katthaci aṭṭhatvā anisīditvā vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgato, satthāraṃ passitvāva vissamissāmī”ti. So evaṃ vatvā taramānarūpo sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā bhagavantaṃ anopamāya buddhasiriyā piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā “cirassaṃ vata me gotamo sammāsambuddho diṭṭho”ti diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya onatasarīro gantvā antaravīthiyameva pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā gopphakesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā evamāha – “desetu me, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu sugato dhammaṃ, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “akālo kho tāva, bāhiya, antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā piṇḍāyā”ti paṭikkhipi.

Bāhiya, having heard the words of the deity in the night, had a heart full of alarm. At that very moment, he left Suppāraka and arrived in Sāvatthī in a single night; he traveled the entire journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas in just one night. And as he went, he traveled by the power of the deity. It is also said that it was by the power of the Buddha. At that moment, the Teacher had entered Sāvatthī for alms. He approached many monks who, having finished their morning meal, were walking in the open air to relieve bodily fatigue, and asked, “Where is the Teacher now?” The monks replied, “The Blessed One has entered Sāvatthī for alms,” and then asked him, “But where have you come from?” “I have come from Suppāraka.” “When did you depart?” “Yesterday evening.” “You have come from afar. Sit down, wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest a little. You will see the Teacher when he returns.” “Venerable sirs, I do not know of any danger to the life of the Teacher or to my own. I have come on a journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night without stopping or sitting anywhere. Only after seeing the Teacher will I rest.” Having spoken thus, he hurried into Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One walking for alms with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha. Thinking, “Indeed, after a long time, I have seen Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” from the place he saw him, he went with his body bowed low, and right in the middle of the street, he paid homage with the five-point prostration. Clasping his ankles firmly, he said: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma! May the Sugata teach me the Dhamma, that which would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time!” Then the Teacher refused him, saying, “It is not the time, Bāhiya. We have entered the village for alms.”

Taṃ sutvā bāhiyo, bhante, saṃsāre saṃsarantena kabaḷīkārāhāro na aladdhapubbo, tumhākaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, desetu me dhammanti. Satthā dutiyampi paṭikkhipiyeva. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “imassa maṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā nirantaraṃ ajjhotthaṭaṃ hoti, balavapītivego dhammaṃ sutvāpi na sakkhissati paṭivijjhituṃ, majjhattupekkhāya tāva [P 2.0215] tiṭṭhatu, ekaratteneva vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgatattā darathopissa balavā, sopi tāva paṭippassambhatū”ti. Tasmā dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā tatiyaṃ yācito antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova “tasmātiha te, bāhiya, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī’”tiādinā (udā. 10) nayena dhammaṃ desesi. So satthu dhammaṃ suṇantoyeva sabbāsave khepetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tāvadeva ca pana bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci, “paripuṇṇaṃ te pattacīvara”nti puṭṭho “na paripuṇṇa”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “tena hi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesāhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

Hearing this, Bāhiya said, “Venerable sir, in wandering through saṃsāra, physical food has never not been obtained, but I do not know of any danger to your life or to my own. Teach me the Dhamma!” The Teacher refused a second time. It is said that this was his thought: “From the moment this one saw me, his entire body has been continuously pervaded by rapture. With such a strong surge of rapture, he will not be able to penetrate the Dhamma even after hearing it. Let him first stand in equanimity. Also, having come a journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night, his fatigue is great. Let that too first be calmed.” Therefore, having refused twice, when requested a third time, standing in the middle of the street he taught the Dhamma in the manner beginning: “Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train thus: ‘In the seen, there will be only the seen...’” (Udāna 10). While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he destroyed all the taints and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. At that very moment, he requested the Blessed One for ordination. When asked, “Are your bowl and robes complete?” he replied, “They are not complete.” Then the Teacher, having said to him, “In that case, search for a bowl and robes,” departed.

“So kira vīsati vassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karonto ‘bhikkhunā nāma attanā paccaye [V 1.0367] labhitvā aññaṃ anoloketvā sayameva paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī’ti ekabhikkhussāpi pattena vā cīvarena vā saṅgahaṃ na akāsi[M 1.0412], tenassa iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ na upajjissatī”ti ñatvā ehibhikkhubhāvena pabbajjaṃ na adāsi. Tampi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesamānameva ekā yakkhinī dhenurūpena āgantvā uramhi paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Satthā piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ nikkhanto bāhiyassa [P 2.0216] sarīraṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne patitaṃ disvā bhikkhū āṇāpesi, “bhikkhave, ekasmiṃ gehadvāre ṭhatvā mañcakaṃ āharāpetvā imaṃ sarīraṃ nagarato nīharitvā jhāpetvā thūpaṃ karothā”ti. Bhikkhū tathā kariṃsu, katvā ca pana vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attanā katakiccaṃ ārocetvā tassa abhisamparāyaṃ pucchiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ bhagavā tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ ācikkhitvā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ yadidaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo”ti (a. ni. 1.216) etadagge ṭhapesi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū pucchiṃsu – “bhante, tumhe ‘bāhiyo arahattaṃ patto’ti vadetha, kadā so arahattaṃ patto”ti? “Mama dhammaṃ sutakāle, bhikkhave”ti. “Kadā panassa, bhante, tumhehi dhammo kathito”ti? “Piṇḍāya carantena antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā”ti. “Appamattako hi, bhante, tumhehi antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā kathitadhammo kathaṃ so tāvattakena visesaṃ nibbattesī”ti, atha ne satthā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, mama dhammaṃ ‘appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā’ti mā pamāṇaṃ gaṇhatha. Anekānipi hi gāthāsahassāni anatthanissitāni na seyyo, atthanissitaṃ pana ekampi gāthāpadaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that for twenty thousand years he practiced the ascetic's life, thinking, ‘It is proper for a bhikkhu, having obtained requisites by himself, to use them himself without regard for another.’ He did not offer support to even a single bhikkhu with a bowl or a robe. Knowing, “Because of this, a bowl and robes created by psychic power will not arise for him,” the Buddha did not give him ordination with the ‘Come, bhikkhu’ formula. While he was searching for that bowl and robes, a female yakkha in the form of a cow came and struck him in the chest, causing him to reach the end of his life. The Teacher, having walked for alms and finished his meal, was leaving with many bhikkhus when he saw Bāhiya’s body fallen on a rubbish heap and commanded the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, stand at the door of a house, have a bier brought, take this body out of the city, cremate it, and build a stūpa.” The bhikkhus did so. Having done this, they went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, reported what they had done, and asked about his future state. Then the Blessed One told them of his attainment of final Nibbāna and placed him in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are quickest to attain higher knowledge, Bāhiya Dārucīriya is the chief.” Then the bhikkhus asked him: “Venerable sir, you say that Bāhiya attained Arahantship. When did he attain Arahantship?” “At the time he heard my Dhamma, bhikkhus.” “But when, venerable sir, was the Dhamma taught to him by you?” “While I was standing in the middle of the street, walking for alms.” “Venerable sir, the Dhamma taught by you while standing in the middle of the street was very brief. How did he produce such a special attainment with just that?” Then the Teacher said to them: “Bhikkhus, do not take the measure of my Dhamma as ‘little’ or ‘much.’ For thousands of verses connected with what is unbeneficial are not better than a single verse connected with what is beneficial.” Having thus connected the sequence, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

101.

101.

“Sahassamapi ce gāthā, anatthapadasaṃhitā;

Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammatī”ti.

“Though a thousand verses be composed of unbeneficial words, better is one line of a verse on hearing which one finds peace.”

Tattha [P 2.0217] ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyoti “appamādo amatapadaṃ…pe… yathā mayā”ti (dha. pa. 21) evarūpā ekā gāthāpi seyyoti attho. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Herein, ‘better is one line of verse’ means that even a single verse of this kind is better, such as: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless…” (Dhp. 21). This is the meaning. The remainder should be understood in the same way as before.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Bāhiyadārucīriyattheravatthu dutiyaṃ.

The second story, of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, is concluded.

3. Kuṇḍalakesittherīvatthu

3. The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī

Yo [M 1.0413][V 1.0368] ca gāthāsataṃ bhāseti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuṇḍalakesiṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with the verse ‘Yo ca gāthāsataṃ bhāse,’ concerning Kuṇḍalakesī.

Rājagahe kira ekā seṭṭhidhītā soḷasavassuddesikā abhirūpā ahosi dassanīyā pāsādikā. Tasmiñca vaye ṭhitā nāriyo purisajjhāsayā honti purisalolā. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatale sirigabbhe nivāsāpesuṃ. Ekamevassā dāsiṃ paricārikaṃ adaṃsu. Athekaṃ kulaputtaṃ corakammaṃ karontaṃ gahetvā pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā catukke catukke kasāhi paharitvā āghātanaṃ nayiṃsu. Seṭṭhidhītā mahājanassa saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti pāsādatale ṭhatvā olokentī taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā [P 2.0218] hutvā taṃ patthayamānā āhāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā mañcake nipajji. Atha naṃ mātā pucchi – “kiṃ idaṃ, ammā”ti? “Sace etaṃ ‘coro’ti gahetvā niyyamānaṃ purisaṃ labhissāmi, jīvissāmi. No ce labhissāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthi, idheva marissāmī”ti. “Amma, mā evaṃ kari, amhākaṃ jātiyā ca gottena ca bhogena ca sadisaṃ aññaṃ sāmikaṃ labhissasī”ti. “Mayhaṃ aññena kiccaṃ natthi, imaṃ alabhamānā marissāmī”ti. Mātā dhītaraṃ saññāpetuṃ asakkontī pituno ārocesi. Sopi naṃ saññāpetuṃ asakkonto “kiṃ sakkā kātu”nti cintetvā taṃ coraṃ gahetvā gacchantassa rājapurisassa sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ pesesi – “imaṃ gahetvā etaṃ purisaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti kahāpaṇe gahetvā taṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ māretvā “mārito, deva, coro”ti rañño ārocesi. Seṭṭhipi tassa dhītaraṃ adāsi.

In Rājagaha, it is said, there was a merchant's daughter, sixteen years of age, very beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing. And at that age, women are inclined toward men and are fond of men. Then her mother and father had her dwell on the upper floor of a seven-storied mansion, in a glorious inner chamber. They gave her only one maidservant as an attendant. Then, having seized a certain man of good family who was committing theft, they bound his hands behind his back, beat him with whips at every crossroad, and led him to the execution ground. The merchant’s daughter, hearing the sound of the great crowd, stood on the mansion's terrace and, while looking, wondered, “What could this be?” Seeing that man, her heart became attached, and longing for him, she refused food and lay down on her bed. Then her mother asked her, “What is this, dear daughter?” “If I get that man who is being seized and led away as a ‘thief,’ I will live. If I do not get him, my life is no more; I will die right here.” “Dear daughter, do not act thus. You will get another husband equal to us in birth, lineage, and wealth.” “I have no need for another. Not getting this man, I will die.” The mother, being unable to persuade her daughter, informed the father. He too, being unable to persuade her, thought, “What can be done?” and sent a thousand pieces of wealth to the king's man who was leading the thief away, with the message: “Take this and give that man to me.” He said, “Very well,” and taking the coins, he released that man, killed another, and reported to the king, “The thief has been killed, Your Majesty.” The merchant also gave his daughter to him.

Sā tato paṭṭhāya “sāmikaṃ ārādhessāmī”ti sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā sayameva tassa yāguādīni saṃvidahati, coro katipāhaccayena cintesi – “kadā nu kho imaṃ māretvā etissā ābharaṇāni gahetvā ekasmiṃ surāgehe vikkiṇitvā khādituṃ labhissāmī”ti? So “attheko upāyo”ti cintetvā āhāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā mañcake nipajji, atha naṃ sā upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ te, sāmi, rujjatī”ti pucchi. “Na kiñci me, bhaddeti, kacci pana me mātāpitaro tuyhaṃ kuddhā”ti? “Na kujjhanti, bhadde”ti[M 1.0414]. Atha “kiṃ nāmeta”nti? “Bhadde, ahaṃ taṃ divasaṃ bandhitvā niyyamāno [P 2.0219] corapapāte adhivatthāya devatāya balikammaṃ paṭissuṇitvā jīvitaṃ labhiṃ, tvampi mayā tassā eva ānubhāvena laddhā, ‘taṃ me devatāya balikammaṃ ṭhapita’nti cintemi, bhadde”ti. “Sāmi, mā cintayi, karissāmi balikammaṃ, vadehi[V 1.0369], kenattho”ti? “Appodakamadhupāyasena ca lājapañcamakapupphehi cā”ti. “Sādhu, sāmi, ahaṃ paṭiyādessāmī”ti sā sabbaṃ balikammaṃ paṭiyādetvā “ehi, sāmi, gacchāmā”ti āha. “Tena hi, bhadde, tava ñātake nivattetvā mahagghāni vatthābharaṇāni gahetvā attānaṃ alaṅkarohi, hasantā kīḷantā sukhaṃ gamissāmā”ti. Sā tathā akāsi.

From that time on, thinking, “I will please my husband,” she, adorned with all her ornaments, personally prepared his gruel and other food. After a few days had passed, the thief thought, “When indeed will I get the chance to kill this woman, take her ornaments, sell them in a tavern, and eat and drink?” Thinking, “Here is a stratagem,” he refused food and lay down on his bed. Then she approached him and asked, “What ails you, my lord?” “Nothing ails me, dear lady,” he replied. She then asked, “Are my parents perhaps angry with you?” “They are not angry, dear lady,” he said. “Then what is this about?” she asked. “Dear lady,” he explained, “on that day, when I was bound and being led away, I promised an offering to the deity who resides at the Robbers' Cliff and thus obtained my life. You also were obtained by me through the power of that very deity. I am thinking, dear lady, that my offering to the deity has been neglected.” “My lord, do not worry. I will make the offering. Tell me, what is needed?” “There is a need for honey-rice-pudding made with little water, and for flowers which have parched grain as the fifth item.” “Very well, my lord, I will prepare it.” Having prepared the entire offering, she said, “Come, my lord, let us go.” “In that case, dear lady, send your relatives back, take your valuable garments and ornaments, and adorn yourself. Laughing and playing, we shall go happily.” She did so.

Atha naṃ so pabbatapādaṃ gatakāle āha – “bhadde, ito paraṃ ubhova janā gamissāma, sesajanaṃ yānakena saddhiṃ nivattāpetvā balikammabhājanaṃ sayaṃ ukkhipitvā gaṇhāhī”ti. Sā tathā akāsi. Coro taṃ gahetvā corapapātapabbataṃ abhiruhi. Tassa hi ekena passena manussā abhiruhanti, ekaṃ passaṃ chinnapapātaṃ. Pabbatamatthake ṭhitā tena passena core pātenti. Te khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hutvā bhūmiyaṃ patanti. Tasmā “corapapāto”ti vuccati. Sā tassa pabbatassa matthake ṭhatvā “balikammaṃ te, sāmi, karohī”ti āha. So tuṇhī ahosi. Puna tāya [P 2.0220] “kasmā, sāmi, tuṇhībhūtosī”ti vutte taṃ āha – “na mayhaṃ balikammenattho, vañcetvā pana taṃ ādāya āgatomhī”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā, sāmī”ti? “Taṃ māretvā tava ābharaṇāni gahetvā palāyanatthāyā”ti. Sā maraṇabhayatajjitā āha – “sāmi, ahañca ābharaṇāni ca tava santakāneva, kasmā evaṃ vadesī”ti? So, “mā evaṃ karohī”ti, punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi “māremi evā”ti āha. “Evaṃ sante kiṃ te mama maraṇena? Imāni ābharaṇāni gahetvā mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dehi, ito paṭṭhāya maṃ ‘matā’ti dhārehi, dāsī vā te hutvā kammaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, when they had gone to the foot of the mountain, he said to her: “Dear lady, from here on, we two shall go alone. Send the remaining people back with the vehicle, and you yourself lift up and carry the offering vessel.” She did so. The thief took her and climbed the Robbers' Cliff Mountain. On one side of that mountain, people ascend; the other side is a sheer precipice. Standing on the mountain summit, they push thieves down from that side. They fall to the ground, having become shattered into pieces. Therefore, it is called the “Robbers' Cliff.” Standing on the summit of that mountain, she said, “My lord, make your offering.” He was silent. When she again said, “Why, my lord, are you silent?” he said to her, “I have no need for an offering. I have brought you here by deceiving you.” “For what reason, my lord?” “I have come to kill you, take your ornaments, and flee.” Terrified by the fear of death, she said, “My lord, both I and the ornaments are your property indeed. Why do you speak thus?” Though she pleaded again and again, saying, “Do not do so,” he said, “I will kill you indeed.” “If that is so, what benefit is there for you in my death? Take these ornaments and give me my life. From now on, consider me as dead. Or, becoming your slave, I will do your work.” Having said this, she spoke this verse:

“Idaṃ suvaṇṇakeyūraṃ, muttā veḷuriyā bahū;

Sabbaṃ harassu bhaddante, maṃ ca dāsīti sāvayā”ti. (apa. therī 2.3.27);

“Here is a golden armlet, and many pearls and beryl gems; take it all, my good lord, and proclaim me as your slave.”

Taṃ [M 1.0415] sutvā coro “evaṃ kate tvaṃ gantvā mātāpitūnaṃ ācikkhissasi, māressāmiyeva, mā tvaṃ bāḷhaṃ paridevasī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the thief, saying, “If this is done, you will go and tell your parents. I will surely kill you. Do not wail so intensely,” spoke this verse:

“Mā bāḷhaṃ paridevesi, khippaṃ bandhāhi bhaṇḍikaṃ;

Na tuyhaṃ jīvitaṃ atthi, sabbaṃ gaṇhāmi bhaṇḍaka”nti. –

“Do not wail intensely; quickly take off your ornaments. Your life is no more; I will take all your adornments.”

Sā [P 2.0221] cintesi – “aho idaṃ kammaṃ bhāriyaṃ. Paññā nāma na pacitvā khādanatthāya katā, atha kho vicāraṇatthāya katā, jānissāmissa kattabba”nti, atha naṃ āha – “sāmi, yadā tvaṃ [V 1.0370] ‘coro’ti gahetvā nīyasi, tadāhaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ācikkhiṃ, te sahassaṃ vissajjetvā taṃ āharāpetvā gehe kariṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ tuyhaṃ upakārikā, ajja me sudiṭṭhaṃ katvā attānaṃ vandituṃ dehī”ti. So “sādhu, bhadde, sudiṭṭhaṃ katvā vandāhī”ti vatvā pabbatante aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ sā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā, “sāmi, idaṃ te pacchimadassanaṃ, idāni tuyhaṃ vā mama dassanaṃ, mayhaṃ vā tava dassanaṃ natthī”ti purato ca pacchato ca āliṅgitvā pamattaṃ hutvā pabbatante ṭhitaṃ piṭṭhipasse ṭhatvā ekena hatthena khandhe gahetvā ekena piṭṭhikacchāya gahetvā pabbatapapāte khipi. So pabbatakucchiyaṃ paṭihato khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ hutvā bhūmiyaṃ pati. Corapapātamatthake adhivatthā devatā tesaṃ dvinnampi kiriyaṃ disvā tassā itthiyā sādhukāraṃ datvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

She thought: “Oh, this deed is heavy. Wisdom, indeed, is not made for cooking and eating, but rather it is made for deliberation. I shall know what must be done to him.” Then she said to him: “Master, when you were seized and led away as a thief, I informed my parents. They, having given up a thousand, had you brought and established you in our home. From that time on, I have been your benefactress. Today, allow me to look upon you well and pay homage.” He said, “Very well, good lady, look well and pay homage,” and stood at the edge of the precipice. Then she, having circumambulated him three times and paid homage at four points, said: “Master, this is the last sight of you for me. From now on, there will be no seeing of me for you, nor of you for me.” Then, embracing him from the front and from the back, when he had become heedless while standing at the edge of the precipice, she stood behind him, and taking his shoulders with one hand and his lower back with the other, she threw him down the precipice. He, striking the side of the mountain, broke into pieces and fell to the ground. The deity dwelling on the summit of the Robber’s Precipice, having seen the actions of them both, gave her applause and spoke this verse:

“Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, puriso hoti paṇḍito;

Itthīpi paṇḍitā hoti, tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā”ti. (apa. therī 2.3.31);

“Indeed, a man is not wise in all situations; a woman too is wise, being discerning in each and every case.”

Sāpi [P 2.0222] coraṃ papāte khipitvā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ gehaṃ gamissāmi, ‘sāmiko te kuhi’nti pucchissanti, sacāhaṃ evaṃ puṭṭhā ‘mārito me’ti vakkhāmi, ‘dubbinīte sahassaṃ datvā taṃ āharāpetvā idāni naṃ māresī’ti maṃ mukhasattīhi vijjhissanti, ‘ābharaṇatthāya so maṃ māretukāmo ahosī’ti vuttepi na saddahissanti, alaṃ me gehenā”ti tatthevābharaṇāni chaḍḍetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā anupubbena vicarantī ekaṃ paribbājakānaṃ assamaṃ patvā vanditvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ santike pabbajjaṃ dethā”ti āha. Atha naṃ pabbājesuṃ. Sā pabbajitvāva pucchi – “bhante, tumhākaṃ pabbajjāya kiṃ uttama”nti? “Bhadde, dasasu vā kasiṇesu parikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ nibbattetabbaṃ[M 1.0416], vādasahassaṃ vā uggaṇhitabbaṃ, ayaṃ amhākaṃ pabbajjāya uttamattho”ti. “Jhānaṃ tāva nibbattetuṃ ahaṃ na sakkhissāmi, vādasahassaṃ pana uggaṇhissāmi, ayyā”ti. Atha naṃ te vādasahassaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā “uggahitaṃ te sippaṃ, idāni tvaṃ jambudīpatale vicaritvā attanā saddhiṃ pañhaṃ kathetuṃ samatthaṃ olokehī”ti tassa hatthe jambusākhaṃ [P 2.0223] datvā uyyojesuṃ – “gaccha, bhadde, sace koci gihibhūto tayā saddhiṃ pañhaṃ kathetuṃ sakkoti, tasseva pādaparicārikā bhavāhi, sace pabbajito sakkoti, tassa santike pabbajāhī”ti.

She, too, having thrown the thief down the precipice, thought: “If I go home, they will ask, ‘Where is your husband?’ If, being asked thus, I say, ‘He has been killed by me,’ they will pierce me with verbal spears, saying, ‘You wicked woman! Having given a thousand to have him brought here, you have now killed him!’ Even if I say, ‘He wanted to kill me for my ornaments,’ they will not believe me. Enough of home for me.” Discarding her ornaments right there, she entered the forest. Wandering on in due course, she reached a hermitage of female wanderers, paid homage, and said, “Venerable ladies, please give me the going forth in your presence.” Then they gave her the going forth. Immediately after going forth, she asked, “Venerable ladies, what is the highest in your life of going forth?” “Good lady, one should develop jhāna after performing the preliminary work on the ten kasiṇas, or one should learn the thousand doctrines. This is the highest goal in our life of going forth.” “Venerable ladies, I will not be able to develop jhāna just yet, but I shall learn the thousand doctrines.” Then they had her learn the thousand doctrines and said: “You have learned the art. Now, wander throughout the land of Jambudīpa and look for someone capable of discussing questions with you.” Giving a rose-apple branch into her hand, they sent her off, saying: “Go, good lady. If any householder is able to discuss questions with you, become an attendant at his feet. If one who has gone forth is able, go forth in his presence.”

Sā nāmena jambuparibbājikā nāma hutvā tato nikkhamitvā diṭṭhe diṭṭhe pañhaṃ pucchantī vicarati. Tāya saddhiṃ kathetuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. “Ito jambuparibbājikā āgacchatī”ti [V 1.0371] sutvāva manussā palāyanti. Sā gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā bhikkhāya pavisantī gāmadvāre vālukarāsiṃ katvā tattha jambusākhaṃ ṭhapetvā “mayā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ samattho jambusākhaṃ maddatū”ti vatvā gāmaṃ pāvisi. Taṃ ṭhānaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Sāpi milātāya jambusākhāya aññaṃ jambusākhaṃ gaṇhāti, iminā nīhārena vicarantī sāvatthiṃ patvā gāmadvāre vālukarāsiṃ katvā jambusākhaṃ ṭhapetvā vuttanayeneva vatvā bhikkhāya pāvisi. Sambahulā gāmadārakā jambusākhaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tadā sāriputtatthero piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco nagarā nikkhanto te dārake jambusākhaṃ parivāretvā ṭhite disvā “kiṃ ida”nti pucchi. Dārakā therassa taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhiṃsu. “Tena hi dārakā imaṃ sākhaṃ maddathā”ti. “Bhāyāma, bhante”ti[P 2.0224]. “Ahaṃ pañhaṃ kathessāmi, maddatha tumhe”ti. Te therassa vacanena sañjātussāhā tathā katvā maddantā jambusākhaṃ ukkhipiṃsu. Paribbājikā āgantvā te paribhāsitvā “tumhehi saddhiṃ mama pañhena kiccaṃ natthi, kasmā me sākhaṃ maddathā”ti āha. “Ayyenamhā maddāpitā”ti āhaṃsu. “Bhante, tumhehi me sākhā maddāpitā”ti? “Āma, bhaginī”ti. “Tena hi mayā saddhiṃ pañhaṃ kathethā”ti. “Sādhu kathessāmī”ti.

She became known by the name Jambuparibbājikā, the Rose-Apple Wanderer. Leaving that place, she wandered about, asking a question of everyone she saw. There was no one capable of discussing with her. Just hearing, “Jambuparibbājikā is coming,” people would flee. When entering a village or town for alms, she would make a heap of sand at the gate, plant a rose-apple branch in it, and say, “Whoever is capable of discussing with me, let them trample this rose-apple branch,” and then she would enter the village. No one was capable of even approaching that spot. When the rose-apple branch withered, she would get another. Wandering in this manner, she arrived at Sāvatthī. At the city gate, she made a heap of sand, planted the rose-apple branch, spoke as before, and entered for alms. Many village children gathered around the rose-apple branch and stood there. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, having completed his alms round and meal, was leaving the city. Seeing the children standing around the rose-apple branch, he asked, “What is this?” The children told the elder what was happening. “In that case, children, trample this branch,” he said. “We are afraid, venerable sir.” “I will discuss the question; you trample it.” Encouraged by the elder’s words, they did so, and after trampling the rose-apple branch, they tossed it aside. The female wanderer returned, scolded them, and said, “I have no business concerning questions with you. Why did you trample my branch?” They said, “The noble elder had us trample it.” “Venerable sir, did you have my branch trampled?” “Yes, sister.” “In that case, please discuss the question with me.” “Very well, I shall discuss it.”

Sā vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya pañhaṃ pucchituṃ therassa santikaṃ agamāsi, sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. “Dvinnaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ suṇissāmā”ti nāgarā tāya saddhiṃyeva gantvā theraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Paribbājikā theraṃ [M 1.0417] āha – “bhante, pucchāmi te pañha”nti. “Puccha, bhaginī”ti. Sā vādasahassaṃ pucchi, pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ thero vissajjesi. Atha naṃ thero āha – “ettakā eva te pañhā, aññepi atthī”ti? “Ettakā eva, bhante”ti. “Tayā bahū pañhā puṭṭhā, mayampi ekaṃ pucchāma, vissajjissasi no”ti? “Jānamānā vissajjissāmi pucchatha, bhante”ti. Thero “ekaṃ nāma [P 2.0225] ki”nti (khu. pā. 4.1) pañhaṃ pucchi. Sā “evaṃ nāmesa vissajjetabbo”ti ajānantī “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, bhante”ti pucchi. “Buddhapañho nāma, bhaginī”ti. “Mayhampi taṃ detha, bhante”ti. “Sace mādisā bhavissasi, dassāmī”ti. “Tena hi maṃ pabbājethā”ti. Thero bhikkhunīnaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbājesi. Sā pabbajitvā laddhūpasampadā kuṇḍalakesittherī nāma hutvā katipāhaccayeneva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

She went to the Elder in the afternoon to ask a question, and the whole city was stirred up. 'We shall listen to the discussion between the two wise ones,' thought the townspeople, and they went with her, paid homage to the Elder, and sat down to one side. The female wanderer said to the Elder, 'Venerable sir, I shall ask you a question.' 'Ask, sister,' he replied. She asked a thousand points of debate, and the Elder answered every question that was asked. Then the Elder said to her, 'Are your questions only this many, or are there others?' 'Only this many, venerable sir,' she said. 'You have asked many questions; we too shall ask one—will you answer it?' 'If I know, I will answer. Ask, venerable sir,' she replied. The Elder asked the question, 'What is the one?' Not knowing how it should be answered, she asked, 'What is that called, venerable sir?' 'It is called the Buddha-question, sister.' 'Give that to me also, venerable sir,' she said. 'If you become like me, I will give it,' he replied. 'In that case, ordain me,' she said. The Elder, having informed the bhikkhunīs, had her ordained. Having been ordained and having received the higher ordination, she became known as the Therī Kuṇḍalakesī. Within just a few days, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “kuṇḍalakesittheriyā dhammassavanañca bahuṃ natthi, pabbajitakiccañcassā matthakaṃ pattaṃ, ekena kira corena saddhiṃ mahāsaṅgāmaṃ katvā jinitvā āgatā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā [V 1.0372] “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, mayā desitadhammaṃ ‘appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā’ti pamāṇaṃ mā gaṇhatha, anatthakaṃ padasatampi seyyo na hoti, dhammapadaṃ pana ekampi seyyova. Avasesacore jinantassa ca jayo nāma na hoti, ajjhattikakilesacore jinantasseva pana jayo nāma hotī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'The Therī Kuṇḍalakesī has not heard much of the Dhamma, yet the task of one gone forth has reached its culmination for her. It is said she fought a great battle with a certain thief, conquered him, and returned.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered together now?' When they replied, 'Regarding this matter,' he said, 'Bhikkhus, do not measure the Dhamma taught by me as ‘little’ or ‘much.’ A hundred verses connected with what is meaningless are not excellent, but a single verse of the Dhamma is indeed more excellent. Victory over other thieves is not called victory; only for one who conquers the internal defilement-thieves is there what is called victory.' Having said this, and connecting the narrative, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

102.

102.

“Yo ca gāthāsataṃ bhāse, anatthapadasaṃhitā;

Ekaṃ dhammapadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammati.

Though one should recite a hundred verses connected with meaningless words, better is one verse of the Dhamma, hearing which one is calmed.

103.

103.

“Yo [P 2.0226] sahassaṃ sahassena, saṅgāme mānuse jine;

Ekañca jeyyamattānaṃ, sa ve saṅgāmajuttamo”ti.

Though one should conquer a thousand thousands of men in battle, yet he who conquers his own self is indeed the supreme victor in battle.

Tattha gāthāsatanti yo ca puggalo sataparicchedā bahūpi gāthā bhāseyyāti attho. Anatthapadasaṃhitāti ākāsavaṇṇanādivasena anatthakehi padehi saṃhitā. Dhammapadanti atthasādhakaṃ khandhādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ, “cattārimāni paribbājakā dhammapadāni. Katamāni cattāri? Anabhijjhā paribbājakā dhammapadaṃ, abyāpādo paribbājakā dhammapadaṃ, sammāsati paribbājakā dhammapadaṃ[M 1.0418], sammāsamādhi paribbājakā dhammapada”nti (a. ni. 4.30) evaṃ vuttesu catūsu dhammapadesu ekampi dhammapadaṃ seyyo. Yo sahassaṃ sahassenāti yo eko saṅgāmayodho sahassena guṇitaṃ sahassaṃ mānuse ekasmiṃ saṅgāme jineyya, dasamanussasatasahassaṃ jinitvā jayaṃ āhareyya, ayampi saṅgāmajinataṃ uttamo pavaro nāma na hoti. Ekañca jeyyamattānanti yo rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu ajjhattikakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasanto attano lobhādikilesajayena attānaṃ jineyya[P 2.0227]. Sa ve saṅgāmajuttamoti so saṅgāmajinānaṃ uttamo pavaro saṅgāmasīsayodhoti.

Therein, 'a hundred verses' means: a person might speak many verses, numbering one hundred. 'Connected with meaningless words' means: connected with words that are without benefit, by way of praising the sky and so forth. 'A verse of the Dhamma' means: that which accomplishes the goal, connected with the aggregates and so forth. As it is said: 'These are the four Dhamma-verses for a wanderer. Which four? Non-covetousness is a wanderer's Dhamma-verse, non-ill-will is a wanderer's Dhamma-verse, right mindfulness is a wanderer's Dhamma-verse, right concentration is a wanderer's Dhamma-verse.' Among these four Dhamma-verses thus stated, even one is more excellent. 'Though one should conquer a thousand by a thousand' means: if a single warrior were to conquer in a single battle a thousand multiplied by a thousand men—that is, defeating a million men and achieving victory—even he would not be called the supreme or excellent one among victors in battle. 'And should conquer oneself' means: one who, in the places of practice by night and by day, while comprehending the internal meditation subject, conquers oneself by the conquest of one's defilements such as greed and so forth. 'He indeed is the supreme victor in battle' means: he is the supreme and excellent one among victors in battle, the chief warrior.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Kuṇḍalakesittherīvatthu tatiyaṃ.

The Story of the Therī Kuṇḍalakesī, the third.

4. Anatthapucchakabrāhmaṇavatthu

4. The Story of the Brahmin Who Asked About What is Unbeneficial

Attā haveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anatthapucchakaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse beginning with “Attā have” concerning the brahmin who asked about what is unbeneficial.

So [V 1.0373] kira brāhmaṇo “kiṃ nu kho sammāsambuddho atthameva jānāti, udāhu anatthampi, pucchissāmi na”nti satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “bhante, tumhe atthameva jānātha maññe, no anattha”nti? “Atthañcāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, jānāmi anatthañcā”ti. “Tena hi me anatthaṃ kathethā”ti. Athassa satthā imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that brahmin thought: “Does the Perfectly Enlightened One know only what is beneficial, or also what is unbeneficial? I shall ask him.” He approached the Teacher and asked: “Venerable sir, I suppose you know only what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial?” “Brahmin, I know both what is beneficial and what is unbeneficial,” replied the Teacher. “In that case, tell me what is unbeneficial,” he said. Thereupon the Teacher spoke this verse to him:

“Ussūraseyyaṃ ālasyaṃ, caṇḍikkaṃ dīghasoṇḍiyaṃ;

Ekassaddhānagamanaṃ paradārūpasevanaṃ;

Etaṃ brāhmaṇa sevassu, anatthaṃ te bhavissatī”ti.

“Sleeping until sunrise, laziness, harshness, habitual drunkenness, travelling a long road alone, and associating with others' wives—these, O brahmin, if you indulge in them, will be unbeneficial for you.”

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo sādhukāramadāsi “sādhu sādhu, gaṇācariya, gaṇajeṭṭhaka, tumhe atthañca jānātha anatthañcā”ti[P 2.0228]. “Evaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, atthānatthajānanako nāma mayā sadiso natthī”ti. Athassa satthā ajjhāsayaṃ upadhāretvā, “brāhmaṇa, kena kammena jīvasī”ti pucchi. “Jūtakammena, bho gotamā”ti. “Kiṃ pana te jayo hoti parājayo”ti[M 1.0419]. “Jayopi hoti parājayopī”ti vutte, “brāhmaṇa, appamattako esa, paraṃ jinantassa jayo nāma na seyyo. Yo pana kilesajayena attānaṃ jināti, tassa jayo seyyo. Na hi taṃ jayaṃ koci apajayaṃ kātuṃ sakkotī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the brahmin gave his approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent, teacher of the group, leader of the group! You know both what is beneficial and what is unbeneficial.” “Indeed, brahmin, there is no one like me who knows what is beneficial and what is unbeneficial.” Then the Teacher, discerning his inclination, asked, “Brahmin, by what activity do you make a living?” “By gambling, Venerable Gotama.” “But do you have victory or defeat?” “I have both victory and defeat,” he replied. Then the Teacher said, “Brahmin, that is insignificant. The victory of one who conquers others is not better. But the victory of one who conquers himself through the conquest of defilements—that victory is better. For no one can turn that victory into defeat.” Having said this, and connecting the narrative, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

104.

104.

“Attā have jitaṃ seyyo, yā cāyaṃ itarā pajā;

Attadantassa posassa, niccaṃ saññatacārino.

“Indeed, conquering oneself is better than conquering other people. For a person who is self-tamed, ever restrained in conduct,

105.

105.

“Neva devo na gandhabbo, na māro saha brahmunā;

Jitaṃ apajitaṃ kayirā, tathārūpassa jantuno”ti.

“neither a deva nor a gandhabba, nor Māra together with Brahmā, could turn into defeat the victory of such a being.”

Tattha haveti nipāto. Jitanti liṅgavipallāso, attano kilesajayena attā jito seyyoti attho. Yā cāyaṃ itarā pajāti yā panāyaṃ avasesā pajā jūtena vā [P 2.0229] dhanaharaṇena vā saṅgāmena vā balābhibhavena vā jitā bhaveyya, taṃ jinantena yaṃ jitaṃ, na taṃ seyyoti attho. Kasmā pana tadeva jitaṃ seyyo, idaṃ na seyyoti? Yasmā attadantassa…pe… tathārūpassa jantunoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā hi yvāyaṃ nikkilesatāya attadanto poso, tassa attadantassa kāyādīhi niccaṃ saññatacārino evarūpassa imehi kāyasaññamādīhi saññatassa jantuno devo vā gandhabbo vā māro vā brahmunā saha uṭṭhahitvā “ahamassa jitaṃ apajitaṃ [V 1.0374] karissāmi, maggabhāvanāya pahīne kilese puna uppādessāmī”ti ghaṭentopi vāyamantopi yathā dhanādīhi parājito pakkhantaro hutvā itarena jitaṃ puna jinanto apajitaṃ kareyya, “evaṃ apajitaṃ kātuṃ neva sakkuṇeyyā”ti.

Herein, 'have' is a particle. 'Jitaṃ' is a change of gender; the meaning is, 'the self conquered by the conquest of one's own defilements is better.' As for 'than this other populace,' it means that whatever other people might be conquered by gambling, or by seizing wealth, or by battle, or by overpowering with force—the victory achieved by conquering them is not better. But why is that conquest better, and this not? Because of the phrase 'For a person who is self-tamed... of such a being.' This is what is said: Because for this person who is self-tamed through being free from defilements, for this self-tamed person who is ever restrained in conduct with respect to body and so on, for such a being who is restrained by these means such as bodily restraint—neither a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Māra together with Brahmā, even if they were to rise up and strive and exert themselves with the thought, 'I will make his victory a defeat; I will cause the defilements abandoned by the development of the path to arise again,' they could not make it a defeat. Just as one who was defeated in terms of wealth and so on, becoming a partisan, might turn the other's victory into defeat, so they could not in that way make this victory a defeat.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Anatthapucchakabrāhmaṇavatthu catutthaṃ.

The Story of the Brahmin Who Asked About What is Unbeneficial, the fourth.

5. Sāriputtattherassa mātulabrāhmaṇavatthu

5. The Story of the Brahmin who was the Maternal Uncle of the Elder Sāriputta

Māse [M 1.0420][P 2.0230] māseti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto sāriputtattherassa mātulabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Māse māse' concerning the maternal uncle of the Elder Sāriputta.

Thero kira tassa santikaṃ gantvā āha – “kiṃ nu kho, brāhmaṇa, kiñcideva kusalaṃ karosī”ti? “Karomi, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ karosī”ti? “Māse māse sahassapariccāgena dānaṃ dammī”ti. “Kassa desī”ti? “Nigaṇṭhānaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ patthayanto”ti? “Brahmalokaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ pana brahmalokassa ayaṃ maggo”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Ko evamāhā”ti? “Ācariyehi me kathitaṃ, bhante”ti. “No tvaṃ brahmalokassa maggaṃ jānāsi, nāpi te ācariyā, satthāva eko jānāti, ehi, brāhmaṇa, brahmalokassa te maggaṃ kathāpessāmī”ti taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ netvā, “bhante, ayaṃ brāhmaṇo evamāhā”ti, “taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā sādhu vatassa brahmalokassa maggaṃ kathethā”ti. Satthā “evaṃ kira, brāhmaṇā”ti pucchitvā “āma, bho gotamā”ti vutte, “brāhmaṇa, tayā evaṃ dadamānena vassasataṃ dinnadānatopi muhuttamattaṃ pasannacittena mama sāvakassa [P 2.0231] olokanaṃ vā kaṭacchubhikkhāmattadānaṃ vā mahapphalatara”nti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Elder, it is said, approached him and asked: “Brahmin, do you perform any meritorious deed?” “I do, venerable sir.” “What do you do?” “Every month I give alms, spending a thousand.” “To whom do you give?” “To the Nigaṇṭhas, venerable sir.” “What do you aspire to?” “The Brahma-world, venerable sir.” “But is this the path to the Brahma-world?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Who said so?” “My teachers told me, venerable sir.” “You do not know the path to the Brahma-world, nor do your teachers; only the Teacher knows. Come, brahmin, I will have the path to the Brahma-world taught to you.” Taking him along, he brought him to the Teacher and said: “Venerable sir, this brahmin speaks thus.” Having related the matter, he added: “It would be good if you would explain to him the path to the Brahma-world.” The Teacher, having asked, “Is it so, brahmin?” and receiving the reply, “Yes, Master Gotama,” said: “Brahmin, more fruitful by far than the alms you have given in this way for a hundred years is looking upon my disciple with a confident mind for just a moment, or giving a mere ladleful of alms-food.” Then, making a connection, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

106.

106.

“Māse māse sahassena, yo yajetha sataṃ samaṃ;

Ekañca bhāvitattānaṃ, muhuttamapi pūjaye;

Sāyeva pūjanā seyyo, yañce vassasataṃ huta”nti.

Should one sacrifice a thousand, month after month for a hundred years, yet should one honor, even for a moment, one who has cultivated themselves—that honor is indeed better than the sacrifice of a hundred years.

Tattha [V 1.0375] sahassenāhi sahassapariccāgena. Yo yajetha sataṃ samanti yo vassasataṃ māse māse sahassaṃ pariccajanto lokiyamahājanassa dānaṃ dadeyya, ekañca bhāvitattānanti yo pana ekaṃ sīlādiguṇavisesena vaḍḍhitaattānaṃ heṭṭhimakoṭiyā sotāpannaṃ, uparimakoṭiyā khīṇāsavaṃ gharadvāraṃ sampattaṃ kaṭacchubhikkhādānavasena vā yāpanamattaāhāradānavasena vā thūlasāṭakadānamattena vā pūjeyya. Yaṃ itarena vassasataṃ hutaṃ. Tato sāyeva pūjanā seyyo. Seṭṭho uttamoti atthoti.

Therein, 'by a thousand' (sahassena) means by the expenditure of a thousand. 'Whoever should sacrifice for a hundred years' (yo yajetha sataṃ samaṃ) means: whoever, for a hundred years, month by month, giving up a thousand, should give alms to the worldly multitude. And 'one who has cultivated themselves' (ekaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ) refers to one whose self has been developed by special qualities such as virtue—at the lowest level, a stream-enterer, and at the highest level, a canker-freed one (an arahant). Whoever should honor such a one who has arrived at their house door, whether by means of giving a ladleful of alms-food, or by giving food just sufficient for sustenance, or by giving even a coarse cloth. That which was offered by the other for a hundred years—than that, this very honoring is better (seyyo). 'Better' means supreme, excellent; this is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne [M 1.0421] so brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphalaṃ patto, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also attained the fruits beginning with stream-entry.

Sāriputtattherassa mātulabrāhmaṇavatthu pañcamaṃ.

The fifth story is that of the brahmin who was the maternal uncle of the Elder Sāriputta.

6. Sāriputtattherassa bhāgineyyavatthu

6. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta's Nephew

Yo [P 2.0232] ca vassasataṃ jantūti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto sāriputtattherassa bhāgineyyaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching regarding the nephew of the Elder Sāriputta, beginning with: “Though a person for a hundred years…”

Tampi hi thero upasaṅkamitvā āha – “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, kusalaṃ karosī”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ karosī”ti? “Māse māse ekaṃ ekaṃ pasuṃ ghātetvā aggiṃ paricarāmī”ti. “Kimatthaṃ evaṃ karosī”ti? “Brahmalokamaggo kireso”ti. “Kenevaṃ kathita”nti? “Ācariyehi me, bhante”ti. “Neva tvaṃ brahmalokassa maggaṃ jānāsi, nāpi te ācariyā, ehi, satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti taṃ satthu santikaṃ netvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “imassa, bhante, brahmalokassa maggaṃ kathethā”ti āha. Satthā “evaṃ kirā”ti pucchitvā “evaṃ, bho gotamā”ti vutte, “brāhmaṇa, vassasatampi evaṃ aggiṃ paricarantassa tava aggipāricariyā mama sāvakassa taṅkhaṇamattaṃ pūjampi na pāpuṇātī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Indeed, the Elder approached him and asked: “Brahmin, do you perform any wholesome deed?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What do you do?” “Every month, having killed one animal, I tend the fire.” “For what purpose do you do this?” “This, it is said, is the path to the Brahma-world.” “By whom was this said?” “By my teachers, venerable sir.” “Neither you nor your teachers know the path to the Brahma-world. Come, let us go to the Teacher.” Having led him to the Teacher and reported the matter, he said: “Venerable sir, please explain the path to the Brahma-world to this man.” The Teacher asked, “Is it so?” When it was said, “Yes, Master Gotama,” the Teacher said: “Brahmin, your tending of the fire in this way for a hundred years cannot match even a moment's offering to my disciple.” Then, connecting the sequence, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

107.

107.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jantu, aggiṃ paricare vane;

Ekañca bhāvitattānaṃ, muhuttamapi pūjaye;

Sāyeva pūjanā seyyo, yañce vassasataṃ huta”nti.

Though a person were to tend the fire in the forest for a hundred years, yet if one were to honor for just a moment one who has developed oneself, that very honor is better than the sacrifice of a hundred years.

Tattha [V 1.0376][P 2.0233] jantūti sattādhivacanametaṃ. Aggiṃ paricare vaneti nippapañcabhāvapatthanāya vanaṃ pavisitvāpi tattha aggiṃ paricareyya. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

In that verse, 'jantu' is a term for a being. 'Tend the fire in the forest' means that even after entering the forest with the wish for the state free from proliferation, one might tend the fire there. The rest is just as before. This is the meaning of the verse.

Desanāvasāne so brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also attained the fruits beginning with stream-entry.

Sāriputtattherassa bhāgineyyavatthu chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth story, the Story of the Elder Sāriputta's Nephew.

7. Sāriputtattherassa sahāyakabrāhmaṇavatthu

7. The Story of the Brahmin Friend of the Elder Sāriputta

Yaṃ [M 1.0422] kiñci yiṭṭhaṃ vāti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto sāriputtattherassa sahāyakabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the brahmin friend of the Elder Sāriputta, beginning with: “Whatever sacrifice or offering…”

Tampi hi thero upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, kiñci kusalaṃ karosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ karosī”ti? “Yiṭṭhayāgaṃ yajāmī”ti. “Tadā kira taṃ yāgaṃ mahāpariccāgena yaja”nti. Ito paraṃ thero purimanayeneva pucchitvā taṃ satthu santikaṃ netvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “imassa, bhante, brahmalokassa maggaṃ kathethā”ti āha. Satthā, “brāhmaṇa, evaṃ kirā”ti pucchitvā “evaṃ, bho gotamā”ti vutte, “brāhmaṇa, tayā saṃvaccharaṃ yiṭṭhayāgaṃ yajantena lokiyamahājanassa dinnadānaṃ pasannacittena [P 2.0234] mama sāvakānaṃ vandantānaṃ uppannakusalacetanāya catubhāgamattampi na agghatī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Elder approached him and asked: “Brahmin, do you do any wholesome deed?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What do you do?” “I perform the Yiṭṭha sacrifice.” At that time, it is said, that sacrifice was performed with great expenditure. After this, the Elder, having questioned him in the same way as before, led him to the Teacher, reported the matter, and said: “Venerable sir, please explain the path to the Brahma-world to this man.” The Teacher asked: “Brahmin, is it so?” When it was said, “Yes, Master Gotama,” the Teacher said: “Brahmin, the gift given to the worldly populace by you performing the Yiṭṭha sacrifice for a whole year is not worth even a quarter of the wholesome volition that arises for one who, with a confident mind, pays homage to my disciples.” Then, connecting the sequence, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

108.

108.

“Yaṃ kiñci yiṭṭhaṃ va hutaṃ va loke,

Saṃvaccharaṃ yajetha puññapekkho;

Sabbampi taṃ na catubhāgameti,

Abhivādanā ujjugatesu seyyo”ti.

Whatever sacrifice or offering there is in the world, if one seeking merit should sacrifice for a year, all of that is not worth a quarter; paying homage to the upright is better.

Tattha yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānavacanametaṃ. Yiṭṭhanti yebhuyyena maṅgalakiriyādivasesu dinnadānaṃ. Hutanti abhisaṅkharitvā kataṃ pāhunadānañceva, kammañca phalañca saddahitvā katadānañca. Saṃvaccharaṃ yajethāti ekasaṃvaccharaṃ nirantarameva vuttappakāraṃ dānaṃ sakalacakkavāḷepi [V 1.0377] lokiyamahājanassa dadeyya. Puññapekkhoti puññaṃ icchanto. Ujjugatesūti heṭṭhimakoṭiyā sotāpannesu uparimakoṭiyā khīṇāsavesu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “evarūpesu pasannacittena sarīraṃ onamitvā vandantassa kusalacetanāya yaṃ phalaṃ, tato catubhāgampi sabbaṃ taṃ dānaṃ na agghati, tasmā ujugatesu abhivādanameva seyyo”ti.

Therein, 'whatever' is a term of complete inclusion, without remainder. 'Yiṭṭha' (sacrifice) is, for the most part, a gift given on occasions such as auspicious rites. 'Huta' (offering) is both a gift for guests prepared with effort, and a gift given with faith in kamma and its fruit. 'If one should sacrifice for a year' means one might give the aforesaid kind of gift continuously for one whole year to the worldly populace, even in the entire universe. 'Seeking merit' means one who desires merit. 'To the upright' means, at the lower limit, to stream-enterers, and at the upper limit, to those whose cankers are destroyed. This is the meaning: All that gift is not worth even a quarter of the fruit that comes from the wholesome volition of one who, with a confident mind, pays homage to such persons by bowing the body. Therefore, paying homage to the upright is indeed superior.

Desanāvasāne [P 2.0235] so brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphalaṃ patto, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also attained the fruits beginning with stream-entry.

Sāriputtattherassa sahāyakabrāhmaṇavatthu sattamaṃ.

The seventh story, the Story of the Brahmin Friend of the Elder Sāriputta.

8. Āyuvaḍḍhanakumāravatthu

8. The Story of the Youth Āyuvaḍḍhana

Abhivādanasīlissāti [M 1.0423] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā dīghalaṅghikaṃ nissāya araññakuṭiyaṃ viharanto dīghāyukumāraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in a forest hut near Dīghalaṅghika, delivered this Dhamma discourse, which begins with the words 'Abhivādanasīlissa,' concerning the youth Dīghāyu.

Dīghalaṅghikanagaravāsino kira dve brāhmaṇā bāhirakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni tapacaraṇaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu eko “paveṇi me nassissati, vibbhamissāmī”ti cintetvā attanā kataṃ tapaṃ paresaṃ vikkiṇitvā gosatena ceva kahāpaṇasatena ca saddhiṃ bhariyaṃ labhitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Athassa bhariyā puttaṃ vijāyi. Itaro panassa sahāyako pavāsaṃ gantvā punadeva taṃ nagaraṃ paccāgami. So tassa āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā puttadāraṃ ādāya sahāyakassa dassanatthāya agamāsi. Gantvā puttaṃ mātu hatthe datvā sayaṃ tāva vandi, mātāpi puttaṃ pitu hatthe datvā vandi. So “dīghāyukā hothā”ti [P 2.0236] āha, putte pana vandāpite tuṇhī ahosi. Atha naṃ “kasmā, bhante, amhehi vandite ‘dīghāyukā hothā’ti vatvā imassa vandanakāle kiñci na vadethā”ti āha. “Imasseko antarāyo atthi, brāhmaṇā”ti. “Kittakaṃ jīvissati, bhante”ti? “Sattāhaṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti. “Paṭibāhanakāraṇaṃ atthi, bhante”ti? “Nāhaṃ paṭibāhanakāraṇaṃ jānāmī”ti. “Ko pana jāneyya, bhante”ti? “Samaṇo gotamo jāneyya, tassa santikaṃ gantvā pucchāhī”ti. “Tattha gacchanto tapaparihānito bhāyāmī”ti. “Sace te puttasineho atthi, tapaparihāniṃ acintetvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā pucchāhī”ti.

It is said that two brahmins who lived in the city of Dīghalaṅghika went forth into an external religious order and practiced asceticism for forty-eight years. One of them thought, 'My lineage will be lost; I will return to the lay life.' Having thought thus, he sold the ascetic practice he had performed to others, and obtaining a wife along with a hundred cows and a hundred kahāpaṇas, he established a household. Then his wife gave birth to a son. His other companion, however, went on a journey and then returned to that city. Hearing of his arrival, the brahmin took his wife and son and went to see his companion. Upon arriving, he placed his son in the mother's hands and first paid homage himself. The mother also placed the son in the father's hands and paid homage. The ascetic said, 'May you live long.' But when the son was made to pay homage, he remained silent. Then the brahmin asked him, 'Venerable sir, why is it that when we paid homage, you said, "May you live long," but when this child paid homage, you said nothing?' 'There is a danger for this child, brahmin.' 'How long will he live, venerable sir?' 'For seven days, brahmin.' 'Is there a means to prevent it, venerable sir?' 'I do not know the means to prevent it.' 'Who then would know, venerable sir?' 'The ascetic Gotama would know. Go to him and ask.' 'Going there, I fear the decline of my ascetic practice.' 'If you have love for your son, do not think about the decline of your ascetic practice. Go to him and ask.'

So [V 1.0378] satthu santikaṃ gantvā sayaṃ tāva vandi. Satthā “dīghāyuko hohī”ti āha, pajāpatiyā vandanakālepi tassā tatheva vatvā puttassa vandāpanakāle tuṇhī ahosi. So purimanayeneva satthāraṃ pucchi, satthāpi tatheva byākāsi. So kira brāhmaṇo sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ apaṭivijjhitvāva attano mantaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇena saṃsandesi, paṭibāhanūpāyaṃ pana na jānāti. Brāhmaṇo satthāraṃ pucchi – “atthi pana, bhante, paṭibāhanūpāyo”ti? “Bhaveyya, brāhmaṇā”ti. “Kiṃ bhaveyyā”ti? “Sace tvaṃ attano gehadvāre maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā tassa majjhe [P 2.0237] pīṭhikaṃ kāretvā taṃ parikkhipanto aṭṭha vā soḷasa vā āsanāni [M 1.0424] paññāpetvā tesu mama sāvake nisīdāpetvā sattāhaṃ nirantaraṃ parittaṃ kātuṃ sakkuṇeyyāsi, evamassa antarāyo nasseyyā”ti. “Bho gotama, mayā maṇḍapādīni sakkā kātuṃ, tumhākaṃ pana sāvake kathaṃ lacchāmī”ti? “Tayā ettake kate ahaṃ mama sāvake pahiṇissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bho gotamā”ti so attano gehadvāre sabbaṃ kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Satthā bhikkhū pahiṇi, te gantvā tattha nisīdiṃsu, dārakampi pīṭhikāyaṃ nipajjāpesuṃ, bhikkhū sattarattindivaṃ nirantaraṃ parittaṃ bhaṇiṃsu, sattame divase sāyaṃ satthā āgacchi. Tasmiṃ āgate sabbacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatiṃsu. Eko pana avaruddhako nāma yakkho dvādasa saṃvaccharāni vessavaṇaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tassa santikā varaṃ labhanto “ito sattame divase imaṃ dārakaṃ gaṇheyyāsī”ti labhi. Tasmā sopi āgantvā aṭṭhāsi.

He went to the Teacher's presence and first paid homage himself. The Teacher said, 'May you live long.' When his wife paid homage, He spoke to her in the same way, but when the son was made to pay homage, He became silent. The brahmin asked the Teacher in the same way as before, and the Teacher also explained in the same way. It is said that the brahmin, without having penetrated omniscient knowledge, compared his own mantra-knowledge with the omniscient knowledge, but he did not know the means of prevention. The brahmin asked the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, is there a means of prevention?' 'There could be, brahmin.' 'What could it be?' 'If you could have a pavilion built at the door of your house, have a platform made in the middle of it, and arranging eight or sixteen seats surrounding it, have my disciples sit on them and cause the protective chants to be recited continuously for seven days, in this way the danger to him would be dispelled.' 'Venerable Gotama, I am able to have the pavilion and other things made, but how shall I get your disciples?' 'When you have done that much, I will send my disciples.' 'Very well, Venerable Gotama.' Having completed all the tasks at the door of his house, he went to the Teacher's presence. The Teacher sent the monks. They went and sat there. They also had the child lie down on the platform. The monks recited the protective chants continuously for seven days and nights. On the evening of the seventh day, the Teacher came himself. When He arrived, all the deities of the Cakkavāḷa assembled. Now, a certain yakkha named Avaruddhaka, having attended upon Vessavaṇa for twelve years and receiving a boon from his presence, had obtained it thus: 'On the seventh day from now, you may take this child.' Therefore, he also came and stood there.

Satthari pana tattha gate mahesakkhāsu devatāsu sannipatitāsu appesakkhā devatā osakkitvā osakkitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā dvādasa [P 2.0238] yojanāni paṭikkamiṃsu. Avaruddhakopi tatheva paṭikkami, satthāpi sabbarattiṃ parittamakāsi. Sattāhe vītivatte avaruddhako dārakaṃ na labhi. Aṭṭhame pana divase aruṇe uggatamatte dārakaṃ ānetvā satthāraṃ vandāpesuṃ. Satthā “dīghāyuko hohī”ti āha. “Kīvaciraṃ pana, bho gotama, dārako ṭhassatī”ti? “Vīsavassasataṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti. Athassa “āyuvaḍḍhanakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vuddhimanvāya pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto vicari. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “passathāvuso, āyuvaḍḍhanakumārena kira sattame divase maritabbaṃ abhavissa, so idāni vīsavassasataṭṭhāyī hutvā pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto vicarati, atthi maññe imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyuvaḍḍhanakāraṇa”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, na kevalaṃ āyuvaḍḍhanameva, ime pana sattā guṇavante vandantā abhivādentā catūhi kāraṇehi vaḍḍhanti, parissayato [V 1.0379] muccanti, yāvatāyukameva tiṭṭhantī”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

But when the Teacher arrived there, and the deities of great power had assembled, the deities of lesser power, retreating again and again and not finding a space, withdrew for twelve yojanas. Avaruddhaka also withdrew in the same way. The Teacher also recited the protective chants for the entire night. When the seven days had passed, Avaruddhaka did not get the child. Then on the eighth day, just as the dawn was rising, they brought the child and had him pay homage to the Teacher. The Teacher said, 'May you live long.' 'Venerable Gotama, for how long will the child live?' 'For one hundred and twenty years, brahmin.' Then they gave him the name 'Āyuvaḍḍhanakumāra.' Having reached maturity, he went about surrounded by five hundred lay disciples. Then one day in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a topic of conversation: 'Venerable sirs, look! It is said that the youth Āyuvaḍḍhana was to have died on the seventh day, but now, being one who will live for one hundred and twenty years, he goes about surrounded by five hundred lay disciples. It seems there is a cause for the increase of longevity for these beings.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what topic of conversation are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'For this one,' He said: 'Monks, it is not merely the increase of longevity. But these beings, by paying respect and revering those endowed with virtue, increase in four ways, are freed from danger, and live for their full lifespan.' Having thus connected the sequence, while teaching the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

109.

109.

“Abhivādanasīlissa[M 1.0425][P 2.0239], niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino;

Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti, āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ bala”nti.

For one who is habitually respectful, who constantly honors the elders, four things increase: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.

Tattha abhivādanasīlissāti vandanasīlissa, abhiṇhaṃ vandanakiccapasutassāti attho. Vuḍḍhāpacāyinoti gihissa vā tadahupabbajite daharasāmaṇerepi, pabbajitassa vā pana pabbajjāya vā upasampadāya vā vuḍḍhatare guṇavuḍḍhe apacāyamānassa, abhivādanena vā niccaṃ pūjentassāti attho. Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhantīti āyumhi vaḍḍhamāne yattakaṃ kālaṃ taṃ vaḍḍhati, tattakaṃ itarepi vaḍḍhantiyeva. Yena hi paññāsavassaāyusaṃvattanikaṃ kusalaṃ kataṃ, pañcavīsativassakāle cassa jīvitantarāyo uppajjeyya, so abhivādanasīlatāya paṭippassambhati, so yāvatāyukameva tiṭṭhati, vaṇṇādayopissa āyunāva saddhiṃ vaḍḍhanti. Ito uttaripi eseva nayo. Anantarāyena pavattassāyuno vaḍḍhanaṃ nāma natthi.

Herein, 'abhivādanasīlissa' means to one who has the habit of veneration, to one who is constantly diligent in the duty of paying homage. 'Vuḍḍhāpacāyino' means, in the case of a householder, to one who shows reverence to those who are older in age or greater in virtue, and even to a young novice ordained that very day; or, in the case of one who has gone forth, to one who shows reverence to those senior in the lower ordination or the higher ordination, constantly honoring them through reverential salutation. 'Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti' means that when the lifespan increases, for however long it increases, for that long the other qualities also increase. Indeed, if a person has performed a wholesome deed that brings about a fifty-year lifespan, and a danger to their life were to arise at the age of twenty-five, that danger is pacified by their habit of paying homage. That person then lives for the full extent of their lifespan, and their qualities such as beauty also increase along with their lifespan. Beyond this, the same principle applies. For a lifespan that proceeds without danger, there is no such thing as an increase.

Desanāvasāne āyuvaḍḍhanakumāro pañcahi upāsakasatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the discourse, the youth Āyuvaḍḍhana, together with five hundred lay disciples, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also attained the fruits, beginning with stream-entry.

Āyuvaḍḍhanakumāravatthu aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Eighth Story: The Youth Āyuvaḍḍhana.

9. Saṃkiccasāmaṇeravatthu

9. The Story of the Novice Saṃkicca

Yo [P 2.0240] ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto saṃkiccasāmaṇeraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve,' concerning the novice Saṃkicca.

Sāvatthiyaṃ kira tiṃsamattā kulaputtā satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajiṃsu. Te upasampadāya pañcavassā hutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā ganthadhuraṃ vipassanādhuranti dve dhurānīti sutvā “mayaṃ mahallakakāle pabbajitā”ti ganthadhure ussāhaṃ akatvā vipassanādhuraṃ pūretukāmā yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā, “bhante, ekaṃ araññāyatanaṃ gamissāmā”ti satthāraṃ āpucchiṃsu. Satthā “kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ gamissathā”ti pucchitvā “asukaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “tattha tesaṃ [V 1.0380] ekaṃ vighāsādaṃ nissāya bhayaṃ uppajjissati, tañca pana saṃkiccasāmaṇere gate vūpasamissati, atha nesaṃ pabbajitakiccaṃ pāripūriṃ gamissatī”ti aññāsi.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, about thirty sons of good family, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, dedicated themselves to the Dispensation and went forth. Having been of five rains since their higher ordination, they approached the Teacher. Having heard of the two duties—the duty of study and the duty of insight meditation—they reasoned, 'We went forth in old age.' Making no effort in the duty of study, they wished to fulfill the duty of insight meditation. Having had a meditation subject leading up to Arahantship taught to them, they took leave of the Teacher, saying, 'Venerable Sir, we will go to a forest abode.' The Teacher asked, 'To what place will you go?' When they replied, 'To such-and-such a place,' He knew: 'There, a danger will arise for them on account of one who eats leftovers, but that danger will be pacified when the novice Saṃkicca goes there. Then their duty as renunciants will reach fulfillment.'

Saṃkiccasāmaṇero [M 1.0426] nāma sāriputtattherassa sāmaṇero sattavassiko jātiyā. Tassa kira mātā sāvatthiyaṃ aḍḍhakulassa dhītā. Sā tasmiṃ kucchigate ekena byādhinā taṅkhaṇaññeva kālamakāsi. Tassā jhāpiyamānāya ṭhapetvā gabbhamaṃsaṃ sesaṃ jhāyi. Athassā gabbhamaṃsaṃ citakato otāretvā dvīsu tīsu ṭhānesu sūlehi vijjhiṃsu. Sūlakoṭi dārakassa akkhikoṭiṃ pahari. Evaṃ gabbhamaṃsaṃ [P 2.0241] vijjhitvā aṅgārarāsimhi khipitvā aṅgāreheva paṭicchādetvā pakkamiṃsu. Gabbhamaṃsaṃ jhāyi, aṅgāramatthake pana suvaṇṇabimbasadiso dārako padumagabbhe nipanno viya ahosi. Pacchimabhavikassa sattassa hi sinerunā otthariyamānassapi arahattaṃ appatvā jīvitakkhayo nāma natthi. Punadivase “citakaṃ nibbāpessāmā”ti āgatā tathānipannaṃ dārakaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittajātā “kathañhi nāma ettakesu dārūsu khīyamānesu sakalasarīre jhāpiyamāne dārako na jhāyi, kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti dārakaṃ ādāya antogāmaṃ gantvā nemittake pucchiṃsu. Nemittakā “sace ayaṃ dārako agāraṃ ajjhāvassissati, yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā ñātakā duggatā bhavissanti? Sace pabbajissati, pañcahi samaṇasatehi parivuto vicarissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Tassa saṅkunā akkhikoṭiyā bhinnattā saṃkiccanti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So aparena samayena saṃkiccoti paññāyi. Atha naṃ ñātakā “hotu, vaḍḍhitakāle amhākaṃ ayyassa sāriputtassa santike pabbājessāmā”ti posiṃsu. So sattavassikakāle “tava mātukucchiyaṃ [P 2.0242] vasanakāle mātā te kālamakāsi, tassā sarīre jhāpiyamānepi tvaṃ na jhāyī”ti kumārakānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “ahaṃ kira evarūpā bhayā mutto, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, pabbajissāmī”ti ñātakānaṃ ārocesi. Te “sādhu, tātā”ti sāriputtattherassa santikaṃ netvā, “bhante, imaṃ pabbājethā”ti adaṃsu. Thero tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā pabbājesi. So khuraggeyeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Ayaṃ saṃkiccasāmaṇero nāma.

The novice named Saṃkicca was the novice of the Elder Sāriputta, and was seven years of age. It is said his mother was the daughter of a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. While he was in her womb, she died in that very moment from an illness. When she was being cremated, the rest of her body burned, except for the flesh of the womb. Then, taking the womb-flesh from the pyre, they pierced it in two or three places with stakes. The tip of a stake struck the corner of the boy’s eye. Having pierced the womb-flesh thus, they threw it onto a heap of embers, covered it with more embers, and departed. The womb-flesh burned, but on top of the embers, the boy, like a golden image, was as if lying in the calyx of a lotus. Indeed, for a being in his final existence, there is no such thing as the destruction of life before attaining Arahantship, even if crushed by Mount Sineru. The next day, people who came to extinguish the pyre saw the boy lying thus and, their minds filled with wonder and amazement, they thought, 'How is it that while so much wood was consumed and the entire body was cremated, the boy did not burn? What can this be?' Taking the boy, they went into the village and asked the fortune-tellers. The fortune-tellers said, 'If this boy lives the household life, his relatives for seven generations will become poor. If he goes forth, he will wander surrounded by five hundred ascetics.' Because the corner of his eye was pierced by a stake, they gave him the name Saṃkicca. In time, he became known as Saṃkicca. Then his relatives raised him, thinking, 'So be it. When he is grown, we will have him go forth under our master, the Elder Sāriputta.' When he was seven years old, upon hearing his relatives say, 'When you were in your mother’s womb, your mother died. Even when her body was being cremated, you did not burn,' the boy, having heard their words, thought, 'It seems I was freed from such a great danger. What use is the household life to me? I will go forth,' and he informed his relatives. They said, 'Excellent, dear boy,' and taking him to the Elder Sāriputta, they said, 'Venerable Sir, please give this boy the going forth,' and handed him over. The Elder gave him the meditation subject on the five parts of the body and gave him the going forth. At the very tip of the razor, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. This is the novice named Saṃkicca.

Satthā “etasmiṃ gate taṃ bhayaṃ vūpasamissati, atha nesaṃ pabbajitakiccaṃ pāripūriṃ gamissatī”ti ñatvā, “bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātikaṃ sāriputtattheraṃ oloketvā gacchathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti vatvā therassa [M 1.0427] santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, āvuso”ti vutte mayaṃ satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitukāmā hutvā āpucchimhā, atha no satthā evamāha – “tumhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātikaṃ oloketvā gacchathā”ti? “Tenamhā idhāgatā”ti. Thero “satthārā [V 1.0381] ime ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā idha pahitā bhavissanti, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti āvajjento tamatthaṃ ñatvā āha – “atthi pana vo, āvuso, sāmaṇero”ti? “Natthi, āvuso”ti. “Sace natthi, imaṃ saṃkiccasāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti. “Alaṃ, āvuso, sāmaṇeraṃ nissāya no palibodho bhavissati, kiṃ araññe vasantānaṃ sāmaṇerenā”ti? “Nāvuso[P 2.0243], imaṃ nissāya tumhākaṃ palibodho, apica kho pana tumhe nissāya imassa palibodho bhavissati. Satthāpi tumhe mama santikaṃ pahiṇanto tumhehi saddhiṃ sāmaṇerassa pahiṇanaṃ paccāsīsanto pahiṇi, imaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti adhivāsetvā sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ ekatiṃsa janā theraṃ apaloketvā vihārā nikkhamma cārikaṃ carantā vīsayojanasatamatthake ekaṃ sahassakulaṃ gāmaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

The Teacher, knowing, "When this one has gone, that danger will be pacified, and then their duty as renunciants will reach fulfillment," said, "Bhikkhus, go after seeing your elder brother, the Elder Sāriputta." They said, "Very well," and went to the Elder. When asked, "What is it, friends?" they replied, "We received a meditation subject from the Teacher and, wishing to enter the forest, took our leave. Then the Teacher told us, 'Go after seeing your elder brother.' That is why we have come here." The Elder, reflecting, "The Teacher must have sent them here having seen some reason—what could it be?" understood the matter and said, "Do you have a novice, friends?" "No, friend." "If not, take this novice Saṃkicca with you." "Enough, friend! On account of a novice, there will be an impediment for us. What use is a novice to those dwelling in the forest?" "Friends, on account of him, there will be no impediment for you. Rather, on account of you, there will be an impediment for him. The Teacher, in sending you to me, sent you expecting that the novice would be sent with you. Take him and go." They consented, saying, "Very well," and the thirty-one of them, together with the novice, after taking leave of the Elder, departed from the monastery. While wandering on tour, they reached a village of a thousand families at a distance of over one hundred and twenty yojanas.

Manussā te disvā pasannacittā sakkaccaṃ parivisitvā, “bhante, kattha gamissathā”ti pucchitvā “yathāphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ, āvuso”ti vutte pādamūle nipajjitvā “mayaṃ, bhante, ayyesu imaṃ ṭhānaṃ nissāya antovassaṃ vasantesu pañcasīlaṃ samādāya uposathakammaṃ karissāmā”ti yāciṃsu. Therā adhivāsesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ manussā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamanapaṇṇasālāyo saṃvidahitvā “ajja mayaṃ, sve maya”nti ussāhappattā upaṭṭhānamakaṃsu. Therā vassūpanāyikadivase katikavattaṃ kariṃsu, “āvuso, amhehi dharamānakabuddhassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahitaṃ, na kho pana sakkā aññatra paṭipattisampadāya buddhe ārādhetuṃ, amhākañca apāyadvārāni vivaṭāneva, tasmā aññatra pāto bhikkhācāravelaṃ, sāyaṃ therūpaṭṭhānavelañca [P 2.0244] sesakāle dve ekaṭṭhāne na bhavissāma, yassa aphāsukaṃ bhavissati, tena ghaṇḍiyā pahaṭāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā bhesajjaṃ karissāma, ito aññasmiṃ rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā appamattā kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjissāmā”ti.

The people, seeing them, with pleased minds, respectfully served them with food and asked, "Venerable sirs, where will you go?" When they were told, "To a suitable place, friends," they prostrated themselves at their feet and requested, "Venerable sirs, if the noble ones would dwell here relying on this place for the duration of the rains-retreat, we will undertake the five precepts and perform the Uposatha observance." The Elders consented. Then the people prepared for them places for the night and for the day, walking paths, and leaf-huts, and with great enthusiasm, they attended upon them, saying, "Our turn today, our turn tomorrow." On the day of entering the rains-retreat, the Elders made an agreement: "Friends, we have received a meditation subject in the presence of the living Buddha. It is not possible to please the Buddha except through the accomplishment of the practice. And for us, the doors to the woeful states are still open. Therefore, except for the time of the morning alms-round and the evening time for attending to the elders, two of us shall not be in one place at any other time. Should anyone feel unwell, when the bell has been struck by him, we will go to him and administer medicine. At any other time, whether in a portion of the night or a portion of the day, we will diligently apply ourselves to our meditation subject."

Tesu [M 1.0428] evaṃ katikaṃ katvā viharantesu eko duggatapuriso dhītaraṃ upanissāya jīvanto tasmiṃ ṭhāne dubbhikkhe uppanne aparaṃ dhītaraṃ upanissāya jīvitukāmo maggaṃ paṭipajji. Therāpi gāme piṇḍāya caritvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantā antarāmagge ekissā nadiyā nhatvā vālukapuline nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ kariṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so puriso taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ therā “kahaṃ gacchasī”ti pucchiṃsu. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Therā tasmiṃ kāruññaṃ uppādetvā, “upāsaka, ativiya chātosi, gaccha, paṇṇaṃ āhara, ekamekaṃ te bhattapiṇḍaṃ dassāmā”ti vatvā tena paṇṇe āhaṭe attanā attanā bhuñjananiyāmeneva sūpabyañjanehi sannahitvā ekamekaṃ piṇḍaṃ adaṃsu. Etadeva kira vattaṃ, yaṃ bhojanakāle āgatassa [V 1.0382] bhattaṃ dadamānena [P 2.0245] bhikkhunā aggabhattaṃ adatvā attanā bhuñjananiyāmeneva thokaṃ vā bahuṃ vā dātabbaṃ. Tasmā tepi tathā adaṃsu. So katabhattakicco there vanditvā pucchi – “kiṃ, bhante, ayyā, kenaci nimantitā”ti? “Natthi, upāsaka, nimantanaṃ, manussā devasikaṃ evarūpameva āhāraṃ dentī”ti. So cintesi – “mayaṃ niccakālaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya kammaṃ karontāpi evarūpaṃ āhāraṃ laddhuṃ na sakkoma, kiṃ me aññattha gatena, imesaṃ santikeyeva jīvissāmī”ti. Atha ne āha – “ahaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā ayyānaṃ santike vasituṃ icchāmī”ti. “Sādhu, upāsakā”ti. So tehi saddhiṃ tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sādhukaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ karonto bhikkhū ativiya ārādhetvā dvemāsaccayena dhītaraṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā “sace, ayye, āpucchissāmi, na maṃ vissajjissanti, anāpucchā gamissāmī”ti tesaṃ anācikkhitvāva nikkhami. Ettakameva kirassa oḷārikaṃ khalitaṃ ahosi, yaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anārocetvā pakkāmi.

While they were living thus, having made their agreement, a certain poor man who was living dependent on his daughter, when a famine arose in that place, set out on a journey, desiring to live dependent on another daughter. The elders, too, having gone for alms in the village and while returning to their dwelling place, bathed in a river along the way, and having sat down on a sandbank, they attended to their meal. At that moment, that man arrived at the place and stood to one side. Then the elders asked him, “Where are you going?” He told them the matter. The elders, arousing compassion for him, said, “Lay follower, you are very hungry. Go, fetch a leaf; we will give you one morsel of rice each.” When he had brought the leaves, they each, in the same manner as they themselves were eating, prepared a morsel with sauces and curries and gave it to him. Indeed, this is the proper conduct: when a bhikkhu is giving food to someone who arrives at mealtime, he should not give the first portion, but should give a little or much, prepared in the same manner as he himself is eating. Therefore, they too gave in that way. Having finished his meal, he paid respects to the elders and asked, “Venerable sirs, have the noble ones been invited by anyone?” “There is no invitation, lay follower. The people give food like this every day.” He thought, “Even though we are always striving and endeavoring, working, we are not able to get such food. What is the use of my going elsewhere? I will make my living right here in the presence of these bhikkhus.” Then he said to them, “I wish to stay in the presence of the noble ones, performing the major and minor duties.” “Very well, lay follower.” He went with them to their dwelling place and, performing the major and minor duties well, he greatly pleased the bhikkhus. When two months had passed, desiring to see his daughter, he thought, “If I ask the noble ones for permission, they will not release me. I will go without asking.” Without informing them, he departed. This, it seems, was his only gross fault: that he left without informing the bhikkhus.

Tassa pana gamanamagge ekā aṭavī atthi.
