Tattha pañcasatānaṃ corānaṃ “yo imaṃ aṭaviṃ pavisati, taṃ māretvā tassa maṃsalohitena tuyhaṃ balikammaṃ karissāmā”ti devatāya āyācanaṃ katvā vasantānaṃ sattamo divaso hoti. Tasmā sattame divase corajeṭṭhako rukkhaṃ āruyha [P 2.0246] olokento taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā corānaṃ saññamadāsi. Te tassa aṭavimajjhaṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā parikkhipitvā taṃ gaṇhitvā gāḷhabandhanaṃ katvā [M 1.0429] araṇisahitena aggiṃ nibbattetvā dārūni saṅkaḍḍhitvā mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ katvā sūlāni tacchiṃsu. So tesaṃ taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā, “sāmi, imasmiṃ ṭhāne neva sūkarā, na migādayo dissanti, kiṃ kāraṇā idaṃ karothā”ti pucchi. “Taṃ māretvā tava maṃsalohitena devatāya balikammaṃ karissāmā”ti. So maraṇabhayatajjito bhikkhūnaṃ taṃ upakāraṃ acintetvā kevalaṃ attano jīvitameva rakkhamāno evamāha – “sāmi, ahaṃ vighāsādo, ucchiṭṭhabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vaḍḍhito, vighāsādo nāma kāḷakaṇṇiko, ayyā pana yato tato nikkhamitvā pabbajitāpi khattiyāva, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne ekatiṃsa bhikkhū vasanti, te māretvā balikammaṃ karotha, ativiya vo devatā tussissatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā corā “bhaddakaṃ esa vadeti, kiṃ iminā kāḷakaṇṇinā, khattiye māretvā balikammaṃ karissāmā”ti cintetvā “ehi, nesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dassehī”ti tameva maggadesakaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā vihāramajjhe bhikkhū adisvā “kahaṃ bhikkhū”ti naṃ pucchiṃsu. So dve māse vasitattā tesaṃ katikavattaṃ jānanto evamāha [P 2.0247] – “attano divāṭṭhānarattiṭṭhānesu nisinnā, etaṃ ghaṇḍiṃ paharatha, ghaṇḍisaddena sannipatissantī”ti. Corajeṭṭhako ghaṇḍiṃ pahari.

Now, on that man’s path of travel, there was a forest. In that place, it was the seventh day for five hundred bandits who were dwelling there, having made a plea to a deity, saying: “Whoever enters this forest, we will kill him and make a sacrificial offering to you with his flesh and blood.” Therefore, on the seventh day, the chief of the bandits climbed a tree and, while looking out, saw him approaching and gave a signal to the other bandits. Knowing that he had entered the middle of the forest, they surrounded him, seized him, bound him tightly, kindled a fire with a fire-drill, gathered firewood, made a great pyre, and sharpened stakes. Seeing their activity, he asked, “Masters, in this place neither boars nor deer and other animals are seen. For what reason are you doing this?” “We will kill you and make a sacrificial offering to the deity with your flesh and blood.” Terrified by the fear of death, without considering the help he had received from the bhikkhus and seeking only to protect his own life, he said this: “Masters, I am a refuse-eater, raised on leftover food. A refuse-eater is an inauspicious person. The noble sirs, however, though they have gone forth from various places, are indeed Khattiyas. In such-and-such a place, thirty-one bhikkhus are dwelling. Kill them and perform the sacrificial offering; the deity will be exceedingly pleased with you.” Hearing this, the bandits thought, “He speaks well. What use is this inauspicious person? We will kill the Khattiyas and perform the sacrificial offering.” And thinking thus, they said, “Come, show us their dwelling place.” Making him their guide, they reached that place. Not seeing the bhikkhus in the middle of the monastery, they asked him, “Where are the bhikkhus?” As he had lived there for two months, he knew their customary practice and said, “They are seated in their day-places and night-places. Strike this bell; at the sound of the bell, they will assemble.” The chief of the bandits struck the bell.

Bhikkhū [V 1.0383] ghaṇḍisaddaṃ sutvā “akāle ghaṇḍi pahaṭā, kassaci aphāsukaṃ bhavissatī”ti āgantvā vihāramajjhe paṭipāṭiyā paññattesu pāsāṇaphalakesu nisīdiṃsu. Saṅghatthero core oloketvā pucchi – “upāsakā kenāyaṃ ghaṇḍi pahaṭā”ti? Corajeṭṭhako āha – “mayā, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Amhehi aṭavidevatāya āyācitaṃ atthi, tassā balikammakaraṇatthāya ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā gamissāmā”ti. Taṃ sutvā mahāthero bhikkhū āha – “āvuso, bhātikānaṃ uppannakiccaṃ nāma jeṭṭhabhātikena nittharitabbaṃ, ahaṃ attano jīvitaṃ tumhākaṃ pariccajitvā imehi saddhiṃ gamissāmi, mā sabbesaṃ antarāyo hotu, appamattā samaṇadhammaṃ karothā”ti. Anuthero āha – “bhante, jeṭṭhabhātu kiccaṃ nāma kaniṭṭhassa bhāro, ahaṃ gamissāmi, tumhe appamattā hothā”ti. Iminā upāyena “ahameva ahamevā”ti vatvā paṭipāṭiyā tiṃsapi janā uṭṭhahiṃsu, evaṃ te neva ekissā mātuyā puttā, na [M 1.0430] ekassa pituno, nāpi vītarāgā, atha ca pana avasesānaṃ atthāya paṭipāṭiyā jīvitaṃ pariccajiṃsu. Tesu ekopi “tvaṃ yāhī”ti vattuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi.

The bhikkhus, hearing the sound of the bell, thought, “The bell has been struck at an improper time; someone must be in distress.” They came and sat down in rows on the prepared stone slabs in the middle of the monastery. The elder of the Sangha, looking at the bandits, asked, “Lay devotees, by whom was this bell struck?” The chief of the bandits said, “By me, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “We have made a plea to the forest deity. For the purpose of making a sacrificial offering to her, we will take one bhikkhu and go.” Hearing this, the great elder said to the bhikkhus, “Friends, a duty that has arisen among brothers should be discharged by the eldest brother. I will give up my life for you and go with these men. Let there be no danger to all of you. Be heedful and practice the duties of a recluse.” The next elder said, “Venerable sir, the duty of the elder brother is the burden of the younger. I will go. You all be heedful.” In this manner, saying, “I myself will go, I myself,” all thirty men stood up in succession. Thus, they were not sons of one mother, nor of one father, nor were they free from passion, and yet for the sake of the others, they successively gave up their lives. Among them, there was not even one who was capable of saying, “You go.”

Saṃkiccasāmaṇero tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “bhante, tumhe tiṭṭhatha[P 2.0248], ahaṃ tumhākaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā gamissāmī”ti āha. Te āhaṃsu – “āvuso, mayaṃ sabbe ekato māriyamānāpi taṃ ekakaṃ na vissajjessāmā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā, bhante”ti? “‘Āvuso, tvaṃ dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa sāmaṇero, sace taṃ vissajjessāma, sāmaṇeraṃ me ādāya gantvā corānaṃ niyyādiṃsū’ti thero no garahissati, taṃ nindaṃ nittharituṃ na sakkhissāma, tena taṃ na vissajjessāmā”ti. “Bhante, sammāsambuddho tumhe mama upajjhāyassa santikaṃ pahiṇantopi, mama upajjhāyo maṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ pahiṇantopi idameva kāraṇaṃ disvā pahiṇi, tiṭṭhatha tumhe, ahameva gamissāmī”ti so tiṃsa bhikkhū vanditvā “sace, bhante, me doso atthi, khamathā”ti vatvā nikkhami. Tadā bhikkhūnaṃ mahāsaṃvego uppajji, akkhīni assupuṇṇāni hadayamaṃsaṃ pavedhi. Mahāthero core āha – “upāsakā ayaṃ daharako tumhe aggiṃ karonte, sūlāni tacchante, paṇṇāni attharante disvā bhāyissati, imaṃ ekamante ṭhapetvā tāni kiccāni kareyyāthā”ti. Corā sāmaṇeraṃ ādāya gantvā ekamante ṭhapetvā sabbakiccāni kariṃsu.

Hearing their conversation, the novice Saṅkicca said, 'Venerable sirs, you stay. I will go, having given up my life for you.' They said, 'Friend, even if we were all being killed together, we would not send you away alone.' 'For what reason, venerable sirs?' 'Friend, you are the novice of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. If we were to send you away, the Elder would rebuke us, saying: "They took my novice and handed him over to the bandits." We would not be able to overcome that censure. For that reason, we will not send you away.' 'Venerable sirs, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when sending you to my preceptor, and my preceptor, when sending me with you, sent me having foreseen this very reason. You stay. I myself will go.' Then, having paid homage to the thirty monks, he said, 'Venerable sirs, if there is any fault in me, please forgive me,' and he departed. At that moment, a great sense of urgency arose in the monks; their eyes filled with tears, and the flesh of their hearts trembled. The great elder said to the bandits, 'Lay devotees, this young one will be frightened seeing you making a fire, sharpening stakes, and spreading leaves. Place him to one side and then perform those tasks.' The robbers took the novice, placed him to one side, and performed all their tasks.

Kiccapariyosāne corajeṭṭhako [P 2.0249] asiṃ abbāhitvā sāmaṇeraṃ upasaṅkami. Sāmaṇero nisīdamāno jhānaṃ samāpajjitvāva nisīdi. Corajeṭṭhako asiṃ parivattetvā sāmaṇerassa khandhe pātesi, asi namitvā dhārāya dhāraṃ pahari, so “na sammā pahari”nti maññamāno puna taṃ ujukaṃ [V 1.0384] katvā pahari. Asi tālapaṇṇaṃ viya veṭhayamāno tharumūlaṃ agamāsi. Sāmaṇerañhi tasmiṃ kāle sinerunā avattharantopi māretuṃ samattho nāma natthi, pageva asinā. Taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā corajeṭṭhako cintesi – “pubbe me asi silāthambhaṃ vā khadirakhāṇuṃ vā kaḷīraṃ viya chindati, idāni ekavāraṃ nami, ekavāraṃ tālapattaveṭhako viya jāto. Ayaṃ nāma asi acetanā hutvāpi imassa guṇaṃ jānāti, ahaṃ sacetanopi na jānāmī”ti. So asiṃ bhūmiyaṃ [M 1.0431] khipitvā tassa pādamūle urena nipajjitvā, “bhante, mayaṃ dhanakāraṇā aṭaviṃ paviṭṭhāmhā, amhe dūratova disvā sahassamattāpi manussā pavedhanti, dve [P 2.0250] tisso kathā kathetuṃ na sakkonti. Tava pana santāsamattampi natthi, ukkāmukhe suvaṇṇaṃ viya supupphitakaṇikāraṃ viya ca te mukhaṃ virocati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

At the conclusion of their tasks, the chief of the robbers, drawing his sword, approached the novice. The novice, while sitting, remained having just entered into jhāna. The chief of the robbers swung his sword and brought it down on the novice's shoulder; the sword bent, and its edge struck its own edge. Thinking, “I did not strike properly,” he straightened it and struck again. The sword, coiling like a palm leaf, went to its hilt. Indeed, at that time, there was no one capable of killing the novice even by crushing him with Mount Sineru, let alone with a sword. Seeing this miracle, the chief of the robbers reflected: “Previously, my sword would cut through a stone pillar or an acacia-wood stump as if it were a lotus shoot, but now, one time it bent, and another time it became like a coiled palm leaf. This sword, though insentient, knows his virtue, while I, though sentient, do not.” He threw the sword to the ground, prostrated with his chest at the novice's feet, and wishing to ask, “Venerable sir, we entered this forest for the sake of wealth. Seeing us even from afar, as many as a thousand men tremble; they are unable to speak two or three words. But for you, there is not even a trace of fear. Your face shines like gold fresh from the mouth of a furnace and like a fully bloomed Kanikara flower. What could be the reason?” he spoke this verse:

“Tassa te natthi bhītattaṃ, bhiyyo vaṇṇo pasīdati;

Kasmā na paridevesi, evarūpe mahabbhaye”ti. (theragā. 706);

“For you there is no state of being frightened, your complexion brightens all the more; why do you not lament in the face of such great danger?”

Sāmaṇero jhānā vuṭṭhāya tassa dhammaṃ desento, “āvuso gāmaṇi, khīṇāsavassa attabhāvo nāma sīse ṭhapitabhāro viya hoti, so tasmiṃ bhijjante vā nassante vā tussateva, na bhāyatī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The novice, arising from jhāna, taught him the Dhamma, saying, “Friend chieftain, for one whose taints are destroyed, the body is like a burden placed on the head. When it breaks up or perishes, he is only content and is not afraid.” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

“Natthi cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ, anapekkhassa gāmaṇi;

Atikkantā bhayā sabbe, khīṇasaṃyojanassa ve.

“There is no mental suffering, O chieftain, for one who is without longing; all fears are overcome, indeed, for one whose fetters are destroyed.

“Khīṇāya bhavanettiyā, diṭṭhe dhamme yathātathe;

Na bhayaṃ maraṇe hoti, bhāranikkhepane yathā”ti. (theragā. 707-708);

“With the guide to becoming destroyed, having seen things as they truly are in this very life, there is no fear at death, just as in the laying down of a burden.”

So tassa kathaṃ sutvā pañca corasatāni oloketvā āha – “tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Tumhe pana, sāmī”ti. “Mama tāva, bho, ‘evarūpaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā agāramajjhe kammaṃ natthi, ayyassa santike pabbajissāmī’ti. Mayampi tatheva karissāmā”ti. “Sādhu, tātā”ti tato pañcasatāpi corā sāmaṇeraṃ vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu[P 2.0251]. So tesaṃ asidhārāhi eva kese ceva vatthadasā ca chinditvā tambamattikāya rajitvā tāni kāsāyāni acchādāpetvā dasasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā te ādāya gacchanto cintesi [V 1.0385] – “sacāhaṃ there adisvāva gamissāmi, te [M 1.0432] samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissanti. Corānañhi maṃ gahetvā nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya tesu ekopi assūni sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhi, ‘mārito nu kho sāmaṇero, no’ti cintentānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ abhimukhaṃ na bhavissati, tasmā disvāva ne gamissāmī”ti. So pañcasatabhikkhuparivāro tattha gantvā attano dassanena paṭiladdhaassāsehi tehi “kiṃ, sappurisa, saṃkicca, laddhaṃ te jīvita”nti vutte, “āma, bhante, ime maṃ māretukāmā hutvā māretuṃ asakkontā mama guṇe pasīditvā dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajitā, ahaṃ ‘tumhe disvāva gamissāmī’ti āgato, appamattā samaṇadhammaṃ karotha, ahaṃ satthu santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti te bhikkhū vanditvā itare ādāya upajjhāyassa santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ saṃkicca, antevāsikā te laddhā”ti vutte, “āma, bhante”ti taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Therena “gaccha saṃkicca, satthāraṃ passāhī”ti vutte, “sādhū”ti theraṃ vanditvā te ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthārāpi [P 2.0252] “kiṃ saṃkicca, antevāsikā te laddhā”ti vutte, “āma, bhante”ti taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “evaṃ kira, bhikkhave”ti pucchitvā, “āma, bhante”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ corakammaṃ katvā dussīle patiṭṭhāya vassasataṃ jīvanato idāni sīle patiṭṭhāya ekadivasampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the chief of the robbers looked at the five hundred thieves and asked, “What will you do?” They replied, “And what about you, master?” “For my part, friends,” he said, “having seen such a miracle, there is no more work for me in the household life. I will go forth in the presence of the noble one.” “We too shall do the same,” they said. “Very well, dear sirs,” he replied. Then the five hundred thieves paid homage to the novice and requested the going forth. He cut their hair and the fringes of their garments with the edges of their own swords, dyed them with reddish earth, and had them put on those ochre robes. After establishing them in the ten precepts, he led them away. As they were going, he thought: “If I go without the elders seeing them, they will not be able to practice the ascetic’s duties. Indeed, from the time the robbers seized me and departed, not one of those elders could hold back his tears. While they are thinking, ‘Has the novice been killed or not?’ their minds will not be directed towards their meditation subject. Therefore, I will go only after they have seen them.” With his retinue of five hundred monks, he went there. When those elders, who were comforted by the sight of him, said, “Well, good man, Saṅkicca, have you been able to keep your life?” he replied, “Yes, venerable sirs. These men, intending to kill me, were unable to do so. Pleased by my virtues and having heard the Dhamma, they have gone forth. I came thinking, ‘I will leave only after you see them.’ Be diligent in the ascetic’s duties. I will now go to the Teacher.” After paying homage to those monks, he took the others and went to his preceptor. When asked, “Saṅkicca, have you gained disciples?” he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” and recounted the events. The elder said, “Go, Saṅkicca, and see the Teacher.” “Very well,” he said, paid homage to the elder, and took them to the Teacher. The Teacher also asked, “Saṅkicca, have you gained disciples?” “Yes, Blessed One,” he replied and recounted the events. The Teacher, after inquiring, “Is it so, monks?” and hearing their confirmation, said, “Monks, better than living for a hundred years, having done the work of thieves and being established in immoral conduct, is a single day’s life now established in virtue.” Then, connecting the discourse, he spoke this verse:

110.

110.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, dussīlo asamāhito;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, sīlavantassa jhāyino”ti.

“Though one should live a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated, better is a single day of life for one who is virtuous and meditative.”

Tattha dussīloti nissīlo. Sīlavantassāti dussīlassa vassasataṃ jīvanato sīlavantassa dvīhi jhānehi jhāyino ekadivasampi ekamuhuttampi jīvitaṃ seyyo, uttamanti attho.

Herein, 'dussīlo' means one without virtue. As for 'sīlavantassa': a life of even a single day, or even a single moment, for one who is virtuous and meditative with the two jhānas is better—that is, supreme—than a life of a hundred years for one who is without virtue. This is the meaning.

Desanāvasāne te pañcasatāpi bhikkhū saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sampattamahājanassāpi sātthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, those five hundred monks attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for the great assembly that had gathered.

Aparena samayena saṃkicco upasampadaṃ labhitvā dasavasso hutvā sāmaṇeraṃ gaṇhi. So pana tasseva bhāgineyyo adhimuttasāmaṇero nāma. Atha naṃ thero paripuṇṇavassakāle āmantetvā “upasampadaṃ te karissāmi, gaccha, ñātakānaṃ santike vassaparimāṇaṃ pucchitvā [M 1.0433] ehī”ti uyyojesi. So mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ [P 2.0253] gacchanto antarāmagge pañcasatehi corehi balikammatthāya māriyamāno tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā pasannacittehi tehi “na te imasmiṃ ṭhāne amhākaṃ [V 1.0386] atthibhāvo kassaci ārocetabbo”ti vissaṭṭho paṭipathe mātāpitaro āgacchante disvā tameva maggaṃ paṭipajjantānampi tesaṃ saccamanurakkhanto nārocesi. Tesaṃ corehi viheṭhiyamānānaṃ “tvampi corehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā maññe, amhākaṃ nārocesī”ti paridevantānaṃ saddaṃ sutvā te mātāpitūnampi anārocitabhāvaṃ ñatvā pasannacittā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Sopi saṃkiccasāmaṇero viya te sabbe pabbājetvā upajjhāyassa santikaṃ ānetvā tena satthu santikaṃ pesito gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “evaṃ kira, bhikkhave”ti pucchitvā, “āma, bhante”ti vutte purimanayeneva anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imameva gāthamāha –

At a later time, Saṅkicca received the higher ordination and, having been a monk for ten years, accepted a novice. That novice was his own nephew, named Adhimutta. Then, when the novice had reached the proper age, the elder summoned him and said, 'I will give you the higher ordination. Go to your relatives, inquire about the measure of your age, and then return.' So he sent him off. As the novice was going to his parents, he was seized on the way by five hundred robbers to be used for a sacrificial offering. He taught them the Dhamma, and with minds filled with faith, they released him, saying, 'You must not tell anyone of our presence in this place.' Having been released, he saw his parents coming along the path. Though they were traveling that very same path, he protected his promise and did not inform them. Hearing the sound of his parents lamenting as they were being harassed by the robbers—'It seems you too have sided with the robbers, since you did not inform us!'—the robbers, realizing that he had not informed even his parents, with minds filled with faith, requested ordination. He, like Saṅkicca the novice had done, ordained all of them and brought them to his preceptor. Having been sent by his preceptor to the Teacher, he went and reported the matter. The Teacher asked, 'Is it so, monks?' and when they replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' he connected the narrative in the same way as before and, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this very verse:

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, dussīlo asamāhito;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, sīlavantassa jhāyino”ti.

Though one should live a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated; better is a single day of life for one who is virtuous and meditative.

Idampi adhimuttasāmaṇeravatthu vuttanayamevāti.

This Story of the Novice Adhimutta is also told in the same way as previously stated.

Saṃkiccasāmaṇeravatthu navamaṃ.

The ninth story, that of Saṅkicca the Novice, is finished.

10. Khāṇukoṇḍaññattheravatthu

10. The Story of the Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña

Yo [P 2.0254] ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto khāṇukoṇḍaññattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling in Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve' concerning the Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña.

So kira thero satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharanto arahattaṃ patvā “satthu ārocessāmī”ti tato āgacchanto antarāmagge kilanto maggā okkamma ekasmiṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇe nisinno jhānaṃ samāpajji. Athekaṃ gāmaṃ vilumpitvā pañcasatā corā attano balānurūpena bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā sīsenādāya gacchantā dūraṃ gantvā kilantarūpā “dūraṃ āgatāmha, imasmiṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇe vissamissāmā”ti maggā okkamma [M 1.0434] piṭṭhipāsāṇassa santikaṃ gantvā theraṃ disvāpi “khāṇuko aya”nti saññino ahesuṃ. Atheko coro therassa sīse bhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapesi, aparopi taṃ nissāya bhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapesi. Evaṃ pañcasatāpi corā pañcahi bhaṇḍikasatehi theraṃ parikkhipitvā sayampi nisinnā niddāyitvā aruṇuggamanakāle pabujjhitvā attano attano bhaṇḍikaṃ gaṇhantā theraṃ disvā “amanusso”ti saññāya palāyituṃ [V 1.0387] ārabhiṃsu. Atha ne thero āha – “mā bhāyittha upāsakā, pabbajito aha”nti. Te therassa pādamūle nipajjitvā “khamatha, bhante, mayaṃ khāṇukasaññino ahumhā”ti theraṃ khamāpetvā corajeṭṭhakena “ahaṃ ayyassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti vutte sesā “mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti [P 2.0255] vatvā sabbepi ekacchandā hutvā theraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Thero saṃkiccasāmaṇero viya sabbepi te pabbājesi. Tato paṭṭhāya khāṇukoṇḍaññoti paññāyi. So tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthārā “kiṃ, koṇḍañña, antevāsikā te laddhā”ti vutte taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “evaṃ kira, bhikkhave”ti pucchitvā, “āma, bhante, na no aññassa evarūpo ānubhāvo diṭṭhapubbo, tenamhā pabbajitā”ti vutte, “bhikkhave, evarūpe duppaññakamme patiṭṭhāya vassasataṃ jīvanato idāni vo paññāsampadāya vattamānānaṃ ekāhampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that the Elder, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, was dwelling in the forest when he attained arahantship. Thinking, 'I will inform the Teacher,' he was coming from there when, weary on the way, he stepped off the path, sat down on a flat rock, and entered into jhāna. Then, five hundred robbers, having plundered a village, were carrying their bundles on their heads according to their strength. Having gone a long way, they became weary and thought, 'We have come far; let us rest on this flat rock.' Stepping off the path, they went to the vicinity of the flat rock, and though they saw the elder, they perceived him to be a tree stump. Then one robber placed his bundle on the elder's head, and another also placed his bundle leaning against him. In this way, all five hundred robbers surrounded the elder with five hundred bundles, and they themselves sat down, fell asleep, and awoke at dawn. As they were taking their respective bundles, they saw the elder and, perceiving him to be a non-human, began to flee. Then the elder said to them, 'Do not be afraid, lay disciples, I am a monk.' They prostrated at the elder's feet and, asking for forgiveness, said, 'Forgive us, venerable sir, we perceived you to be a tree stump.' When the chief robber said, 'I will go forth in the presence of the noble one,' the remaining robbers said, 'We too will go forth.' All being of one accord, they requested ordination from the elder. The elder, like Saṅkicca the novice had done, ordained all of them. From that time on, he became known as Khāṇukoṇḍañña ('Stump-Koṇḍañña'). He went with those monks to the Teacher's presence, and when the Teacher asked, 'Koṇḍañña, have you obtained disciples?' he related the matter. The Teacher asked, 'Is it so, monks?' and when they replied, 'Yes, venerable sir, we have never before seen such power in another; for that reason, we went forth,' he said, 'Monks, better than living for a hundred years established in such an act of little wisdom, is a single day of life for you who are now endowed with the accomplishment of wisdom.' Having said this, he connected the narrative and, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

111.

111.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, duppañño asamāhito;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, paññavantassa jhāyino”ti.

Though one should live a hundred years, unwise and unconcentrated; better is a single day of life for one who is wise and meditative.

Tattha duppañño nippañño. Paññavantassāti sappaññassa. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

In that verse, 'unwise' (duppañño) means one without wisdom (nippañño). 'Of one who is wise' (paññavantassa) means of one possessing wisdom (sappaññassa). The rest is just as before.

Desanāvasāne pañcasatāpi te bhikkhū saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sampattamahājanassāpi sātthikā dhammadesanā ahosīti.

At the end of the discourse, those five hundred monks attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The Dhamma discourse was also of benefit to the great assembly that had gathered.

Khāṇukoṇḍaññattheravatthu dasamaṃ.

The tenth story, that of the Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña, is finished.

11. Sappadāsattheravatthu

11. The Story of the Elder Sappadāsa

Yo [P 2.0256] ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sappadāsattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

This Dhamma teaching, which begins, “Though one should live a hundred years,” was spoken by the Teacher while he was dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the Elder Sappadāsa.

Sāvatthiyaṃ [M 1.0435] kireko kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado aparena samayena ukkaṇṭhitvā “mādisassa kulaputtassa gihibhāvo nāma ayutto, pabbajjāya ṭhatvā maraṇamhi me seyyo”ti cintetvā attano maraṇūpāyaṃ cintento vicarati. Athekadivasaṃ pātova [V 1.0388] katabhattakiccā bhikkhū vihāraṃ gantvā aggisālāya sappaṃ disvā taṃ ekasmiṃ kuṭe pakkhipitvā kuṭaṃ pidahitvā ādāya vihārā nikkhamiṃsu. Ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhupi bhattakiccaṃ katvā āgacchanto te bhikkhū disvā “kiṃ idaṃ, āvuso”ti pucchitvā “sappo, āvuso”ti vutte iminā “kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Chaḍḍessāma na”nti. Tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “iminā attānaṃ ḍaṃsāpetvā marissāmī”ti “āharatha, ahaṃ taṃ chaḍḍessāmī”ti tesaṃ hatthato kuṭaṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nisinno tena sappena attānaṃ ḍaṃsāpeti, sappo ḍaṃsituṃ na icchati. So kuṭe hatthaṃ otāretvā ito cito ca āloleti, ghorasappassa mukhaṃ vivaritvā aṅguliṃ pakkhipati, neva naṃ sappo ḍaṃsi. So “nāyaṃ āsīviso, gharasappo eso”ti taṃ pahāya vihāraṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū “chaḍḍito te, āvuso, sappo”ti āhaṃsu. “Na so, āvuso, ghorasappo, gharasappo eso”ti. “Ghorasappoyevāvuso, mahantaṃ [P 2.0257] phaṇaṃ katvā susuyanto dukkhena amhehi gahito, kiṃ kāraṇā evaṃ tvaṃ vadesī”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ, āvuso, tena attānaṃ ḍaṃsāpentopi mukhe aṅguliṃ pakkhipentopi taṃ ḍaṃsāpetuṃ nāsakkhi”nti. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain man of good family, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, went forth and received the higher ordination. At a later time, he became discontented and thought, 'For a man of good family like me, the state of a householder is unsuitable; it is better for me to die while remaining in the monastic life.' Thinking thus, he went about contemplating a means for his own death. Then, one day, early in the morning, some monks who had finished their meal went to the monastery and, seeing a snake in the fire hall, put it into a pot, closed the pot, and, taking it, left the monastery. The discontented monk, having also finished his meal and coming along, saw those monks and asked, 'Friends, what is this?' When they said, 'A snake, friend,' he asked, 'What will you do with it?' 'We will release it.' Hearing their words, he thought, 'I will have this snake bite me and die.' He said, 'Bring it here; I will release it.' Taking the pot from their hands, he sat down in a certain place and tried to make that snake bite him, but the snake did not want to bite. He put his hand into the pot and stirred it about, and opening the mouth of the fierce snake, he inserted his finger, but the snake did not bite him at all. He thought, 'This is not a venomous snake; it is a house snake.' Leaving it, he went to the monastery. Then the monks asked him, 'Friend, have you released the snake?' He replied, 'Friends, that was not a fierce snake; it is a house snake.' They said, 'Friend, it was indeed a fierce snake! Making a large hood and hissing, it was caught by us with difficulty. For what reason do you speak thus?' He answered, 'Friends, even when I tried to make it bite me and put my finger in its mouth, I was not able to make it bite me.' Hearing that, the monks became silent.

Athekadivasaṃ nhāpito dve tayo khure ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā ekaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ekena bhikkhūnaṃ kese ohāreti. So bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ khuraṃ gahetvā “iminā gīvaṃ chinditvā marissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ rukkhe gīvaṃ upanidhāya khuradhāraṃ galanāḷiyaṃ katvā ṭhito upasampadāmāḷato paṭṭhāya attano sīlaṃ āvajjento vimalacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya sudhotamaṇikhandhamiva ca nimmalaṃ sīlaṃ addasa. Tassa taṃ olokentassa sakalasarīraṃ pharantī pīti uppajji. So pītiṃ vikkhambhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā khuraṃ ādāya vihāramajjhaṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū “kahaṃ gatosi, āvuso”ti pucchiṃsu. “‘Iminā khurena galanāḷiṃ chinditvā [M 1.0436] marissāmī’ti gatomhi[P 2.0258], āvuso”ti. Atha “kasmā na matosī”ti? Idānimhi satthaṃ āharituṃ abhabbo jāto. Ahañhi “iminā khurena galanāḷiṃ chindissāmī”ti ñāṇakhurena sabbakilese chindinti. Bhikkhū “ayaṃ abhūtena aññaṃ byākarotī”ti bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā āha – “na, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavā nāma sahatthā attānaṃ jīvitā voropentī”ti. Bhante, tumhe imaṃ “khīṇāsavo”ti vadatha, evaṃ arahattūpanissayasampanno panāyaṃ kasmā ukkaṇṭhati, kimassa arahattūpanissayakāraṇaṃ “kasmā so sappo etaṃ na ḍaṃsatī”ti? “Bhikkhave, so tāva sappo imassa ito tatiye attabhāve dāso ahosi, so attano sāmikassa sarīraṃ ḍaṃsituṃ na visahatī”ti. Evaṃ [V 1.0389] tāva nesaṃ satthā ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca so bhikkhu sappadāso nāma jāto.

Then one day, a barber, taking two or three razors, went to the monastery. Placing one on the ground, he began to shave the monks' hair with another. That monk took the razor placed on the ground and, thinking, 'With this, I will cut my throat and die,' went to a tree, placed his neck against it, and set the razor's edge to his throat. Standing there, he reflected on his own virtue from the time of his higher ordination onwards and saw his virtue to be as immaculate as a spotless full moon disc and a well-polished gem. As he contemplated this, joy arose, suffusing his entire body. Suppressing that joy and developing insight, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then, taking the razor, he entered the middle of the monastery. The monks asked him, 'Friend, where have you been?' He replied, 'Friends, I went thinking, “I will cut my throat with this razor and die.”' Then they asked, 'Why then did you not die?' 'Now I have become unfit to wield a weapon. For while intending, “I will cut my throat with this razor,” I have instead cut off all defilements with the razor of wisdom.' The monks, thinking, 'This one is making a false declaration of final knowledge,' reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having heard their words, said: 'Monks, those whose cankers are destroyed do not, with their own hands, deprive themselves of life.' 'Venerable Sir, you call this one “one whose cankers are destroyed.” Since he was endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship, why then was he discontented? What was the cause of his supporting condition for Arahantship? And why did that snake not bite him?' 'Monks, in the third existence from this one, that snake was this monk's slave. He could not bring himself to bite his master's body.' Thus the Teacher first explained one reason to them. And from that time on, that monk became known as Sappadāsa.

Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kireko kulaputto satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā uppannasaṃvego pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado aparena samayena anabhiratiyā uppannāya ekassa sahāyakassa bhikkhuno ārocesi. So tassa abhiṇhaṃ gihibhāve ādīnavaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā itaro sāsane abhiramitvā pubbe anabhiratakāle malaggahite samaṇaparikkhāre ekasmiṃ soṇḍitīre nimmale karonto nisīdi. Sahāyakopissa santikeyeva nisinno. Atha naṃ so evamāha – “ahaṃ, āvuso, uppabbajanto ime parikkhāre tuyhaṃ dātukāmo [P 2.0259] ahosi”nti. So lobhaṃ uppādetvā cintesi – “iminā mayhaṃ pabbajitena vā uppabbajitena vā ko attho, idāni parikkhāre gaṇhissāmī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya “kiṃ dānāvuso, amhākaṃ jīvitena, ye mayaṃ kapālahatthā parakulesu bhikkhāya carāma, puttadārehi saddhiṃ ālāpasallāpaṃ na karomā”tiādīni vadanto gihibhāvassa guṇaṃ kathesi. So tassa kathaṃ sutvā puna ukkaṇṭhito hutvā cintesi – “ayaṃ mayā ‘ukkaṇṭhitomhī’ti vutte paṭhamaṃ gihibhāve ādīnavaṃ kathetvā idāni abhiṇhaṃ guṇaṃ katheti, ‘kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa’”nti cintento “imesu samaṇaparikkhāresu lobhenā”ti ñatvā sayameva attano cittaṃ nivattesi. Evamassa kassapasammāsambuddhakāle ekassa bhikkhuno ukkaṇṭhāpitattā idāni anabhirati [M 1.0437] uppannā. Yo pana teneva tadā vīsati vassasahassāni samaṇadhammo kato, svassa etarahi arahattūpanissayo jātoti.

It is said that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, a certain man of good family, having heard the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, felt a sense of spiritual urgency. Having gone forth and received the higher ordination, at a later time, when discontent arose in him, he informed a certain companion bhikkhu. That bhikkhu repeatedly spoke to him of the peril in the household life. Hearing this, the other bhikkhu took great delight in the Dispensation. Previously, during his time of discontent, his monastic requisites had become soiled; he sat down near a certain lime pool, making them clean. His companion was also seated right near him. Then that one said this to him: 'Friend, when I was about to disrobe, I was desirous of giving these requisites to you.' That one, having given rise to greed, thought: 'What use is it to me whether this one remains ordained or disrobes? I will get the requisites now.' From then on, saying such things as, 'Now, friend, what is the use of our life, we who wander for alms in the families of others with bowls in hand, and do not engage in conversation with wife and children?' he spoke of the virtues of the household life. Hearing his talk, that bhikkhu became discontented again and thought: 'When I said, “I am discontented,” this one first spoke of the peril in the household life, but now he repeatedly speaks of its virtues. What, I wonder, is the reason?' Thinking thus, he realized, 'It is because of greed for these monastic requisites,' and he himself turned his mind back from disrobing. Thus, because he had caused a certain bhikkhu to become discontented in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, discontent arose in him now. But the ascetic practice that was performed by him for twenty thousand years at that time, that for him has now become a supporting condition for Arahantship.

Imamatthaṃ te bhikkhū bhagavato santikā sutvā uttariṃ pucchiṃsu – “bhante, ayaṃ kira bhikkhu khuradhāraṃ galanāḷiyaṃ katvā ṭhitova arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, uppajjissati nu kho ettakena khaṇena arahattamaggo”ti. “Āma, bhikkhave, āraddhavīriyassa bhikkhuno pādaṃ ukkhipitvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapentassa pāde bhūmiyaṃ asampatteyeva arahattamaggo uppajjati. Kusītassa [P 2.0260] puggalassa hi vassasataṃ jīvanato āraddhavīriyassa khaṇamattampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard this matter from the Blessed One, those bhikkhus asked further: 'Venerable Sir, it is said that this bhikkhu, having placed a razor's edge on his windpipe, attains Arahantship while still standing. Will the path to Arahantship indeed arise in such a short moment?' 'Yes, bhikkhus. For a bhikkhu with aroused energy, while lifting a foot and placing it on the ground, the path to Arahantship arises even before the foot reaches the ground. Indeed, for a lazy person, better than living for a hundred years is even a single moment of life for one with aroused energy.' Having said this, he connected the sequence of the discourse and spoke this verse:

112.

112.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, kusīto hīnavīriyo;

Ekāhaṃ jīvikaṃ seyyo, vīriyamārabhato daḷha”nti.

Though one may live a hundred years, lazy and of weak effort, better is a single day's life of one who rouses energy firmly.

Tattha [V 1.0390] kusītoti kāmavitakkādīhi tīhi vitakkehi vītināmento puggalo. Hīnavīriyoti nibbīriyo. Vīriyamārabhato daḷhanti duvidhajjhānanibbattanasamatthaṃ thiraṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhantassa. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

In that verse, 'lazy' refers to a person who passes the time with the three kinds of thoughts, such as sensual thoughts and so on. 'Of weak effort' means one without energy. 'Rousing energy firmly' refers to one who undertakes the steadfast energy capable of producing the two kinds of jhāna. The rest is just as before.

Desanāvasāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and so on.

Sappadāsattheravatthu ekādasamaṃ.

The Eleventh Story: The Elder Sappadāsa.

12. Paṭācārātherīvatthu

12. The Story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.

Yo ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paṭācāraṃ theriṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this discourse, beginning with 'Though one may live a hundred years...', concerning the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.

Sā kira sāvatthiyaṃ cattālīsakoṭivibhavassa seṭṭhino dhītā ahosi abhirūpā. Taṃ soḷasavassuddesikakāle sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatale rakkhantā vasāpesuṃ. Evaṃ santepi sā ekena attano cūḷūpaṭṭhākena saddhiṃ vippaṭipajji[P 2.0261]. Athassā mātāpitaro samajātikakule ekassa kumārassa paṭissuṇitvā vivāhadivasaṃ ṭhapesuṃ. Tasmiṃ upakaṭṭhe sā taṃ cūḷūpaṭṭhākaṃ āha – “maṃ kira asukakulassa nāma dassanti, mayi patikulaṃ gate mama paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgatopi tattha pavesanaṃ na labhissasi, sace te mayi sineho atthi, idāneva [M 1.0438] maṃ gahetvā yena vā tena vā palāyassū”ti. “So sādhu, bhadde”ti. “Tena hi ahaṃ sve pātova nagaradvārassa asukaṭṭhāne nāma ṭhassāmi, tvaṃ ekena upāyena nikkhamitvā tattha āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā dutiyadivase saṅketaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi pātova kiliṭṭhaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā kese vikkiritvā kuṇḍakena sarīraṃ makkhitvā kuṭaṃ ādāya dāsīhi saddhiṃ gacchantī viya gharā nikkhamitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ ādāya dūraṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ gāme nivāsaṃ kappetvā araññe khettaṃ kasitvā dārupaṇṇādīni āharati. Itarā kuṭena udakaṃ āharitvā sahatthā koṭṭanapacanādīni karontī attano pāpassa phalaṃ anubhoti. Athassā kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā paripuṇṇagabbhā “idha me koci upakārako natthi, mātāpitaro nāma puttesu muduhadayā honti, tesaṃ santikaṃ maṃ nehi, tattha me gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti sāmikaṃ [P 2.0262] yāci. So “kiṃ, bhadde, kathesi, maṃ disvā tava mātāpitaro vividhā kammakāraṇā kareyyuṃ, na sakkā mayā tattha gantu”nti paṭikkhipi. Sā punappunaṃ yācitvāpi [V 1.0391] gamanaṃ alabhamānā tassa araññaṃ gatakāle paṭivissake āmantetvā “sace so āgantvā maṃ apassanto ‘kahaṃ gatā’ti pucchissati, mama attano kulagharaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ācikkheyyāthā”ti vatvā gehadvāraṃ pidahitvā pakkāmi. Sopi āgantvā taṃ apassanto paṭivissake pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “nivattessāmi na”nti anubandhitvā taṃ disvā nānappakāraṃ yāciyamānopi nivattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Athassā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne kammajavātā caliṃsu. Sā ekaṃ gacchantaraṃ pavisitvā, “sāmi, kammajavātā me calitā”ti vatvā bhūmiyaṃ nipajjitvā samparivattamānā kicchena dārakaṃ vijāyitvā “yassatthāyāhaṃ kulagharaṃ gaccheyyaṃ, so attho nipphanno”ti punadeva tena saddhiṃ gehaṃ āgantvā vāsaṃ kappesi.

It is said that she was the beautiful daughter of a great merchant in Sāvatthī, possessing forty crores of wealth. When she was sixteen years of age, they kept her guarded on the uppermost floor of a seven-storied mansion. Even so, she transgressed with one of her own junior attendants. Then her parents, having promised her to a young man from a family of equal birth, set the wedding day. As that day approached, she said to that junior attendant: 'They say they will give me to a man of such-and-such a family. Once I have gone to my husband’s house, even if you come with a gift for me, you will not gain entry there. If you have any love for me, take me now and flee by whatever means you can.' He replied, 'Very well, lady.' He then said, 'In that case, tomorrow at dawn I will wait at such-and-such a place by the city gate. You, by some means, should leave and come there.' Having said this, on the next day he stood at the appointed place. She too, early in the morning, put on a soiled cloth, disheveled her hair, smeared her body with rice-bran powder, and carrying a pot, left the house as if going with the female servants and went to that place. He took her and went far away, and they made their dwelling in a certain village. He plowed a field in the forest and would bring firewood, vegetables, and so on. The other, she would fetch water with a pot and, with her own hands, did the pounding, cooking, and other chores, experiencing the fruit of her own evil deed. Then a conception was established in her womb. When her pregnancy was full-term, she begged her husband, saying: 'Here I have no one to help me. Parents are tender-hearted toward their children. Take me to their presence; there I will give birth.' He refused, saying: 'What are you saying, lady? If your parents see me, they might inflict various punishments. It is not possible for me to go there.' Though she begged him again and again, she did not receive permission to go. So, when he had gone to the forest, she informed the neighbors, saying, 'If he returns and, not seeing me, asks, "Where has she gone?" you should tell him that I have gone to my own family home.' Having said this, she closed the house door and departed. He too, having returned and not seeing her, asked the neighbors. Hearing the news, he followed after her, thinking, 'I will make her return.' Having caught up to her, though he pleaded in various ways, he was not able to make her turn back. Then, at a certain place, her labor pains stirred. She entered a thicket and said, 'Husband, my labor pains have stirred.' Having lain down on the ground and tossing and turning, she gave birth to a child with difficulty. Thinking, 'The purpose for which I was going to my family home has been accomplished,' she once again returned with him to their house and they made their dwelling there.

Tassā aparena samayena puna gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sā paripuṇṇagabbhā hutvā purimanayeneva sāmikaṃ yācitvā gamanaṃ alabhamānā puttaṃ aṅkenādāya tatheva pakkamitvā tena anubandhitvā “tiṭṭhāhī”ti vutte nivattituṃ na icchi. Atha nesaṃ gacchantānaṃ mahā akālamegho udapādi samantā vijjulatāhi [P 2.0263] ādittaṃ viya meghatthanitehi, bhijjamānaṃ viya [M 1.0439] udakadhārānipātanirantaraṃ nabhaṃ ahosi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tassā kammajavātā caliṃsu. Sā sāmikaṃ āmantetvā, “sāmi, kammajavātā me calitā, na sakkomi sandhāretuṃ, anovassakaṭṭhānaṃ me jānāhī”ti āha. So hatthagatāya vāsiyā ito cito ca upadhārento ekasmiṃ vammikamatthake jātaṃ gumbaṃ disvā chindituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ vammikato nikkhamitvā ghoraviso āsīviso ḍaṃsi. Taṅkhaṇaññevassa sarīraṃ antosamuṭṭhitāhi aggijālāhi ḍayhamānaṃ viya nīlavaṇṇaṃ hutvā tattheva pati. Itarāpi mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamānā tassa āgamanaṃ olokentīpi taṃ adisvāva aparampi puttaṃ vijāyi. Dve dārakā vātavuṭṭhivegaṃ asahamānā mahāviravaṃ viravanti. Sā ubhopi te urantare katvā dvīhi jaṇṇukehi ceva hatthehi ca bhūmiyaṃ uppīḷetvā tathā ṭhitāva rattiṃ vītināmesi. Sakalasarīraṃ nillohitaṃ viya paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇaṃ ahosi. Sā uṭṭhite aruṇe maṃsapesivaṇṇaṃ ekaṃ puttaṃ aṅkenādāya itaraṃ aṅguliyā gahetvā “ehi, tāta, pitā te ito gato”ti vatvā sāmikassa gatamaggena gacchantī [P 2.0264] taṃ vammikamatthake kālaṃ katvā patitaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ thaddhasarīraṃ disvā “maṃ nissāya mama sāmiko panthe mato”ti rodantī paridevantī pāyāsi.

After some time, she conceived again. When her pregnancy was full-term, she begged her husband as before, but being unable to obtain permission to go, she took her son on her hip and departed just as she had done previously. He followed her, and when he called out, 'Stop!' she did not wish to turn back. As they were going, a great untimely storm arose. The sky was as if ablaze with lightning on all sides and breaking apart with the sound of thunder, and became incessant with the downpour of rain. At that moment, her labor pains began. She called to her husband, saying, 'Husband, my labor pains have begun—I cannot bear them. Find me a place sheltered from the rain.' With an adze in his hand, he looked here and there and saw a thicket growing on top of an anthill. He began to cut it down. Just then, a viper of terrible venom emerged from the anthill and bit him. Instantly, his body turned blue, as if being burned by flames from within, and he collapsed right there. Meanwhile, she, experiencing great suffering and looking for his return, did not see him and gave birth to another son. The two children, unable to endure the force of the wind and rain, wailed loudly. She placed both of them between her breasts and, supporting herself over them on the ground with her two knees and hands, remained that way throughout the night. Her entire body became as pale as a yellow leaf, as if devoid of blood. At dawn, she rose. Taking the one son, who was the color of a lump of flesh, in her arms, and holding the other by the finger, she said, 'Come, dears, your father has gone this way.' Walking along the path her husband had taken, she saw his body on the anthill—dead, fallen, blue, and stiff. She wailed, 'Because of me, my husband is dead on the road!' Weeping and lamenting, she went on.

Sā sakalarattiṃ devena vuṭṭhattā aciravatiṃ nadiṃ jaṇṇuppamāṇena kaṭippamāṇena thanappamāṇena udakena paripuṇṇaṃ disvā attano mandabuddhitāya dvīhi dārakehi saddhiṃ udakaṃ otarituṃ avisahantī jeṭṭhaputtaṃ orimatīre ṭhapetvā itaraṃ ādāya paratīraṃ gantvā sākhābhaṅgaṃ attharitvā [V 1.0392] nipajjāpetvā “itarassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti bālaputtakaṃ pahāya tarituṃ asakkontī punappunaṃ nivattitvā olokayamānā pāyāsi. Athassā nadīmajjhaṃ gatakāle eko seno taṃ kumāraṃ disvā “maṃsapesī”ti saññāya ākāsato bhassi. Sā taṃ puttassatthāya bhassantaṃ disvā ubho hatthe ukkhipitvā “sūsū”ti tikkhattuṃ mahāsaddaṃ nicchāresi. Seno dūrabhāvena taṃ asutvāva kumārakaṃ gahetvā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā gato. Orimatīre ṭhitaputto mātaraṃ nadīmajjhe ubho hatthe ukkhipitvā mahāsaddaṃ nicchārayamānaṃ disvā [M 1.0440] “maṃ pakkosatī”ti saññāya vegena udake pati. Itissā bālaputtaṃ seno hari, jeṭṭhaputto udakena vūḷho.

She, because it had rained the entire night, saw the Aciravatī river filled with water to the depth of the knee, the waist, and the breast. Due to her own dull-wittedness, not venturing to enter the water to cross with both young sons, she placed the eldest son on the near shore, and taking the other, went to the far shore. Having spread out a tree branch and made him lie down, thinking, 'I will go to the other one,' she left the infant son. Being unable to cross without anxiety, she went on, repeatedly turning back to look. Then, at the time when she reached the middle of the river, a hawk saw the young boy and, with the perception 'it is a piece of meat,' swooped down from the sky. Seeing it swooping down for her son, she raised both hands and uttered a great sound, 'Sū! Sū!', three times. The hawk, due to the distance, did not hear her, and seizing the young boy, flew up into the sky and was gone. The son standing on the near shore, seeing his mother in the middle of the river raising both hands and uttering a great sound, with the perception 'She is calling me,' quickly fell into the water. Thus, a hawk carried away her infant son, and the eldest son was swept away by the water.

Sā “eko me putto senena gahito, eko udakena [P 2.0265] vūḷho, panthe me pati mato”ti rodantī paridevantī gacchamānā sāvatthito āgacchantaṃ ekaṃ purisaṃ disvā pucchi – “kattha vāsikosi, tātā”ti? “Sāvatthivāsikomhi, ammā”ti. “Sāvatthinagare asukavīthiyaṃ evarūpaṃ asukakulaṃ nāma atthi, jānāsi, tātā”ti? “Jānāmi, amma, taṃ pana mā pucchi, sace aññaṃ jānāsi pucchā”ti. “Aññena me kammaṃ natthi, tadeva pucchāmi, tātā”ti. “Amma, tvaṃ attano anācikkhituṃ na desi, ajja te sabbarattiṃ devo vassanto diṭṭho”ti. “Diṭṭho me, tāta, mayhameveso sabbarattiṃ vuṭṭho, na aññassa. Mayhaṃ pana vuṭṭhakāraṇaṃ pacchā te kathessāmi, etasmiṃ tāva me seṭṭhigehe pavattiṃ kathehī”ti. “Amma, ajja rattiṃ seṭṭhiñca seṭṭhibhariyañca seṭṭhiputtañcāti tayopi jane avattharamānaṃ gehaṃ pati, te ekacitakasmiṃ jhāyanti. Esa dhūmo paññāyati, ammā”ti. Sā tasmiṃ khaṇe nivatthavatthaṃ patamānaṃ na sañjāni, ummattikabhāvaṃ [P 2.0266] patvā yathājātāva rodantī paridevantī –

She, weeping and lamenting as she went, said: 'One son of mine was seized by a hawk, one was swept away by the water, and on the path my husband died.' Seeing a certain man coming from Sāvatthī, she asked: 'Where do you reside, dear sir?' 'I am a resident of Sāvatthī, mother.' 'In the city of Sāvatthī, on such-and-such street, there is a family of such-and-such name; do you know it, dear sir?' 'I know it, mother, but please do not ask about that family. If there is another you know of, please ask.' 'I have no business with any other; I ask only about that one, dear sir.' 'Mother, since you do not permit me to remain silent: today, did you see the rain falling all night?' 'I saw it, dear sir. This rain fell the entire night for me alone, not for another. But I will tell you the reason for the rain later. First, tell me the news concerning that merchant's house.' 'Mother, tonight the house fell, overwhelming the three people: the merchant, the merchant's wife, and the merchant's son. They are being burned on a single funeral pyre. That smoke is visible, mother.' At that moment, she did not perceive that the garment she was wearing was falling. Having reached a state of madness, just as she was born, she went on weeping and lamenting:

“Ubho puttā kālakatā, panthe mayhaṃ patī mato;

Mātā pitā ca bhātā ca, ekacitamhi ḍayhare”ti. (apa. therī 2.2.498) –

Both my sons are dead; on the path my husband is dead. My mother, father, and brother are being burned on a single funeral pyre.

Vilapantī paribbhami. Manussā taṃ disvā “ummattikā ummattikā”ti kacavaraṃ gahetvā paṃsuṃ gahetvā matthake okirantā leḍḍūhi paharanti. Satthā jetavanamahāvihāre aṭṭhaparisamajjhe nisīditvā dhammaṃ desento taṃ āgacchamānaṃ addasa kappasatasahassaṃ pūritapāramiṃ abhinīhārasampannaṃ.

Wailing, she wandered about. Seeing her, people exclaimed, 'A madwoman! A madwoman!' and taking rubbish and dust, they scattered it on her head and struck her with clods of earth. The Teacher, seated in the midst of the eightfold assembly in the Jetavana Mahāvihāra, was teaching the Dhamma when he saw her approaching—one who for a hundred thousand kappas had fulfilled the perfections and was endowed with the great aspiration.

Sā [V 1.0393] kira padumuttarabuddhakāle padumuttarasatthārā ekaṃ vinayadharattheriṃ bāhāya gahetvā nandanavane ṭhapentaṃ viya etadaggaṭṭhāne ṭhapiyamānaṃ disvā “ahampi tumhādisassa buddhassa santike vinayadharattherīnaṃ aggaṭṭhānaṃ labheyya”nti adhikāraṃ katvā patthanaṃ ṭhapesi. Padumuttarabuddho anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pattharitvā patthanāya samijjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “anāgate gotamabuddhassa nāma sāsane ayaṃ paṭācārā nāmena vinayadharattherīnaṃ aggā [M 1.0441] bhavissatī”ti byākāsi. Taṃ [P 2.0267] evaṃ patthitapatthanaṃ abhinīhārasampannaṃ satthā dūratova āgacchantiṃ disvā “imissā ṭhapetvā maṃ añño avassayo bhavituṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti cintetvā taṃ yathā vihārābhimukhaṃ āgacchati, evaṃ akāsi. Parisā taṃ disvāva “imissā ummattikāya ito āgantuṃ mā daditthā”ti āha. Satthā “apetha, mā naṃ vārayitthā”ti vatvā avidūraṭṭhānaṃ āgatakāle “satiṃ paṭilabha bhaginī”ti āha. Sā taṃ khaṇaṃyeva buddhānubhāvena satiṃ paṭilabhi. Tasmiṃkāle nivatthavatthassa patitabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdi. Athassā eko puriso uttarasāṭakaṃ khipi. Sā taṃ nivāsetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇesu pādesu pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, avassayo me hotha, patiṭṭhā me hotha. Ekañhi me puttaṃ seno gaṇhi, eko udakena vūḷho, panthe me pati mato, mātāpitaro ceva me bhātā ca gehena avatthaṭā ekacitakasmiṃ jhāyantī”ti.

It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, she saw the Teacher Padumuttara placing a certain Theri who was a master of the Vinaya in the foremost position, as if taking her by the arm and placing her in the Nandana Grove. Seeing this, she made an aspiration and established her wish, saying: 'May I, too, in the presence of a Buddha such as you, obtain the foremost position among the Theris who are masters of the Vinaya.' The Buddha Padumuttara, extending his knowledge of the future and knowing that her aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: 'In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha named Gotama, this one, by the name of Paṭācārā, will be the foremost among the Theris who are masters of the Vinaya.' The Teacher, seeing her—who had made such an aspiration and was endowed with the great aspiration—coming from afar, thought: 'For this one, apart from me, there is no other who is capable of being a refuge.' He then acted in such a way that she would come facing the monastery. The assembly, upon seeing her, said: 'Do not allow this madwoman to come here.' The Teacher said: 'Stand aside, do not obstruct her.' When she had come to a place not far off, he said: 'Sister, regain your mindfulness.' At that very moment, through the Buddha's spiritual power, she regained mindfulness. At that time, having noticed that the garment she was wearing had fallen off, she established moral shame and moral dread and sat down squatting. Then a certain man threw her an upper robe. Having put it on, she approached the Teacher and, at his feet which were the color of gold, paid homage with the five-point prostration, saying: 'Venerable Sir, be a refuge for me, be a support for me. For a hawk seized one of my sons, one was swept away by the water, my husband is dead on the path, and my mother, father, and brother, having been crushed by the house, are being burned on a single funeral pyre.'

Satthā tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “paṭācāre, mā cintayi, tava tāṇaṃ saraṇaṃ avassayo bhavituṃ samatthasseva santikaṃ āgatāsi. Yathā hi tava idāni eko puttako senena gahito, eko udakena vūḷho, panthe [P 2.0268] pati mato, mātāpitaro ceva bhātā ca gehena avatthaṭā; evameva imasmiṃ saṃsāre puttādīnaṃ matakāle tava rodantiyā paggharitaassu catunnaṃ mahāsamuddānaṃ udakato bahutara”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having heard her words, said: 'Paṭācārā, do not worry. You have come into the presence of one who is indeed capable of being a protection, a refuge, and a support for you. For just as now one of your sons was seized by a hawk, one was swept away by water, your husband is dead on the path, and your mother, father, and brother were crushed by a house; even so in this cycle of existence, the tears you have shed while weeping at the time of death of your sons and others are more abundant than the water of the four great oceans.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

“Catūsu samuddesu jalaṃ parittakaṃ,

Tato bahuṃ assujalaṃ anappakaṃ;

Dukkhena phuṭṭhassa narassa socanā,

Kiṃ kāraṇā amma tuvaṃ pamajjasī”ti.

In the four oceans, the water is little; more than that, the water of tears is abundant and immeasurable. For a being afflicted by suffering, there is grief. For what reason, dear daughter, are you heedless?

Evaṃ satthari anamataggapariyāyaṃ kathente tassa sarīre soko tanuttaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ tanubhūtasokaṃ ñatvā puna satthā āmantetvā “paṭācāre puttādayo nāma paralokaṃ gacchantassa tāṇaṃ vā leṇaṃ vā saraṇaṃ vā bhavituṃ na sakkonti, tasmā vijjamānāpi te na santiyeva, paṇḍitena [V 1.0394] pana sīlaṃ visodhetvā attano nibbānagāmimaggaṃ khippameva sodhetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

When the Teacher was thus teaching the Anamatagga discourse, the grief within her diminished. Then, knowing that her sorrow had lessened, the Teacher called to her again and said, 'Paṭācārā, those called sons and so forth cannot be a protection, a shelter, or a refuge for one who is going to the next world. Therefore, even though they exist, they are as if they do not exist. But for a wise person, having purified virtue, it is proper to quickly purify one's own path leading to Nibbāna.' Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

“Na [M 1.0442] santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā nāpi bandhavā;

Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā. (dha. pa. 288; apa. therī 2.2.501);

Sons are no protection, nor a father, nor even relatives. For one who is overcome by the Ender, there is no protection among kinsmen.

“Etamatthavassaṃ ñatvā, paṇḍito sīlasaṃvuto;

Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ, khippameva visodhaye”ti. (dha. pa. 289);

Knowing the significance of this matter, the wise person, restrained by virtue, should quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna.

Desanāvasāne [P 2.0269] paṭācārā mahāpathaviyaṃ paṃsuparimāṇe kilese jhāpetvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti. Sā pana sotāpannā hutvā satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. Satthā taṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ santikaṃ pahiṇitvā pabbājesi. Sā laddhūpasampadā paṭitācārattā paṭācārātveva paññāyi. Sā ekadivasaṃ kuṭena udakaṃ ādāya pāde dhovantī udakaṃ āsiñci, taṃ thokaṃ gantvā pacchijji. Dutiyavāre āsittaṃ tato dūrataraṃ agamāsi. Tatiyavāre āsittaṃ tatopi dūrataranti. Sā tadeva ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā tayo vaye paricchinditvā “mayā paṭhamaṃ āsittaṃ udakaṃ viya ime sattā paṭhamavayepi maranti, tato dūrataraṃ gataṃ dutiyavāre āsittaṃ udakaṃ viya majjhimavayepi maranti, tatopi dūrataraṃ gataṃ tatiyavāre āsittaṃ udakaṃ viya pacchimavayepi marantiyevā”ti cintesi. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova obhāsaṃ pharitvā tassā sammukhe ṭhatvā kathento viya “evametaṃ paṭācāre, pañcannampi khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ apassantassa vassasataṃ jīvanato tesaṃ udayabbayaṃ passantassa ekāhampi ekakkhaṇampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti [P 2.0270] vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento gāthamāha –

At the end of the teaching, Paṭācārā, having burned away defilements equal in measure to the dust on the great earth, became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. Having become a stream-enterer, she requested ordination from the Teacher. The Teacher sent her to the presence of the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained. Having received the higher ordination, she became known as Paṭācārā on account of her skillful conduct. One day, taking water with a pot and washing her feet, she poured out the water; it went a short distance and was cut off. The water poured the second time went farther than that. The water poured the third time went even farther than that. Taking that very object of meditation, she discerned the three ages and thought: 'Like the water I first poured, these beings die in the first age. Like the water poured the second time which went farther, they also die in the middle age. And like the water poured the third time which went even farther, they die in the last age.' The Teacher, while seated in the perfumed chamber, radiated light and, standing in her presence as if speaking, said: 'So it is, Paṭācārā. Better than living for a hundred years for one who does not see the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, is the life of even a single day or a single moment for one who sees their arising and passing away.' Having said this and connecting the context, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

113.

113.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato udayabbaya”nti.

And one who might live a hundred years, not seeing arising and passing away, better is a single day's life of one who sees arising and passing away.

Tattha apassaṃ udayabbayanti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ pañcavīsatiyā lakkhaṇehi udayañca vayañca apassanto. Passato udayabbayanti tesaṃ udayañca vayañca passantassa. Itarassa jīvanato ekāhampi jīvitaṃ seyyoti.

Therein, 'not seeing arising and passing away' means not contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates with their twenty-five characteristics. 'Of one who sees arising and passing away' refers to one who contemplates their arising and passing away. Than the life of the other, even a single day's life is more excellent.

Desanāvasāne [V 1.0395] paṭācārā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

At the end of the teaching, Paṭācārā attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Paṭācārātherīvatthu dvādasamaṃ.

The twelfth story, the Story of the Elder Paṭācārā, is concluded.

13. Kisāgotamīvatthu

13. The Story of Kisāgotamī

Yo [M 1.0443] ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kisāgotamiṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma discourse concerning Kisāgotamī, beginning with the words: 'He who should live a hundred years.'

Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekassa seṭṭhissa gehe cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ aṅgārā eva hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Seṭṭhi taṃ disvā uppannasoko āhāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā mañcake nipajji. Tasseko sahāyako gehaṃ gantvā, “samma, kasmā socasī”ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā, “samma, mā soci, ahaṃ ekaṃ upāyaṃ [P 2.0271] jānāmi, taṃ karohī”ti. “Kiṃ karomi, sammā”ti? Attano āpaṇe kilañjaṃ pasāretvā tattha te aṅgāre rāsiṃ katvā vikkiṇanto viya nisīda, āgatāgatesu manussesu ye evaṃ vadanti – “sesajanā vatthatelamadhuphāṇitādīni vikkiṇanti, tvaṃ pana aṅgāre vikkiṇanto nisinno”ti. Te vadeyyāsi – “attano santakaṃ avikkiṇanto kiṃ karomī”ti? Yo pana taṃ evaṃ vadati “sesajanā vatthatelamadhuphāṇitādīni vikkiṇanti, tvaṃ pana hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vikkiṇanto nisinno”ti. Taṃ vadeyyāsi “kahaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇa”nti. “Ida”nti ca vutte “āhara, tāva na”nti hatthehi paṭiccheyyāsi. Evaṃ dinnaṃ tava hatthe hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ bhavissati. Sā pana sace kumārikā hoti, tava gehe puttassa naṃ āharitvā cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ tassā niyyādetvā tāya dinnaṃ valañjeyyāsi. Sace kumārako hoti, tava gehe vayappattaṃ dhītaraṃ tassa datvā cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ niyyādetvā tena dinnaṃ valañjeyyāsīti. So “bhaddako upāyo”ti attano [P 2.0272] āpaṇe aṅgāre rāsiṃ katvā vikkiṇanto viya nisīdi. Ye pana naṃ evamāhaṃsu – “sesajanā vatthatelamadhuphāṇitādīni vikkiṇanti, kiṃ pana tvaṃ aṅgāre vikkiṇanto nisinno”ti? Tesaṃ “attano santakaṃ avikkiṇanto kiṃ karomī”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. Athekā gotamī nāma kumārikā kisasarīratāya kisāgotamīti paññāyamānā parijiṇṇakulassa dhītā attano ekena kiccena āpaṇadvāraṃ gantvā taṃ seṭṭhiṃ disvā evamāha – “kiṃ, tāta, sesajanā vatthatelamadhuphāṇitādīni vikkiṇanti, tvaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vikkiṇanto nisinno”ti? “Kahaṃ, amma, hiraññasuvaṇṇa”nti[V 1.0396]? “Nanu ‘tvaṃ tadeva gahetvā nisinnosī’ti, āhara, tāva naṃ, ammā”ti. Sā hatthapūraṃ gahetvā tassa hatthesu ṭhapesi, taṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇameva ahosi.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, in the house of a certain wealthy merchant, forty crores of wealth turned into charcoal. Seeing this, the merchant, overcome with sorrow, refused food and lay down on his bed. A friend of his went to the house and, having asked, 'Friend, why do you grieve?' and having heard the matter, said, 'Friend, do not grieve. I know a stratagem—do this.' 'What should I do, friend?' 'Spread out a mat at your shop, pile those charcoals there, and sit as if selling them. Among the people who come and go, should any say, "Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but you sit selling charcoal," you should reply to them, "If I do not sell my own property, what am I to do?" But should someone say to you, "Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but you sit selling gold and silver," you should say to that person, "Where is the gold and silver?" And when it is said, "Here it is," you should say, "Then bring it here," and receive it with your hands. What is thus given into your hands will become gold and silver. If that person is a young woman, bring her to your house for your son, entrust the forty crores of wealth to her, and you should make use of what is given by her. If it is a young man, give your grown-up daughter in your house to him, entrust the forty crores of wealth, and you should make use of what is given by him.' He, thinking, 'This is a good stratagem,' made a pile of charcoal at his own shop and sat as if selling it. To those who said to him, 'Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but why do you sit selling charcoal?' he gave the reply, 'If I do not sell my own property, what am I to do?' Then a certain young woman named Gotamī, who was known as Kisāgotamī on account of her slender body, the daughter of a ruined family, went to the shop door on some errand of her own. Seeing the merchant, she said thus, 'Father, other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but you are sitting selling gold and silver.' 'Where, dear girl, is the gold and silver?' he asked. 'Are you not sitting holding that very thing?' she replied. 'Then bring it here, dear girl,' he said. She took a handful and placed it in his hands, and it became gold and silver itself.

Atha [M 1.0444] naṃ seṭṭhi “kataraṃ te, amma, geha”nti pucchitvā “asukaṃ nāmā”ti vutte tassā assāmikabhāvaṃ ñatvā dhanaṃ paṭisāmetvā taṃ attano puttassa ānetvā cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ paṭicchāpesi. Sabbaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇameva ahosi. Tassā aparena samayena gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi. So padasā gamanakāle kālamakāsi. Sā adiṭṭhapubbamaraṇatāya taṃ jhāpetuṃ nīharante vāretvā “puttassa me bhesajjaṃ pucchissāmī”ti matakaḷevaraṃ aṅkenādāya “api nu me puttassa bhesajjaṃ [P 2.0273] jānāthā”ti pucchantī gharapaṭipāṭiyā vicarati. Atha naṃ manussā, “amma, tvaṃ ummattikā jātā, matakaputtassa bhesajjaṃ pucchantī vicarasī”ti vadanti. Sā “avassaṃ mama puttassa bhesajjaṃ jānanakaṃ labhissāmī”ti maññamānā vicarati. Atha naṃ eko paṇḍitapuriso disvā, “ayaṃ mama dhītā paṭhamaṃ puttakaṃ vijātā bhavissati adiṭṭhapubbamaraṇā, mayā imissā avassayena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā āha – “amma, ahaṃ bhesajjaṃ na jānāmi, bhesajjajānanakaṃ pana jānāmī”ti. “Ko jānāti, tātā”ti? “Satthā, amma, jānāti, gaccha, taṃ pucchāhī”ti. Sā “gamissāmi, tāta, pucchissāmi, tātā”ti vatvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā pucchi – “tumhe kira me puttassa bhesajjaṃ jānātha, bhante”ti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Accharaggahaṇamatte siddhatthake laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Labhissāmi, bhante”. “Kassa pana gehe laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Yassa gehe putto vā dhītā vā na koci matapubbo”ti. Sā “sādhu, bhante”ti satthāraṃ vanditvā mataputtakaṃ aṅkenādāya antogāmaṃ pavisitvā paṭhamagehassa dvāre ṭhatvā “atthi nu kho imasmiṃ gehe siddhatthako, puttassa kira [P 2.0274] me bhesajjaṃ eta”nti vatvā “atthī”ti vutte tena hi dethāti. Tehi āharitvā siddhatthakesu diyyamānesu “imasmiṃ gehe putto vā dhītā vā matapubbo koci natthi, ammā”ti pucchitvā “kiṃ vadesi, amma? Jīvamānā hi katipayā, matakā eva bahukā”ti vutte “tena hi gaṇhatha vo siddhatthake, netaṃ mama puttassa bhesajja”nti paṭiadāsi.

Then the merchant asked her, 'Dear girl, which is your house?' When she replied, 'Such and such a place,' he, knowing that she was without a husband, had the wealth collected and brought her for his own son, making him accept the forty crores of wealth. All of it became gold and silver itself. After some time, she conceived. At the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son. The child died when he was able to walk. She, never having seen death before, prevented them from taking him out to be cremated, saying, 'I will ask for medicine for my son.' Carrying the dead body on her hip, she went from house to house asking, 'Do you know any medicine for my son?' Then people said to her, 'Dear woman, you have gone mad, wandering about asking for medicine for your dead son.' But she, thinking, 'I will surely find someone who knows the medicine for my son,' kept wandering. Then a certain wise man saw her and thought, 'This dear daughter of mine must have given birth to her first child and has never seen death before. It is right that I should be a refuge for her.' So he said, 'Dear girl, I do not know the medicine, but I do know one who knows the medicine.' 'Who knows it, father?' 'The Teacher knows, dear girl. Go and ask him.' She said, 'I will go, father; I will ask,' and having approached the Teacher, she paid homage and, standing to one side, asked, 'Venerable sir, is it true that you know the medicine for my son?' 'Yes, I know it.' 'What must be obtained?' 'A mere pinch of mustard seeds must be obtained.' 'I will get it, venerable sir. But from whose house must it be obtained?' 'From a house where no one—neither son nor daughter—has ever died.' She said, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and having paid homage to the Teacher, she took her dead son on her hip, entered the village, and stood at the door of the first house. She said, 'Are there any mustard seeds in this house? It is said to be the medicine for my son.' When they said, 'There are,' she said, 'Then please give them to me.' As they were bringing the mustard seeds to give to her, she asked, 'Dear woman, in this house, has no one at all—neither son nor daughter—ever died?' When they replied, 'What are you saying, dear woman? The living are but few, while the dead are many,' she said, 'Then take back your mustard seeds; this is not the medicine for my son,' and returned them.

Sā iminā nīyāmena ādito paṭṭhāya naṃ pucchantī vicari. Sā ekagehepi siddhatthake agahetvā sāyanhasamaye cintesi – “aho bhāriyaṃ [M 1.0445] kammaṃ, ahaṃ ‘mameva putto mato’ti saññamakāsiṃ, sakalagāmepi pana jīvantehi matakāva bahutarā”ti. Tassā evaṃ cintayamānāya puttasinehaṃ mudukahadayaṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ agamāsi. Sā puttaṃ araññe chaḍḍetvā satthu santikaṃ [V 1.0397] gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “laddhā te ekaccharamattā siddhatthakā”ti āha. “Na laddhā, bhante, sakalagāme jīvantehi matakāva bahutarā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “tvaṃ ‘mameva putto mato’ti sallakkhesi, dhuvadhammo esa sattānaṃ. Maccurājā hi sabbasatte aparipuṇṇajjhāsaye eva mahogho viya [P 2.0275] parikaḍḍhamānoyeva apāyasamudde pakkhipatī”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

She, by this method, went about asking from the very beginning. Not having obtained mustard seeds in even one house, in the evening she reflected: “Alas, what a heavy task! I had the perception that ‘only my son has died,’ but in the entire village, the dead are indeed more numerous than the living.” As she was thus reflecting, her tender heart, full of affection for her son, became firm. Having abandoned her son in the forest, she went to the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then the Teacher asked her, “Have you obtained a pinch of mustard seeds?” “They were not obtained, venerable sir. In the entire village, the dead are far more numerous than the living.” Then the Teacher said to her, “You perceived that ‘only my son has died.’ This is the constant nature of beings. Indeed, the King of Death, like a great flood, drags away all beings whose intentions are still unfulfilled and casts them into the ocean of the woeful states.” Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

“Taṃ puttapasusammattaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ;

Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahoghova, maccu ādāya gacchatī”ti. (dha. pa. 287);

Death seizes and carries away that person who is infatuated with children and cattle, whose mind is attached, just as a great flood carries away a sleeping village.

Gāthāpariyosāne kisāgotamī sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsūti.

At the end of the verse, Kisāgotamī was established in the fruition of stream-entry, and many others also attained the fruition of stream-entry and so forth.

Sā pana satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci, satthā taṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ santikaṃ pesetvā pabbājesi. Sā laddhūpasampadā kisāgotamī therīti paññāyi. Sā ekadivasaṃ uposathāgāre vāraṃ patvā dīpaṃ jāletvā nisinnā dīpajālā uppajjantiyo ca bhijjantiyo ca disvā “evameva ime sattā uppajjanti ceva nirujjhanti ca, nibbānappattā eva na paññāyantī”ti ārammaṇaṃ aggahesi. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova obhāsaṃ pharitvā tassā sammukhe nisīditvā kathento viya “evameva, gotami, ime sattā dīpajālā viya uppajjanti ceva nirujjhanti ca, nibbānappattā eva na paññāyanti, evaṃ nibbānaṃ apassantānaṃ vassasataṃ jīvanato nibbānaṃ passantassa khaṇamattampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

She then requested the going forth from the Teacher. The Teacher sent her to the presence of the nuns and had her go forth. Having received the higher ordination, she became known as the Elder Kisāgotamī. One day, when it was her turn in the Uposatha hall, she lit a lamp and sat down. Seeing the lamp flames arising and ceasing, she took as her meditation object: “Even so do these beings arise and cease; only those who have attained Nibbāna are no longer perceived.” The Teacher, while seated in the Perfumed Chamber, projected a radiance and, as if seated in her presence and speaking, said: “Even so, Gotamī, these beings arise and cease like the flame of a lamp; only those who have attained Nibbāna are no longer perceived. Thus, the life of even a single moment for one who sees Nibbāna is better than a life of one hundred years for one who does not.” Having said this and making the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

114.

114.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ amataṃ padaṃ;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato amataṃ pada”nti.

Though one should live a hundred years, not seeing the Deathless State, better is life for a single day seeing the Deathless State.

Tattha amataṃ padanti maraṇavirahitakoṭṭhāsaṃ, amatamahānibbānanti attho. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Therein, 'the deathless state' (amataṃ padaṃ) means the portion free from death; the meaning is the great deathless Nibbāna. The rest is similar to the former.

Desanāvasāne [M 1.0446] kisāgotamī yathānisinnāva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahatte patiṭṭhahīti.

At the end of the discourse, Kisāgotamī, while still seated, became established in arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Kisāgotamīvatthu terasamaṃ.

The story of Kisāgotamī is the thirteenth.

14. Bahuputtikattherīvatthu

14. The Story of the Elder Bahuputtikā

Yo [V 1.0398][P 2.0276] ca vassasataṃ jīveti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bahuputtikaṃ theriṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this discourse on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Bahuputtikā, beginning with 'And one who should live a hundred years...'

Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekasmiṃ kule satta puttā satta ca dhītaro ahesuṃ. Te sabbepi vayappattā gehe patiṭṭhahitvā attano dhammatāya sukhappattā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ aparena samayena pitā kālamakāsi. Mahāupāsikā sāmike naṭṭhepi na tāva kuṭumbaṃ vibhajati. Atha naṃ puttā āhaṃsu – “amma, amhākaṃ pitari naṭṭhe tuyhaṃ ko attho kuṭumbena, kiṃ mayaṃ taṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ na sakkomā”ti. Sā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā tuṇhī hutvā punappunaṃ tehi vuccamānā “puttā maṃ paṭijaggissanti, kiṃ me visuṃ kuṭumbenā”ti sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ majjhe bhinditvā adāsi. Atha naṃ katipāhaccayena jeṭṭhaputtassa bhariyā “aho amhākaṃ, ayyā, ‘jeṭṭhaputto me’ti dve koṭṭhāse datvā viya imameva gehaṃ āgacchatī”ti āha. Sesaputtānaṃ bhariyāpi evameva vadiṃsu. Jeṭṭhadhītaraṃ ādiṃ katvā tāsaṃ gehaṃ gatakālepi naṃ evameva vadiṃsu. Sā avamānappattā hutvā “kiṃ imesaṃ santike vuṭṭhena, bhikkhunī hutvā jīvissāmī”ti bhikkhunīupassayaṃ gantvā [P 2.0277] pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tā naṃ pabbājesuṃ. Sā laddhūpasampadā hutvā bahuputtikattherīti paññāyi. Sā “ahaṃ mahallakakāle pabbajitā, appamattāya me bhavitabba”nti bhikkhunīnaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ karontī “sabbarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti heṭṭhāpāsāde ekaṃ thambhaṃ hatthena gahetvā taṃ āviñchamānāva samaṇadhammaṃ karoti, caṅkamamānāpi “andhakāraṭṭhāne me rukkhe vā katthaci vā sīsaṃ paṭihaññeyyā”ti taṃ rukkhaṃ hatthena gahetvā taṃ āviñchamānāva samaṇadhammaṃ karoti, “satthārā desitadhammameva karissāmī”ti dhammaṃ āvajjetvā dhammaṃ anussaramānāva samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Atha [M 1.0447] satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova obhāsaṃ pharitvā sammukhe nisinno viya tāya saddhiṃ kathento “bahuputtike mayā desitaṃ dhammaṃ anāvajjentassa apassantassa vassasataṃ jīvanato mayā desitaṃ dhammaṃ passantassa muhuttampi jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that in Sāvatthī, in a certain family, there were seven sons and seven daughters. All of them, having come of age, were established in households and lived happily according to their nature. After some time, their father passed away. The great laywoman, even after her husband’s death, did not yet divide the property. Then her children said to her, “Mother, now that our father has passed away, what use is the property to you? Are we not able to support you?” Hearing their words, she remained silent. But when they repeatedly urged her, she thought, “My children will look after me; what need have I for separate property?” and she divided all the property in the middle and gave it to them. A few days later, the wife of the eldest son said, “Oh, our lady, as if having given two shares thinking ‘he is my eldest son,’ she comes only to this very house.” The wives of the other sons also spoke in the same way. When she went to the houses of her daughters, beginning with the eldest, they also spoke to her in this same manner. Feeling disrespected, she thought, “What is the use of living with them? I shall become a bhikkhunī and live.” She went to the bhikkhunīs’ residence and requested the going forth. They gave her the going forth. Having received the higher ordination, she became known as Bahuputtikā Therī. She reflected, “I have gone forth in old age; I must be diligent.” While performing the duties for the bhikkhunīs, she resolved, “I will practice the ascetic’s duties all night long.” Holding onto a pillar in the lower part of the building, she practiced the ascetic’s duties while circling it. Even while on her walking path, thinking, “In a dark place, my head might strike a tree or something,” she held onto a tree and practiced the ascetic’s duties while circling it. Thinking, “I will practice only the Dhamma taught by the Teacher,” she reflected on the Dhamma and continually recollected it while performing the ascetic’s duties. Then the Teacher, while seated in the Perfumed Chamber, projected a radiance and, as if seated before her, spoke with her, saying: “Bahuputtikā, for one who does not reflect on the Dhamma I have taught, who does not see it, a life of a hundred years is inferior to even a moment’s life for one who sees the Dhamma I have taught.” Having said this and making the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

115.

115.

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ dhammamuttamaṃ;

Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato dhammamuttama”nti.

And one who should live a hundred years, not seeing the supreme Dhamma—better is life for a single day, seeing the supreme Dhamma.

Tattha [V 1.0399][P 2.0278] dhammamuttamanti navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ. So hi uttamo dhammo nāma. Yo hi taṃ na passati, tassa vassasatampi jīvanato taṃ dhammaṃ passantassa paṭivijjhantassa ekāhampi ekakkhaṇampi jīvitaṃ seyyoti.

Therein, 'the supreme Dhamma' (dhammamuttamaṃ) refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. For that is indeed called the supreme Dhamma. For one who does not see it, a life of a hundred years is inferior to even a single day or a single moment of life for one who sees and penetrates that Dhamma.

Gāthāpariyosāne bahuputtikattherī saha paṭisambhidāhi arahatte patiṭṭhahīti.

At the end of the verse, the Elder Bahuputtikā was established in Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Bahuputtikattherīvatthu cuddasamaṃ.

The fourteenth story is that of the Elder Bahuputtikā.

Sahassavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of Thousands is concluded.

Aṭṭhamo vaggo.

The Eighth Chapter.
